t: Read the shop tables and choose columns
sum: Use the shop keys to identify customers, products, orders and their lines.
x: SQL queries are declarative: you describe the rows you want and the database works out how to fetch them. A SELECT does not require a loop in your application. That is why one short query can replace much procedural code, and also why small slips in a query can quietly give you the wrong answer. Every lesson in this module uses the same small shop database. Learn its shape once and the examples will make sense straight away. The example schema customers city referred_by --------- 1 Asha London NULL 2 Ben Leeds 1 3 Chloe NULL 1 4 Dev London 2 5 Erin Bristol NULL products price category --------- 1 Kettle 30 kitchen 2 Toaster 25 kitchen 3 Lamp 40 home 4 Rug 90 home 5 Mug 8 NULL orders customer date / status --------- 101 1 2026-01-05 shipped 102 1 2026-02-11 shipped 103 2 2026-02-14 pending 104 3 2026-03-02 shipped 105 4 2026-03-09 cancelled 106 NULL 2026-03-10 pending order_items links orders to products with a quantity. Here is the complete fixture; the pair of order and product ids identifies each line. order_id product_id qty --------- 101 1 1 101 5 4 102 3 2 103 2 1 103 5 2 104 1 1 104 3 1 105 2 1 106 5 1 Prices are whole pounds to keep the arithmetic easy. Order 106 is a guest checkout with no customer, Erin has never ordered, and nobody has bought the Rug. Those gaps matter in later lessons. The original fixture uses integer primary keys, required names and prices, and enforced foreign keys from orders and lines; the final units show a redesigned schema. Result tables illustrate the expected SQLite behaviour of the small shop examples. Differences from PostgreSQL are called out. Unless ORDER BY specifies otherwise, a displayed result table shows the returned rows in a convenient illustrative order. SQLite and PostgreSQL can emit those same rows in a different order. An ordinary equality comparison with a NULL city is unknown, so WHERE does not keep it; this matters for the quoting question at the end of this unit. SELECT and FROM The smallest useful query names some columns and a table: SELECT returns every column. It is handy at the prompt but a bad habit in application code: adding a column to the table silently changes what your code receives, and you pull more data than you need. You can compute new columns and name them with AS: The name after AS is an alias. Strings use single quotes: 'London'. Double quotes are for identifiers, such as a column called "order" that clashes with a keyword. Double quotes in SQLite When legacy double-quoted-string compatibility is enabled, SQLite has a quirk: if "London" is not a column name, it treats it as the string 'London'. PostgreSQL raises column "London" does not exist. Worse, WHERE city = "city" in SQLite compares the column with itself. Always use single quotes for strings. Key takeaways Use the shop keys to identify customers, products, orders and their lines. SELECT chooses output columns; AS names a computed column. Single quotes mean text; double quotes name identifiers. Further reading SELECT — PostgreSQL documentation The SELECT statement — SQLite documentation Quirks, caveats and gotchas in SQLite

sum: WHERE keeps only true conditions.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. WHERE: filtering rows WHERE keeps only the rows for which a condition is true. name price ------ Rug 90 Lamp 40 Kettle 30 The comparison operators are =, <> (or!=), <, <=, > and >=. Combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT. A few shorthands save typing: Shorthand Means ------ x IN ('a','b') x = 'a' OR x = 'b' x BETWEEN 25 AND 40 x >= 25 AND x <= 40 name LIKE 'K%' starts with K name LIKE '_ug' any one char, then ug BETWEEN includes both ends. % in a LIKE pattern matches any run of characters (including none) and _ matches exactly one, so '_ug' finds Rug and Mug. AND binds tighter than OR This is the most common filtering bug. Suppose you want kitchen or home products over £50: name price ------ Kettle 30 Toaster 25 Rug 90 AND is evaluated first, so this means "kitchen (any price), or home over £50". Kettle and Toaster sneak in. Brackets fix it: Now only Rug is returned. When a condition mixes AND and OR, always add brackets, even when you know the precedence. The next reader may not. Key takeaways WHERE keeps only true conditions. BETWEEN includes both bounds; LIKE uses % and _ as wildcards. Bracket mixed AND and OR conditions to state the intended groups. Further reading SELECT — PostgreSQL documentation Pattern matching (LIKE, ILIKE) — PostgreSQL documentation The SELECT statement — SQLite documentation

t: Match text and include whole date ranges
sum: LIKE case behaviour depends on the database and collation.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. Case sensitivity differs With the ordinary case-sensitive text collations used for these examples, 'Kettle' = 'kettle' is false in both databases. Text equality can change with a case-insensitive collation. LIKE also differs: In SQLite, LIKE ignores case for ASCII letters by default, so name LIKE 'k%' finds Kettle. In PostgreSQL, LIKE is case-sensitive with a deterministic collation using case-sensitive text rules; PostgreSQL 18 also supports LIKE with nondeterministic collations such as case-insensitive ones. Use ILIKE, or lower(name) LIKE 'k%'. Moving a query from SQLite in tests to PostgreSQL in production can therefore change its results. Dates as text SQLite has no date type. This schema stores ISO-8601 text like '2026-02-14', which sorts and compares correctly as a string. Watch the upper bound once times appear, though: The string with a time comes after '2026-02-28', so the last afternoon of February falls outside the range. The robust pattern is a half-open range, which works for consistently formatted SQLite text and PostgreSQL date and timestamp columns. This WHERE fragment follows SELECT FROM orders: It selects orders 102 and 103 from the shop fixture. The lower bound includes midnight on 1 February; the upper bound excludes midnight on 1 March. Every time on 28 February is inside the interval. Adjacent monthly ranges meet at a boundary without a gap or overlap. In PostgreSQL, a bare date-like string compared with a timestamp is converted to midnight at the start of that date. With timestamptz, decide the reporting time zone explicitly: local calendar months and UTC months can start at different instants. The half-open range pattern still applies, but its bounds must represent the intended instants. SQLite's LIKE case folding is limited to ASCII by default. It does not make all Unicode upper- and lower-case letters equivalent. PostgreSQL ILIKE follows the active locale; it is not a guarantee of identical Unicode behaviour across engines. Choose a collation and test representative names before treating either pattern as a general case-insensitive search. Key takeaways LIKE case behaviour depends on the database and collation. Consistently formatted ISO date text sorts chronologically. Use an inclusive start and exclusive start of the next reporting period for timestamp ranges. Further reading Pattern matching (LIKE, ILIKE) — PostgreSQL documentation The SELECT statement — SQLite documentation Quirks, caveats and gotchas in SQLite

t: Sort rows and remove duplicate results
sum: ORDER BY is necessary for a guaranteed result order.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. ORDER BY: sorting Without ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed. It often looks stable on a small table, then changes after a database index is added, the table grows or the planner picks a parallel plan. If order matters, say so. name category price --------- Mug NULL 8 Rug home 90 Lamp home 40 Kettle kitchen 30 Toaster kitchen 25 Rows are sorted by category first and price DESC breaks ties within a category. DESC applies only to the column it follows; category is still ascending. Where do NULLs sort? SQLite treats NULL as smaller than any value, so NULLs come first in ascending order. PostgreSQL treats NULL as larger, so they come last. Both accept ORDER BY category NULLS LAST (SQLite since 3.30) if you need the same result everywhere. You can also sort by an alias (ORDER BY double_price) or a column position (ORDER BY 2). Positions are fragile: reorder the select list and the sort silently changes. DISTINCT SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers removes duplicate rows from the result: London, Leeds, Bristol and one NULL. DISTINCT applies to the whole row, not one column. SELECT DISTINCT city, name would return all five customers, because every (city, name) pair is unique. Reaching for DISTINCT to hide duplicates you did not expect is a warning sign. The duplicates usually come from a join that multiplies rows (next lesson), and the real fix is the join. Key takeaways ORDER BY is necessary for a guaranteed result order. Each sort direction applies only to its own column. DISTINCT removes duplicate whole rows and retains one NULL. Further reading Sorting rows (ORDER BY) — PostgreSQL documentation The SELECT statement — SQLite documentation

t: Page through a stable ordered result
sum: Use a unique final sort key when page boundaries can cut through ties.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. LIMIT and OFFSET LIMIT caps the number of rows and OFFSET skips some first: name price ------ Lamp 40 Kettle 30 Pages of a fixed size are the usual reason to use OFFSET. To show a given page, you skip every row on the earlier pages, and the database still has to produce the skipped rows before it can throw them away: With 20 rows per page, page 3 is LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40: skip two earlier pages, then return the next 20 rows. That means producing 60 result rows to return 20. Page 1 needs 20 result rows, but page 5,000 needs 100,000 if enough rows exist. The skipped-result work grows with the page number; sorting and filtering can inspect additional data. This assumes nothing is inserted or deleted between page requests; otherwise the pages shift. Two rules: LIMIT without a deterministic ORDER BY returns an arbitrary set of rows. If two rows tie on the sort key, add a tiebreaker such as id, or a page boundary can show one row twice and another never. Large offsets are slow. OFFSET 100000 still reads and discards 100,000 rows. For deep paging, use keyset pagination: remember the last key you showed and ask for WHERE price <:last_price (plus an id tiebreaker). The database can then seek straight to the right place using an index. PostgreSQL also supports the SQL-standard spelling FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY. SQLite does not, but both understand LIMIT. Key takeaways Use a unique final sort key when page boundaries can cut through ties. OFFSET still makes the database produce skipped result rows. Keyset pagination uses a remembered key to seek into an index. Further reading SELECT — PostgreSQL documentation Sorting rows (ORDER BY) — PostgreSQL documentation Paging through results without OFFSET — Use The Index, Luke

t: Reason about aliases and SQL arithmetic
sum: Logical clause order explains which aliases are visible.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. The order a query is evaluated in You write clauses in one order, but the database evaluates them, logically, in another: This explains several rules at once: ORDER BY can use a SELECT alias, because it runs after SELECT. WHERE cannot, in standard SQL, because it runs before SELECT. In PostgreSQL, WHERE double_price > 60 fails with column "double_price" does not exist. SQLite is lenient and accepts it, which is another way a query can work in tests and fail in production. Repeat the expression instead: WHERE price 2 > 60. LIMIT applies to the sorted result, so "top 3" queries work as expected. This is the logical order. The optimiser may physically do things differently, for example by using an index to read rows already sorted, but the result must be the same as if it had followed these steps. Arithmetic surprises SELECT 7/2 returns 3, not 3.5, in both SQLite and PostgreSQL: dividing two integers gives an integer. The digits after the decimal point are dropped, and the % operator gives back what was left over: These small integer examples assume a nonzero divisor and a representable result. PostgreSQL raises an error on integer overflow; SQLite can promote overflowing arithmetic to floating point. Because the result is truncated rather than rounded, SELECT 9/10 is 0, not 1. Write 7/2.0 or CAST(x AS REAL) (PostgreSQL: x::numeric) when you want a fraction: one non-integer operand makes the whole division non-integer. String concatenation uses: name ' (' city ')' gives Asha (London). For Chloe it gives NULL, because this operator propagates a NULL operand in SQLite and PostgreSQL. Other functions, such as COALESCE and concat, have different rules; the NULL units explain them. Key takeaways Logical clause order explains which aliases are visible. Integer division truncates towards zero in SQLite and PostgreSQL. The concatenation operator propagates NULL in these engines. Further reading SELECT — PostgreSQL documentation Quirks, caveats and gotchas in SQLite

t: Trace matching pairs in an inner join
sum: An inner join returns one row per matching pair.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. A relational database splits data across tables so each fact is stored once. A customer's name lives in customers; their orders live in orders and point back with customer_id. A join puts the pieces back together for one query. Every join does the same thing underneath. Conceptually it pairs each row of one table with each row of another, then keeps the pairs that satisfy the join condition. The join type decides what happens to rows that find no partner. The shop schema This module uses one small shop throughout. Here are the parts that matter for joins. customers city referred_by --------- 1 Asha London NULL 2 Ben Leeds 1 3 Chloe NULL 1 4 Dev London 2 5 Erin Bristol NULL orders customer_id status --------- 101 1 shipped 102 1 shipped 103 2 pending 104 3 shipped 105 4 cancelled 106 NULL pending Two details are deliberate. Erin has no orders, and order 106 is a guest order with no customer. Those two rows are what make the join types behave differently. Products are Kettle (1, £30), Toaster (2, £25), Lamp (3, £40), Rug (4, £90) and Mug (5, £8). order_items has nine rows; the Rug has never been ordered. INNER JOIN: only matching pairs name id ------ Asha 101 Asha 102 Ben 103 Chloe 104 Dev 105 JOIN means INNER JOIN. Only pairs where the condition is true survive. Erin vanishes (no order points at her) and order 106 vanishes (its customer_id is NULL, and NULL = anything is never true). Notice that Asha appears twice. A join produces one row per matching pair, not one per customer. Keep that in mind; it causes the biggest bug in this lesson. The letters c and o are table aliases. Always qualify columns (o.id, not id) once more than one table is involved; both tables here have an id column, so a bare id would be ambiguous and rejected. Row order Results above are shown in a tidy order, but SQL guarantees no order without ORDER BY. SQLite and PostgreSQL may return the same rows in different orders. Key takeaways An inner join returns one row per matching pair. Asha appears twice because she has two orders. Qualify shared names with table aliases. Further reading Joins between tables — PostgreSQL tutorial Table expressions and joined tables — PostgreSQL docs

t: Keep customers with no matching order
sum: LEFT JOIN preserves every left row.
x: In the shop, customers Asha, Ben, Chloe, Dev and Erin have ids 1–5. Orders 101 and 102 belong to Asha, 103 to Ben, 104 to Chloe and 105 to Dev. Guest order 106 has customer_id NULL; Erin has no order. LEFT JOIN: keep everything on the left name id ------ Asha 101 Asha 102 Ben 103 Chloe 104 Dev 105 Erin NULL A LEFT (OUTER) JOIN keeps every row of the left table. If a left row has no partner, it appears once with NULLs in all the right table's columns. Erin is back, with id NULL. This is the join for questions like "all customers, with their orders if any". It is by far the most common outer join. You can predict how many rows a LEFT JOIN returns from two counts: the matching pairs, which are exactly the rows the inner join gave, plus one padded row for each left row that matched nothing. Unmatched rows of the right table (guest order 106) add nothing, because a LEFT JOIN doesn't preserve them. Key takeaways LEFT JOIN preserves every left row. Unmatched right-hand columns are filled with NULL. The result contains matching pairs plus one row per unmatched left row. Further reading Joins between tables — PostgreSQL tutorial Table expressions and joined tables — PostgreSQL docs

sum: ON decides which pairs match before outer padding.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. ON versus WHERE in an outer join This is the classic outer join bug. Say you want every customer, plus their shipped orders. Where does the status filter go? name id status --------- Asha 101 shipped Asha 102 shipped Ben NULL NULL Chloe 104 shipped Dev NULL NULL Erin NULL NULL name id status --------- Asha 101 shipped Asha 102 shipped Chloe 104 shipped Why the difference? The logical order is: build the join (using ON), then apply WHERE. In ON, the filter decides which right rows count as a match. Ben's only order is pending, so he has no match and is padded with NULLs, but he is kept. In WHERE, the filter runs after the padding. Ben has status pending, Dev has cancelled, and only Erin is NULL-padded. None satisfies status = 'shipped', so all three are removed. The LEFT JOIN has quietly become an INNER JOIN. The rule of thumb: Conditions on the optional (right) table go in ON if you want to keep unmatched left rows. Conditions that should remove left rows go in WHERE. The reverse surprise exists too. Putting AND c.city = 'London' in the ON of a LEFT JOIN does not remove Ben, Chloe or Erin. It just stops them matching any order, so they come back padded with NULLs. To keep only London customers, that test belongs in WHERE. For an INNER JOIN, ON and WHERE filters give the same result. Key takeaways ON decides which pairs match before outer padding. A NULL-rejecting WHERE predicate removes padded rows. A predicate on the left table belongs in WHERE when it should remove left rows. Further reading Table expressions and joined tables — PostgreSQL docs SELECT — SQLite docs

t: Keep both sides or find missing matches
sum: RIGHT JOIN preserves the right side; FULL JOIN preserves both sides.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN A RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image: keep every row of the right table. This returns the five matched rows plus NULL 106: the guest order is kept, Erin is not. Any right join can be rewritten as a left join by swapping the tables, and most teams do exactly that so queries read consistently left to right. A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides. name id ------ Asha 101 Asha 102 Ben 103 Chloe 104 Dev 105 Erin NULL NULL 106 A full join adds the unmatched rows of both sides to the matching pairs: Full joins are rarer. They suit reconciliation jobs: "compare yesterday's export with today's and show rows missing from either side". Engine support PostgreSQL supports RIGHT and FULL joins. SQLite only added them in version 3.39 (2022), so older SQLite builds reject them. MySQL still has no FULL OUTER JOIN; a duplicate-preserving emulation uses a LEFT JOIN plus UNION ALL of only the unmatched right-side rows. A plain UNION removes duplicate output rows. The anti-join: rows with no match "Which customers have never ordered?" is a LEFT JOIN followed by a test for the NULLs it creates. The result is just Erin. The same pattern finds products nobody has bought (Rug). Test a column that can never be NULL in a real match, such as the right table's primary key. If you tested a nullable column like o.status, a genuine match with a NULL status would be misreported as "no match". NOT EXISTS expresses the same idea and is often clearer; subqueries come in the next module. Avoid NOT IN against a nullable column; the NULL units show why it can silently return nothing. Key takeaways RIGHT JOIN preserves the right side; FULL JOIN preserves both sides. A FULL JOIN adds unmatched rows to the matching pairs. Find missing matches by testing a non-nullable right-hand key after LEFT JOIN. Further reading Table expressions and joined tables — PostgreSQL docs SQLite 3.39.0 release notes (RIGHT and FULL JOIN) Join (SQL) — Wikipedia)

t: Trace join chains and multiplied child rows
sum: A link table connects the two sides of a many-to-many relationship.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. Joining through a link table Orders and products have a many-to-many relationship, resolved by order_items. Getting product names for an order means two joins in a chain. id name qty --------- 101 Kettle 1 101 Mug 4 102 Lamp 2 Each join adds one table and one condition. Joins are associative for inner joins, so the database is free to execute them in any order it thinks is cheapest; how it chooses is the subject of the query processing module. Mixing LEFT and INNER customers LEFT JOIN orders... JOIN order_items... drops Erin again. Her padded row has o.id NULL, so the inner join to order_items finds no match. Once a table is optional, every join that hangs off it usually needs to be a LEFT JOIN too. Fan-out: when joins multiply rows For the examples below, GROUP BY c.name collects the joined rows for each customer name. COUNT(o.id) counts non-NULL order ids in that group; COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) counts each different known order id once. Names happen to be unique in this fixture; use the customer primary key for identity in real reporting. The aggregate units later explain these operations in depth. Because a join produces one row per matching pair, joining a parent to a child repeats the parent once per child. That is fine until you aggregate. name n d --------- Asha 3 2 Ben 2 1 Chloe 2 1 Dev 1 1 Asha has two orders, but joining to items gives three rows (order 101 has two items). COUNT(o.id) says 3. It gets worse when you join two independent child tables to the same parent. Asha has 2 orders and referred 2 customers. Neither child table says which order goes with which referral, so the join pairs every one with every other: So both counts come out as 4. With three orders and four referrals it would be 12 rows. With an inner join, a parent with zero rows in either child gives 0 rows and disappears; with LEFT JOINs an unmatched child counts as one NULL-padded row instead. Fixes, in order of preference: Aggregate each child table separately (in a subquery or CTE), then join the one-row-per-parent results. Use COUNT(DISTINCT...) for counts. This does not work for SUM, because two different items can have the same value. A useful habit: before trusting a total, ask "what is one row of this result?" If the answer is "one order item", a sum of order totals is wrong. Key takeaways A link table connects the two sides of a many-to-many relationship. An inner join hanging from an optional table can remove padded rows. Independent child relationships multiply rows; count or total the intended entity. Further reading Table expressions and joined tables — PostgreSQL docs Join (SQL) — Wikipedia)

t: Join a table to itself and build combinations
sum: Two aliases let one customer row match another as its referrer.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. Self joins A table can be joined to itself. customers.referred_by points at another customer, so listing each customer with the name of whoever referred them needs two copies of the table with different aliases. name referrer ------ Asha NULL Ben Asha Chloe Asha Dev Ben Erin NULL The aliases are what make it work: c is "the customer", r is "the referrer". With an inner join, Asha and Erin would disappear because nobody referred them. Self joins also find pairs within a table. ON a.city = b.city AND a.id < b.id lists customers sharing a city (just Asha and Dev). The a.id < b.id stops each pair appearing twice and stops a row pairing with itself. Self joins handle one level of a hierarchy; walking a whole tree needs a recursive CTE. CROSS JOIN: every combination A cross join (Cartesian product) pairs every row with every row, so its size is the product of the two tables' sizes: The same product is the most an inner join can ever return: it keeps some of these pairs and drops the rest, so its row count can be zero or anything up to the cross join's count. A cross join is useful on purpose, for example to build a grid of every product for every store or date, which you then LEFT JOIN real sales onto so missing combinations show up as zero. It is dangerous by accident. The old comma syntax FROM customers c, orders o is a cross join (5 × 6 = 30 rows here) until a WHERE o.customer_id = c.id turns it into an inner join. Forget the condition on two tables of a million rows each and you have asked for 1,000,000 × 1,000,000 = 1,000,000,000,000 rows: a trillion. SQLite versus PostgreSQL SQLite (and MySQL) accept JOIN with no ON and treat it as a cross join. PostgreSQL rejects it as a syntax error: an inner or outer join must have ON, USING or NATURAL. Only CROSS JOIN may omit a condition. SQLite also treats CROSS JOIN as an instruction not to reorder the two tables, which PostgreSQL does not. Key takeaways Two aliases let one customer row match another as its referrer. CROSS JOIN returns every left/right pair. Write CROSS JOIN explicitly when every combination is intended. Further reading Table expressions and joined tables — PostgreSQL docs SELECT — SQLite docs

t: Choose explicit join keys over NATURAL
sum: USING joins identically named keys and merges their output column.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. USING and NATURAL When the join columns have the same name in both tables, USING is shorthand. For this inner join, USING (product_id) means ON order_items.product_id = products_v.product_id. A SELECT result contains one merged product_id column instead of two. The explicit select list above chooses just order id, product name and quantity; it returns the nine order lines. A view is a named stored query, so products_v provides the same products with a renamed key. This distinction matters when reading or changing a select list. ON retains both input key columns in SELECT, whereas USING merges them. With an outer join, the merged key represents the preserved side's value; a FULL JOIN can take that value from either side. Prefer explicit output columns so callers do not depend on a layout that changes when a table gains a column. The key being named alike is only a naming convenience. Verify that both columns represent the same relationship before choosing USING. Our order and customer tables both have id, but those ids identify different entities. The foreign key is orders.customer_id, so the correct join is ON orders.customer_id = customers.id. NATURAL JOIN goes further and joins on every column name the two tables share. It is fragile. In our schema the only shared name between customers and orders is id, so customers NATURAL JOIN orders matches customer ids against order ids and returns 0 rows, with no error. Adding a column like created_at to both tables later would silently change the meaning of every natural join. Prefer explicit ON. Choosing a join Question Join ------ Rows with a match INNER All of A, B if any LEFT Matches and both leftovers FULL A with no B LEFT + IS NULL Every combination CROSS Row to row in one table self Key takeaways USING joins identically named keys and merges their output column. NATURAL JOIN uses every shared column name, even an unintended id. Choose the join type from the rows the result must preserve. Further reading Table expressions and joined tables — PostgreSQL docs SELECT — SQLite docs

t: Compute order totals and mean product prices
sum: An order total adds each quantity times its product price.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. Most business questions are about totals, not individual rows. How many orders are pending? What has each customer spent? Which category earns the most? Aggregate functions collapse many rows into one value, and GROUP BY decides which rows get collapsed together. This lesson uses the same shop schema as the rest of the module. An order's total is worked out from its lines in order_items: multiply each line's quantity by its product's price, then add the lines up. The same sum in SQL is SUM(oi.qty p.price) grouped by order. The totals come out as 101 = £62, 102 = £80, 103 = £41, 104 = £70, 105 = £25 and 106 = £8. Aggregates over the whole table With no GROUP BY or HAVING filter, an aggregate treats the whole filtered table as one group and returns exactly one row: SUM MIN MAX AVG ------------ 193 8 90 38.6 SUM adds the values, MIN and MAX pick the smallest and largest, and AVG is the ordinary mean: the sum divided by how many values there are. Key takeaways An order total adds each quantity times its product price. SUM, MIN, MAX and AVG reduce a whole input to a summary row. AVG shares the total across the known input values. Further reading Aggregate functions — PostgreSQL documentation Built-in aggregate functions — SQLite documentation

t: Count rows and avoid truncated averages
sum: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts known values.
x: The shop has six orders: five known customer ids (1, 1, 2, 3, 4) and one guest NULL. Its nine order lines contain fourteen items in total. Prices are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. Three kinds of COUNT COUNT is the one people trip over, because it has three forms that answer different questions: form result counts --------- COUNT() 6 rows COUNT(customer_id) 5 non-NULL values COUNT(DISTINCT...) 4 distinct non-NULL values Guest order 106 has a NULL customer_id, so COUNT(customer_id) skips it. Asha placed two orders, so the distinct count drops to 4. The numeric aggregates shown here, along with COUNT(column), ignore NULLs; the NULL units looks at what that means for averages. Integer arithmetic SUM of integers is an integer, and dividing two integers truncates. SUM(qty) / COUNT() over order_items divides the 14 items by the 9 lines: AVG(qty) gives 1.555... instead. Use AVG, or multiply by 1.0 first (SUM(qty) 1.0 / COUNT()), so the division is no longer between two integers. PostgreSQL differs in a useful way here: AVG of an integer column returns numeric, so you see 38.6000000000000000 rather than SQLite's floating-point 38.6. SUM of an integer column returns bigint, which widens the range but can still overflow at the 64-bit limit. Key takeaways COUNT() counts rows; COUNT(column) counts known values. COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts distinct non-NULL values. AVG avoids the truncation of integer SUM divided by integer COUNT. Further reading Aggregate functions — PostgreSQL documentation Built-in aggregate functions — SQLite documentation

t: Group rows and choose one value per group
sum: GROUP BY emits one result row per grouping key.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. GROUP BY: one row per group GROUP BY splits the rows into groups that share the same values in the listed columns, then runs the aggregates once per group: category n avg_p --------- NULL 1 8.0 home 2 65.0 kitchen 2 27.5 All NULL categories form one group, even though NULL = NULL is not true elsewhere in SQL. You can group by an expression. Monthly order counts: That gives 2026-01: 1, 2026-02: 2 and 2026-03: 3. In PostgreSQL, with a real date column, you would write date_trunc('month', ordered_on) instead. Both databases allow GROUP BY to use a select-list alias; check support and name-resolution rules when moving to another SQL engine. The single-value rule After grouping, each output row stands for a whole group. Every column in SELECT must therefore have one value per group: either it is in the GROUP BY list, or it is inside an aggregate. Asha has two orders with different dates. Which ordered_on should her row show? PostgreSQL refuses: column "orders.ordered_on" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function. SQLite accepts it and picks the value from some row in the group. Here it showed 2026-01-05, but nothing guarantees which one. (MySQL behaves the same unless ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY is on, which it is by default since 5.7.5.) SQLite has one documented special case. If the query uses exactly one MIN() or MAX(), the bare columns come from the row that holds that minimum or maximum. SELECT category, MAX(price), name... GROUP BY category returns Rug for home and Kettle for kitchen. It is convenient, but it is not portable. In PostgreSQL, the standard "row with the max per group" tool is DISTINCT ON or a window function (module 2). PostgreSQL does relax the rule in one sensible case. If you group by a table's primary key, you may select any other column from that table, because the key determines them: Key takeaways GROUP BY emits one result row per grouping key. Use an aggregate when an ungrouped column has several values per group. PostgreSQL recognises columns determined by a grouped primary key. Further reading GROUP BY and HAVING — PostgreSQL documentation Bare columns in aggregate queries — SQLite documentation

t: Filter source rows before filtering groups
sum: WHERE selects the rows that enter groups.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. WHERE versus HAVING Both filter, but at different moments: WHERE filters rows before grouping. It cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. It can. Who spent more than £50 on orders that were not cancelled? customer_id spent ------ 1 142 3 70 Asha (1) spent 62 + 80. Chloe (3) spent 70. Ben's 41 fails the HAVING. Dev's only order was cancelled, so WHERE removed it before grouping and he never forms a group. Recall the logical order from the SELECT units: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. Two consequences: Put row conditions in WHERE to state their intent clearly. Adding status to this query's GROUP BY changes its groups: a customer with both shipped and pending orders can produce two totals. It is not equivalent to filtering status before grouping by customer. The optimiser may also push eligible HAVING predicates down, so the logical order of clauses does not dictate execution cost. HAVING runs before SELECT, so in PostgreSQL you must repeat the aggregate: HAVING spent > 50 fails with column "spent" does not exist. SQLite accepts the alias. ORDER BY spent works in both. Key takeaways WHERE selects the rows that enter groups. HAVING selects groups from their aggregate results. In PostgreSQL repeat an aggregate in HAVING instead of its SELECT alias. Further reading GROUP BY and HAVING — PostgreSQL documentation

t: Count conditions and handle empty input
sum: CASE and FILTER let different aggregates select different inputs.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. Conditional aggregation You often want several counts side by side. Put a condition inside the aggregate: shipped pending ------ 3 2 The CASE form works because summing 1s and 0s is counting. Each row contributes 1 if it meets the condition and 0 if it doesn't: The CASE form works in both engines and is widely portable. FILTER is standard SQL; PostgreSQL has supported it since 9.4 and SQLite since 3.30. This one-pass "pivot" avoids issuing a separate query per status and can avoid repeated scans. Actual performance depends on the plan and available indexes. Joining strings To list the names in each group, PostgreSQL has string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name). SQLite has long had group_concat(name, ', ') and added string_agg with in-aggregate ORDER BY in 3.44. Without the ORDER BY inside the call, the order of the joined names is unspecified. Empty input What does SUM(price) return when no rows match? COUNT of nothing is 0, but SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX of nothing are NULL. Wrap them in COALESCE(SUM(price), 0) when a report needs a zero. (SQLite also has a non-standard TOTAL() that returns 0.0.) Add GROUP BY and the behaviour changes: no rows means no groups, so the query returns zero rows, not one row of NULL. Key takeaways CASE and FILTER let different aggregates select different inputs. Specify ordering inside string aggregation when name order matters. An ungrouped empty input still gives one aggregate row; GROUP BY gives no groups. Further reading Aggregate functions — PostgreSQL documentation Built-in aggregate functions — SQLite documentation Aggregate expressions and FILTER — PostgreSQL documentation

sum: A count after joining lines counts lines rather than orders.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. Fan-out: the silent double count The most expensive aggregate bug in real reporting comes from joins. A join repeats each row on the "one" side once per matching row on the "many" side. Aggregating after that repetition counts things more than once. Counting orders per customer after joining order_items: name n ------ Asha 3 Ben 2 Chloe 2 Dev 1 Asha has two orders, not three. The count is of order lines. COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) fixes this case, but there is a nastier version that DISTINCT cannot always rescue. Joining two independent one-to-many relationships at once multiplies them: name orders refs --------- Asha 4 4 Ben 1 1 Erin 0 0 (Chloe and Dev, with one order and no referrals, are left out to save space.) Asha has 2 orders and 2 referrals. The join produces 2 × 2 = 4 rows for her, so both counts say 4. COUNT(DISTINCT...) would happen to fix counts here, but a SUM cannot be repaired that way. Every value from one child table is repeated once per matching row of the other, so the sum is multiplied: SUM(DISTINCT...) is no fix either: it would merge two genuinely equal values, such as two different order lines that are each worth £30. The reliable fix is to aggregate each relationship separately, then join the results, using subqueries or CTEs (module 2): This gives Asha 2 and 2. A quick sanity check is to compare a grouped total with the same total computed without the join. If the numbers disagree, something is fanning out. LEFT JOIN plus COUNT To include customers with zero orders, use a LEFT JOIN and count a column from the right-hand table: name COUNT() COUNT(o.id) --------- Asha 2 2 Erin 1 0 (Ben, Chloe and Dev show 1 and 1.) Erin's row survives the outer join with NULLs in the order columns. COUNT() counts that row and reports 1. COUNT(o.id) skips the NULL and correctly reports 0. Key takeaways A count after joining lines counts lines rather than orders. Aggregate independent child relationships separately before joining. After LEFT JOIN count a right-hand key to report zero matches. Further reading Aggregate functions — PostgreSQL documentation GROUP BY and HAVING — PostgreSQL documentation

t: Compare unknown values and trace three-valued logic
sum: Ordinary scalar comparisons with NULL give UNKNOWN.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. NULL often makes a correct-looking query return the wrong rows. Treat NULL as a missing or unknown value, rather than zero or an empty string. An application may use it for "unknown" or "not applicable"; SQL does not record which interpretation you intended. If Chloe's city is unknown, is she in London? We don't know. Is she not in London? We don't know that either. SQL encodes that "don't know" as a third truth value, UNKNOWN, alongside TRUE and FALSE. The shop schema has three kinds of NULL that this lesson uses: Chloe's city, the referred_by of Asha and Erin, and the customer_id of guest order 106. Comparisons with NULL are unknown The ordinary scalar comparisons used here, such as = and <>, give UNKNOWN if either operand is NULL (SQL shows UNKNOWN as NULL). Arithmetic and the operator in these examples also propagate NULL: Even NULL = NULL is unknown: two unknown values might or might not be equal. So this finds nobody: Use the dedicated predicates instead: Three-valued logic AND, OR and NOT extend naturally. Treat UNKNOWN as "could be either" and ask whether the answer would change: AND T F U ------------ T T F U F F F F U U F U OR T F U ------------ T T T T F T F U U T U U NOT U is U. The short-cuts are worth memorising: FALSE AND anything is FALSE, and TRUE OR anything is TRUE. In both cases the unknown side can't change the result. There is a compact way to remember both tables. Assign zero to FALSE, one half to UNKNOWN and one to TRUE; the three operators then become simple arithmetic: For example, pairing TRUE with UNKNOWN gives UNKNOWN under AND, while pairing FALSE with UNKNOWN gives FALSE. NOT leaves UNKNOWN unchanged. This numerical encoding describes Kleene's three-valued logic for AND, OR and NOT; it is a memory aid, not SQL's internal storage format. The ordinary scalar equality comparisons in this unit return UNKNOWN whenever either side is NULL. WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. It discards UNKNOWN just as it discards FALSE. To trace a nested condition, evaluate its comparisons first, then AND or OR, then an enclosing NOT. For Erin, referred_by = 1 is UNKNOWN but city = 'London' is FALSE. Their AND is therefore FALSE, and negating that AND gives TRUE. For Chloe the pair is TRUE and UNKNOWN, so its AND and its negation are both UNKNOWN. The quiz uses this contrast. Key takeaways Ordinary scalar comparisons with NULL give UNKNOWN. FALSE AND UNKNOWN is FALSE; TRUE OR UNKNOWN is TRUE. NOT UNKNOWN stays UNKNOWN. Further reading Null (SQL) — Wikipedia) Comparison functions and operators — PostgreSQL documentation Three-valued logic — Modern SQL

t: Filter unknowns and compare nullable values
sum: WHERE keeps TRUE and discards FALSE and UNKNOWN.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. WHERE keeps only TRUE This is the rule that turns three-valued logic into missing rows. WHERE and HAVING retain only rows or groups whose condition is TRUE. An ON condition produces a matching pair only when TRUE; an outer join can subsequently preserve unmatched rows by padding. FALSE and UNKNOWN do not satisfy any of these conditions. name --- Ben Erin Chloe disappears. For her, NULL <> 'London' is UNKNOWN. Worse, WHERE NOT (city = 'London') gives the same two rows, because NOT UNKNOWN is still UNKNOWN. A row can fail both a condition and its negation. Together, city = 'London' and city <> 'London' cover only four of the five customers. If you want Chloe included, say so: IS DISTINCT FROM The standard has a NULL-safe comparison that treats NULL as an ordinary, comparable value: a b a <> b a IS DISTINCT FROM b ------------ 1 2 T T 1 1 F F 1 NULL U T NULL NULL U F WHERE city IS DISTINCT FROM 'London' returns Ben, Chloe and Erin. PostgreSQL has supported it for many years. SQLite added it in 3.39, and has long had its own shorter spelling: IS and IS NOT also compare ordinary values, so city IS NOT 'London' means the same thing here. Boolean literals on the right of SQLite IS have special truth-testing rules. In PostgreSQL, write IS DISTINCT FROM or IS NOT DISTINCT FROM to compare arbitrary values; the separate predicates IS NULL, IS TRUE, IS FALSE and IS UNKNOWN test missingness or truth. IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the NULL-safe equality. It is handy for comparing two nullable columns, for example when checking whether a row has changed. In SQLite, the boolean-literal exception also applies to the long spelling: 2 IS NOT DISTINCT FROM TRUE is true, because it tests truthiness; PostgreSQL rejects this integer-versus-boolean comparison. For the nullable text columns here, both spellings perform the intended value comparison. Key takeaways WHERE keeps TRUE and discards FALSE and UNKNOWN. Add an explicit IS NULL branch when unknown values should pass. IS DISTINCT FROM detects changes involving NULL. Further reading Comparison functions and operators — PostgreSQL documentation NULL handling in SQLite versus other database engines

t: Avoid NULL poisoning in NOT IN
sum: A NULL in a nonempty scalar NOT IN list prevents a TRUE result.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. The NOT IN trap This query looks like "customers who have never ordered": It returns no rows at all, even though Erin has never ordered. The reason is the guest order's NULL customer_id. The subquery produces (1, 1, 2, 3, 4, NULL), and x NOT IN (list) expands to: For Erin (id 5), every comparison is TRUE except the last, which is UNKNOWN. TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN, so WHERE drops her. For everyone else one comparison is FALSE. An AND chain is only as true as its weakest term, so one NULL in the list means NOT IN can never be TRUE. Positive matches with IN still work: 1 IN (1, NULL) is TRUE. A nonmatch can still be UNKNOWN: 3 IN (1, NULL) is UNKNOWN, rather than FALSE. The especially surprising loss of every row occurs when a NULL prevents a NOT IN result from becoming TRUE. The empty-set case is different. If the subquery returns zero rows, IN is FALSE and NOT IN is TRUE, even for a NULL left operand. Both engines accept an empty subquery; PostgreSQL rejects the literal syntax IN (), which SQLite accepts. Do not confuse an empty result with a one-row result containing NULL. The fix is NOT EXISTS, which asks whether a matching row exists, a question that is always TRUE or FALSE: The LEFT JOIN... WHERE o.id IS NULL anti-join from the joins lesson also works. Adding WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL to the subquery fixes NOT IN too, but it is easy to forget, and the bug only appears once the first NULL arrives in production. Prefer NOT EXISTS by habit. PostgreSQL's planner also handles NOT EXISTS well (as an anti-join), while it often can't turn NOT IN over a subquery into one, precisely because of these NULL rules. Key takeaways A NULL in a nonempty scalar NOT IN list prevents a TRUE result. NOT EXISTS asks whether any matching row exists. An empty subquery makes NOT IN true even for a NULL left operand. Further reading Subquery expressions (NOT IN, EXISTS) — PostgreSQL documentation

t: Choose fallback values and CASE branches
sum: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. Functions that tame NULL COALESCE(a, b,...) returns the first argument that isn't NULL: That shows Chloe's city as unknown. NULLIF(a, b) does the reverse: it returns NULL when a = b, otherwise a. Its classic use is avoiding division by zero. total / NULLIF(n, 0) returns NULL instead of failing when n is 0. PostgreSQL raises division by zero; SQLite already returns NULL, so the guard matters most for portability. String concatenation with is NULL if either side is NULL. PostgreSQL's concat() function skips NULL arguments instead (concat('a', NULL) is 'a'), and SQLite added the same function in 3.44. CASE and NULL A searched CASE follows the WHERE rule: a branch is taken only if its condition is TRUE. Chloe falls through both branches to '?'. The simple form, CASE city WHEN NULL THEN..., compares with =, so its NULL branch can never match. Write CASE WHEN city IS NULL THEN... instead. Key takeaways COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument. NULLIF can turn a zero divisor into NULL. Use searched CASE with IS NULL to handle missing values. Further reading Conditional expressions: CASE, COALESCE and NULLIF — PostgreSQL Built-in scalar functions — SQLite Comparison functions and operators — PostgreSQL documentation NULL handling in SQLite versus other database engines

t: Distinguish unknown ratings from zero ratings
sum: AVG divides by the number of known inputs.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. NULL in aggregates SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX and COUNT(column) skip NULLs. This is not universal: PostgreSQL array_agg includes NULL elements. That is usually what you want, but it changes what an average means. Suppose we add a rating column where only three products have been rated: name rating ------ Kettle 5 Toaster 3 Lamp NULL Rug NULL Mug 4 expression result ------ AVG(rating) 4.0 SUM(rating)1.0/COUNT() 2.4 AVG(COALESCE(rating, 0)) 2.4 The two answers divide the same total by different counts: AVG is the mean of the ratings we know. Treating unrated products as 0 gives the lower figure. Neither is wrong, but they answer different questions, so decide which one you mean. Replacing NULL with 0 is a claim that the value is zero, and it is often false. Recall from the previous lesson that SUM over no rows returns NULL, not 0. Grouping, DISTINCT and sorting Here SQL switches rules. For grouping and duplicate removal, NULLs are treated as equal to each other: SELECT DISTINCT referred_by gives NULL, 1, 2: one NULL, not two. GROUP BY city puts all NULL cities in one group. For sorting, NULLs are treated as either smaller or larger than every value. As the SELECT units showed, SQLite puts them first in ascending order and PostgreSQL puts them last. NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST make it explicit. MIN and MAX ignore NULLs: MIN(city) is Bristol, not NULL. Key takeaways AVG divides by the number of known inputs. Replacing NULL with zero changes the question being answered. Grouping and duplicate removal gather NULLs together, while sorting is engine-dependent. Further reading Comparison functions and operators — PostgreSQL documentation NULL handling in SQLite versus other database engines

t: Trace NULL through constraints and outer joins
sum: CHECK rejects FALSE but permits UNKNOWN; add NOT NULL when required.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. Customers are Asha (1, London), Ben (2, Leeds), Chloe (3, unknown city), Dev (4, London) and Erin (5, Bristol). Asha has orders 101 and 102, Ben 103, Chloe 104, Dev 105; guest order 106 has no customer, and Erin has no orders. NULL in constraints Constraints also lean towards letting NULL through. UNIQUE allows many NULLs. Two rows with a NULL email don't violate email UNIQUE, because neither is known to equal the other. Both SQLite and PostgreSQL behave this way by default. PostgreSQL 15 added UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT for when you want at most one NULL. CHECK fails only when the condition is FALSE. With age INTEGER CHECK (age >= 18), inserting age 10 fails, but inserting NULL succeeds, because NULL >= 18 is UNKNOWN, not FALSE. Add NOT NULL when the value is required: This asymmetry, where WHERE rejects UNKNOWN but CHECK accepts it, catches people out. Both follow the same principle: only reject on evidence. NULLs from outer joins A LEFT JOIN fills unmatched right-hand columns with NULL. Filtering on those columns in WHERE quietly turns the outer join back into an inner one: name ref ------ Ben Asha Chloe Asha Asha and Erin have no referrer, so r.city is NULL, the test is UNKNOWN and they vanish. Dev's referrer is Ben, from Leeds. If you meant "keep everyone, but only show referrers outside Leeds", move r.city <> 'Leeds' into ON. Replacing the WHERE condition with r.city IS DISTINCT FROM 'Leeds' keeps unmatched rows but still removes Dev, whose referrer is in Leeds; it does not preserve everyone. Design advice Use NOT NULL by default and allow NULL only where "unknown" or "not applicable" is a real state. Every nullable column makes every query on it harder to reason about. Don't invent stand-in values such as '', 0 or 1900-01-01 for unknown. They take part in comparisons and aggregates as if they were real. When a column is nullable, ask for each query: what happens to the NULL rows here? Key takeaways CHECK rejects FALSE but permits UNKNOWN; add NOT NULL when required. Default UNIQUE rules permit multiple NULLs in SQLite and PostgreSQL. Move a referrer eligibility test into ON to retain every customer. Further reading Constraints — PostgreSQL documentation Null (SQL) — Wikipedia) Comparison functions and operators — PostgreSQL documentation NULL handling in SQLite versus other database engines

t: Insert named columns and read generated values
sum: Name INSERT columns so a schema change cannot shift the values.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. Examples of writes start from that original data unless a block explicitly groups statements together. Reading data can only give you a wrong answer. Writing data can destroy it. This lesson covers the three statements that change rows, known together as DML (data manipulation language): INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. It also covers the constraints that make the database refuse changes that would break your rules. The examples use the module's shop schema. Each one starts from the original data. INSERT Always name the columns you are filling: Columns you leave out get their default, which is NULL unless the table says otherwise. Here referred_by is NULL. id is an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, so SQLite assigns the next number, 6. (PostgreSQL uses an identity column or sequence for the same job; see the next lesson.) INSERT INTO customers VALUES (...) without a column list also works, but it depends on the column order in the table. Add a column later and every such statement breaks, or worse, puts values in the wrong columns. Several rows, and RETURNING One statement can insert many rows. This usually reduces parsing and round-trip work compared with many single-row statements. In autocommit mode it also avoids a separate commit for each row; inside an explicit transaction those statements already share a commit: id name ------ 6 Jug 7 Tray RETURNING hands back the rows as they were written, including generated ids and defaults, without a second query. PostgreSQL has had it for a long time; SQLite added it in 3.35. INSERT... SELECT The rows can come from a query instead of VALUES: This adds "Lamp XL" at £80 and "Rug XL" at £180. The copy happens inside the database, so no data travels to your application and back. If a row might already exist, INSERT... ON CONFLICT (an upsert) can update it instead. Module 2 covers upserts properly. Key takeaways Name INSERT columns so a schema change cannot shift the values. Omitted columns use defaults, including generated ids. Multi-row INSERT and RETURNING can reduce database round trips. Further reading Data manipulation — PostgreSQL documentation

t: Update rows using their previous values
sum: UPDATE expressions read the previous row values.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. Examples of writes start from that original data unless a block explicitly groups statements together. UPDATE UPDATE changes columns in every row that matches WHERE: name price ------ Kettle 35 Toaster 30 The right-hand side of SET sees the old row values. SET a = b, b = a swaps two columns in standard SQL and in PostgreSQL and SQLite, because both expressions read the values from before the update. WHERE can use a subquery: The subquery's average is the ordinary mean of the five prices: This uncorrelated average subquery has no reference to the outer product row. SQLite evaluates it once and reuses its result; PostgreSQL evaluates it against the statement's snapshot. Only Lamp (£40) and Rug (£90) exceed £38.6 and get doubled. The threshold stays fixed for this query. Do not generalise that to a correlated subquery reading the table being changed: SQLite can see changes made earlier by the same statement. To update using another table, PostgreSQL and SQLite (3.33+) both support UPDATE... FROM. Mark every London customer's orders: That updates 101, 102 and 105. MySQL spells this differently (UPDATE orders JOIN customers...), so this is one place where portable SQL is hard. Key takeaways UPDATE expressions read the previous row values. A scalar average subquery here uses the pre-statement data. An UPDATE matching no rows succeeds with an affected count of zero. Further reading Data manipulation — PostgreSQL documentation The UPDATE statement — SQLite documentation

t: Check destructive writes and roll them back
sum: A DELETE removes rows; an UPDATE can clear an individual nullable value.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. Examples of writes start from that original data unless a block explicitly groups statements together. DELETE DELETE removes whole rows. To remove a value, UPDATE it to NULL instead. To empty a table quickly, TRUNCATE (PostgreSQL) skips per-row work, but it is all-or-nothing and doesn't fire row-level triggers. SQLite has no TRUNCATE; it optimises an unfiltered DELETE FROM t instead. The missing WHERE UPDATE products SET category = 'sale'; changes every product. DELETE FROM order_items; removes all nine order lines. Both are valid statements and can finish before you notice in this tiny shop; large tables can instead take substantial time and hold locks. A safe routine for risky changes 1. Write the WHERE clause first, as a SELECT, and check the rows and count. 2. Start a transaction with BEGIN. 3. Run the UPDATE or DELETE with the same WHERE. Check the affected row count it reports. 4. COMMIT if it matches, ROLLBACK if it doesn't. Until COMMIT, other sessions don't see your changes, and ROLLBACK undoes them. How the database keeps transactions isolated from each other is covered in System Design. Some tools add safeguards: MySQL's --safe-updates option restricts UPDATE and DELETE unless they use a key condition or a LIMIT; large queries can be restricted further. Many GUI clients warn about unfiltered writes. In PostgreSQL's psql, autocommit is on by default, so each statement commits immediately unless you type BEGIN first. Key takeaways A DELETE removes rows; an UPDATE can clear an individual nullable value. Omitting WHERE changes or removes every qualifying table row. Inspect the target rows and affected count within a deliberate transaction. Further reading Data manipulation — PostgreSQL documentation

t: Enforce required values, uniqueness and row rules
sum: NOT NULL requires a known value.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. Examples of writes start from that original data unless a block explicitly groups statements together. Constraints A constraint is a rule enforced when relevant data changes. With the default immediate constraint handling used here, a violation fails the statement and undoes its row changes. Deferred constraints are checked later, and SQLite has alternative conflict policies, covered next. Constraints are your last line of defence: application code has bugs, and data is often written by more than one program. constraint rejects ------ NOT NULL a missing value UNIQUE a duplicate PRIMARY KEY duplicate key; normally NULL FOREIGN KEY a reference to nothing CHECK (...) a rule returning FALSE The shop uses SQLite's special INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, which generates an id for an omitted or NULL key. Ordinary non-STRICT rowid tables also have a historical quirk: other primary-key declarations can allow NULL unless explicitly NOT NULL. PostgreSQL primary keys, SQLite STRICT tables and WITHOUT ROWID tables require non-NULL keys. The errors from SQLite on the shop schema: PostgreSQL's messages name the constraint, for example duplicate key value violates unique constraint "customers_pkey" and insert or update on table "orders" violates foreign key constraint "orders_customer_id_fkey". Naming constraints yourself (CONSTRAINT price_positive CHECK (price > 0)) makes those messages easier to act on. DEFAULT isn't a constraint, but it sits alongside them: created TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE fills in today's date when the insert omits the column. INSERT INTO t DEFAULT VALUES inserts a row made entirely of defaults. CHECK Inserting 6 fails with CHECK constraint failed: stars BETWEEN 1 AND 5. Remember from the NULL lesson that a CHECK passes when its result is UNKNOWN, so pair it with NOT NULL if the value is required. A CHECK can only see the row being written. Rules across rows or tables need a UNIQUE constraint, a foreign key, a trigger or application logic. Key takeaways NOT NULL requires a known value. CHECK rejects FALSE but permits UNKNOWN. Use UNIQUE for cross-row uniqueness, rather than a row CHECK. Further reading Constraints — PostgreSQL documentation SQLite foreign key support

t: Protect references and choose delete actions
sum: Foreign keys protect references in both insertion and deletion directions.
x: The shop's orders.customer_id references customers.id, and order_items.order_id references orders.id. Original order 105 is cancelled and has one Toaster line. Each independent write example starts from fresh original data. Foreign keys orders.customer_id REFERENCES customers(id) says every order's customer must exist (or be NULL, like the guest order). The database checks both directions: Inserting an order for customer 99 fails: there is no such customer. Deleting customer 1 fails while orders 101 and 102 still point at her. What happens on delete is your choice: ON DELETE deleting the parent ------ NO ACTION (default) fails if children exist RESTRICT fails, checked at once CASCADE deletes the children SET NULL sets children's FK to NULL NO ACTION and RESTRICT differ only in timing: NO ACTION can be deferred to the end of the transaction, RESTRICT cannot. CASCADE suits rows that have no meaning without their parent, such as reviews of a product or the items of an order. Be wary of using it widely: one DELETE of a customer could silently remove years of order history. For records you must keep, RESTRICT plus a soft-delete flag is safer. SET NULL fits optional links, such as referred_by: if the referrer is deleted, the customer remains, unreferred. SQLite doesn't enforce foreign keys by default For backwards compatibility, SQLite's usual default leaves foreign key enforcement off, though a build can choose a different default. Explicitly run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; for each connection, before starting a transaction, and check its setting; changing it inside an active transaction has no effect. With enforcement off, the order for customer 99 is accepted, and deleting Asha leaves orders 101 and 102 pointing at nobody. PostgreSQL enforces declared foreign keys on ordinary writes. Deferred constraints Sometimes rows that refer to each other must be inserted in an awkward order. A constraint declared DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED is checked at COMMIT instead of after each statement. Both PostgreSQL and SQLite support this for foreign keys, and PostgreSQL also for UNIQUE. If the reference is still broken at commit time, the commit fails. Key takeaways Foreign keys protect references in both insertion and deletion directions. Choose CASCADE, RESTRICT or SET NULL to fit the relationship. Enable SQLite foreign keys per connection and distinguish deferred checks. Further reading Constraints — PostgreSQL documentation SQLite foreign key support

t: Recover from failed statements and transactions
sum: Default constraint handling undoes the failed statement.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. Examples of writes start from that original data unless a block explicitly groups statements together. Statements are atomic With the default constraint-error handling used here, a failed statement undoes its row changes. SQLite has other conflict policies: FAIL can retain earlier row changes from the same statement, and IGNORE can skip offending rows. PostgreSQL sequence increments and external side effects are also not undone by a ROLLBACK: Jug was valid, but it is not inserted either. The products table still has five rows. Inside a transaction, the two databases differ after an error: SQLite, for the default ABORT constraint policy used here, undoes the failed statement. Earlier statements in the transaction remain pending, and COMMIT keeps them. Other conflict policies and errors can have different effects. PostgreSQL marks the whole transaction as failed. Every further statement errors with current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block, and COMMIT acts as a ROLLBACK. Use a SAVEPOINT if you want to recover from an error and carry on. Application code that catches a constraint error and carries on within the same transaction works in SQLite but fails in PostgreSQL. For PostgreSQL, put the part that may fail after a savepoint. If it fails, roll back to that savepoint before continuing. The rollback removes changes made since the savepoint and clears the failed state for that portion of the transaction; earlier work remains pending. A minimal example uses a duplicate primary key in the shop: In application code the error handler must actually send the rollback-to-savepoint command. Merely catching the driver exception does not repair PostgreSQL's transaction state. Do not commit earlier work by accident in SQLite either: choose whether the business operation should survive as a whole, and explicitly roll back the whole transaction if it should not. Key takeaways Default constraint handling undoes the failed statement. SQLite ABORT leaves earlier successful transaction statements pending. PostgreSQL needs rollback or rollback to a savepoint before more work. Further reading Data manipulation — PostgreSQL documentation Constraints — PostgreSQL documentation

t: Model relationships and preserve sale prices
sum: Use a foreign key for one-to-many and a junction table for many-to-many.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. Queries come and go, but a schema lasts for years. A badly chosen type or key turns into thousands of lines of defensive code and a data-cleaning project. This lesson is about writing DDL (data definition language): CREATE, ALTER and DROP. It also covers the decisions behind those statements. We'll redesign the module's shop schema from its requirements, then look at how to change it once it's live. Normalisation theory gets its own module (Relational Theory). How tables and indexes are stored on disk is covered in System Design. From requirements to tables The shop's requirements, stated plainly: A customer has a name, an optional city, and may have been referred by another customer. A product has a name, a price and an optional category. A customer places many orders. A guest can also order with no account. An order contains many products, each with a quantity, and a product appears in many orders. Each noun that has its own facts becomes a table. Each relationship becomes a foreign key: relationship how it's stored ------ one-to-many FK on the "many" side many-to-many a junction table self-reference FK to the same table optional link nullable FK orders.customer_id is the one-to-many link, and it is nullable for guests. order_items is the junction table that resolves orders-to-products many-to-many. Its primary key is the pair (order_id, product_id): a composite key. It also enforces a business rule, because adding a second Kettle to order 101 fails with UNIQUE constraint failed. You increase qty instead. A flaw in our schema The module's order_items stores only a quantity, so an order's total is computed from products.price today. Raise the Kettle's price and every historical order containing a Kettle changes value. That's wrong for invoices, refunds and accounting. The fix is to copy the price at the moment of sale into the line item (unit_pence). This looks like duplication, but it's a different fact: "what this customer paid" rather than "what the product costs now". Many apparent duplicates in a well-designed schema are really snapshots like this. Key takeaways Use a foreign key for one-to-many and a junction table for many-to-many. A composite line key makes each order/product pair unique. The sale price is a historical fact distinct from the current product price. Further reading Data definition — PostgreSQL documentation

t: Store money without binary rounding errors
sum: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. Choosing types Money: never floating point In PostgreSQL, those uncast decimal literals are exact numeric values, so the equality above is TRUE. To demonstrate binary floating point there, cast the operands explicitly: Binary floating point can't represent most decimal fractions exactly. The reason is in how a floating-point number is built: it is a whole number scaled by an integer power of two. The stored 0.1 and 0.2 are each a tiny bit off, and their sum lands next to, not on, the stored 0.3. Those small errors build up in sums. Store money either as: integer minor units (pence): price_pence INTEGER, where £10.99 is 1099. This is exact, fast and portable, and it's how payment processors such as Stripe represent amounts. exact decimals: PostgreSQL numeric(10,2). This is exact, and SUM of it stays exact. Converting between pounds and pence is a single multiplication, done once, when the application reads a price typed by a person or displays one: Parse typed amounts as exact decimals or split the decimal digits into whole pence before storing them. Multiplying an already rounded binary float by 100 can carry a rounding error into the conversion. A fixed-scale numeric column also rounds inputs with extra decimal places, so choose and apply a rounding rule. Three £10.99 items then sum to 1099 + 1099 + 1099 = 3297 pence, exactly £32.97, with no rounding at any step. Avoid real, float and double precision for money. Also avoid PostgreSQL's money type, whose formatting depends on a server locale setting. Key takeaways Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly. Store money in integer minor units or exact numeric values. PostgreSQL uncast decimal literals are numeric, unlike SQLite floating-point literals. Further reading Data definition — PostgreSQL documentation Don't do this — PostgreSQL wiki

sum: PostgreSQL date stores calendar dates; timestamptz stores instants.
x: Choosing a column type also determines how dates, instants and text will compare. The shop started with zero-padded ordered_on text; these examples distinguish SQLite representations from PostgreSQL's dedicated types. Dates and times PostgreSQL has real types. Use date for calendar dates and timestamptz (timestamp with time zone) for moments in time. timestamptz stores an absolute instant, internally in UTC, and converts to the session's time zone on display. Plain timestamp stores a wall-clock reading with no zone, which becomes ambiguous the moment two servers or users disagree on time zone or a daylight-saving clock change happens. PostgreSQL's own wiki says to prefer timestamptz. SQLite has no date type. Store ISO-8601 text ('2026-03-09', or '2026-03-09T14:30:00Z' in UTC). It only sorts correctly if every value uses the same zero-padded format: A CHECK can reject badly formatted values at write time, but beware the NULL lesson. SQLite's date('2026-3-9') returns NULL, so CHECK (d = date(d)) is UNKNOWN and passes. Use the NULL-safe form: This rejects '2026-3-9', and also '2026-02-30', which date() turns into '2026-03-02'. Text In PostgreSQL, text and varchar(n) are stored the same way and perform the same. varchar(n) just adds a length check. Use text, and add a CHECK (length(name) <= 200) where a limit is a real business rule. Avoid char(n), which pads with spaces. Key takeaways PostgreSQL date stores calendar dates; timestamptz stores instants. Consistent zero-padded UTC text sorts correctly in SQLite. Use a NULL-safe date check to reject unparseable input. Further reading Data definition — PostgreSQL documentation Don't do this — PostgreSQL wiki

t: Enforce types and separate identity from business keys
sum: Ordinary SQLite type affinity can store text in an INTEGER column.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. SQLite's type affinity versus strict typing PostgreSQL rejects a value of the wrong type. SQLite, by default, treats the declared type as a preference, called type affinity: n typeof(n) d typeof(d) ------------ abc text 12 text 42 integer 3.5 text '42' was converted to an integer because it looked like one. 'abc' couldn't be converted, so SQLite stored text in an INTEGER column without complaint. Since 3.37, a STRICT table rejects incompatible stored values, although its supported type names and conversion rules still differ from PostgreSQL: '42' is still converted to 42, which is a lossless change. Use STRICT for new SQLite tables. Keys A natural key is a real-world identifier: an email address, an ISBN, a vehicle registration. A surrogate primary key is a meaningless generated number or UUID. Natural keys look attractive, but real-world identifiers change (people change email; registrations are transferred) and are rarely as unique as promised. A primary key is copied into every referencing table, so changing it means updating them all. The common pattern is: a surrogate primary key for identity and foreign keys, and a UNIQUE constraint on the natural key to enforce the business rule. Watch case: 'Asha@x.com' and 'asha@x.com' are different strings, so both pass a plain UNIQUE. A unique index on lower(email) catches it (PostgreSQL also offers the citext extension). Key takeaways Ordinary SQLite type affinity can store text in an INTEGER column. STRICT tables require compatible values, including lossless conversions. Keep mutable business identifiers UNIQUE beside a stable surrogate primary key. Further reading Datatypes in SQLite (type affinity) STRICT tables — SQLite documentation

t: Generate ids without collisions or unwanted reuse
sum: Identity sequences do not advance when an explicit id bypasses generation.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. Generating ids database declaration ------ PostgreSQL 10+ GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PostgreSQL (older) serial / bigserial SQLite INTEGER PRIMARY KEY In PostgreSQL, prefer identity columns to serial. They are standard SQL, and ALWAYS rejects hand-written ids unless the insert says OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE. That matters because inserting explicit ids into a serial or BY DEFAULT column doesn't advance the sequence, and a later generated id collides with duplicate key value violates unique constraint. Use bigint for ids of any table that might grow large. A signed integer column spends one bit on the sign, so its largest value is: Running out of 32-bit ids has caused real outages.
