At 1,000 new rows a second, 2.1 billion ids last about 2,147,483,647 / 1,000 ≈ 2.1 million seconds, under 25 days; the same rate would take about 290 million years to exhaust a bigint. Gaps from rolled-back inserts use up ids faster than the row count suggests. In SQLite, an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY column becomes an alias for the table's internal rowid. New ids normally follow a simple rule: (An empty table starts at 1.) This ordinary rule assumes the current largest rowid is below the signed 64-bit maximum; at that maximum SQLite tries unused positive ids instead. So deleting the newest row lets its id be reused. Delete product 5 and the next insert gets id 5 again. Adding AUTOINCREMENT prevents automatic reuse of IDs from previously committed rows, at a small cost. IDs from rolled-back transactions can still be reused, and explicit IDs require separate care. It's only needed when old ids might linger elsewhere, in logs, caches or URLs. UUIDs make sense when ids are generated outside the database. Random UUIDv4 values can make identifiers difficult to guess, but an id is never a substitute for authorisation. They scatter inserts across a B-tree index. Time-ordered UUIDv7 improves insertion locality, while exposing approximate generation time; PostgreSQL 18 added a built-in uuidv7() function. Key takeaways Identity sequences do not advance when an explicit id bypasses generation. Choose an identifier capacity that fits growth and consumed sequence values. SQLite normally reuses a deleted highest rowid unless AUTOINCREMENT prevents it. Further reading Data definition — PostgreSQL documentation SQLite autoincrement

t: Read a constrained PostgreSQL shop schema
sum: Constrain prices, quantities and statuses in the schema.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. The redesigned schema in PostgreSQL Notice the decisions: orders.customer_id is nullable (guests) and uses the default NO ACTION, so a customer with orders can't be deleted by accident. order_items cascades: lines don't exist without their order. unit_pence snapshots the price. The status list is a CHECK. The alternatives are a PostgreSQL ENUM type (compact; values can be renamed with ALTER TYPE, but removing one requires a more involved migration) or a statuses lookup table with a foreign key (best when statuses carry their own data, or business users add them). Use lower-case snake_case names. PostgreSQL folds unquoted identifiers to lower case, so a table created as "OrderItems" must be double-quoted in every query forever. Index your foreign keys Neither PostgreSQL nor SQLite automatically adds a database index merely because a column is referencing a foreign key. Both provide indexed enforcement for primary and UNIQUE keys; SQLite's INTEGER PRIMARY KEY uses the rowid structure. Without an index beginning with customer_id, finding "orders for customer 1" can require a full table scan. In this SQLite fixture, EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows SCAN orders before the index and SEARCH orders USING INDEX after. A missing FK index can also force scans of the child table when a parent is deleted. order_items already has indexed access by order_id, the first column of its primary key. Real planners can still choose a scan when a small table makes it cheaper. Key takeaways Constrain prices, quantities and statuses in the schema. Snapshot unit_pence on each order line. Add suitable indexes on referencing foreign key columns. Further reading Data definition — PostgreSQL documentation Don't do this — PostgreSQL wiki

t: Evolve SQLite tables within supported ALTER operations
sum: Migrations apply versioned schema changes in order.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. Changing a live schema Schemas change for as long as the application lives, through migrations: versioned DDL scripts applied in order by tools such as Flyway, Alembic or Rails migrations. Developers can rely on a few rules of thumb. What SQLite can ALTER SQLite has long supported RENAME TO, RENAME COLUMN (3.25), ADD COLUMN, and DROP COLUMN (3.35). Version 3.53.0 (April 2026) added ALTER COLUMN... SET NOT NULL and DROP NOT NULL, plus adding and dropping named CHECK constraints. Anything else, such as changing a type or adding a foreign key, still means the documented rebuild: create a new table, copy the rows across, drop the old table and rename the new one, all in one transaction. For a populated table, adding an ordinary NOT NULL column needs a non-NULL value for existing rows, commonly supplied by a default. PostgreSQL can add it without a default to an empty table; SQLite imposes its documented default restriction: For these two alternatives, use separate copies of the original populated customers table. The failed phone addition leaves its schema unchanged. The tier addition succeeds and gives each of its five existing rows the value std; later inserts that omit tier receive the same default. A default is used for omission, so it does not turn an explicitly supplied NULL into std. Before a rebuild, inspect the original schema's constraints, indexes, triggers and dependent views. Copying just its column names can silently drop protection or break dependencies. Follow SQLite's documented rebuild sequence, preserve the objects that still apply, and run PRAGMA foreign_key_check before committing. If a step fails, explicitly roll back instead of committing the earlier successful steps. Rehearse the migration on a copy and verify both the resulting schema and row counts. Key takeaways Migrations apply versioned schema changes in order. SQLite ALTER support depends on the engine version. A new required column needs values for existing rows; a default can provide them. Further reading ALTER TABLE — SQLite documentation

sum: Metadata changes can still wait for and hold blocking locks.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. PostgreSQL: watch the locks Most ALTER TABLE forms take an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which blocks reads and writes on that table. Whether that matters depends on how long the lock is held: Fast, metadata only: adding a nullable column, or (since PostgreSQL 11) adding a column with a non-volatile default such as 'std' or now(). This avoids work that grows with the number of rows, but lock waits and catalogue work still determine the elapsed time. Slow, rewrites or scans: changing a column's type, adding a column with a volatile default such as clock_timestamp(), or SET NOT NULL, which scans every row to check. Even a fast ALTER can cause an outage. If a long-running query holds a lock on the table, the ALTER waits for it, and every new query queues behind the ALTER. Set lock_timeout (for example SET lock_timeout = '2s') so the migration fails fast and can be retried. For slow changes, split the work so that the long validation phase permits ordinary reads and writes. The short catalogue changes still take locks: This migration assumes an existing nullable customers.email column whose older rows have already been populated. It upgrades that older schema to require email; the completed redesign in the earlier unit already makes email required. Indexes follow the same idea. Plain CREATE INDEX blocks ordinary writes for the whole build. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY permits ordinary writes, but requires extra scans and waits, cannot run inside a transaction block, and can leave an INVALID index after a failure. Inspect a failed build and normally drop or rebuild the invalid index before retrying. Renaming or dropping a column that running code still uses breaks that code instantly. The safe pattern is expand and contract: add the new column, deploy code that writes both while still reading the old one, and wait until every writer uses that code or a synchronisation trigger covers older writers. Backfill in batches, verify agreement, switch reads, and keep dual writes until every reader has migrated. Only then stop writing and drop the old column in a later release. Switching reads while older writers still update only the original column exposes stale data. Key takeaways Metadata changes can still wait for and hold blocking locks. Use lock_timeout to fail a waiting migration promptly. Validate constraints separately and expand-and-contract incompatible column changes. Further reading ALTER TABLE — PostgreSQL documentation

t: Use stored queries and roll back schema changes
sum: A normal view stores a query; a materialised view stores its result.
x: The examples continue the shop database introduced in the first unit. The original products are Kettle £30, Toaster £25, Lamp £40, Rug £90 and Mug £8. Views and DROP A database view is a named, stored query: SELECT FROM order_totals WHERE total > 60 returns 101 (62), 102 (80) and 104 (70). A view stores no data; it runs its query each time. PostgreSQL's MATERIALIZED VIEW stores the result and needs REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW to update it. The view inherits the price-history flaw discussed earlier: changing today's product price changes a total recomputed from products.price. On the redesigned schema, total the saved qty unit_pence instead. Naming a query does not change which facts it reads or turn a live calculation into a historical snapshot. Transactional DDL lets you rehearse a small change and undo it. This complete example works in SQLite and PostgreSQL: After rollback, selecting from migration_probe raises a missing-table error. The original shop tables are unaffected. This guarantee concerns supported transactional operations: PostgreSQL's CREATE DATABASE and CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, for example, cannot run inside a transaction block. Check the command's documentation instead of assuming every administrative statement is transactional. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t tolerates a missing table, so that particular drop can be repeated. It does not make an entire migration safe to repeat. In PostgreSQL, DROP TABLE t CASCADE also removes dependent views and foreign key constraints without a separate approval prompt; the referencing tables remain. SQLite and PostgreSQL support transactional DDL for operations such as these. Explicitly roll back a failed migration: PostgreSQL normally aborts the transaction after an error, whereas SQLite can leave earlier successful statements pending and a later COMMIT could retain them. Most MySQL DDL implicitly commits, which is one reason migrations there need extra care. Key takeaways A normal view stores a query; a materialised view stores its result. DROP CASCADE can remove dependent views and constraints. Transactional DDL needs explicit transaction error handling; MySQL most DDL implicitly commits. Further reading Data definition — PostgreSQL documentation ALTER TABLE — PostgreSQL documentation

t: Scalar subqueries and the Advanced SQL fixture
sum: A scalar subquery supplies one value; zero rows becomes NULL.
x: A subquery is a complete SELECT placed inside another statement. It lets you ask a question whose answer depends on another question: "which orders are bigger than the average order?" You can't write the average as a constant because you don't know it yet, so you compute it in a subquery. Every lesson in this module uses the same small shop. Result tables show values for the stated data; only an explicit final ORDER BY guarantees row order. The shop schema Schema notation (column names, not executable SQL): id name city --------- 1 Ana London 2 Ben Leeds 3 Cat London 4 Dev York 5 Eve Leeds id cust date total ------------ 101 1 01-05 120 102 2 01-09 45 103 1 02-11 60 104 3 02-14 200 105 4 02-20 45 106 2 03-02 90 107 1 03-15 60 108 3 03-28 30 Treat customers.id, products.id and orders.id as primary keys. orders.customer_id is NOT NULL and references customers.id. The displayed totals, prices and quantities are non-NULL integers; ordered_on is ISO date text in SQLite and a date in PostgreSQL. These declarations matter for the grouped queries and integer arithmetic that follow. All dates are in 2026. Products are Kettle (30), Toaster (25), Mug (10) in Kitchen, and Lamp (40), Rug (90), Vase (35) in Home. Eve has never ordered, and nobody has bought a Vase. Those two gaps will matter. Where a subquery can go A subquery's shape decides where it is allowed: Shape Returns Used in --------- Scalar 0–1 rows, 1 col SELECT, WHERE, HAVING Column Many rows, 1 col IN, ANY, ALL Table Many rows and columns FROM Existence anything EXISTS Scalar subqueries id total ------ 101 120 104 200 106 90 This uncorrelated aggregate can be evaluated once and reused. It yields the mean order total: The outer query then compares each row with 81.25 and keeps 120, 200 and 90. AVG skips NULL totals, so the denominator counts only non-NULL values. This is an uncorrelated subquery: it doesn't mention the outer query at all, so the database can evaluate it once and reuse the value. A "scalar" subquery that returns two rows If a scalar subquery returns more than one row, PostgreSQL raises an error: more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression. SQLite silently uses the first row it happens to find. A query that "works" in SQLite can fail in production on Postgres, and the SQLite answer was arbitrary anyway. Key takeaways A scalar subquery supplies one value; zero rows becomes NULL. PostgreSQL rejects several scalar rows; SQLite takes the first, without a guaranteed order. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: functions subquery PostgreSQL 18: sql expressions SQLite reference

sum: IN keeps a row of the enclosing query at most once, regardless of matching duplicates.
x: Use the Advanced SQL fixture introduced in Scalar subqueries: customers Ana, Ben, Cat, Dev and Eve; orders total 650. Ana spends 240, Ben 135, Cat 230 and Dev 45. Eve has no orders. London contains Ana and Cat; Leeds contains Ben and Eve; York contains Dev. IN with a column subquery Customers who have bought a Rug (product 4): The result is Ana, Ben and Cat. Each has one Rug order line in the Advanced SQL fixture, so a plain join happens to return the same three customers. IN is a semi-join: it keeps each outer customer row at most once even if there are several matching lines. For example, switching the product to Kettle (id 1) finds Ana in orders 101 and 103; IN still returns her once, while the corresponding join returns her twice. Derived tables in FROM A subquery in FROM acts like a temporary table. Average spend per customer, by city: city avg_spend ------ Leeds 135.0 London 235.0 York 45.0 London's figure, for example, averages Ana's and Cat's spend. Eve has no orders, so the inner join drops her and Leeds averages Ben alone: You need two levels of aggregation (sum per customer, then average per city), and SQL does not let you nest aggregates like AVG(SUM(...)) directly. A derived table is the classic fix. The later CTE units show a named version of the same two-stage calculation. Postgres before version 16 required the alias (AS per_cust); SQLite and Postgres 16+ accept it without one. Always alias anyway. Key takeaways IN keeps a row of the enclosing query at most once, regardless of matching duplicates. A derived table separates aggregation per customer from aggregation per city. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: functions subquery PostgreSQL 18: sql expressions SQLite reference

sum: A correlated subquery binds an inner expression to a row of the enclosing query; aliases make the binding clear.
x: The shop has Ana with orders 120, 60 and 60; Ben with 45 and 90; Cat with 200 and 30; Dev with 45; Eve with none. Order dates are ISO dates in 2026, with each customer’s latest dates shown below. Correlated subqueries A correlated subquery refers to a column of the outer query. Its result is defined relative to the current row of the enclosing query, with that row’s values plugged in. This does not guarantee a separate physical execution for each row: an optimiser may rewrite the query. Each customer's most recent order: id name ordered_on --------- 107 Ana 2026-03-15 106 Ben 2026-03-02 108 Cat 2026-03-28 105 Dev 2026-02-20 Trace it for order 103 (Ana, 11 Feb): the inner query becomes "max date among customer 1's orders", which is 15 March. 11 Feb doesn't equal it, so 103 is dropped. For 107 the dates match, so it stays. The aliases o and o2 are essential. Without them, customer_id = customer_id inside the subquery would refer to orders inside the subquery on both sides and be true for every row. Correlated subqueries in SELECT This returns Ana 3, Ben 2, Cat 2, Dev 1 and Eve 0. COUNT() over zero rows is 0, so customers with no orders still appear. An equivalent LEFT JOIN... GROUP BY works too; the subquery form is often clearer when you want one extra figure per row. A join rewrite needs the same empty-match behaviour. Join customers to orders with LEFT JOIN, group by the customer key and count o.id. Counting instead counts Eve’s padded row as one. An inner join omits her entirely. These are changes in meaning, even if an execution plan happens to be cheaper. Key takeaways A correlated subquery binds an inner expression to a row of the enclosing query; aliases make the binding clear. COUNT() inside a scalar aggregate yields zero when no orders match. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: functions subquery PostgreSQL 18: sql expressions SQLite reference

t: EXISTS and the NOT IN NULL trap
sum: NOT EXISTS keeps rows of the enclosing query without a match and tolerates nullable inner keys.
x: The shop customer ids are Ana 1, Ben 2, Cat 3, Dev 4 and Eve 5. Only Eve has no orders. The orders table has eight rows, and customer_id is NOT NULL in the Advanced SQL fixture. EXISTS and NOT EXISTS EXISTS (subquery) is true if the subquery returns at least one row. What it selects is irrelevant, so SELECT 1 is the convention. Customers who have never ordered: Result: Eve. The same pattern on products and order_items finds Vase. This is an anti-join: keep rows of the enclosing query with no match. The NOT IN trap NOT IN looks like it should be the same as NOT EXISTS. It isn't, because of NULL. Work through it for Ana (id 1). 1 NOT IN (2, 3, NULL) means 1 <> 2 AND 1 <> 3 AND 1 <> NULL. The last term is UNKNOWN, and TRUE AND UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN. WHERE keeps only TRUE rows, so Ana is dropped. So is everyone else. In real code the NULL arrives through a subquery: WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT referrer_id FROM...) where one row has a NULL referrer_id. The query silently returns nothing. Prefer NOT EXISTS NOT EXISTS compares row by row with = inside the subquery, and a NULL there simply fails to match. It does not make unrelated nonmatches UNKNOWN. If you use NOT IN, filter NULLs from its subquery and decide how a nullable outer key should behave: filtering the subquery result alone does not make NULL outer values match NOT EXISTS semantics. IN with a NULL in the list still gives UNKNOWN for nonmatching values; in this positive WHERE filter that does not change which rows survive: id IN (2, 3, NULL) still returns Ben and Cat, because OR with one TRUE term is TRUE. Key takeaways NOT EXISTS keeps rows of the enclosing query without a match and tolerates nullable inner keys. A NULL in a NOT IN list prevents any nonmatching value from becoming TRUE. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: functions subquery PostgreSQL 18: sql expressions SQLite reference

sum: ALL over an empty subquery is TRUE; ANY over it is FALSE.
x: The shop has six products and eight non-NULL order totals. Ana, customer 1, ordered totals 120, 60 and 60. Order 104 totals 200. There are no Garden products. ANY, ALL and row values PostgreSQL supports quantified comparisons. Orders bigger than every one of Ana's: In maths notation, the two quantifiers say: Order 104 (200) beats all three of Ana's totals, so it is the only result. If the subquery is empty there is no comparison value to fail against, so x > ALL(S) is TRUE (it is vacuously true) and x > ANY(S) is FALSE. = ANY (...) is the same as IN. SQLite does not support ANY/ALL; for a nonempty set of non-NULL values, > (SELECT MAX(...)) gives the same result as > ALL (...). NULLs also matter: MAX ignores them, while ALL can return UNKNOWN. Watch the empty-set edge case: > ALL of an empty set is TRUE, whereas comparing with MAX of an empty set gives NULL, which filters everything out. Both databases accept row-value comparisons such as WHERE (id, city) IN (SELECT...). Key takeaways ALL over an empty subquery is TRUE; ANY over it is FALSE. Replacing ALL by MAX also changes NULL behaviour. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: functions subquery PostgreSQL 18: sql expressions SQLite reference

sum: Subquery meaning constrains rewrites; EXPLAIN reveals the chosen plan.
x: A semi-join keeps a row of the enclosing query with at least one match; an anti-join keeps one with no match. These describe result semantics, while an execution plan describes how the database obtains those rows. How databases actually run them "Re-evaluated for every row of the enclosing query" is the meaning, not necessarily the plan. Optimisers rewrite subqueries into joins whenever the semantics allow. These are possible PostgreSQL plan shapes, not a guarantee for this small dataset: Query form Postgres plan ------ IN (subquery) Hash (semi) join NOT EXISTS Hash anti join NOT IN (subquery) Hashed SubPlan Correlated scalar SubPlan per row The interesting row is NOT IN. Because of the NULL semantics above, PostgreSQL 18 generally keeps this nullable form as a SubPlan rather than an ordinary anti-join. When the subquery result is small it builds a hash table of it (a "hashed SubPlan"). The memory a hash table may use is set by two configuration settings: If the planner estimates that the hashed subquery will exceed this budget, it uses a plain SubPlan that rescans the subquery for each row of the enclosing query, which can be catastrophically slow on large tables. That is a second reason to prefer NOT EXISTS. A correlated scalar subquery in SELECT typically runs as a SubPlan once per row of the enclosing query. An index on orders(customer_id) can make each probe cheap. Many rows of the enclosing query can make repeated probes expensive; a single GROUP BY and join may then be cheaper. Compare actual plans and preserve missing matches and NULLs rather than using a fixed row-count threshold. Which form should you write? Write whichever form states the question most clearly, then check the plan with EXPLAIN. EXISTS and IN can use semi-joins; an ordinary join can return duplicates and need a different plan. Investigate expensive NOT IN and per-row scalar subqueries, preserving their intended NULL and duplicate semantics when rewriting. Key takeaways Subquery meaning constrains rewrites; EXPLAIN reveals the chosen plan. In PostgreSQL 18 a large NOT IN subquery can use a repeatedly scanned SubPlan. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: functions subquery PostgreSQL 18: sql expressions SQLite reference

sum: An ordinary SELECT CTE names an intermediate result within one statement.
x: The shop orders total 650: Ana 240, Ben 135, Cat 230 and Dev 45. Eve has none. Monthly revenue is January 165, February 305 and March 180. A common table expression (CTE) is a named subquery written up front with WITH. An ordinary SELECT CTE provides a reusable name for a subquery and changes how a query reads: top to bottom, one step at a time, instead of inside out. Recursive CTEs are different. They add something plain SQL can't otherwise express: a query that refers to its own output, which lets you walk trees and graphs of unknown depth. This unit uses customers and orders from the Advanced SQL fixture. The later hierarchy unit introduces staff. The basic shape name spent ------ Ana 240 Cat 230 Spend per customer is Ana 240, Ben 135, Cat 230 and Dev 45. The scalar subquery averages those four figures: Eve never ordered, so she has no row in spend and isn't counted: the average is per ordering customer, not per customer. Notice that spend is used twice, once in FROM and once in the subquery. With separate derived tables for those two uses, you would repeat the aggregation text. A window aggregate is another possible formulation. You can chain several CTEs, each able to use the ones before it: Monthly revenue is January 165, February 305 and March 180. In Postgres, write to_char(ordered_on, 'YYYY-MM') or date_trunc('month', ordered_on) instead of SQLite's strftime. Why CTEs win code review Each CTE is a step you can name, read and test alone: replace the final SELECT with SELECT FROM monthly to inspect an intermediate result. This is the main reason analytics SQL (dbt models, for example) is written as a chain of CTEs. Key takeaways An ordinary SELECT CTE names an intermediate result within one statement. The average over spend counts ordering customers, excluding customers absent from spend. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: queries with SQLite reference

sum: PostgreSQL 12+ normally folds eligible once-referenced SELECT CTEs.
x: A common table expression (CTE) is a subquery named by WITH for one statement. Naming it does not alone tell you how much of its output the database computes or stores. Inlined or materialised? A CTE can be executed two ways: Inlined: substituted into the outer query like a derived table, so the optimiser can push filters into it and use indexes. Materialised: computed once into a temporary result, then read from there. Good if it is expensive and used many times; bad if the outer query only needs a few rows of a huge result. The rules differ by database and version: Database Default ------ Postgres 11 and earlier No SELECT CTE folding Postgres 12+ Eligible non-recursive, side-effect-free SELECT CTEs: inlined if referenced once, otherwise materialised by default SQLite Planner's choice Both Postgres 12+ and SQLite 3.35+ accept WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (...) or AS NOT MATERIALIZED (...). PostgreSQL ignores NOT MATERIALIZED for recursive or side-effecting CTEs, including SELECTs with volatile functions. SQLite treats these as planner hints; NOT MATERIALIZED does not forbid materialisation. The old Postgres behaviour was famous as an optimisation fence. For this query the outer filter cannot restrict the base scan, so it reads every order while filtering the CTE output: Before version 12, the id = 104 filter couldn't reach the index on orders.id. People deliberately used CTEs as fences to stop the planner from making a bad choice; since 12 you need MATERIALIZED to get that effect. Postgres never inlines CTEs that are recursive or that have side effects (data-modifying CTEs, below). Key takeaways PostgreSQL 12+ normally folds eligible once-referenced SELECT CTEs. SQLite NOT MATERIALIZED is a hint and does not forbid materialisation. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: queries with SQLite reference

sum: Each recursive pass reads the preceding working table.
x: Recursive CTEs A recursive CTE has two parts joined by UNION ALL (or UNION): The anchor member (non-recursive term): the starting rows. The recursive term: a query that references the CTE itself. For UNION ALL, PostgreSQL conceptually runs it as a loop over a working table (SQLite describes a row queue; the examples have the same results): Each pass sees only the rows produced by the previous pass, not the whole result so far. The loop stops when a pass produces no rows. In set notation: With UNION instead of UNION ALL, each pass also discards rows already in the result before they go into the next working table. Counting Pass 1 sees {1} and makes {2}; pass 2 sees {2} and makes {3}; and so on until the pass that sees {5} makes nothing, because 5 < 5 is false. The WHERE is the termination condition. Without it there is no logical stop condition; execution may eventually error or be cancelled. Pass by pass: SQLite accepts recursive self-reference without the RECURSIVE modifier, but PostgreSQL requires it. Write it explicitly for both engines. A NULL-valued row is still a row: termination depends on an empty working table, not on a particular value. PostgreSQL has no built-in default recursion-depth cap; use a terminating predicate and a suitable statement timeout when testing. Key takeaways Each recursive pass reads the preceding working table. UNION removes repeated complete rows; UNION ALL keeps them. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: queries with SQLite reference

sum: Choose the anchor and join direction to walk down or up a hierarchy.
x: A recursive CTE starts with anchor rows and repeatedly joins the newest rows to find more. Here staff has Mia 1, Raj 2, Sam 3, Tom 4, Uma 5 and Vic 6, with managers shown in the tree. Walking a hierarchy Populate staff from the tree: Mia’s manager is NULL; Raj and Sam report to Mia; Tom and Uma to Raj; Vic to Tom. The whole org chart, with depth and path: depth path ------ 0 Mia 1 Mia > Raj 2 Mia > Raj > Tom 3 Mia > Raj > Tom > Vic 2 Mia > Raj > Uma 1 Mia > Sam The depth column follows a simple rule: The anchor is Mia. Pass 1 joins staff to {Mia} and finds Raj and Sam. Pass 2 finds Tom and Uma (Sam has no reports). Pass 3 finds Vic. Pass 4 finds nothing, so the loop ends. Reverse the join to walk up: start from Vic and join s.id = up.manager_id. That gives Vic, Tom, Raj, Mia, the chain of command. Postgres is strict about types If the staff.name column were varchar(10), Postgres rejects the query above: recursive query "chain" column 4 has type character varying(10) in non-recursive term but type character varying overall. The concatenation operator returns text, and resolving the UNION removes the varchar length constraint; that result does not match the anchor's varchar(10). Cast the anchor: name::text AS path. SQLite has no such check. Key takeaways Choose the anchor and join direction to walk down or up a hierarchy. PostgreSQL checks recursive output types; cast a growing varchar path to text. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: queries with SQLite reference

sum: Generate the required months before a LEFT JOIN so months without orders survive.
x: A sparse sales table cannot produce a row for a month it never recorded. The shop has orders in January, February and March 2026, totalling 165, 305 and 180; April has none. A recursive CTE can supply the calendar independently. Filling gaps in a series Reports need a row for every month, even months with no sales. Generate the months, then LEFT JOIN: month rev ------ 2026-01 165 2026-02 305 2026-03 180 2026-04 0 Postgres has a built-in for this, so you rarely need recursion there: The LEFT JOIN is doing essential work: the generated April row has no matching order, so its order columns are NULL. SUM ignores NULL values and has no contributing value there, so it returns NULL. COALESCE supplies zero. Putting an order-date filter in WHERE after the join could discard that calendar row again; restrict matching orders in ON. The termination test reads the previous month. April is generated from March, then April fails the test and creates no May row. This example deliberately starts on the first of a month. Calendar arithmetic at the end of a month needs a separate rule because month lengths differ. PostgreSQL generate_series returns a set of timestamps here; the cast presents the date. Key takeaways Generate the required months before a LEFT JOIN so months without orders survive. SUM over an empty match is NULL; COALESCE turns it into a reporting zero. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: queries with SQLite reference

sum: UNION stops repeated identities only if the full projected row repeats.
x: Use staff ids Mia 1, Raj 2, Sam 3, Tom 4, Uma 5 and Vic 6. Mia manages Raj and Sam; Raj manages Tom and Uma; Tom manages Vic. A recursive anchor is the starting row; the recursive term finds its reports. Cycles Hierarchies in real data are not always trees. Suppose someone sets Mia's manager to Vic, creating a loop. The earlier root-based anchor (manager_id IS NULL) would now find no rows. To demonstrate the cycle, start explicitly at Mia (WHERE id = 1); then the recursive term keeps finding rows: Mia, Raj, Tom, Vic, Mia, Raj... Three defences: UNION instead of UNION ALL. UNION discards rows already produced. If the rows are just (id, name), the second Mia is a duplicate and the loop stops (6 rows). But add a depth column and every row is unique again, so UNION no longer saves you. Track the path and refuse to revisit: with the anchor's path starting as ',1,'. Postgres users can keep a SQL integer array and test s.id <> ALL(c.path). Postgres 14+ CYCLE clause, which does the path tracking for you: On the looped data this returns the six staff plus one extra Mia row with is_cycle = true, then stops. A depth limit (WHERE c.depth < 20) bounds this traversal, though it can truncate legitimate deep paths. PostgreSQL 14+ also has SEARCH DEPTH FIRST or SEARCH BREADTH FIRST clauses: these produce an ordering value, which you must use in the final ORDER BY. The SEARCH clause does not control the physical visitation order. A final LIMIT is useful during experiments but may not stop recursion when a sort or join first demands all rows. Key takeaways UNION stops repeated identities only if the full projected row repeats. Track visited identities or use PostgreSQL CYCLE clause to prevent infinite walks. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: queries with SQLite reference

sum: PostgreSQL data-modifying CTEs communicate changed rows through RETURNING.
x: An ordinary common table expression (CTE) names a SELECT result for one statement. PostgreSQL also allows data modification in WITH; SQLite only allows SELECT bodies there. Examples use orders, order_items and a matching orders_archive table. Differences that bite Feature SQLite Postgres --------- RECURSIVE modifier Optional Required CYCLE clause / SEARCH clause No 14+ DML inside WITH No Yes generate_series No Yes \ SQLite builds can include a generate_series table-valued function as an extension, but don't rely on it being present. Leaving out RECURSIVE in Postgres gives relation "n" does not exist... Use WITH RECURSIVE. SQLite accepts the recursive self-reference anyway, for compatibility with SQL Server and Oracle, which don't use that modifier. Data-modifying CTEs (Postgres) Postgres lets a CTE contain INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE with RETURNING, so you can move rows atomically in one statement: All parts of the statement see the same snapshot, so a SELECT elsewhere in the same WITH won't see the deletion. SQLite rejects DELETE inside WITH. Key takeaways PostgreSQL data-modifying CTEs communicate changed rows through RETURNING. Sibling statements share a snapshot and cannot observe one another’s table changes. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: queries with SQLite reference

sum: A window aggregate preserves every input row while computing over related rows.
x: GROUP BY answers questions like "total per customer", but it collapses rows: you get one row per group and lose the detail. Often you want both: every order, and that customer's running total, and the order's rank. That's what window functions do. A window function computes a value for each row from a set of related rows (its window), and leaves every row in place. Examples use the shop's 8 orders, whose totals are 120, 45, 60, 200, 45, 90, 60 and 30 (650 in all). Anatomy of OVER This is a syntax template; dots mark omitted expressions: PARTITION BY splits rows into independent groups, like GROUP BY without collapsing. Omit it and the whole result is one partition. ORDER BY orders rows within each partition. Ranking and LAG/LEAD need a meaningful order for predictable results (the syntax also permits omitting it); for aggregates it also changes the default frame (examined in Running totals and peer-sensitive frames). The window frame picks which rows of the partition, relative to the current row, an aggregate sees. Window functions run after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, and before the final ORDER BY and LIMIT. That ordering explains several rules below. Aggregates as window functions Ordinary aggregates such as SUM and AVG become window functions when you add OVER; PostgreSQL ordered-set and hypothetical-set aggregates are exceptions. An empty OVER () means "all rows": id total pct --------- 101 120 18.5 102 45 6.9 104 200 30.8......... Each row gets its share of the 650 total. The query computes this percentage for every row: Note the 100.0 in the SQL. With total stored as SQLite integers or PostgreSQL integer (not bigint/numeric), 100 total / SUM(...) does integer division, which throws away the fraction: Writing 100.0 makes one operand a decimal, so the division keeps its fraction and 45 gives 6.9. Comparing a row with its group: Each row's diff is its own total minus the average of its partition: So Ana's three orders (120, 60, 60) show +40, −20 and −20. For exact non-NULL arithmetic these differences sum to zero; floating-point calculations can have rounding error. A window sees the rows that survive WHERE. Filtering to customer 1 before computing SUM(total) OVER () makes that window total 240, not the shop’s 650. To display Ana’s orders with the grand total, compute the window in an inner query and filter the customer in an outer query. An explicit frame from UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING also covers a whole partition even when the window has ordering. Key takeaways A window aggregate preserves every input row while computing over related rows. Use decimal division for percentage shares; integer operands truncate in these examples. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: tutorial window PostgreSQL 18: functions window SQLite reference

sum: ROW_NUMBER numbers rows; RANK and DENSE_RANK give peers equal ranks.
x: The shop order totals are 200, 120, 90, 60, 60, 45, 45 and 30 in descending order. A window partition is the independent group of rows visible to a window function. Ranking: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK The three differ only in how they treat tied rows: rows with the same sort value. Our totals contain two ties (60 twice, 45 twice): total rn rnk dr ------------ 200 1 1 1 120 2 2 2 90 3 3 3 60 4 4 4 60 5 4 4 45 6 6 5 45 7 6 5 30 8 8 6 ROW_NUMBER: always 1, 2, 3... Ties get different numbers, in an arbitrary order unless you add a tie-breaker such as ORDER BY total DESC, id. RANK: ties share a rank and leave a gap (4, 4, then 6). Like a sports table. DENSE_RANK: ties share a rank with no gap (4, 4, then 5). Use it for "the Nth highest distinct value". You can work out either rank by counting what sorts ahead of the row: So DENSE_RANK can never be larger than RANK, and the two agree up to and including the first group of tied rows; they differ from the row after it. The WINDOW w AS (...) clause names a window so you don't repeat it. Both SQLite and Postgres support it. NTILE(k) splits the rows of each partition into k NTILE groups, numbered 1 to k, as equally as possible (quartiles with NTILE(4)). When the rows don't divide evenly, the leftover rows go one each to the first NTILE groups: So 8 rows in 3 NTILE groups have sizes 3, 3 and 2. NTILE works on row positions, so two tied values can land in different NTILE groups. PERCENT_RANK and CUME_DIST give relative SQL ranking positions as fractions between 0 and 1. Key takeaways ROW_NUMBER numbers rows; RANK and DENSE_RANK give peers equal ranks. NTILE balances row counts and can split tied values across NTILE groups. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: tutorial window PostgreSQL 18: functions window SQLite reference

t: Keeping the latest row per group
sum: Compute window values before filtering them in an outer query.
x: The shop has eight orders across four ordering customers. A window function leaves rows in place. PARTITION BY customer_id restarts the calculation for each customer, and ORDER BY inside OVER sets the window order. Top-N per group The most common real use of ROW_NUMBER: each customer's latest order. cust id ordered_on --------- 1 107 2026-03-15 2 106 2026-03-02 3 108 2026-03-28 4 105 2026-02-20 Why the wrapping subquery? Because window functions are computed after WHERE. Writing WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1 fails in both databases (Postgres says window functions are not allowed in WHERE). Some warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, DuckDB) add a QUALIFY clause for exactly this; SQLite and Postgres do not. Choose the function to match the business rule: ROW_NUMBER returns exactly one row per group even on ties, while RANK()... = 1 returns all tied rows. The secondary id sort chooses a repeatable winner if two latest orders share a date. It does not mean ids encode event time: the date remains the primary rule. To return every order tied on the latest date, rank by date alone; adding id would make those rows cease to be peers. Customers without orders are absent from this input and never get a row number. Start from customers and use a separate outer join if the report must include Eve. The inner query computes all candidate rankings before the outer filter is applied logically. That separation explains correctness but does not require a physically stored intermediate table; the optimiser can combine or simplify operations while preserving results. Key takeaways Compute window values before filtering them in an outer query. Use ROW_NUMBER for one row and RANK for every tied winner. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: tutorial window PostgreSQL 18: functions window SQLite reference

t: LAG and LEAD across reporting rows
sum: LAG and LEAD read previous and next rows in window order.
x: The shop orders have monthly revenue January 165, February 305 and March 180. ordered_on is an ISO date. First aggregate orders into one row per observed month; then compare neighbouring monthly rows. LAG and LEAD LAG(x) reads x from the previous row in the window order; LEAD(x) reads the next. Month-over-month revenue: month rev prev diff ------------ 2026-01 165 NULL NULL 2026-02 305 165 140 2026-03 180 305 -125 The diff column is a month-over-month change: The first row has no predecessor, so LAG returns NULL, and NULL minus anything is NULL. Supply a default with the third argument, LAG(rev, 1, 0), and an offset with the second (LAG(rev, 12) for year-over-year when every calendar month is present). Note the pattern: aggregate in a CTE first, then apply the window. Windows run after GROUP BY, so you can write LAG(SUM(total)) OVER (...) in one query, but the two-step form is easier to read. The offset counts rows, not calendar time. If February is missing, March’s preceding row is January. A year-over-year chart therefore needs a complete month series before applying a twelve-row offset. Generate calendar months and left join sales first, as in the series unit, and decide whether a missing month means zero sales or unavailable information. A supplied default applies only when the requested row is outside the partition. If a predecessor exists but its revenue is NULL, LAG returns that NULL; its third argument does not replace stored NULLs. LEAD has the same boundary rule in the forward direction. Neither function’s offset is constrained by the window frame used by an aggregate. Key takeaways LAG and LEAD read previous and next rows in window order. A missing predecessor produces NULL unless an explicit default is supplied. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: tutorial window PostgreSQL 18: functions window SQLite reference

sum: The ordered default frame includes all peers of the current row.
x: The shop orders sum to 650. Ana, customer 1, has 120 on 5 January, 60 on 11 February and 60 on 15 March 2026. Window frames choose which rows contribute to each aggregate. Running totals and frames Add ORDER BY to an aggregate's window and it becomes cumulative: cust ordered_on total running ------------ 1 2026-01-05 120 120 1 2026-02-11 60 180 1 2026-03-15 60 240 2 2026-01-09 45 45 2 2026-03-02 90 135 The running total restarts for each partition. Written as a sum: These are customer 1's rows: 180 on the second row, 240 on the third. The default frame and the ties trap When a window has ORDER BY but no explicit frame, the SQL standard default is: RANGE means "up to and including all peer rows of the current row", where peer rows (peers) are rows with an equal ORDER BY value. With unique ordering values you never notice. With ties you do: id total range_sum rows_sum ------------ 108 30 30 30 102 45 120 75 105 45 120 120 103 60 240 180 107 60 240 240 106 90 330 330 The table shows one possible ordering of ties; without a tie-breaker the ROWS totals assigned to ids 102/105 or 103/107 can swap. Under RANGE, both 45s include each other, so both show 120. Under ROWS, each row adds exactly one row. The two frames sum different sets of rows: A peer-group running total is useful for totals per price band or per day. A per-order total needs ROWS plus a deterministic ordering, such as ORDER BY total, id; ROWS alone does not decide which tied row goes first. The window ORDER BY controls the calculation, while a final query ORDER BY controls the displayed result order. A later LIMIT does not redefine which rows contributed. Key takeaways The ordered default frame includes all peers of the current row. ROWS needs a deterministic tie-breaker for a repeatable per-row running total. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: tutorial window PostgreSQL 18: functions window SQLite reference

sum: A ROWS moving frame counts rows, not elapsed days.
x: The shop orders in date order total 120, 45, 60, 200, 45, 90, 60 and 30. Their dates are distinct. A window frame is the subset of a partition used for the current row’s calculation. Moving averages Explicit ROWS frames give sliding windows. A three-order moving average: The frame holds the current row and up to two before it, so the average divides by however many rows the frame actually has: Partial windows at the start are a common source of misleading charts. Frame modes: ROWS counts physical rows, RANGE uses value distance (RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW in Postgres), and GROUPS counts peer groups. Both databases support all three. The third frame averages 120, 45 and 60, producing 75. The sixth averages 200, 45 and 90, producing about 111.67. Those are three orders, which may span very different durations. A seven-day average asks a different question and needs a date-based RANGE or calendar aggregation. PostgreSQL supports interval offsets on suitable ordered date/time values; SQLite RANGE offsets need a suitable single numeric ordering expression for numerical distance. AVG ignores NULL totals. If one of three rows has a NULL total, the divisor is two; a frame with no non-NULL total returns NULL. If incomplete frames should not be charted, calculate a matching COUNT(total) window and keep only rows with the required count in an outer query. Key takeaways A ROWS moving frame counts rows, not elapsed days. AVG divides by the number of non-NULL values actually present in its frame. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: tutorial window PostgreSQL 18: functions window SQLite reference

sum: LAST_VALUE reads the end of the current frame, not automatically the partition.
x: The shop has eight orders with unique dates. The first is order 101, total 120; the last is order 108, total 30. With an ordered window and no explicit frame, the frame ends at the current row’s last peer. The LAST_VALUE trap You might expect the last order's total (30) on every row. Here dates are unique, so each row returns its own total. With tied dates, the default frame also includes peers and LAST_VALUE can come from another tied row. With unique dates, the current row is the end of that frame. Fix it by extending the frame: FIRST_VALUE with this default frame reaches the partition’s first row. Explicitly bounded or excluded frames can change that, so reason from the frame rather than the function’s name. SQLite and Postgres differences Window function semantics are standard and match closely (SQLite added them in 3.25, 2018). The differences you hit are in surrounding types: Topic SQLite Postgres --------- AVG of ints float, 82.5 numeric, 82.5000... ROUND(x, n) any number numeric only Window in WHERE error error QUALIFY no no In Postgres, ROUND(some_double, 1) fails with function round(double precision, integer) does not exist; cast to numeric first. Performance notes Each distinct PARTITION BY/ORDER BY combination typically needs a sort. Several windows sharing one definition (use WINDOW w) can share the sort. An index matching (partition cols, order cols) can let Postgres skip the sort. Top-N per group via ROW_NUMBER may still read or sort many input rows, although PostgreSQL 15+ can stop computing window values when an eligible run condition fails. For a few rows per group over a large table, a LATERAL join with LIMIT on an index can be far cheaper (see the interview problems lesson). Key takeaways LAST_VALUE reads the end of the current frame, not automatically the partition. An index may avoid a window sort; inspect the plan before assuming it does. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: tutorial window PostgreSQL 18: functions window SQLite reference

sum: Set operators match columns by position and take names from the first branch.
x: Joins combine tables side by side: more columns. Set operations combine query results end to end: more (or fewer) rows. Pivoting goes sideways again, turning row values into columns for reports. This lesson uses the shop's orders by month: month products bought ------ Jan Rug, Kettle, Toaster, Mug Feb Kettle, Rug, Mug, Toaster Mar Rug, Lamp, Mug, Kettle The three operators The three operators are the set operations from maths: union, intersection and difference. Call January's products A and March's B: Set difference depends on operand order, just as numeric subtraction does. The card above shows Toaster in one direction and Lamp in the other. In SQL: "Sold in January but not March" is Toaster. EXCEPT is not symmetric: swap the sides and you get Lamp. Oracle traditionally spells this MINUS; newer releases also accept EXCEPT. The rules Same number of columns, matched by position, not by name. The first query's column names become the result's names. Compatible types. Postgres resolves a common type and errors if it can't (SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 'y' fails with invalid input syntax for type integer). SQLite, with its dynamic typing, happily mixes integers and text in one column. Duplicates are removed by UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT. ALL variants preserve copies according to each operator’s rule; SQLite supports only UNION ALL. ORDER BY and LIMIT apply to the whole result and go at the end. To order one branch, wrap it in a subquery. UNION vs UNION ALL Illustrative output from branches of distinct names: The row counts follow from the sizes of the sets: These counts treat each month as a list with no repeats. If a branch repeats a row, UNION ALL keeps every copy, while UNION also removes repeats within a branch. UNION must remove duplicates, often using sorting or hashing; already ordered input can instead feed a Unique plan node. UNION ALL just appends. Use UNION ALL when duplicates are wanted, or when the projected rows are unique both within each branch and across branches. Disjoint date filters alone do not prove projected names or totals are distinct; a source tag distinguishes branches but does not remove duplicates within one. This is one of the cheapest performance wins in SQL. Key takeaways Set operators match columns by position and take names from the first branch. Use UNION ALL when every copy is required or projected rows are already unique. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: queries union PostgreSQL 18: queries table expressions SQLite reference

t: Set equality, NULLs and copy counts
sum: Set operators treat two NULLs as not distinct, unlike equality predicates.
x: A set operator combines complete rows from two SELECT results. UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT remove duplicate rows by default; PostgreSQL additionally supports the ALL variants discussed here. NULLs are "not distinct" Set operations compare rows using distinctness, not =. Two NULLs count as the same: Contrast WHERE NULL = NULL, which is UNKNOWN. This makes EXCEPT a handy way to diff two tables that contain NULLs, where a join on = would miss matching rows. INTERSECT ALL and EXCEPT ALL With ALL, rows are treated as a multiset: EXCEPT ALL removes one copy per matching row. The PostgreSQL documentation states the rule as counts of copies: Postgres supports INTERSECT ALL and EXCEPT ALL; SQLite supports only UNION ALL. Set operations versus joins Several set operations have join equivalents: Set operation Join form ------ A INTERSECT B EXISTS semi-join A EXCEPT B NOT EXISTS anti-join Products never ordered, two ways: They differ in two ways. EXCEPT deduplicates the output, and it treats NULLs as equal. Use EXCEPT when you're comparing whole rows; use NOT EXISTS when you want other columns from the row being tested in the result. Key takeaways Set operators treat two NULLs as not distinct, unlike equality predicates. EXCEPT ALL subtracts copies; INTERSECT ALL keeps the smaller copy count. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: queries union PostgreSQL 18: queries table expressions SQLite reference

t: Portable grouping of mixed set operators
sum: PostgreSQL binds INTERSECT more tightly; SQLite evaluates left to right.
x: UNION keeps rows found on either side; INTERSECT keeps rows present on both sides. These operators remove duplicates. Mixing them without explicit grouping can change the answer between engines. The precedence trap What does this return? Database Parses as Result --------- Postgres INTERSECT first 1 SQLite UNION first empty Using the set symbols from earlier: The SQL standard (followed by Postgres and SQL Server) gives INTERSECT higher precedence than UNION and EXCEPT, the way binds tighter than +. SQLite evaluates compound selects strictly left to right. The two documented precedence rules give different answers. Don't rely on precedence When mixing operators, make the order explicit. Postgres allows parentheses around whole queries; SQLite doesn't, so use subqueries: SELECT FROM (... UNION...) INTERSECT.... Key takeaways PostgreSQL binds INTERSECT more tightly; SQLite evaluates left to right. A derived table makes the desired grouping portable. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: queries union PostgreSQL 18: queries table expressions SQLite reference

sum: A portable pivot gives each output category its own conditional aggregate.
x: The shop has products in Kitchen and Home. orders holds the date; order_items holds quantity; products holds the unit price. Revenue below is the sum of line quantities times those listed product prices, not the independently stored order total. Pivoting: rows to columns Reports often want categories across the top. Revenue by month and category: month kitchen home --------- 2026-01 75 90 2026-02 125 180 2026-03 50 130 This is conditional aggregation: each output column is an aggregate over only the rows matching its condition. It works on every SQL database, which is why it is the portable way to pivot. Each cell of the pivot is a sum over just the order lines that match its month and its column's category: Check that cell against the data: January's Kitchen revenue is order 101's Kettle (30) plus order 102's Toaster (25) and two Mugs (20), giving 75. FILTER: the cleaner spelling Both Postgres (9.4+) and SQLite (3.30+) support the standard FILTER clause: One difference: if an existing group has rows but none match, FILTER with SUM gives NULL while CASE with ELSE 0 contributes zeros. Over entirely empty input, an ungrouped SUM returns NULL even with CASE ELSE 0, because there is no row on which to evaluate CASE. Neither grouped form creates a missing month. COUNT() FILTER (...) gives 0 either way. ELSE 0 versus no ELSE Counting orders per customer per month with a LEFT JOIN from customers: name jan feb mar ------------ Ana 1 1 1 Dev 0 1 0 Eve 0 NULL NULL The jan column used SUM(CASE... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), so Eve's NULL-padded row counts as 0. The others used SUM(o.ordered_on LIKE '2026-02%'), which relies on SQLite treating booleans as 0/1. For Eve, the LIKE on NULL is NULL, so the sum is NULL. With ordered_on as PostgreSQL date, use a date-range condition or to_char before LIKE; PostgreSQL also rejects SUM(boolean) outright (function sum(boolean) does not exist); write COUNT() FILTER (WHERE...) or cast with::int. Key takeaways A portable pivot gives each output category its own conditional aggregate. FILTER plus SUM can produce NULL; COUNT with FILTER produces zero. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: queries union PostgreSQL 18: queries table expressions SQLite reference

sum: A static PostgreSQL or SQLite SELECT has a fixed output shape.
x: Pivoting turns category values into columns. Unpivoting turns columns into rows. These are changes to report shape, so first decide whether a consumer really needs a wide table or can accept named metric rows. Dynamic pivots In PostgreSQL and SQLite, a static pivot has fixed output columns. Generating "one column per category, whatever categories exist" therefore needs an additional step. Other engines may offer dynamic-pivot syntax. Options: Generate the SQL in application code after querying the distinct values. Postgres's tablefunc extension provides crosstab(), but you still declare the output columns. SQL Server and Oracle have a PIVOT operator, also with a fixed column list. Often best: return long (unpivoted) rows and pivot in the reporting tool or with pandas pivot_table. Unpivoting: columns to rows The reverse turns a wide row into several narrow ones. The portable way is UNION ALL: The straightforward plan scans the table once per branch; inspect the actual plan. Postgres can do it in one pass with LATERAL and VALUES: LATERAL lets a subquery in FROM refer to columns of tables to its left. SQLite doesn't support it. LATERAL explains the scope of each expression: for one outer order row, the VALUES list makes a total metric and a customer metric from that row. Eight orders therefore produce sixteen metric rows. No ORDER BY is present, so their display order is unspecified. The val column must have a common type; these two source columns are integers. For unrelated types, choose a deliberate representation rather than relying on an accidental cast. When generating a dynamic pivot, category names become SQL identifiers rather than bound data values. Use the database driver’s identifier-quoting facilities, keep values parameterised, and keep the report’s output contract clear. Returning long rows avoids rebuilding a query whenever a category is added. Key takeaways A static PostgreSQL or SQLite SELECT has a fixed output shape. UNION ALL unpivots portably; PostgreSQL LATERAL can reference an earlier FROM item. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: queries union PostgreSQL 18: queries table expressions SQLite reference

t: ROLLUP, grouping sets and real NULLs
sum: ROLLUP makes successive prefix subtotals and a grand total.
x: The shop has customers in Leeds, London and York. Its eight orders total 650. A grouping set is a list of columns that defines one aggregation level; an empty grouping set makes a grand total. Subtotals: ROLLUP and GROUPING SETS A report with a grand-total row: city n revenue --------- Leeds 2 135 London 5 470 York 1 45 NULL 8 650 The NULL row is the total (Postgres sorts NULLs last in ascending order). The number of rows follows from the groupings ROLLUP asks for: Use the GROUPING(c.city) function to tell "total" NULLs apart from real NULL cities. GROUPING SETS and CUBE generalise this to any combination of groupings, within one query; the physical plan can use multiple sorts or aggregation phases. SQLite has none of these. The equivalent is a UNION ALL of the grouped query and an ungrouped one, whose straightforward plan reads the inputs for both branches; a stored intermediate result can change that. A real NULL city and the grand total can both display as NULL. Add GROUPING(c.city) to the SELECT list: zero means the grouping includes city, even when that city value is NULL; one means city was omitted for that subtotal. Do not infer the level by testing city IS NULL. For ROLLUP(city, name), there is one row per city/name pair, one subtotal per city and one grand total. Five distinct customers across three cities therefore produce nine rows. This counts output groups, not just the three grouping sets. On an empty input the empty grouping set still produces a grand-total aggregate row, whereas nonempty grouping sets have no groups. Key takeaways ROLLUP makes successive prefix subtotals and a grand total. GROUPING distinguishes a subtotal placeholder from a real NULL key. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: queries union PostgreSQL 18: queries table expressions SQLite reference

t: Nth highest: distinct values and empty results
sum: Decide whether Nth means a distinct value or a row position.
x: The shop totals are 200, 120, 90, 60, 60, 45, 45 and 30. They are non-NULL. Before solving an interview problem, agree its tie rule and whether insufficient data should return NULL or no row. 1. The Nth highest value "Find the second-highest order total." Three standard answers: All three give 120 for the non-NULL totals shown. To ignore missing totals on arbitrary data, filter total IS NOT NULL before OFFSET or ranking; PostgreSQL DESC sorts NULLs first by default. Now the probes: Generalise to N. The nested MAX form shown is specifically the second-highest pattern; arbitrary positions need further nesting or another method. OFFSET skips one fewer row than the requested position, and DENSE_RANK can filter on the desired rank. The fourth distinct total is 60. Forgot DISTINCT? With ties, the 5th highest via ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 4 without DISTINCT lands on the second 60 rather than 45. ROW_NUMBER makes the same mistake; DENSE_RANK is the ranking that means "Nth distinct value". Fewer than N values. A returns one row containing NULL. B and C return no rows. If the spec says "return NULL", wrap it as a scalar subquery: SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT total... OFFSET 8) AS nth gives a single NULL. OFFSET counts the rows to skip, which is why B skips one fewer row than the requested position: Key takeaways Decide whether Nth means a distinct value or a row position. A scalar wrapper converts an empty result into one NULL. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: sql select PostgreSQL 18: functions aggregate SQLite reference

t: Top rows per group and indexed probes
sum: Choose a tie rule before choosing a SQL ranking function.
x: products has id, name, category and price. order_items has product_id, order_id and qty. orders has id, customer_id, ordered_on and total. Its dates are distinct in the Advanced SQL fixture. 2. Top N per group "Top two products by revenue in each category." Product revenue: Rug 360, Kettle 120, Mug 80, Toaster 50, Lamp 40, Vase 0. category name revenue --------- Home Rug 360 Home Lamp 40 Kitchen Kettle 120 Kitchen Mug 80 Vase doesn't appear at all because the inner join drops products with no sales. If unsold products should compete (with revenue 0), use a LEFT JOIN and COALESCE. Swap ROW_NUMBER for RANK or DENSE_RANK depending on the tie rule you agreed. Postgres offers two more tools: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row of each group according to the ORDER BY. It's concise but Postgres-only. Here product_rev is the aggregate product-revenue query above saved as a database view, without its later ranking step. LATERAL makes the inner query depend on the current category; a typical nested-loop plan executes it for each category. An ordinary aggregate view cannot itself have an index on its computed revenue. If product_rev is instead a maintained table or materialized view with an index on (category, revenue DESC), each group can seek to its highest rows and stop after two visible matches. Obtaining the category list and computing or refreshing revenue also have a cost. Ties at the cut-off For the global top N, Postgres 13+ supports FETCH FIRST 4 ROWS WITH TIES. On our totals that returns 5 rows (200, 120, 90, 60, 60) because the 4th and 5th tie. For a repeatable exact count, break revenue ties with a stable unique product key. If all tied winners matter, rank by revenue alone using RANK; DENSE_RANK instead means the highest distinct revenue bands. Those rules can return different row counts. A global LIMIT is not a per-category limit. An indexed strategy still needs its outer category list. Computing SELECT DISTINCT category from millions of products may dominate the few inner probes. A small maintained categories table avoids that scan. Neither an ordinary aggregate view nor its computed revenue has a separately stored index; a maintained summary table or materialized view introduces refresh and consistency work. Key takeaways Choose a tie rule before choosing a SQL ranking function. LATERAL with an index can stop early for each known group. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: sql select PostgreSQL 18: functions aggregate SQLite reference

sum: COUNT(DISTINCT ...) avoids counting repeat purchases as new required products.
x: The shop has customers, orders, order_items and products. Kettle and Mug are product names. Ana bought Kettle twice and Mug once; Cat bought both. Ben bought Mug but no Kettle. 3. Relational division: "all of" "Customers who bought both Kettle and Mug." A WHERE name = 'Kettle' AND name = 'Mug' can never be true on one row. Filter to the candidates, group, and count: In set terms the HAVING clause tests that the customer's products cover the whole required set: The WHERE p.name IN (…) filter builds the intersection and COUNT(DISTINCT p.name) = 2 compares its size. DISTINCT matters: Ana bought Kettle in two different orders, so a plain COUNT gives her 3 and wrongly excludes her. Worse, a customer who bought Kettle twice and no Mug would count 2 and wrongly pass. The same shape answers "customers who ordered in every month that had orders": The textbook alternative is a double NOT EXISTS ("there's no month in which this customer has no order"). The counting version returns only customers represented by the inner join. If there are no required months, it returns nobody, whereas double NOT EXISTS returns every customer (the empty requirement is vacuously satisfied). Choose the intended empty-set behaviour. Key takeaways COUNT(DISTINCT...) avoids counting repeat purchases as new required products. An empty requirement needs an explicit business rule. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: sql select PostgreSQL 18: functions aggregate SQLite reference

t: Removing duplicates and preventing their return
sum: Keep a chosen survivor before deleting other rows with the same email.
x: signups has id as a primary key and email declared NOT NULL. ids 1, 3 and 6 use a@x.io; ids 2 and 5 use b@x.io; id 4 uses c@x.io. 4. Duplicates "Find emails that appear more than once, then delete all but the earliest." With six signups where a@x.io appears three times and b@x.io twice, that returns those two emails. Assume email is NOT NULL and id is a non-NULL primary key. To delete, keep the lowest id per email (this means earliest only if ids encode insertion order): NOT IN is safe here because MIN(id) of a primary key is never NULL. A Postgres-idiomatic version uses a self-join: Every row with a lower-id twin is deleted. Then add a UNIQUE constraint so the duplicates can't come back, which is the answer interviewers actually want to hear. Without it, two concurrent sign-ups can still race past an application-level check. Key takeaways Keep a chosen survivor before deleting other rows with the same email. A UNIQUE constraint protects against future concurrent duplicates. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: sql select PostgreSQL 18: functions aggregate SQLite reference

t: Gaps and islands in login dates
sum: Subtracting a row number gives one key for a consecutive-day run.
x: logins(user_id, day) stores ISO calendar dates. A login streak is a run of consecutive days. This example has one row per day and finds one user’s streaks; timezone boundaries must be settled before producing the day column. 5. Gaps and islands "Find each user's streaks of consecutive login days." User 1 logged in on 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 9 March. The trick: subtract a row number from the date. Within a run of consecutive days, both go up by one each row, so the difference is constant. A gap changes it. day row position island key --------- 03-01 1 02-28 03-02 2 02-28 03-03 3 02-28 03-05 4 03-01 03-06 5 03-01 03-09 6 03-03 Group by that difference: start finish len --------- 2026-03-01 2026-03-03 3 2026-03-05 2026-03-06 2 2026-03-09 2026-03-09 1 In Postgres, date minus integer is a date, so the group key is just day - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY day)::int. For several users, add PARTITION BY user_id and group by both user_id and grp. The trick assumes one row per day. Two logins on the same day would break the arithmetic, so de-duplicate first (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, day). DENSE_RANK also fixes the island key with repeated days, but COUNT() would still count logins; use COUNT(DISTINCT day) for streak length. An alternative that also handles "gaps of up to N days" is to compare each row with LAG(day), flag a new island when the gap exceeds the limit, and take a running SUM of the flags as the island id. Key takeaways Subtracting a row number gives one key for a consecutive-day run. Deduplicate days before numbering or count distinct days after dense ranking. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: sql select PostgreSQL 18: functions aggregate SQLite reference

t: Finding the first cumulative threshold crossing
sum: Calculate running revenue before filtering for the threshold.
x: orders has eight distinct dates in 2026 with totals 120, 45, 60, 200, 45, 90, 60 and 30. The dates are 5 and 9 January; 11, 14 and 20 February; 2, 15 and 28 March. 6. Running totals and thresholds "On what date did cumulative revenue first reach 400?" The query finds the first row whose running total reaches the threshold: The window must be computed before filtering, hence the CTE. If two orders could share a date, decide whether the running total should step per order (ROWS, with a tie-breaker) or per day (the default RANGE). Key takeaways Calculate running revenue before filtering for the threshold. Choose per-day peers or per-order stepping explicitly. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: sql select PostgreSQL 18: functions aggregate SQLite reference

t: Medians from the middle one or two rows
sum: Number only the non-NULL observations before selecting middle rows.
x: The shop non-NULL totals sorted ascending are 30, 45, 45, 60, 60, 90, 120 and 200. A median splits sorted observations in half; with an even count this lesson averages the two middle observations. 7. Median Postgres has an ordered-set aggregate: percentile_cont interpolates between the two middle values; percentile_disc returns an actual value from the data. The SQLite/PostgreSQL version below assumes non-NULL totals and averages the middle one or two rows. Filter NULL totals before numbering to match percentile_cont, which ignores them; other SQL engines may require explicit integer division: The two IN positions come from integer division: With eight rows the positions are fourth and fifth (both 60), so the median is 60. With seven rows both expressions select the fourth row, the single middle observation. Key takeaways Number only the non-NULL observations before selecting middle rows. Continuous percentiles can interpolate; discrete percentiles return observed values. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: sql select PostgreSQL 18: functions aggregate SQLite reference

t: Filtering optional matches without losing customers
sum: An ON filter limits matches while retaining the outer customer.
x: The shop customers are Ana, Ben, Cat, Dev and Eve. Ana ordered 120, 60 and 60; Ben 45 and 90; Cat 200 and 30; Dev 45; Eve none. orders.id is a non-NULL primary key. 8. The LEFT JOIN filter trap "List every customer with their orders over 100." Where the filter goes changes the answer: This returns all five customers: Ana 120, Cat 200, and NULLs for Ben, Dev and Eve. Move o.total > 100 to WHERE and the join first includes every real order plus Eve's padded row. WHERE rejects Ben and Dev's small orders and Eve's NULL, leaving Ana and Cat. This NULL-rejecting predicate makes the result equivalent to an inner join; other WHERE predicates can preserve padded rows. For counts, keep the same ON condition but select COUNT(o.id) and group by the customer key. Ana has one qualifying order over 100, Cat one, and Ben, Dev and Eve zero. COUNT() would count every padded row and incorrectly give those three customers one. The predicate’s purpose determines placement. A condition restricting which optional orders qualify belongs in ON when every customer must survive. A condition deciding which customers belong in the report can still go in WHERE. For example, a filter on the customer’s city deliberately removes other customers. Moving predicates mechanically between clauses can therefore change the business question. Key takeaways An ON filter limits matches while retaining the outer customer. COUNT(o.id) counts actual orders and ignores the padded NULL row. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: sql select PostgreSQL 18: functions aggregate SQLite reference

sum: PostgreSQL json preserves input text; jsonb stores a decomposed representation.
x: Two features that started as vendor extensions and became everyday tools. JSON columns let a database table hold semi-structured data: event payloads, third-party webhooks, per-customer settings. Upserts ("insert, or update if it already exists") support atomic insert-or-update operations for sync jobs and counters. An additive counter is not idempotent: replaying its message increments again, so deduplicate requests when retries must not double-apply. Both differ between SQLite and Postgres in ways that matter, so each example notes what changes. Storing JSON Four events: SQLite stores JSON as ordinary text (or, since 3.45, in an internal binary form called JSONB via functions such as jsonb()). SQLite’s binary representation is private to SQLite and is not readable as PostgreSQL jsonb. A TEXT column alone does not validate JSON; a CHECK using json_valid(payload) can enforce valid text documents. PostgreSQL’s JSON types validate input. Postgres has two types: json jsonb --------- Stored as Exact text Decomposed binary Duplicate keys Kept Last wins Key order Kept Not kept Indexable (GIN) No Yes Operators @>,? No Yes Use jsonb unless you must preserve the exact input text. It costs a little more on insert (JSON decoding) and avoids decoding the original input again for JSON processing; the performance difference depends on the operation and workload. Key takeaways PostgreSQL json preserves input text; jsonb stores a decomposed representation. SQLite JSONB and PostgreSQL jsonb are different binary representations. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: datatype json PostgreSQL 18: functions json PostgreSQL 18: sql insert PostgreSQL 18: sql merge SQLite reference

sum: PostgreSQL ->> returns text; cast before numerical comparisons.
x: events(id, payload) contains JSON documents. Event 1 is a view of product 4 on iOS; event 2 is a cart for product 4, qty 2, on Android; event 3 is a view of product 1 on iOS with tags sale and new; event 4 is a cart for product 5 with qty 1 and no device key. Reading values Both databases spell extraction with arrows, but the details differ: SQLite Postgres --------- -> JSON text jsonb ->> SQL value text Path '$.device.os' -> 'device' ->> 'os' id type os --------- 1 view iOS 2 cart Android 3 view iOS 4 cart NULL A missing key gives NULL, not an error. That is convenient, but it also means a typo in a key name silently returns NULL everywhere. The type trap In SQLite, ->> returns a native SQL value: payload ->> '$.qty' is the integer 2. In Postgres, ->> always returns text: For the demonstrated lexicographic ordering assume C collation. The second form is the dangerous one: it runs, and compares strings character by character. Cast before comparing numbers or dates, and validate incoming shapes: a non-numeric string will make an integer cast fail rather than silently become a number. PostgreSQL -> returns json when the input is json and jsonb when it is jsonb; the table above assumes the payload is jsonb. JSON null is distinct from a missing key when using ->, but ->> turns either into SQL NULL. SQLite ->> also returns 1 or 0 for JSON true or false. Key takeaways PostgreSQL ->> returns text; cast before numerical comparisons. SQLite ->> can return an integer, real, text or NULL SQL value. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: datatype json PostgreSQL 18: functions json PostgreSQL 18: sql insert PostgreSQL 18: sql merge SQLite reference

t: Expanding arrays and building JSON results
sum: JSON array expansion produces one result row per element.
x: events(id, payload) has four documents. Only event 3 contains tags, the array ["sale","new"]; the other documents omit tags. The shop customers and orders can also be combined into one JSON array per ordering customer. Arrays: one row per element json_each (SQLite) and jsonb_array_elements_text (Postgres) are table-valued functions that expand an array into rows: Both return (3, sale) and (3, new). Events without tags contribute no rows, as with an inner join. Building JSON Aggregates turn rows into JSON, which is handy for APIs that want nested output in one round trip: Postgres uses jsonb_agg(o.id ORDER BY o.id) and jsonb_build_object('name', name); SQLite has json_object(...). To modify a document, use json_set (SQLite) or jsonb_set and the merge operator (Postgres). An inner expansion removes an event with no tags because the function yields no element rows. If the report must retain such events, PostgreSQL can use LEFT JOIN LATERAL with ON true, while SQLite can left join json_each. Check the shape before expanding: PostgreSQL jsonb_array_elements_text expects an array and errors on objects or scalar JSON values. SQLite json_each also iterates object members, so the two functions are not identical for arbitrary JSON. The ordered SQLite aggregate shown requires SQLite 3.44 or later. Without its internal ORDER BY, [101,103,107] is merely one possible array order. PostgreSQL’s aggregate ORDER BY serves the same purpose. An outer ORDER BY sorts customer result rows and does not order the contents of an aggregate. A LEFT JOIN can produce an array containing a JSON null for an unmatched customer; filter the aggregate input if the contract requires an empty array. Key takeaways JSON array expansion produces one result row per element. Order JSON aggregate inputs explicitly when array order matters. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: datatype json PostgreSQL 18: functions json PostgreSQL 18: sql insert PostgreSQL 18: sql merge SQLite reference

t: Indexing JSON and promoting stable keys
sum: An expression index targets a selected JSON expression.
x: events(id, payload jsonb) contains view events 1 and 3 and cart events 2 and 4. Only event 3 has a tags key. An index is an additional search structure; it changes access cost rather than the meaning of a query. Indexing JSON in Postgres Without a suitable access path, a JSON predicate may require scanning many rows. PostgreSQL jsonb is already decoded; a scan does not reparse the original JSON text, and other indexed predicates may narrow the rows first. Two options: Expression index on one frequently queried JSON key: The query must use a matching expression that the planner recognises (payload ->> 'type' = 'cart').
