SQLite supports the same idea with indexes on expressions. GIN index for containment and key-existence queries: @> means "contains this sub-document" and? means "has this top-level key". A default GIN index on jsonb supports @>,?,? and?&. The jsonb_path_ops operator class often yields a smaller and more selective index, depending on the documents and query. It supports @>, @? and @@ but not the key-existence operators. The default jsonb_ops class supports those JSON path operators too. Index support means the predicate is eligible for that access path; a small table or unselective filter can still favour a scan. When JSON is the wrong tool If every row has the same keys and you filter, join or aggregate on them, they should be columns. Columns get types, NOT NULL and foreign keys, ordinary column statistics, and a deliberately chosen scalar representation. JSON shines for genuinely variable data you mostly store and return whole. A common pattern is promoting a frequently queried JSON key to a generated column. Key takeaways An expression index targets a selected JSON expression. GIN operator classes support different JSON predicates. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: datatype json PostgreSQL 18: functions json PostgreSQL 18: sql insert PostgreSQL 18: sql merge SQLite reference

sum: ON CONFLICT combines insert-or-update through a unique key.
x: stock(product_id PRIMARY KEY, qty) initially holds product 1 with 10 and product 4 with 3. Each example starts afresh from its stated initial rows. An additive stock adjustment needs request deduplication if replaying a message must have no extra effect. Upserts The problem: insert a stock row for a product, or add to it if the row already exists. The naive approach races: INSERT... ON CONFLICT makes the check and the write one atomic operation. The syntax is the same in Postgres (9.5+) and SQLite (3.24+): Inside DO UPDATE, excluded (the excluded row) is the row you tried to insert, and the table name refers to the existing row. So the SET line computes: Starting from (1, 10) and (4, 3), product 1 already exists, so it becomes 15. Product 2 is new and is inserted with 7, and product 4 is untouched. Useful variations: Add RETURNING (Postgres, SQLite 3.35+) to get the resulting rows back. When the WHERE rejects the update, no row is returned. For DO UPDATE, the conflict target must match an eligible non-deferrable unique index or constraint. PostgreSQL exclusion constraints cannot arbitrate DO UPDATE. ON CONFLICT (qty) with no unique index on qty fails in Postgres with there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification. Key takeaways ON CONFLICT combines insert-or-update through a unique key. The proposed excluded row and existing target row have different meanings. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: datatype json PostgreSQL 18: functions json PostgreSQL 18: sql insert PostgreSQL 18: sql merge SQLite reference

t: Duplicate batch keys and replacement deletes
sum: PostgreSQL DO UPDATE cannot affect the same target row twice in one command.
x: stock(product_id PRIMARY KEY, qty, note) tracks quantity and an optional note. PostgreSQL and SQLite share ON CONFLICT syntax but differ when one input batch repeats a key. Each example is isolated from the others. Duplicate keys in one statement Database Result ------ SQLite row 5 has qty 3 Postgres error Postgres refuses: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time. Within one statement, it won't update a row it has already inserted or updated, because the outcome would depend on processing order. SQLite processes the rows one at a time, so the second updates the first. Batch loaders for Postgres must de-duplicate keys in the batch first (for example, GROUP BY product_id with SUM(qty)). INSERT OR REPLACE is not an upsert SQLite also has INSERT OR REPLACE (and MySQL has REPLACE). It resolves a conflict by deleting the old row and inserting a new one: The note column was lost because the new row didn't supply it. In SQLite, delete triggers fire for that deletion only if recursive triggers are enabled, and foreign keys with ON DELETE CASCADE can remove child rows. Use ON CONFLICT... DO UPDATE to change only the columns you name. A related SQLite parsing quirk: in INSERT... SELECT... FROM t ON CONFLICT..., the parser reads ON as a join condition on t and fails with near "DO": syntax error. Give the SELECT a WHERE clause (even WHERE true) to fix it. Key takeaways PostgreSQL DO UPDATE cannot affect the same target row twice in one command. SQLite REPLACE deletes the old row and inserts a new one. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: datatype json PostgreSQL 18: functions json PostgreSQL 18: sql insert PostgreSQL 18: sql merge SQLite reference

t: MERGE actions, concurrency and returned row versions
sum: MERGE chooses the first applicable WHEN clause for each candidate row.
x: stock(product_id PRIMARY KEY, qty) starts with product 1 at 15 for the MERGE example. PostgreSQL 15 introduced MERGE; version 17 added its RETURNING clause, and version 18 added old/new row references for INSERT RETURNING. MERGE (Postgres 15+) The SQL-standard MERGE handles matched and unmatched rows with separate actions, including deletes: The first WHEN MATCHED clause tests the quantity the row would end up with: Product 1 (qty 15) would drop to 0, so it is deleted; product 3 has no match and is inserted with 4. MERGE tries the WHEN clauses in order and uses the first one whose condition is true, which is why the DELETE clause comes before the plain UPDATE. Postgres 17 added RETURNING with merge_action() to report which branch each row took. SQLite has no MERGE. Prefer ON CONFLICT for concurrent upserts in Postgres. It is built on the unique index and, in the absence of independent errors, resolves a concurrent conflict by inserting or updating (unless an update WHERE rejects the row). Other constraints, deadlocks or serialization failures can still require error handling or retries. MERGE joins first and can still fail with a unique violation if another transaction inserts the same key concurrently. Other upsert details SQL sequences still advance. In Postgres, an insert that ends in DO UPDATE or DO NOTHING has usually already taken a serial/identity value, so ids get gaps. That is normal; don't rely on contiguous ids. Inserted or updated? Postgres users often test xmax = 0 in RETURNING, but that relies on an internal system column. Postgres 18 adds RETURNING old., new.; the old values are all NULL when the row was freshly inserted, which is the supported way to tell. Key takeaways MERGE chooses the first applicable WHEN clause for each candidate row. Use ON CONFLICT for PostgreSQL concurrent upserts and handle independent transaction errors. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: datatype json PostgreSQL 18: functions json PostgreSQL 18: sql insert PostgreSQL 18: sql merge SQLite reference

sum: Relations as typed facts, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: In 1970 Edgar F. Codd, a researcher at IBM, published A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks. Many contemporary database interfaces were navigational: programs followed prescribed paths between records, coupling applications to access structures. Codd argued that applications should be insulated from representation changes. Codd's idea was to describe data purely as sets of facts, with no pointers and no visible storage order. Programs say what they want, and the system works out how to fetch it. That separation, called data independence, is why you can add an index to a Postgres table today without touching a single query. This lesson defines the vocabulary precisely. Every later lesson (algebra, dependencies, normal forms) builds on it. Relations, relational tuples and attributes A database relation is a set of relational tuples that all share the same heading. Informally it is a table, but the precise definition matters. The drawing names the relation Student; its attributes are student id sid, student name and study year. This is the named-attribute presentation of the model: position in a printed table is a display choice. Codd’s original mathematical presentation used ordered domains; naming attributes avoids making that displayed order part of the meaning. Theory SQL Meaning --------- Relation Table A set of relational tuples Tuple Row One fact Attribute Column A named role Domain Type Allowed values The relation heading assigns each attribute name a domain. For example, year draws values from the integers one through four. A relational tuple assigns exactly one value from the correct domain to every attribute; a student name cannot occupy the year attribute. An attribute domain is the set of values an attribute may take. Codd required atomic relational values, indivisible from the database's point of view (more on that in the normal forms lesson). The relation degree (or arity) is the number of attributes: 3 above. The cardinality is the number of relational tuples: 3 above. It changes as rows are inserted; the degree does not. Each relational tuple is a true statement The most useful way to read a relation is as a relational predicate with blanks: Student sid is called name and is in year year. Every relational tuple fills in the blanks to make a true proposition. The relational tuple (2, Ben, 1) asserts "Student 2 is called Ben and is in year 1." Under the closed-world assumption, the stored relation contains every true instance of its stated relational predicate. Only with that completeness assumption does an absent student relational tuple mean that the student does not exist in the population being modelled. SQL NOT EXISTS tests for returned rows regardless of whether the database is complete. A missing holiday booking can establish “no recorded holiday”; it cannot establish attendance, because illness and weekends are different facts. Key takeaways A relational tuple assigns one correctly typed value to each named attribute. Degree counts attributes; cardinality counts relational tuples. Conclusions under the closed-world assumption require a complete relational predicate. Further reading Codd: A Relational Model of Data (1970) PostgreSQL 18: constraints Reiter: On Closed World Data Bases

sum: Sets, bags and SQL results, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Consequences of "a set of relational tuples" Because a relation is a mathematical set, three properties follow directly: No duplicate relational tuples. Stating the same fact twice adds nothing. A set cannot contain an element twice. No relational tuple order. Sets are unordered. "The first row" has no meaning; only ORDER BY imposes an order on a result. No attribute order. The heading is a set too, so attributes are identified by name, not position. SQL tables are not quite relations SQL is a pragmatic descendant of the model, and it deviates in ways that bite: - Tables and query results can be bags (multisets). Without a key, INSERT can add the same row twice, and SELECT dept FROM emp returns duplicates unless you write DISTINCT. - Columns have a position. SELECT and INSERT INTO t VALUES (...) depend on it. - SQL has NULL, which the original model did not, giving three-valued logic. - Stored PostgreSQL row versions occupy physical locations, but those locations provide no guaranteed order in results. Postgres can return rows in a different order between two runs of the same query. Chris Date and Hugh Darwen have criticised SQL’s duplicate rows and three-valued logic as departures from the relational model. In practice you get close to the model by giving every table a key and writing DISTINCT when you want a set. Common pitfalls Tables without keys. A log table with no primary key accumulates exact duplicates after a retried insert, and a predicate using only those stored attribute values cannot distinguish the copies; removing one may require a physical row identifier or a dialect-specific technique. Relying on row order. SELECT... LIMIT 1 without ORDER BY returns some row. It may change after a VACUUM, an index change or a parallel plan. Mistaking current data for a rule. Declaring UNIQUE (name) because today's names are unique will reject a legitimate insert later. Pointers in disguise. Storing "row 5 of the other table" or array positions as references reintroduces the navigational coupling Codd removed. Refer to rows by key value. Key takeaways Relations have neither duplicates nor intrinsic order; SQL can retain duplicates. Use deliberate duplicate removal and an ORDER BY with a unique tie-breaker when order matters. Further reading Codd: A Relational Model of Data (1970) PostgreSQL 18: constraints Darwen: SQL language design and relational departures

sum: Choosing keys from legal states, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Keys A relation has no duplicate relational tuples, so the full set of attributes always identifies a relational tuple uniquely. Usually a smaller set does too. A superkey is any set of attributes whose values are unique across every relational tuple the relation could legally contain. A candidate key is a minimal superkey: remove any attribute and it stops being unique. The primary key is the candidate key you choose as the main way to identify relational tuples. The others are alternate keys, normally enforced in SQL with UNIQUE plus NOT NULL on their attributes. Consider employees described by identifier emp_id, email address email, personal name and department dept. The domain guarantees that each identifier and each email belongs to only one employee: Attribute set Superkey? Candidate key? --------- identifier alone Yes Yes email alone Yes Yes identifier and name together Yes No, not minimal name and department together No No Keys are about rules, not current data A key is a claim about every legal state of the relation, not the rows you happen to have. If today no two employees share a name, the name alone is still not a key, because the business allows two people called Sam. Keys come from the domain, and you find them by asking "can this ever repeat?" Key takeaways A candidate key is a superkey minimal under inclusion. Choose keys from rules for every legal state, not uniqueness in a sample. Further reading Codd: A Relational Model of Data (1970) PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Enforcing relational integrity, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Foreign keys A foreign key is a set of attributes in one relation whose values must appear as a key in another (or the same) relation. An enrolment carries student id sid and course code cid. Its student id refers by value to the key of Student, and its course code to the key of Course. The arrows say that every sid in Enrolled must be the sid of some existing student. Foreign keys are how relations refer to each other without pointers: the reference is a value, matched at query time by a join. Integrity rules The model comes with constraints that every database state must satisfy. Entity integrity: no attribute of a primary key may be NULL. A fact about "a student whose id is unknown" cannot be identified, so it cannot be referred to. Referential integrity: in the null-free theory, a foreign key must match a referenced key value. SQL adds nullable references. PostgreSQL’s default MATCH SIMPLE waives a composite reference when any referencing column is NULL; MATCH FULL permits a reference with all columns NULL but rejects a mixture of NULL and non-NULL. Use NOT NULL on every referencing column when participation is mandatory. relational domain constraints: values come from the attribute's domain (year is an integer from 1 to 4, say). Relational key constraints: no two relational tuples agree on a candidate key. In PostgreSQL these map to DDL (create the referenced course table first). SQLite ordinary rowid tables have a historical exception allowing NULL in some declared primary keys; use explicit NOT NULL, STRICT or WITHOUT ROWID as appropriate: The composite primary key on enrolled does two jobs. It identifies each enrolment, and it stops the same student enrolling on the same course twice. When a referenced row is deleted, the foreign key's ON DELETE action decides what happens: NO ACTION (the PostgreSQL default, with checking deferrable if declared so), RESTRICT (reject immediately, without deferring), CASCADE (delete the referencing rows), SET NULL or SET DEFAULT. A PostgreSQL UNIQUE constraint alone allows multiple NULLs by default. Use UNIQUE together with NOT NULL for a conventional alternate key. NULLS NOT DISTINCT changes uniqueness treatment, but still permits a missing value and is not a replacement for NOT NULL. A CHECK accepts true or unknown, so a domain range check by itself does not forbid NULL. Key takeaways Keys, domain rules and references constrain which database states are legal. PostgreSQL CHECK, nullable UNIQUE and nullable foreign keys need explicit NULL decisions. Further reading Codd: A Relational Model of Data (1970) PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Data independence and query interfaces, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Why the model won The navigational databases of the 1960s, such as IBM's IMS (hierarchical) and CODASYL (network) systems, were fast for the access paths they were built for, and painful for everything else. The relational model made three goals central to its interface. Physical data independence. Indexes, partitioning and storage format can change without changing queries. Logical data independence. Views let you restructure tables while keeping old queries working. Declarative queries. Because queries are expressed over sets with well-defined operators (the next lesson), an optimiser can rewrite them into equivalent, cheaper forms. The doubt in the 1970s was whether a declarative system could ever be fast enough. IBM's System R and Berkeley's Ingres answered that by the late 1970s; System R also produced SQL and a pioneering cost-based optimiser. Oracle, DB2, Postgres (a descendant of Ingres research) and SQLite all follow. NULL, briefly SQL uses NULL to represent missing information. Comparisons with NULL yield unknown, so WHERE x = NULL matches nothing, and NOT IN against a list that contains a NULL returns no rows. The SQL fundamentals module covers the details. For theory, the key point is that NULL breaks the clean "each relational tuple is a true proposition" reading, which is one reason designers try to minimise nullable columns. Key takeaways Physical data independence isolates applications from storage choices. Logical data independence can preserve a query interface through views while tables change. Further reading Codd: A Relational Model of Data (1970) PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Restrict, project and rename, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Relational algebra is a small set of operators that each take one or two relations and return a new relation. That last part is the whole trick: because the output is always a relation, you can feed it into another operator, and build any query expressible in ordinary relational algebra by composing a few simple pieces. You never type relational algebra into Postgres. But the database translates your SQL into a tree of algebra-like operators, transforms that tree into a cheaper equivalent, and then executes it. An EXPLAIN plan shows physical implementations of algebra-like operations, along with SQL extensions such as sorting and aggregation. Each operator has a one-character symbol, mostly Greek letters. Every symbol is explained in the formula card where it first appears, and again in each card that uses it, so you can read any card on its own. Local relations Four students, three courses, six enrolments. Dev is not enrolled on anything. (Course also has a title column, left out here for width.) sid is the student id, cid the course code, and dept the department that runs the course. Unary operators: selection, projection and rename A unary operator takes one relation as input. There are three. Selection (σ) keeps the relational tuples that satisfy a condition. It filters rows. It is written σ, the Greek letter sigma, followed by the condition and then the input relation in brackets: The result has the same attributes as the input; only rows have gone. Projection (π) keeps only the named attributes. It chooses columns, and because the result is a set, duplicates disappear. It is written with the Greek letter π (pi), followed by the attributes to keep: Six enrolments, but only three relational tuples in the result. SQL's SELECT cid FROM enrolled returns six rows; you need SELECT DISTINCT cid to match the algebra. Rename (ρ) changes a relation's or an attribute's name. It is written with the Greek letter ρ (rho), in one of two forms: For a self-join, make the two headings distinct before a Cartesian product. Here we use qualified names as shorthand for renaming every attribute in each copy: the first has S1.sid, S1.name, S1.year; the second has the corresponding S2 names. Merely giving a relation a new label is insufficient in a strictly named-attribute algebra. Name clash: σ is not SELECT SQL's SELECT list is a projection (π). The selection σ corresponds to WHERE. The names are a historical accident that confuses almost everyone once. Key takeaways Selection keeps rows; projection keeps attributes and removes duplicate relational tuples. Give self-join copies distinct attribute names before forming a product. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational model and algebra PostgreSQL 18: constraints

t: Set operators and an algebraic basis
sum: Set operators and an algebraic basis, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Local relations Four students, three courses, six enrolments. Dev is not enrolled on anything. (Course also has a title column, left out here for width.) sid is the student id, cid the course code, and dept the department that runs the course. Set operators: union, difference, intersection Union, difference and intersection work as they do on any sets, with one rule: the two inputs must be union-compatible, meaning the same attributes with the same domains. Students who are not enrolled on anything: Students taking both DB and course labelled OS: In SQL these are UNION, EXCEPT and INTERSECT, which remove duplicates by default; UNION ALL and friends keep them (bag semantics). The six primitive operators Six operators are enough to express everything else: selection σ, projection π, rename ρ, union ∪, difference − and Cartesian product ×. The rest are shorthand: Check the intersection rule on small sets of numbers: Division is also derived; the neighbouring division unit works through its construction. This is a conventional complete basis of six operators, rather than a claim that every presentation uses this exact primitive list. A language expressing all pure-algebra queries is relationally complete. SQL can express them using appropriate duplicate removal and null-free inputs, and adds ordering, aggregation and recursion. Key takeaways Union, difference and intersection require compatible headings and domains. “On course labelled OS but not LA” needs a difference between student sets, not a contradictory row predicate. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational model and algebra PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Products and joins, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Local relations Four students, three courses, six enrolments. Dev is not enrolled on anything. (Course also has a title column, left out here for width.) sid is the student id, cid the course code, and dept the department that runs the course. Product and joins The Cartesian product pairs every relational tuple of one relation with every relational tuple of another, so its size is the product of the two sizes: On its own the product is rarely what you want; it is the raw material for joins. A theta join is a product followed by a selection: When θ uses only equality it is an equijoin. A natural join, written with a bare bow-tie and no condition, is the equijoin on all attributes with the same name, keeping one copy of each: Dev vanishes: an inner join keeps only relational tuples with a partner. The extended algebra adds outer joins, which keep unmatched relational tuples padded with NULLs, plus the semijoin and antijoin, which optimisers use constantly: Semijoin R ⋉ S is SQL's WHERE EXISTS. Antijoin R ▷ S is SQL's WHERE NOT EXISTS. Left outer join R ⟕ S is SQL's LEFT JOIN. Natural join is fragile Natural join matches on every shared column name. If someone later adds updated_at to both Student and Enrolled, NATURAL JOIN silently starts requiring equal timestamps and returns almost nothing. Production SQL should spell out JOIN... ON or USING (sid). For a natural join, shared attribute names must have compatible domains. With no shared names, the matching condition is vacuously true, and the result is the Cartesian product: four students paired with three courses give twelve relational tuples. Adding a same-named column later changes a SQL NATURAL JOIN predicate, so explicit join conditions are safer in application SQL. The outer-join operators above belong to an extension with missing-value markers, rather than the null-free algebra. Key takeaways A product contains every pair; a theta join retains pairs satisfying its predicate. Natural joins match all shared names; outer joins preserve unmatched rows with missing-value markers. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational model and algebra PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Division and universal conditions, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Local relations Four students, three courses, six enrolments. Dev is not enrolled on anything. (Course also has a title column, left out here for width.) sid is the student id, cid the course code, and dept the department that runs the course. Division: "for all" Division answers questions with every in them: which students take all CS courses? A student qualifies if, for every course in the divisor relation, the pair (student, course) appears in Enrolled. Ada (1) and Cat (3) take both; Ben takes only DB. Result: {1, 3}. Division is derived from the basic operators, which shows how "for all" becomes "there is no counterexample": SQL has no division operator. The standard idiom is a double NOT EXISTS: there is no CS course that the student is not enrolled on. The empty divisor relation If the CS department had no courses, the inner condition is vacuously true, and the SQL above returns every student, including Dev. The algebraic version returns only the students in A, those with at least one enrolment. Both are logically defensible ("all of nothing" is true), but they differ. Decide which you intend before shipping a "customers who bought every item in the promotional bundle" report. Key takeaways Division removes candidates with any missing required pair. An empty divisor qualifies every candidate; choose whether candidates come from enrolments or all students. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational model and algebra PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Equivalent query plans, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Local relations Four students, three courses, six enrolments. Dev is not enrolled on anything. (Course also has a title column, left out here for width.) sid is the student id, cid the course code, and dept the department that runs the course. From SQL to an expression tree A simple SQL block maps onto algebra almost mechanically: Written as one algebra expression, read from the inside out: The same expression as a tree, with S for Student and E for Enrolled: Read from the bottom up: join, filter, project. The result is {Ada, Ben, Cat}. Equivalences: why optimisers work Because operators have precise meanings, there are rules that transform one expression into another that is guaranteed to give the same result. Four of the most important: Cascade selections: a selection on two conditions joined by "and" is the same as two selections, one after the other. Commute joins: the order of a join's inputs does not matter, and joins are associative, so join order is free to choose. Push selection below a join: if a condition mentions only one input's attributes, filter that input before joining. Push projection down: drop columns early, keeping any needed by later joins or filters. Rule 3 is the big one. Take the tree above with 10,000 students and 200,000 enrolments, 1,000 of them for DB: The pushed plan feeds 1,000 enrolments into the join instead of 200,000. Every cost-based optimiser (Postgres, SQL Server, Oracle, the Spark SQL Catalyst optimiser) applies these algebraic rewrites, then uses statistics to choose among the equivalent trees. The query processing module covers how it picks. Key takeaways Rewrites must preserve values, multiplicities and the output heading under the intended semantics. Push one-input filters below inner joins and keep needed join and output attributes. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational model and algebra PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Where pure algebra stops, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Local relations Four students, three courses, six enrolments. Dev is not enrolled on anything. (Course also has a title column, left out here for width.) sid is the student id, cid the course code, and dept the department that runs the course. Pitfalls and limits Bags versus sets. SQL works on bags, so some algebraic equivalences need care. For sets, a relation unioned with itself is unchanged; in SQL, R UNION ALL R has twice as many rows. An optimiser may only apply a rewrite if it holds under bag semantics, or if a DISTINCT makes the difference invisible. NULL. The pure algebra has no NULL. SQL's three-valued logic means "the rows where p is true" plus "the rows where p is false" does not always give back the whole table: rows where p is unknown appear in neither. Aggregation is an extension. Grouping (written with the Greek letter γ, gamma) is not part of Codd's original algebra; textbooks add it as an extended operator. No recursion. A fixed finite expression in ordinary relational algebra cannot compute reachability for arbitrary graph size or unbounded depth. A known fixed depth can be expanded into a fixed number of joins; WITH RECURSIVE handles the unbounded case. Key takeaways Bag multiplicities and NULL can invalidate pure-set identities. Aggregation extends the algebra; unbounded reachability needs recursion. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational model and algebra PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: What functional dependencies claim, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Normalisation, covered in the later normal-form units, can sound like a list of rules to memorise. It is not. The normal forms 2NF, 3NF and BCNF are defined using functional dependencies (FDs); higher forms also involve multivalued or join dependencies. Once you can reason about FDs, normal forms become mechanical checks. This unit establishes what an FD claims and how to refute a proposed one. The following units derive consequences, compute attribute closures and find every candidate key. We use single capital letters for attribute names in abstract examples. Adjacent letters in a card denote an attribute set, never a numeric product; every card defines that convention locally. What a functional dependency says A functional dependency is a universal rule comparing pairs of relational tuples, not a claim about one row in isolation: Any two relational tuples that agree on X must also agree on Y. Take a spreadsheet of enrolments that someone has imported as one table: The business rules say a student id identifies one name, a course code identifies one title, and there is one grade per student per course. As FDs: An FD is a constraint on every legal state, exactly like a key. You get it from the domain, not from the data. Data can refute an FD, never prove one If two rows share a cid but have different titles, the FD from cid to ctitle is false (or the data is dirty). But if today's rows all happen to have unique surnames, that does not make surname a determinant of anything. Data-profiling tools that "discover" FDs find candidates that a human must confirm. Trivial and non-trivial FDs An FD is a trivial FD if its right side is part of its left side. Trivial FDs hold in every relation and tell you nothing. The interesting ones are non-trivial. Keys are FDs too A set K is a superkey of R exactly when K determines every attribute of R: Here the student id and course code together determine name, title and grade, so it is a superkey. Neither attribute alone determines everything, so it is also a candidate key: a superkey with nothing that can be removed. The inference examples treat their stated FDs as the complete basis being analysed. Extra rules such as a singleton domain or a fixed maximum row count can imply additional dependencies; include those assumptions when deciding which states are legal. Key takeaways An FD constrains every pair of relational tuples in every legal state. Data can refute a proposed rule; a clean sample cannot establish it as a business constraint. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Inferring dependencies with Armstrong rules, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Armstrong's axioms Given some FDs, which others must also hold? William Armstrong gave three inference rules in 1974. For attribute sets X, Y and Z: Reflexivity: a set determines any subset of itself. Augmentation: adding the same attributes to both sides keeps an FD true. Transitivity: if X determines Y and Y determines Z, then X determines Z. The rules have soundness (every conclusion follows from the given FDs) and completeness (every FD that follows from those premises can be derived). Three useful rules follow from them: the FD union rule, the decomposition rule and pseudotransitivity. The left side does not decompose A right side can be split, but a left side cannot. Grade depends on student and course together, not on either alone. The FD closure contains every functional dependency implied by a given basis: F⁺ can be exponentially large, so in practice you never list it. You compute attribute closures instead. Key takeaways Reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity derive exactly the implied FDs. Right sides split; left sides generally do not. Counterexamples refute invalid inference. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Computing attribute closure, with complete worked examples and local definitions.
x: The attribute-closure algorithm An attribute closure collects every attribute determined by a chosen starting set under the given FD basis. Compute it with a fixpoint loop: Start with the requested attribute set as the result. Find any FD in F whose whole left side is already inside result. Add its right side to result. Repeat until nothing changes. The same algorithm in Python, with a set of letters standing for attributes: Trace the attribute closure of {A, D} for R(A, B, C, D, E): The first dependency adds B to the known A and D. The second then adds C; with C and D available, the third adds E. A sequential Python pass can fire a later rule using an attribute added earlier in that same pass. The card uses simultaneous rounds instead: both schedules reach the same least fixed point. Each pass of the loop either adds at least one attribute or changes nothing and stops, so the number of passes is bounded by the number of attributes: Key takeaways Start from known attributes and apply every available FD until a full pass adds nothing. Sequential firing and simultaneous rounds reach the same least fixed point. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Applying attribute closure, with complete worked examples and local definitions.
x: Three jobs for attribute closure Does F imply a given FD? Compute the attribute closure of its left side and check that the right side is inside it. Is X a superkey? Yes exactly when its attribute closure is every attribute of R. Are F and G equivalent? Yes if every FD in G follows from F, and every FD in F follows from G. In practice you test equivalence FD by FD: compute each FD's left-side attribute closure under the other set, rather than ever listing F⁺. Key takeaways The attribute closure of a determinant tests both implication and superkeys. Two FD sets are equivalent exactly when each derives all dependencies of the other. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Finding every candidate key, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Finding candidate keys A candidate key is a superkey with no unnecessary attributes: Searching every subset is exponential, but two observations prune it hard: An attribute that never appears on any right-hand side cannot be derived, so it must be in every key. An attribute that appears only on right-hand sides, and in no determinant, is in no candidate key: starting with it cannot help derive anything else, so a superkey containing it can derive it from the other attributes. This assumes the stated FDs are the complete constraint basis being analysed. One key Use the five-attribute closure example from the preceding unit: A fixes B, B fixes C, and C together with D fixes E. A and D cannot be derived, so every key includes both. Their attribute closure reaches all five attributes; therefore that pair is the only candidate key. The exact FD basis and attribute closure are restated in the card below. Several keys In the four-attribute example below, B cannot be derived and therefore belongs to every key. B alone reaches only itself; adding any one of A, C or D reaches the whole heading. The candidate keys are B with A, B with C, and B with D. Each is a prime attribute (belongs to some candidate key), a fact the 3NF test in the next lesson cares about. A relation with n attributes can have exponentially many candidate keys. For schemas specified by an FD basis, Lucchesi and Osborn showed that deciding whether a given attribute is prime is NP-complete. Exhaustive enumeration can be practical for a small schema; larger ones may need pruning. This explains why identifying every prime attribute for the 3NF test can be harder than computing one attribute closure. “Minimal” means minimal under set inclusion, not smallest cardinality among keys. There can be candidate keys of different sizes. When checking minimality of a superkey, it suffices to remove each member in turn: if any proper subset were a superkey, some single-member removal would also be one. Do not stop after finding the first candidate key; prime attributes depend on the union of all of them. Key takeaways Every key must include attributes that cannot be derived from right sides. Check every candidate for inclusion minimality; all candidate keys contribute prime attributes. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design PostgreSQL 18: constraints

t: Minimal FD covers and FD equivalence
sum: Minimal FD covers and FD equivalence, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Minimal FD cover Two FD sets can say the same thing with different amounts of redundancy. A minimal FD cover here means an equivalent set with singleton right sides and no remaining redundancy. Some texts call a grouped-right-side version a canonical FD cover; these presentation conventions differ, while the implied dependencies agree. Our singleton convention requires: Every right side is a single attribute. No left side has an extraneous determinant attribute (one you could drop and still derive the FD). No FD is redundant (derivable from the others). The card below starts with a dependency fixing two right-side attributes, a duplicate implied dependency, and an unnecessarily large determinant. Work through it in three stages: Split the two-attribute right side into two dependencies; merge the duplicate dependency fixing B from A. Test B in the two-attribute determinant. A alone already reaches C through B, so B adds nothing to that determinant. Reducing it produces another duplicate. The remaining one-step functional dependency from A to C is implied by the two-step chain through B, so remove it. The two dependencies in the final card line form a minimal FD cover. Four FDs became two, with exactly the same meaning. The 3NF synthesis algorithm in the next lesson starts from a minimal FD cover, which is why this step matters. Minimal FD covers are not always unique; different removal orders can give different, equally valid answers. Key takeaways A singleton-right-side minimal FD cover removes extraneous left attributes and redundant dependencies. Equivalent covers have the same implications and need not be unique. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Dependencies in PostgreSQL queries, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Where FDs show up in real systems Keys and UNIQUE constraints directly enforce key-based dependencies. SQL has no general FUNCTIONAL DEPENDENCY declaration for an arbitrary dependency between two sets of columns; some special dependencies can be enforced with CHECK or exclusion constraints, and others need triggers or schema decomposition. Normalisation avoids storing the same dependent fact in many rows. Postgres uses FDs in GROUP BY. If you group by a table's primary key, PostgreSQL 16–18 lets you select that table's other columns without listing them, because it knows the key determines them: Optimisers use FDs to drop redundant grouping or sorting columns and to prove that a join cannot multiply rows. Data-quality checks test candidate FDs against stored rows. With both cid and ctitle constrained NOT NULL, grouping by course code and requiring more than one distinct title finds violations. COUNT(DISTINCT...) ignores NULLs; do not silently treat its result as an FD proof when missing titles are allowed. Common mistakes Reading FDs off sample data. A coincidence in 50 rows is not a rule. Splitting the left side. Two attributes determining a third together does not imply that either one does alone. Forgetting transitivity. When asked for keys, compute the attribute closure; do not eyeball it. Chains through two FDs are easy to miss. Stopping at one key. A relation can have several candidate keys, and normal-form tests depend on all of them. Key takeaways PostgreSQL recognises its base-table primary-key grouping rule, not every logically inferable FD. Distinct-value checks can refute an FD when missing values are handled explicitly. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Anomalies and first normal form, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Normalisation is the process of splitting a badly structured relation into smaller ones so that each fact is stored once. When a fact is stored in many rows, the copies can disagree unless additional constraints or coordinated writes keep them consistent. Each normal form forbids one kind of redundancy, defined precisely with the functional dependencies (FDs) from the previous lesson. Kent’s informal summary says that non-key facts should depend on the key, its whole value, and no unrelated determinant. It is a mnemonic; the precise prime-attribute conditions in the following units handle cases the mnemonic misses. The formula below states the business rules. Every card defines its notation locally; an arrow expresses a rule across all legal states, rather than a coincidence in these three rows. The problem: anomalies A shop imports its order spreadsheet as a single table: The business rules, as FDs: The only candidate key is the pair of order id and product id. Three kinds of trouble follow. Update anomaly. Ann changes her name. It is stored on every line of every order she has placed, and an update that misses one leaves the data contradicting itself. Insertion anomaly. You cannot record a new product until someone orders it, because oid is part of the key and cannot be NULL. Deletion anomaly. Delete order 11, Raj's only order, and you lose the fact that customer C9 is called Raj. All three come from FDs whose left side is not a key: the table is storing facts about customers and products inside rows about order lines. First normal form (1NF) A relation is in 1NF when every attribute value is an atomic relational value: a single value from its domain, with no repeating groups. Ordinary column constraints and joins do not directly represent the individual items; string-splitting expressions or custom constraints are more complex than storing a row per item. The fix is one row per product per order, as in OrderLine above. What counts as atomic? Atomicity is relative to the chosen domains and relational presentation. Decomposability by a function does not alone violate 1NF: dates and text have inspectable parts. Under the classical flat-relation convention used here, a repeating collection of phone numbers or order lines is represented by separate relational tuples. SQL arrays and JSON are valid SQL values with useful operators, but calling them automatically in or out of 1NF merely because an application searches inside them is too broad. For this design, separate rows let each phone or line have ordinary keys, foreign keys and indexes. Key takeaways Mixing order, customer and product facts creates update, insertion and deletion anomalies. Use separate relational tuples for repeating phone or item facts under the flat relational convention. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form

t: Second normal form and partial dependence
sum: Second normal form and partial dependence, with complete worked examples and local definitions.
x: This unit continues the shop design: an order line stores order id oid, product id pid, date odate, customer id cid, customer name cname, product name pname, current product price price, and quantity qty. An order has one customer and date; a product has one current name and price. One line per order and product is the business rule. Second normal form (2NF) A relation is in 2NF when it is in 1NF and no non-prime attribute depends on part of a candidate key. (A prime attribute is one that belongs to some candidate key.) In the usual case with no constant non-prime attributes, a single-attribute candidate key has no non-empty proper part, so partial dependence needs a composite key. Formally the empty attribute set is also a proper subset; a non-prime attribute forced constant can therefore violate the fully general predicate even with a singleton key. The worked schemas have no such constant dependencies. OrderLine’s key is the order/product pair, and each half determines attributes on its own: Both are partial dependencies. Fix them by moving each one into its own relation: Key takeaways 2NF forbids a non-prime attribute depending on a proper part of any candidate key. Separate order and product facts from order-line facts to remove partial dependencies. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form

t: Third normal form and indirect facts
sum: Third normal form and indirect facts, with complete worked examples and local definitions.
x: The shop has already separated order lines from product facts. Its remaining Order relation stores order identifier oid, order date odate, customer identifier cid and customer name cname. An order fixes its date and customer; a customer fixes one current name. The only candidate key of Order is its order identifier. Third normal form (3NF) A relation is in 3NF when, for every non-trivial FD whose right side is a single attribute A, either the left side X is a superkey or A is prime: The Order relation containing order id, date, customer id and customer name is in 2NF under these rules (its only candidate key is the single order id) but still repeats Ann's name on every order. The cause is a transitive dependency: cid is not a superkey of Order and cname is not prime, so 3NF is violated. Split again: Now every FD's left side is a key of its relation. Ann's name lives in one row, products can exist before anyone orders them, and deleting an order loses nothing else. Price is a different fact The current price of a product (one per product) can hold in every database state even when prices change over time. It does not imply that the price paid on every historical order line equals today's price. In a real shop, the price charged on an order is a separate fact from the current list price, and it belongs to the order and product together: the order id and product id together determine price_paid. Store it on Line. That is not denormalisation; it is modelling a time-dependent fact correctly. Normalising away the price paid is a classic bug that silently alters old invoices. Key takeaways 3NF checks every non-trivial singleton-right-side FD for a superkey determinant or prime result attribute. Customer name and historical price paid belong to different facts and require different determinants. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form

sum: BCNF and prime attributes, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Boyce–Codd normal form (BCNF) A relation is in BCNF when, for every non-trivial FD that holds in it, the left side is a superkey. BCNF drops 3NF's escape clause "or A is prime": 3NF and BCNF differ only when a relation has overlapping candidate keys. The classic example: each teacher teaches one course, and each student has one teacher per course. Teaching records student, course and teacher: The FD from teacher to course has a left side that is not a superkey, so BCNF fails. But course is prime (it is in the first candidate key), so 3NF holds. The redundancy is real: "Smith teaches DB" is repeated for every student Smith teaches. Key takeaways BCNF requires a superkey determinant for every non-trivial FD. Teaching passes 3NF through a prime course attribute while still failing BCNF. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form

sum: Lossless joins and dependency preservation, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Decomposing safely Splitting a relation has two possible costs, and you should check both. Lossless join A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 has a lossless join if joining the parts always gives back exactly R. If not, the join invents spurious tuples. The test for two parts: Split Teaching badly into (student, course) and (course, teacher): Joining on course produces four rows, including Ann, DB, Jones, which never happened. Then try the split into (teacher, course) and (student, teacher): Dependency preservation A decomposition preserves dependencies if the FDs that hold inside each part, taken together, imply every FD in F: Enforcing those local dependencies then suffices without checking a join; an original FD can follow transitively across several local dependencies rather than literally fit in one part. The lossless-join BCNF split of Teaching loses the rule that a student and course together fix the teacher: the projected local FDs do not imply that original rule. For example, local keys still allow Ann to reference Smith and Jones while both teach DB. Merely observing that no part contains all three attributes is not a proof of non-preservation: some dependencies can follow transitively across parts. Key takeaways Losslessness concerns reconstructing every legal relation without invented relational tuples. Dependency preservation concerns whether projected local FDs together imply the original rules. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form

sum: BCNF decomposition and 3NF synthesis, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: The BCNF decomposition algorithm Find a non-trivial dependency whose determinant is not a superkey of the current schema. The card calls that determinant X and the current heading S. Replace the current schema with the two parts shown. Repeat until every relation is in BCNF. Each split shares exactly X, and X determines the whole first part, so every step gives a lossless join. In the five-attribute example below, A fixes B, B fixes C, and C together with D fixes E. Its only candidate key is the pair A and D: The same split sequence as a schema sketch, with names grouping attributes: All three are in BCNF and the decomposition is lossless-join, but the original rule that C and D together fix E is lost. The combined projected FDs cannot derive it: starting from C and D adds nothing in the local dependency union, so E is not reached. The 3NF synthesis algorithm 3NF can always be reached losslessly while preserving every FD. The synthesis algorithm (Bernstein, 1976): Compute a minimal FD cover of F. Make one relation for each left side X, containing X and everything it determines in the cover. If no relation contains a candidate key of R, add one that is just a key. Drop any relation that is a subset of another. The original three dependencies are already a singleton-right-side minimal FD cover. Use that cover for the same five-attribute example: Result: AB, BC, CDE, AD. Every FD lives in one relation, the key relation AD makes the decomposition lossless-join, and here each part happens to be in BCNF too. Choosing between 3NF and BCNF 3NF BCNF --------- Lossless join always always FDs preserved always not always Redundancy a little possible none from FDs Check the actual dependencies rather than assuming a frequency of overlapping keys. Many ordinary schemas can reach BCNF while preserving the required FDs; when those goals clash, the choices are: Stay in 3NF and accept some redundancy, enforcing the dependencies locally; keys alone may not express every local FD. Go to BCNF and enforce the lost FD another way, such as a trigger, a carefully synchronised trigger or application protocol that checks the joined rule. PostgreSQL ordinary views do not provide general declarative cross-table assertions; a naive check-then-write can race with another transaction. Key takeaways BCNF decomposition preserves lossless reconstruction but can lose dependencies. 3NF synthesis uses a minimal FD cover and adds a candidate-key relation when needed. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form

sum: Independent facts, 4NF and 5NF, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Beyond BCNF, briefly BCNF removes redundancy caused by FDs, but not all redundancy. If an employee has a set of skills and, independently, a set of languages, storing (emp, skill, language) forces every skill to be paired with every language. That is a multivalued dependency: an employee determines a whole set of skills, independently of the other attributes. 4NF splits it into (emp, skill) and (emp, language). 5NF handles join dependencies across three or more parts. Both are rare in practice, but the "independent facts in one table" smell is worth recognising. The exact condition matters The dependency says more than “an employee can have several skills”. It requires all combinations of independently recorded skills and languages. Consider one employee with SQL and Python skills and English and French languages: There are four combinations. Recording only SQL/English and Python/French would say that the pairs are linked, not independent, and would violate the claimed multivalued dependency. Splitting the independent lists saves repetition while recovering those four rows by a natural join. A multivalued dependency is trivial if its right attributes are already contained in the determinant, or the two sides together cover the whole heading. Fourth normal form requires a superkey determinant for every non-trivial multivalued dependency. Every FD implies an MVD, so this requirement also implies BCNF. A join dependency says that a relation is always exactly the join of specified projections. Fifth normal form, also called project-join normal form, requires every non-trivial join dependency to follow from candidate-key rules. Three-way decompositions can matter even when no useful two-way split exists. Do not infer a join dependency merely because one sample happens to rejoin correctly: it must be a domain rule. Conversely, a supplier/part/project relation with no such rule must keep its three-way facts; splitting can invent combinations. These are constraint-relative definitions. BCNF does not guarantee freedom from MVD redundancy, and 5NF does not promise that every application constraint or temporal fact is now represented correctly. Key takeaways Independent skill and language lists require all combinations in a combined table. 4NF controls non-trivial MVDs; 5NF controls join dependencies not implied by candidate keys. Further reading Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan: relational database design Fagin: multivalued dependencies and fourth normal form Fagin: Normal forms and relational database operators (1979) Fagin: Domains and keys, section 5 definitions

sum: Measuring redundancy and copied values, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Normalisation stores every fact once, which makes writes simple and keeps the data consistent. The price is paid on reads: answering a question may require joining several tables. Denormalisation is deliberately storing a fact more than once, or storing something derivable, so that reads get cheaper. It is not the absence of design. A denormalised schema starts from a normalised one and adds controlled redundancy, together with a plan for keeping the copies in agreement. The rule of thumb: normalise until it hurts, denormalise until it works. And measure before you decide it hurts. First, check you actually need it Joins on indexed keys can be efficient, but their cost depends on row counts, selectivity, caching and the selected join algorithm. A primary-key index can support selective lookups, but a join need not do one lookup per order: the planner may choose a hash, merge or nested-loop join. Cache state, selectivity and output size determine the measured cost. Teams often denormalise to fix a slow query whose real problem was something else. Before adding redundancy, try: An index on the join or filter column. Missing indexes on foreign keys can slow selective joins or parent-row changes, since Postgres does not create them automatically. A covering index (CREATE INDEX... INCLUDE (...)) which can enable an index-only scan; PostgreSQL may still fetch heap pages for visibility checks. Fixing the query: an N+1 loop in the application, a function on an indexed column, or fetching far more rows than needed. A cache in front of the database, which is redundancy too but lives outside the schema. If the read is still too slow, or is run so often that its cost dominates, denormalise. Copied current values and historical facts Store a value from a parent row on its children, so a common read avoids a join: Every change to customer.name must now also update that customer's orders. If one customer has 50,000 orders, a rename becomes a 50,000-row write. Snapshot or cache? Ask whether the copy should follow the original. The shipping address on an invoice should not change when the customer moves: it is a historical fact about the order, and storing it is correct normalised design. A copy of the customer's current display name should follow the original: that is a cache, and true denormalisation. Confusing the two either changes history or leaves stale data. Key takeaways Measure the query and its plan before adding copied-value update fan-out. Historical snapshots model a different fact; a cached current value must follow its source. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: refresh materialised views PostgreSQL 18: generated columns AWS: transactional outbox PostgreSQL 18: covering indexes and index-only scans

sum: Maintaining counters under writes, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Counters and write contention post.comment_count saves a COUNT() over comments on every page view. If a post page is read 1,000 times a second and gets 5 comments a second, you trade 1,000 counts for 5 increments. A trigger keeps it in step within the same transaction: The fixture assumes post.id is a primary key, comment.post_id is a non-null foreign key, and post.comment_count is non-null and initialised to zero. Each inserted comment adds one; rolling back its transaction also rolls back the increment. A production implementation must cover deletion, moving a comment between posts, bulk maintenance and any path that bypasses ordinary row triggers, such as TRUNCATE. This insert-only example intentionally demonstrates drift when another event is omitted. The hidden cost is contention. Every comment on a viral post updates the same row, and each UPDATE holds that row's lock until its transaction commits, so writers queue behind one another. Remedies: split the counter into several rows (say 16) and sum them on read (sharded counters), or buffer increments and apply them in batches. Key takeaways A database counter update avoids a lost increment but makes one parent row a contention point. Cover every mutation event and reconcile stored counts with their source. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: refresh materialised views PostgreSQL 18: generated columns AWS: transactional outbox PostgreSQL 18: row locks PostgreSQL 18: CREATE TRIGGER

sum: Materialised results and generated values, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Materialised views Reports such as daily sales per product scan millions of rows. Precompute them: In Postgres, a materialised view is a stored query result. It does not update itself; REFRESH re-runs the whole query. Plain REFRESH locks out readers while it runs; concurrent refresh lets ordinary reads continue. Concurrent refresh requires an already-populated view and a qualifying unique index on plain columns covering every row, without a partial predicate or expression. Only one refresh can run on a given view at a time. Relative speed depends on how much changed, so it is not correct to promise that concurrent refresh is always slower. Core Postgres has no incremental refresh (extensions such as pg_ivm add it), whereas Oracle's fast-refresh materialised views and SQL Server's indexed views maintain results incrementally, with restrictions on the query shape. The view is as stale as its last refresh. That suits a dashboard refreshed every 15 minutes; it does not suit a stock level shown at checkout. Generated same-row values A value computed from other columns in the same row is the cheapest kind, because there is no fan-out. Postgres generated columns do it declaratively: STORED computes on write and can be indexed. PostgreSQL 16–17 support the stored kind. PostgreSQL 18 also supports VIRTUAL, the default when the kind is omitted, computed on read. Explicit STORED makes this example portable across those versions. Generation expressions must use allowed immutable expressions over the current row: no subqueries, aggregates, other rows or other generated columns. PostgreSQL 18 imposes extra built-in-type/function restrictions on virtual expressions. The SQL assumes orders(id, day) and line(order_id, product_id, qty, price_paid), with quantity an integer and price an exact numeric amount in pounds per item. Multiplying gives pounds for the line; summing gives pounds for that day and product. These are example fixtures, not assumptions that every shop has one timezone or one currency. A materialised view is a stored snapshot from the query’s read snapshot; it is not guaranteed to include writes that commit during its refresh. Key takeaways PostgreSQL materialised views stay unchanged until refreshed. Concurrent refresh needs a populated view and a qualifying unique index; generated values have stricter same-row rules. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: refresh materialised views PostgreSQL 18: generated columns AWS: transactional outbox

sum: Star schemas and embedded records, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Star and snowflake schemas Analytical databases denormalise on purpose. A star schema has a central fact table (one row per sale, with numeric measures and foreign keys) surrounded by wide, denormalised dimension tables: dim_product holds product, category and department names in one row, even though that contains a transitive dependency: Storing it flat repeats each department name on every product row. The snowflake schema variant normalises dimensions back out. Stars can help when controlled data-loading pipelines keep duplicated dimension attributes consistent; batch loading alone does not prevent update anomalies and queries join one big table to a few small ones, which columnar engines handle well. Embedding and access patterns Document and key-value stores push this furthest. In MongoDB you might embed an order's lines inside the order document. In DynamoDB’s native query API, which has no relational join operation, a common pattern stores several entity types in one table, keyed so that one query fetches a customer and their recent orders together. AWS's own guidance is to design around your access patterns first, which is denormalisation as the default. The cost is the same as in SQL: duplicated data must be updated in every place, and changing an access pattern can require rewriting the data. Key takeaways Star dimensions deliberately repeat descriptive attributes for analytical access. Embedding and single-table designs trade simpler reads for maintenance and access-pattern constraints. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: refresh materialised views PostgreSQL 18: generated columns AWS: transactional outbox Kimball: Fact Tables and Dimension Tables AWS: DynamoDB modelling and access patterns MongoDB: embedding and references

sum: Copy consistency and correctness, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Keeping copies consistent Every denormalisation needs an answer to "what updates the copy, and how stale may it be?" Mechanism Staleness Main risk --------- Same transaction one transaction commit slower writes Trigger one transaction commit hidden logic CDC / outbox asynchronous; often seconds, unbounded during failures lag, ordering Batch refresh minutes+ stale reads Application code in the same transaction is explicit, but every code path that writes the source must remember the copy. One forgotten admin script causes drift. Enabled triggers automatically run for their configured events, but uncovered operations or disabled triggers can still leave gaps; they are also invisible to someone reading the application, can cascade, and add lock contention. Change data capture (reading the write-ahead log, for example with Debezium) or a transactional outbox propagates changes asynchronously to other tables, search indexes or services. Writes stay fast, readers see eventual consistency. Batch rebuilds (materialised view refresh, nightly jobs) are simple and self-healing, at the cost of staleness. Whatever you choose, add a copy reconciliation check: a periodic query comparing the copy with the source, such as counts that disagree with COUNT(). Drift happens, through bugs, manual fixes and restores, and you want to find it before customers do. The trade-off in one picture Denormalise when reads vastly outnumber writes to the copied data, the read path is measured to be the bottleneck, and some staleness is acceptable or the sync can be transactional. Avoid it for data that changes often and is copied widely (a username copied into millions of messages), or where a stale value causes real harm (balances, stock). Atomic maintenance still needs a protocol “Same transaction” means the source and copy commit or roll back together when every relevant write uses that protocol. Under PostgreSQL Read Committed, two separate reads can still see different committed snapshots; use one statement or a suitable transaction snapshot when comparing copies. A read-modify-write counter based on an earlier unlocked read can lose increments. An atomic relative update, or appropriate locking, avoids that race. Multi-row maintenance can deadlock when transactions lock parents in different orders; choose a consistent order and handle retries. For stock, keep one authoritative non-null count per product with a non-negative check. Decrement it in the same transaction as creating the order, and require exactly one row to be updated; a missing row must fail the order too. A refreshed dashboard copy cannot enforce no-oversell, however often it refreshes. An outbox makes the data change and event record atomic inside PostgreSQL; it does not make a later search-index write part of that transaction. Retried delivery can duplicate events, consumers must be idempotent, and per-entity ordering or version checks prevent a stale database update replacing a newer one. Lag can be unbounded during failures. Reconciliation and replay remain necessary. Key takeaways One transaction commit, consistent reading and asynchronous delivery are separate guarantees. Correctness-critical stock needs an authoritative transaction protocol; lagging copies suit reports. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: refresh materialised views PostgreSQL 18: generated columns AWS: transactional outbox

sum: Entities, cardinality and participation, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Normalisation tells you whether a set of tables is well formed. It does not tell you which tables to start with. That comes from conceptual modelling: working out, with the people who know the domain, what things exist, how they relate, and which rules always hold. The standard tool is the entity–relationship (ER) model, introduced by Peter Chen in 1976. An ER diagram is small enough to discuss with a product manager and precise enough to turn mechanically into tables. An ER model makes identifiers and relationship rules visible. Mapping it still requires FD and decomposition checks: attributes may depend on non-identifiers, and a diagram alone is not a proof of BCNF. The building blocks An entity type is a kind of thing with its own identity: Artist, Album, User. Each instance is an entity. An ER attribute describes an entity. Its design can distinguish: Simple ER attributes, such as title, from composite attributes, such as an address split into street, city and postcode. Single-valued attributes, such as a title, from multivalued attributes, such as an artist’s genres. Stored attributes, such as birth_date, from derived attributes, such as current age computed from birth date and today’s date. A key attribute (entity identifier) distinguishes instances, just as a candidate key does. A relationship type connects entity types: a User creates a Playlist. Relationship cardinality and participation Each end of a relationship has two constraints: Relationship cardinality (maximum): can one entity relate to one or many on the other side? Written 1:1 (one-to-one), 1:N (one-to-many) or M:N (many-to-many), where N and M just stand for "many". Participation (minimum): must every entity take part (total, minimum 1), or may it not (partial, minimum 0)? Crow's foot notation, the most common in industry tools, draws both at each end of the line: A music service: Read the first line left to right: an artist has zero or more albums; each album belongs to exactly one artist. Each album has one or more tracks. Playlists and tracks are many-to-many: a playlist holds many tracks, and a track appears on many playlists. Ask for counterexamples To pin down relationship cardinality, ask domain experts concrete questions: "Can an album ever have two artists?" (Yes: collaborations. Then Artist–Album is M:N, not 1:N.) "Can a track exist on no album?" (Singles?) Each answer changes the schema, and changing it after launch is expensive. Mapping an ER model to tables These rules turn a diagram into a schema. Strong entity. Create a table. Its entity identifier becomes the primary key; simple ER attributes become columns; composite attributes are flattened (street, city, postcode). One-to-many relationship. Put its foreign key on the many side. If participation is total, the column is NOT NULL. Many-to-many relationship. Create an associative table (junction table). Its key combines both foreign keys, and any attributes of the relationship itself live here. One-to-one relationship. Use a foreign key with UNIQUE, placed on the side with total participation (so it can be NOT NULL). If both sides are total and always created together, consider merging them into one table. Multivalued attribute. Create its own table, keyed by owner plus value: artist_genre with artist_id and genre columns. This is 1NF in action. Derived attribute. Usually compute it instead of storing it. Compute it in queries or views, or as a PostgreSQL generated column if it uses an allowed immutable expression over the same row. Age derived from the current date is not immutable. A foreign key on an album ensures its referenced artist exists; NOT NULL ensures that album has an artist. It does not ensure that each artist has an album. Likewise, declaring a track’s album foreign key cannot enforce the diagram’s “at least one track per album” condition. Parent-side minimum participation needs an additional transaction protocol or carefully designed deferred constraint triggers. PostgreSQL nullable UNIQUE allows several NULLs by default; for a mandatory one-to-one reference use both NOT NULL and UNIQUE, or a shared primary key. Key takeaways Cardinality describes maximum participation; minimum participation is a separate rule. Foreign keys, NOT NULL and UNIQUE enforce different parts of a relationship. Further reading Chen: The Entity-Relationship Model (1976) PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Weak entities and relationship keys, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Weak entities A weak entity cannot be identified on its own, only relative to an owner entity. Track 3 means nothing without saying which album. Its key is the owner's key plus a partial key: ON DELETE CASCADE reflects existence dependency: if the album goes, its tracks go. Many teams give tracks a surrogate track_id anyway, for shorter foreign keys and URLs. That is fine, as long as UNIQUE (album_id, track_no) still enforces the real rule. Relationship attributes and duplicate entries When a user adds a track to a playlist, when they added it and where it sits are facts about the relationship, not about either entity. They belong on the junction table. The following PostgreSQL example assumes the surrogate-key alternative above: track has a single-column primary key track_id, plus NOT NULL album_id/track_no and UNIQUE(album_id, track_no). It is not directly compatible with the preceding composite-key-only track definition: Notice the key. The textbook junction key (playlist_id, track_id) would forbid the same song appearing twice on one playlist, which real playlists allow. The key must reflect the rule you actually want, so here it is position within playlist. Key takeaways A weak entity needs its owner key plus its partial key. Relationship attributes belong on the junction, and its key must reflect whether duplicates are allowed. Further reading Chen: The Entity-Relationship Model (1976) PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Preserving three-way facts, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Ternary relationships Some facts involve three entities at once: supplier S supplies part P to project J. It is tempting to replace this with three binary relationships, but that loses information. Project into the three pairs and join them back: The join returns four rows: the three real ones and an extra one, S1 P1 J1. Each pair in it is true (S1 supplies P1 to someone; P1 goes to J1; S1 supplies J1), but S1 never supplied P1 to J1. Without a business rule guaranteeing reconstruction from the pairs, keep a three-way table with all three foreign keys. The displayed counterexample shows that the proposed join dependency does not hold. Join dependencies are the territory of 5NF; merely having three entities does not establish one, and some specially constrained ternary relationships can be decomposed safely. What each pair forgets The supplier/part projection remembers that S1 supplies P1 somewhere, but forgets the project. The part/project projection remembers that P1 goes to J1 from someone, but forgets the supplier. The supplier/project projection remembers that S1 supplies something to J1, but forgets the part. None of the three remembered pairs says that S1 supplies P1 to J1. Their join nevertheless constructs it because every pair matches. All original triples survive projection and rejoining: each carries three genuine pairs. The failure is additional triples, so the decomposition is called lossy even though its join has more rows. Information about which combinations were absent has been lost. Before choosing binary tables, ask whether the business explicitly permits a triple whenever those three pairwise facts hold. If yes, the join dependency may be an intended rule. If no, neither a diagram with three binary lines nor three independent foreign keys can recover the original three-way meaning. Key takeaways Pairwise projections can forget which triples were actually true. Only a justified join dependency permits reconstructing three-way facts from pairs. Further reading Chen: The Entity-Relationship Model (1976) PostgreSQL 18: constraints

sum: Mapping subtypes to tables, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: Inheritance: specialisation and generalisation Sometimes entities share most attributes but differ in some: a Payment is either a CardPayment (card token, last four digits) or a BankTransfer (sort code, reference). The ER model calls this specialisation. Subtypes can be disjoint subtypes (at most one subtype; exactly one only when also total) or overlapping subtypes, and specialisation can be total (every payment is some subtype) or partial. For portable relational schemas, choose one of three mappings. PostgreSQL also has native table inheritance, with different semantics and limitations; the mappings here do not rely on it.
