They are named in Martin Fowler's Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture: Mapping Tables Main cost --------- Single table one, with type column many NULLs Class table parent + one per subtype joins Concrete table one per subtype no key common to all subtypes Single-table inheritance puts every column in one table with a kind discriminator. It is fast and simple, but subtype columns must be nullable, so declare kind NOT NULL and use CHECK constraints to keep them coherent: Class-table inheritance has payment(payment_id, amount,...) plus card_payment(payment_id PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES payment,...). No NULL columns and clean constraints, at the cost of a join to load a whole payment. Concrete-table inheritance has a full table per subtype. Queries over "all payments" need UNION ALL, and nothing enforces unique ids across the tables. Enforcing subtype membership A subtype primary key that is also a foreign key ensures each subtype row has a parent and appears at most once in that subtype table. It does not ensure that each parent has a subtype, or that the same parent cannot appear in both card and bank tables. For disjoint membership, a parent discriminator plus matching composite foreign keys can prevent the wrong subtype; total participation still needs a suitable creation/deletion protocol or deferred constraint trigger. Choose the constraint strategy along with the table mapping. Avoid presenting class tables alone as an automatic enforcement of “exactly one subtype”. Key takeaways Single, class and concrete tables make different nullability and query trade-offs. Parent/subtype foreign keys alone do not ensure total, disjoint membership. Further reading Chen: The Entity-Relationship Model (1976) PostgreSQL 18: constraints Fowler: Class Table Inheritance Fowler: Single Table Inheritance Fowler: Concrete Table Inheritance

sum: References, evolving models and keys, with explicit examples and the conditions that make the reasoning valid.
x: The polymorphic-association trap Frameworks such as Rails make this easy: One column points at different tables depending on another column. A single ordinary foreign key cannot choose its referenced table from the type value. Without other integrity checks, orphaned references can accumulate, and queries must account for the type. Two relational alternatives: Exclusive arc: one nullable foreign key per target, and a check that exactly one is set. A common supertype: make Photo and Video subtypes of a Commentable entity (class-table inheritance) and reference its key. The related entity–attribute–value (EAV) pattern, a table of (entity_id, attribute_name, value) rows, makes per-attribute types and constraints harder to express, and complicates ordinary queries in exchange for schema flexibility. For truly open-ended attributes, consider PostgreSQL jsonb together with validation and indexes. It is a trade-off, not a general proof that JSON is always better than a carefully constrained typed EAV design. Keys: surrogate or natural? A natural key comes from the domain (ISBN, ISO country code). A surrogate primary key is generated (GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, UUID). Natural keys can change (emails, names) or turn out not to be unique; a generated integer surrogate can give compact references when the application keeps it stable. UUID surrogates are larger, and a surrogate is not inherently immutable. The common practice is a surrogate primary key plus UNIQUE constraints on the natural keys, so the real-world rules are still enforced. Changing a relationship after launch If albums may have several artists with roles, replace the single album foreign key with an album/artist junction holding role. Preserve uniqueness of the pair when each artist has one role per album; choose a different key if several roles per artist are permitted. Backfill existing artist references as the primary role. An online schema migration needs coordinated writers, backfill, validation and a read switch before removing the old column. The junction does not alone enforce “every album has at least one artist”; keep that minimum participation rule explicit. Key takeaways An ordinary foreign key names one target table; polymorphic target columns need another integrity strategy. A surrogate does not replace business uniqueness, and relationship changes need coordinated migrations. Further reading Chen: The Entity-Relationship Model (1976) PostgreSQL 18: constraints

t: From SQL text to a plan
sum: From SQL text to a plan with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. SQL is declarative: you say what rows you want, not how to find them. Something has to turn that description into a concrete program of loops, lookups and sorts. That something is the query processor, and it is the reason the same query can take 2 milliseconds on Monday and 20 seconds on Tuesday. This module uses the shop schema from SQL Fundamentals, scaled up so that performance actually matters: The examples use PostgreSQL 18 plan terminology and assume serial execution (max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0) for readability. Plan fragments are abbreviated. The supplied row and page counts define the illustrative dataset. The pipeline For an ordinary PostgreSQL optimisable query, the stages are as follows. Utility commands can take different paths; other engines use related architectures with different details. Parser. Checks the grammar and builds a parse tree. A typo like SELEC fails here, before any table is touched. Analyser (or binder). Looks names up in the system catalog: does orders exist, does it have a status column, what type is it? It produces PostgreSQL's analysed query tree, with every name resolved. "Column does not exist" errors come from here. Rewriter. Applies rules. The main one is view expansion: a query against a view is rewritten into a query against the view's underlying tables, so the planner can optimise the whole thing together. Row-level security policies are added here too. Planner/optimiser. Considers many ways to run the query and estimates the cost of each. It outputs one plan. Executor. Runs the plan and streams rows back to the client. Planning and execution both have costs. Their relative importance depends on the complexity of the SQL statement, prepared-plan reuse and workload; short OLTP statements can spend a substantial share of their time planning. Prepared statements skip work A prepared statement is parsed and analysed once. Later executions can reuse a cached plan, which can save planning work when a generic plan is reused. A custom plan still plans for each supplied parameter value; the later unit on parameter plans covers the trade-off. Key takeaways Parsing checks grammar; analysis resolves names and types; rewriting expands ordinary views before planning. Prepared statements can reuse a generic plan, but parameter-specific custom plans still incur planning work. sum: Read a tree of physical operators with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. A plan is a tree of operators Take this question: "which three cities have the most pending orders?" EXPLAIN shows the plan PostgreSQL chose. Simplified, it is: Read it from the leaves upwards. Each node is an operator that takes rows from its children and produces rows for its parent: Node Rows out ------ Seq Scan orders 30,066 of 1,000,000 Seq Scan customers 100,000 Hash Join 30,066 HashAggregate 8 (one per city) Sort, Limit 3 The whole query took about 47 ms. Almost all of it went on the two scans, reading 8,382 pages between them. Notice what the planner did with your SQL. You wrote a join and then a filter, but the plan filters orders inside the scan, before the join. That's predicate pushdown: throwing rows away as early as possible so later operators handle less data. The logical order of SQL clauses (FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT) defines what the answer means; the planner is free to compute it in any order that gives the same answer. Logical and physical operators The SQL describes logical operations: scan a table, join two inputs, group. The plan picks a physical algorithm for each one. Logical Physical choices in Postgres ------ Read a table Seq Scan, Index Scan, Index Only Scan, Bitmap Heap Scan Join Nested Loop, Hash Join, Merge Join Group HashAggregate, GroupAggregate Order Sort, Incremental Sort, or an index already in order Choosing between these is the optimiser's job, and the following units are about how it chooses. Key takeaways Read rows from leaves towards the root; control requests flow down the plan tree. A predicate referring only to orders can move below this inner join when semantics are preserved; aggregation reduces rows before the final sort. sum: Pulling rows and breaking pipelines with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. The iterator (Volcano) model How do the operators pass rows to each other? Most row-store databases, Postgres included, use the iterator model, named after Goetz Graefe's Volcano system from around 1990. Every operator implements the same tiny interface: open(): get ready (allocate memory, open children). next(): return the next row, or "done". close(): release resources. The top operator calls next() on its child, which calls next() on its child, and so on down to a scan that reads a row from a page. Rows are pulled up the tree one at a time. Python generators illustrate this pull behaviour. Use a non-negative integer limit; this miniature demonstrates pull control rather than every SQL LIMIT validation rule: The first block defines the operators. Initialise this six-row fixture before running the following plan; only IDs 2, 4 and 5 are pending. The counter counts visits, including rejected rows. Run a LIMIT 2 over this fixture: The scan stopped after four rows, not six. Once limit has its two rows it stops asking, so nobody below it does any more work. Postgres does the same thing. An illustrative plan for SELECT FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending' LIMIT 5: Postgres read 85 rows and 2 pages out of 7,353, and finished in 0.012 ms. Pipelines and blocking operators Some operators can emit their first row before seeing all of their input. A scan, a filter and the probe side of a hash join all stream: rows flow straight through. Others are blocking (also called pipeline breakers). The full operators listed here consume their input before producing results (an Incremental Sort instead blocks only on each presorted group): Sort: the smallest value might be the last row read. Hash (the build side of a hash join): the table must be complete before any probe can trust a miss. HashAggregate: a group's count isn't final until every row is seen. This is why EXPLAIN shows two costs for each node, like cost=0.00..19853.00. The first number is the startup cost (work before the first row), the second the total cost (work for all rows). A Sort has a high startup cost; a Seq Scan's is zero. When a query has LIMIT, the planner prefers plans with low startup cost, because it may never need the total. Key takeaways A LIMIT stops a streaming subtree by ceasing to request rows. Full sorts, hash builds and hash aggregation consume their inputs first; top-N sorting saves memory without avoiding the scan. sum: Pages, caches and scan costs with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. Pages: the unit of cost Tables and indexes are stored in fixed-size database pages (normally 8 KiB in PostgreSQL 18; its block size is selected at build time). MySQL 8.0 InnoDB defaults to 16 KiB pages and permits other sizes when an instance is initialised. The orders table holds about 136 rows per page. The database reads whole pages, never single rows, so the main question for any plan is how many pages does it touch, and are they in memory? MVCC means a scan must also establish whether each tuple version is visible to its snapshot. A sequential scan visits heap pages; an ordinary index scan follows index entries and then checks heap row versions. A covering index still needs heap visibility checks unless the visibility map says the page is all-visible. To turn a row count into the number of pages a full scan must read, divide by how many rows fit on one page: That matches the 7,353 pages in the table at the top of this lesson. It assumes rows are packed evenly; real tables also contain free space and dead row versions, so the true page count is usually a little higher than this ideal. A page found in PostgreSQL's shared buffer cache is a hit. It avoids an operating-system read request; no fixed latency follows from the label. A page that isn't is a read. It might come from the operating system's cache or from storage; measure the latency rather than assigning a fixed time to either case. Reading pages in order (a sequential scan) is cheaper per page than jumping around (random I/O), because the storage and the OS can read ahead. Postgres encodes that by charging seq_page_cost = 1 per sequential page and random_page_cost = 4 per random one by default. The cost-model unit shows how those numbers turn into a plan's cost. Key takeaways A page visit may hit shared buffers, the OS cache, or storage; buffer reads are not necessarily disk reads. The dense rows-per-page calculation estimates storage pages, while planner cost also includes CPU work and visibility checks. sum: Batches, compilation and workers with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. Other execution models The iterator model pays a function call per row per operator. That overhead is noticeable for analytical queries over billions of rows, so other designs exist: Vectorised execution (DuckDB, ClickHouse; Snowflake's 2016 design paper): operators process batches of values instead of one row per call; batch layout and size vary by engine, so loops are tight and CPU-cache friendly. Compiled execution (HyPer, Umbra, SingleStore): the plan is compiled to machine code that fuses operators into a single loop. Postgres has a limited form of this: it can JIT-compile expressions with LLVM for expensive queries. Parallel query: Postgres can split a scan across worker processes and gather their results through a Gather node. You'll see Gather and Parallel Seq Scan in real plans on big tables. Vectorisation batches CPU work; parallelism uses concurrent workers. They are separate choices: either model can run in one process or be combined with parallel work. Compilation is another axis and may fuse several operators. PostgreSQL expression JIT does not compile an entire query into one fused native loop. The ideas in this module (plans as trees, join algorithms, cost estimation) apply to all of them. Key takeaways Vectorised execution amortises per-row calls; compilation can fuse work and reduce interpreter overhead. Workers add parallelism, which is separate from vectorisation and does not guarantee proportional speedup. Snowflake's 2016 paper describes a columnar, vectorised engine with push-based query execution; it is a historical architecture example, rather than a promise about every current implementation detail. x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. A join is logically simple: pair every row of one input with every row of the other, and keep the pairs that satisfy the condition. Doing exactly that is far too slow for big tables, so databases have three main physical algorithms. Slow joins may involve an unsuitable choice among these algorithms, but slow queries can also have other causes. The two inputs are called the outer and inner sides (in a hash join, the probe and build sides). In a Postgres plan, the first child of a join node is the outer and the second is the inner. Nested loop join The obvious algorithm: for each outer row, look through the inner input for matches. The miniature needs a reusable inner iterable, such as a list, rather than a one-shot generator. Its predicate is a Python callable; SQL equality needs a separate test for SQL NULL. Every outer row is tested against every inner row, so the number of tests is the product of the two row counts: Doubling either input doubles the work, and doubling both quadruples it. That's why a plain nested loop is only sensible when at least one side is tiny. It becomes a great algorithm when the inner side is a database index lookup instead of a full scan. Then each outer row costs one index probe, a few page reads: The loops=99 on the inner node means it ran once per outer row. Ninety-nine primary-key probes: 0.4 ms. Nested loop is also the only algorithm that handles any join condition. PostgreSQL hash and merge joins need a suitable hash-joinable or merge-joinable equality clause. A pure condition like p.price < q.price - 199 therefore needs a nested loop in PostgreSQL 18. Other database engines can implement specialised inequality joins. Memoize Since Postgres 14, a Memoize node can sit above the inner side of a nested loop and cache results by join key. If many outer rows share the same key, repeat lookups are served from the cache. You'll see Hits and Misses counts in EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Key takeaways A plain nested loop tests every pair; an indexed inner lookup changes the cost of each outer iteration. PostgreSQL 18 needs a suitable equality clause for hash or merge joins; pure inequality joins use nested loops. x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. Hash join Prefer a build input with a small projected size, subject to join semantics and available paths. Read all of it into an in-memory hash table keyed on the join column (the build phase). Then stream the larger input and look each row up in the table (the probe phase). This miniature joins non-NULL, hashable keys using Python equality. SQL equality does not match NULL keys: a SQL-style inner hash join must omit them rather than treating Python None as an ordinary matching key. Let n and m be the two input row counts. With well-distributed hashing, building and probing cost expected O(n + m): the work grows in proportion to the total number of input rows (big-O notation ignores constant factors). On top of that comes the cost of emitting the result. Duplicate keys can produce the product of the input row counts in output rows, and those cannot be emitted in time that grows only with the inputs. In Postgres: Batches: 1 means the whole hash table fitted in memory. Postgres caps the memory a hash table may use with two settings: The customers hash table used 4,540 kB, about 4.4 MB, so it fits in one batch. The budget applies per operation and can also multiply across concurrent processes and sessions. Actual overhead and skew make it unsafe to treat it as an exact bound on query memory. When the build side doesn't fit If the build side is too large, Postgres uses a hybrid hash join. It splits both inputs into partitions (batches) by hashing the join key, keeps the first batch in memory and writes the rest to temporary files. Matching rows always land in the same batch number on both sides, so each batch can be joined on its own. Rerunning the join of all orders with work_mem cut to 1 MB: Same answer, but 4 batches, temporary file I/O and about 16% slower (160 ms against 138 ms). The effect of spilling on elapsed execution time depends on workload, storage and cache state. Hash joins need a hash-joinable equality clause and do not promise result order. They are often attractive for large unsorted inputs; width, skew, result size and other paths still matter. Key takeaways A hash build retains duplicate keys; output size can dominate input-linear hashing work. Multiple batches and temporary-file traffic indicate spilling; memory budgets multiply across operations and processes. x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. Merge join (sort-merge) If both inputs are sorted on the join key, walk them together like the merge step of merge sort. Advance whichever side has the smaller key; when the keys are equal, emit the match. On equality, keeping the left position allows all duplicate right keys to match it. This miniature does not handle duplicate left keys or SQL NULL semantics; a general merge join must revisit or buffer matching groups and handle unmatched outer rows separately. With the unique-left-key assumption in this miniature, the merge is O(n + m), where n and m are the row counts of the two inputs: each step advances one of the two positions, so the work grows in proportion to the total number of rows. General duplicate-key joins must also account for output size and any repeated processing of matching groups. If an input isn't already sorted, it must be sorted first. Sorting n rows costs O(n log n), where n is the input's row count and log n grows very slowly (about 20 for a million rows in base 2), and a big sort may spill to disk. Merge join is attractive when an index already provides the order, or when the query needs that order anyway (ORDER BY on the join key). An illustrative merge plan for the pending-orders query (disabling hash joins encourages alternatives but does not force a merge, because nested loops remain available): customers comes out of its primary-key index already in id order, and only the 30,066 pending orders need sorting, in memory. The time is essentially the same as the hash join, which is why the planner's estimates for the two were close. Key takeaways Merge joins need compatible sorted inputs and an eligible equality condition in PostgreSQL. The miniature assumes unique left keys; a general implementation must handle duplicate groups and output size. Costing them in page reads Textbook analyses count page I/Os (each page read from or written to disk counts as one), because that's what dominates when data is on disk. They ignore CPU work and, by convention, the cost of writing the final result. Use the classic set-up: Table R has 1,000 pages, with 100 rows per page (100,000 rows). Two buffer pages are kept back: one to read S into and one to collect output. The number of times the inner table is rescanned dominates, so compare both orientations. The smaller outer table wins in this fixture; ceiling effects mean it is a heuristic rather than a universal rule. If it fits in the operating system's cache, real costs are lower. Key takeaways Row nested loop rereads the inner once per outer row; block nested loop does so once per outer block. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. External sort and hash I/O Use the same textbook fixture: R occupies 1,000 pages, S occupies 500 pages and the join has 102 buffer pages. CPU and final output writes are excluded; inputs start on disk. Sort-merge First sort both tables on the join key with an external merge sort, the algorithm databases use for data bigger than memory. Pass 0 reads a memory-load of pages at a time, sorts it and writes it back out as a sorted run. Each later pass merges as many runs as there are available input buffers into one, using one buffer page per run plus one for output. Every pass reads and writes every page once. For a non-empty table and at least three buffer pages, the number of passes in this textbook model is: S, with 500 pages, also needs two passes (5 runs, merged in one pass). With very little memory the number of passes grows: sorting R with only 3 buffer pages, pass 0 would write 334 runs of 3 pages, and merging them two at a time would take 9 more passes, 10 in all. That's why more sort memory helps so much. Two passes, each reading and writing every page, is 4 I/Os per page. The merge join then reads both sorted tables once more: Here R creates 10 runs and S creates 5. Merging both streams together needs one input buffer per run, plus join/output bookkeeping: 15 input buffers fit within the 102-page budget. Duplicate-key groups may need additional buffering or rescans; the following model excludes that extra work. If the final merge pass of each sort feeds the join directly, the fully sorted tables are never written out. Only pass 0 reads and writes, and the merge pass reads once: Key takeaways External sort creates runs and merges them using the available input buffers. A fused final merge can avoid writing sorted inputs, provided both merge streams and matching groups fit the buffer budget. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. Index nested-loop I/O Use a 1,000-page outer table R with 100,000 rows and an indexed inner table S. This deliberately cold, simplified page-I/O model excludes CPU and final output writes. Index nested loop What about index nested loop? Instead of scanning S for each outer row, probe an index on S's join column. With a 3-level B-tree plus a heap page, that's about 4 random reads per outer row. For 100,000 outer rows that's about 400,000 random reads, far worse than hashing. For 100 outer rows it's about 400 probe reads, far better. Index nested loop wins when the outer side is small. Why only 3 levels? Each B-tree page holds hundreds of keys, so every level multiplies the number of reachable entries by hundreds: The upper levels are read on almost every lookup, so they are usually already in memory, and a real probe often needs fewer than four disk reads. Key takeaways A cold index probe pays for B-tree traversal and heap access; cached tree levels can reduce physical reads. Compare the probe model with hashing using the actual outer row count and workload-specific costs. Actual execution depends on version, workload and settings. Choosing between them Nested loop Hash Merge ------------ Join condition Any Equality Equality Best when Small outer, indexed inner Large unsorted inputs Inputs already sorted Memory Little Build side Little (if presorted) Internal path order May preserve outer None promised May preserve merge keys The illustrative plan costs show why an access path can matter. Joining pending orders to customers: Plan Estimated cost ------ Hash join 23,290 Merge join 25,539 Nested loop + index 30,572 Nested loop, no index 46,172,536 Without an index on the inner side, the nested loop is about 2,000 times more expensive. That's the plan you get when an index is missing and no equality condition exists, or when the planner wrongly believes the outer side has one row. At larger scale, joining all 1,000,000 orders to their 3,000,000 order items, the hash join (8 batches, 587 ms) beat a merge join that had to sort 3 million rows through a 35 MB temporary file (850 ms). A physical path may provide useful ordering to another node, but SQL results have a guaranteed order only with ORDER BY. Outer joins and duplicate groups can limit which path ordering is useful. Outer, semi and anti joins All three algorithms come in variants for other join types, and you'll see the names in plans: Hash Left Join, Merge Full Join: outer joins. Postgres can't run a FULL OUTER JOIN as a nested loop, because the nested loop has no cheap way to remember which inner rows never matched. Semi Join: from EXISTS or IN. Stops at the first matching row for each outer row. Anti Join: from NOT EXISTS. Emits outer rows with no match. Hash Right Join: the planner swapped sides so the smaller input is hashed, even though the SQL said LEFT JOIN. Key takeaways Join cost depends on outer cardinality, input ordering, memory and usable access paths. Join variants preserve different rows; input swaps can change the displayed direction, and only ORDER BY promises result order. x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. The optimiser has to choose between plans without running them. It does this by predicting how many rows each step will produce, converting those predictions into a cost, and picking the cheapest plan it can find. This design, the cost-based optimiser, comes from IBM's System R in the late 1970s (Selinger et al., 1979), and remains influential in modern query optimisers. An optimiser has three parts: Cardinality estimation: how many rows will each operator produce? A cost model: given those row counts, how expensive is each operator? A search strategy: which of the possible plans does it actually consider? Cardinality estimation is a major source of poor choices. Leis et al., How Good Are Query Optimizers, Really? (VLDB 2015), found large estimation errors on its evaluated join workloads; that evidence does not establish one cause for every slow query. What the planner knows ANALYZE (run manually or by autovacuum) reads a random sample of each table and stores a summary. Table-level figures live in pg_class; column-level ones are in the pg_stats view. For our orders table: Column Statistic Value --------- status n_distinct 3 status most common values shipped, cancelled, pending status their frequencies 0.8976, 0.0716, 0.0308 customer_id n_distinct 91,709 ordered_on histogram 101 bounds null_frac: the fraction of NULLs. n_distinct: the number of distinct values. A negative number means a fraction of the row count (-1 means "every row is unique", as for a primary key). most_common_vals / most_common_freqs (MCVs): the most frequent values and how often each appears. histogram_bounds: values that split the remaining (non-MCV) rows into buckets holding equal numbers of rows. physical-order correlation: how closely the physical row order follows the column's sort order, from -1 to 1. It affects how expensive an index scan's heap reads will be. For PostgreSQL 18's built-in scalar statistics analysis, the target sample size uses the following model. Special data-type analysers and other requested statistics can affect the required sample: With that default the standard scalar-statistics analyser can retain up to 100 MCVs and about 100 histogram buckets per column. Raising a column's target to 1,000 samples 300,000 rows and keeps up to 1,000 of each, at the cost of a slower ANALYZE and slightly slower planning. The estimates are estimates Because ANALYZE samples, the numbers change slightly each time it runs. That's why the planner said 30,767 pending orders when the true count is 30,066. Key takeaways ANALYZE collects sampled column distributions; the scalar-statistics target controls detail and the requested sample. Physical-order correlation concerns heap ordering, whereas inter-column dependence requires multivariate statistics. x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plans and figures below are illustrative model inputs. Actual execution depends on version, workload and settings. Selectivity: from stats to row counts Selectivity is the fraction of rows a condition keeps. Every row estimate starts from it: The rules below are all ways of working out s, using the illustrative column-frequency statistics. Equality on a common value WHERE status = 'pending': 'pending' is in the MCV list, so the planner uses its measured frequency, 0.030767, as the selectivity: The actual count is 30,066, so the estimate is about 2% high. Equality on any other value WHERE customer_id = 42: there's no MCV list (no value is especially common), so the planner assumes values are evenly spread and every value matches the same share of rows. The column has no NULLs here; if it had, their fraction would be taken off first: The actual count for customer 42 is 14: close enough to choose the right plan. This residual model requires a positive count of remaining distinct non-NULL values. When the column does have an MCV list but the value isn't on it, the planner takes away the rows the MCVs and NULLs account for and shares the rest evenly among the remaining distinct values: For example, if 3 MCVs cover 40% of rows, there are no NULLs and 103 distinct values, the remaining 60% of rows are shared among 100 values, giving 0.6% per value. PostgreSQL also caps this figure so that a value missing from the list is never estimated as more common than the least common value on it. Key takeaways Use MCV frequencies for listed values; share residual probability among the remaining distinct non-NULL values. The estimates assume sampled frequencies and distinct counts represent the current table. Range selectivity and dependencies Selectivity is the fraction of input rows retained by a condition; cardinality is the number retained. The numerical statistics below are illustrative, rather than measurements of the small executable fixtures. A range, from the histogram WHERE ordered_on >= '2026-01-01': the histogram has 100 buckets, each holding 1% of the non-MCV rows. The date leaves one third of the bucket above it; that bucket runs from 2025-12-18 to 2026-01-08, and 8 more buckets lie above it. Count the buckets above the constant, including the part of the bucket it falls in: The planner applies that fraction to the non-MCV rows and adds the frequencies of any MCVs that satisfy the condition, which is why its final estimate, 84,278 rows, is slightly above 8.3%. The actual count is 86,346. Combining conditions: the independence assumption For conditions A and B, PostgreSQL normally multiplies their selectivities when it has no applicable dependency information, assuming the columns are independent: knowing a row's value in one column tells you nothing about the other. For status = 'pending' AND ordered_on >= '2026-01-01': The illustrative calculation assumes status and date are independent; that assumption needs checking on real data. But consider customers, where every Glasgow customer is in Scotland: The eight cities are equally common; Glasgow and Scotland each cover 1/8 of customers in this fixture, so the planner multiplies: The actual count is 12,500, one eighth of the customers. The planner is out by a factor of 8 because knowing the city already tells you the country. Errors like this can affect plan choices for multi-column filters. Extended statistics You can tell Postgres to measure the relationship: ANALYZE then records that city determines country with degree 1.0, and the estimate becomes about 12,700. Other kinds are ndistinct (for GROUP BY a, b estimates) and mcv (common combinations of values). Key takeaways Histograms describe non-MCV rows and interpolate within buckets. Multiplying selectivities assumes independence; suitable extended statistics can measure dependencies or value combinations. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. Missing expression statistics and join estimates The worked estimates use an illustrative million-row orders table and 100,000 customers; IDs are non-NULL and each order references exactly one customer. When there are no statistics For conditions the planner can't analyse, it uses fixed default selectivities: Condition Default Example --------- expr = const 0.5% lower(email) = '...': 500 of 100,000 expr < const 1/3 price 2 > 100: 3,333 of 10,000 The planner has stats on the email column, but not on lower(email). An expression index on lower(email) allows expression statistics as a side effect, because ANALYZE then gathers statistics on the indexed expression. Join estimates For an equijoin (a join on =), the selectivity is the fraction of all possible row pairs that match. Postgres estimates it from the distinct counts of the two join keys, refined using MCV lists where it has them. For orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id: The formula assumes every key value on the side with fewer distinct values has a match on the other side, which is exactly true for a foreign key. Errors multiply as they go up the tree. If each of three joins is out by a factor of 3, the final estimate can be out by 27, and the join algorithm choices near the top are made on wrong numbers. The cost model Postgres costs are in arbitrary units anchored on one sequential page read = 1.0: Parameter Default Charged for --------- seq_page_cost 1.0 Page read in order random_page_cost 4.0 Page read at random cpu_tuple_cost 0.01 Each row processed cpu_index_tuple_cost 0.005 Each index entry cpu_operator_cost 0.0025 Each operator or function call A sequential scan pays for every page it reads, every row it processes and every condition it evaluates on each row. For orders with status = 'pending': EXPLAIN shows cost=0.00..19853.00: exactly this. An index scan's cost depends on how many index and heap pages it expects to touch, charged at random_page_cost, discounted by physical-order correlation and effective_cache_size (the planner's guess of how much data is cached). Tune random_page_cost for SSDs The default of 4.0 dates from spinning disks. On SSDs, or when most data is cached, many teams set it to around 1.1 so the planner is less reluctant to use indexes. Test the change on your workload first. Key takeaways Missing expression statistics can trigger defaults; indexed expressions can collect statistics after ANALYZE. x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. The optimiser predicts cardinalities, applies a cost model, and searches candidate plans. Cardinality errors can dominate plan quality: the Leis et al. study in Further reading documents this on its evaluated workloads. Searching the plan space For each table the planner generates the candidate access paths (seq scan, each usable index, bitmap scans). It then has to choose a join order, and that space explodes: Tables Left-deep orders All tree shapes --------- 3 6 12 5 120 1,680 10 3,628,800 17,643,225,600 Both columns come from counting arrangements: The three-table row follows the same factorial counts: six left-deep orders and twelve ordered, labelled trees. These counts assume unrestricted joins among distinct tables; they exclude physical method choices and illegal reorderings. Postgres uses System R-style dynamic programming. It finds the best way to join every pair of tables, then every set of three built from those, and so on. It keeps the cheapest plan for each subset, plus any plan that produces a useful sort order (an "interesting order") that might avoid a sort later. Working over subsets rather than full orderings is what makes it tractable: The work per subset still varies, because each subset can be split in several ways and each split has several physical join methods, but the count stays far below the number of trees. At or above geqo_threshold (default 12) FROM items, exhaustive search is too slow, so Postgres switches to GEQO, a genetic algorithm that finds a good plan rather than the best. Separately, join_collapse_limit (default 8) caps how many explicit JOINs are merged into one list for reordering. Key takeaways Dynamic programming reuses subset paths and retains useful ordering alternatives. Join restrictions, pruning, collapse limits and GEQO constrain search; the cheapest estimated candidate need not run fastest. x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. Stale statistics Statistics describe the table as it was at the last ANALYZE. Autovacuum re-analyses a table once enough rows have changed since the last ANALYZE: For the 1,000-row table below, more than 150 changes cross the threshold, and a 500,000-row load passes that easily. But autovacuum only checks tables periodically (every minute by default, set by autovacuum_naptime), so a query run straight after the load still sees the old statistics. On a 100-million-row table, more than 10,000,050 changes cross the default threshold. In between, the planner can be badly wrong: The planner did notice that the table had grown, because it scales reltuples by the current number of pages. But the MCV list said every row is 'a', so 'b' looked almost non-existent. Feed that "1 row" into a join and you get a nested loop running hundreds of thousands of loops, like the 600,000-loop example in the next lesson. Practical rules: Run ANALYZE after bulk loads, before querying the new data. Temporary tables are never analysed by autovacuum. Analyse them yourself. For skewed columns, raise the per-column target: ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET STATISTICS 1000; Add extended statistics for correlated columns used together. Key takeaways ANALYZE after a bulk load avoids relying on old column distributions. Temporary tables need manual ANALYZE; autovacuum thresholds make a table eligible rather than scheduling immediate analysis. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. EXPLAIN is the single most useful tool for understanding a slow query. It shows the plan the optimiser chose, with its estimates. EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs the query and shows what actually happened. The skill is reading the output quickly and knowing which numbers matter. The following abbreviated PostgreSQL 18-style plan fragments are illustrative exercises. The variants ANALYZE executes the statement and reports actual figures. BUFFERS reports pages touched. Since Postgres 18 it's included automatically with ANALYZE; on older versions, ask for it. VERBOSE adds output column lists and schema-qualified names. SETTINGS lists any planner settings that differ from the defaults. Very useful when someone sends you a plan. FORMAT JSON gives machine-readable output for visualisers. TIMING OFF keeps row counts but skips per-node timing, which can have noticeable overhead on some systems. EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs the statement EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM orders deletes the orders. Wrap data-changing statements in a transaction you roll back: BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE...; ROLLBACK; Rollback does not undo sequence increments or external side effects from functions or triggers. Use disposable data when those effects are possible. sum: Inclusive time, loops and row errors with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. Three rules for the numbers 1. Costs and times are cumulative A node's cost and time include its children's. To find the time spent in one node itself (its exclusive time), subtract its children. From the illustrative cities query: For serial totals, multiply both the parent's and each child's average time by their own loops before subtracting; the displayed example has one loop at every node. With parallel execution, loops may include executions by several processes. Multiplying averages by loops gives aggregate instrumented execution time, not elapsed wall-clock time; overlapping worker times cannot simply be subtracted from the leader time. Worker details, rescans and instrumentation overhead make exclusive-time subtraction only a diagnostic approximation. So most of the 47 ms went on the orders scan (26 ms), not the join. 2. Multiply by loops actual time and rows are per loop. The inner side of a nested loop runs once per outer row: Buffers are already totals across all loops, not per loop: 1,200 page accesses, 6 per lookup. 3. Compare estimated rows with actual rows This is the most important check. Walk up from the leaves and find the lowest node where the estimate and the actual differ by 10x or more. Everything above it was planned on wrong information. The Seq Scan on imports expected 1 row and got 600,000. When both counts are positive, measure the gap as a ratio, whichever way round is bigger. A zero estimate or zero actual count needs direct inspection instead of division: That's the root cause. The nested loop above it was a reasonable choice for 1 row and a poor one for 600,000: 3.6 million page accesses. After ANALYZE imports, the planner chose a hash join with about 19,000. Estimates the other way are dangerous too An overestimate can make the planner reject an index and scan a whole table. Any big gap is worth explaining. Key takeaways Rows and time are averages per loop; buffers are totals. Serial inclusive-time subtraction is approximate; parallel worker time can overlap. Investigate estimate errors from the leaves upwards. Red flags and what they indicate You see It suggests ------ Estimate off by 10x+ Stale stats, correlated columns, or a function on a column Large Rows Removed by Filter A missing or unusable index Sort Method: external merge Disk: Sort spilled; work_mem too small, or an index could supply the order Batches: greater than 1 Hash spilled to temp files High loops on an expensive inner node Nested loop over too many outer rows Heap Fetches high on an Index Only Scan Pages are not all-visible; investigate updates, snapshots and vacuum Heap Blocks: lossy Bitmap too big for work_mem; rows rechecked per page Buffers:... read dominates Absent from shared buffers; the OS cache may still serve reads Sorts that spill With the default 4 MB work_mem, sorting a million rows wrote 36 MB to temporary files. Interestingly, work_mem = 64MB still spilled: the in-memory quicksort needed 71 MB (Memory: 71451kB at 256 MB), because in-memory sorting carries per-row overhead the compact on-disk format doesn't. With an ORDER BY... LIMIT 10 instead, the plan uses top-N heapsort Memory: 26kB and never spills. Index Cond versus Filter Index Cond is evaluated by the index access method. Leading-key bounds usually narrow a B-tree search; some later-key conditions filter index entries without reducing the contiguous range scanned. Filter is checked on each row after it's fetched. A condition appearing only under Filter does not supply an index access condition in that node. Here the LIKE 'c42@%' prefix was converted into a range for the index, then rechecked as a filter. New in Postgres 18: Index Searches Index Searches counts how many separate descents into the index happened. Normally it's 1 per loop. Here, an index on (ordered_on, customer_id) was used for a query on customer_id alone, and Postgres 18's skip scan made 1,031 descents, across the date groups it checked. The composite-index unit explains how a leading customer key can need one search. Key takeaways Spills, high loops and heap fetches are evidence to investigate, rather than proof of one fix. Index Cond is handled by the index method; a separate Filter is evaluated after that access. For Buffers: shared hit=7011 read=342: Repeated accesses to the same page count again each time, so this is a measure of work, not of distinct data. hit: already in shared buffers. read: requested from the operating system. It might still have come from the OS page cache, so a read is not necessarily a disk read. Enable track_io_timing to measure time spent in I/O calls. It still cannot tell whether those calls were served from the OS cache or physical storage. dirtied / written: pages this query modified or had to write out (for example, setting hint bits on freshly loaded rows). temp read / written: temporary files from spilling sorts and hashes. Buffer access counts complement timing, but they are not independent of system state. The hit/read split depends on cache warmth, and repeated accesses may revisit the same page. The illustrative totals (3.6 million versus 19,000) suggest very different work, but do not imply that every access becomes a separate disk read on a cold cache. A method for slow queries Get the real plan: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) against production-sized data. A plan from a 1,000-row dev table tells you little. Note the total Execution Time. Find the nodes with the largest exclusive time (subtract children, multiply by loops). Walk up from the leaves looking for the first big estimate error. Check the red flags table. Change one thing (an index, ANALYZE, a rewrite), then re-run and compare buffers and time. For long plans, paste the text into a visualiser such as explain.depesz.com or explain.dalibo.com, which compute exclusive times and highlight misestimates for you. To catch slow plans in production without running EXPLAIN by hand, use the auto_explain module, which logs the plans of statements slower than a threshold, and pg_stat_statements, which records total time and calls for each query shape (queries that differ only in their constant values are counted together) so you know which queries to look at first. Other databases MySQL has EXPLAIN ANALYZE (8.0.18+) with a similar tree format. SQLite's EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN is much terser: SCAN o, then SEARCH c USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?), then USE TEMP B-TREE FOR GROUP BY. That was our cities query: a nested loop of primary-key lookups, with a temporary B-tree for the grouping. Caveats EXPLAIN ANALYZE doesn't send the result rows to the client, so network transfer time isn't included. Postgres 17 added a SERIALIZE option to measure the cost of converting rows to output format. Repeated runs change cache warmth. Compare multiple representative runs and inspect read versus hit; two runs do not establish production behaviour. Per-node timing has overhead. If the plan has millions of tiny loops, use TIMING OFF and rely on row counts and buffers. Key takeaways Buffer counters describe accesses, including repeated visits; shared reads can hit the OS cache. Compare representative plans and timings, including client costs omitted by EXPLAIN. t: Selectivity means pages as well as rows
sum: Selectivity means pages as well as rows with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. The System Design module's indexing lesson covers how B-trees and LSM trees work. This lesson takes the planner's point of view: given a query and its plan, which index would change the plan, and is the change worth what the index costs? The examples below assume an illustrative 1,000,000-row orders table and PostgreSQL 18 plan features. Will the planner use the index? An index lets Postgres jump to matching entries, but each match still needs its row fetched from the table (the heap). If the rows are scattered, each fetch can be a different page. The planner compares that random I/O with simply reading the whole table in order. Three queries on ordered_on with an index on that column: Filter Rows Plan Time ------------ One day 438 Bitmap index scan 0.5 ms One quarter 37,390 (3.7%) Bitmap index scan 9.3 ms Since 2021 847,258 (85%) Seq Scan 51 ms The quarter is the interesting one. A sequential scan took 23 ms, so the index halved the time, but look at the plan: Matching 3.7% of the rows touched 7,306 of 7,353 heap pages, nearly all of them. Orders for a given quarter are spread uniformly through the table (physical-order correlation near 0), so almost every 8 KiB page contains a few. You can predict that: if matching rows are scattered at random, the chance that a page has none at all is tiny. The prediction, about 7,309 pages, is close to the 7,306 the plan reported. The model assumes matches are scattered at random; any clustering by date lowers the page count. A bitmap scan visits matching heap pages in physical order. Whether it beats a sequential scan when nearly every page is touched must be measured; the illustrative timing is not a general guarantee. But the benefit of an index depends on how many pages the matching rows occupy, not just how many rows match. If rows were physically clustered by this date column (for example, an append-only log written in date order), the same quarter would occupy about 4% of the pages, and the index would win by far more. Bitmap scans A Bitmap Index Scan collects the locations of all matches into an in-memory bitmap of pages; the Bitmap Heap Scan then reads those pages in physical order. It's the planner's middle ground between an index scan (good for a few rows) and a seq scan (good for many). Bitmaps from different indexes can be combined with BitmapAnd and BitmapOr. Key takeaways Scattered matches can touch most pages even at low row selectivity. Bitmap scans gather tuple locations and visit heap pages in physical order; compare their cost with a full scan. sum: Composite indexes and skip scan with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. Composite indexes: column order is everything A frequent query: a customer's five most recent orders. With an index on (customer_id, ordered_on): The index holds customer 42's entries side by side, already sorted by date. Postgres descends once, walks backwards and stops after five. There's no Sort node at all. Now the same columns the other way round, (ordered_on, customer_id): Customer 42's entries are now scattered across every date. Postgres 18's skip scan rescues the query by making repeated searches across date groups (1,031 illustrative searches before finding five matches). That's about 100 times slower and 390 times more buffers than the right index. Earlier PostgreSQL versions could still use the index and check the later-key condition, but without skip scan might need to read a much larger index range. Other indexes and restrictions could change the choice. Order the columns: equality, then sort, then range 1. Columns compared with = go first. 2. Then the ORDER BY column, so rows come out in order. 3. Then columns compared with ranges (<, >, BETWEEN). Equality on leading keys and a range on the next key establish the usual scan bounds. Later conditions can still be checked within the index, and PostgreSQL 18 skip scan may perform additional searches to narrow work further. Check the actual plan rather than treating the rule as absolute. Skip scan is usually most attractive when the omitted leading key has relatively few distinct values. PostgreSQL 18 chooses repeated searches only when its cost model expects an advantage; the exact search count need not equal the global distinct-value count, especially with LIMIT or additional bounds. With 2,400 dates it gave 2,400 descents for a full lookup (6.4 ms). With a million distinct leading values it would be hopeless. Design for the query; don't rely on skip scan. Key takeaways Leading equality keys followed by the desired ordering can let LIMIT stop an ordered scan early. PostgreSQL 18 skip scan can use repeated searches, but its usefulness depends on omitted-key distinctness and other bounds. sum: Covering and partial indexes with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. Covering indexes and index-only scans If every column a query needs is in the index, Postgres can answer from the index alone: an Index Only Scan. INCLUDE adds columns to the index's leaf entries without making them part of the key: There's a catch. The index doesn't record whether each row version is visible to your transaction, so Postgres must check the table unless the page is marked all-visible in the visibility map. VACUUM can set those bits; unchanged all-visible pages then permit the heap check to be skipped. Here is the query (20,162 rows) straight after updating 2% of the table, and again after a VACUUM: State Heap Fetches Buffers Time ------------ Just after updating 20,000 rows 20,592 20,661 27.6 ms After VACUUM 0 81 1.1 ms The 20,000 updated rows were spread across nearly every page, so nearly every page lost its all-visible bit. The "index-only" scan went back to the heap for every row and became 25 times slower. Index-only scans work best on tables that are mostly read, or where autovacuum keeps up. Partial indexes If queries only ever look at a small subset of rows, index only that subset: The partial index holds 30,066 entries and is 272 kB. The full index on ordered_on is 6.9 MB. It's cheaper to maintain too: a shipped-order insert adds no entry to it. The planner uses a partial index only when it can prove the query's WHERE clause implies the index's predicate. WHERE status = 'pending' matches. WHERE status = $1 with a parameter usually doesn't, because the planner can't prove $1 is 'pending' when building a generic plan. Key takeaways Covering columns enable index-only access only when visibility checks can avoid heap fetches. A partial index is usable only when the planner can establish its predicate; a generic unknown parameter can prevent that proof. IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. Expression indexes and operator classes An index on email does not directly search the lower-case expression in WHERE lower(email) =..., because the index stores email, not lower(email). Index the expression: Index Plan Time --------- None Seq Scan, 99,999 removed 17 ms On lower(email) Index Scan 0.02 ms For the simple equality shown, an ordinary email index cannot supply a selective lower-case-expression lookup. It can still be scanned as a covering path in some queries; a function does not make every use of an index impossible. ANALYZE also gathers statistics on indexed expressions, so the row estimate improves from the 0.5% default (500) to 1. Pattern planning also depends on the collation and operator. These examples assume a deterministic collation; PostgreSQL 18 supports LIKE with some nondeterministic collations, but index support still needs checking for the specific expression and pattern. Operator classes matter for LIKE. In a database whose collation isn't C, a plain B-tree on a text column can't serve LIKE 'abc%', because the collation's sort order doesn't keep prefixes together byte-wise. An index built with text_pattern_ops can: A pattern beginning with a wildcard such as LIKE '%abc' supplies no selective prefix range for an ordinary B-tree. A full or index-only scan can still use that index as a covering access path. For indexed substring search, consider a trigram index (pg_trgm with GIN or GiST). Combining indexes Postgres can combine single-column indexes with bitmaps: It read 4,984 and 63,535 index entries to find 308 rows. A suitable composite index may reduce the work for this exact query, but bitmap combination means a few well-chosen single-column indexes can serve many query shapes reasonably. That's often the better trade when queries are ad hoc. Key takeaways Match an expression index to the expression searched, and check collation and operator-class requirements for prefixes. Bitmap combinations can serve varied predicates but do not preserve B-tree ordering. sum: Index maintenance and tuning a workload with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. What every index costs Index Size ------ orders (the table) 59 MB orders_cust_cov_idx 30 MB orders_pkey 21 MB orders_cust_date_idx 21 MB orders_date_idx 6.9 MB orders_pending_idx 272 kB The illustrative date index is smaller in part because of B-tree deduplication (Postgres 13+), which stores a repeated key once with a list of row pointers: 1,000,000 rows share only 2,400 distinct dates. Costs to weigh: Writes. An INSERT maintains applicable indexes; a partial index excludes rows outside its predicate. Changing a column used by a non-summarising index, including an INCLUDE column, prevents a HOT (heap-only tuple) update. BRIN is a summarising-index exception; HOT also requires room on the original heap page. Memory. Indexes compete with table data for the buffer cache. Vacuum. Vacuum may need index cleanup for dead tuples; its actual work depends on dead-index entries and cleanup settings, and unnecessary scans can be skipped. Planning. More indexes give more paths to consider, and more chances of a surprising choice. Find indexes that are never used: Check over weeks of traffic, and on replicas, before dropping anything. Also look for redundant indexes: an index on (customer_id) is usually redundant next to one on (customer_id, ordered_on), which serves the same lookups. A tuning workflow Find the queries that matter with pg_stat_statements, ordered by total_exec_time (the execution durations of every call added together, so a fast query called a million times can outrank a slow one called once), not just the slowest single run. Get EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on production-sized data. Design an index for the query: equality columns, then sort, then range; add INCLUDE columns only if an index-only scan is worth the size. To permit ordinary writes during the build, use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. It takes additional work, can wait for transactions, and cannot run in a transaction block. A failure can leave an INVALID index that still adds maintenance overhead; inspect and clean up or rebuild it. Re-run EXPLAIN and compare buffers and time. Watch write latency afterwards. Key takeaways INCLUDE columns consume space and can prevent HOT updates when they change. Review usage over a representative window, replicas and constraints before treating an index as redundant. sum: Functions, casts and search predicates with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. Most slow queries aren't exotic. They are a handful of recurring shapes that stop the planner using an index, make it misestimate, or make it do work the application didn't need. Each section below shows the anti-pattern, an illustrative PostgreSQL 18-style plan, and the fix. The indexes on orders at this point are the primary key, (customer_id, ordered_on), (customer_id) INCLUDE (ordered_on, total), (ordered_on) and the partial index on pending orders. 1. Functions on indexed columns Two things went wrong. The index on ordered_on cannot provide a selective search bound for this expression, because it is sorted by ordered_on, not by extract(year...). And the estimate is the default 0.5% (5,000) instead of 152,653, because there are no statistics on the expression. Rewrite the condition as a range on the bare column: That's 7.6 times faster, with an accurate estimate. A condition the database can answer with an index is called sargable (from "search argument"). The same trap catches date(created_at) =..., lower(email) =..., col + 1 = 10 and coalesce(col, 0) = 5. Either rewrite it so the bare column is compared, or create an expression index that matches it. 2. Type mismatches id is an integer and 42.0 is numeric, so Postgres converts every id to numeric to compare them. That removes the selective search bound on the ordinary integer primary-key index; a different query might still scan the index as a covering path. WHERE id = '42' is fine, because an untyped literal is converted to the column's type. This usually comes from application code: a driver that sends a parameter as numeric or text, or a comparison that casts the indexed column to an incompatible representation. PostgreSQL can support indexed cross-type integer/bigint comparisons; integer/text comparisons may instead need an explicit cast or fail operator resolution. Look for:: casts on the column side of a Filter. 3. Leading wildcards There is no selective prefix bound for an ordinary B-tree: matches could start with anything, so they are scattered across the whole index. The plan is a Seq Scan reading all 100,000 customers. A prefix (LIKE 'c42@%') can use a text_pattern_ops index, as in the previous lesson. For substring search, consider a trigram index (CREATE EXTENSION pg_trgm plus a GIN or GiST index). Full-text search instead matches processed words or tokens, so it is a different search behaviour. Key takeaways A half-open range of dates can search an ordinary date index while preserving the intended day or year. A cast on an integer column to numeric can remove a useful index bound; supported cross-type comparisons behave differently. x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. 4. OFFSET pagination To skip 900,000 rows, Postgres has to produce them: it walked 900,020 index entries and fetched their rows, then threw away all but 20. With 20 rows per page, an offset of 900,000 is page 45,001. Page 1 reads 20 rows; page 45,001 reads 900,020. The work grows in step with the page number, so the deeper users go the worse it gets. Keyset pagination remembers where the last page ended: In these illustrative timings the difference is large. Keyset pagination avoids work that grows with the skipped offset, though actual latency still depends on the data, index and system state. For a non-unique sort column, use a tie-breaker: WHERE (ordered_on, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY ordered_on DESC, id DESC. The trade-off is that you can't jump straight to page 371, which most interfaces don't need. Key takeaways OFFSET produces and discards skipped rows; keyset pagination seeks from the previous cursor. Use a unique ordering and match its directions and NULL handling; concurrent changes still require a consistency policy.
