sum: Exclusion, existence and repeated subqueries with worked examples and explicit assumptions.
x: These examples use PostgreSQL 18. SQL Fundamentals supplies the shop relations: customers(id, name, email, city, country), orders(id, customer_id, status, ordered_on, total), products(id, price) and order_items(order_id). IDs join orders to customers and items to orders. Dates use date, IDs use integer, and totals use numeric. Each query fragment uses these names; ellipses and standalone WHERE clauses need the surrounding SELECT shown by their context. All historical plan fragments and timings in this unit are illustrative inputs, not reproduced benchmarks or promises. Their row/page counts describe a hypothetical dataset; actual plans vary with statistics, indexes, settings, cache state and PostgreSQL version. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. 5. NOT IN with a subquery NOT IN has two problems. Semantics. If the subquery returns even one NULL, x NOT IN (...) is never true (it's NULL or false), so no customer rows satisfy the filter. This count() query still returns one result row containing 0. That is almost never the intended count. Performance. For this PostgreSQL 18 subquery form, the plan commonly uses a SubPlan rather than an ordinary anti-join. It runs the subquery once and probes a hash table of its results (hashed SubPlan), which was fine here: 17 ms. But if the subquery's estimated results exceed the applicable hash-memory budget, the plan becomes a plain SubPlan that rescans the retained subquery results for every outer row. With work_mem reduced to 64 kB the estimated cost jumped from about 10,700 to 976 million. For exclusion by absence of an equal key, this simple NOT EXISTS form can become an anti-join: Here it was slightly slower than the hashed NOT IN, but it permits anti-join strategies and avoids this particular NULL trap. It can still be slow for other reasons, and it intentionally differs from NOT IN for NULLs, including NULL outer keys. 6. Correlated subqueries: a nested loop in disguise Postgres runs a scalar subquery in the SELECT list once per outer row: That's a nested loop over 12,500 customers. With an index on orders(customer_id) each loop is cheap and the whole thing took 30 ms. The equivalent LEFT JOIN... GROUP BY actually took 84 ms here, because it hashed all 1,000,000 orders. So correlated subqueries aren't always slow, but they are only as fast as the inner lookup. Without the index, each of the 12,500 loops would be a full scan of orders: an estimated cost of about 248 million, against 23,000 for the join. Check loops on any SubPlan. 7. DISTINCT to hide duplicate rows "Customers in Bath who have ordered" written as a join returns one row per order, so people add DISTINCT: The join produced 125,174 rows, then a HashAggregate collapsed them back to 12,500: 42 ms. The question was really "does at least one order exist?", which is a semi-join: Four times faster: the semi-join stops at each customer's first order instead of producing all ten and de-duplicating. A DISTINCT you added to fix duplicates is a sign the query asks the wrong question. Aggregating before a join A third formulation counts orders once, then joins those counts to customers: The left join retains customers with no orders; coalesce gives them zero. With a direct left join, use count(o.id) rather than count() to avoid counting the NULL-extended unmatched row. This formulation may scan and aggregate every order, while the scalar subquery can make just the indexed customer lookups needed by a selective outer filter. Early aggregation can reduce intermediate rows, but moving it across joins must preserve grouping keys, duplicate multiplicities, NULL behaviour and the requested aggregate. Joining order counts to several item rows and then summing can multiply those counts. Combining partial averages requires their sums and counts, rather than an unweighted average of averages. Compare equivalent answers before comparing plans. Key takeaways NOT IN and NOT EXISTS differ when NULLs are involved; use the intended semantics. A scalar correlated lookup may be efficient with a selective index; EXISTS avoids unnecessary join multiplicity when only existence is needed. Assume serial execution unless a parallel worker process is shown. 10. Generic plans for skewed parameters Prepared statements save planning time by reusing plans. In PostgreSQL 18's default plan_cache_mode = auto, a parameterised prepared statement normally starts with five executions planned using the actual parameter values (custom plans), then compares a generic plan against the custom plans' average estimated cost including planning overhead. Reuse is a cost decision, not a guaranteed switch on the sixth call. A generic plan can't know the parameter: The generic plan doesn't know the value, so it assumes an average one, as if every status were equally common: It also can't use the partial index, because it can't prove the parameter is 'pending'. If most calls ask for rare values, every call now scans the table. Fixes: SET plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan for that session or role, or write separate statements for the rare and common cases. 11. Exact row counts and SELECT SELECT count() FROM orders read every page: 48 ms here, and larger tables require more work; no fixed time follows from a row count. Postgres has no stored row count, because under MVCC different transactions may legitimately see different counts. If an estimate will do (a "~1.2M results" label), read reltuples from pg_class, or the row estimate from EXPLAIN. SELECT requests every output column. It prevents an index-only scan unless a suitable index covers all required columns, and wider results can increase memory use and client transfer work, including fetching large TOASTed values. Name the columns you need. Myths "CTEs are optimisation fences." True before Postgres 12. Since 12, a non-recursive, side-effect-free SELECT CTE used only once in the query is normally inlined into the main query and optimised with it, unless you write AS MATERIALIZED. "Always use a join instead of a subquery." The earlier subquery unit showed a subquery beating a join. Read the plan. "An index on every column is safe." The previous lesson covered the write, cache and HOT costs. Key takeaways Default prepared-plan selection compares generic and custom estimated costs; a sixth-call switch is not guaranteed. An exact MVCC-visible count needs a scan; CTE inlining and output width depend on the query form. Further reading Sargable — Wikipedia Use The Index, Luke: functions in WHERE clauses Use The Index, Luke: paging through results without OFFSET Don't Do This — PostgreSQL wiki Subquery expressions (EXISTS, IN, NOT IN) — PostgreSQL docs PREPARE and plan_cache_mode — PostgreSQL docs Slow counting — PostgreSQL wiki WITH queries (CTEs) — PostgreSQL docs

sum: The server enforces constraints for every client.
x: PostgreSQL, usually called Postgres, is an open-source relational database server. SQL is the language you send it; Postgres is the system that stores rows, enforces constraints, coordinates concurrent sessions and recovers after a crash. It also supports JSON documents, extensible types and PostgreSQL extensions, but those features do not remove the need to design your data carefully. This module brings the pieces together around a small ticket shop. Read the SQL fundamentals first. This module divides the original ticket-shop walkthrough into short, separately completed units. The examples use PostgreSQL 18-compatible SQL; plans and timings depend on your data and installation. Run the examples in order in a fresh, disposable database, not an existing application database. Follow a database request Your application uses a database driver to connect to the server. psql is another client: a terminal for sending SQL and inspecting the results. An ORM is another layer above a driver; it does not replace the database. A PostgreSQL database cluster means a collection of databases managed by a server installation. It does not necessarily involve several machines. A connection selects one database. Inside it, PostgreSQL schemas such as public are namespaces containing tables, functions and other objects. public.orders names a table in a PostgreSQL schema, not a different database. Postgres normally uses a separate backend process for each client connection. Those processes share memory and coordinate access to storage. Connection pools reuse a bounded number of connections, avoiding a new backend process for every web request. Increasing the connection limit is not a substitute for measuring CPU, memory, lock waits and throughput. A typical request follows this path; responses travel back to the client: With transaction pooling, the next transaction may use a different backend process. Do not assume session settings or temporary objects will persist on the connection your application receives next. To connect to a database that already exists locally: Inside psql, \conninfo shows the connection, \dt lists tables and \d events describes a table. SQL statements end with a semicolon; these backslash commands are client commands. Use a PostgreSQL non-superuser role for the application with only the required database privileges, and bind user values through driver parameters rather than joining them into SQL strings. Key takeaways The server enforces constraints for every client. A PostgreSQL cluster can be one server installation. Transaction pooling requires care with session state. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: tutorial arch PostgreSQL 18: connect estab PostgreSQL 18: app psql PostgreSQL 18: role attributes

sum: Use NOT NULL as well as a CHECK enforcing a non-negative count.
x: Build the ticket-shop fixture in a fresh disposable PostgreSQL database. The examples use PostgreSQL 18-compatible SQL and also run on versions 16 and 17. Later units reuse these exact two tables. Enforce rules beside the data Create two tables. An event has available seats; a booking refers to an event and has an application-supplied request key. The identity column generates values, while PRIMARY KEY enforces uniqueness. Generated IDs can have gaps, including after an aborted transaction; do not interpret the highest ID as the number of rows. A foreign key prevents a booking for a missing event. CHECK rejects negative availability, and NOT NULL separately rejects an unknown value: a check expression evaluating to NULL does not reject the row. The unique request key will help identify retries of the same booking. Enforcing this in the database closes the race in which two requests both check for an existing key, find none, then insert duplicates. Postgres automatically creates an index for a primary key or unique constraint. It does not automatically index the referencing side of every foreign key. Later, we will add an index starting with bookings.event_id to support lookups by event. Choose types for their meaning Value Useful type Reason --------- A count integer Exact whole number A monetary amount numeric(12,2) Exact decimal arithmetic An event instant timestamptz Represents a point in time Optional attributes jsonb Queryable structured document timestamptz converts input to an instant and displays it in the session time zone. It does not preserve the original zone name. A recurring “9am Europe/London” schedule needs the named zone and scheduling rules as well as individual occurrence instants. For money, record the currency too; a decimal type cannot tell pounds from euros. Insert the first event and inspect the generated ID: In this fresh database the ID is 1. In an application, use the returned ID instead of assuming it. RETURNING avoids a separate query to discover which row was created. Key takeaways Use NOT NULL as well as a CHECK enforcing a non-negative count. Identity generates values; a primary key enforces uniqueness. Store event instants and recurrence rules separately. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: ddl constraints PostgreSQL 18: ddl identity columns PostgreSQL 18: datatype datetime PostgreSQL 18: datatype numeric

sum: Combine availability testing and decrement in one UPDATE.
x: The ticket-shop fixture has events(id bigint PRIMARY KEY, seats_left integer NOT NULL CHECK (seats_left >= 0)), plus the name, start time and JSONB columns introduced in the schema unit. Use the returned event-table ID; the fresh ticket-shop fixture below assumes event 1 exists. Make the decision inside the write An unsafe application reads seats_left = 1, checks it in application code and later writes seats_left = 0. Two clients can both read 1 and both claim success. Wrapping that read and write in a default transaction alone does not fix the race. Instead, combine the condition and change in one statement: A returned row means a seat was reserved. No returned row means no matching event with available seats. Under Read Committed, transactions updating this same row concurrently wait for each other; after the first commits, the second rechecks the condition against the updated row. Starting with one seat, only one update can succeed. Key takeaways Combine availability testing and decrement in one UPDATE. At Read Committed a competing updater rechecks the updated row. Inspect the returned row count before claiming success. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: transaction iso PostgreSQL 18: sql update PostgreSQL 18: explicit locking

sum: Roll back if the reservation returns no row.
x: Use the ticket-shop events and bookings tables from the schema unit in a disposable database. Event 1 must exist with at least one seat. bookings.event_id references the event; request_key is NOT NULL and UNIQUE. Each new logical booking receives its own request key. Commit the whole booking or none To reserve and record a booking atomically, use a transaction. This example is for a new request key and assumes the update returns one row: The application must inspect the update result. If it returns no rows, issue ROLLBACK and do not insert the booking. If the insert fails, roll back the transaction so the seat decrement is undone. An SQL error normally leaves the transaction aborted until rollback, unless you recover using a savepoint. For a duplicate request key, roll back and then fetch the existing booking, checking that it belongs to the same intended request. Do not decrement a seat, use ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING for the booking and then commit regardless: the duplicate insert might do nothing while the extra decrement persists. A unique key is a building block for idempotency, not a complete workflow. Keep transactions short. Do not hold the row lock while waiting for a customer or payment provider. External effects need their own retry design and checks to resolve uncertain payment outcomes; an SQL rollback does not undo a payment request to an external service. Key takeaways Roll back if the reservation returns no row. A duplicate insert must not leave an extra decrement committed. Database rollback cannot reverse an external payment. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: sql insert PostgreSQL 18: tutorial transactions PostgreSQL 18: sql savepoint

sum: A stable snapshot does not prevent write skew.
x: Postgres uses MVCC: updates create new row versions, and snapshots decide which versions a query can see. Ordinary reads generally do not block ordinary writes, but writers updating the same row can block each other. Schema changes and explicit locks introduce other conflicts. Isolation Read behaviour Remaining responsibility --------- Read Committed New snapshot per statement Protect multi-step decisions Repeatable Read Stable transaction snapshot Handle write skew and retries Serializable Successful work matches a one-at-a-time order Retry aborted transactions Read Committed is the default. Two SELECTs in one transaction can see different committed values. Repeatable Read keeps a snapshot from its first non-transaction-control statement, but it is not equivalent to serial transaction execution. At every level, a transaction can see its own prior writes. Imagine two on-call staff, both active. Each transaction sees two active staff and marks a different person inactive. At Repeatable Read, they can update different rows and both commit, breaking the rule that someone must remain on call. This is write skew. Use a suitable shared locking protocol or Serializable transactions for all operations maintaining that rule. Serializable can reject a conflicting transaction with SQLSTATE 40001. Retry the whole transaction, including its reads and decisions, with a bounded retry policy. Retrying only the last statement can reuse a decision based on an obsolete snapshot. Deadlocks can also require a transaction retry; acquire multiple row locks in a consistent order to reduce them. For a more involved read-then-change operation, SELECT... FOR UPDATE can lock the selected rows. It does not lock an imaginary row that does not exist, so use constraints or a suitable isolation strategy for “insert if absent” rules. Key takeaways A stable snapshot does not prevent write skew. Serializable participants must retry the whole failed transaction. Locking existing rows does not lock an absent row. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: transaction iso PostgreSQL 18: explicit locking PostgreSQL 18: mvcc serialization failure handling

t: Choose indexes and read the plan
sum: A composite B-tree can match equality then ordering.
x: Use the ticket-shop fixture: bookings has an identity primary key id, an event_id foreign key, a unique request_key, and a created_at timestamptz column. Create the tables in the schema unit first; populate representative data for meaningful performance measurements. Match an index to the request Suppose an admin page needs an event's latest bookings: This B-tree index puts the equality filter first and the requested ordering second. Postgres can find one event's entries in the desired order without sorting all its bookings. The index costs storage and maintenance on writes; adding one to every column is rarely a good trade. Different index methods suit different operators: B-tree is the usual choice for equality, ranges and ordered retrieval. GIN supports inverted lookups, including many JSONB and full-text search operations. BRIN stores summaries over page ranges; it can be compact and useful when values correlate with physical order, such as append-heavy timestamp data. Candidate pages still need rechecking. A sequential scan is not automatically bad: reading most rows, or a tiny table, can be cheaper than visiting an index and fetching rows from the table heap. On this tiny example, do not expect the index to win. Use the existing Query Processing & Optimisation lessons for deeper plan analysis. Start with this diagnostic on representative data: EXPLAIN estimates a plan; its ANALYZE option actually executes it. Costs are planner units, not milliseconds. Compare estimated versus actual row counts, inspect repeated loops, and look at buffer activity before changing settings. A shared-buffer read can still be served from the OS page cache, so it is not proof of a physical disk read. Do not add up inclusive timings of parents and children. ANALYZE has two meanings ANALYZE bookings updates planner statistics. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the supplied query and measures execution, including writes if the query modifies data. Use a disposable database for write experiments; even rollback does not undo sequence increments or external side effects. Key takeaways A composite B-tree can match equality then ordering. A tiny table can still favour a sequential scan. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes; buffer reads need not be disk reads. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: indexes types PostgreSQL 18: indexes multicolumn PostgreSQL 18: indexes ordering PostgreSQL 18: using explain PostgreSQL 18: sql explain PostgreSQL 18: brin

sum: Keep required keys and relationships in constrained columns.
x: The ticket-shop events table has name text NOT NULL and details jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}', alongside its identity, availability and start-time columns. The schema unit inserts a workshop with { "format": "online" } in details. Run the following queries after that ticket-shop fixture setup. Keep important rules explicit Use relational columns for important keys, relationships and invariants. Use JSONB for attributes that genuinely vary, such as event presentation settings. The containment operator @> can use this GIN index for selective queries at sufficient scale. JSONB stores a processed representation rather than preserving input whitespace and key order. Duplicate object keys do not remain separate entries. Use json instead if preserving the input text matters more than JSONB's processing and indexing advantages. A JSON document does not automatically enforce the types and relationships your application expects. If every event has a required capacity used in constraints and joins, a typed column is usually easier to validate and optimise than hiding it in JSON. Large document updates also carry write and index maintenance costs. Key takeaways Keep required keys and relationships in constrained columns. GIN can support selective JSONB containment queries. JSONB does not preserve input text or duplicate keys. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: datatype json PostgreSQL 18: gin intro PostgreSQL 18: indexes types

sum: Old snapshots can delay reclamation.
x: Old row versions cannot be removed while a snapshot still needs them. VACUUM makes space from dead versions reusable and helps maintain visibility information and prevent transaction ID wraparound. Plain vacuum usually reuses space inside the table rather than returning all of it to the operating system. ANALYZE samples data to update planner statistics. Postgres uses those estimates to choose scan and join strategies. Autovacuum automates vacuum and analyse work; monitor whether it keeps up rather than treating it as optional background noise. Inspect why cleanup is delayed In our disposable database you can run: Run this outside a transaction block. A session left “idle in transaction” can retain locks and, when holding an old snapshot, prevent cleanup. If a busy table grows unexpectedly, inspect old transactions, dead tuples and autovacuum activity. Disabling autovacuum or routinely running VACUUM FULL is not a general fix: the latter copies the table into a new file and requires a strong lock. An update can sometimes use a heap-only tuple (HOT), avoiding new ordinary index entries when no non-summarising indexed column changes and the original heap page has room. This reduces index maintenance; it does not remove the need for vacuum. In PostgreSQL 16–18, summarising indexes such as BRIN do not by themselves disqualify HOT. Do not assume every update is eligible. Key takeaways Old snapshots can delay reclamation. Plain VACUUM normally makes space reusable inside the table. VACUUM FULL rewrites and strongly locks the table. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: routine vacuuming PostgreSQL 18: sql vacuum PostgreSQL 18: storage hot PostgreSQL 18: sql analyze

sum: The dead-tuple threshold scales with estimated table size.
x: This unit uses PostgreSQL 18 defaults. PostgreSQL 16 and 17 have no autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold cap. These are eligibility thresholds, not promises that a worker starts immediately. Size-dependent cleanup Autovacuum does not clean a table after every update. It waits until enough dead row versions have built up to make the work worthwhile, and the point at which it acts grows with the table. In PostgreSQL 18 the rule is below; the cap, autovacuum_vacuum_max_threshold, is new in version 18. So a 1,000,000-row table passes this dead-tuple threshold when its estimated dead-version count exceeds 200,050. Repeated updates to the same logical row can leave several obsolete versions. This is not a count of distinct rows, and an eligible table may wait for a worker. For anything above a few hundred rows the 20 % term dominates; the fixed 50 only matters for tiny tables. The cap only matters for very large tables: a 1,000,000,000-row table would otherwise wait for about 200 million dead versions, but with the cap the threshold is capped at 100 million dead versions. The threshold is checked, not a start-time guarantee: autovacuum_naptime defaults to one minute between autovacuum runs on a database. Worker availability and a running worker's progress also matter. Similar rules start a vacuum after many inserts (autovacuum_vacuum_insert_threshold, 1,000 rows by default, plus 20 % of the table's not-yet-frozen part) and start ANALYZE (50 rows plus 10 % of the estimated table size by default, counting inserts, updates and deletes). A large, busy table often needs a smaller vacuum scale factor of its own, set per table as a storage parameter, for example ALTER TABLE bookings SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01). Key takeaways The dead-tuple threshold scales with estimated table size. PostgreSQL 18 adds a configurable maximum threshold. Worker availability and checks determine when eligible work runs. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: routine vacuuming PostgreSQL 18: runtime config vacuum PostgreSQL 18: sql createtable

sum: Normal XID comparisons have an approximately two-billion-ID horizon.
x: PostgreSQL assigns a normal transaction ID (XID) when a transaction needs one, commonly when it first writes. A read-only transaction can also request an XID explicitly. Row-version headers use a 32-bit XID; newer SQL functions can expose a 64-bit full ID that includes an XID epoch. MVCC compares XIDs to decide whether a row version was written in the past (possibly visible) or the future (invisible). An XID counter has a fixed number of values and the comparison is circular, so only half of them can count as "the past": If a row version kept its original XID while the counter moved more than about 2.1 billion transactions on, it would suddenly look as if it came from the future, and committed data would vanish from queries. This is transaction ID wraparound. VACUUM prevents it by freezing old row versions: marking their committed insertion as old enough to be visible to every current and future transaction, so that insertion XID no longer needs normal comparison. A later deletion or update still has its own visibility rules. Postgres forces an anti-wraparound vacuum on any table whose oldest unfrozen XID is more than autovacuum_freeze_max_age XIDs old: 200 million by default, about one tenth of the 2.1 billion horizon, leaving a wide safety margin. These limits count allocated IDs rather than elapsed time or a simple number of top-level commits. It launches these even when autovacuum is disabled. If something such as a long-open transaction stops freezing from advancing, the server warns as the limit approaches and eventually refuses to assign new XIDs until vacuum catches up. Key takeaways Normal XID comparisons have an approximately two-billion-ID horizon. Freezing preserves old committed row visibility across wraparound. Anti-wraparound maintenance can run even when autovacuum is disabled. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: routine vacuuming PostgreSQL 18: datatype oid PostgreSQL 18: functions info

sum: Durable commit need not flush every changed table page.
x: Write-ahead logging, or WAL, records changes before corresponding data pages are written to durable storage. With normal durability settings, commit waits for the required WAL to be flushed; all changed table pages need not already be on disk. Recovery can replay logged changes after a crash. A checkpoint bounds recovery work; it is not a fresh backup. This simplified local durability path assumes synchronous commit and normal storage settings: Streaming replication sends WAL to a standby. Asynchronous replication can lag: a user may write on the primary server and immediately read an older value on a standby. A failover can lose acknowledged transactions that never reached the promoted server. Synchronous replication can wait for a configured standby acknowledgement, trading latency and availability for stronger durability; whether replay is awaited depends on configuration. Key takeaways Durable commit need not flush every changed table page. Asynchronous replicas can lag and lose commits on failover. Synchronous replication guarantees depend on its acknowledgement settings. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: wal intro PostgreSQL 18: wal reliability PostgreSQL 18: warm standby PostgreSQL 18: runtime config wal

sum: Replication can copy an accidental deletion.
x: A standby replays the primary's changes, including mistakes. Crash recovery restores logged work; it does not know that a valid DELETE was accidental. This unit separates availability from recoverability. Recover an earlier database state Replication is not a backup. A mistaken DELETE can propagate to the standby. Protect recovery separately: A logical dump with pg_dump captures one database in a form that can be restored with PostgreSQL tools. Database roles and other cluster-wide objects need separate handling. A physical base backup plus an unbroken series of archived WAL files supports point-in-time recovery, for example to just before an accidental deletion. The target must be after that base backup finished; you cannot use a backup still in progress at the desired target. Test restores into a separate environment and measure recovery time. A successful backup command alone does not prove you can recover. Choose a recovery point objective (acceptable lost work) and recovery time objective (acceptable downtime). Those requirements determine backup frequency, WAL retention, replica configuration and the restore procedure. A managed provider automates some of this, but you still need to understand its retention and recovery guarantees. Key takeaways Replication can copy an accidental deletion. PITR needs a suitable base backup and the required continuous WAL. Test restores against both data-loss and downtime objectives. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: backup PostgreSQL 18: app pgdump PostgreSQL 18: continuous archiving PostgreSQL 18: runtime config wal

t: Trace latency and budget query memory
sum: Separate connection waits, lock waits and execution time.
x: The settings and defaults here are for PostgreSQL 18 with standard build options; inspect the running server before relying on them. When a request is slow, first separate time waiting for a connection, waiting for a lock, executing SQL and transferring results. pg_stat_activity exposes current sessions and waits; pg_locks helps investigate blocking. The optional pg_stat_statements extension summarises query behaviour over time when configured. Next, reproduce the query with representative parameters, examine its plan and check statistics. Then consider query shape, indexes, transaction duration and pool size. Avoid tuning memory or connection limits blindly: a per-operation memory allowance can multiply across operations and concurrent sessions. The main setting behind that warning is work_mem: the base memory allowance for an individual sort operation before spilling to temporary files; hash operations have a multiplied allowance. It is a per-operation limit, not a per-server one, so a base sort-memory budget multiplies out: This example excludes hash operations, parallel workers and other query memory. A hash operation may use work_mem times hash_mem_multiplier; parallel workers can each receive their own allowances. This is a capacity-planning illustration, not a guaranteed maximum. Raising work_mem to 64 MB "to speed up sorts" turns the same workload into about 19,200 MB, nearly 19 GB (18.75 GB counting 1024 MB per GB). That comes on top of shared_buffers (PostgreSQL's own shared buffers, typically 128 MB by default) and each backend process's own baseline memory. Raise it for one session or role running a known heavy report, or limit concurrency with a connection pool, rather than raising it globally and hoping. For a slow event booking, a lock wait on one popular event may dominate even when the primary-key lookup is fast. Another index cannot remove the need for competing reservations to coordinate over the same remaining seat count. Key takeaways Separate connection waits, lock waits and execution time. work_mem is per operation, with extra hash and parallel-worker allowances. A fast index cannot remove contention on the same seat count. Further reading PostgreSQL 18: monitoring stats PostgreSQL 18: view pg locks PostgreSQL 18: pgstatstatements PostgreSQL 18: runtime config resource

sum: Count a scan with an explicit model of a basic operation.
x: An algorithm is a precise procedure for carrying out a task. Before comparing speed, establish what inputs are valid and what answer is required. For the terminating problems in this module, a correct solution must finish and return the right answer on every valid input. Passing a few tests is evidence, not a proof of that guarantee. Count the work that repeats Timings tell you how one implementation behaves on one machine. Counting operations explains how its workload changes when the input grows. Here n is the number of list items. This scan adds each item once. Doubling a long list roughly doubles the additions. Initialising and returning the total add fixed overhead; they do not change that linear growth. A cost model states what counts as one step. A simple RAM model treats a bounded-size comparison, arithmetic operation or memory access as constant cost. Counting loop overhead changes the coefficient, but this scan remains linear. A function call also includes the work its body performs. Python integers can grow to many digits, and comparing long strings may inspect many characters. Treating those operations as constant cost is an explicit simplification, not a property of every Python value. Real memory access and allocation also have costs the simple model omits. Real-world analogy: Checking a guest list Checking each printed name once takes more work when the list grows. How it maps: One check per name corresponds to one addition per input item; picking up the list is fixed setup work. Where it stops: Human checks vary in duration. The algorithm model counts specified operations and must state which have constant cost. Key takeaways Correctness and termination come before efficiency. Define input size and the operation being counted. One pass with constant work per item has linear growth. Further reading Erickson: Introduction

sum: Count the comparisons in a duplicate check that visits each distinct pair once.
x: Comparing each item with every other item creates much more work than scanning once. Here n is the number of list items, and equality comparisons are assumed constant cost. Why avoiding repeats still leaves quadratic work Starting the inner loop after the outer position avoids comparing an item with itself and avoids checking a pair in both orders. The first item still meets every later item; later passes become progressively shorter. With no duplicates, none can exit early. Doubling a large list roughly quadruples these comparisons: there are about twice as many items, each with about twice as many possible partners. Checking only half the full square changes the amount of work, but its growth remains quadratic. The exact pair count is useful when budgeting comparisons, but the growth argument does not require calculating it: Do not classify code by counting nested loops alone. Two consecutive full passes are linear. A full pass containing a fixed hundred checks is also linear. A nested inner range proportional to the input gives quadratic work. For large duplicate checks, sorting makes equal values adjacent; an efficient comparison sort followed by a scan takes O(n log n) time. A hash set takes expected O(n) time under suitable hashing assumptions, using extra memory. Neither bound promises a specific runtime. Key takeaways Avoiding repeated pairs reduces work without removing quadratic growth. An early return helps only inputs that reach it early. Improving the search structure can matter more than speeding up each comparison. Further reading Erickson: Introduction

sum: Compare logarithmic, linear, quadratic and exponential operation counts.
x: A growth rate describes how work changes as the input becomes larger. It is a scaling prediction, not a stopwatch reading. Here n is the item count and each counted operation has constant cost. Recognise the behaviour Growth What creates it Effect of a larger input --------- Constant fixed amount of work no input-dependent increase Logarithmic repeatedly discard a fixed fraction doubling adds roughly one halving step Linear visit every item once doubling roughly doubles work Linear times log linear work over logarithmically many levels doubling costs slightly more than twice Quadratic compare all pairs doubling roughly quadruples work Exponential explore independent binary choices each extra choice doubles candidates A base-two logarithm is the power needed to produce a value from two. For powers of two it also counts repeated halvings down to one. Ten halvings reduce 1,024 to one; doubling that starting size adds just one halving. For other sizes, an algorithm rounds its number of steps as its stopping rule requires. The contrast between linear, quadratic and exponential growth is worth seeing directly: The subset model counts candidates. If checking a candidate requires scanning its contents, include that cost too. Small test inputs can conceal an expensive growth rate. Conversely, a small fixed input may make exhaustive search entirely sensible. There is no universal item cutoff for exponential algorithms: candidate cost, pruning, hardware and the available time all matter. Key takeaways Recognise how the work changes before calculating an exact count. Logarithmic growth comes from reducing the remaining problem by a fixed factor. Growth labels help compare scaling; measurements settle practical runtime. Further reading Erickson: Introduction

sum: Translate a hardware speedup into the input size each growth rate can handle.
x: A faster machine can help immediately. How much larger an input it can handle in the same time depends on the algorithm's growth. More work budget, different input gains Assume the new machine performs every counted operation at the same fixed speedup, with memory and other resources sufficient. This deliberately excludes changes in parallel overhead, cache behaviour or algorithm choice. For a linear scan, twice the work budget buys twice as many items. For pairwise work, twice as many items need roughly four times the budget. Input capacity grows more slowly than hardware speed. For a search that checks every subset at constant cost, each additional item doubles the candidate count. A doubling of machine speed therefore buys only one more item. That last rule is additive: repeated hardware doublings add items rather than multiplying the previous item limit. A thousandfold speedup buys about ten extra binary choices under this model. It does not make an arbitrary exponential search practical. Real-world analogy: A growing dinner party Serving one plate per guest and arranging a conversation between every pair scale differently. How it maps: Plates resemble linear work; pair meetings resemble quadratic work. Faster service buys less extra capacity when the number of relationships also grows. Where it stops: Real meetings can overlap. The algorithm comparison assumes a fixed counted-work model and a uniform speedup. A lower growth rate can give a larger long-term improvement than a constant hardware speedup, but that is not a reason to dismiss hardware upgrades. Measure the current bottleneck and expected input range. A better algorithm may have extra setup or memory costs; a practical decision includes those too. Key takeaways Hardware changes the work budget under the stated model. Quadratic work turns a large speed gain into a smaller input gain. Binary-choice exhaustive search gains one item per doubling of speed. Further reading Erickson: Introduction

sum: Choose the right input measure and simplify a cost without forgetting its limits.
x: Calling an algorithm "linear" is incomplete until you say what it is linear in. Choose the measure that drives the work For a list, n usually counts items. For a graph, V counts vertices and E counts edges. A traversal may need O(V + E) work; neither dimension can be dropped without a relationship between them. For an image, count pixels when the algorithm visits pixels. Doubling both dimensions quadruples pixel count. For a number, input length counts its digits or bits, rather than its numeric value. Adding one bit approximately doubles the range of positive integers representable at that length. A primality test that tries every possible divisor up to the number's value can therefore take exponentially many iterations in the bit length. An early exit on composite inputs does not fix the prime-input worst case. Division on large integers also costs more than a single fixed-size operation. Testing only up to the square root reduces work substantially, but remains exponential in bit length. A polynomial bound in numeric value need not be polynomial in the encoded input length; this distinction is called pseudo-polynomial time. What dominant terms tell you An all-pairs comparison has a quadratic main term and a smaller linear correction. For large inputs, the quadratic part determines scaling. Dropping fixed multipliers and lower-order terms produces a useful growth label. It does not produce an exact runtime or a universal winner. A simple quadratic implementation can beat a linear-times-log implementation over a small input range because of lower setup and per-step costs. The slower growth rate wins eventually under comparable fixed cost models, but the crossover must be established rather than assumed. Key takeaways Always name the input measure, including independent dimensions. Numeric value and encoded length can give very different complexity descriptions. Dominant growth predicts scaling, while constants still matter at finite sizes. Further reading Erickson: Introduction

sum: Use fixed constants to prove or disprove a Big-O claim.
x: Big-O gives an eventual upper bound on growth. It does not promise an exact operation count, and it does not itself mean "worst case". First choose the cost function being discussed, such as worst-case comparisons over inputs of each size. One fixed multiplier must keep working For a nonnegative cost, the definition is: The multiplier absorbs constant factors. The threshold allows a finite set of small inputs to behave differently. Neither may keep changing as the input grows. For example, a scan with fixed setup work still has a linear upper bound. Choose a multiplier larger than its per-item cost; beyond some point, the spare allowance covers the setup on every later input. Matching only the per-item cost leaves no allowance for positive setup work. A quadratic cost cannot have a linear upper bound. As inputs grow, work per item keeps increasing, so every proposed fixed linear multiplier is eventually exceeded. True can still be unhelpful Binary search halves a sorted range and has a logarithmic worst-case comparison count, assuming constant-cost indexing and comparisons. It also has a linear upper bound, because linear growth eventually exceeds logarithmic growth. Both statements are true; the logarithmic bound is more informative. Testing a few sizes cannot prove a bound for every later size. Use the mechanism or a mathematical argument. A ratio that grows without bound is one way to disprove an upper bound; oscillating ratios may require returning to the definition. Key takeaways Big-O permits one fixed multiplier and one fixed starting threshold. A valid bound must hold at every sufficiently large input size. Prefer a tight useful upper bound over a needlessly loose one. Further reading Erickson: Introduction

sum: Distinguish lower bounds, tight bounds and input cases.
x: An upper bound says how fast a cost can grow. A lower bound says how slowly it cannot grow. A tight bound combines both for the same cost function. Lower and tight bounds Big-Omega gives an eventual lower bound: Big-Theta puts the cost between two such bounds: Bounds and input cases answer different questions For insertion sort on n items, already sorted input takes Θ(n) time; reverse-sorted distinct input takes Θ(n²). Thus the worst-case function has a tight quadratic bound and the best-case function a tight linear bound. All inputs share a quadratic upper bound and a linear lower bound, but not one common tight bound depending only on item count. O does not mean worst case, and Omega does not mean best case. State the input case separately. Nor must a function fit a familiar growth class. Suppose its cost is one step at every odd size and one step per item at every even size. It has a linear upper bound and constant lower bound. The even sizes defeat a constant upper bound; the odd sizes defeat a linear lower bound. Its piecewise description is still an exact description. Key takeaways Theta needs matching upper and lower growth bounds. Specify best, average or worst case separately from the notation. Irregular costs need not match a familiar monotone growth class. Further reading Erickson: Introduction

sum: Drop dominated terms while preserving distinctions between exponential bases.
x: Simplifying a cost means keeping the part that determines eventual growth. Here n is input size; log denotes a logarithm with a fixed base greater than one. Remove details only when the bound permits it Fixed positive multipliers do not change a tight growth class. In a finite sum of nonnegative familiar growth functions, keep the fastest-growing term. For example, cubic work eventually dominates quadratic-times-log work and fixed overhead. Two sequential phases add their costs. Independent nested phases multiply their counts. Independent input dimensions must remain separate unless their relationship is known. The rule is about growth, not exact equality. Two functions can share a quadratic upper bound while having quite different values, or even different tight growth rates. A linear function and a quadratic function both have a quadratic upper bound. Logarithm bases and exponential bases behave differently Changing between two fixed logarithm bases multiplies the value by a constant. It changes an exact count, but not the logarithmic growth class. The useful conversion is available as reference: Changing an exponential base is different. Choosing among three possibilities per item creates more candidates than choosing among two. Their ratio itself grows exponentially, so a constant multiplier cannot absorb that difference. A fixed power of a logarithm eventually grows more slowly than any positive power of input size. A fixed polynomial eventually grows more slowly than an exponential with fixed base greater than one. "Eventually" matters: a very large polynomial exponent or coefficient can delay that order far beyond practical inputs. Key takeaways Drop coefficients and dominated terms when describing eventual growth. A shared upper bound is not a statement of equal cost. Fixed log bases change constants; exponential bases can change growth classes. Further reading Erickson: Introduction

sum: Use ratios and the growth ladder to compare unfamiliar cost functions.
x: Compare growth by asking whether the gap between two costs keeps widening. Here n is input size; logarithms have a fixed base greater than one. Ratios give a useful test Divide the first eventually positive function by the second and consider increasingly large inputs: Ratio approaches What it establishes ------ Zero the first grows strictly more slowly A fixed positive number the same tight growth rate Infinity the first grows strictly faster A ratio approaching zero is called little-o. These are sufficient conclusions when the limit exists. A tight bound does not require convergence: a ratio can keep oscillating between two positive constants. If there is no limit, inspect bounds directly. A growth ladder Slower to faster Example mechanism ------ Constant index a fixed-size array slot Logarithmic repeatedly halve a search range Square root count up to the square root of a numeric bound Linear scan every item Linear times log merge over logarithmically many levels Quadratic, then cubic all pairs, then all triples Fixed-base exponential enumerate subsets Factorial enumerate all orderings This compares eventual growth with the same input measure. A square-root divisor search measured in numeric value is still exponential when measured in bit length. Factorial counts multiply the positive integers up to the item count. Taking a logarithm turns that product into a sum of logarithms. There are at most n terms each no larger than the logarithm of n, and a constant fraction are within a constant of that largest logarithm. Thus the logarithm of the factorial has Θ(n log n) growth. This underlies the worst-case comparison-sorting lower bound. A quasi-polynomial example raises input size to its logarithm. It eventually outgrows every fixed polynomial yet remains below a fixed-base exponential. Comparing both expressions as powers of the same base reveals the order; a single measured size cannot prove it. Key takeaways Ratio limits reveal relative growth when the limit exists. A finite-range measurement is not a proof of eventual order. Factorial growth is enormous, but its logarithm is linear times log. Further reading Erickson: Introduction

sum: Add sequential work and count the true length of dependent inner loops.
x: Count how many times the meaningful operation runs, not how many loops are visible. Here n and m are independent input sizes. Assume each counted operation has constant cost. Add sequential work; multiply independent nested work A list scan followed by a square-grid scan adds the two workloads. If n is list length and m is the grid's side length, the result is O(n + m²). Without a relationship between the list and grid sizes, neither contribution can be discarded. A loop that restarts a full inner loop on every pass multiplies the two counts. A fixed inner bound, such as a hundred checks, changes the coefficient but leaves a full outer scan linear. Dependent bounds need a sum Here work() stands for one constant-cost operation. The inner lengths grow from zero to one less than the outer bound. Their total is roughly half a full square, so the work is Θ(n²). Halving a quadratic amount does not make it linear. For a direct growth argument, the final half of outer passes each do at least about half the maximum inner work. That already gives a quadratic lower bound; the full square supplies a quadratic upper bound. No exact sum is needed. Three ordered distinct positions similarly occupy a fixed fraction of a full cube, giving cubic growth. But nesting alone proves nothing: different dependent ranges can produce linear or logarithmic totals. Include hidden work A function call costs its body, not one step. sorted() does comparisons and moves elements. Printing can format values and wait for output. State explicitly when counting calls instead of their elapsed costs. For a worst-case branch, analyse the most expensive path that a valid input can actually reach. Key takeaways Sequential phases add; independently repeated phases multiply. Sum actual inner lengths when bounds depend on the outer position. Count the work inside calls and state the cost model. Further reading Erickson: Introduction

sum: Recognise logarithmic loops and sum a geometric series of inner-loop lengths.
x: Repeated multiplication reaches a large bound much sooner than repeated addition. Throughout, n is a positive integer input bound and work() is one constant-cost step. Count doublings, not the final value The values before each update are one, two, four, eight and so on. A bound of sixteen needs four updates; seventeen needs one more. Doubling the bound adds only about one pass, giving logarithmic work. A fixed multiplier greater than one gives the same growth class. Integer division by a fixed factor has a similar effect when its stopping condition guarantees termination. A loop that increments by one while i i <= n instead makes about the square root of the bound in updates. Inspect the update and stopping rule together. Restarting changes the total Restart a full doubling loop for each of n outer iterations and the total is Θ(n log n). But this different pattern is linear: The inner lengths double. All earlier lengths together are smaller than twice the last length, and the last length is a substantial fraction of the bound. This geometric series therefore gives Θ(n) total work. Charging the largest inner loop on every pass overestimates it. Another trap starts the inner doubling variable at the outer value: Most starting values need very few doublings. Almost all permit a first update, about half a second, about a quarter a third. These shrinking groups sum to linear work; the outer scan is also linear. It is Θ(n), not linear times log. Key takeaways Multiplicative updates often give logarithmic iteration counts. Sum the inner loops actually performed, including their starting values. Geometrically changing lengths can give a linear total. Further reading Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Sum the shrinking inner counts in a harmonic loop.
x: An inner loop can become shorter even when its endpoint stays fixed. Here n is a positive input bound and work() is one constant-cost step. Watch the step size With step one, the inner loop visits every position. With step two it visits about half; step three about a third. Each length is the bound divided by the step, rounded up. The total does not equal the largest inner length multiplied by the outer count. These contributions form a harmonic sum, whose growth is logarithmic. Multiplying by the original bound gives Θ(n log n) work. Rounding adds less than one extra step per outer pass, so it cannot change that class. Why a logarithmic factor appears Group step sizes into bands that double: one, then two to three, then four to seven, and so on. A later band has about twice as many step sizes, but each inner loop is about half as long. Each complete band therefore contributes work proportional to the original bound. There are logarithmically many bands. This differs from a geometric sum of inner lengths. In a geometric sum, doubling the index halves the entire next contribution. Here there are many step sizes between successive powers of two, and their combined contributions matter. Inner-loop pattern Total growth ------ Same full range each time quadratic Length grows with outer position quadratic Doubling outer value sets inner length linear Outer value sets the inner step linear times log The shared lesson is to read the actual range. Similar-looking nested loops need not have similar cost. Key takeaways A larger step means fewer inner iterations. Harmonic contributions accumulate across logarithmically many bands. Integer rounding does not change this loop's tight growth bound. Further reading Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Count recursive calls and uncover work hidden inside ordinary Python operations.
x: A short function can perform a large amount of work. Count all recursive calls and the work each call performs outside its children. Here n is the recursive argument or list length, as stated. Repeated subproblems multiply work Both children repeat calculations already performed elsewhere. Drawing the calls for fib(5) reveals repeated fib(3) and fib(2) work. The total call count grows exponentially. More precisely it is Θ(φⁿ), where n is the nonnegative argument and φ is the golden ratio, about 1.618. The branches have different depths, so a full binary tree with base two is a loose upper bound, not the tight call count. Memoisation stores completed answers by argument. Only a linear number of distinct arguments need calculating. This gives a linear number of additions; it does not make arithmetic on increasingly large Python integers constant-time. A line of Python is not one operation For CPython lists, indexing and reading length are constant-cost in the usual model. Membership scans may inspect every item. Front removal shifts remaining references. Slicing creates a new list of references. Appending is constant amortised time, allowing occasional resizing. All-distinct input makes each membership scan longer, giving quadratic comparisons. Replacing seen with a set and using add gives expected linear work for hashable values with constant-cost hashing and equality under a suitable hashing model. Keeping out as a list preserves first-occurrence order. A recursive binary search that slices its chosen half also hides work. Its comparison count is logarithmic, but the copied halves form a linear total in the original list length. Passing index bounds avoids those copies. Key takeaways Count the whole call tree, including repeated subproblems. Include comparison, hashing, copying and shifting costs. Changing the representation can remove repeated work while preserving the result. Further reading CPython 3.14 list implementation Python caching tools

sum: State which inputs or random choices a performance claim describes.
x: Inputs of the same size can follow different paths. Here n is the number of items and equality comparisons have constant cost. State what is being averaged The best case finds the target first: constant work. The worst case finds it last or fails to find it: linear work. If a present target is equally likely to occupy any position, the average search examines about half the list and is still linear. That average depends on its assumptions. A workload that frequently requests the first item differs from one with mostly absent targets. "Average" without an input distribution is incomplete. For a randomised algorithm, expected time can instead average over the algorithm's random choices while holding the input fixed. Quicksort with distinct keys and fresh uniformly random pivots has expected Θ(n log n) time on every fixed input of n items. A first-element pivot on sorted distinct input instead gives quadratic work. An adversary adapting to predictable random choices falls outside the fixed-input model. Early exits need a remaining worst case An early return can improve some inputs dramatically. It changes worst-case growth only if every valid input avoids the previous worst path. To assess a claim, try to construct an input that still forces the full scan or unbalanced recursion. Worst-case guarantees are useful for hostile inputs and deadlines. Average or expected bounds can also be useful, provided their assumptions fit the application. A fast best case alone gives little assurance about an actual workload. Key takeaways Best and worst case select extreme inputs of a given size. Average case requires an input distribution. Expected time can average random choices for each fixed input. Further reading Erickson: Introduction

sum: Distinguish extra storage, output memory and lazy value generation.
x: Space complexity measures the largest amount of memory needed at once. It does not count every object ever created if earlier objects have already been released. Say what the count includes Total space includes the stored input. Auxiliary space measures additional storage. State whether output is included: a function producing a new list has to store that result even if its working variables are few. Streaming input need not remain resident, so reading many items alone does not imply storing them all. Here n is input length or table side length. The following counts treat each value and reference as one memory word and include returned collections: The sum retains a constant number of values. The reverse creates n reference slots. The square table retains n rows each containing n slots, giving quadratic space. A triangle of increasingly long rows still contains a quadratic number of slots, even when every slot refers to the same zero object. Produce values when needed The first expression builds all squares before summing. The second is a generator expression: sum requests one square at a time. Under the atomic-value model, this removes the linear intermediate collection and uses constant auxiliary storage. It still computes every square. Python integers can grow in bit length. A constant number of integer objects therefore does not necessarily mean constant bytes. Also, a generator can retain a large source or other state; its memory saving depends on the particular producer and consumer. Key takeaways Measure peak live storage and state input/output conventions. Shared values still require slots in a collection. Streaming avoids storing all intermediate values when the consumer can process them one at a time. Further reading Python sequence types and integers

sum: Count live stack frames and understand why caching does not remove the first recursive descent.
x: Every call that is waiting for a child needs a frame containing its local state. Space follows the deepest chain of pending calls, together with data those calls retain. For a positive argument n, this creates a chain down to one. Under a model treating each number as atomic and each frame as fixed-size, stack space is Θ(n). An iterative version holds a constant number of values. Actual Python integers grow: the factorial result alone needs Θ(n log n) bits for sufficiently large n. Calls over time are not simultaneous frames Naive Fibonacci makes exponentially many calls but follows one child at a time. Completed branches release their frames before later siblings finish. Its maximum depth is linear in the argument, so its stack is linear in the atomic-value model. Recursive binary search with index bounds has logarithmic depth because it halves the range. Merge sort also has logarithmic depth, but its merge buffer requires linear extra space. Count retained buffers as well as frames. Real-world analogy: A stack of unfinished tasks When a task depends on a smaller task, put a reminder aside until that task finishes. How it maps: Each reminder is a pending frame. The tallest pile matters for space, even if many reminders are used throughout the day. Where it stops: Frames can retain differently sized objects; counting reminders alone assumes fixed-size state. Caching does not shorten the first descent Memoisation avoids repeating completed calculations. With an empty cache, a Fibonacci-style function still descends through consecutive smaller arguments before any result is available. It can hit the configured recursion limit despite doing only linearly many distinct computations. Use sys.getrecursionlimit() to inspect that limit. Raising it is not a substitute for a space analysis and can be unsafe for some interpreter and C-extension call paths. Python does not eliminate recursive Python tail calls. A bottom-up loop avoids the recursive chain; retaining only the previous two values also avoids a full answer cache. Their growing bit lengths remain a separate cost. Key takeaways Count simultaneously live frames and retained data. Exponential call counts can coexist with linear stack depth. A bottom-up loop can remove a cold recursive descent that caching preserves. Further reading Python recursion limits Python caching tools

sum: Mutate an existing list and bound quicksort stack depth by recursing on the smaller side.
x: An in-place transformation reuses the input storage. Under the strict convention it uses only constant auxiliary space; some descriptions allow a logarithmic recursion stack. State which convention you mean. This keeps two positions and swaps within the existing list. It returns None. In contrast, xs[::-1] allocates a new list. Here n is the list length; the first uses O(1) auxiliary words and the copy uses O(n). Mutation has a cost beyond memory Other references to the same list observe the changes. If the caller needs the original order, copying first removes the storage saving. An in-place algorithm can also be harder to implement correctly. Choose it because its trade-offs fit the caller, not merely because its space label is smaller. Mutating an input is not proof of constant auxiliary space. CPython's list.sort() mutates the list but may allocate a merge buffer proportional to its length. Heapsort can sort an array using constant auxiliary words. Bound quicksort's stack separately from its time Ordinary quicksort that recurses on both partitions can build a linear-depth chain with repeatedly unbalanced pivots. Recurse only on the smaller partition and process the larger partition with a loop. Every additional recursive frame then receives at most half its parent's items, bounding stack depth by O(log n). Changing the order of two recursive calls is insufficient: the larger side must become a loop. This change fixes stack growth even with a poor pivot rule, but it does not remove quadratic worst-case comparisons. Random pivots improve expected time under the stated randomness model; a fallback such as heapsort can provide a worst-case time bound. Key takeaways Distinguish mutation from constant auxiliary storage. Check whether other code still needs the original input. Recursing on the smaller side bounds stack depth without necessarily fixing runtime. Further reading CPython 3.14 sorting design Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Choose a representation and balance extra memory against speed.
x: A faster algorithm may need more storage. A smaller representation may let the same algorithm handle a much larger input. Here n is the number of input items. Spend memory where it removes repeated work Checking duplicates with a hash set uses expected linear time and linear extra storage under suitable hashing assumptions. Sorting in place and comparing neighbours trades more computation for less extra storage, but changes input order. A strict constant-space claim needs a suitable sort, such as heapsort. For a pair-sum problem on a reorderable array, sorting followed by two positions moving inward avoids keeping a hash set. When the current sum is too small, advance the lower end; when too large, retreat the upper end. The ordering makes those decisions safe. Precomputation is another trade-off. Prefix sums store the total before each position. A range total is then the prefix at the end minus the prefix at the start. Building the prefixes costs linear work and storage, while each query uses one subtraction for fixed-size values. Updates can invalidate later prefixes, so the benefit depends on the workload. A growth class is not a byte budget A Python list stores references to objects. A packed numeric array stores fixed-width values directly. Both have linear storage growth, but their per-item sizes differ. For a hypothetical representation with eight-byte entries, ten million entries need an 80 MB data buffer, using decimal megabytes. A list of separately allocated Python integers also needs object headers, references and possible spare capacity. sys.getsizeof reports the immediate object size, not recursively all objects it references. Use the actual build and value range when budgeting. The standard array module exposes itemsize; its type widths depend on the C implementation. A signed 64-bit representation cannot hold arbitrary-size Python integers. Leave room for runtime state and temporary buffers during construction or conversion. Key takeaways Compare time, extra storage and permission to mutate together. Precomputed answers help repeated queries but introduce storage and update costs. Measure representation overhead and peak construction memory, not just asymptotic space. Further reading Python packed arrays Python object-size measurement

t: Dynamic arrays and total append cost
sum: Bound the total writes and copies over a sequence of dynamic-array appends.
x: A dynamic array stores items in a contiguous region with spare capacity. Most appends fill a spare slot. When it is full, a resize may allocate a larger region and copy existing items. Analyse a sequence, not just its slowest operation Consider an idealised array that starts empty with capacity one and doubles when full. Count one unit per copied or newly written element; ignore allocator details. Here n is the number of appends. A resize-triggering append can copy every current item, so one operation can be linear in the current length. But it is too pessimistic to charge that cost to every append. After doubling, many spare slots can be filled before the next copy. The copied capacities are one, two, four, eight and so on. This geometric series is bounded by a constant multiple of its largest term. Adding the one write per append therefore gives linear total work. For this model, total work is below three units per append when spread across the sequence. Aggregate analysis establishes a bound for the whole sequence, then divides by its length. Constant amortised append cost means any sequence of n appends from the stated starting state costs O(n) total work. It does not mean every append is fast. Real-world analogy: Moving to a bigger bookshelf Moving books to a shelf with twice the space is expensive, but many later books fit without another move. How it maps: Spare shelf space corresponds to spare capacity; increasingly separated moves explain the linear total copying. Where it stops: The proof counts item moves under a fixed growth policy. Real allocation and item-copy costs may differ. No probability is involved Amortised analysis averages cost across an operation sequence, not across random inputs. The sequence bound is deterministic under its model. Starting with a large full array would require accounting for that initial state; the from-empty proof cannot silently charge its first resize to earlier appends that never occurred. CPython lists grow with spare capacity rather than precisely doubling. The same geometric-growth idea explains their amortised append behaviour; exact capacity sequences are implementation details. Key takeaways Rare expensive appends can coexist with linear total sequence cost. Amortised guarantees need a starting state and operation policy. Amortisation is different from average-case probability. Further reading Erickson: Amortized Analysis CPython 3.14 list implementation

sum: Use the accounting method to save credit during cheap operations.
x: The accounting method explains an amortised bound by saving credit during cheap operations and spending it during expensive ones. Credit is a proof device, measured in counted work units; no actual runtime balance is needed. Charge enough to fund later copies Use the doubling-array model, starting empty with capacity one. Count each copy and new-element write as one unit. Charge three units per append: one pays for the immediate write and two are saved. Before a resize, saved credit pays to copy all existing elements. After doubling, the appends that fill the new half save enough to pay for the next whole-array copy. The first append also creates enough credit for the first small resize. Inductively, the bank never needs to go below zero. Why save for older elements too? At the last resize those elements spent their previous copying credit. New appends must rebuild credit for the whole array, not just themselves. Banking two units per new element covers both halves by the next full state. Real-world analogy: Saving for an annual bill Regular payments can put aside money for an occasional larger bill. How it maps: Cheap appends contribute spare credit; resizing consumes that saved credit. A nonnegative balance proves earlier charges cover the real cost. Where it stops: There is no interest, prediction or random arrival rate. The algorithm proof must cover every allowed sequence from its stated initial state. The balance is the proof obligation If a proposed charge lets the bank become negative, that accounting argument has failed: it is spending work credits never collected. This does not automatically prove the algorithm is slow; it means the proposed charges or invariant are insufficient. Starting from a pre-populated array requires an initial-credit allowance. Supporting deletion requires a separate argument for the shrinking policy. A proof for append-only sequences does not automatically cover arbitrary updates. Key takeaways Cheap operations can prepay future expensive work. Credits must cover every allowed prefix of the sequence. A negative balance invalidates the proposed accounting proof. Further reading Erickson: Amortized Analysis

sum: Use changes in a potential function to prove an amortised bound.
x: A potential function tracks saved work for an entire data structure. It should rise during cheap operations and fall when expensive work consumes that saving. Actual cost plus the change in stored work When these charges are added, every intermediate potential appears once positively and once negatively. Those terms cancel, leaving actual total work plus final potential minus starting potential. Starting at zero and keeping potential nonnegative therefore makes the amortised total an upper bound on actual total work for every sequence prefix. More generally, final potential must not fall below the starting value for that same bound without an extra initial allowance. A doubling-array example Count copies and writes as one work unit each. Start with an empty capacity-zero array, allocate one slot on its first append, then double when full. For this append-only policy the array is at least half full after its first append. One useful reference choice is: A cheap append stores two potential units alongside its one write. A resize costs many copies, but the drop in potential offsets them. The resulting charge is at most three units per append, including the initial append. This is a proof about counted work, not a claim that each append takes the same time. Choosing potential is part of designing the proof. The element count alone need not be suitable, and this append-only potential is not automatically valid after arbitrary deletions. Key takeaways Potential change connects cheap and expensive operations. Intermediate potential values cancel in a sequence total. Check the starting state and nonnegative-balance condition. Further reading Erickson: Amortized Analysis

sum: Choose growth and shrink thresholds that avoid repeated full-array copying.
x: Amortised append performance depends on the growth rule. Assume a resize copies all current items, each copy costs one unit, and the array starts empty with fixed initial capacity. Fixed increments keep resizes too frequent Adding a hundred slots at a time eventually means copying a huge array after only another hundred appends. Copy sizes grow in an arithmetic progression. Across n appends the total copying is quadratic in n, so amortised cost per append grows linearly. Multiplying capacity by a fixed factor greater than one instead creates room for proportionally more appends each time. Copy sizes form a geometric progression and total copying is linear. Doubling, growing by one half, and growing by a fixed one eighth all give constant amortised append cost with suitable integer rounding. A smaller fixed factor saves spare capacity but causes more copying. Exact growth factors are implementation details; CPython 3.14 uses proportional over-allocation with rounding and small-size adjustments. A bulk insertion can follow additional rules, so do not infer its allocation from a single-item append example. Separate growth and shrink thresholds Suppose the array doubles when full and halves as soon as it becomes half full. Append to a full array, then pop: the append grows it, the pop shrinks it, and the next append must grow it again. Every operation can copy nearly the whole array. Use hysteresis: for example, grow when full but shrink only at a quarter full, halving capacity. After shrinking, the array is half full; after growth it is roughly half full. A substantial number of updates must occur before another resize. With a fixed minimum capacity, this supports constant amortised push and pop cost. Real-world analogy: A thermostat's dead band Heating does not switch on and off at exactly the same temperature boundary. How it maps: Separated thresholds prevent tiny reversals from repeatedly triggering an expensive state change. Where it stops: Array guarantees follow counted updates and copying costs, not physical heating dynamics. Key takeaways Fixed-factor growth spaces expensive copies apart. Fixed-increment growth leads to quadratic total copying. Separate growth and shrink thresholds prevent repeated resizing at one boundary. Further reading CPython 3.14 list implementation Erickson: Amortized Analysis

sum: Apply sequence reasoning to counters and queues while recognising latency spikes.
x: A good sequence bound does not guarantee a short delay for each operation. Here n counts operations or stored items, as each example states. Follow each piece of work across its lifetime A binary counter starting at zero flips its lowest bit on every increment, the next about half as often and later bits progressively less often. Across n increments, the total number of flips is linear in n even though a single carry can flip many bits. A queue can use an inbox stack and an outbox stack. Enqueue pushes to the inbox. Dequeue pops the outbox; only when it is empty does it transfer the inbox by repeated pop-and-push operations. The reversal restores first-in-first-out order. Each item enters the inbox once, transfers at most once and leaves the outbox once. Starting empty, total stack operations are proportional to total queue operations, assuming each stack operation is constant cost. One dequeue can still pay for a large transfer. Throughput and deadlines are different requirements A dynamic-array append may relocate all existing elements. An amortised constant bound permits that delay. A system with a strict per-operation deadline must inspect allocation, relocation and other slow paths rather than relying on the average sequence charge. Possible approaches include reserving enough capacity before the hot path, filling a pre-sized container by index, using fixed-size chunks, or spreading migration work across updates. Each has costs: extra memory, more complicated lookup rules or allocation at chunk boundaries. None alone promises a fixed wall-clock deadline. In Python, [None] n creates a list with n actual elements. Fill those slots by index; appending instead adds after them. It is not an empty list with reserved capacity. The proof also assumes updates progress through states. Reusing an old version of a persistent data structure can repeat expensive work without rebuilding credit. Such structures need an analysis of sharing and deferred work, not an automatic reuse of an imperative proof. Key takeaways Count how often each item or bit can incur work over a sequence. Amortised cost bounds total work, not tail latency. Preallocation or incremental work needs its own capacity and latency assumptions. Further reading Erickson: Amortized Analysis Python sequence operations

sum: Separate recursive subproblem costs from each call’s own work.
x: A recurrence describes a recursive call's cost using the costs of its children. Read three things from the code: how many calls it makes, how large their inputs are, and what work remains outside those calls. Read the control flow Only one branch executes.
