The function searches one roughly half-size range and does constant outside work, assuming constant-cost indexing, comparisons and index arithmetic. It passes bounds instead of copying a slice. Merge sort instead solves both halves and merges their results. The merge visits the items in the current range. These different behaviours produce different recurrences: These are asymptotic models with a fixed positive base-case cost. Half sizes are rounded as the actual ranges require; rounding does not change the stated growth for these algorithms. Binary search is logarithmic, while merge sort is linear times log in the original item count. Do not count child work twice: the cost assigned to a child already contains everything it does. Conversely, do not forget copying, scanning or combining work in the parent. A function with two calls followed by a full scan has the same cost shape as merge sort even if its purpose is different. Key takeaways Count executed children, their sizes and outside work separately. Include a stopping rule and base-case cost. Similar recursion shapes can describe different algorithms. Further reading Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Sum level costs to identify whether roots, levels or leaves dominate.
x: A recursion tree turns recursive work into levels you can add. Each node is one call, labelled with only that call's outside work. Here n is the original input size; leaves have bounded positive cost. Three shapes explain many bounds For two half-size children with linear outside work, each level processes the original input amount in total. More nodes are offset by smaller ranges. Halving produces logarithmically many levels, so total work is Θ(n log n). This picture describes equal halves, not all possible recursion trees. For powers of two, the final level consists of n size-one leaves. Those base-case costs must be included in an exact count even though they do not change the linear-times-log bound. With three half-size children and linear outside work, each level has one and a half times the previous level's work. A growing geometric series is controlled by its bottom levels, so the many constant-cost leaves dominate. With two half-size children and quadratic outside work, each level has only half the previous level's work. A shrinking geometric series is controlled by its top levels, giving Θ(n²) total work. Depth alone is not total work A single child on a fixed fraction of the input with constant outside work has logarithmic total cost. Changing from halves to thirds changes only a constant factor. Two half-size children with constant work per node instead create a linear number of nodes. A logarithmic depth does not imply a logarithmic total. If one halving child does logarithmic outside work at each call, those contributions decrease gradually across the chain. Their sum is the square of a logarithm, not just one logarithm. Inspect work per level as well as depth. Key takeaways Add each level's whole cost, including base-case leaves. Equal level costs accumulate across the depth. Geometrically growing or shrinking levels favour leaves or root respectively. Further reading Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Find the critical exponent and recognise leaf-dominated recurrences.
x: The Master Theorem summarises the recursion-tree argument for equal-size fractional children. Use a fixed positive base-case cost and nonnegative outside work. Here n is input size. Compare outside work with leaf growth For exact full trees, take input sizes that are powers of the divisor; ordinary rounding leaves the standard asymptotic results unchanged. Leaves grow as the input raised to the critical exponent. When the leaves dominate The first case requires outside work to be smaller than leaf growth by a fixed positive power of input size. A mere logarithmic difference is insufficient. Four half-size children produce a quadratic leaf count. Linear outside work is smaller by a full power, so the total is quadratic rather than quadratic times log. Reducing child count can improve an algorithm's exponent. Karatsuba integer multiplication uses three half-size products instead of four, with linear outside work in digit count. Strassen matrix multiplication uses seven half-size products instead of eight, with quadratic outside work in matrix side length. Toom-3 uses five roughly third-size integer products instead of nine. These examples reduce the leaf growth; constants and representation still affect practical performance. Key takeaways Check equal fractional children and fixed parameters first. The critical exponent comes from branching and shrinking. A fixed positive power gap lets leaf growth determine the total. Further reading MIT: Master theorem, including power gaps and regularity Erickson: Solving Recurrences GMP: Toom three-way multiplication

sum: Handle matching costs and logarithmic factors with the second case.
x: When outside work matches the recursion tree's leaf growth, work is spread across many levels. The missing logarithm in a guessed answer often comes from forgetting to add those levels. Matching work adds a level factor Four half-size children with quadratic outside work illustrate the idea. Each child does a quarter of the parent's outside work, but there are four children. Their combined cost matches the parent's. Every level therefore has quadratic total work, and there are logarithmically many levels. The result is Θ(n² log n), where n is the original input size. The balanced case also has a useful logarithmic-factor extension: The exact equal-level picture applies when there is no extra logarithm factor. For two half-size children with linear-times-log outside work, the total size across a level stays the same, but the logarithm decreases gradually as subproblems shrink. Adding those declining level costs gives Θ(n(log n)²). This is not the root-dominated case: one extra logarithm is not a fixed positive power gap. Nor does the displayed extension cover a negative logarithm exponent. Check the version of the theorem being used before applying a shortcut. Key takeaways Equal work per level must be multiplied by the number of levels. The nonnegative-log-power extension adds one logarithm power. A logarithmic factor alone is not a polynomial gap. Further reading MIT: Master theorem, including power gaps and regularity Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Check regularity and apply the complete three-case shortcut.
x: The root dominates when outside work is sufficiently large and consistently shrinks down the recursion tree. Here n is input size, with fixed fractional children and bounded positive base cases. Larger is not enough without regularity For the third Master Theorem case, outside work must exceed leaf growth by a fixed positive power. The children's combined outside work must also be at most a fixed fraction less than the parent's, for all sufficiently large inputs: Two half-size children with quadratic outside work satisfy both conditions. Each child's outside work is a quarter of the parent's, so together they cost half. Later levels keep halving. Adding all of them changes only a constant factor: total work is Θ(n²). The regularity condition prevents a wildly varying outside-work function from hiding large costs deeper in the tree. Ordinary power functions with exponent above the critical exponent satisfy it. "Outside work looks bigger" is not a complete proof for an arbitrary function. The three-case picture Comparison with leaf growth Behaviour ------ Polynomially smaller leaves dominate Matching power, covered log factors accumulate across levels Polynomially larger and regular root dominates Use that picture to explain the answer, then check the relevant conditions. A table of remembered recurrence answers is less reliable than understanding where the work sits. Key takeaways Root domination needs a power gap and regularity. Regularity makes level totals shrink geometrically. Explain which part of the tree supplies the dominant work. Further reading MIT: Master theorem, including power gaps and regularity Erickson: Solving Recurrences

t: When the Master Theorem does not fit
sum: Recognise unsupported recurrences and prove a guessed bound by induction.
x: The Master Theorem is a shortcut with assumptions. When a recurrence falls outside them, inspect its actual work instead of forcing it into a case. Recognise the mismatch Subtracting one item is not shrinking by a fixed fraction. A single recursive chain with a full scan at each step has linearly many levels of decreasing linear work, giving quadratic total work. Two calls each one item smaller create exponential branching across a linear depth. Unequal-size children do not fit the equal-size theorem. Recursion trees or Akra–Bazzi may still work. A number of children or shrink factor that varies with input size needs a different analysis. Outside work smaller than the critical growth by only a logarithm falls between the leaf case and the nonnegative-log-power balanced version taught here. For that last example, two half-size calls plus linear work divided by a logarithm give Θ(n log log n), where n is input size. The next lessons explain the slowly accumulating factor. Some stronger theorem statements cover this case directly; the limitation is in the stated version. Guess, then prove with the same constants A recursion tree can suggest a bound. Mathematical induction then checks a base case and shows that assuming the bound for smaller inputs establishes it for the current input with the same fixed multiplier. Here is a failed attempt for two half-size calls plus linear work: Calling the final expression "linear" does not repair the proof. Repeating that multiplier increase through the levels hides the missing logarithmic factor. A linear-times-log guess has enough room for each level's added work. Its proof must cover a suitable base case; the logarithm at one is zero, so handle that size separately. Key takeaways Check the recurrence form and the growth-case conditions. Induction must preserve one fixed bound through every level. A failed proof suggests a better guess but does not prove that guess. Further reading MIT: Master theorem, including power gaps and regularity Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Balance unequal subproblems and account for work across their scales.
x: Unequal subproblems need not have equal depths. Akra–Bazzi extends recurrence analysis to several fixed shrinking fractions and accounts for work across those scales. Balance the recursive structure Use a fixed number of positive child weights and fixed fractions strictly between zero and one. Base-case costs must stay between positive constants. Choose a sufficiently large fixed base threshold so that recursive children stay in the defined domain. The nonnegative outside work must satisfy a polynomial-growth condition: throughout the range from each child size to its parent size, it stays between fixed positive multiples of the work at the parent size. Powers of size and logarithms used here satisfy this above a suitable threshold. Arbitrary oscillations need not. The formula below uses exact fractional sizes; rounded recurrences require the extended theorem’s conditions. The exact integral is reference material. An integral accumulates contributions over a continuous range, much as a sum adds contributions from discrete levels. Choose a fixed base threshold above any singularity, and use constant positive costs below it: For one-third and two-thirds children with linear outside work, the pieces preserve the parent's total size. Complete early levels each cost linear work; every branch still has logarithmic depth. Total work is Θ(n log n). For one-half and one-quarter children, total size falls to three quarters each generation. With linear outside work, this gives a shrinking geometric sum and Θ(n) total work. The root already supplies the matching linear lower bound. Key takeaways Unequal fixed fractions can still have tractable growth. The balancing exponent describes recursion; the correction includes outside work. Check regularity and base cases before applying the formula. Further reading Leighton: Akra–Bazzi assumptions and extensions Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Apply the general method to linear selection and a gap between Master Theorem cases.
x: Use the distribution of work to understand an Akra–Bazzi answer before evaluating an integral. Here n is the current input size, with bounded positive base cases. Selection: leave a fixed fraction out Median-of-medians selection groups items into fives, recursively finds a pivot from the group medians, then recurses only into the relevant partition. Its worst-case analysis bounds child sizes by about one fifth and seven tenths of the parent, with rounding and a constant-sized boundary correction. This is an upper-bound recurrence for the algorithm, not an exact equality for every input. Those fractions total less than the whole input. With linear partitioning work, the recursive contribution shrinks geometrically once inputs are large enough. The resulting worst-case bound is linear. The small rounding corrections are handled by the base threshold; they do not remove the fixed gap below the full parent size. A logarithmic gap accumulates slowly Consider this recurrence for sufficiently large inputs, stopping at a fixed size above one: Each complete level contains the same total item count, but its outside work is divided by the logarithm of the current subproblem size. Looking upward from the base, those denominators grow in roughly consecutive steps. The level contributions therefore form a harmonic sum over logarithmically many levels. That adds the logarithm of a logarithm. The result lies between linear and linear-times-log growth. It is not covered by the nonnegative-log-power balanced case or the leaf case requiring a fixed positive power gap. Akra–Bazzi's accumulated outside-work correction distinguishes it without pretending those conditions hold. Key takeaways A fixed gap below the parent size can support linear selection. Real algorithm recurrences may be upper bounds with rounding corrections. Slightly sublinear outside work can still add a growing factor across levels. Further reading Erickson: Solving Recurrences

sum: Use an explicitly assumed operation rate to screen algorithm choices.
x: Complexity helps reject implausible designs before implementing them. It does not supply a universal number of operations a machine can perform each second. Build a workload-specific budget Start with the largest expected input, the actual operation being counted and the time available. A comparison of two small integers is different from a network request or comparison of long strings. Use measured throughput for representative data, or label a hypothetical rate clearly. Candidate What to investigate ------ All pairs whether quadratic growth fits the largest input Sort then scan comparison cost, allocation and input mutation Hash-based scan memory, hash quality and equality cost Exhaustive subsets candidate count and cost of checking each A quadratic design can look fine on a sample and fail when an upload grows substantially. Sorting or hashing may avoid most of those comparisons. Conversely, exhaustive search can be the simplest exact solution for a tightly bounded small input. There is no universal "twenty to twenty-five items" limit: pruning, per-candidate work, parallelism and the time budget alter feasibility. Treat an estimate as a model to validate Dividing counted work by a representative operations-per-second rate gives an estimated runtime. A range of observed rates produces a range of predicted times. Do not substitute CPU clock frequency for measured iteration throughput. If the larger input crosses a cache or memory boundary, the old rate may no longer apply. Include allocation, parsing, output and peak memory when those are part of the job. Leave headroom instead of relying on a model that only just fits. Big-O is an upper growth bound with hidden constants, not an exact operation count. A label alone cannot justify a particular one-second deadline. Use the mechanism to screen candidates, then benchmark the actual implementation and workload. Key takeaways Feasibility depends on input bounds, operation cost and available time. Exhaustive search has no universal practical item cutoff. Use estimates to choose what to measure, not to replace measurement. Further reading Python timeit Erickson: Introduction

sum: Explain practical performance differences hidden by asymptotic labels.
x: Two implementations can share a growth class yet perform very differently. Asymptotic notation deliberately hides fixed factors and simplifies the memory system. Small pieces can favour simple methods Insertion sort has quadratic worst-case work in its run length, but small pieces can benefit from its simple operations and contiguous access. A hybrid sort can use it only below a fixed run-size cap. Across all pieces, that bounded work remains linear in the total item count; the merging or partitioning stages determine the larger-input bound. CPython 3.14's natural merge sort extends short runs using binary insertion sort and uses a Powersort merge policy. Its tuning choices are implementation details. The useful general idea is to bound expensive small-run work and measure whether it helps. Locality changes the cost per access Contiguous arrays place neighbouring values near one another. Scattered linked-list nodes require following references; the next address may not be known until the previous node is loaded. Both traversals are linear in item count, but their cache misses and memory dependencies differ. For a C-style row-major matrix, neighbouring columns within one row are contiguous. Traversing down a column instead jumps by a row stride. Both orders visit every entry, yet row order usually has better spatial locality for large matrices. Exact timing depends on layout, cache size, associativity, compiler transformations and hardware. Total matrix size alone does not prove every column access misses the cache. Real-world analogy: Reading a shelf in order Reading adjacent book labels can be easier than following instructions to shelves across a building. How it maps: Nearby array elements resemble adjacent labels; dependent pointers resemble directions learned only after reaching each location. Where it stops: CPUs prefetch, cache and overlap work. The comparison suggests locality, not a numerical slowdown. A smaller exponent still needs a practical implementation Some theoretically faster algorithms have large constants or extra storage needs. Compare a proposed matrix-multiplication implementation with a measured baseline using representative sizes, numeric types, memory limits and accuracy requirements. A ratio of powers with assumed unit constants cannot establish a real speedup. Key takeaways Constants and locality matter over finite input ranges. A bounded quadratic subroutine can fit inside a faster-growing overall algorithm. Benchmark time, peak memory and accuracy before replacing a tuned baseline. Further reading CPython 3.14 sorting design What every programmer should know about memory

sum: Recognise when an attacker can force expensive algorithm paths.
x: Typical performance is not enough when someone can choose inputs that expose expensive paths. Ask what the algorithm guarantees under the actual input and randomness model. Three ways input can amplify work Hash collisions: a basic hash table can degrade to a linear scan when many keys collide. Repeated insertion can then take quadratic work in the key count. Keyed hash randomisation makes predictable collision attacks harder; it is not a universal constant-time guarantee for arbitrary keys. Regex backtracking: some patterns force a backtracking engine to explore many alternatives, giving superlinear or exponential behaviour. Cloudflare's July 2019 outage involved excessive backtracking that exhausted CPU capacity. Check the engine and the exact search API: guarantees for one fixed-pattern search do not automatically cover repeated-match iteration or an unbounded pattern size. Predictable quicksort pivots: repeatedly selecting an end element on sorted distinct input leaves one nearly unchanged partition and can cause quadratic work. Randomisation gives an expected guarantee under its assumptions; an introspective fallback to heapsort supplies a worst-case time bound. Match the defence to the source of risk Use a suitable worst-case bound when latency must be bounded by the algorithm. Where randomisation is appropriate, state what remains unpredictable to the input chooser. Apply input and resource limits as well: even a linear scan takes too long or too much memory on an unbounded request. A fixed tiny configuration list and an ordinary fixed-width numeric sum do not have the same shape-dependent amplification as those examples. That does not make all costs irrelevant: huge input, expensive user-defined comparisons or growing integers require their own model. Key takeaways Check who chooses the input and which slow paths remain reachable. Randomised expected guarantees and worst-case guarantees are different. Bound input size and operation cost as well as the growth rate. Further reading Python hash randomisation Cloudflare's July 2019 outage analysis RE2 design guarantees

sum: Use doubling ratios and realistic constraints to choose a suitable implementation.
x: Measurement tests whether the model explains the actual implementation. Use realistic inputs, repeat runs and inspect the operations dominating elapsed time. Doubling is a diagnostic experiment Measure at several successively doubled input sizes while holding the task and environment comparable. A roughly doubled time suggests linear behaviour; quadrupled time suggests quadratic behaviour; eightfold time suggests cubic behaviour. Linear-times-log growth is slightly above doubling over sufficiently large sizes. These are clues over the measured range, not proofs of asymptotic bounds. Startup work, cache transitions, allocation and noise can distort ratios. A backtracking or exponential algorithm need not follow a stable power-law ratio at all. Python's timeit repeats small benchmarks and documents common measurement pitfalls. Decide whether setup and garbage collection belong in the measured workload. Minimum repeated time can help estimate uncontended execution; service latency needs its own distribution, including slow requests. A profiler identifies where time is spent but also adds overhead. Connect the observation to the code One visible loop does not make this linear. Each front removal shifts the remaining list references, so the total work is quadratic in original item count. A consistent fourfold doubling ratio supports that diagnosis. A deque can remove from the front without shifting every remaining element. Copying once and clearing the original may also satisfy the required behaviour; check mutation and aliasing requirements. Choose for the scarce resource To keep the best hundred scores from a stream too large to store, maintain a min-heap of at most a hundred retained scores. Its smallest retained score is the replacement threshold. Read every record once and replace only when necessary. Storage depends on the requested result count, not stream length. A conventional in-memory quickselect requires the items available for partitioning, and sorting all records does more ordering than the request needs. Match the approach to output, memory and streaming requirements, then benchmark it. Key takeaways Doubling ratios suggest where to investigate. Confirm the mechanism behind an observed slowdown. Choose and measure against actual input, output, memory and latency constraints. Further reading Python timeit Python heap selection Python deque

t: Direct indexing with array address arithmetic
sum: Address arithmetic gives direct access to a fixed-width slot.
x: An array is the simplest data structure there is: a fixed number of same-sized slots laid out one after another in memory. Almost every other structure in this course is either built on arrays or defined by how it differs from one. Two properties make arrays special: Contiguous layout. Element at the next index sits immediately after its predecessor. There are no gaps and no pointers between them. Uniform element size. Every slot is the same number of bytes, so the machine can compute where any element lives. Everything good about arrays (instant indexing, cache-friendliness) and everything bad (expensive inserts, fixed size) follows from those two facts. Indexing is arithmetic Memory is a long row of numbered bytes; the number of a byte is its memory address. To read element i, the machine needs that element's address. Because the slots are contiguous and all the same size, it can work the address out directly from where the array starts: For the array drawn below, substitute its 4-byte slots and base address: The formula only works because every slot is the same size and there are no gaps; a structure without those two properties (a linked list, for example) has no such shortcut. That is one multiply and one add, whatever the array's length. This is why indexing is O(1), or constant time: the cost does not grow as the array gets longer. The CPU does not walk to element i, it calculates where it is. This also explains why most languages start indexing at 0: the index is an offset from the start. Element 0 is zero elements past base. O(1) access, O(n) search For an array of n elements: indexing by position is O(1). Finding a value in an unsorted array is still O(n) (linear time: the work grows in proportion to n), because you must look at each slot. If the array is sorted, binary search finds a value in O(log n), where log n means log₂ n, the number of times you can halve n before reaching 1 (about 20 for a million elements). Key takeaways Address arithmetic gives direct access to a fixed-width slot. Position lookup and searching for an unsorted value are different operations. Further reading Array (data structure) — Wikipedia)

sum: Scan the contiguous dimension for sequential memory access.
x: The preceding unit derived an address from the array base, index and fixed slot size. Here n counts array elements, r and c are zero-based row and column indices, cols counts columns per row, and size is the number of bytes per element. Constant-time indexing is a data-structure model; memory locality explains why two linear scans can still differ in real elapsed time. Why contiguous memory is fast Both indexed access and a single pointer load are constant-time operations in the usual RAM model. Their measured latencies can differ because that model abstracts away the memory hierarchy. CPUs do not fetch single bytes from RAM. They transfer a cache line, whose size depends on the processor; this example assumes 64 bytes, and keep it in a small, fast cache. A cache hit can be much faster than a main-memory access; latency depends on hardware, contention and access pattern. Evidence gap Universal nanosecond latency figures are omitted because no measured hardware configuration or reproducible benchmark is provided. When you scan an array, one aligned 64-byte cache line contains sixteen 4-byte integers. A hardware prefetcher can recognise a sequential pattern and fetch later lines ahead of demand; effectiveness depends on the processor, stride and workload. This is spatial locality, and it is why a simple loop over an array is one of the fastest things a computer can do. A linked list (covered later in this module) scatters its nodes around the heap. Each step can be a cache miss. Scanning n elements is O(n) for both on paper; dependent pointer loads can make the list slower, but no speed ratio follows without measuring the workload. 2D arrays: row-major order A rectangular built-in C or C++ array is contiguous and row-major: row 0 first, then row 1. A newly created C-order NumPy array has this layout too; NumPy also supports other strides and orders. Java int[][] is an array of references to separate int[] rows, which may have different lengths. Fortran, MATLAB and R normally use column-major layout. To locate a row-and-column element, count complete earlier rows and then the earlier slots in its row: For the 3-by-4 grid of 4-byte integers starting at address 1000: In a column-major language the roles swap: you skip whole columns first. Loop order matters. Iterating row by row walks memory sequentially. Iterating column by column jumps a whole row's worth of bytes (the column count multiplied by the element size) every step, potentially touching a different cache line each time when that stride is large. Performance depends on dimensions, cache hierarchy and compiler transformations. Key takeaways Scan the contiguous dimension for sequential memory access. A cache-performance claim needs stated hardware and workload assumptions. Further reading Array (data structure) — Wikipedia) Row- and column-major order — Wikipedia

sum: Interior changes shift elements; position lookup does not.
x: An array gives direct indexed access, but its physical neighbours must move when you open or close an interior gap. In this unit n is the number of live elements and i is the zero-based position being changed. Operations and their cost In this table n is the number of elements in the array and i is the position being read or changed. Operation Cost Why --------- Read/write a[i] O(1) Address arithmetic Search (unsorted) O(n) Check every slot Insert/delete at end O(1) No shifting Insert/delete at i O(n − i + 1) without resizing Shift the tail; reallocation may add O(n) For a dynamic array, amortised; see below. Inserting at position i means shifting every later element one slot right to make room. Inserting at the front of a million-element array moves a million elements. Static vs dynamic arrays A fixed-size array has a size chosen when it is created; this is distinct from static storage duration. C's int a[100] and Java's new int[100] are fixed-size: you cannot append a 101st element. A dynamic array (resizable array) wraps a static array and tracks two numbers: length: how many elements are in use. capacity: how many slots the underlying array has. When the length equals the capacity and you append, it allocates a bigger array, copies everything across, and frees the old one. What the Python operations touch A CPython list’s contiguous slots hold references to objects. Indexing chooses one slot directly; membership scans values until a match or the end. An unsorted list does not get fast membership merely because its storage supports direct indexing. Equality comparisons can themselves be expensive; the linear scan bound counts comparisons, assuming each has fixed cost. An append usually writes into spare capacity. Occasionally it reallocates the backing storage, making that individual operation linear in the current length. “Amortised constant time” describes the total cost spread across a sequence, rather than promising identical latency for every append. The next unit proves why geometric growth gives that guarantee. Negative indices are translated relative to the stored length, so replacing the last item is still direct access. Removing the last item needs no shifting, while removing the first shifts the remaining references. CPython may also shrink its allocation on some pops; its end-pop bound is amortised. Key takeaways Interior changes shift elements; position lookup does not. Length counts live elements, while capacity includes spare slots. Further reading Dynamic array — Wikipedia Array (data structure) — Wikipedia)

sum: Multiply capacity by a constant factor greater than one to bound total copying.
x: A dynamic array distinguishes its live length from its backing capacity. When a full array grows, old elements may need copying. This unit counts that copying across a sequence of appends; allocation costs and allocator-specific in-place growth are outside the model. Why growth must be geometric Copying n elements is O(n) work, so you might expect appends to be slow. The trick is how much to grow. To compare growth policies, count the total number of element copies that resizing makes while you append n elements one at a time. If capacity doubles each time, starting from capacity 1, the resizes copy 1, then 2, then 4, and so on, each resize copying the whole old array: For example, 17 appends end at capacity 32 after copying 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 elements, fewer than 2 × 17 = 34. Spread over n appends, that is fewer than two copies per append: amortised O(1). Amortised means averaged over a long run of operations: an occasional append is expensive, but the total for n appends is still proportional to n. Growing by any constant factor greater than 1 works. Going backwards from the last resize, each earlier resize copied 1/r as many elements as the one after it, so the copies form a shrinking geometric series: The series is stated in terms of final capacity, not arbitrary stopping length. At a full-capacity endpoint: Just after a resize, the final capacity can instead approach the growth factor times the live length. The table describes full-capacity endpoints: Growth factor Copies when n fills final capacity ------ 2 about one copy per final item 1.5 about two copies per final item 1.125 about eight copies per final item For instance, with factor 1.5 and a million elements: 1,000,000 / (1.5 − 1) = 2,000,000 copies. Every factor gives a total proportional to n, so append stays amortised O(1); smaller factors just pay a larger constant. Growing by a constant amount (say +10 slots) does not work. Each resize now copies only 10 more elements than the last, so the copies form an arithmetic series whose total grows with the square of n: With ten-slot increments and a million appends, the approximation gives fifty billion copies, against about a million for doubling. That is O(n²), quadratic time. Amortised is not worst case An individual append that triggers a resize is O(n). If you append to a 10-million-element vector in a latency-sensitive loop, that one append copies 10 million elements. When you know the final size, reserve it up front. Key takeaways Multiply capacity by a constant factor greater than one to bound total copying. Distinguish a full-capacity endpoint from stopping just after a resize. Further reading Dynamic array — Wikipedia

t: Array layouts in Python, Java and C++
sum: Python lists and Java generic lists store references; vector stores values directly.
x: The previous units established contiguous slots and amortised growth. The slot may contain a raw value or a reference to a separate object: the language runtime decides. Details below refer to CPython and OpenJDK 21 where named, rather than every implementation of Python or Java. Real implementations Python list A Python list is a dynamic array of pointers to objects (8 bytes each on a conventional 64-bit CPython build), not of the values themselves. [1, 2, 3] stores three pointers to three separate int objects elsewhere on the heap. CPython over-allocates by about 12.5% plus a small constant. When a list needs room for n elements, list_resize in the CPython source picks the new capacity like this: For nine required elements, the extra eighth rounds down to one, producing capacity sixteen. For seventeen, it rounds down to two: the provisional twenty-five slots round down to twenty-four. For incremental single-item growth, the source comments give the capacity sequence as 0, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 52, 64, 76... For a fixed CPython build, sys.getsizeof on an ordinary list can reveal backing-capacity changes. For a large bulk extension, CPython can instead suppress most spare capacity when the requested growth exceeds the proposed spare room. The mild factor saves memory; a conventional GIL-enabled CPython build can use realloc to extend a block in place when the allocator permits. The free-threaded build’s resize path instead allocates replacement storage and copies references. For a list of n elements: append and pop() are amortised O(1). insert(0, x) and pop(0) are O(n). Use collections.deque for a queue (covered later in this module). For dense numbers, array.array or NumPy store raw values contiguously, which is far more compact and cache-friendly. Java ArrayList ArrayList wraps an Object[]. A default-constructed list allocates its 10-slot backing array lazily, on the first add, and uses roughly 1.5x incremental growth in OpenJDK 21. A larger required minimum or an array-size limit can change that result. The source writes this as old + (old >> 1); >> 1 shifts the bits right by one place, which halves a whole number and drops any remainder: From the default 10 slots this gives 15, then 15 + 7 = 22, then 22 + 11 = 33. ensureCapacity(n) or new ArrayList<>(n) pre-sizes it to hold n elements. Because Java generics only hold objects, ArrayList<Integer> stores references to boxed Integer objects. An int[] of a million elements is about 4 MB; an ArrayList<Integer> of a million is several times that, plus the pointer chasing. C++ std::vector vector stores elements directly and contiguously. The standard requires amortised constant push_back but leaves the growth factor to the implementation: common libraries use factors such as 2 or 1.5 for ordinary incremental growth, but those are implementation details rather than portable guarantees. reserve(n) ensures capacity is at least n without changing size; it does not shrink existing capacity. The crucial pitfall is iterator invalidation: a reallocation moves every element, so any pointer, reference or iterator into the vector becomes dangling. Key takeaways Python lists and Java generic lists store references; vector stores values directly. Reserve space before keeping C++ pointers into a vector. Further reading CPython listobject.c (list_resize) std::vector — cppreference ArrayList — Java SE 21 API

sum: Leave a gap between growth and shrink thresholds.
x: Growing a dynamic array pays for occasional copying by leaving spare room for later operations. Shrinking must also leave room between resize boundaries; otherwise a push and pop can undo each other’s expensive allocation. Here n denotes the current number of live elements. Shrinking and other pitfalls Shrink thrash. If you double when full and halve when below half full, a workload that alternates push and pop right at the boundary resizes on every operation. The standard fix is to halve only when the array falls to a quarter full. CPython shrinks only when length drops below half the allocated size, and then reallocates with room to spare. Wasted capacity. After growth, up to half the slots (with doubling) may be empty. C++ shrink_to_fit makes a nonbinding request to reduce capacity; Java trimToSize reduces backing capacity to size. Allocators and garbage collectors determine when memory is reclaimed or returned to the OS. Off-by-one errors. The last valid index is one less than the array length. In C there is no bounds check, so reading or writing a[len] has undefined behavior, which can corrupt memory, crash or behave unpredictably, a classic source of security bugs. Key takeaways Leave a gap between growth and shrink thresholds. Capacity reclamation and bounds safety are separate from append amortisation. Further reading Dynamic array — Wikipedia CPython listobject.c (list_resize) std::vector — cppreference ArrayList — Java SE 21 API

sum: Rebinding a variable leaves other aliases pointing at the old string.
x: A string represents a sequence of text units. Many implementations use arrays, but indexing cost depends on which units are requested and how the string is represented. But strings come with two complications that trip up beginners and experienced engineers alike: In most modern languages they are immutable: you can never change one, only make a new one. A "character" is not as simple as it sounds. How many bytes it takes depends on the character encoding. Both have real performance and correctness consequences. Immutability In Python, Java, JavaScript, C# and Go, a string object can never be modified after it is created. Operations that look like modification (upper(), replace(), +) return an immutable string value and leave the original contents alone; an implementation may reuse an existing object when the result is unchanged. A variable can be re-pointed at a new string, but any other variable still pointing at the old one sees no change. C++ std::string and Rust String are mutable growable buffers with separate borrowed-view types, std::string_view and &str. C char arrays can be mutable but C does not provide those ownership/view types. Why make strings immutable? Safe as hash keys. A dict or HashMap stores a key in a bucket chosen by its hash. If the key could change, it would sit in the wrong bucket forever. Immutable strings can also cache their hash: Python and Java compute it once and store it. Free sharing. Many variables, threads or data structures can point at the same string with no copying and no locks, because nobody can change it. Interning. Identical literals can share one object. Java interns string literals; CPython interns many identifiers and short strings. Security. A checked string value cannot change through an alias. This does not prevent the file, permissions or other external resource named by it from changing between check and use. Changing the text generally requires producing another value; allocation and copying may be optimized when observable immutability is preserved. Key takeaways Rebinding a variable leaves other aliases pointing at the old string. Immutability enables stable hash keys; external resources can still change. Further reading Python built-in types: text sequences String interning — Wikipedia

t: Bytes, code points and grapheme clusters
sum: Byte length, code-unit length and visible-character length can differ.
x: A string represents text, but byte storage and visible characters are different layers. This unit follows the encoding from a byte representation through runtime indexing to grapheme clusters, so you can choose the length limit your application actually needs. Encoding basics Computers store bytes, not letters. A character encoding maps characters to bytes. ASCII covers 128 characters (English letters, digits, punctuation) in 7 bits. Unicode assigns a number, a code point, to over 150,000 characters: U+0041 is A, U+00E9 is é, U+1F600 is 😀. UTF-8 stores each Unicode scalar value in 1 to 4 bytes; surrogate code points are excluded. ASCII characters take 1 byte, so plain ASCII text is valid UTF-8. It is the dominant encoding on the web and in files. UTF-16 uses 2 bytes for most common characters and 4 bytes (a surrogate pair) for the rest, including most emoji. What does "length" mean? Different languages count different things: In Java and JavaScript, "😀".length() / "😀".length is 2, because they count UTF-16 code units. Slicing such a string in the wrong place splits a surrogate pair and produces garbage. Even code points aren't what a reader thinks of as a character. é can be one code point (U+00E9) or two (e plus a combining accent U+0301). The two forms look identical but compare unequal unless you apply Unicode normalisation to both (Python's unicodedata.normalize). A flag emoji like 🇬🇧 is two code points. What users perceive as one character is a grapheme cluster. How runtimes store strings CPython (PEP 393) picks 1, 2 or 4 bytes per code point for each string, based on the widest character it contains. Every code point then has a fixed width, so s[i] stays O(1). One emoji in a long ASCII string makes the whole string 4 bytes per character. Java 9+ uses "compact strings": Latin-1 (1 byte per char) when possible, otherwise UTF-16. Rust String stores valid UTF-8. Go strings are arbitrary byte sequences, conventionally UTF-8 for text. Getting the i-th code point of an n-byte string means scanning from the start, O(n), which is why Rust doesn't let you write s[i] on a String and Go's s[i] gives you a byte. Key takeaways Byte length, code-unit length and visible-character length can differ. Runtime representation determines what an index means and costs. Further reading PEP 393 — Flexible String Representation UTF-8 — Wikipedia The Absolute Minimum Every Software Developer Must Know About Unicode — Joel Spolsky Python built-in types: text sequences

sum: Repeated full-copy concatenation sums growing prefixes.
x: An immutable string cannot be observably changed through an alias. A full-copy concatenation creates the combined value; repeat that operation and you repeatedly copy earlier prefixes. The cost model below explicitly excludes optimisations that extend an unshared buffer in place. Concatenation cost In the full-copy model, joining two immutable strings creates a value with space for both inputs and copies their code units. Observable immutability itself does not forbid optimising an unshared internal buffer; the CPython caveat below matters: So "abc" + "de" copies 5 characters, and appending one character to a 1,000-character string copies 1,001. That is linear in the combined input lengths. Now put it in a loop: Each pass copies everything built so far plus the new word, so the cost of each pass grows. Adding up all the passes gives an arithmetic series: That's quadratic: O(n²) for a fixed word length. For 100,000 one-character pieces, the formula predicts about five billion character copies. CPython sometimes cheats CPython can extend result in place when nothing else references it, which often makes this loop fast in practice. It's an implementation detail: it disappears if another reference exists, and PEP 8 says not to rely on it. It is not a portable guarantee across Python implementations. The fix: collect, then join Gather the pieces in a list (amortised O(1) appends), then join once. join measures the total length, allocates once, and copies each piece once: O(number of pieces + total length). In Java, use StringBuilder, a mutable, growable character buffer (a dynamic array, so appending k units costs amortised O(k + 1)): The compiler won't save you in a loop javac turns a single expression like a + b + c into one efficient concatenation. But s = s + w inside a loop still creates growing immutable results. For n equal-sized pieces and no cross-iteration optimisation, the loop remains O(n²). Key takeaways Repeated full-copy concatenation sums growing prefixes. Collect pieces and join once, or use a mutable builder. Further reading StringBuilder — Java SE 21 API Python built-in types: text sequences PEP 8 — string-concatenation portability

t: String operations, slices and text pitfalls
sum: Repeated slices can make an otherwise linear recursion quadratic.
x: For these bounds, n is the string length in the units the runtime indexes, and basic element comparisons have constant cost. The earlier encoding unit explains why these units are not necessarily bytes or visible characters. Runtime shortcuts can avoid copying a whole unchanged string; bounds here describe general proper slices and changed results. Common operations and their complexity For a string s of length n (Python and Java, which store their length and support O(1) indexing). In the table, a and b in s[a:b] are the start and end positions of the slice, and m is the length of the string t being searched for: Operation Cost Note --------- len(s) O(1) Length is stored s[i] O(1) Fixed-width units s[a:b] O(b − a + 1) Proper nonempty slices copy; unchanged whole slices may reuse a == b O(n) Stops at first difference t in s O(n·m) worst Usually much faster upper O(n + 1) Unicode case conversion; output may expand literal split, replace Depends on search and output size Replacement can expand the output "".join(parts) O(pieces + output length) Must inspect empty pieces too A few details matter here: C's strlen is O(n). C strings are byte arrays ending in a zero byte, and the length is found by scanning for it. Writing for (i = 0; i < strlen(s); i++) makes the loop O(n²) unless the compiler hoists the call. Slices copy. An ordinary nonempty proper CPython slice such as s[1:] generally copies its selected characters; empty and full unchanged slices can reuse objects. Recursive functions that pass s[1:] down at each level copy O(n) per call: O(n²) total. Pass indices instead. Java's substring has also copied since Java 7u6; earlier versions shared the parent's array, which caused memory leaks when a tiny substring kept a huge string alive. Substring search. A naive search tries every start position, O(n·m) in the worst case. Library implementations use cleverer algorithms and are fast on typical text; CPython adopted the linear-time two-way algorithm for longer needles in Python 3.10. Linear-time algorithms such as KMP appear in a later module. Hashing is O(n) the first time, but Python and Java cache the result on the string object. Pitfalls in practice Byte limits vs character limits. A database column, HTTP header or SMS segment limited in bytes can overflow on text that looks short. Truncating UTF-8 at a byte boundary can slice a character in half and produce invalid data. Truncate on code points (or graphemes), then check the byte length. Identity vs equality. In Python, a is b asks "same object?", not "same text?". Interning makes it accidentally true for some literals and false for strings built at runtime. In Java, == on String compares references; use.equals(). Repeated replace or + in hot paths. Each creates a new string. Build once with a builder or join. Reversing user-visible text. s[::-1] reverses code points, which mangles combining accents and multi-code-point emoji. Key takeaways Repeated slices can make an otherwise linear recursion quadratic. Use text equality and preserve encoding or grapheme boundaries. Further reading Python built-in types: text sequences

sum: A node stores a value and a link rather than a positional address shortcut.
x: An array keeps its elements side by side. A linked list gives that up: each element lives in its own node, anywhere in memory, and each node holds a pointer to the next one. That one change flips the trade-offs. For a list of n elements: You can no longer jump to element i; you must walk there. Access becomes O(n). But if you already hold a node, you can insert or remove next to it by rewiring a couple of pointers, with no shifting. That's O(1). Linked lists are a staple of interviews and textbooks. In production code they are less common than you might expect, and knowing why is part of mastering them. Singly linked lists Each node has a value and a next pointer. The list itself is just a reference to the first node, the head node (or just the head). The last node's next is None. Traversal and search Getting the k-th element means following k pointers, so it costs O(k + 1), including the final value read; this is O(n) in the worst case for a list of n nodes. Searching for a value is O(n) too: you may have to look at every node. Avoid repeating positional traversal Calling an indexed accessor repeatedly does not retain the previous traversal position. A Java LinkedList lookup starts from whichever end is nearer the requested position. That is helpful for one lookup but still repeats walking when an index-based loop visits every element. For one hundred thousand nodes, an index loop sums billions of dependent pointer hops. An iterator instead remembers the current node and follows one link per next element, giving a single linear traversal. When you need repeated arbitrary positional lookup, a dynamic array usually matches the access pattern better. This explains an important distinction: a linked list can support a constant-time update next to a handle you already hold, but locating that handle is a different operation. The next unit examines those updates, including the order in which successor links must change. Key takeaways A node stores a value and a link rather than a positional address shortcut. Repeated indexed access to a linked list can repeat the traversal. Further reading Linked list — Wikipedia LinkedList — Java SE 21 API

sum: Preserve the old successor before replacing a link.
x: A singly linked node has a value and a next reference. Use the Node class from the preceding unit. The operations below assume a finite, acyclic list and valid node handles; deletion also needs a successor to remove. Here n is the number of nodes. Insertion Inserting at the head is O(1), and so is inserting after a node you already hold: Order matters. Create the new node pointing at p.next first, then point p at it. Do it the other way round and you lose the rest of the list. Inserting at the tail of an n-node list is O(n), because you must walk to the last node, unless you also keep a tail pointer, in which case it is O(1). Deletion To remove a node you need the node before it, so you can skip over it: This is the singly linked list's big weakness. Given only a pointer to a non-head node, you cannot unlink that node in O(1), because you cannot reach its predecessor without walking from the head. Copying the successor’s value into it and skipping the successor is not the same operation: it changes what existing handles observe and fails at the tail. Removing the head is a special case (head = head.next), and that special-casing is a common source of bugs. Key takeaways Preserve the old successor before replacing a link. Deleting a real node requires its predecessor; copying a value is a different operation. Further reading Linked list — Wikipedia

sum: Unlinking must update both neighbours.
x: A singly linked list has no backwards link. A doubly linked list adds a predecessor reference so both neighbours can be reconnected when a known node is removed. Constant-time claims count pointer operations on valid handles, not allocator or value-destruction time. Doubly linked lists Add a prev pointer to every node and you can walk in both directions, and delete any node in O(1) given only that node: That code crashes when node is the head (node.prev is None) or the tail. Handling those cases with if statements everywhere is tedious and error-prone. Which brings us to sentinels. Sentinel nodes A sentinel (or dummy) node is a node that holds no data and is always present. With a circular doubly linked sentinel, every real node has neighbours on both sides even when there are no other data nodes. The data sequence can be empty while the sentinel remains. The neatest version is a circular doubly linked list with one sentinel: the sentinel's next is the first element and its prev is the last. For valid handles belonging to this list, insertion and removal use a constant number of pointer updates. Do not remove the sentinel or remove a node twice. Allocation and value destruction are outside this pointer-operation model. There is no special case for an empty list, the first node or the last node. The Linux kernel's struct list_head uses exactly this design, with intrusive link fields embedded in containing objects. The cost of a sentinel One extra node of memory per list. For a list with millions of entries that's nothing; for millions of tiny lists it can add up. Key takeaways Unlinking must update both neighbours. A circular sentinel makes every valid data-node removal use the same pointer updates. Further reading Doubly linked list — Wikipedia Linux kernel API: list management Linux — linked-list API and circular sentinels

sum: A tail-only circular list exposes its head through the tail link.
x: The preceding units showed why knowing the node changes a list operation’s cost. Here n is the number of data elements. Circular organisation changes termination rules; practical layout and stable-handle requirements decide whether pointer-based storage is worthwhile. Circular lists In a circular list the last node points back to the first instead of to None. Circular singly linked lists are handy for round-robin scheduling: keep a pointer to the current node and advance it forever. A neat trick: keep only a tail pointer. Then tail.next is the head, so you get O(1) access to both ends from one pointer. The danger with circular lists is the loop condition. while cur: never ends; you must stop when you return to your starting node. Cost summary For a sequence of n elements, keeping both head and tail handles for the doubly linked representation and using constant-time value/allocation operations: Operation Array Singly Doubly ------------ Access i-th O(1) O(n) O(n) Insert/delete at front O(n) O(1) O(1) Insert/delete at back O(1) amortised See below O(1) Delete given node O(n) O(n) O(1) Insert after given node O(n) O(1) O(1) For a singly linked list, inserting at the back is O(1) if you keep a tail pointer, but deleting the last node is O(n), because you have to walk to its predecessor. The hidden costs Big-O makes linked lists look great for insertion-heavy work. Real hardware is less kind. Memory overhead. Every node carries one or two pointers plus allocator bookkeeping. A Java LinkedList node is an object with three references (item, next, prev); for small elements, the overhead dwarfs the data. A Python node object costs tens of bytes before you even count the value. Cache misses. Nodes are scattered around the heap. Walking a list is a chain of dependent loads: the CPU can't fetch node 5 until node 4 tells it where node 5 is. Arrays stream through cache with prefetching. Allocation. Separately allocated nodes add allocation/reclamation work; pools and intrusive lists can avoid a per-insertion allocation. Finding the spot is O(n) anyway (for n elements). "Insert in the middle is O(1)" assumes you already hold the node. If you have to search for the position first, that search is O(n), and on an array it is a fast linear scan. Why locality can outweigh shifting A vector can beat a linked list when both first perform a linear search for the insertion point: contiguous scanning and shifting may outweigh the cost of moving elements. Actual performance requires measurement. Evidence gap A specific historical benchmark result is omitted because its exact dataset, implementation and measurements have not been independently reproduced or sourced here. When linked lists actually win Linked lists earn their place when you already hold a reference to the node you want to change, or when you need properties arrays can't give: O(1) removal from the middle via a handle. An LRU cache pairs a hash map (key to node) with a doubly linked list. On every hit it unlinks the node and moves it to the front in O(1). This is how Python's OrderedDict and Java's LinkedHashMap keep order. Stable references. Inserting into or removing from a std::list never invalidates iterators to other elements. A vector's reallocation invalidates all of them. Splicing. Relinking a run with known boundaries takes a few pointer changes, but maintaining container metadata can add work. C++ std::list range-splice between different lists is linear in the range length; whole-list and single-element splice are constant-time under their allocator preconditions. No reallocation spikes. A linked queue never has to copy everything to grow, but allocation, reclamation and synchronization still need bounded-latency designs for hard real-time use. Intrusive lists. In kernels and game engines, the next/prev pointers live inside the object itself, so membership needs no separate node allocation; simultaneous membership in several lists requires a separate link pair for each list. Immutable sharing. In functional languages (Haskell, Lisp, Scala's List), prepending to a list creates one new node that points at the old list. Both versions remain valid and share the tail. Many practical structures are hybrids. CPython's collections.deque is a doubly linked list of blocks, each holding 64 items. It keeps O(1) operations at both ends while getting most of an array's cache-friendliness. Key takeaways A tail-only circular list exposes its head through the tail link. Known handles, stable references and shared immutable tails are reasons to accept pointer overhead. Further reading Linked list — Wikipedia LinkedList — Java SE 21 API Linux kernel API: list management collections.deque — Python docs

t: Reverse links while preserving the suffix
sum: Save the remaining suffix before flipping a next pointer.
x: Most linked-list problems, in interviews and in real code, reduce to a few patterns. Learn these four and you can assemble the rest: Reversal: turn every arrow around in one pass. Fast and slow pointers: two pointers moving at different speeds. Merging: weave two sorted lists together. Dummy heads: a throwaway node in front so the real head is never a special case. For a list of n nodes, the iterative patterns below use linear time, O(n), and O(1) extra space (a fixed handful of pointer variables, however long the list); recursive reversal is an explicit exception. Unless detecting a cycle, assume finite acyclic lists. That last part is the point: anyone can solve these problems by copying the list into an array first, but then you've spent O(n) memory. Throughout, we use: Reversal Reversing a singly linked list in place means making every next point backwards. You need three pointers: the node you're working on (cur), the part already reversed (prev), and the rest of the list (nxt), which you must save before you break the link to it. The following is an execution-state trace of the Python function on the three-node chain: Each of the n nodes is visited once: O(n) time, O(1) space. Recursive reversal It's elegant, but on an n-node list it uses O(n) stack space, one frame per node. A conventional CPython build commonly starts with a recursion limit of 1,000; inspect sys.getrecursionlimit() rather than assuming an unchanged configuration. Under that setting a 10,000-node recursive reversal raises RecursionError. Prefer the loop. Key takeaways Save the remaining suffix before flipping a next pointer. An iterative reversal keeps a fixed pointer set; recursion retains one frame per node. Further reading Linked list — Wikipedia sys.setrecursionlimit — Python docs

t: Fast and slow pointers: middle and cycles
sum: The loop condition determines which even-length middle is returned.
x: Use the singly linked Node class from the reversal unit. In an acyclic list of n nodes, one- and two-link moves find a middle without counting the length first. On a cyclic list they instead reveal whether the same node is reached at the same time. Fast and slow pointers Move one pointer (slow) one step at a time and another (fast) two steps. The gap between them grows by one each step. That simple fact answers several questions in one pass. Finding the middle When fast reaches the end, slow has gone half as far. The following execution-state trace records the Python pointer values. For an even-length list such as 1..6, this returns 4, the second of the two middle nodes. If you need the first middle (useful for splitting a list in half for merge sort), use while fast and fast.next and fast.next.next to handle empty input too. Floyd's cycle detection A bug or a malicious input can make a list loop back on itself. Walking it with while cur: then never ends. How do you detect a cycle? The obvious answer is a set of visited nodes: for a list of n nodes that is O(n) time but O(n) memory. Floyd's algorithm (the "tortoise and hare") does it in O(1) memory. If there's no cycle, fast falls off the end. If there is, both pointers end up circling the loop, and fast gains one node per step on slow, so it must eventually land exactly on it. It can't jump over slow: if fast is one behind, the next step brings them together. Note is: compare node identity, not values. Two different nodes can hold the same value. Bound the detection phase The first meeting need not be at the entry. In the chain one, two, three, four, five with five linking back to two, the tail is one link and the cycle has four nodes. The pointers first meet at five. In an acyclic chain with three equal values, two different nodes can hold the same value without forming a cycle: identity is what matters. The next unit uses the meeting to locate the entry. Key takeaways The loop condition determines which even-length middle is returned. Detect a cycle by node identity, not repeated values. Further reading Cycle detection — Wikipedia Linked list — Wikipedia

t: Locate the entry of a detected cycle
sum: At a meeting, the fast pointer has gained a whole number of cycle laps.
x: First detect a meeting with the one-step slow pointer and two-step fast pointer. The preceding unit covered that identity test. This unit locates the cycle’s first node and proves why resetting one pointer works; no auxiliary set or list copying is required. Finding where the cycle starts Floyd's algorithm has a second phase. After the pointers meet, put one back at the head and advance both one step at a time. They meet again exactly at the first node of the cycle. Why does that work? Name three distances. By convention they use Greek letters: μ (mu) and λ (lambda). The first card defines these distances in link steps and nodes. They are not memory addresses. Count the steps each pointer has walked when they first meet (not counting the start, where both sit on the head). Slow reaches the cycle after μ steps, goes some number of whole laps, then k more. Fast moves twice as fast, so it has walked twice as far: The last line is the key. Walking μ steps forward from the meeting point means walking μ + k steps from the cycle's start in total, which is a whole number of laps, so it lands exactly back on the cycle's start. Mathematicians write the same fact using modular arithmetic (arithmetic on remainders, like a clock face): In the trace below the tail is two links long and the meeting is two links into a four-node cycle. Both two and negative two have remainder two modulo four, so the rule holds. A pointer walking μ steps from the head also lands on the cycle's start. Both pointers move one step at a time, so they arrive together, and the first node where they meet is the start. The argument also covers a zero-length tail, where the cycle starts at the head; there the initial equality at the head is not treated as a detected cycle. The trace below checks the numbers: the tail is 2 steps and the pointers meet 2 steps into a 4-node cycle, and 2 + 2 = 4 is exactly one lap. Trace List 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> (back to 3), so the tail μ is 2 steps and the cycle length λ is 4. Phase 1: slow visits 2, 3, 4, 5 while fast visits 3, 5, 3, 5. They meet at 5 after 4 steps, 2 steps into the cycle (k is 2). Phase 2: starting from 1 and 5, one step each gives (2, 6), then (3, 3). They meet at 3, the cycle start, after μ (2) steps. To get the cycle's length, hold one pointer at the meeting point and walk the other round until it returns, counting steps. The same idea finds a duplicate in an array of n + 1 values, each between 1 and n, treating each value as a "next" pointer. Brent's algorithm is a variant that typically does fewer pointer moves. Key takeaways At a meeting, the fast pointer has gained a whole number of cycle laps. Reset one pointer to the head and move both one link per step. Further reading Cycle detection — Wikipedia

sum: A dummy supplies a predecessor even for the real head.
x: Use the Node class from the reversal unit and assume a finite, acyclic list. Here n is the requested one-based distance from the end, rather than the list length. A temporary dummy node supplies a stable predecessor even when the target is the real head. Dummy heads Many list operations treat the first node specially: deleting it changes head, and building a new list has no node to attach the first element to. A dummy head (a sentinel placed before the real head) removes the special case. Build or modify the list after the dummy, then return dummy.next. Removing the n-th node from the end Use two pointers with a gap of n between them. When the front one hits the end, the back one is just before the target. Without the dummy, removing the first node (when n equals the length) needs its own branch. With it, back simply stays at the dummy and the general code works. Trace the boundary cases On the five-node chain with values one through five, requesting the last node leaves the back pointer at node four when front runs off the chain. Requesting the fifth node from the end keeps back at the dummy; bypassing its successor removes the real head with the same statement. The extra initial step is intentional: back must end before the target, not on it. Advancing beyond the available chain raises the explicit error before any link is changed. An empty list has no valid positive removal distance. A zero or negative distance is rejected, rather than silently removing an unrelated node. Python treats bool as an int subclass, so the shown type check accepts True as distance one. Callers that must reject Boolean arguments need a stricter validation contract. This teaching example otherwise leaves all non-target node identities intact. Key takeaways A dummy supplies a predecessor even for the real head. Validate the requested position before bypassing a target. Further reading Linked list — Wikipedia

t: Stable destructive merging and merge schedules
sum: Relink node-disjoint sorted inputs and attach an untouched suffix.
x: Use the Node class from the reversal unit. A dummy node provides an initial attachment point, and the current output tail tells you where to append the next selected node. The inputs below must not share nodes: rewiring intersecting inputs can create a cycle. Merging two sorted lists Assume two sorted, acyclic, node-disjoint lists and constant-time value comparison. This destructive merge repeatedly takes the smaller head and attaches it to the result. A dummy head gives you somewhere to attach the first node. For lists of n and m nodes, this is O(n + m) time and O(1) extra space: it relinks existing nodes rather than creating new ones. Using <= keeps equal elements in their original order (a stable merge), which matters for merge sort. Merge is the core of merge sort on linked lists, which is the standard way to sort an n-node list in O(n log n) without random access (log n is log₂ n, the number of times n can be halved before reaching 1; it is how many levels of splitting there are): find the middle with fast/slow pointers, split, sort each half, merge. Several sorted lists Sequentially merging each new list into the whole accumulated result repeatedly revisits earlier nodes. Balanced pairwise rounds instead roughly halve the number of lists per round. With equal-length lists, the total merge-input sizes have the following costs: For eight lists of one thousand nodes each, sequential merge-input sizes total thirty-five thousand nodes; three balanced rounds total twenty-four thousand. Actual comparisons can be fewer because merge attaches an untouched suffix. For non-power-of-two list counts, balanced round counts are rounded up and some lists sit out a round. A heap of current heads also gives O(N log k), with N and k as defined above, but its mechanics belong to the later heaps module. Key takeaways Relink node-disjoint sorted inputs and attach an untouched suffix. Balanced pairwise rounds avoid repeatedly scanning an ever-growing result. Further reading Linked list — Wikipedia Merge sort — Wikipedia

t: Combine pointer patterns and preserve caller state
sum: Split, reverse and compare can test a palindrome with fixed extra space.
x: The previous units established reversal, middle finding, fixed gaps and merging. Combine these patterns without changing their assumptions: ordinary traversal and intersection search below require finite, acyclic inputs. In the complexity bounds n is the number of nodes being processed. Combining patterns Harder problems chain these together. Is the list a palindrome, in O(1) space? Find the middle (fast/slow), reverse the second half, compare the two halves node by node, then reverse it back to restore the list. Reorder 1,2,3,4,5 to 1,5,2,4,3? Find the middle, reverse the second half, then interleave the halves. Where do two lists intersect? Walk pointer A along list A then list B, and pointer B along B then A. Both travel the same total distance, so they arrive at the shared node together (or both reach None). Common bugs - Losing the rest of the list by overwriting next before saving it. - Checking fast.next.next without first checking fast.next, causing an AttributeError on short lists. - Comparing values (==) when you mean identity (is). - Forgetting to restore a list you mutated (for example in the palindrome check), surprising the caller. Intersection by switching routes Use node identity and finite acyclic inputs. Each pointer traverses its own list, then switches to the other head on the iteration after it reaches None. Equal total routes cancel any unequal prefix lengths. If there is no shared node, both eventually reach None together. For distinct prefixes of three and five nodes followed by four shared nodes, the pointers meet after thirteen loop iterations. One pointer traverses seven links to None, spends one iteration switching, then traverses the other five-node prefix. The other traverses nine links, switches, and takes three more. Equal-length inputs can meet earlier; count the explicit null transition when tracing this exact loop. For the palindrome pattern, split so the second half excludes an odd middle node, reverse that second half, compare corresponding values, and reverse it back even after a mismatch. Restoring the original links is part of the function’s contract, rather than an optional cosmetic step. An implementation must also reconnect any link it detached during splitting. Key takeaways Split, reverse and compare can test a palindrome with fixed extra space. Switching list heads equalises two intersection-search routes, including their null transition. Further reading Cycle detection — Wikipedia Linked list — Wikipedia

sum: LIFO uses the newest item first.
x: A stack is a collection where you can only touch the top. You add to the top (push) and remove from the top (pop), so the last thing in is the first thing out: LIFO. Think of a pile of plates. You can't pull one from the middle without disturbing the rest; you take the one on top. That restriction sounds limiting, but it is exactly the shape of a huge number of problems: anything nested, anything you need to undo in reverse order, and anything where the most recent item is the one that matters. The operations Operation What it does Cost --------- push(x) Put x on top O(1) amortised on a dynamic array pop() Remove and return the top O(1) amortised on a dynamic array peek() Return the top without removing O(1) is_empty() Any items left? O(1) Popping or peeking an empty stack is an error (a stack underflow). Pushing onto a full fixed-size stack is a stack overflow. Implementations On a dynamic array Keep the top at the end of the array, so push and pop never shift anything. In Python, a list already is a stack: Push and pop are amortised O(1) in CPython (growth or shrinking can resize the pointer array), and the list’s reference slots are contiguous, so this is fast in practice. Putting the top at the front (insert(0, x) and pop(0)) would make every operation O(n) on a stack of n items, because every other item shifts. Always grow stacks at the cheap end. On a linked list Push and pop at the head: Each operation uses O(1) pointer updates and there is never a resize, assuming constant-time node allocation and reclamation in the data-structure model. The cost is a heap allocation per push and worse cache behaviour. A linked stack is also the basis of the classic lock-free stack (the Treiber stack): push and pop retry compare-and-swap on the head until successful. Lock-free progress is not bounded per-thread latency, and safe memory reclamation/ABA handling requires care. In the standard libraries Python: use list. (collections.deque also works; queue.LifoQueue adds thread-safe blocking, which you only need between threads.) Java: use ArrayDeque via the Deque interface (push, pop, peek). The old java.util.Stack extends Vector, so it inherits synchronized methods and it exposes index-based methods that break the stack abstraction. Oracle's docs recommend Deque instead. C++: std::stack is an adaptor over another container, std::deque by default (you can choose std::vector). Key takeaways LIFO uses the newest item first. Place the top at an array end or linked-list head to avoid shifting. Further reading Stack (abstract data type) — Wikipedia) Deque — Java SE 21 API Using lists as stacks — Python tutorial

sum: A call frame retains the state needed after a nested call returns.
x: A stack serves the last added item first. Nested function calls and nested bracket pairs both require the most recent unfinished task to finish first. For the bracket checker n is the input character count; for call frames depth is the number of active nested calls. The call stack In the ordinary unoptimised call-stack model, each active call has a stack frame retaining its arguments, local state and a return address (where to continue when it finishes). Returning releases that frame. Registers, inlining, tail calls and runtime-managed frames can change the physical layout. This is why recursion uses O(depth) memory, and why unbounded recursion fails: Native thread stacks have implementation- and configuration-dependent limits. Excessive native recursion can exhaust them, often causing a fault; Java can raise StackOverflowError. Compiler optimizations and runtime-managed frames can change this simple model. CPython guards itself with a recursion limit (commonly 1,000 at startup), raising RecursionError; inspect sys.getrecursionlimit() for the actual process setting. Any recursive algorithm can be rewritten with an explicit stack on the heap, which can grow to gigabytes. Depth-first search on a large graph is the usual example (see the graphs module). Balanced brackets Is {[()()]} balanced? Is ([)]? Nesting means the most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed: a stack. Three ways to fail: A closer that doesn't match the top: ([)] fails at ), because the top is [. A closer with an empty stack: ()). Openers left over at the end: ((. For a string of n characters, that is O(n) time, and O(n) space in the worst case (a string of nothing but openers). Compilers, linters, JSON and XML parsers and your editor's bracket matching all use this idea. One bracket type? If there's only ( and ), you don't need the stack itself, just a counter: +1 for (, −1 for ), fail if it goes negative, and require 0 at the end. Key takeaways A call frame retains the state needed after a nested call returns. Each closer must match the newest unfinished opener. Further reading Call stack — Wikipedia Using lists as stacks — Python tutorial

t: Evaluate postfix expressions with a stack
sum: Push operands and replace the last two with each operator result.
x: A stack removes its newest value first. In postfix notation that value is the right operand of a binary operator, and the next value is the left operand. This is a teaching evaluator for numeric tokens, not a complete expression parser. Evaluating expressions Postfix (Reverse Polish notation) In postfix notation, operators come after their operands: 3 4 + means 3 + 4. There are no brackets and no precedence rules, and evaluation is a single stack pass: Number: push it. Operator: pop two values, apply, push the result.
