This teaching evaluator expects numeric tokens and binary operators. Missing operands raise IndexError; invalid numeric tokens raise ValueError. It uses floating-point arithmetic. Note the pop order: the first pop is the right operand. Getting it backwards breaks - and /. HP calculators, the PostScript language, the JVM's bytecode and CPython's bytecode interpreter are all stack machines that work this way. Trace the operand contract For the tokens 10 4 -, push ten, then four. The first pop is four, the right operand; the second is ten, the left operand. Subtracting in that order returns six. For 8 2 /, the same rule returns four. Reversing the order would return negative six and one quarter respectively. The example deliberately leaves several malformed-input errors visible. An operator with too few operands raises IndexError. A nonnumeric operand token raises ValueError during float conversion. Two leftover values raise the final malformed-expression error. Division by zero raises ZeroDivisionError. A production parser would catch and present these errors with token positions. Each token is processed once, so evaluation is linear in the token count when token conversion and arithmetic costs are treated as fixed. The stack can hold a linear number of operands. Very large numeric tokens, precision requirements and arbitrary-precision arithmetic need their own cost and representation model. Key takeaways Push operands and replace the last two with each operator result. The first popped value is the right operand. Further reading Reverse Polish notation — Wikipedia

sum: Hold operators until their operands and precedence permit output.
x: Postfix evaluation needs no operator-precedence rule because each operator follows its operands. To convert ordinary infix text, keep a separate stack of pending operators while emitting the operand order. The conversion trace below concerns expression tokens, not Python source. Infix to postfix: the shunting-yard algorithm Humans write infix (3 + 4 2). Edsger Dijkstra's shunting-yard algorithm converts it to postfix using a stack of pending operators: Operand: send straight to the output. (: push. ): pop operators to the output until the matching (; discard both brackets. Operator o: while the top of the stack is an operator with higher precedence, or equal precedence and o is left-associative, pop it to the output. Then push o. At the end, pop everything left. The result, 3 4 2 +, evaluates to 11, respecting precedence. Associativity matters too: a - b - c becomes a b - c - (left to right), while exponentiation is right-associative, so 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 becomes 2 3 2 ^ ^. Grouping from the right gives a very different answer from grouping from the left: Python's follows the same convention: 2 3 2 == 512. Equal precedence is the deciding test Consider three symbolic operand tokens separated by subtraction. The second subtraction must finish the first subtraction before starting its own right operand. By contrast, a right-associative exponent operator leaves an equal-precedence exponent pending until the right-hand exponent is available. The conversion handles each token once and each operator is pushed and popped at most once. This gives linear total stack work in the token count, assuming fixed-time token classification. The displayed rules describe binary operators; unary minus, functions and argument separators require additional grammar rules. Key takeaways Hold operators until their operands and precedence permit output. Equal precedence pops for left associativity but waits for right associativity. Further reading Shunting yard algorithm — Wikipedia Reverse Polish notation — Wikipedia

sum: Unresolved indices wait until a later value supplies their answer.
x: The preceding stack units used last-in, first-out storage. Here the stack additionally keeps unresolved candidates in nonincreasing value order. In every bound n is the number of input values; equal values may remain together because only a strictly larger value answers the query. The monotonic stack A monotonic stack keeps its contents in sorted order (all increasing or all decreasing) by popping anything that would break the order before each push. It solves "for each element, find the nearest element to the left or right that is bigger (or smaller)" in O(n). Next greater element: for each value, find the first larger value to its right. The stack holds indices still waiting for a bigger value. When x arrives, every waiting element smaller than x has found its answer and is popped. There's a while inside a for, but for n input values it's still O(n). Instead of asking how long one while loop can run, count the work over the whole run: For the five values [2, 1, 2, 4, 3], five pushes, three pops and five loop exits give thirteen counted events, within the fifteen-event bound. One step can pop many items, but then other steps pop none. This is an amortised argument, like dynamic array growth. The same pattern answers "how many days until a warmer temperature", stock span problems and the largest rectangle in a histogram. Other uses Undo in editors: push each action; undo pops it. Redo is a second stack. Browser back button: a stack of visited pages. Backtracking (maze solving, Sudoku): push choices, pop to retreat. Parsers: compilers use a stack to track nested constructs. Key takeaways Unresolved indices wait until a later value supplies their answer. Count pushes and pops over the complete run rather than multiplying nested-loop bounds. Further reading Stack (abstract data type) — Wikipedia)

t: FIFO queues and the cost of front shifting
sum: A queue serves arrivals in their original order.
x: A queue is a line at a shop: people join at the back and are served from the front. The first one in is the first one out: FIFO. Where a stack serves the most recent arrival, a queue serves the one that has waited longest. Queues are everywhere in real systems. Print jobs, network packets in a router, tasks waiting for a thread pool, messages in broker partitions or queue services, keystrokes waiting for your program to read them: all queues. Inside algorithms, the queue is what makes breadth-first search explore nearest-first. The operations Operation What it does Target cost --------- enqueue(x) Add x at the back O(1) dequeue() Remove from the front O(1) peek() Look at the front O(1) is_empty() Anything waiting? O(1) The wrong way: a plain list The obvious Python queue is a list with append and pop(0): pop(0) shifts every remaining element one slot left. Draining a queue of n items this way moves n − 1 elements on the first dequeue, n − 2 on the next, and so on down to 0: For 100,000 items that is about 100,000² / 2 = 5 billion moves; a proper queue would do 100,000 cheap operations. That is O(n²) for the whole drain, or O(n) per dequeue. The bug is invisible in tests with 10 items and catastrophic in production with a million. Two structures fix it: a linked list with head and tail pointers (dequeue at the head, enqueue at the tail, both O(1)), or, usually better, a circular buffer. Key takeaways A queue serves arrivals in their original order. Repeated list-front removal shifts a quadratic total of elements. Further reading collections.deque — Python docs ArrayDeque — Java SE 21 API

t: Ring-buffer indices and constant pointer work
sum: Wrap the write position after the physical array end.
x: FIFO removal should advance a front position rather than shift all waiting elements. A fixed ring keeps a positive capacity and a live count. The example assumes single-threaded access; adding concurrent producers or consumers needs a separate synchronisation protocol. Circular buffers A circular buffer (ring buffer) is a fixed array whose end wraps round to its start. Track the index of the front (head) and the number of items (count). When the buffer is not full, the next free slot at the back is count places after head, wrapping round to slot 0 when it runs off the end: With capacity 4, head 2 and count 1, the next item goes in (2 + 1) mod 4 = slot 3; the one after goes in (2 + 2) mod 4 = slot 0, back at the start. In Python this is (head + count) % capacity. Dequeuing just advances head. Nothing shifts. Key takeaways Wrap the write position after the physical array end. Clear a dequeued slot so its old object need not stay alive. Further reading Circular buffer — Wikipedia

t: Full ring buffers and bounded overload
sum: A count, reserved slot or monotonic counters distinguishes full from empty.
x: The preceding unit implemented a ring with a count. Alternative representations must still distinguish its full and empty states. This unit connects capacity policy to overload: accepting work faster than it can be completed builds a backlog regardless of how cheap an enqueue is. Full or empty? If you store head and tail indices instead of a count, head == tail is ambiguous: it is true both when the buffer is empty and when it is full. The usual fixes: Keep a count (as above). Waste one slot: declare the buffer full when (tail + 1) % cap == head, so a full buffer holds one fewer item than the physical slot count and head == tail can only mean empty. Use ever-increasing head and tail counters and compare tail - head with the capacity, taking indices % cap only when touching the array. Use nonnegative logical counters for this model; fixed-width machine counters need an explicit wraparound and overflow protocol. Option 3 with a power-of-two capacity lets you replace % cap with a cheap bit mask & (cap - 1). When the capacity is a power of two, the remainder is just the lowest bits of the counter, and a bitwise AND keeps exactly those bits: Worked through in binary: 13 is 1101 and 7 is 0111, so the AND keeps 0101, which is 5, the same as 13 mod 8. With a capacity that isn't a power of two, such as 6, the trick fails: 13 mod 6 = 1 but the bitwise result from 13 and 5 is 5. The Linux kernel's kfifo works this way. Growing and bounding A ring buffer can grow like a dynamic array: allocate double the space and copy the items across in queue order, "unwrapping" them. Java ArrayDeque also grows a circular array, but OpenJDK 21 roughly doubles small buffers and grows larger ones by about 50%, with additional adjustments for required capacity. Often you don't want it to grow. A bounded queue configured to block or reject producers provides backpressure: when consumers fall behind, producers block or are refused, instead of memory growing until the process dies. Audio drivers, network card receive rings and high-throughput designs like the LMAX Disruptor all use fixed-size rings. Arrival rate versus service rate With five thousand arrivals and one thousand completions per second, an unbounded queue accumulates four thousand extra items every second. After ten minutes it holds about 2.4 million items if the rates stay constant and it started empty. A new item behind that backlog waits about forty minutes at the same consumer rate. Blocking or rejecting producers at a finite capacity prevents unlimited queue storage, but it does not make consumers faster. Improving throughput requires more service capacity, batching, or reducing accepted work. Storing backlog on disk changes the storage limit and durability policy rather than the basic rate imbalance. Key takeaways A count, reserved slot or monotonic counters distinguishes full from empty. A bound exposes overload but does not increase consumer throughput. Further reading Circular buffer — Wikipedia ArrayDeque — Java SE 21 API Linux — circular-buffer conventions

t: Deques, block layouts and bounded histories
sum: A deque supports both ends; its middle-access cost depends on implementation.
x: A queue adds at one end and removes at the other. A deque allows either operation at either end. Here n is the number of stored items; bounds concern container operations, excluding user-defined finalisers or other work triggered by dropping an object. Deques: both ends A deque (double-ended queue, pronounced "deck") supports O(1) insertion and removal at both ends. It can act as a stack, a queue, or both at once. For a deque holding n items: Python collections.deque Cost ------ append(x), appendleft(x) O(1) pop(), popleft() O(1) d[0], d[-1] O(1) d[i] in the middle O(n) How it's built varies: CPython's deque is a doubly linked list of fixed-size blocks (64 items each), so both ends are O(1) with no resizing, and access near the middle is O(n). Its docs note that appends and pops from either end are thread-safe. Java's ArrayDeque is a growable circular array. It's the recommended general-purpose queue and stack in Java, and usually faster than LinkedList. C++'s std::deque uses an array of pointers to fixed-size chunks. It offers O(1) indexing as well as O(1) pushes at both ends. Bounded deques deque(maxlen=n) keeps only the most recent n items. Appending to a full one silently discards an item from the opposite end. It's perfect for "the last 100 log lines" or a moving average. A bounded history differs from a bounded work queue A deque with a positive maxlen is an eviction policy: a full append removes the oldest item at the opposite end. It does not wait for a consumer to make room. A Queue with maxsize is a coordination policy: a blocking put waits when the queue is full. For the five successive values one through five and a three-item history, the retained values are three, four and five. Adding zero at the left then discards five at the right, leaving zero, three and four. Choose maxlen for recent context that may be discarded, rather than work items that must all be processed. Thread-safe individual deque appends and pops do not make a multi-step check-then-pop protocol atomic. Between checking nonemptiness and popping, another thread could remove the last item. Use a coordinating queue or an explicit lock when several operations form one protocol. Key takeaways A deque supports both ends; its middle-access cost depends on implementation. A maxlen history evicts from the opposite end instead of blocking producers. Further reading Double-ended queue — Wikipedia collections.deque — Python docs ArrayDeque — Java SE 21 API

t: A FIFO frontier finds unweighted distances
sum: Enqueue newly discovered nodes once and record their distance immediately.
x: A FIFO queue processes older discoveries before newer ones. That order gives shortest edge-count distances in an unweighted graph. Use the deque import shown below; each neighbour in the example must also be a key in the adjacency mapping. Queues in BFS Breadth-first search explores a graph in rings: all nodes one edge away, then two, then three. A queue enforces exactly that order, because nodes discovered earlier (closer) are processed before nodes discovered later (further). In an unweighted graph, dist is the shortest number of edges from start to every reachable node. Replacing the queue with a stack removes the shortest-path guarantee. With discovery marked on push, it is a LIFO traversal but does not necessarily reproduce recursive DFS discovery/parent order; standard DFS uses an appropriate marking or iterator-stack strategy. Graph traversal gets a full treatment in the graphs module. Mark nodes when you enqueue them Mark a node as seen when it's added to the queue, not when it's removed. Otherwise the same node can be enqueued many times by different neighbours, blowing up time and memory on dense graphs. Two routes to the same node Suppose A discovers B and C; both lead to D, while C also leads to E. D and E both lead to F. Starting at A, the queue processes A, B, C, D, E, F when neighbours are listed in that order. D is marked when B enqueues it, so C does not enqueue it again. F is similarly discovered once. Its shortest distance is three edges: the queue has processed every one-edge and two-edge discovery before a three-edge node can be removed. This claim depends on equal edge cost. A weighted edge cannot be represented merely by one queue step; weighted shortest paths require another strategy. The returned mapping covers only reachable nodes, and a missing adjacency key raises KeyError in this compact teaching implementation. Graph representation, traversal complexity and weighted shortest paths are explored in later modules. Key takeaways Enqueue newly discovered nodes once and record their distance immediately. FIFO exploration processes reachable nodes in nondecreasing unweighted distance. Further reading collections.deque — Python docs Breadth-first search — Wikipedia

t: Sliding-window maxima with a monotonic deque
sum: Remove dominated candidates at the back and expired indices at the front.
x: Use collections.deque from the preceding units. Here n is the input array length and k is a positive window size. The algorithm keeps only candidates that could still become a future maximum, while recording their indices so expiry is testable. Monotonic deques: sliding window maximum Given an array of n numbers and a window size k, find the maximum of every run of k consecutive numbers (each run is a sliding window). Recomputing each window from scratch looks at k numbers for each of about n windows, O(nk). A monotonic deque does it in O(n). Keep indices in the deque with their values decreasing from front to back. The front is always the current window's maximum. Values are removed from the back when a bigger value arrives (they're dominated: older and smaller) and from the front when they slide out of the window. Each index enters and leaves once, so the whole run is O(n), the same amortised argument as the monotonic stack. Why discarding a candidate is safe For a three-value window over [4, 2, 12, 3, 8, 1], twelve removes the older four and two from the back. They are smaller and expire earlier, so neither can beat twelve in a future window that still contains them. Eight later removes three, but twelve stays at the front until its index leaves the window. Only then does eight become the maximum. The four answers are twelve, twelve, twelve and eight. Equal values use the newer index because it remains eligible longer. The function returns an empty result for empty input or when the requested positive window exceeds the input length: no complete window exists. It rejects zero and negative sizes. Python bool is an int subclass, so True acts like a window of one under this validator. The input must support length, indexing and value comparisons; NaN or a non-total comparison order needs a separately defined policy. Key takeaways Remove dominated candidates at the back and expired indices at the front. Each index enters and leaves at most once. Further reading collections.deque — Python docs

t: Priority queues, heap costs and tie-breaking
sum: A heap serves the best key rather than the earliest arrival.
x: A FIFO queue serves by arrival time. A priority queue instead serves by an ordering key. Here n is the number of queued items, and the complexity model assumes constant-time key comparisons; expensive comparisons add their own cost. Priority queues Sometimes "first come, first served" is wrong. An emergency department treats the most urgent patient first; an OS scheduler runs the highest-priority thread. A priority queue always removes the item with the best priority (smallest or largest key), whenever it arrived. For a queue holding n items, simple implementations make one operation slow. For the sorted-array row, keep descending order and remove the minimum at the end without shifting; insertion bounds are amortised over backing growth. In the table, log n means log₂ n, the number of times n can be halved before reaching 1: about 20 for a million items, so O(log n) operations stay cheap even for huge queues. Implementation insert remove-min --------- Unsorted array O(1) O(n) Sorted array O(n) O(1) Binary heap O(log n) O(log n) The binary heap balances both, and also gives O(1) peek and O(n) construction from an existing list. How it works (a tree packed into an array) is covered in the heaps module; for now, use the library. Practical details: The traditional heapq functions use a min-heap on a list. Python 3.14 adds public max-heap functions such as heappush_max and heappop_max; on older versions, negate numeric keys. With (priority, item) tuples, equal priorities fall back to comparing the items, which fails with a TypeError for dicts and other non-comparable objects (and, for comparable items, silently orders ties by the item rather than by arrival). Add a counter: (priority, next(counter), item). Java's PriorityQueue is also a min-heap by default; pass a Comparator for other orders. Its iterator does not visit items in priority order. Uses include Dijkstra's shortest paths, event-driven simulations, schedulers, merging k sorted lists and keeping the top k items. Model a complete insert-and-drain workload Assume random insertion ranks, constant-time key comparisons, and an initially empty descending sorted array. Each insertion shifts roughly half the items already stored. A heap instead visits a logarithmic number of tree levels per operation. These are different abstract operations, so their ratio is not a measured speedup. A heap pop may compare children and the replacement item at each level; the model does not count every comparison exactly. Bulk heapify is linear and changes the workload if all items are available before processing. Key takeaways A heap serves the best key rather than the earliest arrival. Add a unique sequence counter when payloads cannot be compared. Further reading heapq — Python docs PriorityQueue — Java SE 21 API

t: Hash maps and sets: lookup interfaces
sum: A map associates a value with a key; a set remembers only whether a key is present.
x: A map associates a value with a key; a set remembers only whether a key is present. Before using either, decide whether the query is exact membership or an ordered search. Suppose you have a list of a million customer IDs and you need to check, for each of a million incoming orders, whether the customer exists. Scanning the list each time costs up to a million comparisons per order: a million orders times a million comparisons is around 10¹² (a million million) operations in total. Sorting the list and binary searching cuts each check to about 20 comparisons, because each comparison halves the range still to search and 2²⁰ is about a million. A hash table does better still: on average, each check takes a constant number of steps, no matter how many IDs you store. This makes hash maps and sets useful for many everyday lookup tasks. The idea in one picture The full hash in the drawing is illustrative, not a claim about Python’s process-dependent string hash. Its remainder after division by eight is one. A hash table is an array of hash buckets (or slots). To store a key, you run it through a hash function that turns it into an integer, then reduce that integer to an array index. To look the key up later, you hash it again, jump straight to the same index and check whether it is there. Collision handling can still scan candidates; expected constant work relies on well-distributed hashes, bounded load and constant-cost key operations. Two different keys can land on the same index. That is a hash collision, and every hash table needs a strategy for it (Collision resolution). As long as collisions are rare, each bucket holds about one key and operations stay fast. The interface There are two flavours. A hash map (dictionary, associative array) stores key → value pairs. In the table below, n is the number of keys stored, and O(1) means "a constant number of steps, however large n gets" (Big-O notation, from the Complexity module): Operation Python Average --------- Insert / update d[k] = v O(1) Look up d[k], d.get(k) O(1) Membership k in d O(1) Delete del d[k] O(1) Iterate for k in d O(n) for compact state; retained holes can add work A hash set stores keys only, and answers "have I seen this?": Sets also support set union (a b), set intersection (a & b) and set difference (a - b). An intersection iterates over the smaller set and probes the larger one, so on average its cost grows with the size of the smaller set only: intersecting a 10-item set with a million-item set takes about 10 lookups. Other languages have the same pair: Java's HashMap / HashSet, C++'s std::unordered_map / std::unordered_set and Go's built-in map. JavaScript's Map / Set offer similar interfaces, but the ECMAScript specification only requires average sublinear access (faster than scanning everything), not a particular hash-table representation. Python dicts remember insertion order Since Python 3.7, iterating over a dict returns keys in the order they were first inserted. This is a language guarantee, not an accident. Sets make no such promise: their iteration order depends on the hashes. The constructor dict.fromkeys makes each supplied value a key. Repeated values update an existing entry without moving its original insertion position. Converting the resulting dictionary to a list therefore gives the distinct values in first-appearance order; it does not sort them. This technique is useful when an API requires deduplication while preserving input order. Key takeaways A map stores key–value pairs; a set stores membership. Exact-key access is fast on average under well-distributed hashes and bounded-cost keys. Dict iteration preserves insertion order; sets offer no such ordering promise. Further reading Time complexity of Python operations — Python wiki Mapping types: dict — Python docs

sum: Here n counts stored keys and m counts buckets.
x: Here n counts stored keys and m counts buckets. Separate the cost of hashing and comparing a key, the collision work, and the occasional resize: constant average lookup is a conditional statement, not a latency guarantee. Average case versus worst case The O(1) figure is an average, and it rests on an assumption: the hash function spreads keys roughly evenly across buckets. How full a table is matters more than how big it is. The load factor measures that fullness: the average number of keys per bucket. Tables keep α below a fixed limit (Java uses 0.75, Python's dict about 2/3) by growing the array when it fills up. With α held below a constant, the expected work per operation is constant, whether the table holds ten keys or ten million. This relies on the hash function spreading keys evenly; it says nothing about a bad hash or a deliberate attack. The worst case is very different. If every key hashes to the same bucket, a list-chained table degenerates into one long chain; an unsuccessful lookup or a hit at the end may scan all n keys: That makes a lookup O(n). Inserting n keys is worse, because each new key is first compared with every key already in the chain (to check it is not a duplicate): For 1,000 keys that is half a million comparisons where a good hash needs about 1,000 steps. This happens in practice when: the hash function is poor for your data (for example, hashing integers that are all multiples of the table size), or an attacker deliberately sends keys that collide, a hash flooding attack (Hash flooding and runtime randomisation). There is also an occasional slow insert: when the table grows, every key is re-inserted into a bigger array, which costs O(n). Spread over all the inserts this averages out to O(1) per insert, which is called amortised O(1) (Rehashing and geometric growth). What "O(1) average" really means It is the expected cost under a reasonable hash function, ignoring the occasional resize. Hashing the key itself is not free: computing an uncached hash of a string of L characters ordinarily scans all L of them, so it costs O(L). CPython caches string hashes, and identity shortcuts can avoid equality scans; a repeated lookup using the same long string need not rescan it. Key takeaways Load factor measures keys per bucket rather than total table size. Colliding chains can make each operation linear and a sequence of inserts quadratic. Hash computation, equality and resizing are separate parts of the cost model. Further reading Hash table — Wikipedia Time complexity of Python operations — Python wiki

sum: The equality contract determines which entries a dictionary treats as the same key.
x: The equality contract determines which entries a dictionary treats as the same key. A key is not safe merely because a call to hash succeeds: its equality-relevant state must also remain stable while stored. Keys must be hashable A hash table finds a key by recomputing its hash. If a key's hash could change after insertion, the table would look in the wrong bucket and the entry would be lost. So the contract is: If a == b, then hash(a) == hash(b). Equal keys must land in the same bucket. A key's hash and equality-relevant state must stay stable while it is in the table. The reverse of rule 1 is not required: unequal keys may share a hash. That is just a collision. In Python, immutable built-ins (int, str, tuple of hashables, frozenset) are hashable. The built-ins list, dict and set are not hashable. Mutability alone is not the general test: custom mutable objects can use stable identity equality/hashing, and an immutable class can disable hashing: Equal keys collapse Because 1 == 1.0 == True in Python, they are the same dict key. {1: "a", True: "b"} gives {1: "b"}: the second assignment updates the value, keeping the first key object. If you define __eq__ on your own class, Python sets __hash__ to None, making instances unhashable, unless you also define __hash__. In Java, overriding equals without hashCode is a classic bug: two equal objects can have different hashes, causing lookup to miss even if bucket reduction happens to coincide. Designing a key safely Separate an object’s identity from its current contents. A mutable customer record can be stored as a value while its stable customer ID is the key. Updating the record’s address then leaves the index intact. Using all mutable fields as the key makes every change an index-maintenance operation instead. For a custom value object, choose the same fields for equality and hashing. Two points considered equal by their coordinates must hash from those coordinates as well. If coordinates can change, freeze the key object or remove it before changing the fields and reinsert it afterwards. Defining a hash from one field and equality from another does not satisfy the contract. A tuple is not automatically a safe key just because the outer container is immutable. Its elements must also be hashable; a tuple containing a list fails when hashed. A frozenset, unlike a set, is immutable and hashable. Neither object promises that a bad custom element implementation becomes sound merely by being wrapped. The two assignments in the example intentionally demonstrate an exception. They are not a successful programme that stores both entries: the tuple entry is inserted, then the list-key assignment raises TypeError and execution stops unless the caller handles it. Key takeaways Equal keys must have equal hashes; unequal keys may collide. Hash and equality-relevant state must remain stable while a key is stored. Immutable containers require hashable elements; mutability alone is not the general test. Further reading Python 3.14 data model: hashing

sum: Once key equality is sound, choose a representation from the actual query.
x: Once key equality is sound, choose a representation from the actual query. A prebuilt membership index can save repeated scans, while range queries and small dense integer domains often need a different structure. When to reach for a hash map or set Most uses fall into three patterns. 1. Lookups by key Replace a repeated linear search with one O(n) build (n being the number of items you index) and O(1) average lookups. For m orders and n users (here m counts orders, not buckets) this is O(n + m), instead of O(n × m) with a nested loop. With 10,000 users and 10,000 orders that is about 20,000 steps instead of 100 million. 2. Deduplication and "seen before?" Checking x in some_list inside a loop is a common hidden O(n²): for n items, each of the n checks can scan up to n list entries. Changing the list to a set is often the single biggest speed-up available in a slow script. 3. Counting Counter is a dict subclass. The hand-written version is counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1. A related tool, defaultdict(list), groups items by key without checking whether the key exists first. When not to use one Hash tables are fast at exact-match lookups and nothing else. Reach for something different when: You need order or ranges. "All keys between 100 and 200", "the smallest key" or "the next key after x" need a sorted structure: a balanced binary search tree (Java's TreeMap, O(log n) per operation for n keys, about 20 steps for a million keys), a B-tree in a database, or a sorted array with binary search. A hash table would have to scan everything. Keys are small dense integers. If keys are 0 to 999, a plain array avoids hashing and often reduces overhead; actual performance depends on representation and workload. Memory is tight. Hash tables keep spare empty slots and per-entry overhead. For example, on a 64-bit CPython 3.14 build, sys.getsizeof(list(range(1_000_000))) is about 8 MB and sys.getsizeof(set(range(1_000_000))) about 33.6 MB, excluding integer objects. These sizes are build- and construction-dependent. You need guaranteed worst-case latency. A resize or a burst of collisions can make one operation take far longer than usual. Need Use ------ Exact lookup, membership Hash map / set Sorted order, range query Balanced BST, B-tree Keys are 0..n Plain array Min or max repeatedly Heap Key takeaways Build a membership index once to avoid repeated list scans. Use sorted structures for ordered range queries and direct arrays for dense integer domains. Account for spare slots, representation overhead and latency spikes when choosing a table. Further reading Time complexity of Python operations — Python wiki collections: Counter and defaultdict — Python docs

sum: A full hash and a bucket index are different things.
x: A full hash and a bucket index are different things. Even a valid hash can perform badly if reducing it to a slot preserves patterns in the input. A hash table is only as good as its hash function. Feed it keys that the function spreads evenly and every bucket holds about one key. Feed it keys that the function clumps together and the table turns into a slow list. This lesson covers what "good" means, the classic ways to build a hash, and how languages responded differently to hash-flooding attacks after 2011. What a table hash needs A hash function maps a key of any size to a fixed-size integer. For a hash table it must be: Deterministic. The same key always gives the same hash, at least within one run of the program. Consistent with equality. If a == b, then hash(a) == hash(b). Uniform. Keys spread evenly over the output range, including the patterned keys real programs produce: sequential IDs, multiples of 1,000, strings sharing a long prefix. Fast. It runs on every lookup, so a few nanoseconds matters. A good hash also has the avalanche property: flipping one input bit flips about half the output bits. That stops similar keys (user1, user2) landing in nearby slots. Table hashes are not cryptographic hashes. SHA-256 is designed to make finding two inputs with the same output computationally infeasible, and pays for that in speed. A table only needs a good spread, so it uses fast non-cryptographic functions such as MurmurHash, xxHash or wyhash, or a keyed function such as SipHash when attackers control the keys (see below). From hash to bucket: the division method The simplest way to turn an integer key into one of m buckets is to divide by m and keep the remainder: It is fast, but the choice of m matters enormously. Take keys that are all multiples of 8 (common for memory addresses and aligned sizes): With sixteen buckets, the keys use only 2 of 16 buckets. With thirteen buckets, they spread over 8 different buckets. When m is a power of two (2, 4, 8, 16, …), reducing the integer key modulo the bucket count just keeps the key’s low bits: 40 is 101000 in binary, and the remainder after division by sixteen is eight, its last four bits, 1000. So any pattern in the low bits goes straight into the bucket index. The textbook advice is to choose m as a prime not close to a power of two. Key takeaways Hashing must respect equality and remain deterministic for the table’s lifetime. Power-of-two remainder selection exposes patterns in low bits. A cryptographic collision guarantee is different from useful bucket distribution. Further reading Hash function — Wikipedia

sum: Multiplication hashing separates hash mixing from the choice of table size.
x: Multiplication hashing separates hash mixing from the choice of table size. The example below uses a fixed 32-bit calculation; it improves one patterned input without proving that every input distributes well. The multiplication method Primes are awkward: the table cannot double neatly, and a variable divisor may require division; compilers can optimise division by known constants. The multiplication method lets m be a power of two. Multiply the key by a constant, keep only the part after the decimal point, and scale that up to the table size: Because every key's fraction is scrambled by the multiplication, the size of the table no longer has to be prime. The method still assumes keys are integers; other keys (strings, tuples) are first turned into integers. In integer arithmetic this becomes Fibonacci hashing: multiply by a large odd constant, keep the low 32 bits of the product, and use the top few of those bits as the bucket index (4 bits for a 16-bucket table): The same calculation in Python, where % is mod and >> shifts bits right (dividing by a power of two and rounding down): For a table of 2⁴ = 16 buckets, the aligned keys eight, sixteen, twenty-four, thirty-two, forty, forty-eight, fifty-six and sixty-four map to 15, 14, 13, 12, 11, 10, 9, 8: all different. This fixed 32-bit mapping improves this example; it is not a universal collision or avalanche guarantee. Inputs differing by 2³² (about 4.3 billion) collide because the product is reduced modulo 2³². Key takeaways Multiplication uses a fractional product to choose a bucket. The fixed-width version keeps a word-sized product then extracts high index bits. The worked alignment example does not guarantee good distribution for every key set. Further reading Hash function — Wikipedia

sum: A string hash must preserve enough position information to avoid systematic anagram collisions.
x: A string hash must preserve enough position information to avoid systematic anagram collisions. We build the weighted sum incrementally, retaining the same result with only one running accumulator. Hashing strings: polynomial hashes A string is a sequence of characters, and each character has a numeric code (a is 97 in ASCII and Unicode). A naive hash adds the character codes, but then every anagram collides: "listen" and "silent" both sum to 655. A polynomial hash fixes this by weighting each position by a different power of a base, so character order affects the result without guaranteeing distinct totals: Position weights distinguish many rearrangements, including the examples here, but do not guarantee distinct hashes for every permutation. A remainder has only finitely many possible values. Even before reduction, anagrams can share a weighted total: base thirty-one hashes both BAa and AaB to sixty-five thousand five hundred and thirty-eight. Their code-point sequences are (66, 65, 97) and (65, 97, 66), so these position weights do not uniquely encode every rearrangement. Hash matches therefore remain candidates for equality checks. Computed with Horner's rule, it needs one multiply and one add per character: Java's String.hashCode uses base 31 over UTF-16 code units, with signed 32-bit overflow instead of a prime modulus. Python's ord gives Unicode code points, so the code above differs from Java for supplementary characters (such as emoji) even with a modulus of 2³². Key takeaways Position-dependent weights avoid systematic anagram collisions. Horner’s rule accumulates a weighted hash in one pass. Python code points and Java UTF-16 code units differ for supplementary characters. Further reading String hashing — cp-algorithms

t: Rolling string hashes and collision risk
sum: A rolling hash reuses a previous window hash rather than rescanning every character.
x: A rolling hash reuses a previous window hash rather than rescanning every character. Here the base is 31 and the window contains three characters. The outgoing code is ninety-seven, the incoming code one hundred, and the old hash ninety-six thousand three hundred and fifty-four, corresponding to abc. Fixed-width arithmetic is assumed in the constant-time update claim. Rolling a fixed-length window Polynomial hashes also roll: you can slide a fixed-length window along a string, removing the leftmost character and adding a new one with a constant number of arithmetic operations. With fixed-width arithmetic and the outgoing weight precomputed, this is O(1), independent of the window length: With a modulus M, every step is also reduced mod M (adding M first if the subtraction went negative). That is the idea behind the Rabin–Karp substring search, which compares a pattern's hash with every window of a text in expected linear time. Small moduli collide sooner than you think With a 10⁹-sized modulus, 100,000 strings almost certainly contain a collision. If you compare strings by hash alone, use a 64-bit modulus or two independent hashes, and confirm matches with a real comparison. The estimate comes from the birthday paradox: the number of pairs of strings grows with the square of the number of strings, so collisions appear long before the hash values run out. Assuming each string's hash behaves like an independent, uniformly random value: The approximation is good when n is much smaller than M. Real hashes are not perfectly random, and patterned inputs can do worse. Key takeaways A rolling update removes the outgoing weight, shifts remaining weights and adds the incoming code. Constant update cost assumes fixed-width arithmetic and a precomputed outgoing weight. Collision risk grows with the number of pairs; confirm matching hashes with real comparisons. Further reading String hashing — cp-algorithms

sum: Randomising the choice of hash function gives a probabilistic guarantee for keys chosen independently of that choice.
x: Randomising the choice of hash function gives a probabilistic guarantee for keys chosen independently of that choice. It does not promise that every chosen function has short chains on every input. Universal hashing Any fixed hash function has a bad input. There are infinitely many keys and only m buckets (m being the table size), so infinitely many keys share some bucket. This proves colliding inputs exist; it does not prove they can be found efficiently. Universal hashing defends against this by choosing the function at random from a family (a large set of possible hash functions) when the table is created. A family is universal if, for any two distinct keys, a randomly chosen member collides on them no more often than a truly random bucket choice would: The probability is over the random choice of h, not over the keys. For a fixed key set chosen independently of the random function, these pairwise bounds give short chains on average while the load factor stays bounded. The classic Carter–Wegman family works for integer keys smaller than a chosen prime: Each choice of a and b is a different hash function, so the family has the product of the prime and one less than the prime as its member count. The expectation is over your random choice, not over the keys, so it covers a fixed adversarial key set chosen before the random function. Adaptive queries need a separate adversary analysis; keeping a and b secret alone is not that proof. Key takeaways The probability is over the random function choice, not the keys. Pairwise collision bounds apply to distinct keys chosen independently of the function. An adaptive adversary requires a separate analysis. Further reading Universal hashing — Wikipedia

sum: When a client chooses keys, collisions become a security and latency concern.
x: When a client chooses keys, collisions become a security and latency concern. A public deterministic table hash offers different protection from a keyed hash or a randomly sampled universal family. Hash flooding attacks In 2003, Crosby and Wallach showed that you could slow a server to a crawl by sending keys that all collide in its hash table: an algorithmic complexity attack. Inserting n colliding keys costs O(n²), because each new key is compared with every key already in its chain: 50,000 colliding keys need about 1.25 billion comparisons. In December 2011, at the 28C3 conference, Alexander Klink and Julian Wälde showed it working against PHP, Java, Python, Ruby and ASP.NET web stacks. Web frameworks parse POST parameters into a hash table automatically, so a single request could carry tens of thousands of colliding parameter names. Java's string hash made colliding keys trivial to generate: Any string built from these two blocks collides with every other one of the same length: "AaAa", "AaBB", "BBAa" and "BBBB" all hash to 2,031,744. Thirty blocks gives 2³⁰ (about a billion) colliding keys. Languages responded in several ways: Defence Example ------ Random seed per process Python 3.3+, Ruby, Perl Keyed hash function SipHash: Python, Rust Cap request parameters PHP max_input_vars Tree-shaped buckets Java 8 HashMap SipHash (Aumasson and Bernstein, 2012) is a fast keyed function designed for exactly this job: without the secret 128-bit key, predicting collisions without the secret key is intended to be computationally difficult. Python switched to it for str and bytes in 3.4 (PEP 456), and common CPython builds default to SipHash-1-3 from 3.11; inspect sys.hash_info.algorithm for the actual build. Rust's default HashMap hasher is also SipHash-1-3. Consequences of randomisation In Python, hash("abc") differs between runs unless you set the PYTHONHASHSEED environment variable. Never store hash() results in files or send them between processes. Integers are not randomised. CPython hashes an integer by taking its remainder modulo a fixed prime, read from sys.hash_info.modulus: One special case: the result −1 is replaced by −2, because −1 signals an error inside CPython. So hash(-1) == -2, and hash(-1) == hash(-2). Key takeaways Public deterministic hashes can let attackers construct expensive collision chains. Keyed hashing and per-process randomisation make predicting collisions harder. Python integer hashes remain deterministic, and built-in hash results are unsuitable for persisted placement. Further reading Denial of Service via Algorithmic Complexity Attacks (Crosby and Wallach, USENIX Security 2003) PEP 456: Secure and interchangeable hash algorithm

t: Hash placement when server counts change
sum: This unit applies bucket reduction to server placement.
x: This unit applies bucket reduction to server placement. The issue is not a bad collision rate: changing the divisor can remap data even when the original hash is excellent. Hashing in distributed systems Hashing also decides which server stores a key in a sharded cache or database. The naive rule reduces the key’s stable full hash modulo the server count to select a server. It works until N changes, because the remainder changes for most keys: Doubling N moves about half the keys. Either way a large share of a cache is invalidated at once, which is why distributed systems use consistent hashing, which ideally moves the new server’s balanced share of keys. That is covered in the System Design subject. Why the remapping matters Consider cached customer profiles placed across ten numbered servers. When an eleventh server is added, recomputing a remainder can direct a request to a different server even if the profile’s full hash and contents never changed. The old copy may still be present on its former server, but the new lookup rule will not visit it. A cache must then refill or migrate the entry; a database must coordinate movement and ownership more carefully. Consistent hashing instead assigns positions on a ring. Adding an owner changes only the intervals it takes over. The ideal movement fraction assumes balanced ownership and uniformly distributed keys; finite rings, skewed workloads and replication can change the amount of data or traffic that moves. It is not a guarantee that every physical server receives exactly an equal share. Do not confuse remapping with hash randomisation. A per-process string hash is unsuitable as a stable cross-process placement hash: the clients and servers must agree on the same hash and placement configuration. A stable distributed hash can still need a separate defence if untrusted clients deliberately choose hot keys. This unit concerns placement changes, while the preceding flooding unit concerns pathological collision work. Key takeaways Changing the server-count divisor can remap most keys. Ideal balanced consistent hashing moves only the new owner’s share. Distributed placement needs an agreed stable hash and configuration. Further reading Consistent hashing original paper

sum: A collision is expected once enough keys are stored.
x: A collision is expected once enough keys are stored. Chaining treats it as an ordinary case: the bucket contains a collection and equality identifies the requested key inside that collection. However good the hash function, two keys will eventually want the same bucket. For independent uniform bucket choices, with 23 keys in 365 buckets the chance of at least one collision is already over 50% (the birthday paradox: 23 people in a room probably include two who share a birthday). So the real design question for a hash table is not whether collisions happen but what to do when they do. There are two families of answer. Separate chaining lets a bucket hold many keys. Open addressing keeps one key per slot and, on a collision, looks for another slot in the same array. Separate chaining Each bucket holds a small collection, usually a linked list, of every key that hashed there. Insert: hash, then add to that bucket's list (after checking the key is not already there). Look up: hash, then scan that one list. Delete: unlink the node. Nothing else in the table is affected. How long is a chain? Assume simple uniform hashing (every key is equally likely to land in any bucket, independently of the others) and that the key you look up is chosen at random. Then the average chain length equals the load factor, and the expected cost of a lookup is: The "1" is the cost of computing the hash and reaching the bucket. These are averages: an unlucky or attacked table can still put many keys in one chain. Chaining is simple and degrades gracefully: α can go above 1 (more keys than buckets) and the table still works, just more slowly. Its costs are memory and locality. In a node-based linked-list implementation, each entry has a next pointer and may live in a separate allocation. Following those pointers can incur cache misses; their importance depends on representation and workload. Java's HashMap, common C++ std::unordered_map implementations and many textbook tables use chaining. The C++ standard specifies bucket and reference-stability requirements, without mandating one physical layout. Capacity versus collision strategy Linear probing, double hashing and Robin Hood hashing are all open-addressing designs: one slot holds at most one key. Rearranging keys or changing the next candidate slot does not create extra storage. Separate chaining can store more keys than buckets because each bucket owns a collection rather than a single-key slot. Later units examine how the open-addressing sequences work, but this capacity distinction already follows from where entries live. Key takeaways Each bucket holds a collection, so the load factor can exceed one. Expected chain costs assume uniform hashing and a randomly selected successful key. Per-node pointers and cache misses are important practical costs. Further reading Open addressing — Wikipedia

sum: Open addressing keeps entries inside the slot array.
x: Open addressing keeps entries inside the slot array. This unit uses linear probing and separates a table trace from Knuth’s large-table average model; the trace is exact, while the expected probe formulas rely on their stated assumptions. Open addressing All keys live directly in the array, one per slot. To insert, you follow the key's probe sequence, a fixed list of slots to try in order (first choice, second choice, …), until you find an empty slot. A lookup follows the same sequence until it finds the key or hits an empty slot (which proves the key is absent). Because everything is in one contiguous array, open addressing is compact and cache-friendly. The load factor cannot exceed one: there are no more key positions than slots. A completely full table can still search with a bounded complete probe cycle, but has no room for a new key. Designs that stop misses only at an empty slot keep spare slots, and performance falls off sharply as fullness approaches one. Linear probing Try the key's home slot, then the next slot along, then the next, wrapping round from the end of the array to the start: Example: a 7-slot table where each key's home slot is its remainder after dividing by 7. Insert 10, 17, 24, 3, 5 (home slots 3, 3, 3, 3, 5): Four keys wanted slot 3 and spilled into 4, 5 and 6. Then 5, whose home was slot 5, found 5 and 6 taken and wrapped round to slot 0. Any key hashing anywhere into slots 3 to 6 now has to walk to the end of this run. That is primary clustering: occupied runs grow, and a longer run is more likely to be hit and so grows faster. Donald Knuth worked out how many slots linear probing examines on average. His formulas assume random, uniformly spread home slots, a large table, and keys that are only inserted (no deletions or tombstones): The same formulas at three loads: α Hit Miss --------- 0.50 1.5 2.5 0.75 2.5 8.5 0.90 5.5 50.5 Going from 75% full to 90% full makes the modelled miss cost about six times larger (50.5 ÷ 8.5 ≈ 5.9). This is a model, not a wall-clock benchmark. Despite clustering, linear probing can perform well at moderate load because nearby probes benefit from locality; measure the implementation and workload. Key takeaways Linear probing continues into adjacent slots and wraps at the end. Occupied runs cause primary clustering. Knuth’s probe estimates concern a particular random insertion model without deletions. Further reading Linear probing — Wikipedia

sum: A probe sequence must do more than spread collisions: it must reach a free slot.
x: A probe sequence must do more than spread collisions: it must reach a free slot. The table size and the step sequence together determine coverage. Quadratic probing Jump by growing amounts so runs do not merge so readily: This removes primary clustering but leaves secondary clustering: keys with the same home slot still follow the identical sequence. Quadratic probing also may not visit every slot. For squared-attempt offsets modulo an odd prime, the first half-rounded-up set of probes are distinct. If fewer slots are occupied than that number, one of those candidate slots is free. Arbitrary choices of the quadratic coefficients do not share this guarantee. A popular variant steps by triangular numbers (0, 1, 3, 6, 10, …), which visits every slot when m is a power of two: Double hashing Use a second hash to choose the step size: Keys with the same home slot now usually follow different sequences, reducing clustering when the two hashes distribute keys well; keys sharing both hashes still share a sequence. Two rules: the step h₂(k) must never be 0 (or you probe the same slot forever), and it must be coprime with m (share no factor with it other than 1) so the sequence can reach every slot. For prime m, any step that is not a multiple of m works; for power-of-two m, any odd step works. For the same keys as the linear-probing example, use the second hash defined in the preceding formula: five minus the key’s remainder after division by five. 17 jumps 3 slots to slot 6, and 24 steps 1 slot to slot 4, rather than all queuing behind 10. The price is computing a second hash and losing the cache locality of linear steps. Key takeaways Quadratic sequences need table-size and coefficient conditions for coverage. Double hashing uses a nonzero step coprime to table size. Power-of-two tables need odd double-hash steps for complete coverage. Further reading Open addressing — Wikipedia Double hashing — Wikipedia

sum: An empty slot proves a search can stop only if insertion would also have stopped there.
x: An empty slot proves a search can stop only if insertion would also have stopped there. Deleting an intermediate entry must preserve that argument for entries further along the probe path. Deletion and tombstones Deletion is where open addressing gets subtle. In the earlier seven-slot linear-probing example, keys ten, seventeen and twenty-four occupy slots three, four and five. Suppose you delete 17 by setting slot 4 back to empty. A lookup for 24 starts at slot 3 (10, not a match), moves to slot 4, finds it empty, and concludes 24 is absent. Wrong: 24 sits in slot 5. The fix is a tombstone: a special marker meaning "deleted, keep probing". Lookups skip over tombstones. Inserts may reuse the first tombstone they pass, but must still probe on to an empty slot to be sure the key is not already further along. Here n means the number of live keys when considering operation complexity. The names EMPTY and TOMB are unique marker objects, not stored keys. get and delete are methods of a table class whose _probe(key) yields at most one complete cycle of slot indices in probe order: Tombstones pile up Tombstones count against the load for lookups, since searches must walk past them, but they hold no data. A table with heavy insert and delete churn can fill with tombstones, making misses slow even though it holds few live keys. Implementations track them and rebuild the table (rehash live keys into a fresh array) when they pass a threshold. In CPython 3.14 ordinary combined dicts, GIL-enabled builds can reuse dummy index slots; dense entry holes are generally compacted on rebuild. Free-threaded builds do not reuse dummy index slots, and popitem can trim the dense entry tail. With linear probing there is an alternative: backward-shift deletion. After emptying a slot, scan forward and move back any key that could legally sit in the gap, until you reach an empty slot. No tombstones, at the cost of more work per delete. Follow the stopping proof After deleting a key, ask what a future lookup concludes at that slot. A tombstone says the probe sequence continued here in the past; an empty marker says it did not need to continue. These are different statements even though neither slot contains a live entry. The methods shown are fragments of a table implementation, not a complete map. The supplied probe generator must be finite and follow the same placement sequence used by insertion. Exhausting a full cycle also proves absence, so both methods raise KeyError after the loop. A complete insertion method must update an existing key rather than blindly reuse a tombstone, and must handle a table with no truly empty slot. Key takeaways An empty marker stops lookup; a tombstone does not. Insertion must keep searching for duplicates before reusing a tombstone. Deletion churn can require rebuilding even with few live keys. Further reading Open addressing — Wikipedia

sum: Robin Hood insertion compares how far two keys have travelled.
x: Robin Hood insertion compares how far two keys have travelled. It changes which key keeps a contested slot, aiming to reduce variation in search lengths rather than eliminate collision costs. Robin Hood hashing Linear probing's average is fine, but its variance is the problem: some unlucky keys end up dozens of slots from home. Robin Hood hashing (Celis, Larson and Munro, 1985) evens this out by "taking from the rich and giving to the poor". The insertion fragment requires a nonempty table with a free slot and a key not already stored; a complete map must handle duplicate updates and grow before exhausting capacity. Each key's probe distance is how far it sits from its home slot, counting forward and wrapping round the end of the array: While inserting, if the incoming key has travelled further than the resident of the current slot, they swap: the incoming key takes the slot and the displaced, "richer" key carries on probing. Insert D (home 2), then A, B and C (all home 0): C reaches slot 2 having travelled 2; D there has travelled 0, so C takes the slot and D moves on to slot 3. The total distance is the same (4), but the worst case drops from 3 to 2. Robin Hood hashing can reduce probe-distance variance; worst-case lookup remains O(n) under adversarial collisions. It also speeds up misses. Probing for an absent key, you can stop as soon as you meet a resident whose distance is smaller than your current distance: had your key been present, it would have displaced that resident. Deletion usually uses backward shifting. Rust's standard HashMap used Robin Hood hashing until 2019 (Rust 1.36), when it switched to a Swiss table. Key takeaways A more displaced incoming key takes a slot from a less displaced resident. The swap can reduce probe-distance variance while keeping linear adversarial worst cases. An absent-key search can stop at a resident with smaller distance. Further reading Hash table: Robin Hood hashing — Wikipedia

sum: Metadata can make a table search cheap before it touches a key or value.
x: Metadata can make a table search cheap before it touches a key or value. Swiss tables use short hash fingerprints to reject most slots in a group; a fingerprint match still requires checking the real key. Modern designs: Swiss tables Google's Swiss tables (Abseil flat_hash_map, presented in 2017) are open addressing with a twist. Alongside the slots is an array of one-byte control bytes, each holding "empty", "deleted" or 7 bits of the key's hash. On Abseil's x86 SSE2 path, a lookup loads 16 control bytes and uses SIMD instructions to compare all 16 against the key's 7 bits in a single step, only touching the slots that match. Tables run at up to 7/8 full while lookups stay fast. Rust (via the hashbrown crate) and, since Go 1.24, Go's built-in map use Swiss-table designs; Go uses eight-slot groups, so Swiss-table designs do not all probe 16 slots. Another option is cuckoo hashing, where each key has two possible slots and inserts evict residents to their alternative slot. The classic two-hash, single-slot, no-stash version checks at most two candidate slots; insertion can trigger rehashing. Bucketed or stashed variants have different lookup bounds. Choosing between them Chaining Open addressing --------- Load factor can exceed 1 at most 1; normally kept below it Memory node + pointer each one flat array Cache behaviour pointer chasing contiguous Delete trivial tombstones or shifting Near full slows gently slows sharply Chaining is the safer general-purpose choice when keys are large or the load is unpredictable, and it lets you swap the chain for a tree (Java HashMap: splitting and tree bins). Open addressing can offer good locality and low overhead at controlled load; actual speed depends on key size, hash cost and workload. Fingerprints are candidates, not equality A seven-bit fingerprint has only 128 possible values. Several distinct keys can therefore match the same control byte. The vector comparison creates a shortlist; the table still checks the actual key for every surviving candidate. The control-byte shortcut reduces unnecessary memory accesses without changing the equality contract. Deletion markers and empty markers also remain distinct metadata states. A lookup can use an empty marker to establish a stopping condition according to the table’s probing rules; a deleted slot may require continuing to another group. Group width is a property of the implementation and hardware path, so copying a statement about Abseil’s sixteen-byte comparison to every Swiss-table implementation would be wrong. When comparing designs, measure the workload you actually have. Small inline keys and values benefit from a flat layout differently from large objects reached through pointers. The hash computation itself can dominate when keys are long, and references into a flat container may have different stability guarantees from references into a node-based container. Choose the API contract as well as a favourable average probe count. Key takeaways Swiss-table metadata rejects most candidate slots before touching full keys. Fingerprint matches still need equality checks. Group widths and reference stability depend on the implementation. Further reading Swiss tables design notes — Abseil Cuckoo hashing — Wikipedia Go Swiss-table implementation

sum: Load factor describes fullness, but a useful growth limit depends on collision resolution.
x: Load factor describes fullness, but a useful growth limit depends on collision resolution. A chaining table and a group-probing table need not share the same threshold. A hash table's speed depends on one ratio: how full it is. The load factor is Keep α low and buckets are mostly empty or hold a single key, so operations are fast. Let α creep up and chains lengthen or probe runs grow. Many dynamically growing tables therefore watch α and, when it passes a maximum load factor, allocate a bigger array and move everything across. This lesson is about that move: what it costs, why it is still cheap on average, and how two widely used implementations do it. Choosing the maximum load factor The threshold is a space–time trade-off. A low maximum wastes memory on empty slots; a high one makes operations slower. Table Typical/default growth policy Scheme --------- Java HashMap 0.75 chaining CPython dict about 2/3 open addressing Abseil Swiss table 7/8 open addressing + SIMD Redis dict normally grows near 1; policy can defer growth chaining Chaining tolerates a higher load factor because a slightly longer chain is a mild slowdown. Open addressing is far more sensitive. Knuth's classical estimate for a linear-probing miss (Collision resolution) shows why: The formula assumes random hashing, plain linear probing and no deletions; it is not the formula for every probing design. Swiss tables can run at 7/8 full because they probe whole groups of slots at once, comparing one-byte metadata entries first, so few probes ever touch the slots themselves. Key takeaways Growth limits trade empty capacity against collision work. Chaining, linear probing and group probing need different cost models. Java’s ordinary size-triggered growth occurs after exceeding its threshold. Further reading Hash table: dynamic resizing — Wikipedia Amortized analysis — Wikipedia

sum: Resizing changes bucket selection, so it visits all entries even if their full hashes are cached.
x: Resizing changes bucket selection, so it visits all entries even if their full hashes are cached. We count this copying work separately from collisions and allocation costs. Rehashing: why every key moves When the table grows, you cannot copy the old array across as it is, because a key's bucket depends on the table size: Doubling the table moves about half the keys under uniform hashing. Growing therefore means rehashing: walking every entry and inserting it into the new array. Visiting/copying entries costs O(n); placing them by ordinary probing assumes well-distributed hashes for expected O(n), and collision-heavy reinsertion can cost more. An implementation can retain the full hash in the entry or key object so it does not have to recompute it (which matters for long strings), but every entry still has to be visited and placed. Amortised analysis: why inserts are still O(1) One O(n) insert sounds bad. The trick is that, if the table grows by a constant factor, expensive inserts become rarer as the table grows. Count the copying work for n inserts into a table that starts with one slot and doubles when full. Each resize copies every key present. First assume n is a power of two: The sum works because each term is bigger than all the earlier terms put together: the last resize does about half the total work. For powers of two the preceding exact sum applies. For an arbitrary positive insertion count, the last copied capacity may exceed half that count, but the following bounds still hold: Thus resizing overhead is amortised O(1) per insert for every sequence. Overall hash-table insertion also depends on collision costs: the usual bound is expected amortised O(1), assuming well-distributed hashes and constant-time key operations. Key takeaways Changing capacity changes bucket reduction and requires visiting all entries. Geometric growth keeps total copying proportional to the insertion count. Amortised copying bounds do not prove bounded individual latency or collision cost. Further reading Hash table: dynamic resizing — Wikipedia Amortized analysis — Wikipedia

t: Growth increments, shrinking and pause limits
sum: A constant average over a sequence does not constrain each individual pause.
x: A constant average over a sequence does not constrain each individual pause. This unit contrasts fixed increments, shrink hysteresis and gradual migration between two tables. Fixed increments versus geometric growth Growing by a constant amount does not work. Add 10 slots each time and every resize copies 10 more keys than the last: That is O(n) per insert, amortised. The program below counts the copies exactly (it starts at one slot, so its numbers differ slightly from the formula): The banker's view Charge each insert 3 units instead of 1. One pays for the insert itself; two are saved. Between doublings, half the old capacity in new inserts earns two saved units per insert: enough to pay for moving every key in the full old table. No operation ever runs up a debt, so the average stays at 3. Shrinking without thrashing If a table also shrinks when it empties, do not use the same threshold in both directions. Grow when the table is completely full (load factor 1) and shrink when it drops below half full (load factor ½), and a workload hovering at the boundary (insert, delete, insert, …) would resize on every operation: a doubled table is exactly half full, so one delete shrinks it, and the shrunken table is full, so one insert doubles it again. The textbook fix is a hysteresis gap (a deliberate difference between the grow and shrink points): double when full, halve only when the load factor falls to ¼. After either resize the table is half full, so at least a quarter of its size in operations must happen before the next one. Many real tables simply never shrink automatically; CPython's dict does not shrink when you delete keys. When amortised is not good enough Amortised O(1) still means an occasional O(n) pause. The pause depends on the implementation, key count, allocator and hardware; measure it against the server's latency budget. Incremental rehashing spreads the work out. Redis keeps two tables during a resize and moves a few buckets on each operation (plus a little work in a background timer). Lookups check both tables until the move completes. Go's built-in map used a similar gradual "evacuation" before its Go 1.24 redesign. The cost is complexity and, temporarily, retaining both bucket arrays: when doubling, the old array plus one twice its size, so three times the old bucket count (excluding entries and other overhead). If you know the final size, the simplest fix is to pre-size the table to avoid growth for the planned live-key count. Deletion churn can still require compaction/rebuilds. Key takeaways Fixed capacity increments cause growing amortised copying costs. Different grow and shrink thresholds prevent boundary thrashing. Incremental migration spreads pauses while temporarily retaining two tables. Further reading Hash table: dynamic resizing — Wikipedia Amortized analysis — Wikipedia

sum: These are CPython 3.14 implementation details for an ordinary combined table with general keys.
x: These are CPython 3.14 implementation details for an ordinary combined table with general keys. The language promises dictionary behaviour and insertion order, while other Python implementations can choose different layouts. How CPython's dict works CPython's dict is open addressing with a compact layout, introduced in Python 3.6 and based on a 2012 proposal by Raymond Hettinger. The simplified description below covers an ordinary combined table with general keys. Split/key-sharing tables and Unicode-only entries have different layouts. There are two arrays: The indices array is the hash table proper. Each slot holds an index into entries, and uses 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes depending on the table size, so a small dict's index is tiny. The entries array stores (hash, key, value) in insertion order. That is why dicts preserve insertion order: iteration just walks entries. Compared with the old design, which stored full entries in a sparse array (24 bytes per general entry on the illustrated 64-bit build), this saves a lot of memory, because only the cheap index array is sparse. Further details: Sizes are powers of two, minimum 8, and a table holds at most about two-thirds of its size in entries (the formula below). Growth: when full, the new size is the smallest power of two that is at least 3 × the number of live keys. Without deletions this doubles the table: in CPython 3.14, a dict built key by key resizes on the 6th, 11th, 22nd and 43rd inserts. Probing uses a perturbed sequence, not linear steps. CPython first interprets a signed hash as an unsigned machine word for perturbation; otherwise a negative hash would not shift towards zero. Starting from i = hash & mask, each step is perturb >>= 5 then i = (5i + perturb + 1) & mask. The shifting perturb feeds the high bits of the hash into the sequence, so keys that share low bits soon diverge; once perturb reaches 0, 5i + 1 alone visits every slot. Deletion marks the index slot as a dummy (a tombstone) and the entry as empty. A rebuild compacts empty entries. In GIL-enabled builds a later insertion can reuse a dummy index slot; free-threaded builds avoid that reuse for lookup safety. The size rules, written out (CPython's USABLE_FRACTION and growth calculation): And the probe sequence. Here & with mask (the table size minus 1) is the same as taking the remainder by the table size, and perturb >>= 5 divides perturb by 32, rounding down: For a full hash of 1,234 and eight slots, the first four slot choices are two, one, seven and four. The perturb values after successive shifts are thirty-eight, one and zero. Key takeaways Ordinary combined dictionaries use sparse indices over insertion-ordered entries. Perturbed probing feeds higher hash bits into early probes. Capacity, tombstone reuse and layouts are implementation and build details. Further reading More compact dictionaries with faster iteration — Raymond Hettinger, python-dev CPython 3.14 dictionary implementation

t: Java HashMap: splitting and tree bins
sum: This unit follows OpenJDK 21 ordinary put and resize paths.
x: This unit follows OpenJDK 21 ordinary put and resize paths. Distinguish normal load-triggered growth from a collision-triggered request to resize or treeify a bucket. How Java's HashMap works Java's HashMap uses separate chaining over an array whose length is always a power of two (default 16). Spreading the hash. In Java's source the bucket index is (n − 1) & hash, where n is the table length (not the number of keys) and & is bitwise AND. Because the length is a power of two, this is the same as the remainder: Using only the low bits is fast, but it ignores the high bits. To stop poor hashCode() implementations that differ only in their high bits from colliding, Java first mixes the high half into the low half: Resizing. Java resizes when the number of entries goes above a threshold: It doubles. Because the size is a power of two, each entry in old bucket i goes either to bucket i or to bucket i + oldCapacity in the new table, depending on one bit of its hash (hash & oldCap). Java 8 uses this to split each chain into "low" and "high" lists in a single pass, preserving order. Tree bins (Java 8). JEP 180 added protection against long chains. In OpenJDK 21, ordinary put invokes treeification when adding a ninth node to a chain of eight (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD is 8). Other insertion paths can reach the threshold differently. A tree bin gives logarithmic lookup when hashes or a consistent comparable-key order distinguish keys. Two conditions apply: If the whole table has fewer than 64 buckets (MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY), Java resizes the table instead, since a small table is the likelier cause of the long chain. When a resize splits a tree bin and a part has 6 or fewer entries (UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD), it turns back into a list. The gap between 8 and 6 avoids flipping back and forth. Tree nodes are ordered by hash, then by compareTo if the keys are Comparable. For keys with identical hashes that are not comparable, the tree cannot order them meaningfully, so the guarantee is weaker; String keys, the usual flooding target, are comparable. How rare are tree bins? The HashMap source notes that with random hash codes and a default maximum load factor of 0.75, bucket sizes follow a Poisson distribution with mean about 0.5. Under that approximate model, the probability of exactly 8 entries is about 0.00000006 (worked out below); this is not a measured treeification rate. Tree bins are a defence against bad or malicious hashes, not a normal-case optimisation. The Poisson distribution gives the chance of seeing exactly k events when they happen independently at an average rate λ. Here an "event" is a key landing in a particular bucket: Key takeaways Hash spreading folds high bits into low bucket bits. Doubling separates old chains by one additional hash bit. Tree-bin bounds need distinguishable hashes or comparable ordering; small tables resize first. Further reading HashMap — Java SE 21 API docs JEP 180: Handle Frequent HashMap Collisions with Balanced Trees OpenJDK 21 HashMap source

sum: A constructor’s capacity argument is not the number of entries you can hold at the default load factor.
x: A constructor’s capacity argument is not the number of entries you can hold at the default load factor. Plan for the threshold after power-of-two rounding, and remember the backing array is allocated lazily. Pre-sizing a Java HashMap new HashMap<>(1000) rounds the capacity up to 1,024, whose threshold is 768, so it still resizes once before reaching 1,000 entries. To hold a given number of entries without resizing, the threshold must be at least that number: Java 19 added HashMap.newHashMap(n), which does that calculation for you. Trace the capacity changes With the default threshold policy and well-distributed keys, a map that begins at sixteen buckets first allocates its backing array on insertion. Initial allocation is not a doubling. Its entry limits before successive doublings are twelve, twenty-four, forty-eight, ninety-six, one hundred and ninety-two, three hundred and eighty-four, then seven hundred and sixty-eight. Inserting a thousand distinct keys crosses all seven limits, leaving a capacity of two thousand and forty-eight buckets. Now compare a constructor argument of one thousand.
