A subtree whose root has black-height b holds a number of real (non-NIL) nodes that grows exponentially with its black-height (the first line below), which you can prove by mathematical induction: it holds for a NIL, and each child's black-height is at least the parent's black-height minus one. The third line comes from applying the first line at the root and substituting the second; solving it for h gives the fourth. For a million keys the bound is about 40; actual height depends on the implementation and update history. Java TreeMap uses this red-black structure. Its documented logarithmic get, put and remove guarantees hold for insertion orders such as ascending IDs; ordered arrivals do not turn it into the unbalanced chain studied earlier. Key takeaways NIL child positions count as black for the path invariant. No consecutive red nodes and equal black-height imply logarithmic height. Distinguish inclusive diagram counts from the proof’s exclusive black-height convention. Further reading Red–black tree — Wikipedia Balanced Search Trees — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne) TreeMap (Java SE 25) — Oracle

sum: Repair insertion colours with uncle cases and rotations.
x: The preceding unit defined red-black invariants: a black root, no red parent with a red child, and equal black-height on every path to a NIL child. Start with strict BST ordering and distinct comparable keys. Here n counts stored keys. This is the conventional bottom-up repair outline, rather than an executable insertion implementation; left-leaning and other variants have different repair rules. Insertion and colour repair Insert as in a BST and colour the new node red (this preserves rule 3; rule 2 or the root-colour rule may need repair). If its parent is black, done. If its parent is red, look at the uncle (the parent's sibling): Uncle red: recolour parent and uncle black and the grandparent red, then repeat the check from the grandparent. No rotation; the problem moves up two levels. Uncle black: one or two rotations around the grandparent plus a recolour fix it for good. Colour the root black. For the conventional bottom-up red-black algorithms, insertion uses at most two rotations and deletion at most three. Recolouring and fix-up traversal can take O(log n) steps in one update of a tree of n keys, because the red-uncle case can repeat up the whole path. These rotation bounds do not apply automatically to every red-black variant. Red-black trees are 2-3-4 trees in disguise Glue each black node to its red children and you get a B-tree node with 2, 3 or 4 children. Rule 3 says all leaves of that B-tree are at the same depth. Sedgewick's left-leaning red-black tree (2008) restricts red links further and its 2-3 variant maps onto 2-3 trees, which makes the code much shorter. Key takeaways New nodes start red so existing black counts are unchanged. A red uncle allows recolouring and moves the conflict upward. A black uncle requires rotations and recolouring; restore the root to black. Further reading Red–black tree — Wikipedia Left-leaning Red-Black Trees — Robert Sedgewick (PDF) Red-black Trees (rbtree) in Linux — kernel docs

t: Choosing balanced trees for real workloads
sum: AVL has a tighter worst-case height bound, but speed needs measurement.
x: Start with the distinct-key BST ordering from the previous units. A rotation must keep the same sorted in-order sequence while changing local links. Here n counts stored keys and h measures real-node height in edges; empty subtrees have height minus one unless a NIL-path convention is explicitly given. Height bounds assume constant-cost key comparisons, rather than measuring application latency. AVL versus red-black Side by side, the two height bounds for n keys are: (The exact AVL worst case for a million keys is 27, from the recurrence above.) AVL Red-black --------- Max height Approx. 1.44 times the base-2 logarithm Twice the base-2 log of one more key Lookup height bound Tighter Looser Rotations/insert At most one repair At most two Rotations/delete O(log n) At most three Extra data Height or balance factor 1 colour bit Search and single-key updates are O(log n) for n keys, with constant-cost comparisons; traversing all entries is O(n). Practical tradeoffs: AVL offers a tighter worst-case height bound; actual read performance needs measurement. Write-heavy or general-purpose libraries usually choose red-black: fewer rotations on delete, and a colour bit can be hidden in the low bit of an aligned pointer, as the Linux kernel does. Where they are used Java TreeMap and TreeSet: red-black trees, giving logarithmic get, put, floorKey and ceilingKey operations; full sorted iteration over n entries takes O(n). Java HashMap: since Java 8, when a single bucket grows past 8 colliding entries (in a table of at least 64 buckets), it is converted into a small red-black tree, Comparable keys can use ordering to obtain logarithmic bin searches. Equal-hash keys without usable comparison ordering can still require linear search within a tree bin. C++ std::map and std::set: red-black trees in the major standard libraries (libstdc++, libc++, MSVC). The standard requires logarithmic key lookup and key-based updates for n elements, with other operation-specific bounds; erasing through a known iterator is amortised constant time. Insertion preserves iterators, without requiring a specific representation. Linux kernel: a generic intrusive rbtree (lib/rbtree.c) used widely. The Completely Fair Scheduler kept runnable tasks in a red-black tree ordered by vruntime (virtual runtime) and ran the leftmost task, caching a pointer to it so picking the next task is O(1). Linux began transitioning fair scheduling toward EEVDF in version 6.6; its implementation uses an augmented red-black tree. epoll also stores its watched file descriptors in one. Why CFS wanted a tree, not a binary heap A binary heap gives the minimum just as fast. But the scheduler also removes arbitrary tasks (one blocks on I/O, one is killed) and re-inserts them with new keys. With an intrusive tree, each task embeds its own tree node, so removing a given task from n runnable tasks is O(log n) with no search. A binary heap would need an extra position index to find an arbitrary entry, and it cannot cheaply answer "which task comes next after this one?". Other balanced structures, briefly B-trees and B+ trees use the same idea with hundreds of keys per node, matching disk pages. Many relational database indexes use them; hash, bitmap and other index types also exist (covered in System Design: databases). Skip lists give expected O(log n) search over n keys with randomised towers of linked lists; Redis sorted sets can use a skip list plus dictionary or a compact encoding. Treaps and splay trees balance with randomness or by moving accessed nodes to the root. Python has no built-in balanced tree. sortedcontainers uses a list of sorted lists, which offers different locality and update tradeoffs from pointer-based trees. Evidence gap Universal AVL-versus-red-black lookup wins and sortedcontainers performance wins are omitted because no matching workload, implementation and reproducible benchmark were supplied. Key takeaways AVL has a tighter worst-case height bound, but speed needs measurement. Conventional red-black deletion uses a bounded number of rotations. Library and kernel uses must be distinguished from interface requirements. Further reading Left-leaning Red-Black Trees — Robert Sedgewick (PDF) Red-black Trees (rbtree) in Linux — kernel docs CFS Scheduler — Linux kernel docs TreeMap (Java SE 25) — Oracle HashMap implementation — OpenJDK Associative container requirements — C++ draft EEVDF Scheduler — Linux kernel docs

t: Heap order and implicit array layout
sum: A binary heap combines complete shape with parent-child priority order.
x: Many problems only ever need the smallest (or largest) item: the next job to run, the nearest unvisited city in Dijkstra's algorithm, the earliest timer to fire, the next event in a simulation. A BST can do that, but it keeps far more order than you need. A priority queue is the abstract data type for this job: push(item), pop_min() and peek(). The standard implementation is the binary heap. For a binary heap of n items it gives O(log n) push and pop (work growing with the logarithm of n, about 20 steps for a million items) and O(1) peek (a fixed cost), stored with implicit parent/child indices rather than tree-link pointers. Python lists still store references to their elements. Costs assume constant-time comparisons; dynamic-array resizing makes push/pop bounds amortized when allocation costs are included. The binary heap property A binary min-heap is a binary tree with two rules: Shape: it is a complete binary tree (every level full except possibly the last, which fills from the left). Order: every parent is less than or equal to its children. So the minimum is always at the root. A max-heap flips the order rule. Notice how much weaker this is than a BST. Siblings are unordered (3 is left of 2), and 4 sits deep on the left while 2 is near the top on the right. The binary heap only promises that every path from the root downward is sorted. That weaker promise is what makes it cheap to maintain. The array layout Because the tree is complete, it packs into an array in level order with no gaps (the tree-structure units): The parent and children of any slot are found by arithmetic on its index: So the 3 at index 1 has children at indices 3 and 4 (4 and 8), and the 9 at index 7 has its parent at index 3 (the 4). In the Python code below, the parent index is (i - 1) // 2, where // divides and rounds down. Avoiding explicit tree links saves their storage. The array of slots is contiguous, though referenced payload objects need not be; actual cache behaviour depends on layout and access patterns. The second half of the array is all leaves: In the 8-item example, indices 4 to 7 (values 8, 7, 6 and 9) are leaves: index 4's left child would be at 9, past the end. Key takeaways A binary heap combines complete shape with parent-child priority order. Array indices replace explicit links. Binary heap order does not sort siblings or the entire array. Further reading Binary heap — Wikipedia Priority Queues — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

t: Sift up, sift down and priority removal
sum: Push appends and moves the new key toward the root.
x: Use the complete-tree array layout introduced earlier. The root is array slot zero; absent child positions lie beyond the occupied prefix. Here n counts binary heap entries and comparisons have constant cost. A valid min-heap makes each parent no greater than its children, without ordering siblings. Array allocation and returned output require their own cost accounting. Sift up: push To push, append the new item at the end (the next free slot in the last level, which keeps the shape) and then sift up: while it is smaller than its parent, swap them. Pushing 0 into the binary heap above: it lands at index 8 (child of 4), swaps with 4, then 3, then 1, and becomes the new root. There is at most one swap per level, and a complete tree is short: Pushing 0 made exactly 3 swaps, the most possible. A million-item binary heap needs at most 19, so push is O(log n). Sift down: pop Here n counts entries before the pop; use the sift-up unit's complete-tree height bound. To pop the minimum, you cannot just remove the root: that would leave a hole at the top. Instead, move the last item into the root (keeping the shape), shrink the array, and sift down: swap it with its smaller child until it is no larger than both children. Swapping with the smaller child matters: that child becomes the parent of the other, so it must be the smaller of the two. Pop also makes at most one swap per level, the same height limit as push, so for n items it is also O(log n). Binary Heaps are not sorted Only a[0] is guaranteed to be the minimum. a[1] is not necessarily the second smallest (in the example it is 3, but 2 is smaller), and iterating over a binary heap list does not give sorted order. Popping repeatedly does. Key takeaways Push appends and moves the new key toward the root. Pop moves the final entry to the root and repairs downward. Choose the smaller child to preserve min-heap order. Further reading Binary heap — Wikipedia Priority Queues — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

sum: Build downward from the last internal node.
x: Use the complete-tree array layout introduced earlier. The root is array slot zero; absent child positions lie beyond the occupied prefix. Here n counts binary heap entries and comparisons have constant cost. A valid min-heap makes each parent no greater than its children, without ordering siblings. Array allocation and returned output require their own cost accounting. Heapify in O(n) Given n unsorted items, you could push them one at a time. Each push can climb the full height, so in the worst case: That is O(n log n): n multiplied by log n. There is a faster way. Treat the array as a complete tree already, and sift down every non-leaf from the bottom up: Use the sift_down helper from the preceding unit to execute heapify. Both operate in place on a list of comparable values; heapify does not return a new sorted list. Trace on [9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6, 3] (8 items, so start at index 3): Why is that O(n)? The cost of sifting down a node is at most its node height, and most nodes have tiny heights. A rigorous bound counts nodes able to move down at least a given number of levels: at most half the nodes can move one level, a quarter two levels, an eighth three, and so on. Summing those possible levels gives: The trace above made 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 swaps, within the bound of 7. For the shown sift-down algorithm, this bounds swaps by n and key comparisons by twice the item count (at most two child comparisons per available downward level, including a level where no swap is needed); loop and index checks are additional constant work per step. Pushing one at a time is slower because new items arrive at the bottom, the level with the most nodes, and each may climb the full height. The intuition: sift-down costs are cheap where nodes are plentiful (the bottom) and expensive only where they are rare (the top). Sift-up is the reverse. Heapsort Heapify, then repeatedly swap the root with the last item and sift down over a shrinking prefix. That is heapsort: for n items, O(n log n) worst case (n pops, each sifting down at most the binary heap's height), O(1) extra memory, but not stable and with poor cache locality (child positions roughly double their parent position), which can affect practical performance. One use is the worst-case fallback inside introsort (the usual implementation of C++ std::sort), which switches to heapsort if quicksort recurses too deeply. Key takeaways Build downward from the last internal node. Most nodes can move only a few levels, making bottom-up heapify linear. Heapsort repeatedly repairs a shrinking binary heap and is not stable. Further reading Priority Queues — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

t: Python priority queues and streaming top-k
sum: Use an insertion counter to break equal-priority payload ties.
x: Use the complete-tree array layout introduced earlier. The root is array slot zero; absent child positions lie beyond the occupied prefix. Here n counts binary heap entries and comparisons have constant cost. A valid min-heap makes each parent no greater than its children, without ordering siblings. Array allocation and returned output require their own cost accounting. heapq in Python Python's heapq module implements a min-heap on a plain list. There is no binary heap class. Here n is the number of items in the binary heap (or in the input, for heapify and nlargest), and k is how many items you ask for. Function Cost ------ heappush(h, x) O(log n) heappop(h) O(log n) h[0] (peek) O(1) heapify(h) O(n), in place heapreplace(h, x) pop then push, O(log n) heappushpop(h, x) push then pop, O(log n) nlargest(k, it) O(n log(k + 1)) when k is between 1 and n; implementation may choose max or sorting Practical details: Max-heaps: before Python 3.14, negate the keys (heappush(h, -x)). Python 3.14 added heapify_max, heappush_max, heappop_max and friends. Priorities with payloads: push tuples (priority, item). If two priorities tie, Python compares the items, which fails for objects that don't support <. Add a counter: (priority, next(counter), item). This also makes ties first-in-first-out. Changing a priority ("decrease-key") is not supported. The usual trick is lazy deletion: push a new entry and mark the old one as removed, skipping stale entries when they are popped. Dijkstra's algorithm in Python is normally written this way. Pattern: top-k "Find the k largest of n items" (top 10 search results, the 100 busiest IPs in a log). Sorting is O(n log n). Better: keep a min-heap of size k holding the best k seen so far. Its root is the weakest of the current top k, so each new item only needs comparing with the root. Each item costs one comparison with the root, and at most one replace that sifts through a binary heap of only k items: So for a keeper count between one and the input size, cost is O(n log(k + 1)) time including final sorting, and O(k) memory. The + 1 keeps the logarithm above zero when there is one keeper. Larger k returns all n items; zero keepers returns immediately. With a billion log lines and 100 keepers, that is about 7 binary heap levels per item instead of the 30 a binary heap of all n items would need, and it works on a stream that never fits in memory. heapq.nlargest does this for you. Min-heap for the largest, max-heap for the smallest It feels backwards, but for the k largest you want quick access to the smallest of your keepers, because that is the one a newcomer must beat. If all n items are in memory and you only need the k-th element, quickselect finds it in expected O(n), but it does not stream and reorders the array. Key takeaways Use an insertion counter to break equal-priority payload ties. A min-heap retains the largest stream items by exposing its weakest keeper. Changing priorities requires an extra policy such as lazy deletion. Further reading heapq — Python docs

t: Heap merging and alternative priority queues
sum: Keep only one current head from each sorted input.
x: Use the complete-tree array layout introduced earlier. The root is array slot zero; absent child positions lie beyond the occupied prefix. Here n counts binary heap entries and comparisons have constant cost. A valid min-heap makes each parent no greater than its children, without ordering siblings. Array allocation and returned output require their own cost accounting. Pattern: k-way merge Merge k sorted lists (sorted runs from an external sort, per-shard query results, SSTables in LSM-tree compaction). Put the head of each list in a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest and push the next item from the same list. This function uses heapq; import it as in the previous unit before running the example. The sample call returns a list; the comment shows that returned list, rather than printed script output. The binary heap never holds more than k items, so each of the N output items costs one pop and at most one push through a small binary heap: So the binary heap merge costs O(k + N log(k + 1)), including scanning empty input lists, with O(k) binary heap space plus O(N) returned output. Merging the lists pairwise one after another would cost up to O(N·k), N times k. heapq.merge is a lazy version of this. Beyond binary heaps d-ary heaps (4-ary is common) are shallower, reducing possible upward levels but requiring more child comparisons per downward level. Cache and runtime effects depend on the implementation and workload. Fibonacci heaps support amortised O(1) decrease-key and O(log n) delete-min (for n queued items), giving O(E + V log V) for Dijkstra on a graph with V vertices and E edges, with suitable handles and nonnegative edge weights. Ordinary pairing heaps do not share this combined constant-amortized decrease-key guarantee; their analysis is different. Benchmark concrete implementations before choosing. Real uses: OS timer queues, Go's container/heap, Java's PriorityQueue (a binary heap), job schedulers, and the event queue in network simulators. Key takeaways Keep only one current head from each sorted input. After popping a head, advance only its input. Different priority queue structures trade off child comparisons and update costs. Further reading heapq — Python docs K-way merge algorithm — Wikipedia

t: Trie paths, exact lookup and prefixes
sum: Shared prefixes share a root-to-node path.
x: In this lesson L is the length of a key in characters and n is the number of keys stored. Hash-table lookup uses expected O(1) probes (a fixed number on average) under suitable hashing assumptions; hashing and equality on uncached strings can cost O(L), in proportion to the key's length. They cannot answer "which words start with inte?" without scanning every key. Balanced BSTs can, but each comparison is a string comparison: So a BST lookup costs O(L log n), and the trie below brings that down to O(L). Real string comparisons often stop at the first differing character, so the BST figure is a worst case. A trie (from retrieval, usually pronounced "try") is built for prefix questions. Instead of storing whole keys in nodes, it stores one character per edge. A key is a path from the root, and every key that shares a prefix shares the path for that prefix. The structure Here is a trie holding car, card, care, cat, do and dog. A marks a node where a word ends. Things to notice: The root represents the empty string. Each node represents the prefix spelled by the path to it. car and card share three nodes. Shared prefixes are stored once. do is a word and a prefix of dog, so an end-of-word flag is needed; you cannot rely on "is it a leaf?". Keys are never compared with each other. Lookup cost depends on the length of the key, not on how many keys are stored. Insert, search and prefix queries With the trie above: Call Result Why --------- search(root, "car") True path exists, flag set search(root, "ca") False path exists, no flag starts_with(root, "ca") True path exists search(root, "dot") False no t under do With constant-time child access, insertion, exact lookup and prefix-path lookup take O(L + 1) for a key or prefix of L characters: one step per character, plus the root (the + 1 covers the empty string, for zero characters). The dict-backed example uses expected constant-time child lookups. For an empty prefix, starts_with returns True even on an empty trie because the root exists; this tests path existence, not whether any word is stored. O(L) is not automatically faster than hashing Hashing a previously unhashed string inspects its characters; some runtimes cache string hashes, and equality costs also matter. Tries directly support prefix navigation and can stop early on a miss. Practical exact-match performance depends on representation and workload. Key takeaways Shared prefixes share a root-to-node path. An end flag distinguishes complete words from their prefixes. Lookup follows key characters with expected constant-cost dictionary access. Further reading Trie — Wikipedia Tries — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

sum: Walk to the prefix node before enumerating descendants.
x: A character trie starts at an always-present root representing the empty prefix. Earlier units used Node.kids as a dictionary of character-to-child links and Node.end as the complete-word flag. Here L counts characters in the searched string or prefix and n counts stored keys. Dictionary child access is expected constant time, rather than a worst-case guarantee. Autocomplete Autocomplete is "walk to the prefix node, then enumerate words below it". Run this function with the Node, insert and walk definitions from the lookup unit. Populate the trie with car, card, care, cat, do and dog to obtain the illustrative completion list below. Sorted child traversal produces Python string lexicographic order (code-point order, not locale-aware alphabetical collation). This simple implementation copies path strings and sorts child keys during recursion; enumeration costs include visited nodes, copied characters and output, and deep words can hit Python's recursion limit. An autocomplete design may rank by popularity. Enumerating and sorting every match can be expensive, so one option is to cache top-k word IDs at selected prefix nodes. Looking up such a cached list of k IDs for a prefix of L characters costs expected O(L + k) in this representation, excluding retrieval and transmission of the completion text. The trade-off is memory, and slower updates when popularity changes. Sizing an autocomplete trie In a hypothetical dataset, 10 million queries with mean length exactly 20 have 200 million characters in total, but shared prefixes typically cut the node count substantially. Storing the top 10 completions at every node as 4-byte IDs adds 40 bytes per node, before container overhead. A design can store these lists only at selected shallow nodes and compute other results on demand; the best policy depends on query traffic. Key takeaways Walk to the prefix node before enumerating descendants. Sorted child traversal gives code-point order, not locale-aware collation. Cached top completions exchange update and memory costs for query speed. Further reading Tries — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

sum: Child arrays reserve every alphabet position even when unused.
x: A character trie starts at an always-present root representing the empty prefix. Earlier units used Node.kids as a dictionary of character-to-child links and Node.end as the complete-word flag. Here L counts characters in the searched string or prefix and n counts stored keys. Dictionary child access is expected constant time, rather than a worst-case guarantee. The memory problem Tries are fast but notoriously memory-hungry, because every character of every unshared suffix gets its own node, and each node carries overhead. Common child representations differ in how much they reserve per node. An array of child pointers reserves one slot for every possible character, used or not: Children as Lookup Memory per node --------- Array of 26 (or 256) pointers O(1) index 208 B (or 2 KiB) with 8-byte pointers, mostly empty Hash map / dict O(1) expected Small, but high constant overhead Sorted list O(log σ) Compact O(log σ) is the cost of a binary search among at most σ sorted children. Dictionary and node object sizes vary by interpreter build. Evidence gap The claimed CPython dictionary sizes and 100,000-word, 65 MB benchmark are omitted because the pinned build, word list, measurement code and retained-object accounting were unavailable. No measured tenfold memory ratio is established. With long mostly unshared suffixes, many nonterminal trie nodes have exactly one child: the unshared tail of a single word like...ication. That observation drives the fix. Why uniform hashes share little structure SHA-256 values use 64 hexadecimal characters when encoded as hex. Imagine one million independent, approximately uniform hashes. Each additional character multiplies the possible prefixes by sixteen. At shallow depths many keys collide; farther down, almost every key owns its entire remaining suffix. Counting occupied prefixes at each depth estimates the non-root node count: This model estimates about 59.68 million nodes, not bytes. Allocation overhead remains representation-dependent. A radix tree compresses the long private suffixes; a hash set is usually the first structure to consider when the task needs only exact membership and no prefix queries. Real hashes are modelled as approximately uniform here, rather than assumed to make every finite sample perfectly balanced. Key takeaways Child arrays reserve every alphabet position even when unused. Dictionary and object overhead depends on the implementation. Mostly unshared suffixes make character tries poor exact-match indexes. Further reading Trie — Wikipedia Tries — Algorithms, 4th ed. (Sedgewick & Wayne)

t: Compressed paths, routing and trie variants
sum: Compress single-child chains only when no intermediate key ends there.
x: A character trie starts at an always-present root representing the empty prefix. Earlier units used Node.kids as a dictionary of character-to-child links and Node.end as the complete-word flag. Here L counts characters in the searched string or prefix and n counts stored keys. Dictionary child access is expected constant time, rather than a worst-case guarantee. Compressed tries and radix trees A radix tree (also called a compressed trie, or a Patricia trie in its binary form) merges chains of single-child nodes that do not mark a key end into one edge labelled with a string rather than a character. Except possibly the root, every internal node now has at least two children (or marks a word end), so the node count is at most twice the number of stored keys, independent of key length (the count is below). Lookups compare chunks of characters along each edge, with the same O(L) total for a key of L characters. Inserting can split an edge: adding cab to the tree above splits nothing because ca already exists, but adding co would split ca into c with children a and o. The node bound comes from counting the only kinds of node compression leaves behind: The radix tree drawn above holds those 4 keys in 5 labelled nodes plus the root, within the bound of 8. A plain trie, by contrast, can need one node per character of every key. Radix trees are where tries meet production: IP routing: a router finds the longest prefix match of a destination address against a table of CIDR prefixes. Binary tries over address bits, compressed (Patricia, LC-tries), are a classic implementation; Linux's IPv4 routing table uses an LC-trie (fib_trie). HTTP routers: Go's httprouter and many others match URL paths with a radix tree. Redis Streams use a radix tree of listpacks; a radix-tree entry represents a packed group of stream entries rather than necessarily one node per message. Ethereum stores its world state in a Merkle Patricia trie. The Linux page cache historically used a "radix tree", now the XArray, to map file offsets to pages. Other variants, briefly Here P names the pattern string and P denotes its character count when quoting a Big O lookup bound. Ternary search trees store one character per node with less/equal/greater children, like a BST over characters. They use far less memory than array tries and still support prefix search. Suffix tries and suffix trees hold every suffix of a text, answering "does pattern P occur anywhere?" in time proportional to the length of P, written O(P), where P is the number of characters in the pattern. Suffix arrays are the space-efficient alternative. Aho–Corasick adds failure links to a trie of patterns, finding all occurrences of many patterns in one pass over a text (GNU grep uses it for multiple fixed patterns, and intrusion-detection systems can use it to match many signatures). Finite-state transducers can merge equivalent states and share suitable suffix structure as well as prefixes. Compression depends on the vocabulary and outputs. When to reach for a trie Use one when you need: prefix queries: autocomplete, "all keys under /api/v1/", routing; longest-prefix matching; many patterns matched at once (Aho–Corasick); sorted iteration over strings with shared prefixes. Avoid one when you only do exact-match lookups (use a hash set), when keys share few prefixes (random IDs, hashes: the trie degenerates into one long chain per key), or when memory is tight and a sorted array with binary search on prefixes will do. Key takeaways Compress single-child chains only when no intermediate key ends there. Insertion may split an edge at the first different character. Routing uses the longest matching prefix, while exact membership often suits hashing. Further reading Radix tree — Wikipedia Longest prefix match — Wikipedia Ternary search tree — Wikipedia Aho–Corasick algorithm — Wikipedia Fixed-pattern search performance — GNU grep manual

t: Lowest common ancestors in ordered and general trees
sum: A BST query follows the side containing both keys until they split.
x: Tree problems look endlessly varied, but nearly all of them use one of a few patterns. Learn the patterns and most "new" problems become variations. Post-order combine. Each call returns a summary of its subtree (height, sum, "found it?"), and the parent combines its children's summaries. Often a second value, the global best, is tracked on the side. Pre-order with state passed down. Each call receives information from above (a running sum, a valid range, a depth) and passes an updated version to its children. Level-order when the question mentions levels, widths or nearest anything. This lesson works through the classics. Assume finite acyclic binary trees without shared nodes or concurrent mutation. These recursive examples are limited by Python call depth. Time bounds use unit-cost arithmetic; hashing-based bounds are expected. Throughout, n is the number of nodes and h is the tree's height in edges. Working recursion depth is O(h + 1), but dictionaries, serialized text and returned trees can require additional storage. Lowest common ancestor The lowest common ancestor (LCA) of nodes p and q is the deepest node that has both as descendants (a node counts as its own descendant). It underlies "how are these two related?" questions: the nearest shared directory of two files, merge bases of Git commits (a DAG can have several incomparable best common ancestors, unlike a rooted tree), or the distance between two nodes. The path from p to q climbs from p up to their LCA, then goes down to q, so: The example line uses nodes 3 and 5 in the BST drawn below: both have depth 3 and their LCA, 4, has depth 2, so they are 2 edges apart (3–4–5). In a BST: follow the split If p and q are both smaller than the current node, the LCA is on the left; both larger, on the right. Otherwise they split here (or one of them is this node), so this node is the LCA. Assume unique ordered keys and that both queried keys exist in this tree. The function does not verify membership. lca_bst(root, 3, 5) is 4, lca_bst(root, 2, 8) is 6 and lca_bst(root, 0, 5) is 2. This is O(h) time for a tree of height h, with O(1) space (a fixed amount, just the current node). In any binary tree: post-order Without ordering, ask each subtree "did you find p or q?": If both sides report a find, this node is where the paths diverge. If only one does, pass its result up. When p is an ancestor of q, the search returns p as soon as it reaches it without looking below, which is correct because p is then the LCA. (This version assumes both nodes are in the tree; if either might be missing, count the finds explicitly.) Key takeaways A BST query follows the side containing both keys until they split. A general tree combines findings from its two children. The simple algorithms assume both requested nodes belong to the tree. Further reading Lowest common ancestor — Wikipedia

sum: Binary lifting stores power-of-two ancestor jumps.
x: Use the binary Node with val, left and right fields introduced earlier. Assume a finite acyclic tree with no shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Throughout this unit n counts nodes and h is the tree height in edges. Recursive examples are limited by Python call depth; arithmetic has unit cost and hash-table operations have expected constant cost. Each example distinguishes working storage from returned output. Many queries For millions of LCA queries on a fixed tree of n nodes, each O(n) walk is too slow. Two standard upgrades: Binary lifting: precompute, for every node, its ancestors 1, 2, 4, 8, … levels up (see the table recurrence below), in O(n log n) time. Then lift the deeper node to the same depth and jump both up together in powers of two: O(log n) per query. Euler tour + range minimum: record a node and its depth on entry and again after returning from each child (not just DFS preorder); the LCA is the shallowest node between the first visits of p and q. With a sparse table, queries become O(1) after O(n log n) preprocessing. (Range-query structures such as segment and Fenwick trees are covered in the advanced module.) The binary-lifting table is built from itself: two half-size jumps make one full-size jump. Give the root itself as its parent, or handle a missing-ancestor sentinel consistently, so upward jumps remain defined. The displayed level count applies to trees with at least two nodes; handle a one-node tree directly. For 100,000 nodes that is 17 levels, 1.7 million table entries, and any climb of up to 99,999 levels takes at most 17 jumps (one per 1-bit in its binary form). Key takeaways Binary lifting stores power-of-two ancestor jumps. An Euler depth tour converts ancestor queries to range minima. Preprocessing pays off when a fixed tree serves many queries. Further reading Lowest Common Ancestor (Euler tour) — cp-algorithms LCA with binary lifting — cp-algorithms Euler tour technique — Wikipedia

sum: A longest path can bend below the root.
x: Use the binary Node with val, left and right fields introduced earlier. Assume a finite acyclic tree with no shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Throughout this unit n counts nodes and h is the tree height in edges. Recursive examples are limited by Python call depth; arithmetic has unit cost and hash-table operations have expected constant cost. Each example distinguishes working storage from returned output. Diameter The diameter is the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. The trap: that path need not pass through the root. The longest path here is 5–4–3–2–6–7–8: 6 edges, bending at node 2. The root is not on it. Every path has a single highest node where it bends. At that node it goes down one edge into each subtree and then as deep as that subtree allows: At node 2 above, both subtrees have height 2, giving the 6-edge path; at a leaf such as 5 the empty sides give 0. So compute heights in post-order and track the best bend seen: In the code, hl + hr + 2 is the formula above, and returning −1 for None makes a leaf contribute 0 edges, as it should. This is the archetype of "return one thing, track another": the function returns the height (useful to the parent) but records the diameter (useful only globally). The O(n²) version Computing height(left) + height(right) separately at every node recomputes heights from scratch, which is O(n²) on a chain of n nodes (about half the square of the node count in descendant visits). Combining both in one post-order pass keeps it O(n). Key takeaways A longest path can bend below the root. Return height to the parent while recording the best two-sided path. Avoid recalculating full subtree heights at every node. Further reading Tree traversal — Wikipedia

sum: A root-to-leaf test must verify that its endpoint is a leaf.
x: Use the binary Node with val, left and right fields introduced earlier. Assume a finite acyclic tree with no shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Throughout this unit n counts nodes and h is the tree height in edges. Recursive examples are limited by Python call depth; arithmetic has unit cost and hash-table operations have expected constant cost. Each example distinguishes working storage from returned output. Path sums Three questions with similar names and different techniques. Root-to-leaf sum: pass state down "Is there a root-to-leaf path summing to target?" Subtract as you descend; check at the leaves. The leaf check matters: without it, a node with one child could "succeed" at its empty side, counting a path that does not end at a leaf. Any downward path: prefix sums "How many downward paths (starting anywhere, ending anywhere below) sum to target?" Checking every start node is O(n²) on a chain of n nodes. Instead, borrow the prefix-sum trick from arrays. Keep the running total from the root down to each node; a downward segment's sum is then a difference of two running totals: For example, on the path 10 → 5 → 3 with target 8, the running sums are 10, 15 and 18. At node 3, 18 − 8 = 10 is the running sum at the root, so the segment 5 → 3 sums to 8. In the code, run is R(v) and seen counts the running sums on the current path. The backtrack line is essential: the map must only contain prefixes on the current path, so a node's prefix is removed when the recursion leaves it. Without it, sums from a sibling branch leak in. Removing zero-count entries keeps O(h + 1) distinct active prefixes for a tree of height h; expected time is O(n) for n nodes with constant-cost integer arithmetic and hashing. Key takeaways A root-to-leaf test must verify that its endpoint is a leaf. Prefix differences count segments that start below an ancestor. Backtrack prefix counts so sibling branches do not contaminate each other. Further reading Tree traversal — Wikipedia

t: Maximum path sums with one-sided gains
sum: Clamp a negative extension to zero rather than taking it.
x: Use the binary Node with val, left and right fields introduced earlier. Assume a finite acyclic tree with no shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Throughout this unit n counts nodes and h is the tree height in edges. Recursive examples are limited by Python call depth; arithmetic has unit cost and hash-table operations have expected constant cost. Each example distinguishes working storage from returned output. Maximum path sum: post-order with clamping "Largest sum over any path" (values may be negative). At each node, a path can bend here using the best downward gain from each side, but it can only pass one side up to the parent, because a path cannot fork. Negative gains are clamped to 0 (just don't extend that way). The example line is a node of value 2 whose children are leaves of value 1 and 3: the bend sums to 6, and the node offers its parent a one-sided gain of 5. Initialise best to minus infinity (float('-inf'), smaller than any number), not 0: in a tree of all-negative values the answer is the largest single node, which is negative. Same shape as diameter: return the one-sided gain, record the two-sided best. Key takeaways Clamp a negative extension to zero rather than taking it. Pass only one downward side to a parent because a path cannot fork. Initialise the global best below all values to handle all-negative trees. Further reading Tree traversal — Wikipedia

sum: Values alone omit shape; empty-child markers make shape explicit.
x: Use the binary Node with val, left and right fields introduced earlier. Assume a finite acyclic tree with no shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Throughout this unit n counts nodes and h is the tree height in edges. Recursive examples are limited by Python call depth; arithmetic has unit cost and hash-table operations have expected constant cost. Each example distinguishes working storage from returned output. Serialise and deserialise To send a tree over a network or save it to disk you must flatten it so it can be rebuilt exactly. A traversal of values alone is not enough: the trees 1 → left 2 and 1 → right 2 both have pre-order 1, 2. The fix is to record the empty children too. This teaching format supports integer node values. Truncated input raises StopIteration, invalid integer text raises ValueError, and extra tokens are rejected; untrusted input also requires size and depth limits. Runtime and storage depend on encoded character length, not just node count. Deserialising consumes the tokens in the same pre-order they were written, so each recursive call knows exactly where its subtree begins and ends. A tree of n nodes produces one value per node plus one more null marker than nodes (the tree-structure units): The example string 3,9,#,#,20,15,#,#,7,#,# has 5 values and 6 markers: 11 tokens. Level-order with nulls (the format LeetCode displays) works too. A JSON or Protocol Buffers schema can encode nested child relationships explicitly; the format alone does not choose a tree representation. Key takeaways Values alone omit shape; empty-child markers make shape explicit. Read tokens in the same recursive order as they were written. Validate untrusted input and account for encoded text length. Further reading Tree traversal — Wikipedia

t: Reconstructing a tree from traversal pairs
sum: In-order splits the values into left and right subtrees once the root is known.
x: Use the binary Node with val, left and right fields introduced earlier. Assume a finite acyclic tree with no shared nodes or concurrent mutation. Throughout this unit n counts nodes and h is the tree height in edges. Recursive examples are limited by Python call depth; arithmetic has unit cost and hash-table operations have expected constant cost. Each example distinguishes working storage from returned output. Constructing a tree from traversals Given traversals without null markers, when can you rebuild the tree? With distinct values: Given Unique tree? ------ Pre-order + in-order Yes Post-order + in-order Yes Pre-order + post-order Only if full Pre-order alone No (but yes for a BST) In-order is the key: once you know the root, its position in the in-order sequence tells you exactly which values are in the left and right subtrees. Pre-order tells you the root (its first element), then the left subtree's root, and so on. For distinct hashable values with consistent equality, the dictionary gives expected O(1) index lookup. For n values, the build takes expected O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary dictionary/set space plus the returned nodes; invalid traversal pairs raise an error. The left subtree must be built before the right because that is the order pre-order lists them. Pre-order and post-order alone are ambiguous whenever a node has a single child: 1 → left 2 and 1 → right 2 both give pre-order 1 2 and post-order 2 1. And a BST can be rebuilt from pre-order alone, because sorting the n values supplies its in-order, at O(n log n) comparison cost, where n counts keys; a bounds-based reconstruction can avoid sorting. Key takeaways In-order splits the values into left and right subtrees once the root is known. Distinct values and a value-to-position map enable linear expected work. Pre-order and post-order leave one-child directions ambiguous in general. Further reading Tree traversal — Wikipedia

sum: Stability preserves the input order of equal keys.
x: Bubble sort is rarely the right general-purpose library sort. So why learn the three "simple" sorts? Because they are small enough to hold in your head, and each one makes a different trade-off visible. Selection sort minimises writes. Insertion sort exploits order that is already there. Bubble sort shows why "obviously correct" can still be slow. And the vocabulary they introduce (stable, in-place, adaptive) is exactly the vocabulary you need to choose between production sorts later. Insertion sort is not just a teaching tool either: it runs inside Timsort, introsort and pdqsort for small sub-arrays. The vocabulary Before the algorithms, a note on notation. Throughout this lesson, n is the number of elements being sorted. Costs are written in Big O notation, which describes how a cost grows as n grows and ignores constant factors: O(1): a fixed amount, however large n is. O(n): grows in proportion to n. Twice the elements, about twice the cost. O(n²): grows with the square of the input size. Twice the elements, about four times the cost. O(log n): grows with the logarithm of n, the number of times you can halve n before reaching 1. It is about 20 for a million elements. O(...) is an upper bound ("at most this fast-growing"). Θ (Big Theta) means "exactly this growth rate, up to a constant factor", and Ω (Big Omega) means "at least this growth rate". Now the four properties that every sort in this module will be judged on. In-place: uses O(1) extra memory beyond the input (some definitions allow O(log n) for a recursion stack). Bubble, selection and insertion are all in-place. Stable sort: equal keys keep their original relative order. If you sort orders by date and two orders share a date, a stable sort leaves them in the order they arrived. Adaptive: runs faster when the input is already partly sorted. Online algorithm: can sort a stream, accepting elements one at a time. We also count two different costs: key comparisons (is a[i] < a[j]?) and moves (swaps or writes). They matter in different settings. Comparing two long strings is expensive; writing to flash memory wears it out. Inversions: a measure of disorder An inversion is a pair of positions i < j with a[i] > a[j]: an earlier element that is bigger than a later one. A sorted array has 0 inversions. How many inversions can there be? An array of n elements has a fixed number of pairs of positions, and in a reversed array of distinct items every one of those pairs is out of order. That gives the maximum: So [4, 3, 2, 1] has 6 inversions, and a reversed array of 1,000 items has 499,500. Inversions matter because swapping an out-of-order adjacent pair removes exactly one inversion; swapping an ordered pair can instead add one. So a sort that only swaps neighbours must do at least as many swaps as there are inversions. On a typical shuffled input, that is about half the maximum: This only holds for a uniformly random permutation (every ordering equally likely) of distinct keys. Real data is often far less disordered, which is exactly what adaptive sorts exploit. Still, this single fact explains why bubble and insertion sort are quadratic on average: a quadratic average number of bubble swaps or insertion shifts. Key takeaways Stability preserves the input order of equal keys. Inversions measure pairwise disorder, and adjacent swaps remove one inversion at a time. Further reading Elementary sorts — Princeton Algorithms

sum: A pass fixes the largest remaining element at the right.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Bubble sort Repeatedly walk the array, swapping neighbours that are out of order. After the first pass the largest element has "bubbled" to the end; after the second pass the last two positions are final, and so on. Each pass compares neighbours across the unsorted part, which is one element shorter each time. Without an early exit, the comparisons add up to: Comparisons: up to that total, 45 for 10 elements. With the swapped flag, a sorted input finishes after one pass of one comparison per adjacent input pair (9 for 10 elements), so it is adaptive in the best case. Swaps: exactly the number of inversions. Stable, because it only swaps when strictly greater (>). Change that to >= and equal elements leapfrog each other: no longer stable. Bubble sort has an asymmetry. A large element near the start (a "rabbit") races to the end in one pass. A small element near the end (a "turtle") moves only one position left per pass. Four passes to move one element. Cocktail shaker sort (alternating direction) helps with turtles, but it is still O(n²). Key takeaways A pass fixes the largest remaining element at the right. A swap-free pass proves the array is sorted; small trailing values still move slowly left. Further reading Elementary sorts — Princeton Algorithms

sum: Minimum scans always make the same comparison count.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Selection sort Find the minimum of the unsorted part and swap it into the next position. The scan for the minimum always covers the whole unsorted part, so the counts never depend on the input: Comparisons: always exactly that total, whatever the input. It is not adaptive: a sorted array costs the same as a reversed one. Swaps: at most one fewer than the input size (499 for 500 elements). This is its one virtue. If writes are far more expensive than reads, selection sort has a linear worst-case swap bound, while bubble and insertion can require quadratic data movement. It need not use the fewest writes on every particular input. Not stable in its usual array form. The long-distance swap can jump an element past its equal twin: You can make it stable by shifting instead of swapping (insert the minimum and slide the rest right), but that costs O(n) writes per step and throws away its only advantage. Key takeaways Minimum scans always make the same comparison count. Long-distance swaps save data movement but can reverse equal-key records. Further reading Elementary sorts — Princeton Algorithms

sum: Each shift removes an inversion; nearly ordered inputs can be much cheaper.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Insertion sort Keep a sorted prefix. Take the next element and slide it left until it sits in the right place, like sorting a hand of cards. Trace on [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3] (the bar marks the end of the sorted prefix): Total shifts: 9, which is exactly the number of inversions in the input. That is the key insight: Insertion sort is O(n + inversions) Each shift removes one inversion, and each element costs at most one extra comparison to stop. So the running time grows with the number of elements plus the number of inversions. The trace has six elements and nine shifts. The sum of six and nine illustrates the growth model, rather than an exact count of executed instructions. Sorted input has zero displacement. The bound assumes shifting one place costs constant time, which is true for arrays. Insertion sort is: Stable, because it stops at the first element that is not strictly greater (a[j] > key). Adaptive, in the strong sense above. Online algorithm: you can feed it elements one at a time and the prefix is always sorted. Fast for small n. Its inner loop is a tight compare-and-shift with sequential memory access and no recursion. At small ranges (often thresholds of tens of elements) it can beat merge sort and quicksort, whose overheads (function calls, extra buffers, pivot selection) dominate at that size. A variant, binary insertion sort, finds the insertion point with binary search. That cuts comparisons to O(n log n), but shifting is still O(n²). It pays off when comparisons are expensive, which is why CPython uses it to build short runs in its list sort. Key takeaways Each shift removes an inversion; nearly ordered inputs can be much cheaper. Strictly greater comparisons preserve stability and the sorted prefix supports online insertion. Further reading Elementary sorts — Princeton Algorithms

sum: Compare writes, comparisons and existing order before choosing a simple sort.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Comparison Sort Comparisons Swaps/writes Stable? ------------ Bubble O(n²), O(n) if sorted One per inversion Yes Selection Fixed quadratic count At most one swap per pass No Insertion O(n + I) One per inversion Yes Here n is the number of elements and I the number of inversions in the input. The exact selection comparison and swap bounds are: All three are in-place with O(1) extra space and O(n²) average and worst case. Where these appear in real systems Hybrid sorts. Timsort (Python, Java objects, V8) extends short runs with binary insertion sort. C++'s std::sort in libstdc++ finishes with insertion sort over the nearly sorted array that introsort leaves behind. pdqsort switches to insertion sort for partitions below about 24 elements. Nearly sorted data. Maintaining a sorted list with occasional appends, or re-sorting a leaderboard after a few scores change, is close to O(n) with insertion sort. Shell sort generalises insertion sort by first sorting elements far apart (gaps like 701, 301, 132,... 1), removing many inversions with each long move. It is still used in some embedded code because it is tiny and needs no recursion. Pitfalls Breaking stability by accident. Using >= instead of > in bubble or insertion sort silently makes them unstable. Stability is a property of the implementation, not just the algorithm's name. Assuming "simple" means "fine for small inputs" without measuring what small is. With 10,000 elements, a quadratic sort makes about 50 million comparisons (10,000 × 10,000 / 2). Content gap: cross-language millisecond/second timings are omitted because no reproducible benchmark, hardware or implementation was supplied. Judging by comparisons alone. On 10,000 reversed elements, selection sort and insertion sort both make about 50 million comparisons, but insertion sort also does about 50 million writes while selection sort does at most 9,999 swaps. Which is cheaper depends on what your "write" costs. Key takeaways Compare writes, comparisons and existing order before choosing a simple sort. Hybrid sorts use insertion sort for small ranges, but the threshold requires measurement. Further reading Elementary sorts — Princeton Algorithms

sum: Each comparison consumes one front element.
x: The simple sorts are slow because each step makes only a tiny amount of progress: one adjacent swap removes one inversion. Merge sort makes progress in bulk by using divide and conquer: Divide the array into two halves. Conquer: sort each half recursively. Combine: merge the two sorted halves into one sorted array. The magic is that step 3 is cheap. Merging two sorted lists takes linear time, and that is enough to get O(n log n) overall, guaranteed, on every input. Here n is the number of elements, O(...) is Big O notation (how cost grows with n, ignoring constant factors) and the logarithm notation in each card is base two: how many times n can be halved before reaching 1, about 20 for a million. The merge step Picture two sorted piles of cards face up. Repeatedly take the smaller of the two top cards. When one pile empties, append the rest of the other. Each comparison outputs one element, and once one list runs out the rest of the other is copied with no comparisons at all. That gives the cost of a merge: Five comparisons for six elements: 3 + 3 − 1, the maximum. Why <= makes it stable When the two front elements are equal, we take the one from the left half. Everything in the left half came earlier in the original array, so equal keys keep their original order. Write < instead and equal elements from the right half jump ahead: the sort is no longer stable. One character decides it. Key takeaways Each comparison consumes one front element. Taking ties from the left keeps earlier equal-key records first. Further reading Merge sort and its complexity — Princeton Algorithms

t: Merge sort and its recursion tree
sum: Balanced recursive halves and linear merging give a logarithmic number of full-data levels.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. The full sort Proof of O(n log n): the recursion tree A recurrence describes a cost in terms of the same cost on smaller inputs. Merge sort's running time obeys this one: Draw it as a tree. The root does the merge constant times the input size in work. Its two children each do half that, so that level also totals the merge constant times the input size. Every level works the same way: Subproblem sizes halve each level, so they reach 1 after a base-two logarithmic number of levels. That gives one more than a base-two logarithmic number of levels, each costing the per-element merge constant times the input size. For 1,024 elements that is 11 levels. The proof assumes the input size is a power of two; for other sizes the halves differ by at most one element and the result is the same. Key takeaways The balanced recursion tree has logarithmically many levels, each touching the full input. Further reading Merge sort and its complexity — Princeton Algorithms

t: Merge recurrence tools and exact counts
sum: The master theorem connects recursive halves to the linear combine step.
x: Here n is the number of input elements. This unit builds on the preceding decision-tree or recurrence proof. The master theorem, a general recipe for divide-and-conquer recurrences, gives the same result: The theorem gives the answer, but the tree shows why: every level touches every element exactly once. Concrete numbers for a million elements: The operation counts differ greatly. Content gap: absolute runtimes are omitted because no benchmark environment or implementation was verified. Worst, best and average are all linear times logarithmic growth Merge sort always splits in the middle and always merges everything, so its cost hardly depends on the input. Plain merge sort is not adaptive: a sorted input still costs Θ(n log n). Timsort (covered later in this module) fixes that. The exact worst-case comparison count for top-down merge sort is known, and it is very close to the theoretical minimum (covered later in this module): For five elements that is 8 comparisons, one more than the minimum of 7 that the relevant unit in this module derives. Key takeaways The master theorem connects recursive halves to the linear combine step. Exact comparison counts refine asymptotic bounds without establishing measured runtimes. Further reading Merge sort and its complexity — Princeton Algorithms

t: Merge memory, bottom-up runs and inversions
sum: Array merging needs an element buffer; linked lists can relink nodes.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Space: the real cost The array version needs an O(n) auxiliary buffer for merging. You can allocate it once and reuse it, rather than slicing like the teaching code above (which allocates a lot of small lists). The recursion stack adds O(log n). In-place merge algorithms exist, but they are complicated and slower in practice. This is merge sort's main trade-off against quicksort with smaller-side recursion and heapsort, which need O(log n) and O(1) extra space respectively. Naive quicksort can use O(n) stack space. Linked lists are the exception. Merging two linked lists just re-links nodes, so merge sort on a list needs no buffer, and it does not need random access. It is the standard way to sort a linked list. Bottom-up merge sort You can skip recursion entirely. Treat the array as n runs of length 1, merge neighbouring pairs into runs of length 2, then 4, 8 and so on. Same O(n log n), no recursion stack, and the access pattern is simple sequential passes. It is also the idea behind external sorting. A bonus: counting inversions While merging, whenever you take an element from the right half, it is smaller than every element still waiting in the left half. Each of those is an inversion. Adding len(left) - i at that moment counts all inversions in O(n log n), instead of O(n²) by checking every pair. This is used to measure how similar two rankings are (Kendall tau distance). Key takeaways Array merging needs an element buffer; linked lists can relink nodes. Bottom-up merging avoids recursion, and taking a right element counts inversions with remaining left elements. Further reading Merge sort and its complexity — Princeton Algorithms

sum: Generate sorted runs, then merge their buffered fronts with a heap.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. External sorting: data bigger than memory Suppose you must sort 100 GB of records on a machine with 1 GB of RAM. You cannot load it all, and random access to disk is slow. Merge sort's sequential access pattern makes it the natural fit. Phase 1: run generation. For a simplified example, reserve 1 GB for sortable records with additional memory available for overhead, sort each chunk, and write it as a sorted run. That gives 100 runs. On a machine with only 1 GB total, choose smaller chunks and expect more runs. Phase 2: k-way merge. Open all 100 runs at once. Give each a small input buffer (say 8 MB each, reserving the remaining memory for output, heap and process overhead) and repeatedly output the smallest front element. With k runs (here k = 100), finding the smallest of the k fronts efficiently uses a min-heap of size k (covered in the trees module), costing O(log k) per element. The arithmetic of the plan: Total: every record is read and written twice (once per phase), all sequentially. If there are too many runs to merge in one go, you merge in several passes, each multiplying run length by k. PostgreSQL does exactly this When a sort needs more memory than work_mem (default 4 MB), PostgreSQL switches to an external merge sort using temporary files. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Sort Method: external merge Disk:... instead of quicksort Memory:.... Raising work_mem for a big reporting query can keep the sort in memory. The same pattern appears in big-data systems: MapReduce and Spark sort map output into spill files and merge them, and LSM-tree databases (RocksDB, Cassandra) merge sorted files during compaction. Key takeaways Generate sorted runs, then merge their buffered fronts with a heap. Run budgets must leave room for buffers and process overhead; extra merge passes add disk traffic. Further reading Merge sort and its complexity — Princeton Algorithms PostgreSQL memory budgets and temporary files

sum: Merge sort provides stable ordering and a worst-case guarantee.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Trade-offs and pitfalls Property Merge sort ------ Time (all cases) Θ(n log n) Extra space O(n) for arrays Stable Yes, with <= Adaptive No (plain version) Use it when you need guaranteed linear times logarithmic growth, stability, a linked list, or data on disk or arriving as sorted streams. Small sub-arrays. Recursing down to size 1 wastes time. Real implementations switch to insertion sort below roughly 16 to 32 elements. Skip merges that are not needed. If left[-1] <= right[0], the halves are already in order and the merge can be skipped. For an index-range implementation that returns without copying an already ordered range, this makes sorted-input time linear. In the slicing example, creating and concatenating halves still costs Θ(n log n), even if comparisons become linear. Midpoint overflow. In languages with fixed-width integers, (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow on huge arrays. Use lo + (hi - lo) / 2. This bug sat in Java's library for years (covered later in this module). Key takeaways Merge sort provides stable ordering and a worst-case guarantee. Skipping comparisons in a slicing implementation still leaves copying costs. Further reading Merge sort and its complexity — Princeton Algorithms

sum: Lomuto finishes by placing the pivot at its sorted index.
x: Merge sort does its work on the way up: split blindly, then merge carefully. Quicksort does the opposite. It works on the way down: partition carefully, then the two halves need no combining at all. Pick a pivot element. Partition: rearrange the array so everything smaller than the pivot comes before everything larger. Recursively sort the two sides. Done; there is no merge step. Throughout this lesson, n is the number of elements being sorted, and costs use Big O notation (O, Θ and Ω: at most, exactly and at least this growth rate, ignoring constant factors). Quadratic means growing with n², the input size squared. Quicksort is in-place, has tiny inner loops and accesses memory sequentially, which can make it fast on arrays; the fastest choice depends on data, comparator and implementation. Its weakness is that a bad pivot makes the split lopsided, and a run of bad pivots makes it quadratic. Most of the engineering around quicksort is about avoiding that. Lomuto partition The simpler scheme, popularised by Programming Pearls and CLRS. Use the last element as the pivot. Keep a boundary i: everything left of i is smaller than the pivot. Trace on [7, 2, 1, 6, 8, 5, 3, 4], pivot 4: After partitioning, the pivot is in its final sorted position. Recursion handles [2,1,3] and [8,5,7,6]. Key takeaways Lomuto finishes by placing the pivot at its sorted index. Partition swaps can reorder equal keys, so this implementation is unstable. Further reading Quicksort and partitioning — Princeton Algorithms

sum: Hoare returns a split boundary, not the final pivot index.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Hoare partition Hoare's original 1961 scheme uses two pointers moving towards each other, swapping pairs that are on the wrong side. Same input, pivot a[3] = 6: Two differences matter: Under a uniformly random permutation of distinct keys, these classical schemes give Hoare roughly one-third of Lomuto's expected swaps; this is not a bound for every input. Hoare does not put the pivot in its final place. It only guarantees that everything in the left part is no bigger than the pivot and everything in the right part is no smaller. So the recursion is on [lo, p] and [p+1, hi], not p-1. Using Lomuto bounds with Hoare can leave an unsorted boundary element out of recursion. Choosing hi as the pivot index in this Hoare variant can instead fail to shrink a partition and cause infinite recursion. Duplicates On an array where every element is equal, Lomuto with < finds nothing smaller, so every partition is zero keys on one side and every non-pivot key on the other: O(n²). Hoare's pointers stop on equal elements (< and > are strict), swap them, and meet in the middle: balanced splits, O(n log n). Stopping on equal keys looks wasteful but is exactly what saves it. Key takeaways Hoare returns a split boundary, not the final pivot index. Strict scans stop on equal keys and balanced duplicate splits avoid Lomuto’s all-equal degeneration. Further reading Quicksort and partitioning — Princeton Algorithms

sum: Consistently extreme pivots make a quadratic triangle of comparisons.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Pivot choice and the worst case Quicksort's cost depends entirely on how balanced the splits are. Two recurrences (costs written in terms of the same cost on smaller inputs) show the two extremes: With the first or last element as the pivot, already sorted input is the worst case: each partition peels off one element. Lomuto then compares the pivot with every other element of a sub-array that shrinks by one each time: For 100 elements the recursion also goes 99 levels deep. For a million elements that is about 500 billion comparisons and a stack overflow. Sorted and reverse-sorted inputs are common in practice, so this is not theoretical. Defences: Median-of-three: use the median of the first, middle and last elements. Fixes sorted and reverse-sorted inputs and gives slightly better splits on random data. Large arrays can use the "ninther" (median of three medians of three). Random pivot: pick a uniformly random element. Now no particular input is bad; only bad luck is. The expected number of comparisons is given below, for every fixed input of distinct keys, with fresh independent uniform pivots. Randomizing the pivot alone does not rescue Lomuto on all-equal keys. The probability of quadratic behaviour is vanishingly small for large n. Deterministic pivots can be attacked If an attacker knows your pivot rule, they can construct an input that triggers the worst case. McIlroy's 1999 paper "A Killer Adversary for Quicksort" did this against C library qsort implementations. For untrusted input, use randomisation or a sort with a worst-case guarantee. Key takeaways Consistently extreme pivots make a quadratic triangle of comparisons. Independent random pivots give an expected guarantee for distinct keys, not an absolute worst-case bound. Further reading Quicksort and partitioning — Princeton Algorithms

sum: Recursing only on the smaller side bounds stack growth.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Recursion depth Even with good pivots, naive quicksort can recurse O(n) deep on bad luck. The fix is simple: recurse into the smaller side and loop on the larger. Each recursive call is on at most half the elements, so the size halves with every level of nesting: The larger side is handled by the loop, which uses no extra stack. 3-way partitioning Real data often has many duplicates: sorting a million orders by country code, or by a status with five values. Two-way partitioning keeps re-partitioning equal keys. 3-way partitioning (Dijkstra's Dutch national flag problem) splits into < pivot, = pivot and > pivot, and recurses only on the outer two. With k distinct key values among the n elements, randomized 3-way quicksort has an expected O(n(1 + log k)) bound; exact work also depends on key frequencies; with all keys equal, it is a single O(n) pass. Sedgewick and Bentley showed this is optimal up to a constant for inputs with many duplicates. Key takeaways Recursing only on the smaller side bounds stack growth. Three-way partitioning finishes equal keys immediately and recurses on the outer ranges. Further reading Quicksort and partitioning — Princeton Algorithms

sum: A depth budget detects excessive quicksort work and switches to heapsort.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Introsort: a worst-case guarantee David Musser's introsort (1997) combines three algorithms: Run quicksort (median-of-three pivots). Track recursion depth. If it exceeds a limit (formula below), the pivots are going badly, so switch that sub-array to heapsort, which is O(n log n) worst case (covered later in this module). Leave sub-arrays below a threshold (16 elements in libstdc++) unsorted, then finish with insertion sort. The depth limit in libstdc++ is: Since heapsort costs O(n log n) on any sub-array it takes over, the total stays O(n log n). You get quicksort's speed in the common case and an O(n log n) guarantee. C++ requires std::sort to be O(n log n) in the worst case since C++11, and the major standard libraries (libstdc++, MSVC and current libc++) use introsort-style hybrids..NET's Array.Sort is introsort too. pdqsort (covered later in this module) is a modern descendant. Key takeaways A depth budget detects excessive quicksort work and switches to heapsort. Deterministic pivot heuristics alone cannot guarantee safety against adversarial inputs. Further reading Quicksort and partitioning — Princeton Algorithms

sum: Dual pivots change comparisons and swaps; an analytic model does not prove a runtime improvement.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Variants in production Dual-pivot quicksort (Yaroslavskiy, 2009) partitions into three parts using two pivots. Java has used it for Arrays.sort on primitive arrays since Java 7. For the analyzed unsampled algorithm on uniformly random distinct keys, the leading comparison count is slightly lower, while swaps increase (formula below). This model alone does not establish a runtime or cache-miss improvement for a modern Java implementation. Not stable. Partitioning swaps elements over long distances, so equal keys can be reordered. That is why Java uses quicksort only for primitives (where stability is invisible) and a merge sort for objects. Summary Quicksort ------ Average time Θ(n log n), ~expected logarithmic-factor linear comparisons Worst time Θ(n²) (introsort: n log n) Extra space O(log n) stack with smaller-side recursion Stable No Key takeaways Dual pivots change comparisons and swaps; an analytic model does not prove a runtime improvement. Objects with visible ties need a stable sort; quicksort partitioning normally reorders ties. Further reading Quicksort and partitioning — Princeton Algorithms Analysis of Yaroslavskiy’s dual-pivot quicksort

sum: Build a max-heap from the last parent toward the root.
x: Throughout this lesson, n is the number of elements being sorted, and the logarithm notation in each card is base two: how many times n can be halved before reaching 1 (about 20 for a million). O, Θ and Ω are Big O, Big Theta and Big Omega: growth rates of at most, exactly and at least, ignoring constant factors. So far we have two O(n log n) sorts, each with a catch. Merge sort is guaranteed linear times logarithmic growth but needs O(n) extra memory. Quicksort is in place but can go quadratic. Heapsort removes both catches: O(n log n) in the worst case, with O(1) extra space. Then we will ask a deeper question: could some cleverer algorithm do better than linear times logarithmic growth? The answer is no, for any algorithm that sorts by comparing elements, and the proof is one of the most elegant in computer science. Heapsort Heapsort is selection sort with a better data structure. Selection sort spends O(n) finding the maximum each round. A binary max-heap (covered in the trees module) finds and removes the maximum in O(log n). Recall the array layout. The heap is a tree stored level by level in the array, with no pointers; the position of a node's children is computed from its own index: Every parent is at least as large as its children (the heap property). So the maximum is always at index 0. The algorithm has two phases: Build a max-heap in place from the array. Repeatedly swap the root (the maximum) with the last element of the heap, shrink the heap by one, and sift the new root down to restore the heap property. The sorted part grows from the right, exactly like selection sort. Trace Input [4, 10, 3, 5, 1]. Phase 1. Start at the last node that has a child; every node after it is a leaf, which is already a valid one-element heap: Phase 2. Swap root to the end, sift down, repeat. Key takeaways Build a max-heap from the last parent toward the root. Move the root to the sorted suffix and restore the remaining heap by sifting down. Further reading Priority queues and heapsort — Princeton Algorithms

sum: Most heap nodes have short or zero sift-down paths.
x: This unit builds on the preceding sorting units. Here n is the number of input elements; Big O bounds growth up to a constant factor, and logarithms are base two unless stated otherwise. Why the build phase is O(n), not O(n log n) Inserting n elements one at a time would cost O(n log n). The bottom-up build is cheaper because most nodes are near the bottom, where sift-down is short.
