Where these show up Mark-and-sweep garbage collectors mark live objects by traversing the reference graph from the roots (a multi-source traversal), then sweep whatever was not reached. Web crawlers traverse link graphs; their scheduling may use breadth-first ideas, priorities and per-site limits. Degrees of separation can be found with BFS. Bidirectional BFS searches from both ends; in directed graphs the backward search follows reversed edges. In a roughly tree-like model, two half-depth searches are much smaller than one full-depth search: With 100 contacts each and six degrees of separation, that is about two million vertices instead of a trillion. Overlap between friend lists, degree variation and stopping rules affect actual work. Content gap No claim is made about LinkedIn’s current implementation: an authoritative implementation description was not verified. Build tools and package managers use DFS to walk dependency trees. Key takeaways Include keys, fuel or other move-dependent information in visited-state identity. Bidirectional search reverses edges on its backward side in a directed graph. Tree-like frontier estimates are modelling assumptions, not dataset benchmarks. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Breadth-first search — Wikipedia Implicit graph — Wikipedia

sum: Grey vertices remain on the active recursion path.
x: Lesson 2 used DFS just to visit things. Its real power is the structure it leaves behind: which vertices are still "open" on the stack, and the order in which vertices finish. That structure answers questions such as "is there a circular dependency?", "in what order should I build these modules?" and "which pages all link to each other?". Throughout this lesson, n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges, and O(…) is Big O notation: how the running time grows with the graph's size, ignoring constant factors. Every algorithm here runs in O(n + m), the same as one traversal. The three colours Give every vertex a colour during DFS: White: not yet discovered. Grey: discovered, still on the recursion stack (we are somewhere inside its subtree). Black: finished; all its outgoing edges have been examined and all recursive calls it made have returned. When DFS at u looks at an edge u→v, the colour of v classifies the edge: v is Edge type Meaning --------- White Tree edge DFS goes to v Grey Back edge v is u or an ancestor of u Black Forward or cross Already done A back edge points from a vertex to one of its own ancestors, closing a loop. That gives the key theorem: a directed graph has a cycle if and only if a DFS covering all vertices finds a back edge. Cycle detection in directed graphs Why "visited" is not enough A plain visited set reports a cycle in this DAG, which has none: DFS goes 0→1→3, finishes, then 0→2 finds 3 already visited. But 3 is black (finished), not grey. It is a cross edge, not a loop. Grey, not visited Only grey means "on my current path". Checking v in visited instead of color[v] == GREY gives false positives on any DAG where two paths reconverge, such as the diamond above. Key takeaways Grey vertices remain on the active recursion path. A black reconvergence is not a directed cycle. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Depth-first search — Wikipedia

sum: Ignore the particular parent edge, not arbitrary edges to a parent.
x: Directed DFS colours were covered previously. Undirected adjacency lists store each edge at both endpoints, which creates an immediate reverse edge. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. Cycle detection in undirected graphs In an undirected graph every edge appears in both directions, so from u you will always see your parent again. Ignore that one edge; any other already-visited neighbour closes a cycle. Two shortcuts. First, a connected undirected graph with no cycle is a tree, and a tree's edge count is fixed by its vertex count: So a connected graph with 10 vertices and 10 edges must contain a cycle. The test needs the graph to be connected: a triangle plus one separate, isolated vertex has 4 vertices and 3 edges, one fewer than the vertex count, yet it contains a cycle. Second, Union-Find (lesson 6) detects a cycle the moment an edge joins two vertices already in the same set. The code is presented for simple undirected graphs. In a recursive multigraph DFS, distinguish the particular parent edge by edge id: ignoring every edge to the parent can hide a genuine two-edge cycle. Pitfalls Directed cycle detection with a visited set: reports cycles in DAGs (the diamond). Undirected logic on a directed graph or vice versa: the parent trick is only for undirected graphs. Recursion depth: a sufficiently long chain can exceed Python’s configured recursion limit. Use iterative versions or sys.setrecursionlimit with care. Forgetting disconnected parts: every algorithm here needs the outer "for each unvisited vertex" loop. Key takeaways Ignore the particular parent edge, not arbitrary edges to a parent. The edge-count tree test requires connected input. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Cycle (graph theory) — Wikipedia)

t: Ordering dependencies with Kahn and DFS
sum: Orient prerequisite edges consistently.
x: A DAG is a directed graph with no cycle. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. DFS colour-based cycle detection is an earlier prerequisite; recursion-depth limits apply to the DFS implementation below. Topological sort A topological order of a DAG lists the vertices so that every edge u→v has u before v. For prerequisites, orient each edge from prerequisite to dependent: socks before shoes, shirt before tie. If edges instead point from a target to its dependencies, use reverse topological order. It exists if and only if the graph has no directed cycle, and there may be many valid orders. Example DAG (A→C, B→C, B→D, C→E, D→E): Kahn's algorithm (BFS-style) Repeatedly output a vertex with no remaining incoming edges, then delete its outgoing edges. On the example: in-degrees A0, B0, C2, D1, E2. The queue starts [A, B]. Output A (C→1), B (C→0, D→0), C (E→1), D (E→0), E. Order: A, B, C, D, E. If a cycle exists, its vertices never reach in-degree 0, so the output is short. That makes Kahn's a cycle detector for free. Replace the queue with a min-heap to get the lexicographically smallest order. DFS-based Run DFS and record each vertex when it finishes. A vertex finishes only after everything it points to has finished, so reversing the finish order puts every vertex before every vertex it has an edge to. On the example (starting from A): finish order E, C, A, D, B. Reversed: B, D, A, C, E. Different from Kahn's, and equally valid. (This version assumes a DAG; combine it with the grey check to detect cycles.) Both run in O(n + m) for n vertices and m edges. Kahn's DFS-based --------- Style Queue, in-degrees Recursion, finish order Cycle check Built in Needs grey check Parallelism Shows ready tasks No Recursion None Deep on long chains Where it is used GNU Make, Bazel and Gradle order build steps topologically. Package managers order installs. Acyclic spreadsheet formulas can be recalculated in dependency order; circular formulas need error handling or an explicitly supported iterative calculation mode. Python ships graphlib.TopologicalSorter, a Kahn-style sorter whose get_ready() returns every task that can currently run in parallel. Key takeaways Orient prerequisite edges consistently. Kahn detects a cycle when it cannot output every vertex. Reverse DFS finish order is valid only after establishing acyclicity. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Topological sorting — Wikipedia

t: Strong components with Kosaraju and Tarjan
sum: Strong connectivity requires reachability in both directions.
x: DFS discovery and finish order were established in earlier units. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. The recursive examples assume their depth fits Python’s configured recursion limit. Strongly connected components In a directed graph, u and v are strongly connected if each can reach the other. A strongly connected component (SCC) is a maximal set of mutually reachable vertices. Edges: 0→1, 1→2, 2→0, 2→3, 3→4, 4→5, 5→3, 6→5, 6→7, 7→6. SCCs: {0, 1, 2}, {3, 4, 5}, {6, 7}. Collapse each SCC to a single vertex and discard internal edges; you get the condensation, which is always a DAG. That is why SCCs matter: they turn any directed graph into a DAG of "clusters" you can topologically sort. Kosaraju's algorithm DFS the whole graph, recording finish order. Reverse every edge. DFS the reversed graph, taking start vertices in decreasing finish time. Each tree found is one SCC. Why it works: the vertex that finishes last lies in a "source" SCC of the condensation. In the reversed graph that SCC becomes a sink, so a DFS from it cannot leak into other components. Two passes, each O(n + m) for n vertices and m edges, and simple to get right. Tarjan's algorithm One DFS pass. Each vertex gets an index idx (discovery order) and a low value: the smallest index reachable from its subtree using tree edges plus at most one edge to a vertex still on the SCC stack. This separate stack can include vertices whose recursive calls have already returned; it is not the grey recursion stack. Vertices are pushed onto a separate stack as discovered. When a vertex finishes with low[u] == idx[u], it is the root of an SCC: pop the stack down to u. In symbols, the code updates low like this: If even that earliest reachable vertex is u itself (the equality tested in the code), nothing in u's subtree escapes to an older open vertex, so u and everything above it on the stack form one SCC. On the example it returns [5, 4, 3], then [2, 1, 0], then [7, 6]. Tarjan emits SCCs in reverse topological order of the condensation: sinks first. Also O(n + m) for n vertices and m edges, one pass, no reversed graph, but the on_stack check is easy to get wrong. Uses of SCCs 2-SAT is solved by building an implication graph and checking that no variable sits in the same SCC as its negation. Compilers find mutually recursive functions. Garbage collectors and dependency analysers find reference cycles. Key takeaways Strong connectivity requires reachability in both directions. Condensation contracts mutually reachable groups into a DAG. Tarjan’s SCC stack differs from the recursion stack. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Strongly connected components — cp-algorithms Strongly connected component — Wikipedia Tarjan's strongly connected components algorithm — Wikipedia

sum: Colour every component, not just the one containing the first vertex.
x: BFS visits successive distance layers. Import deque from collections for the following function. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges; adjacency lists include every vertex and both directions of every undirected edge. Bipartite check An undirected graph is bipartite if its vertices split into two sides with every edge crossing between them: students and courses, jobs and machines. Equivalently, it can be 2-coloured so no edge joins two vertices of the same colour. Theorem: a graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd-length cycle. A square (4-cycle) is bipartite; a triangle is not. BFS colours by layer parity (whether the layer number is even or odd): For example, a vertex 3 edges from the start gets colour 1. A clash means an edge inside one layer, or between two layers of equal parity, which closes an odd cycle. The check costs O(n + m) for n vertices and m edges, and the outer loop handles disconnected graphs. Key takeaways Colour every component, not just the one containing the first vertex. A same-colour edge proves that the undirected graph is not bipartite. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Bipartite graph — Wikipedia

t: Relaxation and a lazy Dijkstra min-heap
sum: Relaxation improves a distance only when an edge yields a cheaper route.
x: BFS finds the path with the fewest edges. Once edges carry weights (kilometres, milliseconds, pounds), the fewest edges is no longer the cheapest. A motorway detour of 3 roads can beat a single slow lane. This lesson covers the single-source problem: the cheapest distance from one source s to every other vertex. Assume finite graphs, finite numeric weights and valid adjacency entries for every vertex. The Python min-heap examples require mutually orderable vertex labels to break distance ties. Arithmetic and expected dictionary access are treated as constant-time. Throughout, n is the number of vertices, m the number of edges, w(u, v) the weight of the edge from u to v, and O(…) is Big O notation: how the running time grows with n and m, ignoring constant factors. Every algorithm here is built on one operation. Relaxation Keep a tentative distance dist[v] for every vertex, starting at infinity (0 for the source). The following fragment belongs inside a traversal with distances and parents already initialised. To relax an edge u→v of weight w is to ask "is going via u better than what I have?": In the worked line, v's best so far is 9, u is 3 away and the edge costs 4, so v improves to 7. In Python: Distances only ever decrease, and never drop below the true shortest distance. The algorithms differ only in which edges they relax, and in what order. Dijkstra's algorithm Intuition: grow a region of "settled" vertices outward from s, always settling the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance next. It is BFS where the queue is ordered by distance instead of arrival. Python's heapq has no "decrease key", so we push a new entry and skip outdated ones when they surface (lazy deletion). The min-heap holds O(m + 1) entries and can pop stale entries as well as live ones. Each push or pop costs time proportional to the logarithm of the min-heap size, and in a simple graph the min-heap size cannot outgrow n² by much: For a simple graph with one thousand vertices, a min-heap with up to a million entries has a base-two logarithmic factor of about twenty rather than ten: a constant factor, so the bound is unchanged. Arbitrary multigraphs (with repeated edges) can have m far above n², so the logarithmic factor for this lazy implementation depends on the edge count, with one added to keep the argument positive. Key takeaways Relaxation improves a distance only when an edge yields a cheaper route. Skip stale min-heap entries created by earlier tentative distances. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Dijkstra's algorithm — Wikipedia

t: Dijkstra traces, costs and negative edges
sum: Non-negative weights justify settling the closest unsettled vertex.
x: Earlier Dijkstra code uses heapq and tentative distances, re-pushing an improved vertex and skipping obsolete entries. Here n counts vertices, m counts edges, and edge weights have one common cost unit. The worked trace and correctness proof assume non-negative weights unless explicitly stated otherwise. A worked trace Edges: S→A 4, S→B 1, B→A 2, B→C 5, A→C 1, C→T 3. The table lists nonstale pops; obsolete A(4) and C(6) entries are skipped. Pop dist after relaxing ------ S (0) A 4, B 1 B (1) A 3, C 6 A (3) C 4 C (4) T 7 T (7) done The direct edge S→A (4) loses to S→B→A (3), and C improves twice. Final: S 0, B 1, A 3, C 4, T 7. Why it is correct When u is popped with the smallest tentative distance d, could a cheaper path to u exist? Any such path P must leave the settled region somewhere, through some unsettled vertex x: So d is final. The first inequality is exactly where non-negative weights are needed: a negative edge after x could make P cheaper than dist(x). Complexity Here n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges. An indexed binary min-heap extracts each reachable vertex once and uses decrease-key on improvements. The earlier lazy version can also pop stale entries, with at most one new push per successful edge relaxation. On simple graphs, both give this conventional growth bound: A road graph of a million junctions and four million road segments needs on the order of 10⁸ basic steps; that is a scale estimate, not a measured time. Priority queue Time ------ Binary min-heap O((n + m) log n) Fibonacci min-heap O(m + n log n) Unsorted array O(n²) For dense graphs, the O(n²) array bound avoids the binary min-heap bound’s logarithmic factor. Fibonacci min-heaps improve the asymptotic decrease-key bound. Actual speed depends on implementation, successful relaxations and workload; these bounds do not establish a universal winner. Why negative edges break it The correctness argument assumed that extending a path never makes it cheaper. A negative edge breaks exactly that. Pop A: tentative distances are four to B and five to C. Pop B at distance four and settle it: D becomes six. Pop C at distance five: its negative edge improves B to two. But B is already settled and its edge to D has already been used. Textbook settle-once Dijkstra reports six for D; the true A→C→B→D route costs four. "My lazy version handled it" The lazy-deletion code above does re-push B with distance 2 and fixes D, because it never marks vertices as final. That variant gives correct answers with negative edges (but no negative cycles), but a vertex can be re-processed many times, and the worst case becomes exponential. Use Bellman–Ford instead. You cannot fix negative edges by adding a constant to every weight either: a path with more edges gets penalised more, which changes which path is shortest. Key takeaways Non-negative weights justify settling the closest unsettled vertex. A lazy min-heap can pop stale entries; its simple-graph bound does not imply a measured winner. Constant edge shifts alter paths with different edge counts. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Dijkstra's algorithm — Wikipedia Dijkstra — cp-algorithms Johnson's algorithm — Wikipedia

sum: At most one fewer round than vertices suffices without a reachable negative cycle.
x: The previous unit’s negative-edge graph is A→B 4, A→C 5, C→B −3 and B→D 2. From A, correct distances are A:0, B:2, C:5 and D:4. Here n counts vertices and m counts directed edges; the edge list has numbered endpoints for the implementation below. Bellman–Ford Relax every edge for at most one fewer rounds than there are vertices. Why n − 1 rounds? A shortest path without cycles visits each vertex at most once, so it has at most one edge fewer than there are vertices: Each round extends correct paths by one more edge, so after round 3 on the four-vertex example every distance is final. On the negative-edge example above, Bellman–Ford correctly returns A 0, B 2, C 5, D 4. If an n-th round can still improve something, a negative cycle is reachable from the source. Distances are unbounded below for vertices reachable from that cycle; other vertices can still have finite distances. This implementation returns None for the entire result when it detects one. Bellman–Ford detects this; Dijkstra cannot. Time: up to n − 1 rounds, each relaxing all m edges: When there is at least one edge, this is conventionally written O(nm). The 10¹¹ figure counts edge-relaxation opportunities; it is not an elapsed-time prediction. Real uses: distance-vector routing protocols such as RIP are a distributed Bellman–Ford, each router relaxing the routes its neighbours advertise. Currency arbitrage detection turns exchange rates into weights with a logarithm, which turns multiplying rates into adding weights: For example, rates 0.9, 0.9 and 1.25 multiply to 1.0125, a 1.25% profit, so their weights sum to a negative number and Bellman–Ford flags the cycle. SPFA The "Shortest Path Faster Algorithm" only re-relaxes edges out of vertices whose distance just changed, using a queue. Its performance depends on edge order and graph structure; its worst-case bound remains O(nm) (vertices times edges) when m ≥ 1. Key takeaways At most one fewer round than vertices suffices without a reachable negative cycle. The extra relaxation test detects cycles reachable from the source. In-place relaxation can propagate through several edges in one round. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Bellman–Ford algorithm — Wikipedia

t: 0–1 BFS and choosing a shortest-path method
sum: A zero-weight improvement goes to the front of the deque.
x: Earlier units covered unweighted BFS, Dijkstra and Bellman–Ford. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. INF in the snippet is float("inf"). A in the comparison table is introduced in the next two units; its heuristic is an estimate of remaining cost. 0-1 BFS If every weight is 0 or 1, you do not need a min-heap. Use a deque: push to the front for a 0-edge (same distance) and to the back for a 1-edge (one more). Queued distance labels occupy at most two consecutive values in nondecreasing order; obsolete entries are skipped. Thus, it behaves like Dijkstra's min-heap at O(1) per operation: O(n + m) total, for n vertices and m edges. Typical problems: the fewest walls to break in a maze (stepping into a wall costs 1, open floor 0), or a grid where following the printed arrow is free and changing direction costs 1. Choosing an algorithm In the table, n is the number of vertices, m the number of edges, h the A heuristic, and log the logarithm. Graph Use Time --------- Unweighted BFS O(n + m) Weights 0/1 0-1 BFS O(n + m) Non-negative Dijkstra, simple graph O((n + m) log(n + 1)) One target + h A Depends on heuristic, ties and reopening Negative edges Bellman–Ford O(n + nm) DAG, any weights Topo order O(n + m) The last row: in a DAG, relax edges in topological order and each vertex is final when you reach it, even with negative weights. Key takeaways A zero-weight improvement goes to the front of the deque. Match edge-weight assumptions to the algorithm before comparing costs. Further reading Primary reference for this unit 0-1 BFS — cp-algorithms

t: A* priorities and a grid implementation
sum: A* orders by cost already paid plus estimated remaining cost.
x: Dijkstra’s min-heap ordering was covered earlier. This unit uses heapq and INF = float("inf"), as in that implementation. The grid has four-direction movement at unit cost; a # character is a wall. A search Dijkstra settles vertices by distance from the source; obstacles, weights and connectivity shape the explored region. If you want one specific target and can estimate how far you are from it, you can steer the search. A orders the min-heap by a priority that adds a guess of the remaining distance to the distance already travelled: A vertex six steps from the start and estimated four from the goal has priority ten, so it is expanded before one three steps from the start and estimated nine from the goal (priority twelve). On a grid the usual estimate is the Manhattan distance, the number of up/down/left/right steps ignoring walls: Key takeaways A orders by cost already paid plus estimated remaining cost. The grid implementation rejects blocked endpoints and ragged inputs. Manhattan distance fits four-way unit-cost movement. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Introduction to A — Red Blob Games

sum: Admissibility and consistency make different guarantees.
x: A ranks vertices using known cost plus a heuristic estimate; these quantities and edge weights share one cost unit. A heuristic’s guarantee depends on the graph and movement rules, not its name alone. Heuristic quality For finite graphs with non-negative edge costs, a zero heuristic at the reachable goal, and a heuristic expressed in the same cost units, two properties matter: For example, Manhattan distance on a 4-way grid with cost-1 moves is consistent: one move changes it by at most 1, the cost of the move. Admissible: h never overestimates the true remaining cost (the first line). A that reopens a vertex when a better g is found and stops when the goal is popped returns an optimal path. Merely discovering the goal is not a safe stopping condition. Consistent heuristic (monotone): the second line holds for every edge. With a zero heuristic at the goal this implies admissibility, and no settled vertex needs reopening. A zero heuristic gives Dijkstra’s ordering. A perfect-distance heuristic can still expand many vertices lying on different optimal paths; ties matter. Movement Admissible h ------ 4-way grid, cost 1 Manhattan 8-way grid, straight cost 1 and diagonal cost the square root of 2 Octile 8-way grid, all moves cost 1 Chebyshev Geometric edges costing at least their Euclidean length Euclidean Travel time with a valid global speed upper bound Straight-line distance ÷ that speed Trading optimality for speed Weighted A search inflates the heuristic to search more greedily towards the goal. It can reduce expansions, but a speedup is not guaranteed. The price is a bounded loss of optimality, shown below. On a finite graph with non-negative costs, an admissible heuristic that is zero at the goal, reopening on improved known cost, and stopping when the goal is popped, weighted A returns a cost within a known factor of the best: With an inflation factor of 1.5 and a true shortest cost of 100, the path found costs at most 150. Route-planning methods include contraction hierarchies and landmark heuristics (ALT). Content gap Product-specific implementations and millisecond/vertex-count performance claims are omitted: no identified dataset, implementation and reproducible measurement support them here. Key takeaways Admissibility and consistency make different guarantees. Stop on a popped goal, with the stated reopening policy. Weighted A trades an optimality bound for more goal-directed ordering. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Admissible heuristic — Wikipedia A search algorithm — Wikipedia Thayer and Ruml: Faster Than Weighted A

sum: The outer loop unlocks one possible intermediate vertex.
x: Sometimes one source is not enough. A delivery company wants the driving time between every pair of its 300 depots. A network tool wants every router's distance to every other to find the network's graph diameter (the longest shortest path). A game precomputes distances between all waypoints so that AI agents can look them up instantly. That is the all-pairs shortest paths (APSP) problem: fill an n × n table where d[i][j] is the shortest distance from i to j. Just writing the answer down takes a lot of work: For 300 depots that is 90,000 distances. A compressed or query-only representation is a different task. Throughout, m is the number of edges and O(…) is Big O notation: grows at most this fast, up to a constant factor. Assume finite weights and constant-time arithmetic in the complexity bounds below. Floyd–Warshall Floyd–Warshall is a short, elegant piece of dynamic programming. The idea Number the vertices 0 to n − 1. The DP table has one layer per number of "unlocked" vertices: The initial layer allows no intermediates: use minimum direct edge weights, also allowing the zero-length diagonal walk (so a negative graph self-loop can make the diagonal negative), and ∞ for absent connections. The final layer allows every vertex: it is the answer. For the finite shortest-distance recurrence, assume no negative cycles. Going from k to k + 1, we unlock vertex k. A shortest path using intermediates from {0..k} either avoids k (cost dₖ[i][j]) or passes through k exactly once (cost dₖ[i][k] + dₖ[k][j]). So: For the worked line, suppose there is an edge 2→0 costing five and an edge 0→1 costing three: before any vertex is unlocked, 2 cannot reach 1, but via vertex 0 it costs 5 + 3 = 8. The code drops the k subscript and updates one table in place. Key takeaways The outer loop unlocks one possible intermediate vertex. Initialise minimum parallel-edge weights and preserve negative self-loops. A negative diagonal reveals a negative cycle. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Floyd–Warshall algorithm — Wikipedia Floyd–Warshall — cp-algorithms

t: Implementing Floyd–Warshall in the right order
sum: Keep the intermediate vertex loop outermost.
x: Earlier units defined the distance table by permitted intermediate vertices. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. The recurrence below assumes no negative cycles; affected pairs need the separate interpretation covered next. The worked graph used in this unit’s loop-order question has edges 0→1 3, 0→3 7, 1→0 8, 1→2 2, 2→0 5, 2→3 1 and 3→0 2. A wrong loop order can leave the 1→0 result at seven rather than the true five. The code A single matrix updated in place is safe: during round k, row k and column k do not change, because going through k to reach k adds nothing: So it does not matter whether you read old or new values. Time: O(m + n³), including edge initialisation, for n vertices and m edges; O(n³) for simple graphs. Skipping rows i that have no route to k can reduce actual iterations. Space: O(n²). Negative edges: fine. Negative cycles: afterwards some d[i][i] < 0. k must be the outermost loop The DP is over k. If you write for i: for j: for k:, then d[i][j] is finalised before the entries it depends on are ready. The code still runs and still looks plausible, but gives wrong answers on some graphs. Key takeaways Keep the intermediate vertex loop outermost. The diagonal identifies negative cycles after relaxation. In-place updates preserve the recurrence when shortest distances are finite. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Floyd–Warshall algorithm — Wikipedia Floyd–Warshall — cp-algorithms

sum: A next-hop table reconstructs only valid unaffected shortest paths.
x: The previous unit’s floyd_warshall(n, edges) returns distance and next-hop matrices. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. Each outer round permits one more intermediate vertex, and row/column indexing uses numbered vertices. A worked example k Key improvements ------ via 0 2→1: eight; 3→1: five; 1→3: fifteen via 1 0→2: five; 3→2: seven via 2 0→3: six; 1→0: seven; 1→3: three via 3 1→0: five; 2→0: three; 2→1: six Final matrix: Notice 1→0 improves twice: 8 directly, then 7 via 2, then 5 via 2 and 3 (1→2→3→0). Reconstructing paths Only reconstruct a pair after confirming no negative cycle lies on a route between its endpoints; affected pairs have no shortest path. For valid unaffected pairs, nxt stores the first hop. The guard below catches a cyclic or malformed table, but is not itself a complete negative-cycle test: This is a simplified shortest-path next-hop table. Real forwarding tables can aggregate destinations into network prefixes, use policy and offer multiple next hops. Why people like it Floyd–Warshall is four lines of logic, handles negative weights, has no min-heap, and array-based implementations can exploit contiguous rows and vectorised inner loops. The Python list implementation here does not itself guarantee those optimisations. For n up to a few hundred it is often the simplest correct choice. The three nested loops make the cost easy to count: Content gap CPython, C and NumPy runtime estimates are omitted because the project has no reproducible benchmark with specified hardware, data and implementation. Pitfalls Wrong loop order in Floyd–Warshall: k must be outermost. INF + INF overflow in C, Java or Go when INF is INT_MAX. Skip addition if either operand is the infinity sentinel, and establish bounds that keep every finite sum representable. A large infinity sentinel alone does not prevent overflow or spurious finite paths from adding a negative value to infinity. Memory. The table grows with the square of the vertex count: Negative cycles make some distances undefined (−∞). Check the diagonal and propagate: any pair whose path can touch a negative cycle is −∞. Key takeaways A next-hop table reconstructs only valid unaffected shortest paths. An explicit all-pairs table has quadratic storage. Infinity sentinel addition and negative cycles need handling beyond the basic recurrence. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Floyd–Warshall — cp-algorithms Floyd–Warshall algorithm — Wikipedia

sum: Boolean closure tracks reachability rather than route cost.
x: Earlier Floyd–Warshall units established the intermediate-vertex recurrence. Here n counts vertices, m counts edges, and vertices are numbered from zero. The example graph has 2→0 of weight 5 and 0→1 of weight 3, so 2 can reach 1 through 0. Transitive closure Sometimes you only care whether j is reachable from i. Replace min/+ with OR/AND (Warshall's algorithm): In the example graph, 2 has no edge to 1, but 2 reaches 0 and 0 reaches 1, so unlocking vertex zero marks that pair reachable. Pack each row into a bitset, and a whole row updates in one operation: "if i reaches k, then i reaches everything k reaches". Python's arbitrary-size integers make this easy: This computes reflexive transitive closure: every vertex reaches itself via a zero-length walk. A row of n bits is stored in machine words of w bits each, so OR-ing two rows costs one operation per word: A row OR is therefore not constant time, but 157 word operations is far fewer than 10,000 single-bit ones. Python integers use implementation-specific internal digits (sys.int_info.bits_per_digit), not necessarily 64-bit payloads. Uses: "can this permission/role reach that resource?", "does module A transitively depend on B?", and query optimisers deriving implied joins. For sparse graphs, a BFS from every vertex costs O(n(n + m)), n traversals of O(n + m) each, which beats n³ when m is small. On a DAG you can compute closures in reverse topological order by OR-ing together the bitsets of the vertices each one has edges to. Key takeaways Boolean closure tracks reachability rather than route cost. The implementation includes each vertex’s zero-length walk to itself. A Python integer row operation is not constant time as row width grows. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Transitive closure — Wikipedia

t: Sparse all-pairs searches and selected sources
sum: Sparse non-negative graphs often favour repeated single-source searches.
x: BFS handles unit-cost edges; Dijkstra handles non-negative weights; Floyd–Warshall allows negative edges but no finite answer for pairs affected by a negative cycle. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. Johnson’s negative-edge method is explained next. When to run Dijkstra n times instead APSP with non-negative weights can also be done by running single-source Dijkstra from every vertex. In the table, n is the number of vertices, m the number of edges and log the base-2 logarithm. Method Time ------ Floyd–Warshall O(n³) n × Dijkstra (min-heap) O(n (n + m) log n) n × BFS (unweighted) O(n (n + m)) Johnson's, binary min-heaps O(n(n + m) log(n + 1)) On a sparse graph the edge count is a small multiple of the vertex count, and n Dijkstras win: For a road network with ten thousand vertices and forty thousand edges: The ratio of these growth expressions is roughly 150; it is not a measured speedup or a count of equivalent machine instructions. On a dense graph (m close to n²) the min-heap version becomes O(n³ log n), worse than Floyd–Warshall. You also often do not need all pairs. If you only need distances between 300 depots in a road graph with ten million vertices, run 300 Dijkstras (or a bidirectional/contraction-hierarchy query per pair) rather than any all-pairs algorithm over the whole road graph. Key takeaways Sparse non-negative graphs often favour repeated single-source searches. Compare growth expressions separately from runtime measurements. Compute only the requested sources when a full table is unnecessary. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Shortest paths — NetworkX docs Floyd–Warshall algorithm — Wikipedia

sum: Bellman–Ford potentials make reweighted edges non-negative.
x: Earlier units covered Bellman–Ford’s negative-cycle test and Dijkstra’s non-negative-weight requirement. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. Graphs and weights are finite, with constant-time arithmetic assumed for the growth bounds. Johnson's algorithm: negative edges on sparse graphs Dijkstra cannot handle negative edges, and Floyd–Warshall is O(n³). Johnson's algorithm gets the best of both: Add a new vertex q with a 0-weight edge to every vertex. Run Bellman–Ford from q to get h(v) for each v (O(n(n + m)) for the augmented graph). If it finds a negative cycle, stop. Reweight each edge by adding the potential of its start and subtracting the potential of its end (formula below). Because the potentials are shortest-path distances, every new weight is non-negative. Run Dijkstra from every vertex on w'. Undo the shift on each answer. Steps 3 and 5 in full: For example, with a zero potential at the start, a potential of minus three at the end, and an edge weight of minus three, the reweighted edge costs zero: Why step 3 preserves shortest paths: along any path u → x₁ → … → v, each middle potential is added once and subtracted once, so the h terms telescope (cancel in pairs) and every u→v path changes by exactly h(u) − h(v). The ranking of paths is unchanged. (Compare adding a constant to every edge, which penalises long paths more and breaks the ranking.) With binary min-heaps on simple graphs, total time is O(n(n + m) log(n + 1)), including the augmented Bellman–Ford run. When the edge count grows at least proportionally to the vertex count, this is commonly simplified to O(nm log n). Key takeaways Bellman–Ford potentials make reweighted edges non-negative. Intermediate potentials cancel along a path. Recover original distances after running Dijkstra. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Johnson's algorithm — Wikipedia

t: Minimum spanning trees and safe cut edges
sum: An MST minimises the sum of chosen edge weights.
x: You need to connect 6 offices with fibre. Assume each possible link has a positive installation cost. Every office must be reachable from every other, and you want to spend as little as possible. You will never buy a link that closes a loop, because a loop always contains a link you could drop while keeping everything connected. So the answer is a tree that spans every vertex: a minimum spanning tree (MST). For a connected undirected graph it has a fixed number of edges and the smallest possible total weight: Throughout this lesson, n is the number of vertices, m the number of edges, and O(…) is Big O notation: how the running time grows, ignoring constant factors. The example Edges: A–B 4, A–C 1, B–C 2, B–D 5, C–D 8, C–E 10, D–E 2, D–F 6, E–F 3. The MST is A–C 1, B–C 2, D–E 2, E–F 3, B–D 5, with total weight 13. Why greedy works: the cut property A cut splits the vertices into two non-empty groups. An edge crosses the cut if it has one end on each side: For example, putting A and C on one side cuts the example graph; the crossing edges are A–B 4, B–C 2, C–D 8 and C–E 10, and the lightest is B–C. Cut property For any cut, the lightest edge crossing it belongs to some MST. If it is strictly the lightest, it belongs to every MST. Proof sketch: take an MST T that does not contain the lightest crossing edge e. Adding e to T creates a cycle, and that cycle must cross the cut a second time at some edge f. Exchange f for e: T′ is still a spanning tree, so some MST contains e. The companion cycle property says the heaviest edge on any cycle is never needed (if it is strictly heaviest). Both Kruskal and Prim are just ways of repeatedly applying the cut property. A consequence: if all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique. Every spanning tree uses the same number of edges. Therefore adding one constant to every edge shifts every tree total equally and preserves the MST ranking. A globally heaviest edge can still be necessary if it is the only link joining two regions. Key takeaways An MST minimises the sum of chosen edge weights. The cut exchange argument justifies greedy edge choices. Distinct weights ensure uniqueness; ties need not. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Minimum spanning tree — Wikipedia Kruskal's algorithm — Wikipedia

sum: Find returns a set representative; successful union merges sets.
x: The previous unit introduced Kruskal: process edges in increasing weight and reject an edge whose endpoints already belong to the same component. Here n is the number of elements. This unit implements that component test. Union-Find (disjoint set union) Union-Find maintains a partition of the vertices into disjoint sets, with two operations: find(x): which set is x in? (Returns the set representative, the set's root.) union(a, b): merge the sets containing a and b. Each set is a tree of parent pointers; the root represents the set. find(2) follows 2 → 1 → 0. union(2, 5) links root 3 under root 0 (or vice versa). Done naively, these trees can degenerate into long chains and find becomes O(n). Two tricks fix that. Union by rank Attach the lower-rank root under the higher-rank root. After path compression, rank need not equal the current height. Each root keeps a rank, an upper bound on its tree's height. A rank only goes up when two trees of equal rank are joined, which at least doubles the smaller size: So heights stay O(log n) even without the second trick. Path compression During find, point every vertex on the path straight at the root. Until later unions change the root, a subsequent find from one of those non-root vertices follows one parent link. The code Union by rank keeps recursion depth O(log n), much smaller than a naive chain; it must still fit the runtime’s configured recursion limit. Ordinary DSU supports incremental undirected connectivity: start with one component per vertex and reduce the count after every successful union. It cannot split a component after deletion. It also ignores direction, so it is not a directed-cycle detector. Key takeaways Find returns a set representative; successful union merges sets. Rank is an upper height bound after compression, not the current height. Ordinary Union-Find merges and does not support arbitrary deletion. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Disjoint Set Union — cp-algorithms Disjoint-set data structure — Wikipedia

t: Amortised Union-Find costs and complete Kruskal
sum: Inverse-Ackermann amortised cost is not a four-instruction per-call promise.
x: The DSU class from the previous unit provides find and union with rank and path compression. Kruskal’s input tuples are (weight, start, end), with numbered vertices. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges except where a card explicitly uses m for operation count. Kruskal's algorithm Sort all edges by weight. Walk through them, adding each edge unless it would form a cycle with edges already chosen. On the example: Edge Weight Action --------- A–C 1 add B–C 2 add D–E 2 add E–F 3 add A–B 4 skip: A, B joined B–D 5 add (5 edges: done) Each added edge is the lightest edge crossing the cut between its endpoint's current component and everything else, so the cut property guarantees it is safe. The only hard part is the cycle test: "are u and v already connected by chosen edges?" Running a BFS each time would cost O(n) per edge, for n vertices. That is what Union-Find is for. Inverse Ackermann Initialising n singleton sets costs O(n). With rank and compression, the total cost is: So a million operations on a million elements cost on the order of a few million steps in total. Inverse-Ackermann definitions vary by small constants; the function grows extremely slowly. This is an amortised growth bound, not a claim that each call performs at most four instructions. Individual calls can take O(log n). Variant Cost per op ------ Naive O(n) worst Union by rank only O(log n) Path compression only O(log n) amortised Both O(α(n)) amortised Kruskal in full Time: sorting dominates: The last line holds for connected simple graphs. For a million edges, the base-two logarithm of the edge count is about twenty, giving a sorting growth expression of twenty million; this is not an exact comparison count. Key takeaways Inverse-Ackermann amortised cost is not a four-instruction per-call promise. Include initialisation and sorting in the full algorithm cost. Disconnected input yields a forest. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Disjoint-set data structure — Wikipedia

t: Prim keys, dense graphs and Borůvka rounds
sum: Prim uses an attaching-edge cost, while Dijkstra uses a path cost.
x: The running example has A–B 4, A–C 1, B–C 2, B–D 5, C–D 8, C–E 10, D–E 2, D–F 6 and E–F 3. Its MST weighs 13. The code numbers vertices from zero; letter names are used for the explanatory trace. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. Prim's algorithm Prim grows one tree from a start vertex. At each step it adds the lightest edge leaving the tree. (Cut property again: the cut is "tree versus everything else".) From A on the example: A, then C (1), B (2 via C), D (5 via B), E (2 via D), F (3 via E). Total 13, the same tree found in a different order. It looks almost exactly like Dijkstra. The one difference is the key used to order the min-heap: In the example, D reached from B (distance three from A via C) gets Dijkstra key eight but Prim key five. Time: for n vertices and m edges, the shown lazy min-heap uses O(n + m log(m + 1)) time and O(n + m) space. For connected simple graphs this is O(m log n). An indexed decrease-key min-heap gives O((n + m) log(n + 1)); array selection gives O(n² + m), attractive for dense graphs without guaranteeing the fastest measured runtime. Kruskal or Prim? In the table, n is the number of vertices and m the number of edges. Kruskal Prim --------- Input Edge list Adjacency list Time, connected simple graph O(m log(m + 1)) O(m log(n + 1)) Dense graphs Sort hurts O(n²) array Grows A forest One tree Disconnected Gives forest One component Both are fine for most problems. Kruskal is simpler to write if you have a DSU handy; Prim with an array is the choice for complete graphs, such as points in the plane where every pair is an edge. A third algorithm, Borůvka's, selects a cheapest outgoing edge from every component. Resolve equal weights consistently or use Union-Find to discard cycle-forming selected edges. On a connected graph, every component joins at least one other in each round, so the count at least halves: A thousand vertices need at most 10 rounds. Isolated components in a disconnected graph cannot merge. Its per-component edge choices expose parallel work, and distributed and GPU MST implementations use variants of this approach. Synchronisation, communication and hardware determine their performance. Key takeaways Prim uses an attaching-edge cost, while Dijkstra uses a path cost. Array selection is a useful dense-graph alternative to min-heaps. Borůvka merges components in logarithmically many rounds on connected input. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Prim's algorithm — Wikipedia GPU MST research implementation Engineering massively parallel MST algorithms

t: MST clustering, updates and tour bounds
sum: MST paths do not minimise every source-to-target distance.
x: The running six-vertex example has MST edges A–C 1, B–C 2, D–E 2, E–F 3 and B–D 5, total 13. Its other edges are A–B 4, C–D 8, C–E 10 and D–F 6. A cut separates two non-empty vertex groups; a lightest crossing edge is safe to add. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. Where MSTs are used Network design: cabling, pipelines, power grids (the problem Borůvka originally studied in 1926, for electrifying Moravia). Single-linkage clustering: run Kruskal but stop when k components remain (k is the number of clusters you want). For a complete graph of pairwise dissimilarities, the result is single-linkage clustering, maximising the minimum distance between clusters. On a sparse graph, spacing refers only to edges present in that graph. Approximation algorithms: doubling an MST and shortcutting repeated vertices gives a tour at most 2× optimal for metric TSP (where going direct is never longer than a detour). See the formula after this list. Union-Find on its own: incremental undirected connectivity, image segmentation, percolation simulations, and type unification in compilers. The 2× bound for the travelling salesman problem comes from two inequalities: So if the MST weighs 100 km, the tour is at most 200 km, and the best tour is at least 100 km. Pitfalls MST is not a shortest-path tree. The MST minimises total weight; the path between two vertices inside it can be much longer than their shortest path. Directed graphs need a minimum spanning arborescence (Chu–Liu/Edmonds' algorithm). Kruskal and Prim do not apply. Disconnected input: no spanning tree exists. Kruskal returns a minimum spanning forest; check len(tree) == n - 1. Negative weights are fine. Only the relative order of weights matters, unlike Dijkstra. For a single edge-weight decrease, compare that edge with the heaviest edge on the unique tree path between its endpoints. If it is lighter, replacing that heaviest edge reduces the spanning-tree weight. This is the cycle exchange principle; the surrounding graph and its other weights are assumed unchanged. Key takeaways MST paths do not minimise every source-to-target distance. Stopping Kruskal early produces single-linkage clusters under the stated input assumptions. The doubled-tree tour bound requires metric distances. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Minimum spanning tree — Wikipedia Kruskal's algorithm — Wikipedia Borůvka’s original 1926 paper Nešetřil and Nešetřilová: MST history and original-paper translation

sum: Flow respects capacities and conservation at interior vertices.
x: This lesson covers three ideas that turn up in real systems and senior interviews: how much can a network carry (max flow), how to pair things up optimally (graph matching), and which single link or vertex would break a network if it failed (bridges and articulation points). Network flow The model A flow network is a directed graph where each edge has an edge capacity: the most it can carry, in litres per second, Gbit/s, lorries per day. There is a source vertex s where everything starts and a distinct sink t where it ends. Assume finite capacities. A flow assignment assigns an amount to each edge, obeying two rules: For example, a pipe with an edge capacity of 10 litres per second can carry 0 to 10, and a junction receiving 7 must send out 7. The maximum flow problem asks for the largest possible value. Edges: s→a 10, s→b 10, a→b 2, a→t 4, a→c 8, b→c 9, c→t 10. The maximum flow is 14. Why greedy fails The obvious approach: find any s→t path with unused edge capacity, push as much as you can, repeat. It can get stuck. Edges s→a, s→b, a→b, a→t, b→t, each with edge capacity 1. If greedy first picks s→a→b→t, it uses up s→a and b→t. Now s→b leads only to b, whose exit is full. Greedy stops at 1, but the max is 2 (s→a→t and s→b→t). The residual graph The fix is to allow undoing flow. The following card describes one original edge’s residual contributions, assuming no original opposite-direction edge. With antiparallel edges, add the contributions in each direction: So: the forward residual u→v is the unused edge capacity; this edge contributes a backward residual on v→u equal to its flow, meaning “you may cancel up to that many units”. With an original antiparallel edge, aggregate residual capacity also includes that opposite edge’s unused edge capacity. An augmenting path is any s→t path in this residual graph. In the example, after the bad first path, the residual has s→b (1), the backward edge b→a (1), and a→t (1). Pushing along s→b→a→t cancels the a→b flow and reroutes it, giving 2. Key takeaways Flow respects capacities and conservation at interior vertices. Backward residual edges cancel a previous forward decision. Account for original antiparallel edges when aggregating residual capacities. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Ford–Fulkerson algorithm — Wikipedia Edmonds–Karp — cp-algorithms

sum: Augment by a residual path’s bottleneck.
x: The preceding unit defined residual edges: unused edge capacity in the forward direction and cancellable backward flow. Its running directed network has s→a 10, s→b 10, a→b 2, a→t 4, a→c 8, b→c 9 and c→t 10. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. Ford–Fulkerson and Edmonds–Karp Ford–Fulkerson is the method: while an augmenting path exists, push its bottleneck edge capacity along it. With integer capacities each augmentation adds at least 1, so the number of augmentations is at most the answer itself: That can be awful if capacities are large: in the classic bad case, paths alternate back and forth across a middle edge with edge capacity 1, needing two million augmentations when the other capacities are a million. With irrational capacities a bad path choice may never terminate. Edmonds–Karp fixes the choice: always use the shortest augmenting path (fewest edges), found by BFS. That bounds the number of augmentations, whatever the capacities: So the total is O(n m²), in the unit-cost arithmetic model, independent of how large the edge capacities are. The 10¹¹ figure is a worst-case growth expression; real runs usually need far fewer augmentations. Integer bit lengths and floating-point error require separate consideration. On the first example it returns (14, residual_graph): the flow value and the final residual capacities. Faster algorithms Dinic's algorithm pushes many shortest paths at once using BFS levels and DFS blocking flows: O(n²m) in general and O(m√n) (√ is the square root; n vertices, m edges) on unit networks such as the standard bipartite matching reduction. Arbitrary unit-capacity networks need a different bound; edge capacity 1 alone does not establish O(m√n). Push-relabel is another family whose performance depends on the instance and implementation. A useful fact: with integer capacities there is always an integer maximum flow, and these algorithms find one. This is what makes flow usable for counting and assignment problems. Key takeaways Augment by a residual path’s bottleneck. Shortest augmenting paths bound the number of searches independently of edge capacity magnitude. Exact integer capacities avoid the floating-point complications omitted here. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Max-flow min-cut theorem — Wikipedia Ford–Fulkerson algorithm — Wikipedia

sum: A cut upper-bounds every feasible flow.
x: The previous two units introduced feasible flow and residual cancellation. The example network is s→a 10, s→b 10, a→b 2, a→t 4, a→c 8, b→c 9 and c→t 10. Its feasible maximum flow is 14. Capacities and flows share the same throughput unit. Max-flow min-cut An s–t cut splits the vertices into S (containing s) and T (containing t). Its cut capacity is the total edge capacity of edges going from S to T (edges from T back to S do not count): The worked line places s, a, b and c on the source side and only t on the sink side. Max-flow min-cut theorem The maximum flow value equals the smallest cut capacity over all s–t cuts. The intuition: every unit of flow must cross every cut, so the flow value is at most any cut capacity (the last line above). When Ford–Fulkerson stops, let S be the vertices still reachable from s in the residual graph. Every edge S→T is a saturated edge, full to its edge capacity (or it would be in the residual), and every edge T→S carries 0 (or its backward residual would be usable). So the flow equals that cut capacity, and both are optimal. In the first example, after the algorithm finishes, s, a, b and c lie on the source side, with only t on the sink side. The cut edges are a→t (4) and c→t (10): cut capacity 14, matching the flow. Increasing only links outside this cut cannot raise the maximum flow while its cut capacity stays 14. Other engineering objectives or coordinated upgrades can still justify those changes. Uses of min cut: Image segmentation: pixels are vertices, the source means "foreground", the sink "background", and edge capacities penalise cutting between similar neighbours. The min cut optimises the specified representable segmentation energy (the basis of "graph cuts" in computer vision). Network reliability: the minimum number of links whose failure disconnects two data centres equals the max flow with unit capacities. Baseball elimination and project selection reduce neatly to min cut. Key takeaways A cut upper-bounds every feasible flow. Residual reachability yields a matching optimal cut after augmentation stops. Upgrading an edge outside a still-tight cut cannot increase the maximum flow. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Maximum flow problem — Wikipedia Max-flow min-cut theorem — Wikipedia

t: Bipartite matching, reassignment and vertex covers
sum: Unit-capacity flow enforces one partner per vertex.
x: Earlier graph units established bipartite colouring; flow units established integer max flow. The two sides of a bipartite graph represent different sets of entities, and every eligible pairing crosses between them. Bipartite matching A graph matching is a set of edges with no shared vertex. In a bipartite graph (workers and jobs, riders and drivers), a maximum matching pairs up as many as possible. As a flow problem Add a source joined to every worker and a sink joined from every job, all capacities 1, and direct the worker→job edges. An integer max flow is a maximum matching: each worker sends at most 1 unit, each job receives at most 1. Kuhn's algorithm (augmenting paths) The flow view specialises into a short DFS. For each left vertex u, try to find a right vertex v that is free, or whose current partner can be moved elsewhere. With Ann→{X, Y}, Bob→{X}, Cat→{Y, Z}: Ann takes X. Bob wants X, so Ann is asked to move, and moves to Y. Cat tries Y: Ann would have to move back to X, which would need Bob to move, and Bob has nowhere else to go. That fails, so Cat takes Z. Result: 3 pairs. With n vertices and m edges in the bipartite graph: Kuhn's bound counts one search per left vertex; these are growth expressions, not measured times. Kuhn: O(n_L + m + n_L m), where n_L counts left vertices and m counts eligible pairs. Including the input scan keeps the bound meaningful when there are no edges. Hopcroft–Karp: finds many shortest augmenting paths per phase, O((n + m) √n), conventionally O(m √n) after isolated vertices are removed. Weighted assignment (minimise total cost while assigning every item on the required side, e.g. driver ETA, the estimated time of arrival): the Hungarian algorithm, O(n³) for an n × n assignment, or min-cost flow. Without a required cardinality, an empty matching can minimise non-negative cost. König's theorem In a bipartite graph, the size of a maximum matching equals the size of a minimum vertex cover (the fewest vertices touching every edge). So max matching also answers "fewest guards to watch every corridor" when the graph is bipartite. In general graphs, minimum vertex cover is NP-hard. Key takeaways Unit-capacity flow enforces one partner per vertex. Augmenting paths can move existing partners to admit a new one. König’s vertex-cover equality is specific to bipartite graphs. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Maximum flow problem — Wikipedia Matching (graph theory) — Wikipedia) Hopcroft–Karp algorithm — Wikipedia

t: Bridges and articulation points from low links
sum: Strict versus non-strict low-link comparisons answer different failure questions.
x: DFS discovery order was covered earlier. This low-link calculation is for a simple undirected graph; Tarjan’s SCC low links earlier served a different directed-graph purpose. Here n counts vertices and m counts edges. Bridges and articulation points In an undirected network: A bridge is an edge whose removal increases the number of connected components. An articulation point (cut vertex) is a vertex whose removal, with its incident edges, increases that number. These are single points of failure: the one fibre link between two regions, the one router everything passes through. Low-link values Run DFS and record tin[u], the time u was discovered. Define low[u] as the smallest tin reachable from u's subtree using tree edges downwards plus at most one back edge. In symbols: For the example below, with adjacency lists in increasing order, DFS from 0 visits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 in that order. Vertex 3 has discovery and low-link values of three, while vertex 1 has discovery value one. The strict bridge test therefore identifies 1–3. For a tree edge u→v (v a child of u): If low[v] > tin[u], nothing in v's subtree can get back to u or above without using u–v. So u–v is a bridge. If low[v] >= tin[u] and u is not the root, v's subtree cannot get above u without passing through u. So u is an articulation point. The tree root is an articulation point if and only if it has two or more DFS children. The implementation below assumes a simple undirected graph on vertices 0..n−1, with both directions present in adjacency lists. Two triangles {0, 1, 2} and {3, 4, 5}, joined by 1–3, with 6 hanging off 5. The function returns bridges 5–6 and 1–3 and articulation points {1, 3, 5}. Edges inside a triangle are never bridges: each has a detour. One DFS: O(n + m) for n vertices and m edges. As with undirected cycle detection, skip the parent by edge id rather than vertex if parallel edges are possible, because a doubled link is not a bridge. In practice Network engineers run exactly this on topology graphs to find links and routers that need redundancy. Removing all bridges splits a graph into 2-edge-connected components; grouping edges around articulation points gives biconnected components, which are used in planarity testing and circuit analysis. Key takeaways Strict versus non-strict low-link comparisons answer different failure questions. The DFS root needs its own articulation-point test. Parallel-edge inputs need parent edge identities. Further reading Primary reference for this unit Bridge (graph theory) — Wikipedia) Finding articulation points — cp-algorithms Finding bridges — cp-algorithms

sum: State a domain, a base case and a measure that cannot decrease forever.
x: A function is recursive when its execution can call itself, directly or through other functions. To make a terminating recursive algorithm, use a well-founded progress measure: it can never decrease forever (no infinite decreasing chain). A common design has these two properties: There is at least one base case: an input small enough to answer directly, with no further calls. Every recursive call makes progress towards a base case. Recursion is the foundation for the rest of this module. Divide and conquer, backtracking and (in a later module) dynamic programming are all recursive ways of thinking, even when the final code uses a loop. The shape of a recursive function Summing the digits of a non-negative integer is a small example. The numerical functions below validate that domain; trees are assumed finite and acyclic. Each call strips one digit, so the input shrinks and must eventually fall below 10. That is the progress guarantee. Almost every recursive function follows the same recipe: Identify the smallest inputs (empty list, 0, a leaf node, a single character) and answer them directly. Assume the function already works for anything smaller than the current input. Combine that smaller answer with a little local work to answer the current input. The leap of faith The second step is the one beginners resist. When you write digit_sum(n // 10), you should not try to trace every call in your head. Instead, trust that it returns the right digit sum for the shorter number, and only check that your combining step is correct. This is exactly proof by induction: Induction Recursion ------ Base case holds Base case returns correctly Assume true for k Trust the smaller call Prove for k + 1 Combine into the answer Thinking this way scales. To count nodes in a binary tree, you say: an empty tree has 0 nodes; otherwise it has 1 plus the count of the left subtree plus the count of the right subtree. The correctness argument need not trace every depth; resource usage still depends on the height. Define the function's contract first Write one sentence: "count(node) returns the number of nodes in the subtree rooted at node." The leap of faith is only safe if the contract is precise and every call respects it. Common pitfalls Missing base case, or one that is never reached. fact(-1) with base case n == 0 recurses forever (until RecursionError). Reject negative input: changing the base case to n <= 1 alone terminates but incorrectly returns 1 for negative factorials. Not shrinking the input. Calling f(n) from f(n) with a different flag still needs a measure that strictly decreases. Repeated subproblems. Exponential blow-up, as with naive fib. Expensive arguments. For a copied slice of length n, slicing lists or strings per call adds hidden O(n) work. Shared mutable state. Appending to one list across calls is fine, but remember every frame sees the same object (this matters a lot in backtracking). Key takeaways State a domain, a base case and a measure that cannot decrease forever. Trust smaller calls only after establishing their contract and progress. Further reading Recursive algorithms — Erickson Recursion)

sum: Pending work resumes after a recursive call returns.
x: What the call stack actually does The leap of faith is how you design recursion. To debug it, and to understand its cost, you need the machine's view. Conceptually, a pending call has a stack frame holding parameters, local state and where execution resumes. Implementations can inline calls or eliminate tail calls; the examples here use ordinary CPython frames. A returned frame may remain referenced by debugging or traceback objects. Here is fact(3) at its deepest point: Then the stack unwinds: fact(1) returns 1, fact(2) computes 2 × 1 = 2, fact(3) computes 3 × 2 = 6. Two consequences follow: Space is proportional to depth. With constant-sized frame state, a recursion that is d calls deep at its deepest point costs O(d) control-stack space: d frames, each of fixed size. Retained lists, arbitrary-size integers and other objects must be counted separately. A recursive function over a linked list of length n uses O(n) space; over a balanced tree of n nodes, O(log n). Work after the call happens on the way back up. Along a single call chain, code before the call runs on descent and code after it runs on return; multiple recursive branches are completed in the order the code calls them. Python's recursion limit CPython limits active recursion and raises RecursionError when the configured allowance is exhausted. The usual default is 1000; inspect sys.getrecursionlimit() rather than assuming how many calls remain. Since CPython 3.11, most Python-to-Python calls no longer consume C stack per call. Raising the limit still increases memory/resource exposure, and calls involving C code can have separate stack limits; the documentation warns that an excessively high setting can crash the process. In practice: a million-node binary tree with near-minimum height has about 20 levels, well below the usual recursion allowance when entered from a shallow call stack. Recursion over a list, a string, or a tree that might degenerate into a chain is a bug waiting for large input. Key takeaways Pending work resumes after a recursive call returns. Control-stack space depends on maximum nesting, not on the number of nodes visited. Further reading Python recursion allowance CPython 3.11 call changes

t: Repeated calls and hidden slice costs
sum: A recursion tree counts repeated work, not just distinct arguments.
x: The cost of recursion: recursion trees When a function makes more than one recursive call, draw the recursion tree to estimate its cost. Each non-base invocation of naive Fibonacci makes two recursive calls: fib(4) makes 9 calls, fib(5) 15, fib(30) over 2.6 million. Counting the calls gives a recurrence of its own, because each call is itself plus the calls its two children make: The total grows that fast because the same subproblems are solved again and again. Caching results (memoisation) reduces this to O(n) additions; integer bit costs grow with n, so this is not an O(n) bit-time claim; that idea is the heart of the dynamic programming module. Hidden O(n) work per call Here n is the original list length. return xs[0] + total(xs[1:]) looks linear, but each slice copies the list. Because every frame holds its slice until it returns, memory grows the same way. Pass an index instead of slicing. Adding up the copies on a list of n items: That gives O(n²) time (assuming constant-cost element addition) and, because the slices are all alive at the deepest point, O(n²) memory at its peak. Key takeaways A recursion tree counts repeated work, not just distinct arguments. A copied slice retained by each frame can turn linear-looking recursion into quadratic work and storage. Further reading Recursive cost analysis — Erickson Python lists and slices

sum: A tail call returns its result without pending work.
x: Tail recursion A call is a tail call if it is the very last thing a function does: its result is returned directly, with no work left to do afterwards. return n fact(n - 1) is not a tail call: the multiplication happens after the call returns. return fact_acc(n - 1, acc n) is a tail call. You can often make a function tail-recursive by passing an accumulator that carries the partial result down: Why care? Because a tail call needs nothing from the current frame afterwards, so a language can reuse the frame instead of pushing a new one. This is tail-call optimisation (TCO), and it turns tail recursion into a loop with O(1) stack space. The Scheme programming language requires it by its standard; many functional language implementations rely on it; C compilers such as GCC and Clang often perform it at higher optimisation levels, but the C standard doesn't guarantee it. Python does not do TCO CPython does not eliminate Python-level tail calls. fact_acc(10000) still raises RecursionError with the usual default allowance, accumulator or not. Guido van Rossum explained the decision in 2009: eliminating frames would destroy useful tracebacks, and he considers recursion a less fundamental tool than iteration in Python. So in Python, rewriting as tail recursion does not by itself eliminate control-stack growth; its value is that it makes the next step, converting to a loop, mechanical. Key takeaways A tail call returns its result without pending work. An accumulator does not remove Python call frames; tail-call elimination is an implementation property. Further reading Guido van Rossum: Tail Recursion Elimination Scheme standard

sum: Self tail calls become parameter updates in a loop.
x: Converting recursion to iteration Tail recursion becomes a loop A tail-recursive function maps directly onto a while loop: the parameters become variables, and the tail call becomes reassignment. General recursion needs an explicit stack When there are several recursive calls or work after the call, replace the call stack with your own list. This pre-order traversal avoids the interpreter recursion limit; its maximum usable input is still constrained by memory and execution time: A Python list stores pending work in dynamically allocated memory. General simulations can retain a resume point or a visited flag; specialised traversals sometimes need fewer entries. This routine also stores O(n) output. Here depth is the maximum nesting of pending work. The following table counts control-stack entries, assuming constant-sized entries; it excludes retained data and output. Approach Stack space Clarity --------- Plain recursion O(depth), capped High Tail rec. + TCO O(1) High Loop replacing self tail calls O(1) Medium Explicit stack O(depth), heap Lower Key takeaways Self tail calls become parameter updates in a loop. General recursion needs explicit pending work; push right before left to reproduce pre-order. Further reading Recursive algorithms — Erickson Python recursion allowance

sum: Independent smaller pieces can be solved separately and combined.
x: Divide and conquer is recursion with a plan. You divide the input into smaller subproblems, solve them recursively, and combine their answers. Balanced pieces often give efficient recurrences, but unequal splits also count as divide and conquer. The payoff comes from the cutting. Halving an input of a million items takes only about 20 levels to reach size 1, so even if every level does work proportional to the input size, the total stays small. Compare that with an algorithm that pairs every item with every other item: These growth expressions are scale estimates, not exact instruction counts or timings. The three steps Divide the input into some number of smaller subproblems, each a fixed fraction of the original size. Conquer each subproblem recursively (with a base case for tiny inputs). Combine the sub-answers into the answer for the whole. The cleanest examples have independent subproblems that can be solved separately. Repeated equivalent subproblems can waste work; caching them leads toward dynamic programming. Independence alone neither guarantees balanced splits nor eliminates all coordination costs in parallel implementations. Analysing it: recurrences The cost of a divide-and-conquer algorithm is a recurrence: an equation that gives the running time on an input in terms of the running time on smaller inputs. Draw the recursion tree to see where the time goes: Whether the total is dominated by the root, the leaves or spread evenly depends on how fast the number of calls grows compared with how fast the per-call work shrinks. Key takeaways Independent smaller pieces can be solved separately and combined. Repeated equivalent subproblems call for caching rather than repeated plain recursion. Further reading Recursive algorithms — Erickson Divide and conquer

sum: Compare the exponent of local work with the critical leaf-growth exponent.
x: The previous unit defined a recurrence as the work of smaller calls plus the work outside them. Here n is input size, a is the fixed number of calls per split, and b is the fixed shrink factor. We now compare those calls with local work to solve this restricted recurrence family. The master theorem (simplified) The master theorem answers that race in one step for recurrences of this shape. It applies when a and b are fixed numbers, the base case costs a constant, and the work outside the recursion is a power of n. This simplified form ignores the rounding of subproblem sizes to whole numbers: Case Who dominates ------ combine exponent bigger the root's combine exponents equal every level equally leaf exponent bigger the leaves More general recurrences (uneven splits, or local work growing linearly times a logarithm) need other tools, such as the full master theorem or the Akra–Bazzi method. The algorithm names below are an overview; their implementations appear in later units. Each card uses input size n, counting unit-cost arithmetic operations or comparisons as appropriate. Key takeaways Compare the exponent of local work with the critical leaf-growth exponent. The simplified theorem assumes fixed branching and shrink factors and power-shaped local work. Further reading Recursive cost analysis — Erickson Master theorem)

t: Binary search and one shrinking subproblem
sum: Use the master theorem to count midpoint probes when only one half survives.
x: Here n is the number of sorted items. The previous unit compared local work with leaf growth; binary search is its equal-exponent case with just one surviving half at each step. Binary search Compare the target with the middle element and discard the half that can't contain it. That is one subproblem of half the size, with a constant amount of work per call: A three-way comparator can classify a probe in one comparison; separate equality and ordering tests may perform more. Binary search is the degenerate case where "combine" is free and one half is thrown away entirely. Some people call this decrease and conquer. Key takeaways A midpoint comparison discards one half and leaves no costly combination. Count midpoint probes separately from language-level equality and ordering tests. Further reading Recursive cost analysis — Erickson

t: Merge sort as divide and conquer
sum: Two sorted halves can be merged in linear work per level.
x: For this unit n is the number of items being sorted. Merge sort is a concrete example of two independent half-size problems followed by linear combination. Merge sort Split the list in half, sort each half, and merge the two sorted halves in linear time. Each level does linear work in total (every item is merged once per level), and there are about log₂n + 1 levels: For a million items, the linear-times-logarithm scale is roughly twenty million. This is neither an exact element-move count nor a timing; copied slices and concatenations also contribute work. The <= ensures a stable sort (equal keys stay in their original order). The price is O(n) extra memory for merging. Key takeaways Two sorted halves can be merged in linear work per level. Stable merging uses the left element on equal keys, and ordinary merging needs linear extra storage. Further reading Recursive sorting — Erickson

sum: Compute the half-power once, then square it.
x: Fast exponentiation To raise a number x to a non-negative whole-number power n, straightforward powering multiplies by x one time after another, which is O(n) multiplications. The bounds here count arithmetic operations; large-integer bit costs are additional. Divide and conquer notices that a power splits into two equal halves: Each call halves n, so there are about log₂n calls, each doing at most two multiplications: Compute the half once Writing return power(x, n // 2) power(x, n // 2) makes two recursive calls instead of one. You've rebuilt the slow algorithm with extra overhead. The recurrence shows why: two calls on half the exponent, with constant work each, is the "leaves dominate" case. The iterative version reads the bits of n from least significant upwards: square x at every step and multiply it into the result when the bit is 1. With a modulus applied after every multiplication, this is modular exponentiation, the workhorse of RSA and Diffie–Hellman. Taking the remainder after each step keeps the numbers small, and it gives the same final remainder: Python’s built-in pow(base, exp, mod) performs efficient modular powering; CPython 3.14 uses binary powering and a sliding-window method depending on exponent size. It is not literally this loop. Fixed-size matrix powering can compute the nth Fibonacci number using O(log n) matrix multiplications, with growing integer bit costs. Key takeaways Compute the half-power once, then square it. Reducing products modulo a positive modulus preserves the final remainder. Further reading Python pow Pinned CPython 3.14 integer implementation

sum: Three recursive half-products replace the four products of schoolbook splitting.
x: Karatsuba multiplication Schoolbook multiplication of two n-digit numbers multiplies every digit by every other digit: O(n²). In 1960 Anatoly Karatsuba found a faster way, published with Ofman in 1962. Split each number into a high half and a low half around a power of ten: That looks like four half-size multiplications (a × c, a × d, b × c and b × d), which gives no gain: The trick is that the middle term can be had with one extra multiplication: So three multiplications suffice: An exponent-only scale expression for 1000 digits is about 57,000, compared with one million for a square. These are growth-model expressions, not exact digit-product counts: rounding, base cases and half-sum carries matter. A worked example on 1234 × 5678: Key takeaways Three recursive half-products replace the four products of schoolbook splitting.
