Know which one you need "Number of combinations" (coin change) puts items in the outer loop. "Number of sequences" (climbing stairs with step set S, or LeetCode's "combination sum IV", which despite its name counts orderings) puts the target outer. Pitfalls Mixing up combinations and orderings in coin counting. Forgetting dp[0] = 1 in counting problems: the empty selection is one way to make zero. Integer overflow in counting problems outside Python: counts can grow exponentially; use arbitrary precision or a modulus only when the requested answer is modular. Key takeaways Coins outside and amounts increasing count combinations. Amounts outside count ordered sequences. The empty selection gives one way to make zero. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming MIT algorithms course

sum: Fixing the end position supplies the value needed to extend a subsequence.
x: Longest increasing subsequence Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (not necessarily next to each other). For [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18], one LIS is [2, 3, 7, 18], length 4. A quadratic DP over end positions State: L[i] records length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at index i. Recurrence: the element before a[i] is some earlier a[j] < a[i], or there is none and a[i] stands alone. Answer: max(L), not L[n-1], because the LIS can end anywhere. For the input [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7], the final value 7 can follow the earlier values 2, 5 or 3. Their ending lengths are 1, 2 and 2: For the example, L = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4], so the answer is 4. "Ending at i" is a common trick: "the best subsequence in a[:i]" doesn't give you a usable recurrence, because you need to know the last element to decide whether a[i] can extend it. Fixing the end fixes that. To reconstruct, store parent[i] = j for the j that gave the best value and follow parents back from the argmax. Key takeaways Fixing the end position supplies the value needed to extend a subsequence. The best subsequence can end anywhere. Parent links can reconstruct the chosen subsequence. Further reading Python bisect Longest increasing subsequence

sum: Sorted minimum tails allow binary search for each new value.
x: Minimum tails with binary search Keep an array tails where tails[k] is the smallest possible last element of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1 seen so far. tails is always sorted, so you can binary-search it. For each x: If x is bigger than every tail, append it: you've extended the longest subsequence. Otherwise replace the first tail that is not smaller than the new value: you have found a subsequence of that same length with a no-larger ending, making future extension at least as easy. Trace: Length 4. Here n is the number of input elements. Each costs one binary search on tails, plus an amortised O(1) append or O(1) replacement: The memory is O(n) slots for tails. tails is not the LIS On [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6] the final tails is [1, 2, 5, 6]. That isn't a subsequence at all: the 2 comes after the 5 in the input. The length is right (4, e.g. [3, 4, 5, 9]), but the contents of tails mix different subsequences. To reconstruct, store for each element the index of the element before it in the subsequence (the tail at position k − 1 when it was placed). Non-strict (non-decreasing) LIS: use bisect_right instead, so equal elements extend rather than replace. With bisect_left, [2, 2, 2] gives 1; with bisect_right it gives 3. Real-world use LIS underlies patience diff (used by Bazaar and available in Git as git diff --patience), which matches unique lines between files and keeps a longest increasing subsequence of unique-line matches, not necessarily an unbroken run. A return-value pitfall The LIS can end before the final input position: return the largest ending length, not merely the final entry. Key takeaways Sorted minimum tails allow binary search for each new value. Replacing a tail improves future extension opportunities without changing that length. The tails array need not itself be an input subsequence. Further reading Python bisect Longest increasing subsequence

t: Count paths on an empty grid
sum: A path into a cell came from above or from the left.
x: When the state needs two numbers, the DP becomes a table. Two shapes dominate: Grids: the state is a cell (r, c), and moves go right or down. Two strings: the state is a pair of prefix lengths (i, j), meaning "the first i characters of A and the first j of B". The second is really the first in disguise. Comparing two strings is walking a grid, where a diagonal step means "use a character from both" and a horizontal or vertical step means "use a character from only one". Unique paths A robot starts in the top-left of a grid with m rows and n columns and can move only right or down. How many paths reach the bottom-right? State: P[r][c] records number of paths from the start to (r, c). Recurrence: you arrived from above or from the left. Base: every cell in the top row and left column has exactly one path. A 3 × 7 grid has 28 paths. That's Pascal's triangle on its side, and there is a closed form (a direct formula with no table): Key takeaways A path into a cell came from above or from the left. On an empty grid, choosing the downward moves gives a binomial closed form. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming Dynamic programming

t: Grid obstacles and rolling path costs
sum: Blocked cells reset their path count to zero.
x: The empty-grid path count adds the answers from above and left. Preserve that dependency shape while adding blocked cells or cell costs. The DP earns its keep once the closed form stops working, for instance with obstacles: For a 3 × 3 grid with the centre blocked, this returns 2 (around the top-right or around the bottom-left). Notice the single row array. Before the update, row[c] still holds the value from the row above; row[c-1] has already been updated to the current row. So row[c] += row[c-1] is exactly above + left. That's the rolling array trick, and it takes memory from O(m·n) to O(n). Minimum path sum (each cell has a cost; find the cheapest right/down path) uses the same shape with min instead of +: A neighbour that doesn't exist (above the top row or left of the first column) counts as +∞ (positive infinity), so it is never chosen. Path counts use integer slots whose bit sizes can grow; the usual grid time bounds count additions as unit cost. Key takeaways Blocked cells reset their path count to zero. A rolling row holds above before update and left after update. Minimum-cost paths use the same dependency shape with min. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming Dynamic programming

sum: The table compares pairs of prefix lengths.
x: Edit distance (Levenshtein) The minimum number of unit-cost insertions, deletions and substitutions to turn A into B. Python strings are sequences of Unicode code points here; user-perceived characters may contain several code points. kitten → sitting is 3: substitute k→s, substitute e→i, insert g. State: D[i][j] records edit distance between A[:i] and B[:j]. Recurrence: look at the last characters A[i-1] and B[j-1]. If they're equal, no edit is needed for them: D[i][j] = D[i-1][j-1]. Otherwise take the cheapest of three edits, each costing 1: delete A[i-1]: D[i-1][j] + 1 insert B[j-1]: D[i][j-1] + 1 substitute: D[i-1][j-1] + 1 Base: D[i][0] = i (delete everything), D[0][j] = j (insert everything). For horse → ros, the first nonempty prefixes have different letters, h and r: The table for horse → ros: Answer D[5][3] = 3: horse → rorse (substitute h→r) → rose (delete r) → ros (delete e). To reconstruct the edits, start at the bottom-right and step back to whichever neighbour produced the value: diagonal with equal characters (match), diagonal +1 (substitute), up +1 (delete), left +1 (insert). Complexity: one constant-time step per table cell: Two 1,000-character strings need about 1,000,000 cells. The O(m × n) form is the usual shorthand for nonempty strings. Why "matching characters → take the diagonal" is safe When the last characters match, there's always an optimal alignment that pairs them. You might worry that deleting or inserting could be better, but any such solution can be rearranged into one that pairs the matching ends at no extra cost. Many implementations still take min over all three for safety; it gives the same answer. Check basic distance bounds Useful sanity checks follow directly from reversible edits, required length changes, and substituting the shared-length portion: These bounds permit substitutions. The separate LCS identity later applies only when substitutions are forbidden. Key takeaways The table compares pairs of prefix lengths. Matching ends cost nothing; otherwise try insertion, deletion and substitution. Empty-prefix costs provide the first row and column. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming Levenshtein distance

sum: Matching ends extend the diagonal subsequence; mismatches drop one end.
x: Longest common subsequence The longest sequence of characters that appears, in order but not necessarily next to each other, in both strings. The LCS of "ABCBDAB" and "BDCABA" has length four, for example "BCBA". State: L[i][j] records LCS length of A[:i] and B[:j]. Recurrence: If A[i-1] == B[j-1]: use the character, and extend the LCS of both shorter prefixes. Otherwise: drop one of the last characters and keep the better result. Base: row 0 and column 0 are all 0. For A = "ABCB", B = "BDCAB": L[4][5] = 3 ("BCB"). Reconstruction: from (m, n), if the characters match, emit the character and go diagonal; otherwise move to whichever of up or left has the larger value. You collect the LCS backwards, so reverse it at the end. LCS and edit distance are cousins. If only insertions and deletions (indels) are allowed (no substitutions), every character not in the LCS must be deleted from A or inserted from B: The example compares "ABCB" with "BDCAB" from the table above, with LCS length 3. Key takeaways Matching ends extend the diagonal subsequence; mismatches drop one end. Trace back through the full table to recover characters in reverse order. Insert/delete-only distance is determined by the LCS length. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming Levenshtein distance Hirschberg’s algorithm

sum: A substring must be unbroken, so a mismatch resets its matching run.
x: A subsequence can skip characters, whereas a substring must form one uninterrupted run. That difference changes the state, the mismatch rule and the answer location. Subsequence vs substring The longest common substring (one unbroken run of characters) is a different DP: The 0 on a mismatch is the difference from LCS, and it is why the answer is the maximum cell anywhere in the table, not the bottom-right. Key takeaways A substring must be unbroken, so a mismatch resets its matching run. The longest matching run can end at any table cell. Further reading Longest common subsequence Longest common substring

sum: Only the previous row is needed to compute the next one.
x: Space optimisation: rolling rows Create each mutable table row separately. In Python, [[0] n] m repeats references to one row: changing one row also changes all the others. The list comprehension used in the full-table examples creates independent rows; the rolling version likewise allocates a fresh current row. All three recurrences only look at the current row and the previous row. So keep two rows and swap them: With m the length of a and n the length of b, memory falls from O(m·n) to O(n). Make the shorter string the columns to get O(min(m, n)), where min picks the smaller length. You can go down to a single row, but recurrences that read the diagonal [i-1][j-1] need a saved copy, because by the time you reach column j you've overwritten column j − 1 with the current row: The catch: with rolling rows you lose the stored history for a direct traceback, because the earlier rows are gone. If you need both linear memory and the alignment itself, use Hirschberg's algorithm, which finds the midpoint of the optimal path with a forward and a backward pass and recurses. For nonempty strings it retains O(mn) time and O(m + n) space including output; the exact constant depends on the implementation. Repeated full recomputation is another space/time tradeoff. Key takeaways Only the previous row is needed to compute the next one. One-row updates must save the old diagonal before overwriting it. Recovering an alignment needs stored history or additional computation. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming Levenshtein distance Hirschberg’s algorithm

t: String DP applications and threshold bands
sum: Edit and alignment DPs underpin several real text and biological applications.
x: In the real world Line diff is related to LCS and shortest insertion/deletion scripts. Myers’ algorithm has an O(N × (D + 1)) bound, where N is the total input length and D is the insertion/deletion distance, so it is fast when the files are similar. GNU diff and Git use related algorithms and heuristics; default output need not be minimal. Git offers --minimal and alternative algorithms such as --patience. Spell checkers and fuzzy search rank suggestions by edit distance; PostgreSQL's fuzzystrmatch extension provides levenshtein(). Bioinformatics: Needleman–Wunsch (global alignment) and Smith–Waterman (local alignment) are sequence-alignment DPs with scores for matches, mismatches and gaps; local alignment also allows restarting at zero. Aligning two 100,000-base sequences is 100,000 × 100,000 = 10¹⁰ (ten billion) cells, which is why real tools use heuristics (like BLAST) and banding. Quadratic is real Edit distance of two 100,000-character strings is 10¹⁰ cell updates. It's widely believed that no algorithm can do it in strongly subquadratic time: a 2015 result by Backurs and Indyk showed that would refute the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis. In practice, if you only care whether the distance is at most some threshold k, a banded DP fills only a narrow band around the diagonal. That works because every step off the diagonal costs at least one insertion or deletion. With a threshold of twenty edits and two 100,000-character strings, the band is 41 cells wide: about 4 million cells instead of 10 billion. This includes a zero threshold (a band one cell wide, an equality check). Pitfalls Off-by-one between string and table indices. D[i][j] covers A[:i], so the last character is A[i-1]. Pad the table with an extra row and column for the empty prefix. Using L[m][n] for longest common substring. The answer can be anywhere in the table. Overwriting the diagonal in a single-row optimisation. Building [[0] n] m in Python: that's m references to the same row, so writing one cell writes the whole column. Use a list comprehension. Key takeaways Edit and alignment DPs underpin several real text and biological applications. A small distance threshold restricts useful cells to a diagonal band. The exact worst-case lower bound is conditional on SETH. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming Levenshtein distance Backurs and Indyk: conditional edit-distance lower bound Git diff algorithms PostgreSQL fuzzystrmatch

t: Indivisible items and the knapsack table
sum: Ratio-based greedy solves fractional knapsack but can fail for whole items.
x: You have a bag that holds weight W and a set of items, each with a weight and a value. Which items should you pack to maximise the total value? That's the knapsack problem, and a surprising number of real problems are knapsack in disguise: choosing which features fit in a sprint, which ads fill a slot, which jobs fit on a machine, which files fit on a disk, how to split a bill evenly. Learn this family well and you'll recognise it everywhere. Why greedy fails The obvious greedy is "take items in order of value per unit weight". With a weight limit of 7 kg and items: Item Weight Value Value/kg ------------ A 1 1 1.00 B 3 4 1.33 C 4 5 1.25 D 5 7 1.40 Greedy takes D (5 kg, value 7), then B doesn't fit, C doesn't fit, takes A: total 8 for 6 kg. The optimum is B + C: 7 kg, value 9. Greedy is optimal for the fractional knapsack, where you can take part of an item (gold dust rather than gold bars). For indivisible items this greedy rule is not generally exact; DP is one option alongside exhaustive search, branch and bound and other methods. 0/1 knapsack Each item can be taken at most once. The code assumes positive integer weights, nonnegative integer values and a nonnegative integer weight limit; choosing nothing is allowed. State: K[i][c] records best value using only the first i items with weight limit c. Recurrence: decide about item i (weight w, value v). Skip it: K[i-1][c]. Take it, if it fits: K[i-1][c-w] + v. No items give zero value. With the items above: For the items above (rows count considered items; columns give weight limits zero through seven): Answer K[4][7] = 9. Reconstruction: walk up from K[n][W]. If K[i][c]!= K[i-1][c], item i was taken; subtract its weight. Here, at capacity 7, rows D and C both give 9, so skip D. Row C improves the previous value from 5 to 9, so take C and leave capacity 3. Row B improves the previous value from 1 to 4 there, so take B and leave capacity zero. Result {B, C}. Key takeaways Ratio-based greedy solves fractional knapsack but can fail for whole items. A state records items considered and the remaining weight limit. Compare skipping an item with taking it once. Further reading Knapsack recurrences Erickson: dynamic programming

t: Use each item once with a backward loop
sum: Descending capacities read the previous item row.
x: The previous table used one row per item. Compressing it to one row is correct only when each read still represents the earlier item row. One row, iterated backwards Each row only reads the previous row, at the same or a smaller weight limit. So use a single array and loop the weight limit downwards: Why downwards? When you update best[c], you read best[c - w]. Going downwards, best[c - w] hasn't been touched yet in this round, so it still holds the "previous row" value: item i hasn't been used. Going upwards, best[c - w] may already include item i, so you'd use it twice. The one-character bug Loop direction is the only difference between 0/1 and unbounded knapsack in the 1-D form. With one item of weight 2 and value 3 and weight limit 6, the downward loop gives 3 (one copy), and the upward loop gives 9 (three copies). Get the direction wrong and your 0/1 solution silently becomes unbounded. Key takeaways Descending capacities read the previous item row. Ascending capacities can reuse the same item and change the problem. Further reading Knapsack recurrences Erickson: dynamic programming

sum: Ascending capacities deliberately allow repeated copies.
x: Unbounded knapsack Unlimited copies of each item. Same array, loop the weight limit upwards: Now best[c - w] may already contain copies of this item, which is exactly what we want. Example: items (3 kg, 4), (4 kg, 5), (5 kg, 6), weight limit 10 kg. 0/1 gives 11 (4 + 5 kg); unbounded gives 13 (3 + 3 + 4 kg). The earlier coin-change problem is unbounded knapsack: "minimum coins" is min-count knapsack, "number of ways" is counting knapsack. Bounded knapsack (item i available up to a limited number of times) can be solved by splitting each item into bundles of 1, 2, 4,... copies, plus a final remainder, so that every count from 0 to the limit is a sum of distinct bundles: With 13 copies, bundles of 1, 2, 4 and 6 replace 13 separate items with 4; any count from 0 to 13 is a sum of distinct bundles (for example 9 = 1 + 2 + 6). A limit of 0 contributes no items. Key takeaways Ascending capacities deliberately allow repeated copies. A bounded supply can be represented by doubling bundles and a remainder. Further reading Knapsack recurrences Erickson: dynamic programming

sum: A Boolean table records exactly reachable sums.
x: Knapsack can ask whether a total is possible rather than what its best value is. Each input position remains available at most once, including repeated equal values. Subset sum For nonnegative integer nums and target T, is there a subset of positions that sums exactly to T? It's 0/1 knapsack where each item's value equals its weight and we only ask about feasibility. subset_sum([3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2], 9) is True (4 + 5). For target 30 it is False. Variants change only the combiner: Count subsets summing to T: cnt[s] += cnt[s - x], with cnt[0] = 1. Minimum items to reach T: +∞ sentinel value and min(..., dp[s - x] + 1). Bitset trick A Python integer can encode reachable sums. Start with mask = 1 and limit = (1 << (T + 1)) - 1; for each nonnegative input not exceeding the target, update mask = (mask (mask << x)) & limit. Skip inputs greater than the target, then test (mask >> T) & 1. Masking bounds retained and temporary lengths by O(T + 1) bits. Without masking, storage instead grows with the sum of all inputs. Packed word operations can improve constants, but a shift is not constant-time on arbitrary-size integers. Content gap: fixed 64× or Python speedup claims are omitted because no pinned benchmark supports them. Key takeaways A Boolean table records exactly reachable sums. Descending sums keep each position available at most once. Bitsets pack reachability, but arbitrary-sized shifts still cost work. Further reading Knapsack recurrences Erickson: dynamic programming

t: Split totals into equal or near-equal groups
sum: An equal partition needs an even total and a reachable half-total.
x: Subset sum answers whether a chosen group can reach an exact total. Partition uses that answer to balance two groups without changing the input domain. Partition Can nums be split into two groups with equal sums? If the total is odd, equal integer sums are impossible. Otherwise use subset sum with half the total as the target: For [1, 5, 11, 5], the total is 22 and selecting the single 11 reaches half, so the answer is True. For [1, 2, 3, 5], the total is odd at 11, so the answer is False. Minimum difference partition (split into two groups as evenly as possible): compute all reachable sums up to S / 2 and take the largest one. For [1, 5, 11, 5], the reachable half-total gives difference zero. For [1, 2, 3, 5], the best smaller group has sum 5 (5 alone, or 2 plus 3); the other group has sum 6, so the difference is 1. Key takeaways An equal partition needs an even total and a reachable half-total. The largest reachable sum at most half the total gives the smallest gap. Further reading Knapsack recurrences Erickson: dynamic programming

t: Numeric value versus encoded input size
sum: A numeric capacity can be exponentially larger than its bit length.
x: Pseudo-polynomial time 0/1 knapsack takes O(n · W) time, where n is the number of items and W the weight limit. That looks polynomial. It isn't, quite. Complexity is measured against the size of the input: the number of bits needed to write it. The input includes every weight and value as well as W, so their bit lengths all matter. Writing W in binary takes far fewer bits than W itself: For a capacity of 1,000: The capacity-based bound is therefore not polynomial in the full binary encoding length. Capacity Bits Work proxy: 100 items --------- 1,000 10 100,000 1,000,000 20 100,000,000 1,000,000,000 30 100 billion 10¹⁸ 60 10²⁰ Adding ten bits to W multiplies the work by about 1,000 (2¹⁰ = 1,024). An algorithm that's polynomial in the numeric value but not in its bit length is called pseudo-polynomial. This is consistent with knapsack, subset sum and partition being NP-complete (as decision problems). These decision versions are weakly NP-complete: they have pseudo-polynomial algorithms, unlike strongly NP-complete numeric problems, unless every problem whose solutions can be checked in polynomial time can also be solved in polynomial time, a statement widely believed to be false. Large numbers do not make every individual instance difficult. When the numbers are small (bounded by a polynomial in n), DP solves them efficiently. Contrast with strongly NP-hard problems like the travelling salesman, whose decision versions remain NP-complete even with polynomially bounded weights. Key takeaways A numeric capacity can be exponentially larger than its bit length. Capacity-indexed DP is pseudo-polynomial. Small numeric bounds can make weakly NP-complete problems manageable. Further reading Knapsack recurrences Erickson: dynamic programming

sum: Small total values suggest indexing by value instead of weight.
x: A weight-indexed table can be too large even for a modest item count. Choose a different state or a different guarantee according to which quantity is small. What to do when W is huge DP over value instead of weight: minW[v] records minimum weight needed to achieve value exactly v. It takes O(n · V) time, where V is the total of all values. Useful when values are small but weights are big. Meet in the middle: for n up to about 40, split the items in half, enumerate all subsets of each half, sort one side and binary-search it: With forty items, the displayed work proxy is about twenty million steps, compared with about 1.1 trillion subsets for full enumeration. These estimates omit implementation constants and integer bit costs. Approximation algorithms: scale and round the values, then run the value DP. Pick an allowed relative error ε (epsilon) between 0 and 1. For nonnegative values, discard individually overweight items, choose an appropriate scaling factor and handle the zero-optimum case separately. The appropriately scaled value DP has the following guarantee: For a one-percent tolerance the returned value is at least 99 percent of the optimum. With n items, its work is polynomial in n and the reciprocal of the tolerance, plus input bit costs: an FPTAS. The correct scaling construction is required; arbitrary rounding does not establish this guarantee. Branch and bound / integer programming solvers can exploit structure in some large instances, but retain exponential worst-case risks. Key takeaways Small total values suggest indexing by value instead of weight. Meet in the middle reduces dependence on the item count. Approximation and exact solvers have different guarantees. Further reading Knapsack recurrences Erickson: dynamic programming

sum: A subset choice under an additive budget often has a knapsack state.
x: Recognising knapsack Ask: "Am I choosing a subset of items, subject to a budget on some additive quantity, while optimising or counting another additive quantity?" If so, the state is (items considered, budget used), and it's knapsack. Examples: Target sum ("assign + or − to each number to reach T"): it turns into subset counting for nonnegative integer inputs. The example is five ones with target three: count the subsets of sum 4, of which there are 5 (choose which four 1s are positive). The reduction needs a valid integer subset target: If either check fails, no assignment exists; equal-valued positions still count as distinct. Last stone weight II: minimum-difference partition. Ones and zeroes: knapsack with a two-dimensional budget (count of 0s and 1s), state dp[zeros][ones]. Key takeaways A subset choice under an additive budget often has a knapsack state. Target sum becomes subset counting with a parity and range check. Equal-valued input positions remain distinct choices. Further reading Knapsack recurrences Erickson: dynamic programming

t: Intervals, split points and cubic work
sum: Interval dependencies are smaller ranges.
x: So far every state has been a prefix, a suffix or a pair of prefixes. Two more shapes cover a large class of harder problems: Interval DP: the state is an unbroken range [i, j], and the recurrence splits it at some point k. Tree DP: the state is a node (often with a small flag), and the answer combines the answers of its children. Interval DP: the pattern States: O(n²) intervals. Transitions: O(n) split points each. Total: usually O(n³) time and O(n²) slots, for n sequence elements. The cubic bound is not an exact transition count. For the classic matrix-chain loops: Order: every interval depends on strictly shorter ones, so loop by length, from short to long. Recognise the interval boundary For an optimal search tree over sorted keys, the chosen root divides a key interval into the ranges on its left and right. CYK parsing splits a substring and combines two grammar symbols allowed by a rule. Cutting a rod at fixed marks chooses a first cut inside a piece; the two resulting marked intervals are independent, and that cut costs the original piece’s length. These have range states and split choices. LIS ending states and ordinary tree include/exclude states have different dependency shapes. Key takeaways Interval dependencies are smaller ranges. Increasing interval length is a valid evaluation order. Count all split candidates rather than equating a cubic bound with an exact count. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming Matrix chain multiplication

sum: Exact matrix multiplication is associative, but evaluation costs differ.
x: Matrix chain multiplication With the classical dense algorithm, multiplying a matrix with p rows and q columns by one with q rows and r columns has the following scalar-multiplication count (multiplications of single numbers): Matrix multiplication is associative in exact arithmetic, so for a chain A·B·C you can choose the bracketing, and the costs can differ wildly. With A: 10 × 30, B: 30 × 5, C: 5 × 60: For the two bracketings: Six times as many scalar multiplications in this cost model, just from the brackets. The number of possible bracketings of a chain of n matrices is the (n − 1)th Catalan number, which grows exponentially (about 4ⁿ, divided by a polynomial in n): 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42,... for chain lengths one, two, three and onwards, and 1,430 already for 9 matrices. So trying them all is out. Key takeaways Exact matrix multiplication is associative, but evaluation costs differ. The classical dense model counts multiplications of individual numbers. Choose brackets without changing the exact result. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming Matrix chain multiplication

sum: The final multiplication defines two independent subchains.
x: The previous unit counted the scalar multiplications for a particular bracketing. Now minimise that count across every bracketing without enumerating them all. Represent the chain by a dimension list p: each matrix’s row count is its entry in the list, and its column count is the following entry. Neighbouring matrices therefore share their inner dimension. State: C[i][j] records minimum cost to multiply matrices i through j. Recurrence: the last multiplication splits the chain into (i..k) and (k+1..j). The left product’s rows come from the first matrix and its columns from the split. The right product shares that inner dimension and ends with the final matrix’s column count. The final cost is their three dimensions multiplied together: A single matrix needs no multiplications. For the dimensions [10, 30, 5, 60], try the two final splits: matrix_chain([10, 30, 5, 60]) returns 4,500. For [40, 20, 30, 10, 30] (four matrices) it returns 26,000, via ((A(BC))D). Store the best k in a parallel split table to print the bracketing recursively. The table fills diagonal by diagonal: Where this matters Numerical libraries face this directly: numpy.linalg.multi_dot chooses the multiplication order for a chain of arrays using this DP, and numpy.einsum with optimize=True uses its greedy contraction-order search, which need not find the global optimum. Database query optimisers solve a harder cousin when ordering joins. Key takeaways The final multiplication defines two independent subchains. Keep the cheapest split and optionally store it for reconstruction. A single matrix has zero multiplication cost. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming Matrix chain multiplication NumPy multi_dot NumPy einsum

t: Burst balloons by choosing the last move
sum: An early burst changes the adjacency of the remaining pieces.
x: Burst balloons: think about the last move Balloons in a row have numbers. Bursting balloon k earns the product of its value and both neighbours’ values, where left and right are its current neighbours (or 1 past the ends). Maximise total coins. The obvious state, "which balloon do I burst first in [i, j]?", fails: after bursting it, its neighbours become adjacent, so the two halves aren't independent. The trick is to ask which balloon is burst last in an open interval (i, j). The subproblem keeps boundary balloons i and j present. If k is last, then when it is burst its neighbours are exactly i and j (everything between has gone). And the balloons in (i, k) and (k, j) never interact with each other, because k stands between them the whole time. Pad the array with 1s at both ends: a = [1] + nums + [1]. The base case says there is nothing to burst when no balloons lie strictly between i and j. For [3, 1, 5, 8] the answer is 167: burst 1 (3·1·5 = 15), then 5 (3·5·8 = 120), then 3 (1·3·8 = 24), then 8 (1·8·1 = 8). First vs last When a choice changes the neighbours of what's left, try defining the recurrence by the last action in the interval instead of the first. The last action sees a fixed boundary; the first one doesn't. Key takeaways An early burst changes the adjacency of the remaining pieces. Choosing the last burst fixes both boundary neighbours. Two open subintervals can then be solved independently. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming MIT algorithms course

sum: Matching ends enclose a smaller palindrome.
x: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. First require a unbroken range; the next unit will allow gaps between retained characters. Counting palindromic substrings P[i][j] records True if s[i..j] (characters i to j inclusive) is a palindrome, a string that reads the same backwards. It is exactly when the ends match and the inside is a palindrome (or there is no inside): "aaa" has 6 (three as, two aas, one aaa); "abc" has 3; "racecar" has 10. For a string of n characters this is O(n²) time and space. Note the loop order: i descending, j ascending, because P[i][j] reads P[i+1][j-1] (next row down). Looping by length works too. Expand around centre gets the same O(n²) time in O(1) space: a nonempty string has one centre per character and one per gap: For each one, grow outwards while the ends match. Manacher's algorithm computes a compact array of palindrome radii in O(n), reusing mirror information. That suffices to find a longest palindrome or count occurrences; explicitly listing all occurrences can require Θ(n²) output. Key takeaways Matching ends enclose a smaller palindrome. Single characters and matching pairs are base cases. Compact palindrome radii can be linear-sized even when occurrences are quadratic. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming Longest palindromic substring

sum: Matching ends contribute two characters around the inner answer.
x: A palindromic subsequence may skip input characters. Keep an interval state, but compare dropping either end when they cannot both join the palindrome. Longest palindromic subsequence The characters need not be next to each other, so it's a classic interval DP: An empty range, whose left endpoint is past its right endpoint, counts as zero. For "bbbab" the answer is 4 ("bbbb"). Its length equals the LCS length of s and its reverse; an arbitrary reconstructed LCS need not itself be palindromic. For "acbac" and its reverse "cabca", the maximum common-subsequence length is three. Both "aba" and "abc" are longest common subsequences, but only the first is a palindrome. The equality of optimal lengths does not make every reconstructed sequence valid. Key takeaways Matching ends contribute two characters around the inner answer. A mismatch drops one end and keeps the better subproblem. Empty ranges and single positions need distinct base cases. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming Longest palindromic substring

t: Choose non-adjacent nodes on a tree
sum: Include and exclude states separate the effect of choosing the parent.
x: DP on trees Once boundary information such as the parent’s selected status is represented in the state, the relevant child subtrees can be combined independently. That makes the tree itself the DP order: compute every child before its parent (a post-order traversal). Maximum independent set on a tree Choose as many nodes as possible so that no two chosen nodes are adjacent. (Or, weighted: maximise total weight. This is "house robber on a tree".) On general graphs this is NP-hard. On a tree with n nodes it's O(n). State: two values per node v: inc[v] records best in v's subtree if v is chosen. exc[v] records best in v's subtree if v is not chosen. Recurrence: If v is chosen, none of its children may be. If v isn't chosen, each child is free to be chosen or not. Bottom-up on the tree above: Answer 4: nodes {0, 3, 4, 5}. For the stated valid simple undirected tree (symmetric adjacency lists, integer vertices 0..n−1), each node is visited once and each edge twice: O(n) work. The routine assumes this tree structure; cycles or disconnected inputs require validation or a different traversal. Recursion depth on trees A tree can be a path of 100,000 nodes. A cold recursive Python DFS can exceed its configured call-depth limit; CPython usually starts with a limit of 1,000, but the actual threshold depends on existing call depth and implementation. For large inputs, compute an order with an explicit stack (or BFS), then process nodes in reverse order so children come before parents. Key takeaways Include and exclude states separate the effect of choosing the parent. Compute children before combining their answers. Use an explicit traversal order when recursion would be too deep. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming MIT algorithms course

t: Tree covers, rerooting and interval applications
sum: Excluding a vertex forces every child into a vertex cover.
x: Other tree DPs with the same shape Tree diameter: for each node, the two longest downward paths through different children. Minimum vertex cover (the fewest nodes such that every edge touches at least one of them): the same two states, with min instead of max. Rerooting: for suitable constant-sized states and O(1)-per-edge combination/exclusion (often using prefix/suffix aggregates), a second top-down pass can compute every root’s answer in O(n). More expensive transitions change the bound. In the real world Parsing: CYK uses an interval DP for a grammar in Chomsky normal form, in O(n³ · G) time for a nonempty string of n words, where G is the size (number of rules) of the grammar; handle an allowed empty string separately. RNA secondary structure prediction in noncrossing base-pair models (such as Nussinov and Zuker formulations) uses interval DP; unrestricted pseudoknots need other treatment. Optimal binary search trees (given access frequencies) are interval DP; Knuth's observation that the optimal root index is monotone cuts it from O(n³) to O(n²) for n keys. Compilers use tree DP for instruction selection: tiling an expression tree with machine instructions at minimum cost. Key takeaways Excluding a vertex forces every child into a vertex cover. Rerooting is linear only with suitably cheap state combination. Parsing, RNA models, search trees and instruction selection use related DPs. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming MIT algorithms course

t: Represent a small set with bits
sum: Each bit records whether one item is present.
x: Every DP so far has had states indexed by positions, lengths or weight limits. The following units cover three less obvious state spaces, then tie everything together with one idea: a finite, acyclic DP can be evaluated over a DAG of states. The module ends with a practical checklist for spotting DP in an interview. Bitmask DP When the state needs to know which items from a small set have been used, encode that set as the bits of an integer (a bitmask): bit j is 1 if item j is in the set. Each item is either in or out, so: With n items there are 2ⁿ subsets, so practical limits depend on the number of dimensions, transitions, representation and available resources; the following table shows growth, not a hardware guarantee. Items Subsets Endpoint slots Work proxy ------------ 10 1,024 ~10⁴ ~10⁵ 16 65,536 ~10⁶ ~1.7 × 10⁷ 20 ~10⁶ ~2 × 10⁷ ~4 × 10⁸ 25 ~3.4 × 10⁷ ~8 × 10⁸ ~2 × 10¹⁰ For example, start with cities zero, one and three included. Setting the bit for city two adds it; testing that bit before adding it reports absence. The following expression fragment assumes mask holds decimal 11, j is 2 and n is 5. It shows operations rather than printing their results. The bit operations you need: Key takeaways Each bit records whether one item is present. The number of subsets doubles with every extra item. State and transition dimensions determine feasibility. Further reading Held–Karp algorithm Erickson: dynamic programming

t: A visited-set state for travelling salesman
sum: Visited cities and current city determine the remaining tour choices.
x: Held–Karp: the travelling salesman Given distances between n cities, find the shortest tour that starts at city 0, visits every city exactly once, and returns. Brute force fixes city 0 as the start and tries every order of the rest: That is 120 quadrillion tours for just 20 cities. Hopeless. The key observation: once you've visited a set of cities and are standing at city j, the order you visited them in no longer matters for the rest of the tour. Only the set and the current city do. That's the state. State: dp[mask][j] records length of the shortest path that starts at 0, visits exactly the cities in mask, and ends at j. Recurrence: extend a path by one unvisited city k. Written "pulling" from the state before k was added: Base: dp[1][0] = 0 (only city 0 visited, standing at 0). The code below "pushes" forwards instead: from each finished state it tries every unvisited k and keeps the minimum, which computes the same values. Why does increasing mask order work? Adding a city sets a bit, so the new mask is numerically larger. Every state is final before anything reads it. For the four-city distance matrix it returns 80 (0 → 1 → 3 → 2 → 0: 10 + 25 + 30 + 15). Key takeaways Visited cities and current city determine the remaining tour choices. Adding a bit moves to a larger numeric mask. Close the full-set path by returning to city zero. Further reading Held–Karp algorithm Erickson: dynamic programming

sum: Held–Karp reduces factorial enumeration to exponential DP.
x: The visited-set recurrence is exact for the stated cost matrix. Its resource requirements depend on the table representation and on which states are reachable. Let n be the number of cities. The allocated table has one slot per subset and endpoint, and each reachable state tries up to n next cities: So O(n² · 2ⁿ) time, O(n · 2ⁿ) space. Compare 4.2 × 10⁸ with the 1.2 × 10¹⁷ brute-force tours: about 300 million times fewer. It is a work-bound proxy, not this implementation’s exact transition count: many allocated states are unreachable. Content gap C++/Python running-time predictions and a universal city-count cutoff are omitted because no pinned implementation, machine and benchmark support them. Held–Karp remains exponential, but its bound is much smaller than factorial enumeration. NP-hardness does not prove that every exact TSP algorithm must take exponential time; even a proof that polynomial-time solving differs from polynomial-time verification would rule out polynomial time, not every subexponential possibility. Concorde uses branch-and-cut techniques and has solved particular large benchmark instances, which is not a worst-case guarantee. Content gap A claim that this is the current best exact worst-case TSP bound is omitted: that research frontier requires a separately scoped, up-to-date comparison of weight models and algorithm variants. Key takeaways Held–Karp reduces factorial enumeration to exponential DP. Allocated table states and executed transitions are different counts. Memory layout and available resources matter as much as the growth bound. Further reading Held–Karp algorithm Erickson: dynamic programming

sum: A job mask can describe which assignments remain.
x: Bitmasks also represent assigned jobs or the occupied boundary of a grid. The mask must retain every fact needed by later choices, not merely count how much work is done. Other bitmask DPs Assignment problem: n workers, n jobs, cost matrix. dp[mask] records minimum cost to assign the first popcount(mask) workers (popcount is the number of 1 bits in the mask) to the jobs in mask. O(n · 2ⁿ). (The Hungarian algorithm does it in O(n³), but the bitmask DP generalises to constraints Hungarian can't handle.) Set cover / partition into groups: iterate submasks with sub = (sub - 1) & mask, stopping explicitly after zero (otherwise it wraps back to mask). Including the empty submask, the number of pairs is: By comparison, independently choosing two arbitrary masks gives: Transitions may still add work per pair. Profile DP (broken-profile, e.g. tiling a grid with dominoes): the mask records which cells of the current column boundary are already filled. When assignments interact The plain job mask is sufficient only when assignment costs depend on the current engineer and chosen project. If adjacent engineers’ project choices interact, also retain the previous engineer’s project. The engineer index is the mask’s set-bit count; the last-project flag supplies the missing boundary information. With n projects this gives O(n × 2ⁿ) allocated states and up to n next choices each, hence O(n² × 2ⁿ) transition work. A mask alone would incorrectly merge histories with different neighbouring costs. Key takeaways A job mask can describe which assignments remain. Extra interaction constraints may require additional boundary state. Stop a submask loop after zero to avoid wrapping around. Further reading Held–Karp algorithm Erickson: dynamic programming

t: Count digit properties below a bound
sum: The tight flag records whether the prefix still matches the bound.
x: Digit DP How many integers in [0, N] have digits summing to k? (Or contain no "4", or have no two equal adjacent digits,...) N can be up to 10¹⁸. Enumerating every integer up to a bound of 10¹⁸ is impractical. Instead, build the number digit by digit from the left and count how many completions satisfy the property. State: (pos, acc, tight) pos: which digit we're placing. acc: whatever the property needs to remember (here, the digit sum so far). tight: whether every digit so far has equalled N's digit. If so, the next digit can be at most N's digit at this position; otherwise any digit 0–9 is allowed. count_digit_sum(100, 5) is 6 (5, 14, 23, 32, 41, 50). count_digit_sum(2024, 10) is 120. Complexity: count the states: Many of those states are unreachable, and exceeding the target digit sum prunes more. Exact counts may require growing integers. Content gap The original microsecond running-time prediction is omitted because no reproducible benchmark supports it. Two standard moves: Ranges: count in [L, R] using the counts up to each end: Leading zeros: if the property cares about them (e.g. "no two adjacent equal digits", where 007 shouldn't count as having adjacent zeros), add a started flag to the state. The intuition Once you've placed a digit smaller than N's digit, you're "free": every remaining combination is below N. That's why the tight=False states are shared between many prefixes and get cached. tight=True is a single path that hugs N. Key takeaways The tight flag records whether the prefix still matches the bound. Cache repeated free suffix states instead of enumerating every integer. Subtract prefix counts for ranges and track leading-zero state when needed. Further reading Digit DP Python caching

t: Evaluate path recurrences on a DAG
sum: A topological order finalises every predecessor before its outgoing edges.
x: DP over DAGs: the unifying view Draw each state as a node and each "depends on" relation as an edge. For the finite recurrences here, dependencies are acyclic, so this graph is a DAG. More general cyclic Bellman equations may instead require iterative methods. Then: Bottom-up evaluation is processing nodes in topological order. Memoisation is DFS on that DAG with caching. Some optimisation DPs, such as sequence alignment, are shortest/longest path problems in that DAG. Some counting DPs count paths in the DAG. Others combine independent child choices by multiplication, so the dependency graph alone is not a path-counting recurrence. Edit distance, for example, is the shortest path through a grid DAG from the pair of empty prefixes to the pair of complete strings, with edges of weight 0 or 1. Knapsack is a longest path through a DAG of (item, weight limit) nodes. When the problem itself is a DAG, apply this directly: The inner line is the relaxation step: Given consecutively numbered vertices starting at zero, valid edges with integer weights and a complete topological order, this computes the best path starting anywhere, allowing a zero-edge path of value 0. For single-source shortest paths, initialise only the source to 0 and all other distances to +∞, use min-relaxation, and return the distance array rather than its maximum. Negative edge weights are valid in a DAG. Real uses: critical path method in project scheduling (longest path through task dependencies), scheduling lower bounds with unlimited parallel resources, and the Viterbi algorithm (most likely path through a layered DAG of hidden states over time). For shortest paths with nonnegative weights, the correctness proof of Dijkstra's algorithm gives a safe order for finalising distances even on cyclic graphs. This is not a topological order of all graph edges. Key takeaways A topological order finalises every predecessor before its outgoing edges. DAG longest and shortest paths support negative edges. Acyclic DP dependencies and safe shortest-path settling orders are different ideas. Further reading Topological sorting Erickson: dynamic programming

t: Choose a DP state from the problem
sum: Constraints suggest candidate state spaces, then you must estimate their work.
x: Recognising DP in an interview Wording signals "Count the number of ways..." → counting DP (often reported modulo 10⁹ + 7, the remainder after dividing by the prime 1,000,000,007, to keep numbers small). "Minimum cost / maximum value / longest / shortest..." with choices at each step → optimisation DP. "Is it possible to..." over subsets or partitions → feasibility DP. Greedy feels natural but you can construct a counterexample → DP. Constraint signals The input limits often tell you the intended complexity. Here n is the input size (number of items, string length and so on), N is a numeric bound on a value, and the O(...) entries are Big-O growth rates: Constraint Likely approach ------ Up to 20 items Bitmask, O(2ⁿ · n) Up to 500 items Interval, O(n³) Up to 5,000 items 2-D, O(n²) Up to 100,000 items 1-D, O(n log n) Values up to 10,000 Knapsack on values Decimal bound up to 10¹⁸ Digit DP These are prompts to estimate work and storage, not running-time guarantees. Transition costs, memory layout, hardware and language can change feasibility substantially. A process that works Brute force first: write the recursive "try every choice" solution. It defines the recurrence. Identify the state: which arguments does the recursion actually depend on? Small integer parameters suggest a manageable table, but you must still prove that they determine a subproblem and that dependencies and transitions are valid. Check for overlap: can two different paths of choices reach the same arguments? If yes, memoise. Count: states × transitions. Compare with the constraints. Convert to bottom-up only if you need the speed, the space optimisation, or to avoid recursion limits. When it's not DP The best choice is provably always the same local choice → greedy (interval scheduling by earliest finish, Huffman coding). The subproblems don't overlap → memoisation saves no repeated calls. Plain recursion or divide and conquer may suffice; tree DP can still combine disjoint subtrees. The state would have to include an unbounded history → look for a different formulation, or the problem may be NP-hard with no good DP (general longest path, general TSP for large n). Key takeaways Constraints suggest candidate state spaces, then you must estimate their work. Start with brute force, identify sufficient state, and check overlap. Greedy needs a proof; caching cannot rescue an enormous history state. Further reading Erickson: dynamic programming MIT algorithms course

t: Clarify the problem and work an example
sum: Clarify input domains, permitted mutations and the required return value before choosing an algorithm.
x: A routine can help you clarify the requested behavior, develop a correct approach, explain your reasoning and test boundary cases. Treat the following as practical advice, not a guarantee of interview success; interview formats and scoring vary. Content gap Population-wide claims about why most candidates fail are omitted because no reliable survey or causal evidence is provided. This module is a catalogue of patterns. These first units cover the routine you run before picking one. The five steps One possible allocation for a 45-minute practice session is: 5 minutes clarifying and on examples, 5–10 on the approach, 15–20 coding, 5–10 testing. Adjust this to the task and interviewer; a short or familiar problem may need less planning. Step 1: clarify Restate the problem in your own words, then ask about anything that would change the algorithm. Input size. "How large can n be?" Here, and throughout this module, n means the number of elements in the input (the length of the array or string) unless a problem says otherwise. Use the answer to compare growth against the resource budget (see the following input-growth unit). Value ranges. Negative numbers? Zeros? Can values cause integer overflow in 32 bits? Sortedness and duplicates. Is the array sorted? Can values repeat? Output shape. Indices or values? One answer or all? What if there is no answer: return -1, None, raise? Mutability. May I modify the input in place? Ties. If several answers are valid, does it matter which? Questions are signals "Is the array sorted?" is not small talk. A yes points straight at binary search or two pointers. "Can values be negative?" matters for monotone sum-window rules (the sliding-window units), though fixed-size windows and other window predicates can still handle negatives. Step 2: examples Write one ordinary example and work it by hand. Then list the edge cases you'll test at the end: empty input, a single element all values equal, all distinct already sorted, reverse sorted negatives, zeros, the largest allowed values the answer at the very start or very end Working an example by hand often reveals the algorithm. Watch what you do: if you keep scanning back over the same elements, that repeated scan is the thing to optimise. Key takeaways Clarify input domains, permitted mutations and the required return value before choosing an algorithm. Work a normal case by hand and record boundary cases for later tests. The five-step routine is practical advice; interview timing and scoring vary. Further reading Coding interview techniques — Tech Interview Handbook Coding interview cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook How to Solve It (Pólya) — Wikipedia Time complexity — Wikipedia

t: From brute force to a lookup
sum: A brute-force solution supplies a correctness baseline and exposes repeated work.
x: The input has n elements. This unit turns a scan of all pairs into a lookup of earlier values, preserving original indices. Step 3: brute force State the obvious solution and its complexity out loud, even if it is slow. It proves you understand the problem, gives you a fallback, and is often the starting point for the optimisation. Classic example, two sum: given an unsorted array and a target, return the indices of two numbers that add up to the target. The two loops look at every pair of positions once. The number of pairs tells you the cost: That is O(n²) time and O(1) extra space: the work grows with the square of n, while the memory used beyond the input stays fixed. You don't always need to code the brute force; saying it and its cost is usually enough. Step 4: optimise Look for wasted work. Three useful questions are: What is the bottleneck? In two sum, the inner loop: for each a[i], we search the rest of the array for target - a[i], the one value that would complete the pair: That single partner is what makes a lookup structure useful in the next question. Is there a data structure that answers that inner question faster? "Have I seen value v?" is a hash-set lookup: O(1) on average. Am I recomputing something? Running totals, window contents and "best so far" values can usually be carried forward instead of recomputed. Now it is expected O(n) time under constant-cost, well-distributed hashing and O(n) space. Numeric examples assume exact arithmetic; large Python integers add bit-length costs. We traded memory for time, which is the most common trade in this whole module. Why check before inserting? If x is exactly half the target (say target 6 and a current value of 3), inserting first would let x pair with itself. Checking first means a value can only pair with an earlier element. Reuse the lookup idea for duplicates To detect any duplicate, keep a hash set of values already scanned. Check membership before adding each value. A repeated value answers yes; exhausting the input answers no. Under expected constant-cost hashing, one pass takes expected O(n) time and up to O(n) set entries, where n is the input length. Sorting then comparing neighbouring values is another option with an O(n log n) comparison bound. It changes the data order, and Python’s in-place list sort can still need O(n) temporary references. Neither bound alone predicts the faster implementation for a particular input. If the optimal approach is unclear, stating a correct brute-force baseline exposes the bottleneck and gives a concrete direction to discuss. The routine does not require discovering the optimum before explaining any solution. Key takeaways A brute-force solution supplies a correctness baseline and exposes repeated work. Check the complement before inserting the current value so two sum uses distinct positions. Hash-based acceleration trades memory for expected speed under stated hashing and numeric-cost assumptions. Further reading Coding interview techniques — Tech Interview Handbook Coding interview cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook How to Solve It (Pólya) — Wikipedia Time complexity — Wikipedia

sum: Compare candidate growth expressions at the largest permitted input.
x: Input limits tell you which growth expressions deserve investigation. Here n is the number of input elements; constants, memory and the deadline still matter. Let the constraints choose the complexity Interview and contest problems specify limits on input size. For example, an array may contain between one and one hundred thousand elements: That is a heavy hint. Input size helps compare growth, but whether an approach is fast enough also depends on the algorithm’s constants, operation types, numeric sizes, memory, hardware and deadline. Content gap Generic C++/Python operations-per-second figures and universal pass/fail thresholds are omitted because no pinned benchmark or judge configuration establishes them. The table uses a few growth expressions you may not have met. Each one describes how the work grows with n: For zero items there is one empty ordering and one empty subset. The factorial product displayed above uses the usual continuation pattern for at least two items; its zero-input value is defined as one. The table also uses Big-O notation: O(f(n)) supplies an asymptotic upper bound, up to a constant factor, for a nonnegative cost function f(n). It need not be tight or count exact operations. A base-2 logarithm measures the exponent needed to produce its argument; for 100,000 it is about 16.6. The whole number of successive halvings needed to reach one or less is 17. The table lists growth expressions to investigate for illustrative input sizes, not guaranteed feasible limits. Example n Growth to investigate Candidate technique --------- ≤ 10 O(n!) Permutations ≤ 20 O(2ⁿ) Subsets, bitmasks ≤ 500 O(n³) Triple loop, DP ≤ 5,000 O(n²) Pairs, 2-D DP ≤ 10⁶ O(n log n) Sort, heap > 10⁶ O(n), O(log n) One pass, math Plugging the largest allowed n into two of these expressions shows the gap: These are work expressions, not exact operation counts inferred from big-O. Compare them with the actual resource budget before choosing. Key takeaways Compare candidate growth expressions at the largest permitted input. Factorial counts orderings; powers of two count subsets. Big-O expressions are not exact instruction counts or promises about runtime. t: Use problem cues to form a hypothesis
sum: A problem cue suggests a technique; its preconditions decide whether the technique is valid.
x: Before selecting a template, identify the input shape, the requested output and what information must be maintained. This short catalogue previews the concrete patterns that follow. Spotting the pattern Once you understand the problem, match its shape against the patterns in this module. Cue in the problem Try ------ Sorted array, pair/triple Two pointers Contiguous subarray/substring Sliding window Many range-sum queries Prefix sums Sum equals k, negatives allowed Prefix sum + hash map Next greater/smaller Monotonic stack Max of every window Monotonic deque Overlapping ranges, schedules Sort intervals k largest / k-th / stream Heap Merge k sorted inputs Heap (k-way) "Appears once", at most 20 items Bits, masks "Have I seen this?" Hash map/set Other modules cover the rest of the toolkit: binary search, BFS/DFS, backtracking and dynamic programming. Patterns are hypotheses A cue suggests a pattern; it doesn't prove it fits. "Longest subarray with sum at most k", where k is a limit the problem gives you, looks like a sliding window, but if values can be negative the window logic breaks. Check the pattern's preconditions before you commit. Key takeaways A problem cue suggests a technique; its preconditions decide whether the technique is valid. Signed sum problems often call for prefix values and an appropriate lookup structure. Other modules cover graph search, backtracking, binary search and dynamic programming. t: Test the code and audit hidden costs
sum: Trace representative and boundary inputs, then state an invariant or correctness argument.
x: Testing complements a correctness argument. Here n is the number of input elements; the earlier two-sum implementation checks a hash map before inserting the current element. Step 5: test Don't announce "done" and wait. Test like an engineer: Trace your normal example through the code line by line, tracking variables. This can reveal off-by-one errors; examples supplement an invariant or correctness argument rather than proving correctness for all inputs. Run the edge cases from step 2: empty input, one element, duplicates. Check the complexity you claimed against the code you wrote. A hidden in list check or slice inside a loop can turn O(n) into O(n²). For two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6): Note that 3 + 3 = 6 was correctly not returned, because there is only one 3. Talking through it Make your reasoning available for discussion. Useful ways to narrate include: Before coding: "Brute force is O(n²) by checking every pair. The inner loop is a lookup, so a hash map should get us to O(n) with O(n) space. Shall I go with that?" Getting a nod before coding avoids building the wrong thing. While coding: say what each block is for, not every keystroke. Use clear names (seen, lo, hi), not a1, tmp2. When stuck: say what you're trying. "Sorting would help, but we need original indices... we could sort pairs of (value, index)." Explaining the sticking point gives the interviewer something concrete to respond to. When you spot a bug: say so and fix it. Finding and explaining a bug makes the correction available for discussion. Hints are not failure. Take them, acknowledge them and build on them. Common pitfalls Solving the wrong problem. Returning values when indices were asked for; assuming sorted input when it wasn't. Premature optimisation. Spending 20 minutes hunting an O(n) trick and running out of time with nothing written. A correct O(n log n) beats an unfinished O(n). Skipping the complexity. Always state time and space, and justify them. Ignoring Python costs. x in some_list is O(n); s[1:] copies; list.pop(0) is O(n). Use sets, indices and collections.deque. Recap of the pattern family Run the same routine every time: clarify, examples, brute force, optimise, test. Ask about input size, value ranges, sortedness and duplicates; each changes the algorithm. Use constraints to compare growth and resource needs; an input of about 100,000 elements makes a quadratic scan a significant concern, not a universal impossibility. Optimise by finding the bottleneck, then asking which data structure answers it faster. Narrate your reasoning, get agreement before coding, and test by tracing, not by hoping. Key takeaways Trace representative and boundary inputs, then state an invariant or correctness argument. Python list membership, front removal and slices can add hidden linear work. Explain time and space costs alongside your reasoning.
