t: Discard impossible pairs in sorted input
sum: Sortedness proves which endpoint cannot participate in a remaining answer.
x: Many brute-force solutions look at every pair of positions (i, j) in an array of n elements: roughly half the square of the input length in pairs, which is O(n²) work (the work grows with the square of n). The two-pointer pattern keeps two indices and moves each one only forwards (or only backwards), so each pointer makes O(n) moves and together they make O(n) moves. Two same-direction pointers can together make nearly twice as many moves as there are elements. Costs below assume constant-time numeric operations and indexing. It works when there is a rule that tells you, after looking at the current pair, which pointer can safely move: that some whole set of pairs can be discarded without checking them. Usually that rule comes from the input being a sorted sequence, or from an invariant you maintain about the region each pointer has passed. There are three common flavours: Opposite ends: pair sum in a sorted array Problem. Given a sorted array and a target, find two elements that add up to the target. Start with the smallest and largest elements. Compare their sum with the target: Too small? Among the two allowed inward moves, moving lo right can increase the sum. a[lo] paired with any other remaining element gives a sum no larger, so a[lo] can't be in any answer: discard it. Too big? Symmetrically, a[hi] paired with any other remaining element is too big: move hi left. Trace with a = [1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11], target 10: Each step discards one element for good, so at most one fewer step than the array length: O(n) time, O(1) space. Compare the hash-map version of two sum (the earlier approach units), which is expected O(n) under constant-time, well-distributed hashing but needs O(n) extra memory and works on unsorted input. Three sum "Find all triples summing to 0" is: sort (O(n log n)), then for each i, run pair sum on the part after i with target -a[i]. That's O(n²) total for this algorithm, excluding integer bit costs. Skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicate triples. Other safe opposite-end moves A palindrome scan compares the two outer values. If they differ, the sequence is not a palindrome; if they match, discard both and check the inner range. Each inward move is justified by an equality already checked. A merge of two sorted sequences instead keeps one forward index per input and takes the smaller current value. For the existing count_less question, if the two endpoint values sum below the target, the left endpoint pairs successfully with every remaining position up to the right endpoint. Count that whole block, then discard the left endpoint. Otherwise discard the right endpoint. This rule depends on sortedness just as pair-sum search does. Key takeaways Sortedness proves which endpoint cannot participate in a remaining answer. Use distinct positions: stop when the pointers meet. Sorting then fixing one element reduces three sum to repeated pair scans. Further reading Two pointers — USACO Guide Dutch national flag problem — Wikipedia Array cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook

sum: A container is limited by its shorter endpoint and the distance between endpoints.
x: Here n is the number of nonnegative heights. The input need not be sorted: the move rule follows from a bound on all pairs involving one endpoint. Opposite ends: container with most water Problem. h[i] is a nonnegative height of a vertical line at position i. Choose two lines that, with the x-axis, hold the most water. The water a pair of lines can hold is limited by the shorter line: The formula assumes the lines are thin and the water's surface is flat, so only the shorter line matters; it holds for any nonnegative heights. The array isn't sorted, so why do two pointers work? Start with the widest container (lo = 0, hi = n - 1). Suppose h[lo] < h[hi]. Any other container using lo with a partner inside the range: is narrower (the partner is closer), and has height at most h[lo] (the shorter line caps it). So it can never beat the current one. Every pair involving lo is discarded in one move: advance lo. Move the shorter line; if heights tie, either endpoint can be discarded. For fewer than two lines, the code returns 0. For [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7] the answer is 49, from the lines at positions 1 and 8: The proof is the pattern Two pointers are only correct when you can argue that the move discards nothing useful. If you can't say why a move is safe, you don't yet have a two-pointer solution; you have a guess. Key takeaways A container is limited by its shorter endpoint and the distance between endpoints. Discarding the shorter endpoint cannot remove an improvement inside the current range. Equal heights allow either endpoint to move; fewer than two lines give zero area. Further reading Two pointers — USACO Guide Dutch national flag problem — Wikipedia Array cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook

t: Filter a sorted array with read and write indices
sum: The kept prefix contains the distinct values seen so far; the list itself is not resized.
x: Here n is the sorted array length. A read index scans the input and a write index marks the next kept position; constant extra space requires avoiding temporary slices. Same direction: remove duplicates in place Problem. Given a sorted array, remove duplicates in place so each value appears once, and return the length of the distinct prefix. The list is not resized; ignore the tail after that prefix. Extra space must be O(1). Use a read pointer r that scans every element and a write pointer w marking where the next kept element goes. The invariant: a[0:w] holds the distinct values seen so far, in order. The same read/write shape solves "move all zeros to the end", "remove all copies of value v" and "keep at most two of each value" (keep an item when w < 2 or it differs from a[w - 2]). Another same-direction variant is fast and slow pointers on a linked list: the slow pointer moves one step, the fast one two. Check equality after advancing: they eventually meet if there's a cycle (Floyd's algorithm). On an acyclic list, stop when fast cannot take another two-step advance; the chosen loop convention determines which middle node is returned for an even-length list. Key takeaways The kept prefix contains the distinct values seen so far; the list itself is not resized. Keep at most two copies by comparing with the value two kept positions back. Fast and slow linked-list pointers use a related movement pattern with a different invariant. Further reading Two pointers — USACO Guide Dutch national flag problem — Wikipedia Array cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook

t: Partition the unknown region into three categories
sum: Dutch flag keeps known zero, one and two regions around an unknown region.
x: Here n is the input length. For the Dutch flag example every element must be 0, 1 or 2; the code sorts in place in one scan. Partitioning: the Dutch national flag Problem. An array contains only 0s, 1s and 2s. Sort it in one pass, in place. (Dijkstra posed it with the red, white and blue of the Dutch flag.) Keep three pointers and four regions: Look at a[mid], the first unknown element: 0: swap it into the 0s region (a[lo]), advance lo and mid. 1: already in place; advance mid. 2: swap it with a[hi], shrink hi. Don't advance mid: the element that just arrived from hi hasn't been examined yet. Why is it safe to advance mid after swapping with lo? If lo < mid, the swapped-in value comes from the known 1s region. If lo == mid, the swap is with itself and the current value has just been identified as 0. In either case advancing is safe. Each step either advances mid or shrinks hi, so the unknown region shrinks every iteration: O(n) time, O(1) space. Three-way partitioning is also how quicksort copes with many duplicate keys. Recognising the pattern Cue Flavour ------ Sorted array, find pair/triple Opposite ends Palindrome check Opposite ends Pick two ends to maximise Opposite ends In place, O(1) space, filter Read/write Linked list middle or cycle Fast/slow Gather by category in place Partition Merge two sorted arrays One pointer each Pitfalls Unsorted input. Pair sum's move rule depends on sortedness. If the input isn't sorted, either sort it (O(n log n), and you lose original indices unless you sort (value, index) pairs) or use a hash map. lo < hi vs lo <= hi. Pair problems need two distinct elements, so stop when they meet. Dutch flag uses mid <= hi because the element at hi is still unknown. Advancing after a swap from the right. In partitioning, the element swapped in from the right is unexamined; advancing past it is the classic bug. Duplicates in three sum. Without skipping equal values you'll report the same triple many times. Recap of the pattern family Two pointers replace an O(n²) scan of pairs with O(n) by proving each move discards only useless pairs. Opposite ends suits sorted arrays and "choose two ends" problems: move the pointer that can't be part of a better answer. Same direction (read/write, fast/slow) does in-place filtering and linked-list tricks in O(1) space. Partitioning keeps regions with invariants; the Dutch flag sorts three values in one pass. Always be able to state the invariant or the reason a move is safe. Key takeaways Dutch flag keeps known zero, one and two regions around an unknown region. A value swapped from the right is unexamined, so do not advance the middle index. State the invariant behind a pointer move rather than applying a template blindly. Further reading Two pointers — USACO Guide Dutch national flag problem — Wikipedia Array cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Dijkstra on the Dutch National Flag

t: Maintain the sum of a fixed-size window
sum: A fixed window updates its sum by adding the entering value and subtracting the leaving value.
x: A sliding window is two pointers that bound a contiguous range a[lo..hi]. Instead of recomputing something about every subarray from scratch (an array of n elements has O(n²) subarrays, often with O(n) work each), you update the window's summary as the edges move: add the element entering on the right, remove the one leaving on the left. It is a candidate when a problem says subarray or substring (consecutive) and asks for the longest, shortest, maximum or count of windows satisfying some condition. The code uses random-access sequences. Arithmetic, equality and hashing costs are treated as constant; dictionary bounds are expected/amortised, not adversarial worst-case guarantees. Python string elements are Unicode code points, which need not be complete displayed characters. Fixed-size windows Problem. Find the maximum sum of any k consecutive elements. Brute force sums each window from scratch: about n windows of k elements each, so O(n × k) work, where n is the array length. But consecutive windows share all but one of their elements. Slide by adding the new element and subtracting the one that fell off: The worked line uses the example below: the window [2, 1, 5] sums to 8; sliding one step brings in a[3], whose value is 1, and drops a[0], whose value is 2. This only works because addition can be undone by subtraction; a window maximum can't be "un-added" like this (the monotonic stack and deque units handles that with a deque). For a = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], k = 3: Each slide costs a constant amount of work, so the whole scan is O(n) time, O(1) space. The same idea handles "average of every window", "count anagrams of p in s" (a window of length len(p) with a character count) and rolling hashes (Rabin–Karp). Counts that update with the window For distinct values, keep a map from value to occurrence count. Increment the entrant, decrement the leaver and delete a key when its count becomes zero. The number of remaining keys is the current distinct count, read in constant time. For anagrams, compare counts against the pattern’s required counts. Maintain how many character counts currently disagree: when one count changes, update that mismatch count from its old and new equality status. This avoids scanning the whole alphabet on every slide. Build the target counts once and update a bounded number of keys per slide, assuming expected constant-time hashing. Account for both source and pattern lengths in the total cost. Key takeaways A fixed window updates its sum by adding the entering value and subtracting the leaving value. Maintain counts and a constant-time mismatch counter for anagram windows. A median needs order information; a running total alone does not suffice. Further reading Sliding window — USACO Guide String cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Two pointers — USACO Guide

sum: Longest-window validity must survive taking subwindows; shortest covering validity must survive expansion.
x: A variable window changes length to restore or preserve a predicate. Here n is the input length. A subarray or substring occupies a contiguous range; an arbitrary subsequence may skip positions. Variable-size windows Here the window grows and shrinks. The template: hi - lo + 1 is the window's length, because both ends are included: If the empty window is valid and add/remove/valid/record each cost O(1), both pointers only move forwards, so each element is added once and removed no more than once: O(n) total, even with the inner while. That amortised argument is the reason the pattern is fast. The precondition: monotonicity These variable-window templates need monotonic validity: every subwindow of a valid window stays valid for the longest/shrink-when-invalid template; every superwindow of a valid window stays valid for the shortest/shrink-while-valid template. Merely being able to make some invalid window valid by growing is insufficient. "Sum at most k", with non-negative numbers and a non-negative limit k, qualifies. With negative numbers, removing an element can increase the sum, so the window can't tell which way to move. Use prefix sums instead (the prefix-sum units). When to record a candidate For a longest valid window, shrink until validity is restored, then record its length. Typical downward-closed predicates are at most a specified number of distinct values, at most a specified number of zeros, or a sum at most a nonnegative limit when all values are nonnegative. For products of integers at least one and a limit greater than one, removing values cannot increase the product; the same longest/counting shape is valid. For a shortest window whose positive values sum to at least a positive target, expansion cannot destroy validity. Once valid, record a candidate inside the shrink loop, then remove from the left. Stop shrinking when the sum falls below target. Each endpoint still moves only forwards. For [2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 3] with target 7, the final [4, 3] is the shortest qualifying range. A negative value can rescue an earlier sum that looked too large. For [3, -2, 1] with a limit of 2, removing the initial 3 immediately loses the valid whole-array answer. Use a prefix-based method that retains the needed starts instead. For counting under a downward-closed predicate, keep the smallest valid left edge. Every starting position from that edge through the current right edge then gives a valid ending subarray. Adding the number of such starts counts those subarrays once. Key takeaways Longest-window validity must survive taking subwindows; shortest covering validity must survive expansion. With constant-cost updates, forward-only endpoints give linear total work. Negative values can break monotone sum rules; consecutive positions alone does not prove a window solution. Further reading Sliding window — USACO Guide String cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Two pointers — USACO Guide

sum: Store each character’s last position to jump past a duplicate.
x: The earlier variable-window rule now tracks unique characters. Here n is the string length measured in Python code points; dictionary operations use the expected constant-cost hash model. Longest substring without repeating characters Problem. Return the length of the longest substring of s with all distinct characters. Window condition: no character appears twice. When s[hi] is already in the window, move lo just past its previous occurrence. Storing each character's last index lets lo jump instead of stepping. Trace for "abcabcbb": Answer 3. O(n) time; O(min(n, alphabet)) space, where n is the length of s, alphabet is the number of different characters that can occur, and min picks the smaller of the two: the map never holds more keys than either. Why >= lo matters For "abba": at the final a, last['a'] = 0, but lo is already 2 (moved by the second b). The old a is outside the window, so lo may never move backwards to 1. Without the >= lo check, the code returns 3 instead of 2. Key takeaways Store each character’s last position to jump past a duplicate. Ignore occurrences before the left edge so the edge never moves backwards. Python strings are scanned by code point, which can differ from displayed characters. Further reading Sliding window — USACO Guide String cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Two pointers — USACO Guide

t: Shrink a covering substring to its minimum
sum: A counter records missing occurrences, including repeated target characters.
x: Find the shortest contiguous substring covering every target occurrence. Hashing and character comparisons are assumed constant-cost, and each Python character is a code point. Minimum window substring Problem. Given s and t, find the shortest substring of s containing every character of t (with multiplicity). For s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC", the answer is "BANC". An empty target has answer ""; when no covering substring exists the answer is also "". This is a "shortest" problem: grow until the window is valid, then shrink while it stays valid, recording the best. Keep need[c]: how many more of c the window still needs (negative means surplus), and missing: the total number of required characters not yet covered. How it plays out on the example: Each character enters and leaves once. Writing s for the length of s and t for the length of t, that gives expected O(s + t) time, O(alphabet) auxiliary space plus the returned substring. The missing counter is what keeps the validity check O(1); comparing two full count maps each step would cost O(alphabet) per move. Key takeaways A counter records missing occurrences, including repeated target characters. Record a covering candidate before removing its leftmost character. An empty target or absence of a covering substring returns the empty string. Further reading Sliding window — USACO Guide String cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Two pointers — USACO Guide

sum: Every valid start between the left and right edges contributes one ending window.
x: Here n is the input length and k is an integer distinct-value budget. Values must be hashable; count-map operations have expected constant cost. Counting windows: the at-most trick "Count subarrays with exactly k distinct values" is awkward for a window: removing an element can keep the count at k or drop it, so there's no single clean shrink rule. But "at most k" is monotonic. For each hi, after shrinking, every window ending at hi and starting anywhere in [lo, hi] qualifies: that's hi - lo + 1 windows. These functions count nonempty subarrays; a negative distinct budget gives 0, and exactly(a, 0) gives 0. Values must be hashable. The subtraction works because every subarray with at most k distinct values has either exactly k or at most k − 1: For [1, 2, 1, 2, 3] with k = 2: twelve subarrays have at most two distinct values (all 15 except the three that end with 3 and also contain both 1 and 2), and five have at most one (the five single elements, since no two neighbours are equal). So exactly 7 subarrays have exactly two distinct values. Recognising the pattern Cue Kind of window ------ "every k consecutive" Fixed "longest... such that" Variable, shrink when invalid "shortest... containing" Variable, shrink while valid "count subarrays at most k" Variable, add hi-lo+1 "exactly k" Subtract two at-most counts Max/min of each window Monotonic deque (the monotonic stack and deque units) Sum equals k, negatives allowed Not a window: prefix sums Pitfalls Non-contiguous sequence problems. "Subsequence" means elements need not be adjacent; a contiguous window alone does not enumerate arbitrary subsequences. DP, greedy or other methods may apply. Negative numbers break sum-based windows, as above. Recording at the wrong time. For "longest", record after shrinking (window valid). For "shortest", record inside the shrink loop before removing. Expensive validity checks. Keep a counter (missing, len(count)) so each check is O(1). Stale map entries. Delete keys whose count hits 0, or len(count) overstates the distinct count. Recap of the pattern family A sliding window maintains a contiguous range's summary incrementally, turning O(n²) or O(n × k) into O(n), where n is the input length and k the window size. Each element enters and leaves the window no more than once, so the inner while doesn't make it quadratic. Variable windows need monotonic validity; negative numbers usually break sum conditions. "Longest" shrinks until valid then records; "shortest" records while shrinking a valid window. Count exactly a budget by subtracting the at-most-previous-budget count from the at-most-budget count. Key takeaways Every valid start between the left and right edges contributes one ending window. Subtract the at-most-lower-budget count from the at-most-budget count. Delete zero-count map keys; these examples count nonempty subarrays. Further reading Sliding window — USACO Guide String cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Two pointers — USACO Guide

t: Subtract prefixes to answer static range sums
sum: The padded prefix table starts with zero and totals elements before each position.
x: If you'll ask "what's the sum of a[l..r]?" many times, adding up the range each time costs O(n) per query. Here a[l..r] means the elements from index l to index r, both included, and n is the length of the array. A prefix sum array costs O(n) once and then answers every range query in O(1). The idea underpins far more than range queries: subarray-sum counting, difference arrays for batched updates, 2-D summed-area tables and cumulative frequency tables all reuse it. Examples use exact integer arithmetic. The O(1) arithmetic/hash model assumes values fit the chosen word size; Python arbitrary-precision costs grow with bit length. Floating-point prefix subtraction can lose accuracy through rounding and cancellation. The prefix array Build the prefix array one running total at a time: The prefix at an index totals that many earlier elements. The table has one more entry than the input because it includes the empty prefix. Any range sum is then one subtraction: The leading zero, P[0] = 0 in the implementation, is what makes ranges starting at index 0 work without a special case. This relies on subtraction undoing addition exactly, so it holds for integers but only approximately for floating-point numbers, and it does not work for operations like max that can't be undone. Off-by-one insurance Use the length-n + 1 array with P[0] = 0. Think of P[i] as the sum of the elements before index i. Then "sum of a[l..r]" is always "everything before r + 1 minus everything before l". Python provides these values as an iterator: itertools.accumulate(a, initial=0). Materialise it with list(...) for indexed range queries. Integer width and numeric limits Forgetting the leading zero: misses ranges that start at index 0. In frequency-counting variants, seed seen = {0: 1} for the same reason. Integer overflow in fixed-width languages: a prefix sum can be as large as the count times the largest value, which blows past a 32-bit integer: Key takeaways The padded prefix table starts with zero and totals elements before each position. Inclusive range queries subtract the prefix before the left edge from the prefix after the right edge. Use a suitable integer width and account for floating-point cancellation. Further reading Prefix sums — USACO Guide More on prefix sums (2-D, difference arrays) — USACO Guide Prefix sum — Wikipedia Summed-area table — Wikipedia

sum: Count frequencies of earlier running totals, including one empty prefix.
x: Here n is the array length and k is a target sum. The preceding padded prefix convention represents the empty prefix with total zero. Subarray sum equals k Problem. Count the nonempty contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly k. Values may be negative. A sliding window fails because of the negatives (the sliding-window units). Prefix sums turn the question around: So as we scan, for each running total run, the number of subarrays ending here with sum k equals the number of earlier prefix values equal to run − k. Keep a hash map counting prefix values seen so far. Trace for a = [1, 2, 3], k = 3: The two subarrays are [1, 2] and [3]. Expected O(n) time with well-behaved constant-cost hashing, O(n) space. Why seen = {0: 1}? It represents the empty prefix P[0] = 0. Without it, subarrays that start at index 0 (like [1, 2] above, where the required earlier prefix is zero) are never counted. Key takeaways Count frequencies of earlier running totals, including one empty prefix. Query before inserting the current prefix so empty subarrays are excluded. Prefix-frequency counting handles signed values under expected constant-cost hashing. Further reading Prefix sums — USACO Guide More on prefix sums (2-D, difference arrays) — USACO Guide Prefix sum — Wikipedia Summed-area table — Wikipedia

t: Use first indices and normalised remainders
sum: Store the first occurrence to maximise the length of a matching subarray.
x: Different prefix problems retain different information: counts for counting, earliest positions for longest ranges, or normalised remainders for divisibility. Here n is the number of elements. Prefix summaries for different questions The same "complement in a hash map" trick, borrowed from two sum, solves several variations: Problem Store in map ------ Count sum equals k prefix → count Longest sum equals k prefix → first index Sum divisible by positive k prefix % k → count Equal 0s and 1s map 0→−1, find sum 0 For "longest", seed first = {0: -1} and store the first ending index at which each running total appears (do not overwrite it). At ending index j, a match gives the length: Remainder and update caveats Negative modulo: in Python -1 % 5 == 4, which is what you want; in C, Java and JavaScript, -1 % 5 == -1, for positive k. In fixed-width code, the extra + k can itself overflow: compute r = x % k, then add k only if r is negative; ensure the preceding sum fits too. Java also provides Math.floorMod. Mutable data: prefix sums go stale after an update; rebuilding is O(n). Use a Fenwick tree if updates are frequent. Remainder frequencies For a positive modulus, reduce each running prefix sum to its canonical remainder between zero and one less than the modulus. Two prefixes in the same remainder class differ by a multiple of the modulus, so the subarray between them has divisible sum. Keep a frequency map, seeded with one empty prefix at remainder zero, and look up a remainder before inserting it. Python’s remainder has the positive divisor’s sign. Java’s remainder follows the dividend’s sign, so a negative running total can produce a negative key for the same class. With positive Java int modulus and int input values, widen the sum to long before Math.floorMod; merely normalising after an overflowing int addition does not repair that lost value. Key takeaways Store the first occurrence to maximise the length of a matching subarray. Equal normalised prefix remainders identify sums divisible by a positive modulus. Widen before Java addition and normalise remainders consistently. Further reading Prefix sums — USACO Guide More on prefix sums (2-D, difference arrays) — USACO Guide Prefix sum — Wikipedia Summed-area table — Wikipedia

t: Record starts and stops for batched updates
sum: An inclusive update switches on at its first index and off just after its last index.
x: Here n is the array length and u is the number of updates. The batch starts with zeros; updates are applied before the final array is read. Difference arrays: batched range updates Prefix sums make range queries cheap. The inverse trick makes range updates cheap. Problem. Start with n zeros. Apply many updates "add v to every element in [l, r]", then report the final array. Doing each update directly is O(r − l + 1). Instead, record only where each update starts and stops: Each update touches two cells of the difference array: Each update is O(1); one prefix-sum pass at the end rebuilds the array. Total O(n + u) for u updates instead of O(n × u). Check index 2: covered by +2 and -1, so 1. Correct. Where you see this "Car pooling" (can a car with C seats take every trip?) and "flight bookings" are difference arrays over time or flight number. For positive-duration start-inclusive, end-exclusive bookings start,end), mark +1 at the start and −1 at the end, then sweep. Inclusive discrete ranges instead cancel just after the last included index. The interval units calls this a sweep line. The efficient batch use applies updates before rebuilding the values. Interleaved queries are possible but a plain difference array may need O(n) work per read. A Fenwick tree over differences supports range-add/point-query in O(log n); two Fenwick trees or an appropriately lazy segment tree support range-add/range-sum. Key takeaways An inclusive update switches on at its first index and off just after its last index. One final prefix pass reconstructs all batch-updated values. Efficient interleaved updates and queries need an appropriate tree rather than repeated rebuilding. Further reading [Prefix sums — USACO Guide More on prefix sums (2-D, difference arrays) — USACO Guide Prefix sum — Wikipedia Summed-area table — Wikipedia

sum: A zero row and column simplify rectangle boundaries.
x: The earlier prefix-subtraction idea extends to grids. The example uses exact integer arithmetic with constant-cost operations; returned and auxiliary storage must both be counted. 2-D prefix sums For a grid, let P[r][c] be the sum of the rectangle from (0, 0) up to but not including row r and column c. Build it with inclusion–exclusion: The query subtracts the strip above and the strip to the left, then adds back the corner that was subtracted twice: The drawing’s letters identify four regions. In the formula below, each letter denotes that region’s cell sum: For the grid the prefix table is and the rectangle rows 1–2, columns 1–2 (the cells 6, 3, 2, 0) comes from four lookups: This is the summed-area table from computer graphics, introduced for texture mapping in 1984. The Viola–Jones face detector used it (as the "integral image") to evaluate rectangular features in constant time, which helped make real-time face detection practical in the early 2000s. Recognising the pattern Many range-sum queries on a static array or grid. "Subarray sum equals / is divisible by k", especially with negatives. "Equal number of X and Y in a subarray" (map one to −1, look for sum 0). Many range updates followed by reads: difference array. Products work too (prefix products, or "product of array except self" with prefix and suffix passes), but watch out for zeros. Recap of the pattern family A padded prefix totals the elements before its index; an inclusive range subtracts the prefix before its start from the prefix just after its end. "Subarray sum equals k" becomes "count earlier prefixes equal to run − k", O(n) with a hash map and safe with negatives. Difference arrays make each range update O(1); one prefix pass recovers the final values. 2-D prefix sums answer any rectangle sum in O(1) with inclusion–exclusion. For interleaved updates and queries, move to a Fenwick or segment tree. Key takeaways A zero row and column simplify rectangle boundaries. Remove the upper and left strips, then restore their doubly removed corner. Static grid queries take constant arithmetic work after a table build. t: Fix endpoint semantics before merging ranges
sum: Closed intervals include both endpoints; positive-duration start-inclusive, end-exclusive meetings exclude the end.
x: Interval problems describe things that occupy a range: meetings, bookings, reservations, IP ranges, genome regions, time-series gaps. Each interval is a pair [start, end]. Throughout this lesson, n is the number of intervals. The questions are variations on "which ones overlap?", "how many at once?" and "how do I combine them?" Many interval algorithms begin with sorting. For merging, tracking the current merged block makes a linear scan sufficient. Individual intervals can overlap non-neighbours even after sorting (a long interval may contain many others). Other tasks need heaps, trees or even quadratic output when listing every overlapping pair. Overlap, precisely For valid closed intervals [a, b] and [c, d] (each start no later than its end), the overlap test is: That is, each starts before (or when) the other ends. The predicate uses two endpoint comparisons, whatever the interval lengths, and works for any ordered values: integers, times or real numbers. It's easier to remember the negation: they do not overlap if either interval ends strictly before the other starts. Closed or start-inclusive, end-exclusive? Do [1, 3] and [3, 5] overlap? Under the closed interval convention (both ends included), yes: they share the point 3. For meetings, usually no: a meeting ending at 3:00 frees the room for one starting at 3:00. That's a start-inclusive, end-exclusive interval [start, end), and for nonempty intervals the test becomes strict (see the formula below). The meeting and scheduling code below assumes positive duration and finite, consistently ordered numeric endpoints. Empty intervals require separate handling. Endpoint semantics affect overlap tests and event ties; merging adjacent half-open intervals is a separate policy, since their union can be consecutive even though they do not overlap. For half-open intervals the touching case no longer counts: Merging overlapping intervals Problem. Merge all overlapping intervals. [[1,3], [2,6], [8,10], [15,18]] becomes [[1,6], [8,10], [15,18]]. Sort by start. Walk through, keeping the last merged interval. If the next one starts no later than the last one ends, extend; otherwise start a new one. Why max when extending? For [[1, 10], [2, 3]], the second interval is entirely inside the first. Setting the end to 3 instead of max(10, 3) would shrink the merged interval: a classic bug. Why does sorting by start make one pass enough? After sorting, any interval that overlaps the current merged block must start before the block ends, and all such intervals come next in the order. Once you see a start beyond the block's end, no later interval (they all start even later) can touch it. Key takeaways Closed intervals include both endpoints; positive-duration start-inclusive, end-exclusive meetings exclude the end. Sorting by start permits a scan of the current merged block. Use the larger end when absorbing a contained interval. t: Insert a range in three ordered phases
sum: Copy intervals before the new range, absorb overlaps, then copy the remainder.
x: Here n is the number of valid closed intervals. The input is already sorted by start and internally non-overlapping, so one scan suffices. Inserting into a sorted list Problem. Given non-overlapping intervals sorted by start, insert a new one, merging as needed. A generic comparison sort gives an O(n log n) upper bound after appending. Python’s adaptive list sort can exploit the existing run and added interval to take O(n), but this explicit three-phase scan establishes O(n) without depending on sorting adaptivity: Inserting [4, 8] into [[1,2], [3,5], [6,7], [8,10], [12,16]]: The returned outer list is new, but unmerged intervals are shared with ivs; copy those pairs too if the caller needs independent mutable intervals. Output and slicing use O(n) space. Key takeaways Copy intervals before the new range, absorb overlaps, then copy the remainder. The linear scan relies on sorted, internally non-overlapping input. Unmerged interval pairs are shared unless explicitly copied. t: Count rooms with end times or events
sum: A room-count heap retains one last end time per allocated room.
x: Here n is the number of positive-duration, start-inclusive, end-exclusive meetings with finite consistently ordered endpoints. A room is reusable at exactly its previous end time. Meeting rooms I: any conflict? "Can one person attend all these meetings?" Sort by start; if any meeting starts before the previous one ends, there's a clash. O(n log n). Meeting rooms II: how many rooms? Problem. Given meetings [start, end), find the minimum number of rooms so that no two overlapping meetings share a room. For [[0,30], [5,10], [15,20]] the answer is 2. The answer equals the maximum number of meetings in progress at any instant. Two standard ways to find it. With a min-heap of end times Process meetings by start time. The heap holds the last scheduled end time of every room allocated so far, including rooms already free. Its minimum identifies a room whose availability time is earliest. O(n log n) time, O(n) space. The heap's size never shrinks, so at the end it equals the peak number of simultaneous meetings. To produce an allocation, extend the heap entries to (end_time, room_id) and record each assignment; this end-times-only version returns just the count. With a sweep line Turn each meeting into two events: +1 at its start and −1 at its end. Sort the events by time, sweep left to right, and track the running count. The peak is the answer. The tie-break is where the start-inclusive, end-exclusive semantics live. Sorting (time, delta) tuples puts (10, -1) before (10, 1), so a meeting ending at 10 frees its room before one starting at 10 claims it. For closed intervals you'd want starts first. The sweep line is a difference array (the prefix-sum units) over time, done with sorting instead of an array, so it works for huge or real-valued times. Geometric segment-intersection algorithms also sweep events, but they need additional ordering and intersection logic beyond this concurrency counter. A bounded integer timeline If every start and end is an integer minute in a known day, allocate one difference slot for each boundary. Add one at a start and subtract one at an end, then sweep the slots with a running sum. Aggregating all changes at the same boundary respects start-inclusive, end-exclusive semantics. The maximum running count is the room requirement. This takes O(n + T) work and O(T) slots, where T is the largest permitted integer boundary and n is the number of meetings. A 1,440-minute day needs 1,441 boundary slots when the final end is included in the sweep. Arbitrary real-valued times instead use sorted events or another ordered representation. Key takeaways A room-count heap retains one last end time per allocated room. Half-open event ties process ends before starts. A bounded integer timeline allows a difference-array scan without sorting. sum: Choose the compatible activity that finishes earliest.
x: Here n is the number of positive-duration half-open intervals. Touching endpoints are allowed; minimise removals by maximising the number retained. Non-overlapping intervals: the greedy choice Problem. Remove the fewest intervals so the rest don't overlap. Equivalently, keep as many as possible: the unweighted activity selection problem. Weighted scheduling generally requires a different method, such as dynamic programming. Sort by end time and greedily keep each interval that starts after the last kept one ends. Finishing earliest leaves the most room for everything else; an exchange argument shows no other choice can do better. Sorting by start instead fails: [[1, 100], [2, 3], [4, 5]] would keep [1, 100] first and block the other two. Why replacing the first choice is safe Take an optimal compatible schedule and compare its first interval with the earliest-finishing interval. Replacing that first choice with the earliest-finishing one leaves no later finish time, so every later selected interval remains compatible. The replacement keeps the same number of intervals. Apply the argument again to the intervals that can start after that finish. This is a statement about unweighted counts and positive-duration half-open intervals. An early-finishing interval with a small reward need not belong to an optimal weighted interval schedule, whose objective is total reward rather than interval count. The algorithm sorts in O(n log n) time and scans in O(n), where n is the interval count. The scan uses constant extra state; Python’s in-place sort may still allocate linear temporary storage. Key takeaways Choose the compatible activity that finishes earliest. An exchange argument supports the greedy choice for unweighted activity counts. Weights change the objective and generally require a different method. sum: An intersection begins at the later start and ends at the earlier end.
x: Each input list contains valid closed intervals, sorted by start and internally non-overlapping. Here m and n are the two list lengths. Intersecting two sorted lists For two sorted lists of internally non-overlapping closed intervals, keep one current interval from each list. Their shared range begins at the later start and ends at the earlier end. Keep it when its start is no later than its end: a single-point overlap is valid for closed intervals. Advance whichever interval ends first. That interval cannot meet any later interval in the other list: later intervals start beyond the current one's end. If the two end times tie, advancing either is safe; advancing both is also safe under the strict internal non-overlap contract for closed intervals. For A = [[0, 2], [5, 10]] and B = [[1, 5], [8, 12]], the intersections are [[1, 2], [5, 5], [8, 10]]. First advance A past its end at 2, then B past its end at 5, then A past its end at 10. The pointer scan costs O(m + n) time, where m and n are the two list lengths, plus space for the returned intersections. This is an intersection, not a union: gaps in either input remain gaps in the result. With positive-duration half-open intervals, discard an equal-endpoint candidate because it contains no point. Recognising the pattern Cue Approach ------ Merge / union of ranges Sort by start, extend Insert in a sorted list Three-phase O(n) Any overlap at all? Sort, compare neighbours Max simultaneous / rooms Heap of ends or sweep Keep most / remove fewest Sort by end, greedy Intersect two sorted lists Two pointers Pitfalls Unsorted input. Most algorithms assume sorted by start; sort first unless the problem guarantees it. Inclusive vs exclusive ends. Decide early, then use < or <= consistently, including in sweep-line tie-breaks. Forgetting max on merge when one interval contains another. Mutating the caller's list. intervals.sort() sorts in place; use sorted() if the caller needs the original. Sorting by the wrong key in greedy selection: by end, not start or length. Recap of the pattern family Sort first: after sorting by start, overlaps involve only the current merged block, so one pass suffices. Merging extends the last block's end with max; insertion into a sorted list is O(n) in three phases. Minimum rooms equals peak concurrency: a min-heap of end times or a sweep over +1/−1 events. Keep the most non-overlapping intervals by sorting on end time and choosing greedily. Pin down closed vs half-open intervals; it decides every comparison and tie-break. Key takeaways An intersection begins at the later start and ends at the earlier end. Advance the interval ending first because it cannot intersect later intervals in the other list. Closed intervals can intersect at a single point; do not drop that endpoint. t: Answer waiting indices with the next greater value
sum: Keep indices of unanswered positions with non-increasing values.
x: A monotonic stack is an ordinary stack with one rule: its contents stay sorted (all increasing or all decreasing from bottom to top). Before pushing a new element, you pop everything that would break the order. The magic is in the pops. In the left-to-right next-element scan, a pop can identify the first later value satisfying the chosen strict or non-strict comparison. Other scan directions and previous-element variants use different invariants. Questions of the form "for each element, find the nearest element to the left/right that is greater/smaller" all fall to this. Each element is pushed once and popped no more than once, so the whole scan of n elements is O(n), even though there's a while inside the for. Next greater element Problem. For each element, find the first element to its right that is strictly greater, or −1 if none. Brute force scans right from every element: O(n²). Instead, keep a stack of indices that are still waiting for their next greater element. Their values are non-increasing from bottom to top (if a smaller one sat under a bigger one, the bigger one would already have answered it). Trace for a = [2, 1, 2, 4, 3]: (The stack holds indices; values are shown for readability.) Note a[2] = 2 doesn't pop a[0] = 2: the problem says strictly greater, so the comparison is <. Using <= would answer "next greater or equal". Getting this right matters a lot with duplicates. Key takeaways Keep indices of unanswered positions with non-increasing values. A strictly larger arrival answers all smaller waiting values on top. Use a deliberate strict or non-strict comparison for duplicates. t: Adapt nearest-element answers to distance and wraparound
sum: Daily temperatures records an index gap rather than the warmer value.
x: Use the preceding next-greater stack as the prerequisite. Here n is the input length; comparisons and indexing are treated as constant-cost. Nearest-element variants Want Scan Pop while top is --------- Next greater (right) L→R < x Next smaller (right) L→R > x Previous greater L→R <= x, then top Previous smaller L→R >= x, then top For "previous" variants, the answer for x is whatever is left on top of the stack after popping (or none if empty). Circular arrays (the element after the last is the first): loop i over range(2 n) and use a[i % n], only pushing during the first pass. Here % is Python's remainder operator, so i % n wraps index n back to 0, n + 1 to 1, and so on. Daily temperatures ("how many days until a warmer day?") is the same algorithm storing i - j instead of the value, where j is the index being popped (the colder day) and i the index of the warmer day that pops it. Stock span uses the previous greater element. Translate the answer, retain the waiting invariant For temperatures [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73], days at indices 3 and 4 remain waiting when 72 arrives at index 5. It answers both: the waits are two days and one day respectively. The later 76 answers the earlier 75 at index 2 with a four-day wait. Initialise unanswered waits to zero rather than the next-value example’s minus-one marker. For circular next greater on [5, 4, 3, 2, 1], the first pass leaves every index waiting. On the second pass, 5 answers the four smaller values. The original 5 stays unanswered because equality is not strictly greater. Push only first-pass positions so the second pass supplies answers without duplicating work. For stock span, count today and all immediately preceding no-higher prices. After discarding no-greater stack candidates, subtract the previous strictly greater price’s index from today’s index; use minus one for that earlier index if no such price exists. This includes today in the returned span. Key takeaways Daily temperatures records an index gap rather than the warmer value. A second circular pass supplies wraparound answers without pushing indices twice. Previous-element variants answer from the remaining stack top after discarding unsuitable values. t: Measure histogram rectangles at pop time
sum: Rectangle widths come from limiting bars on both sides.
x: Here n is the number of nonnegative integer bar heights, each bar has width one, and empty input returns zero. Numeric operations are treated as constant-cost. Largest rectangle in a histogram Problem. Bars of width 1 have heights h. Find the area of the largest rectangle that fits under the histogram. For h = [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] the answer is 10: height 5 across the bars of height 5 and 6. Insight. The best rectangle uses some bar i as its shortest bar, and then extends as far as possible on both sides: until the previous smaller bar on the left and the next smaller bar on the right. So for each bar: The answer is the largest A_i over all bars. Every rectangle under the histogram has some shortest bar, so checking each bar as "the shortest" covers every candidate. The code below uses strictly increasing stack heights and pops on >=. Its left boundary is the previous strictly smaller bar; its right boundary is the first smaller-or-equal bar (or the end histogram flush sentinel). An equal bar therefore takes ownership of a span from an earlier equal bar. This asymmetric tie rule still measures a maximum-area representative for every possible height. The histogram flush sentinel height 0 at i = n flushes every remaining bar off the stack so they all get measured. Trace the key moment, at i = 4 (height 2), with stack holding indices [1, 2, 3] (heights 1, 5, 6): O(n) time, O(n) space. It's also the core of maximal rectangle in a binary matrix: treat each row as the base of a histogram of consecutive 1s above, and run this per row for O(R × C), where R is the number of rows and C the number of columns. >= versus > here With equal heights, popping on >= means an earlier equal bar is measured with a too-short right boundary. That's fine: the last equal bar in the run gets the full width, so the maximum is still correct. Key takeaways Rectangle widths come from limiting bars on both sides. The implementation uses previous strictly smaller and next smaller-or-equal tie ownership. A zero histogram flush sentinel flushes remaining bars, and row histograms extend the method to a binary matrix. Further reading All nearest smaller values — Wikipedia Minimum stack / minimum queue — cp-algorithms Sliding window — USACO Guide Amortized analysis — Wikipedia

t: Discard dominated values and expire old indices
sum: Keep decreasing candidate values so the front answers the current maximum.
x: Here n is the array length and k is an integer window length from one to n. A deque supports removals at both ends. Monotonic deque: sliding window maximum Problem. Return the maximum of every window of size k. A heap with only lazy deletion of expired roots can retain O(n) entries and take O(n log n). A bounded indexed heap or periodic rebuilding can instead give O(n log(k + 1)). A monotonic deque gives O(n). Keep indices in a deque whose values are decreasing from front to back. The front is always the current window's maximum. Push at the back: before adding i, pop smaller-or-equal values from the back. They need not represent any future maximum: a[i] is at least as large and expires later. Equal maxima are interchangeable when returning only values. Expire at the front: if the front index has slid out of the window, pop it. Result [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7], one value per full window: Each index enters and leaves the deque once: O(n) time, O(k) auxiliary space, plus O(n − k + 1) output space. The same structure powers DP optimisations where dp[i] depends on the max or min of dp over a sliding range (for example "jump game VI"). A related dominance argument solves "shortest subarray with sum at least k" with negative values, using a deque of increasing prefix sums; that is not simply the same fixed-range DP recurrence. Key takeaways Keep decreasing candidate values so the front answers the current maximum. A newer no-smaller value dominates an older value for future windows. Expire candidates by position and count the separate returned-output storage. t: Prove linear total stack and deque work
sum: Count total pushes and pops across the scan rather than multiplying loop bounds.
x: Here n is the input length. The preceding examples remove each stored candidate at most once; all stated linear bounds use constant-cost comparisons and amortised container operations. Why it's O(n): the amortised argument Count operations per element rather than per loop iteration: each index is pushed exactly once: n pushes; each index is popped no more than once: at most n pops. So the combined pushes and pops number at most twice the input length; loop tests, comparisons and output writes add O(n) more work. A single step may pop many elements, but then those elements are gone and can't be popped again. Recognising the pattern Cue Structure ------ "next/previous greater/smaller" Monotonic stack "days until warmer", "span" Monotonic stack Area bounded by shortest bar Increasing stack Max/min of each window Monotonic deque DP over a sliding max/min Monotonic deque Remove k digits for smallest Increasing stack (greedy) Pitfalls Storing values instead of indices. You usually need the index for widths, distances or window expiry. Store indices; look values up. Strict vs non-strict comparisons. Decide what duplicates should do and pick < or <= deliberately. Forgetting leftovers. Elements still on the stack at the end have no next greater; use a suitable flushing value or a final pass. Expiry check in the deque. Compare the front index with i - k, not the value with anything. Recap of the pattern family A monotonic stack keeps elements sorted; each pop reveals a "next greater/smaller" relationship. Every element is pushed and popped no more than once, so the scan is O(n) amortised. Largest rectangle uses smaller-height boundaries; the code assigns equal heights asymmetrically (previous strictly smaller, next smaller-or-equal) to cover their full span. A monotonic deque gives the max or min of every sliding window in O(n), while a heap with unbounded lazy deletion can take O(n log n). Store indices, choose strict or non-strict comparisons deliberately, and flush leftovers. Greedy digit removal uses a deletion budget To make a nonnegative decimal number as small as possible after removing a fixed number of digits, scan its digits left to right. While deletions remain and the kept last digit is larger than the incoming digit, delete that last digit. At the first differing position, keeping the smaller incoming digit wins lexicographically for equal-length digit strings. If deletions remain after the scan, remove that many trailing digits. Strip leading zeros for the returned numeric representation and return zero if nothing remains. The deletion budget matters: after it is exhausted, the retained digits need not stay monotonic. Each digit is still appended once and removed at most once, so the scan is linear in the number of input digits. This greedy use shares the stack’s total-operation proof, not every invariant of next-greater search. Key takeaways Count total pushes and pops across the scan rather than multiplying loop bounds. Permanent dominance supports nearest-element, sliding-extremum and greedy digit patterns. Indices retain position information needed for output, widths and expiry. t: Use heap roots and safe priority tuples
sum: A min-heap exposes its minimum at the root without sorting every element.
x: A binary heap gives you the minimum (or maximum) of a changing collection in O(1), and inserts or removes the root in O(log(n + 1)) heap comparisons, where n is the number of items in the heap. The log is there because a heap is a balanced tree a number of levels logarithmic in its size, and an insert or removal walks one path from top to bottom; the + 1 just keeps the bound meaningful when n is 0 or 1. Removing an arbitrary item needs a way to locate it. Python list resizing makes individual operations occasionally linear; the standard bound is amortised and assumes constant-cost comparisons. Many problems that look like "sort everything" only need the best few items, or the current best, and a heap can avoid sorting the entire collection. The following units develop three patterns built on that one idea. Python's heapq in 60 seconds heapq turns a plain list into a min-heap: h[0] is always the smallest. In the table, n is the number of items in the heap (or in the input iterable it), and k is how many items you ask for. Call Cost ------ heappush(h, x) O(log(n + 1)) heappop(h) O(log(n + 1)) h[0] (peek) O(1) heapreplace(h, x) O(log(n + 1)): pop, then push heapify(h) O(n) nlargest(k, it) O(n log(k + 1)), k from 1 to n Python 3.14 provides public max-heap functions such as heapify_max and heappush_max. The examples use the older-compatible negation technique for ordered numeric values: push -x, and -h[0] is the maximum. NaN values are excluded because they do not provide the required ordering. Tuples compare element by element, so (priority, item) works. If priorities can tie and the items aren't comparable (say, linked-list nodes), add a tie-breaking counter: (priority, i, item). Key takeaways A min-heap exposes its minimum at the root without sorting every element. Heapify builds bottom-up in linear time. A unique tie-breaker avoids comparing non-comparable records. t: Retain the strongest values in a size-budget heap
sum: For the largest values, the minimum root is the weakest retained member.
x: Here n is the number of scored numeric inputs and k is the requested number to keep. Comparisons have constant cost; values must provide consistent ordering. Pattern 1: top-K Problem. Find the k largest elements of n (or the k-th largest). Options: Approach Time Extra space --------- Sort, take last k O(n log n) Python sort: O(n) auxiliary, plus output Min-heap of size k O(n log(k + 1)) O(k) Max-heapify all, pop k O(n + k log(n + 1)) O(n) storage; O(1) heapify auxiliary Randomised quickselect O(n) expected O(1) auxiliary with iterative in-place partition To see why the size-k heap pays off when k is much smaller than n, compare the dominant terms: These are rough counts that ignore constant factors; the memory saving (k items instead of n) is often the bigger win. The size-k heap is a standard option. The counter-intuitive part: to keep the k largest, use a min-heap. Its root is the smallest of your current top k, the "weakest member", which is exactly what a newcomer must beat. Quickselect Quickselect partitions like quicksort but recurses into only the side containing the k-th position: expected O(n) with independent random pivots, O(n²) worst case for ordinary quickselect. It is a useful option for a one-off order statistic, but universal speed claims require benchmarks. The usual in-place implementation needs the array resident and reorders it. Key takeaways For the largest values, the minimum root is the weakest retained member. The result is heap-ordered rather than sorted and may have fewer values than the requested budget. Quickselect suits a one-off resident order statistic; a small heap supports streams. t: Count frequencies before selecting the leaders
sum: A heap of scored items does not by itself count query frequencies.
x: Here n is the number of inputs, u is the number of distinct keys and k is a selection budget between one and u. Hashing is expected constant-cost; ties need a consistent policy. Frequency selection The size-k heap works on a stream of already scored items: keeping the 100 largest numeric observations needs O(100) stored items. Exact top-100 query frequencies are different: frequencies must first be counted, which can require memory proportional to the number of distinct queries or external/distributed storage. Top-K frequent elements: count with a Counter (expected O(n), O(u) entries for u distinct values), then take the top k by count with heapq.nlargest(k, counts, key=counts.get). Since counts are bounded by n, a bucket sort (a list of buckets indexed by frequency) gets O(n) total. Exact leaders when counts exceed memory A frequency table needs space for every distinct key, even if only a hundred leaders will be returned. Partition queries by a deterministic hash of the key across machines or files. Every occurrence of a key must reach the same partition. Count each partition exactly, select its local leaders with a size-budget min-heap, then select the global leaders from the union of local results. The same total ranking must apply locally and globally: order first by frequency, then by a consistent key tie-breaker when the identity of tied results matters. A globally top-100 key cannot have a hundred better-ranked keys inside its own partition; if it did, it would not be globally top-100. Therefore the union of local top-100 results contains every global top-100 key. Hash partitioning does not guarantee balanced distinct-key counts. Check partition sizes and repartition oversized groups or use external aggregation. A popular key can create large traffic while using only one counter; distinct-key count is a separate memory consideration. External sorting and counting groups is another exact approach that avoids loading all keys at once. A Count-Min Sketch estimates frequencies but does not enumerate candidate keys by itself. A complete approximate heavy-hitter design needs candidate recovery plus error and probability parameters. This unit makes no turnkey accuracy claim for a sketch-plus-heap recipe. Key takeaways A heap of scored items does not by itself count query frequencies. Exact frequency counting retains one count per distinct key or uses external storage. Heap, sorting and frequency-bucket selection offer different time and space trade-offs. t: Merge sorted streams through their current heads
sum: Keep one current head per nonempty input list.
x: Here k is the number of sorted input lists, N_nonempty the number of nonempty lists and N their total element count. Numeric comparisons and list indexing have constant cost. Pattern 2: k-way merge Problem. Merge k sorted lists (total N elements) into one sorted list. At every step, the next output element is the smallest among the k list heads. A heap of those heads finds it in O(log(k + 1)), not O(k). Let N_nonempty be the number of nonempty lists. Inspecting all k inputs and heapifying their heads costs O(k); each of the N outputs then costs one pop and at most one push on a heap of at most N_nonempty heads: So total time is O(k + N log(N_nonempty + 1)), with O(N_nonempty) heap space plus O(N) returned output. Concatenating and a generic comparison sort has an O(N log N) bound, but adaptive sorting can exploit the k existing runs. Sequentially merging into a growing result has O(Nk) worst-case movement. The list index i in the tuple breaks ties and tells us which list to advance. Python ships this as heapq.merge(lists), which is lazy. Where this runs in production External sorting (sorting files bigger than RAM) sorts chunks that fit in memory, writes them as sorted "runs", then k-way merges the runs. LSM-tree databases such as RocksDB and Cassandra do the same during compaction, merging sorted SSTable streams, often writing multiple output SSTables and applying version/tombstone rules. Related problems: "k-th smallest element in a sorted matrix" (rows are sorted lists; pop k times), "smallest range covering one element from each of k lists" (track the max of the heads alongside the heap's min). Key takeaways Keep one current head per nonempty input list. A list identifier breaks equal-priority ties and selects which input to advance. Account for inspecting empty inputs and storing the returned result. t: Balance two halves around the running median
sum: The lower-half maximum and upper-half minimum straddle the median.
x: Here n is the number of finite numeric observations seen so far. Values must be consistently ordered, so NaN is excluded; heap operations use amortised constant-cost comparisons. Pattern 3: two heaps for a running median Problem. Numbers arrive one at a time. After each, report the median. Re-sorting each time is O(n log n) per query. Instead, split the numbers into two halves: lo: a max-heap of the smaller half (its top is the largest small number); hi: a min-heap of the larger half (its top is the smallest large number). Keep every element of lo no larger than every element of hi, and keep the sizes balanced: len(lo) equals len(hi) or exceeds it by one. Then the median sits at the tops: Pushing through lo and then moving its top to hi guarantees the ordering invariant without any comparisons of our own; the rebalance step fixes the sizes. Each add takes O(log(n + 1)) amortised heap work; median reads O(1) heap entries, and the two heaps together store O(n) values. The numeric example returns a floating-point mean for even sizes: very large integers can lose precision or overflow conversion, and finite floats can overflow their sum. For exact integer medians, replace (a + b) / 2 with Fraction(a + b, 2) from fractions, accounting for integer bit costs. The two-heaps shape also solves IPO / maximise capital (a min-heap of projects by cost, a max-heap of affordable profits) and, with deletion support, sliding window median. Naive lazy heaps may accumulate stale entries; O(k) storage and O(n log(k + 1)) total time require bounded heaps, rebuilding or indexed deletion. Recognising the pattern Cue Pattern ------ "k largest/smallest/closest" Size-k heap "k-th largest in a stream" Size-k min-heap "top k frequent" Counter + heap/buckets "merge k sorted" Heap of heads "k-th smallest in sorted matrix" K-way merge "median of a stream" Two heaps Repeatedly take the best option Heap (greedy) Pitfalls Wrong heap direction. k largest → min-heap of size k; k smallest → max-heap of size k. Comparing uncomparable items. (5, node_a) vs (5, node_b) raises TypeError when the priorities tie; add an index. Forgetting to negate back when using -x for a max-heap. Assuming the heap list is sorted. Only h[0] is guaranteed; the rest is in heap order. Integer vs float medians. The even case returns an average, which may need to be a float. Recap of the pattern family A size-k min-heap keeps the k largest of n items in O(n log(k + 1)) time and O(k) space (for k from 1 to n), and works on streams. K-way merge holds one head per list in a heap: O(k + N log(N_nonempty + 1)) for N_nonempty nonempty inputs, a technique behind external sorting and LSM compaction. Two heaps (max-heap of the low half, min-heap of the high half) give a running median with O(log(n + 1)) amortised inserts. Python's heapq is a min-heap; negate for max, and use tie-breakers in tuples. Quickselect finds a one-off k-th element in O(n) average when all data is in memory. Key takeaways The lower-half maximum and upper-half minimum straddle the median. Preserve both ordering and the size difference of at most one. Even medians use a mean; numeric accuracy and empty-stream behavior need explicit handling.
