t: Read shifts and manipulate individual flags
sum: Bitwise operators combine bit patterns rather than treating values as logical conditions.
x: A fixed-width machine word is a row of bits. Many CPUs provide bitwise AND, bitwise OR, XOR and shifts on a native word with one instruction; width, latency and available instructions depend on the architecture. Python integers can span many machine words, so their bitwise operations are not constant-time for arbitrarily large values. Bit manipulation problems exploit that: they treat a number as a tiny set or a packed array of booleans, and use identities that turn loops into one-liners. In interviews the cues are "without extra space", "every element appears twice except one", "at most 20 items" (so item positions can be represented by bits in a mask), "power of two" or "count the 1 bits". In production the same tricks show up in permission flags, Bloom filters, bitmap indexes, chess engines and network masks. The operators The two shift rows are arithmetic in disguise. For a nonnegative integer: The ~ row is two's complement, explained next: Python bitwise operations behave as if integers had infinitely many two’s-complement sign bits: -x == ~x + 1. This specifies the result, not Python’s internal storage representation. In Python, >> on a negative number is arithmetic (it rounds down, towards minus infinity): -5 >> 1 == -3. Single-bit operations For a nonnegative integer bit index i, treat bit i of integer x as a boolean flag: This is how flag sets work in practice: Unix file permissions (0o755 is rwxr-xr-x), Linux open() flags (O_CREAT O_TRUNC), and feature flags packed into one integer column. Key takeaways Bitwise operators combine bit patterns rather than treating values as logical conditions. Python shifts have exact integer semantics and nonnegative shift distances. Test, set, clear or toggle one position with a single-bit mask. Further reading Bit manipulation — cp-algorithms Enumerating submasks — cp-algorithms Bit Twiddling Hacks — Sean Eron Anderson, Stanford Hamming weight — Wikipedia Binary cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Python integer bitwise semantics

t: Clear or isolate the lowest set bit
sum: Clearing the lowest set bit gives one popcount loop visit per set bit.
x: These examples use nonnegative Python integers and nonnegative bit positions. Python integers can span multiple machine words; bit-operation costs grow with bit length. The two workhorse tricks x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit Subtracting 1 flips the lowest 1 to 0 and every 0 below it to 1. ANDing with the original wipes all of those out. Uses: Power of two: a power of two has exactly one set bit, so x > 0 and x & (x - 1) == 0. Counting set bits (Kernighan's method): clear the lowest bit until zero; the loop runs once per set bit, not once per bit position. Python provides x.bit_count() (3.10+), which counts the ones in abs(x); the lesson loop instead rejects negative input. GCC provides width-specific extensions such as __builtin_popcount for unsigned int and __builtin_popcountll for unsigned long long; C++20 also has std::popcount for unsigned types. Whether the compiler emits a hardware popcount instruction depends on the target and compiler settings. x & -x isolates the lowest set bit Since -x == ~x + 1, the bits above the lowest 1 are flipped and the bits from there down match. Bitwise AND keeps only that one bit. That is the step a Fenwick tree uses to advance update indices (i += i & -i, with i > 0); prefix queries subtract it. In C/C++, use unsigned arithmetic for such fixed-width tricks: negating the minimum signed value can overflow. Key takeaways Clearing the lowest set bit gives one popcount loop visit per set bit. A positive power of two has exactly one set bit; zero requires a separate guard. The isolated lowest bit advances a positive Fenwick update index. Further reading Bit manipulation — cp-algorithms Enumerating submasks — cp-algorithms Bit Twiddling Hacks — Sean Eron Anderson, Stanford Hamming weight — Wikipedia Binary cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook GCC bit-operation builtins

t: Cancel pairs and separate two single values
sum: XOR cancels equal pairs regardless of order or grouping.
x: Here n is the sequence length. Multiplicity contracts are part of correctness: do not apply cancellation when counts differ from those promised. XOR: the cancelling operator XOR has three properties that make it look like magic: The four lines are self-inverse, identity, commutative and associative. So XOR-ing a list together cancels every value that appears an even number of times. Single number. Every element appears twice except one. Find it in O(n) time, O(1) space: Missing number. nums contains n distinct values from 0..n with one missing. XOR all indices 0..n with all values; everything present cancels, leaving the missing one: No integer overflow risk, unlike summing. Two single numbers Assume a reusable sequence of integers in which every value appears twice except two distinct singles, x and y. XOR-ing everything gives x ^ y, which is non-zero because x!= y. Any set bit in it is a position where x and y differ, so split the numbers into two groups by that bit; each group contains exactly one of them, and duplicates stay together. For [1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 5], the total XOR is 6, whose lowest set bit has value 2. The group with that bit contains 2, 3 and 2, cancelling to 3; the other single is 5. Key takeaways XOR cancels equal pairs regardless of order or grouping. Missing-number XOR needs the exact distinct-value domain. A differing bit partitions two unique singles while duplicates stay together. Further reading Bit manipulation — cp-algorithms Enumerating submasks — cp-algorithms Bit Twiddling Hacks — Sean Eron Anderson, Stanford Hamming weight — Wikipedia Binary cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook

t: Recover one value when all others occur three times
sum: Count each of the 32 bit positions modulo three.
x: XOR cancels pairs, so tripled values require a different summary. This unit counts each bit position independently under the signed 32-bit input contract. Every element thrice except one For this code, input is a reusable sequence of signed 32-bit integers, with every value occurring three times except one occurring once. XOR does not cancel triples. Instead, count each bit position modulo 3: the bits of the tripled values contribute multiples of 3, so the remainder is the single number's bit. O(32n) time, O(1) space. The last two lines convert the 32-bit pattern back to a negative Python int. Key takeaways Count each of the 32 bit positions modulo three. The reconstruction assumes signed 32-bit input values and a reusable sequence. Convert a set sign bit back from an unsigned pattern to a negative Python value. Further reading Bit manipulation — cp-algorithms Enumerating submasks — cp-algorithms Bit Twiddling Hacks — Sean Eron Anderson, Stanford Hamming weight — Wikipedia Binary cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook

sum: An item-position mask describes one of all possible subsets.
x: Here n is the number of item positions, or the number of cities when explicitly stated. Mask complexity assumes unit-cost word operations; Python arbitrary-precision masks add bit-length costs. Bitmasks as subsets With n items, an integer mask ranging from zero through the largest n-bit pattern represents a subset: bit i set means item i is in. This enumerates all subsets of item positions with no recursion (equal item values can therefore produce equal-looking lists). The returned nested lists take Θ(n·2ⁿ) element references for n of at least 1, and enumeration also takes Θ(n·2ⁿ) tests in the unit-cost mask model. Θ (big-Theta) means the cost grows exactly at that rate, up to constant factors: here n bit tests for each of the 2ⁿ masks. Union is a b, intersection a & b, "is a a subset of b?" is a & b == a. Bitmask DP uses the mask as a DP state. The Held–Karp algorithm for the travelling salesman problem stores dp[mask][last] = shortest path from a fixed start visiting exactly the cities in mask, ending at last (add the edge back to the start to complete a tour): O(2ⁿ · n²) time instead of O(n!), where n is the number of cities: The 4.2 × 10⁸ figure is an upper-work expression, not an exact transition count. Content gap A C++ promise that this runs in time and a universal practical size limit are omitted because no implementation, hardware, deadline or benchmark supports them. Key takeaways An item-position mask describes one of all possible subsets. Materialising all subsets counts both bit tests and returned element references. Held–Karp also stores an endpoint and closes the tour back to its fixed start. Further reading Bit manipulation — cp-algorithms Enumerating submasks — cp-algorithms Bit Twiddling Hacks — Sean Eron Anderson, Stanford Hamming weight — Wikipedia Binary cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook

t: Walk nonzero submasks in descending order
sum: Subtract one then intersect with the original mask to get the next submask.
x: The preceding subset representation is the prerequisite. Here n is the number of mask bits, and the illustrative loop visits nonzero submasks under a unit-cost mask model. Iterate nonzero submasks For nonnegative mask, iterate over every nonzero submask: Over all n-bit masks, there are 3ⁿ (mask, submask) pairs including zero submasks, since each element is in the submask, in the mask only, or in neither. This loop omits one zero submask per mask: That is O(3ⁿ) in the unit-cost mask model. Recognising the pattern Cue Trick ------ "appears twice except one" XOR everything "power of two" x > 0 and (x & (x - 1)) == 0 "count 1 bits" Kernighan / DP Lowest set bit x & -x At most 20 items, choose a subset Enumerate position masks Visit all of at most 20 nodes Bitmask DP Many boolean flags Pack into an int Key takeaways Subtract one then intersect with the original mask to get the next submask. The shown loop excludes zero and requires a nonnegative original mask. Across all masks, excluding empty submasks removes one visit per mask. Further reading Bit manipulation — cp-algorithms Enumerating submasks — cp-algorithms Bit Twiddling Hacks — Sean Eron Anderson, Stanford Hamming weight — Wikipedia Binary cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook

t: Reuse smaller bit counts in a dynamic-programming table
sum: Dropping the lowest bit reaches an already computed table entry.
x: Here n is a nonnegative integer upper bound. The table stores counts for every value through that bound; arithmetic and indexing use a unit-cost word model. Counting bits for 0..n Problem. Return the number of 1 bits in every integer from 0 to n. Calling a bit-at-a-time or set-bit-clearing routine on every integer through n takes O(n log n) word operations overall; a constant-time native-word popcount changes that comparison. The following DP uses O(n) table operations and O(n) entries: i >> 1 is i with its last bit dropped, and we've already computed it. The alternative recurrence bits[i] = bits[i & (i - 1)] + 1 reuses the lowest-bit trick. Key takeaways Dropping the lowest bit reaches an already computed table entry. The last bit adds either zero or one to that smaller count. A hardware popcount and a bit-clearing loop have different cost models. Further reading Bit manipulation — cp-algorithms Enumerating submasks — cp-algorithms Bit Twiddling Hacks — Sean Eron Anderson, Stanford Hamming weight — Wikipedia Binary cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook

t: Account for integer width and operator precedence
sum: Python complement behaves with indefinitely extended sign bits.
x: The preceding bit operators use Python integer semantics. This unit contrasts them with fixed-width Java and C-family expressions; explicit width and sign assumptions are essential. Language traps Python ints are unbounded. ~5 is -6, not 4294967290, and there's no overflow to rely on. To emulate 32-bit unsigned results, mask with & 0xFFFFFFFF. Operator precedence differs. In Python, comparisons bind looser than &, so x & 1 == 0 means (x & 1) == 0. In C, C++ and Java, == binds tighter, so the same text means x & (1 == 0), which yields 0 in C/C++ but is a type error for integer x in Java (int & boolean). Always parenthesise. Shifts and arithmetic. In both Python and C, + and - bind tighter than <<, so 1 << n - 1 is 1 << (n - 1). Fixed-width overflow. In Java, 1 << 31 is negative and 1 << 32 == 1 (the shift count is taken mod 32). 1L << k uses 64-bit long, but its shift distance is still masked modulo 64 and its sign bit is bit 63. Recap of the pattern family x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit (powers of two, popcount); x & -x picks it out (Fenwick trees). XOR cancels pairs: single number and missing number in O(n) time and O(1) space; split by a differing bit for two singles. An n-bit mask is a subset: enumerate all 2ⁿ, use it as a DP state, or walk submasks in O(3ⁿ) total. bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1) counts bits for 0..n in O(n), where n is the largest number. Mind the language: Python ints are unbounded, and & vs == precedence differs between Python and C-family languages. Key takeaways Python complement behaves with indefinitely extended sign bits. Parentheses avoid precedence changes between Python and C-family languages. Java masks shift distances; a long value changes the width but does not remove the masking rule. Further reading Bit manipulation — cp-algorithms Enumerating submasks — cp-algorithms Bit Twiddling Hacks — Sean Eron Anderson, Stanford Hamming weight — Wikipedia Binary cheatsheet — Tech Interview Handbook Python operator precedence

sum: Choose one structure for each required operation.
x: Most "design a data structure" problems share one idea: no single structure gives you every operation cheaply, so you glue two together. Each structure covers the other's weakness, and the hard part is keeping them in sync. Costs in this lesson are written in big-O notation, which says how the number of steps grows as the structure fills up. The card below defines the notation and shows what the gap means for a million items: A hash map offers expected O(1) lookup but does not automatically maintain sorted-key or access-recency order. Python dictionaries do preserve insertion order. A linked list keeps order and can splice in O(1), but finding a node is O(n). An array gives O(1) access by position, but deleting from the middle is O(n). Combine them and you can often get O(1) for everything. The method: List the operations and the cost each must have. For each operation, ask what it needs: lookup by key, an ordering, access by position? Pick a structure for each need, and decide what the hash map's values point at (a node, an index). Write down the invariants that tie them together, and check every operation preserves them. Complexities below assume constant-time key hashing/equality and word-sized values. Hash operations are expected amortised O(1), and dynamic-array append/pop can resize; these are not worst-case per-operation guarantees. Key takeaways Choose one structure for each required operation. Write down the invariant joining the structures before implementing updates. Further reading Cache replacement policies — Wikipedia functools.lru_cache — Python docs LinkedHashMap — Java SE 21 API docs

sum: A key-to-node lookup reaches the matching recency-list node.
x: LRU cache: hash map + doubly linked list An LRU (least recently used) cache holds at most cap items. get(key) returns a value and marks it as recently used; put(key, value) inserts or updates, evicting the least recently used item when full. Both must be O(1). Lookup by key needs a hash map. Ordering by recency, with "move to front" and "remove oldest", needs a list we can splice in O(1). So the map stores key -> node, and the nodes form a doubly linked list ordered from most to least recent. Why doubly linked? To unlink a node you must update its predecessor's next. With only next pointers, finding the predecessor is O(n), where n is the number of nodes in the list, because you must walk from the head. The prev pointer makes removal O(1). Why store the key in the node? When you evict the tail you must also delete it from the map, and the node is all you have. Sentinel nodes The dummy head and tail nodes mean every real node always has a real prev and next. That removes every "is this the first node?" special case, which is where most hand-written linked-list bugs live. The invariant: a key is in the map if and only if its node is in the list, and list order is recency order. Every branch of put maintains it: an update moves an existing node, an insert adds to both, an eviction removes from both. In practice you rarely write this by hand. Python's OrderedDict (with move_to_end and popitem(last=False)) and Java's LinkedHashMap (with accessOrder = true and an overridden removeEldestEntry) are exactly this structure. CPython's positive, bounded functools.lru_cache uses a dict plus a circular doubly linked list; the unbounded mode does not need recency eviction. Key takeaways A key-to-node lookup reaches the matching recency-list node. Unlink and relink on hits; eviction removes a node from both structures. Further reading Cache replacement policies — Wikipedia functools.lru_cache — Python docs LinkedHashMap — Java SE 21 API docs CPython 3.14 cache implementation

sum: Move an accessed key exactly one frequency bucket upwards.
x: LFU cache: hash map + buckets of lists An LFU (least frequently used) cache evicts the key with the fewest accesses, breaking ties by evicting the least recently used of those. Again, get and put should be O(1). The obvious design is a min-heap of keys ordered by count, so the least-used key sits at the top. The catch is that every get raises a count, and the heap must then sift that key to its new place: At most nineteen swaps is not much, but it is not O(1), and some hits require no swaps at all. The O(1) trick is to notice that a frequency only ever goes up by one. So instead of sorting, keep a bucket for each frequency: val: key to value. freq: key to its access count. by_f: count to an ordered set of keys with that count, oldest first. min_f: the smallest count currently present. When a key is touched, its count goes up by exactly one, so it moves to the next bucket up. Two update rules keep min_f correct without ever searching: Worked example, using the bucket picture above: touch D, whose count f is 1. D moves to bucket 2, but bucket 1 still holds E, so min_f stays 1. Now touch E: bucket 1 empties and min_f was 1, so min_f becomes 2, and bucket 2 is guaranteed non-empty because E has just landed in it. No smaller bucket can be non-empty, because min_f was the smallest. The rules rely on counts only rising by one at a time; a design that could decrement or reset counts would need a real search. Evict before you insert In put, evict first and only then add the new key. If you insert first, min_f becomes 1 and the new key may be the only member of bucket 1. Evicting "the oldest key in the minimum bucket" then throws away the key you just added, while a stale key with count 2 survives. Production caches seldom use exact LFU. Counts never decay in this design, so a formerly popular key can linger long after its usefulness ends. Redis uses an approximate, decaying 8-bit counter instead, and Caffeine uses a frequency sketch. Key takeaways Move an accessed key exactly one frequency bucket upwards. An emptied minimum bucket advances by one because the touched key just entered that next bucket. Further reading Cache replacement policies — Wikipedia functools.lru_cache — Python docs LinkedHashMap — Java SE 21 API docs Constant-time LFU design paper

sum: Swap the last array item into a deleted slot and repair its map index.
x: Insert, delete and getRandom in O(1) Design a set supporting insert(x), remove(x) and get_random() (each element equally likely), all in O(1) average. A hash set gives O(1) insert and remove, but no way to pick a uniform random element without walking it. An array gives O(1) uniform random choice (items[randrange(n)]), but removing from the middle is O(n), where n is the number of elements, because every later element shifts left. Combine them: an array of values plus a map from value to index. The clever step is deletion. Instead of shifting everything left, move the last element into the hole and pop the end, which is O(1). The order of the last two map operations matters. If x is itself the last element, last == x: we set pos[x] = i and then delete pos[x], which is correct. Do it the other way round (delete, then set pos[last]) and you resurrect a map entry for a value that is no longer in the array. get_random() requires a non-empty set; Python raises IndexError on an empty one. The array does not preserve insertion order after a removal. That is fine here because a set has no order, but it is the price of O(1) deletion. With duplicates (a multiset), map each value to a set of indices. Removal picks any index of x, moves the last element there, and updates the last element's index set. get_random still picks one array slot uniformly, so a value that fills more slots comes up more often: For items = [1, 1, 2], the value 1 has 2 copies out of 3 slots, so it is returned about two times in three and 2 about one time in three. Returning each value with probability proportional to its count is usually what is wanted from a multiset; if you need each distinct value equally often, you need a separate array of distinct values to sample from. Key takeaways Swap the last array item into a deleted slot and repair its map index. Sampling array slots weights duplicate values by their number of copies. Further reading Cache replacement policies — Wikipedia functools.lru_cache — Python docs LinkedHashMap — Java SE 21 API docs

sum: Match lookup, ordering and sampling needs to complementary structures.
x: Recognising the pattern Need Structure ------ Find by key Hash map Recency or insertion order Doubly linked list Uniform random / by index Dynamic array Min or max, changing Heap Sorted order, ranges Balanced BST Other classics built the same way: Min stack: a stack of (value, min so far) pairs gives O(1) get_min. Time-based key-value store: map from key to a list of (timestamp, value) appended in time order, then binary search, for O(log n) "value at time t", where n is the number of timestamps stored for that key and t is the time asked about. All O(1) data structure (increment, decrement, get max key, get min key): the LFU bucket idea, with a doubly linked list of count buckets. Pitfalls Forgetting one side. Every bug in these designs is the two structures drifting apart: a key left in the map after its node was evicted, or an index pointing at a moved element. Average, not worst case. The O(1) relies on hash map operations being O(1) on average. Adversarial keys can degrade them. Capacity edge cases. Capacity 0, updating an existing key when full (no eviction should happen), and removing the last element are where interview solutions break. Concurrency. A cache-hit get on this LRU implementation writes recency pointers. Concurrent access needs a correct synchronisation strategy, commonly a lock around operations; a miss does not move a node. This is one reason high-throughput caches approximate LRU instead. Key takeaways Match lookup, ordering and sampling needs to complementary structures. Capacity limits and concurrent recency writes must preserve every structure together. Further reading Cache replacement policies — Wikipedia functools.lru_cache — Python docs LinkedHashMap — Java SE 21 API docs

t: Representing disjoint sets with parent forests
sum: A root represents its entire connected component.
x: Union-Find (also called a disjoint-set union, or DSU) keeps track of elements split into non-overlapping groups. It supports two operations: find(x): which group is x in? It returns a set representative element for the group. union(a, b): merge the groups containing a and b. Two elements are in the same group exactly when find(a) == find(b). That one comparison answers "are these connected?" for road networks, friend circles, pixels in an image or accounts that share an email address. It is tiny to implement, and with two simple tricks each operation costs so little that for any input you could ever store it is effectively constant. The idea: a forest of parent pointers Each group is a tree. Every element points to a parent; the root points to itself and is the group's representative. All you store is one array, parent. find(x) follows parent pointers up to the root. union(a, b) finds both roots and makes one the parent of the other. The naive version has a problem. Union in an unlucky order (union(1, 0), union(2, 1), union(3, 2) and so on, always hanging the old tree under the new element) builds a chain, and find on the bottom element walks every link in it: one fewer link than there are elements. If n is the number of elements, a sequence of operations can cost O(n) each in the worst case (O(n) means "grows in proportion to n"). Key takeaways A root represents its entire connected component. Compare roots rather than immediate parents. Further reading Disjoint-set data structure — Wikipedia Disjoint Set Union — cp-algorithms Kruskal's algorithm — Wikipedia Ackermann function — Wikipedia

t: Balancing Union-Find by size and rank
sum: Attach smaller trees under larger ones to limit depth.
x: Fix 1: union by size or by rank When merging, hang the smaller tree under the larger one. "Smaller" can mean: size: number of elements in the tree, or rank: an upper bound on the tree's height. Every element starts with rank 0. The rank rule for merging two roots fits in two lines: So two rank-2 trees make a rank-3 tree, while a rank-1 tree hung under a rank-3 root leaves the rank at 3. For union by size, an element only gets deeper when its tree is merged under a tree at least as big. Each time that happens, the size of the tree containing it at least doubles. A tree can never hold more than all n elements, which caps how many doublings there can be: With a million elements, no find walks more than 19 parent steps. That makes find O(log n) in the worst case: its cost grows in proportion to the logarithm of n. The bound assumes every union goes through the size rule; a single careless parent[b] = a breaks it. For union by rank, a separate induction (a proof that the claim holds for rank 0 and stays true after every merge) bounds the tree size by its rank. Rank rises only when two equal-rank roots merge, which at least doubles the smaller one: For a thousand elements, the base-two logarithm is about 9.97, so the card’s floor bound limits every rank to nine. Parent ranks strictly increase on every path up the tree, which is why the height can be no larger than the root's rank. Size is often more useful in practice, because you get the group sizes for free ("how big is the largest friend circle?"). Key takeaways Attach smaller trees under larger ones to limit depth. Rank grows only when equal-rank roots merge and remains an upper bound after compression. Further reading Disjoint-set data structure — Wikipedia Disjoint Set Union — cp-algorithms Kruskal's algorithm — Wikipedia Ackermann function — Wikipedia

t: Path compression and the DSU implementation
sum: Find the root, then repoint the visited path at it.
x: Fix 2: path compression find already walks from x to the root. While doing so, repoint every node on the path directly at the root. Without an intervening union, the next find on a non-root node on that path takes one parent step. Variants such as path halving (point each node at its grandparent as you go) achieve the same bounds in a single pass. The full structure Iterative find in Python The textbook recursive find (parent[x] = find(parent[x])) is elegant, but an unbalanced variant can create a chain exceeding the interpreter's recursion limit. Union by size or rank already prevents such linear-depth chains. The two-pass loop above has no such limit. Note that union returns whether a merge actually happened. That boolean is what most applications use. Key takeaways Find the root, then repoint the visited path at it. Union returns false when its two arguments already share a root. Further reading Disjoint-set data structure — Wikipedia Disjoint Set Union — cp-algorithms Kruskal's algorithm — Wikipedia Ackermann function — Wikipedia

sum: Initialisation and later operations have separate costs.
x: How fast is it? In this table n is the number of elements and m counts the complete sequence of finds and unions, including the unions that create any long path. Initialisation is charged separately. O(f) means "grows at most in proportion to f". Version Cost per operation ------ Naive O(n) worst case Union by size or rank O(log n) worst case Path compression only O(log n) amortised Both O(α(n)) amortised α(n) is the inverse Ackermann function. The Ackermann function A grows so absurdly fast that its inverse barely moves. Under one common convention it is defined like this: The last line is the worked example: a billion elements is more than the diagonal’s sixty-one at argument three, but far below its value at argument four, so alpha of a billion is 4. Other textbooks use slightly different conventions and get 3 or 5 instead, but always a tiny constant. In practice, treat each operation as constant time; just say "amortised inverse Ackermann" when asked. This bound, proved by Robert Tarjan in 1975, is also tight: Fredman and Saks showed in 1989 that a matching inverse-Ackermann lower bound holds in the cell-probe model with logarithmic-size words for suitable operation sequences. "Amortised" matters. An individual find can still walk a long path once, but it flattens that path as it goes. Averaged over a whole sequence, the total is bounded: For example, 10 million operations on a million elements give an illustrative scaling factor of about forty million, plus linear initialisation. This is a substitution into an asymptotic model, not a measured or guaranteed count of primitive operations. One unlucky find inside that run may be slow; the bound is only on the total. Rank after compression Path compression changes heights but never updates ranks. That is fine: rank was only ever an upper bound on height, but the inverse-Ackermann proof also uses rank-growth and node-count invariants, not just this upper bound. Key takeaways Initialisation and later operations have separate costs. Inverse-Ackermann bounds apply to a sequence, not a fixed operation-step count. Further reading Disjoint-set data structure — Wikipedia Disjoint Set Union — cp-algorithms Kruskal's algorithm — Wikipedia Ackermann function — Wikipedia Tarjan’s original Union-Find analysis

sum: Kruskal accepts exactly the edges that join different components.
x: Application 1: Kruskal's minimum spanning tree Kruskal's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree by taking edges cheapest first and keeping an edge only if it joins two different components. "Different components?" is exactly find(u)!= find(v), and keeping the edge is union(u, v). Here V is the number of vertices and E the number of edges. The three phases add up: A connected graph needs at least one edge fewer than it has vertices (the third line), so the sort outgrows both other terms. The last two lines are a worked example with 1,000 vertices and 10,000 edges: illustrative scaling terms near 133,000 for sorting and 40,000 for DSU processing. These are substitutions into growth models, not predicted comparison or pointer-step counts; each union includes two finds and the constants differ. Disconnected graphs may instead be dominated by initialisation; the code returns a minimum spanning forest. You can stop early once used has one fewer edge than the graph has vertices. Application 2: connectivity and cycle detection Number of connected components: start with count = n and decrement on every successful union. Edges can arrive one at a time ("number of islands II", or a network where links come up over time), and you can answer after each one. Cycle detection in an undirected graph: adding edge (u, v) when find(u) == find(v) closes a cycle. union returning False is the signal. This is the "redundant connection" problem. Percolation: a grid percolates when a virtual top node and a virtual bottom node end up in the same set, a classic Monte Carlo experiment. Compared with BFS or DFS, union-find shines when edges arrive incrementally. A straightforward BFS test of graph reachability may traverse the current graph for each request; union-find just absorbs each new edge. Key takeaways Kruskal accepts exactly the edges that join different components. A failed union detects a cycle in an undirected incremental graph. Further reading Disjoint-set data structure — Wikipedia Disjoint Set Union — cp-algorithms Kruskal's algorithm — Wikipedia Ackermann function — Wikipedia

sum: Shared identifiers create a transitive closure of account groups.
x: Application 3: accounts merge Each account is a name plus a list of emails. In this exercise, sharing an email is a trusted signal to merge accounts, and we take its transitive closure: A shares with B and B shares with C, so all three join one component. Directly sharing an email is not itself transitive. Assume each account has at least one email and merged accounts have consistent names; real entity resolution needs stronger domain rules. Union the account indices through shared emails: The same shape appears in entity resolution (deduplicating customer records that share a phone number or address), clustering, and compilers: type inference in ML-family languages unifies type variables with a union-find structure. Variants worth knowing Weighted union-find stores, for each node, a value relative to its parent (an offset, a ratio, a bit recording whether a path length is odd or even). find accumulates values along the path. This solves "evaluate division" (given some ratios between variables, work out others, as in the block below) and "is this graph bipartite?" online. Offline deletion: union-find cannot split a set. For a known deletion-only history, first build the final graph, then process removals backwards as additions. Mixed additions and deletions need extra machinery. Hash-map parents: when elements are strings or sparse coordinates, use a dict instead of a list, creating entries on first sight. Pitfalls Comparing parents, not roots. parent[a] == parent[b] is not the same as being connected. Always compare find(a) and find(b). Linking non-roots. parent[b] = a instead of parent[find(b)] = find(a) loses the rest of b's tree. Forgetting it is undirected. Union-find has no notion of direction, so it cannot detect cycles in a directed graph or find strongly connected components. Use DFS-based algorithms for those. Key takeaways Shared identifiers create a transitive closure of account groups. Weighted parents carry relations; known deletion-only histories can be processed backwards. Further reading Disjoint-set data structure — Wikipedia Disjoint Set Union — cp-algorithms Kruskal's algorithm — Wikipedia Ackermann function — Wikipedia

t: Answering ranges from stored tree pieces
sum: Each node summarises one contiguous range.
x: Here n is the non-empty input array’s length. Big-O bounds count constant-time combines of constant-size summaries on word-sized values. Suppose you have an array and two kinds of request arriving in any order: "what is the sum (or minimum, or maximum) of a[l..r]?" and "change a[i]". Throughout this lesson n is the number of elements in the array, and O(f) means "the work grows at most in proportion to f". a[l..r] means the elements from index l to index r, both included. A plain array makes updates O(1) (a fixed amount of work) but queries O(n). A prefix-sum array makes sum queries O(1) but every update O(n), because every later prefix changes. On large arrays, many O(n) operations can become expensive. A segment tree makes both operations O(log n). For a million elements the difference is stark: A segment tree does a few nodes of work per level, so the real count is a small multiple of 20, still tens of thousands of times less than a scan. It works for any operation that combines associatively, not just sums. The idea: store answers for halves, quarters, eighths... Each node of a segment tree is responsible for a contiguous range of the array and stores the answer for that range. The root covers everything; each node splits its range in half between its two children; the leaves are single elements. For a = [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7, 4] with sums: Any range can be assembled from a handful of these precomputed pieces. Writing S(l, r) for the sum of a[l..r]: That is two nodes instead of four elements. For long ranges the saving is enormous: any range needs at most about two nodes per level of the tree. Key takeaways Each node summarises one contiguous range. Fully covered pieces combine into the requested range without scanning all elements. Further reading Segment Tree — cp-algorithms Segment tree, the interval-stabbing version — Wikipedia Range minimum query — Wikipedia

t: Laying out a segment tree in an array
sum: Use one-based child indices in a flat array.
x: Here n is the non-empty input array’s length. Big-O bounds count constant-time combines of constant-size summaries on word-sized values. Storing it in an array Like a binary heap, the tree lives in a flat array, with the root at index 1. The children of a node are found by arithmetic, so no pointers are stored: How big must the array be? Each level can hold twice as many nodes as the one above, and the leaves must fit on the bottom level: That is why implementations allocate 4 n. When n is already a power of two, the bottom level holds exactly n leaves and 2n slots are enough. Key takeaways Use one-based child indices in a flat array. Round the leaf capacity up to a power of two when bounding allocated slots. Further reading Segment Tree — cp-algorithms Segment tree, the interval-stabbing version — Wikipedia Range minimum query — Wikipedia

t: Building, querying and updating segment trees
sum: Disjoint, covered and partial overlap are the three query cases.
x: Here n is the non-empty input array’s length. Big-O bounds count constant-time combines of constant-size summaries on word-sized values. Query, update and build The examples require non-empty arrays and valid inclusive ranges or point indices: For an 8-element array, query(2, 5) is valid and query(5, 2) or update(8, x) is not. Complexity assumes constant-size summaries and constant-time combines on word-sized values. Integer sums are associative; floating-point sums need numerical-error considerations. The query has three cases at each node: Disjoint: the node's range misses [l, r] entirely. Return the identity (0 for sum, +infinity for min). Covered: the node's range lies inside [l, r]. Return its stored value without going deeper. Partial overlap: recurse into both children and combine. The update walks one root-to-leaf path, then recomputes each node on the way back up. Why O(log n)? Build: every node (twice the element count, minus one) is computed once: O(n). Update: one root-to-leaf path, O(1) work per node: O(log n). Query: at each level, at most two nodes are partially overlapped (the ones containing the ends of [l, r]). Everything between them is fully covered and stops immediately. So at most four nodes are visited per level. Counting levels gives the bounds: For a million elements that is at most 21 nodes per update and at most 84 per query, which is why both are O(log n). The bounds assume combining two summaries takes constant time. Key takeaways Disjoint, covered and partial overlap are the three query cases. Point updates recompute summaries on one root-to-leaf path. Further reading Segment Tree — cp-algorithms Segment tree, the interval-stabbing version — Wikipedia Range minimum query — Wikipedia

sum: An associative combine and an empty-range identity define a valid range summary.
x: Here n is the non-empty input array’s length. Big-O bounds count constant-time combines of constant-size summaries on word-sized values. Beyond sums: what can a node store? The structure works whenever the combine operation is associative, with an identity element for the empty range: The worked line shows min is associative. Sum, min, max, gcd (greatest common divisor), bitwise AND, bitwise OR, bitwise XOR and matrix products all qualify. Subtraction does not: subtracting three and then two from eight gives three, while subtracting their difference from eight gives seven. Associative is enough; commutative is not required. The recursive code always combines the left child before the right, so non-commutative operations like matrix multiplication or string concatenation work, as long as you keep that order. Actual string concatenation is not constant-time, and matrix costs depend on dimension; their runtimes include combine costs. You can also store a small struct per node. The famous example is the maximum subarray sum over a range, with point updates. Each node stores four numbers: Field Symbol Meaning --------- sum s total of the range pre p best prefix sum suf q best suffix sum best b best subarray sum Combining a left child L and a right child R: For example, take the left half [2, −1] and the right half [3, −5]: You can check every line by listing the prefixes and suffixes of [2, −1, 3, −5] by hand. These rules assume subarrays must be non-empty. The best subarray is either entirely in one half or crosses the middle, in which case it is a suffix of the left plus a prefix of the right. Kadane's algorithm cannot handle updates; this can, in O(log n) each. Key takeaways An associative combine and an empty-range identity define a valid range summary. Maximum-subarray nodes retain total, best prefix, best suffix and best interior sum. Further reading Segment Tree — cp-algorithms Segment tree, the interval-stabbing version — Wikipedia Range minimum query — Wikipedia

t: Lazy range updates and deferred tags
sum: A fully covered node updates its summary immediately.
x: Here n is the non-empty input array’s length. Big-O bounds count constant-time combines of constant-size summaries on word-sized values. Lazy propagation: updating whole ranges Now add a third request: "add x to every element of a[l..r]". Doing it as one point update per element is slow for a big range: Lazy propagation applies a range update the same way a query reads a range: stop at fully covered nodes. At such a node, update its stored sum and leave a pending tag saying "my children still owe +x": The third line describes a fully covered node spanning indices zero through three, initially holding zeros. The next unit traces the complete tree update. The tag is pushed down to the children only when some later operation needs to go below that node. Key takeaways A fully covered node updates its summary immediately. A pending tag records work still owed to the children. Further reading Segment Tree — cp-algorithms Segment tree, the interval-stabbing version — Wikipedia Range minimum query — Wikipedia

sum: Push pending updates before descending into children, including during queries.
x: Here n is the non-empty input array’s length. Big-O bounds count constant-time combines of constant-size summaries on word-sized values. Implementing deferred updates The following complete sum-tree example starts from zeros and uses valid inclusive ranges. Its pending tag has the meaning introduced in the previous unit. Tracing a lazy update On 8 zeros, add(0, 3, 5) reaches node [0,3], which is fully covered. It sets that node's sum to 20 and its tag to 5, and the root's sum to 20. The four leaves are not touched at all. A later add(2, 5, 1) must go inside [0,3], so it first pushes the tag: [0,1] and [2,3] each get sum 10 and tag 5. Both operations now visit O(log n) nodes, so range update and range query are both O(log n). Lazy propagation needs two properties: You can update a node's summary without looking at its children. Pending tags compose: two adds become one add. Mixing "assign" and "add" works too, but the tag must record the order (an assignment wipes out earlier adds). For a range add, both properties are one line each: So a node covering 4 elements with sum 20 and minimum 3 becomes sum 28 and minimum 5 after adding 2. Some updates fail the first test. "Replace each range element with its remainder after division by a positive integer" changes a sum in a way that depends on every element, so plain lazy propagation cannot do it. Key takeaways Push pending updates before descending into children, including during queries. Tag composition must preserve update order when assignments and additions mix. Further reading Segment Tree — cp-algorithms Segment tree, the interval-stabbing version — Wikipedia Range minimum query — Wikipedia

t: Iterative segment trees and practical choices
sum: A bottom-up tree puts leaves in the second half of its array.
x: Here n is the non-empty input array’s length. Big-O bounds count constant-time combines of constant-size summaries on word-sized values. The iterative bottom-up version For point updates and commutative operations there is a compact, fast, non-recursive form. It needs only 2n slots, with the leaves in the second half: In Python, i // 2 is exactly the floor of i / 2 for non-negative i. It avoids recursive-call overhead. Content gap: performance multiplier No fixed speedup is supplied because the original “several times faster” claim lacked a reproducible benchmark for a specified implementation and workload. Where segment trees are used Competitive programming and interviews: range sum/min/max with updates, "count of smaller numbers after self" (after coordinate compression), and booking problems such as "maximum number of overlapping events" (range add plus range max). Computational geometry: sweep-line algorithms, such as computing the area of a union of rectangles, keep a segment tree over the y-coordinates. Huge index ranges: a dynamic (sparse) segment tree creates nodes only when touched, so it can cover indices up to 10^9 with memory proportional to the operations performed. A name clash In computational geometry, "segment tree" traditionally names a related structure that stores a set of intervals and answers "which intervals contain point x?" in O(log n + k), where n is the number of stored intervals and k is the number of intervals reported. The Wikipedia article describes that version. The array-based segment tree in this lesson is the meaning used in competitive programming and interviews. Pitfalls Inclusive vs half-open ranges. Pick one convention and stick to it; mixing them is the most common bug. Wrong identity. Returning 0 for a disjoint range in a min tree silently corrupts answers. Use +infinity. Forgetting to push. In a lazy tree, every operation that descends past a node must push its tag first, including queries. Overkill. If you only need prefix sums with point updates, a Fenwick tree (next lesson) is shorter and often has lower overhead; measure the actual workload. If the array never changes, a prefix-sum array or sparse table is simpler still. Key takeaways A bottom-up tree puts leaves in the second half of its array. Keep half-open ranges distinct from inclusive ranges and choose the simplest structure for the workload. Further reading Segment Tree — cp-algorithms Segment tree, the interval-stabbing version — Wikipedia Range minimum query — Wikipedia

sum: Subtract two prefix totals to answer a range sum.
x: Here n is the number of input elements. Fenwick positions start at 1; the empty prefix is valid, but an update at zero is not. Arithmetic costs assume word-sized values. A Fenwick tree, or binary indexed tree (BIT), solves a narrower problem than a segment tree: maintain an array under point updates and answer prefix sums: the total of the first i elements. Range sums then follow by subtraction: The last line adds the three elements directly and matches. The trick only works because addition can be undone by subtraction; it fails for operations such as minimum (see below). What it gives up in generality it repays in simplicity. The whole structure is one array of n + 1 numbers and two loops of about four lines each. Historical accounts commonly credit Boris Ryabko’s 1989 coding work. Peter Fenwick’s 1994 paper presents the binary indexed tree for cumulative-frequency tables in arithmetic-coding compression. The intuition: binary decomposition of a prefix Any positive whole number is a sum of distinct powers of two. Thirteen uses eight, four and one. In the same way, the prefix of the first 13 elements can be split into blocks whose lengths are powers of two, longest first: A Fenwick tree stores exactly these blocks. Entry t[i] holds the sum of a block ending at i whose length is the lowest set bit of i (the value of the rightmost 1 when i is written in binary). A prefix sum then needs one block per set bit of i: For a million elements that is at most 20 blocks per query. Key takeaways Subtract two prefix totals to answer a range sum. A prefix decomposes into one block for each set bit in its index. Further reading Fenwick Tree — cp-algorithms Fenwick tree — Wikipedia Segment Tree — cp-algorithms

sum: Bitwise AND of a positive index and its negation extracts its lowest set bit.
x: Here n is the number of input elements. Fenwick positions start at 1; the empty prefix is valid, but an update at zero is not. Arithmetic costs assume word-sized values. The lowbit trick The lowest set bit of i is i & -i in code. This works because of two's complement, the way computers store negative integers: So lowbit(12) is 4: 12 is 1100 in binary, and its rightmost 1 is worth 4. For any odd number the answer is 1. Python integers behave as if they had infinitely many sign bits, so i & -i works there too. Each entry therefore covers this block: For an eight-element array: i binary lowbit t[i] covers ------------ 1 0001 1 a[1] 2 0010 2 a[1..2] 3 0011 1 a[3] 4 0100 4 a[1..4] 5 0101 1 a[5] 6 0110 2 a[5..6] 7 0111 1 a[7] 8 1000 8 a[1..8] Odd indices hold single elements; powers of two hold whole prefixes. Key takeaways Bitwise AND of a positive index and its negation extracts its lowest set bit. Each tree entry stores the block of that length ending at its index. Further reading Fenwick Tree — cp-algorithms Fenwick tree — Wikipedia Segment Tree — cp-algorithms

sum: Queries remove the lowest set bit to move to an earlier block.
x: Here n is the number of input elements. Fenwick positions start at 1; the empty prefix is valid, but an update at zero is not. Arithmetic costs assume word-sized values. The code Assume n (the array length) is zero or more, update positions and ranges are valid 1-based positions, and a prefix query asks for anything from 0 to n elements. add(n + 1, delta) is an intentional no-op used by range-update boundaries. Complexity counts constant-time word arithmetic; arbitrary-size integer arithmetic has additional bit costs. Querying: strip the lowest bit prefix(i) adds t[i], then removes i's lowest bit to jump to the end of the previous block, and repeats until i is 0: In binary the walk clears the lowest set bit at each step: the prefixes visit indices thirteen, twelve, eight and then zero. The earlier block-count bound shows this is logarithmic in the array length. Updating: add the lowest bit add(i, delta) must change every block that contains position i. Those are t[i], then t[i + lowbit(i)], and so on: adding the lowest bit jumps to the next larger block that also covers i. So add(5, d), with d the value added, changes t[5] (element 5), t[6] (elements 5 to 6), t[8] (elements 1 to 8) and t[16] (elements 1 to 16). Each step moves the lowest set bit at least one place left, so this is also O(log n): the number of steps grows with the logarithm of the array length n. Fenwick trees are 1-indexed Index 0 has lowbit 0, so i += i & -i would loop forever on add(0,...). Store a[k] at k + 1 if your data is 0-indexed, and do the shift in one place. Key takeaways Queries remove the lowest set bit to move to an earlier block. Updates add the lowest set bit to visit enclosing blocks; index zero is invalid for updates. Further reading Fenwick Tree — cp-algorithms Fenwick tree — Wikipedia Segment Tree — cp-algorithms

sum: A forward pass builds block totals in linear time.
x: Here n is the number of input elements. Fenwick positions start at 1; the empty prefix is valid, but an update at zero is not. Arithmetic costs assume word-sized values. Building in O(n) For an array of n elements, calling add n times builds the tree in O(n log n). There is a linear, O(n), method: copy the array in, then push each entry's total up to its immediate parent block once. By the time the loop reaches i, t[i] already contains everything from its smaller sub-blocks, so a single forward pass suffices. Worked application: counting inversions An inversion is a pair of positions whose values violate ascending order: A sorted array has 0 inversions; a reversed array of n distinct elements has the most possible, I_max, 10 for five elements. Walk left to right, keeping a Fenwick tree of how many times each value has been seen. For each element, the number of earlier elements greater than it is "elements seen so far" minus "seen elements ≤ it". Each element adds the number of earlier elements bigger than it: For [3, 1, 2, 5, 4] the three inversions are the pairs (3, 1), (3, 2) and (5, 4). For an array of n elements it runs in O(n log n), the same as the merge-sort method, and the same pattern answers "count of smaller numbers after self" and rank queries in leaderboards. Coordinate compression (mapping values to ranks) is what keeps the tree size equal to the number of distinct values rather than the largest value. Key takeaways A forward pass builds block totals in linear time. Coordinate-compressed counts reveal how many earlier elements exceed each value. Further reading Fenwick Tree — cp-algorithms Fenwick tree — Wikipedia Segment Tree — cp-algorithms

sum: A range addition changes only two difference-array boundaries.
x: Here n is the number of input elements. Fenwick positions start at 1; the empty prefix is valid, but an update at zero is not. Arithmetic costs assume word-sized values. Variations Range update, point query Store a difference array in the tree: each entry holds how much an element differs from the one before it. Then a range add touches only two entries, and an element's value is a prefix sum: In code that is add(l, x) and add(r + 1, -x), and prefix(i) returns the current value of a_i. Example: on 6 zeros, adding 5 to positions 2 to 4 gives differences [0, 5, 0, 0, −5, 0], whose running totals are [0, 5, 5, 5, 0, 0]. Key takeaways A range addition changes only two difference-array boundaries. A prefix sum of the differences reconstructs one current element. Further reading Fenwick Tree — cp-algorithms Fenwick tree — Wikipedia Segment Tree — cp-algorithms

t: Range sums with two Fenwick trees
sum: One tree stores differences and the other corrects their prefix weighting.
x: Here n is the number of input elements. Fenwick positions start at 1; the empty prefix is valid, but an update at zero is not. Arithmetic costs assume word-sized values. Range update, range query Use two trees, b1 and b2. For the code’s range-add arguments l, r and x, b1 stores the difference-array boundaries and b2 stores their position-weight corrections. The complete calls below show both updates to each tree. The prefix sum is then: Before the range both trees read 0, so the prefix sum is 0, as it should be. The last two lines are a worked example: add 5 to positions 3 to 6 of an 8-element array of zeros. At position 4 the answer is 10 (two elements of 5 so far); at position 7 it is 20 (all four elements of 5). Several range adds simply add up, because both trees are linear. b1 is the difference array; b2 is a correction so that positions before l and after r come out right. Key takeaways One tree stores differences and the other corrects their prefix weighting. Subtract prefix totals to recover any inclusive range total. Further reading Fenwick Tree — cp-algorithms Fenwick tree — Wikipedia Segment Tree — cp-algorithms

sum: Order-statistic walks require non-negative counts so prefixes are monotone.
x: Here n is the number of input elements. Fenwick positions start at 1; the empty prefix is valid, but an update at zero is not. Arithmetic costs assume word-sized values. Finding the k-th element If the tree stores non-negative counts and k is between 1 and the total count, "find the smallest i with prefix(i) >= k" (the k-th smallest element) can be done in O(log n) by walking down powers of two, where n is the tree size. Binary searching over prefix instead costs O(log² n), meaning (log n) squared: about log n prefix queries of about log n steps each. Two dimensions Nest the loops (t[i][j], each loop using lowbit) for 2D prefix sums with point updates on an n-by-m grid in O(log n · log m): about log n steps in one direction, each doing about log m steps in the other. Fenwick tree vs segment tree In this table n is the number of array elements. Fenwick Segment tree --------- Memory One extra slot beyond array length About two to four times array length Code ~10 lines ~40+ lines Operations Commutative group (sum, XOR) Any associative Range min/max Awkward Natural Range updates Tricks above Lazy tags The key limitation: range queries come from prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1), which needs an inverse element. For the standard point-delta update shown here, combining must also be associative and commutative, with an identity: an abelian group. Sum has subtraction, XOR is its own inverse, but min and max have no inverse: knowing the minimum of a[1..r] and of a[1..l-1] tells you nothing about the minimum of a[l..r]. A Fenwick tree can maintain prefix minima if values only decrease, but for general range min with updates, use a segment tree. Fenwick trees are also fast in practice: the loops are tight, the array is compact, and there is no recursion. Pitfalls zero-based indexing: an infinite loop on index 0, or off-by-one errors at the ends. Keep the shift in one place. Assigning instead of adding: add adds a delta. To set a[i] = x, keep a copy of the array and add x - a[i]. Using it for min/max range queries: subtraction does not work for them. Overflow in fixed-width languages: prefix sums of many large values can exceed 32 bits. Choose a width justified by the maximum total, or use arbitrary-precision integers; even 64 bits can overflow. A quick check: Here a 64-bit integer (limit about 9.2 × 10^18) is plenty. Key takeaways Order-statistic walks require non-negative counts so prefixes are monotone. General range sums need an inverse; min and max require different restrictions or a segment tree. Further reading Fenwick Tree — cp-algorithms Fenwick tree — Wikipedia Segment Tree — cp-algorithms

t: Why naive string search repeats work
sum: Repeated prefixes make naive matching retry the same successful comparisons.
x: Here n is the text or indexed-string length, m is the pattern length, and positions count from zero. Costs count constant-time character and word operations unless noted. The naive way to find a pattern p (length m) in a text t (length n) tries every start position and compares character by character. In the worst case every start position compares the whole pattern: The second line is the classic bad case: searching for aaaab (five characters) in a million as matches four as and fails on the b at every start, about five million comparisons, and finds nothing. When mismatches come early (typical English text), naive matching is much closer to n comparisons. The algorithms in this lesson avoid that waste in different ways. KMP and the Z-function reuse previous matches instead of restarting the search at every position. Rabin–Karp compares hashes instead of strings. Suffix arrays pre-process the text once so that many later queries are fast. The waste in naive matching Suppose we search for abab and have matched aba before a mismatch: Naive matching slides the pattern one place and starts again from scratch. But we already know the last three text characters were aba. The end of what we matched (a) is also a start of the pattern, so the next possible match can begin there, with one character already matched. Nothing before it can work. KMP precomputes, for every prefix of the pattern, exactly this "how much can I keep?" number. Key takeaways Repeated prefixes make naive matching retry the same successful comparisons. A border tells a matcher which already-matched characters it can retain. Further reading Prefix function and Knuth–Morris–Pratt — cp-algorithms Rabin–Karp algorithm — Wikipedia Z-function — cp-algorithms Suffix Array — cp-algorithms Suffix array — Wikipedia

t: KMP borders, prefix tables and overlapping matches
sum: The prefix function stores the longest proper border of each prefix.
x: Here n is the text or indexed-string length, m is the pattern length, and positions count from zero. Costs count constant-time character and word operations unless noted. KMP: the prefix function For a pattern p, pi[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of p[0..i] that is also a suffix of it. ("Proper" means not the whole string.) A string that is both a proper prefix and a suffix is called a border, so pi is often called the failure function or border array. As a formula: For example, ababa (positions 0 to 4) ends with aba, which is also how it starts, so the value at position 4 is 3: the last line of the block. The border must be proper, so ababa itself does not count. When p[i] does not extend the current border of length k, the next candidate border is the border of that border, pi[k - 1]. The loop keeps falling back until something extends or k reaches 0. Searching with it The search uses the same loop, with the text in place of the pattern: kmp_search("abababab", "abab") returns [0, 2, 4], including overlapping matches. Key takeaways The prefix function stores the longest proper border of each prefix. After a full match, falling back to its border retains overlapping matches. t: Why KMP is linear and when to use it
sum: Every fallback spends an earlier increase in matched-border length.
x: Here n is the text or indexed-string length, m is the pattern length, and positions count from zero. Costs count constant-time character and word operations unless noted. Why it is linear The text index i only moves forward. Each step raises k by at most 1, and each fallback lowers it by at least 1. k can never go below 0, so it cannot fall more often than it rose: For a 1,000,000-character text and a 100-character pattern that is at most about 2,000,000 loop steps plus 200 for the table, however repetitive the input. Memory is O(m) for pi, excluding the returned list of match positions. The empty pattern matches at every text boundary. A concatenation trick Compute the prefix function of p + "#" + t, where # appears in neither string. Every position where pi equals m is the end of a match. The separator stops a border from running past the pattern. KMP vs Rabin–Karp vs Z Here n is the text length, m the pattern length and C the number of Rabin–Karp hash candidates. Time Best for --------- KMP O(n + m) worst Streams, one pattern Rabin–Karp O(n + m + mC), C candidates Many patterns, substring hashing Z O(n + m) worst Prefix-matching questions KMP processes the text one character at a time and never looks back, so it works on a stream. The Z trick needs the whole text concatenated in memory. What real libraries do CPython's forward string search combines Boyer–Moore/Horspool-style skipping with a two-way algorithm and adaptive selection based on input sizes and observed work. The two-way path has a linear worst-case bound. Content gap: no universal fastest-algorithm ranking is given; that requires reproducible benchmarks for the workload and implementation. Key takeaways Every fallback spends an earlier increase in matched-border length. Choose deterministic matching when collision verification or stream access matters. t: Building and sliding a rolling hash
sum: Remove the outgoing character contribution before shifting the hash.
x: Here n is the text or indexed-string length, m is the pattern length, and positions count from zero. Costs count constant-time character and word operations unless noted. Rabin–Karp: compare hashes, not strings Treat a window of m characters as a number in base B, modulo a large prime M: The last line is a toy example: with base ten, digits as characters and a modulus large enough to ignore, the window 123 hashes to the number 123. Sliding the window one place removes the leading character and appends one. That is O(1) arithmetic, a rolling hash: In the toy example, sliding from 123 to 234 removes 1 × 100, shifts 23 to 230 and adds 4. Real code does each step modulo M so the numbers never grow, and must keep the subtraction non-negative (see Pitfalls). Key takeaways Remove the outgoing character contribution before shifting the hash. Hash equality is only a candidate; compare actual characters for exact matching. t: Hash candidates, prefix fingerprints and modulo
sum: Candidate verification adds a cost per matching window, including genuine matches.
x: Here n is the text or indexed-string length, m is the pattern length, and positions count from zero. Costs count constant-time character and word operations unless noted. Candidate verification and substring fingerprints Equal strings always have equal hashes, but different strings can produce a hash collision. So a hash match is only a candidate, confirmed by a direct comparison. For this implementation the time is: The last line is a worked example: searching aaa (a 3-character pattern) in a million as gives about a million genuine matches, so the checks alone cost about three million comparisons. Repeated text and pattern characters can require Θ(nm) verification even without collisions when the pattern is at most half the text length. When the pattern nearly fills the text, use the actual candidate count instead. Linear expected time needs assumptions controlling false positives and genuine matches. Content gap: collision probabilities No numeric collision probability is provided for the fixed public B and M above: a prime modulus alone does not justify a 1/M probability for arbitrary inputs. Porting negative remainders Negative modulo: in C or Java, (h - x) % M can be negative. For positive M, Python's % returns a non-negative result, which hides this bug until you port the code. For this fixed modulus near one billion, a sufficiently wide integer type can safely add the modulus before reducing again. For arbitrary fixed-width values, the intermediate addition must also avoid overflow: Both −7 and 4 leave the same remainder class (they differ by exactly 11), but only 4 equals a correctly computed hash. Key takeaways Candidate verification adds a cost per matching window, including genuine matches. Normalise negative remainders so equivalent hashes compare equal when porting. sum: Extract substring fingerprints from two prefix hashes and understand their collision limits.
x: Here n is the string length and k is the number of patterns. Hash values are fingerprints, so exact equality still needs verification. Rabin–Karp's real strengths are elsewhere: Many patterns at once: group k equal-length patterns by hash and look up each window in expected O(1), plus verification of candidate patterns. Substring equality in O(1): with prefix hashes of a string of length n, any two substrings' fingerprints can be compared after O(n) set-up (formula below). This is probabilistic equality unless verified. Hashing and binary search can give an expected O(n log n) Monte Carlo longest-repeated-substring algorithm under an appropriate random-hash model; collision checks add costs. Content-defined chunking: backup tools such as restic use rolling fingerprints to choose boundaries. Rsync instead searches at every offset for matches to fixed-size blocks of the basis file. The prefix-hash trick stores the hash of every prefix, then cuts any substring's hash out of two of them: The last line is a toy example with base ten, digits as characters and a modulus large enough to ignore: for the string 5123, the prefix hashes are 5 (first character) and 5123 (all four), so the substring 123 hashes to 123, exactly what hashing it directly gives. Each comparison is O(1) once the H array and powers of B are precomputed in O(n). Hash collisions can be attacked With a fixed, public B and M, an adversary can build inputs that collide on purpose. Randomised fingerprints can reduce collision risk under a stated model, but fixed double hashing is not an adversarial guarantee. Verify candidates; use KMP or Z when deterministic linear bounds matter. Key takeaways Shift the shorter prefix hash by the substring length before subtracting it. Fingerprint equality is probabilistic under a stated hash model and is not an adversarial guarantee. t: Reusing prefix matches with the Z-function
sum: A Z-value measures agreement with the whole string prefix.
x: Here n is the text or indexed-string length, m is the pattern length, and positions count from zero. Costs count constant-time character and word operations unless noted. The Z-function z[i] is the length of the longest substring starting at i that is also a prefix of the whole string. By convention z[0] = 0. In the table, the value 3 at position 4 is because aab starting at 4 matches the prefix aab, then the suffix reaches the end of the string. The algorithm keeps the rightmost window [l, r) known to match a prefix. For a new i inside that window, the character run from i mirrors the run from i − l, so it can reuse the earlier value, capped at the window's edge: The last line is the worked example for aabxaab: after position 4 the window runs from 4 up to 7, so position 5 mirrors position 1 and starts at 1. One more comparison (a against b) fails, so the value stays 1, with no wasted comparisons. Each successful comparison in the inner loop pushes r to the right, and r never moves left, so the total work is O(n), where n is the length of s. To search, compute z of p + "$" + t, choosing $ absent from both strings: every position with z[i] == m is a match. The Z-function is often the simplest tool for "which suffixes match a prefix?" questions, such as finding a string's period. Key takeaways A Z-value measures agreement with the whole string prefix. Reuse an earlier mirrored Z-value only within the already-known matching window. sum: Sorting suffix positions groups all occurrences of one pattern together.
x: Here n is the text or indexed-string length, m is the pattern length, and positions count from zero. Costs count constant-time character and word operations unless noted. Suffix arrays: pre-process the text once The algorithms above take O(n) per query, where n is the text length. If the text is fixed and queries are many (a genome, a corpus, a code base), we can do better by indexing the text. The suffix array of s is the list of starting positions of all its suffixes, in sorted order: Every occurrence of a pattern is a prefix of some suffix. Because the suffixes are sorted, all suffixes starting with p form one contiguous range, which two binary searches find in O(m log n), where n is the text length and m the pattern length: each binary-search comparison checks at most the pattern’s length. Searching ana finds the block ana, anana: occurrences at 3 and 1. Building it Sorting the n suffixes of an n-character string directly costs O(n log n) comparisons of up to n characters each, O(n² log n) in the worst case (for example, a string of all as, where suffixes share long prefixes). Prefix doubling sorts by the first 1, 2, 4, 8... characters. The rank of a suffix by its first 2k characters is the pair (rank of first k, rank of the k after that), so each round is a sort of integer pairs: Each round doubles the number of characters compared, so the rounds run out quickly: For a million-character string that is at most 20 rounds. Specialised algorithms (SA-IS, DC3) achieve O(n) with a suitable bounded integer alphabet. Arbitrary comparison-based alphabet ordering has its own cost. Key takeaways Sorting suffix positions groups all occurrences of one pattern together. Prefix doubling ranks increasingly long prefixes through pairs of shorter ranks. t: LCP arrays and indexed substring questions
sum: Adjacent longest-common-prefix values expose repeated substrings.
x: Here n is the text or indexed-string length, m is the pattern length, and positions count from zero. Costs count constant-time character and word operations unless noted. The LCP array The LCP array stores, for each adjacent pair in the suffix array, the length of their longest common prefix. For banana, with lcp[0] = 0 by convention: Kasai's algorithm builds it in O(n), where n is the string length. The LCP array turns many problems into array scans: Longest repeated substring: the maximum LCP value. For banana that is 3 (ana). Number of distinct substrings: every substring is a prefix of some suffix, and each suffix's first lcp characters were already counted by its sorted neighbour: Longest common substring of two strings: build over a + "#" + b with # absent from both inputs, and take the largest LCP between adjacent suffixes from different strings. Suffix arrays vs suffix trees A suffix tree is a compressed trie of all suffixes. It can answer the same queries, and builds in O(n) with Ukkonen's algorithm for a constant-size alphabet and constant-time edge lookup. Space overhead depends on node representation; no universal bytes-per-character estimate is supplied without measurement. A suffix array is n integers. Together with the LCP array it can simulate most suffix-tree algorithms, which is why bioinformatics tools favour suffix arrays and the related FM-index (built on the Burrows–Wheeler transform, as in the BWA and Bowtie read aligners). Pitfalls Forgetting overlaps in KMP: after a match, set k = pi[k - 1], not 0, or you miss overlapping occurrences. Trusting a hash match: without the final comparison, Rabin–Karp is a probabilistic algorithm that can report false positives. Separators that occur in the input: the # in p + "#" + t must be a character neither string contains. Quadratic suffix sorting: sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: s[i:]) is fine for tests but builds O(n²) characters of slices. Key takeaways Adjacent longest-common-prefix values expose repeated substrings. Subtract those repeated prefixes from the total substring count to count distinct substrings. sum: Expected costs average over the structure’s own random choices for a fixed independent input.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. Balanced binary search trees such as red–black and AVL trees guarantee O(log n) operations (time growing in proportion to the logarithm of n, the number of keys stored), but their rebalancing rules are fiddly to get right. Randomised structures take another route: make a few random choices, and the structure is balanced with high probability, whatever order the keys arrive in. The second half of this lesson goes the other way: using randomness as the output. Picking k items uniformly from a stream of unknown length, and shuffling an array so every order is equally likely, both have short algorithms that are easy to get subtly wrong. Expected vs worst case A randomised structure's bounds are over its own independent random draws, not over the input. For any fixed input sequence independent of the random choices, suitably random priorities or promotion levels give expected logarithmic bounds. This is not a worst-case guarantee against every adaptive adversary. You would need to be unlucky, and the probability of being much slower than O(log n), where n is the number of keys, shrinks very quickly as n grows. That is a stronger guarantee than "average case over random inputs", which a plain BST also has, and which sorted input breaks. Skip lists A sorted linked list of n nodes has O(n) search, because you can only walk forward one node at a time. A skip list, introduced by William Pugh in 1990, adds express lanes: extra levels of linked lists, each containing a random subset of the level below. When a key is inserted, it gets level 1, then flips a coin: heads, also join level 2; heads again, level 3; and so on. The chance of heads is called the promotion probability. Three numbers follow from it: So with a million keys and fair coins, about half the nodes reach level 2, a quarter level 3, and the list is about 20 levels tall. These are averages over the independent random draws; any single run can be a little taller or shorter. Key takeaways Expected costs average over the structure’s own random choices for a fixed independent input. Geometric promotion creates progressively sparser express lanes. t: Searching and inserting in a skip list
sum: Search moves right below the target, then drops down a level.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. Search Start at the top-left. Move right while the next key is smaller than the target. When you cannot, drop down a level. At level 1, the next node is the target if it is present. Insert Search as usual, but remember the last node visited on each level (update[i]). Those are the nodes whose pointers must change. Then pick a random level and splice the new node in on each of its levels. This insert method continues the SkipList class from the search example. It permits duplicate keys; it is an ordered membership demonstration rather than a distinct-key set API. Delete is symmetrical: find update, then unlink the node on each level it occupies. No rotations, no colour rules. Key takeaways Search moves right below the target, then drops down a level. Remember each level’s predecessor before splicing a new tower.
