t: Skip-list pointer costs, caps and uses
sum: Promotion probability trades pointer memory against search constants.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. Cost Read the search path backwards: from the found node, each step either goes up (if that node was promoted, which happens with the promotion probability) or left. Pugh's analysis turns that into an expected step count: O(log n) means the cost grows in proportion to the logarithm of n. Lower p means fewer, longer hops per level but fewer levels, so at a million keys both settings take about 40 steps. Pugh's full formula adds a small constant; the estimate ignores it. The memory cost is the number of forward pointers, one per level each node occupies (not counting the head): A million keys therefore cost about 2 million pointers with fair coins and about 1.33 million with a promotion probability of 1/4. Lower p saves pointers; search constants and variance also depend on the workload and implementation. The code caps levels at 32 for a bounded practical capacity. The number of nodes expected to reach the cap shows when that stops being enough: Well below that scale the capped top level has a small expected population. This is a probabilistic practical estimate, not a guarantee that the cap never affects a particular run. An asymptotic O(log n) guarantee for unbounded n requires a cap that grows with log n; a fixed cap eventually leaves too many nodes on its top level. Where skip lists are used Redis sorted sets (Redis 8.2 implementation) (ZADD, ZRANGE, leaderboards) pair a hash table with a skip list, using a promotion probability of 1/4 and a cap of 32 levels. Each forward pointer also stores a skip-list span, so rank queries (ZRANK) are O(log n) too, where n is the number of members in the set. Small sorted sets use a compact listpack instead. LevelDB uses a skip-list memtable. RocksDB uses a skip list by default and also offers other memtable representations. Java's ConcurrentSkipListMap is a sorted concurrent map. Its Java SE 21 API documents safe concurrent access and expected average logarithmic lookup and updates. That public contract does not promise lock-free progress; the hand-written example above is not a concurrent implementation. Key takeaways Promotion probability trades pointer memory against search constants. A fixed level cap is a practical capacity choice, not an unbounded logarithmic guarantee. t: Treaps, random priorities, split and merge
sum: A treap keeps BST order on keys and heap order on priorities.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. Treaps A treap is a binary search tree where each node also has a random priority, and the tree is a heap on priorities: every parent's priority beats its children's. (The name is tree + heap.) For distinct keys and priorities, there is exactly one tree satisfying both rules. And it is the same tree you would get by inserting the keys in decreasing priority order into a plain BST. Since priorities are random, that is a random insertion order, and a BST built from random insertions has expected depth O(log n), where n is the number of keys: The average depth is about 14 for 5,000 keys (the leading term 2 ln(n) alone gives 17); the deepest node is somewhat deeper, but still logarithmic in expectation. So the treap's shape no longer depends on the order keys actually arrived. Inserting 5,000 sorted keys into a plain BST gives a chain of height 4,999 edges; a treap with independent random priorities has expected logarithmic height, though a linear-height outcome remains possible. Split and merge The cleanest treap implementations use two operations: split(t, key) returns two treaps: keys below key, and the rest. merge(a, b) joins two treaps when every key in a is smaller than every key in b. The root is whichever root has the higher priority. Assume distinct keys and independent priorities; insert below requires a key not already present. TNode generates a random priority, with a counter to break rare finite-precision ties. The ideal analysis assumes independent continuous priorities; this finite implementation approximates that model. The example uses import random, introduced with the skip-list implementation; run that import when using this excerpt separately. The recursive implementations can hit Python’s recursion limit on a sufficiently tall outcome; expected balance is not a hard stack bound. Each runs in expected time proportional to the tree’s depth, which is O(log n) for n keys. Delete is two splits (cutting out the key) and one merge. Split and merge are what make treaps popular in competitive programming. An implicit treap keys nodes by position (subtree sizes) instead of by value, giving a sequence that supports insert at index, delete range, moving a sequence fragment and reversing a range, with expected O(log n) tree work for a sequence of n items when properly augmented; reversal needs lazy tags. Inserting m fresh items costs at least O(m), and deleting nodes can add reclamation work. That is the same job a rope does, which the next lesson covers. Tree vs list Skip lists and treaps solve the same problem with the same expected bounds. Skip lists are simpler to make concurrent. Treaps are a real BST, so augmenting nodes (subtree sums, sizes) and split/merge come naturally. Key takeaways A treap keeps BST order on keys and heap order on priorities. Merge requires all left-treap keys to precede every right-treap key. sum: A later item enters a size-k reservoir with k divided by the number of items seen.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. Reservoir sampling You are reading a log stream of unknown length and want a uniform random sample of k lines, using O(k) memory. You cannot store the stream, and you cannot know n in advance. Algorithm R keeps the first k items. Then, for each later item i (counting from 0), it draws j = randint(0, i); if j < k, the new item replaces sample[j]. Why it is uniform Assume independent uniform draws and a sample size no bigger than the stream. Follow one item: it must first enter the sample, then survive every later step, where it is evicted only if the draw picks exactly its slot. Multiplying those chances, most factors cancel (the product telescopes): The first k items start in with probability 1, and the same telescoping gives k/n: with 10 slots and 1,000 lines, every line has a 1 % chance. If the stream is shorter than k, the code returns everything it saw; a negative k is outside its contract. Equal inclusion probabilities alone do not prove uniform subsets. Algorithm R additionally gives every possible sample the same probability, by induction over each replacement step: Key takeaways A later item enters a size-k reservoir with k divided by the number of items seen. Uniform subsets need a replacement induction as well as equal item-inclusion probabilities. Further reading Skip list — Wikipedia Treap — Wikipedia Treap (Cartesian tree) — cp-algorithms Reservoir sampling — Wikipedia Fisher–Yates shuffle — Wikipedia Vitter’s reservoir-sampling paper

sum: Weighted sampling without replacement does not give simply proportional inclusion probabilities.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. Reservoir variants Algorithm L computes how many items to skip before the next replacement, so it draws far fewer random numbers than one per item: For a 100-line sample from a billion lines, the displayed growth term is about 1,712. It illustrates scaling rather than predicting 1,712 actual draws: a common Algorithm L implementation uses three draws per selected replacement, as well as initialisation and termination work. Scanning a non-skippable input stream can still take linear time even when the random-draw count falls. Weighted sampling (Efraimidis–Spirakis): give each item a random key based on its weight and keep the k items with the largest keys, as below. This is sequential weighted sampling without replacement. It does not promise that each item's inclusion probability is k times its share of the total weight. Distributed: for a single-item sample, choose one shard's sample with probability proportional to its shard size. For larger reservoirs, simple repetition is insufficient: allocate shard counts with a hypergeometric distribution and subsample each local uniform reservoir without replacement. Each local reservoir must hold up to k items, or the whole shard if it is smaller. Key takeaways Weighted sampling without replacement does not give simply proportional inclusion probabilities. Shard samples must be combined with their shard sizes, not by a fair shard coin. sum: Draw from the remaining prefix, including the current position.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. The Fisher–Yates shuffle To shuffle an array uniformly, walk from the end. At each position i, swap a[i] with a[j] for j = randint(0, i), which can pick i itself. Think of it as drawing cards from a hat: the last position gets any of the items, the one before it any of the items left, and so on. Count the equally likely runs: For three items there are 6 runs and 6 orderings, each with probability 1/6. It takes O(n) time (proportional to n) and works in place. This is the version Durstenfeld published in 1964 and Knuth gives as Algorithm P; Python's random.shuffle uses it. Key takeaways Draw from the remaining prefix, including the current position. Each permutation corresponds to one equally likely sequence of draws. t: Shuffle bias, seed limits and adversaries
sum: Swapping with any array position creates unequal permutation counts.
x: Here n is the number of keys or stream items, and k is the requested sample size when sampling. Random draws are assumed independent and uniform under the stated model. The classic bug A tempting variant swaps every position with any position: Count its runs against the possible orderings: Counting them: three permutations appear 5 times in 27 and three appear 4 times, so some come out with probability 5/27 ≈ 18.5 % instead of 1/6 ≈ 16.7 %. Unpredictability matters A fair permutation algorithm does not make a predictable generator secure. Use an operating-system-backed generator such as secrets.SystemRandom when choices must be unpredictable. Content gap: the specific historical poker incident is omitted because a reliable primary account establishing the exact loop and seed was not verified in this audit. Two more pitfalls: Sorting with a random comparator, such as JavaScript's arr.sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5), gives biased, implementation-dependent results, because the sort assumes comparisons are consistent. Sorting by a random key drawn once per element is unbiased (ignoring ties), but O(n log n) for n elements. Too little randomness: a generator can only produce as many shuffles as it has possible seeds, as below. So a generator seeded with 32 bits can reach at most about 4 billion of the deck's orders, a vanishingly small fraction. Pitfalls Off-by-one ranges: randint(0, i) is inclusive in Python, randrange(i) is not. Drawing j with randrange(i) in Fisher–Yates, so position i can never keep its own item, is Sattolo's algorithm: it produces only single-cycle permutations, uniformly within that restricted class, rather than uniformly over all permutations. Ignoring the high-probability fine print: expected O(log n), for n keys, is extremely reliable at scale, but individual operations vary. Systems needing hard per-operation bounds use deterministic trees. Predictable seeds: if attackers can predict your priorities or independent random draws, they can build bad inputs for skip lists and treaps after all. Key takeaways Swapping with any array position creates unequal permutation counts. Unbiased algorithms still require enough unpredictable randomness for security-sensitive uses. t: Building sparse tables for static ranges
sum: Store every fitting power-of-two block summary.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. This index assumes a non-empty array and valid inclusive query endpoints. This unit builds a static range-minimum index from overlapping power-of-two blocks. Later units separately cover historical versions and editable text. Range minimum queries A range minimum query (RMQ) asks for the smallest value in a[l..r], the elements from index l to index r inclusive. The options so far, for an array of n elements (O(n²) means growing with n × n): Method Build Query Updates ------------ Scan none O(n) O(1) Every range O(n²) O(1) rebuild Segment tree O(n) O(log n) O(log n) Sparse table O(n log n) O(1) rebuild The sparse table is the right choice when the array never changes and there are many queries: for example, LCA queries on a fixed tree, or the LCP array of a suffix array. The sparse table Precompute the minimum of every block whose length is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, …). Each row holds minima for one block length, twice the previous row’s length. Combine two adjacent half-size blocks from the preceding row to obtain each larger block: The worked lines use the example array below, a = [5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 6, 8]: the length-2 block starting at index 3 covers 7 and 1, so its minimum is 1. The recurrence only works for operations where combining two halves gives the answer for the whole, which holds for min. The code builds row after row (table is T, j is k and half is h): Each row fits as long as its block length is at most n, which fixes how many rows there are and bounds the size: The 8-element example below has 4 rows and 21 entries. A million elements need at most 20 million entries, about 80 MB as 4-byte integers (the exact count, about 18.95 million entries, is about 76 MB), and far more as Python objects. So the build is O(n log n) time and memory, and that memory is the main limit on how large an array a sparse table suits. For a = [5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 6, 8]: Key takeaways Store every fitting power-of-two block summary. Sparse-table preprocessing is worthwhile for many queries on unchanged data. Further reading Sparse Table — cp-algorithms Range minimum query — Wikipedia

sum: Two largest-fitting blocks cover any range.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. This index assumes a non-empty array and valid inclusive query endpoints. The O(1) query: overlap is fine Any range can be covered by two blocks of the same power-of-two length: the largest power of two that fits inside the range. One block starts at the left end and one ends at the right end. They may overlap in the middle. The worked lines are query(2, 6) on the example array: two length-4 blocks, a[2..5] and a[3..6], overlapping at indices 3 to 5: Overlap does not matter for min, because counting an element twice does not change a minimum. The overlap query needs an associative combine that is also an idempotent operation: combining a value with itself gives the value back. Min, max, gcd (greatest common divisor), bitwise AND and bitwise OR all qualify. Sums are not idempotent Overlapping blocks would double-count the middle for a sum. You can still answer range sums from a sparse table in O(log n), with n the array length, by decomposing the range into disjoint power-of-two blocks (like a Fenwick prefix), but a prefix-sum array does that job in O(1) with O(n) memory. A disjoint sparse table stores the table differently to give O(1) queries for any associative operation. In the Python, bit_length() - 1 computes k, the base-2 logarithm of the range length rounded down: 5 is 101 in binary, 3 bits long, so k is 2. C++ code often uses __builtin_clz or precomputes a log array. Key takeaways Two largest-fitting blocks cover any range. Overlap requires an associative idempotent combine; summation double-counts. sum: An Euler-tour depth minimum gives a lowest common ancestor.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. Where it is used Lowest common ancestor: record an Euler tour of a tree (the nodes visited by a DFS, including returns) and their depths. The LCA of u and v is the shallowest node between their first appearances: an RMQ. For a tree of n nodes (the tour records the root once and one entry for each outward and return edge traversal), that is O(n log n) build and O(1) per LCA. Suffix arrays: the longest common prefix of two distinct suffixes is the minimum of the LCP array between their positions, so an RMQ structure answers it in O(1). Very large static data: specialised micro/macro RMQ constructions combine small in-block tables with summaries of block minima to obtain O(n) build and O(1) query, where n is the array length. Whether the more specialised implementation is worthwhile depends on memory limits and workload; compare those costs before choosing it. Pitfalls Sparse tables on changing data: a point update can affect O(n) blocks across all levels, where n is the array length. Use a segment tree instead. The count adds up like this: For a million elements, the top row is nineteen. The geometric bound allows up to 1,048,575 affected entries, about a million, against roughly twenty nodes in a segment tree. This is an upper bound, not the exact number affected at any chosen position. Using the overlap trick for sums: it double-counts. The combine must be associative and idempotent. Key takeaways An Euler-tour depth minimum gives a lowest common ancestor. A point change can affect linearly many sparse-table entries. sum: Copy the changed path and share untouched subtrees.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. Persistent data structures Ordinary structures are ephemeral: an update destroys the old version. A persistent structure keeps old versions usable. A partially persistent structure lets you read every version but update only the newest; a fully persistent one lets you update them too, forming a tree of versions. This sounds expensive, but most of each version is shared with the previous one. Shared nodes must remain immutable: changing one in place corrupts every version that still references it. Path copying In a tree, an update only changes nodes on one root-to-leaf path. Copy just those nodes, and point the copies at the unchanged subtrees of the old version: Inserting 45 into the tree with keys 20, 30, 40, 50 and 70: v2 created four nodes (50', 30', 40' and 45); everything else is shared. Both roots remain valid. In a balanced tree, the copied root-to-leaf route is only as long as the tree is tall: So each update costs O(log n) time and memory: about 20 new nodes per insertion into a million-key tree, instead of copying a million. This only holds if the tree stays balanced; a badly unbalanced tree would copy a path as long as the whole chain. Other techniques: Fat nodes: each field stores a list of (version, value) pairs. Reads binary-search for the version. Good for partial persistence. Driscoll, Sarnak, Sleator and Tarjan (1989) showed how to make linked structures with a constant number of fields per node and bounded in-degree persistent with O(1) amortised extra space per primitive field-update step. A whole operation may contain many such steps. Key takeaways Copy the changed path and share untouched subtrees. Logarithmic update overhead requires a balanced tree and immutable shared nodes. Further reading Sparse Table — cp-algorithms Range minimum query — Wikipedia Persistent data structure — Wikipedia Rope (data structure) — Wikipedia) Text Buffer Reimplementation — VS Code blog Making Data Structures Persistent

sum: Subtract two prefix versions’ counts to query one array slice.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. What persistence buys you Cheap undo and snapshots: retaining roots keeps historical nodes alive. Selecting a previous root is O(1), but storing history and reclaiming it have costs. Safe sharing between threads: immutable, safely published nodes need no mutation locks for readers. Publishing roots and keeping nodes alive still require the language's synchronisation and memory-reclamation rules. Queries on history: a persistent segment tree over value ranks, with one version per array prefix, answers "k-th smallest value in a[l..r]" in O(log n), with n the array length. It subtracts one version's counts from another's, node by node (shown below). In the worked lines, a = [5, 2, 4, 7] and v covers the values 1 to 4: the four elements a[0..3] contain two such values (2 and 4), a[0] contains none, so the slice a[1..3] has 2. Walking down, the query goes left when the left child's count is at least k and right otherwise. It needs a static array; changing an element would change every later version. Where you meet it Functional languages: Haskell, Clojure, Scala and Erlang default to immutable collections. Clojure’s vectors use a wide branching tree plus a tail buffer; hash maps use hash-array mapped tries with collision handling and specialised small forms. Path copying shares unchanged structure. For an idealised full 32-way tree, the height estimate is: In a model of full-width array nodes, copying six 32-slot nodes moves roughly 192 references. Actual Clojure copies depend on tails, occupied branches and hash collisions; this is not a universal copy count. Git: a commit points to a tree of blobs. Changing one file creates new blob and tree objects up the path to the root; unchanged subtrees are shared by hash. That is path copying. Databases and filesystems: LMDB and Btrfs use copy-on-write trees. Retaining old pages supports snapshots; publication, reader coordination and page reclamation still follow each system's synchronisation rules. Persistence vs MVCC PostgreSQL's MVCC keeps old row versions for concurrent transactions, which is persistence at the row level, but it is not path copying: it keeps old row versions in the table's own storage and cleans them up with VACUUM. LMDB's copy-on-write B-tree is the closer analogue. Key takeaways Subtract two prefix versions’ counts to query one array slice. Root publication and memory reclamation still need coordination even when nodes are immutable. sum: Rope leaves hold chunks; internal weights count left-subtree characters.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. Ropes Inserting into a single flat text buffer can copy or shift a large part of a 100 MB document. The amount depends on the representation and edit position. A rope (Boehm, Atkinson and Plass, 1995) stores the text as a binary tree whose leaves hold short string chunks. Each internal node stores a rope weight: the total length of its left subtree. Indexing To find character i, compare it with the weight: go left if smaller, otherwise subtract the weight and go right. Tracing char_at(root, 10) on the rope above: Character 10 of Hello_my_name_is_Simon is indeed a. The cost is one step per level, so a balanced rope finds any character in O(log n) steps for n characters. Key takeaways Rope leaves hold chunks; internal weights count left-subtree characters. A right descent subtracts the skipped left-subtree length from the index. t: Rope edits, balancing and practical trade-offs
sum: Split and concatenate around edits while maintaining balance.
x: Here n is the array length, tree size or text length specified in the section. Big-O costs assume fixed-size summaries and constant-time word operations. Operations Here n is the length of the text in characters and m the number of characters inserted: Operation Flat string Balanced rope --------- Index O(1) O(log n) Concatenate O(n) O(log n) Insert m new characters O(n + m) O(log n + m) Delete a range O(n) Implementation-dependent Iterate all O(n) O(n) These bounds assume balanced trees and bounded leaf sizes, and constant-time character indexing in the flat representation. UTF-8 byte offsets and Unicode character positions need additional care. Inserting new text must read/copy its m characters; deletion can also incur work to reclaim removed nodes. Concatenation creates a new root over two ropes, then rebalances. Insert is split at the position, then two concatenations. Immutable rope nodes can share unchanged structure between versions, making undo history proportional to changed paths plus inserted text. Retaining roots keeps that shared storage alive. Real-world use Editors: the Xi editor and Zed use rope-like B-trees of text chunks. VS Code instead uses a piece table stored in a red–black tree (the "piece tree"), which records edits as references into the original file and an append-only buffer. Both avoid copying the document on each keystroke. Libraries: the SGI STL shipped rope, and Rust crates such as ropey provide them. Ropes are not always better. For short strings, pointer overhead and lost cache locality can outweigh the editing benefit. Chunking keeps substantial work on contiguous memory; chunk sizes are implementation and workload choices, rather than a universal recommendation. Shared-node and balancing pitfalls Mutating a "persistent" node: one in-place write corrupts every version sharing that node. Persistence relies on discipline or immutable types. Unbalanced ropes: repeated appends without rebalancing make a chain with O(n) indexing, where n is the number of leaves. Key takeaways Split and concatenate around edits while maintaining balance. Read or copy inserted characters and account for reclamation and pointer overhead. sum: Read a sample record’s timing and distinguish its last timestamp from its duration.
x: A signal records how a quantity changes. A sensor might measure temperature over time; a synthetic test might contain plain numbers with no physical unit. Digital signal processing (DSP) changes or analyses such sequences of values. A sample is one value. A sample index counts positions, starting at zero here; it is not itself a time in seconds. A record such as [2, 4, 1, 3] contains four samples. Its third value has index 2 because counting starts at zero. The values alone do not say whether the measurements are a second apart or a millisecond apart. From count to seconds For uniform sampling, consecutive values are separated by the same sample period. The sample rate counts samples per second. A higher rate means shorter gaps. This course assumes an exact constant rate unless stated otherwise. At 4 samples per second, four samples starting at zero have timestamps 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 seconds. Interpreting the same values at twice the rate halves every gap and makes the record pass twice as quickly. Keep the rate, start time and physical units with the data. Real-world analogy: Regular snapshots Imagine taking a photograph every quarter of a second. How it maps: Each photograph is a sample; its position in the stack is its index. The schedule supplies its time. Where it stops: A sample need not be an image, and equally spaced measurements do not guarantee that fast motion between them can be recovered. Duration versus timestamp span For a non-empty record, this course calls the number of sample periods represented by the record its record duration. The last period ends one interval after the final timestamp. The timestamp span measures only the gap between the first and last sample. State which one an application needs. Those four samples represent a one-second record interval, although the last timestamp is 0.75 seconds. Four sample periods fill that interval; the recorded instants have only three gaps. Adding a sample at exactly one second would start the next interval rather than fill a missing slot in the first. This half-open interval includes its start and excludes its end. A one-sample record has one period of duration and zero timestamp span. An empty record has no first or last timestamp. The reference relationships below collect the timing rules. They assume a non-empty, uniformly sampled record whose first timestamp is zero. Timing metadata does not reveal everything that happened between measurements. Irregular measurements need their actual timestamps rather than one assumed rate. Key takeaways A sample index is a position; the sample rate converts it to time. Record duration counts sample periods, while timestamp span counts gaps. Keep timing and physical units alongside a numerical array. Further reading Steven W. Smith: signal values and sample indices

sum: Describe a sampled sinusoid using amplitude, frequency and phase.
x: A sinusoid is a smooth repeating wave described by sine or cosine. It is useful as a controlled test signal: its amplitude, frequency and timing can be varied separately. Amplitude here means the maximum magnitude of the ideal wave relative to its centre. Frequency counts cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz). A 2 Hz wave repeats twice per second. Phase tells us where in the cycle a wave starts. An angle in radians measures arc length divided by radius. A full turn is twice pi radians; pi is about 3.14159. A quarter turn is half pi radians. At zero starting phase, sine starts at zero and rises; cosine starts at its positive maximum. A wave sampled at regular instants Imagine sampling one complete cycle at four equally spaced positions. A unit-amplitude sine starting at zero phase gives approximately [0, 1, 0, -1]. The next sample begins the next cycle. Changing amplitude scales the height without changing the repetition rate. Changing frequency changes how far through a cycle each new sample advances. Changing starting phase chooses a different starting point without changing that advance. A quarter-turn starting phase makes this sine start at its positive maximum. A finite set of samples need not hit the ideal wave’s maximum. Its largest recorded sample can therefore be smaller than the stated amplitude. That alone does not show that the generator used the wrong amplitude. This reference expression describes the same three controls for a sampled sine: Real-world analogy: A hand on a clock Picture a hand turning at a steady rate. How it maps: Its turning rate represents frequency and its starting direction represents phase. The vertical height of its tip behaves like a sine wave. Where it stops: The rotating hand is a geometric aid; a measured signal does not need to be a physical rotating object. Frequency per sample Normalised frequency must name its convention. Here it means cycles per sample; some other texts instead use radians per sample or a fraction of the Nyquist frequency. Never transfer a bare number between these conventions. One cycle every four sample intervals means one quarter of a cycle per sample. At a fixed frequency in hertz, sampling more often reduces the advance between samples. At a fixed cycles-per-sample frequency, interpreting the same sequence at a higher sample rate makes it repeat faster in physical time. Always keep the sample rate with a test signal. A waveform’s appearance alone cannot establish its frequency in hertz, and sampling can make different continuous waves look identical, as the next lesson explains. Key takeaways Amplitude controls height, frequency controls repetition and phase controls the cycle’s starting point. Recorded samples can miss the ideal wave’s maximum. Always label a normalised-frequency convention. Further reading Steven W. Smith: relevant chapter

sum: Recognise aliases and place anti-alias filtering before sampling.
x: Uniform samples can agree even when their underlying continuous waves differ. This ambiguity is aliasing. Once two possible inputs produce the same samples, analysing those samples alone cannot tell which input occurred. Sampling faster is useful only if it is fast enough for the signal content arriving at the sampler. Keep baseband content below half the rate A baseband signal occupies frequencies from zero up to some highest frequency. A band-limited ideal signal has no content above that limit. The Nyquist frequency is half the sample rate. To preserve arbitrary phase at the upper edge of this baseband signal, its highest frequency must stay strictly below that boundary: Why exclude the endpoint? A sine at exactly half the sample rate, with zero starting phase, is sampled at its zero crossings. Every sample is zero in exact arithmetic. A cosine at that same frequency alternates positive and negative values. Merely having two samples per cycle does not preserve every possible phase and amplitude at the boundary. A finite record is also not the infinite sequence assumed by ideal reconstruction theory. The condition prevents spectral overlap for the ideal band-limited case; it does not promise recovery of arbitrary data from a few samples. An explicit fold At 1000 samples per second, a 700 Hz cosine produces the same samples as a 300 Hz cosine, with equal amplitude and zero starting phase. The higher frequency appears below the 500 Hz Nyquist limit. If both tones arrive together, their stored contributions overlap: a later analysis cannot reliably assign the combined values back to the two original tones. In this frequency interval the alias behaves like a reflection around half the sample rate. Higher frequencies can fold repeatedly, and phase can change during folding. The example specifies cosine and starting phase to avoid suggesting that every sine keeps its original sign. Real-world analogy: A wheel in a film A wheel turning quickly can appear to turn slowly or backwards in regularly spaced film frames. How it maps: The frames sample position. Different numbers of turns between frames can produce the same visible positions, just as different frequencies can produce the same samples. Where it stops: A real wheel has visual features and exposure blur. The DSP claim concerns mathematical sample values, not every detail of a video. Prevent the ambiguity before it happens An analogue anti-alias filter reduces high-frequency content before an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) takes samples. Real filters need a transition band, so leave room between wanted frequencies and the Nyquist limit. The filter reduces unwanted content to an acceptable level rather than forming an ideal brick-wall cutoff. A digital filter after this sampling step cannot separate a wanted 300 Hz component from a 700 Hz component already folded onto it. When later reducing a digital sample rate, filtering must likewise precede the rate reduction. Key takeaways Different continuous frequencies can produce identical samples. Use a strict upper frequency margin and account for real anti-alias filter transitions. Filtering must act before the sampling operation that would cause the alias. Further reading Steven W. Smith: relevant chapter MIT 6.003: sampling theorem and aliasing

sum: Separate rounding to levels from losing values beyond the range.
x: Sampling chooses times. Quantisation chooses representable amplitude levels. These are different restrictions: increasing the sample rate does not make the amplitude steps finer. A digital value may represent volts, temperature or a unitless normalised amplitude; know the conversion before interpreting its size. A bit has two possible states. Three bits can label eight different codes. The voltage range, coding and rounding rules still need specification: a bit count alone does not define a complete converter. Small rounding errors and lost peaks Imagine a toy quantiser with levels spaced by 0.25, from −1 to 0.75. An input of 0.30 rounds to 0.25. Small input changes can leave the output unchanged until it crosses the boundary to the next level. Finer steps can preserve smaller amplitude changes within the available range. An exact halfway input needs a stated tie rule. If this toy chooses the more positive neighbour, −0.375 becomes −0.25 rather than −0.5. Another rule could choose differently. Specify the spacing, endpoints and rounding rule before predicting exact output values; the bit count alone is insufficient. For nearest-level rounding without range limiting, error magnitude is at most half a step. That bound does not protect over-range inputs. Clipping, also called saturation, caps excessive values at an endpoint. In this toy, inputs of 1.0 and 1.5 both become 0.75. Their different peak heights are lost. Real-world analogy: Marks and ends on a ruler A short ruler has marked divisions and also a final endpoint. How it maps: Rounding a length to the nearest mark resembles quantisation. Reporting every length beyond the ruler as its maximum resembles clipping. Where it stops: Real measurements can have other errors; the ruler comparison does not make quantisation error random or independent. Choose the remedy for the problem If small changes disappear between amplitude levels, consider finer quantisation over the required range. Increasing sample rate alone changes the time spacing, not those levels. Increasing bit depth can provide more levels, but the chosen input range still matters. If peaks reach the endpoint, reduce input gain before the range-limited stage or choose an appropriate input range. Making an already clipped record quieter only shrinks its flat peaks; it cannot infer their original heights. Quantisation error also depends on the signal and rounding scheme. A repeated input can produce a repeated error, so do not automatically treat that error as independent white noise. These lessons distinguish the mechanisms rather than assuming a noise model that fits every input. Key takeaways Sampling selects times; quantisation selects amplitude levels. Specify the grid, endpoints and tie rule before predicting a quantiser. Clipping can cause errors far larger than half a step and loses information. Further reading Steven W. Smith: relevant chapter

sum: Measure a finite record’s offset and overall level with the correct units.
x: One number cannot describe every property of a signal. A sensor record can have a steady offset, a fluctuating component and occasional large excursions. Record mean, peak magnitude and root mean square (RMS) answer different questions. This lesson uses a non-empty finite record of real values; these are exact record descriptions, not estimates of an unknown infinite process. Mean and DC offset The mean adds all samples and divides by the count. DC originally means direct current; in DSP a DC component is a constant offset. The record mean is the constant you subtract to centre that record at zero. For [1, 3] volts the mean is 2 volts and the centred samples are [-1, 1] volts. The offset might be unwanted sensor bias, or it might be the actual quantity being measured. Do not remove it automatically. A short slice of a changing signal can have a nonzero mean without the underlying source having a permanent offset. Peak and RMS Peak magnitude is the largest absolute sample value. RMS squares the samples, averages the squares and takes a square root. Squaring prevents positive and negative values cancelling. The final root restores the original units. Mean zero does not mean no signal. A record alternating between −1 and +1 volt has zero mean, but its RMS is 1 volt. The signs cancel in the mean; they do not cancel when squared. Adding a constant offset increases this record’s RMS even though its fluctuations around its own mean stay the same. Real-world analogy: A commuter around home A commuter travels equal distances east and west of home. Their average signed position can be home even though they spend time far from it. How it maps: Mean uses signed positions, which can cancel. RMS measures distance from zero using squares, so opposite signs cannot erase the excursions. Peak records the farthest position reached. Where it stops: RMS is a particular squared-distance measure, not the average distance travelled or the length of the journey. These reference expressions show how mean and RMS treat the same record differently: Choose the measurement for the decision Use mean to examine offset, peak to check stored excursions against a limit, and RMS to describe overall squared level. Records with the same RMS can have different peaks, so an RMS limit alone does not guarantee freedom from clipping. Use the same measurement window when comparing records. RMS has a connection to physical power only with a specified model, such as voltage across a fixed resistor. Squared temperature values are not automatically watts. Peak sample magnitude also need not equal the maximum of a continuous waveform between sampling instants. Key takeaways Mean describes offset; subtracting it changes the measured signal. Peak checks extremes; RMS includes both offset and fluctuations. Mean, peak and RMS retain the original signal units. Further reading Steven W. Smith: relevant chapter

sum: Interpret level changes by naming the measured quantity and its reference.
x: A decibel (dB) expresses a ratio on a logarithmic scale. It makes large ratios manageable and turns successive multiplicative gains into additive level changes. A bare decibel value is incomplete unless you know what is compared: power, amplitude, or a level relative to a named reference. Zero decibels means equal numerator and reference, not silence. Negative decibels mean the numerator is smaller than its reference. They do not mean a negative amplitude or negative physical power. Power and amplitude are different For positive powers, a tenfold increase is +10 dB and a tenfold decrease is −10 dB. For amplitude magnitudes such as voltage, a tenfold increase is +20 dB. Do not apply an amplitude rule to a power ratio. The different scales agree when power is proportional to amplitude squared with the same proportionality factor. For example, halving an RMS voltage across the same resistance quarters the power; both describe about a 6 dB decrease. Across different resistances, the voltage ratio alone does not establish the power ratio. The reference expressions use a logarithm, which asks which power of ten produces a ratio. They are useful for converting a measured ratio, rather than memorising separate answers for every possible change. For positive amplitude magnitudes of the same kind, the conventional amplitude-ratio expression uses twenty: Successive gains add as decibel changes: a 6 dB increase followed by a 6 dB decrease returns to the original level if the stages apply those gains without clipping or other changes. That does not mean adding the decibel readings of two separate signals predicts their mixed level; their timing and phase also matter. Do not compare peak amplitude to an RMS reference without saying so. A reference of 1 volt RMS produces a different statement from a reference of 1 unitless peak amplitude, even if both ratios happen to have the same number. Zero and digital full scale The logarithm of zero has no finite real value. As a positive amplitude approaches zero, its decibel level decreases without a finite lower limit. For a display, report silence separately or choose and label a display floor. A floor is a display policy, not a measured nonzero signal. dBFS means decibels relative to digital full scale. Metering conventions differ, especially for RMS sine references. In this course’s simple unitless peak meter, full-scale peak magnitude is 1 and the amplitude reference is that same value. A peak of 0.5 is about −6 dB relative to full-scale peak. This definition does not assert a universal sine-RMS convention. Write the ratio and reference in measurement reports so another person can reproduce the level. Key takeaways Use ten for power ratios and twenty for amplitude ratios under the stated interpretation. Name the reference and whether amplitude means peak or RMS. Zero needs deliberate handling; a display floor is a policy. Further reading Steven W. Smith: power and amplitude decibels Analog Devices AN-938: full-scale and RMS conventions

sum: Change values and timing while stating what happens at record edges.
x: Many DSP tasks begin with simple operations: scale one record, add two records, or shift a record in time. Specify units and timing before combining arrays. Adding a temperature in degrees to an acceleration in metres per second squared has no physical meaning without an explicit model or conversion. Scale and mix aligned records Gain multiplies every sample by a factor. A negative gain reverses polarity, swapping positive and negative values. Mixing here means adding aligned samples, possibly with separate gains. It does not mean interleaving two arrays or appending one after another. For the unitless records [1, -1] and [1, 1], adding corresponding values gives [2, 0]. Equal positive samples reinforce; opposite samples cancel. Two records each within a normalised limit of 1 can therefore sum beyond that limit. Scaling before a range-limited output provides headroom, a margin below the allowed peak. For example, reducing both inputs before mixing can leave room for aligned peaks. Reducing gain after a range-limited stage has already clipped does not restore the original sum. The point at which gain is applied matters. Equal array lengths alone do not establish that timestamps agree. Two sensors can store the same number of values at different rates or with different starting times. Align what each position represents before adding it. Appending one record after another is concatenation, a different operation from mixing. Delay with explicit boundaries A sample delay makes an event occur later. For an integer delay, retrieve an earlier input value at each output index. This lesson treats values outside the finite input record as zero, called zero extension. For input [1, 2, 3] and a two-sample delay, retaining only three output samples gives [0, 0, 1]. Retaining the complete delayed finite record gives [0, 0, 1, 2, 3]. This is a storage choice: the last two original values were cropped in the short output, not destroyed by the delay itself. A delay measured in samples needs a sample rate to become a time. At a higher rate, the same number of delayed samples represents a shorter wait. A pure delay changes when events occur without changing their order or playing them more slowly. Real-world analogy: A recording with a later start Imagine placing a recorded announcement two seconds later on a timeline. How it maps: A delay changes the announcement’s position. Saving only the original time window can crop the end, while extending the timeline retains it. Where it stops: This models a pure shift, not echoes, speed changes or the physical propagation of sound. Shifting values from the end back to the start would be a circular shift, a different boundary convention. It can create a value at the beginning where a delayed recording should still be silent. Fractional-sample delay requires estimating values between sample positions and is outside this lesson. Key takeaways Mixing adds aligned compatible samples; gains control their contributions. Sample addition can exceed individual input peaks. State the delay’s boundary convention and whether the output retains its tail. Further reading Steven W. Smith: relevant chapter

sum: Read real and imaginary parts, magnitude, conjugation and a rotating phasor.
x: A complex number stores two real components in one mathematical object. The real part lies on a horizontal axis and the imaginary part lies on a perpendicular vertical axis. Imaginary does not mean erroneous or physically impossible: it names a second mathematical direction. DSP uses these pairs to retain the strength and phase of sinusoidal components. Two coordinates, one number The imaginary unit is the number whose square is negative one. Engineers often write it as j. Think of the components as coordinates, rather than two ordinary magnitudes to add. The complex magnitude is the straight-line distance from the origin. Its units are the same as the components’ units. For a real part of 3 and an imaginary part of 4, the magnitude is 5, not 7. Adding complex values instead adds the two real parts and the two imaginary parts separately. The complex conjugate keeps the real part and reverses the imaginary part’s sign. Our example becomes real part 3 and imaginary part −4. It reflects across the real axis while keeping the same magnitude. These reference expressions collect the coordinate rules: Real-world analogy: Directions on a map A location three blocks east and four blocks north has two coordinates. Its straight-line distance from the starting point is five blocks. How it maps: The two map directions represent real and imaginary components. Reflecting north to south resembles complex conjugation. Where it stops: Complex multiplication has specific rotation and scaling rules; map coordinates alone do not explain all complex arithmetic. A rotating phasor A phasor represents a magnitude and a phase angle together. Picture an arrow from the origin to a complex point. Its length is magnitude and its direction is phase. When an arrow of fixed length rotates, its horizontal and vertical components change even though its magnitude does not. One component alone therefore cannot describe the complete arrow. At one cycle per four samples, starting along the positive real axis, the phasor visits right, up, left and down. Its real part follows cosine, its imaginary part follows sine. Reversing the imaginary sign reverses the direction of rotation. Later Fourier lessons use complex weights to compare data against such rotations; no transform knowledge is needed yet. The zero complex number has magnitude zero but no unique direction. An angle returned for zero by software should not be treated as evidence of a meaningful physical phase. Key takeaways A complex number has real and imaginary components. Magnitude combines perpendicular components; conjugation flips the imaginary sign. A rotating phasor packages cosine and sine while retaining phase information. Further reading Steven W. Smith: relevant chapter

sum: Interpret a sliding template match without mistaking a large score for proof.
x: Cross-correlation scores how well a known template matches data at different shifts. A distinctive sensor pulse may be recognisable even when its starting position is unknown. At each shift, multiply aligned values and add them. A strong positive score can indicate a positive match, but raw score also depends on amplitude, offset and overlap length. Define the lag before interpreting it This lesson uses real, unitless finite sequences and the sign convention of SciPy’s correlate(data, template). Treat values outside either stored record as zero. Lag is the integer shift of the template relative to the data origin; a positive lag places the template’s start later in the data. For data [0, 0, 1, -1, 0] and template [1, -1], the complete pattern starts at data index 2. The best positive match is therefore at lag +2 samples. At that position, positive aligns with positive and negative with negative; both products contribute positively. Shifting the template one place either way aligns opposite signs and gives a negative score. For complex inputs, SciPy conjugates the shifted template before multiplying. Conjugation reverses the imaginary sign; it leaves a real template unchanged, so the real-valued example needs no extra operation. Reversing the input order reverses the lag interpretation. Never guess the sign from the word correlation alone. Real-world analogy: Sliding a transparent pattern Slide a transparent strip with a distinctive pattern across a longer strip and look for alignment. How it maps: The short strip is the template; its position is lag. Correlation combines agreement over corresponding positions into one score. Where it stops: Numerical products allow negative values, amplitude weighting and cancellation. A visual match alone does not define those arithmetic rules. Do not assume that the position in a returned score array is the lag. Full correlation includes partial overlaps before the template reaches the data’s start, so its lag labels can begin below zero. Obtain the labels explicitly; SciPy provides correlation_lags for this purpose. Similarity is not a guarantee Doubling the data amplitude doubles every raw score, including negative scores. An increased peak therefore does not necessarily mean a closer match in shape. A large DC offset can dominate scores when the template has a nonzero mean. Subtracting appropriate means can help compare fluctuating shape, but also changes what is being detected. Normalising by the overlapping magnitudes can reduce amplitude dependence. The method must specify which overlap is measured and what happens when it contains only zeros, where division by its magnitude would fail. No such normalisation is applied here. At extreme full-mode lags only a few samples overlap. Their scores are not automatically comparable to a full-template overlap. valid mode excludes positions requiring zero padding, provided the data is at least as long as the template. Repeated patterns or noise can produce misleading peaks; report ambiguity rather than assuming a single physical delay. Correlation compares a sliding template in its original order. Convolution, introduced next module, uses a reversal in the sliding sum and describes how a system combines shifted responses. They share arithmetic ingredients but have different index definitions and purposes. Key takeaways State input order, lag convention and record boundaries. Obtain lag labels explicitly rather than using an output array index. Raw correlation depends on shape, amplitude, offset and overlap; a peak is evidence to interpret. Further reading SciPy: correlation definition and boundary modes SciPy: explicit correlation lag labels

t: Two tests for a predictable system
sum: Test linearity and time invariance, and understand why initial state belongs in the assumptions.
x: A discrete-time system takes an input sequence and produces an output sequence. Multiplying every sensor reading by two is a system. So is smoothing several readings or clipping values above a limit. Before choosing a filter, ask which mathematical shortcuts its behaviour permits. Linearity means preserving combinations A linear system preserves scaling and addition together. Processing a mixture must give the same result as processing its components separately and then mixing their outputs with the same weights. This property is superposition. It must hold for every allowed pair of inputs and every allowed constant weight; one successful example cannot prove it. Think of two sensors feeding a mixer. A linear filter lets you filter each sensor separately and then mix, or mix first and filter once, with the same result. This is useful because a complicated signal can be understood through simpler components. It is a property of the processing rule, not a claim that the output graph looks like a straight line. The optional notation records that same test for entire sequences. Doubling every reading passes this test. Squaring fails because doubling an input makes its squared result four times as large, rather than twice as large. Adding a constant offset also fails: zero input produces a nonzero output. Zero input producing zero output is necessary for linearity, though it is not a sufficient test by itself. Clipping is another common failure: a quiet mixture may pass unchanged while a louder mixture hits the limit. Time invariance means the same rule later A time-invariant system gives an equally shifted output when its entire input is shifted. A fixed one-sample delay passes: sending a pulse three samples later moves the delayed pulse three samples later too. Multiplying each sample by its absolute sample index fails: an identical pulse gets a different gain when it arrives later. Linearity and time invariance are separate tests. A fixed squaring operation is time invariant but nonlinear. Multiplication by the sample index is linear but time varying. A system that passes both is linear time-invariant, or LTI. Fixed weighted sums of present and past inputs are important examples. Real-world analogy: an unchanged recipe Doubling two ingredients and combining batches works predictably when the recipe scales consistently. Preparing the same batch tomorrow should also give the same result. How it maps: Scaling and combining batches suggest linearity; applying the same recipe on a later day suggests time invariance. Where it stops: Real cooking is rarely linear. Temperature, vessel size and chemical changes can break both predictions. Include the initial state Filters may remember earlier samples. Zero state means their stored history is initially zero. An input/output linearity test must include that assumption: a filter already holding a nonzero output can respond even to zero new input. For time-shift comparisons, shift the complete input history and use the corresponding zero-state setup. Restarting a device midway through one run changes the experiment. Likewise, finite-array truncation can hide a delayed output; compare the whole relevant output, including its tail. Key takeaways Linearity preserves weighted combinations; time invariance preserves shifts. One counterexample disproves either property. State and record boundaries must be part of an LTI claim. Further reading Smith: linear systems, Chapter 5 Julius O. Smith: LTI digital filters

t: Learn a system from one impulse
sum: Use an isolated unit impulse to reveal an LTI system's weights, memory and causality.
x: A unit impulse is a discrete sequence containing 1 at sample zero and 0 everywhere else, including negative sample indices. It is a single nonzero sample, rather than a narrow continuous-time spike of unspecified height. The impulse response is the output produced by this input when a system starts at rest. For an LTI system, it tells us how every input sample contributes to future output. Each sample can be viewed as its own scaled, shifted impulse. Linearity lets us add their responses; time invariance lets us shift the same response to each arrival time. Reveal the weights Consider a system that takes three quarters of the present reading and one quarter of the previous reading, then adds them. All input values before sample zero are zero. The impulse produces 0.75 at sample zero, 0.25 at sample one, then zeros. That two-sample response exposes the two weights directly. A pulse with amplitude 4 produces 3, then 1. A pulse arriving five samples later produces that same pair five samples later. The output depends on both the pulse and what the system remembers, so the system must start in zero state for this interpretation. This reveals filter memory without a long test signal. The first response value tells you how much acts immediately; later values show how an input continues to matter. Here the influence ends after two outputs. Other systems have longer responses, including tails that decay without reaching exact zero in the mathematical model. For an established LTI system, doubling a pulse doubles its whole response, and delaying the pulse delays the whole response. If either prediction fails, the measured response cannot serve as one fixed description of all its behaviour. Causality is about available information A causal system uses only present and past inputs. For a zero-state LTI system this means its impulse response is zero at every negative sample index. It cannot produce a response before the impulse arrives. A filter that needs tomorrow's sensor reading is noncausal in a live stream, although a saved recording may make that future sample available for offline processing. Real-world analogy: a single clap A clap in a room is followed by reflections that become quieter over time. How it maps: The isolated event is the test input; the sequence of reflections suggests how a system can spread one event through time. Where it stops: A clap is not an exact discrete unit impulse, and a real room measurement includes the microphone, source and background noise. It does not prove the room is LTI. What one experiment cannot establish An impulse response fully characterises an already established LTI system under its initial-state assumptions. It does not prove an unknown system is linear or time invariant. A clipper may look like an unchanged connection for a small impulse yet distort larger signals. A changing system may respond differently tomorrow. A short measurement can also miss a long, quiet tail. Key takeaways A discrete unit impulse has one sample of amplitude 1 and zeros elsewhere. Its zero-state response characterises an LTI system. Causality excludes response before the input; one test cannot prove LTI behaviour. Further reading Julius O. Smith: impulse-response representation Smith: convolution and impulse responses, Chapter 6

sum: Predict convolution by following overlapping responses, including zero extension and the output tail.
x: Linear convolution combines an input with an impulse response to predict the output of a zero-state LTI system. Each input sample launches a scaled copy of the response. When copies overlap, add their contributions. Unlike correlation, convolution models a system's response; it is not a template-similarity score. First add the copies Suppose each input reading contributes its full value immediately and half its value one sample later. A single reading of 2 therefore produces 2 now and 1 next time. If another reading arrives before that response ends, the new response overlaps the old one. The output at that moment includes both contributions; the newer reading does not erase the earlier reading's influence. There are two useful views of the same operation. Follow one input forward to see every output it affects, or stand at one output position and collect the input contributions that reach it. Keeping the timing aligned is what makes these views agree. The last output remains after the final nonzero input. That filter tail is part of full convolution. This is linear convolution with zero extension: values outside either stored sequence are treated as zero. There is no wrapping from one end of an array to the other. Real-world analogy: overlapping payment plans Each purchase creates a payment today and a smaller payment next month. Several purchases can contribute to the same month's bill. How it maps: A purchase maps to an input sample; its fixed payment pattern maps to the impulse response. Adding the bills due in one month maps to adding overlapping contributions at one output sample. Where it stops: Real payment plans can include fees or changing terms. Convolution here assumes the same fixed linear response to every input, and sample values may also be negative. Keep the tail and the timing If an input record contains four readings and each reading launches a three-position response, the last reading still has two positions of influence left after the record ends. Full convolution keeps those positions. Some may happen to contain zero; the full output length describes positions, not a count of nonzero values. The optional reference below writes the output-side view. It also gives the full array length for two nonempty finite sequences. Choose which outputs to retain NumPy's convolve with mode="full" computes this discrete linear convolution for one-dimensional arrays. Other modes select fewer output positions; they do not create a physically different filter. Always choose which part of the full result your application needs. In particular, “same” length is an array-selection policy, not a guarantee of causal alignment. Key takeaways Convolution adds shifted, scaled impulse responses. Finite linear convolution uses zeros beyond the records and preserves a tail. State the output mode and alignment whenever comparing implementations. Further reading Smith: convolution, Chapter 6 NumPy: convolve and its boundary modes

t: Smooth a stream with a moving average
sum: Build a causal moving average and distinguish smoothing, startup effects and delay.
x: A moving average gives equal weight to a fixed number of neighbouring samples. It can reduce rapid fluctuations when the useful quantity changes slowly. For a live sensor stream, choose present and past samples so the operation is causal. A centred average on a saved recording is a different timing choice because it also uses future samples. A three-sample average This causal version includes the present reading and two older ones. It starts with zero history, and its divisor stays three even during startup. At every update, add the current reading and the two previous readings, then divide by three. When a new sample enters, the oldest leaves. A one-sample spike therefore affects three successive outputs before leaving the window completely. A sustained change gradually replaces every old reading. Suppose a sensor suddenly changes from zero to 6 and stays there. The first outputs are 2, 4 and 6. The filter needs three nonzero input samples to fill its window. This startup transient follows from the declared zero history; it is not a calculation error. A program that instead divides the first sum by one and the second by two outputs 6 immediately. That may be a useful boundary policy, but it is not the same fixed-coefficient LTI filter at the beginning of the record. Initialising past samples to the first reading also changes the initial state. Real-world analogy: a three-day spending average A daily dashboard averages today's spending with the previous two days. One expensive day affects three successive dashboard entries. How it maps: The sliding set of days maps to the filter's sample window; equal shares map to equal coefficients. A sharp event spreads across several outputs. Where it stops: Days without records are often omitted in a dashboard. This filter explicitly fills missing earlier history with zeros and keeps its divisor fixed. Smoothness has a timing cost The three coefficients are symmetric, so this filter has a linear phase response and a group delay of one sample wherever its frequency response is nonzero. Group delay describes how the phase changes across a small frequency interval. It does not mean every output sample is simply the input shifted by one place: smoothing changes amplitudes and shapes, and response sign changes can add phase jumps. At 100 samples per second, one sample is 0.01 seconds. An abrupt event spreads across three output samples. For an alarm, that spreading can matter more than how quiet the line looks on a plot. A longer average generally smooths more rapid variation and spreads a change over more samples. Choose a window by asking how much rapid fluctuation you can suppress while still noticing useful changes promptly. A quiet-looking trace can conceal a brief event that matters. If useful signal and interference occupy the same frequencies, averaging reduces both; it cannot recognise which source you wanted. The end of a stored record also needs a policy. Assuming later input is zero reveals a falling tail as the last readings leave the window. A live block boundary is different: the next block continues the signal, so its first outputs must still include the previous block's history. Key takeaways A causal moving average uses present and past readings. Zero history and a fixed divisor create a predictable startup transient. Smoothing changes amplitudes and timing; choose the window for the task. Further reading Smith: moving average filters, Chapter 15 Julius O. Smith: symmetric linear-phase filters

sum: Interpret steady-state gain and phase, and turn a vague smoothing goal into frequency requirements.
x: A filter can preserve a slowly varying trend while reducing faster oscillations. Its frequency response describes how a stable LTI system scales and shifts sinusoids at each frequency after startup effects have passed. Amplitude response gives the amplitude ratio; phase response gives the phase shift. A negative output value at one instant is not a negative amplitude ratio: amplitude ratios are nonnegative. A steady 7 Hz sinusoid remains a 7 Hz sinusoid after filtering, unless the response removes it completely. Half amplitude means a smaller oscillation, not a slower one. A phase shift moves the peaks within each cycle. Different input frequencies can receive different gains and shifts, so a mixture can change shape even though none of its steady sinusoidal components changes frequency. At a response zero, that frequency is cancelled completely and the output's phase is undefined. During startup, the stored history can add a transient, so measuring the first few output samples may give a misleading picture of steady-state response. Measure a simple response A two-sample equal-weight average passes a constant input unchanged once its history is filled. Slow changes make neighbouring readings similar, so averaging changes them relatively little. At half the sample rate, the readings alternate positive and negative with equal magnitude; each neighbouring pair cancels exactly. Between these cases, gain and phase vary with frequency. These different outcomes are the same fixed filter acting on different inputs. To investigate a filter, compare sustained test tones at several frequencies after startup, or evaluate its coefficients with a response tool. Record both amplitude and timing behaviour. A few measurements can illustrate the trend but do not prove that every frequency in a band meets a requirement. Specify useful and unwanted bands The passband is the frequency region intended to pass within a specified gain tolerance. The stopband is intended to be sufficiently reduced. The transition band lies between them. A low-pass filter passes low frequencies and reduces higher ones, but no finite filter here makes an instantaneous jump between perfect passage and perfect rejection. For a 100-sample-per-second sensor, an illustrative requirement might preserve 0–2 Hz within a chosen tolerance and strongly reduce frequencies above 15 Hz. The tolerated gain error and required reduction must also be stated before deciding whether a design succeeds. A moving average has cancellation frequencies but also unwanted lobes between them. Increasing its length does not turn it into a universal frequency separator. It also cannot recover information already lost to aliasing, and it reduces useful signal components occupying the same frequencies as unwanted noise. Define the task before choosing the filter. Key takeaways Stable LTI filtering changes steady-state sinusoidal amplitude and phase, not frequency. Startup behaviour must be excluded or modelled when measuring response. Passband, stopband, tolerances and timing requirements guide filter choice. Further reading Julius O. Smith: frequency response Julius O. Smith: steady sinusoidal response Smith: moving average frequency behaviour, Chapter 15

t: Design and inspect a small FIR filter
sum: Design a low-pass FIR, check its actual response, and account for symmetric-filter delay.
x: A finite impulse response, or FIR, filter has an impulse response that becomes exactly zero after a finite number of samples. A direct FIR implementation multiplies present and past inputs by fixed filter coefficients and adds them. Each coefficient is often called an FIR tap. A moving average is an FIR with equal taps; useful FIR filters need not use equal or positive coefficients. Ask a design tool a precise question Begin with requirements: which frequencies matter, how much their gain may vary, how strongly unwanted frequencies must be reduced, and how much delay is acceptable. A filter that makes a graph look smooth may still erase useful changes or delay an alarm too much. SciPy's signal.firwin designs FIR coefficients using the window method: it limits and shapes an ideal response's coefficient sequence. For example, you can request 31 taps, a Hamming window, a low-pass response and an explicit sample rate of 100 samples per second. The sample rate tells the tool how to interpret frequencies; this filter does not change how many samples arrive each second. The cutoff of 10 Hz is this API's half-amplitude point, approximately minus 6 dB, rather than a promise that every frequency below 10 Hz has gain 1. scale=True normalises this low-pass design to unity gain at DC. Always check an API's convention before treating a parameter as a passband edge. Inspect what was actually designed Use a tool such as freqz to evaluate the returned coefficients, then compare the measured gains with the requirements. Check the passband, transition and stopband rather than inspecting only the named cutoff. Four chosen frequencies establish the response at those points; they do not prove that the whole band meets a tolerance. Peaks between checked points can matter. Filter ripple is the unwanted variation of gain within a band. Increasing tap count with a comparable window usually narrows the transition; window choice trades transition width against ripple and stopband attenuation. More taps also require more work in a direct implementation and, for this symmetric design, introduce more delay. If a design fails, change the design choices and recheck; a reassuring parameter name is not evidence of success. Symmetry gives a specific delay Real, symmetric FIR coefficients give linear phase. Their group delay is constant wherever the response is nonzero and the phase can be followed continuously. This describes the slope of phase with frequency: frequency components locally share the same delay. It does not say their amplitudes are unchanged. Phase can jump when the corresponding zero-phase response changes sign, and phase is undefined at exact response zeros. The symmetry centre sets the delay. A causal symmetric 31-tap filter has a delay of 15 sample intervals, or 0.15 seconds at 100 samples per second. Adding more symmetric taps moves that centre farther into the past. The optional reference gives the general relationship. An even number of symmetric taps gives a half-integer delay in sample intervals, which is valid. Arbitrary FIR coefficients need not have constant group delay. Nor does “FIR” mean “zero delay”. Shifting a saved output backwards can align a recording, but cannot make future samples available to a live system or undo changed amplitudes. Startup and the finite tail still need a policy. Key takeaways FIR taps describe finite memory; a design parameter needs an API convention. Inspect response, including transition and ripple, against actual requirements. Real symmetric FIRs have a known group delay where their response is nonzero. Further reading SciPy: firwin design and cutoff convention SciPy: freqz response evaluation Julius O. Smith: symmetric linear-phase filters

t: A smoother that remembers its output
sum: Trace a one-pole feedback smoother and distinguish stored state from an FIR's finite history.
x: Feedforward paths use present or previous inputs. Feedback paths use previous outputs. With feedback, an input's influence can be passed forward repeatedly rather than ending after a fixed number of taps. An infinite impulse response, or IIR, filter can therefore have a theoretically endless impulse-response tail, even when that tail becomes extremely small. Mix a new reading with the old result A one-pole smoother keeps one previous output. Each update takes a share of the new reading and a share of that remembered output, with positive shares that add to one. The result becomes the remembered value for the next update. Unlike a moving average's fixed window, an older input fades gradually through repeated updates instead of leaving after a fixed number of samples. Here the coefficient names follow an explicit convention: the memory weight is on the previous output, and the complementary weight is on the current input. With equal shares, a sudden sustained change makes the output move halfway towards the new level at each update. More weight on the old output means a slower response and longer retention; more on the new input means a faster response and less smoothing. The optional recurrence records that convention precisely. With equal shares, the output approaches a sustained new level but does not reach it in a finite number of updates in exact arithmetic. This is different from a three-sample moving average, whose window eventually contains only the new level. Choose between them by considering both noise reduction and how promptly useful changes must be seen. After an isolated pulse, equal shares make the remaining output halve at each zero input. The decreasing tail explains the IIR name. A real computer eventually rounds very small changes away or encounters its representation limits; “infinite” describes the mathematical response, not an infinite array stored in memory. Real-world analogy: a slowly updated estimate A person revises an estimate halfway towards each new observation rather than replacing it immediately. How it maps: The old estimate maps to the previous output; the new observation maps to the current input. Repeated partial updates retain past information with decreasing influence. Where it stops: A person may change their judgement rules. This filter uses fixed numerical weights, and its state is exactly specified. Check the convention before implementing The previous output is the whole persistent state for this particular implementation. Resetting it at each input destroys the feedback history. Initialising it differently changes startup behaviour, so state must be part of the specification. SciPy's lfilter uses denominator coefficients with a subtraction convention. This same smoother is represented by numerator [0.5] and denominator [1.0, -0.5]. Copying a positive memory weight into the denominator without changing its sign gives a different filter. Other authors may call the current-input weight “alpha”; compare the recurrence, not just the name. This smoother needs little state, but its phase delay generally varies with frequency. Choosing IIR over a symmetric FIR changes more than coefficient count. Stability and numerical precision need separate attention next. Key takeaways Feedback reuses earlier outputs; a decaying influence can continue indefinitely. Name which weight multiplies which value before comparing coefficients. Resetting the remembered output changes the signal being computed. Further reading Julius O. Smith: the one-pole filter SciPy: lfilter coefficient and state conventions

sum: Separate bounded-output mathematics from overflow, coefficient rounding and finite test evidence.
x: Bounded-input bounded-output stability, or BIBO stability, means every bounded input produces a bounded output for the stated system and initial conditions. “Bounded” means there is a finite ceiling on absolute magnitude for all time; it does not mean “small enough for this particular computer type”.
