Here we analyse causal filters in zero state with exact arithmetic first. Why the convex smoother stays bounded The previous lesson's smoother uses positive weights that add to one. If the new reading and previous output both lie within a fixed magnitude bound, their weighted average stays inside it too. It cannot exceed both values or fall below both. Zero initial output starts inside the bound, so the same reasoning applies at the first update, the second and every later update. This proves a useful property for this specific normalised smoother. Negative feedback coefficients require a different magnitude argument. A fixed FIR with finitely many finite coefficients is also BIBO stable: each output adds only a fixed finite number of bounded contributions. A one-pole condition, with its scope Now consider a different rule: add the whole current input to a fixed multiple of the previous output. Here the input weight stays one; it is not reduced to complement the memory weight. Its filter pole is the memory multiplier: an existing disturbance is repeatedly multiplied by it. If the multiplier's magnitude is below one, old contributions shrink fast enough for every bounded input to give a bounded output. A negative multiplier can be stable too: its sign alternates the old contribution while its magnitude shrinks. This condition belongs to this specific one-pole rule; more complicated recursive filters need their own analysis. The optional reference records the rule and its strict stability boundary. At a multiplier of one, constant positive input accumulates without limit. At minus one, an alternating bounded input can likewise make the output's magnitude grow. Beyond either boundary, even a single impulse leaves a growing response. A finite test that happens to look quiet cannot prove stability for every bounded input: the choice of test signal and how long you observe it both matter. The computer is a separate constraint Numerical overflow occurs when a result exceeds a representation's range. A stable filter with gain 100 can still overflow a narrow integer type when a large bounded input arrives. Rounding error occurs because many values have no exact finite representation. Rounding coefficients can also change the implemented filter, so check its actual stored coefficients, especially near a stability boundary. For example, doubling is a stable mathematical operation: any finite input bound gives a finite output bound. A narrow integer representation can still fail to hold the doubled value. Depending on the arithmetic rules, overflow may wrap to an unexpected value, saturate at a limit or raise an error. None of those outcomes turns the exact mathematical gain into an unstable system; they show that the implementation needs a separate range check. Use suitable types, scaling, numerical range validation and representative stress inputs. Floating-point arithmetic also has finite precision and range. SciPy recommends second-order-section filtering for most general IIR tasks because it reduces numerical problems; our one-state example does not establish safety for high-order direct forms. Key takeaways Mathematical stability concerns all bounded inputs over unlimited time. The stated one-pole condition belongs to a specific nondegenerate recurrence. Stable mathematics does not eliminate representation limits or implementation errors. Further reading MIT: convolution models and BIBO stability Julius O. Smith: one-pole stability NumPy: numerical scalar types and overflow SciPy: filtering and numerical recommendations

sum: Preserve filter state between blocks and separate computation deadlines from total latency.
x: Devices and files often deliver samples in processing blocks rather than one at a time. A block boundary is a software boundary, not a break in the underlying signal. If coefficients, sample order and arithmetic stay the same, a sample-by-sample recurrence gives the same outputs regardless of how its input is divided into blocks, provided its filter state survives between them. Pass the state forward This complete Python example processes the one-pole smoother with a previous-output weight of 0.5. The function accepts its initial state and returns its final state alongside the output list. It does not reset itself secretly. Resetting the second block to zero produces two zeros there, losing the previous block's tail. This error often looks like a jump at every boundary. A direct FIR instead retains the required previous inputs; a library may store an equivalent transformed state. SciPy's lfilter exposes initial and final delay states as zi and zf. Retain its returned state in that API's representation; it is not generally just the last output sample. Real-world analogy: reading across pages Turning a page does not restart a story. You carry the relevant context into the next page. How it maps: Pages correspond to blocks; retained context corresponds to filter state. The amount printed on a page changes how the material is delivered, not its order or meaning. Where it stops: A digital filter needs a precisely defined finite state for these implementations, rather than a reader's flexible recollection. Decide what the end means Zero state is one explicit startup policy. Another initial state may be justified by known earlier history. At the end of a finite recording, full convolution of an FIR can be obtained by appending enough zeros to flush the tail: one fewer zero than its number of taps. Keep only as many outputs as the chosen policy requires. An IIR generally has no exact finite tail length. A finite application chooses a justified stopping tolerance or records a fixed additional duration. Do not flush with zeros between ordinary live blocks: the next block supplies the actual continuation. Startup, normal continuation and end-of-record handling are different decisions. A deadline is not total latency For a regular incoming stream, one block's sample duration gives a recurring processing interval. At 48000 samples per second, each 64-sample block represents about 1.33 milliseconds of stream time. Larger blocks arrive less often but contain more work; raising the sample rate while keeping the block size fixed makes the interval shorter. In a simple single-worker pipeline, sustained processing must keep up with this arrival interval, with margin for other work and scheduling variation. A worker that regularly takes longer accumulates a backlog even if each individual result is numerically correct. A host timing test cannot guarantee a real device will meet every deadline. End-to-end latency also includes collecting samples into buffers, queues, computation, filter delay and output hardware. Smaller blocks reduce some buffering delay but increase call overhead. State continuity establishes numerical correctness; timing measurements and a complete pipeline model address separate requirements. The Python example allocates lists and prints results to make state passing visible. It is a teaching example, not an audio callback to copy into a live device. Real-time callbacks need bounded work and must avoid operations such as allocation or console output that can take unpredictable time on their platform. Key takeaways Retain state across normal blocks and use explicit startup and tail policies. Processing block size should not alter the recurrence's numerical result. Processing budget, filter delay and end-to-end latency measure different things. Further reading SciPy: lfilter initial and final states Smith: convolution and output length, Chapter 6 PortAudio: processing callbacks and bounded work PortAudio: streams, buffers and buffering latency PortAudio: buffering, scheduling and timing model

sum: Turn a finite sample record into frequency components and label its bins correctly.
x: A time plot shows when samples rise and fall. A discrete Fourier transform, or DFT, describes that same finite record as a combination of regularly spaced sinusoidal patterns. Each frequency bin tests one of those patterns across the whole record. A strong match produces a large coefficient. Each coefficient is complex: its two parts preserve both magnitude and phase. The raw magnitude is not yet a calibrated tone amplitude. The fast Fourier transform, or FFT, is an efficient way to calculate these same DFT coefficients; it adds no observations. What a bin tells you Imagine comparing the samples with a steady oscillation. At the matching rhythm, contributions reinforce each other. At many mismatched rhythms, positive and negative contributions cancel. The DFT does this with both cosine and sine components, so it can also describe where the oscillation is within its cycle. Real-world analogy: checking a rhythm Clap at a chosen steady rhythm while watching a repeating movement. A matching rhythm stays aligned; a mismatched rhythm drifts. How it maps: Each DFT bin tests one rhythm across the full record. Adding contributions reinforces a matching pattern and cancels many mismatched ones. Where it stops: A DFT uses signed and complex arithmetic to measure phase as well as strength; simply counting claps cannot reproduce it. The transform describes the finite record exactly, within numerical error. It does not establish that a physical machine contains only the bin frequencies. A single tone between bins can produce several large coefficients. Do not count non-zero bins as separate physical oscillators. Label the frequency axis The sample rate sets the physical time scale. The transform length sets how many frequency positions share that scale. With no padding, recording more samples at the same rate gives closer bin labels. Changing the sample rate without updating the labels gives the wrong frequency axis. Eight samples taken at 800 samples per second give non-negative labels of 0, 100, 200, 300 and 400 Hz. These labels exist even when a bin's coefficient is zero. Choose the transform for the input For real input, the negative-frequency coefficients are complex conjugates of the positive-frequency coefficients: they carry redundant information. NumPy's rfft keeps the non-negative half. Interior coefficients can still be complex even though the samples are real. An even-length real record includes DC and an exact Nyquist endpoint; an odd-length record has no bin exactly at Nyquist. For arbitrary complex input, negative frequencies can hold independent information, so use the full fft. Use matching frequency-label functions. rfftfreq labels the real-input output; fftfreq labels the full output in stored order: zero, positive frequencies, then negative frequencies. For an even length, the full transform labels its Nyquist slot negative while the real-input transform labels it positive. Both describe the same sampled endpoint. Key takeaways A bin measures a pattern across a finite record; it is not proof of a separate physical tone. An FFT calculates a DFT efficiently, with no extra information. Match the frequency axis to the sample rate, transform length and real or complex input. Further reading NumPy: DFT definitions and conventions NumPy: real-input FFT NumPy: real-input frequency labels

sum: Recover real-tone amplitudes without doubling DC or Nyquist, and distinguish amplitude from power density.
x: A raw FFT magnitude is a sum over samples. A longer record can therefore produce a larger raw peak even when the physical tone has stayed equally strong. Before interpreting a spectrum, ask what its vertical axis measures and how the software normalises it. An amplitude spectrum reports tone size in the input's units, such as volts. A power spectral density, or PSD, reports mean-square content per unit bandwidth. They answer different questions and need different scaling. Turn a raw peak into a tone amplitude Start with a controlled case: NumPy's default unnormalised forward FFT, a real record, no tapering window and an isolated tone exactly centred on an interior bin. A bin-centred tone completes a whole number of cycles in the record. Divide the coefficient magnitude by the acquired sample count. Then double it for an ordinary positive-frequency tone: a real sinusoid has matching positive and negative frequency contributions, and a one-sided amplitude plot combines that pair. If the same steady tone is recorded for twice as long, the raw magnitude doubles under these assumptions; the calibrated amplitude stays the same. That is a useful check for a length-dependent calibration bug. Treat the endpoints separately DC has no separate negative-frequency partner. Neither does the Nyquist bin in an even-length real record. Divide their magnitudes by the sample count without doubling. For odd lengths, every returned real-FFT bin after DC has a partner because there is no exact Nyquist bin. DC magnitude gives the absolute mean. To preserve the sign of an offset, use the signed real DC coefficient instead. The Nyquist component describes an alternating sampled sequence; it cannot establish an arbitrary continuous sinusoid's amplitude because sampling exactly at Nyquist has phase ambiguity. Changing the FFT normalisation or applying a window changes the calibration. An off-bin tone spreads across bins, so its largest bin alone generally underestimates its peak even after this simple correction. Choose the quantity you need Peak amplitude is useful for asking how large an isolated vibration or voltage tone is. Mean-square power describes a signal's average squared size. An ordinary sinusoid, averaged over whole cycles, contributes half its squared peak amplitude to mean square. Electrical watts require an additional circuit relationship; square volts alone are not watts. PSD distributes mean-square power over frequency. For voltage input, its units are square volts per hertz. Multiplying each density by its bin width and summing estimates mean square under the estimator's window and detrending conventions. More densely spaced bins must not create extra total power. SciPy's periodogram offers scaling="density" for PSD and scaling="spectrum" for a squared-magnitude spectrum. Its default detrending removes the mean; use detrend=False if DC must remain. Tapered PSD uses window-energy normalisation, so simply squaring doubled tone amplitudes is not a general PSD recipe. A tapered estimate also need not match the unweighted finite record's mean square exactly. Key takeaways Record the FFT normalisation, window, sample count and units before interpreting a peak. Combine paired bins for one-sided tone amplitude; leave DC and an even-length Nyquist bin undoubled. Choose amplitude for tone size and PSD for mean-square content per bandwidth. Further reading NumPy: FFT normalisation conventions SciPy: periodogram scaling and units

sum: Choose a named window, understand its trade-offs and correct coherent tone amplitude.
x: A noiseless single tone can produce many non-zero FFT bins. The transform describes a finite record as a repeating pattern. If the tone does not complete a whole number of cycles, joining repeated copies can create an abrupt boundary. Several bin patterns are needed to represent that record: spectral leakage. This does not mean the FFT created sensor noise or discovered a separate oscillator at every bin. It means the finite observation affects the spectrum you can measure. A window changes the leakage pattern An unweighted record uses a rectangular window. A spectral window multiplies the samples by a chosen set of weights before transforming. A taper gives less weight to the ends, reducing the effect of the repeated boundary. The central feature around a tone is its main lobe; smaller surrounding features are side lobes. Compared with a rectangular window, a Hann window lowers side lobes but widens the main lobe. A weak tone far from a strong one can become easier to see, while two close tones can become harder to separate. Choose according to the distinction the measurement needs. Real-world analogy: a photograph's soft edge A hard-edged cut-out draws attention to its boundary. Fading the edge makes that boundary less abrupt, but blurs where it ends. How it maps: A taper reduces abrupt record boundaries and distant spectral leakage, while broadening a tone's central spectral feature. Where it stops: The broadening comes from Fourier mathematics, not optical focus. A window cannot reveal unrecorded samples or guarantee separation of nearby tones. Name the finite window you used SciPy distinguishes a periodic Hann window, requested with sym=False, from a symmetric Hann, requested with sym=True. The periodic version is intended for spectral analysis; the symmetric version is commonly used for FIR design. A periodic window's final stored value need not be zero. Their finite arrays have different sums. The average weight, called coherent gain, describes how the window scales a coherent tone under the usual separated-tone assumptions. For a periodic Hann with more than two samples, that average is one half. A symmetric Hann's average differs, so calculate the actual weight sum instead of assuming both conventions are interchangeable. Calibrate the tone you actually measured For an isolated, bin-centred real tone at an interior frequency, replace the unwindowed sample-count denominator with the sum of the weights. This is exact when the mirrored negative-frequency tone contributes zero at the measured positive bin, and approximate when that contribution is negligible. Check the condition near DC or Nyquist and when changing windows. This corrects window attenuation; it does not fix every peak error. A tone between bins can still have an underestimated largest bin, called scalloping loss. Nearby signals can also affect the peak. Noise PSD needs a different calibration based on squared weights and sample rate; use a documented estimator rather than reusing the coherent-tone correction. Key takeaways Leakage comes from finite observation and does not require noise. Hann suppresses side lobes while broadening the central response. State the window convention and distinguish coherent-tone correction from off-bin estimation and PSD scaling. Further reading SciPy: Hann conventions Steven W. Smith: applications of the DFT SciPy: window sums and spectral scaling

t: More bins do not mean more observation
sum: Use zero padding to sample a spectrum more finely without mistaking it for new resolving power.
x: Zero padding appends zeros to an acquired record before its FFT. The longer transform evaluates the same finite-record spectrum at more closely spaced frequencies. A plotted peak looks smoother and a grid-based peak search can land closer to its true location. No new measurements have been made. The important distinction is between the spacing of the displayed frequency grid and the ability to distinguish neighbouring tones. Both are sometimes called frequency resolution, so say which you mean. Keep observation and transform length separate The acquired sample count and sample rate determine how long you observed the signal. The FFT length includes any appended zeros and determines the grid spacing. Padding changes the second length while leaving the first unchanged. For example, acquire 64 samples at 640 samples per second: a tenth-second record. Its unpadded bins are 10 Hz apart. Pad it to 256 points and the grid becomes 2.5 Hz apart, but the acquired observation remains a tenth of a second. Real-world analogy: enlarging a photograph Enlarging an existing photograph can make its shapes easier to inspect. It does not capture details that the camera never recorded. How it maps: Extra FFT points sample the existing finite-record spectrum more densely; extra acquired samples can supply new observation information. Where it stops: Zero padding is exact evaluation on a denser frequency grid, not a camera's pixel interpolation algorithm. Its usefulness and limitations follow from the record's transform. Choose the change that solves the problem If a peak falls between coarse grid points, padding can improve the display and the search grid. For a 73 Hz cosine in the example above, the largest unpadded bin is labelled 70 Hz and the padded one 72.5 Hz. The closer label does not establish exact frequency or measurement uncertainty: leakage, noise, the finite record and other tones can bias the estimate. If two tones blend into one broad feature, padding alone cannot narrow the window's main lobe in hertz. Collect a longer record if the tones stay steady long enough. That can narrow the spectral features, but window shape, relative tone levels and noise still govern whether the tones can be separated. A longer observation can also mix changes that happen during it. Preserve amplitude calibration Appending zeros should not make the same tone physically smaller. For coherent-tone calibration, retain the original acquired sample count when there was no taper, or the original window-weight sum when there was a taper. Dividing by the longer padded length would falsely reduce amplitude. Keep that calibration issue separate from off-bin peak error. Key takeaways Padding gives a denser grid without a longer observation. More acquired time can narrow spectral features when the signal remains steady; padding cannot. A peak's grid label is an estimate, and padding must not change coherent-tone amplitude scaling. Further reading NumPy: FFT length and zero padding Steven W. Smith: Fourier transform properties

sum: Build a short-time spectrum and distinguish frame duration, hop spacing and frequency-grid spacing.
x: A single FFT describes everything in its record together. If a machine first vibrates at one frequency and later another, that spectrum does not show their order. A short-time Fourier transform, or STFT, instead analyses successive short, windowed records called analysis frames. A spectrogram displays a squared-magnitude or power-related version of those transforms: time on one axis, frequency on another and strength shown by colour. Check what the colours mean. A coloured plot is not automatically a calibrated PSD. Frame length controls what gets blended Each frame observes a span of time. A longer frame gives narrower spectral features for steady tones, making close frequencies easier to distinguish under suitable conditions. It also combines events across a longer interval. If a tone changes inside the frame, both its earlier and later frequencies can contribute to that frame. A shorter frame localises changes more closely in time, but broadens its frequency features. Choose the frame length for the event you want to understand rather than assuming a more detailed-looking plot has resolved everything. Hop controls how often you look The hop is the distance in samples between neighbouring frame starts. A hop shorter than the frame length makes the frames overlap. Reducing the hop gives more frequent spectra by sharing more samples. It does not shorten each frame's observation or remove its time-frequency trade-off. For example, a frame can observe 125 milliseconds while another frame starts every 31.25 milliseconds. The frequent updates still each mix information over a 125-millisecond span. Real-world analogy: overlapping snapshots Take long-exposure photographs at frequent intervals. Starting another exposure sooner creates more photographs, but each photograph still blends movement over its own exposure. How it maps: Frame length is the observation span and hop is the interval between observations. Overlapping frames share samples. Where it stops: The STFT measures oscillation components using a window, rather than brightness. A smaller hop cannot improve the window's intrinsic frequency discrimination. Read a spectrogram's contract Before comparing two plots, establish the window and frame length, hop, FFT length, time labels and boundary policy. Extra zero padding gives more frequency-grid positions inside each frame; it does not lengthen the acquired frame. Some implementations label frames by their centres, others by their starts. Some extend the signal at the edges, while others omit incomplete frames. A centred window near an edge can include assumed samples outside the actual record. These choices affect apparent event timing and edge content. Finally match the strength normalisation and colour units. Amplitude, squared magnitude and PSD use different normalisations. SciPy's ShortTimeFFT exposes frame, hop and scaling choices; record the settings with the plot so another reader can interpret it. Key takeaways An STFT follows changing spectra using successive windowed frames. Frame length controls the observation span; hop controls update spacing. Match time labels, boundaries and scaling before comparing spectrograms. Further reading SciPy: short-time Fourier transform SciPy: ShortTimeFFT

t: Reduce sample rate without folding signals
sum: Set a new Nyquist limit, low-pass first and understand why keeping every second sample is insufficient.
x: Keeping every second or third sample lowers the sample rate. It also lowers the range of frequencies that can be represented without ambiguity. A tone that was safe at the original rate can exceed the new Nyquist limit and appear as a different, lower-frequency tone. Decimation combines low-pass filtering with retaining samples at a lower rate. The order matters: suppress the unwanted high frequencies before discarding samples. Design for the output rate Reducing a 1200-sample-per-second signal by a factor of three gives 400 samples per second. Its new Nyquist boundary is 200 Hz, even though the original boundary was 600 Hz. Design the prefilter for the reduced rate. Wanted baseband content must lie strictly below that boundary. A practical low-pass also needs a transition band in which its response falls from passing wanted content to rejecting unwanted content. Do not put the wanted passband edge exactly at Nyquist and expect an instantaneous cut-off. Choose enough stopband attenuation for the alias level the application can tolerate. Why filtering afterwards is too late A 350 Hz cosine is below the original Nyquist boundary in this example. Keep every third sample without filtering, and it appears as a 50 Hz cosine at the output. Discarding samples has folded the unwanted tone into the useful band; it has not erased it. Now an actual 50 Hz input and the aliased 350 Hz input can be indistinguishable from the output samples alone. A later low-pass cannot selectively remove the alias while preserving every genuine 50 Hz component. Filter before the ambiguity occurs. Real-world analogy: checking before a narrow doorway Remove oversized items before sending a mixed delivery through a narrow doorway. Sorting afterwards cannot recover information lost when items were forced together. How it maps: The new rate has a smaller unambiguous frequency range. The prefilter suppresses components outside it before samples are discarded. Where it stops: Aliasing is an exact ambiguity between sampled oscillations, not physical damage or a queue. A real filter only attenuates unwanted components by a finite amount. Specify the whole rate-change operation SciPy's decimate filters before reducing. resample_poly also combines FIR filtering and rate conversion efficiently. An API is useful, but its default filter is not evidence that your required passband and stopband specification has been met. Test across the unwanted band and inspect finite-record edges. Record the timing convention too. A causal streaming filter has delay and startup behaviour; an offline centred or zero-phase operation has different alignment and boundary assumptions. Neither should silently substitute for the other when event times matter. This digital prefilter protects a later digital rate reduction. It cannot repair aliasing that already happened at the original analogue-to-digital conversion, which needs its own anti-alias protection. Key takeaways The output rate sets the relevant Nyquist boundary. Filter before reducing, leaving a transition band and enough unwanted-band rejection. Record timing and edge assumptions, and keep original ADC aliasing separate from later decimation. Further reading SciPy: decimation includes an anti-alias filter SciPy: polyphase resampling and boundary assumptions

sum: Follow zero insertion, spectral images and the low-pass gain needed to reconstruct between samples.
x: Interpolation estimates samples at new time positions from an existing record. Increasing the output sample rate gives more values to pass to another system, but they are computed estimates, not extra physical measurements. It cannot recover frequency distinctions already lost to aliasing. Integer-rate interpolation has two conceptual steps: insert zero placeholders between the original samples, then apply a reconstruction low-pass filter. Efficient implementations can combine these steps without explicitly calculating every zero. New positions preserve the original times To double the rate, put each original sample in every other output position. Interpret the result at twice the original sample rate. Original values then retain their original time positions; the extra positions fall between them. For a constant sequence of ones, the intermediate sequence alternates ones and zeros. Those zeros do not claim the physical signal stopped between observations. They reserve positions for the filtering step. Real-world analogy: filling a timetable Put the known appointments into a timetable with twice as many time slots. Empty slots reserve positions; they do not mean the activity stopped. How it maps: Original samples retain their timing while zero placeholders create new positions. The filter estimates values at and around those positions. Where it stops: Signal interpolation depends on a bandwidth assumption and a numerical filter, not judgement about appointments. It cannot invent unknown high-frequency information. Filter images and restore the scale Zero insertion produces spectral images: copies of the original baseband spectrum within the enlarged frequency range. A reconstruction low-pass retains the wanted band and suppresses those images. They are still separated from the wanted baseband, so filtering can remove them before any later reduction folds them together. The filter must also have appropriate gain. With one zero after every original sample, the constant sequence's average is halved. A unity-DC-gain low-pass would keep that reduced average. If no other scale correction is present, a factor-two interpolator needs a filter with DC gain two. More generally, the required DC gain equals the zero-insertion factor, with corresponding passband gain where faithful reconstruction is wanted. A three-coefficient filter with weights [0.5, 1.0, 0.5] illustrates this for doubling. Their sum is two. It fills the interior constant sequence back to one and provides linear interpolation between successive original values after accounting for delay. Its image suppression is too gradual for demanding applications; it is a useful model rather than a production specification. Compare implementations fairly That toy filter used causally has one high-rate-sample delay and edge transients. An offline centred API can produce different timing and edge values while still performing its documented operation. Match the filter, scaling, output-length and boundary conventions before comparing arrays. Resampling can increase by one integer factor and decrease by another. SciPy's resample_poly combines zero insertion, FIR filtering and reduction using polyphase computation. It supplies the required internal amplitude scaling, so do not multiply its default output by the insertion factor again. Its default boundary model assumes zeros beyond the finite input. A filter for the intermediate increased rate must both suppress interpolation images and protect the final reduced rate from aliasing. Inspect timing and boundary behaviour as well as the interior frequency response. Key takeaways Zero placeholders reserve time positions; low-pass filtering forms the interpolated signal. Reconstruction needs the right gain as well as image suppression. More output values cannot undo original aliasing or replace new measurements. Further reading SciPy: upsample, FIR filter and downsample SciPy: polyphase resampling

t: FFT convolution without wrapping the tail
sum: Turn circular FFT multiplication into full linear convolution and preserve block tails with overlap-add.
x: FFT multiplication can calculate convolution efficiently, but the transform's boundary model matters. A fixed-length DFT treats its input as repeating. Multiplying the transforms and taking an inverse FFT therefore gives circular convolution: contributions beyond the chosen length wrap back to the beginning. Ordinary finite filtering with zero extension needs linear convolution instead. The solution is to reserve space for the complete output, including its filter tail, before transforming. Make room before multiplying For a four-sample input and a three-coefficient FIR, the full output occupies six positions. Pad both transforms to at least that full length. Using only the length of the longer input generally leaves too little room. A longer FFT can be chosen for efficiency. After the inverse transform, keep the full linear output length; extra padded positions are not additional physical output. Small floating-point errors can remain. Real-world analogy: a circular calendar Write a long task schedule on a repeating weekly calendar. Anything that spills past Sunday appears back under Monday unless you reserve enough distinct dates. How it maps: Circular convolution wraps the tail into earlier positions. Sufficient padding reserves space for every linear-convolution contribution before the repetition begins. Where it stops: The FFT combines numeric contributions by addition, and its wrap is an exact mathematical boundary rule. Padding removes that wrap for finite linear convolution; it does not remove a filter's actual tail. Recognise wraparound in a result For input [1, 2, 3, 4] and FIR [1, 1, 1], full linear convolution is [1, 3, 6, 9, 7, 4]. A four-point FFT product instead returns [8, 7, 6, 9]. The final tail has been added into the beginning, not discarded or substituted for the first samples. This gives a useful diagnosis: if the end of a filtered record contaminates its beginning, inspect transform length and padding before changing the filter coefficients. Compare with direct full convolution on a small input to check the boundary behaviour. Add block responses at their original positions For a long signal, overlap-add processes input blocks separately with the same FIR. Each block needs sufficient FFT padding for its own full convolution. Place that result at the output position corresponding to the block's original start. Adjacent results overlap because each block keeps producing a filter tail after its last input sample. Add contributions at shared positions. Concatenating full block outputs shifts later responses; overwriting the overlap loses contributions. When full finite output is requested, retain the last tail after the final input block. A streaming implementation also needs buffering, latency and flushing policies. Overlap-add does not guarantee zero latency. SciPy provides fftconvolve for FFT convolution and oaconvolve for overlap-add; actual speed depends on lengths and hardware. Key takeaways FFT multiplication naturally uses circular boundaries. Pad both transforms for the full linear output to prevent wraparound. Overlap-add combines shared positions and keeps the final tail when full output is required. Further reading Steven W. Smith: FFT convolution and overlap-add SciPy: full FFT convolution SciPy: overlap-add convolution

sum: Combine known timing, RMS, causal filtering and a calibrated spectrum with explicit synthetic checks.
x: Before trusting a measurement chain, test it on a synthetic signal with known truth. A real vibration sensor adds calibration uncertainty, noise, drift and timing error. A generated record lets you first ask whether the processing behaves as intended. This experiment uses an acceleration offset, a wanted 64 Hz tone and a 192 Hz interferer. The task is to preserve the wanted tone, reduce the interferer and explain the measured output. It tests numerical processing on a host computer; it does not establish physical sensor accuracy or device timing performance. State a reproducible contract Use the following fixed setup, with no random noise or external files. Acceleration values are in metres per second squared. Setting Choice ------ Sample rate 1024 samples per second Acquired length 1280 samples Constant offset 0.4 Wanted cosine peak 2 at 64 Hz Interfering cosine peak 0.6 at 192 Hz Start both cosines at their positive peak at sample zero. They complete whole cycles over this acquired record, so their mean is zero and the measured mean should be the stated offset, allowing numerical rounding. Remove that measured mean before analysing AC RMS, so the constant offset does not count as vibration around the mean. Both oscillating tones remain. RMS describes average squared size followed by a square root; it is not the sum or average of the tone peaks. For these whole-cycle, orthogonal cosines, mean-square contributions add because their cross-products average to zero. Separate filter behaviour from measurement behaviour Apply a causal three-tap moving average with equal weights and zero initial state. Each output averages the current input and two preceding inputs. SciPy's lfilter can implement this causal operation; an offline zero-phase filter would be a different contract. Discard the first 256 outputs, then analyse the remaining 1024. This keeps filter startup outside the analysed segment. Both tones complete whole cycles there too. The symmetric three-tap filter has one input-sample delay: discarding startup does not remove that delay when interpreting time events. Apply a periodic Hann to the analysed segment. Use its actual weight sum for coherent-tone amplitude calibration, doubling only paired interior bins. Both test tones are interior bins, well away from DC and Nyquist. Use a separate frequency-response calculation to predict each output tone before comparing with the measured spectrum. Interpret the checks The wanted output peak is approximately 1.899 and the interferer's approximately 0.353, in the same acceleration units as the input. The interferer is reduced, not eliminated. The wanted tone is also attenuated, so its output peak must not be reported as the original input peak. Make separate checks for mean removal, RMS, filter response and spectrum scaling. A coherent-amplitude assertion can reveal a scaling or filtering error, but it cannot by itself prove time alignment, physical calibration or real-time performance. Inspect time events as well if timing matters. A longer, suitably designed filter may reject the interferer better, with different delay and transition behaviour. On a real record, document sample-clock accuracy, calibration, detrending, window, bandwidth and transient handling. A peak's bin label alone does not supply an uncertainty interval. Key takeaways Known synthetic input lets you check each processing stage against a stated contract. Predict the filter's effect before interpreting an output peak as an input measurement. Numerical agreement establishes the tested behaviour; physical calibration and timing need their own evidence. Further reading SciPy: causal filtering and initial conditions SciPy: frequency response of a digital filter SciPy: periodic and symmetric Hann windows NumPy: FFT conventions

sum: Identify the inputs, decisions, outputs and constraints of a small firmware system.
x: A room sensor reads a measurement, decides whether a threshold has been crossed and changes an indicator. The program has the familiar ingredients of any software system: data, conditions, functions and state. What changes is its relationship with the physical device. Embedded software runs as part of a device's particular purpose. Firmware is the software stored for that device to execute, often in memory that retains its contents without power. The term does not mean that the software can never be updated. The vendor's supported update process determines how a particular device changes its firmware. This course concentrates on small microcontrollers, or MCUs. You can learn their software structure and test decision logic on a computer before choosing a development board. Start with behaviour For an illustrative sensor indicator, write the behaviour before writing code: Part Example requirement ------ Input A new measurement and whether it is valid Decision Compare a valid measurement with a limit Output Update the indicator Fault Show a distinct indication when data is invalid The threshold and the fault indication are choices for this example, not universal sensor rules. A first useful test is a sequence of inputs: below the threshold, above it, then invalid. The expected outputs are normal, alert, then fault. That sequence can be tested without connecting an actual sensor. Real-world analogy: a receptionist following a procedure A receptionist receives information, checks a rule and gives an appropriate response. If the information is missing, the procedure can specify a different response. How it maps: Incoming information represents sensor input, the rule represents firmware logic and the response represents an output. An explicit missing-information rule represents fault handling. Where it stops: A microcontroller cannot use human judgement to fill in an omitted rule. Firmware must define its inputs, timing and failure behaviour precisely. What changes from desktop development A bare-metal application runs without an operating system managing its application execution. Its startup support and libraries still do real work. A real-time operating system is still an operating system; an application running under one is not bare metal. Other embedded devices use an operating system, so embedded does not automatically mean bare metal. Hardware places constraints on available memory, supported signals and the time allowed for a response. A real-time requirement concerns meeting a timing requirement, not simply running as fast as possible. A program that eventually gives the right answer can still fail if that answer arrives too late for its intended job. For this course's small project, success means the logic is correct, operations return control promptly, and invalid input has a defined outcome. Later modules add device interfaces and timing methods to that foundation. Key takeaways Describe observable inputs, decisions, outputs and fault behaviour before choosing implementation details. Firmware can be updateable; embedded systems can run with or without an operating system. Correct timing can be part of correct behaviour. Further reading Firmware definitions — NIST Bare metal excludes an OS or RTOS — Altera Pico microcontroller boards — Raspberry Pi RP2040 datasheet: system description

sum: Separate instruction execution, persistent storage, working memory and hardware interfaces.
x: A microcontroller combines one or more processor cores, memory and hardware interfaces in a chip. The exact mixture varies. The development board around it may add more memory, power circuitry, connectors and other components. The CPU, or central processing unit, executes instructions. It uses RAM, random-access memory, for working data such as changing variables and temporary buffers. The SRAM commonly used by small MCUs is volatile memory: its contents are not retained when power is removed. Flash memory is non-volatile storage that can hold firmware and persistent data. It may be inside the MCU or on a separate chip. As a concrete distinction, RP2040 has on-chip SRAM and accesses external flash through its flash interface. Do not assume that a board's advertised flash capacity describes memory inside its processor. Give each part a job For the sensor indicator introduced earlier: Part Job in the example ------ CPU Execute the measurement decision Firmware storage Retain the program when power is removed RAM Hold the current measurement and state Peripheral Exchange signals with the sensor or indicator A peripheral is a dedicated hardware block such as a timer or a serial controller. Software configures it and observes or supplies data. The peripheral can perform its configured hardware work between CPU instructions; it does not decide the application's requirements for you. Real-world analogy: a workshop with instructions and a workbench A workshop keeps instructions in a cupboard, places the current job on a workbench and uses specialised tools for particular operations. How it maps: Stored instructions represent firmware storage; the workbench represents working RAM; the worker following instructions represents the CPU. Specialised tools represent peripherals. Where it stops: Actual memory has defined addresses and access rules. Some systems execute code from RAM, and a peripheral's registers are not ordinary storage just because software accesses them by address. Addresses describe different kinds of access A memory map describes which addresses refer to memory and which refer to hardware. A peripheral register is a location used to control or observe a hardware function. For example, one register can select a pin's function while another reports an input value. Access can cause register side effects: reading or writing a peripheral register is not automatically equivalent to reading or writing a RAM variable. Later lessons use the relevant device manual or SDK rather than guessing addresses. Try a mental power cycle. The saved firmware can remain in flash, but the current working measurement is not a persistent record merely because it was stored in RAM. To retain a setting, the application needs an appropriate supported storage mechanism and a defined loading process. Key takeaways Distinguish firmware storage from the RAM used while the program runs. MCU and board memory are different descriptions; check the actual device. Peripherals and their registers have device-specific behaviour. Further reading RP2040 datasheet: memory and peripheral descriptions Pico board memory and storage — Raspberry Pi

t: Read the chip, board and SDK documentation
sum: Use the chip datasheet, board wiring and SDK configuration together before controlling a pin.
x: An example says it blinks an LED, but your board stays dark. Before changing code at random, distinguish three sources of information. The datasheet describes a component: its supported functions, electrical limits, registers and required operating conditions. A board manual and schematic describe how a particular circuit board connects those components. The SDK, or software development kit, supplies libraries, header files, examples and build support for a supported target. None replaces the others. A chip may support a function on several pins, while the board uses one of those pins for another purpose. A library may also require a specific board selection so it chooses the correct implementation. Work from the device outward For an onboard indicator, follow this sequence: Identify the exact board model and revision, not just the processor family. Read its manual or schematic to find how the indicator is connected. Check which component controls that connection. Use the official SDK example for that board and check its build configuration. Observe the intended result before adding external circuitry. The Pico SDK's blink example illustrates why this matters. Its ordinary Pico LED path and Pico W wireless-chip LED path differ. The example selects the supported path using board configuration. Copying a pin number from a different board is not a substitute for that selection. Real-world analogy: an appliance manual and a room plan An appliance manual explains what the appliance can do. A room plan shows where it is installed and how it is connected. A control panel provides the supported way to operate it. How it maps: The component datasheet describes the device's capabilities, the board schematic describes actual connections and the SDK provides a software interface to those capabilities. Where it stops: A board's connections can constrain what is usable. Neither a convenient API nor a familiar connector overrides the component's electrical limits or the board's wiring. Keep the first experiment simple Use a board's documented onboard indicator for the first hardware observation. If an example builds but does not work, check the selected board, the actual firmware image loaded and the documented indicator connection before concluding the MCU is broken. Keep any later experiments to low-voltage development hardware. Before connecting an external signal, check the electrical limits for inputs, ground reference and power arrangement in the exact manuals. Do not connect unknown voltage sources or high-current loads directly to MCU pins. This course does not require external wiring to understand or test its first logic examples. Key takeaways A component's capabilities, a board's connections and an SDK's configuration answer different questions. Match an example to the exact board before assuming a particular pin controls its indicator. Electrical limits remain hardware requirements even when an API accepts a value. Further reading SDK board selection and first examples — Raspberry Pi Official blink implementation — Raspberry Pi RP2040 datasheet

t: From source code to a running device
sum: Distinguish compiling, linking, transferring firmware and observing its behaviour.
x: Writing a source file changes a file on your computer. It does not change the program already running on a board. A firmware workflow must turn that source into an appropriate image, transfer it using a supported method and then observe what actually runs. A toolchain is the collection of development tools used for that target. A cross-compiler runs on one system while producing code for another target. Choosing the wrong target can produce perfectly valid machine code that the intended MCU cannot execute. Follow the stages This is a simplified development sequence, not a set of shell commands: The compiler translates source into target code, often producing object files. In a C toolchain, preprocessing handles items such as header inclusion before compilation proper. The linker combines object files and libraries, resolves references between them and lays out the result according to the target's build configuration. A successful compile does not prove that linking will succeed. A function can have a declaration that allows compilation while its implementation is missing from the link. Similarly, successful linking does not prove that the resulting program satisfies the device's behaviour requirements. Real-world analogy: preparing and delivering a printed instruction pack Different people prepare pages, someone assembles the complete pack, and a delivery step takes it to the place where it will be used. Finishing a page does not prove the pack was delivered or followed correctly. How it maps: Preparing pages represents compilation; assembling the pack represents linking; delivery represents transferring the firmware. Observing the device checks the behaviour of the delivered result. Where it stops: Firmware must match the processor, code and data locations, and transfer format. A successfully delivered image can still contain decision bugs or initialise the wrong hardware. A concrete supported route For an original Pico running an appropriate Pico SDK blink image, the official documentation describes entering BOOTSEL mode, which exposes a USB mass-storage interface, then copying a UF2 image through that interface. The bootloader interprets the transfer and the board restarts into the application. This is a Pico workflow, not a universal way of programming MCUs or an ordinary storage drive for arbitrary files. Other supported routes use a debug interface and a programming tool. Follow the board's current guide for the required image format and procedure. Record the board selection, build configuration and image you transferred so an observation can be tied to a particular build. Key takeaways Build, transfer and observation are separate steps; success at one does not prove success at the next. A cross-compiler and linker must target the actual device and build configuration. Use an official board-specific programming method rather than assuming all MCUs accept the same file. Further reading Overall compilation and linking options — GCC First binaries and BOOTSEL workflow — Raspberry Pi Debug probe programming and debugging — Raspberry Pi

sum: Trace a documented reset path without assuming every MCU begins directly at main.
x: Resetting a device is not the same operation as flashing new firmware. A reset restarts execution through a defined hardware and software path. Programming flash changes stored contents. Either operation may be part of a development tool's sequence, but one does not automatically imply the other. Your application's first visible action may be turning an indicator on. Before that action, the processor and its support code need a way to locate executable code and establish an environment in which that code can run. Trace one documented startup model Arm's CMSIS Cortex-M startup template describes a reset handler, an initial stack pointer, and an interrupt vector table containing handler addresses. The reset handler typically calls system initialisation, then transfers control to a C runtime that performs its initialisation and calls the application's main function. Here main is the entry function used by that runtime; it is not the first instruction executed after reset. This names a particular Cortex-M software model. The exact sequence comes from the chip, toolchain and project. Another processor or startup package can use a different arrangement. C variables with static storage duration have storage for the whole program execution; program-wide variables are an example. C requires these variables to receive their specified starting values before C program startup. The described runtime completes this initialisation before calling main. This is a software initialisation rule, not a claim that reset hardware erases all physical RAM. C does not require every microcontroller project to use an entry function named main. Real-world analogy: opening a shop before serving customers A shop can need its entrance opened, workspace prepared and equipment checked before the first customer is served. How it maps: The opening procedure represents the reset and startup path; serving the first customer represents entering application code. A fault during preparation can prevent the application's first visible action. Where it stops: There is no universal startup checklist for every MCU. Hardware-defined entry rules and vendor startup routines determine the real order, and a reset need not erase every memory region. Boot code and application code are distinct A bootloader is code that loads or starts another program and may support a programming or recovery interface. Some devices begin in manufacturer ROM, read-only memory containing fixed boot code. Others enter an application image more directly. These arrangements are device-specific. RP2040 is one concrete example: its boot ROM participates in startup and supports the documented USB boot interface. That example should not be expanded into a claim that every MCU has a USB bootloader. When diagnosing a board that never reaches the application, ask which milestone failed. Did the programming tool report a successful transfer? Can the debug tools reach the target? Does execution reach application startup? Does hardware initialisation finish? These observations separate a startup failure from a failure in the later decision logic. Treat retained settings deliberately. Some reset conditions can preserve RAM contents or special retention storage, while startup routines may reinitialise application data. Check the specific device and runtime rather than using a reset as a general promise to erase all data. Key takeaways Reset, flash programming, startup and application entry are distinct operations. main is reached through supporting code in the described CMSIS startup model. Boot behaviour and retention depend on the target and its startup configuration. Further reading Cortex-M startup file and reset handler — Arm CMSIS System initialisation — Arm CMSIS C11 draft: execution environments, sections 5.1.2 and 5.1.2.1 RP2040 datasheet: boot sequence

t: Keep a main loop responsive with explicit state
sum: Trace bounded main-loop work and distinguish a button state from a new button event.
x: A main loop, sometimes called a superloop, repeatedly performs the application's foreground work. In a cooperative design, each operation returns control so the loop can visit its other jobs. One operation that waits indefinitely can prevent all later foreground jobs from running. An explicit state machine records the current mode and defines how an input changes it. It replaces vague instructions such as "handle the button somehow" with a rule that can be traced and tested. Separate an event from a level For this teaching example, a button toggles an indicator between OFF and ON. The input is an already accepted press event, not the raw electrical signal and not a button-held level. The later debounce lesson explains how to derive such events from real input. This is illustrative pseudocode, not C or an SDK API. Each input check and output update is assumed to return promptly. The assignments initialise or change the remembered state. One loop pass consumes at most one event. With an initial state of OFF, the sequence below gives a deterministic trace: Pass Accepted event State after pass --------- 1 none OFF 2 PRESS ON 3 none, button still held ON 4 PRESS after another press OFF Using the held-button level as the event would toggle again on every pass while the button stayed down. A fast loop would then produce behaviour unrelated to the number of deliberate presses. Real-world analogy: one person checking several service desks A person visits several desks in order, handles a small piece of work at each and returns for the next round. Waiting forever at one desk prevents visits to the others. How it maps: The person represents foreground execution, desks represent loop jobs and each short visit represents work that returns control. The remembered indicator mode represents the application's explicit state. Where it stops: Real MCU interrupts can run between foreground instructions, and another core may run simultaneously. A loop structure alone proves neither how soon work will finish nor safe access to shared data. Test decisions separately from hardware The event-to-state rule can be tested on a computer with a list of input events. That checks the defined transitions; it does not validate the physical button, signal levels or output wiring. To reason about responsiveness, list the maximum work each foreground job can do before returning. Avoid an unbounded wait for input inside a loop job. Later timing and debugging lessons add elapsed-time scheduling, bounded communication and observation methods. They also explain why merely adding interrupts or more scheduling machinery does not establish a timing guarantee. Key takeaways Cooperative jobs must return control for the loop to service other foreground work. Remember explicit state and consume an accepted event once. A trace can test decision logic without claiming to validate hardware or deadlines. Further reading Cooperative superloop model — Quantum Leaps Official blink application and its main loop — Raspberry Pi Cortex-M interrupt model — Arm CMSIS

t: C values, declarations and small functions
sum: Choose a value type deliberately and follow a small C function call.
x: Firmware spends much of its time representing things: a sampled value, a count, a setting and whether an operation succeeded. C makes the representation part of the program. A declaration gives an object a type and a name; an initialiser gives it its starting value. A semicolon ends the declaration. Read a small complete program This is a complete C11 program for a computer, using a target that provides the exact-width integer types. The headers make library declarations and type names available; they do not initialise a microcontroller. main is this hosted program's entry function. The braces enclose a function's statements. It prints 1. The function accepts one function argument, named sample inside the function. return sends the comparison result to the caller. bool represents false or true; <stdbool.h> supplies the convenient C11 names. The u suffix makes a literal unsigned. The cast (unsigned) gives printf the argument type its %u conversion expects. A function call does not automatically share a caller's local variable: here the value is passed into the function parameter. Size and meaning are separate An unsigned integer represents non-negative integers. <stdint.h> provides names such as uint16_t when the implementation supports the corresponding exact-width type. uint16_t has exactly 16 value bits and no padding; it can represent 0 through 65,535. These exact-width names are optional in C11, so check the target toolchain. Plain int is not guaranteed to be 32 bits. const means this declaration does not permit modifying limit through that name. It does not promise storage in flash. A type also does not encode a measurement unit: a count in milliseconds and a count in microseconds may have the same C type. Put the unit in the name and document the range. Real-world analogy: choosing a labelled measuring jar A labelled jar tells you what belongs inside and how much it can hold. Choosing a bigger jar does not tell you whether its contents are flour or sugar. How it maps: An integer type defines a representable range; a name and contract explain what that value means. Choose both before using the value in control decisions. Where it stops: C does not enforce a physical unit just because a name includes it. Conversions and arithmetic still follow language rules and can lose information. Do not treat narrowing as validation Converting 256 to uint8_t, where that type exists, produces 0 under C's unsigned conversion rules. It does not report an invalid input. A cast requests a conversion; it is not a range check. Check a value's allowed range before storing it in a narrower type. Signed overflow is a different case and must not be assumed to wrap. Key takeaways Declarations name a type and an object; function parameters receive argument values. Exact-width unsigned types make a chosen representation explicit when the target provides them. Keep units and valid ranges in the program's names and contracts; casts do not validate input. Further reading C11 draft: declarations, functions and integer types

t: Pointers and memory mapped device registers
sum: Separate an address, the object it refers to and a hardware register access.
x: A pointer is a value that can refer to an object or function. This lesson uses object pointers. A null pointer refers to neither, and a pointer one past an array's end cannot be used to access an element. Taking an object's address does not copy the object. Dereferencing the pointer accesses the referred-to object, provided that access is valid for its type, alignment and lifetime. Address and value are different In a declaration, uint32_t p means that p is a pointer to a uint32_t object. In an expression, &status obtains status's address, while p accesses the object referred to by p. The same character has different jobs in a declaration and an expression. This complete C11 host program deliberately uses an ordinary RAM object as a model. It does not touch a device or invent a peripheral address: It prints 1 2 on the host used for this exercise. snapshot is an independent stored value; changing status through the pointer does not retroactively change the earlier snapshot. In these examples the printed values fit unsigned, so those output casts preserve them. Real-world analogy: a room number and the room's noticeboard A room number tells you where to go; a note copied from the room's noticeboard records what it said at the time you visited. How it maps: A pointer identifies an object to access, while a copied value is a snapshot. Keeping the pointer does not make an old snapshot update itself. Where it stops: A pointer must satisfy C's validity rules. A plausible-looking number is not permission to access memory, and real hardware accesses can have effects that reading a noticeboard does not. When an address belongs to hardware With memory-mapped I/O, accesses to specified addresses communicate with peripheral registers. A register can expose status, accept a configuration or trigger an operation. The device manual defines its address, access width, permitted operations and effects. Reading one register might consume queued data; writing another might clear a reported event. It need not behave like normal RAM. Use the vendor SDK's documented accessors or register definitions. A pointer fabricated from a number in a tutorial is not a portable way to locate a peripheral. Never run a raw device-address sketch on a host computer. What volatile contributes Hardware register definitions often use volatile to express that accesses have externally observable significance under the implementation's rules. GCC documents its volatile-access behaviour and explains that non-volatile accesses are not ordered by a volatile object. volatile does not make a multi-step update atomic, protect shared state, validate a pointer or synchronise threads. Later timing lessons handle concurrent access explicitly. Key takeaways A pointer refers to an object; a copied value remains a separate snapshot. A device register is defined by its manual and can have effects when read or written. Volatile access is one part of a hardware interface, not a concurrency solution. Further reading C11 draft: address, indirection and qualifiers GCC: volatile accesses and ordering RP2040 datasheet: register access and side effects

sum: Use unsigned masks without assuming every device register permits read modify write.
x: A bit mask selects positions within an integer. Number positions from zero at the least-significant bit, the rightmost position in a binary display. Bit zero has the value one, bit one the value two, and bit two the value four. Hexadecimal notation is a compact way to write the same pattern; C writes hexadecimal literals with a 0x prefix. Four useful operations Bitwise AND (&) keeps a position set only when both inputs have it set. Bitwise OR () sets a position when either input has it set. Bitwise XOR (^) sets a position when the inputs differ. Bitwise NOT (~) flips the bits of its promoted operand. These are integer operations, distinct from C's logical && and, which test truth and short-circuit evaluation. This complete C11 host program operates on a local integer, not a device register. On the checked host, uint32_t and the constant macros used here operate as 32-bit unsigned values. Check the target's promoted operand types before generalising the inverted-mask expression: It prints 4. = means update the left object with the OR result; the corresponding compound assignments do the same for the other operations. The comments show the intermediate values. To test a selected bit, use a condition such as (value & bit1)!= 0u; the parentheses make the intended grouping explicit. A left shift moves a pattern towards higher positions. UINT32_C(1) supplies a constant suitable for the corresponding least-width unsigned type; the operand used by the shift can undergo integer promotion. The shift by one here is defined on implementations providing the exact-width types. Never shift by a negative amount or by the width of the promoted left operand or more. General code also needs to avoid invalid signed shifts. Real-world analogy: changing labelled switches A row of labelled switches lets you change one selected position while keeping the others as they were. How it maps: A mask identifies the selected positions. OR sets them, AND with an inverted mask clears them, and XOR flips them in an ordinary integer value. Where it stops: A peripheral register may not store switches in this simple way. Reads can have effects, writes can use special meanings, and another execution context can change a value between your read and write. Ordinary integers and registers have different contracts Compound assignment is a read-modify-write operation. It is not automatically an indivisible hardware update. A write-one-to-clear status register interprets a written one as a request to clear an event, rather than a new stored value. Reading its old bits and writing them back may clear events unintentionally. Some chips provide separate set and clear accessors; the RP2040 is one named example with documented atomic register aliases and exceptions. Use the actual register's contract, not a generic masking recipe. Key takeaways Masks select positions; bitwise operations differ from logical truth operators. Check the promoted operand type and valid shift range. Apply register-specific access rules before using read-modify-write on hardware. Further reading C11 draft: integer promotions and bitwise operators RP2040 datasheet: atomic register access and register definitions

t: GPIO direction, pulls and logical levels
sum: Configure a pin for the intended signal and interpret its level using the board circuit.
x: A general-purpose input/output pin, or GPIO, connects software to a digital signal. In input mode the peripheral samples the pin's level. In a typical output mode it drives a level. Many pins also have alternate peripheral functions, so naming a GPIO is only the first part of configuring it. Decide what each end is allowed to do Before connecting anything, check the chip's allowed input range and the development board's actual wiring. Work only with known low-voltage development hardware. Do not connect a motor, relay coil, mains source, unknown voltage or high-current load directly to a GPIO. An onboard LED with its existing circuit is sufficient for this course. An input is often high impedance: it should not strongly drive the wire it observes. If nothing determines the level, the input may float and produce unreliable readings. A pull-up resistor weakly connects it towards the permitted high reference; a pull-down resistor weakly connects it towards ground. Whether an internal pull is available, its strength and its suitability depend on the device and circuit. For the following input model, the manual specifies a pull-up and a switch that connects the input to ground when pressed: Switch state Sampled level Logical pressed state --------- Released High False Pressed Low True This is an active-low input: the active condition uses the low level. It is not a universal button convention. The phrase "write high" also does not universally mean "turn the onboard LED on"; some indicators are wired active-low or controlled through another device. Real-world analogy: a door sign with an agreed meaning A door sign can use either side to mean occupied, provided everyone follows the same convention. Looking at its colour without knowing the convention is ambiguous. How it maps: The sampled electrical level and the application's logical meaning are separate. The board circuit determines whether high or low means pressed or illuminated. Where it stops: A label cannot enforce voltage limits or prevent two outputs fighting one another. Electrical compatibility and correct direction must be established before software interprets the level. Keep hardware access at the boundary This complete C11 host example tests the logical interpretation without wiring hardware: It prints 0 1. The! operator negates a truth value. On a real target, a small driver obtains the electrical level through its SDK, then applies this interpretation. For example, the SDK for RP2040 documents separate operations for initialising GPIO, selecting direction, selecting pulls and reading or writing values. The correct sequence and pin assignment still depend on the exact board. Key takeaways Configure the signal function, direction and required pull before interpreting readings. Derive active-high or active-low meaning from the circuit, not a pin number. Test interpretation separately from the device driver and obey the actual electrical limits. Further reading Raspberry Pi SDK: GPIO configuration and level access RP2040 datasheet: GPIO and electrical specifications

t: Debounce a button without stopping the loop
sum: Accept a new input state after repeated matching samples and report one stable transition.
x: A mechanical switch can make and break contact several times during a press or release. Software that treats every raw transition as an action may report several presses. Debouncing separates an unstable raw input from the stable state the application is allowed to use. State that survives each call This example requires three consecutive matching samples. It is a teaching policy, not a claim that every real switch settles after three samples. A struct groups related fields. The typedef declaration gives the grouped type the name Debounce. A pointer to that structure lets the update function modify the same state on successive calls; d->seen accesses a field through that pointer. This is a complete C11 host model. The update runs in one foreground context, takes bounded work per sample, and does not sleep: It prints 5, the zero-based sample index at which the stable state changes to true. Here the raw values already represent "pressed", after active-low interpretation. The first attempted true run is interrupted by a false sample. The final three true samples form one accepted change. Further true samples produce no additional stable-change notification. Real-world analogy: waiting for a repeated answer When a noisy announcement keeps changing, you can wait for the same answer several times before acting on it. How it maps: The candidate records the latest possible answer, the count records consecutive agreement and the stable state is the accepted result. Reporting only a stable change avoids repeating the same action every sample. Where it stops: Agreement at sample instants does not prove the contact stayed steady between them. A real debounce interval must suit the switch, sampling schedule and how quickly the application must react. Sampling schedule is part of the policy Three matching samples span two gaps between sample instants. Taking the same number of samples faster shortens the observed interval; taking them irregularly means the count no longer represents a fixed duration. Neither case proves that the contact stayed steady between samples. The later timing module schedules calls using a timer. Do not poll this function as fast as the CPU allows and then treat its count as milliseconds. Measure the actual switch behaviour and choose a stable-time requirement. If the application wants only presses, additionally require that the new stable state is true; a release is also a stable change. Key takeaways Keep raw input, candidate state and accepted state distinct. Consecutive sample counts need an explicit sampling schedule. Emit an action on the desired stable transition rather than on every matching sample. Further reading C11 draft: structures, pointers and iteration Microchip AN2805: how contact bounce creates multiple triggers

sum: Keep storage alive for every pointer use and pass a buffer capacity explicitly.
x: A pointer can refer to the correct kind of object and still be unsafe to use. Two further questions matter: is that object still alive, and is the requested element inside its bounds? C generally leaves these checks to the program. A local array belongs to its scope An ordinary local array has automatic storage duration. Its lifetime ends when execution leaves its enclosing block. Returning a pointer to that local array does not keep the array alive. Reading or writing the former object afterwards has undefined behaviour: the language does not promise an outcome, even if one test appears to work. An object declared with static storage duration lasts for the execution of the program. That does not mean it is non-volatile storage or that its contents survive a reset. Static objects can also introduce shared state, so they are not an automatic replacement for a clear ownership contract. Real-world analogy: a key to a borrowed workbench Keeping the key to a borrowed workbench does not extend your booking. You need both the key and permission to use the bench at that time. How it maps: A pointer alone does not extend an object's lifetime. The caller must know who owns the storage and how long it remains available. Where it stops: C does not check the booking for every access. A stale pointer can cause undefined behaviour rather than a helpful refusal. Let the caller provide the storage This complete C11 host example writes three readings into an array supplied by its caller. size_t is an unsigned type suitable for object sizes and array counts. NULL is a null pointer constant; the function rejects it here before dereferencing. It prints 3 30. The array's valid indexes are 0, 1 and 2. Index 3 is one past its end and cannot be dereferenced. Passing an array to this function supplies a pointer to its first element, not a copy of the whole array or its capacity. The separate cap parameter records the caller's promise about writable elements. The check is useful but cannot discover whether that promise is true: a non-null pointer and a large claimed capacity do not prove a valid buffer exists. The caller must supply a live writable array of at least that capacity. In this example the caller's own array remains alive for the whole call and subsequent print. Prefer explicit ownership before allocation tricks For a small controller, fixed buffers with documented owners often make memory use easier to reason about. They still require bounds checks. Dynamic allocation has additional ownership and failure handling, but it is not needed for this beginner example. Decide who may change each buffer, when it may be reused and whether another context can still be using it. Key takeaways A pointer does not extend the lifetime of its object. Pass buffer capacity and return how much valid data was produced. Bounds checks depend on an honest caller contract as well as checks on each array index. Further reading C11 draft: object lifetime, arrays and pointer arithmetic

sum: Distinguish an ideal quantised code from the accuracy of a physical voltage measurement.
x: An analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) turns an analogue input into a finite integer code. Software must know the selected channel, conversion configuration, result's bit layout and reference before interpreting that code. A valid numeric result does not itself prove the sensor wiring or measurement is correct. Resolution describes available codes For an illustrative ideal unipolar converter, divide the reference span into equally wide bins. Assume the input lies from zero up to the reference, with the upper endpoint excluded, and use a floor-quantiser model. The real ADC transfer function may position transitions differently; use its datasheet for an actual design. A 12-bit result has 4096 possible codes, numbered 0 through 4095.
