With an assumed reference span of exactly 3.3 volts, each ideal bin is about 0.806 millivolts wide. More bits make the bins finer for the same span; they do not guarantee a more accurate physical measurement. The number of codes and the highest code are different. Dividing the reference span by the highest code makes an endpoint-normalised display scale; it is not automatically the converter's physical voltage interval. Real-world analogy: reading a ruler with finite marks A ruler gives you a finite spacing between marks. Adding more marks can make the reading more detailed, but it does not fix a ruler that was printed at the wrong scale. How it maps: The ADC's code spacing describes resolution. Reference error, converter error and the rest of the measurement circuit affect accuracy separately. Where it stops: An ADC also has noise, timing and an input circuit. More displayed digits do not remove these effects or prove that a sensor voltage has settled before sampling. Interpret a code under explicit assumptions Under this model, code 2048 starts the bin halfway through the reference span, at 1.65 volts. The input could lie elsewhere inside that bin: the code identifies an interval, not a unique exact voltage. Reference error and converter error add further uncertainty on real hardware. If the reference span increases while the code stays the same, its estimated voltage increases too. The same integer therefore need not mean the same voltage on two differently configured converters. The relationships below are useful when implementing a conversion. They describe the stated ideal model, not an accuracy promise: On hardware, check the input's permitted range, source impedance and acquisition requirements before connecting a known low-voltage signal. Do not assume a digital-tolerant pin has the same permitted analogue range. A reference may differ from its nominal value, and averaging cannot remove a fixed scale error. RP2040 is a concrete example whose advertised code width and measured effective resolution differ; this does not make its numbers universal for other devices. Key takeaways Code count, highest code and real measurement accuracy are different quantities. State the reference and converter model behind any voltage estimate. Use the actual analogue input and settling requirements before wiring or sampling. Further reading Raspberry Pi SDK: ADC operation and effective resolution RP2040 datasheet: ADC transfer behaviour and electrical limits

sum: Explain how pulse repetition and active time change an output without producing a steady analogue voltage.
x: Pulse-width modulation (PWM) repeatedly switches an output between digital levels. Its period is the time for one complete cycle. Its duty cycle is the fraction of that cycle spent in the chosen active state. Frequency and duty cycle answer different questions: how often the waveform repeats and how much of each cycle it is active. Change the active fraction or the repetition rate An active-high waveform that is high for one quarter of every cycle has a 25 percent duty cycle. Increasing that duty cycle makes the output spend more of each cycle high. It need not change how often the cycles repeat. Increasing frequency while keeping duty cycle unchanged makes each full cycle shorter, including both its high and low parts. The active fraction stays the same. For example, a signal repeating at 1,000 hertz has a one-millisecond period; if it is high for a quarter of that period, its high time is 0.25 milliseconds. When configuring timing, these relationships are useful reference: The output is still a sequence of high and low levels. It does not become a constant quarter-scale analogue voltage merely because the duty cycle is 25 percent. A filter and load can respond to its average under suitable conditions, but their behaviour must be designed and measured. A dedicated digital-to-analogue converter is another way to obtain a controlled analogue output; it also has its own settling and load requirements. Real-world analogy: opening a tap for part of each cycle Imagine a tap opened for one quarter of every repeating interval and closed for the rest. Over many intervals it passes less water than a tap left open continuously. How it maps: The repeating interval represents the PWM period, and the open fraction represents duty cycle. Changing that fraction changes the average delivered activity without adding intermediate digital output levels. Where it stops: An electronic pin is not an unlimited power source, and a load does not necessarily average pulses harmlessly. Voltage, current, switching behaviour and the actual circuit remain design constraints. Check the timer's counting rules A hardware PWM peripheral normally keeps counting without the CPU writing every edge. Its counter mode, clock divider and compare rule determine the waveform. A compare value is checked against the counter to choose when the output changes state. For a simple active-high model, the counter visits positions 0 through 99 and the output is high at positions below 25. That means 100 positions per cycle, with the first 25 high. Increasing the compare value while keeping the counter clock and range fixed lengthens the high part without changing the cycle length. This is a reasoning model, not code to run fast enough to create accurate pin timing. RP2040's SDK documents a normal wrap counter whose maximum is inclusive: a maximum of 99 means 100 positions. Its normal counting mode can implement this model, but other modes and output inversion change how settings map to pulses. Check the actual mode before interpreting a configuration. Use an onboard LED through its documented board interface for a first observation. For hardware PWM, first confirm that the board exposes a PWM-capable route to that indicator; an LED driven through another device may need a different interface. Confirm whether its circuit is active-high or active-low. Perceived brightness is not generally proportional to the duty percentage. Never attach a high-current load directly to a pin; this course does not design motor or relay drivers. Key takeaways Period and duty cycle describe different aspects of the pulse train. A PWM pin switches levels; it is not automatically a steady analogue output. Count the actual timer positions and check the board's output circuit before configuration. Further reading Raspberry Pi SDK: PWM counter, wrap and compare behaviour RP2040 datasheet: PWM operation Different onboard LED paths in the official blink example — Raspberry Pi

sum: Choose how to notice an event without hiding work or assuming every edge is retained.
x: A button has changed or a serial byte has arrived. Firmware needs to notice, preserve any information that matters, and decide what work to perform. Polling and interrupts are two ways to arrange that work; neither automatically makes an application responsive. Check explicitly or handle an interrupt With polling, the main loop repeatedly checks a status value. For example: check whether a receive buffer contains a byte, process a bounded amount of work, then check other devices. A blocking driver call can still prevent the next check, even if the rest of the loop looks simple. With an interrupt, a configured hardware condition requests a processor exception. When the processor accepts it, execution enters an interrupt service routine (ISR), then later returns to interrupted work. An interrupt can be pending while another operation runs; masking, priority and current execution context affect when its handler executes. It is not an instantaneous callback. An ISR should do the necessary bounded work: preserve data or record progress, acknowledge the source as the device requires, and defer longer processing to the main loop. Clearing a processor's pending bit and clearing the peripheral's underlying condition are not necessarily the same operation. Read that peripheral's procedure. Real-world analogy: checking a door or hearing a bell Someone can repeatedly look at the entrance or respond when a doorbell rings. How it maps: Looking is polling; the bell represents an interrupt request. A short response can record that someone arrived before the person returns to their main task. Where it stops: Hardware has precise masking, priority and acknowledgement rules. Several arrivals can produce one pending indication, and a bell does not guarantee that each arrival is counted. Trace the information you can lose Suppose firmware checks a pin every 5 ms, at 0 ms, 5 ms and 10 ms. A pulse starts at 1 ms and ends at 2 ms. Every check sees the inactive level: polling the level misses that pulse. An edge-capable peripheral may latch a request, but its behaviour must be configured and checked. A single pending flag can merge several events before service. A serial receive FIFO can retain several bytes but eventually fill. Choose the mechanism by the information required: latest state, a count of events, or every received byte. Start with a cooperative loop when its measured check intervals meet the device's needs. Add an interrupt where hardware support and response requirements justify it. Measure the longest interval under realistic load, including driver calls and logging, rather than treating an average loop speed as a guarantee. Key takeaways Polling checks explicitly; an ISR runs when the processor accepts an interrupt request. Keep interrupt work bounded and acknowledge the actual device condition correctly. A pending indication need not preserve every event. Further reading Arm CMSIS interrupt controller interfaces Raspberry Pi SDK interrupt handling

sum: Use unsigned elapsed-time subtraction with an explicit counter width and observation bound.
x: A delay that stops the main loop can stop button checks and communication work too. A non-blocking timer instead asks whether enough time has elapsed, performs a small action when due, and lets the loop continue. A counter that eventually wraps Assume an abstract time source supplies a uint32_t tick count, advancing once per millisecond. uint32_t, when provided by the C implementation, is an unsigned integer type with exactly 32 bits. The code below accepts the tick count as input; it does not configure a hardware timer. A wrapping counter returns to zero after its largest representable value. Comparing now >= start + interval is unreliable when the addition wraps. Instead, subtract the saved starting count and convert the result to the counter's unsigned type. This is valid when the actual elapsed time since the saved marker is less than one whole counter cycle. The counter alone cannot distinguish a short interval from the same interval plus one or more complete cycles. Arrange regular checks so a due timer is handled before that ambiguity arises. This example uses a 10 ms interval, with checks much more frequent than a full 32-bit millisecond cycle. Real-world analogy: a mileage display rolling over A limited-digit mileage display returns to zero after its highest reading. Two nearby readings can still reveal the distance travelled across that rollover. How it maps: Unsigned subtraction recovers a small elapsed count across one rollover of the displayed number. The saved reading is the timer's starting marker. Where it stops: The readings cannot reveal how many complete display cycles were missed. Firmware must also know the tick duration and how long it can go without observing the timer. Run a portable C example This is a complete C11 host program. bool is a true/false type; >= compares values; return passes the result to the caller. The cast (uint32_t) converts the difference back to the counter's unsigned width. It prints 1: moving from four counts before zero to count six takes ten ticks. UINT32_MAX names the largest value of the type, and u marks an unsigned integer literal. After an action, saving the current time starts a new interval from that observation; a late check shifts the schedule. Advancing a saved deadline by fixed periods is another policy, but then late work needs an explicit catch-up or skip policy. Neither policy makes execution occur at the exact intended instant. Check the time between counter increments and the longest loop delay. Key takeaways Ask whether time has elapsed instead of stopping the whole loop. Unsigned subtraction handles rollover only within a known observation bound. Decide whether late work shifts, catches up or skips the schedule. Further reading C11 committee draft: unsigned arithmetic and exact-width types Raspberry Pi SDK time interfaces

t: Share events with an interrupt safely
sum: Protect a read-and-clear operation under explicit single-core interrupt assumptions.
x: An ISR can update a value between two instructions in the main loop. Correctness depends on the whole operation being performed, not just whether each individual access fits in one machine instruction. Volatile is one part of the contract A volatile access tells the compiler that the access has observable behaviour according to its implementation's rules. It is commonly part of an SDK's contract for hardware registers and interrupt-shared state. It does not make a multi-step update indivisible, synchronise ordinary threads, or order unrelated memory as a memory barrier would. A flag answers a yes/no question such as “has work arrived?”. Setting it three times before the foreground reads it still leaves one true flag. If every event matters, use a suitable counter or bounded queue and an explicit overflow policy; hardware may already merge events before the ISR runs. How a read-and-clear loses an event Suppose a counter contains three. The main loop copies three into a local variable. An ISR increments the shared counter to four. The main loop then clears it to zero. It processes three events and forgets the fourth. Declaring the counter volatile does not prevent this sequence. A short critical section can exclude the specific ISR during the copy-and-clear. This is a Pico SDK fragment illustrating a single-core execution design on RP2040, not a portable host program. Include the SDK headers, install and acknowledge the device-specific handler separately, and assume no other core, DMA engine or non-maskable handler accesses this counter. Assume it cannot overflow between drains. The SDK functions save the previous interrupt state, disable interrupts on the calling core, and later restore that saved state. Do not unconditionally enable interrupts on exit: the caller may already have disabled them. The handler comment is a placeholder for the peripheral's required acknowledgement, not a complete ISR implementation. Real-world analogy: collecting order slips A clerk briefly closes a collection hatch, takes the accumulated order slips and restores the hatch to its previous state. How it maps: The brief pause represents excluding the relevant interrupt while shared work is taken and cleared. Processing the collected work happens after the pause ends. A hatch that was already closed stays closed, just as a previously disabled interrupt state stays disabled. Where it stops: Masking interrupts on one core does not stop other cores or every hardware actor. A counter also has finite capacity and cannot reconstruct events that the device never retained. Keep the protected work short; process the copied count afterwards. If the no-overflow assumption cannot be justified, choose and test a policy such as counter saturation with an overflow indicator. Language atomics are another tool, but their availability, lock-free implementation and suitability inside an ISR must be checked for the actual target and SDK. Key takeaways Volatile does not make read-and-clear indivisible or a flag count events. A critical section must exclude every competing actor relevant to its data. Restore the previous interrupt state and plan for overflow. Further reading GCC: what volatile does and does not guarantee Pico SDK interrupt state helpers Pico SDK calling-core interrupt scope

t: Read a UART frame and budget its bytes
sum: Separate UART framing, payload rate and the receive buffer that software must drain.
x: A UART, or universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter, converts bytes into a serial bit stream and reconstructs received bytes. A common full-duplex connection uses a transmit signal in each direction, plus the electrical reference required by the interface. Asynchronous means there is no separate shared bit-clock wire; each end uses its configured timing. Both ends must agree on baud rate, data bits, parity and stop bits. Pin functions and electrical levels are separate requirements. Work only with low-voltage development hardware. Use a board-approved adapter and the device manuals: a UART framing setting does not establish a safe voltage, and an RS-232 electrical interface is not directly interchangeable with a microcontroller's logic-level pins. Framing uses time too Assume an ordinary binary UART link with 8N1 framing: one start bit, eight data bits, no parity and one stop bit. That is ten transmitted bit periods for one payload byte, before any gaps between frames. Counting only the eight data bits underestimates how long transmission takes. More payload or more framing bits takes longer at the same line rate; a higher line rate shortens the ideal wire time. Gaps between frames and software delays can add to that time. Use this relationship when you need a transfer estimate: For example, 96 payload bytes take 100 milliseconds at 9600 baud with 8N1 and no extra gaps. This is a wire-time estimate, not a promise about the time an application call takes. A UART's FIFO and any software receive buffer provide temporary storage. They do not increase the sustained drain rate. If input keeps arriving faster than software consumes it, a finite buffer eventually overflows. An overrun can lose data; check the hardware and driver error reporting. Real-world analogy: letters arriving in a tray A tray can hold letters while someone is busy, but it eventually fills if letters arrive faster than they are opened. How it maps: UART receive buffers hold a bounded amount of incoming data until firmware reads it. A larger buffer buys time during a pause, not unlimited sustained capacity. Where it stops: Real UARTs have framing and error flags, and their buffers retain bytes rather than whole application messages. A tray does not define when one command ends. Give the byte stream a meaning For a first text command protocol, agree a terminator such as a newline and a maximum command length. Accumulate bytes until the terminator, reject an overlong command, and decide how to resynchronise. For binary messages, use a specified length and framing scheme. Receiving one byte is not the same as receiving a complete valid command. Trace O, N, newline: the parser stores the first two bytes and handles the command only when the terminator arrives. A receive call may return before, at or after those three bytes have arrived; preserve the parser's partial state across calls. Keep interrupt receive work short and perform command interpretation outside the ISR where possible. Key takeaways UART timing and framing must agree at both ends; electrical compatibility is separate. Include start, data, parity and stop bits when estimating wire time. Buffers are finite, and application messages need their own framing rules. Further reading TI: RS-232 electrical interface and logic-level conversion Pico SDK UART framing and receive interfaces RP2040 datasheet: UART peripheral

sum: Distinguish a seven-bit target address, wire address byte and the final read NACK.
x: Ordinary bidirectional I2C uses two shared signals: SDA for data and SCL for the clock. Devices pull a signal low or release it; pull-up resistors bring released lines high. Work only with low-voltage development hardware. Check the board, target-device and bus specifications for suitable levels and pull-ups rather than assuming a universal resistor value. A controller initiates a transfer and addresses a target. We use a single-controller bus with seven-bit addressing in this lesson. Device-specific commands and register layouts still come from the target's datasheet: “uses I2C” does not specify how to read its measurements. A fictional one-byte sensor register Assume a fictional target has seven-bit address 0x48, selects a register by a one-byte write, and returns that register on a following read with a repeated START. Its register 0x01 currently contains 0x7A. This is a protocol exercise, not a claim about an actual sensor. Step Sender What happens --------- START Controller Begin transfer 0x90 Controller Address 0x48, write direction ACK Target Accept address 0x01 Controller Select the fictional register ACK Target Accept register byte Repeated START Controller Begin another address phase 0x91 Controller Address 0x48, read direction ACK Target Accept address 0x7A Target Return the fictional register byte NACK, then STOP Controller Finish this one-byte read The first wire byte combines the seven address bits and the read/write bit. The Pico SDK's I2C API accepts the seven-bit address separately; it supplies the direction bit. Passing 0x90 where that API expects 0x48 confuses two different representations. ACK means the receiving side acknowledged that byte. It is not proof that a measurement is fresh or meaningful. A NACK at the end of the controller's last read byte is the normal way to decline another byte, whereas an address NACK can indicate that the selected target did not respond. Real-world analogy: addressing a letter and asking for a reply A sender identifies the recipient, delivers a request and then allows the recipient to reply before ending the exchange. How it maps: The address selects a target; the write selects the fictional register; the repeated START changes the transfer direction without ending that combined exchange. Where it stops: I2C has precise clocked byte and acknowledgement rules, and a target's command sequence is device-specific. An acknowledged address does not identify which of two incorrectly duplicated-address devices replied. Stop failures becoming a frozen loop Use a driver operation with a suitable timeout and check its result and returned byte count. Devices may stretch the clock in modes that allow it; a broken connection or stuck signal also needs a bounded failure path. A timeout is a software decision to stop waiting, not proof that the underlying wiring has recovered. Retry only under a deliberate policy; report the fault if recovery fails. Key takeaways Distinguish a seven-bit API address from the address-and-direction byte on the wire. Read the target's command protocol; there is no universal sensor register map. Interpret NACK in context and bound failed transfers. Further reading NXP UM10204: I2C protocol and acknowledgement Pico SDK I2C addressing and timeout APIs

t: Match SPI clocks and chip selection
sum: Use a peripheral datasheet to set SPI sampling edges, selection and exchange boundaries.
x: A common four-signal SPI, or serial peripheral interface, connects a controller and a peripheral with a clock, data in each direction and chip select. The controller supplies clock pulses. The two data directions can shift bits during the same clocks, although a particular command may use only one direction's useful result. Signal names vary. A controller's data output is often called COPI or MOSI; its data input is CIPO or MISO. Follow the actual device labels and directions, not just familiar wire colours. Work only with low-voltage development hardware. Check electrical compatibility and the board's pin-function configuration before connecting devices. Agree which edge means sample Clock polarity (CPOL) chooses the idle clock level. Clock phase (CPHA) chooses which clock edge samples a bit relative to that idle level. In the commonly named mode 0, the clock idles low and the receiver samples on the leading, rising edge; subsequent data changes happen on trailing, falling edges. The first transmitted bit must already be valid before the first sampling edge. Do not memorise “always read on rising edges”: a different required mode can use different edges. Configure the mode, bit order, number of bits per transfer and maximum clock rate specified by the peripheral. Also respect chip select setup and hold times; lowering the clock rate does not fix the wrong sampling mode. Real-world analogy: a leader setting the beat Two people pass items in time with a leader's beat. They must agree which part of the beat means present an item and which means take it. How it maps: The controller's clock sets the transfer rhythm, and the configured sampling edge determines when a bit must be valid. Chip select identifies the intended exchange. Where it stops: Real devices specify exact timing, bit order and chip select behaviour. Matching a beat does not establish a shared command language or prove that the receiver accepted a command. Trace a command without inventing a device Assume a fictional peripheral uses an active-low chip select and requires a command byte followed by one dummy byte, all within one selection. It returns status while the dummy byte is clocked. This is that fictional device's rule, not a universal SPI frame format. Drive its chip select active using the required timing. Transfer the command byte and discard the simultaneously received placeholder. Transfer the dummy byte while collecting the returned status. Wait for the transfer to finish, then deassert chip select at the allowed time. A transmit function returning can mean data entered a buffer rather than that the last clock finished; use the documented driver semantics. The Pico SDK's blocking transfer operations are one concrete example to inspect, rather than assuming every API means the same thing. SPI itself does not provide I2C-style addressing and per-byte ACK. Check the returned device status or other documented evidence. For multiple peripherals sharing a data-return wire, each unselected device must release it as its datasheet requires; chip-select wiring alone does not prove the bus is electrically shareable. Key takeaways Match polarity, phase, bits per transfer, bit order and rate to the device's specification. Chip select timing and command framing belong to the peripheral's protocol. Clocking bits does not itself prove successful application-level communication. Further reading Pico SDK SPI format and transfer semantics RP2040 datasheet: SPI peripheral timing

sum: Choose an observation that can answer the actual debugging question.
x: An indicator did not change when expected. Before rewriting the driver, turn the symptom into a question: did the input arrive, did the state change, or did the output operation reach the device? Each question needs different evidence. Choose an observation Question Useful observation ------ Did this branch execute? A bounded log or breakpoint Who changed this variable? A watchpoint, when supported Which bytes did the driver report? A bounded receive trace and errors Did the expected signal appear? A suitable instrument and device timing specification A breakpoint stops execution at a chosen location. A watchpoint can stop when a watched expression changes. Support depends on the target and debugger; hardware watchpoints have target-specific limits, and software watchpoints can add substantial overhead. Optimisation can also make a source variable unavailable or harder to interpret at a particular stopping point. GDB is one debugger with these facilities. A host debugger can inspect the portable project in this module; build with suitable debug information when inspecting source variables. Inspecting a microcontroller instead requires a supported probe, connection and target configuration; there is no universal debug command or pinout. Real-world analogy: investigating a missed delivery A delivery record can show when a parcel was handed over; watching a doorway can show who actually moved it. Different records answer different questions. How it maps: Logs record selected events, a breakpoint checks execution at a point, and a watchpoint helps identify a data change. Choose the evidence that can distinguish competing explanations. Where it stops: A debugger can stop the processor and logging consumes execution time and storage. These observations can change the timing of the fault being investigated. Use one hypothesis at a time For the hypothetical missing indicator, inspect the decoded input first. If it is correct, inspect the resulting application state. If that is also correct, check the driver result and the actual output configuration. This separates a parsing defect from a state-rule defect or an incorrectly configured output. Add a short trace containing the state, event, driver failure result and timestamp you actually need. Bound its buffer and output rate; do not print without limit inside an ISR. A fault that disappears after adding logging needs investigation: the change may affect timing or memory use without correcting the defect. Halting a processor changes its relationship with external devices and deadlines. A watchdog may continue running or pause under a configured debug option; check that device's behaviour. Use non-halting observations when you need timing evidence, and record how the observation affects the system. Key takeaways Start with a question that an observation can answer. Debugger and logging overhead can change timing and behaviour. Separate decoded input, application state and physical output evidence. Further reading GDB breakpoints and watchpoints GDB watchpoint support and limits GDB: optimisation and source-variable visibility Zephyr: logging overhead and bounded output Pico SDK watchdog debug-pause option

t: Test decision logic without a board
sum: Separate deterministic decisions from hardware access and test boundary inputs on a computer.
x: A sensor driver has electrical and timing dependencies. The rule deciding whether its decoded value should light an indicator often does not. Put that decision in a small function with explicit inputs and outputs, then test it without a board. Give the logic a narrow contract Our fictional sensor reports whole numbers from 0 to 100. For this learning project, values below 70 mean normal, values from 70 to 100 mean alert, and values outside the range are invalid. These are invented application requirements, not a real sensor's units or accuracy specification. This complete C11 host program implements that rule. A comparison in C produces integer zero or one; assert checks that the expected expression is true and stops a test that fails. Build these tests with assertions enabled, without defining NDEBUG. Assertions are test checks here, not the production policy for handling a failed device. It prints logic checks passed. The cases on both sides of 70 distinguish “greater than” from “greater than or equal”, while the range endpoints expose an incorrect validity check. Real-world analogy: rehearsing with prepared cue cards An actor can rehearse responses using prepared cue cards before the rest of the production is ready. How it maps: Controlled readings replace unpredictable live inputs, letting a test repeat the same decision and check its result. Where it stops: Prepared inputs cannot prove that a physical sensor, driver, clock or electrical connection works. Hardware integration still needs its own observations. Introduce controlled failures too Keep acquisition outside this function: the driver returns a decoded sample or an explicit failure. A fake supplies chosen results for tests, including an unavailable sample or a timeout. Do not silently substitute an in-range reading for failure; that would make the logic mistake “nothing was read” for “the reading was normal”. Use host tests for boundary cases and state transitions. Later, compare a known device input with the reported driver result on the real board. Compiling on a computer does not check the target's register access, interrupt behaviour or timing budget. Keep both kinds of evidence. Key takeaways Make application decisions deterministic and independent of hardware access. Test endpoints, threshold neighbours and explicit failures. Host tests complement rather than replace hardware integration checks. Further reading C11 draft: expressions, assertions and test behaviour GCC warning options

t: Plan timeouts, watchdogs and reset recovery
sum: Separate a handled device timeout from whole-system loss of progress, then define recovery.
x: A timeout limits how long one operation may wait. A watchdog can reset parts of a device when required software progress stops being reported. They address different failure levels: a disconnected sensor should first become a handled application fault, not an excuse to retry forever. Feed only for meaningful progress A hardware watchdog is commonly a counter that software periodically refreshes. If it expires, its configured reset action occurs. Exact clocks, reset coverage, timeout limits and debug behaviour are device-specific. The Pico SDK watchdog interface is one concrete example; it is not a universal timer API. Define a health policy before choosing where to feed it. For a small application, a supervisor can require evidence that the main loop ran, the acquisition work reached a completed result, and the indicator/status work completed during the monitoring window. A completed result can include a correctly handled timeout; it need not mean that an unplugged sensor became healthy. Observed progress Policy decision in this example ------ Loop, acquisition outcome and status all progressed Refresh watchdog Sensor timed out, fault status published, loop responsive Continue documented degraded operation Main loop stopped, but an ISR still runs Do not let that ISR hide the stalled loop Blindly feeding from a periodic ISR can keep the watchdog satisfied while the main application is stuck. Each progress report should refer to the current monitoring window; stale “healthy” flags are not evidence of fresh progress. Real-world analogy: a scheduled check-in A worker checks in after completing the agreed checks. Missing the check-in triggers a predefined response rather than an endless wait. How it maps: A watchdog refresh represents current progress evidence, and expiry requests the configured recovery action. The health policy defines what the check-in actually proves. Where it stops: A reset cannot repair broken wiring or prove the software correct. A badly chosen check-in can report success while the important work is stalled. Make reset a controlled transition On boot, read the documented reset-cause information before clearing or overwriting relevant evidence. Initialise the application's outputs and state deliberately, then enter the documented start state. Do not immediately restore a remembered output command without validating whether it is still appropriate. For this course's indicator project, reset returns to WAITING until a fresh valid sample arrives. A timeout latches a visible FAULT state; the chosen recovery event clears it back to WAITING, not straight to a stale NORMAL reading. If repeated resets occur, preserve enough diagnostic evidence and a recoverable maintenance path to investigate them rather than hiding a reboot loop. Test the watchdog intentionally on a supported board using its official example and recovery instructions. Check whether it pauses during debugging; a halted processor is not a normal workload. Tests of the host model can check the chosen recovery policy but cannot validate the hardware watchdog clock or reset circuitry. Key takeaways A timeout bounds one operation; a watchdog supervises selected progress. Refresh only from current, meaningful health evidence. Plan reset cause, initial outputs and a recoverable startup path. Further reading Pico SDK watchdog and reset-cause interfaces Official Pico watchdog example

sum: Compare a cooperative loop with scheduled tasks without treating priority as a deadline proof.
x: A small cooperative loop can remain easy to inspect when every operation is bounded. As communication, sampling and reporting become independent activities, an RTOS, or real-time operating system, can help organise their scheduling and waiting. Adding an RTOS does not make an unbounded driver call or an overloaded processor meet a deadline. Work can wait without consuming the processor An RTOS task has execution state and a task stack. In a single-core system, only one task executes on that core at an instant. A task can be ready to run, running, or blocked while waiting for a supported event or time condition. Other states and exact scheduling rules depend on the kernel and configuration. With preemption enabled in a priority-based FreeRTOS configuration, a higher-priority ready task can preempt a lower-priority one. A blocked high-priority task is not ready; lower-priority ready work can run. Equal-priority time sharing and other details depend on configuration. Consider a deliberately simplified single-core trace with preemption enabled. The sensor task has higher priority than the logger: Event Sensor task What can run --------- Waiting on a supported event Blocked Ready logger Event makes sensor ready Ready Sensor can preempt logger Sensor finishes bounded work and waits Blocked Logger can resume Real-world analogy: a shared workshop bench Several workers need one bench. Someone waiting for a delivery can step aside; an urgent ready job can be given the next use of the bench. How it maps: The bench is one CPU core, tasks are the workers, and a blocking wait removes work from the ready set until its event occurs. Priority helps choose among ready work. Where it stops: The kernel follows exact scheduling rules rather than social judgement. Shared resources, interrupt work and execution time can still delay an urgent task beyond its deadline. Add ownership before adding tasks Assign one owner to a peripheral or protect its use with the appropriate mechanism. A queue can carry commands or results between tasks, but its finite capacity needs a rule for handling a full buffer. Kernel scheduling does not make every SDK driver safe for simultaneous calls. Each task also needs a stack budget, and scheduling adds its own configuration and debugging work. Measure the actual workload, check blocking behaviour and bound competing work. If the small indicator application already meets its requirements with a measured loop, keeping that loop is a valid choice. Introduce tasks when they simplify explicit waiting, ownership and coordination enough to justify their costs. Key takeaways A blocked task is not ready work competing for the CPU. Priority does not establish a worst-case deadline guarantee. Tasks still need bounded work, shared-device ownership and stack capacity. Further reading FreeRTOS task states and task API contracts FreeRTOS scheduling implementation FreeRTOS queues and wait timeouts

t: Build a small sensor and indicator model
sum: Run a complete C model that validates samples, indicates a threshold and latches faults.
x: Now connect the pieces into a small project: accept a sensor result, validate it and choose an indicator state. The hardware adapter will supply events; the application rules will remain testable on a computer. Write the contract before the code Use the fictional whole-number sensor from the previous testing lesson: valid values are 0 to 100 inclusive, and the alert threshold is 70. A SAMPLE event carries a decoded value. TIMEOUT means the acquisition did not finish within its chosen bound; FAILED means the driver reported an acquisition error. RESET is an explicit application recovery event; it is not an automatic C restart or a promise about a physical reset pin. Current state or event Result ------ Reset event WAITING for fresh data Already FAULT, without reset Remain FAULT Timeout, failed read or invalid sample Latch FAULT Valid sample below 70 NORMAL Valid sample at least 70 ALERT WAITING, NORMAL, ALERT and FAULT are application states, not electrical pin values. The later adapter must map each state to the chosen onboard indicator and reported status. It must not map missing data to a normal measurement. Run the complete host model An enum gives names to alternatives. enum mode is a type; current and event are function inputs. The conditional expression condition? first: second selects one result. Each call below performs only bounded comparisons and returns a state; it never waits for hardware. With assertions enabled, it prints project checks passed. The test shows that a valid sample cannot silently clear a latched fault; explicit recovery returns to WAITING. Boundary values and a timeout are part of the normal test plan. Real-world analogy: a parcel inspection station A station waits for a parcel, inspects its label and selects a normal, alert or fault indicator. A fault remains recorded until an operator performs the defined reset action. How it maps: The event is an arriving result, validation checks the allowed input contract, and the resulting state selects the application's indication. Explicit recovery prevents a later arrival from silently erasing a fault. Where it stops: These states are software policy. The model does not validate a real sensor's electrical interface, measurement accuracy or timing, and it is not a safety-certified controller. Keep acquisition outside the model A board adapter starts a read at the chosen sampling interval, bounds its wait using a deadline, and produces SAMPLE, TIMEOUT or FAILED as appropriate. The state function also rejects out-of-range decoded samples. The adapter applies the returned state to a documented onboard indicator and exposes the fault through status output. This host model deliberately simulates those events. It is a complete executable model of the application rules, not complete firmware for an unspecified board. Its rules can be reused after adding and checking an adapter for a particular board and sensor. Key takeaways State the input range, threshold, timeout and recovery policy explicitly. Test invalid inputs and fault latching as well as normal readings. Keep device acquisition and output mapping outside the deterministic state function. Further reading C11 draft: enum, selection statements and assertions Official Pico I2C timeout API contracts

t: Take the first project from tests to a board
sum: Use concrete acceptance cases and a documented board adapter to complete the learning project.
x: Finish the sensor-and-indicator project in two stages: first make its application rules repeatable on a computer, then check a specific board adapter. Keep a record of the source revision, build settings, board identity and expected observations so a later change can be compared with the same baseline. Run the portable program first Save the complete program from the preceding lesson as project.c. With a C11-capable compiler supporting these warning options, this command builds the host test. The backslash continues the shell command onto the next line; -o names its output file. Expect project checks passed. Keep assertions enabled for this test build. A warning-free compilation and passing examples are useful evidence, not proof of every input or of target timing. Add more cases before changing the project rules. Acceptance case Expected application result ------ Fresh valid 50 NORMAL Fresh valid 70 ALERT Invalid 101 FAULT Valid 20 after a latched fault Still FAULT Explicit recovery WAITING Acquisition timeout FAULT Add a board adapter deliberately Choose an existing supported low-voltage development board and use its official setup and example for the exact variant. Confirm the board's schematic, SDK pin functions, power method and signal limits before connecting a sensor. Start with its onboard indicator; do not connect motors, relays, mains or other loads directly to MCU pins. The following is integration pseudocode, not a universal SDK or a second runnable program: Give an attempt one terminal outcome. If completion and deadline are both observed in one pass, use a documented rule based on the driver's result and timing contract; do not dispatch a successful sample and then a stale timeout for the same attempt. A failed read must not retry forever and prevent the cooperative loop from continuing. Observe and recover Flash using the official workflow for that board and inspect the expected startup state. Exercise valid readings, threshold neighbours, invalid results and a deliberately controlled timeout. Use a host fake for faults that cannot be injected safely or reliably on the board. Check the expected indicator/status path and return to a known state after each case. Real-world analogy: a rehearsal followed by a venue check Rehearsal checks the sequence of actions; a venue check confirms that the real equipment and controls work together. How it maps: Host tests check repeatable application logic, while board checks establish the chosen adapter's actual behaviour under the tested conditions. Where it stops: A successful demonstration covers only the exercised inputs and conditions. It does not establish production reliability, all timing bounds or suitability for a safety-critical use. Keep a recovery path: the official flash or debug connection, a known-good image and a record of reset causes. Once the baseline is repeatable, change one requirement at a time and rerun the same acceptance cases. More advanced bootloaders, updates and power characterisation belong after this introductory project. Key takeaways Make the host acceptance cases pass before adding physical integration. Bind each acquisition attempt to one valid result or explicit failure outcome. Keep a documented flash, observation and recovery workflow for the actual board. Further reading GCC warning options and their limits Official Pico SDK board configuration and build workflow Official Pico examples

sum: Distinguish the OSI, TCP/IP and five-layer models and identify each layer’s responsibility.
x: Sending a web page from a server in Frankfurt to your phone involves electrical pulses, radio waves, error checks, addresses, routing decisions, retransmissions, encryption and HTTP. Dividing these responsibilities makes the system easier to build and reason about. Networks tame this by layering. In the model, each layer groups related responsibilities, relies on services below, and offers a cleaner service to the layer above. Ethernet does not care whether it carries a web page or a video call. HTTP does not care whether the bits travel over fibre or Wi-Fi. This lesson sets up the vocabulary used for the rest of the subject. The two models There are two reference models you will meet constantly. The OSI reference model has seven layers. Its numbering survived: engineers still say "layer 2 switch" or "layer 7 load balancer". The TCP/IP model (described in RFC 1122) has four layers and describes the protocols the internet actually runs. # OSI layer TCP/IP layer Examples ------------ 7 Application Application HTTP, DNS, SMTP 6 Presentation Application TLS, encodings 5 Session Application (rarely distinct) 4 Transport Transport TCP, UDP; QUIC over UDP 3 Network Internet IP, ICMP 2 Data link Link Ethernet, Wi-Fi 1 Physical Link Cables, radio Many textbooks (Kurose and Ross, Tanenbaum) teach a hybrid five-layer model: physical, link, network, transport, application. That is the model this subject follows. A basic Ethernet bridge doing ordinary layer-2 forwarding within one VLAN looks up the destination MAC address. It does not need an IP destination or an application header for that lookup. What each layer is responsible for: Physical: turn bits into signals on a medium and back again. Link: move a frame across one link or LAN to the next device, using link-specific framing and, on Ethernet or Wi-Fi, MAC addresses. Network: move a packet from source host to destination host across many links, using IP addresses and routing; not all IP addresses are globally routable or uniquely identify one host. Transport: deliver data between transport endpoints using ports and addresses. Services vary: TCP offers an ordered reliable byte stream and congestion control; UDP itself does not. Application: whatever the program needs: fetching pages, resolving names, sending mail. Hop-by-hop versus end-to-end Layers 1 and 2 operate on a single hop. Layer 3 crosses the whole path, but every router along the way inspects it. Layers 4 and up are, in principle, only looked at by the two end hosts. Remembering this explains a lot about which devices touch which headers. Key takeaways The OSI numbering describes seven responsibilities; this course uses the five-layer teaching model. Link delivery is local to a hop or LAN; network routing crosses links. Further reading RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts — Communication Layers OSI model — Wikipedia Internet protocol suite — Wikipedia Encapsulation (networking) — Wikipedia) RFC 3439: Some Internet Architectural Guidelines and Philosophy IANA IP protocol number registry RFC 9001: QUIC packet and header protection RFC 7348: VXLAN framing

sum: Follow a payload through headers and learn how receivers select the next protocol.
x: Encapsulation On the way down the stack, each layer takes what the layer above handed it, treats it as an opaque payload, and adds its own header in front (and sometimes appends a trailer). On the way up at the receiver, each layer strips its header, acts on it, and passes the payload up. Each layer's unit has a name, the PDU (protocol data unit): Layer PDU name ------ Application Message Transport Segment (TCP) / datagram (UDP) Network Packet (or datagram) Link Frame Physical Bits / symbols How the receiver knows what is inside Several headers and endpoint identifiers allow demultiplexing, selecting the next protocol or recipient. Not every protocol header contains an explicit next-protocol field: Ethernet's EtherType field: 0x0800 means IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x0806 ARP. IPv4's Protocol field (IPv6 calls it Next Header): 6 is TCP, 17 UDP, 1 ICMPv4 and 58 ICMPv6. IPv6 Next Header can also identify an extension header. TCP and UDP port numbers, together with addresses and other socket context, select transport endpoints. Port 443 conventionally serves HTTPS and 53 serves DNS; port numbers alone do not prove the application protocol or uniquely identify one process. Without these fields a receiver would see an undifferentiated stream of bytes. For ordinary forwarding without NAT or a tunnel, each router replaces the incoming link-layer frame for the next link while preserving the source and destination IP addresses. It decrements IPv4 TTL (or IPv6 Hop Limit); an IPv4 router also updates the IPv4 header checksum. These changes do not normally change the transport ports. A basic bridge forwarding within one VLAN instead looks up the destination MAC address. Key takeaways EtherType and IP protocol fields identify payload protocols. Each routed Ethernet hop needs its own local frame; end hosts interpret transport endpoints. t: Count useful bytes and wire time
sum: Explain why headers and wire overhead affect small requests more than full frames.
x: An application pays for more than its own bytes. Transport, network and link layers add headers, and Ethernet also uses a trailer and time between frames. Link efficiency is the share of link occupancy that carries useful data at the boundary you choose. A small request and a full frame Assume a 100-byte HTTP request fits in one TCP segment: no TLS, minimal TCP/IPv4 headers and untagged Ethernet. Ignore acknowledgements, retransmissions and PHY coding. Part Bytes ------ HTTP request 100 TCP header 20 IPv4 header 20 Ethernet header and FCS 18 The resulting frame is 158 bytes from destination MAC to FCS. Ethernet's header contains two 6-byte MAC addresses and a 2-byte EtherType; its FCS is a 4-byte CRC trailer. Wire occupancy also includes an 8-byte preamble/start delimiter and a nominal 12-byte-time inter-frame gap. A byte-time is the time to send one byte. The gap is a time allowance, not extra frame payload; the PHY may send idle signalling during it. This request therefore costs 178 byte-times, of which only 100 carry HTTP: about 56% efficiency. A full 1500-byte IPv4 packet with minimal headers carries 1460 bytes of TCP data and occupies 1538 byte-times under the same accounting. About 95% carries TCP data. The fixed overhead has been spread across much more useful data. Small messages are still useful: waiting to fill a frame can add latency. The point is to understand the cost, rather than always choose the largest message. Count the right boundary The IP MTU counts the IP packet; Ethernet frame size counts destination MAC through FCS; wire occupancy additionally counts preamble and gap. Confusing these boundaries produces misleading rates. TCP options use some space inside the same IP MTU, leaving less for data. Tags, encryption and tunnels can add further overhead. A calculated payload ceiling is not a measured application rate: host limits, congestion, acknowledgements and loss can reduce goodput. Key takeaways Fixed overhead takes a larger share of a small frame's wire time. Distinguish useful payload, IP packet size, Ethernet frame size and wire occupancy. sum: Decode a synthetic header with Python and identify what the limited parser cannot validate.
x: Parsing headers in code Many header fields have defined byte layouts; optional and variable-length fields need additional parsing. Python's struct module can unpack them (! means network byte order, which is big-endian): The tuple contains the destination, source and EtherType. The final return value is the bytes after the fixed header; the displayed slice deliberately omits it. The length check rejects an incomplete fixed header before struct.unpack reads it. This is a synthetic header followed by placeholder bytes, not a valid complete ARP frame. Its all-ones destination denotes broadcast and its EtherType selects ARP, which you will meet in the ARP units. This parser demonstrates an untagged Ethernet II header only. It does not handle VLAN tags, 802.3 length/LLC framing, frame length validation or FCS stripping/verification; packet-capture APIs may omit the FCS. Key takeaways Network byte order puts the most significant byte first. Parsing 14 header bytes does not validate the whole frame or its FCS. sum: Recognise checksum, NAT, MTU and middlebox interactions across layer boundaries.
x: Why layering works Independent evolution. A faster Ethernet link does not inherently require a new TCP wire format. An application protocol can evolve without redesigning link framing. Interchangeable parts. IP runs over Ethernet, Wi-Fi, 5G, satellite and (famously, in RFC 1149) carrier pigeons. Anything that can carry a packet can be part of the internet. The narrow waist. Many link technologies below and many applications above all meet at a single network protocol, IP. IP is the common internetworking service in this model; applications normally use higher-level APIs, while lower-layer devices need not implement an IP endpoint. Each device does only what it needs. Basic bridging uses link-layer information, while IP routing uses network-layer information. Real switches and routers can also inspect higher layers for filtering, load distribution or other functions. Where layering leaks In theory a layer knows nothing about the others. In practice the boundaries leak, and many real problems live in those leaks. TCP checksums cover IP addresses. The TCP checksum includes a "pseudo-header" of source and destination IP. So address translation must preserve checksum correctness by adjusting or recomputing it; particular changes can cancel numerically. Address/port translation. A home gateway can use network address and port translation to share a public address. It may preserve a source port when possible or rewrite it when required by its mapping policy. MTU. The network layer needs the link MTU: the maximum network-layer packet that fits, rather than the whole Ethernet frame including its header and FCS. An oversized packet may be fragmented when permitted, or rejected with an ICMP message. If the required signalling or discovery fails, a path-MTU black hole can make larger traffic fail while smaller packets work. Middleboxes inspect layer 4. Firewalls and load balancers parse TCP headers and drop what they do not recognise. Such ossification can impede new transports and extensions. QUIC uses UDP to improve deployability and protects packet contents and selected header fields to limit unwanted dependencies; some headers remain visible and some networks block UDP or QUIC. Wireless loss looks like congestion. Loss-based TCP congestion control treats loss as a congestion signal, even when a particular loss comes from corruption rather than queue overflow. Reducing the rate may not address that radio error, and link-layer retransmissions can recover some radio loss before TCP sees it. Wi-Fi retry mechanisms also benefit other traffic; TCP is not their sole reason for existing. Layers that do not fit. MPLS is often called "layer 2.5". TLS sits between transport and application. Some tunnels, such as VXLAN, carry an inner Ethernet frame inside UDP (without the original FCS); other VPNs tunnel IP packets or application data instead. Layering is a model, not a law Treat the layers as a way to reason about responsibilities. Expect real systems to cross them for performance, security or historical reasons, and expect bugs where they do. Key takeaways Layering allows independent evolution but practical boundaries can interact. NAT, MTU discovery, encrypted transports and tunnels need coordinated accounting. sum: Distinguish link capacity from latency and predict how packet size and link rate affect transmission.
x: A connection can move a lot of data each second yet respond slowly. Buying more bandwidth helps when capacity is the constraint; it cannot make a signal travel a fixed route faster. Bandwidth and latency Bandwidth, also called link rate or capacity here, is how many bits a link can put onto the medium per second. Latency is the time a bit or packet takes to reach its destination, using the timing boundary specified. Real-world analogy: More lanes Adding lanes to a road lets more vehicles travel at once. It does not shorten the route. How it maps: Link capacity is like the number of lanes; propagation time is like the journey along the route. More capacity can reduce congestion and the time needed to send a whole packet. Where it stops: Packets are serialised into signals, and routers add processing and queueing. A road journey does not model all those delays. Bits and bytes Network rates use decimal SI units and bits: 1 Mbit/s is 1,000,000 bits per second. One byte is 8 bits. File sizes may use decimal bytes (MB) or binary units (KiB, with 1024 bytes per KiB). A 100 Mbit/s link has an ideal ceiling of 12.5 MB/s before overhead; a browser's displayed rate requires measurement. Transmission delay Transmission delay is the time to put all of one packet's bits onto the link, from its first bit to its last. Larger packets take longer. A higher link rate sends the same packet in less time. Cable length plays no part in this particular delay. For example, putting a 1500-byte packet onto a 100 Mbit/s link takes 120 microseconds, ignoring additional framing and encoding. At 1 Gbit/s it takes 12 microseconds. The signal still needs time to travel after the first bit enters the medium. Overhead, server work, congestion and host limits can make a file transfer slower than the raw rate suggests. Keep the units and the measured boundary explicit. Key takeaways Capacity describes a rate; latency describes a time. Packet size and link rate determine transmission delay; route length determines a different delay. sum: Explain the propagation floor and distinguish route length from link rate.
x: Propagation delay is how long a signal takes to travel through the medium. A longer route takes longer; a medium with a higher signal speed takes less time. Distance sets a floor In this model, propagation depends on route length and signal speed, rather than packet size or bit rate. Increasing the rate alone puts bits onto the link faster but does not make each bit travel faster. A useful teaching approximation for ordinary solid-glass fibre is about 5 microseconds per kilometre, or 1 millisecond per 200 km. The precise value depends on fibre construction and wavelength; some cables also have different speeds. For a hypothetical 5,600 km fibre route at 200,000 km/s, propagation takes 28 ms each way. If the return follows the same route and speed, propagation alone contributes 56 ms to the round-trip time (RTT, there and back). Processing, transmission and queueing add more. These are specified-model results, not measured city-pair latencies. A real route may be longer than the distance on a map. What can improve it? A shorter route or a faster propagation medium can reduce propagation delay. Radio in air travels faster than light in typical solid-glass fibre, but a real radio link has its own capacity, reliability and equipment constraints. A higher bit rate or smaller packet can reduce transmission delay while leaving propagation unchanged. An upgrade that also changes the route, wavelength or medium may change both; identify which property actually changed. Key takeaways Propagation follows route length and signal speed. A faster link rate alone leaves propagation time unchanged. sum: Diagnose four delay components and explain store-and-forward packet pipelining.
x: A packet can be delayed before transmission, during transmission, while travelling, and while a device examines it. Separating these costs helps identify which change could improve a slow path. Four contributions Queueing: waiting behind traffic that shares the output link. An idle link can have no queueing delay; a congested one can add hundreds of milliseconds. Transmission: putting every packet bit onto the link. Packet size and link rate determine this. Propagation: the signal travelling along the route. Distance and medium determine this. Processing: examining headers, checking errors and deciding what to do. Hardware, software, enabled features and load affect the time. Variation in packet delay is commonly called jitter. Queueing contributes to jitter, but is not its only possible source. To model one hop, add the relevant waiting, transmission, propagation and processing times. For a whole path, account for each link and each device once at the chosen timing boundary. Store-and-forward and pipelining With store-and-forward, a device receives the complete packet before sending it onward. One packet crossing two such links therefore pays a transmission delay on each link. Cut-through forwarding can overlap reception with onward transmission and needs a different model. For a concrete two-link example, assume a 1500-byte packet, two 100 Mbit/s links spanning 200 km and 800 km, one router taking 20 microseconds, no queues and no framing overhead. At the assumed 5 microseconds per kilometre, propagation contributes 5 ms; both transmissions and processing together contribute 0.26 ms. The total is about 5.26 ms. Increasing link rate addresses only part of this example's delay. Splitting a message into packets lets different links work on different packets simultaneously. On equal-rate, initially idle links, later packets can follow the first one at one packet-transmission interval apart. For this illustration, ignore propagation and processing; each row is one packet-transmission interval: Interval Link 1 Link 2 Link 3 ------------ First P1 — — Second P2 P1 — Third P3 P2 P1 Fourth — P3 P2 Fifth — — P3 Each router still receives a whole packet before forwarding it; work overlaps across links. Two packets do not transmit simultaneously on the same serial link. Extra per-packet headers are excluded from this illustration: splitting too finely can waste capacity. Key takeaways Different delay components respond to different improvements. Store-and-forward repeats transmission per link; packet pipelining overlaps work across links. sum: Explain why queues grow near capacity and why high throughput can hide bufferbloat.
x: A link with spare capacity on average can still build queues. Bursts temporarily arrive faster than the link can serve them; spare capacity between bursts is what lets that backlog drain. Why delay grows near full load Traffic intensity, often called utilisation in the simple model, compares the average incoming work with the link's service capacity. Traffic asking for 90 Mbit/s on a 100 Mbit/s link represents 90% load. With sustained offered work above service capacity, an ideal infinite queue has no stable finite backlog. A real finite buffer eventually fills and drops or rejects excess traffic. Below capacity, the average load alone still does not determine delay: burstiness, packet sizes, scheduling and competing traffic matter. Near full load there is little spare service capacity to drain bursts. A small rise in average traffic can therefore produce a much larger rise in waiting time. An illustrative queue model The M/M/1 queue makes this effect precise under particular assumptions: Poisson arrivals (independent random arrivals at a steady average rate), independent exponentially distributed service times, one server, infinite waiting space and offered load below capacity. In that model the mean queueing wait is one mean packet-service time at 50% load, four at 80%, nine at 90% and 99 at 99%. Delay grows much faster than the offered load near capacity. The mean is finite below full load under these assumptions. Fixed-size packets have fixed transmission times rather than exponential ones. Real arrival patterns and schedulers also differ. This model is neither a universal prediction nor a bound for routers. Bufferbloat Very large buffers can keep throughput high while allowing hundreds of milliseconds of persistent queueing. This bufferbloat hurts calls and games during a bulk upload. Active queue management, including CoDel and FQ-CoDel, addresses persistent queues; FQ-CoDel also separates traffic into flow queues. Measure latency under load as well as throughput. An impressive bulk-transfer rate does not establish that interactive traffic is responsive. Key takeaways Average spare capacity does not prevent transient queues. Near capacity, waiting can grow sharply; exact values depend on the queue model. Throughput and latency under load reveal different aspects of a link. t: Data in flight and window limits
sum: Explain why long, high-capacity paths need more data in flight and can be window-limited.
x: A sender learns that data arrived only when an acknowledgement (ACK) returns. A high-capacity path with a long round trip can therefore hold a lot of sent-but-unacknowledged data. Keeping enough data in flight To sustain a target payload rate, a steady sender needs permission to keep roughly a round trip's worth of payload in flight. This is the bandwidth-delay product. A higher target rate or longer acknowledgement round-trip time increases the required flight allowance. At a hypothetical 1 Gbit/s payload rate and 70 ms acknowledgement RTT, about 8.75 MB would be unacknowledged. This is a payload target, not a universal socket-memory setting: actual operating-system buffer accounting differs. A window can be the bottleneck The TCP send window limits how much data may remain unacknowledged. If it is too small for the target rate and RTT, the sender must wait even when the path has spare capacity. ACKs can advance a sliding window continuously; the sender need not stop after each batch. Nevertheless, in a steady window-limited model, its delivered rate is bounded by about one window's worth per round trip. Without negotiated window scaling, TCP's 16-bit receive-window field represents at most 65,535 bytes. If this is the active limit over a 70 ms RTT, it caps steady payload throughput near 7.5 Mbit/s. Window scaling allows larger advertised receive windows when negotiated; sender congestion limits, receiver space and other constraints still apply. Paths with large bandwidth-delay products are called long fat networks. They need adequate flight allowances, appropriate buffering and recovery that handles many packets in flight. Simply increasing a physical link's rate may leave the limiting window unchanged. Key takeaways Higher target rates and longer feedback delays need more payload in flight. A small active window can limit throughput despite spare link capacity. Window scaling increases representable receive windows; it does not remove all throughput limits. sum: Separate bottleneck capacity, achieved throughput and useful payload goodput.
x: A link's nominal capacity, the traffic it actually carries, and the useful data delivered to an application are different measurements. The bottleneck sets a ceiling Throughput is the rate actually achieved at a stated boundary. A path cannot carry traffic faster than its slowest link, the bottleneck. A 1 Gbit/s home LAN behind a 100 Mbit/s broadband link can reach the internet at no more than 100 Mbit/s through that route. Competition with other flows, active window limits, host performance and congestion can make the achieved rate lower still. A bottleneck capacity is a ceiling, not a promised result. Goodput counts useful data once Goodput counts useful application data delivered per second. It excludes headers, duplicate transmission attempts, pure acknowledgements and handshakes. State the boundary: TCP payload rate can still include TLS or application-protocol overhead that file goodput excludes. For the earlier one-direction, untagged full-duplex Ethernet model, a 1500-byte IPv4 packet with minimal TCP/IP headers carries 1460 bytes of TCP payload in 1538 byte-times of wire occupancy. On 1 Gbit/s Ethernet that allows about 949 Mbit/s of TCP payload. Twelve bytes of TCP options lower it to about 941 Mbit/s. These are ideal framing ceilings. They assume hosts, acknowledgement handling, congestion and loss do not constrain the rate, and exclude additional application/TLS overhead. What retransmissions change A retransmission may finally deliver data that was lost, but delivering that payload then consumed more than one attempt. Goodput counts the useful payload once. In a saturated-link accounting model with equal payload sizes and 2% of attempts being extra retransmissions, useful rate falls by another 2% after framing overhead. Real loss can additionally trigger congestion control, idle time or timeouts, so this accounting is not a general loss-to-throughput prediction. When a transfer is slow, measure the bottleneck, retries, window limits and host work. A higher line-rate label alone does not explain the outcome. Key takeaways Bottleneck capacity bounds throughput; other constraints can reduce it further. Goodput excludes overhead and counts useful delivered bytes only once. Retransmission accounting alone does not predict TCP's congestion response. sum: Choose between reducing round trips and increasing sustained goodput for different workloads.
x: Small exchanges are often dominated by round trips; sufficiently large transfers can be dominated by sustained goodput. Server work, congestion and host performance can dominate either, so diagnose the workload first. Compare two workloads Assume a hypothetical path with a 100 Mbit/s payload rate and a 40 ms round-trip time. Ignore DNS, server work, loss, slow start and additional overhead. Use fresh TCP plus a full TLS 1.3 handshake with no resumption, early data or retry. A 20 KB API response waits through TCP setup, TLS setup and the request/response round trip. Those three round trips cost about 120 ms, while response transmission takes only about 1.6 ms. A 1 GB download needs about 80 seconds of payload transmission. The same setup cost is small beside that. Sending the small response at a higher payload rate removes little of its delay. Reducing RTT or avoiding repeated setup addresses the larger cost in this model. For the large download, improving sustained goodput can make a substantial difference. Avoid unnecessary round trips Connection reuse avoids repeating setup for every request. A server location with a lower measured RTT shortens each required round trip. A conventional full TLS 1.2 handshake without resumption or False Start takes two TLS round trips before the request. With one TCP setup round trip and one request/response round trip, that simplified fresh-connection model needs four RTTs. TLS 1.3 reduces the TLS part to one unless retry adds another exchange. TLS/QUIC early data (0-RTT) requires prior connection state and replay-safe application handling. It is not available for every first connection, and replay risk matters when a request changes state. These examples isolate mechanisms. Real workloads can involve parallel requests, caching, congestion, server computation and connection limits. There is no universal bandwidth threshold beyond which pages stop benefiting. Key takeaways Small exchanges can benefit most from fewer or shorter round trips. Large transfers can benefit most from higher sustained goodput. Reuse and handshake choices depend on protocol and application constraints. sum: Distinguish symbol rate from bit rate and explain why denser signalling needs reliable distinction.
x: The physical layer turns bits into signals that travel as voltages, light or radio waves. It chooses from distinguishable symbols, such as voltage levels or combinations of amplitude and phase. Symbols and bits measure different things The baud rate counts symbols per second. The bit rate also depends on how much information each symbol distinguishes. With two states, one symbol can distinguish 0 from 1. With four states it can distinguish 00, 01, 10 and 11: two bits per symbol. Each extra bit requires twice as many states for an uncoded fixed mapping. Scheme States Bits per symbol --------- Two voltage levels 2 1 PAM-4 4 2 16-QAM 16 4 1024-QAM, used in Wi-Fi 6 1024 10 A 1 Gbaud PAM-4 mapping therefore represents 2 Gbit/s before overhead. Coding, framing and pilots (known reference symbols used by the receiver) reduce the useful payload rate. Why more levels have a cost At a fixed signal range, putting states closer together makes them harder to distinguish in noise. More states can raise bits per symbol while also making the mapping less robust. A receiver also needs suitable pulse shaping and timing: the waveform need not stay constant during a symbol interval. Choosing modulation means balancing rate against the channel conditions, coding and implementation limits. Key takeaways Baud counts symbols; bit rate also counts the bits represented by each symbol. Denser signal states increase raw rate but require reliable distinction in noise. sum: Explain the ideal symbol-rate limit, bandwidth conventions and limits of adding levels.
x: A physical channel passes a limited range of frequencies. Here bandwidth means that frequency range in hertz, rather than a network's advertised bit rate. Symbols must remain distinguishable Pulses can spread into neighbouring symbol intervals, causing intersymbol interference. Ideal pulse shaping can arrange for neighbouring pulses to contribute zero at the receiver's sampling instants. For a noiseless real low-pass channel, one-sided bandwidth is measured from zero frequency to the upper limit. The ideal Nyquist zero-intersymbol-interference model supports a maximum real symbol rate of twice that bandwidth. This is a model with particular bandwidth and signalling conventions, not a universal factor to apply to every radio rate. More distinguishable levels allow more bits in each symbol. Four levels carry two bits per symbol; increasing the number of levels does not increase bits per symbol in direct proportion. For example, a hypothetical noiseless 3.1 kHz baseband channel with four levels permits 6,200 real symbols per second, each carrying two bits, for 12.4 kbit/s. These values illustrate the assumptions; finite implementations and overhead require separate accounting. Noise changes the problem The noiseless model does not decide how many closely spaced levels a real receiver can reliably distinguish. Noise can blur them together. Shannon's noisy-channel limit addresses that additional constraint. Increasing the number of levels on an unchanged noisy channel therefore does not guarantee a usable rate increase. Both bandwidth and reliable distinction matter. Key takeaways The Nyquist zero-ISI model constrains real symbol rate for its stated one-sided baseband bandwidth. More levels carry more bits per symbol, but noise constrains usable signalling. sum: Explain noisy-channel capacity, decibel power ratios and bandwidth-versus-power trade-offs.
x: A receiver must distinguish signal from noise. Choosing more modulation states cannot create unlimited reliable capacity when noise blurs those states. A limit for a specified noisy channel For a band-limited additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel, noise is modelled as random Gaussian variation added to the signal, with equal average noise power in equal-width frequency bands across the channel. Shannon capacity gives the highest reliable information rate in this model under its average-power constraint. At rates below capacity, suitable coding can make error probability arbitrarily small as coding length grows. This is not a promise of zero errors for finite packets. The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compares signal power with noise power. Engineers often express it in decibels (dB): every additional 10 dB multiplies the power ratio by ten. Thus 30 dB represents a signal power 1000 times the noise power. A dB value is not itself the power ratio. What can improve capacity? For a hypothetical single flat AWGN channel, 20 MHz at 30 dB SNR has about 199 Mbit/s capacity. At the same SNR, doubling bandwidth doubles capacity. Doubling signal power while holding noise and bandwidth fixed gives a much smaller proportional improvement at this high SNR. Keeping SNR fixed while widening a channel is an explicit assumption. If total signal power stays fixed and noise spectral density stays constant, a wider channel admits more noise and reduces SNR. Actual Wi-Fi systems also involve multiple spatial channels, contention, pilots, coding and protocol overhead. Independent spatial channels can add capacity, but simply adding antennas does not guarantee independence. Attenuation, interference, propagation paths and equipment affect achievable rates. Key takeaways Capacity depends on channel bandwidth and signal-to-noise power ratio. More modulation levels cannot defeat the stated channel limit. The asymptotic theorem does not promise error-free finite packets or model a complete Wi-Fi network.
