ARC (RFC 8617) helps forwarders and mailing lists: each intermediary records the authentication results it saw and signs them, so the final receiver can choose to trust a known forwarder's verdict even though email SPF and DKIM now fail. Pitfalls Forgotten senders. Moving to p=reject before every SaaS tool signs with your domain can cause legitimate invoices and password resets to be rejected when they lack any aligned authentication pass. email SPF lookup limit. Evaluated nested terms can exceed the ten-term budget and produce permerror. Short DKIM keys. RFC 8301 requires RSA signing keys of at least 1024 bits and recommends at least 2048; key rotation and supported algorithms need an operational policy. Plaintext relay. Opportunistic relay without an effective authenticated-TLS requirement is vulnerable to downgrade; local mandatory-TLS policies are another possible protection. Key takeaways One aligned email SPF or DKIM pass can satisfy DMARC; unaligned authentication does not. Enforcement rollout must include every legitimate sender and account for forwarding or content changes. Further reading RFC 9989 RFC 9990 RFC 8617 Google sender policy

t: SMTP parser agreement and enforced relay TLS
sum: Relay security depends on both consistent framing and an effective authenticated-TLS policy.
x:
An SMTP sender transmits an envelope followed by message headers and body. email SPF authenticates a connecting IP for an envelope domain; DKIM binds covered content to a signing domain, and DMARC checks alignment with the visible From. Those authentication results do not replace safe SMTP framing or confidential, authenticated transport. Dot-stuffing and SMTP smuggling The message ends with a line containing just.. A body line that starts with. is sent with an extra. (as..), which the receiver strips. That is dot-stuffing. In 2023, researchers showed SMTP smuggling: some servers accepted a bare 
.
 as end of data while others required 
.
. An attacker could hide a second, forged message inside the first, which the receiving server then treated as a separate message from the sending provider. Same lesson as HTTP request smuggling: when two parsers disagree on framing, attackers live in the gap. TLS between servers With opportunistic STARTTLS on port 25 and no policy requiring authenticated TLS, stripping the offer can induce plaintext delivery. Enforcing senders instead defer or fail delivery. Two policy mechanisms are: MTA-STS (RFC 8461): an HTTPS policy in enforce mode requires authenticated TLS to approved MX hosts. Cached policies protect against stripping; initial DNS policy discovery can still be suppressed before a sender has a policy. DANE (RFC 7672): DNSSEC-authenticated TLSA records associate acceptable certificates or keys, including supported trust-anchor forms, to the SMTP service. Key takeaways Dot-stuffing preserves message boundaries only when both hops apply compatible end-of-data parsing. Opportunistic STARTTLS and enforced authenticated TLS have different downgrade guarantees. MTA-STS and SMTP DANE constrain relay security under different discovery and trust assumptions. Further reading RFC 5321 RFC 8461: MTA-STS RFC 7672: SMTP DANE SMTP smuggling original research

sum: Four NTP timestamps estimate clock offset and network round-trip delay under an explicit timing model.
x: NTP: agreeing on the time Clocks drift. A clock's error rate is quoted in parts per million (ppm): how many microseconds it gains or loses per second. Multiplying by the time elapsed gives the accumulated error: This is an illustrative rate; actual oscillators and environmental conditions differ. Clock synchronisation matters for logs, certificates, Kerberos tickets, TOTP codes and lease timeouts. Acceptable error depends on each protocol and application policy. NTP (version 4, RFC 5905) runs over UDP port 123. Servers are arranged in strata: reference clocks (such as GPS or atomic sources) are informally called stratum 0, stratum 1 is a server attached to one, stratum 2 syncs from stratum 1, and so on. Stratum 16 means "unsynchronised". In an NTP packet, a stratum field of zero instead means unspecified/invalid and can identify a Kiss-o'-Death response; it is not an ordinary reference-clock server reply. Four timestamps One request/response gives the client four times: The first and fourth timestamps come from the client's clock; the middle two come from the server's clock. From them the client estimates how far its clock is from the server's, and how long the network took: Round-trip delay is the round trip minus the server processing time. Clock offset estimates server time minus client time under the model that each clock runs at a steady rate and the path delay is symmetric; it is not an instruction to step the clock immediately. Why does averaging work? Subtracting the client-send timestamp from the server-receive timestamp gives the offset plus outbound travel time. Subtracting the client-receive timestamp from the server-send timestamp gives the offset minus return travel time. Adding them cancels the travel times only when the two are equal. The same arithmetic in Python: Check it: the client sends at its 10.000, which is server time 10.130; 20 ms later the server receives at 10.150. It replies at 10.152; 20 ms later it is server time 10.172, which on the client's clock is 10.042. Substituting: The ideal arithmetic recovers 130 ms; floating-point computation has rounding error. Key takeaways Four NTP timestamps estimate clock offset and network round-trip delay under an explicit timing model. The delay calculation subtracts the time spent handling the request at the server. Further reading RFC 5905

t: NTP path asymmetry, slewing and monotonic time
sum: Unequal one-way delays bias an NTP offset estimate; low delay does not prove symmetry.
x: NTP estimates server time minus client time by averaging the apparent difference in each direction. It estimates network round-trip delay by subtracting server handling time from the complete exchange. Those estimates cannot by themselves identify one-way path asymmetry. The symmetry assumption The formula assumes the outbound and return trips take equal time. If they don't, the error in the offset is half the difference: So in this example the offset estimate is biased by −15 ms. Those four timestamps alone cannot distinguish this from clock offset. With nonnegative delays and otherwise ideal timestamps, the error magnitude is at most half the measured network round-trip delay. Low-delay samples reduce that bound but do not prove symmetry; multiple sources and filtering can help reject bad measurements. Disciplining the clock Clock-discipline behaviour depends on implementation and configuration. Wall-clock steps can disrupt duration calculations and timestamp ordering: Slewing: run the clock slightly fast or slow until the offset is gone. The time needed is the offset divided by the slew rate; at an illustrative 500 ppm, correcting 1 second takes 1 ÷ 0.0005 = 2,000 seconds, about 33 minutes (see the formula below). This is not a universal Linux limit: chrony supports higher slew rates on Linux. Stepping the clock: set the time directly when policy permits. Classic ntpd uses a 128 ms step threshold with state-machine safeguards; stepping is not inherently restricted to boot. Programs should measure durations with a monotonic clock (time.monotonic() in Python), which is never stepped, and use wall-clock time only for timestamps. Leap seconds add a further wrinkle. Google documents a 24-hour leap smear centred on a leap second; it changes the clock's rate instead of presenting an abrupt insertion. Its offset from unsmeared UTC reaches half a second. Different smear policies need not agree, so do not mix incompatible sources. CGPM Resolution 4 (2022) calls for increasing the permitted UT1−UTC difference by or before 2035, allowing much longer intervals without leap adjustments; it does not specify an unconditional permanent abolition date. Key takeaways Unequal one-way delays bias an NTP offset estimate; low delay does not prove symmetry. Slew and step policies differ, while duration measurements should use a monotonic clock. Further reading RFC 5905 chrony configuration Google leap smear CGPM resolution 4

t: NTP timestamp fields, eras and authentication
sum: NTP timestamps split seconds and fractions into 32-bit fields, so era context matters at wraparound.
x: Wire format and security The basic NTP header is 48 bytes (extensions/authentication can add bytes): leap indicator, version, mode, stratum, poll, precision, root delay and dispersion, reference ID, then four 64-bit timestamps. Each timestamp is 32 bits of seconds since 1 January 1900 and 32 bits of fraction. Both limits follow from the field width: So the seconds field wraps in February 2036; era-aware implementations use contextual date information to disambiguate it. Correct era handling is not guaranteed by the 32-bit field alone. Plain NTP is unauthenticated, so an on-path attacker can shift your clock and, for example, make expired certificates look valid. NTS (Network Time Security, RFC 8915) uses TLS key establishment (TCP port 4460), then protects NTP exchanges with negotiated AEAD keys and authenticators. Opaque cookies carry server state; they are not themselves the per-packet integrity check. Authentication does not prevent an on-path attacker from delaying valid packets. Legacy ntpd's unauthenticated monlist response could amplify spoofed requests, documented as CVE-2013-5211. Exposure depends on implementation, version and access controls. A universal amplification ratio and present-day deployment prevalence are omitted because this review did not establish reliable measurements. PTP (IEEE 1588) can achieve sub-microsecond synchronisation in appropriately engineered networks. Hardware timestamping and PTP-aware transparent clocks reduce timestamp and switch-residence errors; the protocol name alone does not guarantee a particular accuracy. Key takeaways NTP timestamps split seconds and fractions into 32-bit fields, so era context matters at wraparound. NTS authenticates exchanges but cannot stop an on-path attacker delaying valid packets. Further reading RFC 5905 RFC 8915 NTP amplification advisory

t: SSH transport, host trust and authentication
sum: SSH establishes a protected transport, authenticates users and then multiplexes useful channels.
x: SSH: three protocols in a stack SSH (RFCs 4251 to 4254) runs over TCP port 22 and is really three protocols layered on top of each other: Transport layer Both sides send a version string in plaintext, such as SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6. Both send KEXINIT listing supported algorithms in preference order: key exchange, host key types, ciphers, message authentication codes, compression. Negotiation generally follows client preference among mutually supported choices, subject to compatibility rules between key-exchange and host-key algorithms. Key exchange: an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange, these days curve25519-sha256 or a post-quantum hybrid. OpenSSH 9.0 made sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com the default, and OpenSSH 10.0 switched to mlkem768x25519-sha256. The server signs the exchange hash with its host key. The client checks that key against ~/.ssh/known_hosts. Without a preconfigured trusted host key or host-certificate authority, a first connection can prompt for trust on first use (TOFU). Independently checking the fingerprint avoids blindly trusting that first peer. Session keys are derived from the shared secret and the exchange hash. The first exchange hash becomes the permanent SSH session ID. After the version strings, SSH already uses the binary packet protocol; initial key-exchange packets are unencrypted. NEWKEYS activates the negotiated protection. The base packet structure is: In the base RFC 4253 format, packet length including its four-byte length field but excluding the message authentication code is aligned to the cipher block size or 8 bytes, whichever is larger. Negotiated AEAD/Encrypt-then-MAC formats alter some framing and authentication details. Padding provides limited length hiding. Modern ciphers such as chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com and AES-GCM are AEADs, so integrity comes from the cipher's tag. Each direction tracks an implicit SSH sequence number. Base RFC 4253 MACs and some negotiated modes use that counter; SSH AES-GCM instead uses its IV-based invocation counter (RFC 5647). Integrity protection normally detects invalid packet manipulation, but the handshake interaction below exposed an exception for affected modes. Terrapin (2023) Sequence numbers were not reset after the handshake. With affected encryption modes (notably ChaCha20-Poly1305 or CBC with Encrypt-then-MAC), an on-path attacker could inject a message during the unencrypted phase and delete one afterwards, keeping the counts consistent, and so silently strip extension negotiation. The fix, "strict KEX", resets sequence numbers at NEWKEYS and forbids stray messages during the handshake; both client and server must support it. User authentication Within the encrypted transport, the client requests the ssh-userauth service and tries methods: publickey, password, keyboard-interactive (for OTPs). For publickey, the client signs a blob containing the SSH session ID, so a captured signature can't be replayed on another connection. A server talking to an attacker in the middle would have a different session ID, so the signature would not verify. Agent forwarding (ssh -A) lets a remote host ask your local agent to sign for you. A privileged attacker on that host can request signatures through an unconstrained forwarded agent while it remains accessible. Confirmation, destination and hardware constraints can limit use; forwarding does not normally reveal the private key itself. ProxyJump (ssh -J) is safer for hopping through bastions: the end-to-end session is negotiated from your laptop. Key takeaways SSH establishes a protected transport, authenticates users and then multiplexes useful channels. Host-key trust and session-bound public-key authentication solve different impersonation and replay problems. Further reading RFC 5647: SSH AES-GCM RFC 4253 RFC 4252 OpenSSH 10.0 release Terrapin original research

t: SSH channel credit and pipelined SFTP
sum: SSH channels have separate credit but still share one ordered TCP transport.
x: SSH runs an encrypted transport, authenticates a user and multiplexes channels inside that transport. A session channel can run a command or a subsystem; port forwarding uses other channel/request types. Connection layer: channels Everything useful happens in SSH channels multiplexed over one transport: session channels run a shell, a command (exec) or an SSH subsystem such as sftp. direct-tcpip channels carry ssh -L local port forwards. tcpip-forward global requests set up ssh -R remote forwards. Each channel has its own channel window, adjusted with CHANNEL_WINDOW_ADJUST, just like HTTP/2 streams. A small channel window caps throughput at the window divided by the round-trip time (the same window-over-round-trip ceiling as HTTP/2 flow control), which is why bulk transfers over high-latency SSH links can be slow even on fast networks (HPN-SSH exists to raise these limits). Ordinary SSH port forwarding relays application bytes between separate TCP connections; it does not encapsulate complete inner TCP packets. Loss on the shared SSH TCP connection can nevertheless stall delivery for every multiplexed channel. SFTP: not FTP SFTP is not FTP over SSH. It is a separate binary protocol (draft-ietf-secsh-filexfer; OpenSSH implements version 3) that runs as the sftp subsystem inside one SSH session channel. Since OpenSSH 9.0, the scp command uses the SFTP protocol by default too. It works like a remote file system API: (Simplified; the real messages are binary.) File-operation requests carry an SFTP request ID (the INIT/VERSION negotiation is an exception), so a client can have many READs outstanding at once. That pipelining is what makes SFTP fast: OpenSSH's client keeps up to 64 requests in flight by default. A naive client that issues one 32 KiB read and waits for the reply gets at most one block per round trip: Key takeaways SSH channels have separate credit but still share one ordered TCP transport. SFTP is a separate binary file-operation protocol; request IDs permit pipelined reads. Further reading RFC 4254 SFTP v3 protocol draft OpenSSH SFTP manual

t: gRPC requests and protobuf message bytes
sum: A native gRPC call uses an HTTP/2 stream containing length-prefixed messages; this example uses protobuf.
x: gRPC on the wire This section describes native gRPC over HTTP/2. Each call is one HTTP/2 stream. Knowing the framing helps you debug it with ordinary HTTP tools. The request The path is /package.Service/Method, which is how proxies route and authorise per method. te: trailers tells proxies the client understands trailers, which gRPC needs. grpc-timeout carries the gRPC deadline: 250m means 250 milliseconds (units are H, M, S, m, u, n). Applications should propagate the remaining budget downstream; automatic support and configuration differ by language/library. Message framing The gRPC framing is independent of its message encoding; protobuf is the usual default, rather than a requirement of this wire protocol. Inside DATA frames, each encoded message is prefixed with 5 bytes: a 1-byte compressed flag and a 4-byte big-endian length. Take this message: Protobuf encodes each field as a protobuf tag followed by the value. The tag packs the field number and the wire type into one varint: shifting left by 3 bits (<< 3 in code) multiplies by 8, leaving the low 3 bits for the wire type. 08 = field 1, varint. 96 01 = 150. Each varint byte carries 7 bits of the number, least significant group first, and its top bit (worth 128) means "more bytes follow" (see the formula below). 12 = field 2, length-delimited. 02 = 2 bytes. 68 69 = "hi". The 5-byte prefix 00 00 00 00 07: not compressed, 7 bytes. This helper demonstrates nonnegative values; signed int32 negatives use sign-extended varints, while sint32 uses ZigZag encoding. The message boundaries are independent of DATA frame boundaries: one message can span many DATA frames, and one DATA frame can carry several messages. Streaming RPCs simply send more length-prefixed messages on the same stream. Key takeaways A native gRPC call uses an HTTP/2 stream containing length-prefixed messages; this example uses protobuf. A message has a five-byte gRPC prefix, independent of HTTP/2 DATA frame boundaries. Further reading gRPC HTTP/2 protocol Protobuf encoding

t: gRPC trailers, deadlines and connection balancing
sum: HTTP success and RPC success are separate; grpc-status in trailers gives the RPC outcome.
x: A native gRPC call is one HTTP/2 stream. Requests carry a method path, a content type and optionally grpc-timeout; 250m means a 250-millisecond remaining budget. Messages have a one-byte compression flag and four-byte length before each encoded body; these examples use protobuf. The final call result is separate from those bytes. The response and trailers The status is in the trailers, because a streaming server only knows whether the call succeeded at the end. A conforming gRPC response uses HTTP status 200 even for a gRPC error; HTTP intermediaries and protocol errors can produce other HTTP statuses. A call that fails immediately can send a single "Trailers-Only" HEADERS frame. Common codes: Code Name Retry? --------- 0 OK n/a 3 INVALID_ARGUMENT No 4 DEADLINE_EXCEEDED Maybe 5 NOT_FOUND No 8 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED Depends on quota/resource cause 13 INTERNAL Rarely 14 UNAVAILABLE Consider retry if safe and budget permits Retry decisions need method semantics, duplicate-effect protection, retry policy and remaining deadline. A timeout can occur after a server has committed a change. Deadlines and cancellation Pass the remaining deadline budget to downstream calls, reserving any time needed to finish the current response. Starting with 300 ms and spending 50 ms leaves about 250 ms; giving every downstream hop a fresh 300 ms timeout can keep work running after the caller has stopped waiting. Propagation support differs between language libraries and configuration. When a client deadline expires, it can report DEADLINE_EXCEEDED and signal cancellation. Server handlers must cooperate by checking cancellation and stopping unnecessary work; cancellation is not an instantaneous distributed stop and cannot roll back an already committed side effect. Operational consequences Browsers can't read HTTP/2 trailers or control framing through fetch, so browsers use gRPC-Web, which moves trailers into the body and needs a proxy (or server support) to translate. Load balancing. A client using one long-lived HTTP/2 connection sends its streams to the backend chosen for that connection by a connection-oriented layer-4 balancer. A channel can also use multiple connections; the backend assignment lasts for that connection. Use a layer-7 (HTTP/2-aware) proxy such as Envoy, or client-side balancing across several connections. gRPC keepalives are HTTP/2 PING frames. Pinging more often than the server allows gets a GOAWAY with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM and the debug data too_many_pings. Message size. Receive limits are configurable and implementation-specific; exceeding an enforced limit can produce RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED. A cross-language table of current defaults is absent because this review did not verify every supported implementation. Key takeaways HTTP success and RPC success are separate; grpc-status in trailers gives the RPC outcome. Retry safety and deadline propagation depend on effects and remaining budget, not just a status name. Further reading gRPC HTTP/2 protocol gRPC deadlines gRPC load balancing gRPC keepalive

t: BitTorrent metadata, bencoding and peer discovery
sum: BitTorrent v1 hashes the bencoded info dictionary, which commits to piece hashes rather than publisher identity.
x: BitTorrent The metainfo file and the info-hash For BitTorrent v1, a.torrent file is a bencoded dictionary. Bencoding has four types: Type Example Encodes --------- Integer i42e 42 String 4:spam "spam" List l4:spami42ee ["spam", 42] Dict d3:cow3:mooe {"cow": "moo"} Dictionary keys are byte strings and must be sorted by raw bytes. Canonical integer and string-length encodings also matter; hash the original encoded info substring or fully validate input before re-encoding. That matters because of the info dictionary: name, length (or a list of files), piece length, chosen when the torrent is created (256 KiB is one example), pieces: the SHA-1 hashes of every piece, 20 bytes each, concatenated. The info-hash is the SHA-1 of the bencoded info dictionary. It identifies the torrent everywhere: to trackers, in the DHT, in the peer handshake and in magnet links (magnet:?xt=urn:btih:<info-hash>). It ties the metadata to the piece hashes, subject to SHA-1's security limitations. An info-hash is not a publisher identity or proof that downloaded content is safe. BitTorrent v2 (BEP 52) replaces SHA-1 with SHA-256 Merkle trees per file, with 16 KiB leaves (the final block can be shorter). With the necessary hashes/proofs, blocks can be verified against the per-file root; identical file contents share that root. The v2 info-hash is SHA-256, with protocol-specific truncation where a 20-byte identifier is required. Finding peers A client finds others through a BitTorrent tracker (an HTTP or UDP server returning peer lists for an info-hash), the DHT (below) or peer exchange with already-connected peers. A magnet link can carry an info-hash and optional parameters such as tracker URLs or a display name; the client fetches the info dictionary itself from peers (BEP 9) and verifies it against the hash. Key takeaways BitTorrent v1 hashes the bencoded info dictionary, which commits to piece hashes rather than publisher identity. Trackers, DHT lookups and peer exchange discover suppliers; magnet metadata must match its hash. Further reading BEP 3 BEP 9 BEP 52

t: BitTorrent wire messages, verification and choking
sum: BitTorrent peers handshake, pipeline block requests and verify completed pieces against trusted metadata.
x: A BitTorrent v1 torrent identifies pieces through SHA-1 hashes in trusted metainfo. Peers advertise what they have and trade blocks; the wire protocol and selection policies perform different jobs. The peer wire protocol Peers talk over TCP (or uTP, a UDP-based protocol with delay-based congestion control designed to yield to other traffic). The connection starts with a 68-byte handshake: The field sizes add up to the fixed length: After that, every message except the zero-length keep-alive carries a 4-byte big-endian length, a 1-byte ID and a payload: ID Message Payload --------- 0 / 1 choke / unchoke none 2 / 3 interested / not interested none 4 have piece index 5 bitfield pieces I have 6 request index, offset, length 7 piece index, offset, block 8 cancel as request A length of 0 is a keep-alive. Ordinary request blocks are 16 KiB blocks, with shorter blocks where a piece ends, and clients keep several requests outstanding per peer (pipelining again, for the same window/RTT reason as SFTP). Each completed piece is hashed and compared with the metainfo. A mismatch means the piece is discarded and re-downloaded, and the peers that supplied it may be banned. This detects mismatching content without trusting each supplier, but still depends on trusted metadata and hash assumptions. A mixed-source bad piece does not identify which contributor supplied a bad block. Piece selection and choking Two policies make swarms work: Rarest first. Download the pieces that the fewest of your peers have. This promotes availability of scarce pieces but cannot guarantee that every piece remains online and makes you useful to others sooner. Tit-for-tat choking. You upload only to a few peers at a time. BEP 3 describes decisions on a 10-second cadence and rotation of an optimistic slot every 30 seconds. The optimistic interested peer counts within the four allowed interested downloaders, rather than being an unconditional fifth slot; new connections receive selection bias. Seeders use upload performance rather than download reciprocation. Client policies can differ. Near the end, endgame mode requests the last few blocks from every peer that has them and cancels duplicates on arrival, so one slow peer doesn't hold up completion. Key takeaways BitTorrent peers handshake, pipeline block requests and verify completed pieces against trusted metadata. Rarest-first and optimistic unchoking improve exchange without guaranteeing piece availability. Further reading BEP 3 BEP 29

t: Kademlia XOR distance and bounded routing buckets
sum: Kademlia ranks node and key IDs by XOR distance in one shared identifier space.
x: Kademlia: the XOR metric A distributed hash table (DHT) maps keys to values with no central server. BitTorrent's Mainline DHT (BEP 5) is based on Kademlia (Maymounkov and Mazières, 2002) and stores "which peers have info-hash X". A current population estimate is absent because this review did not establish a reliable measurement. Nodes and keys share a 160-bit ID space (info-hashes are 160 bits, so they fit). The distance between two IDs is their XOR (exclusive or: compare the IDs bit by bit, writing 1 where they differ and 0 where they match), read as an integer. With 4-bit IDs: In Python the XOR operator is ^, so 0b0110 ^ 0b0011 gives 5. A difference in a high bit outweighs all the lower bits together, so IDs that share a longer prefix are always closer. XOR distance is a true metric, meaning it behaves like ordinary distance: Crucially, for any point and any distance there is exactly one ID at that distance, so all nodes can consistently rank IDs for a target. Completing a lookup also requires adequate live routing information. Original Kademlia replicates each value on a small, fixed number of the closest nodes (the contact/replication parameter k); Mainline DHT stores peer contact information associated with the hash. k-buckets Each node keeps a DHT routing table made of k-buckets. In the basic distance-bucket model, each bucket covers a band of distances twice as wide as the one before: Each bucket holds a fixed maximum number of contacts, the contact-capacity parameter k: 20 as the original paper's example, and 8 in Mainline DHT. The capacity per bucket is bounded by k; contact density falls across exponentially larger distance regions. Mainline DHT uses a splitting routing-table implementation rather than a literal permanently allocated array of 160 buckets. It's like knowing every house on your street, a few people in your town and one person in each country. When a bucket is full and a new contact appears, Kademlia pings the least recently seen contact and drops the newcomer if the old one answers. The paper's analysis of Gnutella traces motivated favouring older responsive contacts; current networks need not have the same uptime distribution. This impedes an attacker simply displacing old contacts with a flood of new IDs, but does not eliminate Sybil or eclipse attacks. Key takeaways Kademlia ranks node and key IDs by XOR distance in one shared identifier space. Bounded k-buckets retain contacts across distance scales; Mainline DHT uses a splitting table. Further reading BEP 5 Original Kademlia paper

t: Kademlia lookup progress and hostile identities
sum: A lookup queries progressively closer candidates and completes its closest responsive candidate set.
x: Kademlia gives each node and key an identifier, using XOR as distance. A node retains bounded contact lists called k-buckets across distance scales. Mainline BitTorrent DHT uses 160-bit IDs and a contact-capacity parameter of eight. Lookup To find the nodes closest to a target identifier (called T in the API examples): Pick the few closest contacts you know (the paper calls this concurrency parameter α, alpha, with 3 as its example) and send each find_node(T) (or get_peers(T) in BitTorrent) in parallel. Each reply contains the k closest contacts it knows. Query the closest ones you haven't asked yet. If a round finds no closer contact, query the remaining unqueried contacts among the k closest seen. Complete when the closest responsive candidates have been checked; handle failed contacts/timeouts rather than stopping after the first non-improving round. With populated, maintained routing buckets and the model's ID-distribution assumptions, prefix progress supports O(log n) lookup scaling, where n is the number of nodes in the network. Big O notation describes how a cost grows as n grows, ignoring constant factors; log n is the logarithm of n, which grows very slowly. Roughly, each round fixes at least one more bit of shared prefix, and the number of bits needed to single out the closest nodes among n is about the base-2 logarithm of n: how many times you can halve n before reaching 1, about 20 for a million nodes. It is not a guarantee that every response halves numeric XOR distance or that an unavailable key will be found. Churn, timeouts, sparse tables and adversaries matter. Measured round counts are omitted because no representative current deployment measurement was verified. XOR distance is symmetric: a query sender can also be a useful routing contact for its receiver. Subject to routing-table admission and maintenance rules, learning from incoming messages improves coverage without contacting every node. This is an opportunity to learn a contact, not evidence that the sender is honest. Mainline DHT messages are bencoded dictionaries over UDP (KRPC): ping, find_node, get_peers (returns peers, or closer nodes) and announce_peer. To stop arbitrary IPs being announced, get_peers replies include an IP-bound announce token that the requester must return to the issuing node when announcing. It limits announcement of other IP addresses; it does not prove the announcing peer actually has the content. Sybil attacks Anyone can choose a node ID. An attacker who creates many IDs close to a target info-hash can hide or censor it ("eclipse"). Mitigations include tying IDs to IP addresses (BEP 42) and querying several disjoint paths. Key takeaways A lookup queries progressively closer candidates and completes its closest responsive candidate set. Logarithmic scaling needs routing/distribution assumptions; Sybil and eclipse attacks remain risks. Further reading BEP 5 BEP 42 Original Kademlia paper

t: WebRTC signalling, candidate checks and TURN
sum: WebRTC leaves signalling transport to the application while ICE tests candidate-pair reachability.
x: WebRTC: browsers talking directly WebRTC lets two browsers exchange audio, video and data directly. The hard part isn't the media; it's getting a packet from one to the other when both are behind NATs. Signalling is your problem WebRTC deliberately does not specify signalling. Peers exchange SDP offers and answers (session descriptions: codecs, ICE credentials, DTLS fingerprints) through any channel you like, usually a WebSocket to your server. The browser peer-connection API follows JSEP's offer/answer processing. The following fragment is illustrative and wrapped for display: candidate attributes are single lines on the wire, and the fingerprint/password here are abbreviated placeholders. ICE, STUN and TURN ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment, RFC 8445) gathers ICE candidates, addresses where a peer might be reachable: Host candidates: the device's own interface addresses. Server-reflexive (srflx) candidates: the externally observed address and port a NAT has mapped, learned by asking a STUN server "what address do you see me as?". Relayed candidates: an address on a TURN server that forwards packets for you. Each side sends its candidates to the other (with trickle ICE, as they're found rather than all at once). ICE forms compatible candidate pairs and checks them in a prioritised process using authenticated STUN requests. Type/local preferences and both candidate priorities matter; peer-reflexive candidates may be discovered during checks. The controlling agent nominates a valid pair, rather than every first-success pair being automatically selected. Why this works through NATs: when A sends a check to B's srflx address, A's NAT creates an outbound mapping. When B's check arrives at A's srflx address, the relevant mapping and filtering state may permit it. Success depends on both NATs' mapping and filtering behaviour; a STUN-observed mapping is not guaranteed to apply to every destination. This is UDP hole punching. STUN messages are tiny: a 20-byte header with the magic cookie 0x2112A442 and a 96-bit transaction ID, plus attributes. The server reports your address in XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS, with the port XORed against the cookie's high 16 bits and IPv4 address against the cookie: IPv6 additionally uses the STUN transaction ID, because some NATs "helpfully" rewrote IP addresses they spotted inside packet payloads. Endpoint-dependent NAT mappings (often called symmetric NAT) and restrictive filtering can defeat direct UDP hole punching, but NAT labels alone do not prove that every direct path fails. TURN provides a relay path when one is reachable and permitted. A 1 Mbit/s stream relayed once accounts for about 1 Mbit/s ingress and 1 Mbit/s egress, excluding overhead; provider charging varies. Client-to-TURN transport can use TCP or TLS, including a configured port 443, but this does not guarantee firewall traversal. A universal percentage of calls requiring TURN is absent because no reliable representative measurement was established. Key takeaways WebRTC leaves signalling transport to the application while ICE tests candidate-pair reachability. STUN discovers or checks addresses, and TURN offers a relay when a permitted direct path fails. Further reading RFC 8445 RFC 8489 RFC 8656 RFC 9429

sum: WebRTC protects media and data using DTLS-derived keys, SRTP and SCTP channels.
x: After ICE has checked candidates and nominated a path, WebRTC establishes protected media/data transport. The signalling exchange includes DTLS certificate fingerprints; the trustworthiness of that exchange is part of the security model. Security: DTLS-SRTP and SCTP Encryption is mandatory in WebRTC: After ICE, peers run a DTLS handshake (TLS for UDP) over the chosen path. Each checks that the other's certificate matches the a=fingerprint received over signalling. So the signalling channel must be trustworthy; whoever controls it can swap fingerprints and sit in the middle. Media keys are exported from DTLS into SRTP (DTLS-SRTP, RFC 5764). Data channels run SCTP over DTLS over UDP (RFC 8831), giving multiple streams with reliable or unreliable, ordered or unordered delivery per channel. With BUNDLE and RTP/RTCP multiplexing, several protocols share an ICE transport. First-byte ranges distinguish outer STUN, DTLS and RTP/RTCP packets; SCTP is inside DTLS, not a separate outer packet type. Connectivity-check headers and ordinary RTP headers are not all encrypted. TURN/TCP paths add their own transport framing. Group calls A two-party call is naturally peer-to-peer. With more people: Topology Each client uploads Server work --------- Mesh One per other participant No media forwarding if paths are direct SFU 1 (or a few) Forward packets MCU 1 Decode, mix, encode In a mesh, each client sends its own copy of its stream to every other participant, so upload grows with the size of the call: So with five people at 1.5 Mbit/s video, a full mesh needs each client to upload 6 Mbit/s, before protocol overhead; whether an uplink supports this is deployment-specific. An SFU (selective forwarding unit) takes one upload per client and forwards copies, and with simulcast each client sends, say, three resolutions so the SFU can give each receiver the one that suits its bandwidth. An SFU reduces client upload replication at the cost of server forwarding. With ordinary per-hop DTLS-SRTP, the SFU holds media keys; an additional mechanism such as SFrame is needed to hide media content from it. Key takeaways WebRTC protects media and data using DTLS-derived keys, SRTP and SCTP channels. Mesh upload grows with other participants; SFUs reduce replication but ordinary per-hop media keys expose content. Further reading RFC 8827 RFC 8831 RFC 5764 RFC 9605

t: RTP packet fields and media-clock timestamps
sum: RTP sequence numbers count packets while timestamps follow payload-specific media clocks.
x: RTP: real-time media packets Media in WebRTC (and VoIP, IPTV and many broadcast systems) rides on RTP (RFC 3550) over UDP. UDP allows late media to be discarded without transport head-of-line blocking. RTP can also use other transports; TCP-based fallback can be useful on restrictive networks despite its latency tradeoffs. Whether a late packet is useful depends on the playout deadline. The fixed header is 12 bytes: Payload type (PT, 7 bits) says which codec, mapped in SDP (a=rtpmap:111 opus/48000/2). RTP sequence number (16 bits) increases by 1 per packet: detects loss and reordering. Timestamp (32 bits) is in media clock units, not wall time: 48,000 Hz for Opus audio and 90,000 Hz for common video payload formats such as H.264. The advance per packet is the clock rate times the time the packet covers (see the formula after this list). Packet timestamp and marker rules are defined by the payload format. Marker bit (M) typically flags the last packet of a video frame. SSRC identifies the stream source; CSRC lists contributing sources when a mixer combined streams. This header fixture decodes as version 2, PT 111, sequence 6699 and timestamp 960. By hand, the top two bits of the first byte are the version, and the low 7 bits of the second byte are the payload type: The sequence bytes 1a 2b give 26 × 256 + 43 = 6,699, and the timestamp bytes 00 00 03 c0 give 3 × 256 + 192 = 960. PT 111 means Opus only if negotiated that way. With an illustrative initial timestamp of zero and one 20 ms Opus frame per packet, 960 is the second frame; real initial timestamps and sequence numbers are randomised. This snippet parses only the fixed header, not a complete validated RTP packet. Key takeaways RTP sequence numbers count packets while timestamps follow payload-specific media clocks. A fixed-header parser illustrates fields but does not validate a complete RTP packet. Further reading RFC 3550 RFC 7587 RFC 6184

t: RTCP reports, jitter and round-trip timing
sum: RTCP sender reports relate independent media clocks to wall time for synchronisation.
x: RTP carries a packet sequence number, media-clock timestamp and source identifier. RTCP is its companion control protocol. RTP clock rates depend on the payload format: Opus uses 48,000 ticks per second, while common video formats use 90,000. RTCP: feedback RTP's companion, RTCP, sends periodic reports. In the cards below, i and j label consecutively received packets, which need not have consecutive sequence numbers: Sender reports map the RTP timestamp to wall-clock (NTP format) time, which is how receivers lip-sync audio and video streams that have unrelated RTP clocks. Receiver reports give fraction lost, cumulative loss and interarrival jitter, a running estimate of how much packet transit times vary (formula below). Round-trip time: the sender works out the network round trip from the report it gets back, subtracting the time the receiver held it (formula below). The jitter estimate is updated for every packet, moving one sixteenth of the way towards the latest measurement: The round-trip time uses three values carried in or measured around the reports: A and LSR come from the sender's own clock, so the two machines' clocks need not agree. On the wire A and LSR use the same compact representation, so the subtraction needs modular arithmetic (it must handle the counters wrapping round) and assumes the clocks run at stable rates. WebRTC adds RTCP feedback messages: NACK (please resend packet 6702, if there's time), PLI (picture loss indication, allowing an encoder to respond with recovery information such as an intra picture) and transport-wide congestion feedback, which drives Google Congestion Control in adjusting the encoder's bitrate. On the receiving side, a jitter buffer holds packets briefly to reorder them and smooth out variable delay. It is a direct trade: a bigger buffer survives more jitter but adds latency. A suitable latency budget depends on the application; a universal 150 ms cutoff is omitted because this review did not establish one applicable to every interactive call. Key takeaways RTCP sender reports relate independent media clocks to wall time for synchronisation. Receiver reports describe loss, jitter and timing; a jitter buffer trades added latency for tolerance. Further reading RFC 3550 RFC 4585

sum: An address in a packet is a claim, not cryptographic proof of the sender.
x: Basic IPv4, ARP, UDP and traditional DNS do not by themselves cryptographically authenticate every sender or encrypt application data. Checksums detect some accidental corruption, but do not prove identity. Security extensions and deployment controls can add protections. Missing authentication and encryption enable several important network attacks. These threat units sort attacks into five families. For each one, ask two questions: what security property does it break, and what is the standard defence? The classic properties are often summarised as CIA: Property Meaning Broken by --------- Confidentiality Only the intended party reads it Eavesdropping Integrity Nobody alters it undetected MITM, injection Authenticity It came from who it claims Spoofing, replay Availability The service stays up DoS / DDoS (Strictly, CIA is confidentiality, integrity and availability; authenticity is usually grouped with integrity. It is listed separately here because so many network attacks target it.) Eavesdropping Eavesdropping (passive sniffing) means reading traffic you were not meant to see. The attacker changes nothing, which makes it very hard to detect. Where can an attacker listen? Shared media. Wi-Fi is radio: a nearby receiver may capture frames on a monitored channel, subject to signal, interference and radio capabilities. An Ethernet repeater hub repeated received signals onto its other ports, subject to physical-layer error and collision handling. Switched LANs. A switch normally forwards known unicasts toward the learned destination port, while broadcasts and some unknown traffic are flooded. MAC-table exhaustion or ARP poisoning may expose additional traffic, depending on switch protections and topology. On the path. Any ISP, transit provider, café router or compromised router between you and the server sees your packets. Even when the payload is encrypted, metadata leaks: source and destination addresses, packet sizes, timing, and often the server's hostname (in DNS queries and the TLS SNI field, covered in the TLS units). The defence is encryption in transit: TLS for application traffic, VPNs for whole networks, WPA2/WPA3 for Wi-Fi. The maths behind the ciphers is covered in the Security & Cryptography subject; here we care about where encryption sits and what it leaves exposed. Spoofing Spoofing means forging an identifier. Many packet fields can be written by a sender. Whether a forgery is accepted depends on filtering, cryptographic validation and protocol state. What is forged How Classic use --------- Source IP Write any value in the header Reflection DDoS MAC address Change the NIC setting Bypass MAC filters ARP reply Send unsolicited replies LAN MITM DNS answer Race the real reply Redirect a domain Email sender Set the From header Phishing IP spoofing has a catch for the attacker: replies go to the forged address, not to them. So it is mostly useful for one-way attacks where the attacker does not need the answer. That is exactly what reflection attacks need, as covered in the later amplification units. An off-path attacker who cannot observe replies has an additional obstacle when forging a TCP handshake: the acknowledgment must match the server's initial sequence number plus one in the ordinary no-data handshake. Unpredictable sequence-number generation makes blind guessing harder. BCP 38: stop spoofing at the source RFC 2827 (BCP 38) recommends filtering customer traffic against permitted source prefixes. This blocks spoofing outside those prefixes, but does not by itself stop one host impersonating another inside an allowed prefix. More granular source validation and reflector controls are also useful. Key takeaways An address in a packet is a claim, not cryptographic proof of the sender. Encryption hides protected content but leaves observable metadata. BCP 38 filters unauthorised source prefixes; it does not identify every individual sender. Further reading UDP-Based Amplification Attacks — CISA RFC 2827 (BCP 38): Network Ingress Filtering RFC 4987: TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations Amplification Hell: Revisiting Network Protocols for DDoS Abuse (NDSS 2014) February 28th DDoS incident report — GitHub blog Understanding the Mirai Botnet (USENIX Security 2017)

sum: An encrypted channel to an impostor still exposes data to that impostor.
x: A passive observer reads traffic; an active attacker may relay it or resend an earlier valid message. The objective here is to distinguish peer authentication from message freshness. Man-in-the-middle A man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacker sits between two parties, relaying and possibly altering traffic while each side believes it is talking directly to the other. An unmitigated MITM can threaten confidentiality, integrity and authentication; correctly authenticated encryption can prevent reading or modifying protected content even when traffic is relayed. Ways to get in the middle: ARP spoofing on a LAN: tell the victim "the gateway's IP is at my MAC address". Rogue Wi-Fi access points ("evil twins", the wireless units). DNS spoofing: make the domain resolve to the attacker's IP. BGP hijacking: an unauthorised announcement may redirect traffic in networks that accept and select it. Encryption alone does not stop MITM. If Alice does a key exchange with Mallory, she has a perfectly encrypted channel to the attacker. What stops MITM is authentication: Alice must verify she is talking to the real bank. In TLS that is the certificate check (the TLS units). This is why clicking through a certificate warning is so dangerous. Replay In a replay attack the attacker captures a valid message and sends it again later. They do not need to read or change it. A replayed payment A client sends an encrypted, signed message: "pay merchant £50". The attacker cannot read it, but captures it and sends it ten more times. If the server only checks the signature, it pays out £550. The signature is valid every time, because it is the same message. The defence is to make each message usable once: Nonces: include a unique value in the authenticated request; atomically reject reuse in the relevant session or account. Timestamps: an authenticated timestamp can limit the timestamp validity interval, but a replay inside that window still needs duplicate detection. Clock and expiry rules must be defined. Sequence numbers: authenticate counters and track accepted values. An ordered channel can require the next counter; an IPsec-style anti-replay window can accept unseen out-of-order packets while rejecting duplicates and packets that are too old. TLS early data has separate replay caveats (the TLS units). Key takeaways An encrypted channel to an impostor still exposes data to that impostor. Preventing replay needs authenticated freshness information and receiver state. A timestamp bounds age; duplicate detection handles reuse inside that bound. Further reading UDP-Based Amplification Attacks — CISA RFC 2827 (BCP 38): Network Ingress Filtering RFC 4987: TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations Amplification Hell: Revisiting Network Protocols for DDoS Abuse (NDSS 2014) February 28th DDoS incident report — GitHub blog Understanding the Mirai Botnet (USENIX Security 2017)

t: Which resource does a denial of service exhaust?
sum: Volumetric, protocol-state and application attacks exhaust different resources.
x: Traffic can be authentic and still exhaust a service. Identify the constrained resource before choosing a defence: link capacity, retained state and expensive application work need different controls. Denial of service A denial-of-service (DoS) attack stops a service working for its legitimate users. A distributed DoS (DDoS) uses many sources, typically a botnet of compromised machines. The Mirai botnet of 2016, built from hacked cameras and routers, disrupted DNS resolution at Dyn and access to many customer websites. DDoS attacks are classified by the resource they exhaust: Class Exhausts Measured in Example ------------ Volumetric Link bandwidth bits/s UDP reflection Protocol State tables packets/s SYN flood Application Server CPU / app requests/s HTTP flood Volumetric Fill the victim's pipe with more traffic than it can carry. If the link is 10 Gbps and 50 Gbps arrives, legitimate packets are dropped upstream, before your servers ever see them. You cannot filter your way out on your own equipment; mitigation must happen upstream, at your ISP or a scrubbing service (Cloudflare, Akamai, AWS Shield) with sufficient capacity and filtering for the particular attack. Cloudflare reported a 29.7 Tbps attack in its 2025 Q3 report; this is a provider-reported measurement, not a guaranteed limit on future attacks. Protocol Exhaust a stateful resource with relatively little bandwidth. The classic is the SYN flood: send many TCP SYNs (often with spoofed sources) and never complete the handshake. Each one occupies a slot in the server's half-open connection queue until it times out. The standard defence is SYN cookies. For a SYN handled with a cookie, the server avoids retaining a per-request half-open connection entry. It encodes limited information in the SYN-ACK's initial sequence number; the client's acknowledgment is that number plus one. The server validates the cookie and reconstructs connection state. Shared keys, counters and transient packet processing still exist. Firewalls and load balancers with connection tables are also protocol-attack targets. Application layer Send requests that look legitimate but are expensive: searches, logins, uncached pages. A few thousand requests per second hitting a slow database query can do more damage than gigabits of junk. Slowloris is the low-and-slow variant: open many HTTP connections and send headers one byte at a time, never finishing. Thread-per-connection servers (classic Apache) run out of workers. Defences include rate limiting, CAPTCHAs or challenges, caching, and event-driven servers or reverse proxies with short deadlines for receiving headers. Key takeaways Volumetric, protocol-state and application attacks exhaust different resources. A SYN handled by a cookie avoids a retained per-request half-open entry. A saturated access link needs mitigation before that link. Further reading UDP-Based Amplification Attacks — CISA RFC 2827 (BCP 38): Network Ingress Filtering RFC 4987: TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations Amplification Hell: Revisiting Network Protocols for DDoS Abuse (NDSS 2014) February 28th DDoS incident report — GitHub blog Understanding the Mirai Botnet (USENIX Security 2017)

sum: Reflection directs replies to a forged victim address.
x: Source-address spoofing becomes a bandwidth problem when public UDP servers send large replies to small requests. This unit traces that path and calculates its idealised byte budget. Amplification attacks One important family of volumetric attacks combines spoofing with reflection and amplification: The attacker sends a small UDP request to a public server (DNS resolver, NTP server, memcached instance), with the source IP forged as the victim's. The server replies, to the victim, with a much larger response. Thousands of reflectors do the same, all aiming at the victim. UDP is used because there is no handshake to verify the source. The reflectors are innocent and the victim sees traffic from thousands of legitimate servers, which is hard to block. The amplification factor To compare reflectors, and to estimate how big an attack can get, you need one number: how many bytes come back for every byte the attacker sends. That ratio is the bandwidth amplification factor (BAF): For example, a 40-byte request that triggers a 1,400-byte response has a payload BAF of 35. The ratio depends on which bytes you count (payload only, or headers too; the next unit compares them) and on the particular query and server, so published figures are measurements, not constants. The following historical examples use UDP-payload ratios. Rossow's 2014 measurements report sample means for particular queries and servers; GitHub's 2018 incident report cites an upper memcached example. They are not fixed protocol constants or current guarantees: Protocol Approx. BAF ------ DNS 28.7 (open resolvers), 54.6 (authoritative servers) SSDP 30.8 NTP (monlist) 556.9 CharGEN 358.8 Memcached Up to 51,000 in the cited 2018 report If every reflector answers every request, the traffic arriving at the victim is the attacker's sending rate multiplied by the BAF. The attacker's sending rate is in turn the number of bots times each bot's upload rate: This assumes a payload-rate model: reflectors have enough capacity, nothing is lost on the way, and every request is answered. Real attacks fall short of it, because reflectors' own links and rate limits cap what they can send. Working it out. A botnet has 2,000 devices, each able to send 5 Mbps, reflected through open DNS resolvers with a BAF of 50: Through exposed memcached servers even a 1 Gbps attacker could, in principle, generate tens of Tbps (terabits per second; 1 Tbps = 1,000 Gbps); in practice the reflectors' own links cap it. In 2018 GitHub absorbed a 1.35 Tbps memcached attack. The same calculation as Python code: This prints 500.0. Key takeaways Reflection directs replies to a forged victim address. Specify which bytes a bandwidth amplification factor counts. The bot-rate model assumes sufficient reflector capacity and no loss. Further reading UDP-Based Amplification Attacks — CISA RFC 2827 (BCP 38): Network Ingress Filtering RFC 4987: TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations Amplification Hell: Revisiting Network Protocols for DDoS Abuse (NDSS 2014) February 28th DDoS incident report — GitHub blog Understanding the Mirai Botnet (USENIX Security 2017)

sum: Headers and fragmentation change amplification measured at the IP or link layer.
x: The previous unit counted response payload bytes per request payload byte. This unit compares that number with the IP-packet ratio, then identifies controls at senders, reflectors and the victim’s upstream network. Two subtleties: Headers dilute the factor in this unfragmented example. A UDP datagram carried in one IPv4 packet with no options has 28 bytes of IP and UDP headers (20 for IPv4, 8 for UDP); link-layer overhead is additional. For a 40-byte request and 1,400-byte response, the payload BAF is 35, but counting the IP and UDP headers too gives a lower ratio: A full link-level ratio also needs link-layer framing and packetisation, which dilute it further. Packet amplification matters too. One request producing many response packets multiplies the packets per second, which stresses routers and firewalls as well as links. Defending against amplification Do not be a reflector: close open resolvers, disable NTP monlist, never expose memcached (UDP 11211) to the internet. Memcached disabled UDP by default from version 1.5.6 after the 2018 attacks. BCP 38 ingress filtering at ISPs, so spoofed packets never leave the attacker's network. Protocol design: cap amplification before validating a peer's address. QUIC permits up to three times the received UDP payload bytes before address validation; this bounds amplification rather than eliminating it. Upstream scrubbing and anycast to spread and absorb the flood. Content omitted after review Universal attack-success rates, firewall mistake rankings and provider capacity guarantees are absent: this review has no representative measurement supporting those claims. Historical amplification figures in the preceding unit retain their original measurement scope. Key takeaways Headers and fragmentation change amplification measured at the IP or link layer. Source validation and closing reflectors reduce the available attack paths. QUIC bounds pre-validation amplification; it does not eliminate amplification. Further reading UDP-Based Amplification Attacks — CISA RFC 2827 (BCP 38): Network Ingress Filtering RFC 4987: TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations Amplification Hell: Revisiting Network Protocols for DDoS Abuse (NDSS 2014) February 28th DDoS incident report — GitHub blog Understanding the Mirai Botnet (USENIX Security 2017)

sum: A first-match filter stops at its first matching rule.
x: The earlier threat units showed why receiving a packet does not, by itself, establish a trustworthy identity. A firewall is the first answer to that: a device or piece of software that sits on a boundary and decides, packet by packet or connection by connection, what is allowed through. The second answer is to have more boundaries. Network segmentation splits a network into zones so that a compromise in one zone does not hand over all of them. The third answer, zero trust, says that network location alone never grants implicit trust. This unit focuses on rule matching and its default policy. What a firewall decides on Every firewall matches traffic against a list of firewall rules. The more of the packet it understands, the more precise the rules can be: Type Looks at Example rule --------- Stateless filter Headers of one packet Drop TCP to port 23 Stateful Headers plus connection state Allow replies to my requests Application (L7) Protocol content Block HTTP POST /admin Most rules are written in terms of the 5-tuple: protocol, source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. Add the direction (inbound or outbound) and the interface, and you can express most network policy. Rule order and default policy The toy filter below uses top-to-bottom, first-match evaluation. Real products differ: AWS security groups combine allow rules, while nftables can continue across chains after an accept verdict. Anything that matches no rule gets the default policy, which should be deny. This prints allow, deny, deny. SSH from inside 10.0.0.0/8 matches rule 1. SSH from the internet skips rule 1 and hits rule 3. DNS matches nothing and falls through to the default. Swap rules 1 and 3 and internal SSH breaks too, because the broad deny now matches first. Order bugs and broad rules that shadow narrow ones can contradict the intended policy. Good tooling flags shadowed rules that can never match. Default deny, both ways Explicit inbound and outbound allowlists can reduce exposure. Egress restrictions can obstruct some command-and-control and exfiltration paths, but allowed services may still be abused; default-deny adoption is not universal. Key takeaways A first-match filter stops at its first matching rule. A broad earlier rule can shadow a later specific rule. Explicit defaults and outbound controls make permitted paths easier to review. t: Connection state and cloud return traffic
sum: Connection state lets policy recognise reply traffic but consumes finite memory.
x: Rule order is only part of a firewall’s behaviour. A packet may be a reply in an existing flow, or a new attempt requiring another state entry. This unit follows that distinction into AWS subnet and interface controls. Stateless versus stateful A stateless filter judges each packet alone. That causes a problem with replies. When your web server at port 443 answers a client, the reply goes to the client's ephemeral port, some random number such as 51,812. A stateless filter needs a rule covering the intended return traffic. For clients anywhere on the internet this often includes a range of destination ephemeral ports; source ports, addresses and protocol flags may further constrain a rule, but do not prove connection state. A stateful firewall keeps a connection table. When it sees an allowed outbound SYN, it records the flow. Connection tracking supplies state that filtering rules can match. A known flow is accepted only when the applicable policy permits it: On Linux this is conntrack. This abbreviated nftables input-chain example explicitly accepts established and related traffic: The inet family covers both IPv4 and IPv6; the ip saddr condition is specifically IPv4. A new IPv6 SSH attempt matches neither the IPv4 SSH allow rule nor the web-port rules and falls through to drop. This is an input-chain fragment, not a complete deployment ruleset: it omits IPv6 neighbour discovery, router advertisements, other required ICMP handling, and forwarding and outbound policy. Blindly applying it can break connectivity. UDP and ICMP tracking uses protocol-specific tuples and timeouts; a UDP reply does not establish application-level authentication. The cost of state State is memory, and memory can run out. The connection table is itself a DoS target: a SYN flood or many short UDP flows can fill it, after which the firewall drops new connections, including legitimate ones. Timeouts matter too. Linux keeps an idle established TCP entry for five days by default, while many cloud load balancers and NAT gateways drop idle flows after minutes, which is why long-lived idle connections mysteriously die unless they send keepalives. Firewalls in the cloud AWS is a good case study because it gives you both kinds side by side: Security group Network ACL --------- Applies to Network interface Subnet State Stateful Stateless Rules Allow only Allow and deny Evaluation All rules together Numbered order, first match Because NACLs are stateless, you must explicitly allow return traffic to ephemeral ports (AWS suggests 1024 to 65535). Forgetting the outbound ephemeral rule is a classic cause of "the security group is open but nothing works". Security groups can also reference other security groups: "allow port 5432 from members of sg-web". Within supported AWS connectivity arrangements, the reference resolves to associated interfaces' private addresses and updates automatically as interfaces join or leave the group. It is a network policy reference, not cryptographic proof of application identity; traffic through a middlebox can require different rules. Key takeaways Connection state lets policy recognise reply traffic but consumes finite memory. AWS security groups combine stateful allow rules; NACLs are ordered and stateless. Return ports and idle timeouts matter even when the service port is open. sum: An open HTTPS port does not identify the application behind it.
x: A firewall can inspect protocol content when it is available, while segmentation limits where traffic can go. Use both to ask which resources remain reachable after a compromise. Beyond ports: application-layer firewalls Port 443 tells you almost nothing in a world where everything is HTTPS. Next-generation firewalls (NGFWs) identify the application, user and sometimes the content. Web application firewalls (WAFs) sit in front of HTTP services and block patterns such as SQL injection. Reading encrypted HTTP content requires authorised decryption, such as TLS termination or interception with a trust anchor accepted by the client. Some application identification instead uses exposed metadata; installing a root certificate alone does not intercept traffic. Interception breaks certificate pinning, adds a high-value target and can weaken TLS if the middlebox is poorly implemented. It is a trade-off, not a free upgrade. Segmentation A flat network, where every machine can reach every other machine, means one compromised laptop can probe every server. An attacker may move laterally from the initial foothold toward other resources. The Target breach (2013) A March 2014 Senate staff analysis described an apparent path from compromised HVAC-vendor credentials into sensitive network areas. It cited Target's confirmation that around 40 million payment-card accounts were exposed. The report explicitly relied on then-available reports and expert analysis, not a completed public forensic reconstruction. Its segmentation lesson is to restrict supplier access to necessary resources rather than grant broad internal reachability. Segmentation draws internal boundaries: A DMZ holds internet-facing services, so a compromised web server is still outside the internal network. VLANs and subnets separate departments, guest Wi-Fi, IoT devices and management interfaces. Microsegmentation goes down to individual workloads: each service can talk only to the specific services it needs, typically enforced on the host or by the hypervisor rather than by a central box. The design question is always blast radius: if this machine falls, what else can the attacker reach? Each allowed path is a possible route for lateral movement. Key takeaways An open HTTPS port does not identify the application behind it. Inspecting encrypted HTTP requires appropriate decryption and introduces trust costs. Segmentation restricts the paths available after one workload is compromised. sum: Network location alone grants no trust in the zero trust model.
x: Segmentation provides network boundaries. Zero trust adds resource access decisions based on identity, device context and policy, with monitoring that can change those decisions over time. Zero trust Traditional design is castle and moat: hard perimeter, soft inside. In this simplified perimeter-only model, internal location grants broad trust; real perimeter designs can also enforce internal controls. That model fails when: An attacker gets one foothold inside (phishing, a vendor, a stolen VPN password). Staff work from home, cafés and phones, and data lives in SaaS and the cloud, so there is no single inside. Zero trust (NIST SP 800-207) rejects trust based solely on network location. Its core ideas: Evaluate access to each resource using subject and device identity and policy. NIST describes per-session access and ongoing reevaluation, not a requirement to make the user perform fresh MFA for every HTTP request. Check the device: is it managed, patched and encrypted? Least privilege: limit the resources and operations accessible for the task. Monitor and reevaluate: collect relevant security telemetry and restrict or revoke access as risk changes. Shorter sessions limit some stolen-token exposure but do not automatically expire a stolen password or private key. Google's BeyondCorp is an influential published implementation example, described in its 2014 paper. Employees reach internal applications through an identity-aware proxy on the public internet; being in a Google office grants nothing extra. Between services, mutual TLS can authenticate service identities, with authorisation enforced separately; a service mesh is one implementation option (the TLS units). Zero trust is not "no firewalls" Zero trust adds identity checks; it does not remove network controls. Segmentation still limits blast radius when an identity is stolen, and an exposed management port is still exposed. Buying a product labelled "zero trust" while leaving a flat network behind it changes little. Pitfalls Rule sprawl: thousands of rules nobody dares delete. Tag each rule with an owner and a ticket, and review hits; a rule with zero hits for a year is a candidate for removal. Any-any rules added "temporarily" during an incident. Forgotten paths: management interfaces, backup networks and monitoring agents often bypass the segmentation everything else respects. Trusting the VPN as if it were the office (the tunnel and VPN units). IPv6: a reachable IPv6 path can bypass IPv4-only filtering when a service listens on IPv6 and no other control prevents it. Content omitted after review No ranking of the most common firewall errors, universal default-policy adoption rate or single zero-trust deployment recipe is supplied: the review has no representative measurement establishing those generalisations. Key takeaways Network location alone grants no trust in the zero trust model. Identity, device context and least privilege inform access and reevaluation. Review alternate paths, including IPv6, management networks and VPN access. sum: TLS protects connection contents, not every observable address, size or timing signal.
x: TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the protocol behind the padlock: HTTPS and configured secure SMTP/IMAP use TLS. QUIC version 1 uses the TLS 1.3 handshake for authentication and key establishment, while QUIC applies its own packet protection. The earlier threat units showed that encryption alone does not stop a man-in-the-middle; you also need to know who you are talking to. Correctly configured TLS can provide both; peer verification and the negotiated authentication mode matter. These TLS units take the network engineer's view: what is on the wire, what each message proves, and what goes wrong in production. How the ciphers and key exchanges work mathematically is covered in the Security & Cryptography subject. What TLS does and does not protect TLS gives a connection three properties: Confidentiality: only the two endpoints can read the data. Integrity: protected records reject unauthorised changes under the cryptographic assumptions; this does not prevent packet loss, delay or all denial of service. Authentication: in the certificate-based mode illustrated in the next unit, the client validates the server identity and proof of its private key. PSK modes use a different credential. Client certificate authentication is optional (mTLS, covered later). It does not hide: IP addresses and ports (they are in the IP and TCP headers). Sizes and timing of records, which can leak which page you visited. Traditionally, the hostname, sent in clear in the SNI (Server Name Indication) extension so a server hosting many sites knows which certificate to present. ECH can hide the inner SNI; a later unit covers its remaining metadata limits. Why TLS 1.3 was needed The pre-TLS-1.3 ecosystem retained legacy protocol versions, cipher suites and implementations with weaknesses. TLS 1.2 CBC suites were exposed to timing and padding-oracle implementation attacks; original POODLE targeted SSL 3.0. RSA key transport also lacks forward secrecy: later compromise of its decryption key can expose recorded handshakes using that key. A conventional full TLS 1.2 handshake takes two TLS round trips before client application data, excluding TCP setup and False Start. TLS 1.3 was originally specified by RFC 8446 (2018), now superseded by RFC 9846 (July 2026). Its core redesign took a hard line: Removed Why ------ RSA key transport, static DH No forward secrecy CBC modes, RC4 Padding and bias attacks SHA-1, MD5 in signatures Hash collisions Compression CRIME attack Renegotiation Complex, attacked What is left is small. RFC 8446 originally defines five cipher suites, all AEAD (authenticated encryption), the common ones being TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256. Certificate-authenticated TLS 1.3 uses ephemeral key establishment. RFC 8446 also permits PSK-only psk_ke, which lacks forward secrecy against later PSK compromise; PSK with ephemeral DH can provide it for post-handshake traffic. The later resumption unit covers early data’s separate limitations. Secure erasure of ephemeral/session secrets is part of the model. Key takeaways TLS protects connection contents, not every observable address, size or timing signal. TLS 1.3 removed legacy choices and separates record protection from key exchange. Forward secrecy depends on the negotiated mode and erasure of temporary secrets. sum: The illustrated certificate handshake needs one TLS round trip before client application data.
x: This unit follows a full certificate-authenticated TLS 1.3 connection. Its message order explains both the latency improvement and how authentication binds the agreed keys to the intended peer. The 1-RTT handshake This diagram shows a full certificate-authenticated handshake without HelloRetryRequest, client certificates or early data. It excludes TCP setup; implementation scheduling and transport loss can add delay. Step by step: ClientHello. The client lists versions, cipher suites and signature algorithms, and, crucially, sends a key share straight away. It guesses which group the server will accept (for example, X25519 when supported). It also sends SNI and ALPN (for example h2 for HTTP/2). ServerHello. The server picks the options and sends its own key share. Both sides can now compute a shared secret, and subsequent handshake messages in this flow are encrypted; record headers and optional compatibility ChangeCipherSpec records are exceptions. EncryptedExtensions: the rest of the server's choices, such as the agreed ALPN. Certificate: the server's certificate chain. In TLS 1.2 this went in clear; now a passive observer cannot see which certificate was presented. CertificateVerify: a signature using the certificate's private key over a context-bound transcript value (including a fixed prefix, role-specific context string and transcript hash). This proves the server holds the key right now, and ties the key exchange to that identity, which is what defeats a man-in-the-middle. Finished message: a keyed message authentication code over the whole transcript, computed with a key derived from the handshake. If an attacker altered any earlier message (say, deleted the strongest cipher suites to force a weak one), the transcripts differ and Finished fails. The client sends its own Finished and can send application data immediately in this successful flow: one TLS round trip versus two for the conventional full TLS 1.2 flow. If the client guessed the wrong group, the server can send a HelloRetryRequest naming a supported group. A retry can also request a cookie. The revised ClientHello costs an extra round trip. Downgrade protection and ossification A downgrade can expose older protocol choices or weaker permitted configurations; a correctly configured TLS 1.2 connection is not automatically vulnerable to every historical attack. So a TLS 1.3 server that ends up negotiating 1.2 puts a fixed sentinel (DOWNGRD plus one byte) in the last 8 bytes of its random value, which 1.3 clients check. Deployment showed a different problem: middleboxes that inspected TLS broke on anything unfamiliar. TLS 1.3 therefore disguises itself. The legacy version field still says 1.2 (0x0303), the real version goes in a supported_versions extension, and dummy ChangeCipherSpec messages are sent so the handshake looks like a resumed 1.2 session. QUIC reduces exposed protocol details with packet encryption and partial header protection, while fields such as connection IDs and version remain visible. Key takeaways The illustrated certificate handshake needs one TLS round trip before client application data. CertificateVerify binds proof of a private key to the handshake context. Finished authenticates the transcript; compatibility fields support older middleboxes. sum: A session ticket identifies a resumption PSK; it is not simply the raw key.
x: A full TLS handshake establishes secrets that may support a later resumed connection. The shortcut matters because sending application data before that later handshake finishes changes the security guarantees. Consider two operations at a shop: viewing a public catalogue and charging a card. Repeating a catalogue read may be acceptable under the application’s stated semantics. Repeating an unprotected charge is not. Naming an endpoint GET or POST does not prove which side of that boundary it belongs on. Resumption and 0-RTT After a handshake, the server can issue a session ticket: an opaque identity associated with a resumption PSK. The client derives that PSK from resumption secrets and the ticket nonce; the ticket is not simply the raw key. A resumed handshake skips the certificate. With a ticket, the client may also send 0-RTT early data in its very first flight, encrypted with a key derived from the PSK. The catch is serious: 0-RTT data can be replayed An attacker can capture the first flight and send it again. TLS does not inherently guarantee non-replay of early data. Servers can implement anti-replay state, but applications must account for the remaining risk across instances and retries. Early data lacks forward secrecy against later compromise of its PSK. Permit only requests whose actual semantics tolerate replay; an HTTP method label or idempotence alone is not a complete safety argument. A server can answer HTTP 425 Too Early to make the client retry after the full handshake. This revisits the earlier threat units’ replay problem, accepted deliberately in exchange for speed. Key takeaways A session ticket identifies a resumption PSK; it is not simply the raw key. 0-RTT early data has replay and forward-secrecy limitations. Permit early data only when the actual operation tolerates the remaining replay risk.
