t: Building and checking a certificate path
sum: A certificate path connects the leaf certificate identity to an independently trusted anchor.
x: A server proving possession of a private key is useful only if the client can associate that key with the intended service. Certificate path validation and name checks supply that link. Certificate chains A certificate ties a public key to names, and is signed by a certificate authority (CA). Clients use configured trust anchors, often from a browser, operating system or application root store. Store membership varies. Root private keys can be kept offline while intermediate CAs perform routine issuance; this is an operational design, not a property of every CA. The following chain-shaped example illustrates a leaf certificate, intermediate and cross-signed root. It is not a live assertion of what www.rfc-editor.org currently serves: The server sends its leaf certificate and needed intermediates. A client must independently trust a suitable anchor. Item 2 illustrates a cross-signed certificate for the same subject/key, with a different issuer and potentially different constraints, enabling an alternate path where supported. Certificate validation includes the following checks (this is not an exhaustive validation algorithm; path-length/name constraints and unsupported critical extensions also matter): Each signature verifies with the issuer's public key, up to a root it trusts. The leaf certificate and intermediate certificates in the validation path are within their validity dates; trust-anchor handling is a separate client-policy input. The leaf certificate's Subject Alternative Name matches the hostname. (Browsers ignore the old Common Name field.) Intermediates are marked as CAs (basicConstraints CA:TRUE) and allowed to issue. The leaf certificate is allowed for server authentication (extended key usage). Applicable browser policies require Certificate Transparency evidence for publicly trusted certificates. A signed certificate timestamp is a log's promise to include the certificate, not itself an inclusion proof; SCTs need not be embedded in the certificate. Monitoring helps detect misissuance. "It works in Chrome but not in curl" The server sends only its leaf certificate, not the intermediate. Desktop browsers often cope, because they cache intermediates or fetch them from a URL in the certificate. Other clients may fail with "unable to get local issuer certificate"; fetching and caching depend on the TLS backend, trust store and configuration, not just the application name. The fix is on the server: serve the full chain (leaf certificate plus intermediates). Key takeaways A certificate path connects the leaf certificate identity to an independently trusted anchor. Names, validity, permitted uses and CA constraints all matter. Serving required intermediates avoids depending on a particular client’s cache or fetching behaviour. t: Revocation, renewal and verified TLS clients
sum: Revocation mechanisms and client failure policy vary.
x: Certificate trust must survive routine operations as well as the first connection. This unit covers leaked keys, validity limits and a Python client that keeps chain and hostname verification enabled. Revocation and short lifetimes If a private key leaks, the certificate must be revoked. The two classic mechanisms are CRLs (lists of revoked serial numbers) and OCSP (ask the CA about one certificate). Direct OCSP requests can reveal certificate lookups to the responder. Some clients soft-fail when status cannot be retrieved; others use different revocation mechanisms or policies. Blocking a responder can therefore undermine a soft-fail check. OCSP stapling lets the server attach a recent signed OCSP response itself. The industry's answer has shifted to short-lived certificates. Let's Encrypt shut down its OCSP service in 2025 in favour of CRLs. The CA/Browser Forum has cut the maximum lifetime of public certificates from 398 days to 200 days (from March 2026), falling to 100 days in 2027 and 47 days in 2029. Short lifetimes limit the damage of an unrevoked key, and make reliable renewal and monitoring more demanding. Automated renewal (for example ACME) is a practical approach, not a mathematical requirement imposed by the lifetime alone. Checking a server by hand: The negotiated version, cipher and certificate subject depend on the live endpoint and local TLS stack; no fixed output is guaranteed. create_default_context() turns on chain and hostname verification; passing server_hostname sets SNI and the name to check. Code that sets verify=False (in requests) or CERT_NONE throws all of that away and is open to any MITM. Key takeaways Revocation mechanisms and client failure policy vary. The public certificate lifetime schedule makes reliable renewal and monitoring valuable. Use a verified TLS context and an explicit server name; live outputs are environment dependent. t: ECH and the visible server name
sum: ECH encrypts the inner ClientHello, including its real SNI.
x: TLS 1.3 encrypts the server certificate in the ordinary full handshake, but its initial ClientHello is normally visible. ECH addresses that remaining name exposure. Distinguish the actual server name from the provider’s visible public name. For example, when several sites share the public name and externally visible configuration in this unit’s model, an observer can identify the provider without reading the inner SNI. A unique destination IP or a separate plaintext DNS lookup may still reveal which site the user requested. Encrypted Client Hello Even with TLS 1.3, the ClientHello is sent in clear, so the SNI reveals the site to anyone on the path, and is widely used for censorship and filtering. Encrypted Client Hello (ECH, RFC 9849, 2026) closes that gap: The client looks up the site's DNS HTTPS record, which carries an ECHConfig: a public key and a public name for the provider's client-facing server. It encrypts the real ClientHello with that key and wraps it in an outer ClientHello naming only the public name. The provider decrypts the inner hello and completes the handshake for the real site. ECH hides the inner ClientHello from passive observers, but the practical anonymity set depends on shared configuration, IP addresses and other metadata; a CDN is not a protocol requirement. Plaintext DNS can independently disclose the requested name. Encrypted DNS protects that hop but does not conceal it from the chosen resolver. For defenders it is a trade-off: firewalls and filters that block by SNI (the detection units) lose that signal. Key takeaways ECH encrypts the inner ClientHello, including its real SNI. A visible public name, server IP and DNS observations can still constrain privacy. ECH privacy depends on deployment and anonymity sets, not merely enabling one extension. sum: Full certificate-based mTLS proves possession of both server and client private keys.
x: The certificate handshake so far authenticated the server. A service-to-service connection can also require a client certificate. This unit tracks where that proof ends and where application authorisation begins. Mutual TLS In a full server-certificate TLS handshake, the client need not supply a certificate and may authenticate at the application layer later. For certificate-based mutual TLS (mTLS), the server requests a client certificate and the client supplies Certificate and CertificateVerify when authenticating. PSK resumption does not repeat these certificate messages. Where it is used: Service-to-service traffic in zero trust designs (the earlier firewall and segmentation units). Configured service meshes can issue workload certificates and apply mTLS. For example, Istio uses SPIFFE-style identities and separate authentication/authorisation policies; permissive modes and unenrolled workloads require attention. APIs for banks and payment networks, IoT devices and internal admin tools. Trade-offs and pitfalls: You usually run a private CA, and must issue, rotate and revoke certificates for every client. Automation is the whole game. A certificate proves who the caller is, not what they may do. You still need authorisation: "service checkout may call POST /charge". TLS terminated at a load balancer ends the mTLS there; the backend must trust the balancer to pass on the verified identity, usually in a header that clients must be prevented from setting themselves. Content omitted after review A universal trusted-root count, live endpoint chain/output, certificate-outage frequency and current key-exchange adoption percentages are not asserted: no reproducible dated measurements were available for those claims in this review. The handshake and chain examples are explanatory models. Key takeaways Full certificate-based mTLS proves possession of both server and client private keys. Identity authentication and permission to perform an operation are separate decisions. When a trusted proxy terminates mTLS, protect the identity it forwards to the backend. sum: Plain encapsulation provides reachability without proving confidentiality or authenticity.
x: A tunnel carries packets of one network as the payload of packets on another. Wrap a packet addressed to 10.20.0.5 inside a packet addressed to your office's public IP, send it across the internet, unwrap it at the far end, and the office network sees what looks like a local packet. Tunnels on their own provide reachability, not security. Here, VPN means a cryptographically protected IP tunnel: it authenticates the two ends, and encrypts and integrity-protects what flows between them. The tunnel units cover the plain tunnels (GRE, VXLAN), two examples of protected VPN protocols (IPsec and WireGuard), and the practical problem they all share: overhead and MTU. Encapsulation and the MTU tax Every tunnel adds headers. The physical link's MTU (usually 1,500 bytes for Ethernet) does not change, so the inner packet must shrink: Because the outer packet still has to fit the link, the room left for the inner packet is the link MTU minus every header the tunnel adds: Applying it to three common tunnels, with the header sizes used in the code below: The same arithmetic as code, with a header-size table you can extend: This prints 1476, 1420 and 1450: inner IP size budgets for these exact header assumptions: basic GRE over IPv4, WireGuard over IPv6, and untagged VXLAN over IPv4. They are not universal interface defaults. Options, VLAN tags, extra tunnels and path MTU change the budget; WireGuard padding is bounded so it does not exceed the selected MTU. GRE: a plain tunnel GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation, IP protocol 47) has a 4-byte base header, with optional fields adding overhead, and can encapsulate different payload protocols. It is simple and widely supported by routers, and it gives no confidentiality or authentication at all. Anyone on the path can read it, and forged traffic may be accepted if it reaches an endpoint without effective filtering or other validation. GRE is therefore often run inside IPsec when routing protocols need a tunnel interface. Key takeaways Plain encapsulation provides reachability without proving confidentiality or authenticity. Subtract every added byte from the underlay IP MTU to obtain the inner budget. Header models and padding rules matter more than a memorised tunnel default. Further reading RFC 4301: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol RFC 4303: IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) WireGuard: Next Generation Kernel Network Tunnel (whitepaper) WireGuard: protocol and cryptography RFC 7348: Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN) RFC 4459: MTU and Fragmentation Issues with In-the-Network Tunneling

sum: Small successful requests do not prove the path can carry full-size packets.
x: A tunnel can authenticate correctly and still stall on large transfers. Its added headers reduce the inner IP packet budget. This unit follows what happens when the sender does not learn that smaller budget. When the MTU is wrong If an inner packet exceeds the tunnel’s selected MTU, the encapsulating endpoint must handle that limit; implementations may fragment where permitted or reject it and report the smaller budget. At a forwarding router, an oversized IPv4 packet with Don’t Fragment set is dropped and can trigger an ICMP fragmentation-needed message; IPv6 routers do not fragment and use ICMPv6 Packet Too Big. The error lets the source adapt its packet size. This is path MTU discovery (PMTUD). Firewalls that block all ICMP break it. The result is a PMTU black hole: the TCP handshake and small requests work, but anything large stalls. "SSH connects but git clone hangs" through a VPN is the classic symptom. The usual fixes: Set the tunnel interface MTU correctly (using the actual underlay budget; wg-quick can infer an initial value). Clamp the TCP MSS at the tunnel edge to advertise an appropriate data budget. The maximum segment size (MSS) is how much TCP data fits in one packet once the IP and TCP headers are taken out (the formula follows this list). Senders must account for options, and an MSS clamp does not fix UDP or later path changes. Allow ICMP "packet too big" (ICMPv4 type 3 code 4, ICMPv6 type 2) through firewalls. The MSS to clamp to, with minimum-size IPv4 and TCP headers: Over IPv6 the subtraction is 60 bytes instead of 40, and TCP options such as timestamps reduce the data further. Key takeaways Small successful requests do not prove the path can carry full-size packets. Permit necessary Packet Too Big signalling and configure the tunnel MTU correctly. MSS clamping changes TCP’s advertised data budget and does not repair all UDP traffic. t: IPsec negotiation, ESP and NAT traversal
sum: IKEv2 authenticates peers and negotiates SAs; ESP protects data according to those SAs.
x: IPsec separates negotiation from packet protection. Follow both roles before debugging an apparently connected VPN: successful initial IKE messages do not prove that later negotiation and ESP data can pass. IPsec IPsec secures IP packets at the network layer, and can protect selected traffic without application changes, according to configured policies. It is the standard for site-to-site VPNs between offices, data centres and cloud VPCs (AWS Site-to-Site VPN, Azure VPN Gateway). It has two halves: IKEv2 (UDP 500) is the control plane. The peers authenticate each other (with certificates or a pre-shared key), agree on algorithms and derive keys. IKE establishes a bidirectional IKE SA (with separate 64-bit initiator/responder SPIs) and negotiates Child SAs for data traffic. An ESP Child-SA pair contains unidirectional SAs with 32-bit SPIs. ESP (IP protocol 50) is the data plane: it protects the selected data packets using the negotiated SA algorithms. The encrypted-and-authenticated examples here use AEAD; ESP also permits other protection combinations, including integrity without encryption. There is also AH (protocol 51), which authenticates without encrypting. AH also authenticates relevant immutable IP-header fields; mutable fields receive special treatment. Address-rewriting NAT normally conflicts with that authentication. Transport and tunnel mode For these confidentiality-enabled ESP examples, tunnel mode encrypts the original IP packet, including its inner addresses, and is suitable for site-to-site VPNs. Transport mode leaves the original IP header outside encryption. The ESP trailer is encrypted; the ESP header and authentication tag are not. Actual protection follows the negotiated algorithms. With a 16-byte tag, no extra options or traffic-flow padding, ESP tunnel mode using AES-GCM adds 54 to 57 bytes over IPv4. Padding varies because ESP must make the encrypted part end on a 4-byte boundary: NAT traversal ESP has no TCP/UDP ports, complicating port-based NAT multiplexing; some devices implement ESP-specific passthrough. When IKE detects a NAT on the path, both peers switch to NAT-T: ESP is wrapped in UDP on port 4500, adding another 8 bytes. If a site-to-site VPN negotiates but no traffic flows, check that UDP 500 and 4500 (and protocol 50, if there is no NAT) are allowed. Key takeaways IKEv2 authenticates peers and negotiates SAs; ESP protects data according to those SAs. Confidentiality-enabled tunnel mode encrypts inner addresses; transport mode leaves the original IP header visible. NAT-T wraps ESP in UDP and changes the byte budget. sum: A replay window accepts unseen recent packets while rejecting duplicates and stale counters.
x: IPsec sequence numbers protect against replay only when the receiver tracks which authenticated packets it already accepted. Reordering makes a bounded window more useful than requiring one strictly consecutive counter. Anti-replay Each ESP packet carries a sequence number. The receiver keeps an anti-replay window (RFC 4303 recommends 64 packets) so that it tolerates packets arriving slightly out of order but rejects duplicates and anything too old. WireGuard and DTLS use the same idea. The receiver accepts an authenticated packet only when both conditions on the first line hold, and then updates its highest-seen number: For example, a four-packet window with highest accepted sequence number five covers sequence numbers two through five. Packet three is accepted if unseen; packet one is stale; packet nine is accepted and moves the highest accepted number to nine. Trace it with a window of 4: seq top before Result Why ------------ 1, 2, 5 0, 1, 2 accept new 3 5 accept recent and unseen 5 5 reject duplicate 1 5 reject below current window 9 5 accept new top 6 9 accept recent and unseen This toy handles already authenticated positive sequence numbers for one SA, without wrapping. Never update replay state before integrity verification: a forged high counter could otherwise evict legitimate packets. Its set pruning takes time proportional to the replay-window width for every accepted packet. Efficient implementations can use bitmaps. The replay-window width is a trade-off: too small and legitimate reordering (common with multi-core senders or ECMP paths) causes drops; too large costs memory per SA. Key takeaways A replay window accepts unseen recent packets while rejecting duplicates and stale counters. Authenticate packets before changing replay state. The teaching set model omits counter wrapping and costs work proportional to its window. sum: WireGuard fixes its cryptographic suite rather than negotiating cipher suites.
x: WireGuard ties public-key identities to address prefixes. This unit distinguishes the operating system’s route decision, the peer chosen for an outbound packet, and the source check on a decrypted inbound packet. WireGuard WireGuard (in the Linux kernel since 5.6, 2020) is a deliberately minimal VPN. Its design choices are the opposite of IPsec's: IPsec WireGuard --------- Algorithms Negotiated Fixed set Configuration model Many suites and policy choices Fixed cryptographic suite Identity Certs or PSK Public keys Transport ESP or UDP UDP only There is no cipher negotiation: WireGuard uses Curve25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and BLAKE2s inside a Noise-protocol handshake. If those ever need replacing, the protocol version changes. This removes cipher-suite negotiation as a downgrade surface, while key distribution, routing, access policy and implementation security still matter. A data packet carries a 16-byte header (type, receiver index, 64-bit counter) and a 16-byte authentication tag: 32 bytes, plus outer UDP and IP. Rekeying uses message and time thresholds. For example, an active initiator triggers a new handshake when sending after a session key reaches the 120-second threshold; this is not a guarantee of a handshake every two minutes while idle. Cryptokey routing Each peer is a public key with AllowedIPs prefixes. OS routing must first select the WireGuard interface; its cryptokey table then selects a peer. The following is a wg-quick-style configuration; the wrapper normally installs routes derived from AllowedIPs: Outbound: a packet routed into WireGuard selects the peer by longest-prefix match on its destination in the cryptokey table. Inbound: after authentication, the inner source address must select that same sending peer in the cryptokey table. Merely matching one of its broader prefixes is insufficient if a more-specific prefix selects a different peer. This laptop uses a split tunnel: only the two internal ranges go through the VPN. With suitable OS routes, AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0,::/0 supports a full tunnel for ordinary IPv4/IPv6 destinations. Endpoint, local and policy-route exceptions still need handling. PersistentKeepalive = 25 enables periodic authenticated empty packets when needed during idle periods, intended to keep a NAT mapping open when its timeout and policy permit (the earlier firewall units’ idle timeouts again). WireGuard avoids replies to random invalid probes. This is not absolute invisibility: under load, a packet with a valid MAC derived from the responder's public key can elicit a cookie reply before full peer authentication. Other network behaviour can also leak information. Key takeaways WireGuard fixes its cryptographic suite rather than negotiating cipher suites. OS routing selects the interface before AllowedIPs selects the peer. Inbound source lookup must select the authenticated sending peer; split and full tunnels also depend on OS routes. sum: A VXLAN VNI names an overlay network; it is not an authentication credential.
x: Cloud overlays need many separate layer 2 networks. VXLAN supplies the identifier space and transport, while operators must supply the security boundary around tunnel endpoints. VXLAN and overlays Data centres and clouds need far more isolated layer 2 segments than VLANs allow. VXLAN (RFC 7348) carries whole Ethernet frames in UDP (port 4789), with a 24-bit VNI (VXLAN network identifier). The number of network segments an ID field can name doubles with every bit: The VXLAN encapsulation looks like this: For the inner IP budget, subtract outer IPv4 (20), UDP (8), VXLAN (8), and inner Ethernet (14): 50 bytes, leaving a 1,450-byte inner IP budget on this 1,500-byte underlay, as calculated in the earlier tunnel budget unit. The outer Ethernet header shown above is outside the underlay IP MTU. Under these assumptions, either the underlay MTU is raised (data centres often run 9,000-byte jumbo frames) or the overlay MTU drops to 1,450. The devices that wrap and unwrap are VTEPs, usually hypervisors or top-of-rack switches. Fabrics can use BGP EVPN to distribute MAC address reachability, reducing flood-based learning; broadcast, unknown-unicast and multicast handling may still involve copying packets or flooding. Geneve (RFC 8926, UDP 6081) is a more extensible successor, used for example by AWS Gateway Load Balancer. VXLAN has no security VXLAN has no authentication and no encryption; RFC 7348 says so explicitly. An untrusted sender may inject frames if a VTEP accepts its packets and the selected VNI is configured. The VNI alone is not authentication; underlay filtering and endpoint policy can reject the traffic. Keep the underlay private and filtered, never expose VTEPs to the internet, and run VXLAN over IPsec or WireGuard if it must cross untrusted links. Key takeaways A VXLAN VNI names an overlay network; it is not an authentication credential. The untagged IPv4 model costs 50 bytes of the inner IP budget. Filtering and protected underlay paths provide security absent from VXLAN itself. t: VPN access without broad internal trust
sum: A remote-access VPN creates a network path, not unlimited authority.
x: A VPN can protect traffic across an untrusted path while still granting too much access at its destination. The relevant question is what a stolen remote-access identity can reach after login. Consider an employee who needs only one internal dashboard. If VPN membership permits access to every database and administration interface, encryption has protected a much broader path than the employee needs. Restrict the reachable resources or use a suitable identity-aware application proxy; the precise design depends on the application and administration requirements. VPNs in a security architecture A remote-access VPN puts a device "on the network", which is exactly the location-based trust the earlier firewall and segmentation units warned about. Stolen VPN credentials or vulnerabilities in exposed VPN gateways can give attackers a way in. Internet-facing VPN gateways therefore require restricted administration, monitoring and timely fixes. Content gap A vendor-by-vendor list of recently exploited VPN vulnerabilities and an incident-frequency claim are omitted here because the individual advisories and a comparable incident dataset were not verified. Good practice: MFA for remote access, and certificate-based device authentication. Prioritise fixes for known exploitation and high-risk exposed vulnerabilities; follow the applicable vendor advisory and incident response process. Treat VPN users as a separate, segmented zone, not as the office LAN. Prefer per-application access (identity-aware proxies) for most users, and keep network-level VPNs for site-to-site links and administrators. Content omitted after review A universal WireGuard/IPsec code-size comparison, protocol popularity ranking and fixed tunnel-MTU defaults are not asserted: implementation versions, options and path configurations were not specified for those claims. The earlier tunnel units instead give explicit header-budget models. Key takeaways A remote-access VPN creates a network path, not unlimited authority. Segment remote users and combine identity, device authentication and least privilege. Patch and monitor exposed VPN endpoints according to verified advisories. t: Radio exposure and WEP IV reuse
sum: Radio reception extends the observation boundary beyond a cable.
x: Wired networks have a physical boundary: to sniff a cable you need to reach it. Wi-Fi signals may extend beyond the intended premises. Capture depends on channel, signal, interference and receiver capabilities; being nearby does not guarantee reception of every frame. So Wi-Fi security has to provide in protocol what walls provide for Ethernet: Access control: only authorised devices may join. Confidentiality and integrity for protected data, with separate protection rules for management traffic; many headers and control frames remain exposed. Authentication of the network, so clients do not join an impostor. The history of Wi-Fi security is a tour of how to get these wrong, and it is worth studying because the same mistakes recur in other protocols. WEP: what not to do WEP, introduced with the original 802.11 standard, encrypted the payloads of protected 802.11 data frames with the RC4 stream cipher, using a key built from a shared 40- or 104-bit secret plus a 24-bit initialisation vector (IV) sent in clear. Integrity came from a CRC-32 checksum. Its flaws compound: IV reuse Stream ciphers must never reuse a keystream. A 24-bit IV has only about 16.8 million possible values, and repeats come much sooner than that. If each frame picks an IV independently and uniformly at random (repeats allowed), the birthday approximation says when the chance that some two frames share an IV reaches 50 %: This is why it is called the birthday problem: in a room of just 23 people, two probably share a birthday. Counter-based IV choices have different repeat behaviour until wraparound. For equal IVs under the same WEP key, XORing the encrypted payloads cancels their keystream and reveals the XOR of the plaintexts; recovering either plaintext needs further information. Key takeaways Radio reception extends the observation boundary beyond a cable. WEP’s small IV space can repeat keystreams under the same key. The birthday estimate assumes independent uniform random IV choices. t: Why WEP keying and CRC integrity fail
sum: WEP’s weak RC4 key scheduling enabled practical key-recovery attacks.
x: WEP combines a shared secret and a public 24-bit IV for RC4 data encryption. The previous unit explained IV reuse. This unit examines two additional problems: weak key scheduling and an unkeyed integrity check. Weak RC4 key scheduling The Fluhrer–Mantin–Shamir attack (2001), and the much faster PTW attack (2007), recover the key from captured traffic. The 2007 PTW paper reports recovery of a 104-bit WEP key with fewer than 40,000 frames in half its cases, using an active attack. Its sub-minute collection result involved reinjection on an 802.11g network; this is an experiment-specific result, not a guarantee for any busy network. CRC-32 is not a keyed MAC A message authentication code (keyed MAC) is a checksum computed with a secret key, so only key holders can produce a valid one. CRC-32 has no key, and its algebraic structure permits predictable checksum adjustments when chosen bits are modified. For two messages of the same length: So an attacker who flips chosen bits of a WEP frame (RC4 encryption is XOR with a keystream, so flipping ciphertext bits flips the same plaintext bits) can also fix up the encrypted checksum. CRC-32 has no key, so it cannot prove that the frame is genuine. Shared-key management makes individual revocation and safe rotation difficult; WEP does not require that operators literally never change keys. WEP is obsolete; never use it. The lessons: never reuse a nonce, use a keyed MAC, and derive fresh per-session keys. Key takeaways WEP’s weak RC4 key scheduling enabled practical key-recovery attacks. CRC-32 detects accidental errors; it does not authenticate a sender. The equal-length CRC relation includes the affine correction term. t: WPA2 passphrase and session key derivation
sum: WPA2-Personal derives a PMK with the SSID as salt and 4,096 PBKDF2 iterations.
x: Replacing WEP requires authenticated encryption and a sound key hierarchy. This unit separates the passphrase-derived pairwise key-derivation secret from the keys used for one client’s protected traffic. WPA2 WPA (2003) was a stop-gap (TKIP) that ran on WEP hardware. WPA2 (IEEE 802.11i, 2004) is the real fix, using AES in CCMP mode for authenticated encryption. It comes in two flavours: Mode Authentication Used in --------- Personal (PSK) Shared passphrase Homes, small offices Enterprise 802.1X / EAP per user Companies, eduroam In Personal mode the passphrase is stretched into a 256-bit Pairwise Master Key (PMK). Stretching means deliberately repeating a hash thousands of times, so that each guess an attacker tries costs thousands of hash computations too: The same derivation in Python: This ASCII-only passphrase example (not raw hexadecimal PSK provisioning) prints f42c6fc52df0ebef, the beginning of the derived 256-bit key for those inputs. Note that the SSID is the salt, so a table for one exact SSID can be reused on other networks with that same SSID, not across arbitrary different names. The four-way handshake The PMK is never used to encrypt traffic directly. Instead, after association, the access point (authenticator) and client (supplicant) run the four-way handshake to derive a fresh Pairwise Transient Key (PTK) for this session: Both sides then derive the session key from the PMK and values exchanged in the clear: Fresh nonces separate PTK derivations for distinct handshakes under the same PMK; secure nonce generation and correct key-installation state are required. The MIC on M2 proves the client knows the PMK; the MIC on M3 proves the AP does. That mutual proof is what resists a stranger's AP completing this authenticated handshake as yours, as long as the stranger does not know the passphrase. M3 also delivers the Group Temporal Key (GTK) used for broadcast and multicast frames. Key takeaways WPA2-Personal derives a PMK with the SSID as salt and 4,096 PBKDF2 iterations. The four-way handshake derives per-session key material from nonces and addresses. MICs confirm key possession; correct nonce generation and installation still matter. Further reading Key Reinstallation Attacks (KRACK) — Mathy Vanhoef Dragonblood: analysing WPA3's Dragonfly handshake Wi-Fi Protected Access — Wikipedia Wired Equivalent Privacy — Wikipedia IEEE 802.1X — Wikipedia RFC 7664: Dragonfly Key Exchange

t: WPA2 offline guessing and search budgets
sum: Captured handshake data can verify passphrase guesses without a live login.
x: The WPA2 handshake does not send the passphrase, yet it can give an observer enough information to check a guessed passphrase. Trace that distinction before estimating the work of a search. The offline cracking problem Look at what an eavesdropper captures: ANonce, SNonce, both MAC addresses, and a MIC computed from a PTK that depends only on those values and the PMK. So they can mount an offline guessing attack, testing passphrase guesses on their own hardware: No further contact with the network is needed, so there is no lockout. The 4,096 PBKDF2 iterations add work per guess. The rate depends on hardware and implementation; the next example uses a hypothetical rate. In some configurations, a captured PMKID, derived using the PMK, a fixed label and both MAC addresses, supplies another offline verifier without a victim client handshake: How long does a password last? The search space is the number of choices per position raised to the number of positions, and the time to search it all is that space divided by the guessing rate: This assumes the passphrase was chosen uniformly at random. Human choices are often not, and a dictionary ordered by popularity finds them far sooner. Uniformly choosing five words from a specified large list gives a much larger finite search space (calculated in the quiz); security still depends on the list, selection process and attacker resources. WPA2-Personal's resistance to this offline guessing attack depends on passphrase strength. An observer who knows the shared passphrase and captures the needed WPA2-Personal handshake can derive that client's link-layer keys; application TLS can still protect the application payload. Implementation and management-frame security also matter. Key takeaways Captured handshake data can verify passphrase guesses without a live login. SSID salting restricts reuse of precomputed tables to the same salt. The worked duration is a hypothetical uniform-search model, not a hardware benchmark. Further reading Key Reinstallation Attacks (KRACK) — Mathy Vanhoef Dragonblood: analysing WPA3's Dragonfly handshake Wi-Fi Protected Access — Wikipedia Wired Equivalent Privacy — Wikipedia IEEE 802.1X — Wikipedia RFC 7664: Dragonfly Key Exchange

sum: A retransmitted handshake message must not reset an in-use key’s security state.
x: Fresh key derivation is insufficient when a device later reinstalls the same key and resets its packet-number state. KRACK connects a reliability retransmission to that security failure. KRACK In 2017 Mathy Vanhoef published KRACK (Key Reinstallation Attacks), a flaw in the WPA2 protocol itself rather than in any one product. The handshake has a reliability feature: if the AP does not receive M4, it retransmits M3. The standard said the client should install the PTK on receiving M3, and vulnerable implementations reinstalled a key on a retransmitted M3. Reinstalling the key reset the CCMP packet number, which forms part of the CCMP nonce. Now the client encrypted new frames with a nonce, and therefore keystream, it had already used: the same mistake that killed WEP. Nonce reuse can expose relationships between plaintexts and enable decryption with additional known or predictable data; the exact capability depends on cipher and traffic. KRACK also enabled forgery in affected TKIP/GCMP cases. Worst hit were Linux and Android devices using affected wpa_supplicant versions 2.4 and later before fixes, which installed an all-zero key after the reinstall, making traffic trivially decryptable. Fixes ensure keys are not reinstalled in a way that resets their security state. Patch every affected device: client patches do not fix vulnerable AP-side Fast BSS Transition behaviour, nor do ordinary AP patches automatically fix clients. Patched and unpatched devices interoperate, so no new protocol was needed. KRACK showed that even a protocol with a formal security proof can fail where the proof's model (a single key installation) does not match the key-installation logic engineers actually built. Key takeaways A retransmitted handshake message must not reset an in-use key’s security state. KRACK capabilities depended on the affected cipher and implementation. Patch affected client and AP roles; one side’s fix does not cover every attack variant. t: SAE, management frames and WPA3 transition risks
sum: Correctly implemented fresh SAE resists passive offline password verification and provides forward secrecy under its assumptions.
x: WPA3-Personal changes password authentication, while protected management frames address another attack surface. Open networks use the separate OWE design. Keep those roles distinct when evaluating an access point’s advertised mode. WPA3 WPA3 (2018) addresses WPA2's structural weaknesses: WPA2 problem WPA3 answer ------ Offline guessing SAE handshake No forward secrecy SAE derives fresh keys Spoofed deauth frames PMF mandatory Open Wi-Fi in clear Separate Enhanced Open programme: OWE SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, based on the Dragonfly key exchange) replaces the PSK step. Both sides prove knowledge of the password through a Diffie-Hellman-style exchange that is designed to resist passive offline dictionary verification when correctly implemented. Each guess requires a live exchange with the AP, which can rate-limit. A fresh SAE exchange derives new key material and provides forward secrecy against later password disclosure under its security assumptions. Caching and roaming can reuse key material across associations. Protected Management Frames (802.11w) protect robust management frames such as deauthentication/disassociation once the relevant security association is established. They do not prevent radio jamming or protect every pre-association/control frame. Under WPA2 without PMF, anyone can forge a "deauth" from the AP, kicking clients off to capture their handshake or push them towards an evil twin. WPA3 is not flawless. The 2019 Dragonblood attacks (Vanhoef and Ronen) found timing and cache side channels in SAE implementations, and downgrade attacks against transition mode, where an AP accepts both WPA2 and WPA3 so old devices can connect: an attacker advertises a WPA2-only copy and captures a crackable WPA2 handshake. Fixes followed (including the hash-to-element method), but transition mode remains a weak spot. Wi-Fi certification requirements for 6 GHz call for WPA3 or Enhanced Open (OWE) with PMF, without WPA2 on that band. This does not prohibit a multi-band SSID from separately serving legacy clients on 2.4 or 5 GHz. OWE encrypts open networks (cafés, airports) with an unauthenticated key exchange. It stops passive sniffing, but not an evil twin, because nobody's identity is checked. Key takeaways Correctly implemented fresh SAE resists passive offline password verification and provides forward secrecy under its assumptions. PMF protects selected management frames after keys exist, not all radio traffic. WPA2 transition support and implementation side channels can weaken the intended protections. Further reading Key Reinstallation Attacks (KRACK) — Mathy Vanhoef Dragonblood: analysing WPA3's Dragonfly handshake Wi-Fi Protected Access — Wikipedia Wired Equivalent Privacy — Wikipedia IEEE 802.1X — Wikipedia RFC 7664: Dragonfly Key Exchange

sum: 802.1X separates the supplicant, authenticator and authentication server roles.
x: A shared Wi-Fi passphrase makes individual user revocation awkward. Enterprise authentication supplies separate credentials, but its protection still depends on the EAP method and the client’s server validation policy. 802.1X and WPA-Enterprise In Enterprise mode there is no shared passphrase. 802.1X splits authentication across three roles: The controlled data port remains unauthorised while authentication proceeds; EAPOL and necessary link-management traffic are separate. The client and the RADIUS server run an EAP method through the AP. With a key-generating EAP method and the illustrated RADIUS deployment, exported keying material reaches the authenticator over the AAA channel; the link layer derives/selects its PMK. RADIUS is a common backend, not a requirement of every 802.1X deployment. The normal four-way handshake follows. Independent authentication credentials and pairwise key derivation prevent one ordinary user's credentials from deriving another's unicast keys. Group traffic can still use a shared GTK, and caching/roaming can reuse PMKs; isolation is not a claim that every frame has a unique per-user key. Access can be revoked per user and logged per user, and the RADIUS server can assign VLANs by role, which ties Wi-Fi into the segmentation of the earlier firewall and segmentation units. The same 802.1X runs on wired switch ports. The EAP method matters: Method Client proves with Risk --------- EAP-TLS Certificate Needs a client PKI PEAP / EAP-TTLS Password in a TLS tunnel Weak if server cert not checked The PEAP evil twin PEAP wraps a password exchange (usually MSCHAPv2) inside TLS from the RADIUS server. If clients do not check that server certificate against the right CA and name, an attacker runs an evil twin AP with their own RADIUS server, clients happily complete the tunnel, and the attacker captures MSCHAPv2 exchanges. Captured MSCHAPv2 challenge responses permit offline attacks on its DES-based construction, which can recover an NT password hash without necessarily recovering the plaintext password. Deploy a profile validating the intended CA and server name. EAP-TLS avoids password-based inner authentication but still requires server validation. Defending a wireless network Use WPA3, or WPA2 with long random passphrases where you must, and enable PMF. Prefer 802.1X with EAP-TLS for organisations; validate server certificates on every client. Put guest and IoT devices on separate SSIDs and VLANs, isolated from internal networks. Run wireless intrusion detection to spot rogue APs, evil twins and floods of deauth frames. Treat Wi-Fi, even WPA3, as one layer: TLS and VPNs on top mean a Wi-Fi compromise does not expose application data. Content omitted after review Universal GPU guessing rates, claims that dictionary attacks usually finish in minutes, and an absolute guarantee that a five-word passphrase is uncrackable are omitted. No hardware benchmark, password distribution or attacker budget was specified; the numerical exercise uses explicit hypothetical assumptions. An exact WEP introduction/deprecation chronology and attribution of the PBKDF2 output to a particular IEEE test-vector publication are also omitted because those original records were not retrieved; the key output itself was executed. Key takeaways 802.1X separates the supplicant, authenticator and authentication server roles. Individual credentials enable individual access decisions and pairwise key separation; group keys remain shared. Validate the intended server CA and name for PEAP and EAP-TLS deployments. sum: Passive IDS sensors analyse a copy; inline IPS devices can block traffic.
x: The earlier units focused on preventive controls. Prevention can fail: a password is phished, a VPN appliance is unpatched, a firewall rule is too broad. The question then is how quickly you notice. Dwell time is the interval from intrusion to detection. Content gap No industry-wide dwell-time estimate, rule-count estimate or typical retention period is supplied: a dated, comparable measurement was not verified for this lesson. Detection on the network rests on three kinds of evidence, which trade detail against cost: Source Detail Cost to keep --------- Packet capture Captured packet bytes, subject to truncation and loss Potentially high Protocol logs (Zeek) Selected connection, protocol-exchange or file events Depends on logging Flow records Aggregated traffic sharing selected attributes Depends on export On top of the evidence sit detection systems that raise alerts. This unit introduces alerting engines; the following units examine alert precision and the evidence those engines consume. IDS and IPS An intrusion detection system (IDS) watches traffic and raises alerts. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) sits inline and can also drop traffic. An IDS is fed a copy of traffic from a switch SPAN (mirror) port or a network TAP, or in the cloud via traffic mirroring. A passive sensor is outside the forwarding path; automatic response integrations can still affect traffic. A mirror can lose packets when the copied traffic exceeds its monitoring-port capacity. An IPS can stop an attack in progress, but it adds latency and becomes a point of failure. You must choose fail-open (traffic flows if the IPS dies, unprotected) or fail-closed (the network goes down with it). A false positive on a blocking rule can disrupt legitimate traffic; alert-only rules do not themselves block it. Network IDS (NIDS) watch the wire; host IDS (HIDS) and EDR agents watch processes and files on each machine. They complement each other: hosts see what happened inside encrypted sessions, networks see machines that have no agent, such as printers, cameras and anything the attacker brought. Signatures and anomalies Signature-based detection matches known patterns. Snort and Suricata are examples of open-source engines. A Suricata rule (backslashes continue a rule across lines): The header (alert http any any -> $HOME_NET any) says what traffic to consider; the options say what to look for. flow:established,to_server selects traffic towards the server in a flow the engine considers established. This is connection tracking, not cryptographic peer authentication or a guarantee against forged traffic; midstream handling also depends on configuration. http.uri selects the normalised URI buffer. The string match is only a teaching example, not a complete SQL-injection detector. Signatures match specified patterns, which can occur in both known and previously unseen attacks, or in benign traffic. Anomaly-based detection learns a baseline (normal hosts, ports, volumes and times) and alerts on deviations: a workstation suddenly talking SMB to fifty others, a server uploading gigabytes at 3 a.m. It can flag previously unseen behaviour, but deviations can be legitimate. Relative false-positive rates depend on the detector, data and threshold. Key takeaways Passive IDS sensors analyse a copy; inline IPS devices can block traffic. Inline failure policy trades continued connectivity against unfiltered passage. An established flow is connection state, not cryptographic sender authentication. t: Why a rare attack creates many false alerts
sum: Alert precision depends on attack prevalence as well as detector sensitivity.
x: A detector with a small false-positive rate can still create a large investigation workload. The denominator matters: rare malicious events may be outnumbered by benign events by many orders of magnitude. The base-rate problem Even a small false-positive rate can overwhelm true alerts when malicious events are rare. The question an analyst cares about is: when an alert fires, how likely is it to be real? That fraction is the detector's alert precision, and it depends on how common attacks are (the base rate) as well as on the detector: This is Bayes' theorem applied to alerts. It assumes the rates are constant across events, and it is undefined if the detector never alerts (the bottom line is zero). Working it out. A network sees 10,000,000 connections a day, of which 100 are malicious. A detector catches 99 % of attacks and flags only 0.1 % of benign connections: About 99 % of alerts are false in this model. That workload can make triage difficult; it does not prove that every analyst will miss the true alerts. This is why mature teams tune aggressively, suppress noisy rules, correlate network alerts with host and identity signals in a SIEM, and measure precision in their own environment. Malware-domain and honeypot alerts can be useful, but shared infrastructure, research traffic and mistakes can still create false positives. Key takeaways Alert precision depends on attack prevalence as well as detector sensitivity. The worked counts are expected values, not guaranteed daily outcomes. Tune and correlate evidence using the actual operating environment. t: Capture filters, display filters and TCP flags
sum: tcpdump capture filters and Wireshark display filters use different syntax.
x: Packet captures preserve observations at one point in a path. This unit shows how to choose packets and read TCP flag output without confusing a reset, silence or a heuristic retransmission label with a complete diagnosis. Packet capture with tcpdump When you need ground truth, capture packets. tcpdump uses BPF capture filters. On supported live-capture platforms filtering can run in the kernel; offline capture-file filtering runs in userspace: -nn matters on a busy box: name resolution can add delay and generate DNS traffic. Cached results and local host databases mean this is not necessarily a DNS query for every address. A line of output looks like this (wrapped to fit): The flags are the quickest way to read a conversation: Flags Meaning ------ [S] SYN, opening [S.] SYN-ACK [.] ACK flag; payload may still be present [P.] PSH and ACK flags; inspect length for payload [F.] FIN, closing [R] RST, refused or aborted SYNs to many ports can indicate a scan, but may also be authorised diagnostics. A reset indicates active rejection or abort somewhere along the path, possibly by a middlebox. Silence could reflect filtering, loss, an unavailable host or replies travelling by a path the sensor cannot see; it does not identify a firewall by itself. Wireshark Wireshark decodes hundreds of protocols and is the tool for understanding a capture. Its display filters use a different syntax from BPF capture filters, a constant source of confusion: Capture (libpcap) Display (Wireshark) ------ tcp port 80 tcp.port == 80 host 10.0.0.5 ip.addr == 10.0.0.5 Useful display filters for investigations: tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0: connection attempts. tcp.analysis.retransmission: packets Wireshark heuristically classifies as retransmissions; investigate capture loss and reordering before inferring network loss. dns.flags.rcode == 3: NXDOMAIN answers. Bursts of random-looking names can indicate malware using domain-generation algorithms. tls.handshake.type == 1: visible ClientHellos; ECH can hide the real server name in the encrypted inner ClientHello. "Follow TCP Stream" reassembles a conversation. For TLS you can decrypt your own captures if the client writes its session secrets to a file: browsers and many libraries honour the SSLKEYLOGFILE environment variable, and Wireshark reads it. Key takeaways tcpdump capture filters and Wireshark display filters use different syntax. Flags and lengths describe packet observations rather than proving intent. Name-resolution controls, capture loss and TCP stream reconstruction context affect interpretation. Further reading Suricata rules format — Suricata docs tcpdump and libpcap Wireshark display filters — Wireshark wiki Logging IP traffic using VPC Flow Logs — AWS RFC 7011: IPFIX Protocol Specification Zeek documentation Base rate fallacy — Wikipedia

sum: Host offloads can expose large buffers and incomplete checksums before wire transmission.
x: A packet capture is shaped by its observation point and retention settings. Before diagnosing impossible packet sizes or promising a month of retention, separate host-buffer artefacts from bytes actually stored. Capture pitfalls - Offloads. Depending on the capture hook and enabled offloads, host captures can show large buffers before transmit segmentation or after receive coalescing, and outbound checksums before hardware fills them in. Such apparent errors need not occur on the wire. - Drops. A busy capture can drop packets; tcpdump reports "dropped by kernel" on exit. - Storage. Recording bytes at a constant 1 Gbps is 125 MB/s, or 10.8 decimal TB/day before capture-file overhead (calculated below). A physical link rate is not identical to recorded packet bytes because link-layer framing and gaps also consume capacity. Choose retention from measured volume and budget. - Privacy and law. Captures contain personal data and credentials; handle them as sensitive. The storage a full capture needs is the recorded rate, converted from bits to bytes, multiplied by how long you record: Keeping 30 days of that is about 324 TB, which is why full capture usually has short retention or is triggered only when needed. Key takeaways Host offloads can expose large buffers and incomplete checksums before wire transmission. Capture volume uses recorded bytes, not physical link capacity alone. Storage calculations exclude file overhead, replication and compression unless stated. Further reading Suricata rules format — Suricata docs tcpdump and libpcap Wireshark display filters — Wireshark wiki Logging IP traffic using VPC Flow Logs — AWS RFC 7011: IPFIX Protocol Specification Zeek documentation Base rate fallacy — Wikipedia

sum: Encrypted application payloads require appropriate keys to inspect.
x: A passive sensor without session secrets cannot read protected application contents. It can still correlate observable traffic patterns, provided each conclusion respects what was actually captured. Encrypted traffic When traffic is encrypted, a passive sensor without decryption keys cannot inspect application plaintext. Defenders lean on metadata: Who talks to whom, how often and how much. Malware beaconing to its command server at regular intervals shows up in timing even when encrypted. Visible TLS handshake metadata: ordinary ClientHello SNI can reveal a requested name; ECH hides the inner name while an outer public name can remain visible. TLS 1.3 encrypts certificate messages, so a passive observer without keys cannot generally read them. TLS fingerprints: features of the ClientHello can help group similar clients, but are not authenticated software identities. Different clients may share a fingerprint, and an attacker can imitate one. Changes in parameter ordering can also affect order-sensitive fingerprints. DNS logs, which can reveal names looked up through the observed resolver. Cached answers, direct IP connections and unobserved encrypted DNS create gaps. The alternative is TLS interception at a proxy, which restores payload visibility at the cost of the risks described in the earlier firewall and segmentation units. Any interception policy must define which traffic it can inspect and which traffic it exempts. Zeek sits in between: it parses traffic into structured logs (conn.log, dns.log, http.log, ssl.log, files.log) whose record units depend on the log type. These logs retain selected metadata; encrypted application contents remain unavailable without decryption. Storage and usefulness depend on the enabled analysers and traffic. Key takeaways Encrypted application payloads require appropriate keys to inspect. Visible names, addresses, timing and fingerprints are useful but incomplete signals. ECH, caching and unobserved DNS paths limit what a passive sensor can infer. Further reading Suricata rules format — Suricata docs tcpdump and libpcap Wireshark display filters — Wireshark wiki Logging IP traffic using VPC Flow Logs — AWS RFC 7011: IPFIX Protocol Specification Zeek documentation Base rate fallacy — Wikipedia

t: Flow records and bounded scan heuristics
sum: Flow definitions, sampling and time windows vary across export systems.
x: Flow records trade raw packet detail for selected counters and attributes. This unit uses that summary to investigate communication patterns while keeping sampling, logging gaps and legitimate scanning in view. Flow records A flow record summarises packets grouped by selected attributes within an observation interval. Common fields include a 5-tuple, timestamps, counters and TCP flags, but templates and the rules for grouping packets into records vary. One TCP connection can produce multiple records. NetFlow (Cisco, v5 and v9) and its IETF standard successor IPFIX (RFC 7011): routers or probes export flow records to a collector. sFlow statistically samples packets at a configured average rate and exports sampled packet-header data plus counters. This is not necessarily a strict count such as exactly every 1,000th packet; sampled header bytes can include some payload. Where flow export uses packet sampling (for example an average of 1 in 1,000 packets), it reduces observation volume but can miss short flows and introduces uncertainty into estimates. In AWS, VPC Flow Logs record traffic on network interfaces. A default-format record looks like this (shown one field per line): action reports ACCEPT or REJECT. A rejection can arise from security groups, NACLs or packets arriving after a connection has closed; this field alone does not identify a particular rule. They have blind spots: traffic to the Amazon-provided DNS resolver, DHCP and the instance metadata service is not logged, so DNS-based activity needs Route 53 Resolver query logs instead. The default maximum time window for each record is 10 minutes, with a 1-minute option; Nitro interfaces use at most 1 minute regardless. Publication adds delay, and SKIPDATA records disclose some logging gaps. A simple scan detector over simplified flow records (source, destination, port, action): Ignoring the trailing space on the unflagged line, this prints 10.0.2.7 1 0 and 203.0.113.9 5 4 SCAN?. The app server's two connections go to one (host, port) pair; the external address probes five pairs, mostly rejected. Real detectors add a time window, thresholds tuned to the environment and allowlists for legitimate scanners, and distinct destination pairs per source are one useful heuristic, not proof of a malicious scan. Within its coverage, flow data can help investigate questions such as: which hosts did this compromised machine talk to? Did anything inside send unusual volumes to the internet (exfiltration)? When did this start? Retention depends on record volume, cost and policy; small individual records do not guarantee months of affordable storage. Putting it together A practical network-detection stack for a medium organisation: Flow logs at relevant observation points (budgeted retention) for investigation and anomaly detection. DNS and proxy logs for destinations. Zeek and Suricata at key choke points (internet edge, between major network segments). Short-retention or triggered full capture where the detail is worth the storage. Everything into a SIEM, correlated with host (EDR) and identity logs, with detections tuned for precision. Segmentation (the earlier firewall and segmentation units) helps detection too: a denied connection between network segments can merit investigation, but configuration errors and legitimate discovery can also produce it. Key takeaways Flow definitions, sampling and time windows vary across export systems. VPC Flow Logs have documented coverage gaps and aggregation behaviour. Distinct destination pairs are a useful scan heuristic, not proof of malicious intent. Further reading Suricata rules format — Suricata docs tcpdump and libpcap Wireshark display filters — Wireshark wiki Logging IP traffic using VPC Flow Logs — AWS RFC 7011: IPFIX Protocol Specification Zeek documentation Base rate fallacy — Wikipedia

sum: Compare streams, channel width, modulation and scheduling as different improvements.
x: Switched Ethernet commonly gives each device a dedicated wired link. Wi-Fi stations share radio resources, but not every station can hear every other. Modern multi-user techniques allow coordinated simultaneous transmissions, and spatial reuse can allow concurrent transmissions in different coverage areas. Radio conditions change with interference, motion and obstacles. Almost everything distinctive about Wi-Fi follows from that: how devices take turns, why they cannot detect collisions, how a slow active client can consume airtime needed by another client, and why a product’s aggregate advertised PHY rates do not predict one client’s application throughput. The 802.11 generations Wi-Fi is the Wi-Fi Alliance's brand for the IEEE 802.11 standards. In 2018 the Alliance introduced generation numbers so people did not need to remember letters. Name Standard Bands Key additions ------------ Legacy 802.11b/a/g b/g: 2.4; a: 5 GHz b up to 11 Mbit/s; a/g up to 54, with OFDM for a/g Wi-Fi 4 802.11n (2009) 2.4, 5 GHz MIMO, 40 MHz, frame aggregation Wi-Fi 5 802.11ac (2013) 5 GHz 80/160 MHz, 256-QAM, DL MU-MIMO Wi-Fi 6 802.11ax; certification began 2019 2.4, 5 GHz OFDMA, 1024-QAM, TWT Wi-Fi 6E 802.11ax adds 6 GHz additional spectrum, subject to local rules Wi-Fi 7 802.11be; certification began 2024 2.4, 5, 6 GHz 320 MHz, 4096-QAM, MLO What each change buys: MIMO (multiple-input multiple-output): several antennas send independent spatial streams on the same frequency at once. Two streams roughly double the rate. The usable count depends on both endpoints and the radio channel; antenna count alone does not establish it. Wider channels: rate scales roughly with width, so 80 MHz carries about four times a 20 MHz channel. Denser modulation (QAM): 256-QAM carries 8 bits per symbol, 1024-QAM 10, 4096-QAM 12. Each step needs a much cleaner signal, so achievable modulation depends on signal quality, interference and hardware, not a fixed distance boundary. OFDMA (Wi-Fi 6): the channel is split into resource units, so the AP can send to or receive from several clients in one transmission instead of one at a time. This can reduce per-client access overhead, depending on scheduling, compatible clients and workload. Target Wake Time (Wi-Fi 6): devices negotiate when to wake, saving battery for phones and IoT sensors. 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E and 7): additional spectrum for capable devices, subject to national power, indoor/outdoor and coexistence rules. It is not interference-free. Country allocations change: for example, Ofcom published a July 2026 upper-6-GHz sharing decision, so an undated “UK has only 500 MHz” statement is inadequate. Multi-Link Operation (Wi-Fi 7): coordinates multiple links; concurrent transmission/reception depends on the MLO mode and hardware. It does not require every device to transmit on three bands simultaneously. Key takeaways Compare streams, channel width, modulation and scheduling as different improvements. A generation label does not establish supported modes, spectrum permission or measured throughput. Further reading IEEE 802.11 — Wikipedia Wi-Fi 6 — Wikipedia Wi-Fi 7 — Wikipedia Wi-Fi Alliance: Wi-Fi CERTIFIED 7 launch, January 2024

sum: More constellation points add bits logarithmically and need cleaner signals.
x: This unit focuses on modulation, signal quality and capacity. It builds on the earlier units in this module; the examples below state their additional assumptions. Why denser modulation needs a cleaner signal A QAM symbol is one of a fixed number of possible points (amplitude-and-phase combinations). The number of bits one symbol carries is the base-2 logarithm of the number of points: So 256-QAM carries 8 bits (eight doublings of 1 give 256), 1024-QAM 10 bits and 4096-QAM 12 bits. Going from 1024 to 4096 points adds only 2 bits (+20%), but squeezes four times as many points into the same space, so the receiver must tell apart points that sit much closer together. Noise that a 256-QAM receiver shrugs off makes a 4096-QAM receiver pick the wrong point. The Shannon–Hartley theorem sets the theoretical ceiling on any channel, whatever the modulation. It applies to a channel disturbed by random (Gaussian) noise: At 30 dB SNR this ideal Gaussian-noise ceiling is about 10 bits per second per hertz. It is not a minimum SNR specification for 1024-QAM: modulation, coding, error targets, interference and hardware determine an actual radio’s requirements and usable locations. SNR is usually quoted in decibels: Real radios fall short of the Shannon limit and also lose rate to coding and guard intervals, so the later PHY-rate unit’s table sits below it. Key takeaways More constellation points add bits logarithmically and need cleaner signals. The Gaussian-noise capacity model is a theoretical bound, not a radio throughput measurement. Further reading Shannon: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (original paper)

sum: Count down backoff only while the channel is idle; failure grows the contention window up to its cap.
x: This unit focuses on Wi-Fi contention, backoff and acknowledgments. It builds on the earlier units in this module; the examples below state their additional assumptions. Sharing the air: CSMA/CA Classic shared Ethernet used CSMA/CD: listen before sending, and if you detect a collision while transmitting, stop, jam and back off. Wi-Fi cannot do the "CD" part: Ordinary Wi-Fi radios do not implement Ethernet-style collision detection while sending; their own transmit signal makes simultaneous sensing of weak incoming signals difficult. A collision may happen at the receiver but not be audible at the sender at all (covered in the next unit). So Wi-Fi tries to avoid collisions instead, and uses missing expected acknowledgments as an indication of failure; not every frame is individually acknowledged. The following is a simplified DCF contention example for acknowledged unicast using 5 GHz OFDM timings. Modern QoS traffic commonly uses EDCA with access-category parameters; broadcast/multicast and scheduled multi-user exchanges differ: Carrier sense. Listen. If the channel is busy, wait until it goes idle. Wait DIFS. After the channel goes idle, wait a fixed gap (34 µs on 5 GHz). Random backoff. Pick a random whole-number count between zero and the current contention window, inclusive (9 µs slots; the window starts at 15). Count down only while the channel stays idle; freeze the counter if someone else starts sending. Transmit when the counter hits zero. ACK. The receiver replies after a shorter gap, SIFS (16 µs). The shorter gap gives priority over compliant contenders that sense this exchange; interference and hidden terminals can still corrupt the ACK. No ACK? Assume a collision or corruption, grow CW (here 15, 31, 63... up to 1023) and try again. After a retry limit, drop the frame. The contention window roughly doubles after each failure, capped at a maximum: For example, drawing seven slots on the first attempt gives a 63-microsecond idle countdown. After three failures the count is drawn from zero through 127, giving up to 1.143 milliseconds of counted idle slots. Busy periods and interframe waits add wall-clock time. The interframe gaps follow the same slot arithmetic: In the timeline, k is the random slot count from the formula above. There is also virtual carrier sense: eligible frames carry Duration/ID information that can reserve remaining exchange time. Stations update their NAV (network allocation vector) according to protocol rules. Some fields are zero or have other meanings; physical carrier sensing still applies. Why the random backoff matters If two stations both wait for a busy channel to end and then send immediately, they can collide when their transmissions overlap at the receiver. The random countdown spreads them out, and the doubling makes stations back off harder when the channel is congested. Key takeaways Count down backoff only while the channel is idle; failure grows the contention window up to its cap. SIFS gives immediate replies priority over ordinary DCF contention under the stated sensing assumptions. Further reading Carrier-sense multiple access with collision avoidance — Wikipedia ns-3 Wi-Fi model: DCF, EDCA and protection mechanisms

sum: A hidden sender can interfere at a receiver it cannot hear directly.
x: This unit focuses on hidden and exposed terminals. It builds on the earlier units in this module; the examples below state their additional assumptions. The hidden terminal problem and RTS/CTS Carrier sense only works if every station can hear every other. Often they cannot. A and C both sense an idle channel and transmit at once. Their frames can interfere at the AP, causing missing ACKs and retries. Capture effects or different timings can allow some frames to succeed; throughput need not collapse in every such topology. RTS/CTS can mitigate this when the relevant contenders receive the protection frames: A sends a short Request To Send to the AP, with the duration of the exchange. The AP replies Clear To Send, carrying the remaining protected exchange time. C cannot hear A's RTS, but it can hear the AP's CTS, so it sets its NAV and stays quiet. A sends its data; the AP ACKs. This reduces the chance of wasting a long data transmission on a hidden-terminal collision. Missed CTS frames, other interferers and overlapping reservations still permit data/ACK loss. The cost is two extra frames and gaps per exchange, so implementations can select protection using an RTS threshold and other policies; defaults are device-specific. Wi-Fi 6 also uses RTS/CTS-style protection automatically in some situations, such as before multi-user transmissions. The mirror image is the exposed terminal: a station that hears a nearby transmission and defers, even though its own transmission would not have interfered at its intended receiver. RTS/CTS does not fix this; it is one reason dense networks waste airtime. Key takeaways A hidden sender can interfere at a receiver it cannot hear directly. Received RTS/CTS protection can mitigate hidden-terminal collisions; it does not solve exposed-terminal deferral. Further reading Hidden node problem — Wikipedia

sum: Start with a permitted, surveyed channel plan; overlapping energy and coordinated co-channel sharing differ.
x: This unit focuses on channels, interference and radio propagation. It builds on the earlier units in this module; the examples below state their additional assumptions. Channels and interference 2.4 GHz has channels only 5 MHz apart, but each transmission is about 20 MHz wide. Neighbouring channels therefore overlap, and 1, 6 and 11 is a conventional conservative 20 MHz plan where those channels are permitted. Available channels, PHY spectral masks and interference determine other viable plans; this is not the only possible set worldwide. The centre frequency of each 2.4 GHz channel follows a simple rule (channels 1 to 13; Japan's channel 14 is a special case): Channels 1 and 3, by contrast, are only 10 MHz apart, so their 20 MHz-wide signals overlap by about half. Two kinds of interference behave very differently: Co-channel: your neighbour's AP is also on channel 6. When networks can sense each other, contention helps them share airtime. Collisions, hidden terminals and decoding failures can still occur. Adjacent-channel: your neighbour is on channel 3. Overlapping energy may interfere without successful frame decoding. Energy detection can still cause deferral, depending on thresholds. The result depends on power, frequency separation, placement and equipment; it is not a universal ranking of channel plans. Rule of thumb In a dense deployment using channels 1–11, 20 MHz with a coordinated 1/6/11 plan is a useful starting point. Check the regulatory domain and survey neighbouring use; wider channels reduce the number of separate channels available. 5 GHz has many more 20 MHz channels, enough for several 80 MHz channels. Some are DFS channels shared with radar: an AP must listen for radar before using them and vacate if it detects any, which can cause a sudden channel change. 6 GHz excludes older 2.4/5-GHz-only Wi-Fi clients, but compatible clients can still use low rates or consume substantial airtime. Other authorised services and neighbouring networks may share spectrum. At fixed antenna gains and distance, free-space path loss grows with frequency. It is the loss between two ideal antennas with nothing in the way, so it is a best case: So at 10 m the 5.5 GHz signal arrives about 7 dB weaker, roughly one fifth of the power, than the 2.4 GHz one. Wall losses depend on material, construction, angle and frequency; the free-space equation does not predict them. Actual coverage also depends on permitted power, antenna patterns, wall materials, bandwidth and receiver sensitivity; a frequency label alone does not establish range or throughput. Other things share 2.4 GHz too: Bluetooth, microwave ovens and baby monitors. Key takeaways Start with a permitted, surveyed channel plan; overlapping energy and coordinated co-channel sharing differ. Free-space path loss compares frequencies under fixed gains and distance, not arbitrary indoor coverage. Further reading List of WLAN channels — Wikipedia Ofcom: 6 GHz spectrum sharing decisions

t: PHY rates and the number on the box
sum: An aggregate router label sums separate radios, while a single-link client uses one link at a time.
x: This unit focuses on PHY rates and the number on the box. It builds on the earlier units in this module; the examples below state their additional assumptions. Why real throughput is far below the advertised rate The number on the box is the maximum PHY rate, often summed across bands. A PHY rate is just bits per symbol, times the number of subcarriers carrying data, times the number of spatial streams, divided by how long each symbol lasts. For Wi-Fi 6 (HE, "high efficiency"): Take an "AX3000" router, using 1024-QAM with rate-5/6 coding and a 0.8 µs guard interval on both radios: A conventional single-link client connection does not obtain this sum. Multiple-radio devices and other link-bonding arrangements existed before Wi-Fi 7; MLO standardises coordinated multi-link operation. PHY rate excludes channel-contention waits, interframe gaps, PHY preamble airtime, MAC acknowledgments, headers and retransmissions. Ordinary single-link uploads and downloads also consume shared airtime, including TCP acknowledgments. Other active stations share those resources. These effects explain why useful application throughput can fall below the negotiated PHY rate; the next units quantify particular simplified cases. Now compare this model with a hypothetical phone’s negotiated PHY rate. The next units examine airtime overhead, sharing and retries. 1. The client's link rate is lower For an example client with two spatial streams using an 80 MHz HE channel and 0.8 µs guard interval, full-channel single-stream PHY rates are approximately: MCS Modulation 1 stream, 80 MHz --------- 0 BPSK 1/2 36 Mbit/s 7 64-QAM 5/6 360 Mbit/s 9 256-QAM 5/6 480 Mbit/s 11 1024-QAM 5/6 600 Mbit/s Each row comes from the PHY-rate formula with 980 data subcarriers and a 13.6 µs symbol. For an illustrative negotiated MCS 7 on two streams, the arithmetic is: Rate adaptation selects rates using link feedback; the illustrated room count does not predict a particular MCS. Key takeaways An aggregate router label sums separate radios, while a single-link client uses one link at a time. Compute a PHY rate from streams, data subcarriers, modulation, coding and symbol duration. Further reading Cisco: Wi-Fi throughput validation and PHY-rate tables

sum: A fixed channel-access cost overwhelms a short frame but can be shared by an aggregate.
x: This unit focuses on frame aggregation and airtime efficiency. It builds on the earlier units in this module; the examples below state their additional assumptions. 2. MAC overhead Every transmission pays a fixed cost in airtime: DIFS, average backoff, the PHY preamble, SIFS and the acknowledgement. For the calculation below, assume 200 µs per channel access and omit per-MPDU delimiters, padding and variable protocol costs. This is a supplied teaching value, not a universal measured overhead. The fraction of airtime that carries data is the efficiency: Frame aggregation amortises access costs; Block Ack can acknowledge multiple MPDUs. It is an important efficiency mechanism, but no single TCP/PHY efficiency percentage holds for every link. Key takeaways A fixed channel-access cost overwhelms a short frame but can be shared by an aggregate. The supplied 200-microsecond model omits variable per-frame overhead and is not a measured efficiency guarantee. Further reading WiFi — High Performance Browser Networking Cisco: Wi-Fi throughput validation and PHY-rate tables

t: Sharing airtime and diagnosing slow Wi-Fi
sum: Equal frame opportunities can give a slow active client disproportionate airtime in the simplified DCF model.
x: This unit focuses on sharing airtime and diagnosing slow Wi-Fi. It builds on the earlier units in this module; the examples below state their additional assumptions. 3. Half duplex and sharing An ordinary single radio link cannot simultaneously transmit and receive on that link. Uploads and downloads consume radio resources; scheduling, OFDMA/MU-MIMO, spatial reuse and multiple links make modern sharing more complex than a single global turn-taking sequence. 4. The performance anomaly In a simplified saturated, equal-priority DCF model with comparable frame sizes, stations obtain similar access opportunities rather than equal airtime. Slow transmissions can then reduce faster stations’ throughput. QoS, frame aggregation, AP scheduling and airtime policies change this model. One slow client A fast client at 54 Mbit/s and a slow one at 6 Mbit/s alternate 1,500-byte frames, ignoring overhead. Each cycle moves one frame for each, so both get the same throughput, about 5.4 Mbit/s. The fast client loses 90% of its throughput. The calculation behind the example: The fast client gets 5.4 of its possible 54 Mbit/s. The model assumes both clients always have a frame waiting and get equal turns. Some APs implement airtime fairness policies to mitigate this; capabilities and effectiveness vary. Moving compatible clients to another band can separate contention, but does not guarantee high rates there. 5. Loss and retries Interference and fading cause corrupted frames. Wi-Fi retries at the link layer, which can hide some radio losses from TCP but adds latency and jitter. Under load, large buffers in the AP add more: an illustrative loaded link might show 5 ms idle RTT and 200 ms during a download; this is not a universal measurement or unique diagnosis. Practical consequences Survey placement, interference, client capabilities and backhaul before changing configuration. Wired backhaul avoids consuming wireless backhaul airtime; a dedicated radio still has coexistence and capacity constraints. Compare permitted bands for the actual devices and coverage needs. Extra APs need channel and power planning; more is not automatically better. Wired connections can remove active traffic from radio contention. An idle device’s removal need not produce a measurable improvement. Compare local wired and wireless tests, RSSI/SNR, negotiated rates, retries, airtime use and loaded latency to locate the bottleneck. Evidence limits Universal handset stream counts, fixed TCP efficiency ratios, driver defaults and guaranteed channel-plan outcomes are omitted because they need device-specific evidence. Regional spectrum rules are time-sensitive; consult the regulator before deployment. No RF, coverage, interference or throughput measurements were performed for this lesson. Key takeaways Equal frame opportunities can give a slow active client disproportionate airtime in the simplified DCF model. Separate airtime, retries, queueing and backhaul with measurements before changing a deployment.
