It might be a heading, a task row or an entire screen. Starting with small named parts makes a larger screen easier to read and reuse. This course assumes basic JavaScript variables, functions, arrays and objects. It explains the extra syntax as it appears. Examples belong in a React-enabled project or playground whose build tool transforms JSX into JavaScript; pasting JSX directly into an ordinary browser script will not work. Project installation is outside this course. A function that describes UI A function component returns a description of what should appear. JSX is the HTML-like syntax inside the JavaScript below. HTML is the browser's document markup language; JSX is JavaScript syntax that a tool transforms. They look similar but are not interchangeable. This complete component file can be used as the root component in that prepared environment. export default makes StudyPage available for another file to import. The environment mounts that root component into the page. StudyPage returns one main element containing a heading and two uses of Welcome. Each use describes an h2 with the same text. The browser therefore displays the main heading followed by two smaller headings. Writing a function definition alone does not put it on the screen: some rendered component must use it. <Welcome /> tells React to use the JavaScript component named Welcome. <main> and <h1> refer to built-in browser elements. Names used as custom JSX tags must begin with a capital letter. Writing <welcome /> would describe a lowercase element rather than call the Welcome component. The parentheses after return group several lines into one returned expression. Keep the opening parenthesis on the same line as return; JavaScript can otherwise end the return statement before the markup. Compose a screen from parts Composition means combining smaller components to make a larger one. A component can contain ordinary elements and other components. Keep component definitions at the top level of a file, rather than defining one inside another component's function. This gives the component a stable definition; later lessons explain why component identity matters for state. Real-world analogy: A reusable recipe A recipe for a sandwich can be used twice when preparing two lunches. How it maps: The component function is the reusable description; each JSX use asks React for another instance of that part of the interface. Where it stops: A component returns a UI description, not a physical object. React decides when to run it and how to update the browser. Choose a component when a part has a clear responsibility or is reused. You do not need to make every single tag a separate component. A useful boundary lets you understand its purpose from its name and inputs. Key takeaways A function component describes a piece of UI by returning JSX. Capitalised JSX names refer to components; lowercase names are treated as browser element names. Nesting and reusing components is composition. Use a React-enabled environment that transforms JSX before the browser runs it. Further reading Your first component — React Importing and exporting components — React

sum: Connect JavaScript expressions, destructuring, callbacks and module imports to readable JSX.
x: JSX does not replace JavaScript. Use JavaScript to calculate a value, then insert that value where the UI needs it. An expression is code that produces a value, such as a variable name, a function call or an arithmetic operation. A statement such as if controls execution and cannot go directly inside JSX braces. Read values with braces Quotes pass literal text. Braces evaluate a JavaScript expression. title="name" passes the text name; title={name} passes the value held by the variable. In JSX children, {name} displays that value. A plain object is not itself a valid text child: choose one of its properties instead. Destructuring extracts named properties into local variables. In a function parameter, { name } reads the name property from its argument. The value of that property is not another object merely because braces appear around the parameter. An arrow function is a compact function expression. name => name.toUpperCase() takes one input and returns the expression after the arrow. A function passed into another operation is a callback. Array map calls its callback for each item and collects the returned values into a new array. This component excerpt receives person, an object with a name string. No imports are needed inside this excerpt in a project using the modern JSX transform. Given a person named Sam, the heading reads Hello, Sam; the paragraph reads ADA, GRACE. map has not changed the original strings in names. Here it produces strings which the array join method combines into one string; a later lesson maps data directly to JSX elements. If an arrow callback has a block body with braces, write an explicit return to return a value. Parentheses around JSX group an expression; braces after the arrow begin a block. Mixing these up can make a list silently contain undefined instead of the intended elements. Move components between files An export makes a value available outside its file. An import obtains it from another module. A JavaScript module is a file executed under JavaScript's module rules; imports and exports let it share values. A default export is imported without braces and can be given a local name. A named export is imported with braces and its exported name, unless explicitly renamed. The following two labelled files form one example../Badge.jsx is the relative path to the neighbouring file. Named-import braces select an export; they are not object destructuring, despite the similar appearance. These are ordinary JavaScript module rules, not a special React data flow. The earlier Greeting function can similarly be exported and imported. Imports run at the file level; they do not belong inside a component body. Key takeaways Quotes give literal strings; JSX braces evaluate expressions. Destructuring reads object properties into local names. An arrow expression returns implicitly; a block body needs return. Default imports and named imports use different syntax. Further reading JavaScript in JSX with curly braces — React Importing and exporting components — React Arrow functions — MDN Destructuring — MDN

sum: Use fragments, closed tags, className and style objects without confusing JSX with HTML.
x:
JSX describes elements using familiar tag shapes, but a JavaScript tool must be able to read it as an expression. A few consistent rules prevent most beginner syntax errors. React and JSX are separate ideas: React is the UI library; JSX is an optional way of writing its element descriptions. Group and close the markup A component returning several neighbouring elements must group them into one returned value. A wrapper such as section works when that element belongs in the page structure. A fragment, written <>..., groups neighbouring elements without adding a wrapper element to the browser's DOM. The DOM, or Document Object Model, is the browser's live tree of DOM nodes. A fragment changes the JSX grouping without creating a new node in that tree. It is useful when a wrapper would be meaningless, but it does not supply layout or styling of its own. Every JSX tag must close. Write
rather than
and
  • Read
    • rather than leaving the closing tag out. Paired tags must nest properly: close the inner element before the outer one. This is stricter than some HTML shorthand. Use JavaScript attribute names Use className for an element's CSS class. CSS, Cascading Style Sheets, controls appearance; a class name chooses styling rules defined elsewhere. Most React DOM property names use camelCase: words join with later words starting in capitals. onClick is an example you will meet in the events lesson. Accessibility attributes such as aria-label, and custom data- attributes, retain their hyphens. For an inline style, pass a JavaScript object rather than an HTML style string. Its property names are generally camelCase, such as backgroundColor. The outer braces enter JavaScript from JSX; the inner braces create the object. They are two separate uses of JavaScript syntax, not a special double-brace operator. This component excerpt uses a fragment and explicit CSS string values. The notice class can be defined in the project's stylesheet. The DOM contains a heading and a paragraph as siblings. The line break is a child of the paragraph. The fragment does not become an extra div. className="notice" sets the heading's class; it does not create a new component called notice. A common debugging sequence is to check the returned grouping, then matching tags, then attribute names. A syntax error prevents the file being transformed at all, so do this before investigating state or event behaviour. Valid JSX describes structure; visual layout still depends on the browser and CSS. Key takeaways Group neighbouring returned elements with a meaningful wrapper or a fragment. Close every JSX tag, including tags such as br. Use className and camelCase style properties. A style value is an object; a fragment adds no DOM wrapper. Further reading Writing markup with JSX — React JavaScript in JSX with curly braces — React

sum: Pass read-only inputs and nested children into a reusable card component.
x: A reusable component should describe the same kind of UI with different content. Props, short for properties, are the inputs that a parent passes to a child component. A prop can hold a string, number, boolean, object, array, function or JSX value. Props are not limited to HTML attributes. Read inputs without changing them A component receives one props object. Destructuring its parameter gives local names to chosen properties. Props are read-only: treat both the props object and values passed through it as immutable inputs. Do not assign a different title or change an array received from a parent while rendering. Read-only is a programming rule, not a claim that every JavaScript object is deeply frozen. A parent can later render the child with different props. When that happens, the child describes the UI using those new inputs. If the child needs an interaction to request a change, the parent can pass a callback; later lessons develop that pattern. Let the caller supply the inside children is the prop containing JSX nested between a component's opening and closing tags. A wrapper can place those children inside its own layout without knowing their detailed content. This is composition: the caller decides the content and the wrapper decides the surrounding structure. This complete component file renders two cards. title = 'Untitled' is a JavaScript default parameter inside destructuring. That default is used when the prop is missing or undefined, but not when it is null or an empty string. The first card shows Today and a paragraph. The second shows Untitled and a button. Card does not need separate branches for paragraphs and buttons: it simply includes its children where the content belongs. The button is presentational here; a later lesson gives it an event handler. The parent uses an explicit title prop and nested JSX for different jobs. title supplies one named value; children supplies the flexible content region. Neither changes who owns the data: the parent chooses what it passes, while the child reads it. Real-world analogy: A picture frame One frame design can surround different pictures and carry different captions. How it maps: The wrapper component supplies the frame, a named prop supplies the caption and children supplies the picture placed inside. Where it stops: Children are React values describing content, not objects physically inserted into a frame. The parent can provide new values on another render. Prefer clear named props over passing a large object that the component does not need. If a card only needs a title, receiving that title directly makes its contract easier to see. Composition helps avoid a single component accumulating a different boolean prop for every possible layout. Key takeaways Props flow from parent to child as read-only inputs. Nested JSX arrives through the children prop. Defaults apply to missing or undefined props, not null. Compose a reusable wrapper with caller-supplied content. Further reading Passing props to a component — React

sum: Use JavaScript conditions to show alternatives and avoid rendering an accidental zero.
x: A screen often has alternatives: a ready message or a loading message, a result list or an empty state. Conditional rendering means describing different UI for different inputs. React uses normal JavaScript decisions rather than a separate template condition language. Choose an entire return value Use an if statement before the JSX when a condition changes the whole result. Returning null tells React that this component contributes no visible content. It does not remove its parent's other children. This component excerpt receives a boolean visible and a numeric count. If visible is false, nothing appears from ResultSummary. If it is true with a count of zero, the paragraph says No results. A positive count produces Results available.!visible means the boolean opposite of visible. The ternary operator has a condition before?, a value for the true case after it, and a value for the false case after:. It is an expression, so it can go inside JSX braces. An if statement itself cannot go there. Prefer an early return or a named variable if several nested ternaries make the JSX difficult to read. Show one optional element carefully The JavaScript logical AND operator, &&, returns an operand value. When the left operand is falsy, it returns that left value; otherwise it evaluates and returns the right value. It does not always return a boolean. React renders no text for boolean children, null or undefined. A number is different: React can display the number zero. This intentional pitfall is a valid component excerpt, but its UI is wrong for a badge that should disappear when the count is zero. At zero, count &&... returns zero. React receives that number and displays it. Use a boolean condition on the left instead. This corrected component excerpt hides the badge entirely at zero. Now the condition is false at zero, so React receives false and displays no child text. At a positive count, the condition is true and the b element appears. The condition makes the intended threshold explicit, including for negative numbers. Conditional UI should handle meaningful empty cases, rather than leaving an unexplained blank area. If showing nothing would confuse someone waiting for results, use an explicit empty message instead of null. Choosing between these is a product decision; both are valid React values. Key takeaways Use if outside JSX or a ternary expression inside it. Returning null produces no visible content from that component. && returns operand values, so numeric zero can become visible text. Compare a numeric count with a threshold before using &&. Further reading Conditional rendering — React

sum: Transform arrays into elements and choose keys that keep each item associated with its identity.
x: A task list should come from task data rather than repeated handwritten tags. JavaScript array methods choose which records to show and transform them into JSX. React also needs a reliable way to match items between renders when a list changes. Filter records, then map them Array filter returns a new array containing items whose callback returned a truthy value. Array map returns a new array containing each callback's result. Neither method inherently changes the source array, although a callback can still incorrectly mutate the objects it receives. This component excerpt receives a tasks array. Each record has a stable string id, a title and a boolean done. The arrow callback with parentheses implicitly returns its JSX. Suppose the records are a: Read (open), b: Rest (done) and c: Practise (open). Filtering keeps records a and c. Mapping returns two list elements, displaying Read and Practise. The original array still contains all three records. Give each sibling a stable React key A React key is an identity hint for an element in a collection of siblings. It helps React match a record's previous UI to its next UI when items are inserted, removed or reordered. Put the key on the element returned directly from map; a key buried inside a child component is too far down. Keys must be unique among siblings and stable for the same item across renders. They need not be globally unique across separate lists. Use an identifier from the data. Create an identifier when creating a new record, rather than generating a random key during rendering. Random keys change on each render and can cause React to recreate items, losing user input or component state. The array index is an item's current position, not its identity. Imagine rows A and B each have a text input. Someone edits A's input, then inserts C before A. With index keys, the first position still has key zero but now represents C; input or component state can become associated with the wrong record. Stable record ids let React follow A as it moves. Index keys can be acceptable for a truly fixed list, but become risky when insertion, deletion or reordering is possible. Real-world analogy: A cloakroom ticket A ticket follows one person's coat even if staff rearrange the pegs. How it maps: A stable key identifies the same list item when its position among siblings changes; a peg position alone is like an array index. Where it stops: Keys only identify items within a particular sibling list. They do not globally locate components or preserve state after an item is removed. key is special React information, not a normal prop delivered to the child. If a TaskRow needs its record id, pass it separately, for example as an id prop as well as the key. Reusing the same data value for those two purposes is fine. Key takeaways filter selects records; map transforms them into elements. Put a stable key on the element returned directly by map. Use data identity rather than changing positions or random values. Pass an id separately if the child needs it; it cannot read key as an ordinary prop. Further reading Rendering lists — React Array map — MDN

sum: Separate rendering from committing and keep component calculations free of external changes.
x: Writing JSX describes a desired result. It does not mean every function call immediately changes the page. Understanding React's render and commit stages makes it easier to avoid bugs caused by code that does work at the wrong time. Calculate first, update the DOM later A render is React calling components to calculate what their UI should look like. On an initial render React calls the root and the components it returns. On later updates, it calls components as needed to calculate a new result. A parent rendering can cause its children to render too. A commit is React applying the necessary changes to the browser's DOM. On an update, React compares the new description with the previous result; rendering does not mean replacing every DOM node. The browser then paints what is visible. Do not use the number of component function calls as a count of user actions or committed updates: React may repeat or discard render work. Keep render calculations pure A pure render returns the same UI for the same props, state and context inputs, without changing things that existed before it ran. State is a component's remembered data; the next lesson introduces it. Context is another React input mechanism covered later. A render calculation should read those inputs and return its description. Do not change received props, modify a module-level counter, send a request or write to the DOM during render. Those changes would be side effects, observable work beyond producing the returned value. Repeating a render could then repeat the work even without another interaction. Local mutation can be fine: a fresh array created during this render belongs only to this calculation. This component excerpt creates such an array, fills it and returns elements built from it. It leaves tasks and its records untouched. Given tasks titled Read and Practise, it displays READ, PRACTISE. Repeating the calculation with the same input gives the same result. The local names array starts fresh on every call; it does not accumulate titles across renders. By contrast, pushing into the tasks prop would modify data owned elsewhere. Sorting that same array in place would also modify it, even if the component only meant to change the display order. Later lessons show how to make copies for updates. Real-world analogy: A draft shopping list You can work out a shopping list on fresh paper without buying anything yet. How it maps: Rendering calculates a description; committing applies the agreed changes to the DOM. Work on a fresh local draft does not alter the shared starting information. Where it stops: React controls scheduling and may repeat calculations. A commit changes browser objects, not a real shopping basket, and is distinct from the browser painting pixels. Put actions at the right boundary An event handler is a natural place for work caused by a user action, such as submitting a request after a button press. Some synchronisation with outside systems belongs in an Effect, taught later. Moving every calculation into an Effect is not the goal: computing a title or filtered list from current inputs belongs in render. Key takeaways Rendering calculates a description; committing updates the DOM. A render can happen without a distinct committed change. Treat props as immutable and avoid external changes during render. Fresh local arrays can be built during a pure calculation. Further reading Render and commit — React Keeping components pure — React

sum: Pass a function as an event handler and use state to remember interaction results.
x: A rendered button needs a way to respond when someone uses it. An event handler is a function React calls in response to an interaction. A component can then update state, its remembered data, so that its next render describes the changed screen. Pass a function for React to call The built-in button's onClick prop receives a function. Pass the function itself, such as onClick={handleClick}. Writing onClick={handleClick()} calls it while rendering and passes its return value instead. If that call updates state during render, it can cause repeated rendering rather than waiting for a click. An arrow callback is also useful when a handler needs an argument: the arrow function can call another function when the event happens. The key question is whether JSX is receiving a function to run later or the result of running it now. Remember a value with useState useState is a React Hook, a function that gives a component a React feature. Call it at the top level of the component, before any conditional return; do not call it inside a loop, condition or handler. Later lessons explain the Hook rules in more detail. useState(0) supplies an initial value. It returns an array with two entries: the current state value and a setter function. Array destructuring gives them local names. Calling the setter requests an update; it does not change the current render's variable in place. This complete component file has two independent counter instances. The named import obtains useState from React. An arrow updater receives the pending previous value and returns the next value; later lessons explain update queues. Both buttons initially display Completed: 0. Click the first twice and the second still displays zero while the first displays two. React keeps state for each component instance. Two uses of the same function do not automatically share memory. For one click, React calls the handler, the setter requests the update, React renders using the new state, then commits any necessary DOM change. The component function can run again without resetting state to the initial value. The initial value starts that instance's state; it is not an instruction to overwrite it every render. Why a normal variable is insufficient A local variable inside a component starts fresh when the function runs again. Changing it also does not request a React render. State solves both needs: React retains the value between renders and its setter tells React there is an update to process. State lasts while React preserves that component instance in the UI; a later lesson explains removal and resetting. Real-world analogy: Separate scorecards Two players using identical scorecard designs still keep separate scores. How it maps: The component function is the shared design; each rendered instance has its own state value and setter. Where it stops: React manages that memory according to component identity in the UI. It is not permanent storage and does not survive every removal or page reload. Key takeaways Pass event handlers as functions; do not invoke them during render. useState returns the current value and a setter that requests an update. A normal local variable neither persists nor schedules a React update. Separate component instances have independent state. Further reading Responding to events — React State: a component’s memory — React

sum: Predict what a handler reads before and after requesting a state update.
x: A state setter requests a future render; it does not rewrite the state variable in the function already running. Each render receives a state snapshot. The JSX and event handlers created by that render use that snapshot. This distinction answers a common beginner question: “Why did I read the old number immediately after setting it?” You read the number that belongs to the current render. React will call the component again with the next value and create new handlers for that render. Trace a single click The following component function assumes useState is imported from React and JSX is transformed by a React-enabled build. Its report prop is a function supplied by the parent; it records the value passed to it. It is a teaching example inside an event handler, not logging during render. Initially the button displays 0. The first click requests 1, then reports 0. After React processes the update, the button displays 1. A second click uses the new handler: it requests 2 and reports 1. Calling the setter is not an instruction to change the existing count binding halfway through the handler. A normal local variable also does not remember values between component calls. React state supplies that memory. Directly assigning to a local variable will not tell React to display a new result. Delayed work keeps its captured values A JavaScript closure lets a function retain access to the variables from where it was created. A delayed callback created by a handler therefore keeps that render's state values. It does not automatically switch to values from a later render. For example, suppose a Send handler schedules a message using the currently selected recipient. Changing the selection before the callback runs does not change the already captured recipient. Decide whether the operation should use the value at the time of the click or a later value; do not assume those are interchangeable. We will use functional updates next when an update needs the latest pending state. Real-world analogy: A printed order slip A waiter prints the order as it stood when you pressed Send. Later edits make a new order slip. How it maps: The printed slip is a render snapshot; its handler reads those recorded values even after requesting another render. Where it stops: React state is held by React, and JavaScript closures capture bindings. There is no literal copy of every object: mutating shared objects can corrupt older snapshots. Key takeaways A handler reads the state snapshot of the render that created it. Setters request another render; they do not change the current state binding. Delayed callbacks retain their captured values unless you deliberately design another mechanism. Further reading State as a snapshot useState reference Closures — MDN

sum: Choose replacement or functional updates and trace their order.
x: Sometimes one event needs several changes to the same state. React processes queued updates to calculate the next value. Batching groups updates so React can display the resulting state together after the event handler finishes. Do not expect the screen to update between two setter calls in that handler. A value requests a replacement Here is a handler excerpt inside a component whose count state is initially 0. Both lines evaluate their argument using the same snapshot. Both requests mean “replace with 1”, so the next displayed count is 1, not 2. The second line does not read the result of the first request. A function transforms the pending value An updater function receives the pending value from React's update queue. This handler excerpt uses arrow functions: n => n + 1 means “take a value named n and return one more”. Starting at 0, the first updater returns 1. React passes that pending result to the second updater, which returns 2. This expresses two increments without depending on the handler's older snapshot. Prefer this form when the next state depends on the previous state. Replacement and functional updates can be mixed. Starting at 0, trace this excerpt from top to bottom: The replacement chooses 5. The updater transforms that to 6. The final replacement chooses 2, so the next count is 2. This is an ordered queue, not a rule that all increments must win. Keep updaters pure A pure updater calculates and returns the next state without modifying old state or doing external work. Do not send requests, change another state variable, or write to external arrays inside an updater. Put event-specific external work in the handler instead. In development Strict Mode, React may call updater functions twice to expose accidental impurities; one result is ignored. Correct logic must not depend on the number of updater calls. React does not batch separate intentional clicks into one event. For this lesson, trace each handler in order, then consider the next interaction with the newly displayed state. Batching is useful behaviour, not a timer you should attempt to exploit for correctness. Real-world analogy: Editing instructions in order A clerk receives “use 5”, “add one”, then “use 2” before updating a display. How it maps: Replacement updates choose a pending value; updater functions transform the current pending value in queue order. Where it stops: The clerk is only a model of this queue. React can perform additional internal work, and pure updater functions must tolerate repeated development checks. Key takeaways Repeating a snapshot-based replacement does not accumulate increments. Functional updates receive the pending value and compose in order. Updaters must only calculate state; keep external work outside them. Further reading Queueing state updates useState caveats

sum: Copy changed object paths and preserve previous state snapshots.
x: Objects stored in state are ordinary JavaScript objects, but React code should treat them as immutable: never edit an existing state object. Instead, create a replacement and pass it to the setter. A mutation changes an existing object in place, potentially affecting every variable that refers to it. React can skip an update if the next value is the same according to Object.is. More fundamentally, mutation damages the old snapshot that earlier handlers or other components might still use. A new outer object is not sufficient if you have already changed one of its shared nested objects. Copy the changed path Object spread syntax, written...previous, copies an object's own enumerable properties into a new object. Later properties override earlier ones. It is a shallow copy: nested objects remain shared references unless you copy them too. This component-body excerpt assumes useState is imported. renameCity is an event handler that would be passed to a button's onClick prop. The parentheses after the arrow make the object literal the function's return value. Without them, braces would begin a function body instead. Trace the update: the callback receives the pending profile; the outer spread preserves name; the nested spread preserves postcode; the final city property overrides Leeds with York. Both the profile and address become new objects. The earlier profile still contains Leeds. Copying is selective You do not need to copy every value in your application. Copy each object along the path from the changed field back to the state root. Unchanged branches may keep their existing references because nothing writes into them. This deliberately wrong excerpt shows why an outer copy alone cannot repair a mutation. Assume profile and setProfile exist: The first line already edits the address used by the old profile. The second line changes only the outer object. A new outer reference may trigger rendering, but it does not restore the old data. Avoid the mutation rather than trying to force a render afterwards. Real-world analogy: Editing a folder of documents To change an address while preserving an old application, make a new address page and a new folder pointing to it. Reuse unchanged pages. How it maps: The folder is the outer object; the address page is a nested object. Copying only the folder still points at the same old page. Where it stops: JavaScript objects are references, not physical paper. A shallow copy intentionally shares unchanged values; it does not recursively duplicate everything. Key takeaways Replace state objects instead of editing them in place. Spread copies one level; copy nested objects on the changed path. Put overrides after spreads and preserve fields you did not change. Further reading Updating objects in state Spread syntax — MDN

sum: Use spread, filter and map to change lists without editing old state.
x: A task list is often an array of objects. There are two separate things to protect: the array and the objects stored inside it. Creating a new array does not automatically create new item objects. Use stable item IDs to describe which task changed. An ID identifies the task even if the array is filtered or reordered. The array index only describes its current position. Add, remove and replace Array spread, written [...previous], places the previous elements into a new array. filter returns an array containing the elements that pass its test. map returns an array containing one callback result per original element. These operations can preserve the original array when your callbacks do not mutate its items. This component-body excerpt assumes useState is imported. Its functions handle task changes within the component. A UI event handler would call addTask with a newly created task whose ID is unique in the list. The ternary operator chooses the expression after? when its condition is true, otherwise the expression after:. Suppose the list contains task 7, “Read”, and task 8, “Practise”, both unfinished. Finishing 7 makes a new array and a new object for task 7. Task 8 keeps its existing object because it did not change. Removing 7 then keeps only task 8. The previous arrays and the original object for task 7 remain unchanged. The shallow-copy trap This intentionally wrong excerpt assumes tasks is non-empty and setTasks exists: The array is new, but its first element still refers to the old task object. The assignment mutates that shared object. Copy the changed item with object spread instead, as finishTask does. Methods such as push, splice, sort and reverse mutate the array on which they are called. If you need sorting, first copy the array, then sort that copy. Sorting a fresh array is safe provided the comparison function itself does not mutate shared items. For small study projects, a clear immutable update is usually the most valuable first goal. Real-world analogy: A guest list of contact cards A new guest list can refer to the same contact cards. Editing a shared card still changes what the old list sees. How it maps: The list is an array and each contact card is an item object. Updating one item requires a new array plus a replacement for that card. Where it stops: Arrays contain references rather than actual cards. Reusing unchanged item objects is intentional and safe when they remain read-only. Key takeaways Add with spread, remove with filter and replace with map. Copy changed item objects as well as the containing array. Treat mutating array methods carefully; operate on a fresh copy. Further reading Updating arrays in state Updating objects in state

sum: Connect labelled text and checkbox inputs to state and handle submission.
x: A controlled input displays a value supplied by React state. User edits call an event handler, which immediately updates that state. React then renders the accepted value. For text, connect value to a string and read event.target.value. For a checkbox, connect checked to a boolean and read event.target.checked. An uncontrolled input instead keeps its current value in the browser; defaultValue or defaultChecked supplies only its initial value. Both approaches have uses. This lesson uses controlled inputs so the application can calculate what to display from state. A small complete component This component function assumes useState is imported and JSX is transformed. The parent supplies an onSave callback; it receives a plain object. Wrapping each input in a visible label associates the control with its name. Typing “Read” updates title through the text change handler. Clicking Complete updates done through the checkbox handler. Submitting then passes { title: 'Read', done: true } to onSave. This example saves through a callback; it does not make a network request or guarantee persistence after a reload. Submission and input pitfalls The form's onSubmit handles submission, including keyboard submission where supported by the browser. preventDefault stops the form's normal navigation; it does not automatically stop event propagation. A submit button is explicit here. Give any other button inside the form type="button" if it should perform a local action without submitting. A controlled text input needs a string throughout its lifetime. Initialise it to an empty string instead of undefined or null; otherwise it can switch between uncontrolled and controlled behaviour. Its change handler must synchronously update the state used by value. Passing a fixed value without such an update makes the field effectively read-only. A checkbox uses checked, not its value string, for the selected state. For a separate label, JSX uses htmlFor to match an input's unique id. A placeholder is not a replacement for a visible label. The association helps users understand and activate the control. Key takeaways Control text with value/string and checkboxes with checked/boolean. Update the controlling state immediately in onChange. Use visible labels and handle form submission deliberately. Further reading Input reference preventDefault — MDN

sum: Coordinate sibling controls through a common parent and callback props.
x: Two components may need to display and update the same information. Giving each a separate useState variable creates two independent copies, not shared state. If they must agree, choose a single owner and pass the value down through props. Lifting state up moves state to the closest common parent of the components that need it. The parent owns the value; children receive it plus a callback prop to request changes. Data travels down, and events travel up through function calls. A child does not edit its props or reach into a sibling. Two editors, one value The following component functions assume useState is imported. Editor has no local state for this value. Its label prop supplies a visible name and its onChange prop accepts the next string, not the browser event. Type “Hello” into First. Its handler calls setText('Hello') through the prop. The parent receives the update and renders again. Both editors now receive “Hello”, and the paragraph displays it too. Editing Second follows exactly the same route. No extra synchronisation step is necessary because only one string is stored. Controlled is a design relationship An application component is often described as a controlled component when its important behaviour is determined by props. Here the parent controls the editors' text. A component can still have unrelated local state, such as whether a help message is open. Controlled and uncontrolled are useful design descriptions, not strict categories imposed on every custom component. Lift only as high as necessary. If no other component needs a temporary draft, keeping it local makes the relationship easier to understand. Moving every variable to the top of the application makes distant components responsible for details they do not use. Do not automatically initialise a child's state from a prop and expect it to follow later changes. useState(initialValue) uses that initial value when the component first mounts; subsequent prop updates do not overwrite the stored state. Keep the value controlled, or deliberately design an independent draft and its reset behaviour. Real-world analogy: Two displays, one thermostat Two wall displays show one thermostat setting. Each sends adjustment requests to the same controller. How it maps: The parent is the owner of the setting; props show the current value and callback props request updates from either child. Where it stops: React does not require physical messages or a central owner for all data. Independent settings can stay in independent components. Key takeaways Shared values need one owner at the nearest useful common parent. Pass current data down and change-request callbacks to children. Keep independent data local; do not mirror props into state by default. Further reading Sharing state between components Choosing state structure

sum: Derive display values and represent statuses that cannot be active together directly.
x: State should store information that must be remembered between renders. If a value can be calculated from current props and state, usually calculate it during render instead. Derived state such as a filtered list or full name does not need a separate setter merely because it appears on screen. Every duplicated value creates another update that you might forget. A search box with query, tasks and a separately stored visibleTasks can become inconsistent when tasks change but the filtered copy does not. Derive a filtered result This component-body excerpt assumes useState is imported and tasks is an array prop containing objects with string title fields. The query starts empty. toLowerCase returns lower-case text. The string method String.prototype.includes, used as title.includes(needle) below, tests whether the title string contains the search text. The callback has a block body, so its result needs an explicit return. With “Read React” and “Buy tea”, the query “READ” produces just “Read React”, and the count is 1. If the parent later removes that task, the next render recalculates an empty result. There is no second stored list to repair. The original task array is unchanged. The calculation belongs in render because it only reads inputs and produces a result. It does not contact a server, change the DOM directly, or request state updates. For a small list, start with this simple calculation; performance tools and optional caching belong later. Avoid impossible combinations A submit workflow can be idle, submitting, successful or failed. Four booleans allow contradictory combinations, such as successful and failed simultaneously. One status string restricts the current mode to one chosen value. This component-body excerpt defines the initial status: Use setStatus('submitting') when starting an operation and an appropriate terminal status when it finishes. This does not start or finish a submission by itself; it supplies a representation that is easier to reason about. An error message can still be stored separately if the application needs to remember its content. When selecting one task, prefer storing its ID over a duplicate task object. Find the current object from the task array during render. If the ID is absent after deletion, handle that case explicitly, for example by showing no selection. This avoids a selected copy silently keeping an old title while the main list has a new one. Real-world analogy: One bill, calculated totals A receipt stores its line items and calculates the total from them. Keeping a second editable total invites disagreement after an item changes. How it maps: Tasks and query are the inputs; the filtered result and count are calculations from those inputs. Where it stops: Some values really are independent records, such as a historical price agreed earlier. Only derive values whose meaning is determined by current inputs. Key takeaways Derive display values from current inputs during render. Represent modes that cannot be active together with one status value. Store an identity rather than a duplicate object when selecting existing data. Further reading Choosing state structure Reacting to input with state

sum: Use position, component type and keys to preserve or reset local state deliberately.
x: React associates state with a component's identity in the rendered tree. Rendering a fresh JSX expression does not necessarily create fresh state. When the same component type stays in the same position with the same key, React normally preserves its state through updates. A remount replaces a component instance with a new one and starts its local state again. Removing a component, changing its type at that place, or changing its key can discard the old state. Consider the resulting tree, not the location of the JSX text in a file. A draft for a recipient These component functions assume useState is imported. The parent supplies recipientId and recipientName as props. This example keeps a local draft while the same recipient remains selected; it does not implement a submit action or contact a recipient. Type a draft for recipient 7. Updating only the name of recipient 7 leaves the key and component type unchanged, so the draft survives. Switching to recipient 8 changes the key: React removes the old Draft and creates a fresh one with an empty string. Switching back to 7 creates another fresh Draft; a key does not cache removed state. Without a key that changes, changing the name prop alone would keep the existing draft at this position. That can be useful for cosmetic prop changes and dangerous when the draft belongs to a different person. Decide whether preserving or resetting matches the interaction. Stable keys and stable definitions Keys distinguish siblings within their parent, not components throughout the whole application. A task's stable ID is usually suitable. An array index can attach a row's local state to the wrong task after insertion or reordering. A random key generated on every render forces replacement repeatedly, losing input state rather than fixing identity. Define component functions at the top level of their module. Defining a child component inside a parent's function creates a different function object on every parent render. React sees a different component type and can reset the child's state unexpectedly. Move the child definition outside and pass needed data as props. Real-world analogy: A labelled cubby Belongings for a child stay in the same labelled cubby. Reassigning that cubby to a different child means clearing it before use. How it maps: The location and label help model component identity; changing a key requests a fresh state holder in that parent. Where it stops: Keys are local to siblings and do not store discarded state somewhere else. Returning to an old key does not retrieve an archived draft. Key takeaways State follows identity in the tree, using position, type and key. Change a key deliberately when a new entity needs fresh local state. Stable IDs and top-level component definitions prevent accidental resets. Further reading Preserving and resetting state Rendering lists

sum: Move related update rules into a pure reducer and trace dispatched actions.
x: Several handlers may update the same related state. A reducer gathers those update rules in one pure function. It receives the current state and a reducer action, then returns the next state. An action describes what happened; by convention it is an object with a type string plus any data needed for that event. useReducer is an alternative to useState, not a global store. Each mounted component instance has its own reducer state, preserved across its renders. It is useful when several events must follow consistent rules, while a simple text field may remain clearer with useState. A pure reducer This complete JavaScript function needs no React import. The object spread preserves other fields while replacing count. The switch statement selects a branch from action.type; the throw statement reports an unexpected action instead of silently losing the state. The reducer must not mutate its inputs, send network requests or produce random identifiers. It calculates the next value from the given state and action. If an event needs an ID or the current time, create that event information in the handler and put it in the action. Then repeated reducer evaluation produces the same result. Connect an event to the reducer This component function assumes useReducer is imported from React and the reducer above is in scope. Call useReducer at the top level of the component. Dispatch is the function React returns for requesting a transition. Clicking Add two dispatches { type: 'added', amount: 2 }. React passes that action and current state to the reducer. Starting at 0, two separate Add two clicks produce 2, then 4. Reset produces 0. The component displays each resulting state; the handler does not assign to state.count directly. Dispatch requests a future update, so code after dispatch still reads its render's existing snapshot. In development Strict Mode, React may call a reducer twice to expose impurities and ignore one result. Keep reducers pure and test state transitions rather than assuming an exact call count. Real-world analogy: A scorekeeper with event cards A scorekeeper follows written rules for “add two” and “reset” cards. The same score and card always produce the same next score. How it maps: The current score is state, a card is an action, and the rulebook is the reducer. Dispatch submits an event for React to process. Where it stops: The reducer itself must only calculate. It does not physically update a display, send messages or create event information. Key takeaways Reducers centralise related update rules as pure transitions. Actions describe events; dispatch asks React to apply one. Return new state, preserve required fields and keep external work in handlers. Further reading Extracting state logic into a reducer useReducer reference

sum: Keep ordinary Hook calls in a stable order inside components and custom Hooks.
x: You have already used useState. It is a Hook: a React function that connects a component to a capability such as state. A custom Hook is your own function that calls Hooks to reuse logic. Its name starts with use followed by a capital letter, such as useCounter. These rules apply to the ordinary Hooks in this course, including useState, useRef and useEffect. React has other APIs with different rules; you do not need those APIs here. Keep the calls predictable Make each top-level Hook call directly in a function component or custom Hook body, before any conditional return. Do not call them inside conditions, loops, event handlers, nested callbacks or ordinary utility functions. React must be rendering the component when these Hooks are called. React associates a component's Hook state with the order of its calls. If a conditional Hook disappears on a later render, subsequent calls no longer line up. Giving the variables different names does not solve that problem. Real-world analogy: Labelled seats Imagine handing out numbered seats in the same order at each rehearsal. How it maps: A component's successive Hook calls need a consistent ordering, like the same people receiving the same numbered seats. Where it stops: React tracks calls within component instances; it does not inspect variable names or literally allocate theatre seats. Put the condition after the Hook This complete component example assumes the React-enabled JSX environment from the first module. The import makes useState available; the environment transforms JSX before the browser executes it. When hidden changes from false to true, the component still calls its Hook and then returns nothing. When it becomes false again at the same tree position, its count is preserved. Moving the Hook below the conditional return would break the ordering rule. An event handler may call setCount, because a setter is an ordinary function React returns to you. Calling useState inside that handler would be a new Hook call outside rendering. Distinguish creating the state during render from requesting an update later. If each row needs local state, make a Row component and render rows with stable keys. Put its Hooks at the top of Row, rather than calling a Hook inside the parent's map callback. A React Hooks linter can catch many ordering and dependency mistakes before you run the app. Key takeaways Call ordinary Hooks at the top level of components or custom Hooks, before conditional returns. Hook order belongs to each component instance; variable names do not identify its state. Handlers may call setters; ordinary Hook calls belong in rendering. Further reading React: Rules of Hooks React: State is tied to a position in the tree

sum: Use a ref for a value that survives rendering without driving the displayed output.
x: State describes information used to render the screen. A ref, created with useRef, holds a mutable value that survives re-renders without scheduling a render when changed. React returns the same ref object on later renders of that component instance. Its current property starts with the argument passed to useRef. Store a timer identifier or a DOM element in a ref. Store a displayed count, input value or selected task in state. If changing a value should change JSX, a ref alone is the wrong tool. Ask the DOM to focus The DOM is the browser's tree of objects describing the page. A DOM element's focus() method moves keyboard focus to it. React supports attaching a ref to an element so a handler can perform this small browser operation. Complete component example for a React-enabled JSX environment: The?. operator is optional chaining. It skips the method call if current is null or undefined. Initially the ref contains null. When React commits the input to the DOM, it sets current to the actual element. Clicking the button reads the ref in the handler and focuses that input. When React removes the element, it clears this object ref to null. The label gives the input an accessible name; focus does not replace the need for a label. Here focusing responds directly to a click, so no effect is necessary. An escape hatch with boundaries Refs give controlled access outside React's normal data flow. Do not read or write current to calculate the displayed output during rendering. Keep those accesses in event handlers or effects. A ref mutation does not notify React; an unrelated future render might reveal a changed value, which makes display behaviour unreliable. Real-world analogy: A bookmark A bookmark remembers a place without rewriting the book's contents. How it maps: A ref remembers a value between renders, while changing it does not request a new screen. Where it stops: A ref can hold any JavaScript value, and a DOM ref is managed by React during commit rather than by a reader. Use a DOM ref for focus or scrolling. Avoid manually removing React's children or changing text that React manages; React's next update assumes control of that structure. React should describe the content, while the ref handles the narrow browser operation. Key takeaways Ref changes persist but do not request a render; state changes are for displayed data. Read DOM refs in handlers or effects after the element exists. Focus is a useful escape hatch; keep React in charge of rendered content. Further reading React: useRef React: Manipulating the DOM with refs MDN: Optional chaining MDN: HTMLElement focus

sum: Connect to external systems after commit and undo the connection with cleanup.
x: An effect, declared with useEffect, synchronises a component with something outside React: a browser event subscription, a connection or a non-React widget. Rendering calculates JSX; an effect performs external work after React commits a render. Effects run in the browser, not during server rendering. Do not use an effect merely because state changed. Calculating a filtered list belongs in rendering. A purchase triggered by a particular click belongs in that event handler. An event subscription that must exist while a component is present is a good effect. Pair setup with cleanup This complete component reports the last key pressed while it is mounted. window.addEventListener registers a browser callback. removeEventListener unregisters that same function. The setup function registers the callback. The returned function is cleanup: React calls it when stopping this synchronisation. Return the function rather than calling it immediately. Removing a different function with similar code would not remove the original listener. The empty dependency array means the effect reads no changing props or state. setKey has a stable identity, so it can be omitted here. The callback gets the key from the browser event instead of closing over key. Trace the behaviour: mount the component, press A, and its state shows A. Remove the component, then press B. Cleanup has removed its listener, so that removed component no longer responds. A new mount creates its own subscription. Reconnecting and Strict Mode For an effect with changing dependencies, React stops the previous setup before starting the new one: cleanup uses the old render's values, then setup uses the new values. Final removal also runs cleanup. Cleanup is therefore more than an unmount notification. Real-world analogy: A library loan Borrow a book when you need it, return it before replacing it, and return the last book when you leave. How it maps: Setup acquires an external resource; cleanup releases that particular resource before replacement or removal. Where it stops: Some effects require no cleanup, and React schedules these steps around commits rather than human visits. When Strict Mode is enabled at the root during development, React runs an extra setup-and-cleanup cycle for effects before the ongoing setup. This helps expose missing cleanup. It is a development check, not a production promise about how many times a component renders. Correct code leaves only the intended active subscription and cleans it up when removed. Do not hide the check with a ref that prevents a later setup. Key takeaways Effects synchronise external systems; calculations and direct event responses usually belong elsewhere. Cleanup undoes the matching setup before replacement and on removal. Development Strict Mode helps find effects that do not clean up correctly. Further reading React: Synchronising with Effects React: useEffect React: StrictMode MDN: removeEventListener

sum: Identify the values an effect reads and avoid stale subscriptions or unnecessary effects.
x: An effect's dependency array lists the reactive values its setup reads: props, state, and variables or functions declared in the component body. React compares each listed value with its previous value using Object.is. For objects and functions this compares identity, not a deep inspection of their contents. Dependencies describe the code. They are not a menu of when you would like an effect to run. Use a React Hooks linter and fix a missing dependency by changing the code or including the value; suppressing the warning can leave behaviour tied to an old render. Reconnect to the selected room Component example: connectRoom is a stable imported helper defined outside components supplied by the teaching environment. It takes a room name, opens an external connection and returns an object with disconnect(). Its internal network implementation is outside this example. Mount with room set to music: setup connects to music. Change it to books: React first runs cleanup for music, then setup connects to books. Re-render with books again: that dependency has not changed, so this update does not require re-synchronisation. Removing the component disconnects books. If you replace [room] with [], the connection remains with music after the prop changes. This is a stale closure: the original setup and its functions retain the values from the render that created them. The visible JSX may say books while the external connection still uses music. Three dependency choices Argument Behaviour ------ [room] Re-synchronise when room changes [] No reactive inputs to compare Omitted Re-run after this component commits All three run setup when the effect first starts; cleanup and development checks still apply. An empty array does not mean that an effect can never start again after a component is removed and mounted afresh. An object created inside rendering is a fresh object each time. If an effect only needs room, build its connection options inside setup and depend on room, instead of depending on an unnecessary fresh options object. This reduces unnecessary reconnecting without hiding a real input. Remove the effect when possible To show tasks matching a search query, call tasks.filter(...) during rendering. Both tasks and query are already available inputs; a second state variable and an effect introduce another value to keep consistent. For sending a message after a click, use the click handler. First decide whether there is an external synchronisation to maintain; only then design its dependencies. Key takeaways Include the reactive inputs actually read by an effect. Missing dependencies can leave external behaviour using an old render's values. Reduce dependencies by simplifying the code, and derive render data directly when possible. Further reading React: Removing Effect Dependencies React: Lifecycle of Reactive Effects React: You Might Not Need an Effect MDN: Object.is

sum: Model loading, error, empty and success states, and ignore results from obsolete requests.
x: Network responses can arrive in a different order from requests. Request list A, then list B: if B finishes first and A finishes later, blindly storing both results makes A overwrite B. This race condition depends on timing, so a quick test on a fast connection may miss it. This lesson uses a deliberately small client-only fetch example to teach effect lifecycle. Production applications may use a framework's data facilities or a data library for caching, request sharing and other needs. This example does not provide those facilities. Represent the request's outcome The Fetch API's fetch(url) returns a Promise, an object representing a result that may arrive later. In an async function, await waits for that result without blocking the browser's whole JavaScript execution. try...catch handles failures: a thrown error in its try block transfers control to its catch block, including a rejected Promise encountered by await. The Error constructor creates the error object used with throw in this example. An HTTP error such as 404 does not itself reject fetch: check response.ok. response.json() asynchronously parses the response body as JSON. Assume a same-origin teaching endpoint whose URL arrives as a string prop. It returns an array of objects with stable unique id and string text fields. The data contract is assumed; a real application should validate untrusted data. Complete component example, with JSX transformed by the environment: The inner async function handles the asynchronous work. The effect itself returns an ordinary cleanup function, not a Promise. A single status distinguishes loading, error and success; an empty successful array gets its own message. The stored URL prevents displaying a previous URL's data during a render before the new effect has started. Trace overlapping requests Each setup gets its own local ignore variable. Changing from A to B runs A's cleanup, setting A's flag to true, and starts B with a separate false flag. If B succeeds first, its data is stored. If A later succeeds or fails, its flag prevents either branch from changing state. Unmounting similarly marks the active request obsolete. Real-world analogy: An old takeaway order You replace an order and disregard a later message about the cancelled choice. How it maps: Cleanup marks an earlier request obsolete so its late reply cannot replace the current result. Where it stops: The flag does not cancel network traffic or undo server work. It only prevents applying an obsolete result. Ignoring and cancelling are different: AbortController can cancel a supported fetch, but this example only ignores obsolete outcomes. Test response order explicitly, including stale errors, loading, an empty array, a current error and removal before completion. Key takeaways Fetch needs an explicit HTTP success check and separate loading, error and empty handling. Cleanup marks obsolete work so late responses cannot replace the active result. This teaching pattern is not a complete production data layer. Further reading React: Fetching data with Effects MDN: Using Fetch MDN: async function

sum: Extract useful behaviour into named Hooks while keeping each call's state independent.
x: A custom Hook is a function that uses React Hooks to provide a reusable behaviour. Name it for what it does, beginning with use followed by a capital letter. Give it clear inputs and return values. Calling it is part of rendering the caller; it must follow the same top-level ordering rules as built-in Hooks. Do not turn every utility into a Hook. A plain function that only filters an array needs no special Hook name. Extract a Hook when it packages stateful or external synchronisation logic with a useful purpose. Share the recipe, not the state Complete module example for a React-enabled JSX environment. A returned object's shorthand { count, increment } means properties named count and increment containing those local values. Click the first button twice: its value becomes 2 while the second stays 0. Click the second once: it becomes 2 without changing the first. Each call uses its own state, even though both execute the same Hook function. To share one count, move one Hook call to a common parent and pass its value and handlers down. Real-world analogy: One recipe, two kitchens Two cooks can follow the same recipe while keeping separate ingredients and meals. How it maps: A custom Hook shares the instructions for behaviour; each call has its own state and effects. Where it stops: A Hook may deliberately connect to a shared external source, so independent local state does not imply the outside world is separate. Keep synchronisation inside the Hook A Hook that installs a browser listener must also remove it. The following complete Hook definition extracts the previous lesson's keyboard behaviour. A component calls useLastKey() at its top level and renders the returned string. Two components using this Hook both respond to the same keyboard because they observe the same browser, not because they share a state variable. Removing one component removes its subscription while the other continues working. Extraction should preserve the original behaviour, dependencies and cleanup. The step input in useCounter is read from each current render. If a parent changes it, future clicks use the new step without resetting the count. Initial state is only initial state; passing different inputs to a Hook does not automatically mean resetting every value inside it. Key takeaways Custom Hooks share stateful logic; separate calls have independent state. Clear inputs and outputs make a Hook easier to read and test. Keep effect cleanup and accurate dependencies with the behaviour being extracted. Further reading React: Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks React: Rules of Hooks MDN: Object initialiser shorthand

sum: Use the nearest provider to supply a value without manually passing it through every layer.
x: Start with props: a child gets a value and callbacks from its parent. If many distant components need the same value, passing it through intermediate components can become repetitive. Context lets a component read a value supplied by an ancestor without each intermediate component forwarding a prop. createContext(defaultValue) creates a context object outside components. A provider supplies its value to descendants. A consumer reads it with useContext. The context object identifies the channel; it does not hold a global state variable. Put changing data in state owned by an appropriate parent and provide that value. Read the nearest provider Complete React 19 module example for a React-enabled JSX environment. React 19 supports <ThemeContext value={...}> as provider syntax. You may also see <ThemeContext.Provider value={...}> in existing code. Read the three labels in order. The first has no provider above it, so reads the default light. The second reads the outer provider's initial dark. The third reads the nearer inner provider's light. After switching the outer theme, the second becomes light; the first and third still read light for their original reasons. React searches upwards from the component calling useContext. A provider returned by that same component is below the call, so it cannot affect that call. The default is a fallback when there is no matching provider, not a value that gets merged into every provider. Real-world analogy: A room's noticeboard A building has general notices, while an individual room can supply its own local notice. How it maps: A nearer provider overrides the value a consumer would otherwise get from a more distant ancestor. Where it stops: Context follows the React component tree, not physical distance or DOM styling rules. Updates still matter When a provided value changes according to Object.is, React updates components reading that context. Wrapping a consumer in memo does not block fresh context. A new object used as a provider value has a new identity even if its fields look the same, so careless object creation can cause unnecessary updates. Context transports a value; it does not decide state ownership or make mutation safe. Keep ordinary immutable state updates. Prefer a small relevant context over placing every unrelated app value in one changing object. For two nearby siblings, lifting state and passing props may be simpler and more explicit. Key takeaways Try props first; context is useful for values needed across distant descendants. Consumers read the nearest matching provider above them, or the default if none exists. Context updates reach consumers; context does not replace state ownership or immutability. Further reading React: Passing Data Deeply with Context React: useContext React: createContext

sum: Understand what memoisation can save while keeping rendering correct without it.
x: A component can render because its own state changes, a parent renders it, or context it reads changes. A render recalculates the description of UI; it does not mean React rewrites every DOM element. First keep rendering pure, put state near the components that need it, and remove unnecessary effects. If an interaction feels slow, reproduce it with realistic data and inspect it with React Developer Tools' Profiler or the browser's performance tools. Compare the same interaction before and after a change. Development checks can add work, so development timing is not a reliable substitute for production measurement. Small examples here teach behaviour, not a measured speedup. Three different things to cache Memoisation reuses a previous result when its inputs are unchanged. Tool What it may reuse ------ memo A component's previous render work useMemo A calculated value useCallback A function identity memo wraps a component and normally compares each prop using Object.is. It can skip parent-driven re-rendering with unchanged props, but this is an optimisation, not a guarantee. Its own state and consumed context still update it. A freshly created array, object or callback is a different identity, even when its contents or code look the same. Cache a calculation only when worthwhile Complete component example, assuming tasks is an array of objects with done booleans. This tiny calculation is illustrative; it has not been shown to need caching. The calculation must be pure. Replacing a task means copying the changed object and array: if you mutate the existing array, its identity may stay the same and the cached result can become stale. useMemo does not make mutation safe. Removing useMemo and calculating the filter directly must preserve correctness. useCallback returns a function without calling it. Component-body excerpt, assuming useCallback is imported and setTasks is the stable useState setter: The functional update receives current tasks, so this callback does not read a captured tasks value. If a callback reads changing props or state, those inputs belong in its dependencies. A stable callback can help when passed to a memoised child; adding one everywhere adds complexity without establishing a benefit. Keep caches optional React may discard cached values or render a memoised component again. Do not put an essential connection or side effect inside useMemo, or rely on it to retain application state. An optimisation must preserve behaviour if React recalculates it. React Compiler can automatically memoise components, values and functions when configured in a supporting build. It is a build tool, not something guaranteed merely by importing React. Check the project's build configuration before adding manual memoisation. Correctness, immutability and useful measurements still come first. Key takeaways Reproduce and measure slow interactions before adding caches. memo, useMemo and useCallback cache different things and do not guarantee correctness or render counts. Immutable updates and accurate dependencies matter with or without memoisation. Further reading React: memo React: useMemo React: useCallback React: React Developer Tools React: Compiler introduction

sum: Combine minimal state, immutable updates, derived search results and stable keys in one small app.
x: Build a task list that filters by text and toggles completion. Keep one source of truth: the task array and search query. The visible rows are derived during rendering, so they do not need their own state or effect. This project has no network connection or external subscription to maintain. Each task has an immutable, stable identifier independent of its text or filtered position. A checkbox is controlled by done. The parent owns the state and passes each row its task plus a callback that requests a toggle. A complete small app This module exports a component for the React-enabled JSX environment used throughout the course. It needs no CSS or external service. The includes string method tests whether text contains the query; both are lowercased for a case-insensitive match. The state setter uses an updater function so each toggle works from the current task array. map creates a new array and spread creates a new object for the changed task. Unchanged task objects can be reused because this code never mutates them. Filtering creates a display selection without deleting anything from state. Check observable behaviour Initially see Read, Walk and Review; only Review is checked. Type re: see Read and Review. Type RE: see the same two rows. Toggle Read while filtered, then clear the query. Read is still checked and Walk is unchanged. Type zzz: see the empty message. Clear it: all tasks return with their saved completion state. Toggle a checkbox twice: its completion returns to its starting value. These checks test user-visible behaviour rather than a particular number of renders. The stable keys describe sibling identity; state preservation here also relies on storing completion in the parent task objects. A row hidden by filtering is removed from the tree, so any additional local row state would be lost on removal unless stored elsewhere. No custom Hook or context is necessary for a single parent and its rows. Add them only when they solve an actual sharing or synchronisation need. No memoisation is justified by the size of this example. State is held in memory: reloading or remounting this app starts again from the initial tasks; persistence is a separate feature. As an extension, design an Add task form. Generate each id once when the task is created, reject blank text, and append immutably. Do not generate keys during rendering. That is a design exercise, not behaviour implemented above. Key takeaways Own tasks and query once, and calculate the visible list during rendering. Use stable ids, controlled inputs and immutable functional updates. Test filtering, toggling and empty results; add architecture only when a real need appears. Further reading React: Thinking in React React: Updating Arrays in State React: Preserving and Resetting State MDN: String includes

sum: Name the property attacked before choosing a control.
x: "Is this system secure?" has no answer until you say secure against what, protecting which property. A bank's public interest-rate page has no secrets, but it matters a great deal if someone changes the numbers. A hospital's patient records must stay private, but they also must be available at 3 a.m. in A&E. Security people use two small frameworks to make that question precise. The CIA triad names the properties you want to protect. AAA names the machinery that enforces who may do what, and records what happened. The CIA triad Property Question it asks Typical attack --------- Confidentiality Who can read it? Data breach Integrity Can it be changed undetected? Tampering Availability Can it be used when needed? DDoS, ransomware Confidentiality Only authorised parties can read the information. Breaches of confidentiality are the ones that make headlines: a leaked customer database, an S3 bucket left public, a laptop stolen from a car. Controls include encryption (at rest and in transit), access control, data minimisation (don't store what you don't need) and classification so people know what is sensitive. Confidentiality also covers metadata. Even if a message is encrypted, the fact that a journalist contacted a particular source at 2 a.m. may be the real secret. Integrity Integrity protects information against improper modification or destruction. It does not prove that the original information was factually true. A payment where an attacker changes the destination account number has not leaked anything; it has broken integrity. Controls include cryptographic hashes and MACs, digital signatures, database constraints, version control, and access control on writes. Integrity has a subtle sibling: authenticity, meaning the data came from who it claims to. A perfectly intact email that was forged by an attacker has integrity in the narrow sense, but not authenticity.
