It fits less well for exploratory work, UI layout or spikes where you do not yet know what you want. Many practitioners write a throwaway spike, then TDD the real version. It does not by itself produce good design or good tests. Tests written in tiny steps can still couple to implementation. Research on productivity and quality has mixed findings across tasks and study designs. For example, industrial case studies reported defect reductions with extra initial development time, while a six-month study found no effect on quality or productivity. Neither establishes a universal effect. Outside-in TDD A popular variant starts with a failing acceptance test for a whole feature, then uses unit-level TDD to build the pieces until the outer test goes green. This is the "London school" style from the earlier interaction-verification unit, and it often uses mocks for collaborators not yet written. Key takeaways Watch each new test fail for the intended reason, then implement enough to pass. Fake it and triangulation motivate generalisation without uniquely specifying an implementation. TDD provides design feedback and regression checks, with limits for exploratory work. Further reading Test Driven Development — Martin Fowler Self Testing Code — Martin Fowler Industrial TDD case studies — IBM Research Six-month TDD study — original research Equality and triangulation — Kent Beck

t: Find missing cases with properties and shrinking
sum: A property states an expected rule; generated cases try to falsify it.
x: Example tests check inputs you choose. Property-based testing lets a library generate inputs against a rule you expect to hold; it then simplifies failures so that you can understand them. Property-based testing Example-based tests check specific inputs you chose. Their blind spot is the inputs you didn't think of. Property-based testing flips this: you state a rule that must hold for all inputs, and a library generates inputs trying to break it, within configured search limits. The idea comes from Haskell's QuickCheck (Claessen and Hughes, 2000). In Python, the Hypothesis library provides it; it is third-party, so install it separately. A bug examples miss Here is a merge of two sorted lists with a subtle bug: The obvious example tests pass: Now state a property: merging two sorted lists must give the same as sorting their concatenation. A Hypothesis run can expose the error and shrink it to a simple counterexample such as the following; time needed to find a failure and the exact report are not guaranteed: When both lists contain the same value, one copy is dropped. Shrinking An illustrative first failure might use messy lists such as a=[-91, 3, 3, 17], b=[3, 40]. It then shrinks: it repeatedly tries simpler inputs (shorter lists, smaller numbers) and keeps any that still fail. Shrinking seeks a simpler failure but does not guarantee a globally smallest input. Shrinking is a big part of why property testing is practical; a random 300-element failing list would be nearly useless. With an example database enabled, Hypothesis saves useful failing inputs and reuses them on later runs. The default local profile uses a.hypothesis/ database; current CI-profile settings can disable the database and use deterministic generation. Explicit @example cases are more durable regression checks. Key takeaways A property states an expected rule; generated cases try to falsify it. The buggy merge loses equal values even though its hand-picked examples pass. Shrinking simplifies failures; the example database can reuse them when enabled. Further reading Hypothesis documentation What is property-based testing? — Hypothesis

t: Design useful properties and reach difficult inputs
sum: Use round-trip properties, test oracles, test invariants, idempotence and metamorphic relations for different contracts.
x: A property test needs both a truthful rule and generators that reach useful cases. Assume from hypothesis import given, example, assume and from hypothesis import strategies as st for the API examples below. User stands for an application class with an age constructor argument. Strategies A Hypothesis strategy describes how to generate values: st.integers(min_value=0), st.floats(allow_nan=False), st.text(), st.booleans() st.lists(st.integers(), max_size=50), st.dictionaries(...), st.tuples(...) st.sampled_from(["GBP", "EUR"]), st.builds(User, age=st.integers(0, 120)).map(...) and.filter(...) to transform; assume(cond) inside a test to discard unsuitable inputs. Finding good properties "What property?" is the hard part. Common patterns: Pattern Example ------ Round-trip property Decode the encoded value; recover the original Test oracle Fast implementation agrees with simple reference Test invariant sort keeps length and items Idempotence Repeating the operation changes nothing Metamorphic Add a restrictive filter: no new results The first and fourth rows are mathematical statements about functions. Written as maths, they say what must hold for every generated input: For example, trimming " hi " gives "hi", and trimming "hi" again still gives "hi", so trimming is idempotent. Doubling a number is not: 3 becomes 6, then 12. The round-trip property rule holds only for inputs the encoder represents faithfully and that compare equal to themselves. The float NaN ("not a number") fails the second condition: it is not equal even to itself, so the decoded copy never compares equal to the original, and such inputs are usually excluded from the strategy. Python’s json.dumps returns JSON text as a str, and json.loads reads it back. Acyclic JSON-native values within recursion and memory bounds can recover the original value after encoding and decoding: string-keyed dictionaries, lists, strings, booleans, None, supported integers and finite floats. Tuples instead decode as lists, and non-string dictionary keys can change. With the unchanged default formatting, serialising a decoded serialisation is stable for this restricted domain. The test oracle pattern used for merge is particularly strong: a simple, obviously correct implementation (here sorted) checks a fast, clever one. Limits of property-based testing Generation is strategy-guided, not uniform random sampling, and can be deterministic under the CI profile or explicit settings. The default max_examples=100 limits satisfying generated cases in a successful search, not necessarily all calls including rejected inputs and shrinking. Some bugs need rare inputs. A run-length encoder that writes "aaab" as "3a1b", with a decoder that reads one digit then one character, breaks on any run of 10 or more (it treats 0 as the character for a one-character run, leaving a unmatched). The round-trip property is useful, but a generic text strategy is not a guarantee of reaching long repeated runs. Generate such runs deliberately and pin the known counterexample. No measured rate of finding a failure is asserted here. Remedies: Design strategies that reach the interesting region (small alphabets, boundary values, long runs). Pin known-tricky cases with @example("a" 10), which runs in the explicit-example phase (enabled by default) before generated inputs. Raise max_examples for important properties, perhaps in a nightly run. Property tests also run slower than single examples and need more thought to write. They complement example tests rather than replace them: examples document specific expectations clearly, properties hunt for what you forgot. Stateful testing Hypothesis can also generate sequences of operations (add, remove, query) against a system and a simple model of it, checking they agree after every step. This is how bugs in caches, databases and data structures that only appear after a particular series of calls get found. Key takeaways Use round-trip properties, test oracles, test invariants, idempotence and metamorphic relations for different contracts. A generic strategy may miss rare regions; deliberately generate interesting shapes. Pin known cases with explicit examples and keep example tests alongside properties. Further reading Hypothesis documentation What is property-based testing? — Hypothesis Useful property patterns — Hypothesis JSON encoding and decoding — Python docs

t: Diagnose flaky suites and shared-state failures
sum: A flaky outcome can arise from the test setup or a real intermittent product bug.
x: A test suite is only useful if people trust it. Two things destroy that trust. Flaky tests have inconsistent outcomes on unchanged code; they may reveal real intermittent defects as well as test or environment problems. Weak tests pass when something is wrong, so green means little. This unit diagnoses intermittent failures; the following units cover clock control, coverage and mutation testing. Flaky tests A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. Google's testing blog reported in 2016 that about 1.5% of all its test runs produced a flaky result, that almost 16% of its tests showed some flakiness, and that about 84% of the pass-to-fail transitions its CI observed involved a flaky test. Those figures describe that 2016 Google dataset. A transition involving a flaky test does not itself establish that no new product bug exists. The damage compounds. A full run is clean only if every test passes. When tests flake independently of each other, the chance of that is one copy of the per-test pass chance for each test, all multiplied together: Doubling the suite to 400 such tests drops the clean-run chance to 0.995 to the power 400, about 13 %. The formula assumes the flakes are independent. In practice many share a cause (a slow CI machine, a shared database), so they cluster, but the lesson holds: tiny per-test flake rates add up across a big suite. In the independent 200-test illustration, most runs contain a spurious test failure. Re-running by reflex can then hide real failures in the noise. Common causes Cause Typical example ------ Async and timing sleep(1) then assert Order dependence Shared module state Time and dates now(), midnight, DST Randomness Unseeded random data Shared resources Fixed port, shared DB row Concurrency Real race in the code External services Network, rate limits Order dependence, concretely Run the file and test_add_two fails (add("plum") returns 3, because "apple" is still in the cart). Run pytest test_order.py::test_add_two alone and it passes. Reverse the order and the other test fails. Order-dependent tests often look stable for months, then break when someone adds a test, renames a file or turns on parallel execution. Tools that expose them: pytest-randomly shuffles test order on every run (and reseeds random), so hidden dependencies surface quickly. It prints the seed, so a failing order can be replayed. pytest-xdist (pytest -n 4) runs tests in parallel processes, which exposes shared files, ports and database rows. Key takeaways A flaky outcome can arise from the test setup or a real intermittent product bug. Independent small flake rates can make large suites mostly red. Shared state explains tests that pass alone but fail after another test. Further reading Flaky Tests at Google — Google Testing Blog Flaky tests — pytest docs

t: Control test time and repair intermittent failures
sum: Inject a fixed clock to test exact expiry boundaries.
x: A test can depend on hidden inputs such as the clock, test order or the operating environment. The earlier global-cart example exposed order dependence; this unit controls time and turns intermittent failures into an actionable repair. Assume from datetime import datetime in the code below. Control the clock A test that creates a token "expiring in 1 second" and checks it is not expired is flaky on a slow CI machine. Passing the clock in makes it exact: Libraries such as freezegun or time-machine can freeze the clock for code you can't change, but injecting the clock is clearer. Also watch for time-zone assumptions (a test written in London fails in a CI region on UTC-8) and for tests that only fail on 29 February or across a daylight-saving change. Changing test order and process grouping can reveal shared-state problems. Raising line coverage only asks which statements ran; it does not establish that each test owns its state. The later coverage units explain the measurement in detail. What to do with a flaky test Reproduce: run it many times in a loop, with random ordering and in parallel, until it fails. Record the seed. Find the root cause, using the causes table in the preceding diagnosis unit. Often the bug is in the code (a real race), not the test. Fix: inject clocks and randomness, give each test its own data, wait on conditions instead of time, use ephemeral ports (port 0). If you can't fix it today, quarantine it: move it out of the blocking suite, with an owner and a deadline, and keep running it to collect data. Automatic retries Retrying failed tests (e.g. pytest-rerunfailures) turns red builds green, but it also hides real intermittent bugs, such as a race condition that will hit users. If you retry, track every test that needed a retry and treat that list as a bug backlog, not as a pass. Key takeaways Inject a fixed clock to test exact expiry boundaries. Investigate the root cause before quarantining or retrying a flaky test. Wait on conditions, isolate data and record reproduction details. Further reading Eradicating Non-Determinism — Martin Fowler Flaky tests — pytest docs

t: Read line and branch coverage reports
sum: Coverage records execution rather than the adequacy of assertions.
x: Once failures are trustworthy, ask which code the suite actually exercises. Coverage helps locate missing execution, but a high percentage cannot establish that assertions detect wrong results. Code coverage Code coverage measures which parts of the code ran while the tests ran. In Python the standard tool is coverage.py (pytest --cov via pytest-cov). Line versus branch coverage Every line runs, so line (statement) coverage is 100%. Line coverage is the share of executable statements that ran at least once: Yet we never tested an order under £50, or a non-express order. Branch coverage tracks alternatives between measured source lines; for these two if statements, each has a true and false outcome. It does not necessarily distinguish every short-circuited boolean subexpression. Our test only took the true side of both. If only the seven-statement function is in shipping.py and a separately measured driver invokes it, coverage.py can report the following. Including the test function or driver in the measured file changes the statement total: 4->7 means "line 4’s if never jumped straight to line 7" (the condition was never false), and similarly for 7->9. In branch mode, coverage.py puts statements and branch outcomes into one percentage: Counting branch outcomes alone, the test took 2 of 4, which is 50 %. The combined figure sits between the two because it mixes statements (all run) with branch outcomes (half taken). Key takeaways Coverage records execution rather than the adequacy of assertions. Line coverage counts executed statements; branch measurement also tracks alternative transitions. coverage.py combines statement and branch opportunities in its branch-mode percentage. Further reading Branch coverage measurement — coverage.py Code Coverage Best Practices — Google Testing Blog

t: Find the gaps left by full branch coverage
sum: Full branch coverage can miss combinations of decisions and their path-specific faults.
x: The preceding shipping example starts with a cost of 5, makes the base free for totals of at least 50, and adds 10 for express shipping. A single test exercised both true outcomes; now consider what remains untested even after both outcomes of each decision have run. Even full branch coverage doesn't cover every execution path, a complete route from the function's entry to its exit. Two independent ifs give four paths (under or over £50, times express or not). Each extra independent if doubles the number of paths but adds only two branch outcomes: Two tests, (60, True) and (10, False), take all four branch outcomes but only two of the four paths. If cost += 10 becomes cost = 10, those tests still pass: the first starts express pricing from zero and the second skips it. Only a paid-base express case such as (10, True) distinguishes 15 from the incorrect 10. The formula assumes every combination of outcomes is possible; when conditions depend on each other, some paths are infeasible and the real count is lower. Loops can produce unbounded paths. Full path coverage is often infeasible, though finite small regions can be exhaustively exercised. What coverage tells you, and what it doesn't Coverage is excellent at one thing: showing code no test executes. If the error-handling branch for a failed payment has 0% coverage, you know it is untested. It cannot tell you that covered code is well tested. Coverage counts execution, not checking. A test that calls every function and asserts nothing has high coverage and catches almost nothing. Goodhart's law "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Mandate 90% coverage and you get tests written to raise the number: assertion-free calls, tests of trivial getters, tests coupled to implementation. Google's published guidance offers 60% as "acceptable", 75% "commendable" and 90% "exemplary", but explicitly avoids organisation-wide mandates. Practical uses that work well: Look at uncovered lines in the diff during code review, and ask whether they matter. Watch for coverage dropping on a change, which often means new code arrived without tests. Use branch coverage, not just line coverage. Key takeaways Full branch coverage can miss combinations of decisions and their path-specific faults. Path counts grow quickly only when the model’s decision combinations are feasible. Use uncovered code to guide review instead of treating a percentage as proof. Further reading Branch coverage measurement — coverage.py Code Coverage Best Practices — Google Testing Blog Test Coverage — Martin Fowler

t: Use mutations to discover missing boundary checks
sum: Mutation testing asks whether tests distinguish deliberate code changes.
x: Coverage tells you where code ran. Mutation testing changes that code deliberately and asks whether a test notices. A missed boundary is a useful example of the extra information it supplies. Mutation testing Coverage asks "did the tests run this code?" Mutation testing asks the question you actually care about: "if this code were wrong, would a test fail?" The tool makes many small changes to your code, called mutants, one at a time, and runs the tests against each: >= becomes >, <, <= or == + becomes -, and becomes or a constant 18 becomes 19 or 17 return x becomes return None; a condition becomes True If some test fails, the mutant is killed: your tests noticed the change. If all tests pass, the mutant survived: the suite did not detect that change; it may be a meaningful missed fault, an equivalent change or outside the required behaviour. The mutation score summarises a run as the share of mutants your tests killed, leaving out mutants that no test could ever kill (equivalent mutants, examined in the next unit): The fraction requires at least one non-equivalent mutant; otherwise there is no killable population to divide by. Tools cannot generally tell which mutants are equivalent, so until a human marks them, a reported score may divide by all generated mutants and read lower than the true value. A surviving mutant Coverage is 100%. Now mutate: Mutant 30 10 Result ------------ age > 18 T F survives age >= 19 T F survives age >= 17 T F survives age < 18 F T killed True T T killed Three mutants survive, all at the boundary. The tests cannot tell 18 from 17 or 19. One more test kills all three: age > 18 fails on 18, age >= 19 fails on 18, age >= 17 fails on 17. This is the boundary-testing advice from the earlier boundary-testing unit, discovered mechanically. Counting only the five mutants in the table, none of which is equivalent, the boundary test moves the mutation score from 40 % to 100 %: Key takeaways Mutation testing asks whether tests distinguish deliberate code changes. Surviving mutants may indicate a missed fault, equivalence or behaviour outside the contract. Inputs at 17 and 18 distinguish boundary changes that tests at 10 and 30 miss. Further reading Mutation testing basics — PIT State of Mutation Testing at Google — Google Research mutmut documentation

t: Triage equivalent mutants and measure suite health
sum: Equivalence depends on the observed contract and input domain.
x: The previous unit showed mutants that missing boundary tests could kill. Some survivors cannot be killed under the intended contract; others are too costly to analyse across an entire codebase. Triage turns the result into useful work. Equivalent mutants and cost Some mutants don't change behaviour at all, so no test can kill them. These are equivalent mutants: For ordinary integer inputs under a value-only maximum contract, equal inputs give equal output values. The mutant is equivalent under that contract, but not universally in Python: callers can observe object identity, and equal-valued floats such as -0.0 and 0.0 have distinguishable signs. Deciding equivalence is undecidable in general, so a human has to judge surviving mutants, which takes time. Mutation testing is also expensive: each mutant means re-running (part of) the suite, and a large codebase has hundreds of thousands of potential mutants. Tools reduce the cost by running only the tests that cover each mutated line, and by mutating only changed code. Google's approach, described in State of Mutation Testing at Google (2018), mutates only lines changed in a code review, skips "arid" lines unlikely to matter (such as logging), and shows a few surviving mutants to the author and reviewer as review comments. That turns an expensive batch metric into targeted, actionable feedback. Tools: mutmut and Cosmic Ray for Python, PIT (Pitest) for the JVM, Stryker for JavaScript, C# and Scala. Putting it together A healthy team watches all three, uses them to find weak spots, and never turns any of them into a target to game. Key takeaways Equivalence depends on the observed contract and input domain. Changed-line mutation analysis makes expensive test-strength checks more actionable. Read coverage, mutation results and flake rates together without gaming a target. Further reading Code Coverage Best Practices — Google Testing Blog Mutation testing basics — PIT State of Mutation Testing at Google — Google Research mutmut documentation

sum: A blob stores bytes; its containing tree stores the filename and mode.
x: Most people learn Git as a list of commands. That works until something goes wrong: a rebase eats a commit, a branch "disappears", or a merge produces something nobody expected. At that point the commands stop making sense, because they are thin layers over a very simple data model. Learn the model and nearly every command becomes obvious. Git is two things: A content-addressed object store: a key-value database where the key is a hash of the value. A small set of refs: human-readable names that point at objects in that store. Everything else (branches, merges, rebases, tags, git log) is built from those two pieces. Snapshots, not diffs Git models committed project state as snapshots. This logical model is separate from delta compression used to store or transfer objects. Every commit stores the complete state of the project tree at that moment. That sounds wasteful, but it is not. If a file has not changed, the new snapshot simply points at the same stored copy as the previous one. Diffs are computed on demand when you ask for them (git diff, or git log with -p); they are not the logical representation of commits. Packfiles can nevertheless store object deltas, as described below. The four object types Every object has a type, a size and some content. There are exactly four types. Type Holds Points to --------- blob File bytes Nothing tree A directory listing Blobs, trees, submodule commit IDs commit Snapshot + metadata One tree, parents tag Annotated tag Usually a commit Blobs A blob is just the bytes of a file. It has no filename, no permissions and no timestamp. Two files with identical contents, anywhere in the history, are the same blob. Trees A tree is a directory listing. Each entry has a mode, a type, a hash and a name. You can inspect one with git cat-file -p. The following is an illustrative excerpt: hashes are shortened and depend on the repository contents. Common modes are 100644 (normal file), 100755 (executable), 120000 (symlink), 040000 (subdirectory) and 160000 (a submodule commit). For ordinary files, Git tracks the executable bit rather than general permission bits. File type is represented separately by the mode. Commits A commit points at exactly one tree (the root of the snapshot), zero or more parents, and records who and when. This is an illustrative excerpt whose object IDs are shortened to fit; identity fields record claims rather than establishing a person's identity: A root commit has no parent; a repository can contain multiple roots. A normal commit has one parent. A merge commit has two or more. The author is who wrote the change; the committer is who last applied it. Rebase and cherry-pick normally preserve authorship while recording the current committer and time; the two identities can still be the same person. When one nested file changes, Git needs its new blob, a replacement tree for each containing directory up to the root, and a new commit. Unchanged blobs and subtrees are reused. For src/lib/util.py, that means three replacement trees: lib, src and the root. Annotated tags An annotated tag (git tag -a v1.0 -m "...") is a real object with a tagger, date, message and optionally a GPG or SSH signature. A lightweight tag (git tag v0.1) is not an object at all: it is a ref pointing directly at an object, usually a commit. The commands here default to HEAD. You can check with git cat-file -t v1.0 (prints tag) versus git cat-file -t v0.1 (prints commit). Key takeaways A blob stores bytes; its containing tree stores the filename and mode. A commit names one root tree and its parents, preserving a complete logical snapshot. Annotated tags are objects; lightweight tags are refs. Further reading Git Internals: Git Objects — Pro Git

sum: Git hashes the object header as well as the content.
x: The previous unit introduced blobs, trees, commits and tags. Here the objective is to connect their identities: how Git names an object and why rewriting history creates new commits. Content addressing: the hash is the name In a SHA-1-format repository, an object's name is the SHA-1 hash of a small header followed by its content. A hash function turns any sequence of bytes into a fixed-size fingerprint; the same bytes always give the same fingerprint, and a change normally gives a different fingerprint. Different inputs can collide; tamper-evidence assumes an attacker cannot feasibly find a suitable collision. Written as a formula: For a file containing hello and a newline, t is blob and n is 6, so Git hashes blob 6, a NUL byte, then the six content bytes. You can reproduce Git's hashes yourself: Those match git hash-object hello.txt and git write-tree in a SHA-1 repository whose index contains just that file, with the shown mode and no content-conversion filters. Content addressing has three big consequences. 1. Deduplication is free. Copy hello.txt to copy.txt and commit: Git writes only two new objects, a new tree and a new commit. The tree has two entries pointing at the same blob hash. 2. History is tamper-evident. A commit's hash covers its tree hash and its parent hashes. The tree hash covers every blob and subtree hash. To record different bytes in an old snapshot, Git needs replacement hashes along that tree and each rewritten descendant, assuming collision resistance. Existing objects are not modified, and the hash chain proves neither authorship nor code safety. This structure is a Merkle DAG, the same idea behind blockchains and certificate transparency logs. 3. Objects are immutable. You cannot edit a commit. Amend and a replaying rebase create replacement commits and move a ref. A commit-level reset instead moves a ref and may update the index and working tree without creating a replacement commit. --amend makes a new commit Illustratively, run git commit --amend -m "copy file" on a commit whose shortened hash is 375494. The result has a different hash, shown here as a08133, because the message is part of the hashed content. The old commit 375494 still exists in Git's object store; the branch simply points somewhere else now. Key takeaways Git hashes a Git object header together with its content. Tree and parent hashes bind a commit to its snapshot and history, assuming collision resistance. Amend creates a replacement commit and moves a ref rather than editing the old object. Further reading Git Internals: Git Objects — Pro Git Hash function transition — Git docs Upcoming breaking changes in Git 3.0 — Git docs

sum: SHA-1 and SHA-256 encode 160 and 256 bits as 40 and 64 hexadecimal characters.
x: A commit binds its tree and parent IDs into its own hash. That tamper-evidence depends on the hash function; this unit examines the object format and its limits. SHA-1, collisions and SHA-256 SHA-1 is broken for collision resistance: the 2017 SHAttered attack produced two different PDFs with the same SHA-1. Git responded in two ways: Since Git 2.13 it uses SHA-1DC, a hardened SHA-1 that detects the known collision-attack patterns and refuses them, while producing the same hashes for normal data. Git 2.29 added an experimental SHA-256 object format (git init --object-format=sha256). SHA-256 repositories cannot yet freely exchange objects with SHA-1 ones, and check the intended Git clients and hosting service for SHA-256 interoperability before choosing it. Why is a SHA-1 object ID 40 characters long, and a SHA-256 one 64? Git prints IDs in hexadecimal (base 16, digits 0–9 then a–f), and each hexadecimal digit carries exactly 4 bits: So a SHA-1 ID is 20 raw bytes inside tree objects and 40 characters when printed, and a SHA-256 ID is 32 bytes or 64 characters. Commands accept a shorter unique prefix (git show 5870310), which is why abbreviated hashes of 7 or more characters appear throughout this module. As checked on 2026-10-15, Git's published plan for 3.0 is to make SHA-256 the default for new repositories, along with main as the default branch name (Git 2.x still defaults to master unless init.defaultBranch is set). Key takeaways SHA-1 and SHA-256 encode 160 and 256 bits as 40 and 64 hexadecimal characters. SHA-1DC detects known attack patterns; it does not restore SHA-1 collision resistance. Check client and hosting support before selecting SHA-256; the Git 3.0 defaults remain a published plan. Further reading Git Internals: Git Objects — Pro Git Hash function transition — Git docs Upcoming breaking changes in Git 3.0 — Git docs

t: Refs, HEAD and staging the next commit
sum: A branch ref names a tip; HEAD normally names the current branch.
x: Git objects store immutable content and history. Refs give that history useful names, while the index describes what the next snapshot should contain. Refs, branches and HEAD Hashes are unfriendly, so Git keeps refs: names that map to a hash. A branch is a ref under refs/heads/. With the files backend and a loose SHA-1 ref,.git/refs/heads/main is a 40-hex-digit object ID plus a newline. Packed refs, SHA-256 and the reftable backend use different representations; an unborn branch has no commit ref yet. A tag is a ref under refs/tags/. A remote-tracking branch such as origin/main lives under refs/remotes/ and records the last known remote position, normally updated by fetch and also by successful pushes with a matching tracking mapping. HEAD is a symbolic ref saying which branch you are on:.git/HEAD contains ref: refs/heads/main. Creating a branch records a ref rather than copying the project or its history, so it is normally inexpensive. That is why Git encourages branching where older systems discouraged it. When you commit, Git writes the new objects, then updates the branch that HEAD points to. The symbolic target stored in HEAD stays the branch name; resolving HEAD now reaches the new commit. Detached HEAD git switch --detach <commit> (or git checkout <hash>) makes HEAD contain a raw hash instead of a branch name. git status reports HEAD detached at 5870310. New commits made now are not on any branch. Switch away without a durable ref and they may no longer be reachable from branches or tags. Retained reflogs can still protect them temporarily; the next unit covers that recovery window. Packed refs With the files backend, maintenance can pack refs into.git/packed-refs to reduce loose-file overhead; not every branch ref is necessarily packed. Do not rely on reading.git/refs/ directly in scripts; use git rev-parse or git for-each-ref. Git also supports the reftable ref storage backend; use Git commands rather than depending on its on-disk representation. The index (staging area) Between your working tree (the files you edit) and Git's object store sits the Git index, also called the staging area: the file.git/index. It is a flat list of paths, modes and blob hashes describing the next commit. git add f applies configured content conversions (such as line-ending or clean filters), stores the resulting blob and records its hash in the index. git commit turns the index into tree objects, writes a commit pointing at the root tree, then moves the branch. So blobs are created at git add time, not at commit time. If you git add a file and later discard it, that blob lingers until git gc removes it. Key takeaways A branch ref names a tip; HEAD normally names the current branch. Detached HEAD commits need a durable ref if you want to retain them. git add stores converted content and records it in the index before git commit builds trees. Further reading Git Internals: Git References — Pro Git

sum: Packfile deltas compress stored snapshots without changing their logical model.
x: A branch ref identifies a commit; trees and parent links lead to other objects. This unit connects that graph to disk use, retention and recovering committed work. How objects are stored Ordinary local object creation usually writes a loose object: zlib-compressed, at.git/objects/ce/013625... (the first two hex characters become a directory name). That is fine for a few objects but wasteful for millions. git gc (which also runs automatically from time to time) combines objects into a packfile. Inside a pack, Git stores some objects as deltas against similar objects, often another version of the same file. So Git's model is snapshots, while its storage uses delta compression. The two ideas are independent. Network transfers (fetch, push, clone) normally transfer packs based on negotiated wants and common history. Negotiation, filtering and transport choices determine the set; it need not equal every and only missing object. Reachability, reflog and git gc An object is reachable if you can get to it by following pointers from some ref. Git's garbage collection prunes only objects outside its retention roots. Reflogs and configurable age thresholds can retain objects that no branch or tag reaches; explicit immediate pruning can remove that protection after reflog expiry. When enabled and retained, a reflog records local updates to a ref. This illustrative excerpt shows the amended tip followed by the previous commit; your hashes and entries will differ: Reflog entries keep old commits alive. By default, entries for commits that are still reachable expire after 90 days and entries for unreachable ones after 30 days (gc.reflogExpire, gc.reflogExpireUnreachable). The usual prune grace period is two weeks (gc.pruneExpire), including expiry when using modern cruft packs. These are configurable age thresholds, not an extra guaranteed two weeks after a reflog entry expires. Recovering "lost" work Bad rebase or hard reset? Run git reflog, find the hash from before the mistake, and git branch rescue <hash>. The reflog is local only: it is not pushed, and a fresh clone has none of your history of moves. Common pitfalls Thinking a branch is a series of commits. A branch is one pointer to one commit. "The commits on a branch" means everything reachable from that pointer. Committing secrets. Deleting the file in a later commit does not remove its blob from history. Anyone with a clone has it. Rotate the secret first, then rewrite history if you must (for example with git filter-repo). Huge binaries. Each distinct version is a blob, and a full clone normally retains reachable versions. Compression, partial/shallow clones and deliberate history removal affect actual disk use and retention. Use Git LFS or keep artefacts out of the repository. Panicking after a reset. A retained reflog may recover committed work. It is not a backup and does not recover arbitrary uncommitted changes discarded by a hard reset. Key takeaways Packfile deltas compress stored snapshots without changing their logical model. Reflogs can retain old committed work, but expiry and pruning are configurable. Deleting a secret from the current tree leaves its old blob in history; rotate it immediately. Further reading Git Internals: Packfiles — Pro Git git-gc documentation

sum: A fast-forward moves a ref; a divergent merge normally records two parents.
x: Two people start from the same commit and each make changes. Sooner or later the work has to come back together. Git gives you two fundamentally different ways to do that: Merge: keep both lines of history as they happened and join them with a new commit. Rebase: replay one line of work on top of the other, as if it had been written later. For straightforward independent changes, both often produce the same final files. This is not guaranteed: rebase replays intermediate commits, may skip already-applied patches and can expose different conflicts. What differs is the shape of the history and which commits exist. With the object model from the last lesson, each is easy to reason about. The merge base In this simple history there is one merge base, the best common ancestor of the two branches (git merge-base main feat). Git compares three snapshots: the base (B), "ours" (E, the branch you are on) and "theirs" (D). That is why it is called a three-way merge. Complex histories can have multiple best bases; the ort strategy (and its earlier Git recursive strategy) can combine them into a virtual base. A line changed on only one side takes that side's version. A line changed differently on both sides is a merge conflict. Fast-forward merges If main has not moved since feat branched off, there is nothing to combine. main is an ancestor of feat, so Git just moves the main pointer forward: The command output is illustrative; object abbreviations depend on your repository. No new commit is created. This integration leaves no merge commit recording the feature boundary. The branch ref and local reflogs can still exist. git merge --no-ff feat forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible. Teams use it to keep a visible record of each feature as a unit. Three-way merges and merge commits When both sides have moved, a successful ordinary two-head merge creates a merge commit with two parents: This illustrative excerpt omits the remaining commit metadata and message. The two parent lines establish the merge ancestry. Parent order matters. The first parent is the branch you were on (main); the second is the branch you merged in. git log --first-parent follows only first parents, giving a view that skips merged side-branch internals while retaining direct mainline commits of main even in a merge-heavy history. Since Git 2.34 the default two-head merge strategy is ort (you will see "Merge made by the 'ort' strategy"), a faster replacement for the older Git recursive strategy. Since Git 2.50, selecting the option -s recursive uses ort; earlier releases had a separate implementation. Conflicts Suppose both branches change timeout = 30. main sets 45 and feat sets 60: The default markers do not show what the line was before. Turn on git config merge.conflictStyle zdiff3 (or diff3) and you also see the base: Now you can see that both sides raised the timeout, which is often the context you need to resolve it correctly. To resolve: edit the file, git add it, then git commit (or git merge --continue). To give up: git merge --abort. Remember resolutions with rerere git config rerere.enabled true makes Git record how you resolved each conflict. If the same conflict appears again, for example when you redo a rebase, Git prints "Resolved 'cfg.py' using previous resolution" and applies it for you. Key takeaways A fast-forward moves a ref; a divergent merge normally records two parents. Three-way merging compares the base with both tips; textual success does not prove semantic correctness. diff3-style markers expose the base; resolve deliberately, stage, then continue. Further reading Basic Branching and Merging — Pro Git git-merge documentation git-rerere documentation

sum: Rebase normally creates new commits on the chosen base, changing their parents and hashes.
x: A merge retains existing ancestry. Rebase instead replays a selected sequence of commits onto another base; this unit follows that replay and its conflict handling. Rebasing git rebase main (run on feat) does this: Find the commits on feat that are not on main (C and D). Check out main's tip (E). Re-apply each commit's change, one at a time, creating new commits C' and D'. Move feat to point at D'. C' has the same change and message as C but a different hash, because its parent is different. The originals can be found via retained reflogs. ORIG_HEAD initially records the old branch tip, but other commands during the rebase can overwrite it. main can now fast-forward to feat, giving a perfectly linear history. Conflicts during rebase Each replayed commit can conflict. Git stops, you resolve, git add, then git rebase --continue. Other options are --skip (drop this commit) and --abort (go back to how things were). "Ours" and "theirs" swap during a rebase A rebase works by checking out the upstream and applying your commits onto it. So during a rebase of feat onto main, git checkout --ours gives you the upstream side including commits already replayed and --theirs gives you the commit being replayed from feat. This is the opposite of what people expect. Interactive rebase git rebase -i main opens a to-do list where you can pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup or drop each commit, and reorder them. It is how you turn a messy branch ("wip", "fix typo", "actually fix it") into a tidy series before review. A neat workflow uses fixup commits. This is a command template: replace <sha-of-target> with the commit to correct, after adding the correction to the Git index. --fixup creates a commit titled fixup! <original title>, and --autosquash moves it next to its target and marks it fixup, so it melts into that commit. Rebase --onto git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> takes the commits after <upstream> and replays them onto <newbase>. The classic use: you branched feat2 off feat, then feat was rewritten. git rebase --onto feat <old-feat-tip> moves just your feat2 commits onto the new feat. Key takeaways Rebase normally creates new commits on the chosen base, changing their parents and hashes. During rebase, ours is the upstream plus replayed work and theirs is the feature commit being replayed. Interactive rebase cleans a private sequence; --onto can move only the commits after a known old base. Further reading Git Branching: Rebasing — Pro Git git-rebase documentation

t: Shared history, force leases and squash merges
sum: Rewriting commits colleagues use makes their ancestry diverge.
x: Rebase can tidy private commits, but replacing published ancestry affects everyone using it. This unit covers that coordination boundary, force-update checks, and alternatives for integrating or copying changes. The golden rule of rebasing Don't rebase commits other people have built on Rebasing replaces commits with new ones. If a colleague has pulled your old commits and built on them, their history and yours now diverge, with duplicated changes under different hashes. Rebase freely on private branches; do not rewrite main or a shared branch. Rewriting your own pushed feature branch (for example, after review) is common and fine, but it needs a force-push, which brings its own hazard. Force-pushing safely After rewriting a pushed branch, a normal git push is rejected as a non-fast-forward. If server policy permits it, git push --force can replace the remote branch tip and remove a teammate's commits from that branch's ancestry. Those objects may still be retained elsewhere. git push --force-with-lease is safer: it only overwrites the remote if the remote branch is still where your remote-tracking ref (origin/feat) says it is. If someone pushed since your last fetch, you get! [rejected] (stale info). There is a subtle trap. If you (or your editor, in the background) run git fetch, your origin/feat is updated to include the teammate's commit, and the lease passes, so their work is overwritten anyway. Adding --force-if-includes (Git 2.30+) closes that gap: it checks whether the remote-tracking tip is reachable from an entry in the local branch reflog used for the rewrite. This prevents the illustrated unseen-update overwrite; it does not prove the rewritten code preserved every remote change. This assumes an upstream-configured feature branch and permission to rewrite it. These checks limit particular overwrites; they do not review the replacement code. Squash merges Platforms such as GitHub and GitLab offer squash and merge: all the branch's changes become a single new commit on main, with one parent. Locally it is git merge --squash feat followed by git commit. History on main is linear with one commit per pull request, which is easy to read, bisect and revert. The branch's individual commits are not ancestors of main. git branch -d feat may refuse if checking against main; if feat has an upstream it checks that upstream instead, and continuing to work on the same branch afterwards produces confusing repeated conflicts. Why linear history helps bisect git bisect finds the commit that introduced a bug by binary search. You mark one commit as good (bug absent) and a later one as bad (bug present). Git checks out a commit halfway between them; you test it and answer git bisect good or git bisect bad, and the suspect range halves. Because the range halves every time, the number of tests grows only with the logarithm of the number of commits: So 1,000 commits take about 10 tests and 1,000,000 take about 20. The estimate assumes every commit can be built and tested: a commit that does not build has to be skipped (git bisect skip), which costs extra steps. With squash merges each candidate is one whole, reviewed pull request, so bisect lands on a meaningful unit; merge-heavy history works too, but bisect may test side-branch commits that never ran CI. Cherry-pick git cherry-pick <sha> applies one commit's change on top of the current branch as a new commit. It is mostly used to backport a fix to a release branch. Use -x to append "(cherry picked from commit...)" to the message so the link is traceable. Key takeaways Rewriting commits colleagues use makes their ancestry diverge. An implicit force lease can be weakened by a background fetch; --force-if-includes adds a reflog-based check. Squash merges record one combined commit without preserving the feature commits as ancestors. Bisect needs buildable, testable candidate commits; cherry-pick copies a change for a backport. Further reading git-rebase documentation git-push documentation (force-with-lease)

t: Reading ranges and undoing shared changes
sum: Log ranges select reachable commits; diff ranges compare snapshots.
x: After choosing how to integrate history, you need to inspect which commits and file changes differ, and undo mistakes without confusing ancestry with file contents. Pull is fetch plus integrate git pull is git fetch followed by a merge or a rebase. If your branch and the remote have both moved, recent Git versions refuse with "Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches" until you choose: pull.rebase true, pull.rebase false (merge) or pull.ff only. Many teams set pull.rebase true so routine pulls do not create "Merge branch 'main' of..." noise. Reading ranges: two dots and three dots Command Means ------ git log A..B On B, not on A git log A...B On either, not both git diff A..B Tip A vs tip B git diff A...B Base vs tip B git diff main...feat compares a merge base with feat, as GitHub's PR comparison does. The merge base can advance after integrations; it need not be the original branch point. Undoing things Mistake Fix ------ Bad local merge/rebase Inspect ORIG_HEAD/reflog, preserve current work, then choose a recovery commit Lost local committed history Inspect git reflog and create a rescue branch at a retained commit Pushed bad commit git revert <sha> Pushed bad merge git revert -m 1 <merge> A hard reset discards tracked working-tree and staged changes, so it is not a general undo operation. Reflogs record ref changes, not every edit. Reverting a merge commit needs -m <parent-number> to select the mainline parent; it is parent 1 for the merge shown here. There is a catch: once a merge is reverted, merging the same branch again brings in only newer commits, because the old ones are already ancestors. To bring the reverted work back, revert the revert. Merge or rebase? Merge Rebase --------- History Original ancestry retained Replayed ancestry; normally linear Hashes Preserved Rewritten Conflicts Once Per commit Safe if shared Yes No A widely used compromise: rebase your private branch onto main to keep it current and tidy, then integrate it via a merge commit or squash merge on the platform. You get readable history without rewriting anything other people depend on. Key takeaways Log ranges select reachable commits; diff ranges compare snapshots. Revert records a new inverse change, while reset moves refs and can discard local edits. Reverting a merge leaves its ancestry in place, so a later merge brings only newer work. Further reading git-rebase documentation git-merge documentation gitrevisions: specifying ranges

sum: Integration frequency controls how soon incompatible changes are discovered.
x: Git lets you branch any way you like. A workflow (or branching strategy) is the team's agreement about which branches exist, how long they live, and how work flows into the code you ship. There are many named workflows, but they mostly differ on one variable: how often each developer's work is integrated with everyone else's. Get that right and the rest is detail. Why integration frequency matters When two people work apart, their changes drift. Longer separation can increase integration work and delay discovery of incompatibilities; there is no universal mathematical growth law: Evidence gap No numerical integration-cost growth curve is included: this project has no reproducible evidence establishing a universal relationship between branch age and effort. The risks below are qualitative. More lines changed on each side means more textual conflicts. Worse, semantic conflicts appear: changes that merge cleanly but break each other. One person renames a function's meaning while the other adds a new caller relying on the old meaning. Git cannot detect this; review, static analysis and tests of the combined code may detect it. Feedback arrives late. You learn your design clashes with a colleague's after a week of work rather than after an hour. Martin Fowler calls the dreaded end-of-project phase integration hell. The fix is counter-intuitive: if integrating hurts, do it more often, so each integration is small. Key terms Mainline / trunk: the single branch that represents the current state of the product, usually main. Healthy branch: a branch where every commit builds and passes tests, providing a baseline for further work. Passing tests alone does not establish release readiness. Feature branch: a branch for one piece of work, merged back when finished. Release branch: a branch cut to stabilise and maintain a particular release. GitHub flow The simplest common workflow, popularised by GitHub: main is always deployable. Create a descriptively named branch from main for each change. Push it and open a pull request; CI runs and colleagues review. Merge to main once approved and green. Deploy main (often automatically, right after merge). There are no develop or long-lived release branches. It suits web services that deploy continuously and only ever run one version in production. Its main risk is feature branches that live too long: GitHub flow does not force branches to be short, so teams must keep them short by habit. Key takeaways Integration frequency controls how soon incompatible changes are discovered. A semantic conflict can survive a clean textual merge. GitHub flow uses one deployable main branch with reviewed change branches. Further reading Patterns for Managing Source Code Branches — Martin Fowler GitHub flow — GitHub Docs

sum: GitFlow keeps released code on main and ongoing integration on develop.
x: GitHub flow keeps a deployable main branch. GitFlow instead separates released history from ongoing integration, with explicit branches for stabilisation and urgent fixes. GitFlow Vincent Driessen's 2010 model, often called git-flow, uses two permanent branches plus three kinds of temporary ones: Branch Purpose Merges into --------- main Released code only — develop Integration — feature/ New work develop release/ Stabilise main, develop hotfix/ Urgent prod fix main, develop A hotfix, in commands. This template assumes existing main, develop and v1.0 references; the comment marks where the actual fix and commit must be made. Where GitFlow fits and where it hurts GitFlow was designed for software released in discrete, numbered versions, where several versions may be supported at once: desktop apps, libraries, firmware, on-premises products. Its costs: Two integration points (develop and main), with frequent merges in both directions and a real chance of forgetting to merge a hotfix back into develop, so the bug reappears in the next release. Feature branches tend to be long, which brings back late integration. main is usually a release behind the code being worked on, so "what is in production?" and "what is being tested?" are separate questions. In 2020 Driessen added a "note of reflection" to the original post: for teams doing continuous delivery of web apps he recommends a much simpler workflow such as GitHub flow, while GitFlow may still suit explicitly versioned software or multiple supported versions. Key takeaways GitFlow keeps released code on main and ongoing integration on develop. Hotfixes must reach both release history and future development. The model adds coordination cost; its author recommends simpler flows for continuously delivered web applications. Further reading A successful Git branching model — Vincent Driessen

sum: Integrate small changes at least daily rather than parking a whole feature on a long branch.
x: A workflow helps only if integration is frequent enough to reveal incompatible work. Trunk-based development turns that into a daily practice, including while a large feature remains unfinished. Trunk-based development In trunk-based development (TBD), everyone integrates into one trunk at least daily. There are two styles: Commit straight to trunk: common in small teams with strong tests and pairing. Short-lived feature branches: a branch lives hours to a day or two, is reviewed in a small pull request, and merged. This is the usual style in companies that require review. The rule is not "no branches"; it is "no long-lived development branches apart from trunk; maintained release branches are a separate case". DORA's research (from its 2016 and 2017 data) found that teams with higher delivery performance tended to have three or fewer active branches, merge into trunk at least daily, and have no code freezes or integration phases. Shipping unfinished work safely If you merge daily, half-built features reach trunk. Two techniques keep that safe: Feature flags. New code paths ship switched off and are enabled when ready, possibly for a percentage of users first. This application sketch assumes a flag service, both pricing implementations and a charging function. It shows routing, not a complete checkout system. A disabled flag does not make incompatible initialisation or data changes safe. Branch by abstraction. To replace a large component (say, an ORM), introduce an interface in front of it, move callers onto the interface, build the new implementation behind it step by step, switch over, then delete the old one. Every step is a small, releasable commit on trunk. Every flag is a fork in the code's behaviour, and forks multiply. With independent on/off flags, each extra flag can double the number of combinations the code might run in: This is an upper bound: constraints and paths that can never be on together reduce the combinations that can actually happen, and teams test the ones that matter rather than all of them. But the trend is why old flags must go. Flags are debt Give each flag an owner and an expiry date, and delete it once the feature is fully launched. Stale flags cause real incidents: The SEC's account of Knight Capital's 2012 incident reports losses exceeding $460 million and describes a repurposed old flag that reactivated dead code on one server. Key takeaways Integrate small changes at least daily rather than parking a whole feature on a long branch. Feature flags and branch by abstraction let incomplete work integrate safely when compatibility is maintained. Independent flags multiply configurations; assign owners and remove completed release flags. Further reading Trunk Based Development Trunk-based development — DORA capabilities Branch by abstraction — Martin Fowler Feature Toggles — Pete Hodgson on martinfowler.com

t: Release branches, forks and workflow choices
sum: When a defect affects trunk, fix and test there first, then backport to the maintained release.
x: Trunk-based development can maintain older numbered releases without using them as development branches. This unit follows fixes across that boundary and compares workflow choices. Release branches in trunk-based development Teams that must support a release for a while (mobile apps, versioned products) cut a release branch from trunk shortly before release. Fixes are made on trunk first and then cherry-picked to the release branch: This command template assumes both branches exist and the bug affects trunk. Replace abc123 with the actual tested fix commit. Fixing trunk first avoids forgetting to forward-port that fix. Later edits can still regress the behavior, so retain a regression test. Release branches only receive fixes, never features, and are deleted when that release is no longer supported. The forking workflow Open-source projects cannot give push access to every contributor. Instead each contributor forks the repository, pushes branches to their fork, and opens a pull request against the upstream. Maintainers review and merge. The branching inside the upstream can be GitHub flow, trunk-based or anything else; forking is about access, not branch structure. Comparing the options GitHub flow GitFlow Trunk-based ------------ Long-lived main main, develop trunk Branch life Days Days–weeks Hours–1 day Releases Continuous Versioned Either Needs CI, review Discipline CI, flags Choosing a workflow One version in production, deployed often (most web services): GitHub flow or trunk-based development with short-lived branches. Several supported versions (libraries, mobile apps, on-premises products): trunk-based development with release branches, or GitFlow if you really need a separate integration branch. Large monorepo, many engineers: trunk-based development, typically with a merge queue so that main stays green while dozens of changes land per hour (covered in the CI lesson). Whatever you pick, measure branch age. If pull requests regularly stay open for a week, you are living with the costs of late integration whatever the workflow is called. Common pitfalls Long-lived "feature" branches for big projects. Use flags or branch by abstraction instead, and merge small slices. Environment branches (dev, staging, prod) where code is promoted by merging between branches. Each environment's branch drifts, and you end up deploying a merge result that was never tested. Promote the same build artefact through environments instead. Code freezes. A freeze can reflect weak integration confidence or an explicit operational/business constraint. Improve feedback and release controls rather than treating a longer freeze as a substitute for them. Fixing the release branch only, then forgetting trunk. Fix trunk first, then backport. Key takeaways When a defect affects trunk, fix and test there first, then backport to the maintained release. Forking controls contribution access independently of the upstream branching model. Promote the same tested artefact through environments rather than treating drifting environment branches as proof of equivalence. Further reading Patterns for Managing Source Code Branches — Martin Fowler Trunk Based Development A successful Git branching model — Vincent Driessen

t: Review goals, change size and priorities
sum: Review supports knowledge transfer and coherent design as well as defect detection.
x: Many teams review code before it reaches the main branch; others use pairing or selective post-merge review. Done well, review spreads knowledge, keeps the codebase coherent and catches real problems. Done badly, it is a queue where changes sit for days while people argue about brace placement. This lesson covers what review actually achieves, how to be a good author and reviewer, and the process choices that decide whether review helps or hurts delivery. What review is for Ask engineers why they review and most say "to find bugs". Research suggests the picture is broader: A 2013 Microsoft study by Bacchelli and Bird found that finding defects was the top stated motivation, but only a minority of review comments were actually about defects. Much of the value came from knowledge transfer, team awareness and alternative solutions. Google's 2018 case study of about 9 million reviewed changes ("Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google") found education and maintaining norms (readability, consistency) to be central motivations alongside correctness. So review is a bug filter, but also: Collective ownership: review can help more people understand a change; approval alone does not guarantee understanding. Consistency: the codebase stays readable to everyone, not just its author. Mentoring, in both directions. A security and design checkpoint before something is hard to undo. Review does not replace tests. A targeted boundary test can catch an off-by-one that a reviewer misses; CI only detects what its checks actually exercise. Let machines check what machines can check, so reviewers spend attention on what only humans can judge. The standard: better, not perfect Google's published engineering practices put it plainly: reviewers should favour approving a change once it definitely improves the overall code health of the system, even if it is not perfect. There is no perfect code, only better code. That principle cuts both ways. A reviewer should not demand polish on every line. But a reviewer should block a change that makes the system worse: unclear design, missing tests, a new abstraction that does not pull its weight. Size is the biggest lever Small changes get better reviews, faster. Large ones get skimmed. Google's guidance suggests around 100 lines is usually a reasonable size for a change and 1,000 lines is usually too large, while noting that the number of files matters too: 200 lines in one file can be fine; spread over 50 files it usually is not. Ways to keep changes small: Separate refactoring from behaviour change. A pure rename across 40 files is easy to approve on its own; mixed with logic changes it hides them. Split by layer or step: schema migration, then backend, then UI. Stack changes: open PR 2 on top of PR 1, so review of the first does not block writing the second. Use feature flags so a partial feature can merge safely (see the workflows lesson). What reviewers look for, in order Google's list of what to look for is a useful checklist. Review from the top down: there is no point polishing names in code whose design is wrong. Area Question ------ Design Does this belong here? Functionality Does it do what's intended? Complexity Could it be simpler? Tests Correct, useful tests? Naming, comments Clear? Explain why? Style, docs Guide followed? Docs updated? Also read every line you are asked to review, look at the context (the whole file, not just the diff) and say what is good. Praise for a clean test is information too. Key takeaways Review supports knowledge transfer and coherent design as well as defect detection. Approve definite improvements to code health without requiring personal perfection. Separate refactoring from behaviour changes and review design before details. Further reading Google Engineering Practices: Code Review The Standard of Code Review — Google Small CLs — Google Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google

t: Working through a review and giving feedback
sum: Mutable defaults retain state across calls; interpolated SQL values allow injection.
x: Review design before details, and separate mechanical changes from behaviour changes. Now apply that priority to a concrete Python function and communicate the findings so the author can act. A worked review Here is an example function that looks fine at a glance. It assumes a SQLite connection and an orders table; the next version keeps that interface while fixing the query construction. Useful comments, in priority order: Security (blocking). The query builds SQL with an f-string, so an email such as x' OR 1=1 -- can turn this SQLite query into an unconditional selection while commenting out the malformed trailing clause. Use parameters: db.execute(sql, params). Bug (blocking). statuses=[] is a mutable default. It is created once, so "open" is appended on every call and the list grows forever. Use statuses=None. Bug (blocking). With an empty list plus "open", tuple(statuses) renders as ('open',). That trailing comma is invalid SQL. Parameterising fixes this too. Tests. No test covers this function. A test calling it twice would have caught point 2. Nit: SELECT couples callers to every column; consider listing the ones you need. A fixed version for Python sqlite3 (other drivers can use different placeholder syntax): Only the placeholders are interpolated; every value goes through the driver as a parameter. Writing good comments Comment on the code, not the person. "This loop re-reads the file each time" rather than "you wrote a slow loop". Explain why. "This needs a lock because two workers can call it at once" teaches; "add a lock" just instructs. Label severity. Google suggests prefixes like Nit: (minor, take or leave), Optional: or Consider:, and FYI: (for future reference). Some teams use the Conventional Comments format (suggestion:, issue (blocking):, question:). Ask questions when unsure. "What happens if items is empty here?" invites the author to check, and you may learn they already handled it. Big disagreements go to a call. After two rounds of back and forth in comments, talk. Then write the outcome in the PR for posterity. Being a good author Write a description that says what changed, why, and how it was tested. Link the ticket. Reviewers should not have to reverse-engineer intent from the diff. Review your own diff first. Debug prints, commented-out code and unrelated formatting changes are easy to spot in the PR view. Make CI green before asking. Do not spend a reviewer's attention on something the robot will reject. Respond to every comment, even if only "Done". If you disagree, explain why; reviewers can be wrong too. Key takeaways Mutable defaults retain state across calls; interpolated SQL values allow injection. Bind SQL values through the driver and build only placeholder syntax dynamically. Explain the reason and severity of comments, and supply intent and validation as the author. Further reading Google Engineering Practices: Code Review Conventional Comments

t: Fast review, code owners and approval policy
sum: Slow review encourages batching, which makes review slower.
x: Small changes and useful feedback still need a responsive process. This unit connects review turnaround with automated checks, ownership routing and approval controls. Making review fast Slow review quietly destroys trunk-based development: if a review takes two days, people bundle work into bigger changes to "make the wait worth it", which makes reviews slower still. Google's guideline is that one business day is the maximum time to respond to a review request, and that if you are not in the middle of a focused task you should review shortly after a request arrives. Responding does not have to mean finishing; an initial response can clarify expectations, but approval-dependent merges remain blocked until the required review is complete. Ship, Show, Ask Rouan Wilsenach's model, published on martinfowler.com, classifies changes: Ship (merge directly, e.g. a typo fix), Show (open a PR, wait for automated checks, then merge without waiting for human feedback) and Ask (open a PR and wait for review). It suits teams with strong CI and high trust, and it is a reminder that not every change needs the same gate. Tooling and policy Formatters and linters (Black, Ruff, Prettier, gofmt) end style arguments. Run them in CI and pre-commit hooks so style never reaches a human. Automate import ordering, known-vulnerable dependency checks, recognised bug patterns such as mutable defaults, and tests across supported interpreter versions. Scanners and linters depend on their configured rules and data; green results do not establish that a design fits the product. Branch protection on GitHub or GitLab can require N approvals and passing status checks before merging, and can dismiss stale approvals when new commits are pushed. CODEOWNERS maps paths to owners who can be requested for review; requiring owner approval is a separate protection setting. On GitHub the file lives in.github/, the repository root or docs/, and the last matching pattern wins: With required code-owner review enabled, billing/api.py needs an eligible payments owner approval, and billing/main.tf an infra owner approval because.tf matches last. Listing several owners on one line permits approval by any one of them; it does not require every listed team. Pair or mob programming is continuous review. Many teams accept pairing as satisfying the review requirement. Pitfalls Rubber-stamping: "LGTM" on a 2,000-line diff after two minutes. The fix is smaller changes, not stricter rules. Bikeshedding: long review discussions on trivia while the design question goes unasked. Automate style; review design first. Gatekeeping: one senior engineer must approve everything, and becomes the bottleneck. Spread ownership. Approving what you did not understand. If you cannot explain the change, ask. That is the review working. Ignoring dependencies. A one-line lockfile bump can pull in thousands of lines of third-party code. Review new dependencies deliberately. Key takeaways Slow review encourages batching, which makes review slower. Use automated checks for mechanical work and route human review by relevant ownership. On GitHub the last matching CODEOWNERS pattern wins; required owner review and stale-approval dismissal are separate policies. Ship / Show / Ask varies the feedback gate with the change and team context. Further reading Google Engineering Practices: Code Review Ship / Show / Ask — Rouan Wilsenach About code owners — GitHub Docs

sum: CI is frequent integration verified by automated checks, together with prompt repair of failures.
x: Continuous integration (CI) is often confused with "having a CI server". The tool is the easy part. CI is a practice: everyone integrates their work into the mainline frequently, at least daily, and every integration is verified by an automated build and test run. When the build breaks, fixing it is the team's top priority. The tooling (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, Buildkite, CircleCI) exists to make that practice cheap. A team running a sophisticated pipeline on week-old feature branches is not doing CI in this sense. Why CI works Small integrations are cheap. Problems surface within minutes of the change that caused them, while the author still remembers it. The mainline stays healthy. If main always builds and passes tests, developers have a tested baseline for branching and diagnosis. Release readiness also depends on deployment, compatibility and operational checks. It replaces fear with evidence. The pipeline supplies repeatable evidence about the behaviors and properties its checks cover; a green run is not proof that nothing breaks. The cost is discipline: tests must be good enough to trust, and a red build must be fixed (or the change reverted) quickly. A common rule is that if a fix is not obvious within about ten minutes, revert first and investigate afterwards. Anatomy of a pipeline A typical pipeline runs on every push to a pull request and every merge to main: Two principles shape the order: Fail fast. Run the cheapest, most likely-to-fail checks first. A lint error should not wait behind a 20-minute integration suite. Run independent jobs in parallel. Independent jobs (unit tests, scans, docs build) run in parallel; only true dependencies are sequential. A GitHub Actions example This workflow is a configuration template for a Python repository with requirements.txt, tests and Ruff configuration. It requires GitHub-hosted execution; it does not show a measured run or guarantee these durations. This teaching example uses readable version tags and a moving runner label; production policy should pin reviewed action commits and control tool/dependency versions. requirements.txt must include the test and lint dependencies. What each part does: on: run for pull requests, pushes to main, and merge_group (the event a GitHub merge queue sends, covered below). concurrency with cancel-in-progress: a new push to the same branch cancels the run for the previous push, saving minutes. (Many teams exclude main so that every commit on main gets a full result.) permissions: contents: read: the job's GITHUB_TOKEN gets read-only access, following least privilege. timeout-minutes: a hung test fails after 15 minutes instead of the default 360. strategy.matrix: the job runs once per Python version, in parallel. cache: pip: restores downloaded packages keyed on dependency files and environment details; pip installation still runs, and speed depends on whether a useful dependency cache entry was restored and on the remaining work. Key takeaways CI is frequent integration verified by automated checks, together with prompt repair of failures. Order cheap likely failures early and parallelise independent jobs. The workflow example supplies trigger, permission, cancellation, timeout and Python-version controls; tags remain mutable. Further reading Continuous Integration — Martin Fowler Secure use reference — GitHub Actions

sum: Test sharding reduces elapsed time while repeating setup on every runner.
x: A CI pipeline is useful when developers receive feedback soon enough to act on it. This unit studies test time, compute cost, test layers and intermittent failures. Speed is a feature Extreme Programming's ten-minute build is still a good target: fast enough that developers wait for the result rather than context-switching. As pipelines slow down, people stop running them locally, batch changes and ignore results. Techniques, roughly in order of effort: Cache dependencies and build outputs. Key caches on lockfile hashes so they invalidate correctly. Parallelise the test suite. Split a test suite into test shards that run on separate machines. Run only what changed. Monorepo build tools (Bazel, Nx, Pants, Turborepo) compute which targets are affected by a change and skip the rest. Push slow tests later. Run end-to-end suites after merge or on a schedule, not on every push, as long as failures are acted on. How much does test sharding help? Splitting a suite into test shards divides the test time but not the setup each CI runner must do first, and you pay for every runner for the whole wait: test sharding arithmetic A suite of 2,400 tests averaging 0.5 s each takes 1,200 s, or 20 minutes, on one runner; with 60 s of setup that is 1,260 s, or 21 runner-minutes. Split across 8 test shards the wait drops to about 3.5 minutes, at the price of 28 runner-minutes instead of 21. You trade compute for feedback time, usually a good deal. The sum assumes even test shards: one slow test file can make one test shard much longer than the rest, so balance test shards by measured duration. The test pyramid Not all tests cost the same: Lots of fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a thin layer of end-to-end tests. A suite shaped like an ice-cream cone (mostly end-to-end) is slow and flaky, and when it fails it tells you little about where the problem is. Key takeaways Test sharding reduces elapsed test time while repeating setup on every runner. Balance test shards by measured duration and use caches keyed to declared inputs. Keep many focused unit tests, some integration tests and a small end-to-end layer. Further reading The Practical Test Pyramid — Ham Vocke Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them

t: Flaky tests and compounded failure risk
sum: A flaky test can pass and fail on unchanged code, sometimes revealing a real race.
x: A fast suite still needs trustworthy feedback. This unit distinguishes intermittent test outcomes from reliable evidence, then calculates how many small flake risks combine. Flaky tests A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. Google reported in 2016 that about 1.5% of all test runs gave a flaky result, that almost 16% of tests had some flakiness, and that about 84% of pass-to-fail transitions they observed involved a flaky test. That last number is the real damage: many transitions involved tests known to be flaky. This does not establish that most red builds were misleading alerts: intermittent failures can expose real races or other defects. Typical causes are timing (sleep(1) and hope), test order dependence, shared state, real network calls and unseeded randomness. Why does a small flake rate per test hurt so much? A run goes red if any test flakes, so with many tests the chances compound. If each test flakes independently: Even a 0.1 % flake rate per test leaves about 18 % of 200-test runs red. Real flakes are not perfectly independent, so treat this as a model of how the risk compounds, not a prediction. What to do: Test quarantine: move a known-flaky test out of the blocking suite, file a ticket and fix it soon. Track flakiness per test; many CI systems can detect pass-after-retry.
