Update status and add explicit corrections where needed, without silently rewriting what was decided. The log is a history, including the decisions you reversed. Keep them short: one or two pages. An ADR that takes a week to write won't get written. Write one when a decision is significant: costly to reverse, affecting structure, or likely to be questioned. Choosing Postgres, adopting hexagonal architecture or splitting a module qualifies; naming a variable doesn't. Variants such as MADR (Markdown Architectural Decision Records) add a considered options section with pros and cons for each alternative, which helps reviewers see what was rejected and why. ADRs as a review tool Write the ADR with status Proposed and open it as a pull request. Discussion can happen on the PR; define whether merging marks acceptance in your team's workflow. The decision and its debate are then preserved together. Key takeaways An ADR records one significant decision, its forces and its consequences. Keep accepted decision history while updating status and linking replacement records. A proposed ADR can support review before the decision is accepted. Explicit downsides explain why a future reader should not casually reverse the choice. Further reading Documenting Architecture Decisions — Michael Nygard Architectural Decision Records MADR Lightweight ADRs — Thoughtworks

sum: Match review effort to reversibility and turn architectural properties into executable checks.
mt: Software Architecture at the Code Level
x: An ADR preserves why a choice was made. Next decide how much care that choice needs, and which properties automated checks must preserve while the system changes. Reversible and irreversible decisions Not every decision deserves the same care. Jeff Bezos's 2015 shareholder letter split them into Type 1 (one-way doors, consequential and hard to reverse) and Type 2 (two-way doors, which you can walk back through). Decision Door ------ Name of an internal helper Two-way Choice of logging library behind an adapter Two-way Public library API at 1.0 One-way-ish Main database for 10 years of data One-way-ish Splitting into separately deployed services One-way-ish Two consequences for architecture: Spend ADR and review effort on one-way doors. Make two-way decisions quickly. Turn one-way doors into two-way ones where you can. Putting the database behind a repository port, or a vendor SDK behind an adapter, can reduce call-site changes, but the cost of migrating also depends on data and semantic compatibility. Much of good architecture is buying reversibility. The related idea of the last responsible moment says to delay irreversible decisions until you have the most information, but no later, since not deciding is also a decision. Evolutionary architecture Neal Ford, Rebecca Parsons and Patrick Kua's Building Evolutionary Architectures defines an evolutionary architecture as one that supports guided, incremental change across multiple dimensions. The key word is guided: change is constant, but some properties must be protected while it happens. Fitness functions A fitness function is an objective, preferably automated, check of an architectural characteristic. Rather than hoping the layering survives, you test for it. Examples: Characteristic Fitness function ------ Layering import-linter contract in CI No cycles Acyclic import check Latency p99 latency under 0.2 seconds in a load test Dependency hygiene No package more than 1 major version behind Bundle size Fail if over 250 KB gzipped A fitness function can be an ordinary test: This small example checks direct absolute import statements, requires at least one source file, and matches the top-level package exactly. It does not resolve relative or dynamic imports and can include imports guarded by TYPE_CHECKING. A dedicated tool like import-linter also follows indirect chains, which is why it's usually the better choice. The point is that architecture rules become executable and fail the build like any other bug. Key takeaways Spend greater care on costly, hard-to-reverse decisions. Adapters can reduce call-site changes but cannot guarantee an easy data or semantic migration. A fitness function checks an architectural property rather than merely describing it. A direct-import AST check has explicit limits; dedicated tools can follow indirect dependencies. Further reading 2015 Letter to Shareholders — Amazon Building Evolutionary Architectures — authors’ site Import Linter: contract types ast — Python documentation

sum: Use strangler fig routing, branch by abstraction and parallel runs to reduce migration risk.
mt: Software Architecture at the Code Level
x: With decisions recorded and fitness checks guarding constraints, architecture can change in smaller steps. These techniques preserve feedback and reduce the size of each risky cutover. Changing structure incrementally A long all-at-once rewrite can delay feedback and lose undocumented behavior. Joel Spolsky's essay Things You Should Never Do argues against this approach using Netscape as a cautionary example. Evidence gap A universal rewrite failure rate and a precise single-cause Netscape chronology are omitted; an opinion essay is not sufficient evidence for those claims. The alternative is a set of techniques for changing structure in small, safe steps. Strangler fig. Named by Martin Fowler after vines that grow around a host tree until they replace it. Put a routing layer in front of the old code; move one capability at a time to the new implementation; route to it; delete the old part. The aim is to keep the system serving throughout, but each cutover still needs compatible data, operational checks and a recovery plan. Branch by abstraction. For replacing a component used throughout the code (an ORM, a payment provider) without a long-lived feature branch: Introduce an abstraction (a port) over the existing component. Move all callers onto the abstraction. Build the new implementation behind the same abstraction. Switch over, often with a feature toggle, a slice of traffic at a time. Delete the old implementation, and the toggle. Every step is a small commit on the main branch, so you avoid a months-long merge. Parallel run. For risky logic like pricing, run old and new implementations side by side, return the old result, and log differences. GitHub's open-source Scientist library (Ruby, with ports in other languages) does exactly this. Switch only when relevant differences are understood. Shadow execution must isolate side effects and cap additional load; Scientist evaluates both behaviors but does not inherently run them concurrently. Key takeaways Strangler fig replaces capabilities gradually behind a routing facade. Branch by abstraction moves callers onto a seam while implementations change in small main-branch commits. Parallel runs compare results before serving the replacement. Shadow execution needs isolated side effects and controlled load. Incremental cutovers still require compatible data, monitoring and recovery. Further reading Strangler Fig Application — Martin Fowler Branch By Abstraction — Martin Fowler Scientist — GitHub Things You Should Never Do — Joel Spolsky

sum: Relate architecture to domain learning and team structure, and control the configuration cost of old toggles.
mt: Software Architecture at the Code Level
x: Incremental replacement depends on the surrounding code and organisation. This unit connects evolutionary design to domain learning, team ownership and the cleanup of migration toggles. Other evolutionary ideas Monolith first. In his 2015 essay, Fowler reported that almost all successful microservice stories he had heard began with monoliths, while many from-scratch stories involved trouble. This is practitioner experience, not a representative success-rate study; because boundaries are hard to get right before you understand the domain. A well-modularised monolith keeps the option open. Sacrificial architecture. Sometimes the right design for today is one you expect to throw away when you reach 10× scale. Fowler's example is eBay, which moved from Perl to C++ to Java as it grew, as recounted in his essay. Knowing it's temporary changes how much you invest. Conway's law. "Organizations which design systems are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations." Ownership shared between teams can affect boundaries, but Conway's observation does not deterministically predict that any shared module will blur. The inverse Conway manoeuvre shapes teams to match the architecture you want. Pitfalls ADRs written after the fact for show. If they don't influence decisions, they become stale paperwork. Write them at decision time. ADR as a design document. ADRs record a decision. Long technical designs belong elsewhere and can be linked. Fitness functions nobody runs. A check outside CI is a suggestion. Evolution as an excuse for no design. "We'll refactor later" works only if the code is testable and modular enough to refactor, and if later actually comes. Toggles that never die. Every independent on/off flag doubles the number of configurations the code could run in (see the formula below); dependencies, and flags that can't both be on, can reduce the reachable combinations. Put a removal date on them. Each toggle has two states, and independent toggles can be combined freely, so the possible configurations multiply: This is an upper bound: toggles that depend on each other, or can't both be on, rule some combinations out. It still shows why old toggles should be deleted rather than left to accumulate. Key takeaways A modular monolith keeps boundaries movable while the domain is being learned. A sacrificial architecture is a conscious temporary investment. Conway’s observation motivates aligning team communication with intended ownership. Independent on/off flags create exponentially many configurations; remove obsolete toggles. Evolution needs testable boundaries and checks that actually run. Further reading Monolith First — Martin Fowler Sacrificial Architecture — Martin Fowler Conway’s original paper Inverse Conway manoeuvre — Thoughtworks

sum: Build a safety net and separate structural changes from feature and bug fixes.
x: Refactoring is changing the structure of code without changing what it does. Martin Fowler's definition has two parts: a refactoring is a small change that makes code easier to understand and cheaper to modify, without changing its observable behaviour; and refactoring (the activity) is applying a series of those small changes. The key word is behaviour-preserving. If you rename a function and fix a bug in the same commit, you have done two things, and when something breaks you will not know which one caused it. Kent Beck's image is the two hats: when you add a feature you wear one hat, when you refactor you wear the other, and you swap often but never wear both at once. Why bother? Code is read far more than it is written. Every feature you add lands in the shape the code already has. If that shape is awkward, the feature is slow to add and easy to get wrong. Beck's advice sums up the workflow: "make the change easy (warning: this may be hard), then make the easy change." Refactoring is the first half. You reshape the code so the new feature fits naturally, then add it. There are a few common moments to refactor: Preparatory: just before a feature, to make room for it. Comprehension: while reading confusing code, rename and extract until it makes sense, so the next reader gets your understanding for free. Litter-pickup: small improvements as you pass through (the "boy scout rule": leave the code a bit better than you found it). Planned: a dedicated chunk of work when neglect has made an area painful. Healthy teams need this less, because the other three keep it in check. Prioritise restructuring where code changes frequently and those changes cause regressions or slow reviews. A stable, rarely changed module may offer little change-related return, while still needing assessment for security, operational and knowledge risks. The safety net: tests You cannot claim behaviour is unchanged unless something checks it. Before refactoring, you need tests that cover the code you are about to touch, and they should be fast enough to run after every small step. If the code has no tests, write characterisation tests first (Michael Feathers' term from Working Effectively with Legacy Code). You do not assert what the code should do; you record what it currently does, bugs included. If a refactoring changes one of these outputs, you have changed behaviour, deliberately or not. Fix bugs afterwards, as a separate, visible change. Commit at every green Make one small move, run the tests, commit. If the next step goes wrong you can discard the intended tracked-file edits with git restore <paths> after checking the diff (unrelated uncommitted work must be preserved) instead of debugging a half-finished restructure. Key takeaways Refactoring preserves observable behaviour; bug fixes and new features are separate changes. Use tests around the affected code, and characterisation tests when intended legacy behaviour is unclear. Prefer small green steps and prioritise areas where structure causes real cost. Further reading Definition of Refactoring — Martin Fowler Workflows of Refactoring — Martin Fowler

t: Recognise smells and make small moves
sum: Use code smells to select focused refactorings and preserve arithmetic behaviour.
x: A safe refactoring starts from the tests and behaviour boundary established in the preceding unit. This unit connects design symptoms to small changes you can verify. Code smells: when to refactor A code smell is a surface symptom that often (not always) signals a deeper design problem. Some common ones from Fowler's catalogue: Smell Typical fix ------ Long function Extract Function Duplicated code Extract, then reuse Feature envy Move Function Data clumps Introduce Parameter Object Primitive obsession Replace Primitive with Object Shotgun surgery Move related code together Divergent change Split the module Two of these are worth telling apart. Shotgun surgery is when one change forces edits in many places. Divergent change is the opposite: one module changes for many unrelated reasons. Both are coupling and cohesion problems seen from different directions. The core moves Most day-to-day refactoring uses a handful of moves. Here is a function definition for a fictional surcharge. The snippets are partial examples: no order is constructed or invoice called, so executing the definitions prints nothing. A call prints a formatted total; the numeric policy is invented for this exercise. Extract Function pulls a coherent piece into a named function. The name documents intent: For the supported numeric inputs, the arithmetic and printed output are preserved. This is a fictional country-tagged surcharge, not a VAT implementation or tax guidance. Keep the original accumulation loop: replacing it with sum can change floating-point results on Python 3.12 and later. Now each part can be tested and reused, and adding a new country's rate touches one small function. Other moves you will use constantly: Rename (variable, function, class). The cheapest, most valuable refactoring. If you have to read a function's body to know what it does, its name is wrong. Inline Function / Inline Variable: the reverse of extract, when the indirection no longer earns its keep. Extract Variable: give a complicated expression a name. Move Function: put a function next to the data it uses most (the fix for feature envy). Introduce Parameter Object: (start, end) passed everywhere becomes a DateRange. Replace Conditional with Polymorphism: a match on type repeated in several places becomes one class per case. Separate Query from Modifier: a function that both returns a value and changes state is split, so reading never surprises you. Modern IDEs (IntelliJ, PyCharm, VS Code with a language server) automate rename, extract and move. Automated refactorings are much safer than hand edits because the tool can resolve many references consistently, though dynamic code like getattr(obj, name) can still escape it. Key takeaways A smell suggests investigation, rather than proving that code needs replacement. Shotgun surgery spreads one change across modules; divergent change gives one module unrelated reasons to change. Extract, rename, move and introduce parameter objects in behaviour-preserving steps. Further reading Catalog of Refactorings Python sum changes

sum: Use expand and contract, branch by abstraction and strangler routing to replace systems incrementally.
x: Tests protect local changes, but public contracts also include callers, schemas, stored formats and operational consumers. Incremental migration keeps compatible versions working together. Refactoring code you do not fully control Renaming a function is easy when you can update every caller in one commit. It is hard when callers live in other services, other teams or other companies. Parallel change (expand and contract) Change an interface in three phases, each safe to deploy on its own: For columns, expand the schema and deploy atomic dual writes while still reading the old column. Drain every old-only writer, including jobs, before a race-safe backfill from the current row values; alternatively use database synchronization that also covers old writers. Validate equality before switching reads. Keep dual writes through the rollback window, then retire all old readers/writers before dropping the old column. Locks, transactions and conditional updates must prevent stale backfill data from overwriting newer values. Branch by abstraction To replace a large internal component (say, an ORM or a payment library) without a long-lived branch: Put an abstraction layer (an interface) in front of the old component. Move all callers to use the abstraction. Build the new implementation behind the same abstraction, switched by a flag. Flip callers over gradually, then delete the old implementation and, if it no longer helps, the abstraction. The aim is to keep changes integrated on the main branch, with each step building and remaining deployable; the pattern does not guarantee this without tests of component compatibility and behaviour. Strangler fig For a whole legacy system, Fowler's strangler fig pattern (named after a vine that grows round a tree until it replaces it) routes traffic through a facade. New functionality goes into the new system; old routes are moved across one at a time until the legacy system handles nothing and can be switched off. The big-bang rewrite is the alternative, and it has a poor record: the old system keeps changing while you rebuild it, the rewrite delivers nothing until it is finished, and hidden behaviour in the old code is rediscovered as production bugs. Pitfalls Refactoring without tests is just editing and hoping. Mixing refactoring with behaviour change in one commit makes review and bisecting much harder. Separate commits, ideally separate PRs. Refactoring for its own sake. Spend effort where code changes often. A stable module may have little change-related cost, but still assess operational, security and knowledge risks. Big-bang refactors on a long-lived branch drift from main and end in painful merges. Prefer small steps merged daily. Breaking public contracts. Anything other code depends on (APIs, serialised formats, database schemas, even log formats parsed by alerts) is behaviour. Use parallel change. Speculative generality. Refactoring towards a flexibility nobody needs yet adds indirection. Refactor for the change in front of you. Key takeaways Expand an interface before migrating callers, then contract after all old dependencies are gone. Database backfills must account for concurrent and old-version writers, validation and rollback. Branch by abstraction replaces a component; strangler routing replaces system capabilities incrementally. Further reading Parallel Change — Martin Fowler Branch By Abstraction — Martin Fowler Strangler Fig Application — Martin Fowler

t: Understand technical debt and its kinds
sum: Distinguish principal and interest, classify debt and recognise risks beyond messy code.
x: Every codebase has parts the team wishes were different: a module everyone is scared to touch, a dependency three major release versions behind, a test suite that takes 40 minutes. Technical debt is the name for the gap between the code you have and the code that would make today's work easy. The phrase is useful because it is a metaphor the whole business understands. It is also widely misused, so it is worth knowing what it originally meant. The original metaphor Ward Cunningham coined it in a 1992 experience report about a financial product called WyCash: Shipping first time code is like going into debt. A little debt speeds development so long as it is paid back promptly with a rewrite... The danger occurs when the debt is not repaid. Every minute spent on not-quite-right code counts as interest on that debt. Three ideas are packed in there: Debt principal: the work needed to bring the code up to the design you now know you want. Debt interest: the extra time every future change costs because you have not done that work. Borrowing can be smart. Shipping early to learn from real users is valuable. The mistake is never repaying. Cunningham later stressed that he meant code written with your best current understanding, which becomes "debt" as you learn more about the problem. He did not mean permission to write sloppy code. Fowler's debt quadrant Martin Fowler sorted debt along two axes: was it deliberate or inadvertent, and was it prudent or reckless? Reckless Prudent --------- Deliberate "We don't have time for design." "Ship now, deal with the consequences." Inadvertent "What's layering?" "Now we know how we should have done it." Prudent, deliberate: a conscious trade-off with a repayment plan. Hitting a trade-show deadline with a hard-coded config, ticketed for next sprint. Reckless, deliberate: skipping tests and design because of pressure, knowing better. The timing and size of the cost depend on the project. Reckless, inadvertent: the team did not know good practice. Training and review fix the cause. Prudent, inadvertent: can emerge even after careful design. Even excellent teams only learn the best design by building the thing. This is Cunningham's original sense. The quadrant matters because the response differs. Prudent debt needs a repayment plan; reckless debt needs a change in how the team works. Kinds of debt Debt is not only messy code: Kind Example ------ Code Copy-pasted logic, 500-line functions Design Wrong module boundaries Test Missing or flaky tests Dependency Libraries years out of date Infrastructure Hand-built servers Documentation Runbooks nobody updated Knowledge Only one person understands it Dependency debt compounds silently. Regular small upgrades can reduce accumulated migration work, though even a minor release can require investigation and testing. Skipping five years of versions means a migration project, often forced at the worst moment by a security vulnerability or an end-of-life date. Python 2 reached end of life in January 2020, and many organisations spent years paying that bill at once. Key takeaways Technical debt describes costs created by a gap between current implementation and current understanding. Principal is repayment work; interest is the ongoing cost of carrying the debt. Deliberate versus inadvertent and prudent versus reckless debt need different responses. Further reading The WyCash Portfolio Management System — Ward Cunningham Technical Debt Quadrant — Martin Fowler Sunsetting Python 2

t: Find expensive debt and estimate payback
sum: Compare carrying costs and repayment effort, then investigate frequently changed complex code.
x: Technical debt is useful as an economic metaphor when it guides a decision. The following figures are hypothetical engineering-effort estimates, not measured productivity rates. The interest is what matters Not all ugly code is costly debt. Frequent changes expose design costs, but unchanged code can also incur incident response, security maintenance, runtime cost and knowledge risk. Compare those costs as well as change friction. A worked example makes the trade-off concrete. Two quantities matter: the debt interest (the extra time you pay over a period because of the debt) and the payback period (how long the fix takes to earn back its own cost in saved interest): Is it worth paying down? The checkout module's structure adds about 2 extra days to each feature that touches it, and the team ships 8 such features a quarter. A restructure is estimated at 20 days. A legacy reporting module also adds 2 days per change, but changes once a year. The same 20-day fix would apply. The checkout fix pays for itself in under two quarters and keeps paying after that. Ignoring other costs, the reporting fix takes ten years to repay through change savings alone; deferring it may make sense if security, operational and knowledge risks are also acceptable. The model assumes the interest stays constant and that the fix removes it completely; in practice both are estimates. This is why "the code is ugly" is a weak argument and "this costs us 16 days a quarter" is a strong one. Finding hotspots Adam Tornhill's hotspot analysis combines two signals you already have: how often a file changes (from version control) and how complex it is (lines of code or a complexity metric). Files that are both complex and frequently changed are candidates for expensive change friction; the two signals alone do not prove causation. File change frequency from git: This command is an illustrative history query, not fixed output. Run it in the repository you are investigating. It counts appearances of paths in the selected Git history and sorts larger counts first; merge history, renames and Git’s path-display conventions can affect interpretation. Cross-check the top entries with complexity, bug reports and the files developers complain about. You usually find that a small fraction of files accounts for most of the pain. Other useful signals: lead time for changes in an area, how often a module appears in incident reports, and how long reviews take for PRs touching it. Key takeaways Compare change friction together with operational, security and knowledge risks. Payback estimates depend on how much cost the fix actually removes and how long savings continue. Hotspots combine complexity and file change frequency; confirm the signal against real delivery and incident evidence. Further reading Technical Debt — Martin Fowler Hotspot analysis — CodeScene Git log documentation

t: Make debt repayment part of delivery
sum: Record repayment triggers, choose incremental strategies and explain the business cost.
x: The previous unit estimated carrying cost and payback. Now turn that evidence into owned work instead of a vague list of disliked code. Paying it down There is no single right approach; most teams combine several. Continuous cleanup. Refactor as part of every feature that touches the area (the preparatory refactoring from the previous lesson). This keeps interest low and needs no permission because it is just how features are built. Reserved capacity. A fixed share of each sprint (for example, a locally chosen 10–20%; illustrative, not an established industry rate) goes to debt items. It stops the work being permanently pushed back by features. Targeted projects. For a big structural problem (splitting a module, replacing a framework), a planned project with a clear goal and an end date. Use branch by abstraction or strangler fig so value arrives incrementally. Deliberate debt with a plan. When you choose to borrow, record it: a ticket with the shortcut, why it was taken, the trigger for repaying it ("before we onboard a second customer") and an owner. The comment links the shortcut to owned work and a trigger; a bare # TODO: fix gives no such repayment mechanism. Things that do not work well The "tech debt sprint" once a year. Debt accumulates daily. As the only repayment strategy, a yearly cleanup can defer valuable fixes for months and may be displaced by deadlines. A debt backlog with hundreds of vague items. Nobody can prioritise "clean up utils". Each item needs a location, a cost (interest) and a rough fix size. Rewriting from scratch to escape the debt. Rewrites have their own debt from day one and lose the hidden knowledge in the old code. Incremental replacement often reduces cutover risk, but compare its compatibility and replacement effort with the specific rewrite. Talking to the business Product managers and executives do not want to hear "the code is bad". They do respond to: Speed: "Features in billing take three times longer than elsewhere; this would bring them closer to average." Risk: "This library is out of security support; one CVE and we are doing an emergency upgrade under pressure." Reliability: "Four of last quarter's six incidents came from this module." Options: "We cannot launch in the EU until VAT handling is generalised." Fowler's design stamina hypothesis gives the long-run picture: with little attention to design, a team is faster at first, but there is a point (Fowler judges it can arrive within weeks, but explicitly calls its position a judgement rather than a measured universal bound) after which the team with better internal quality delivers more. Debt is a choice to move faster now and slower later. Make the choice consciously and know when "later" arrives. Pitfalls Calling every disagreement "debt". If you would design it differently but it costs nothing to work with, it is a preference, not debt. Ignoring interest. Prioritise by cost of carrying the debt, not by how ugly it looks. Borrowing without recording it. Deliberate debt that is not written down becomes inadvertent debt for the next person. Hero repayments. One engineer quietly rewriting a module over a weekend creates a knowledge silo, which is itself debt. Evidence gap A universal time until debt becomes costly and a measured industry-wide percentage of capacity reserved for debt are not included: this review did not establish reliable evidence for those population claims. The examples are illustrative. Key takeaways Combine continuous cleanup, selected maintenance capacity and targeted incremental projects. Record deliberate shortcuts with a reason, owner and repayment trigger. Explain debt using delivery cost, risk and lost options; design stamina is a hypothesis rather than a universal timetable. Further reading Design Stamina Hypothesis — Martin Fowler Is High Quality Software Worth the Cost? — Martin Fowler

sum: Replace guesses with falsifiable hypotheses, a reliable reproduction and a careful traceback reading.
x: Debugging can consume substantial engineering time. The usual approach is to stare at the code, guess, change something, and rerun. Sometimes it works. When it does not, you can lose a day. Methodical debugging replaces guessing with a process. A structured investigation can reduce wasted experiments; its benefit depends on the problem. Debugging is the scientific method A bug is a gap between what you expect the program to do and what it actually does. Somewhere, one of your beliefs about the system is false. Debugging is finding which one. The loop: Observe: gather facts. What exactly happens? What did you expect? Hypothesise: propose a specific cause. "The cache returns a stale price after an update." Predict: if that is true, what else must be true? "Clearing the cache should fix it; the database row should be correct." Test: run the experiment that would disprove the hypothesis. Conclude: keep or discard it, and loop. Two habits make this work. First, change one thing at a time, to make the effect easier to attribute. Second, write things down: hypotheses tried, results, commands run. After two hours you will not remember whether you tested with the cache off. David Agans' book Debugging condenses this into nine rules worth memorising (paraphrased here): understand the system; make it fail; quit thinking and look; systematically narrow the search; change one thing at a time; keep an investigation record; check the plug; get a fresh view; and if you didn't fix it, it ain't fixed. Step 1: reproduce it A reliable reproduction provides strong evidence for evaluating a fix; without one, confidence must come from other evidence and remains harder to establish. Aim for a reproduction that is: Reliable: fails every time, or at a known rate. Fast: seconds, not a 20-minute deploy. Automated: ideally a failing test. Collect everything: the exact error message, the full stack trace, inputs, versions, environment and time. "It's broken" is not a bug report; "POST /orders with an empty basket returns 500 since Tuesday's deploy" is. Read the stack trace properly Python prints frames oldest first and says so: Traceback (most recent call last). The bottom line is the exception; the frame just above it is where it was raised. Work upwards to find the first frame in your code, which is usually where the wrong value came from or was passed in. The following traceback is illustrative, with source filenames and line numbers chosen for the example. Here the crash is in order_total, but the real question is why n was zero, and whether handle should have rejected an empty basket before calling it. Key takeaways Write down observations, hypotheses, experiments and actual results. A useful reproduction records inputs, expected and actual behaviour, versions and environment. Read the exception and raising frame, then trace the wrong value back through your own code. Further reading Python errors and exceptions Methodical debugging — MIT The Debugging Book — Andreas Zeller

sum: Shrink reproductions and use deterministic good/bad tests to localise regressions.
x: Start from the reliable reproduction and recorded evidence established in the preceding unit. Smaller inputs and a narrower history reduce the number of plausible causes. Step 2: minimise it A bug that appears with a 3 MB input file and 40 config flags is hard to reason about. Shrink it: remove half the input; if it still fails, keep the smaller version; if not, try the other half. If neither half fails, test smaller removals from the original failing input; an interaction may require pieces from both halves. Continue until no individual remaining piece can be removed while preserving the failure. This is delta debugging, formalised by Andreas Zeller, and tools automate it. Property-based testing libraries like Hypothesis do the same thing automatically, "shrinking" a failing random input toward simpler cases that still fail; shrinking does not guarantee the globally smallest case. A minimal reproduction often makes the cause obvious. It also makes a perfect regression test. Step 3: localise it by binary search When you do not know where the bug is, halve the search space with each experiment. In an ideal binary search, 20 yes/no tests distinguish roughly a million candidates (20 halvings cover 1,048,576). Arbitrary code, configuration interactions and non-monotonic failures need not provide such a partitioning oracle. You can binary-search almost anything: Code path: log or assert at the midpoint of the pipeline. Is the value already wrong there? Data: does it fail on the first half of the records or the second? Configuration: revert half the changed settings. History: which commit introduced it? git bisect If something used to work, git bisect finds the commit that broke it by binary search over history. The commands below are a workflow template. They depend on the repository’s revisions and tests and temporarily change the checkout; they are not a standalone reproducible output example. How many tests does bisect need? Each test halves the range of suspect commits, so the question is how many halvings it takes to get from all the candidates down to one: This assumes a linear history with one deterministic good-to-bad transition and no skipped commits. Merges, flaky tests, reversions and untestable commits complicate this bound. Doubling the history to 2,000 commits adds only about one more test. Better still, automate it with a script whose exit code tells git the answer: Exit code 0 means good, 1 to 127 (except 125) means bad, and 125 means "cannot test this commit, skip it" (for example, when it does not build). With pytest, exit codes for interruption, internal errors, usage errors or no collected tests must not be interpreted as evidence of the target regression. Use a wrapper that maps an untestable revision to 125 or aborts the run, and returns 1 only for the relevant test failure. Key takeaways Shrinking finds a smaller failure, not necessarily the globally smallest input. Binary-search bounds require a reliable partition; interactions and flaky failures can break the model. In git bisect run, distinguish target failures from untestable revisions and tooling errors. Further reading Git bisect documentation pytest exit codes Reducing Failure-Inducing Inputs — Andreas Zeller

t: Inspect state and fix the cause
sum: Use debugger stops and regression tests to explain and repair a failure.
x: After reproducing and localising a failure, inspect actual values. A debugger and a small failing test help distinguish the cause from a plausible patch. Tools: print, logs and debuggers Print debugging is fine. It is quick, works everywhere, and leaves a trail. Use logging rather than print for anything that may stay, and print repr() so you can tell "1" from 1 and spot trailing whitespace. A debugger lets you stop the program and inspect everything without recompiling or adding prints. In Python, put breakpoint() (Python 3.7+) where you want to stop: pdb command Does ------ n Next line (step over) s Step into a call c Continue to next breakpoint p expr Print an expression w Where: show the stack u / d Move up / down the stack b file:line, cond Conditional breakpoint Post-mortem debugging is underused. Run python -m pdb script.py, then enter c at the initial stop; after an uncaught exception, you land in the frame that raised, with every local variable available. In a REPL, import pdb; pdb.pm() does the same after an exception. Conditional breakpoints filter execution stops: b pricing.py:12, n == 0 stops only on the bad iteration out of thousands. Step 4: fix the cause, not the symptom Once you have found the bad line, resist the quickest patch. Ask why the value was wrong. Write a failing test that reproduces the bug. Fix the root cause. If an empty basket should be impossible, reject it at the boundary, rather than adding if n == 0: return 0 deep inside pricing. Watch the test pass, and run the full suite. Look for siblings. The same mistake is often made in several places. Search for the pattern. Explain it. If you cannot say why the bug happened and why the fix works, you have probably found a coincidence. "If you didn't fix it, it ain't fixed." Example: a classic Python trap Default arguments are evaluated once, when the function is defined, so a mutable default is shared between calls. Symptom versus cause The symptom (a list "remembering" earlier values) looks like a caching bug. Knowing the language's evaluation rules finds it in seconds. The fix is tags=None, then if tags is None: tags = [] inside the function. Key takeaways A conditional breakpoint stops at the interesting state rather than every iteration. Post-mortem debugging inspects the failure frame after an uncaught exception. A fix should satisfy the intended rule, pass its regression test and address similar mistakes. Further reading pdb — The Python Debugger Default argument values — Python tutorial

sum: Handle heisenbugs, environment drift and production-only failures without confusing correlation for cause.
x: Some failures resist a deterministic reproduction. Keep the same observe–hypothesise–test discipline, but make uncertainty and the failure rate explicit. The hard cases Heisenbugs A heisenbug changes or disappears when you try to observe it. Adding a print or attaching a debugger alters timing, so a race condition stops happening. Typical causes are concurrency (data races, unsynchronised shared state), uninitialised memory in C and C++, and timing-dependent code. Approaches: Use tools built for the job: ThreadSanitizer for supported C/C++ toolchains detects data races; AddressSanitizer detects classes of memory-safety errors. Go offers -race on supported platforms. Rust sanitizer support depends on the toolchain and target; none of these detects every bug. Increase the failure rate: run the test 10,000 times in a loop, add load, or insert deliberate sleeps to widen race windows. Consider a bounded, thread-safe in-memory event buffer to reduce synchronous I/O, while recognising that any instrumentation can alter timing. "Works on my machine" The code is the same, so something else differs. Diff the environments methodically: dependency versions (compare lock files), OS and architecture, environment variables, configuration, locale and time zone, data, and file system case-sensitivity (default macOS volumes are commonly case-insensitive, while common Linux configurations are case-sensitive; inspect the actual mounted volume). Containers reduce this class of bug by making environments reproducible. Bugs only in production You cannot attach a debugger to production easily, so you rely on what the system already records: structured logs with a request or trace ID, metrics, and traces. Correlate by time ("what changed at 14:05?"). Recent deploys and config changes are useful initial hypotheses; correlate them with evidence rather than assuming that a recent change caused the failure. Pitfalls Shotgun debugging: changing several things at once until it works. You learn nothing and may introduce new bugs. Trusting assumptions. "That function can't return None." Check it. Agans' "check the plug" rule: is the service you are testing the one you changed? Is the config file the one being loaded? Stopping at the first plausible cause. Confirm it: turn the bug off and on again by reverting and reapplying the fix. Not asking for help. Explaining the problem to someone (or to a rubber duck) forces you to state your assumptions, and the faulty one often jumps out. After an hour stuck, get a fresh view. Key takeaways Instrumentation can change timing; a disappearing failure is not evidence of a repair. Compare versions, configuration, data, locale and platform when environments disagree. Use logs tied together by request identifiers, metrics and traces in production, then test hypotheses one at a time. Further reading ThreadSanitizer — Clang AddressSanitizer — Clang Data race detector — Go Traces — OpenTelemetry

t: Choose a target and calculate the ceiling
sum: Use user-facing metrics and Amdahl’s law to decide which performance change can matter.
x: A useful rule for performance work is: measure before you change anything. Intuition can misidentify where time goes. In a hypothetical profile, a suspected loop might take only 2% of runtime while a database call hidden inside a helper dominates. Those figures illustrate a possibility, rather than measurements from this course. This lesson covers a disciplined workflow: define the goal, measure, find the bottleneck, change one thing, and measure again. When to optimise Donald Knuth's famous line, from a 1974 paper, is usually quoted only in part: We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil. Yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%. The point is not "never optimise". It is: do not contort code for speed before you know it matters, and when it does matter, measure which parts matter and work there. The quoted percentages are rhetorical guidance, not measured proportions for every program. Start with a concrete target tied to users or cost: Latency: "p99 of /search under 300 ms" (the 99th percentile, roughly 1% of observations lie above it, depending on ties and the percentile convention). Completion time: "the nightly import finishes within its 2-hour window". A throughput target would instead name work per unit time, such as rows imported per second. Resources: "fit in a 512 MB container", "halve the CPU bill". Without a target you cannot tell when to stop, and performance work has no natural end. Use percentiles, not averages A mean of 80 ms can hide a p99 of 2 seconds. Users making more requests have more opportunities to encounter slow requests, though request types and latency dependence also matter. Amdahl's law: where the ceiling is Amdahl's law (Gene Amdahl, 1967) answers the question "if I speed up one part of a program, how much faster does the whole thing get?" It applies to a fixed amount of work, assuming the rest of the runtime is unchanged. Suppose a function takes 30% of runtime and you make it 10 times faster: The untouched part sets a ceiling. Even if the improved part became infinitely fast, its time would shrink to nothing and only the untouched part would remain: The 70% you did not touch caps the gain. The lesson: work on the biggest slice first, and a profiler tells you which slice that is. Key takeaways Define a concrete latency, completion-window or resource target before optimising. Amdahl’s law assumes a fixed workload and an unchanged remainder. Improving a small runtime fraction has a strict ceiling under that model. Further reading Amdahl’s law — NVIDIA CUDA Best Practices Structured Programming with go to Statements — Donald Knuth

sum: Compare repeated measurements and recognise load tests that omit queued requests.
x: The target from the preceding unit determines what to measure. A benchmark is useful only if its data, timing boundary and arrival model represent that target. Step 1: benchmark honestly A benchmark measures how long something takes, so you can compare before and after. Easy to do, easy to do badly. For small snippets, Python's timeit runs code many times and handles timer details: The printed number is runtime-dependent; there is no fixed expected duration. It is a total for 100,000 lookups, not seconds per lookup. The timeit docs recommend looking at the minimum of the repeats: higher values are usually caused by other processes interfering, not by your code. Common benchmarking mistakes: Unrealistic data. An algorithm that is fine with 100 rows can be quadratic at 100,000. Use production-sized inputs. Mismatched warm-up. Warm up for steady-state measurements; measure cold starts separately if that is the target. The first run can pay for cold caches, lazy imports, connection setup and JIT compilation (in PyPy, the JVM or V8). Noise. Laptops slow their CPUs when hot (thermal throttling), browsers steal CPU. Repeat runs and compare distributions, not single numbers. Measuring the wrong thing. A micro-benchmark of string concatenation tells you nothing if the request spends 90% of its time waiting for Postgres. Match the arrival model Load tests that omit queued waits. A load generator that waits for each response before sending the next one sends fewer requests exactly when the system slows down, so it under-reports bad latency. This is coordinated omission; for an independently arriving production workload, tools like wrk2 schedule a target arrival rate and measure latency from intended send times. Constant rate alone is insufficient if delayed sends are omitted from latency. A closed-loop model can be appropriate when the real workload is closed-loop. Key takeaways Use representative data, repeated measurements and comparable machines and load. Warm steady-state tests consistently; measure cold starts separately when they matter. For independently arriving traffic, account for latency from intended arrival times. Further reading timeit — Python docs wrk2 arrival-time latency accounting

t: Read profiles and separate CPU from waiting
sum: Interpret call timings and sampled stacks, then choose tools for off-CPU delays.
x: Once a representative benchmark exposes the expensive execution path, profile that workload. The question is where time goes, including time when the request is not computing. Step 2: profile to find the bottleneck A profiler tells you where time goes. There are two main kinds. Kind How it works Example --------- Deterministic Hooks calls and returns in scope cProfile Sampling Records stacks at a fixed rate py-spy, perf Deterministic profilers count observed call events in the profiled execution scope, with overhead that can disproportionately affect tiny functions. Sampling profilers periodically capture stacks; some interrupt execution while tools such as py-spy read another process externally. Sampling is approximate and often lower overhead, but production use requires suitable permissions and validation of workload impact. py-spy can attach to a running Python process by PID without restarting it. Reading cProfile This command is a template: app.py must exist and the resulting profile depends on that program, its inputs and the runtime. Illustrative output, with some columns trimmed: ncalls: how many times it was called. tottime: time spent in the function itself, excluding functions it called. cumtime: time including everything it called. Read it like this: main takes 9.8 s cumulatively but almost none itself. Nearly all of it is under load_order, and within that db.query has a tottime of 9.1 s from 5,000 calls. Repeated per-order queries suggest an N+1 query pattern if an initial query fetched the orders. Investigate batching or joining and measure the resulting database work; the profile alone does not guarantee the saving. fmt_price is called 200,000 times but costs only 0.3 s; optimising it cannot remove more than its measured contribution under these assumptions. Reading a flame graph A flame graph (Brendan Gregg's visualisation) aggregates stacks. This schematic demonstrates the parent/callee layout; its widths are not drawn to match the cProfile numbers above: Each box is a function; the box above it is something it called. Width is the share of samples that included that function: for a CPU-time graph, wider estimates more CPU time. Other flame graphs can encode off-CPU time or allocation volume. The x-axis is not time. Boxes are sorted (often alphabetically) so identical stacks merge. Look for wide plateaus near the top: in a CPU-sampled graph with complete stack unwinding, these indicate self CPU time rather than just callees. CPU time versus waiting A request can be slow while the CPU is idle. It may be waiting for a database, a network call, a lock or the disk. This is off-CPU time, and a CPU-only profiler will not show it, because a sleeping thread is not on the CPU to be sampled. Compare wall-clock time (what the user experiences) with CPU time (what the process actually computed). If a request takes 800 ms of wall time and 20 ms of CPU time, optimising Python code cannot help much; look at what it waits for, including time runnable but waiting for CPU scheduling. A low CPU time for one request does not show that the whole machine is idle. Distributed tracing, database slow-query logs and wall-clock profiling modes are the right tools there. For whole machines, Gregg's USE method is a quick checklist: for each resource (CPU, memory, disk, network), check Utilisation, Resource saturation (queued work) and Errors. Key takeaways cProfile self time excludes callees; cumulative time includes them. A CPU flame graph aggregates samples and stack relationships rather than showing a timeline. Low per-request CPU time can indicate I/O, locks or scheduler delay; validate attachment permissions and profiler overhead. Further reading The Python Profilers — Python 3.14 docs py-spy Flame Graphs — Brendan Gregg Off-CPU Analysis — Brendan Gregg The USE Method — Brendan Gregg

sum: Evaluate algorithms, batching, caching and concurrency against measured bottlenecks.
x: The profile identifies a candidate, not the correct intervention. Preserve ordering, values and side effects while testing whether less work meets the target. Step 3: the wins that matter Candidate improvements to evaluate against measurements: Do less work. Remove repeated computation, unneeded fields, duplicate calls. Better algorithms and data structures. Reducing quadratic work to O(n log n), where n is the number of input items, improves scaling under comparable constant-time operations. Constants, memory use and workload size still determine the practical crossover. Batch I/O. One query for 5,000 rows instead of 5,000 queries. Batch remote service requests, buffer writes. Cache results that are expensive and reused, with a plan for invalidation. Concurrency for I/O-bound work (asyncio, threads): overlap the waits. Move hot loops to optimised code: NumPy vectorisation, a C extension, or a compiled language. Micro-optimisations (local variable lookups, avoiding attribute access) last, and only in a proven hot loop. A very common example of point 2: With 10,000 items in each list, the two versions differ enormously in the work they do: These function definitions do not print anything. Both retain the order and duplicates from list a when values in b match; the set version changes lookup mechanics. For the Django scenario, one query to fetch 300 orders followed by a separate customer lookup per order makes 301 queries. With a ForeignKey pointing to one related customer, Order.objects.select_related("customer") fetches the related customers using a join in the orders query. That queryset is an incomplete application example: it requires the actual model and database, and the one-query statement covers this access pattern only. Django many-to-many relationships instead need prefetch_related, normally adding a separate batched query. Query counts do not determine execution time: measure the joined or batched query too. This is an asymptotic comparison, not a measured timing guarantee. It assumes stable, hashable values and effectively constant-time equality/hashing; the set uses extra memory proportional to the length of b (m in the code comments). Unhashable values or unusual equality semantics can invalidate this replacement. No universal seconds-to-milliseconds result is included because it cannot be reliably established without a specified workload and benchmark. Key takeaways Reduce unnecessary computation and round trips before tuning tiny operations. A set can replace repeated list scans for stable hashable values, at an extra memory cost. Average-case operation counts are not a measured speedup or a worst-case hash-table guarantee. Further reading Python data model — hashing Django select_related and prefetch_related

t: Trace retained memory and protect gains
sum: Compare allocation snapshots, distinguish Python allocations from process memory and guard against regressions.
x: Performance includes memory as well as latency. A growing resident footprint needs allocation evidence and a workload with a clear observation window. Compare allocations Memory problems show up as growing RSS, memory swapping, or the container being OOM-killed. Python's tracemalloc takes snapshots of allocations; comparing two snapshots shows which lines allocated the memory that grew: Typical culprits are unbounded caches, lists that grow for the lifetime of a process, and objects retained by callbacks or other references. Python normally collects unreachable reference cycles; cycles alone do not establish a leak. tracemalloc covers traced Python allocations, not every native allocation or all RSS. Step 4: verify and protect After a change, re-run the same benchmark, on the same machine and data. Keep the change only if it moved the target metric meaningfully. Then protect the gain: a performance test in CI with a generous threshold, or production dashboards that alert on regressions. Speed lost a little at a time in later commits is common and hard to notice. Pitfalls Optimising without a profile. The most common mistake, and the most wasted effort. Trusting micro-benchmarks for macro decisions. Measure the real workload too. Ignoring the tail. Improving the median while p99 gets worse can make the product feel slower. Sacrificing clarity for tiny gains. Unreadable code has its own cost. Comment any non-obvious optimisation with the measurement that justified it. Key takeaways Compare snapshots to identify growing traced allocations and inspect who still retains the objects. Python allocation tracking does not cover every native allocation or all resident process memory. Re-run the same benchmark after a change and protect a meaningful gain with appropriate monitoring. Further reading tracemalloc — Python docs gc — Python docs

t: Agile values and Scrum’s feedback cycle
sum: Read the Agile values alongside Scrum accountabilities, events and quality commitments.
x: The label "Agile" is used for a variety of software processes. In practice that word covers everything from small, self-organising teams shipping daily to heavyweight processes with more meetings than releases. To work well in any of them, it helps to know what the ideas actually are and why they exist. The problem Agile was solving The traditional waterfall model runs in phases: gather all requirements, design everything, build it, test it, release. Sequential planning is easier when requirements are stable, but safety-critical or contractual work does not by itself justify deferring integration, feedback or validation. Software requirements can change or remain uncertain. Users only know what they want once they see something; markets move; technical unknowns surface mid-build. A waterfall project discovers these problems at the end, when changing course is most expensive. (Winston Royce's 1970 paper, often cited as the origin of waterfall, actually described the purely sequential version as risky and recommended iteration.) The Agile Manifesto In 2001, seventeen practitioners met in Snowbird, Utah, and wrote the Manifesto for Agile Software Development. It is four lines: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools Working software over comprehensive documentation Customer collaboration over contract negotiation Responding to change over following a plan It adds: "while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more." Agile does not mean no documentation or no plan. It means you deliver working software in short cycles, get feedback, and adjust, because that is cheaper than being wrong for a year. Scrum and Kanban are two approaches used to organise work and feedback. Scrum Scrum is a framework for working in fixed-length iterations called Scrum Sprints, usually just called Sprints. The official definition is the Scrum Guide by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, in its November 2020 version. It is short (under 15 pages) and much of what people call "Scrum" is not in it. The Scrum Team A small team, typically 10 or fewer people, with three accountabilities: Product Owner: maximises the value of the product; owns and orders the Product Backlog. Scrum Master: helps the team and organisation use Scrum effectively; causes the removal of impediments to team progress. This accountability is not a project-manager role. Scrum Developers: everyone doing the work of creating a usable Increment each Sprint, including testers and designers. Events Event Timebox (1-month Sprint) ------ Sprint One month or less Sprint Planning Up to 8 hours Daily Scrum 15 minutes Sprint Review Up to 4 hours Sprint Retrospective Up to 3 hours For shorter Sprints, Planning, Review and Retrospective are usually shorter; the Daily Scrum remains a 15-minute event. The Guide does not prescribe a most-common Sprint length. Sprint Planning answers why this Sprint is valuable (the Sprint Goal), what can be done, and how. Daily Scrum is for the Developers to inspect progress towards the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan. The 2020 Guide dropped the old "three questions" format. Sprint Review shows stakeholders what was done and decides what to do next. It is a working session, not a demo for applause. Sprint Retrospective looks at how the team works and picks improvements. Scrum is founded on empiricism: make work transparent, inspect what happens and adapt. Product Backlog refinement means continually breaking down and clarifying work items; it is an ongoing activity, not a sixth Scrum event. Artefacts and commitments Artefact Commitment ------ Product Backlog Product Goal Sprint Backlog Sprint Goal Increment Definition of Done The Definition of Done is a shared, explicit quality bar (for example tested, reviewed and documented; exact criteria depend on the product and organisation). Work that does not meet it is not part of the Increment, however close it is. Not in the Scrum Guide Story points, velocity, user stories, burndown charts and planning poker are all common practices, but none is required by Scrum. Key takeaways Agile values feedback and working software while retaining value in plans, tools and documentation. Scrum defines three accountabilities, five events and three artefacts with commitments. The Definition of Done governs the Increment; popular estimation rituals are not required by Scrum. Further reading Manifesto for Agile Software Development The Scrum Guide (2020)

t: Control work in progress and reason about flow
sum: Use pull policies and Little’s law with consistent boundaries and long-run averages.
x: Scrum creates a regular inspection rhythm. Kanban focuses on the flow of work and can be used alongside it, especially when arrivals are unpredictable. Kanban Kanban comes from Toyota's production system, where cards ("kanban" means signboard) signalled when to produce more. David J. Anderson adapted it for software in the mid-2000s. Kanban does not prescribe roles or iterations. Useful practices include: Visualise the workflow on a board, with a column per stage. Control work in progress (WIP) with explicit policies; limits may cover individual stages or a larger part of the workflow. Manage flow: measure how work moves and remove blockages. Make policies explicit, such as what "ready for review" means. Improve continuously using data and feedback loops. The numbers are WIP limits. Dev is full at 3, and Review is full at 2: A and B occupy its two slots. Help finish Review work first. Review may then pull C when its policy allows; finishing C alone does not create Dev capacity until it leaves that stage. Pull from To do only after a Dev slot opens. Keep the card and any delivery blockage visible. This is a pull system, not push: work moves when there is capacity downstream. Stop starting, start finishing. Little's law Why limit WIP? Little's law, proved by John Little in 1961 for queueing systems, links three averages. It answers the question "if we keep this much work open, how long will each item take on average?" It holds for a stable system over the long run, meaning work leaves at about the rate it arrives, so the queue is not growing without limit: The second line is the same law rearranged. All three must use the same workflow boundary (say, "from Dev to Done") and the same time unit. The law says nothing about any single item, and a short filling or draining interval cannot be treated as a steady-state forecast without accounting for boundary effects. Temporary variation does not disprove the long-run identity. Halving WIP In a stable workflow, average throughput is 4 items a week and average WIP is 12. Then average WIP falls to 6 while throughput stays at 4. A WIP cap is not the measured average, and this does not promise that every item finishes twice as fast. Lower WIP may reduce context switching, but excessive restriction can starve stages and reduce throughput. Measure both flow and capacity. Scrum versus Kanban Scrum Kanban --------- Cadence Fixed Sprints Continuous flow Roles PO, SM, Developers None required Planning focus Sprint Goal and evolving plan Flow and WIP policies Useful measures Goal outcomes and product value WIP, throughput, work-item age, cycle time Kanban suits work that arrives unpredictably (operations, support, platform teams). Scrum suits product development where a regular rhythm of planning and review helps. Kanban can also complement Scrum. Sprint scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as learning occurs without endangering the Sprint Goal. Key takeaways Pull work only when the receiving stage has capacity under its explicit policies. Little’s law links compatible long-run averages; a WIP cap is not the measured average. Reducing WIP reduces average cycle time only if throughput remains fixed under the model. Further reading The Kanban Guide (May 2025) The official Kanban Guide — Kanban University

t: Use relative estimates without making false promises
sum: Separate estimates from targets and commitments, and understand team-local velocity and coordination costs.
x: Forecasts support decisions under uncertainty. Relative sizing can expose different understandings, while staffing changes introduce their own uncertainty. Estimation Every business needs some answer to "when will it be ready?" Estimation is hard for well-understood reasons. Unknowns. Much of software work is discovering what needs doing. The cone of uncertainty. Steve McConnell, building on Barry Boehm's work, illustrates a possible early range of 0.25× to 4× in his cone model. It is not a universal statistical confidence interval. Reducing uncertainty requires decisions and learning; elapsed time alone does not narrow it. The planning fallacy. Kahneman and Tversky described the tendency to underestimate task durations despite contrary experience; later experiments found evidence for it. Hofstadter's tongue-in-cheek law is commonly quoted as: "It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take into account Hofstadter's law." McConnell also separates three things that are often confused. An engineering estimate is a prediction ("probably 6–10 weeks"). A delivery target is a desired outcome ("launch by the conference"). A delivery commitment is a promise. Conflating them turns honest estimates into negotiations. Relative estimation: story points Relative estimation is one technique for discussing size and uncertainty. Story points size work relative to a reference item ("this is about twice the password-reset page"), often on a rough Fibonacci-like scale: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. The growing gaps express growing uncertainty: the scale deliberately avoids debating adjacent large values as if the estimates were precise. Planning poker uses simultaneous revelation to reduce anchoring on the first spoken estimate: everyone reveals a card at once. If one person says 2 and another 13, they discuss, and usually one of them knows something the other does not. That conversation is the most valuable part. A team's velocity (sprint velocity) is the number of story points it completes per Sprint, used to forecast how much the team can take on. It is usually averaged over the last few Sprints, and a rough forecast divides the remaining backlog by it: This illustrative forecast assumes the backlog stays the same size and the team's capacity stays stable. Because the past Sprints varied from 18 to 24 points, a range (about 4.4 to 5.8 Sprints, so 5 or 6) is more honest than the single number. Velocity only works within one team: points are not comparable across teams. Ranking teams by velocity can reward inflated point assignments rather than delivered value; use it for local planning, not as a productivity target. Scrum’s feedback practices also require acting on significant Review findings and following through on retrospective improvements, as introduced earlier. Brooks's law Fred Brooks, in The Mythical Man-Month (1975): "Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later." New people need training from existing members, and the number of possible pairwise communication links grows much faster than the team. Each person can pair with every other person, and that counts every pair twice (Ann–Bob and Bob–Ann), so divide by 2: These are possible links, not a claim that every pair communicates or that actual overhead must be quadratic. Adding people can help on separable work; evaluate onboarding and coordination costs. Key takeaways An estimate predicts, a target expresses a desire and a commitment makes a promise. Story points and velocity are local planning tools; compare shared assumptions rather than ranking teams. Possible communication pairs grow faster than team size, but actual overhead depends on the work. Further reading The Purpose of Agile Planning — Mike Cohn Planning Poker — Mike Cohn Velocity — Mike Cohn

sum: Calculate a PERT weighted estimate and make its modelling assumptions explicit.
x: A single date hides the shape of uncertainty. The following illustrative calculation makes one modelling choice visible so stakeholders can question its inputs. Ranges and three-point estimates A single number hides uncertainty. A three-point estimate gives three values for one task: an optimistic one, a most likely one and a pessimistic one. PERT (the Program Evaluation and Review Technique, developed for the US Navy's Polaris programme in the late 1950s) combines them into a single expected duration by weighting the most likely value four times as heavily as either extreme: A beta distribution can model durations between chosen optimistic and pessimistic bounds. The PERT weighted mean is an additional modelling assumption, not a consequence of choosing any beta distribution; its parameters must be chosen to give that mean. Under this PERT weighting model the estimated mean (5) is above the mode (4), reflecting the asymmetric inputs. Three inputs alone do not establish the true distribution, and not every duration distribution is right-skewed. Key takeaways Three-point estimation records optimistic, most likely and pessimistic durations. PERT weights the most likely value four times as heavily as either extreme. The weighted result is a model estimate, not a deadline or proof of the true duration distribution. Further reading PERT in the PMI Practice Standard for Scheduling

sum: Compare average-rate forecasts with a seeded Monte Carlo model and explain the limits of its percentiles.
x: If work items are sufficiently comparable, completed-item history can support a forecast without estimating every item separately. This model is an example, not a guaranteed probability for a real team. Forecasting from data: Monte Carlo If the team tracks how many items it finishes each week, it can forecast without estimating individual items. Simulate the future by sampling from past throughput: For comparison, the simple average gives a single-number answer: The average says nothing about how likely a miss is; the simulation does. On CPython 3.14.4, this seeded example prints 50%: 11 and 85%: 13. The sequence can depend on the Python implementation and version; record those when reproducing it. These are model outputs, not guaranteed real-world probabilities. Resampling assumes this short history represents future throughput, weeks can be sampled independently, remaining items are comparable and the backlog stays fixed. Changes in scope, staffing or dependence can invalidate the forecast. Some teams take this further with #NoEstimates: split work into small, similar-sized items and forecast purely from throughput. Pitfalls Cargo-cult Scrum. All the ceremonies, none of the feedback. Ignoring feedback that requires adaptation undermines the Review; it need not change the backlog on every occasion. Velocity as a performance target. Goodhart's law warns that using points as a productivity target can encourage inflation. Velocity is a planning tool for the team. Treating points as fixed hours. A rule such as “one point always means eight hours” hides uncertainty and team-local sizing. Empirical team-level forecasts should retain those assumptions and variation. Ignoring the retrospective. A retro that picks no action, or never checks last time's action, is a wasted hour. Single-number estimates treated as promises. Give ranges with a confidence level, and re-forecast as you learn. Key takeaways Sampling historical throughput creates a distribution of modelled completion times. Percentiles describe the simulation under its assumptions, rather than guaranteed real-world probabilities. Re-forecast when scope, staffing, item comparability or dependence changes. Further reading random — Python docs The Kanban Guide — flow metrics and forecasts

t: Shape ownership and write useful documentation
sum: Spread critical knowledge and separate design decisions from task guides and reference material.
x: Past a certain size, the hardest problems in software are not technical. A brilliant engineer who leaves no documentation, blocks every review and burns out on call creates less value than a merely good engineer who makes the whole team faster. This unit connects team responsibilities, shared knowledge and documentation. The following units cover review, sustainable on-call and learning from incidents. (The System Design module covers SLOs, error budgets and service-level incident response; here the focus is the team.) Teams shape systems Conway's law (Melvin Conway, 1968): organisations that design systems "are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations". Eric Raymond's tongue-in-cheek restatement: "If you have four groups working on a compiler, you'll get a 4-pass compiler." It works in both directions: If two teams must coordinate on every change to a shared module, consider whether module boundaries or team responsibilities create avoidable coordination. Some coordination may be inherent in the domain. The inverse Conway manoeuvre deliberately shapes teams to match the architecture you want. Align team ownership with business capabilities and appropriate service boundaries; a team can own several services, and organisation alone does not guarantee independence. The bus factor (or truck factor) is the number of people who would have to disappear before a project stalls. A bus factor of one is a single point of failure: holidays, illness or a resignation stop work, and that person cannot take a real break. Raise it deliberately with pairing, rotating ownership, documentation and review. Writing things down Spoken knowledge does not scale and does not survive staff changes. Good teams write. Design docs Before building anything substantial, write a short design doc and have it reviewed. The goal is to find the expensive mistakes while they are still cheap to fix: on paper, not in production. A common structure, used widely at Google and elsewhere: Context and scope: what problem, for whom, and why now. Goals and non-goals: non-goals are as important; they stop scope creep and endless debate. The design: APIs, data model, key flows, a diagram. Alternatives considered: and why they lost. This is often the most valuable section for future readers. Cross-cutting concerns: security, privacy, observability, migration, cost. Keep it as short as the problem allows. A two-page doc that people actually read beats a 30-page doc that they skim. Once decided, record significant choices as Architecture Decision Records (covered in the architecture module) so the why outlives the meeting. The four kinds of documentation The Diátaxis framework points out that documentation serves four different needs, and mixing them makes each worse: Kind Reader wants to ------ Tutorial Learn by doing How-to guide Achieve a specific task Reference Look up facts Explanation Understand why A README that mixes a walkthrough, exhaustive API details and a long architecture essay can make each task harder. A short overview can still link to those distinct resources. Separate them, and keep docs next to the code (docs as code) so they are reviewed and updated in the same pull request as the behaviour they describe. Runbooks are a special case of how-to guide: step-by-step instructions for operational tasks and alerts. Every alert that can page someone should link to a runbook that says what it means, how to check impact and what to try first. Key takeaways Team communication and system boundaries influence each other; organisation alone does not guarantee independence. Raise the bus factor through collective code ownership, pairing, review and maintained documentation. Separate tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation; record goals, non-goals and alternatives in design docs. Further reading Conway’s original observation Design Docs at Google — Malte Ubl Diátaxis documentation framework Docs as Code — Write the Docs

sum: Keep code review focused on code health and create conditions for shared learning.
x: Documentation spreads context before work starts; review spreads it as code changes. The same respect and willingness to ask questions matter in both. Code review Code review catches defects, but its bigger benefits are spreading knowledge (raising the bus factor) and keeping the codebase consistent. Google's published engineering practices give a useful standard: reviewers should favour approving a change once it definitely improves the overall health of the code, even if it is not perfect. Perfectionism in review slows everyone and drives people to accumulate changes into huge, unreviewable changes. Practical habits: Small changes. Smaller coherent changes are easier to understand and review; line counts alone do not determine review quality. Split refactoring from behaviour change (see the refactoring lesson). Fast responses. Google's guide says one business day is the maximum time to respond to a review request. Slow reviews are a hidden tax on every engineer. Comment on the code, not the person. "This loop is O(n²); a set would make it O(n)" (where n is the number of items) rather than "why would you do this?". Label severity. Prefix optional suggestions with Nit: so the author knows what blocks approval. Automate the trivial. Formatters and linters in CI settle style, so humans spend review time on design and correctness. Explain the why in the PR description: context, approach, how it was tested, and what the reviewer should focus on. Team health in general Psychological safety means the team believes it is safe to ask questions, acknowledge mistakes and take interpersonal risks. It helps people expose uncertainty during reviews and shared work. Onboarding is a test of your docs. Have every new joiner fix whatever confused them. Pairing and mobbing spread knowledge fast, especially on unfamiliar code. Async by default for things that do not need a meeting: written proposals, recorded decisions, threads rather than calls. Protect focus time. Rotate ownership of components and of on-call so expertise is not concentrated. Key takeaways Review small coherent changes promptly and distinguish blocking concerns from optional nits. Automate routine style so review can concentrate on design and correctness. Psychological safety, onboarding and shared work help people expose uncertainty and spread knowledge. Further reading The Standard of Code Review — Google Speed of Code Reviews — Google Five dynamics of effective teams — Google

sum: Plan rotation capacity, actionable alerts, escalation and recovery for responders.
