x: Running a service includes supporting the people who respond when it fails. Staffing arithmetic is a starting constraint; sustainable workload requires explicit policies and regular review. On-call that people can sustain If your team runs production services, someone needs to respond when they break at 3 a.m. Done badly, on-call burns people out and drives them away. Done well, it is a manageable part of the job that also teaches people how the system really behaves. Rotation design Google's SRE book gives concrete guidelines worth knowing: No more than about 25% of an engineer's time should be spent on call. With a primary and a secondary on call around the clock and week-long shifts, the ideal coverage calculation gives eight engineers for a single-site team, before leave and other resilience needs. Google separately recommends about six per site for dual-site teams, considering both coverage and critical team mass. Google reports around 6 hours of work per incident in its experience, including diagnosis and follow-up, and uses at most 2 incidents per 12-hour shift as a workload guideline. This is not a universal incident-duration estimate. Response expectations cited by Google: about 5 minutes for user-facing, time-critical services, about 30 minutes for less time-sensitive ones. Where does eight come from? Two roles must be filled at every moment, and nobody may spend more than a quarter of their time in either of them: With week-long shifts, each of the eight is on call (primary or secondary) for one week in every four, as the SRE book puts it. Real teams need more, to cover leave, illness and training. The incident limit follows the same kind of reasoning: A follow-the-sun rotation across suitable time zones and shift lengths can avoid night duty, with clear handovers. Check that the roster covers all 24 hours: London and San Francisco each working an ordinary eight-hour day do not provide complete coverage. Other essentials: A secondary and a clear escalation path, so nobody is alone with a problem beyond them. Handover notes at the end of each shift: what fired, what is still open, what to watch. Compensation and recovery: pay or time off for on-call, and a lie-in after a bad night. Training: shadow shifts and practice incidents before someone carries the pager alone. Alert hygiene The SRE book's test for a page: it should detect something urgent, actionable and actively or imminently user-visible. Every page should require human judgement; if a script could handle it, automate it. Common failures and fixes: Problem Fix ------ Pages on CPU > 80% without service risk Tie pages to actionable current or imminent service risk Same alert fires daily Fix the cause; downgrade or remove only if paging is unnecessary Alert with no runbook Add a runbook; keep necessary service-risk detection 20 alerts for 1 outage Group and deduplicate Alert fatigue is dangerous: when most pages are noise, people stop treating them as urgent, and the real one gets missed. Review every page from the last rotation in a weekly meeting and ask "was this worth waking someone for?". Key takeaways Two simultaneous duty roles at a 25% duty fraction require at least eight people in the simplified single-site model. That arithmetic excludes leave and says nothing about incident volume or recovery needs. Page for urgent actionable threats to users and use runbooks, escalation and alert review. Further reading Being On-Call — Google SRE book Monitoring Distributed Systems — Google SRE book

sum: Write blameless incident reviews and make owned prevention work part of normal delivery.
x: The on-call unit focused on response capacity. After a significant incident, use the evidence to improve both the service and the conditions in which people operate. Postmortems: learning, not blame After a significant incident, the team writes a postmortem: what happened, the impact, the timeline, contributing factors and follow-up actions. The service-level mechanics (severity levels, incident command, SLO triggers) are in the System Design reliability module. What matters at team level is the culture around it. A postmortem is blameless. It assumes everyone acted reasonably given what they knew at the time, and asks why the system made the mistake easy. "Alice ran the wrong migration" leads nowhere; "the migration tool runs against production by default with no confirmation" leads to a fix. Blamelessness is not about being nice. It is practical: if people are punished for honest mistakes, they hide them, and the organisation stops learning. Amy Edmondson's research on psychological safety (a shared belief that it is safe to admit mistakes and take interpersonal risks) found an association with team learning (not a guarantee of causation in every team), and Google's internal Project Aristotle study of team effectiveness reported it as the most important factor of the five it identified. What makes a postmortem worth writing: Action items with owners and dates, tracked like any other work. Untracked actions can create false confidence and leave preventable risks unaddressed. Contributing factors, not a single root cause. Real incidents usually involve several: a bug, a missing alert, a confusing dashboard. Sharing. Other teams learn from your failures cheaply. Many companies hold a regular postmortem review. Pitfalls Hero culture. Celebrating the person who fixes everything at 2 a.m. rewards the bus factor of one that caused the problem. Docs written once and never updated. Outdated instructions can mislead responders; flag uncertainty and maintain important procedures. Keep docs near the code and change them in the same PR. Review as gatekeeping. Blocking on style preferences, or leaving reviews for days, teaches people to avoid review. Paging on causes rather than symptoms. High CPU alone need not page, but imminent exhaustion that threatens users and requires urgent human action can justify a page. Blameless in name only. If a postmortem's real outcome is someone being quietly sidelined, the next incident will be reported later and less honestly. Key takeaways A blameless review explains decisions using the information available at the time. Record impact, timeline, contributing conditions and concrete preventive actions. Assign owners and track completion in the ordinary work system so the review changes practice. Further reading Postmortem Culture — Google SRE book

sum: Distinguish wave size, repetition time and wavelength, and predict how they change.
x: Every sound your synth makes ends up as a speaker cone pushing air back and forth. The air pressure at your ear rises and falls around normal atmospheric pressure, and your ear turns that pattern into what you hear. Inside the synth there is no air. There is first a sequence of numbers, then a voltage on a wire. The vocabulary is the same at every stage, though. Here, a waveform describes how a quantity (pressure, voltage, or a number in memory) changes over time, and we describe it by how big the change is, how often it repeats and where in its cycle it is. Start by distinguishing how large a wave is, how often it repeats and how far it travels. The four basic measurements Picture one repeating cycle of a wave plotted against time: Amplitude (A) is how far the wave swings from its centre line. In air that's a pressure difference; in a circuit it's volts; in software it's a number, conventionally between −1 and +1. Bigger amplitude sounds louder, though loudness perception is more complicated than amplitude alone. Period (T) is the time one full cycle takes, in seconds. Frequency (f) is how many cycles happen per second, in hertz (Hz). It's the reciprocal of the period (one divided by the period). Wavelength (λ) is the distance one cycle covers as it travels through a medium such as air. Frequency and period are two views of the same thing: if you know how long one cycle takes, you know how many fit in a second. For scale, a 440 Hz wave completes each cycle in about 2.27 milliseconds (ms). The relationship is exact for any repeating wave; it only stops being meaningful for sounds that don't repeat, such as noise. Wavelength needs one more ingredient, the speed at which the wave travels. In the time of one period, the wave moves forward by one wavelength: The speed of sound depends on the medium and its temperature (it is faster in warmer air and much faster in water or steel), so wavelength depends on the conditions in which sound travels. Wavelength matters for room acoustics and speaker design, including room resonances and how sound diffracts around obstacles. Inside a synth it barely matters at all: your signals live as samples and voltages, where only time and frequency count. Don't confuse wavelength with period. One is metres, the other seconds. Human hearing is usually quoted as roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz (20,000 Hz). The top end falls with age, and that range is a rule of thumb rather than a hard limit. In air, those frequencies have wavelengths of roughly 17 m down to 1.7 cm. Key takeaways Amplitude measures the size of the swing; frequency measures cycles per second. Frequency and period are reciprocals: doubling one halves the other. Wavelength is a distance in a medium; period is a time. Inside a synth, work with time and frequency. Further reading Sine wave — Wikipedia Speed of sound — Wikipedia Sound speed, frequency and wavelength — OpenStax

sum: Measure position within a cycle and explain reinforcement, cancellation and phase jumps.
x: Phase and radians The phase of a wave says where in its cycle it is at a given moment. You can measure it in fractions of a cycle (0 to 1), degrees (0° to 360°), or radians (0 to 2π). Maths libraries use radians, so get comfortable with them. A radian measures an angle by comparing arc length with circle radius. One full turn is about 6.283 radians. Cycle fractions, degrees and radians are three units for the same position: Cycles Degrees Radians --------- 0.25 90° π/2 ≈ 1.571 0.5 180° π ≈ 3.142 1 360° 2π ≈ 6.283 Phase matters most when you combine waves. Two identical sines in phase add up to double the amplitude. Shift one by half a cycle (π radians, 180°) and they cancel completely. Anywhere in between gives partial reinforcement or partial cancellation. That's why detuned oscillators "beat", and why some layered sounds go thin when a phase relationship shifts. Phase on its own, for a single steady tone, is mostly inaudible. Your ear can't tell a sine from the same sine starting a quarter-cycle later. What you can hear is a sudden phase jump in the middle of a tone: the waveform can jump to a new value instantly, creating a click. A phase change at a specially chosen point can leave the value unchanged, so a click is not inevitable. Pitfalls Degrees passed to sin. If phase is in degrees, convert it with math.radians before calling math.sin. A quarter-cycle should reach the positive peak, rather than an arbitrary value. Key takeaways One full cycle is 2π radians; maths-library sine functions expect radians. Relative phase controls how two waves reinforce or cancel. A sudden phase change can create a discontinuity and a click. Further reading Sinusoids — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA) Phase (waves) — Wikipedia)

t: Build a sine from its parameters
sum: Explain how frequency, elapsed time, phase and amplitude determine a sine’s value.
x: The sine wave formula The purest tone is a sine wave. This formula gives its value at any moment, and it is the starting point for every oscillator in the project: Read it from the inside out: f·t is the number of cycles completed after t seconds. At 440 Hz, after 0.01 s you've done 4.4 cycles. 2π·f·t converts cycles to radians, because sin wants radians. φ (phi) is the starting phase, in radians. A starting phase of π/2 turns a sine into a cosine. A scales the result, which otherwise swings between −1 and +1. For a sine starting at zero, a quarter-cycle reaches the positive peak, a half-cycle returns to zero and three quarters reaches the negative peak. An amplitude of 0.5 makes those peaks +0.5 and −0.5, whatever the frequency. Frequency determines how quickly you reach them. The formula describes an ideal, never-ending tone; real notes start, stop and change, which is what the rest of the module deals with. Frequency can also be measured in radians per second, called angular frequency. One cycle contains two pi radians, so angular frequency is about 6.283 times the cycles-per-second value. Why the sine is special A sine contains exactly one frequency. An ideal periodic waveform (a sawtooth, a square, or a repeating approximation to a sustained violin tone) can be built by adding sines at whole-number multiples of its fundamental frequency. Those whole-number components are its harmonics, and their amplitude recipe is a big part of its timbre. A real recorded note also changes over time and can contain noise. The synthesis module builds on this. Pitfalls Forgetting the 2π. sin(f·t) produces a tone 2π times too low (440 Hz becomes about 70 Hz). Key takeaways Frequency and elapsed time determine the number of cycles completed. Convert cycles to radians, add starting phase, then take the sine and scale its amplitude. Angular frequency measures radians per second; harmonics build richer periodic waveforms. Further reading Sinusoids — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA) Sine wave — Wikipedia Python sine and angle functions — Python documentation

t: Samples per cycle and phase increment
sum: Predict how pitch and sample rate change samples per cycle and per-sample phase advance.
x: From time to samples A digital synth computes values only at evenly spaced sample instants. The sample rate says how many of these occur each second; 48,000 per second is a common rate. Each sample uses the sine’s value at that instant. The first sample is at the start, the next is one sample period later, and so on; samples need not land on peaks or whole-cycle boundaries. Two practical quantities describe how an oscillator moves through those instants. Samples per period tells you how many numbers describe one cycle: Phase increment is how far round the cycle you move between one sample and the next. It's the reciprocal of samples per period: At 48 kHz, a 440 Hz cycle spans about 109 sample periods, while a 3520 Hz cycle spans fewer than 14. Those spans need not be whole numbers. Notice: Samples per period is rarely a whole number. A 440 Hz cycle at 48 kHz takes 109.09 samples, so the samples land at slightly different points of each cycle. That's fine; the phase is tracked as a real number. Higher pitches get fewer samples per cycle. At 3520 Hz you have under 14 points per cycle. The Nyquist-limit unit shows where this runs out. The phase increment depends on both tone frequency and sample rate. Change the rate to 44.1 kHz and the step for every note changes. If a synth assumes the wrong sample rate, every note comes out at the wrong pitch. Pitfalls Hard-coding the sample rate. Compute the increment from the actual rate the audio hardware is running at. Key takeaways Sample time is the sample index divided by the sample rate. Samples per period is sample rate divided by tone frequency; it need not be a whole number. Phase increment is tone frequency divided by sample rate in cycles per sample. Use the hardware’s actual rate. Further reading Sinusoids — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA) Numerically controlled oscillator (phase accumulator) — Wikipedia

sum: Preserve phase through frequency changes and processing blocks without an ever-growing counter.
x: The phase accumulator A sine can be evaluated using each sample’s elapsed time. Many real oscillators instead keep the phase of a wave in a running variable and add the increment each sample, wrapping it back into range after each full cycle: This phase accumulator is the core of many digital oscillators. It has three advantages over recomputing phase from a growing sample counter. 1. Frequency changes preserve phase. Recomputing phase from total elapsed time with a new frequency can make the phase jump. Switch from 440 Hz to 450 Hz at 0.525 s: At the switch time, the two formulas give values of 0 and full scale. Switching directly between them can introduce an abrupt waveform jump and an audible click; the exact adjacent samples and audibility depend on the switch and playback conditions. With an accumulator, you just change inc and the phase carries on from where it was. Vibrato, pitch bends and glides can use this. An abrupt increment change can still make a transient by changing the waveform’s slope; ramping the increment makes the transition gentler. 2. Precision stays bounded. The phase is always between 0 and 1, so its spacing stays bounded instead of getting coarser with elapsed time. Rounding of the increment and additions can still introduce a small frequency error. A sample counter n only grows. A 32-bit float (common on embedded chips) represents integers exactly only up to 2²⁴ = 16,777,216. At 48 kHz that's about 349.5 seconds, under six minutes. At that boundary, adding one to a float32 counter can leave it unchanged. An oscillator relying on that counter can stall; other ever-growing time calculations can also lose phase accuracy. 3. It's cheap. One add and a compare per sample, then a waveform lookup. The waveform part can be sin, a table, or simple arithmetic for a sawtooth (the phase itself, rescaled, is a naive saw). Keep the state between blocks Audio is processed in blocks (say 48 samples at a time). The phase must persist from one block to the next. Resetting it to zero each block repeats the same 48-sample segment. At 48 kHz, that repeated segment has a 1 kHz repetition rate, with spectral components on a 1 kHz grid, rather than the intended 440 Hz sine. Boundaries can jump and the result can buzz or click; the exact spectrum and audibility depend on the waveform, reset timing and playback conditions. Real-world analogy: A clock hand changing speed A clock hand can speed up without jumping to a new position. It continues from wherever it has reached. How it maps: The hand’s position is oscillator phase; its speed is frequency. Changing the phase increment changes future progress while keeping the current phase. Where it stops: An oscillator’s phase wraps every cycle, and digital updates introduce rounding. A continuous phase also does not guarantee a perfectly smooth slope when its speed changes abruptly. Why absolute-time glides go wrong Frequency is the rate at which phase advances. If you multiply a changing frequency by all the elapsed time, earlier cycles are effectively recalculated at the new frequency. This is the practical failure during a glide: The oscillator can run much faster than the setting suggests, and the error depends on when the glide begins. Frequencies pushed beyond Nyquist also alias in sampled playback. Accumulating only the new phase step avoids this recalculation of the past. An accumulator adds each sample’s current increment to the phase already earned. It therefore follows the requested frequency sample by sample, subject to ordinary rounding error. Pitfalls Ignoring wrap. Without the wrap, a float phase eventually loses precision like the counter does. Key takeaways Keep phase as oscillator state and add the current increment for every sample. Changing the increment preserves phase; recomputing from absolute time can cause jumps. Wrap phase to keep numerical spacing bounded, and retain it between audio blocks. Rounding error still remains. Further reading Sinusoids — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA) Numerically controlled oscillator (phase accumulator) — Wikipedia Changing frequency requires accumulated phase — CMU Introduction to Computer Music

sum: Use doublings and logarithms to explain octaves and equal-tempered semitones.
x: A synth receives "play note 60" and has to turn it into a phase increment. Between those two is a formula you'll write in your first afternoon and use for the rest of the project. Understanding it properly also explains why pitch bends, detune and vibrato are specified in semitones and cents, not hertz. Pitch is a ratio, not a difference Frequency is physical: cycles per second. Pitch is perceptual: how high or low a note sounds. For a steady periodic tone, the pitch we hear closely tracks the fundamental frequency (the rate at which the whole waveform repeats). The crucial fact is that our ears judge pitch by ratios. Going from 110 Hz to 220 Hz sounds like the same step as going from 440 Hz to 880 Hz, even though the first is a 110 Hz difference and the second is 440 Hz. Both are a doubling, and a doubling of frequency is an octave. So pitch is logarithmic in frequency: equal steps in pitch are equal multiplications of frequency. This is the basis of musical pitch arithmetic. Exponentials and logarithms, briefly An exponential turns a pitch offset into a frequency ratio. One octave means doubling; two octaves means doubling twice. Fractional octaves fill the spaces between those steps. A base-2 logarithm works backwards: it counts how many doublings a positive frequency ratio represents. Adding pitch offsets combines their ratios by multiplication. Up an octave and then up another octave doubles twice, regardless of the starting note. You do not need to memorise a logarithm identity to use this idea. The practical rule follows: do pitch arithmetic in note space, then convert to hertz once at the end. In note space, transposing, bending and modulating are simple additions. In hertz they're multiplications, and mixing the two up is a classic bug. Semitones and equal temperament Western chromatic music commonly divides the octave into 12 semitones. In twelve-tone equal temperament (12-TET), every semitone has the same frequency ratio. Twelve of them must make an octave (×2), so each one is the number that gives 2 when 12 copies of it are multiplied together. Each semitone up multiplies frequency by about 1.0595; twelve such steps exactly double it. For example, the note one semitone above A4 (440 Hz) is A♯4, at about 466.16 Hz. Equal temperament gives every key the same interval pattern. That flexibility means most intervals differ slightly from pure whole-number ratios. Simple whole-number ratios such as 3:2 (the pure ratio of a perfect fifth) don't land exactly on a 12-TET note: Interval Just ratio 12-TET ratio Difference ------------ Octave 2.000 2.000 0 cents Fifth 1.500 1.4983 12-TET 1.96 cents flat Major third 1.250 1.2599 12-TET 13.69 cents sharp The difference column uses cents: hundredths of a semitone, explored in the tuning unit. 12-TET is a common default tuning; alternative tunings are a later feature. Pitfalls Adding hertz for musical intervals. "Up a fifth" is ×1.4983, not +220 Hz. Key takeaways An octave doubles frequency; musical intervals use ratios rather than fixed hertz differences. Exponentials turn octave offsets into ratios, and base-2 logarithms count doublings. In 12-TET, twelve identical semitone ratios multiply to two. Just intervals differ slightly. Further reading Equal temperament — Wikipedia Cent (music) — Wikipedia) Notes, MIDI numbers and frequencies — UNSW

sum: Turn note numbers into hertz, invert the conversion and avoid integer-division and octave-label bugs.
x: MIDI note numbers MIDI identifies notes with a number from 0 to 127. Note 60 is middle C, and 69 is the A above it, which is tuned to 440 Hz by convention. Each step of 1 is one semitone. Your synth needs to turn a note number into a frequency, and the usual equal-tempered conversion follows those ratios: Going the other way, a tuner or a pitch detector turns a frequency back into a (usually fractional) note number: Both conversions assume 12-TET with A4 at 440 Hz. Changing the reference pitch changes the frequency scale; a different tuning system may require a different mapping altogether. Notes 21 to 108 are the 88 keys of a piano (A0 to C8). Note 0, at about 8.2 Hz, is below hearing; you'd hear it only through its harmonics. Octave labels vary, numbers don't In scientific pitch notation middle C is C4, so note 60 = C4 and 69 = A4. Some software and instruments label note 60 as C3 instead: Ableton Live’s manual gives its full MIDI range as C−2 to G8, which places note 60 at C3. The number on the wire is always 60, so think in note numbers and check how each piece of gear displays them. Keep the 440 as a parameter (a4 above). A "master tune" control is just a different reference. Pitfalls Integer division. In C-family languages, (n − 69) / 12 with integers truncates to whole octaves. Use floating point. Assuming octave labels. Use note numbers between systems. Key takeaways The conventional 12-TET reference is note 69 at 440 Hz, with one semitone per note-number step. Use floating-point division in the exponent and keep the reference pitch configurable. Note 60 is middle C; displayed octave names vary between products. Further reading MIDI Tuning Standard — Wikipedia MIDI 1.0 core specifications — MIDI Association Piano key frequencies — Wikipedia Sampler key range — Ableton Live 12 manual Tuning reference and note mapping — MIDI Association Notes, MIDI numbers and frequencies — UNSW

sum: Express tuning errors in cents and predict the beat rate of two close tones.
x: Cents A cent is 1/100 of a 12-TET semitone, so there are 1200 cents per octave. To measure how far apart two frequencies are in pitch, count the octaves between them and multiply by 1200: To apply a cents detune, multiply by the ratio for that interval. The reference conversion is: How small is a cent? It is often smaller than a pitch change a listener can reliably distinguish between separate tones. The just-noticeable difference depends on frequency, duration, level, timbre, training and the listener. Research finds substantial variation with test conditions, so use measured results for the particular listening task. Two tones played together are another matter: even a cent or two of mistuning can be heard as slow beating. Cents are the natural unit for detune. Here's a function that finds the nearest note and how far off it is: The n // 12 − 1 gives the octave number in scientific pitch notation, because note 0 is C−1. Detuning and beats Play two oscillators at nearly the same frequency and you hear the level wobble. That's beating: the two sines drift in and out of phase, reinforcing then cancelling. The wobble happens once for every cycle one oscillator gains on the other, so its rate is the difference in frequency. For example, detuning one 440 Hz oscillator by +10 cents produces about 442.55 Hz. The pair beats about 2.55 times per second. The frequency difference describes the interference envelope. A difference of a few hertz sounds like a slow level wobble. As the difference grows into tens of hertz, listeners may hear rapid beats, roughness or two distinct tones rather than a countable wobble. The perceptual boundaries depend on the tones and listener. Because the detune is in cents, the beat rate grows with pitch: the same 10 cents at 880 Hz beats at about 5.1 Hz. This is why a fixed-cents detune sounds "wider" in the high register, and some synths offer a fixed-Hz detune as an alternative. Key takeaways A semitone contains 100 cents, and an octave contains 1200. Use a logarithm to measure an interval and an exponential to apply detune. Two close tones beat at their frequency difference; fixed-cents detune beats faster on higher notes. Further reading Cent (music) — Wikipedia) Pitch discrimination and harmonicity — Micheyl, Ryan & Oxenham Beats and their perception — UNSW Physclips Beat (acoustics) — Wikipedia)

sum: Compare fixed-hertz and fixed-cents vibrato and combine bend, detune and modulation before conversion.
x: Linear vs exponential modulation Suppose an LFO adds vibrato. Two ways to do it: Linear (in Hz): add a fixed number of hertz. Exponential (in pitch): multiply by a fixed ratio, set in cents. A fixed 10 Hz swing is a much larger fraction of a 110 Hz bass note than of a 440 Hz note. Its musical interval is therefore wider in the bass. Specifying a fixed cents depth instead gives the same pitch interval in each register. Option 2 is what players expect for vibrato and pitch bend. MIDI pitch bend, for example, is normally interpreted as a number of semitones (the bend range), added in note space. Analogue synths face the same problem in hardware. The common 1 volt per octave standard, used by Moog instruments, makes control voltage linear in pitch: each extra volt doubles the oscillator frequency, using an exponential converter inside the oscillator. For example, two extra volts request two octaves: a 110 Hz oscillator would ideally become 440 Hz. A semitone needs one twelfth of a volt. Real oscillators follow this law only over a limited range, which is why analogue synths need calibrating. Pitfalls Converting too early. Keep pitch as a float note number (including bend, detune and modulation in semitones), then convert to hertz, then to a phase increment. Key takeaways Fixed-hertz modulation changes its musical depth across the keyboard. Fixed-cents modulation applies the same interval on every note. Add bend, detune and modulation in note space, then convert to frequency and phase increment. Further reading MIDI Tuning Standard — Wikipedia CV/gate — Wikipedia

sum: Separate pitch from harmonic content and explain beating between equal-tempered notes and harmonics.
x: Pitch vs timbre Play a sine and a sawtooth at 220 Hz. They have the same pitch but sound completely different. The difference is timbre, often loosely called "tone colour". A sawtooth at 220 Hz contains sine components at 220, 440, 660, 880 Hz and so on: the harmonic series, every whole-number multiple of the fundamental. In an ideal sawtooth their amplitudes fall off steadily. The second harmonic is twice the fundamental frequency, the third is three times it, and so on. In an ideal sawtooth, the second has half the fundamental’s amplitude and the third one third. Higher harmonics grow weaker but enrich the waveform’s shape. A sine has only the 220 Hz component. Because all the extra components are exact multiples, the waveform still repeats 220 times per second, and the ear still hears 220 Hz. The harmonic series is also where just ratios come from: harmonics 2, 3, 4, 5 give an octave, a fifth above that, another octave, and a major third. The 5th harmonic of 110 Hz is 550 Hz, about 14 cents below the 12-TET C♯5 (554.37 Hz). Timbre also depends on how the sound changes over time: the attack, how harmonics fade, noise. Subtractive synthesis works by starting with a harmonically rich wave and filtering harmonics away, changing timbre while leaving pitch alone. That's the next module. The missing fundamental Pitch perception isn't just "find the lowest component". If you remove the 220 Hz component from a sawtooth and keep 440, 660, 880 Hz and so on, most listeners still hear a pitch of 220 Hz, because the harmonics are spaced 220 Hz apart. This is why small speakers can suggest bass notes they can't reproduce. Key takeaways A periodic waveform’s harmonics lie at whole-number multiples of its fundamental. Harmonic amplitudes and changes over time shape timbre. Listeners can hear a missing fundamental from the spacing of the remaining harmonics. Further reading Equal temperament — Wikipedia Beat (acoustics) — Wikipedia) Timbre — Wikipedia

t: Sample timing, block deadlines and memory
sum: Interpret sample instants and budget processing time, buffer memory and audio data rate.
x: A digital synth handles a timed stream of numbers, and a converter turns it into an analogue voltage. This lesson is about what those numbers are, how precise they need to be, and what goes wrong at the edges. Two separate settings decide the quality of a digital signal. Sample rate sets how often you measure. Bit depth sets how finely each measurement is recorded. Neither of them is the playback volume, which is decided by the numbers' size relative to full scale and by whatever amplifier follows the converter. Discrete-time signals Sampling a signal means measuring a continuous signal at evenly spaced instants. The spacing between instants is the sample period, so each sample index identifies one measurement time. At 48 kHz, sample instants are about 20.8 microseconds apart. Sample indices count these instants from zero; dividing the index by the rate gives its time in seconds. Picture each sample as a lollipop: a value at an instant, with nothing defined in between. A sample is a value at an instant, rather than a little rectangle of constant value. Ideal band-limited reconstruction determines the smooth signal from those samples; real DACs approximate this using their reconstruction filters. Common sample rates: Rate Typical use ------ 44.1 kHz CD audio 48 kHz Video, most pro audio and audio hardware 96 kHz High-resolution recording; some synth internals The sample rate fixes the highest frequency you can represent: half the sample rate, as the Nyquist-limit unit explains. At 48 kHz the ideal reconstruction band lies strictly below 24 kHz, above the roughly 20 kHz limit of hearing. Higher rates mostly buy room for processing that creates high frequencies (distortion, sharp waveforms), not extra audible treble. It also sets your time budget. Synths process audio in blocks (a fixed number of samples handled in one go), and the hardware plays a block in a fixed time: All the work for a block must finish in less time than that, every time. If it doesn't, the hardware runs out of samples and you hear a click or dropout. How much data is that? The numbers add up quickly, which matters on a microcontroller: One second of mono float32 at 48 kHz is 192,000 bytes, about 192 kB (kilobytes). Stereo 24-bit audio data at 48 kHz is 2.304 Mbit/s (megabits per second). On an I²S bus, 24-bit samples often travel in 32-bit slots, giving a 3.072 MHz bit clock for two such slots per sample frame. Check the actual interface configuration. A delay effect with a two-second buffer needs 384,000 bytes (384 kB) per channel in float32. Check this against your board's RAM before designing features. Pitfalls Confusing the three settings. Sample rate (how often), bit depth (how finely), level (how big relative to full scale). Turning a synth down in software doesn't change its bit depth, but very quiet integer signals do use fewer effective bits. Key takeaways Sample rate determines the spacing of sample instants and the duration of each processing block. Finish each block before the hardware consumes it or audio can drop out. Buffer memory scales with duration, sample rate, bytes per sample and channel count. Further reading Sampling (signal processing) — Wikipedia)

sum: Explain how bit depth changes level spacing and distinguish rounding error from clipping.
x: Bit depth and quantisation Each sample must be stored with finite precision. Every extra bit doubles the number of patterns available to represent a sample. For example, 16 bits provide 65,536 distinct levels. A signed sample uses some codes for negative values, one for zero and the rest for positive values; it does not lose half its precision by being signed. Bits Levels Integer range --------- 8 256 −128 to 127 16 65,536 −32,768 to 32,767 24 16,777,216 −8,388,608 to 8,388,607 Rounding the true value to the nearest level is quantisation. The levels are evenly spaced, so the step size is the width of the range divided by the number of levels, and rounding to the nearest level is wrong by at most half a step either way: This assumes the signal stays inside full scale; a value beyond the top or bottom level is clipped, and its error can be much larger. Real-world analogy: Rounding a length to ruler marks A ruler with finer marks lets you report a length more closely. Rounding to the nearest mark moves the report by no more than half the gap between marks. How it maps: Ruler marks are integer sample levels; adding a bit makes the marks twice as dense across the same full-scale range. Nearest rounding chooses the closest available level. Where it stops: An audio sample can be negative, and its signed endpoints are asymmetric. Values beyond the available range overload rather than simply rounding to a nearby internal mark. Pitfalls Truncating instead of rounding. Truncation toward zero gives sign-dependent error approaching a full step; it need not add DC to a symmetric signal. Rounding downward instead has a negative bias, averaging about half a step under the uniform-error model. Nearest rounding limits error to half a step away from overload. Key takeaways Each extra bit doubles the number of distinct integer sample values. Nearest rounding stays within half a step away from overload. Signed integer endpoints are asymmetric; overload and truncation require separate care. Further reading Quantization (signal processing) — Wikipedia) Audio bit depth — Wikipedia Taking The Mystery Out of the Infamous Formula "SNR = 6.02N + 1.76dB" — Analog Devices MT-001

sum: Use the six-decibel-per-bit rule and recognise when coarse quantisation violates its assumptions.
x: Quantisation noise and the six-decibel rule For a busy signal much larger than one step, the error behaves like a small random noise added to the signal: quantisation noise. How far that noise sits below the signal is the SQNR, the signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio, measured in decibels (dB, a logarithmic scale for ratios explained in the decibel-gain unit). The standard result, for a full-scale sine wave, is: Each extra bit adds about 6 dB, because it halves the step size and halving an amplitude is −6.02 dB. 16 bits gives about 98 dB; 24 bits about 146 dB. The six-decibel rule assumes a sine that nearly fills full scale without overloading and rounding error that is approximately uniform and unrelated to the signal. A quieter signal sits closer to the same quantisation floor. Coarse periodic signals can instead produce correlated distortion. The Analog Devices tutorial derives the result in detail. You can check this in a few lines: At 12 and 16 bits the formula agrees closely. At 4 bits this example also overloads the positive endpoint: its largest code is 7/8, below the sine's 0.999 peak. That clipping contributes substantial error. In addition, the uniform, signal-independent error model is only an approximation; low-resolution periodic quantisation can produce distortion rather than a gentle hiss. Why 997 Hz? Test tones are often slightly "odd" frequencies like 997 Hz rather than 1000 Hz. With 1000 Hz at 48 kHz, each cycle is exactly 48 samples, so the same few quantisation errors repeat every cycle and pile up at harmonic frequencies. A tone without that short repeating sample pattern can distribute quantisation error more broadly; the relation between test frequency and sample rate matters, rather than whether a number is odd. Key takeaways The uniform-error model predicts about 6.02 dB per bit plus 1.76 dB for a full-scale sine. Lower signal level reduces SQNR even when the file’s bit depth stays fixed. Coarse quantisation and endpoint overload can produce distortion and disagree with the noise model. Further reading Quantization (signal processing) — Wikipedia) Audio bit depth — Wikipedia Taking The Mystery Out of the Infamous Formula "SNR = 6.02N + 1.76dB" — Analog Devices MT-001

sum: Explain why reducing bit depth needs dither and why a converter’s word length exceeds its effective resolution.
x: Dither and real converter noise The same problem returns for very quiet signals, even at 16 bits. A sine whose amplitude is under half a step rounds to zero every time and vanishes completely. A fade-out turns gritty in its last few bits. Dither addresses this by adding a tiny amount of random noise before quantising. Common triangular (TPDF) dither spans two quantisation steps peak-to-peak. With suitable dither and no overload, the output error’s mean and noise power no longer vary with the signal: you trade extra hiss for removal of systematic quantisation distortion, and quiet details survive statistically inside the noise. This does not mean every property of the total error is independent of the signal. Dither matters whenever you reduce bit depth, such as when exporting 16-bit files. Inside a 32-bit float synth it's rarely needed. Real converters A "24-bit" converter outputs 24-bit words, but its analogue noise floor is far above the theoretical 146 dB. Examples from TI’s datasheets are 99 dB typical for the PCM1808 ADC and 112 dB typical for the PCM5102A DAC. These are A-weighted figures under the stated test conditions. The higher-performance PCM1792A specifies 127 dB with a 2 V RMS stereo test output and 132 dB in its mono test configuration. These are different configurations, not a guaranteed range for any board. Board circuitry and power supplies affect the result, so check the datasheet and measure. 24 bits gives a comfortable margin so that converter noise, not quantisation, sets the floor. A noise-only estimate of effective resolution can be obtained by rearranging the full-scale-sine SQNR rule from the preceding unit. Formal ENOB measurements normally use SINAD, which includes distortion as well as noise; substituting an A-weighted dynamic-range figure gives only an estimate. Key takeaways Dither adds noise before quantisation to decorrelate error from quiet signals. Use dither when reducing bit depth; continuous float processing usually does not need it. A 24-bit converter’s analogue noise floor is higher than ideal 24-bit quantisation noise. Check and measure the hardware. Further reading Dither — Wikipedia Taking The Mystery Out of the Infamous Formula "SNR = 6.02N + 1.76dB" — Analog Devices MT-001 PCM5102A audio DAC datasheet — Texas Instruments PCM1808 ADC datasheet — Texas Instruments PCM1792A DAC datasheet — Texas Instruments SINAD, SNR and ENOB — Analog Devices MT-003

sum: Keep internal float headroom and convert safely at fixed-format boundaries.
x: The −1..1 convention and floating point Inside most audio software, samples are floating-point numbers where ±1.0 means full scale. The converter's maximum output corresponds to 1.0. This convention lets the same code work whatever bit depth the hardware uses. Why floats internally? Headroom. A float can hold 3.7 or −12.0 without trouble. Mixing several voices can exceed 1.0 mid-chain and be scaled down later without clipping; normal floating-point rounding still applies. Integers would overflow or clip. Resolution where it matters. A 32-bit float has a 24-bit significand plus an exponent. Quiet signals in the normal range keep their relative precision, because the exponent scales with the value; subnormal values lose significant bits. Simple maths. Gain is a multiply; mixing is an add. Integer and fixed-point arithmetic formats still matter at the edges: WAV files, converter interfaces, and microcontrollers without a floating-point unit. The conversion at the boundary is where bugs live: Three things to notice: 1.7 was clipped to 32767. Over-range floats must be clipped at conversion, never cast directly. In C and C++, converting a float to an integer type that can't hold its value is undefined behaviour. In practice you may get a wrapped value or, on x86, the "integer indefinite" value −2,147,483,648: either way, a loud crack. NumPy is no safer: in testing, np.array([1.7 32767]).astype(np.int16) gave −9833, silently. Asymmetry. Integers run from −32768 to +32767, so full scale isn't symmetric. Libraries choose 32767 or 32768 as the scale factor. Inconsistent scale factors. Here the code multiplied by 32767 but divided by 32768, so a round trip shrinks the signal very slightly. Pick one convention and use it both ways. Pitfalls Casting instead of clipping at float-to-integer conversion. Denormals. Float values extremely close to zero (subnormals, or denormals) are much slower to process on some processors: some x86 instructions on some processors need a slow assist, costing tens or hundreds of cycles. The penalty depends on the processor, instruction and floating-point mode; benchmark the target rather than assuming a fixed cost. Decaying filters and reverbs can produce them. The usual fixes are to switch on the CPU's flush-to-zero (and denormals-are-zero) mode for the audio thread, as many audio frameworks do, or to add a tiny offset or noise so the values never get that small. Key takeaways With floats, ±1 is nominal full scale and intermediate results can exceed it. Clamp over-range values before integer conversion and use consistent scale factors. Float precision follows the signal’s scale, but subnormal values can have processor-specific performance costs. Further reading Single-precision floating-point format — Wikipedia Subnormal number — Wikipedia Subnormal numbers — Intel documentation Floating-to-integer conversion — C++ standard draft

t: The Nyquist limit and ambiguous samples
sum: Explain why sufficiently band-limited signals reconstruct exactly and why frequencies beyond Nyquist become ambiguous.
x: Sampling has a hard limit. Above a certain frequency, a sampled signal stops meaning what you think it means: a 30 kHz tone and an 18 kHz tone can produce exactly the same samples. This is digital aliasing, usually just called aliasing, and it's the most important limitation in digital synthesis. For a synth builder it's not an abstract worry. The classic analogue waveforms (sawtooth, square, pulse) have harmonics that go on for ever. Generate them naively in software and some of those harmonics fold back into the audible range as clangy, out-of-tune tones. This lesson explains why, and how to predict exactly where they'll land. The sampling theorem The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem says: A strictly band-limited signal can be reconstructed ideally when the sample rate is more than twice its highest frequency. This requires all frequency content to remain below the boundary, including harmonics. The practical boundary is half the sample rate, called the Nyquist frequency. At 48 kHz that boundary is 24 kHz; the signal’s content must stay strictly below it for unambiguous ideal reconstruction. Some common rates and their boundaries: Sample rate Nyquist frequency ------ 44.1 kHz 22.05 kHz 48 kHz 24 kHz 96 kHz 48 kHz "Perfectly reconstructed" is a strong claim and it's true. Below Nyquist, samples aren't a rough approximation of the wave: they contain all its information. A 10 kHz sine at 48 kHz has only 4.8 samples per cycle and looks like a jagged mess on a plot, yet ideal reconstruction rebuilds a pure 10 kHz sine from those samples. Real DACs approximate the ideal with finite filters, finite precision and analogue noise. The condition is strict: below half the sample rate, rather than at it. A sine exactly at the boundary gets sampled twice per cycle. Depending on its phase, the samples might be +1, −1, +1, −1 or 0, 0, 0, 0. They can't tell you the amplitude. What aliasing is Take a sine at 30 kHz and sample it at 48 kHz. Its phase moves more than half a cycle per sample. Because whole turns leave no trace in the sine value, the samples can equally describe a lower-frequency sine moving in the opposite phase direction. At this rate, they match an inverted 18 kHz sine: The 30 kHz samples equal the 18 kHz samples with the sign flipped (a phase inversion). Once sampled, nothing can tell them apart. A DAC reconstructing the baseband will output the 18 kHz component. The 30 kHz tone has taken on an alias frequency, or alias. Key takeaways The Nyquist frequency is half the sample rate; the reconstruction condition is strictly below it. A band-limited wave’s samples retain its information even when a plot looks jagged. Above-Nyquist tones can produce the same samples as lower tones, so their original frequency is lost. Further reading Sampling Theorem — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA) Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem — Wikipedia Aliasing — Wikipedia

sum: Wrap a component by the sample rate, reflect it below Nyquist and trace rising-frequency sweeps.
x: Following an alias frequency Picture the frequency axis folded back and forth like a paper fan, with creases at every multiple of the Nyquist frequency (fs/2 in the drawing, where fs is the sample rate): Any frequency maps to the point directly below it on the first segment, from 0 up to the Nyquist frequency. As a procedure: Divide the frequency by the sample rate and keep the remainder (this is "modulo"), giving a value from 0 up to the sample rate. If the result is above the Nyquist frequency, subtract it from the sample rate. This reference rule implements that procedure. It predicts the folded frequency; phase still affects the signed waveform and special fold-point samples. The formula holds for any frequency, sine by sine. A complex sound is a sum of sines, so apply it to each component separately. The examples show that a very high input can appear near the bottom of the audio band. Removing whole sample-rate multiples first handles frequencies beyond the first fold. Notice the behaviour as an input sweeps upwards: the alias rises to 24 kHz, then falls to 0 at 48 kHz, then rises again. A rising pitch whose alias falls is the unmistakable sound of aliasing. Key takeaways Take the frequency’s remainder after division by the sample rate. Reflect remainders above half the sample rate back into the lower half. Compute complex sounds component by component; aliases reverse direction at fold points. Further reading Sampling Theorem — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA) Aliasing — Wikipedia

t: Why naive sawtooths and squares alias
sum: Explain why waveform edges create aliases and why folded harmonics can fall below the note.
x: Why sharp waveforms alias A sine has one frequency. A sawtooth has harmonics at every whole-number multiple of its frequency, and their amplitudes fall slowly. A sawtooth’s second harmonic has half the fundamental’s amplitude, its third one third and so on. Even the twentieth is only about 26 dB below the fundamental, so very high harmonics cannot simply be assumed inaudible. A square has only the odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th, …), whose amplitudes also fall as one over the harmonic number. That fall-off is slow, so a lot of energy sits in very high harmonics. The cause is the waveform's sharp edge. A discontinuity (an instant jump) needs infinitely many harmonics to describe, and a waveform with a jump has harmonic amplitudes that halve per octave of harmonic number (about 6 dB). A triangle wave has corners but no jumps; its harmonic amplitudes fall fourfold per octave (about 12 dB), so it aliases far less. A naive sawtooth is generated directly from the phase accumulator (the phase-accumulator unit) by rescaling the phase. Rescaling the wrapped phase from zero-to-one into minus-one-to-plus-one creates a rising ramp. At each wrap it jumps straight from the top back to the bottom: that is the naive sawtooth’s sharp edge. That jump makes it a sample of the ideal infinite-bandwidth sawtooth. Every harmonic above Nyquist folds back. Take a high note, 1760 Hz (A6), at 48 kHz: Harmonics up to the thirteenth (22,880 Hz) are below 24 kHz and fine. Harmonics 14 and up fold back; many land away from multiples of 1760 Hz. Some higher aliases can also coincide with genuine harmonic bins. Which aliases land low, where they are most audible? Harmonic 27 lands at 480 Hz, below the note's own fundamental, only about 29 dB down. None of these are harmonics of 1760 Hz, so they sound like an inharmonic, metallic ring. As the note bends, they slide in the wrong directions. Low notes are less affected (their high harmonics are much weaker by the time they reach Nyquist), which is why naive oscillators can sound fine in the bass and terrible at the top. You can't filter it out afterwards Once an alias is at 480 Hz, it's indistinguishable from a real 480 Hz component. A low-pass filter after the oscillator can't remove it without removing real content too. Aliasing has to be prevented where the high frequencies are created. Key takeaways Sawtooth and square jumps need slowly decaying harmonics, so high pitches alias strongly. A folded harmonic can fall below the fundamental and become an inharmonic tone. After folding, an alias cannot be distinguished from wanted content at the same frequency. Further reading Alias-Free Digital Synthesis of Classic Analog Waveforms — Stilson & Smith (CCRMA) Aliasing — Wikipedia Sawtooth wave — Wikipedia

sum: Choose input filtering, band-limited oscillators and oversampling where new high frequencies are created.
x: Preventing aliasing in a synth There are two situations. 1. Sampling a real analogue signal (an ADC). Here an anti-aliasing filter removes content above Nyquist before it can fold. Every audio interface input has one. In a modern delta-sigma ADC, the converter samples many times faster than the final sample rate, so a simple analogue low-pass in front is enough, and a steep digital filter does the rest before the rate is reduced to the final rate. 2. Generating a signal digitally (an oscillator). There's no analogue signal to filter: the samples are computed directly. So the oscillator itself must only generate content below Nyquist. Established techniques, at a conceptual level: Additive synthesis: sum sines for each harmonic, stopping below Nyquist. Exact, but costly for low notes with hundreds of harmonics. Band-limited wavetables: precompute a single cycle with only the harmonics that fit, keeping several tables for different pitch ranges and picking one per note. BLIT: construct a band-limited impulse train and integrate it to obtain the desired waveform, taking care with DC and numerical drift. BLEP methods: replace each naive discontinuity with a band-limited step, often by adding a precomputed correction. PolyBLEP uses a cheap polynomial approximation to the step correction. Oversampling: run the oscillator at, say, 4× the output rate, low-pass filter digitally, then discard samples. Aliases still occur, but further up where harmonics are weaker, and the filter removes content outside the output passband before downsampling. Aliases already folded into that passband remain. The roadmap suggests comparing a naive waveform with a library's band-limited version rather than inventing a technique. Stilson and Smith's paper in the further reading is the classic overview. Nonlinear processing aliases too. Clipping, distortion and waveshaping create new harmonics. FM creates sidebands, which need not be harmonics. A hard clipper applied to a 5 kHz sine creates harmonics at 15, 25, 35 kHz and so on, and those above Nyquist fold back. Oversampling around the nonlinear stage is the standard remedy. Key takeaways ADC input filtering removes unwanted high frequencies before sampling or decimation. Digital oscillators need band-limited generation or a suitable correction technique. Nonlinear processing also generates above-Nyquist content. Oversampling helps, but it does not make naive waveforms alias-free. Further reading Alias-Free Digital Synthesis of Classic Analog Waveforms — Stilson & Smith (CCRMA) Oversampling — Wikipedia Hard Sync Without Aliasing — Eli Brandt

sum: Distinguish out-of-band DAC images from in-band aliases and trace the conversion chain.
x: Reconstruction: the DAC side A DAC is given one number per sample period. A crude converter holds each value until the next (a zero-order hold), producing a staircase. That staircase contains the wanted signal plus image frequencies: copies of the spectrum mirrored around multiples of the sample rate. For a 1 kHz tone at a 48 kHz sample rate, the first images sit at 47 and 49 kHz: one kilohertz either side of the sample rate. More sit at 95 and 97 kHz, either side of twice the rate. Images are not aliases. An alias is a folded component inside the represented band, created when sampling; images sit above Nyquist, created when converting back to analogue, and a filter can remove them. A reconstruction filter (anti-imaging filter) removes the images, leaving the smooth wave the theorem promises. Most modern audio converters are delta-sigma designs that internally oversample and do much of this filtering digitally, so their external analogue filtering can be simple. Follow the converter or codec datasheet's recommended output circuit. Key takeaways Holding samples creates image frequencies around multiples of the sample rate. Reconstruction filtering removes images; it cannot undo aliases already in the samples. Modern converters combine internal digital filtering with their specified analogue circuits. Further reading Sampling Theorem — Julius O. Smith, Mathematics of the DFT (CCRMA) Reconstruction filter — Wikipedia PCM5102A audio DAC datasheet — Texas Instruments

sum: Choose amplitude or power decibels and convert a chain of gains to a sample multiplier.
x: A synth that's too quiet is annoying. One that clips is broken: harsh, aliasing distortion every time a chord gets loud. Managing level is a constant job, from the first oscillator to the final converter, and decibels are the language for it. Why decibels Level ratios in audio span an enormous range. An ideal signed 24-bit sample format has millions of steps between zero and full scale. Real converters have a higher analogue noise floor than that ideal resolution suggests. Ratios like that are unreadable as plain numbers, and our perception of loudness is roughly logarithmic anyway, so audio uses a logarithmic unit: the decibel (dB). A decibel is always a ratio to something. There are two formulas, and mixing them up is the most common mistake. For quantities that measure power or energy: For amplitudes (sample values, voltages, sound pressures): Why the different factors? At unchanged impedance, power grows with squared voltage amplitude. At the same impedance, doubling voltage quadruples power. The amplitude and power decibel rules therefore describe the same physical change when applied to the appropriate quantities. Under that condition both formulas give the same dB value for the same change; you just use the one matching the quantity you have. Samples, voltages and pressures are amplitudes, so use the amplitude rule when comparing their magnitudes. Going back from decibels to a multiplier undoes the logarithm: Useful reference landmarks: doubling an amplitude adds about 6 dB, ×10 adds 20 dB, and ×1.414 (the square root of 2) adds about 3 dB. In power terms, doubling power is +3 dB. Gains in dB add where the ratios multiply: A −6 dB stage followed by a −12 dB stage gives −18 dB overall, about one eighth of the original sample amplitude. Add the decibel changes; multiply the corresponding linear gains. Key takeaways Use twenty times the log for amplitude ratios and ten times the log for power ratios. Doubling amplitude adds about 6 dB; doubling power adds about 3 dB. Serial gains add in decibels and multiply as linear factors. Further reading Decibel — Wikipedia Decibels and amplitude ratios — UNSW

sum: Measure digital level, compare crest factors and recognise different RMS meter conventions.
x: dBFS: decibels relative to full scale dBFS measures a digital level relative to a defined full-scale reference. In a fixed PCM output format, that reference corresponds to the largest permitted sample level; floats can also hold values above it. With floats in ±1.0, full scale is 1.0, so the reference amplitude in the decibel formula is 1: 0 dBFS is the nominal sample-peak maximum at a fixed-format output. Smaller peaks read negative: a peak of 0.5 is −6 dBFS, a peak of 0.1 is −20 dBFS. A value of 2.0 would be +6 dBFS: fine inside a float pipeline, but it will clip at the converter. RMS and dBFS conventions differ For peak levels, dBFS is unambiguous. For RMS levels, conventions differ. AES17 (and related IEC and ITU standards) defines the RMS of a full-scale sine as 0 dBFS, so a full-scale square wave reads +3 dBFS. Other meters use the plain maths, where a full-scale sine reads −3 dBFS RMS. When comparing figures, check which convention a meter or datasheet uses. This lesson uses the plain maths. Peak, RMS and crest factor Two measurements describe a signal's level: Peak level: the largest absolute sample value. It decides whether the digital samples exceed the fixed-format limit. Reconstructed analogue peaks can be higher between samples, which needs a separate true-peak check. RMS (root mean square): the square root of the average of the squared samples. It tracks the signal's power, and relates more closely to perceived loudness than peak does. The name describes the recipe, read from right to left: square every sample, take the mean, then the square root. For a steady sine measured over whole cycles, RMS is below peak. For a sine measured over whole cycles, RMS is about 71% of its peak. A sine peaking at 0.5 therefore has RMS about 0.354. This is a waveform-specific relationship, not a rule for arbitrary audio. The ratio of peak to RMS is the crest factor, often given in dB: Waveform Crest factor In dB --------- Square 1 0 Sine 1.414 (square root of 2) 3.01 Saw, triangle 1.732 (square root of 3) 4.77 Music (varies widely) often much higher 12–20 is an example A square wave and a sine with the same peak don't sound equally loud: the square has 3 dB more RMS. Switching from sine to square at the same peak increases RMS by 3 dB and often sounds louder, but perceived loudness also depends on spectrum and listening level. Synths may compensate per waveform. Key takeaways Peak level tells you whether nominal full scale is exceeded; RMS measures average squared signal size. Crest factor is peak divided by RMS: a sine has about 3 dB, a square has 0 dB. RMS dBFS references differ between meters. Check conventions before comparing figures. Further reading dBFS — Wikipedia Crest factor — Wikipedia

sum: Predict in-phase and unrelated sums and compare safe voice scaling with average-level scaling.
x: Summing signals Mixing digital signals is just addition, sample by sample. What happens to the level depends on how the signals relate: Identical, in phase: amplitudes add. Two equal signals give +6.02 dB. Identical, with opposite polarity: they cancel. Unrelated (different frequencies, noise): powers add. Two equal signals give about +3 dB of RMS. The distinction grows as more sources are added: With unrelated equal-level voices, RMS grows more slowly than the worst-case peak: three voices add about 4.8 dB of RMS on average, whereas three identical aligned copies add about 9.5 dB. Average power does not bound the largest sample. But peaks are what clip, and unrelated signals still line up their peaks now and then. Here's an A major triad, each voice a sine at 0.8 (−1.9 dBFS): The RMS rose by the expected amount for three unrelated signals: One of these voices has RMS about 0.566. Three together have RMS about 0.98, as expected for unrelated equal-level signals over this capture. But the three peaks nearly align, reaching about 2.4. Converted to a fixed format, almost a third of the samples would clip. Headroom is the gap between your normal peak level and 0 dBFS. Two common policies scale each voice by the voice count or its square root. They serve different goals. Assuming each voice is bounded by full scale, dividing each by the maximum voice count bounds the mathematical sum at full scale, but makes single notes quiet. Dividing by the square root of the voice count keeps average RMS steadier for unrelated voices but can still peak over. Many designs do this and add a soft clipper or limiter at the end to catch the rare peaks. Real-world analogy: Several taps feeding one drain A drain can carry the flow from any one tap, yet simultaneous surges from several taps can exceed its flow capacity. Average flow alone does not describe a brief surge. How it maps: Tap flow rates are simultaneous voice sample values, and drain flow capacity is the output range. The sample values add, so aligned peaks can exceed that range even when individual voices and average RMS look modest. Where it stops: Audio values can be positive or negative and can cancel; water flow in this picture cannot. RMS power addition also follows signal statistics, rather than adding average tap flows directly. Key takeaways Identical in-phase signals add amplitudes; unrelated signals add power on average. Unrelated signals can still align their peaks and exceed full scale. Dividing by voice count protects against the worst case; square-root scaling needs protection for overshoots. Further reading Decibel — Wikipedia dBFS — Wikipedia Gain stage — Wikipedia Decibels and signal combination — UNSW

sum: Compare clipping curves and measure the new harmonics that require alias control.
x: Clipping: hard and soft When a signal exceeds what a stage can represent, it clips. Hard clipping flattens anything beyond the limit: Values within minus one to plus one pass unchanged; values beyond either endpoint are held at that limit. For example, an input of 1.7 becomes 1.0. Explicit saturating conversion does this. A raw integer cast is not a clipper: out-of-range conversion can wrap or be undefined, so clamp before converting to the DAC format. It creates a sharp corner where the wave meets the ceiling, and sharp corners mean strong high harmonics. A symmetric clip of a sine, or another input with half-wave symmetry, creates only odd harmonics before sampling. Symmetry of the clipper alone does not remove even harmonics already in an arbitrary input. Soft clipping bends the wave gradually towards the limit. A common choice is the hyperbolic tangent: The tanh function is almost straight near zero and flattens towards minus one and plus one. It changes 0.1 only slightly, to about 0.0997, but compresses 2.0 to about 0.964. Small signals pass almost unchanged; big ones are squashed smoothly. It still distorts, but its high harmonics fall away much faster. Compare both on a 1 kHz sine driven 6 dB over full scale (amplitude 2.0). The levels are relative to the fundamental: (The FFT reading is explained in the FFT measurement units. This experiment runs at a very high sample rate to greatly reduce alias contamination of the harmonics measured here. A finite sample rate cannot eliminate every alias from ideal hard clipping.) By the 9th harmonic, soft clipping is about 20 dB cleaner. Inside a synth running at 48 kHz, both clippers' harmonics above 24 kHz will alias, which is why distortion stages are often oversampled. Clipping as a sound Deliberate saturation is a classic synth effect. Accidental clipping at the output is a fault. The difference is whether you chose where it happens and controlled its aliasing. Key takeaways Hard clipping flattens over-range samples; a raw integer cast is not a safe clipper. Soft clipping bends smoothly and usually produces weaker high harmonics for comparable drive. Both introduce nonlinear harmonics; control aliasing around intentional distortion stages. Further reading Clipping (audio) — Wikipedia)

t: Stage gain and protect the output
sum: Place headroom and protection in a float synth and measure worst-case patches.
x: Gain staging inside a digital synth Gain staging means setting the level at each stage so that no stage clips and none is needlessly quiet. Floating-point storage allows intermediate values above nominal full scale, but effects may deliberately limit or saturate them. A typical output path is: Practical rules: Know where the hard limit is. The final fixed-format conversion needs a bound. Intermediate floats can exceed 1.0, but check each effect for its own saturation or input limits. Budget headroom where levels can grow: summing voices, resonant filters (which can boost signals near the cutoff well above the input level) and feedback effects. Protect the output. A soft clipper or limiter just before conversion turns rare overshoots into mild saturation instead of harsh clipping. Measure. Log peak and RMS in an offline render of your worst case: all voices, full resonance, maximum velocity. Change gain smoothly. Jumping a gain value between samples can cause clicks; stepping it in coarse increments when a knob turns causes "zipper noise". Smoothing is covered in the synthesis module. Key takeaways Budget headroom for mixing, resonance and feedback effects. Intermediate float signals can exceed nominal full scale; protect the final fixed-format conversion. Measure worst-case peak and RMS, and smooth control changes to avoid clicks and zipper noise. Further reading dBFS — Wikipedia Gain stage — Wikipedia

t: From digital full scale to line voltage
sum: Convert dBu and dBV to RMS volts and match the synth output to its destination safely.
x: From dBFS to volts The DAC turns 0 dBFS into some maximum output voltage. That voltage is set by the codec and the output circuit, so it's on the board's datasheet, not a universal number. What your audio interface expects is in its manual. Two common nominal line levels use different references: Level Reference RMS voltage --------- +4 dBu (pro) 0 dBu = 0.7746 V ≈ 1.228 V −10 dBV (consumer) 0 dBV = 1 V ≈ 0.316 V Converting either unit to an RMS voltage is the decibel formula run backwards, with that unit's reference voltage: These are nominal levels; real signals peak well above them, and equipment has headroom for that. Check both the synth's maximum output and the interface input's maximum level in their manuals, and set the synth's output level so that its loudest patch doesn't overload the input. Keep to line-level connections Turn the monitor level down before testing a new connection and raise it gradually. Line, instrument, microphone, headphone and speaker connections are not interchangeable. Never connect a power amplifier's speaker output to a line input or to a development board. Work only with low-voltage, battery or USB-powered circuits and the board's documented audio outputs, and add any output protection the board's documentation recommends. Key takeaways dBu and dBV use different RMS voltage references; digital dBFS depends on the actual converter and circuit. Nominal line level leaves headroom for signal peaks. Check both devices’ maximum levels. Use documented line-level outputs and low-voltage circuits; speaker outputs must not feed line inputs. Further reading Line level — Wikipedia RMS voltage references and crest factor — RaneNote 169

t: Check and plot an offline test signal
sum: Build a reproducible Python workbench and check signal length, level, DC and zero-crossing frequency.
x: Ears are good at telling you something is wrong and bad at telling you what. Is that buzz aliasing or clipping? Is the note 3 cents flat, or is it a filter making it sound duller? The roadmap's readiness test for this stage is to "explain each sample's meaning, verify frequency and level from the data". This lesson builds a small offline toolkit for doing exactly that. The tools are standard: numpy for arrays and the FFT, matplotlib for plots, soundfile for WAV files. You're using an FFT, not writing one; FFT implementation is deliberately deferred. Set up Use a virtual environment so the experiments are reproducible from a clean checkout: Commit requirements.txt with your experiments. The outputs below were produced with numpy 2.5, matplotlib 3.11 and soundfile 0.14; numbers in the last decimal place may differ slightly on other versions. Protect your ears and speakers A full-scale sine is very loud and fatiguing. Generate test files at −12 dBFS or lower, turn the monitor level down before playing anything new, and raise it gradually. Never play untested generated audio on headphones at volume. Generate a test signal and check it numerically Start with a known signal and check that the numbers match the theory: Each check has a reason: Length: 1 s at 48 kHz must be 48,000 samples. Off-by-one-block errors show up here. Peak 0.5 is −6.02 dBFS, as requested. RMS 0.3536 is the peak divided by 1.414 (the square root of 2), the sine's crest factor (the peak-and-RMS unit). DC offset (the mean) should be essentially zero for this whole-cycle capture. Partial cycles can have a non-zero mean even when the underlying wave is centred correctly. A persistent offset over complete cycles means the waveform is shifted off centre, which wastes headroom and can thump when audio starts and stops. Other cheap sanity checks are worth wrapping in a function: np.isfinite(x).all() (NaN or infinity anywhere means a bug, often a filter blowing up), and the number of samples at or beyond ±1.0. Plot the waveform A plot shows what summary numbers hide: discontinuities, glitches at block boundaries, asymmetry. Plot short windows (a few cycles) to see the shape, and mark the samples as dots, because they're the real data. The lines joining them are just a drawing aid; recall from the reconstruction unit that the true reconstructed signal is smooth, not straight-sided. Fixing the y-axis at ±1 makes levels comparable between plots. Measure frequency in the time domain For a clean, single-frequency signal, count upward zero crossings: places where a sample is negative and the next one isn't. Average the spacing between them: The frequency is one over the average period, where each period is measured in samples and converted to seconds. Average the gaps between upward crossings to estimate one cycle’s length. More samples between crossings mean a lower frequency; a higher sample rate makes the same sample gap represent less time. This counts whole samples, so it's only accurate to a fraction of a sample per period (here 0.01 Hz after averaging many periods). It's fooled by noise and by waveforms with several crossings per cycle. For anything richer than a sine, use the spectrum. Key takeaways Check sample count, peak, RMS, DC offset and finiteness before listening at a safe level. Plot short windows with sample dots; joining lines are a visual aid. Upward zero crossings estimate a clean sine’s period but are unreliable on noisy or complex waveforms. Further reading numpy.fft.rfft — NumPy documentation python-soundfile documentation

sum: Read FFT frequency axes and choose enough observation time to distinguish nearby tones.
x: Read a spectrum with numpy's FFT The FFT (fast Fourier transform) takes a finite capture of samples and returns how much of each frequency they contain, at evenly spaced frequencies called FFT bins. For real input (ordinary audio), the negative-frequency spectrum mirrors the positive half in magnitude. NumPy's rfft therefore returns only the non-negative bins. For even input lengths these include the Nyquist frequency; for odd lengths the last bin lies just below it. Use np.fft.rfftfreq with the same capture length and actual sample spacing to generate the matching frequency axis: Three facts you need to read it correctly: Bin spacing is the sample rate divided by the number of samples. One second at 48 kHz gives 1 Hz bins; 0.1 s gives 10 Hz bins. Longer captures give finer frequency resolution. Scaling: NumPy’s raw output grows with the number of input samples. For ordinary positive-frequency bins, multiply by 2 and divide by the sum of the window (in the next unit). DC and the even-length Nyquist bin have no negative-frequency partner and are not doubled. Windowing: multiply the capture by a smooth window (Hann is a good default) that tapers its ends to zero. Without it, a frequency that doesn't fit a whole number of cycles in the capture smears energy across the spectrum. That smearing is called spectral leakage. Zero-padding a capture gives more displayed frequency points by interpolating the same transform. It adds no measured information and cannot replace a longer capture when separating nearby tones. Key takeaways For even-length real input, rfft returns half the sample count plus one bins. Bin spacing is sample rate divided by capture length in samples. Longer captures give finer bin spacing; windowing and correct scaling are also needed to read a spectrum. Further reading numpy.fft.rfft — NumPy documentation numpy.fft.rfftfreq — NumPy documentation Zero padding and spectral interpolation — Julius O. Smith

sum: Use a Hann window and the window sum to recover a bin-centred sine’s amplitude.
x: Analyse a real sample array with NumPy's rfft. In this unit, the capture length is the number of input samples and bins are indexed from zero. A bin-centred sine completes a whole number of cycles in the capture. Window and scale an FFT The Hann window NumPy uses is a smooth raised-cosine taper. The window tapers the capture towards zero at both ends, reducing the artificial jump caused by analysing a finite segment. For an even-length Hann window, the centre gets just below one rather than exactly one. Windowing also reduces the measured magnitude. To recover a bin-centred sine’s amplitude, account for the actual window sum. Ordinary positive-frequency bins need doubling because the real sine has a mirrored negative-frequency contribution: The 0 Hz bin and, for even capture lengths, the Nyquist bin have no separate mirror, so they are not doubled; the spectrum function below halves them back. Both the frequency and the level match what we generated: the round trip from theory to data and back works. Key takeaways A Hann window tapers the capture endpoints to reduce abrupt boundaries. Divide FFT magnitude by the window sum and double ordinary positive-frequency bins. DC and the even-length Nyquist bin are not doubled; accurate bin-level readings assume a bin-centred tone. Further reading numpy.fft.rfft — NumPy documentation numpy.fft.rfftfreq — NumPy documentation Spectrum Analysis Windows — Julius O. Smith, Spectral Audio Signal Processing (CCRMA) numpy.hanning — NumPy documentation

sum: Compare rectangular and Hann captures and explain why between-bin peak readings understate amplitude.
x: FFT bin spacing is the sample rate divided by the capture length in samples. The preceding FFT units explain the amplitude scaling; here we compare what happens when a tone falls between bins. Leakage between FFT bins What if the frequency falls between bins? With a 0.1 s capture (10 Hz bins), compare 1000 Hz (exactly on a bin) with 1005 Hz (halfway between two bins), with and without a window: (−120 here means "at or below −120 dB"; the floor hides meaningless rounding noise.) On this bin, both recover the expected level to the displayed precision. Between bins, the unwindowed ("rect") capture loses 3.9 dB at the peak and leaks energy to −52 dB as far as 500 Hz away, which would mask real low-level components such as aliases. The Hann window loses only 1.4 dB at the peak and keeps the far leakage near −118 dB. A between-bin amplitude shortfall is called scalloping loss. For accurate amplitudes, use coherent sampling (whole cycles), a flat-top window (which widens the main peak), or a peak-interpolation method with an amplitude correction matched to the chosen window. Practical consequences: window when leakage is a concern; a rectangular window is suitable for a coherent capture containing whole cycles. Read levels from a capture long enough that the bins are fine; and when you need an exact level, generate test frequencies that land on bins (an integer number of cycles in the capture). Key takeaways An unwindowed, between-bin tone leaks energy into distant bins and can hide faint components. A Hann window reduces distant leakage, but a between-bin peak still underreads amplitude. For an exact level check, capture a whole number of cycles and use the correct scaling. Further reading Spectrum Analysis Windows — Julius O.
