Smith, Spectral Audio Signal Processing (CCRMA) Window function — Wikipedia Spectral leakage — Wikipedia Flat-top amplitude measurement — SciPy documentation

sum: Compare a naive sawtooth’s spectrum with predicted folded harmonics and recognise aliases hidden on harmonic bins.
x: Verify an aliasing prediction The sharp-waveform unit predicted where a naive 1,760 Hz sawtooth's harmonics fold at 48 kHz. Now measure it. A 1 s capture makes each bin exactly 1 Hz, so bin index equals frequency: The predictions were −28.6, −28.9, −28.3 and −29.2 dB for the four aliases (each harmonic's amplitude is one over its harmonic number, here 27, 28, 26 and 29), and −6.0 dB for the 2nd harmonic. The measurements agree to about 0.1 dB, and the small differences come from other, much weaker harmonics folding onto the same bins. This is the "compare a deliberately aliased signal with its predicted apparent frequency" exercise from the roadmap. Later, run the same script against a band-limited oscillator from a library and watch those aliases drop. If the sample rate is an exact multiple of a waveform’s fundamental, aliases can land on existing harmonic bins. They then change harmonic levels rather than appear as extra inharmonic lines. Test awkward frequencies as well as neat ones. Key takeaways Predict alias frequencies and relative levels before measuring the spectrum. Several higher harmonics can fold onto the same bin, changing its observed level. A neat ratio of note frequency to sample rate can hide aliases on existing harmonics; also test awkward frequencies. Further reading numpy.fft.rfft — NumPy documentation Spectrum Analysis Windows — Julius O. Smith, Spectral Audio Signal Processing (CCRMA)

t: Write WAV files and check the round trip
sum: Export with explicit clipping and fades, then verify rate, subtype, length and quantisation error.
x: Write a WAV file with a library Writing a WAV encoder isn't a learning goal; a library handles the format. soundfile (a wrapper for libsndfile) takes float arrays and converts them to the requested subtype: Reading the file back and comparing is the important habit. The sample rate, format and length are as intended, and the error is at most one 24-bit step (2⁻²³ ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻⁷). That's quantisation, not a bug. It's a full step rather than the half step that rounding would give because, in the libsndfile version bundled here (1.2.2), the clipping conversion rounds down: every error lies between 0 and −1 step. At 24 bits that's harmless, but it's exactly the kind of detail a read-back check reveals. Notes: sf.read returns float64 by default; integer PCM files are scaled around ±1.0. Float-format files can contain values outside that range. Pass an integer type, as in sf.read(path, dtype="int16") (or "int32"), to get integers instead. These are scaled to fill the integer type, not the file's raw values: a 16-bit file read as int16 gives its stored samples, but a 24-bit file read as int32 comes back multiplied by 256. Use sf.write(path, x, fs, subtype="FLOAT") to keep a 32-bit float file with headroom above 1.0 for analysis. Use PCM_16 or PCM_24 for files to share or import into a DAW. soundfile switches on libsndfile's clipping option whenever it opens a file, so in testing it clipped 1.7 to full scale when writing PCM rather than wrapping it. Clip explicitly anyway, so your output never depends on a library setting. The fades matter: a file that starts or ends mid-wave clicks, which is easy to mistake for a synth bug. A measurement checklist Before trusting any experiment's audio, check: Check How ------ Length and rate len(x), sf.info Finite values np.isfinite(x).all() Peak level np.max(np.abs(x)), then dBFS RMS and DC np.sqrt(np.mean(x2)), np.mean(x) Full-scale warnings np.sum(np.abs(x) >= 1) Frequency windowed FFT peak Unwanted content FFT, compare with prediction Then listen at a safe level. Measurement tells you what's there; listening tells you whether it matters. Key takeaways Use the library’s subtype to choose PCM or float storage and clip explicitly before PCM output. Short fades prevent start and stop discontinuities. Read each file back to check metadata and sample error; library versions can affect conversion details. Further reading python-soundfile documentation

sum: Choosing a synthesis approach.
x: A synthesiser is a program (or circuit) that turns control information, such as "play note 60, fairly hard", into an audio signal. In a digital synth that signal is a stream of samples; an analogue circuit produces a continuous signal. Every design answers the same two questions: Where does the raw sound come from? A waveform, a recording, a mathematical model. How is it shaped over time? Filters, envelopes and modulation. The different "kinds" of synthesis are mostly different answers to the first question. Before choosing one for your instrument, it helps to know what each costs and what it is good at. The main approaches Approach Raw material Shaped by --------- Subtractive Bright waves (saw, square) Filters remove harmonics Additive Many sine waves Per-partial levels FM / PM Sines modulating sines Modulation index Wavetable Stored single cycles Scanning through tables Sample-based Recordings Pitch shift, envelopes Physical modelling Model of a vibrating object Model parameters Subtractive Start with a waveform rich in harmonics and remove what you don't want with a filter. A sawtooth through a low-pass filter whose cutoff falls over time gives the classic "pluck" or brass sound. The Minimoog Model D is a concrete example of this architecture. We use subtractive synthesis for the learning experiments because its blocks can be tested separately; the project has not selected the finished instrument’s architecture. Additive Under the usual Fourier-series conditions, a periodic sound can be described by a mean plus sine components; at an ideal jump, the series converges to the midpoint of the two limits. Additive synthesis builds the sound directly from those sines, each with its own frequency and level, often with its own envelope. It gives total control, but a low note can need hundreds of sines per voice, and controlling that many parameters musically is hard. For this first instrument, a few oscillator and filter states need little working memory. Recorded sample libraries can consume much more storage, while a large additive bank can cost many oscillator evaluations. These are design trade-offs rather than universal rankings: measure the concrete implementation and target sound. These are offline learning experiments. Later hardware exercises must use documented low-voltage development hardware, with the exact board and audio-interface manuals checked before making connections. Mains construction is outside this course’s project scope. Key takeaways Subtractive synthesis removes harmonics; additive synthesis builds them. Use the target sound, memory and processing cost to choose an approach. Further reading Minimoog Model D user guide — Moog Additive synthesis — Julius O. Smith

sum: FM, PM and sidebands.
x: FM and PM In frequency modulation one signal varies an oscillator’s instantaneous frequency. Here we consider sinusoidal modulation of one sine oscillator (the carrier) by another (the modulator), at constant rates and depth. More general modulation need not have this same simple sideband grid. This creates new frequency components, called sidebands, at the carrier frequency plus and minus multiples of the modulator frequency, so two sine oscillators can produce a complex spectrum. The optional relationship records that spacing: For example, a 400 Hz carrier modulated by a 100 Hz modulator gives sidebands at 300 and 500 Hz (the first pair), 200 and 600 Hz (the second pair), and so on, so the possible components lie on a 100 Hz harmonic grid. Which are audible depends on their levels and cancellation; perceived pitch is not guaranteed to be 100 Hz. A ratio such as 400 Hz to 141 Hz does not give a simple low-order harmonic relationship and can sound metallic. Since those two integer frequencies do share a 1 Hz divisor, it would be wrong to claim they have no common mathematical fundamental. How strong each pair is depends on the modulation index (how hard the modulator pushes); a low non-zero index concentrates most energy in the carrier and first pairs, while a high index usually spreads significant energy over more pairs. More distant sideband terms are generally small rather than exactly absent, and individual terms can have zeros. (A sideband that would land below 0 Hz reflects back to a positive frequency.) John Chowning developed FM synthesis at Stanford from 1967 and Yamaha licensed it; the DX7 (1983) made it famous. Yamaha's commercial "FM" (the DX7 included) is actually implemented as phase modulation (adding the modulator to the carrier's phase rather than its frequency). The two are mathematically closely related: phase-modulating with a signal is the same as frequency-modulating with its derivative, after converting phase units to frequency units. A practical advantage of PM is that a modulator with a DC offset only shifts the carrier's phase, whereas in true FM it shifts the carrier's pitch. A small FM/PM oscillator network can create rich spectra with little work, but cost grows with its operators, oversampling and implementation. Predicting a patch by ear can be difficult because sideband levels change nonlinearly with index. Key takeaways Audio-rate frequency or phase modulation produces sidebands. The modulation index controls their distribution, not just the carrier/modulator ratio. Further reading Sinusoidal FM and PM — Julius O. Smith Frequency modulation synthesis — CMU History of FM synthesis — Yamaha

sum: Stored sound and physical models.
x: Wavetable Store a set of single-cycle waveforms (a wavetable) and play one back with a phase accumulator, optionally sweeping or crossfading through the set to make the timbre evolve. The historical examples distinguish table lookup from later timbre-scanning systems. Hal Chamberlin’s September 1977 BYTE article describes accessing a stored cycle with a fractional table pointer. Julius O. Smith discusses Michael McNabb’s spectral-table interpolation in Dreamsong, while Wolfgang Palm’s PPG instruments made evolving stored-wave sounds a commercial approach in the late 1970s. Waldorf continued that lineage with the Microwave in 1989. These are examples of development, not a claim that any one person invented all table-lookup synthesis. Each table is cheap to play, but high notes alias unless you keep band-limited versions of each table (covered in the neighbouring synthesis units). Sample-based Play back recordings of real sounds, re-pitched by reading them faster or slower, then shape them with envelopes and filters. Recordings can reproduce detailed source sounds, but storage and expressive coverage depend on the recordings, playback method and processing. Elektron’s Digitakt II is a manufacturer-described stereo sampler (product page checked 2026-10-16). The project names a Digitakt without confirming its model, so identify the actual instrument before applying model-specific connection or format advice. Physical modelling Simulate the physics of a string, tube or membrane. The classic small example is Karplus–Strong: fill a short delay line with noise and feed it back through a gentle low-pass filter. The loop's length sets the pitch, and the filter makes high harmonics die first, like a plucked string. The total delay around the loop is roughly one period of the note. A shorter loop repeats sooner and gives a higher pitch. The filter also delays the signal, so accurate tuning must include its delay; a fractional-delay adjustment can fill the gaps between whole-sample lengths. So a 220 Hz string at 48 kHz needs a loop of about 218 samples, and a note an octave up (440 Hz) needs about 109. Julius O. Smith's Physical Audio Signal Processing covers this family in depth. A reasonable first instrument Subtractive is the usual first build because each block (oscillator, filter, amplifier, envelope, LFO) can be built and tested on its own. The project brief suggests a monophonic digital subtractive synth as an option; this module teaches every block it would need without committing you to it. Key takeaways Wavetables store cycles; sample playback uses recordings. A Karplus–Strong loop needs roughly one period of delay, with filter delay included for accurate tuning. Further reading Blofeld user manual — Waldorf Karplus–Strong — Julius O. Smith Digitakt II product description — Elektron Table lookup in BYTE, September 1977 — Hal Chamberlin Digital synthesis taxonomy — Julius O. Smith PPG history — PPG Microwave history — Waldorf

t: Audio and control in one voice
sum: Audio and control in one voice.
x: The classic subtractive voice A voice is everything needed to play one note. The textbook subtractive voice looks like this: Oscillator (VCO/DCO): generates a periodic waveform at the note's pitch. Filter (VCF): usually a resonant low-pass; its cutoff sets brightness. Amplifier (VCA): multiplies the signal by a gain, so the note can start and stop. Envelopes: time-varying control signals started by the key (the gate). One drives the amplifier, another typically sweeps the filter cutoff. LFO: a slow oscillator (below about 20 Hz) that wobbles pitch (vibrato), level (tremolo) or cutoff. The "V" names come from analogue gear where each block was voltage controlled. In software the same structure holds: audio flows left to right, and control signals arrive from below. Notice there are two kinds of signal. Audio signals run at the sample rate and you hear them. Control signals (envelopes, LFOs, knob positions, MIDI) steer the audio blocks. They often change more slowly, but fast modulation can require per-sample updates too. Keeping these separate is central to real-time design, as later lessons show. Key takeaways Follow audio through oscillator, filter and amplifier. Envelopes, LFOs and note events control those blocks. Further reading Minimoog Model D user guide — Moog Blofeld user manual — Waldorf

sum: Held notes and monophonic priority.
x: A monophonic synth plays one pitch at a time. This offline sketch assumes one channel and one held instance per note number. It deduplicates repeated note-ons; a receiver that permits stacked same-pitch events must define matching note-off semantics separately. Monophonic: note priority When you hold two keys on a mono synth, which one sounds? That rule is note priority: Last-note priority: the most recently pressed key wins. Releasing it falls back to a key still held. Low-note or high-note priority: the lowest or highest held key wins. Last-note priority needs a stack of held notes, otherwise releasing the newest note while an older one is held leaves silence or a stuck note: When note_off returns a note, the voice glides or jumps back to it; None means start the release. Stuck notes Every note-on must eventually be matched by a note-off for the same note, or a voice sounds forever. Handle the MIDI convention that a note-on with velocity 0 means note-off, and give yourself an "all notes off" escape. The project brief lists "no stuck notes" as a success criterion. Key takeaways A held-note stack allows last-note priority to return to an older held key. Treat MIDI note-on with velocity zero as a note-off. Further reading Minimoog Model D user guide — Moog MIDI message summary — MIDI Association Zero-velocity note-on discussion — MIDI Association

t: Polyphony, shared filters and voice stealing
sum: Polyphony, shared filters and voice stealing.
x: Monophonic and polyphonic A monophonic synth has one voice: it plays one note at a time. A polyphonic synth has several voices and can play chords. Paraphonic designs share some sound-shaping stages across several pitches, commonly a filter and its envelope. Amplifier and triggering arrangements vary by instrument. Polyphonic: voice allocation A poly synth has a fixed pool of voices (say 4 or 8). The voice allocator decides which voice plays each new note: If a voice is free, use it. If all are busy, steal one. Common choices: the oldest note, the quietest voice, or a voice already in its release phase. This sketch marks a voice free as soon as its key is released, so a voice still sounding its release tail can be reused abruptly. Real voice allocators track the envelope state, prefer voices that have finished, and fade a stolen voice out over a few milliseconds to avoid a click (covered in the neighbouring synthesis units). The following is an offline policy sketch, not callback-ready allocation code. Its note arrays are a fixed voice pool, but the temporary list and Python runtime are unsuitable for a hard real-time callback. Note-off handling here frees a voice immediately rather than waiting for its envelope; repeated same-pitch/channel note matching is deliberately simplified. A production allocator must define that policy and track completion of release tails. Cost and choice For the illustrated design with one oscillator, one filter and two envelopes per voice, 8 independent voices require 8 oscillator states, 8 filter states and 16 envelopes. Shared LFOs and output effects need not multiply with the voice count. On a microcontroller, measure the busiest supported combinations on the target board, including shared effects and control handling. Leave processing headroom for variation; a desktop experiment or average voice cost does not guarantee callback deadlines. A mono synth is the smallest complete instrument, and a well-structured monophonic voice becomes one voice of a poly synth later. Real-world analogy: A room with a fixed number of chairs When every chair is occupied, seating someone new means asking someone else to leave. How it maps: The chairs are the voice pool. An idle voice is an empty chair; stealing chooses an occupied voice to reassign. Where it stops: A released note may still have an audible tail, and fading that tail is an audio transition problem, not just a seating policy. Key takeaways A fixed voice pool prefers idle voices before stealing. Shared filtering shapes all notes together; independent voices permit separate articulation. Budget per-voice work plus shared processing, and fade audible stolen voices. Further reading Matriarch manual — Moog Blofeld user manual — Waldorf

sum: Phase increments and waveform shapes.
x: An oscillator's job sounds trivial: output a repeating waveform at a chosen frequency. The interesting part is state. Audio arrives in blocks (say 32 or 48 samples at a time), the frequency may change between or within blocks, and the oscillator must continue exactly where it left off. Get the state wrong and you hear clicks, buzzes and detuning. Many digital waveform oscillators use one idea: the phase accumulator. Phase as a fraction of a cycle Represent phase as a cycle fraction from zero inclusive to one exclusive: how far through the current cycle you are. 0 is the start of a cycle, 0.5 is halfway, and 1.0 wraps back to 0. Each sample, advance the phase by the phase increment: the fraction of a cycle that passes during one sample. In one second the oscillator must complete as many cycles as its frequency, while the system produces as many samples as the sample rate, so each sample covers the frequency divided by the sample rate of a cycle: At 440 Hz and 48 kHz, the increment is about 0.0091667: one cycle takes about 109 samples, so the output repeats 440 times per second. Double the frequency and the increment doubles, so each cycle takes half as many samples. A waveform is then just a function of phase, with phase running from zero inclusive to one exclusive. A sine rises and falls smoothly, a saw rises then jumps down, and a triangle rises then falls along straight segments. The code below defines their phase positions precisely. For example, a quarter of the way through the cycle the sine is at its peak of +1, the saw is at −0.5 and the triangle is at 0. The square and pulse waves are simpler still: +1 while the phase is below a threshold (0.5 for a square, the chosen width for a pulse), otherwise −1. In code: Separating "where am I in the cycle?" from "what value is there?" is what makes the design flexible: the same accumulator drives a sine, a wavetable lookup or an LFO. Oscillator pulse width A pulse wave is high for a fraction width of each cycle. At 0.5 it is a square wave. Narrower widths sound thinner and more nasal; oscillator pulse-width modulation (sweeping the width with an LFO) gives a chorus-like movement. Avoid widths of exactly 0 or 1: the wave becomes a constant (DC), with no sustained audible tone. Starting, stopping or changing that constant can still create a transient, and DC can use headroom; it is not a safe loudspeaker-drive signal. Key takeaways Frequency divided by sample rate gives cycles advanced per sample. Sine, saw, triangle and pulse are different functions of the same phase. Duty cycle controls oscillator pulse width; exact endpoint widths produce DC. Further reading Digital sinusoid generators — Julius O. Smith Blofeld user manual — Waldorf

sum: Keeping phase across audio blocks.
x: This offline example stores phase in an object and returns newly allocated Python lists. It illustrates persistent DSP state, not real-time memory handling. The single-subtraction wrap assumes a positive frequency below the sample rate; useful audio fundamentals must also respect Nyquist. State carried across blocks Here is a minimal oscillator that processes a block at a time. The phase lives in the object, not in the function: Output: The printed phase describes where the next block will continue: After both blocks, the oscillator has travelled two complete cycles and another two thirds. Its stored phase is the remaining two thirds, ready for the next block. The last sample of block A and the first of block B are consecutive points on the same sine. The block-boundary bug If phase resets at every block with constant frequency and identical processing, the same block repeats. With 64-sample blocks at 48 kHz, the output is periodic on a 750 Hz harmonic grid; it generally replaces the intended tone rather than adding a separate buzz to it. Some frequencies happen to fit an integer number of cycles per block, so do not use one favourable test to establish correctness. Key takeaways Phase belongs to the oscillator, so the next block continues the same sequence. Resetting every block can replace the intended tone with the block repetition spectrum. Further reading Digital sinusoid generators — Julius O. Smith Waveform implementation — PJRC

sum: Musical pitch and frequency control.
x: Frequency control Musical pitch is exponential: each octave doubles the frequency. MIDI note numbers convert to hertz with the twelve-tone equal temperament formula (from module 1): So note 60 (middle C) is 261.63 Hz, and note 81 (an octave above note 69) is 880 Hz. Pitch modulation, pitch bend and detune are added in semitones or cents before this conversion, then the increment is recomputed. Because the increment is just the frequency divided by the sample rate, it can change each sample while phase stays continuous. A sudden frequency step can still make an audible transient or unwanted modulation; smoothing and a suitable band-limited oscillator remain necessary. Key takeaways Equal-tempered note numbers map exponentially to frequency. Changing increment preserves phase continuity, while abrupt frequency changes can still need smoothing. Further reading Tuning and reference note — MIDI Association Notes, octaves and frequency — UNSW Acoustics

sum: Wrapping phase without losing overshoot.
x: Wrapping the phase correctly When the phase passes 1.0, subtract 1. Don't reset it to 0. Setting it to 0 discards the fraction that overshot, so each cycle becomes a whole number of samples long. That quietly detunes the oscillator: With reset-to-zero, each cycle lasts the ideal number of samples rounded up to a whole number. The output therefore repeats too slowly unless the requested cycle already fits a whole number of samples. So resetting makes every 1100 Hz cycle exactly 44 samples, giving 1090.9 Hz: about 14 cents flat, an audible error. The error is worst for high notes, where one extra sample is a large part of a short cycle. Subtracting 1 keeps the fraction, so cycle lengths vary between 43 and 44 samples and approach the requested average pitch in exact arithmetic; finite measurements and floating-point arithmetic introduce small errors. Two more wrapping cases matter: Increment of 1 or more (a very high frequency or extreme modulation): one subtraction is not sufficient for every such overshoot (for example, an overshoot above two cycles). Use p = p - floor(p). Negative increments (through-zero FM, reversed playback): the phase can go below 0, so wrap upwards too. p - floor(p) handles both directions. Beware that some languages' remainder operators (such as C's fmod) return negative results for negative inputs. Here is why p - floor(p) works in both directions: Wrapping does not make frequencies above Nyquist representable. The floor method is a finite-number range operation: reject NaN/infinity, and do not infer numerical accuracy once enormous phases have already lost their fractional bits. Real-world analogy: Keeping your place on a running track After passing the start line, a runner keeps the distance travelled beyond it. How it maps: A whole lap is one cycle. Wrapping removes completed laps while retaining the overshoot; resetting to zero throws away progress. Where it stops: Digital phase advances in discrete steps and does not model physical inertia. Wrapping cannot prevent spectral aliasing. Key takeaways Reset-to-zero wrapping discards overshoot and detunes the oscillator. Subtracting the floor wraps finite positive and negative phases into one cycle. Further reading Digital sinusoid generators — Julius O. Smith C11 committee draft — WG14 Python mathematical functions — Python

sum: Integer phase and table indexing.
x: The preserved C fragment below is a DDS implementation example, not a C lesson. Assume valid positive sample rate, a non-negative frequency below Nyquist, finite arithmetic, an unsigned 32-bit phase, and between one and 31 table-index bits. The shift chooses the sample after the phase advance; that is a consistent one-step phase offset if used throughout. Integer phase accumulators Hardware and many embedded libraries use an unsigned 32-bit integer for phase, where the full range 0 to 2³² − 1 represents one cycle. Storing an unsigned addition back into that 32-bit type wraps it automatically. The increment is still rounded to a finite frequency grid. The high phase bits choose the table entry; the remaining bits track progress between entries: For 1000 Hz at 48 kHz the rounded increment is 89,478,485 counts per sample. In C, using the shift operator >> to keep the top bits: The frequency resolution is the frequency that one count of increment represents. At 48 kHz, changing the increment by one count changes the frequency by about 0.000011 Hz. That fine frequency grid is separate from the table resolution: using more phase bits does not create more stored waveform samples. This is the numerically controlled oscillator at the heart of direct digital synthesis (DDS) chips, and the PJRC Teensy Audio Library's waveform object uses a uint32_t phase accumulator in the same way (source checked 2026-10-04). Key takeaways Unsigned integer phase wraps modulo its range. The high phase bits select a wavetable entry; frequency quantisation is set by one increment count. Further reading Waveform implementation — PJRC C11 committee draft — WG14

sum: Why growing floating-point phase drifts.
x: Floating-point precision drift Single-precision float has a 24-bit significand, about 7 significant decimal digits. That matters in two ways. Wrapping protects precision in these examples. Running a float32 accumulator at 440 Hz for a simulated minute gave 439.99972 Hz on average, an error of about 0.001 cents. The phase stays below 1, where floats are precise. Unwrapped phase in float is a bug. If you never wrap, the stored number grows without limit. A growing floating-point sample counter converted to an ever-larger angle has the same broad risk: its spacing eventually becomes too coarse to represent small changes accurately. This experiment isolates repeated phase addition: Time running Effective pitch ------ 1 s 439.5 Hz 10 s 445.3 Hz 60 s 468.8 Hz 300 s 375.0 Hz The note goes audibly out of tune within seconds and wildly wrong after a few minutes. The reason is the spacing between neighbouring normal float32 values, which doubles when the magnitude crosses the next power-of-two boundary. The ideal unwrapped phase after 60 seconds would be about 26,400 cycles. The accumulated float32 phase differs, but remains in the same binary-exponent interval in this run. Near the phase reached after a minute in this example, adjacent float32 values are about 0.002 cycles apart. The intended step is about 0.0092 cycles, so addition rounds it to about 0.0098. The actual phase step has changed, which changes the pitch. That matches the measured 468.8 Hz. The spacing grows at successive powers of two. Rounding can move the step up or down: after 300 seconds the simulated frequency is 375 Hz. Separately, a float32 counter repeatedly incremented by one can stall at 16,777,216, about 5.8 minutes at 48 kHz, because the next integer is no longer representable. A drone or a held pad would expose this on stage. Always keep phase wrapped to one cycle (or use the integer form). Wrapping means keeping the fractional cycle progress when phase crosses a cycle boundary. Resetting phase to zero at each audio block instead discards progress and can create a discontinuity. Preserve phase between blocks; a frequency change normally changes the increment while leaving the current phase intact. Key takeaways Float32 spacing grows with magnitude, so an unwrapped accumulator changes its effective step. Wrapped phase keeps the number small; a growing float32 counter eventually cannot count every sample. Further reading Floating-point limits — NumPy Python mathematical functions — Python

sum: Choosing an oscillator reset policy.
x: From oscillator to instrument A practical oscillator also needs: Band-limiting for saw, square and pulse, or high notes alias badly (covered in the neighbouring synthesis units). Smoothed or per-sample frequency so pitch changes don't step audibly (covered in the neighbouring synthesis units). A reset policy: resetting phase on each note-on gives a consistent attack; free-running sounds more like analogue oscillators. Both are valid choices. Libraries such as DaisySP (Oscillator) and the Teensy Audio Library (AudioSynthWaveform) provide alias-reducing waveform options and a way to set or reset phase. In the source revisions checked on 2026-10-16 (DaisySP 2c72eaf9eac5, PJRC Audio 3039be2773e8), the basic frequency setters recompute an increment without a pitch smoother, so smoothing remains your job. The roadmap suggests writing your own sine oscillator first, then comparing with a library's. Key takeaways Resetting at silent note starts makes attacks repeatable; free-running phase varies starts. Resetting an audible oscillator can click; band-limiting and smoothing remain separate requirements. Further reading Oscillator interface — DaisySP Waveform interface — PJRC

sum: Periodic sounds as Fourier series.
x: Play a sine, a triangle, a square and a sawtooth at the same pitch and loudness. Each sounds clearly different: the sine pure, the triangle soft, the square hollow, the saw buzzy and bright. Pitch and loudness are equal, so the difference is timbre, and for steady periodic tones timbre is largely set by the spectrum: which frequencies are present, and how strong each one is. This lesson gives you the spectra of the standard waveforms and a way to verify them. Every later block (band-limiting, filters) is easier to reason about in these terms. Fourier series for ordinary periodic audio signals A nonconstant periodic waveform has a fundamental frequency of one divided by its shortest repeating period, and, under the usual Fourier-series conditions for piecewise-smooth signals, it can be represented by a mean plus sinusoidal components at whole-number multiples of that repeat rate. At an ideal jump the series takes the midpoint of the one-sided limits. Each component completes a whole number of cycles during the waveform’s repeat period. Its amplitude sets its contribution; its phase sets where that component starts. A constant mean is represented separately. For example, a wave repeating every 10 milliseconds has a 100 Hz repeat rate. Its non-DC components lie on the 100, 200, 300 Hz grid and so on; some may have zero amplitude. DC is the mean value (zero for the centred waveforms here). The first harmonic is the fundamental; perceived pitch need not equal the strongest component. For this periodic sound, the second and higher harmonics are its overtones: components above the fundamental. “Harmonic” also includes the fundamental, which is not an overtone, and non-periodic sounds can have inharmonic overtones, so these words are not identical labels. Every component has its own amplitude and phase. This is the Fourier series. Intuitively: a single sinusoid has one non-zero positive-frequency component, while a more complicated periodic waveform requires more components (and possibly a DC mean). The sharper the features of a waveform (corners, jumps), the more high harmonics it needs to build them. The component magnitudes plotted against frequency form the magnitude spectrum: a row of spikes on the harmonic grid, each with a height. Key takeaways A periodic sound can be decomposed into a mean plus harmonics with individual phases and magnitudes. Its repeat rate sets the harmonic grid; the strongest component need not be the perceived pitch. Further reading Fourier series — Julius O. Smith Gibbs phenomenon — NIST DLMF

sum: Fourier series and harmonic patterns.
x: A waveform’s harmonic amplitudes explain much of its steady timbre. This unit compares the ideal saw, square and triangle at the same fundamental frequency. The standard waveforms Wave Harmonics present Relative amplitude pattern --------- Sine Fundamental only No upper harmonics Saw All whole harmonics Inverse harmonic number Square Odd harmonics Inverse harmonic number Triangle Odd harmonics Inverse square of harmonic number The important comparison is how quickly the upper harmonics weaken. Peak level and harmonic level are different measurements: Equal waveform peaks do not imply equal fundamental strength. For ideal waves with extrema at minus and plus one, the fundamental amplitudes are about 0.637 for the saw, 1.273 for the square and 0.811 for the triangle. Other components combine with the fundamental to make the final waveform. Changing where a waveform starts in its cycle changes harmonic phases, while leaving its harmonic magnitudes unchanged. Two saws with identical harmonic magnitudes can therefore begin their cycles at different-looking points. To compare harmonics by ear it helps to convert their relative amplitudes into decibels: A halving of amplitude is about a 6 dB reduction. This is why the saw’s second harmonic is about 6 dB below its fundamental, whereas the triangle’s much weaker third harmonic is about 19 dB below its fundamental. What this means for the sound: Saw has every harmonic, falling at 6 dB per octave of harmonic number (each doubling of the harmonic number halves the amplitude). This is the brightest standard wave and the usual starting point for subtractive brass, strings and basses. Square has only odd harmonics with the same reciprocal-harmonic-number decay. Missing even harmonics give its hollow, woody, clarinet-like character. Triangle also has only odd harmonics, but they fall at the reciprocal of harmonic number squared, i.e. 12 dB per octave. The 3rd harmonic is 1/9 of the fundamental (−19 dB), so it sounds close to a sine. Key takeaways Fourier series describes periodic waves using DC and harmonics with magnitudes and phases. Saw harmonics decay by harmonic number; triangle harmonics decay faster than square harmonics. Further reading Blofeld user manual — Waldorf Gibbs phenomenon — NIST DLMF

t: Oscillator pulse width and missing harmonics
sum: Oscillator pulse width and missing harmonics.
x: Pulse waves A pulse wave's harmonics depend on its width (the fraction of each cycle it spends high): A harmonic vanishes whenever its number times the width is a whole number. At half-cycle width, all even harmonics vanish. At quarter-cycle width, every fourth harmonic vanishes, because the fourth harmonic spans a whole cycle during the high interval. This is why sweeping oscillator pulse width changes the timbre so audibly. Key takeaways Oscillator pulse width changes the harmonic strengths. At one-third duty cycle, every third harmonic vanishes in the ideal series. Further reading Blofeld user manual — Waldorf Alias-free classic waveforms — Stilson and Smith

sum: Measuring harmonics with an FFT.
x: Check it with numpy The roadmap asks you to compare spectra with an existing analysis tool rather than writing an FFT. numpy's rfft computes the discrete Fourier transform of a real signal. The FFT reports the signal's content in a row of evenly spaced frequency slots called bins. Their spacing, and which bin holds a given frequency, follow from the sample rate and the number of samples analysed: This is coherent sampling: make the test components complete whole cycles in the capture. A useful trick follows: analyse exactly one second at an integer frequency. Then the FFT bins are exactly 1 Hz apart and every harmonic lands exactly on a bin, so there is no spectral leakage (energy smearing into neighbouring bins) to worry about. Half a second (24,000 samples) would give 2 Hz bins, so 300 Hz would be in bin 150. Output (harmonics 1 to 7, relative to the fundamental): (Spacing tidied to fit; values unchanged.) The inverse-harmonic-number, odd-only and reciprocal-square harmonic patterns appear to the displayed precision. These are sampled naive waveforms, so small discretisation and folded-harmonic effects remain; this experiment does not prove exact band-limiting. The absolute fundamental amplitudes come out as 0.6366, 1.2732 and 0.8106, matching the ideal-wave fundamental strengths from the harmonic-pattern unit to the displayed precision. At a fixed sample rate, raising the fundamental raises every harmonic. Fewer harmonics then fit strictly below Nyquist, half the sample rate. A band-limited oscillator must adjust its harmonic content as pitch rises; a clean-looking low-note test does not establish high-note performance. Note the scaling: rfft returns sums, not amplitudes. For a coherent real sine in an interior positive-frequency bin, multiply its magnitude by twice the reciprocal of the sample count. Do not double DC or the Nyquist endpoint, which do not have separate negative-frequency partners: For example, one second of a 0.5-amplitude sine at 48 kHz gives a raw magnitude of 12,000 in its coherent interior bin; amplitude normalisation recovers 0.5. For non-coherent frequencies or real recordings, a window such as np.hanning reduces sidelobe leakage while broadening peaks. Correct for its coherent gain if estimating amplitudes. Finite recordings and modulated sounds need a measurement method matched to the question. Key takeaways Bin spacing depends on analysis length, not just sample rate. Coherent steady test tones avoid leakage; windowing changes the measurement trade-off. Double interior positive-frequency magnitudes only when converting a real tone to peak amplitude. Further reading Real FFT — NumPy FFT definitions and normalisation — NumPy Spectrum analysis windows — Julius O. Smith

sum: Phase alignment and peak headroom.
x: Equal magnitudes can hide different shapes Two waves can have identical magnitude spectra but different shapes. Build a 39-harmonic saw-like tone twice: once with all harmonics in sine phase, once all in cosine phase. Same harmonic amplitudes, but the cosine-phase version has a peak 2.3 times higher, because all its harmonics reach their crests together at the start of each cycle. For output gain, the cosine-phase version needs about 7.4 dB more peak headroom in this experiment. That extra peak comes from timing, without increasing any component’s amplitude. The experiment proves equal harmonic magnitudes, not equal perception. Human studies of harmonic complexes show that phase differences can be audible, with sensitivity depending on factors such as fundamental frequency, the listener and listening conditions. Listen if timbre matters; do not use a magnitude FFT as proof that two tones must sound identical. Your headroom does not care what it sounds like: the peak is what clips. Filters change phases, which is one reason a filtered signal can peak higher than its input. For a changing note, the harmonic levels and phases can evolve during the attack and decay. One static magnitude spectrum cannot describe all that articulation; the next unit returns to this broader meaning of timbre. Real-world analogy: Several people pushing together The largest combined push happens when everyone pushes at the same moment. How it maps: Harmonic phases determine when peaks line up. Keeping individual amplitudes unchanged can still change the largest combined sample. Where it stops: Different harmonics cycle at different rates; the analogy predicts peak alignment, not how loud or alike two sounds will seem. Key takeaways Equal magnitude spectra can have different time-domain peaks. Phase changes can consume headroom even when the steady-state RMS is unchanged. Further reading FFT definitions and normalisation — NumPy Mathematics of the DFT — Julius O. Smith Phase discrimination in harmonic complexes — Drennan and colleagues

sum: Gibbs ripple and evolving timbre.
x: Gibbs ripple Adding up a finite number of harmonics never quite produces a perfect corner. A square wave built from odd harmonics overshoots each jump by about 9% of the jump size, in the limit of a large Fourier-series term count. A particular short finite sum differs slightly. For an ideal square spanning minus one to plus one, a hard-truncated series with many odd harmonics therefore peaks near 1.179. That is roughly 1.4 dB above unity, so scaling by the intended flat level alone can clip the output. Measure the actual implementation and leave margin. This is the Gibbs phenomenon. It matters later: a hard Fourier truncation of a square or saw shows this ripple even with every retained harmonic below Nyquist. Other smoothing windows and approximate oscillators can change the overshoot, so an overshoot of about 18% above the flat level is not mandatory for every anti-aliased implementation. Timbre is more than the static spectrum The spectrum explains why waveforms differ, but real timbre also depends on how the spectrum changes over time. A piano's high harmonics die faster than its fundamental; a brass note gets brighter as it gets louder. That is why synths pair oscillators with filters, envelopes and modulation, which change the spectrum while the note plays. The DSP learning objectives ask you to describe a target sound in exactly these terms: pitch, spectrum, envelope and modulation. Key takeaways Limiting an ideal jump to finitely many Fourier terms creates ripple and overshoot. More terms narrow the overshoot region; allow peak headroom. Timbre includes changes over time as well as a steady magnitude spectrum. Further reading Gibbs phenomenon — NIST DLMF Blofeld user manual — Waldorf

sum: Where naive oscillator harmonics fold.
x: The earlier harmonic-pattern unit showed that a sawtooth has harmonics at every multiple of its fundamental, forever. A digital system can only represent frequencies below half its sample rate (the Nyquist frequency: 24 kHz at a 48 kHz sample rate). Module 1 covered what happens to anything above: it aliases, folding back to a different frequency. The naive oscillator from the oscillator units, 2.0 p - 1.0, samples an ideal saw directly. It therefore contains all those impossible harmonics, and they fold back into the audible band. This lesson explains how those folded components differ from ordinary brightness; the following units compare ways to prevent or reduce them. Where the harmonics go Take a high-ish note: 1245 Hz (close to D#6) at a 48 kHz sample rate. Nyquist is 24 kHz, so harmonics 1 to 19 (up to 23,655 Hz) are fine. Harmonic 20 is at 24,900 Hz and folds back. A component above Nyquist lands at its distance from the nearest whole multiple of the sample rate: The table tracks each isolated ideal source harmonic using its reciprocal-harmonic-number amplitude. Several harmonics can fold to one sampled frequency and add or cancel, so these levels are not guaranteed total FFT-bin amplitudes. A saw’s higher source harmonics get progressively weaker. Its 31st harmonic is about 30 dB below the ideal fundamental before sampling; that does not make its folded contribution harmless or uniquely determine the combined sampled-bin level. Harmonic Lands at Level (the reciprocal of harmonic number) --------- 20 23,100 Hz −26.0 dB 31 9,405 Hz −29.8 dB 38 690 Hz −31.6 dB 39 555 Hz −31.8 dB Two things make this bad: These aliases are not harmonic. 9,405 Hz and 690 Hz are not multiples of 1245 Hz, so they sound like dissonant, metallic tones rather than brightness. They move the wrong way. Bend the pitch up and a real harmonic rises, but a folded one can fall. Pitch sweeps produce the tell-tale "birdie" whistles moving against the note. A component 30 dB below the fundamental can be audible when it is poorly masked, but audibility depends on the sound, listener and playback level; that number alone is not an audibility threshold. Low notes suffer less, because their harmonics are already weak (the reciprocal of harmonic number is small) by the time they reach Nyquist. Why square waves are no better The naive square also has slowly decaying odd harmonics, so it can alias strongly. The exact folded levels differ from a saw. A naive triangle is much better (the reciprocal of harmonic number squared falls faster), and a fixed sine strictly below Nyquist has no upper harmonics to fold. Pitch modulation, clipping or an above-Nyquist sine requires separate analysis. The problem is discontinuities: a periodic jump requires harmonics extending to arbitrarily high frequencies. Key takeaways Naive sharp waveforms contain harmonics beyond Nyquist. Folded components can be inharmonic and move down while pitch moves up. Further reading Aliasing — Julius O. Smith Alias-free classic waveforms — Stilson and Smith

sum: Harmonic limits and wavetable ranges.
x: Established fixes There is no free lunch. Each method trades CPU, memory, latency or flexibility. 1. Additive synthesis Sum only the harmonics below Nyquist. How many is that? The largest whole number whose harmonic stays strictly below half the sample rate: For a 1245 Hz note at 48 kHz, that is harmonics 1 to 19. For fixed frequencies and amplitudes, the exact sum contains only the selected below-Nyquist components. Changing amplitudes or pitch introduces sidebands that need separate checks. The cost is one sine per harmonic per sample: a 50 Hz note at 48 kHz has 479 harmonics below Nyquist. Fine offline, expensive for a polyphonic synth on a microcontroller. 2. Band-limited wavetables (mipmaps) Precompute single-cycle tables using additive synthesis, offline. Keep several versions: one per octave (say), each containing only the harmonics that stay below Nyquist for the highest note that table will play. At playback, choose the table for the current pitch and read it with a phase accumulator and interpolation. The same counting rule sets each table's harmonic limit, using the highest note the table serves. A table serving higher notes needs fewer harmonics. Design for the highest playback pitch in each range; a table safe only at the bottom of its range will produce above-Nyquist components as pitch rises. Playback replaces many per-sample oscillators with table lookup and interpolation. It can represent many waveform shapes, but finite tables and interpolation can leave residual spectral error; table construction alone is not a guarantee of alias-free playback. The costs are memory, a slight loss of brightness at the bottom of each table's range, and possible audible switching between tables (crossfading helps). Some designs deliberately allow aliases confined near the top of the output band to preserve more brightness. That is a stated error tolerance, not zero aliasing or a universal inaudibility guarantee; verify the full pitch range, modulation and output chain. Real-world analogy: Packing for the smallest bag A shared packing list must fit the smallest bag on the trip, even if larger bags could carry more. How it maps: The table’s highest note has the least harmonic room below Nyquist. Its harmonic limit must fit that note, leaving unused room at lower notes. Where it stops: Playback interpolation and modulation can create additional spectral error; counting stored harmonics is only part of validation. Key takeaways Keep harmonics strictly below Nyquist; exclude exact equality under this policy. Additive generation trades processing work for explicit spectral control; tables trade memory for playback cost. Further reading Alias-free classic waveforms — Stilson and Smith Additive synthesis — Julius O. Smith

sum: Oversampling, BLIT and BLEP methods.
x: 3. Oversampling Run the naive oscillator at a multiple of the sample rate (say 4× or 8×), low-pass filter, then discard samples (decimate). The higher sample rate moves the folding boundary upwards. The low-pass filter removes content above the final Nyquist before decimation, but aliases that already folded into the wanted band survive; oversampling a discontinuous naive waveform does not guarantee zero aliasing. Simple to reason about, costly in CPU, and the decimation filter must be good. 4. BLIT: band-limited impulse train Stilson and Smith (CCRMA, 1996) generate a band-limited train of impulses using a closed-form formula, then integrate it to get a saw (or integrate a bipolar impulse train for a square). It's elegant and accurate, though the integrators need care to avoid DC drift. 5. BLEP and PolyBLEP: correct the jumps Insight: a saw is smooth everywhere except at its jump. Aliasing comes from the jumps. So generate the naive wave, then add a correction around each discontinuity that approximates a suitably low-pass-smoothed step. Ideal band-limited steps have infinite support; practical finite corrections leave some residual aliasing. minBLEP (Eli Brandt, 2001) precomputes a band-limited step, makes it minimum-phase, and stores the difference from an ideal step in a table. At each jump, the oscillator adds the table, aligned to the jump's exact fractional position. PolyBLEP (Välimäki and Huovilainen, 2007) replaces the table with a tiny polynomial that only touches two samples: the one just before the jump and the one just after it. It is cheap and needs no correction lookup table, at the cost of weaker suppression than a long table. Key takeaways Oversampling requires filtering before decimation. BLIT integrates a band-limited impulse train; BLEP methods correct discontinuities. Finite tables and short polynomial corrections reduce rather than guarantee zero aliasing. Further reading Alias-free classic waveforms — Stilson and Smith Hard sync without aliasing — Eli Brandt Antialiasing oscillators — Välimäki and Huovilainen

sum: A measured PolyBLEP saw experiment.
x: This is an offline NumPy experiment requiring NumPy installed in the Python environment. All subsequent NumPy experiments use the same dependency. The test is one second at a fixed integer frequency, so the FFT bins are one hertz apart. It compares this polynomial implementation, not a proof about every BLEP library or about modulated notes. A PolyBLEP saw in Python The code uses the common two-sample PolyBLEP also illustrated in Martin Finke’s tutorial. The correction is zero away from the falling edge. Just before that edge it lowers the saw; just after it, it raises the saw. Spreading the transition across nearby samples reduces the unwanted high-frequency content, while also changing wanted harmonics near Nyquist. The code assumes constant positive frequency strictly below Nyquist, finite values, and one sample-loop evaluation per output sample: Output: Reading it: the strongest alias below 10 kHz is at 9,405 Hz in both cases (harmonic 31 folded), but PolyBLEP pushes it from −29.8 dB to −55.4 dB relative to the fundamental, an improvement of about 25 dB. The last column is the 10th harmonic (12,450 Hz) relative to its ideal inverse-harmonic-number level: PolyBLEP softens it by 1.9 dB. In the same run the 19th harmonic (23.7 kHz) was 7.6 dB low. That is PolyBLEP's trade-off: it gently dulls the very top octave while reducing the measured off-harmonic content. This fixed-note result is not a guarantee for moving pitch or every listening condition. Key takeaways Evaluate the correction relative to the edge and subtract it for a falling saw edge. Measure residual aliases and wanted-harmonic droop together. Further reading Oscillator implementation — DaisySP PolyBLEP oscillator tutorial — Martin Finke Real FFT — NumPy

sum: Pulse corrections and library oscillators.
x: The saw's jump is downwards (+1 to −1), so the correction is subtracted. A square has a rising jump at phase 0 and a falling one at the oscillator pulse width w, so it needs two corrections. This is a Python fragment using the preceding unit’s poly_blep function. Supply phase p, a fixed oscillator pulse width w strictly between zero and one, and a positive increment dt below half a cycle per sample. Extremely narrow pulses and moving edges need additional validation: The same fixed-frequency FFT check, at oscillator pulse widths 0.5 and 0.3, gave −55.4 dB worst off-harmonic bin below 10 kHz for the corrected version (naive: −29.8 and −28.7 dB respectively). Remember that a pulse with a width other than 0.5 also has a DC offset (a non-zero average), which you may want to remove. A pulse held high for less than half the cycle has a negative mean; held high for more than half, it has a positive mean. At a high fraction of 0.3 its mean is −0.4. Remove unwanted DC with a suitable blocker, allowing for its effect on low frequencies. Triangle waves have corners, not jumps. They can be corrected with a band-limited ramp (BLAMP), or made by integrating a PolyBLEP square with a leaky integrator, which is what DaisySP's WAVE_POLYBLEP_TRI does. Using a library You don't need to invent any of this. Source revisions checked 2026-10-16: DaisySP 2c72eaf9eac5 and PJRC Audio 3039be2773e8. These are software-library observations, not a board-revision compatibility claim; confirm your installed library before copying names: DaisySP Oscillator offers naive waveforms plus WAVE_POLYBLEP_SAW, WAVE_POLYBLEP_SQUARE and WAVE_POLYBLEP_TRI. Teensy Audio Library AudioSynthWaveform offers WAVEFORM_BANDLIMIT_SAWTOOTH, WAVEFORM_BANDLIMIT_SAWTOOTH_REVERSE, WAVEFORM_BANDLIMIT_SQUARE and WAVEFORM_BANDLIMIT_PULSE alongside the naive ones. Its source (synth_waveform.cpp, class BandLimitedWaveform) inserts a precomputed band-limited step from a lookup table at each edge, interpolated to the edge's fractional position and spread across a window of about 32 samples (16 either side of the edge): a table-based BLEP approach, not PolyBLEP. The roadmap exercise is exactly this lesson's experiment: generate naive and band-limited versions at a high pitch, run them through the FFT analysis, and listen to a slow upward sweep of each. The fixed-note test also works with the actual checked DaisySP oscillator source compiled on the host: the naive saw’s strongest off-harmonic bin below 10 kHz was about −29.83 dB relative to its fundamental, versus −55.45 dB for its PolyBLEP saw. The tenth-harmonic droop was about −1.95 dB. These measurements agree closely with the offline Python implementation; they do not measure a board’s real-time capacity, output circuit or behaviour under rapidly changing pitch. Choosing a method Method CPU Memory Notes ------------ Additive high low exact fixed-frequency sum; costly for low notes Mipmapped tables low medium any waveform Oversampling high low needs a good decimator PolyBLEP low no correction table some top-end droop minBLEP medium small table longer corrections can improve suppression For a first subtractive voice on a microcontroller, PolyBLEP is the usual pragmatic choice. Key takeaways Pulse waves need opposite corrections at rising and falling edges. Non-half duty cycles have a non-zero mean. Inspect the exact library revision and compare its output with the naive oscillator. Further reading Oscillator implementation — DaisySP Waveform implementation — PJRC Teensy Audio Library — PJRC

sum: ADSR stages and linear segments.
x: A note isn't just a pitch and a timbre; it has a shape in time. A piano note strikes and decays, an organ note starts and stops abruptly, a pad swells. The envelope generates that shape as a control signal, usually driving the amplifier (loudness) and often the filter cutoff (brightness). The same maths solves a second problem: when a knob or MIDI controller changes a parameter in steps, the audio must not step with it. That's parameter smoothing. ADSR The classic envelope has four controls, triggered by the key's gate (on while held): Envelope attack: time to rise from the current level to the peak after the key goes down. Decay stage: time to fall from the peak to the sustain level. Sustain level: a level (not a time), held while the key stays down. Envelope release: time to fall to zero after the key is released. Linear segments The simplest implementation moves the level by a fixed step per sample. For an attack from 0 to 1 the step is the total rise divided by the number of samples the attack lasts. A longer segment spreads the same change across more samples, so each step is smaller. If a retrigger starts partway up, compute the step from the current level rather than assuming the starting level is zero. Decay and release work the same way, using the distance they have to travel. It's easy to reason about, and each segment ends at a precise time. Linear segments have a drawback for amplitude: hearing is roughly logarithmic, so a linear fade in amplitude sounds like it hangs on, then vanishes abruptly at the end. Linear attacks often sound fine; linear releases and decays often sound unnatural. Key takeaways Sustain is a level; attack, decay and release controls describe transitions. Linear ramps spread a chosen distance across a fixed number of samples. Further reading Envelope generators — Nigel Redmon Minimoog Model D user guide — Moog

sum: Exponential segments and time constants.
x: Assume a positive time constant, positive sample rate and a fixed finite target. The envelope values here are dimensionless gain/control values. A zero-time segment needs an explicit immediate-transition branch; the coefficient formula divides by the time constant. Exponential (one-pole) segments Analogue envelope generators charge and discharge a capacitor through a resistor, which gives exponential curves. Digitally, that is a one-pole filter moving towards a target: each sample, the level moves a fixed fraction of the remaining distance. In the code this is y += c (target - y). The time constant is a fixed duration describing how quickly the remaining gap shrinks. After one time constant, about 63.2% of the initial gap has closed. Reaching 99% takes about 4.6 time constants and reaching 99.9% takes about 6.9. A time constant describes the curve, not when the segment finishes. For a release towards zero, the same time constant takes the same time to reach a given fraction of its starting level, regardless of the starting amplitude. A fixed absolute stopping threshold differs: a louder start needs longer to fall to that threshold. For a 10 ms time constant at 48 kHz: Fraction reached Time ------ 63.2% 10.0 ms 99% 46.1 ms 99.9% 69.1 ms An exponential approach never quite arrives, which creates two practical issues: Attack: if the target is 1.0 the attack never ends. Common fix: aim past the peak (say 1.2) and switch to decay when the level crosses 1.0. Release: the level gets ever smaller without reaching 0. Stop at a threshold (e.g. 1e-5, which is −100 dB) and mark the voice idle so the voice allocator can reuse it. Very tiny floating-point values (subnormals) can also be slow on some processors. Real-world analogy: Closing half the remaining gap Imagine taking a fixed fraction of the remaining distance towards a door on every step. The steps become smaller as you approach. How it maps: The one-pole moves a fixed fraction of its remaining error, so it slows near the target and needs an explicit end condition. Where it stops: The fraction need not be one half, real motion is continuous, and finite arithmetic can eventually round to a target. Key takeaways One time constant closes about 63% of a fixed-target gap. State whether a time control means a time constant or a time to a specified threshold. Exponential attack and release need explicit end conditions. Further reading ADSR implementation — Nigel Redmon Time constant of one pole — Julius O. Smith Subnormal floating-point numbers — Intel

sum: An exponential ADSR state machine.
x: This standalone offline state-machine experiment uses positive attack, decay and release time constants, a sustain level between zero and one, and a fixed sample rate. Its “decay” stage asymptotically holds sustain instead of switching to a separate sustain state; gate-off from any stage starts release. A second gate-on attacks from the current level. Notice the numbers. Both follow from one rule: the time an exponential segment takes depends only on how many times smaller the remaining distance must get. The attack aims beyond the peak, so it crosses the stopping level in finite time. Release aims at zero but stops at a small threshold. These end conditions determine stage durations together with the time constants. So with a 5 ms time constant and a 1.2 target, the attack takes about 9 ms, and a 200 ms release time constant takes 2.2 s to fall from 0.6 to −100 dB. "Release = 200 ms" is ambiguous unless you say what it means: time constant, time to −60 dB, or time to silence. Pick a definition, document it, and convert the knob value to a coefficient accordingly. Key takeaways Overshoot the attack target so the peak is reached in finite time. Stop release at a documented small threshold and mark the voice idle. The demonstrated control times are time constants, not complete stage durations. Further reading ADSR implementation — Nigel Redmon Time constant of one pole — Julius O. Smith

sum: Retriggering, clicks and legato.
x: Retriggering and clicks A click can result when a waveform jumps abruptly; its audibility depends on the jump size and signal at that moment. A gain jump produces an output jump when the underlying waveform is non-zero. Envelopes cause clicks in a few classic ways: Abrupt envelope reset on retrigger. A note is releasing at level 0.4 and you press another key on the same voice. If the envelope jumps to 0 before attacking, the output gain drops 0.4 in one sample. Instead, start the attack from the current level, as the exponential ADSR state machine in the neighbouring unit does. Zero-length attack or release. A gain jump from 0 to 1 on a waveform that isn't at a zero crossing is a step. Enforce a minimum of around a millisecond or two (a rule of thumb, not a standard). Voice stealing. Reassigning a sounding voice to a new note jumps both its pitch and its envelope. Fade it out quickly first. Phase reset. Resetting oscillator phase while a voice is audible can change its output abruptly. A reset at matching waveform values need not create a value step. Some percussive patches want a click (a sharp attack). The point is to choose it, not suffer it. Legato and trigger modes On a mono synth, what happens when you press a new key while still holding the old one? Multi-trigger: every new note retriggers the envelopes. Each note is articulated. Single-trigger (legato): if a key is already held, the new note changes pitch only; the envelopes carry on from where they are. Only a fresh press after all keys are up retriggers. Legato is often paired with glide (portamento): the pitch slides to the new note, often controlled in the log-frequency (semitone) domain. A linear ramp in that domain gives equal intervals equal time; an exponential smoother instead slows near its target. Key takeaways Attacking from the current envelope level avoids a hard gain reset. Choose multi-trigger or legato deliberately, and treat phase resets and voice stealing as possible discontinuities. Further reading ADSR implementation — Nigel Redmon Minimoog Model D user guide — Moog

t: Removing zipper noise with ramps and smoothers
sum: Removing zipper noise with ramps and smoothers.
x: Parameter smoothing and zipper noise Controls arrive in steps: A single MIDI 1.0 CC data value has 128 possible values; a sweep can cross 127 adjacent transitions. Paired high-resolution CCs and other protocols can represent more values, and not every step is necessarily audible. A knob read by an ADC is noisy and quantised. Control values often update once per audio block. At 48 kHz with 32-sample blocks, that gives up to 1,500 update opportunities a second; an unchanged target creates no step. Stepwise gain or cutoff changes can create abrupt output changes or other transients, depending on the waveform and filter structure. A sequence can sound like a rasping buzz while the knob moves: zipper noise. The fix is to let the control set a target and move the actual parameter towards it smoothly, every sample. The offline code assumes positive time constant and sample rate, and a positive integer ramp length. A zero-length ramp needs a separately handled jump. These classes demonstrate the curves; they are not synchronisation mechanisms for sharing targets between real threads. The output shows two different timing contracts. After 240 samples (5 ms, one time constant) the one-pole has covered 63.2% of the way; after 480 samples (two time constants) 86.5%. The linear ramp uses equal steps. A fixed-length ramp reaches the target after its allotted samples in exact arithmetic. A one-pole keeps closing the remaining gap and therefore needs a stopping rule when exact arrival matters. The one-pole smoother is the simplest option: one multiply-add per sample, one evolving output state, plus its target and coefficient, and it handles a target that keeps moving gracefully. The linear ramp finishes after its chosen sample count, reaching the target in exact arithmetic. Repeated floating-point addition can leave a small rounding error; explicitly assign the target on the last step when an exact stored endpoint is required. Its fixed duration is useful when you need a guaranteed time (e.g. a voice-steal fade before reuse) but needs recalculating whenever the target changes. Key takeaways Control updates set targets; the audio path changes parameters smoothly. A one-pole approaches; a fixed-length ramp reaches its target after its allotted samples. Further reading SmoothedValue — JUCE One-pole filter — Nigel Redmon

t: Choosing smoothing time and musical units
sum: Choosing smoothing time and musical units.
x: Choosing smoothing times There's no universal value; listen and measure. Useful starting points: Gain and mix levels: a few milliseconds to a few tens of milliseconds. Too short and zipper noise returns; too long and the control feels laggy. Filter cutoff: similar, and smooth it in a perceptual unit (octaves) rather than hertz so its motion is even in musical terms. Only a constant-rate ramp in octaves gives every octave equal time; an exponential smoother still slows near its target. Pitch: small smoothing for knob jitter; deliberate glide is a separate musical control. Noisy ADC knobs: combine smoothing with a small dead-band or hysteresis so a stationary knob doesn't wobble the parameter. Smoothing in the right domain matters. Gain heard in decibels, and frequency heard in octaves, are perceptually logarithmic. A linear ramp in hertz from 100 Hz to 10 kHz spends most of its time in the top octaves. For example, a linear-in-hertz sweep from 100 Hz to 10 kHz spends only about 1% of its duration between 100 and 200 Hz, but about half between 5 and 10 kHz. Both intervals are one octave. A sweep that is linear in octaves instead gives each octave an equal share of the time, rather than allocating most of the duration to the largest hertz spans. JUCE’s SmoothedValue offers linear and multiplicative smoothing. The multiplicative form moves in equal ratios and cannot reach zero: use an appropriate finite fade or explicit threshold for silence. Where this fits on hardware On a microcontroller, the main loop or a timer reads knobs and MIDI and writes targets; the audio callback runs the smoothers per sample. That split keeps slow, irregular work out of the audio path. Embedded lessons later cover how to pass those values safely. Real-world analogy: Equal steps on a musical staircase Treat each octave as one stair, regardless of which note you started on. How it maps: A ramp in octaves gives equal musical intervals equal time; a ramp in hertz allocates more time to the much wider hertz spans at the top. Where it stops: This is a choice of control mapping, not a claim that perceived loudness or every timbre follows a simple octave scale. Key takeaways Balance responsiveness against unwanted steps. A linear ramp in log frequency gives equal musical intervals equal time. Dead-band or hysteresis can complement smoothing for noisy controls. Further reading SmoothedValue — JUCE Notes, octaves and frequency — UNSW Acoustics

sum: Frequency response, cutoff and slope.
x: In a subtractive synth the filter is where most of the character lives. The oscillator supplies a bright, buzzy spectrum; the filter decides how much of it you hear, and sweeping the filter is what makes a sound "open up" or "wow". This lesson builds one filter fully (the one-pole low-pass) and introduces the resonant designs you'll use from a library, so you can choose and drive them sensibly. Frequency response A linear time-invariant filter, after startup transients settle, treats each sine component separately: a sine goes in, a sine at the same frequency comes out, scaled in amplitude and shifted in phase. The frequency response says how much, for every frequency. Magnitude response: gain versus frequency, usually in dB on a log-frequency axis. Phase response: the phase shift versus frequency. A frequency-dependent phase shift is not necessarily one common time delay for the entire waveform. Filter types by shape: Type Passes Removes --------- Low-pass below cutoff above cutoff High-pass above cutoff below cutoff Band-pass (BP) around cutoff both sides Notch both sides around cutoff Cutoff, slope and order A cutoff is a design/reference frequency, often the half-power point for a simple monotonic low-pass. Filters act gradually rather than starting abruptly there; resonant or other families can use a different reference convention. For an analogue-style all-pole low-pass, far into its stopband, each pole contributes about 6 dB per octave of asymptotic filter slope. This is a qualified rule: digital responses near Nyquist, zeros, shelving and other responses need their actual transfer function. The filter order describes the highest relevant delay or derivative after cancellation; here it corresponds to the all-pole design’s pole count: Order Slope Example family --------- 1 6 dB/oct one-pole 2 12 dB/oct two-pole, biquad 4 24 dB/oct four-pole, ladder To estimate how much a low-pass cuts a frequency well above its cutoff, count the octaves and multiply by the slope. A steeper stopband slope reduces distant harmonics more strongly for the same frequency ratio. For example, three octaves above cutoff means three doublings, not three extra hertz. Compare measured response curves when exact rejection matters. This is an asymptote (the straight line the curve approaches): near the cutoff, and with resonance, the real curve differs, so use it only for frequencies well above cutoff. A steep slope separates low and high content more sharply; a gentle slope leaves more upper harmonics. Neither is inherently more natural: choose for the target sound. Key takeaways An LTI filter scales and phase-shifts steady sine components. Use per-pole slope as a qualified asymptotic rule, not a universal digital response formula. Further reading Introduction to digital filters — Julius O. Smith Audio EQ Cookbook — Robert Bristow-Johnson / W3C

sum: Resonance, Q and headroom.
x: Resonance and Q A resonant filter boosts frequencies near the cutoff before rolling off. On a synth this is the resonance (or emphasis) control. Turn it up and the filter "sings" at the cutoff frequency; sweep it and you hear the classic wah. Q (quality factor) controls damping and response shape in the two-pole low-pass family discussed here. A Q of about 0.7071 (one divided by the square root of 2) is the Butterworth value: maximally flat, no peak, −3 dB at cutoff. For this low-pass family, raising Q above the maximally flat value creates an increasingly strong resonance. The maximum generally lies near, rather than exactly at, the design frequency. For the RBJ cookbook low-pass, the gain at the cutoff frequency equals Q. For example, a quality factor of 4 gives four times the input amplitude at the design frequency, about a 12 dB boost. The maximum response may lie elsewhere, so measure peaks across the band when setting output gain. A numerical check at a 48 kHz sample rate with a 1 kHz cutoff confirms it: Q Gain at the design frequency ------ 0.7071 −3.0 dB 2 +6.0 dB 4 +12.0 dB 10 +20.0 dB At high enough resonance, some filters self-oscillate: the peak becomes so strong that the filter rings at its cutoff with no input, effectively becoming a sine oscillator. Analogue players use this deliberately. Key takeaways Q controls the RBJ low-pass response; gain at its design frequency equals Q. Resonance consumes headroom; self-oscillation depends on the design. Further reading Audio EQ Cookbook — Robert Bristow-Johnson / W3C Analysis of the Moog ladder — Stilson and Smith

t: The one-pole recurrence and per-voice state
sum: The one-pole recurrence and per-voice state.
x: This audio filter uses finite input samples and a positive cutoff/sample rate. Its state is independent for each separately filtered voice. Alternatively, sum voices first and intentionally filter the mix once; that shares a filter envelope rather than interleaving unrelated streams through one state. The one-pole low-pass The simplest useful filter. Its difference equation says how each output sample is computed: This is the same remaining-gap rule used by the envelope and smoother, now running on audio. When the input jumps to a new constant value, the output approaches it quickly at first and then more slowly; the step size shrinks as the gap closes. The coefficient comes from the cutoff (one standard choice, also used by EarLevel Engineering): The state is the single number y[n-1]. It must persist across samples and blocks, exactly like oscillator phase, and each voice needs its own. Real-world analogy: A moving average with a memory A cautious tracker moves partway from its previous estimate towards each new observation. How it maps: The stored output is the estimate; the new audio sample is the observation; the coefficient sets how quickly the estimate responds. Where it stops: The filter acts at audio rates and changes phase as well as level. This comparison does not predict an exact cutoff. Key takeaways The recurrence mixes the new input with the previous output. Preserve state across blocks and use separate state for independent voices. A filter on the summed signal is a deliberate shared-filter architecture. Further reading One-pole filter — Julius O. Smith One-pole filter — Nigel Redmon

sum: Measuring the one-pole frequency response.
x: To measure a filter, feed it steady sine waves at several frequencies and wait for startup transients to settle. Compare input and output amplitudes. This standalone offline example uses a positive cutoff and sample rate, with each test sine strictly below Nyquist. This is the roadmap exercise "measure its effect at selected frequencies": feed in sines and measure what comes out. Theory gives the same answers. The filter's magnitude response is: The complex response predicts the steady sine amplitude; the peak-of-samples method can differ at the displayed precision, and filling in more points gives the table below. Measuring only the largest sample is generally phase-dependent; for more accurate sine amplitude estimates, fit sine/cosine coefficients or measure RMS over complete cycles. Input Gain (1 kHz cutoff) ------ 500 Hz −1.0 dB 1 kHz −3.0 dB 2 kHz −7.0 dB 4 kHz −12.2 dB 8 kHz −17.7 dB 16 kHz −22.5 dB The slope settles towards about 6 dB per octave above cutoff, then flattens as it approaches Nyquist (the digital filter is not an exact copy of an analogue one up there). Cutoff accuracy at high frequencies The exp formula puts the −3 dB point very close to the set cutoff when the cutoff is well below Nyquist. At 48 kHz the half-power point (about −3.01 dB) is about 1,001.43 Hz for a 1 kHz setting, 5,188.89 Hz for 5 kHz, and 11.895 kHz for 10 kHz. A 15 kHz setting never reaches half power below Nyquist. A literal −3.000 dB crossing is slightly different; the usual “−3 dB cutoff” label is a rounded half-power convention. If you need accurate high cutoffs, use a design based on the bilinear transform with prewarping (as the RBJ cookbook does). The same structure gives a one-pole high-pass for free. Subtracting the low-pass output from the original input rejects a constant input after settling. The result is a high-pass response whose gain depends on this design; it is not automatically unity-normalised. With a very low cutoff (a few hertz) that is a DC blocker, handy for removing the offset from a pulse wave. Key takeaways Measure settled sines and compare with the response formula. The exponential coefficient approximates the intended cutoff only well below Nyquist. Subtracting low-pass output produces a DC-rejecting high-pass, with a design-dependent gain. Further reading One-pole filter — Julius O. Smith One-pole filter — Nigel Redmon Audio EQ Cookbook — Robert Bristow-Johnson / W3C

sum: Impulse responses, IIR and FIR.
x: IIR and FIR The one-pole filter feeds its own previous output back. Its impulse response is the output after a single input sample of one followed by zeros. After the impulse, each output feeds a fraction of itself into the next output. With the stable coefficient used here, that tail shrinks but never reaches exact zero in ideal arithmetic. That makes it an infinite impulse response (IIR) filter. A conventional feedforward finite impulse response (FIR) filter uses only current and past inputs. It multiplies a finite set of recent inputs by chosen weights, called taps, and adds them. Once an isolated impulse has passed every tap, no copy remains to contribute to later output.
