For example, averaging the current and two previous input samples with equal one-third weights gives a three-tap moving average. It has a low-pass main lobe but also zeros and sidelobes; it is not a monotonic textbook one-pole. IIR FIR --------- Feedback yes no Cost for a steep slope low high (many taps) BIBO stable with fixed finite coefficients Depends on poles Yes Exact non-trivial linear phase Generally incompatible with causal stable IIR Possible with appropriate symmetry The table compares common direct implementations. FIR describes the finite response; equivalent feedback-based implementations of some FIR responses can also exist. Many common synth resonant filters are IIR because feedback produces sharp responses with few operations. Fixed finite-coefficient FIR filters are BIBO stable: bounded input gives bounded output. An FIR can also form a resonant magnitude peak; it simply has no infinite ringing tail. Symmetric FIR designs can give exact linear phase and are useful in resampling. Finite-precision overflow, unbounded changing coefficients and nonlinear processing need separate analysis. Key takeaways A feedback one-pole has an infinite impulse response in exact arithmetic. A fixed finite FIR has bounded output for bounded input. Linear-phase FIR designs are possible; do not infer all IIR responses share one phase rule. Further reading Filter stability — Julius O. Smith Linear-phase FIR filters — Julius O. Smith

sum: Feedback stability and coefficient limits.
x: Stability, intuitively Feedback can run away. If the fraction fed back is too large, every sample adds more than the last and the output grows without limit. For the one-pole, the previous output is multiplied by 1 − a every sample. Strict BIBO stability for the genuine non-cancelled one-pole response requires that multiplier’s magnitude below one. At the limiting coefficient settings, distinguish a non-decaying initial condition from forced growth; the zero-input behaviour alone is not the full BIBO definition: For positive finite cutoff and sample rate, the exponential mapping gives a stable fixed filter in exact arithmetic. The shortcut replaces the exponential mapping with a coefficient proportional to cutoff, which can exceed two: at 48 kHz this occurs above about 15.3 kHz. Instability can therefore occur below Nyquist; checking the audio frequency limit alone is insufficient. In general a digital IIR filter is stable when all its poles lie inside the unit circle. You don't need the theory yet; you need the habits: Clamp cutoff and resonance to the range the design supports. Compute coefficients with the design's own formulas, not approximations. Watch for NaN or infinity in the output during development, and reset the filter state if it appears. Key takeaways For this one-pole, stability requires the feedback multiplier magnitude below one. The shortcut coefficient can violate that condition below Nyquist. Clamp parameters to the actual supported range and detect non-finite output. Further reading One-pole filter — Julius O. Smith Filter stability — Julius O. Smith

t: Choosing a biquad or state-variable filter
sum: Choosing a biquad or state-variable filter.
x: Resonant filter designs (conceptual) You aren't expected to implement these yet. Know what they are, so you can pick one from a library and drive it well. Biquad (RBJ cookbook) A general second-order IIR section, five coefficients: Robert Bristow-Johnson's Audio EQ Cookbook (now a W3C note) gives formulas for low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, notch, peaking and shelving filters from a centre or cutoff frequency (the cookbook’s frequency parameter), Q (or the width of the band) and gain. It's the standard choice for EQs. The cookbook's second-order low/high-pass responses approach 12 dB/oct in their analogue-style stopband region; two cascaded stages give 24 dB/oct. Notch, peaking and shelving biquads do not share that blanket slope rule. Caveat: the common direct-form structures are known to behave poorly when coefficients change rapidly (fast cutoff sweeps): Wishnick (DAFx 2014) documents clicks when Direct Form II coefficients change, and a time-varying filter with feedback (IIR) can go unstable even when every individual coefficient set is stable. That's why synth filters often use other structures. State-variable filter (SVF) A two-integrator loop that produces low-pass, band-pass and high-pass outputs at once, with cutoff and resonance controls that are nearly independent. The classic digital version (Chamberlin's) is very cheap but misbehaves at high cutoffs: its tuning drifts and, especially at low resonance, it goes unstable once the cutoff rises past roughly a seventh to a sixth of the sample rate (about 6.5 to 8.3 kHz at 48 kHz for Q between 0.5 and 0.707), so it is often run oversampled. Modern versions based on trapezoidal integration, such as Andrew Simper's (Cytomic), stay well-behaved when modulated quickly: Simper's paper states the filter remains stable and smooth even with audio-rate modulation, and Wishnick gives a proof of the SVF's stable time-varying behaviour. Those results apply to the specific integrator arrangement analysed in those papers and to supported positive, finite parameter ranges. They do not certify arbitrary SVF code, endpoint values, or finite-precision overflow. Key takeaways An RBJ biquad defines a second-order response through normalised coefficients. Fast coefficient changes require a structure and parameter range with appropriate time-varying stability evidence. Further reading Audio EQ Cookbook — Robert Bristow-Johnson / W3C Trapezoidal state-variable filter — Andrew Simper Time-varying filters — Aaron Wishnick

t: The ladder model and cutoff modulation
sum: The ladder model and cutoff modulation.
x: Ladder Robert Moog's patented transistor ladder: four one-pole low-pass stages in series (24 dB/oct) with negative feedback from the output to the input. Stilson and Smith's analysis models the feedback gain k from 0 to 4: in its ideal linear model, the response becomes marginal at feedback 4, with imaginary-axis poles at the individual stage corner frequency. The ideal response diverges at that frequency as feedback approaches the threshold. Real sustained self-oscillation is amplitude-limited by circuit nonlinearities; the linear model does not predict its final amplitude. Two well-known traits follow from the model: resonance comes with a drop in low-frequency level (explained below), and the feedback loop has no delay, so digital versions need care (a unit delay in the loop, or an implicit/zero-delay-feedback solution). The model's response shows where the bass loss comes from. At very low frequencies, each ideal stage passes the signal without attenuation, but the overall negative feedback still reduces gain. Increasing feedback therefore changes both the resonant peak and the bass level. In this uncompensated model, a feedback gain of 3 leaves one quarter of the original DC amplitude, about 12 dB down. Drive cutoff in octaves Pitch, envelope and LFO modulation of cutoff should add in octaves (log frequency), then convert once, as below. Clamp the result to the range supported by the exact filter implementation before computing coefficients. Being below Nyquist alone does not establish a safe cutoff or resonance. Add cutoff modulation in octaves before converting to frequency: one octave doubles the base cutoff, two quadruple it, and a negative octave halves it. Combining contributions first keeps every route in the same musical unit. Key takeaways The ideal four-stage ladder feedback model explains resonance and bass loss. A marginal self-oscillation threshold is not a bounded practical oscillator model. Combine cutoff contributions in octaves and clamp before using the chosen design. Further reading Analysis of the Moog ladder — Stilson and Smith Trapezoidal state-variable filter — Andrew Simper

t: LFO shapes, ranges and stepped controls
sum: LFO shapes, ranges and stepped controls.
x: A static patch sounds lifeless. Modulation means letting one signal change a parameter of another over time: an LFO wobbling pitch, an envelope sweeping cutoff, key velocity opening the filter. Most of a synth's expressiveness comes from what modulates what, and by how much. This lesson covers the sources, how to scale and combine them in the right units, and where to compute them. LFOs A low-frequency oscillator is the same phase accumulator as an audio oscillator, run below the audible pitch range. Typical rates run from well under 1 Hz (slow sweeps) to around 20 Hz (fast flutter); there's no fixed standard, and many synths go higher. Common shapes: Sine / triangle: smooth, even wobble. Saw / ramp: repeating rise or fall. Square: switches between two values (trills). Sample & hold (S&H): a new random value each cycle, held steady. LFOs drive controls, but their update rate still limits representable modulation; sharp shapes and modulation at audible frequencies require particular care. Slow smooth LFOs usually make aliasing less pressing than abrupt audible parameter changes. The sharp edges of a square or S&H LFO can, however, cause clicks if applied directly to gain or cutoff, so smooth them a little. Bipolar and unipolar Bipolar sources swing from −1 to +1: the parameter moves both up and down around its setting (vibrato around the note). Unipolar sources run from 0 to +1: the parameter only moves one way from its setting (tremolo that only reduces volume, an envelope that only opens the filter). Convert a bipolar value to a unipolar one like this: Shift and scale the source so its lowest value becomes zero, its centre becomes one half, and its highest value becomes one. This preserves the shape while changing the range; taking the absolute value would change the shape instead. In the code below this is the unipolar function. This offline sketch assumes a positive update rate and a non-negative LFO rate below half that update rate. It updates the held random value at a wrap; the initial held value is zero until the first wrap. Random output is nondeterministic; the printed sine/tremolo results do not use those random values. The LFO updates once per 32-sample block, so its increment is based on the block rate, not the sample rate. Base the phase increment on how often the LFO actually runs. A per-block LFO takes larger steps per call than a per-sample LFO at the same musical rate; using the audio sample rate in a per-block update would make it too slow. So the LFO updates 1,500 times a second and a 5 Hz cycle takes 300 updates. The tremolo gain swings between 0.5 and 1.0: depth 0.5 means down to half the signal amplitude, never above the original. Half amplitude is not a guarantee of half perceived loudness. Key takeaways The LFO increment uses the rate at which it is actually updated. Map bipolar to unipolar values when modulation should move one way. Smooth abrupt sample-and-hold LFO transitions if clicks are unwanted. Further reading Blofeld user manual — Waldorf Real FFT — NumPy

sum: Tempo sync and tremolo gain.
x: Two common LFO options: Key sync / retrigger: reset the LFO phase on each note so every note starts its wobble the same way. Without it, a free-running LFO’s phase at note-on depends on timing and can differ between notes. Tempo sync: derive the rate from tempo. When the tempo beat is a quarter note, 120 BPM gives half a second per quarter note, so one cycle per quarter note is 2 Hz. A time signature or tempo marking can assign another note value to the beat; state that convention. The tempo-sync conversion in general: Gain depth is usually specified as a fraction of the level (or in dB). Apply it like this: With a unipolar LFO, subtract a scaled amount from unity gain. Zero depth leaves the signal unchanged; full depth reaches silence at the LFO maximum. Intermediate depths reduce level without raising the original peak. That keeps the peak at the original level and avoids pushing the signal past full scale. Key takeaways State which note value receives the tempo beat before deriving an LFO rate. Unipolar tremolo can reduce level without increasing the original peak. Further reading Blofeld user manual — Waldorf Notes, octaves and frequency — UNSW Acoustics

sum: Vibrato in cents and semitones.
x: Vibrato and tremolo Vibrato is periodic pitch variation; tremolo is periodic amplitude variation. (Some instruments and effects use the names loosely; synths use them precisely.) Pitch depth belongs in cents or semitones, because pitch is heard logarithmically. Add the modulation in semitones (or cents), then convert: Vibrato depth 440 Hz swings between ------ ±50 cents 427.47 – 452.89 Hz ±100 cents 415.30 – 466.16 Hz For vibrato intended to have the same musical interval on every note, a fixed depth in hertz is unsuitable: ±10 Hz is a wide vibrato on a bass note and barely noticeable on a high one. A fixed deviation in hertz is used deliberately in linear FM, where the goal is a chosen modulation index and sideband pattern rather than equal musical width. Key takeaways Vibrato changes pitch; tremolo changes amplitude. Cents and semitones preserve musical width across the keyboard. A fixed hertz deviation has a different purpose in linear FM. Further reading Notes, octaves and frequency — UNSW Acoustics Sinusoidal FM and PM — Julius O. Smith

t: Envelope amounts and a modulation matrix
sum: Envelope amounts and a modulation matrix.
x: Envelope, velocity and other sources The most important modulation in a subtractive synth is the filter envelope: a second ADSR, scaled by an amount, added to the cutoff. Short attack and decay with low sustain give the classic pluck or "squelch". Like pitch, cutoff should be modulated in octaves: Scale the envelope by the requested octave amount. A full envelope with a three-octave amount opens the filter by three doublings; a half-height envelope contributes half that musical interval. Other routes add their own signed octave contributions. Other standard sources: Velocity: an encoded note-attack performance value, often related to how fast a key was pressed; its exact physical mapping depends on the controller. In MIDI 1.0 it's a 7-bit value (1–127 for a sounding note; a note-on with velocity 0 means note-off). Mapping velocity to both level and cutoff makes harder notes louder and brighter, like acoustic instruments. Key tracking: the note number itself, so the filter opens for higher notes and timbre stays consistent across the keyboard. Mod wheel (MIDI CC 1), aftertouch and pitch bend: performance controls often mapped to vibrato depth or cutoff. In conventional MIDI 1.0, pitch bend and CC 1 are per channel; polyphonic key pressure can address a note, while channel pressure applies to the channel. Using separate channels changes how “global” controls should be assigned. Random per note, for subtle analogue-style variation. The modulation matrix Hard-wiring "LFO → pitch" and "env 2 → cutoff" is fine for a first instrument. A modulation matrix generalises it: a list of routes, each with a source, a destination and an amount. Each destination sums its contributions in its own natural unit, then converts once. Here the envelope adds 1.5 octaves, the LFO subtracts 0.5 and velocity 100 adds about 0.787. The full-precision sum is used in the exponent: a displayed rounded octave sum should not be substituted as though it were exact. The result is approximately 1,726 Hz. The useful reading of that result is: The envelope opens the filter, the negative LFO contribution partly closes it, and the positive velocity contribution opens it further. Sum those octave contributions first, then perform one frequency conversion and apply the supported-range clamp. For the modest values shown, the clamp bounds the result between its illustrative endpoints. Arbitrarily large finite octave sums can overflow during exponentiation before that clamp runs; validate inputs and bound the octave sum before conversion in production code. A matrix makes combinations you did not plan for easy. (On a real filter, clamp to the range that design supports, often somewhat below Nyquist.) Design points: Keep amounts signed, so any route can invert. Decide which sources are per voice (envelopes, velocity, key tracking) and which are global (a shared LFO, the mod wheel). Matrices cost CPU per route per update; on small hardware, keep the route list short and fixed-size. Real-world analogy: Several adjustments on one thermostat Several controls can ask for warmer or cooler settings, but their adjustments must share one unit before they can be combined. How it maps: Each route has a signed amount. Contributions to one destination use the same units, are added, and then converted and limited. Where it stops: A modulation matrix is not necessarily a feedback controller; its sources can change much faster than room temperature. Key takeaways Scale sources in each destination’s own units and add contributions before conversion. Distinguish per-voice from channel-wide or global sources. Keep route counts bounded and clamp to the actual filter range. Further reading Blofeld user manual — Waldorf MIDI message summary — MIDI Association MIDI control changes — MIDI Association

sum: Control-rate and per-sample modulation.
x: Control rate versus audio rate Not every signal needs updating 48,000 times a second. Many synths compute modulation at a control rate, once per block, and only the audio path per sample. The important comparison is updates per event. A slow LFO gets many updates within one cycle, while a millisecond attack may span only one or two blocks. Holding one value for each block can make the fast event a handful of abrupt steps. At 48 kHz with 32-sample blocks the control rate is 1.5 kHz, and each block lasts 0.67 ms. That's plenty for a 5 Hz LFO (300 updates per cycle). It's not enough for: Fast envelopes: a 1 ms attack would be about 1.5 control steps, a staircase that can cause a click or buzz, depending on the signal and playback level. Fast or stepped modulation of gain and cutoff: the block-rate staircase is the zipper noise from the envelopes lesson. Audible-frequency pitch modulation: varying oscillator frequency with an audible-frequency modulator is FM (covered in the neighbouring synthesis units). It creates sidebands (below) and needs sufficient update bandwidth; in this voice, compute it per sample. For the sideband example, assume a sine carrier with constant-depth sinusoidal linear FM. This is not the deep exponential pitch mapping discussed next: For constant-depth sinusoidal linear FM of a sine carrier, sidebands are spaced at whole multiples of the modulator frequency on either side of the carrier. Their levels depend on modulation depth, and components can cancel. With modest pitch depth, a 5 Hz LFO is commonly heard as vibrato. Its sidebands are spaced by 5 Hz; perception depends on carrier, depth and listening conditions rather than a universal boundary between “wobble” and “separate tones”. A 220 Hz modulator on a 440 Hz carrier puts them at 220, 660, 880 Hz and so on: new tones, which a block-rate staircase cannot produce correctly. Common compromise: compute modulation sources at control rate, then linearly interpolate the result across the block (or feed it into per-sample smoothers), and run anything fast or audible (amp envelope, audible-frequency FM) per sample. Putting it together A complete basic voice now looks like this, with the per-sample and control-rate parts marked: That's a playable monophonic subtractive synth. The roadmap's suggested exercise for this lesson is to apply an LFO to amplitude or pitch, then explain what you hear in terms of rate, depth and units. Key takeaways Compare the update rate with the fastest relevant event. Interpolate slow controls; fast envelopes and audible-frequency modulation generally belong in the sample loop. Further reading Sinusoidal FM and PM — Julius O. Smith SmoothedValue — JUCE Real FFT — NumPy

t: Deep exponential modulation and mean frequency
sum: Deep exponential modulation and mean frequency.
x: Exponential versus linear FM Applying an oscillator to pitch in octaves (exponential FM, as you would for vibrato) is not symmetric in hertz. In a quick numpy check, a 5 Hz LFO at ±1 octave on 440 Hz gave an average frequency of 494.5 Hz, roughly 2 semitones sharp. At vibrato depths (±1 semitone) the average was about 440.37 Hz, a small but non-zero mean-frequency shift. For deep FM with an audible-frequency modulator, synths use linear FM (or phase modulation), which can keep the mean instantaneous frequency at the carrier (for zero-mean linear modulation). Perceived pitch and tuner readings depend on the resulting spectrum and analysis method; they are not guaranteed by that arithmetic mean. The ±1-octave result follows from the mapping’s asymmetry: One octave below 440 Hz is 220 Hz; one octave above is 880 Hz. Equal time at paired positive and negative octave offsets adds more hertz on the upper side than it removes on the lower side. Over complete cycles, the arithmetic mean frequency therefore rises even though the sine control itself has zero mean. Key takeaways Symmetry in octaves is asymmetric in hertz. Average instantaneous frequency and perceived pitch are different measurements. Zero-mean linear FM preserves mean instantaneous frequency; periodic PM can too. Further reading Sinusoidal FM and PM — Julius O. Smith Frequency modulation synthesis — CMU

sum: Voltage is measured between two points; current passes through a component.
x: Every circuit in a synth, from an LED on the front panel to the board's audio output, obeys a few simple rules. Learn them well now and the rest of this module is mostly applying them. Low voltage only This module covers low-voltage DC work only: USB power, bench supplies of a few volts, and batteries. It does not cover mains wiring or mains power supplies. Use a ready-made, certified supply (a USB charger or a bench supply) and never open or modify anything that plugs into the wall. Four quantities Voltage (written V, measured in volts, also V) is the difference in electrical potential between two points. It is the "push". A voltage is always between two points. "This pin is at 3.3 V" really means "3.3 V higher than ground". Electric current ( written I, measured in amperes or amps, A) is the rate at which charge flows past a point. One amp is one coulomb per second. Current flows through things. Electrical resistance ( written R, measured in ohms, Ω) is how strongly something opposes current. A resistor is a part made to have a known resistance. Electrical power ( written P, measured in watts, W) is the rate at which energy is transferred, for example turned into heat in a resistor or into light in an LED. A water analogy helps at first: voltage is pressure, current is flow rate, and resistance is a narrow pipe. Don't push it too far. It breaks down for capacitors and for anything at audio or radio frequencies. Ohm's law Ohm's law is the rule you use most: it links the voltage across a resistor to the current through it. For an ohmic resistor at roughly constant temperature, the two are proportional. Double the voltage and the current doubles. The resistance is the fixed ratio between them: For example, a 1 kΩ resistor (1000 Ω) with 5 V across it: Ohm's law models ohmic resistors and the resistive part of wires when temperature and other conditions keep their resistance effectively fixed. It does not describe LEDs and diodes. Their current rises steeply with forward voltage rather than following a fixed resistance. Dividing voltage by current describes an operating point; it does not give a constant resistance that predicts another point. Apply Ohm’s law to the resistor in series with the LED, as in the neighbouring LED units. Key takeaways Voltage is measured between two points; current passes through a component. Use Ohm’s law for resistors at the stated operating conditions, not for LEDs. Further reading OpenStax: Ohm’s law OpenStax: electric current

t: Resistor heat and an LED power budget
sum: Check resistor heat as well as current.
x: Check resistor heat as well as current. Power: voltage times current Power tells you how fast a part turns electrical energy into heat (or light). It's what decides whether a resistor survives. For a two-terminal part, instantaneous absorbed power is voltage times current when positive current enters the terminal labelled positive. In steady DC that is also the time-averaged electrical power. With changing signals, average the instantaneous product; multiplying arbitrary RMS voltages and currents is not a universal power rule: For a resistor only, you can substitute Ohm's law into it. Replace V with I × R to get the second line, or replace I with V / R to get the third: The squared forms only work for resistors, because they rely on Ohm's law. For a steady-DC LED, multiply its voltage by its current. A chip can have several supply and signal terminals; budget the relevant power flows rather than assuming one pair describes every path. Power matters because resistors, regulators and chips all have a maximum they can dissipate before they overheat. A typical small through-hole resistor is rated at 0.25 W (check the actual part's datasheet). An LED's resistor A 5 V supply drives an LED through a 330 Ω resistor, and you measure 10 mA. How much voltage does the resistor take, how hot does it get, and what is left for the LED? The same sum as a short Python script: Key takeaways Check resistor heat as well as current. The squared power formulas assume an ohmic resistor with a fixed resistance. Further reading OpenStax: electrical energy and power SparkFun: LED current limiting

sum: Prefix case matters: milli and mega differ by a billion.
x: Prefix case matters: milli and mega differ by a billion. Units and prefixes Electronics spans huge ranges, so SI prefixes are everywhere. Get them wrong and you're off by a factor of a thousand. Prefix Symbol Factor --------- mega M 10⁶ kilo k 10³ milli m 10⁻³ micro µ (or u) 10⁻⁶ nano n 10⁻⁹ pico p 10⁻¹² Tips: Note the case: m (milli) and M (mega) differ by 10⁹. Schematics often put the prefix where the decimal point would be (the RKM code, part of IEC 60062): 4k7 means 4.7 kΩ, 2R2 means 2.2 Ω, and 100n means 100 nF. A handy pairing: volts ÷ kilohms = milliamps. 3.3 V across 1 kΩ is 3.3 mA. Key takeaways Prefix case matters: milli and mega differ by a billion. Read the unit before substituting a value into a calculation. Further reading BIPM: SI prefixes Vishay: resistor colour code

sum: A steady current needs a complete current return path.
x: A steady current needs a complete current return path. Complete circuits In the steady low-voltage DC model, sustained conduction current flows around a closed electrical loop (a complete circuit): from the supply's positive terminal, through the load, and back to the supply's negative terminal. Break the loop anywhere (an open switch, a loose jumper, a cracked solder joint) and the current everywhere in that loop drops to zero. Two consequences: The current return path is part of the circuit. A signal that leaves your synth board on one wire must come back on another. In ordinary unbalanced audio wiring, the sleeve or shield is that return; balanced audio uses a pair of signal conductors. Current is the same everywhere in a single loop. If 10 mA flows through the resistor, 10 mA flows through the LED. This is Kirchhoff's current law in its simplest form. Kirchhoff's voltage law is the other half: around any closed loop, the voltage rises equal the drops. It's how you work out what is left for the LED once the resistor has taken its share: In this lumped, steady-DC model, include any significant wire resistance as another component. Kirchhoff’s laws do not require zero wire resistance. At high frequencies or with changing magnetic flux, the simple lumped model needs additional care. Conventional current and electron flow Circuit diagrams and textbooks use conventional current: current flows from + to −. That convention predates the discovery of the electron. In a metal wire the charge carriers are actually electrons, which are negative and drift the opposite way, from − to +. Both descriptions predict the same voltages, currents and power. Every formula, datasheet and schematic symbol uses conventional current. A forward-biased diode carries conventional current from anode to cathode (the bar). An LED's outward arrows indicate light, not current. Use conventional current and treat electron flow as a physics detail. Key takeaways A steady current needs a complete current return path. Use conventional current from anode to cathode through a forward-biased LED. Further reading OpenStax: Kirchhoff’s rules OpenStax: electric current SparkFun: LED current limiting

sum: Circuit ground is a chosen reference, distinct from protective earth.
x: Circuit ground is a chosen reference, distinct from protective earth. Ground is a reference Circuit ground (GND, 0 V) is the point you choose to measure every other voltage against. In a battery- or USB-powered synth it's usually the supply's negative terminal. It doesn't have to connect to the earth in the soil. Three meanings of "ground" get mixed up: Signal or circuit ground: the 0 V reference and current return path inside your circuit. This is what "GND" on a microcontroller board means. Chassis ground: the conductive case or chassis reference; whether it connects to circuit 0 V depends on the equipment design. Protective earth: the mains safety earth in a wall socket. It belongs to mains equipment and is not something to modify. The later noise and grounding units return to this. Two practical rules follow: Direct, non-isolated single-ended signals need a common voltage reference. For ordinary GPIO/UART links, connect the boards' GND pins. Isolated links such as DIN MIDI deliberately avoid a direct ground connection. A voltage only means something relative to a reference both sides agree on. "0 V" isn't the same everywhere. Ground wires have small resistances. When current flows through them, two "ground" points can differ by a few millivolts. For audio that's enough to hear (the noise and grounding units). Key takeaways Circuit ground is a chosen reference, distinct from protective earth. Real return conductors develop voltage when current flows. Further reading Analog Devices MT-031: converter grounding RaneNote 110: system interconnection

sum: Series resistances add; parallel branches share a voltage.
x: A common analogue knob on a microcontroller synth uses a potentiometer as a voltage divider. The board reads its wiper voltage with an ADC and turns it into a number; encoders and other controls work differently. To wire knobs correctly, and to understand why some readings come out wrong, you need series and parallel resistance and the divider formula. Series: one path, resistances add Components in series (a series circuit) share a single current path. The same current flows through each one, and their voltages add up to the total. Because the current has to push through every resistor in turn, their resistances simply add: For example, a 1 kΩ and a 2.2 kΩ in series: Parallel: several paths, conductances add Components in parallel (a parallel circuit) connect across the same two connection points, so they all have the same voltage. The currents split between the branches and add up to the total. Each extra branch is another path for current, so the combination conducts more easily than any branch alone. The easy way to add them is by conductance, which is one divided by resistance (how easily current flows). Conductances in parallel add: For exactly two resistors this rearranges into a handier "product over sum" form. The symbol ∥ is shorthand for "in parallel with": Three facts are worth memorising: Two equal positive resistors in parallel give half the value: two 10 kΩ parts combine to 5 kΩ. The parallel total is always smaller than the smallest branch. A much larger resistor in parallel barely changes anything: Key takeaways Series resistances add; parallel branches share a voltage. For positive finite resistances, a parallel total is below the smallest branch. Further reading OpenStax: series and parallel resistors

sum: The output is the bottom resistor’s share of the input.
x: The output is the bottom resistor’s share of the input. The voltage divider Two resistors in series across a supply split the voltage in proportion to their resistances. The output is taken from the junction: The formula comes straight from the two laws in the voltage and current units. The resistors are in series, so one current flows through both, set by their total. Ohm's law on R2 alone then gives the voltage across it: Two examples: The ratio sets the output, not the individual resistance values. 1 kΩ/1 kΩ and 100 kΩ/100 kΩ both halve the voltage when unloaded. The individual resistance values still matter in two ways. They set the divider standing current (and so the wasted power), and they determine how badly the output sags when something draws current from it. Key takeaways The output is the bottom resistor’s share of the input. An unloaded ratio says nothing about how well a divider drives a load. Further reading SparkFun: voltage dividers OpenStax: series and parallel resistors

t: Loading, source resistance and divider limits
sum: Combine a resistive load with the bottom resistor first.
x: Combine a resistive load with the bottom resistor first. Loading: the divider's output changes when you use it The divider formula assumes nothing draws current from the output. Anything you connect there is a load (an electrical load), and it sits in parallel with the bottom resistor. That lowers the effective bottom resistance, so the output falls. To find the loaded output, combine the load with the bottom resistor first, then use the divider formula as before: For a 10 kΩ/10 kΩ divider from 3.3 V with a 10 kΩ load: The script below repeats this for several loads: For a resistive load, compare it with the divider’s output resistance and your allowed error: a load ten times that resistance causes about 9.1% sag, while a hundred times causes about 1% sag. These are trade-offs, not universal pass/fail limits. A 1 MΩ load barely moves a 10 kΩ divider. A 10 kΩ load drags it from 1.65 V to 1.10 V. The divider's output resistance (its source impedance) tells you how easily a load can pull it around. Seen from the output, the supply acts like a short for changes, so the two resistors appear in parallel: The lower the output resistance, the less a load disturbs it, but the more divider standing current (the current that flows through the divider all the time) it wastes. Why this matters for ADCs A microcontroller's ADC input isn't a pure open circuit. Many ADCs briefly connect a small sampling capacitor that has to charge through the source's resistance. If the source impedance is too high, the sampling capacitor may not settle to the new input voltage; the error can have either sign depending on its previous charge, and noise can also matter. The chip's datasheet or reference manual states the maximum source impedance for a given sampling time. Check it for your board rather than assuming a value. Dividers are not power supplies A divider can make a reference voltage for a high-impedance input. It can't power anything that draws significant or varying current. Feed a 5 V-to-3.3 V divider into a board's power pin and the voltage collapses as soon as the board draws current. Use a voltage regulator for power. Key takeaways Combine a resistive load with the bottom resistor first. Output resistance and allowed error determine acceptable loading. Further reading TI: linear-regulator fundamentals SparkFun: voltage dividers OpenStax: series and parallel resistors

t: Wiring a potentiometer to an ADC
sum: Use the documented analogue supply and ADC voltage limits.
x: Use the documented analogue supply and ADC voltage limits. The potentiometer: a divider with a moving tap A potentiometer (pot) is a resistive track with a wiper that slides along it. It has three terminals: the two ends of the track and the wiper. Wire one end to the supply, the other to ground, and the wiper is a divider output. Turn the knob and you move the wiper position between the upper part of the track and the lower part. The total stays fixed: For an unloaded linear 10 kΩ pot across 3.3 V, a quarter-track setting leaves 2.5 kΩ below the wiper and gives about 0.83 V. This assumes the ground end is the bottom and the track is ideal. For a microcontroller knob: Points to watch: Use the board's documented analogue supply for the pot, matching the ADC range. Do not load an unbuffered VREF pin unless the documentation explicitly allows it. If the pot is fed from a different voltage, the ADC's full range won't match the knob's full range. Feeding it from a higher voltage could also exceed the input's maximum (the logic and datasheet units). Swapping pins 1 and 3 reverses the direction of the knob. It's harmless and easily fixed in software. Never wire the wiper straight to a supply rail. At one extreme the wiper sits at the end connected to ground, and you'd short the supply through a few ohms of track. The pot's resistance trades divider standing current against source impedance. Values around 10 kΩ are a common choice for microcontroller knobs, but confirm against the ADC's source-impedance limit. Worst-case source resistance Key takeaways Use the documented analogue supply and ADC voltage limits. A pot’s wiper source resistance peaks in the middle of a linear track. Further reading Bourns PDB181-GTR: circuit and taper charts SparkFun: voltage dividers PJRC: Teensy 4.1 signal-voltage limits

sum: Taper describes resistance versus rotation.
x: Taper describes resistance versus rotation. Linear and logarithmic (audio) taper The potentiometer taper (or law) is how resistance changes with rotation. Linear taper: halfway round, the wiper is at half the total resistance. Output voltage is proportional to angle. Logarithmic or "audio" taper: the resistance changes slowly at first, then quickly. A common specification is a 10% log taper, meaning the wiper is at 10% of the total at mid-rotation. Hearing is roughly logarithmic, so a log pot makes an analogue volume control feel even. Rotation Linear 10% log (approx.) --------- 0% 0% 0% 50% 50% 10% 100% 100% 100% Two practical warnings: Markings aren't standardised. For example, Bourns PDB181-GTR uses its A-series audio curves and B0 linear curve. Other manufacturers and legacy parts use different letter schemes. Read the datasheet. Cheap log pots are approximations, often two linear segments joined near the middle. For digital synths, usually choose linear When a pot feeds an ADC, you can apply any curve you like in software. A linear pot gives even resolution across the whole rotation, and code can map it to a logarithmic volume or exponential frequency response. A log pot is mostly useful when it directly controls an analogue audio level. Key takeaways Taper describes resistance versus rotation. Verify the manufacturer’s marking scheme rather than assuming a letter code. Further reading Bourns PDB181-GTR: circuit and taper charts

sum: Read digits, multiplier and tolerance separately.
x: A synth build uses a small set of passive parts over and over. Each one has a value (what it does) and ratings (what it survives). Ignoring ratings or component polarity can damage parts even when the nominal value is correct. Reading the value Through-hole resistors use colour bands defined by IEC 60062. Read from the end where the bands bunch together. The gold or silver tolerance band is usually at the other end, often slightly separated. Colour Digit Multiplier --------- Black 0 ×1 Brown 1 ×10 Red 2 ×100 Orange 3 ×1k Yellow 4 ×10k Green 5 ×100k Blue 6 ×1M Violet 7 ×10M Grey 8 ×100M White 9 ×1G Gold ×0.1 Silver ×0.01 Four-band resistor code: digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance. Yellow-violet-red-gold = 4, 7, ×100 = 4.7 kΩ ±5%. Five-band resistor code (precision): digit, digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance. Brown-black-black-red-brown = 1, 0, 0, ×100 = 10 kΩ ±1%. Tolerance band: brown ±1%, red ±2%, gold ±5%, silver ±10%. The digit bands form a whole number, and the multiplier band scales it: A five-band resistor uses three significant digits. Brown-black-black-red-brown has three digits followed by the red multiplier and brown tolerance: Colours are easy to misread under poor light. Brown, red and orange look alike, and so do violet and grey. Measure with a multimeter before fitting (out of circuit) whenever you're unsure. Key takeaways Read digits, multiplier and tolerance separately. Confirm uncertain colours by measuring the unpowered resistor out of circuit. Further reading Vishay: resistor colour code

sum: Choose an actual preferred value, then recalculate the result.
x: Choose an actual preferred value, then recalculate the result. Preferred values Resistors come in E-series values. E12 (for ±10%) has 12 values per decade (each tenfold range, such as 10 to 100): 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82. E24 adds more in between. You calculate an ideal value, then choose the nearest standard value in the safe direction. The values aren't arbitrary. The underlying ideal sequence uses a constant ratio, so neighbours are approximately evenly spaced in percentage terms. The actual preferred values use a standard table: E24 uses the same idea with 24 steps per decade (n ÷ 24), each about 10% apart. Tolerance and resistor dissipation rating Component tolerance: how far a real part may be from its marked value. A 10 kΩ ±5% part may be anywhere from 9.5 to 10.5 kΩ. For a divider that sets a precise level, use 1% parts. Resistor dissipation rating: the most power the part can turn into heat continuously. Common small through-hole resistors are rated around 0.25 W. Check the datasheet. Calculate the power and leave margin. Running at half the rating or less is a common conservative practice. For the power check, use the resistor form of the power law from the voltage and current units: Key takeaways Choose an actual preferred value, then recalculate the result. Tolerance, temperature and power derating belong in the design check. Further reading Vishay: preferred-value table, IEC 60063 Vishay: resistor colour code OpenStax: electrical energy and power

sum: More capacitance slows voltage change for the same current.
x: More capacitance slows voltage change for the same current. A capacitor stores charge between conductors separated by an insulating dielectric. Capacitance is measured in farads; practical parts span picofarads to thousands of microfarads. The following model assumes ideal capacitance and a fixed charging current where a finite voltage-change per unit time is calculated. Behaviour An ideal capacitor blocks steady DC current once charged; a steady voltage can remain across it. Real capacitors have leakage and other losses. It passes changes, since current flows while its voltage is changing. This is why it can remove a DC offset from an audio signal or short fast noise to ground. Its voltage can't jump instantly. It changes at a rate set by the current: The RC time constant For an initially discharged ideal capacitor charged through a fixed resistor by a DC voltage step, the charging curve is exponential: fast at first, then slower and slower as it nears the supply. The RC time constant sets how long that takes: The time constant is the unit of time for the charging curve: After five time constants it's within 1% of the final voltage (99.3%). The curve assumes an ideal capacitor and a steady source. When the source is removed and it discharges through a resistor, the remaining capacitor voltage decays exponentially, approaching 0 V. Key takeaways More capacitance slows voltage change for the same current. An ideal RC step reaches about 63.2% after one time constant. Further reading OpenStax: ideal RC circuits

sum: An unloaded RC low-pass has its cutoff at one over two pi times RC.
x: An unloaded RC low-pass has its cutoff at one over two pi times RC. An RC low-pass filter RC circuits show up across synth hardware. They smooth a noisy knob and slow a bouncing switch. A resistor followed by a capacitor to ground is also the simplest low-pass filter (an RC low-pass filter): it passes slow changes and shorts fast ones to ground. Its cut-off frequency is: This assumes whatever reads the capacitor draws almost no current. A load across the capacitor changes the cut-off, just as it loads a divider. Key takeaways An unloaded RC low-pass has its cutoff at one over two pi times RC. Loading and nonideal components change the simple model. Further reading TI Precision Labs: passive RC response OpenStax: ideal RC circuits SparkFun: voltage dividers

t: Capacitor types, component polarity and real capacitance
sum: Check component polarity and working-voltage limits for the exact part.
x: Check component polarity and working-voltage limits for the exact part. Types Type Polarised? Typical use --------- Ceramic (MLCC) No Decoupling (100 nF), small values Film No Audio signal paths, filters Ordinary aluminium electrolytic Yes Bulk supply filtering, large µF Tantalum Yes Compact bulk capacitance Things to watch: Component polarity. Ordinary polarised aluminium electrolytic and tantalum capacitors must have their + lead at the higher voltage. Specially specified non-polarised electrolytic types also exist; use each part only as its manufacturer permits. On aluminium electrolytics a stripe marks the negative lead, and the negative lead is usually the shorter one. On tantalum capacitors the marking works the other way: a stripe or bar usually marks the positive lead. Check the datasheet. Reverse them and they can overheat, vent or burst; tantalums can fail short and catch fire. Don't use a polarised capacitor where the voltage across it can reverse, such as a plain AC audio signal with no DC bias. Voltage rating. Every capacitor has a maximum working voltage. Choose one comfortably above the highest voltage it will see. A 6.3 V capacitor on a 5 V rail leaves little margin, so 10 V or 16 V is more comfortable. Margin is a design rule of thumb; check the manufacturer's guidance for the part. Ceramic DC bias. Many high-value ceramics (X7R, X5R and similar Class 2 dielectrics) lose a significant share of their capacitance when a DC voltage is applied, sometimes well over half near the rated voltage. The effect is documented in manufacturers' DC-bias curves. The "X7R" code itself only describes temperature behaviour (±15% from −55 to +125 °C); it says nothing about voltage. C0G/NP0 (Class 1) ceramics barely change with voltage or temperature, but come in much smaller values than Class 2 types of the same size. Markings. Small ceramics often use a three-digit code: two digits, then the number of zeros, in picofarads. 104 means 10 followed by four zeros: Key takeaways Check component polarity and working-voltage limits for the exact part. Use the DC-bias curve for Class 2 ceramic capacitors. Further reading Murata: capacitance under an applied DC voltage Murata: ceramic types and temperature codes Analog Devices MT-101: decoupling techniques

sum: Subtract the LED drop before sizing the resistor.
x: Subtract the LED drop before sizing the resistor. LEDs and the current-limiting resistor An LED is a diode that emits light. It normally conducts strongly under forward bias and carries much less reverse current within its reverse-voltage limits. Its current rises steeply with forward voltage; the quoted forward voltage (written V_f) is measured at a stated current rather than being a fixed switching threshold, so an LED always needs something to limit its current, usually a series resistor. The forward voltage depends on colour and current. For a typical red indicator LED it's around 1.8–2.2 V at 20 mA, and for blue and white around 3–3.5 V. Datasheet maximums are higher: For a concrete example, the Kingbright WP7113ID red LED datasheet and WP7113QBC/D blue LED datasheet give their own forward-voltage figures at specified test currents. WP7113ID revision V.14A dated 8 January 2026 lists 1.9 V typical and 2.3 V maximum at 10 mA; WP7113QBC/D revision V.18B dated 26 March 2025 lists 3.3 V typical and 4.0 V maximum at 20 mA (both checked 16 October 2026). Package size or colour alone is not a specification. Use the figures from your LED's datasheet. Small 3 mm and 5 mm indicator LEDs are usually characterised at 20 mA, with an absolute-maximum continuous current often in the 20–30 mA range. A characterization current is not a recommended default drive current. Use the exact LED’s allowed current and thermal derating; many indicators are useful at only a few milliamps. The resistor's job is to take whatever voltage the LED doesn't. Kirchhoff's voltage law gives that leftover voltage, and Ohm's law on the resistor turns it into a resistance: 260 Ω is not an E12 preferred value, so pick the next E12 value up, 270 Ω, and recalculate what you actually get: Forward voltage varies with device, current and temperature, so this nominal calculation is an estimate. A hardware bound uses maximum supply, minimum LED drop, minimum resistor value and all relevant component and pin limits. The same calculation in Python, including the safe E12 selection: Round up to the next standard value. That gives slightly less current, which is the safe direction. Then check the resistor's power (about 6 mW here) and the source's limits. When a microcontroller pin drives the LED, the pin's maximum output current from the board's datasheet also applies. LED orientation: the longer leg is usually the anode (+). The cathode (−) is often marked by a flat on the rim. Check the datasheet. Reversed, it may stay dark but may also exceed its allowed reverse voltage. Do not apply a reverse voltage beyond the exact LED’s rating. LED reverse ratings are often only a few volts. Key takeaways Subtract the LED drop before sizing the resistor. Use worst-case supply, forward voltage and resistor tolerance for hardware. Further reading Kingbright WP7113ID, revision V.14A Kingbright WP7113QBC/D, revision V.18B SparkFun: LED current limiting

sum: A diode’s current and temperature affect its forward drop.
x: A diode’s current and temperature affect its forward drop. Diodes A forward-biased diode conducts conventional current from anode to cathode (towards the bar in its schematic symbol; an LED’s outward arrows represent emitted light). Reverse-biased, it normally carries a small leakage current until breakdown; respect the exact reverse-voltage rating. The cathode is marked with a band. Type Forward drop (approx.) Common use --------- Silicon (e.g. 1N4148) ~0.6–0.75 V at a few mA Low-current signal switching, diode clamping Silicon rectifier (e.g. 1N400x) ~0.7 V small current, up to ~1 V at 1 A Reverse-polarity protection Schottky ~0.2–0.4 V small current, ~0.45–0.6 V at 1 A Low-drop protection The forward drops are approximate, and they rise with current and fall with temperature. Datasheets give limits at stated test conditions and show typical curves. Checked 16 October 2026: Vishay 1N4148 revision 1.6 (7 November 2024) gives 1 V maximum at 10 mA; Vishay 1N5817 revision 1 July 2020 gives 0.45 V maximum at 1 A, while Vishay 1N4001–1N4007 revision 29 April 2020 gives 1.1 V maximum at 1 A. These are exact documented examples, not a universal diode drop. Uses in a synth: Reverse-polarity protection: a series diode in the supply line blocks current if the supply is connected backwards, at the cost of its forward drop. Diode clamping: diodes to the supply rails catch input overvoltage (the logic and datasheet units). Flyback: a correctly oriented diode across a DC relay or motor coil lets its current recirculate after switch-off, limiting the voltage spike while stored magnetic energy is dissipated. Check the drive circuit and release-time requirements. Key takeaways A diode’s current and temperature affect its forward drop. Check component polarity and reverse ratings; a diode does not eliminate all fault paths. Further reading Vishay 1N4148, revision 1.6 Vishay 1N4001–1N4007, revision 29 April 2020 Vishay 1N5817–1N5819, revision 1 July 2020

sum: Poles and throws describe routing; momentary describes spring return.
x: Poles and throws describe routing; momentary describes spring return. Switches and buttons Switches are described by their poles and throws: switch poles are the independent circuits switched, and switch throws are the positions each pole can connect to. SPST: single pole, single throw. A simple on/off. SPDT: single pole, double throw. A common terminal switches between two others. DPDT: two SPDT switches moved together. Momentary switches spring back when released; a normally open push button connects while pressed, whereas a normally closed one opens. Latching switches stay in the selected state. Toggle describes the actuator, and toggle switches can be latching or momentary. Tactile buttons often have four legs that are internally connected in pairs. Check which pairs with a continuity tester before wiring. Mechanical contacts bounce (contact bounce): for a few milliseconds a press looks like several rapid presses. A microcontroller reading a button also needs a defined idle level from a pull-up or pull-down resistor. Debouncing and pull-ups are covered with the embedded topics. Connectors and pinouts Connectors are where parts are most often wired wrong. Pin headers are commonly on a 2.54 mm (0.1 in) contact spacing. Pin 1 is marked by a square pad, a triangle or a dot. Pinout diagrams can be drawn from either side. "Looking into the socket" and "looking at the solder side" are mirror images. Check which view the diagram shows. Audio jacks: on a 3.5 mm or 6.35 mm TRS stereo jack, the tip carries left, the ring carries right and the sleeve is ground. On a mono TS jack, the tip carries the signal and the sleeve is ground. Connector keying: keyed connectors only fit one way. Unkeyed headers fit both ways, including the wrong one. Product-specific connectors (power inputs, MIDI DIN, board edge headers) have pinouts defined by the product or standard. Take them from that documentation, never from memory. DIN MIDI isn't a direct GPIO connection; it needs the interface circuit from the MIDI specification, covered in a later module. Component polarity and pinout mistakes destroy parts Before power-up, check every polarised part (electrolytics, diodes, LEDs, chips) and every connector orientation against the schematic. It takes a minute and catches the most common fatal mistakes. Key takeaways Poles and throws describe routing; momentary describes spring return. Confirm both internal switch contacts and the view used for a connector pinout. Further reading SparkFun: reading schematics SparkFun: breadboard connections RaneNote 110: system interconnection

t: Supply pins, signal limits and stress ratings
sum: A board’s power input does not specify its I/O voltage tolerance.
x: The fastest way to destroy a microcontroller board is to connect something at the wrong voltage. This lesson covers how to know, from the documents, what each pin will accept, and how to make two parts with different supplies talk safely. Scope Everything here concerns low-voltage DC logic and audio circuits, typically 3.3 V and 5 V. Power your circuits from a certified USB supply or bench supply. Mains power-supply design is out of scope. Supply voltages: 3.3 V and 5 V Two supply voltages dominate hobby digital electronics: 5 V: a common board-input supply, including ordinary USB-powered examples in this module, and the native supply of older logic families and many classic microcontrollers. 3.3 V: a common supply for modern microcontrollers, including the ARM chips on audio-focused boards. Many boards accept 5 V from USB and use an on-board voltage regulator to make 3.3 V for the chip. The board may expose both voltages on pins. The fact that 5 V exists on the board says nothing about whether the chip's I/O pins tolerate 5 V. A real board's limits PJRC’s Teensy 4.1 product documentation (checked 16 October 2026; this page does not identify a separate PCB revision) states that its digital pins accept 0 to 3.3 V signals and "are not 5V tolerant", and that the analogue range is fixed at 0 to 3.3 V. Other boards differ: some microcontrollers have individual 5 V-tolerant pins. Read the exact board and revision's documentation and the microcontroller datasheet, and record the date you checked. Absolute maximum ratings versus recommended operating conditions Every datasheet separates two very different tables. Absolute Maximum Ratings describe stress limits, not guaranteed operation. Exceeding them can cause permanent damage; extended operation at those limits can reduce reliability. TI’s SN74HC00 datasheet SCLS181H (revision H, August 2021; checked 16 October 2026) includes a supply maximum of 7 V and an input clamp current of ±20 mA. Recommended Operating Conditions are where the part is guaranteed to work as specified: for the SN74HC00, a supply (V_CC) from 2 V to 6 V, with inputs between 0 V and the supply voltage. Design inside recommended conditions with margin. Never treat an absolute maximum as a target. Living near it can shorten the part's life even if it doesn't fail at once. Key takeaways A board’s power input does not specify its I/O voltage tolerance. Design inside recommended conditions, not at absolute maximum ratings. Further reading TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H PJRC: Teensy 4.1 signal-voltage limits

sum: Compare worst-case output levels with guaranteed input thresholds.
x: Compare worst-case output levels with guaranteed input thresholds. Logic levels and thresholds A digital input doesn't care about the exact voltage. It decides "high" or "low" using thresholds from its datasheet: Symbol Meaning ------ V_IH(min) Lowest voltage guaranteed read as high V_IL(max) Highest voltage guaranteed read as low V_OH(min) Lowest voltage a high output guarantees V_OL(max) Highest voltage a low output guarantees Between V_IL(max) and V_IH(min) is a forbidden zone where the input's behaviour isn't guaranteed. An output can drive an input reliably only if the worst-case output always lands inside the region the input is guaranteed to accept, in both states: The gaps between the two sides are the noise margins: how much noise (or ground offset) the link can tolerate before a bit is misread: Key takeaways Compare driver and receiver guarantees for both states. A positive static margin is a budget for specified noise and ground offset; electrical stress and timing still need separate checks. Further reading TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H TI SN74HCT00, manufacturer datasheet TI: interpreting standard-logic datasheets, SZZA036C

sum: Compare actual HC and HCT thresholds before translating logic levels.
x: Use the threshold and noise-margin definitions from the preceding unit to choose an interface. The output limits in this example are illustrative driver guarantees: a high of at least 2.4 V and a low of at most 0.4 V. Check the real part’s load, supply, temperature, edge rates and receiving voltage limits. HC and HCT threshold examples Part (supply) Reads high from Reads low up to --------- SN74HC00 (4.5 V) 3.15 V 1.35 V SN74HCT00 (4.5–5.5 V) 2.0 V 0.8 V Checked 16 October 2026: these examples use TI SN74HC00 datasheet SCLS181H (revision H, August 2021) and SN74HCT00 datasheet SCLS062F (revision F, October 2022). The SN74HC00 figures come from its datasheet (Recommended Operating Conditions with a 4.5 V supply). HC input thresholds scale with the supply voltage. The SN74HCT00 figures are "TTL-compatible" thresholds, designed to accept lower-voltage highs. Suppose a 3.3 V microcontroller output guarantees a high of at least 2.4 V and a low of at most 0.4 V. These are illustrative output guarantees for this calculation, not a specification for an arbitrary microcontroller. Take the real ones from your chip's datasheet at your load current. Into each part: The same check in Python: The negative high margin means a 3.3 V output isn't guaranteed to be read as high by a 5 V HC input. It may work on your bench and fail on another day or another chip. The HCT part has positive margins in both states, which is why an HCT buffer powered from 5 V is a standard way to translate 3.3 V logic up to 5 V. TI's HCT application note (SCLA011) recommends HCT parts for the closely related problem of feeding TTL-level outputs into HC logic. The dangerous direction: 5 V into 3.3 V Going down is the real hazard. A 5 V output driving a 3.3 V-only input exceeds that input's rating. Options, depending on speed and direction: A level-shifter chip designed for the job (the robust choice for fast or bidirectional signals). A voltage divider (two resistors) to scale 5 V down to about 3.3 V, for slow, one-way signals. Lesson 2's loading rules apply. An input the datasheet explicitly specifies as 5 V tolerant, under the stated conditions. Key takeaways HCT inputs can accept the example driver’s lower high voltage when every stated condition is satisfied. Going from a 5 V output to a 3.3 V-only input needs documented level conversion; the board supply does not establish I/O tolerance. Further reading TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H TI SN74HCT00, manufacturer datasheet TI: interpreting standard-logic datasheets, SZZA036C

sum: Match part, package, view, temperature, supply and load conditions.
x: Match part, package, view, temperature, supply and load conditions. Reading a datasheet Datasheets follow a predictable layout. In order of usefulness to a beginner: Features and description: what the part is, supply range, key specs. Pin configuration: pin numbers and names. Note which view (top view is standard for ICs) and the pin 1 marking. Absolute maximum ratings: what will damage it. Recommended operating conditions: where to design. Electrical characteristics: guaranteed min/max values under stated test conditions, such as V_OH at a given load current. Typical characteristics (graphs): how the part usually behaves. Not guaranteed. Application and layout information: example circuits, decoupling and layout advice. Often the most practical section. Rules of thumb: Design to min/max, not "typ". Typical values describe representative behaviour under the stated conditions and are not production guarantees. Read the test conditions. A guaranteed minimum high output at 20 µA isn't the same as at 4 mA. TI's SN74HC00 lists 4.4 V and 3.98 V respectively, with a 4.5 V supply at 25 °C. Read the footnotes. They hold the exceptions. Get the datasheet for the exact part number, including suffixes, from the manufacturer. Key takeaways Match part, package, view, temperature, supply and load conditions. Typical curves describe behaviour but are not guaranteed limits. Further reading TI: interpreting standard-logic datasheets, SZZA036C TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H

t: Level conversion, input clamps and back-powering
sum: Use proper level conversion during normal operation.
x: Use proper level conversion during normal operation. Protecting inputs Inputs that connect to the outside world (jacks, long wires, other equipment) see accidents: wrong voltages, static discharge, hot-plugging. Many CMOS inputs, including the SN74HC00, have internal clamp diodes from each input to the supply pin (V_CC) and to GND. When an input goes beyond a rail by a diode drop, the diode conducts and dumps the excess current into the rail. A series resistor limits the current that flows into those clamps during a fault. TI permits particular over-rail cases only when its specified pin-current limits are observed; that exception belongs to this exact device, not every microcontroller. During a fault the clamp holds the pin about one diode drop above the rail, so the resistor takes the rest of the fault voltage: The 0.5 V clamp drop is an assumption: the real drop depends on the chip and the current, and like any silicon junction it is usually somewhat higher at milliamp currents. A lower actual drop would increase the current, so 0.5 V is only an illustrative assumption, not a guaranteed current bound. A real protection design needs the diode curve, resistor tolerance, rail behaviour and chip injection limits. Be conservative: Clamps are fault protection, not a level shifter. Some manufacturers, such as PJRC for Teensy 4.1, say plainly not to drive pins above 3.3 V. Use proper level conversion for normal operation. Microcontrollers specify their own injected-current limits. Check the chip's datasheet rather than borrowing a 74HC figure. Back-powering: a signal driven into an unpowered chip can power it partly through the clamp diodes, causing strange behaviour or damage. Power boards up together, or make sure signals can't arrive before the supply. External Schottky clamps (with a lower forward drop than the internal diodes) are often added on exposed inputs, so they conduct before the chip's internal diodes do. Key takeaways Use proper level conversion during normal operation. Clamp current and supply-rail injection must both remain within documented limits. Further reading TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H TI: interpreting standard-logic datasheets, SZZA036C PJRC: Teensy 4.1 signal-voltage limits

t: Local decoupling and bulk supply storage
sum: A local capacitor shortens the path for switching current pulses.
x: A local capacitor shortens the path for switching current pulses. Decoupling capacitors Digital chips draw current in very short pulses each time their transistors switch. The supply wiring has resistance and inductance, so it can't deliver those pulses instantly. The local supply voltage dips and rings, and that noise spreads to everything sharing the supply, including audio. A decoupling capacitor (bypass capacitor) next to the chip's supply pin acts as a local reservoir, supplying the pulses so the long supply path doesn't have to. For TI SN74HC00, datasheet SCLS181H recommends 0.1 µF at the supply terminal, allows combining it with 1 µF to address different noise frequencies, and places bypass capacitors close to the supply terminal. Practical rules: Use each device’s specified local capacitors. For SN74HC00, the documented 100 nF capacitor goes close to its supply pin, with short connections to the pin and to ground. Distance adds inductance and defeats the purpose. Bulk capacitance (an electrolytic, say 10–100 µF) where power enters a board, for slower load changes. Values are typical, not prescriptive; follow the datasheets. Follow the datasheet where it gives specific values. Audio codecs and regulators often do. The noise and grounding units explain why this matters even more for audio. Key takeaways A local capacitor shortens the path for switching current pulses. Use the exact chip and regulator’s specified values and layout. Further reading TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H Analog Devices MT-101: decoupling techniques

sum: Follow nets, pin numbers, labels and junctions rather than page geometry.
x: A schematic says what connects to what. A breadboard is one physical way to make those connections. The skill is moving between the two without error, and checking your work before power goes on. Common symbols Symbols vary between the US/ANSI style and the IEC style used in Europe. You'll meet both. Part Symbol notes Designator --------- Resistor Zigzag (US) or rectangle (IEC) R1, R2 Capacitor Two parallel plates C1 Polarised capacitor One plate curved or marked + C2 Diode Diode symbol with a cathode bar; not a current arrow D1 LED Diode with outward arrows D2, LED1 Potentiometer Resistor with an arrow (wiper) RV1, VR1 Switch / button Broken line with a lever SW1, S1 IC Box with numbered pins U1, IC1 Connector / jack Varies; pins numbered J1, P1 Ground Downward lines or a triangle GND Supply Arrow, bar or label (+5V, 3V3) VCC The reference designator (R1, C3, U2) links each symbol to the parts list and to the board's silkscreen. Use designators in your notes too: "R3 is wrong" is unambiguous. Reading a schematic Nets, not pictures A schematic is a graph made of schematic nets. Each net is a set of pins joined together electrically. Wire lengths and positions mean nothing; only connections do. Junction dots mark wires that connect. Two wires crossing without a dot don't connect. Many drawing conventions avoid four-way junctions entirely, so a cross is never ambiguous. Net labels: two wires with the same label (for example ADC0 or +3V3) are connected even if no line joins them. Power and ground symbols are net labels too. Matching symbols for the same named ground or supply identify that net within the schematic’s scope. Distinct AGND and DGND symbols or hierarchical labels need the design’s own connection rules. Hidden power pins: some schematics omit an IC's supply pins from the drawing. Check the datasheet pinout so you don't forget to power the chip. Conventions that help Signals usually flow left to right: inputs on the left, outputs on the right. Higher voltages at the top, ground at the bottom. Values sit beside designators: R1 10k, C4 100n. Reading a pot input +3V3 → RV1 pin 3, RV1 pin 1 → GND, RV1 pin 2 → net ADC0, C5 100n from ADC0 to GND, and elsewhere ADC0 → U1 pin 14. That's three nets: +3V3, GND and ADC0. ADC0 has three members: the pot’s wiper, one terminal of the capacitor and U1 pin 14. Key takeaways Follow nets, pin numbers, labels and junctions rather than page geometry. Reference designators identify actual parts. Further reading SparkFun: reading schematics TI SN74HC00, SCLS181H

sum: Verify the board’s internal strips and any split rails unpowered.
x: Verify the board’s internal strips and any split rails unpowered. How a breadboard is connected A solderless breadboard has spring clips under the holes, joined in fixed groups: Terminal strips: in each numbered row, holes a–e are connected to each other, and f–j are connected to each other. The two halves are not connected across the centre channel. Centre channel: DIP chips straddle it, so each pin gets its own strip. Power rails: long strips along each edge, usually marked red (+) and blue or black (−). Rails on opposite sides aren't connected. Bridge them with jumpers if you want the same supply on both sides. Some boards split the rails halfway along. A gap in the red or blue line often marks this. Check with a continuity tester, because a split rail is a classic "half my circuit is dead" bug. From schematic to breadboard A systematic method avoids most wiring errors: Number the nets. Write every net from the schematic as a list: GND, +3V3, ADC0, LED_A, and so on. Give each net a home. Power and ground go on the rails. Each other net gets one terminal strip (or several joined by a jumper). Place ICs across the channel first, with pin 1 in a known row. Then place parts around them. Plug each component lead into the strip for its net. A resistor between ADC0 and GND has one lead in the ADC0 row and one on the − rail. Avoid shorting a component to itself. Both legs of a resistor in the same strip bypass its resistance: both ends are on the same net. Colour code wires: red for positive supply, black or blue for ground, other colours for signals. It's a convention, not a rule, but it makes checking much faster. Tick off each connection on the schematic as you make it. Breadboard limits Breadboards are for low-voltage, low-current, low-frequency prototyping. Spring contacts have some resistance and can loosen. Adjacent strips add stray capacitance whose value depends on the board and wiring. Long jumpers pick up noise. An audio prototype can be noisier than a well laid out finished board. Record the limitation and investigate unexplained hum rather than assuming every noise is unavoidable. Key takeaways Verify the board’s internal strips and any split rails unpowered. Place component ends on the intended different nets. Further reading SparkFun: breadboard connections SparkFun: reading schematics

sum: Keep the schematic, pin table, parts, photos and measurements together.
x: Keep the schematic, pin table, parts, photos and measurements together. Documenting wiring Your future self, or the project's success criteria ("wiring, parts, limitations... documented"), needs enough detail to rebuild the circuit: A schematic with designators and values. A hand drawing photographed is fine early on. A connection table for anything wired to a board's pins: Net From To --------- +3V3 Board 3V3 pin RV1 pin 3 ADC0 RV1 pin 2 Documented ADC input GND Board GND RV1 pin 1, rail − A photo of the breadboard, taken from above in good light. The exact parts: manufacturer part numbers or at least values and types, and the board model and revision. What you measured (expected against actual) and the date. Keep it with the code in version control, so a wiring change and the code that expects it stay together. Key takeaways Keep the schematic, pin table, parts, photos and measurements together. Name the exact board revision and documentation checked. Further reading SparkFun: reading schematics SparkFun: breadboard connections

t: Checking a prototype before first power
sum: Check component polarity, rail resistance and supply voltage before power.
x: Check component polarity, rail resistance and supply voltage before power. Before you apply power Do these checks every time, and they become fast: Visual check: every polarised part (electrolytics, diodes, LEDs, ICs) the right way round. No stray wire ends or component legs touching. Supply to ground, power off: use the meter's resistance or continuity mode across the supply rails. A dead short (a near-zero reading or a continuous beep) means stop and find it. A brief beep that stops can be capacitors charging from the meter. Check rail continuity: each rail connects end to end (or you know where it's split). Check the supply's voltage before connecting it: measure the supply's output on its own. Limit the current if you can: a bench supply with an adjustable current limit, set just above the expected draw, can reduce sustained fault current. It cannot guarantee protection: supply output capacitance, current-limit reaction delay, device limits and wiring still matter. First power-up: observe the supply current and watch for abnormal heat or smell; use a suitable thermometer if needed. Do not touch exposed energised conductors or hot components. Anything getting hot or smelling means disconnect at once. Measure the rails powered: confirm the supply voltage at the chip's pins, not just at the supply. Key takeaways Check component polarity, rail resistance and supply voltage before power. A current limit reduces available fault current but cannot guarantee protection. Further reading Keysight E3633A/E3634A: load and output-capacitance limits Tektronix: bench-supply CV/CC operation SparkFun: breadboard connections Fluke: resistance measurement SparkFun: using a multimeter

t: Voltage measurement, ranges and meter loading
sum: Voltage is measured across two points with the correct jack and range.
x: Measuring tells you whether the circuit is doing what you calculated. Soldering makes a circuit permanent. Both are hands-on skills with a few rules that, if you ignore them, destroy fuses, parts or your lungs. Low-voltage work only Everything here assumes low-voltage DC circuits powered from USB, batteries or a bench supply. Don't use these techniques on mains-powered equipment. Mains measurement needs suitably rated (CAT-rated) instruments and training, and it's outside this project's scope. A digital multimeter (DMM) has a rotary switch and usually three or four input jacks: COM: the common (black) lead. It stays here for everything. VΩ (shared with current only on some meters): red lead for voltage, resistance, continuity and diode test. mA / µA: red lead for small currents, protected by a fuse. A or 10A: red lead for large currents, fused only if the meter’s manual specifies it; some inexpensive meters leave that input unfused. The jack layout differs between meters, so read the manual. Voltage: in parallel Put the probes across the thing you're measuring, black on the reference (usually ground) and red on the point of interest. Nothing gets disconnected. Use DC volts (V⎓) for supply rails and logic. AC volts usually rejects the DC component, so it will not tell you a rail’s steady voltage. An average-responding meter is RMS-calibrated for a sine wave; other waveforms need a suitable true-RMS instrument within its frequency, crest-factor and range limits. A digital meter's voltage input is high-impedance, typically around 10 MΩ on DC volts, though some meters and ranges differ (check your meter's specification). It barely loads most circuits, but on a very high-resistance divider the meter itself pulls the reading down. Lesson 2's loading rule applies to meters too. A negative DC reading means the red probe is below the black probe in voltage. The probes may be reversed, or the measured voltage may genuinely have the opposite polarity. Choosing ranges Autoranging meters choose for you. On a manual meter: Start on a range above the largest value you expect, then step down for resolution. An "OL" or "1" display means meter over-range. Go up a range. For current, start on the highest range if you're unsure, which on many meters means moving the red lead to the A jack. Key takeaways Voltage is measured across two points with the correct jack and range. The meter’s finite input impedance can load high-resistance circuits. Further reading SparkFun: using a multimeter SparkFun: voltage dividers

t: Measuring series current and burden voltage
sum: Power off before inserting the meter in series.
x: Power off before inserting the meter in series. Current: in series To measure current, the current has to flow through the meter. Break the circuit and insert the meter into the gap: Power off. Move the red lead to the mA jack (or the A jack for larger currents) and select the current range. Open the circuit at one point and connect the meter across the gap. Power on and read. Power off and move the red lead back to VΩ before your next measurement. The classic fuse-blower In current mode the meter is almost a short circuit, by design. Put it across a supply (as you would for voltage) and you short the supply through the meter. The meter's fuse is there to blow in that case. Replace it only with the exact type and rating the manual specifies. Forgetting to move the red lead back to VΩ is the commonest way to do this. Meters also have a burden voltage: the small voltage the meter drops while measuring current. It comes from the series resistance of the shunt and other current-path parts, including the fuse and connections. Model their combined resistance to estimate it with Ohm’s law: On sensitive low-voltage circuits that stolen voltage can slightly change what you're measuring. Compare that drop with the voltage left for the current-setting parts and with your allowed error. Even in a 5 V circuit, a 0.1 V drop can matter if an LED leaves little resistor headroom. Key takeaways Power off before inserting the meter in series. Restore the voltage jack after current measurements. Further reading Fluke: current measurement SparkFun: using a multimeter

sum: Remove all power and discharge capacitors before resistance tests.
x: Remove all power and discharge capacitors before resistance tests. Resistance and continuity: only unpowered Resistance mode works by passing a small test current from the meter's own battery and measuring the resulting voltage. So: The circuit must be unpowered.
