sum: Preallocate and perform bounded work without waiting in the audio callback.
x: What must never happen in the callback The callback must have a bounded, predictable execution duration. Anything whose duration is unknown, or that may wait for something else, breaks that. Ross Bencina's essay Time waits for nothing is the classic statement; Electro-Smith's audio guide says the same for Daisy: avoid dynamic allocation like malloc and blocking peripheral calls, and use flags to defer such work to the main loop. Never in the callback Why ------ Memory allocation Unbounded time; can fail; fragments Locks, waits, sleeps May wait on lower-priority code Logging / printf Formatting and I/O take long, variable time File, SD, flash I/O Milliseconds, and may block Bus I/O (I2C display) Blocks for ms (the serial-bus units) Unbounded loops No worst-case time Two subtle ones: Locks and priority inversion. If the callback waits for a lock held by the main loop, it cannot proceed until the main loop runs again. But on a bare-metal single-core MCU the main loop cannot run while the callback's interrupt is executing, so a callback that spins on that lock never gets it: a deadlock, and the audio stops. On an RTOS or a general-purpose OS, a high-priority audio thread blocked on a lock held by a low-priority thread is classic priority inversion: the holder may be descheduled for far longer than your budget. This is why the safe-transfer units uses lock-free techniques. Logging. Even a short print may format numbers, copy into a USB or UART buffer, and block when that buffer is full. Set a flag or write a counter, and print from the main loop. Illustrative pseudocode: peak is the measured absolute output peak for this block, the flag uses verified bounded lock-free atomics, and the queue has an explicit per-block event limit. Platform-specific atomic syntax and initialization are omitted. Key takeaways Preallocate and perform bounded work without waiting in the audio callback. Defer logging and peripheral transfers, and bound queued event processing. sum: A cycle counter or GPIO pulse measures the work included within its boundaries.
x: Measuring CPU load CPU load is the fraction of the budget the callback uses: Measured in cycles instead, divide the cycles the callback used by the cycles per block; the ratio is the same. Measure observed maxima as well as averages; one slow block can be enough for an audible fault, and a finite run does not prove worst-case timing. Cycle counters Most Cortex-M3, M4 and M7 chips include a cycle counter (CYCCNT, in the DWT debug unit) that counts CPU clock cycles. It is optional in the Armv7-M architecture (the NOCYCCNT bit in DWT_CTRL says whether it exists), and Cortex-M0/M0+ parts do not have it, so confirm your part has it. It is also off after reset: firmware must set TRCENA in DEMCR and CYCCNTENA in DWT_CTRL. Teensy 4's start-up code does both, and its audio library reads the counter as ARM_DWT_CYCCNT; PJRC's page notes it counts at the CPU clock (600 MHz). The 32-bit counter wraps every few seconds at these clocks, which unsigned subtraction handles for short intervals: Read it at the start and end of the callback: Libraries wrap this for you: libDaisy CpuLoadMeter: call OnBlockStart() and OnBlockEnd() in the callback; read average, minimum and maximum load from the main loop. (It times blocks with libDaisy's System::GetTick() timer rather than the DWT counter.) Teensy AudioProcessorUsageMax(): an estimate of the maximum percentage of CPU any audio update has used, which PJRC calls "the most useful for assuring the audio processing is operating within acceptable limits". Its implementation uses the cycle counter. GPIO toggle and a scope Set a spare pin high at the start of the callback and low at the end. On an oscilloscope (or a cheap logic analyser): Pulse width is the callback time and the period is the block period, so the load is the width divided by the period (0.8 ms wide every 2.9 ms is about 28%). You see jitter and occasional long blocks directly, using persistence or a trigger on pulse width. The two pin writes and the measurement method add overhead; quantify it on the chosen platform. Know the limits of your measurement The callback's time varies with what the synth is doing. Measure with the worst realistic case: all voices sounding, every effect on, knobs moving. Caches and memory location (lesson 1) change timing; code that is fast in one build may be slower after an unrelated change moves it. Library code outside your callback (format conversion, interrupt entry) also uses the budget. Library meters may or may not include it; a GPIO toggle only measures what lies between the toggles. Decide a margin, record the measured maximum and the conditions, and re-measure after significant changes. Key takeaways A cycle counter or GPIO pulse measures the work included within its boundaries. Record build, workload, maxima and margin; a finite measurement is not a universal timing proof. t: Shared data and the limits of volatile
sum: Identify one writer, one reader and possible preemption for every shared-data connection.
x: The real-time audio units split the firmware into two worlds: the audio callback, which runs from an interrupt once per block and must never wait, and the foreground (main loop and lower-priority work), which reads knobs, parses MIDI and drives the display. Every useful synth needs data to cross between them. A knob moves in the foreground; the filter that reacts lives in the callback. Getting this wrong produces the worst kind of bug: rare, timing-dependent and hard to reproduce. A stuck note once an hour. A click when two parameters change together. This lesson gives you a small set of safe patterns, described in language-neutral terms so they apply whatever language and platform you end up using. The foreground/background split Draw the shared-data connections explicitly. For a simple synth: For each arrow, ask: who writes, who reads, and can the reader interrupt the writer (or run on another core) halfway through? On a single-core MCU, the callback can interrupt the main loop at any instruction. On a multi-core computer such as a Raspberry Pi, both sides may genuinely run at the same time. What can go wrong Torn reads. The main loop is writing a value that takes more than one memory operation (a 64-bit number on a 32-bit core, or a group of related fields). The callback interrupts between the two halves and reads half old, half new. Stale values. The compiler sees that a loop never changes a variable and keeps it in a register, so the loop never sees the other side's update. Reordering. The writer does "write data, then set ready flag". The compiler, and on some processors the hardware, may make the flag visible before the data. The reader sees "ready" and reads garbage. Lost updates. Both sides do read-modify-write on the same variable (count = count + 1). One side's update overwrites the other's. Why volatile is not synchronisation C and C++ (and some other languages) have a volatile keyword. It tells the compiler that every access to that variable must really happen, in program order relative to other volatile accesses, because something outside the program (a hardware register, an interrupt) may change it. It preserves the defined volatile accesses, but it does not make an otherwise unsynchronised C++ thread-sharing program well-defined. Hardware interrupt semantics also depend on the compiler and target. It does not: make a read-modify-write such as x = x + 1 indivisible; prevent a multi-word value from tearing; order ordinary (non-volatile) memory accesses around it, so "write data, then set volatile flag" can still be reordered as far as the data is concerned; provide the memory barriers that multi-core processors need. The diy-synth roadmap states it directly: "volatile alone is not thread synchronisation". The Linux kernel documentation has a whole page explaining why kernel code should not use volatile for this, and the C++ reference says the same for threads: use atomics. volatile remains correct for its real purpose, memory-mapped hardware registers. Key takeaways Identify one writer, one reader and possible preemption for every shared-data connection. Volatile preserves its defined accesses but does not supply atomicity or payload publication. sum: Use an atomic type with target-verified lock-free operations.
x: Pattern 1: atomic single values For one independent parameter (cutoff, gain, a mode number), use your language's atomic type. A supported atomic operation guarantees: the value is read and written in one indivisible step (no tearing); loads and stores obey atomic coherence rules; a compiler cannot simply replace repeated atomic loads with one cached ordinary load. This is not a bounded-time freshness or scheduling guarantee; with the right memory ordering, writes before it are visible to a reader who sees it. One caveat for interrupts: the atomic must be lock-free. If the hardware cannot do the operation natively, the library may fall back to an internal lock, and an interrupt that hits while the foreground holds that lock will deadlock. Armv7-M provides 8-, 16- and 32-bit exclusive access instructions, but no 64-bit exclusive pair. This does not by itself certify a language atomic implementation. Check the exact type, operation, compiler, ABI and alignment: in C++, inspect is_always_lock_free, target documentation and generated code. Even lock-free read-modify-write can retry; prefer documented bounded loads/stores for this pattern. Pseudocode, where store_release and load_acquire stand for the language's atomic operations with release/acquire ordering: For a lone value that no other data depends on, the weakest ("relaxed") ordering is usually enough; release/acquire matters when the value announces other data. On a 32-bit MCU, an aligned 32-bit store is typically one instruction anyway, but write the atomic: it documents intent and stays correct if the code moves to a multi-core platform. Rule of thumb: latest-value-wins data (a knob position) suits an atomic. If the callback misses an intermediate value, nothing is lost, because only the latest matters. Key takeaways Use an atomic type with target-verified lock-free operations. A lone latest value and a published payload need different ordering guarantees. sum: Updating parameters individually does not publish a whole parameter set together.
x: A preset changes several related parameter values. The foreground produces a complete set and the callback adopts it at a block boundary. Each publication and acknowledgement must use an atomic operation that is suitable for the actual platform. A preset generation is a version number for one complete parameter publication; carry it with the buffer index in a target-supported atomic representation. Several parameters that must change together If a preset change sets ten parameters, atomics individually can let the callback see five new and five old. Options: Send the change as one message through a queue (pattern 2). The callback applies all ten at a block boundary. Double buffer with acknowledgement: allow only one unacknowledged publication. Fill the inactive set, then release-store its index and preset generation together. The callback acquire-loads that publication, finishes all reads of the old set, and release-stores the adopted preset generation as its acknowledgement. Only after an acquire-load sees that exact acknowledgement may the producer reuse the old set. A counter increment at block start alone is insufficient: it can advance before the callback loads the new publication. The callback never waits. On Teensy, PJRC's audio library offers AudioNoInterrupts() and AudioInterrupts() around a group of settings so they "all take effect at the same time". That briefly holds off the audio update from the foreground; keep the section short. Key takeaways Updating parameters individually does not publish a whole parameter set together. An immutable queued message or acknowledged buffer ownership protects the full set. sum: Exactly one producer writes the publication index and one consumer writes the release index.
x: Pattern 2: single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer For events (note on, note off, a preset load), every message matters. Dropping or overwriting one causes stuck notes. Use a queue. On real-time systems the standard choice is a lock-free single-producer/single-consumer (SPSC) ring buffer: A fixed array, allocated at start-up. head: the next slot to write. Only the producer writes it. tail: the next slot to read. Only the consumer writes it. Because each index has exactly one writer, no lock is needed: just atomic loads and stores with the right ordering. Why the orderings: the producer must write the item before publishing the new head (release); the consumer must see that head before reading the item (acquire). The same pairing protects the slot being freed in the other direction. The mathematical model uses increasing counters and reduces them modulo capacity for array slots. Real fixed-width unsigned counters wrap: use the same unsigned width for subtraction, use a power-of-two capacity below the counter modulus, and prevent producers from advancing past capacity. The difference between them is how many items are waiting: With a power-of-two capacity and unsigned integers, h - t stays correct even after the counters wrap around, and h mod CAP can be computed cheaply as h & (CAP - 1), as the Python below does. A single-threaded Python simulation of the index logic (it cannot show the concurrency, only the arithmetic): When full, the producer refuses rather than waiting. Count overflow and use an explicit recovery policy: for note-event loss, set a separate lock-free panic/reset flag so the callback can release held voices and discard invalid pending state. Silently dropping note offs is not safe. The callback never waits; an empty queue means no events are available. Sizing the queue DIN MIDI delivers at most 3,125 bytes a second. Complete three-byte messages take 0.96 ms, but running-status note messages need only two bytes (0.64 ms) and real-time events one byte (0.32 ms). Size the queue for the actual event mix, maximum interval between drains and bursts; USB can deliver much larger bursts. A 64-event queue is an example, not a guaranteed bound. Key takeaways Exactly one producer writes the publication index and one consumer writes the release index. Queue arithmetic, memory ordering, capacity and overflow recovery are separate responsibilities. sum: Polled state can lose intermediate transitions; events preserve their order within capacity.
x: Pattern 3: event queues for notes Represent notes as events, not as polled state. If the callback samples "is key 60 down?" once per block, a note-on followed by a note-off within the same block vanishes. A queue preserves transitions in order provided it does not overflow; overflow needs the recovery policy above. Keep parsing (turning raw MIDI bytes into messages) in the UART interrupt or the main loop, and keep the callback's job to applying messages. Pick one place to push from: if both the UART interrupt and the main loop push into the same queue, it is no longer an SPSC arrangement and the lock-free design above is unsafe. The diy-synth roadmap's MIDI exercise asks for exactly this separation, with diagnostic logging outside the callback. To log what arrived, push a copy to a second queue that the main loop prints. The same pattern runs the other way: the callback pushes meter levels or a "clipped" flag to a queue or atomic that the main loop displays. Key takeaways Polled state can lose intermediate transitions; events preserve their order within capacity. Bound the events processed per block and keep a single producer per SPSC queue. sum: Audio-rate smoothing reduces abrupt parameter steps after a safe data transfer.
x: Pattern 4: smooth on the receiving side The callback now receives correct values, but they arrive in steps: knob scans at around 1 kHz, MIDI CCs in 128 coarse steps. Jumping a gain or cutoff by a step at a block boundary makes zipper noise. Smooth again, at audio rate, inside the callback: Per-sample one-pole towards the latest target. This is the same smoother as the knob-reading units', now updated once per audio sample instead of once per knob reading: For a 20 ms time constant, the same formula gives a coefficient of about 0.001041. Compute a once at start-up, not per sample, because the exponential is expensive. In code: Linear ramp per block: step from the old value to the new across the block, adding the same increment each sample: In the mathematical version, apply the increment before each of the 48 output samples: the last parameter value reaches the target. Real code must choose that endpoint convention, retain state across blocks and account for rounding; assigning the exact target after the last step avoids cumulative endpoint error. Other ramp durations can span several blocks. Sample-rate steps can still be audible for large or sensitive changes, so listen and measure rather than promising silence. Why smooth here and not only in the foreground? The foreground can only deliver values as often as it runs. The receiving side knows the sample rate, so it is the only place that can reduce the size and spacing of parameter steps; digital samples remain discrete. The foreground smoothing from the knob-reading units is about rejecting knob noise; this smoothing is about removing steps. Choosing a pattern Data Pattern ------ Single knob value Atomic, smooth in callback Grouped parameter change One message or double buffer Note on/off, program change SPSC event queue Meters, clip flag (back) Atomic or SPSC queue Debug logging Queue to main loop Key takeaways Audio-rate smoothing reduces abrupt parameter steps after a safe data transfer. One-pole curves and linear ramps have different endpoint and timing behavior. sum: Keep a distinct path for MIDI instructions and for the sound the synth creates.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. MIDI (Musical Instrument Digital Interface) lets a sequencer such as a Digitakt tell your synth what to play. These lessons concentrate on MIDI 1.0 performance messages and the separate audio signal route. The most important idea in this lesson is also the simplest: MIDI note events do not carry live audio. MIDI also supports specialised SysEx transfers, including sample data, but that is distinct from an audio stream. It carries short messages such as "key 60 went down on channel 1, quite hard" and "key 60 came back up". The receiving instrument decides what those events sound like. Events, not audio Think of MIDI as a pianist's instructions written down at the moment they happen, not a recording of the piano. MIDI Audio --------- Carries Performance events here Audio waveform Size Often 2–3 MIDI 1.0 bytes For example 48,000 digital samples/s Sound depends on Receiver's synthesis Recorded waveform and playback chain Cable MIDI (DIN, TRS, USB) Audio jack, USB audio This has practical consequences for your build: Your synth needs two separate paths: MIDI in (what to play) and audio out (the sound it makes). Connecting the Digitakt's MIDI OUT to your synth does nothing audible until your synth's audio output reaches a mixer or interface. A recorded MIDI part in Ableton is a list of events. Change the synth patch and the "recording" sounds different. A recorded audio part is fixed. A complete MIDI 1.0 Note On uses three bytes before transport framing. Digital audio storage depends on duration, sample rate, channel count and sample representation; it is usually far larger than the event list. Key takeaways Keep a distinct path for MIDI instructions and for the sound the synth creates. sum: Count start and stop bits as well as data: a back-to-back three-byte DIN message takes 0.96 ms.
x: The serial link Classic MIDI 1.0 runs over a 5-pin DIN cable as an asynchronous serial link. The MIDI electrical specification fixes the format: 31,250 bits per second (±1%). Each byte is framed as 1 start bit, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit, no parity (often written 8-N-1). So each byte costs 10 bit-times, which works out at 320 µs (calculated below). Bytes are sent least significant bit first. How long does one byte take on the wire? Divide the number of bits in its frame by the number of bits the link sends each second. You use this whenever you need to know how quickly MIDI can deliver something. A whole message is just its bytes sent one after another, so its time is the byte count times the DIN framed-byte duration: So a three-byte message takes about 0.96 ms, roughly a millisecond. That figure matters later when we talk about chords and latency: ten three-byte notes "at once" are actually 30 bytes, about 9.6 ms of wire time, so they are spread over roughly 10 ms. This assumes the bytes are sent back to back with no gaps; a slower sender only makes it longer. Your microcontroller's UART (universal asynchronous receiver-transmitter) does this framing for you. You configure it for 31,250 baud, 8-N-1, and it hands you whole bytes. Key takeaways Count start and stop bits as well as data: a back-to-back three-byte DIN message takes 0.96 ms. sum: The top bit distinguishes status from seven-bit data; discard orphan data and preserve interrupted messages around MIDI real-time bytes.
x: Status bytes and data bytes Every MIDI 1.0 byte is one of two kinds, and you can tell which by looking at the top bit: A status byte has bit 7 set. It says what kind of message this is. For channel messages, the top four bits (tttt above, including the 1) are the message type and the bottom four (cccc) are the channel. A data byte has bit 7 clear, so it carries a value from 0 to 127 (7 bits). Why 128 values? Each extra bit doubles the number of patterns, so the count of distinct values is 2 raised to the number of bits: With all 8 bits the same formula would give 256 values (0–255); spending one bit on the status/data flag halves that to 128. This one-bit rule is what makes MIDI robust. If a receiver joins mid-stream or loses a byte, a status byte outside the MIDI real-time class supplies a new message boundary. Real-time bytes also have bit 7 set but may interleave with a message without resetting it. It is also why MIDI values run 0–127 rather than 0–255: the eighth bit is spent on telling status from data. Channel messages have one or two data bytes according to their status, and a receiver waits for that complete message before dispatching it. System messages differ: some have no data bytes, while SysEx has variable length. It also says receivers should ignore data bytes that are not preceded by a valid status byte, apart from one shortcut called running status, which the later running-status unit covers. Key takeaways The top bit distinguishes status from seven-bit data; discard orphan data and preserve interrupted messages around MIDI real-time bytes. sum: Convert displayed channels to a zero-based low nibble when sending, and add one when displaying received channels.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. Channels MIDI 1.0 has 16 channels. They let one cable address up to 16 independent instruments (or parts of a multitimbral instrument). Each receiver is set to listen on one channel (or all of them, "omni") and ignores channel messages for others. The channel is in the low nibble of the status byte, numbered 0–15 on the wire. People and manuals number them 1–16. To build a channel message's status byte, take the message type's base value (whose low nibble is 0) and put the wire channel number into that empty low nibble: This off-by-one causes real bugs: Channel 1 is 0 on the wire When the Digitakt's MIDI track is set to CHAN 1, your synth will see status bytes with channel nibble 0 (for example 0x90 for a note on), not nibble 1 (0x91). Store channels internally as 0–15 and add 1 only when displaying them. Key takeaways Convert displayed channels to a zero-based low nibble when sending, and add one when displaying received channels. sum: MIDI specifies note numbers; the equal-tempered frequency calculation additionally assumes a tuning reference.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. Note on and note off The two messages your synth must handle first: Message Status Data 1 Data 2 ------------ Note Off 0x8n key (0–127) release velocity Note On 0x9n key (0–127) velocity (0–127) The letter in the final hexadecimal position labels the channel nibble; it is not a literal hexadecimal digit. The key number identifies the note: the MIDI specification gives middle C a value of 60. Each step is a semitone, so 61 is C♯, 72 is the C an octave up. Converting a key number to a frequency is a convention from the MIDI Tuning Standard and equal temperament: key 69 is A at 440 Hz, and each semitone multiplies the frequency by the same factor, the twelfth root of 2 (about 1.0595), so that twelve semitones exactly double it. Your oscillator needs this conversion every time a note starts: Worked examples: key 81 is 12 semitones above 69, so the power is 1 and the frequency is 880 Hz; key 57 is 12 below, so the power is −1 and it is 220 Hz. This holds only for standard 12-tone equal temperament tuned to a 440 Hz reference A; a synth with a different tuning reference or a microtonal scale uses a different formula or table. The same calculation in Python: Octave names differ, numbers don't Devices disagree about what to call note 60. Ableton Live's note ruler starts at C-2 (note 0), so Live calls middle C (60) Live C3. Elektron's Digitakt manuals number notes from Digitakt C0 (note 0, through Digitakt G10 for note 127); the original Digitakt manual states outright that MIDI note 60, middle C, is Digitakt C5. Much other software calls it C4. The number 60 is what goes on the wire, so debug with numbers. Key takeaways MIDI specifies note numbers; the equal-tempered frequency calculation additionally assumes a tuning reference. t: Handle velocity and both note endings
sum: Normalise Note On with velocity zero into a note-off event before voice handling.
x: Velocity and note endings are separate from the key number. The synth must recognise both documented ways to release a MIDI note. Velocity For a Note On that starts a note, velocity is a seven-bit performance value from 1 to 127, commonly representing how fast a key was struck. The specification leaves its interpretation to the receiver; it suggests that if velocity controls loudness, the mapping should preferably be exponential, and that devices without velocity sensing should send 64. Note on with velocity 0 means note off This rule trips up nearly every first MIDI implementation. The MIDI 1.0 specification gives two equivalent ways to end a note: A Note Off message: 8n kk vv. A Note On message with velocity zero: 9n kk 00. It says a receiver must be able to recognise either method, and should treat them identically. Many transmitters prefer the second form because, combined with running status, a long run of notes can be sent without repeating the status byte. If your synth treats 9n kk 00 as "start a note very quietly", notes will never end. That is a classic stuck-note bug. Key takeaways Normalise Note On with velocity zero into a note-off event before voice handling. Everything else in MIDI makes it expressive and in time: knobs and wheels (control change), patch selection (program change), pitch bend, pressure, the tempo clock, and manufacturer-specific data (SysEx). This unit maps message lengths and pressure. The following units cover controllers, running status, system messages and MIDI 2.0. The full map Channel messages carry a channel in the low nibble of the status byte (the final placeholder stands for a wire channel from zero to fifteen). System messages (0xF0–0xFF) have no channel. Status Message Data bytes --------- 8n Note Off key, velocity 9n Note On key, velocity An Poly Key Pressure key, pressure Bn Control Change controller, value Cn Program Change program Dn Channel Pressure pressure En Pitch Bend MIDI LSB, MIDI MSB F0…F7 System Exclusive / Common varies F8…FF System Real-Time none Notice that Program Change and Channel Pressure have one data byte; the other channel messages have two. Aftertouch (pressure) Pressing harder on a key after it bottoms out can send: Channel Pressure Dn vv: one value for the whole channel (the MIDI Association's message summary says to send the single greatest pressure of the keys held). sum: Pair the first 32 controller numbers with their fine controllers, and reset the remembered fine value on a new coarse value.
x: 14-bit controllers 128 steps are coarse for something like filter cutoff: you can hear each step as a zipper. The specification pairs controllers so that CC 0–31 carry MIDI coarse parts and CC 32–63 carry the matching MIDI fine parts. The MIDI LSB's controller number is always 32 more than the MIDI MSB's: Together the two 7-bit halves give 14 bits, and the combined value is the MIDI MSB scaled up by 128 plus the MIDI LSB: Multiplying by 128 is the same as applying a bitwise left shift by 7 bits, which is how firmware usually writes it: (msb << 7) lsb. Rules worth implementing exactly: If 128 steps are enough, a transmitter can send only the MIDI MSB. After both have been sent, a fine change may send just the MIDI LSB. When a MIDI MSB arrives, the receiver should reset its MIDI LSB to zero. So B0 01 40 then B0 21 20 means modulation is 8,224: MIDI MSB 0x40 (64) and MIDI LSB 0x20 (32), exactly the worked example above. Key takeaways Pair the first 32 controller numbers with their fine controllers, and reset the remembered fine value on a new coarse value. sum: Use RPN selection before Data Entry, deselect when done, and apply a selected bank when Program Change arrives.

RPN 0,0 is pitch bend sensitivity: Data Entry MIDI MSB is semitones, MIDI LSB is cents. To set ±12 semitones on channel 1, a sender transmits: Sending RPN 127,127 (the "null" RPN) afterwards stops later Data Entry messages changing it by accident. NRPNs (CC 99/98) work the same way for manufacturer-defined parameters; the Elektron manuals list which NRPNs their knobs send. Program change and bank select Cn pp selects patch pp, with a single data byte. Programs are 0–127 on the wire, but many devices display them as 1–128, so the off-by-one appears again. For more than 128 patches, the specification has the sender transmit Bank Select as a pair (CC 0 MIDI MSB, CC 32 MIDI LSB), immediately followed by the Program Change. Bank Select alone must not change the program; the new bank applies when the Program Change arrives. t: Map pitch bend into a pitch offset
sum: Make the bend mapping explicit, keep centre exact, and account for the one-step asymmetry of the raw value range.

To turn the raw value into a pitch offset, measure how far it is from centre as a fraction of half the range, then scale by the bend range: To apply the offset, scale the note's frequency by the same semitone factor as the key-to-frequency formula in the note-frequency unit: Mapping the raw value to semitones in Python: The range is asymmetric by one step (8,192 values below centre, 8,191 above). This is an implementation mapping, not a MIDI-mandated bend law. An implementation can instead divide the upper half by 8,191 to make the maximum reach exactly the configured positive range; keep the centre exactly zero and document the choice. sum: Reuse only channel status; System Common and SysEx clear it, while MIDI real-time bytes leave it and partial messages intact.
x: Running status Running status is a byte-saving rule for channel voice and mode messages: once a status byte has been sent, the transmitter can omit it for following messages of the same type and channel, and send only the data bytes. Nine bytes become seven. Combined with "note on, velocity 0 = note off", a whole melody can go out with a single 90 at the start. The receiver's rules, from the specification and its appendix: Remember the last channel status byte in a running status buffer. A data byte that arrives when a complete message has just ended reuses that status. Any new channel status byte replaces it. System Exclusive and System Common status bytes clear it. Real-time bytes do not touch it, even when they arrive between data bytes. Running status is optional for transmitters but mandatory for receivers. The parser state-machine unit turns these rules into executable code. Key takeaways Reuse only channel status; System Common and SysEx clear it, while MIDI real-time bytes leave it and partial messages intact. sum: MIDI clock has 24 ticks per quarter note; transport and optional Active Sensing have distinct jobs.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. System real-time: clock and transport Real-time messages are single status bytes with no data. They may appear anywhere, even in the middle of another message, so they can keep accurate time. Byte Message ------ F8 Timing Clock FA Start 0xFB Continue 0xFC Stop FE Active Sensing FF System Reset F9 and FD are undefined and should be ignored. Timing Clock is sent 24 times per quarter note (24 PPQN, pulses per quarter note). A receiver measures the gap between clocks to find the tempo. Going the other way, the expected gap at a given tempo is one minute divided by the number of clocks in that minute: Faster tempos give shorter gaps: at 60 BPM the gap is about 41.7 ms. A receiver can turn the formula round (the tempo in BPM is 60 seconds divided by 24 times the measured gap) to estimate tempo; in practice it averages several gaps, because individual clocks jitter. The same calculation in Python: Six clocks make one sixteenth note, which is the unit the Song Position Pointer (F2 ll mm) counts in. Transport details from the specification: Start (FA) means play from the beginning. Continue (0xFB) means resume from the current position. A synced receiver starts on the next F8 after either, and the specification asks senders to leave at least 1 ms between FA and the first F8. Stop (0xFC) should stop playback immediately. Clocks may keep flowing while stopped, so receivers can lock to tempo before Start. Active Sensing (FE) is optional. Once a receiver has seen it, it should expect some message at least every 300 ms. If all MIDI traffic stops for the timeout, it should silence its voices and leave Active Sensing mode; silence can indicate disconnection, but does not prove the physical cause. The detailed specification recommends sending within 270 ms and judging loss after more than 330 ms to leave timing margin around the nominal 300 ms interval. A simple mono synth needs clock only for tempo-synced features such as an arpeggiator or a synced LFO. It must still tolerate clock bytes, because a sequencer like the Digitakt may send them constantly. Key takeaways MIDI clock has 24 ticks per quarter note; transport and optional Active Sensing have distinct jobs. t: Handle SysEx and channel mode messages
sum: Keep SysEx data seven-bit and respect ID allocation; distinguish channel-wide mode messages from ordinary sound controls.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. System Exclusive SysEx carries manufacturer-defined data: patch dumps, firmware, parameter edits. The ID is 1 byte, or 3 bytes starting with 00. Every SysEx payload byte is a data byte (0–127); independent MIDI real-time status bytes may interleave on the wire. 8-bit data must be packed into 7-bit bytes. ID 7D is reserved for non-commercial use (education, research): suitable for a private experiment, not for a product released to the public even free of charge. IDs 7E and 7F are the Universal SysEx messages (7E for Universal Non-Real-Time and 7F for Universal Real-Time) defined by the MIDI specs themselves. Only MIDI real-time bytes may be interleaved inside a SysEx message. Any other status byte terminates it, although senders should always end with F7. The Digitakt uses SysEx to send and receive project, pattern and Sound data (presets on the Digitakt II) through its SYSEX DUMP menu, which is a handy backup route. Channel mode messages CC numbers 120–127 are mode messages: CC Meaning ------ 120 All Sound Off (silence now) 121 Reset All Controllers 122 Local Control on/off 123 All Notes Off 124–127 MIDI omni mode, MIDI monophonic mode and MIDI polyphonic mode Channel Mode messages are recognised on the receiver’s configured Basic Channel, even when Omni is on. MIDI monophonic mode concerns note voices: with Omni off it can allocate one voice per selected MIDI channel; with Omni on it plays one voice across the received channels. MIDI polyphonic mode permits simultaneous voices up to the receiver’s capacity. Neither mode specifies mono or stereo audio output. All Notes Off and the mode changes also perform the specified note-release functions when supported. In particular, the specification says to ignore CC 123 while Omni is on. All Sound Off silences sound promptly, without waiting for the normal release envelope. Sustain deferral and recovery are developed in the stuck-note unit. Key takeaways Keep SysEx data seven-bit and respect ID allocation; distinguish channel-wide mode messages from ordinary sound controls. sum: Receive into bounded storage, count overflow, and keep parsing, waiting and logging outside the audio deadline.
x: The preceding MIDI units established the message formats. The implementation units cover what firmware has to do with them: turn a stream of bytes into events, decide which note a monophonic synth should play, make sure notes always stop, and turn controller values into smooth parameter changes. The code here is Python, so you can run and test the logic on your computer first. On the synth, the same logic runs in firmware. Where timing and threads matter, the lesson uses short language-neutral pseudocode. Where MIDI handling runs A typical embedded synth has three activities: Receiving happens in an interrupt (or via DMA). It should only push each byte into a fixed-size ring buffer. At 31,250 baud successive bytes can complete every 320 µs at the nominal bit rate. Parsing and note logic run outside the audio callback, in the main loop or a control task, draining the buffer. The audio callback consumes a bounded number of queued note events in order, applies them to its voice state, and smooths latest-value control parameters. It must never wait on MIDI, allocate memory, or print logs. How data crosses from the control code to the audio callback (atomics, a lock-free queue, or double buffering) depends on your platform, and is covered with embedded programming. The rule for now: the audio callback must never block. This is architectural pseudocode, not executable Python: buffer, parser and event interfaces must be supplied by the platform. An interrupt may receive batches through a hardware FIFO or DMA rather than one callback per byte. Count overflows rather than ignoring them. A lost note-off byte is a future stuck note, and the counter tells you it happened. Key takeaways Receive into bounded storage, count overflow, and keep parsing, waiting and logging outside the audio deadline. t: Trace a MIDI parser state machine
sum: Test single-data-byte messages, interrupted messages, SysEx termination and orphan data on the computer.
x: Parsing: a small state machine The parser must cope with everything the specification allows: channel messages with one or two data bytes; running status (data bytes with no new status byte); MIDI real-time messages (single bytes F8–FF) arriving anywhere, even mid-message; SysEx of any length without accumulating its payload; garbage: data bytes before any status, undefined status bytes, a device plugged in mid-stream. The state is small: the running status byte, the data bytes collected so far, and whether we are inside a SysEx. Trace the interesting parts: 40 64 has no status byte; running status reuses 90, giving a second Note On. F8 arrives between 3C and 00. It is emitted immediately and the half-built Note On survives, so 90 3C 00 still completes (a note off, since velocity is 0). F2 00 00 is a System Common message (Song Position). System Common clears running status, so the final 3C 00 has no status to attach to and is ignored. This mirrors the receiver rules in the specification's appendix: store the status on channel messages, clear it on System Exclusive and System Common, leave it alone for MIDI real-time messages, and ignore data bytes when there is no status. Undefined System Common bytes (F4, F5) clear it too, and undefined MIDI real-time bytes (F9, FD) are simply ignored. This teaching parser discards SysEx payload rather than implementing patch dumps. Its rs field temporarily holds the current System Common status until that message completes; only channel statuses persist across completed messages. Input to feed is one actual UART byte, an integer from zero to 255. The parser emits raw tuples. A separate dispatcher must handle System Reset by resetting synth and parser state to the chosen documented power-up state. Other recognised real-time events do not disturb an unfinished message. The normalisation step turns channel tuples into events your synth understands, and this is where 9n kk 00 becomes a note off and messages for other channels are dropped. Test the parser on your computer first Feed it recorded streams, hand-written edge cases and random bytes. Random input must never crash it or emit a message with a data value above 127. Bugs found here cost seconds; the same bugs found on hardware cost an evening. Key takeaways Test single-data-byte messages, interrupted messages, SysEx termination and orphan data on the computer. t: Track held notes and choose a target
sum: Track held keys separately from the sounding target, and make priority, retrigger and overflow policies explicit.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. Note priority for a monophonic synth A mono synth has one voice, but a player (or the Digitakt's chord feature) can hold several keys. The note priority rule decides which held key sounds: Last note: the most recently pressed key wins. Releasing it falls back to the previous one still held. It is one possible policy for a sequenced or keyboard-played monophonic voice. Low note: the lowest held key wins, whatever order the keys were pressed in. High note: the highest held key wins. Which to offer is a design decision; some mono synths let the player choose it as a setting. The key data structure is a note stack: the list of held keys in press order. The rule is applied to the stack after every change. None means no keys are held, so the gate closes and the envelope enters release. This example deliberately keeps one entry per key. Repeated Note Ons for the same channel and key are coalesced, so one Note Off removes that key; this is a simplified monophonic allocation policy, not a universal rule for stacked voices. Transmitters still owe a matching Note Off for every Note On. Two further design choices: Retrigger or legato. When the target changes while keys are still held, do you restart the envelope (retrigger) or just glide or jump the pitch (legato)? Many mono synths offer both. Bounded memory. In firmware the stack is a fixed array (say 16 entries, with oldest-dropping on overflow), never a growing list. Removing a key that isn't in the stack must be harmless. Key takeaways Track held keys separately from the sounding target, and make priority, retrigger and overflow policies explicit. t: Prevent and recover from stuck notes
sum: Handle both note endings, channel changes and sustain, then provide a panic action for lost events.
x: Stuck notes and how to prevent them A stuck note is a voice that never receives the note off that should end it. The project brief asks for "no unintended stuck notes", so design against each cause. Cause Defence ------ 9n kk 00 not treated as off Normalise in the parser Note off on another channel Track notes per channel Channel changed while held Release all on change Bytes lost (overflow, unplug) Count overflows; panic Repeated same-key starts Choose and document a matching policy Sustain pedal held Defer offs until pedal up Track held notes, not just "the current note". If the synth remembers only the sounding note, a note off for an earlier key can be misapplied, or missed entirely. A note stack with a documented repeated-key and sustain policy makes those transitions explicit; it does not by itself guarantee that every MIDI use case is covered. Implement the mode messages that silence notes. In supported Omni-Off operation, All Notes Off (CC 123) releases MIDI-started notes on the applicable channel; the specification says to ignore CC 123 while Omni is on. Channel Mode messages are recognised on the configured Basic Channel, and mode changes 124–127 also have the specified note-release effect. The specification says All Notes Off should send voices into their release stage rather than cutting them abruptly. All Sound Off (CC 120) is the hard version: silence as soon as possible. A spec detail worth copying: while the sustain pedal (CC 64) is on, note offs and All Notes Off are remembered but not acted on until the pedal is released. Don't rely on All Notes Off alone. The specification says receivers aren't required to recognise it, and transmitters should send individual note offs first. Treat it as a safety net. Give yourself a panic action. A button (or a documented MIDI control instruction) that clears held and sustain-deferred notes, silences or releases voices according to its policy, and resets pitch bend to centre is invaluable during development. Consider Active Sensing. If your source sends FE and the receiver supports Active Sensing, a receive-activity timeout should silence its voices and leave Active Sensing mode. The nominal interval is 300 ms; the specification recommends a receiver threshold above 330 ms for margin. This detects missing traffic rather than proving the cable physically came out. If the source never sends FE, behave normally. Key takeaways Handle both note endings, channel changes and sustain, then provide a panic action for lost events. t: Map controller steps onto useful ranges
sum: Choose a curve for the parameter; exponential frequency mapping spreads ratios evenly but does not add MIDI resolution.
x: Mapping CC values to parameters A CC gives you 0–127. Your synth parameter has a real range and a natural scale. Mapping has three parts. 1. Choose the curve For frequencies and times, use an exponential curve, so that equal knob movements give equal musical intervals. The idea: instead of adding a fixed number of hertz per step, multiply by a fixed ratio per step, so every step is the same musical interval. The same mapping in Python, with its values across the knob: Compare a linear map over the same range, which adds a fixed number of hertz per step: So the step from 0 to 1 jumps from 20 Hz to about 177 Hz (more than three octaves), and half the knob covers 10–20 kHz where little changes audibly. How evenly does the exponential map spread its steps? Count the octaves in the range, then divide them between the 127 steps: These formulas assume f_lo is above zero (an exponential map can never reach 0 Hz) and that the parameter really is perceived on a ratio scale, as pitch and time are. A linear mapping can suit a control position. A pan control's audible gain law is a separate design choice, so equal position steps need not mean linear channel gains. A decibel-style curve can be useful for mix levels; choose its range and mute behaviour explicitly. For MIDI controllers defined as switches, use the documented convention: values up to 63 are off, and values from 64 are on. Key takeaways Choose a curve for the parameter; exponential frequency mapping spreads ratios evenly but does not add MIDI resolution. sum: Publish control targets safely, then smooth them at audio rate using a coefficient matched to the sample rate.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. 2. Use more resolution where it matters At 128 steps, a slow filter sweep can produce audible stepping. Options: accept 14-bit pairs (each controller from 0 to 31 paired with the controller 32 higher, such as CC 1 with CC 33) where your controller sends them, and in every case smooth the value in the audio callback. 3. Smooth in the audio domain The control code only sets a target. The audio callback moves the real parameter towards it a little each sample (a one-pole smoother is the usual tool, covered with synthesis DSP). This reduces abrupt control changes and can make zipper noise and MIDI arrival jitter less audible; smoothing adds response lag and cannot guarantee that every modulation artefact vanishes. Each sample, the smoother closes a fixed fraction of the remaining gap: For a fixed target and a coefficient strictly between zero and one, each update reduces the remaining gap without overshooting. At zero it never moves; at one it jumps directly to the target. At 48,000 samples per second with a coefficient of 0.01, the gap shrinks to about 37 % of its starting size in about 100 samples, roughly 2 ms. The pseudocode: Keep a single CC map table in one place: CC number, parameter, curve and range. Print it into your project docs. Use it when configuring the Digitakt MIDI track's CC slots. The publish/read mechanism must be appropriate for the actual platform; this pseudocode does not supply synchronisation. t: Trace the DIN MIDI current loop
sum: Check DIN pin numbering from the correct view; current on is logical zero, and MIDI IN keeps its shield free of a DC ground path.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. This lesson is about the wires: how a MIDI byte physically gets from the Digitakt to your synth's microcontroller, and why you can't just connect a DIN socket to a GPIO pin. The project's electronics notes say exactly that: "DIN MIDI is not a direct connection to arbitrary GPIO pins." Here is why, and what to build instead. Low-voltage work only Everything in this lesson runs from your development board's 3.3 V or 5 V supply. Never open or modify mains-powered equipment. Before connecting any circuit to a board, check the pin voltage limits in that board's documentation. The 5-pin DIN connection MIDI uses a 5-pin DIN connector with its pins spread over 180°. The MIDI electrical specification (updated in 2014 as document CA-033) fixes the details: Devices have female sockets labelled MIDI IN, MIDI OUT and (optionally) MIDI THRU. Cables are male-to-male. Only three pins are used: pin 4 (current source), pin 5 (current sink, the data line) and pin 2 (shield). Pins 1 and 3 are left unconnected. The cable is shielded twisted pair, at most 15 m (50 ft), with the shield connected to pin 2 at both ends. Pin 2 is grounded at the transmitter only. At a MIDI IN, pin 2 must have no DC path to the receiver's ground. That last rule is the key to the whole design, and it comes from how the signal is carried. A current loop, not a voltage Most logic signals are voltages measured against a shared ground. MIDI instead sends a current of about 5 mA around a loop through the cable: out of the transmitter on pin 4, through an LED inside the receiver, and back to the transmitter on pin 5. The current enters the receiver on pin 4 and leaves on pin 5, so the LED's anode faces pin 4. RB and the LED are in series, so it makes no electrical difference which leg RB sits on; follow the reference figure when you build it. Logical 0 = current on. When the UART's TX pin goes low, current flows from VTX through the loop into TX. Logical 1 = current off. TX high: no voltage across the loop, no current. The line idles at 1, so an idle UART means no current. So the UART needs no inversion: start bits (0) light the receiver's LED, stop bits (1) turn it off. The spec also says one output drives exactly one input. Key takeaways Check DIN pin numbering from the correct view; current on is logical zero, and MIDI IN keeps its shield free of a DC ground path. t: Protect and isolate the MIDI input
sum: Use the reference isolated input instead of exposing an MCU pin directly to a DIN cable.
x: Why the input needs an optocoupler The receiver's end of the loop is the LED of an optocoupler (opto-isolator): an LED and an electrically isolated light sensor sealed in one package. The only connection between the two sides is light. This gives galvanic isolation: The receiver's circuit ground is never connected to the sender's ground through the MIDI cable. A correctly isolated DIN MIDI input avoids adding a DC ground loop path: a second ground path between two pieces of mains-powered equipment that already share earth through their power leads. Ground loops let current flow in signal grounds, which you hear as hum in audio. It separates the receiver logic from the sender's signal voltage, within the component's and circuit's ratings. It is not an unlimited fault or safety-isolation guarantee. In a studio full of devices connected by audio cables as well as MIDI, this matters. The spec's own words: "To avoid ground loops, and subsequent data errors, the transmitter circuitry and receiver circuitry are internally separated by an opto-isolator." Wiring the DIN pins straight to a GPIO would tie the grounds together, break this isolation, and expose your microcontroller to whatever the sender drives. With a 3.3 V board whose pins are not 5 V tolerant (PJRC states this for the Teensy 4.1, for example), a 5 V MIDI output could damage it. Key takeaways Use the reference isolated input instead of exposing an MCU pin directly to a DIN cable. sum: Check optocoupler supply, pull-up, speed and pin limits together; an optional shield capacitor preserves DC isolation but is not ideal at every frequency.
x: The reference MIDI IN circuit Figure 2 of CA-033 gives the input circuit. The essential parts: Part Role ------ RB = 220 Ω Series resistor in the loop Optocoupler Isolation; e.g. PC900V, 6N138 D1 (1N914) Reverse protection for the LED RD (pull-up) Opto output to VRX Pin 2 No DC path to ground How it works: Loop current flows through RB and the optocoupler's LED. The light detector and output circuitry respond to the LED, pulling the output low against the pull-up RD. That output goes to your UART's RX pin. Current on gives a low (0), current off gives a high (1): the same low/high logic relationship the sender's UART produced. D1, wired across the LED in the reverse direction, stops a reversed or faulty connection from putting a damaging reverse voltage on the LED. Requirements from the spec: the receiver must need less than 5 mA to turn on, and rise and fall times should be under 2 µs. To see why 2 µs is comfortable, compare it with the length of one bit: The spec names the Sharp PC900V and Hewlett-Packard 6N138 as acceptable and notes that other high-speed optocouplers may be. Its only recommended RD value is 280 Ω for the PC900V with a 5 V pull-up supply (VRX). The reference parts use output circuitry requiring an external pull-up (the 6N138's output pin is the bare collector of its output transistor), which is why the pull-up RD is needed. Acceptance in the older CA-033 example does not prove a part works at a 3.3 V output supply. For a 3.3 V receiver, pick an optocoupler whose actual manufacturer datasheet supports that supply and choose RD from that datasheet. Pull the output up to your MCU's supply (3.3 V), never to 5 V on a pin that isn't 5 V tolerant. Optional additions in CA-033: ferrite beads on the signal pins, and a 0.1 µF capacitor from MIDI IN pin 2 (or the jack shield) to ground. A capacitor's opposition to AC (its reactance) falls as frequency rises: Repeat it at a radio frequency of 10 MHz (10,000,000 Hz) and the reactance is about 0.16 Ω, close to a short circuit. This is the ideal-capacitor approximation used in CA-033, not a complete RF model of a real part or cable. At 20 kHz the same ideal capacitor is about 79.6 Ω, so do not call it an open circuit throughout the audio band. The optional connection preserves DC isolation while giving RF interference a lower-impedance path, as the specification intends. Key takeaways Check optocoupler supply, pull-up, speed and pin limits together; an optional shield capacitor preserves DC isolation but is not ideal at every frequency. sum: Use the resistor values for the specified transmitter voltage and account for receiver and driver drops.
x: The reference MIDI OUT circuit, 3.3 V version The original 1983 output used +5 V and two 220 Ω resistors. Most current microcontrollers run at 3.3 V, so the 2014 update adds a 3.3 V variant. In Figure 1, RA connects pin 4 to the supply VTX, and RC connects pin 5 to the UART TX (optionally through a buffer): VTX RA (pin 4) RC (pin 5) --------- +5 V ± 10% 220 Ω 5% 0.25 W 220 Ω 5% 0.25 W +3.3 V ± 5% 33 Ω 5% 0.5 W 10 Ω 5% 0.25 W Pin 2 is grounded at the transmitter. You can check the loop current with Ohm's law, treating the receiver as its 220 Ω RB plus an LED forward voltage drop. All three resistors are in series around the loop, so their resistances add, and the voltage left to push current through them is the supply minus what the LED drops: This ignores the small voltage left across the UART's TX output when it pulls low and the cable's own resistance, which is why the spec quotes ranges rather than one exact figure. The same calculation for all four cases in the spec: These match the spec's own figures: 5 mA for the original design, about 7.2 mA typical and 4.47 mA worst case for the 3.3 V design. The last line shows why you mustn't run the 5 V resistor values from 3.3 V: under 3 mA may not reliably switch every receiver. sum: Normal loop current does not determine the worst resistor heating: check the specified electrical short case and driver limits.
x: Why RA is rated 0.5 W Why is RA rated 0.5 W? If a cable fault shorts pin 4 to ground, RA sits directly across the supply. The spec's worst case is the supply 5% high (3.465 V) and the resistor 5% low (31.35 Ω). Ohm's law gives the current, and the power the resistor must turn into heat follows from the voltage across it: So the result is about 111 mA and 0.38 W, below the nominal 0.5 W rating; actual component temperature and derating requirements still matter. The spec also assumes the buffer driving RC in 3.3 V designs is open-collector or open-drain, and warns not to exceed the driving buffer's short-circuit current rating. Use the published circuit Copy CA-033's figures (or your board vendor's documented MIDI circuit) exactly, and note where each value came from. If you use a MIDI breakout or shield, check its schematic against CA-033 for the voltage your board runs at. Key takeaways Normal loop current does not determine the worst resistor heating: check the specified electrical short case and driver limits. t: Choose TRS wiring and plan THRU chains
sum: Type A puts DIN pin 5 on the tip and pin 4 on the ring; check the actual product, cable and THRU configuration.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. MIDI THRU and daisy chains A THRU socket re-transmits whatever arrives at IN. Each optocoupler slightly distorts the bit edges, and the errors accumulate along a chain. The spec says that for chains longer than three instruments, faster optocouplers help. Your Digitakt has a THRU port (it can also be set to send DIN sync instead). MIDI over TRS minijacks Small devices often replace the DIN socket with a 3.5 mm TRS (tip-ring-sleeve) jack and an adapter cable. The MIDI Association standardised this in 2018 as RP-054, which specifies Type A. RP-054 actually recommends a 2.5 mm TRS connector; its wiring rules also apply when another size such as 3.5 mm is used. Its adapter cable is at most 2 m and uses shielded twisted pair. An ordinary stereo audio cable is not automatically an acceptable direct TRS MIDI cable. Before standardisation, two incompatible wirings spread: TRS Type A (standard) Type B --------- Tip Pin 5 (sink) Pin 4 (source) Ring Pin 4 (source) Pin 5 (sink) Sleeve Pin 2 (shield) Pin 2 (shield) The MIDI Association's article (written before RP-054) lists Akai Pro, IK Multimedia, Korg, Line 6, littleBits and Make Noise as using Type A, and Arturia, 1010music and Novation as using Type B. Wiring varies by product, so check each device's manual rather than assuming by brand. Pins 4 and 5 are swapped between the types, so a Type B adapter on a Type A device drives the loop backwards. The same article says that connecting with incompatible cables "should not damage devices designed in accordance with the MIDI spec": in the reference receiver, the reverse-protection diode D1 conducts instead of the LED, so the loop current stays limited by the resistors, but no data gets through. A device that departs from the reference circuit (for example, one without D1) has no such guarantee. A few devices also use a two-conductor TS jack, sometimes informally called "Type C". If you put a TRS MIDI jack on your synth, use Type A, label it clearly, and never plug it into an audio jack. The official RP-054 document also recommends protection against accidental connection to non-MIDI equipment. Follow its reference circuitry rather than inferring safety from connector shape. Key takeaways Type A puts DIN pin 5 on the tip and pin 4 on the ring; check the actual product, cable and THRU configuration. sum: USB MIDI 1.0 parsed event packets contain a cable/type header and complete MIDI bytes, rather than DIN framing.
x: USB MIDI USB MIDI carries the same MIDI messages over USB, defined by the USB-IF's Device Class Definition for MIDI Devices (release 1.0, 1999). Key facts from that document: MIDI is a subclass of the USB Audio class. A device that follows it is class-compliant: operating systems that include a USB MIDI class driver can use it without a vendor driver. Data travels in fixed 32-bit USB-MIDI Event Packets: a header byte with a 4-bit cable number (up to 16 virtual MIDI cables per endpoint) and a 4-bit Code Index Number (the message type), then three MIDI-byte positions, with unused positions filled with zero. Each packet normally holds one complete message, status byte included, so running status isn't used. (The spec also has a single-byte mode, CIN 0xF, for passing an unparsed byte stream, but that is a special case.) The header byte puts the cable number in its top nibble and the Code Index Number in its bottom nibble: A SysEx message can span multiple USB-MIDI Event Packets. Its packet codes distinguish the start/continuation and the final one, two or three bytes; do not assume a whole patch dump fits in one packet. USB is also much faster than 31,250 bit/s, which helps with dense data. (USB MIDI 2.0, a later class specification, carries MIDI 2.0's packets natively and can fall back to USB MIDI 1.0.) Key takeaways USB MIDI 1.0 parsed event packets contain a cable/type header and complete MIDI bytes, rather than DIN framing. t: Provide a USB host for MIDI devices
sum: A device connector does not provide a host; choose DIN or an explicitly supported host and routing arrangement.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. Host and device: why two USB gadgets can't talk USB is not peer-to-peer. Every USB connection has exactly one host, which schedules all transfers, and one or more devices, which only respond when the host polls them. Devices cannot talk to each other except via the host, and two hosts can't talk over USB directly. (USB On-The-Go and dual-role ports can switch roles, one end must provide a supported host role; the other can be an ordinary USB device.) What this means for your setup: Both Digitakt models have a USB-B socket for connecting to a computer host, so the Digitakt acts as a USB device. Most development boards' main USB port is also a device port. Plug a USB-device synth into a USB-device Digitakt and nothing happens: there is no host. A matching cable shape doesn't mean the connection can work. Ways to connect two USB devices: A computer as host. Both plug into the computer, and software (Ableton, or a MIDI routing utility) forwards messages between them. A board with a USB host port. PJRC's Teensy 4.1, for example, has a second USB port that operates in host mode, separate from its device port, supported by the USBHost_t36 library. A standalone USB MIDI host box that hosts both devices and forwards between them. Use DIN MIDI instead. Point to point, isolated, no host needed. For the illustrated standalone link, DIN avoids the USB host requirement; the final interface remains a project decision. Ordinary USB adds a ground path An ordinary non-isolated USB implementation joins host and device grounds. A product with an isolated USB implementation is an exception; do not infer its internal ground paths just from the connector. DIN MIDI doesn't, because of the optocoupler. That is one reason USB connections between mains-powered studio gear can introduce hum, as Diagnose ground paths and run a test session discusses. (Elektron lists the original Digitakt's USB port as electrically isolated; check your own model's documentation.) Key takeaways A device connector does not provide a host; choose DIN or an explicitly supported host and routing arrangement. sum: Match signal level and load requirements from documentation before connecting outputs to inputs.
x: MIDI tells your synth what to play. This lesson is about the other cable: the audio that leaves your synth and goes into the audio interface. Getting it wrong gives you noise, hum, distortion, a quiet signal or, at worst, damaged equipment. Getting it right is mostly a matter of knowing the level conventions and a few circuit principles. Safety boundaries Everything here concerns low-voltage signal connections. Don't open mains-powered gear, and never "fix" hum by removing a mains earth. Before connecting a home-built circuit to the interface, check the interface manual's maximum input level and connect with the gain turned down. The level hierarchy Audio connections come in families with very different voltages and impedances: Level Typical source Goes into --------- Mic Microphone Mic preamp Instrument Guitar pickup Hi-Z input Line Synth, mixer, DAC Line input Headphone Headphone amp Headphones Speaker Power amplifier Passive speaker Mic level is weak and varies widely between microphones (it is sometimes quoted as around −60 dBV). The required preamp gain depends on the microphone, source and distance; this quoted level is an illustration, not a fixed mic-level standard. Passive-pickup output comes from sources like guitar pickups that can supply very little current. "Hi-Z" instrument inputs present a high input impedance chosen for the pickup; consult the instrument and interface documentation so as not to load them. Line level is the level synths, mixers and interfaces use between each other. It is where your synth's output belongs. Headphone outputs are amplifiers designed for a specified range of headphone loads; check the supported impedance and output ratings. Speaker level outputs from power amplifiers drive passive loudspeakers (usually 4–8 Ω) with much higher voltages and currents. These are not interchangeable. A speaker output into a line input can overload or damage it. A line output into a speaker is nearly a short circuit for the line driver: very weak sound and a possibly damaged output. A headphone output can sometimes feed a line input with a suitable stereo-to-mono breakout and conservative level, but check both manuals: a stereo headphone TRS output is not balanced mono, and its peak voltage can overload an input. Key takeaways Match signal level and load requirements from documentation before connecting outputs to inputs. t: Convert between line levels and volts
sum: Compare dBu and dBV through their level reference voltages; their displayed numbers cannot be subtracted directly.
x: Decibels with a reference: dBV and dBu A decibel figure is a ratio. To describe an absolute voltage it needs a reference: dBV: relative to 1 V RMS. dBu: relative to 0.7746 V RMS, a holdover from 600 Ω telephone practice: the voltage that dissipates 1 mW in 600 Ω. Where does 0.7746 V come from? Power in a resistor is voltage squared divided by resistance, so the voltage that gives a chosen power is the square root of power times resistance: Today the 600 Ω load is history: 0 dBu just means 0.7746 V RMS, whatever the actual load. To turn a level in decibels into a voltage, undo the decibel formula for voltage ratios (which uses 20 times the base-10 logarithm): For −10 dBV the same formula, with a 1 V reference and a power of −10/20, gives about 0.316 V. The two nominal line levels: Professional: +4 dBu. Consumer: −10 dBV. To compare two voltages in decibels, go the other way: You can't just subtract −10 from +4 to get 14 dB, because the two figures use different references (0.7746 V and 1 V); converting both to volts first avoids that trap. The same sums in Python: For a pure sine, peak voltage is about 1.414 times RMS voltage; that relationship explains the peak output line above. The following headroom unit explains why it does not hold for an arbitrary waveform. Key takeaways Compare dBu and dBV through their level reference voltages; their displayed numbers cannot be subtracted directly. sum: Use the square-root-of-two factor only for a sine wave and leave room above the nominal operating level.

Sine-wave peaks and operating level So pro line level is about four times the voltage of consumer line level, about 12 dB higher. The "peak" line uses the relationship between a sine wave's RMS value and its peak: The factor of about 1.414 holds only for a pure sine wave. Other waveforms and music can have a different, including higher, ratio of peak to RMS, which is one reason equipment needs headroom. Two cautions: Nominal is not maximum. The nominal level is the design's operating level; real signals have peaks well above it, and equipment leaves headroom for them. Elektron, for example, specifies the Digitakt II's main outputs and inputs at +18 dBu peak, and the original Digitakt's main outputs at +22 dBu peak. Analogue-to-digital alignment is equipment-dependent; −18 and −20 dBFS are examples used in some systems, not a universal correspondence to a particular dBu voltage. Interfaces differ. Many line inputs are switchable or have enough gain range to handle both conventions. Read your interface manual for its maximum input level (often in dBu) and compare it with your synth's maximum output. Elektron labels these published maximum ratings “dBu peak”. The standard dBu voltage reference is RMS-based; the manufacturer label is quoted here rather than silently converted into waveform peak volts. t: Check the output and input impedances
sum: Model the resistive divider, then check the real output driver’s load and current ratings rather than extrapolating beyond them.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. Impedance bridging Audio line connections are not impedance-matched (that is for power transfer and radio). They use impedance bridging: a low output impedance drives a high input impedance. A line driver is normally specified for a minimum load impedance; the receiver should present a much higher impedance than the source. These are design and product specifications, not fixed universal values. In this resistive Thevenin model, the output and input impedances form a voltage divider: the source's voltage is shared between its own output impedance and the input impedance in proportion to their sizes, and only the input's share reaches the next stage. In decibels a voltage ratio of 0.958 is about −0.4 dB, a negligible loss. The Digitakt's main outputs have a 440 Ω output impedance (Elektron's figure, unbalanced). See what happens to a 1 V signal from a 440 Ω source as the load changes: Into a 10 kΩ line input, almost nothing is lost. Into a 32 Ω headphone or 8 Ω speaker, nearly all the voltage is dropped inside the source, and the output stage is asked for far more current than it was designed for. That is the numerical reason line, headphone and speaker connections are not interchangeable. The calculations are a linear resistive model, not proof that a real driver remains linear into headphones or a speaker. Outside its rated load it can limit current, distort, overheat or become unstable. Design the synth output for the actual receiving input and follow the buffer or codec driver's documented minimum load. Key takeaways Model the resistive divider, then check the real output driver’s load and current ratings rather than extrapolating beyond them. t: Read balanced and stereo jack wiring
sum: A balanced line relies on impedance symmetry and a differential receiver; a TRS connector alone proves neither balance nor signal type.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. Balanced and unbalanced connections An unbalanced connection uses two conductors: signal and ground (which is also the shield). Any noise induced onto the signal wire, or any voltage difference between the two devices' grounds, adds directly to the audio. A balanced connection (a balanced line) uses three: two signal conductors (hot and cold) with equal impedances to ground, plus a shield. Interference couples almost equally onto hot and cold, so much of it appears as a common-mode voltage. A differential receiver responds primarily to the difference between the conductors. Rejection is finite and depends on impedance balance, cable construction and the receiver. Notes that save confusion: Balancing is about equal impedances, not necessarily equal and opposite signals. An "impedance-balanced" output that drives only the hot leg, with the cold leg tied to ground through a matching impedance, can still provide common-mode rejection with a suitable balanced receiver. Elektron describes the Digitakt's main outputs as impedance balanced. Balanced connections usually use XLR or 1/4″ TRS: tip = hot, ring = cold, sleeve = ground and shield. The same TRS plug is also used for unbalanced stereo (headphones: tip = left, ring = right). The connector alone doesn't tell you which; the jack's documentation does. TS (tip-sleeve) plugs are unbalanced mono. Mixing them: a TS plug in a balanced output usually shorts the cold leg to ground. That is normal and fine for impedance-balanced outputs, but for some output designs the cold leg should be left disconnected instead, so check the manual. An unbalanced source can feed a balanced input using the manufacturer's recommended wiring. Noise rejection depends on the resulting impedances and connections; do not assume a particular amount of rejection survives or is lost. For your first build An unbalanced mono output on a 1/4″ TS jack, buffered to a low output impedance, into a balanced line input on your interface, using a short cable, is a perfectly good start. Balanced output stages can come later if hum or noise demands it. Key takeaways A balanced line relies on impedance symmetry and a differential receiver; a TRS connector alone proves neither balance nor signal type.
