t: Block DC without losing low bass
sum: Check actual board bias and coupling, then size the capacitor for the lowest input impedance and its tolerance.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. DC offset and output coupling For the external analogue line connection here, the wanted changing audio signal should have little unintended DC offset. Many DIY synth circuits aren't: An MCU DAC limited to non-negative voltages may have a nominal range from zero towards its positive reference (check actual swing and load limits), so a bipolar waveform can be biased near mid-scale (1.65 V in an ideal 3.3 V range) and swing either side of that. Many single-supply audio codecs likewise bias their analogue outputs to an internal mid-supply reference. Not all do: TI's PCM510x DACs, for example, use an internal charge pump to give ground-centred outputs that need no DC-blocking capacitor. Check your part's datasheet. A single-supply op-amp stage commonly needs bias and coupling too; suitable charge-pump or other circuitry can provide ground-centred outputs. That constant offset is DC. Sent into an interface, it can shift the input stage's operating point, eat headroom, cause thumps when plugging and unplugging, and push speaker cones off centre. So the output is normally AC-coupled: a series coupling capacitor passes the audio and blocks the DC. The capacitor and the next stage's input impedance form a high-pass filter. Its corner frequency, below which the bass starts to roll off, is: This approximation assumes the source's output resistance is much smaller than the input resistance. If it isn't, use the source's output resistance plus the input resistance in place of the input resistance. The same calculation in Python, for three cases: 10 µF into a 10 kΩ input: corner about 1.6 Hz, well below the 20 Hz bottom of hearing. 1 µF into 10 kΩ: about 16 Hz, which already starts to thin the lowest bass, especially as cascaded coupling stages add up. 10 µF into the Digitakt II's 21 kΩ inputs: about 0.8 Hz. Choose C so that the corner sits comfortably below 20 Hz for the lowest input impedance you expect to drive. Account for capacitor tolerance, voltage rating and voltage coefficient, and if it is a polarised electrolytic, orient it for the DC across it (positive towards the side at the higher DC potential; check both ends under normal and transient conditions). Check what your board already does Some audio codec boards already AC-couple and buffer their line outputs; others expose a raw DAC pin. Don't assume. Read the board's datasheet or schematic for the output's DC bias, maximum swing and output impedance before adding (or omitting) a coupling capacitor and buffer. Key takeaways Check actual board bias and coupling, then size the capacitor for the lowest input impedance and its tolerance. t: Measure before the first audio connection
sum: Verify DC and waveform swing with appropriate instruments, then connect a documented line path with phantom power off and levels down.
x: A worked level check Suppose (hypothetically) your synth's output stage swings a full-scale sine between 0 V and 3.3 V, centred on 1.65 V. After AC coupling, that is a 1.65 V peak sine. Convert the peak to RMS, then express the RMS voltage relative to the dBu reference: That's close to pro nominal level at full scale, and well within a line input that accepts, say, +18 dBu. Set the interface gain low and verify actual peak voltage and transients; the ideal sine calculation alone does not prove the hardware cannot overload. For a smaller output, compare clean gain available in the synth and interface. The noise outcome depends on both stages; extra output gain is not automatically quieter. Connecting your synth to the interface safely A checklist for the first connection: Read both manuals. Note the synth's maximum output level and DC behaviour, and the interface's input types, impedances and maximum levels. Use a line input (or a combo jack's 1/4″ line path), not the speaker terminals of anything, and not a mic input with phantom power. Turn off 48 V phantom power on that channel. Phantom power is intended for microphones; with some cables, adapters and electronic instruments it can cause malfunction or even damage. Measure before connecting to the interface. Power the isolated low-voltage synth as documented. Use a DC-voltage meter to check offset, and an oscilloscope (or a suitably rated, frequency-specified AC meter) to check waveform swing. An ordinary meter alone cannot reveal short peaks or clipping. Gain to minimum, monitors down. After the output checks, connect following both devices’ documented power-up and connection procedure. Bring the gain up until peaks sit comfortably below clipping on the interface meter (Leave headroom at every stage covers this). Protect the output. A suitable buffer and documented series resistance can improve fault tolerance, but do not guarantee survival of every short or load. Follow your board vendor's recommended output circuit. Key takeaways Verify DC and waveform swing with appropriate instruments, then connect a documented line path with phantom power off and levels down. x: The project's success criteria say an external device should play the instrument, its audio should be recorded into Ableton through the existing interface, and a test session should run without stuck notes or audio interruptions. Find out which model you own and confirm every port and setting against the current manual for it before buying parts or wiring anything. t: Prove the Digitakt MIDI track path
sum: Check port function, output route, track channel and note length before treating silence or a held note as a firmware fault.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. Step 2: sequence the synth from a Digitakt MIDI track Both manuals give the same procedure (section "Controlling a synthesizer using the MIDI tracks"): Connect Digitakt MIDI OUT to the synth's MIDI IN with a standard MIDI cable. In SETTINGS > MIDI CONFIG > PORT CONFIG, set OUT PORT FUNC to MIDI (not DIN 24/48 sync). In the same menu, set OUTPUT TO to MIDI (or MIDI+USB). Select a MIDI track. On the original Digitakt these are tracks 9–16. On the Digitakt II, first assign the MIDI machine to a track (FUNC + SRC opens the machine menu). Press SRC and set CHAN to the channel your synth listens on (OFF or 1–16). Set the synth to receive on that channel. Then program notes as on any track. Things your synth will see: Note on/off with the trig's note, VEL and LEN. LEN decides when the note off is sent; the original Digitakt manual lists an INF (infinite note length) setting, so a note can be held indefinitely by design. Check LEN before blaming your firmware for a stuck note. Chords: a MIDI trig can send up to four notes (NOT2–NOT4). A mono synth will apply its note priority to them, so keep chords off unless you want that effect. Pitch bend, aftertouch, mod wheel, breath (PB, AT, MW, BC on the SRC page) and assignable CCs, whose values and CC numbers are set on the Digitakt FLTR page and Digitakt AMP page (the layout differs between the two models; see your manual). They're OFF by default; enable each one, then pick its CC number to match the CC map implemented by your synth, introduced in Choose and decode control changes. Parameter locks and LFOs can then automate your synth's parameters. Bank and program change (BANK, SBNK, PROG) if your synth supports presets. Clock and transport, if CLOCK SEND / TRANSPORT SEND are enabled in MIDI CONFIG > SYNC. Your parser must tolerate the F8 stream. Prove the MIDI path in isolation first Before wiring the synth, send the Digitakt's MIDI to the computer (USB MIDI) or through a USB MIDI interface into a MIDI monitor, and check the bytes match what you expect: channel nibble, note numbers, velocity-0 or 8n note offs, CC numbers. Then connect the synth. Key takeaways Check port function, output route, track channel and note length before treating silence or a held note as a firmware fault. Step 3: record into Ableton For the synth's audio, Ableton Live 12's manual describes the essentials: Create an audio track. In its In/Out section, select your interface in Live's Audio settings, then set Audio From to Ext. In and choose the channel the synth is plugged into. Arm the track and record. sum: Block duration is a timing unit, not a complete measured latency; compare direct and software monitoring on the actual setup.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. Monitoring and latency Latency adds up along the chain. Two simple formulas cover most of it. First, an audio buffer (or block) represents a duration given by its sample count divided by the sample rate. That duration is a useful timing budget; a particular buffering architecture determines how much latency it contributes: Second, DIN MIDI delays a message by the time its bytes take on the wire, 0.32 ms per byte: The DIN wire-time result is a minimum for back-to-back bytes. The buffer duration is a model input, not a universal lower bound on each implementation's latency: drivers and converters add their own delays, and other MIDI traffic (clock, CCs) queued ahead of a note delays it further. The same estimates in Python: MIDI transmission: about 1 ms per three-byte message on DIN. Your synth's audio block: if it processes 48-sample blocks at 48 kHz, notes can wait up to 1 ms for the next block, plus the codec's own conversion delay (see your board's documentation). Ableton monitoring: the interface's input buffer, Live's processing and the output buffer, plus converter delays. At 128 samples per buffer and 48 kHz, one buffer represents 2.67 ms. In a simple one-input-buffer plus one-output-buffer model that is about 5.33 ms, before additional delays; use measured or driver-reported audio monitoring latency for the actual hardware. Practical consequences: If you hear the synth through Ableton while playing it from the Digitakt, you add the audio monitoring delay. Use direct monitoring on the interface (and set the track's monitor to Off) when tight feel matters. For recordings, Live compensates: with monitoring In or Auto, "Keep Monitoring Latency in Recorded Audio" aligns the recording with what you heard; with monitoring Off, Live's manual points to the Overall Latency adjustment in its Audio settings. Measure rather than guess: record a Digitakt sound and your synth triggered on the same step, and measure the offset in samples on the waveforms. Key takeaways Block duration is a timing unit, not a complete measured latency; compare direct and software monitoring on the actual setup. Gain staging across the chain Gain staging means setting each stage's level so the signal stays well above that stage's noise floor and well below its clipping point. In order: Synth output: design it to reach line level at full scale (the audio-level units). Don't make it so hot that the interface input can't accept it. Interface input gain: set it with your loudest patch (high resonance, all oscillators, full velocity). A common rule of thumb is to leave peaks around −12 to −6 dBFS: plenty of headroom, and at 24-bit there's still a large margin above the noise floor. Some systems align analogue nominal levels with −18 or −20 dBFS; your interface's alignment is equipment-dependent, so you don't need to record "hot". Ableton track: adjust with the track fader or a utility device, not by going back and changing the input gain mid-session. Digitakt: its outputs can deliver up to +18 dBu (II) or +22 dBu (original) peak. Check those maxima against your interface's maximum input level, and use the Digitakt's master level or the interface pad if necessary. Clipping is a stage, not a song If you hear distortion, find which stage clips: watch the synth's output on a scope, the interface's input meter and Live's track meter in turn. Turning down the end of the chain doesn't fix clipping earlier in it. Elektron labels these published maximum ratings “dBu peak”. The standard dBu voltage reference is RMS-based; the manufacturer label is quoted here rather than silently converted into waveform peak volts. t: Diagnose ground paths and run a test session
sum: Change one signal or low-voltage power connection at a time, preserve protective earth and record the results of stress tests.
x: Product details in this unit refer to the original Digitakt OS 1.53 manual and Digitakt II OS 1.17 manual, fetched on 16 October 2026. Confirm your model, firmware and current manual before wiring or configuring it. Ground loops in a studio setup A ground loop can form when two devices are connected by more than one conductive ground path, for example through their mains earths and an audio cable shield. Interference currents can then create unwanted voltage in signal references, heard as mains hum at the mains frequency (50 Hz in the UK) and its harmonics, often with buzz from digital activity. Common paths in this setup: Audio cables (the shield is ground in unbalanced connections). Ordinary USB connections, which join host and device grounds unless the implementation is electrically isolated. A dev board powered from the computer by USB, with its audio output plugged into the interface (also on that computer), makes a loop through the computer, the interface's USB and the audio cable. Not DIN MIDI: the optocoupler at each MIDI IN breaks that path, by design. Diagnose before you fix: unplug one connection at a time and note which change removes the hum. Running a laptop briefly on battery, or temporarily powering the dev board from a different source, can show whether the USB path is involved. Safe remedies: Prefer balanced connections into the interface (the Digitakt's outputs are impedance balanced; use TRS cables into balanced line inputs). Use DIN MIDI rather than USB to connect devices where you can. Insert a ground loop isolator (an audio isolation transformer) in the offending audio line; it passes the signal while breaking the DC ground path. For a USB-powered dev board, a properly specified USB isolator can break the USB ground path if it supports the required speed, class and power arrangement. A separate documented supply plus DIN MIDI may also remove that path; check remaining connections. Keep audio cables short and away from power supplies. Never lift a safety earth Removing or taping over the mains earth on a device to stop hum also removes its protection against electric shock. Fix the signal-side ground path instead. Putting it together: a first test session Wire the studio connection diagram from Draw the complete studio connection plan. Power up with all gains down. Prove MIDI: a MIDI monitor shows the Digitakt track's notes on the expected channel. Prove audio: the synth's test tone reaches the interface meter at a sensible level, with no DC offset and no hum. Sequence a pattern from the Digitakt; record it into Ableton with direct monitoring. Stress test: fast notes, long notes, chords, CC sweeps, pattern stop/start, cable unplug and replug. Record any stuck notes, clicks or dropouts, and their causes, in the project journal. Key takeaways Change one signal or low-voltage power connection at a time, preserve protective earth and record the results of stress tests. sum: Sound in air is a longitudinal pressure disturbance; molecules oscillate locally.
x: Everything in this module happens in air. Your synth makes a voltage; a loudspeaker turns it into moving air; a room bounces it about; an ear or a microphone turns it back into something useful. Before looking at any of those devices, you need a working model of what sound in air actually is and how it behaves with distance. Module 1 covered decibels as ratios and dBFS, and module 5 covered dBu and dBV for signal voltages. This lesson adds the decibel scale for sound in air: dB SPL. Sound is a pressure wave A loudspeaker cone moving forward squashes the air in front of it slightly (a acoustic compression); moving back, it leaves the air slightly thinner (a rarefaction). Each layer of air pushes on the next, so the disturbance travels outward. The air molecules themselves only jiggle back and forth around where they started. What travels is the pattern of pressure. Two consequences matter for audio engineering: Sound is longitudinal: the air moves along the direction of travel, not across it. The pressure changes are tiny. Atmospheric pressure is about 101,325 Pa. A 120 dB SPL sound has an RMS pressure of 20 Pa; a 60 dB SPL sound has an RMS pressure of 0.02 Pa. These are pressure examples, not hearing-safety thresholds. Speed of sound and wavelength In dry air the speed of sound depends mainly on temperature: warmer air molecules move faster, so they pass the disturbance on faster. For ideal dry air at fixed temperature, static pressure cancels from the sound-speed relation. Humidity also changes the speed, so precise outdoor alignment needs the actual conditions. A standard ideal-gas approximation, good for everyday air temperatures, is: Worked example at a room temperature of 20 °C: The approximation assumes dry air behaving as an ideal gas. Humidity generally raises the speed; its effect depends on temperature and water-vapour content. The dry-air calculation is an approximation, not a measured outdoor value. The same calculation as a short program: The usual working figure is 343 m/s at 20 °C, which is about 1 metre every 2.9 ms. That number turns up everywhere: speaker delay times, room modes, crossover alignment. Wavelength is how far the wave travels in one cycle. In one second the wave travels about 343 metres and completes as many cycles as its frequency, so each cycle covers the speed divided by the frequency: Worked example for a 1 kHz tone (1000 Hz): The same division gives the table below. It applies to any wave, as long as you use the speed for the medium the wave is in (sound in water travels about four times faster, so its wavelengths are four times longer). Frequency Wavelength (at 343 m/s) ------ 20 Hz 17.15 m 100 Hz 3.43 m 1 kHz 34.3 cm 10 kHz 3.43 cm 20 kHz 1.7 cm Audible wavelengths span a factor of 1,000, from longer than a house to shorter than your thumb. Relative size strongly affects diffraction and scattering. Reflection and absorption also depend on material impedance, construction, mounting and incidence angle. Key takeaways Sound in air is a longitudinal pressure disturbance; molecules oscillate locally. Temperature changes sound speed and therefore travel time. At a fixed sound speed, doubling frequency halves wavelength. Further reading Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State

t: Read sound pressure in dB SPL
sum: The air-pressure reference is 20 micropascals RMS.
x: Sound pressure level: dB SPL Sound pressure is the changing pressure around the ambient value, measured in pascals (Pa). For a level measurement, we use its RMS value: an average size over a specified time interval. Because the range is so huge, we use decibels relative to a reference of 20 µPa (20 millionths of a pascal), roughly the quietest 1 kHz tone a young, healthy listener can detect. The sound pressure level is: The multiplier is 20, not 10, because pressure is a field quantity, like voltage: for a progressive wave in the same medium, sound intensity is proportional to pressure squared, and squaring a ratio doubles its logarithm (module 1 explains why). Worked example for a pressure of 1 Pa: As a program, for a few pressures: Remember 1 Pa ≈ 94 dB SPL. Microphone sensitivities are quoted at 1 Pa (the microphone units) and calibrators often produce 94 dB SPL for exactly this reason. Key takeaways The air-pressure reference is 20 micropascals RMS. One pascal RMS is approximately 94 dB SPL. Pressure ratios use twenty times the base-ten logarithm. Further reading Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State

sum: Use the same direction and a source’s free-field far field.
x: The inverse square law A small source in open space (a free field, with no reflections) spreads its power over the surface of a growing sphere. The area of a sphere grows with the square of its radius, so the same power is shared over more and more air: This is the inverse square law. Turning the pressure ratio into decibels (20 × log, because pressure is a field quantity) gives the working form, which predicts the level at one distance from a level measured at another: Each doubling of distance therefore loses the same amount: Worked example: a speaker gives 100 dB SPL at 1 m. What does a listener at 25 m get? Where the law doesn't hold - Indoors, reflections build a reverberant field. Beyond a certain distance (the critical distance) the level stops falling at 6 dB per doubling and levels off. The room-acoustics units cover rooms. - Close to a source, particularly a large one or a line of speakers, the level doesn't fall in neat inverse-square steps (see the later boundaries and fields unit). - Acoustic line sources (long columns of speakers) fall closer to 3 dB per doubling over part of their range, because the energy spreads over a cylinder rather than a sphere. Key takeaways Use the same direction and a source’s free-field far field. Each distance doubling reduces pressure level by about six decibels. Reflections, line-source geometry and near-field behaviour need different models. Further reading Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State

sum: Uncorrelated sources add in mean-square pressure, giving about three decibels for two equal sources.
x: Adding sources Independent sound sources (for example unrelated noise sources) can be treated as incoherent sources over the averaging interval: their waveforms are unrelated, so their mean-square pressures add, with the correlation cross-term averaging to zero. To add levels, turn each one back into a relative mean-square pressure, add those values, and turn the total back into decibels: Worked example, two equal 90 dB SPL sources, then a 90 and an 80: This assumes the sources really are unrelated and you average over a long enough time. The same sum as a program: Two equal incoherent sources: +3 dB. A source 10 dB quieter adds only about 0.4 dB. The loud one dominates. Four equal sources: +6 dB. Coherent sources are different. Two speakers playing the same signal at the same distance add in pressure, so they can give up to +6 dB where they arrive in phase, and deep cancellation where they arrive out of phase. Compare doubling the pressure with doubling the power: For delayed broadband copies, the repeating frequency peaks and notches are comb filtering; a single tone instead shows spatial interference, and it is why the microphone units’ 3:1 rule and the crossover units’ driver alignment exist. Key takeaways Uncorrelated sources add in mean-square pressure, giving about three decibels for two equal sources. Identical in-phase copies double pressure, giving about six decibels. Delayed broadband copies can create comb filtering. Further reading Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State

t: Relating wavelength to boundaries and fields
sum: Size relative to wavelength affects diffraction and acoustic shadows.
x: Reflection, absorption and diffraction At a boundary, sound can be reflected, transmitted or absorbed; diffraction describes spreading around edges and openings. Wavelength, impedance and construction all matter. Sound reflection. A hard, large, flat surface (a wall, a desk, a window) reflects sound like a mirror reflects light: angle in equals angle out. This only works well when the surface is large compared with the wavelength. A stiff 30 cm panel can give a directional reflection at 10 kHz (wavelength 3.4 cm). At 100 Hz (wavelength 3.4 m), diffraction around it is important; its actual reflection and transmission still depend on material and mounting. Sound absorption. Porous materials (mineral wool, thick fabric) turn some of the sound's energy into heat. Each material has an absorption coefficient, the fraction of incident energy not returned as reflected sound in the room-acoustics convention; it may include transmitted energy: For example, a panel that reflects 30 % of the arriving energy has an absorption coefficient of 0.7. The coefficient varies with frequency, so it is quoted per octave band. Thin foam absorbs high frequencies well and does almost nothing to bass, because bass wavelengths are far longer than the foam is thick. Diffraction. Waves bend around obstacles and spread out through openings. When an obstacle is small compared with the wavelength, sound diffracts around it with hardly a shadow. When it's large, it casts an acoustic shadow. This is why you can hear the bass, but not the cymbals, from a band round the corner; why your head shadows high frequencies but not low ones (the hearing units); and why a loudspeaker radiates almost equally in all directions at low frequencies but beams forward at high frequencies (the loudspeaker-driver units). Size vs wavelength Behaviour ------ Object much smaller Sound diffracts round it Comparable Partial, frequency-dependent Object much larger Reflection and shadowing Near field and far field Very close to a source, the sound field is complicated: different parts of the source (the cone, the edges of the cabinet, several drivers) are at noticeably different distances from you, and their contributions interfere. Level can change sharply as you move a few centimetres, and it doesn't follow the inverse square law. Further away, in the far field, the source behaves like a point: level falls 6 dB per doubling, and the balance between drivers settles down. The distance needed depends on source geometry, frequency and the measurement criterion. Several source dimensions alone is not a universal far-field test for a large array; follow the manufacturer's measurement method and verify that distance-scaled responses converge. Datasheet figures are quoted "at 1 m", but large speakers are often measured further away and the result scaled back to 1 m with the inverse square law. "Near-field monitor" means something else Studio "near-field monitors" are small speakers listened to from about 1–2 m, so that you hear more direct sound than room reflections. They aren't about the acoustic near field of the speaker itself. The room-acoustics units cover them. Key takeaways Size relative to wavelength affects diffraction and acoustic shadows. Absorption also depends on material, mounting and incidence angle. A reverberant room and an acoustic near field do not follow a simple distance law. Further reading Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State

t: Why equal SPL is not equal loudness
sum: Hearing sensitivity varies with frequency, listener and sound level.
x: A sound level meter measures pressure. You hear something else: loudness, pitch, direction and timbre, all built by your ear and brain from that pressure. Psychoacoustics studies the gap between the two. For anyone mixing, designing speakers or building instruments it explains why a bass line vanishes at low volume, why a quiet pad disappears under a loud lead, and why a delay speaker can be louder than the stage without pulling the image towards it. It also explains how hearing gets damaged. That part is not optional reading. The range of hearing The commonly quoted range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Treat both ends as soft: The top end falls with age and noise exposure. Many adults hear little above 15–16 kHz. Your synth's 18 kHz content may be inaudible to you and obvious to a teenager (or to your dog). At the bottom, below about 20 Hz, very loud sound is felt more than heard. Hearing is most sensitive roughly between 2 and 5 kHz, partly because the ear canal resonates in that region. In level, hearing spans from the threshold near 0 dB SPL at mid frequencies to very high levels that can cause pain and damage. Pain thresholds vary, and harmful exposure can occur far below pain; a 120 dB level difference represents a millionfold pressure ratio. Equal-loudness contours Play a 100 Hz tone and a 1 kHz tone at the same dB SPL and the 100 Hz tone sounds much quieter. An equal-loudness contour joins up the levels at which pure tones of different frequencies sound equally loud. Each contour is labelled in phons: for example, the forty-phon contour passes through 40 dB SPL at one kilohertz. The standard specifies young, otologically normal listeners, frontal free-field pure tones and binaural listening; it is not a calibration of every listener or broadband music. The first such curves were Fletcher and Munson's (1933). The current international standard is ISO 226. Its 2003 edition replaced older curves that had been shown to be inaccurate, and it was revised again in 2023 with small changes. (A sketch of the shape only: read real values and listening conditions from the applicable ISO 226 edition.) Three things to take from the curves: Bass needs much more SPL than mid frequencies to sound equally loud, especially at low listening levels. The curves flatten as level rises. The difference between bass and mids is smaller at 80 phon than at 20 phon. So a mix sounds different at different volumes. Turn it down and the bass and extreme treble seem to fade first. Mix at one consistent, moderate level, and check at quiet and loud levels. Key takeaways Hearing sensitivity varies with frequency, listener and sound level. Equal-loudness contours describe pure tones under specified conditions. A mix’s perceived balance changes with listening level. Further reading Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore Noise regulations — HSE Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4 WHO safe-listening venues standard summary ISO 226:2023 scope and history — Estonian standards body

t: Understand A, C and Z weighting
sum: A-weighting strongly attenuates low-frequency contributions to a meter reading.
x: A and C weighting Sound level meters apply a frequency weighting to make a single number track human response better. The two that matter, both defined for sound level meters in IEC 61672-1: A-weighting (dB(A) or dBA) strongly reduces low frequencies (about −19 dB at 100 Hz, −30 dB at 50 Hz) and slightly boosts 2–4 kHz. It was based on the 40-phon Fletcher–Munson curve. It is the standard weighting for noise exposure and for many noise-floor specifications. C-weighting (dB(C)) is nearly flat from about 31.5 Hz to 8 kHz (−3 dB points). It is used for peak level measurements, and for loud, bass-heavy sound where A-weighting would hide the low end. Z-weighting is flat ("zero"). The A-weighting curve is defined by a formula in IEC 61672-1. It describes a set of simple filters: two that cut below about 20 Hz, one each near 108 Hz and 738 Hz that shape the low-mid roll-off, and two that cut above about 12.2 kHz. You don't need to memorise it, but it shows that "dB(A)" is a precisely defined filter, not a vague idea: Worked example at 100 Hz: The same formula as a program, evaluated at several frequencies: Why live engineers watch dB(C) as well as dB(A) A kick drum and sub-bass can carry enormous energy at 40–60 Hz while barely moving a dB(A) meter. Venues often monitor both. Key takeaways A-weighting strongly attenuates low-frequency contributions to a meter reading. Great Britain workplace exposure uses A-weighting for dose and C-weighting for peaks. Weightings are measurement filters, not a loudspeaker behaviour. Further reading A-weighting measurement implementation — Son, Kyung and Cho (2019) Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore Noise regulations — HSE Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4 WHO safe-listening venues standard summary

sum: Masking depends on spectrum, timing and level.
x: Masking A loud sound can make a quieter one inaudible. This is masking, and it's the reason a mix "gets muddy": parts that each sound fine alone hide each other when played together. Simultaneous masking is strongest when the two sounds are close in frequency. It spreads upwards: a loud low sound masks higher frequencies much more effectively than a loud high sound masks lower ones. The effect grows with level. That's why a heavy bass part can dull a whole mix. Temporal masking also happens: a loud sound can hide quieter sounds just after it (and, briefly, just before it). Lossy codecs such as MP3 and AAC exploit masking: they spend fewer bits on what masking will hide anyway. Critical bands, intuitively The cochlea behaves like a bank of overlapping band-pass filters. Critical-band measurements and auditory-filter bandwidths both describe frequency selectivity, but their numerical widths depend on how they are measured. ERB is the width of an ideal rectangular filter with the same peak gain and integrated response as the actual filter. Two tones inside one band interact strongly: they mask each other, beat or sound rough. Tones in well-separated bands are heard more independently. The bands are narrow at low frequencies and wider at high frequencies. One standard model, Glasberg and Moore's equivalent rectangular bandwidth (ERB), gives the width of the auditory filter centred on a given frequency. It was fitted to listening-test data from young, normally hearing listeners at moderate levels: Worked example at a centre frequency of 1 kHz (1000 Hz): The formula is an average fit, not a sharp boundary: real filters overlap, and their widths change with level and between listeners. Centre ERB ------ 100 Hz ≈ 35.5 Hz 1 kHz ≈ 133 Hz 4 kHz ≈ 456.5 Hz In practice: two bass parts a few tens of hertz apart are fighting inside the same band, so EQ-ing space between parts (or choosing different octaves) does more for clarity than turning one up. Key takeaways Masking depends on spectrum, timing and level. Auditory filters overlap and generally widen as centre frequency rises. ERB summarizes a filter response; it is not a sharp separation boundary. Further reading Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore Noise regulations — HSE Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4 WHO safe-listening venues standard summary

sum: Time differences dominate low-frequency left–right localisation; level differences matter strongly at high frequencies.
x: Localisation: ITD and ILD You locate a sound left or right mainly from two cues: Interaural time difference (ITD). A sound from the side reaches the near ear first. Maximum adult ITDs are of order 0.6–0.7 ms and vary with head size, frequency and source direction; simply dividing ear spacing by sound speed neglects diffraction around the head. ITD (as phase differences) is the main cue at low frequencies, below about 1 kHz. Interaural level difference (ILD). The head casts an acoustic shadow, but only for wavelengths small compared with the head (the acoustics units’ diffraction rule). So ILD is the main cue at high frequencies, above about 1.5 kHz. Between roughly 1 and 1.5 kHz both cues contribute. This "duplex theory" goes back to Lord Rayleigh (1907). Neither cue separates front from back or up from down; for those the brain uses the filtering of the outer ear (pinna) and small head movements. Why one subwoofer is usually enough At very low frequencies the head casts almost no shadow (so ILD vanishes), the interaural time difference becomes a tiny fraction of a cycle, and in a room the modes and reflections swamp what cues remain. So localisation of deep bass is poor, which is why a single subwoofer can usually be placed off-centre without the bass seeming to come from it. An 80 Hz crossover is a common system choice, not a hard hearing boundary; it only works if the crossover is low and the sub's distortion and port noise don't add higher-frequency content you can locate. The precedence (Haas) effect In a room, you hear the direct sound plus many reflections from other directions, yet you perceive one sound coming from the source. The precedence effect is the reason: the auditory system localises a sound by the first-arriving wavefront and suppresses the direction of early reflections. Precedence depends on signal, level, delay, direction and listening conditions. Fusion (hearing one event), localization dominance (hearing it toward the first source), and suppression of information about the reflection are related but distinct; one can persist after another breaks down. There is no universal delay/level boundary guaranteeing all three. Exact Haas-derived limits are absent here because their original experimental conditions were not reliably established in this review. This has a direct engineering use (the sound-system units): a delay speaker is aligned using the difference between stage-to-listener and fill-to-listener travel times, plus any deliberately chosen precedence offset: For example, if the stage path is 34.3 m longer, the travel-time difference is 34.3 m divided by 343 m/s, which is 100 ms; with a chosen 10 ms offset the starting setting is 110 ms. The formula ignores electronic latency and temperature changes. Account for electronic latency, then measure and listen across the coverage area. A large offset can cause audible echoes or comb filtering rather than guarantee stage localization. Key takeaways Time differences dominate low-frequency left–right localisation; level differences matter strongly at high frequencies. Outer-ear filtering and head movements provide additional direction cues. Delay alignment uses path and electronic-latency differences; an extra offset is a design choice to evaluate. Further reading Auditory pathways and localisation — David Heeger, NYU Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore Noise regulations — HSE Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4 WHO safe-listening venues standard summary

sum: Workplace noise risk depends on level and exposure time.
x: Hearing damage and safe exposure Noise-induced hearing loss is permanent. It depends on level and time together: the dose. Tinnitus (ringing) after a loud session is a warning sign. Great Britain workplaces: Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 (HSE). These apply to music and entertainment work too. Threshold Daily LEP,d / weekly LEP,w Peak (LCpeak) --------- Lower action value 80 dB(A) 135 dB(C) Upper action value 85 dB(A) 137 dB(C) Exposure limit 87 dB(A) 140 dB(C) At the lower action value the employer must assess the risk, provide information and training, and make hearing protection available to anyone who asks for it; at the upper one, hearing protection and hearing protection zones become mandatory. The exposure limit values take account of the reduction given by hearing protection and must not be exceeded; the action values do not (regulation 4(5)), so they're judged on unprotected exposure. Key takeaways Workplace noise risk depends on level and exposure time. Action values use unprotected exposure. The exposure limit takes hearing protection into account; peak exposure also needs assessment. Further reading Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore Noise regulations — HSE Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4 WHO safe-listening venues standard summary

sum: NIOSH’s recommended eight-hour reference is 85 dBA with a three-decibel noise-dose exchange rate.
x: Noise dose and listening guidance NIOSH (US) recommended exposure limit: 85 dB(A) averaged over an eight-hour day, with a 3 dB noise-dose exchange rate: every 3 dB increase halves the allowed time. A 3 dB increase doubles the sound energy, so halving the time keeps the total energy (the dose) the same: Worked example at a steady 100 dB(A): The same calculation for several levels, as a program: A steady 100 dB(A) exposure reaches the NIOSH reference daily dose in 15 minutes, before adding other exposure that day. This is a risk-management limit, not a guarantee of no hearing damage. WHO: The WHO–ITU standard for personal audio devices sets a reference weekly allowance of 80 dB for 40 hours a week for adults (75 dB for children). The WHO Global Standard for Safe Listening Venues and Events (2022) recommends a maximum of 100 dB LAeq over any 15 minutes for audiences, alongside monitoring, hearing protection, quiet zones and other measures. This is a ceiling, not a recommended operating target or a guarantee of safety for an entire event. Protect your hearing while building and testing - Bring levels up gradually. A DIY synth can produce a full-scale square wave or a feedback screech the moment you change a line of code. - Set headphone and monitor volume before putting headphones on, and start low. - Use a limiter on the monitoring path while developing. - Wear musicians' earplugs at gigs and loud rehearsals; they reduce level fairly evenly across frequency. Key takeaways NIOSH’s recommended eight-hour reference is 85 dBA with a three-decibel noise-dose exchange rate. Other daily exposures add to the total dose. WHO venue and personal-device recommendations use different reference periods and additional protective measures. Further reading Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore Noise regulations — HSE Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4 WHO safe-listening venues standard summary Noise exposure and exchange rate — NIOSH Personal-device reference sound allowances — WHO WHO–ITU personal-device reference allowances

sum: Moving-coil and ribbon microphones generate voltage by electromagnetic induction.
x: A moving-coil microphone resembles a moving-coil loudspeaker run backwards: a light diaphragm moved by sound pressure, connected to something that turns motion into voltage. The way it makes that conversion decides its sensitivity, noise, ruggedness and whether it needs power. The way sound reaches the diaphragm decides its directional pattern. Even if you mostly record your synth by plugging it straight in (the sound-system units’ DI box), you'll mic amplifiers, voices and rooms, and you'll need to read microphone specifications. Three ways to make a voltage Dynamic (moving coil) A small coil of wire is glued to the diaphragm and sits in the gap of a permanent magnet. Sound moves the diaphragm, the coil moves through the magnetic field, and electromagnetic induction generates a voltage proportional to its velocity. A traditional passive moving-coil mic needs no power; models with internal active electronics are exceptions. Rugged and tolerant of very high SPL (kick drums, guitar cabs, vocals on stage). The coil adds mass, so transient and high-frequency detail are usually less than a condenser's. Low output: typically around 1–3 mV per pascal. Needs plenty of preamp gain. The Shure SM58 is the classic example. Condenser (capacitor) The diaphragm is one plate of a capacitor; a fixed backplate is the other. Sound changes the gap, so the capacitance changes. A conventional capsule with an external polarising supply is charged through a very large resistance, so charge is approximately constant over the relevant audio timescale. An electret supplies a persistent electric polarisation. Changing capacitance then changes the capsule voltage; the readout electronics and capsule design still matter. The capsule has an extremely high impedance, so a conventional studio condenser microphone uses an impedance converter (a small amplifier). That needs power: usually phantom power, sometimes a battery or a dedicated supply for valve models. The diaphragm is very light, so condensers capture fast transients and high-frequency detail. Often higher output (for example 10–30 mV/Pa). A low-noise condenser can give a quieter recording of a quiet source, but compare the actual microphone and preamp specifications; the operating principle alone does not guarantee lower noise or lower maximum SPL. Ribbon A very thin corrugated metal ribbon hangs in a magnetic field. Sound moves the ribbon, and induction generates a voltage, as in a dynamic mic. The ribbon has a tiny output and very low impedance, so passive ribbons use a step-up transformer. Open at front and back, a ribbon naturally has a figure-8 pattern. Smooth, often darker high end. Physically fragile: a blast of air (wind, a kick drum port, blowing into it) can stretch the ribbon. Ribbons and phantom power A correctly wired balanced cable puts phantom voltage equally on both signal pins, so an ideal floating passive output sees no differential DC. Damage can still happen with a faulty or miswired cable, with unbalanced adapters, or when hot-plugging with phantom on, because the pins don't make contact at the same instant. Switch phantom power off before connecting a passive ribbon (or anything that doesn't need it). Some modern "active" ribbons need phantom: follow the manufacturer's manual. Proximity effect Directional (pressure-gradient) mics have a bass boost when the source is very close, within a few centimetres to tens of centimetres. Close to a small source, the pressure difference between the front and back of the diaphragm contains an extra component that is relatively strongest at low frequencies. The closer the source, the bigger the boost. Singers use it ("eating the mic" for a warm, big voice). It causes boomy, muddy recordings when you didn't want it. Omnidirectional (pure pressure) mics have no proximity effect. Many directional mics have a bass-cut switch to compensate. Key takeaways Moving-coil and ribbon microphones generate voltage by electromagnetic induction. Condenser microphones need power for their impedance-converting electronics. Pressure-gradient microphones can show proximity bass boost; pure pressure microphones do not. Further reading Microphone technology — DPA U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann Phantom power — Schoeps Three-to-one rule — DPA Ribbon microphone phantom precautions — Royer

t: Read microphone patterns and their nulls
sum: Ideal first-order patterns combine omnidirectional and figure-eight responses.
x: Polar patterns How a mic responds to sound from different directions depends on how the diaphragm is exposed: Pressure microphones (diaphragm open only at the front, sealed behind) respond to pressure itself, which has no direction: omnidirectional. Pressure-gradient mics (open at front and back) respond to the difference in pressure between the two sides. Sound from the side reaches both sides equally, giving a null: figure-8. Combining the two (or using an acoustic delay network behind the diaphragm) gives the cardioid family. All the common ("first-order") patterns are a mix of an omni part, which is the same in every direction, and a figure-8 part, which follows the cosine of the angle. One formula covers the whole family; only the mix changes: To compare directions you convert the ratio r into decibels relative to the front. Setting r to zero and solving gives the angle of the null: The logarithmic pickup formula applies only where the sensitivity magnitude is nonzero; at an ideal null its limiting level is negative infinity. A real microphone has finite rejection. The null-angle expression applies only when the omni share is at most one half and less than one; a pure omni has no null. Worked through for a cardioid with omni share 0.5 and a hypercardioid with omni share 0.25: The same sums in Python, for all three directional patterns (the code puts the absolute value in for you): Pattern Side (90°) Null --------- Omni 0 dB none Cardioid −6 dB 180° (rear) Supercardioid ≈ −8.7 dB ≈ 125° Hypercardioid −12 dB ≈ 110° Figure-8 null 90° Super- and hypercardioids are narrower at the front but have a rear lobe (a hypercardioid is only −6 dB directly behind). That matters for stage monitors (the sound-system units): put a wedge at a cardioid's 180° null, but at the 110–125° nulls of a hyper- or supercardioid. Real microphones only follow these shapes approximately. Their directionality can change substantially with frequency; a pressure-gradient design can retain low-frequency directionality, while a pressure microphone becomes more directional at high frequencies as its size matters. Check the polar plots in the datasheet. Key takeaways Ideal first-order patterns combine omnidirectional and figure-eight responses. A cardioid’s rear null differs from the angled nulls of hypercardioid and supercardioid patterns. Measured polar plots vary with frequency and determine practical placement. Further reading Microphone technology — DPA U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann Phantom power — Schoeps Three-to-one rule — DPA

sum: Sensitivity relates output voltage to acoustic pressure, commonly at one kilohertz and one pascal.
x: Reading the specifications Sensitivity The output voltage for a given sound pressure, normally at 1 kHz and 1 Pa (94 dB SPL): mV/Pa: millivolts of output per pascal of sound pressure, or dBV/Pa: the same figure in decibels relative to 1 volt per pascal. Converting between the two is a voltage-ratio decibel calculation: Mic (manufacturer's figures) mV/Pa dBV/Pa --------- Shure SM58 (dynamic) 1.6 −56.0 Neumann U 87 Ai, cardioid 28 ≈ −31 (The SM58 figures follow Shure’s user guide version 6.4 (2024-F), checked October 2026; the −56.0 dBV/Pa figure corresponds to about 1.585 mV/Pa, rounded to 1.6 mV/Pa. Older specifications quote different values, so confirm the revision for the microphone being used. Supercardioid definitions also vary a little between sources; an omni share of 0.366 is one common choice.) How much more preamp gain does the less sensitive mic need for the same output? Take the ratio of the two sensitivities and convert it to decibels: So the dynamic needs about 25 dB more preamp gain for the same output. Gain raises signal and input noise together. For quiet sources, compare microphone sensitivity, its own noise and the preamp’s equivalent input noise; a low-noise condenser often performs well. Self-noise A condenser's electronics produce some noise even in a silent room. Self-noise (or "equivalent noise level") is quoted as the SPL that would produce the same output, usually A-weighted (dB-A). Neumann specifies the U 87 Ai's self-noise as 12 dB-A in cardioid. Below about 10 dB-A is very quiet; above about 20 dB-A can become audible on quiet sources. Passive dynamics and ribbons have no active electronics, but their winding and transformer resistance still generate thermal noise. That noise and the preamp’s input noise both contribute to the recorded noise floor. Maximum SPL and dynamic range Max SPL is the level at which distortion reaches a stated figure (often 0.5% or 1% THD). Neumann gives 117 dB SPL for the U 87 Ai (127 dB with its pre-attenuation pad). The dynamic range is the gap between self-noise and max SPL: Because the self-noise figure is A-weighted, this is an approximate, A-weighted range; with the pad engaged the top end rises to 127 dB SPL. Key takeaways Sensitivity relates output voltage to acoustic pressure, commonly at one kilohertz and one pascal. Compare microphone noise and preamp noise together. Dynamic range requires both a noise reference and a stated overload criterion. Further reading Microphone technology — DPA U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann Phantom power — Schoeps Three-to-one rule — DPA SM58 manufacturer specifications — Shure

sum: P48 uses matched feed resistors to apply common-mode DC to the signal conductors.
x: Phantom power (P48) Condenser microphones are powered through the same balanced cable that carries their signal. IEC 61938 defines P48: +48 V fed through two matched 6.81 kΩ resistors, one to each signal conductor (pins 2 and 3 of an XLR), with the shield (XLR pin 1) as the return. Closely matched feed resistors help preserve the impedance balance of the line. The standard allows up to 10 mA per microphone. Lower-voltage P12 and P24 variants also exist. The equal DC on the signal wires is common-mode, so it does not appear across an ideal floating dynamic coil. A preamp still needs suitable DC blocking, voltage ratings and transient protection: common-mode rejection alone does not make an arbitrary balanced input safe at 48 V. The mic draws its current through both feed resistors at once. Two equal resistors side by side (in parallel) act like one of half the value, and the voltage lost across them follows Ohm's law: The same calculation for three currents, in Python: The feed resistors limit what the mic can draw: a low-current mic like the U 87 Ai (0.8 mA per Neumann) sees nearly the full 48 V; a hungry one sees much less. A supply that can't deliver enough current makes some mics distort earlier. Phantom power and your synth As module 5 said, keep phantom off on any channel your synth or other line-level gear is plugged into. Phantom is for microphones and DI boxes designed for it. Key takeaways P48 uses matched feed resistors to apply common-mode DC to the signal conductors. Feed resistance makes the microphone’s connector voltage depend on current draw. Use compatible inputs and correct cables; turn phantom off for equipment that does not require it. Further reading Phantom supply and XLR contact diagrams — Schoeps CMC/MK manual, October 2015 Microphone technology — DPA U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann Phantom power — Schoeps Three-to-one rule — DPA Ribbon microphone phantom precautions — Royer

sum: Distance changes direct-to-room balance and leakage.
x: Placement basics Distance controls the direct-to-room balance. Close placement gives more direct sound, less room, more proximity effect and more level variation as the performer moves. Further away captures more of the room. Angle controls tone. On a guitar cab, the centre of the cone is brighter; towards the edge it's darker. Small moves matter. Use acoustic nulls. Aim the null of a directional mic at what you don't want (a monitor, a neighbouring drum). Mind sound reflections. A music stand or desk near the mic adds a reflection a few milliseconds late, which comb-filters the sound. The 3:1 rule When several mics are open at once, a source reaches its own mic and, more weakly and later, its neighbours. When the signals are mixed, the delayed copy comb-filters the direct one. The 3:1 rule says the distance between mics should be at least three times the distance from each mic to its source. Why it works: by the inverse square law, sound pressure falls in proportion to distance, so the leakage level drops by: When a copy that much quieter is mixed with the direct sound, it can only nudge the sum up or down a little: That is about +2.5 dB at a peak and −3.5 dB at a notch, rather than the +6 dB peaks and perfect notches of equal-amplitude delayed copies. It's a rule of thumb that assumes omni-like pickup and similar levels. Directional mics aimed well, or very different source levels, change the numbers. Key takeaways Distance changes direct-to-room balance and leakage. The three-to-one spacing rule is a practical starting estimate. Leakage ripple also depends on source geometry, microphone response and channel gains. Further reading Microphone technology — DPA U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann Phantom power — Schoeps Three-to-one rule — DPA

t: From voice-coil current to cone force
sum: A magnetic field and current-carrying voice coil create force.
x: A loudspeaker driver is the motor and diaphragm that actually move air. A loudspeaker system is one or more drivers plus an enclosure (the enclosure units) and usually a crossover (the crossover units). This lesson is about the driver: how it works, and how to read the numbers on its datasheet. The motor structure Nearly all speakers you will meet are moving-coil (electrodynamic) drivers, a design dating from the 1920s. The parts: Magnet and pole pieces (the motor). A permanent magnet (ferrite or neodymium) and steel parts concentrate a strong magnetic field in a narrow ring-shaped magnetic gap. Voice coil. A coil of fine wire wound on a light former, sitting in the gap. It's attached to the cone. Cone (diaphragm). Pushes the air. Paper, polypropylene, aluminium and composites are common. It must be light and stiff. Driver suspension. The driver surround at the outer edge and the driver spider behind the cone keep the coil centred in the gap and provide a restoring force that pulls the cone back to rest. Basket (frame) holds it all together. How current becomes sound A current in a wire in a magnetic field feels a force (the Lorentz force; it's the motor principle). The voice coil is wound so the wire crosses the field at right angles everywhere in the gap, so the force on it is simply: Datasheets quote the product Bl ("BL") because B and l only ever appear together. For example, with 1 A in the coil of a 7 T·m driver: Audio current alternates, so the force alternates and the cone moves back and forth, pushing air (the acoustics units). The cone, coil and the air it carries have mass; the suspension acts as a spring. Mass on a spring has a resonance. That's the driver's free-air resonance, Fs, one of the Thiele–Small parameters in the enclosure units. Below Fs the output falls away. A driver is also an electromagnetic generator: a moving coil in a field produces a voltage (back-EMF), exactly as a dynamic mic does. That back-EMF is why the impedance changes so much near resonance. Key takeaways A magnetic field and current-carrying voice coil create force. Moving mass and suspension compliance establish the driver’s free-air resonance. The moving coil also generates back electromotive force. Further reading Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue Baffled piston radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State Rated impedance — Dynaudio

sum: An impedance label does not mean constant impedance at every frequency.
x: Impedance: nominal vs reality An "8 Ω" speaker isn't 8 Ω. Its impedance depends on frequency: At DC it's just the voice-coil resistance, Re (often around 5–7 Ω for an "8 Ω" driver). Near Fs it rises to a sharp peak, because the back-EMF of the resonating cone opposes the current. Above resonance it falls to a minimum, then rises again at high frequencies because the voice coil is an inductor. A simple model adds up three parts: the coil's resistance, the coil’s inductive impedance (which grows with frequency in this simple model), and a "motional" part that peaks at resonance. Impedance is a complex number, because it also shifts the timing (phase) of the current; the size of the total is what an impedance plot shows. At resonance the frequency-offset variable is zero, so the motional part reaches its full peak. Purdue’s sample uses 6.6 Ω coil resistance, 0.48 mH inductance, 65 Hz free-air resonance, electrical Q of 0.436 and mechanical Q of 2.25: The model is easier to sweep across frequency in Python (2j is Python's way of writing 2 × j): From 6.7 Ω to over 40 Ω across the band. (Real voice-coil inductance is lossy, so the high-frequency rise is usually gentler than this simple model shows.) Nominal impedance is a single rounded label for the region above resonance. The loudspeaker standard IEC 60268-5 says the minimum impedance in the rated frequency range should not fall below 80% of the rated (nominal) impedance: Not every manufacturer follows that rule, and real multi-way speakers with crossovers can dip well below their label, which is why amplifier makers care about the minimum, not the nominal (the power-amplifier units). Key takeaways An impedance label does not mean constant impedance at every frequency. Resonance, coil resistance and inductance shape the curve. Amplifier compatibility requires the load’s magnitude and phase, not just its nominal label. Further reading Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue Baffled piston radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State Rated impedance — Dynaudio

sum: Check whether sensitivity is referred to one watt or 2.83 volts.
x: Sensitivity and the maths of power vs SPL Loudspeaker sensitivity is the SPL on-axis at 1 m for a reference input. Two conventions: dB SPL @ 1 W / 1 m. One watt into the nominal impedance. dB SPL @ 2.83 V / 1 m. 2.83 V is 1 W into 8 Ω. Why 2.83 V? The power a voltage delivers into a resistance is: Using nominal impedance to define the test voltage, the two references agree for 8 Ω. For 4 Ω, 2.83 V corresponds to 2 W nominal, and doubling the power adds about 3 dB (the following power-and-distance unit derives the relationship), making its voltage-sensitivity figure about 3 dB higher. Actual electrical power varies with complex impedance and frequency; compare the measurement conditions. Key takeaways Check whether sensitivity is referred to one watt or 2.83 volts. The voltage reference corresponds to about one watt nominal into eight ohms, and two into four ohms. In the linear regime, doubling power gives approximately three decibels. Further reading Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue Baffled piston radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State Rated impedance — Dynaudio

t: Work backwards from required listener level
sum: Use a consistent reference, spectrum and far-field measurement direction.
x: Power, distance and efficiency To predict how loud a speaker will be, start from its sensitivity, add the decibels gained by using more than 1 W, and subtract the decibels lost by listening further away than 1 m. For a fixed signal spectrum in the linear range, use this approximate on-axis free-field, far-field estimate (neglecting air absorption and power compression): Each doubling of power adds only 3 dB; ten times the power adds 10 dB. For an 87 dB/1 W/1 m speaker at 1 m (so the distance term is zero): The same in Python: Worked example (from Purdue's notes): you want 90 dB SPL at 4 m outdoors from an 86 dB/1 W/1 m speaker. Work backwards: first the distance loss, then the level needed at 1 m, then the power. Every 3 dB of sensitivity halves the amplifier power needed for the same level. Sensitivity is closely related to loudspeaker efficiency, the fraction of electrical power that comes out as sound: The rest becomes heat, mostly in the voice coil. Key takeaways Use a consistent reference, spectrum and far-field measurement direction. Distance loss can demand much more power than a sensitivity comparison alone suggests. Leave appropriate peak margin while respecting driver excursion and thermal limits. Further reading Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue Baffled piston radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State Rated impedance — Dynaudio

sum: A larger piston becomes directional at a lower frequency.
x: Frequency response A frequency response plot shows on-axis SPL (at a fixed input) against frequency. Look for: The usable range, often given as ±3 dB limits, with the low-frequency limit set mainly by Fs and the enclosure. Smoothness: narrow peaks often come from cone breakup or cabinet resonance. Off-axis curves: how the response changes at 30° or 60°. Because of diffraction, a driver radiates widely when its wavelength is large compared with the cone, and shows beaming (narrower dispersion) when the wavelength becomes comparable with the cone. Where does beaming start? Treat the cone as a flat, rigid disc (a "piston"). Directivity becomes significant when the cone's circumference is about one wavelength, which corresponds to a dimensionless wavenumber-radius product of one: Worked for a woofer with a 13 cm effective diameter and a 25 mm tweeter dome: (343 is the speed of sound in m/s; 0.065 m and 0.0125 m are the two radii.) The piston model stops being reliable once the cone breaks up (below), so check measured off-axis curves. That beaming is one reason multi-way speakers hand high frequencies to smaller drivers. Power handling Two separate limits: Driver power handling (thermal). The voice coil heats up. Too much average power for too long burns the coil or its adhesive. Ratings are usually based on long tests with band-limited noise, and the method (and so the number) differs between standards and manufacturers, so read what method a figure refers to. Mechanical (excursion). At low frequencies the cone must move a long way. Xmax describes an excursion limit under a specified geometric or distortion criterion; definitions vary. Motor, suspension and other nonlinearities can limit it. Beyond the useful linear range, distortion increases; far beyond it, the coil can strike the motor structure or the suspension can tear. A driver can be over-excursed at low frequencies with modest power, especially below a ported box's tuning frequency (the enclosure units). Power ratings are not targets A "100 W" speaker doesn't need 100 W, and isn't safe with any 100 W signal. A clipped signal from a small amplifier can damage a tweeter (the power-amplifier units), while the required clean peak capacity and suitable protection must be chosen from actual limits. Driver types Driver Typical job Notes --------- Subwoofer Below ~80–120 Hz Long excursion, big cone Woofer Bass (and mids in 2-way) 13–38 cm common Midrange ~300 Hz–3 kHz Covers the vocal region Tweeter Above ~2–3 kHz Light dome, 19–28 mm Compression driver + horn Mid/high in PA Very high sensitivity In a compression driver, a diaphragm pressurises a small chamber; sound passes through phase-plug channels into a narrow horn throat, and the loudspeaker horn flares out to the room. The horn improves the match between the diaphragm and the air, so far more of the electrical power becomes sound. It also controls dispersion, which PA designers use to aim sound at the audience and away from walls. Horn-loaded systems can reach sensitivities around 110 dB SPL at 2.83 V/1 m; a typical hi-fi speaker is in the mid-80s to around 90 dB. Cone breakup At low frequencies a cone moves as a rigid rigid piston. As frequency rises, the cone stops moving as one piece: bending waves travel across it, and different parts move with different phase. This is cone breakup. It causes: Peaks and dips in the response, often a sharp peak near the top of the driver's range. Changes in dispersion, and sometimes audible coloration and distortion. Stiff, light cones (aluminium, ceramic) push breakup higher but often produce a stronger, sharper peak when it happens. Softer, well-damped cones break up earlier but more gently. Either way, the crossover (the crossover units) is chosen so the driver isn't asked to play much in its breakup region. Key takeaways A larger piston becomes directional at a lower frequency. Cone breakup invalidates a rigid-piston prediction; use measured off-axis data. Thermal power and cone excursion are separate limits. Driver types trade displacement, bandwidth, dispersion and efficiency. Further reading Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue Baffled piston radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State Rated impedance — Dynaudio

sum: A bare driver has dipole cancellation at low frequencies.
x: Hold a bare woofer in the air, play a bass line through it, and you get a thin, tinny sound. Mount the same driver in a box and the bass appears. This lesson explains why, and how the box's design shapes the bass response. It's a deep subject with decades of published theory. The goal here is the concepts and enough of the maths to read a driver datasheet and understand what box-modelling software tells you. The acoustic short circuit When the cone moves forward, it compresses the air in front and rarefies the air behind. The two sides radiate equal and opposite pressure waves: the bare driver is a dipole (Dan Russell's radiation demo in Further reading shows the field). At high frequencies the wavelength is short compared with the path from front to back around the cone's edge, so the two waves don't meet in time to cancel much. At low frequencies the wavelength is long, the rear wave easily diffracts round the edge, and it cancels the front wave. Air just sloshes from front to back. This is the acoustic short circuit, and it's why a bare driver has almost no bass. The cure is to separate front from back: A baffle (a flat board) lengthens the path, so cancellation starts at a lower frequency. An enclosure (a box) traps the rear wave completely, or redirects it so it helps. Baffle step Even in a box, the front baffle has a finite size. At high frequencies, where the baffle is large compared with the wavelength, the driver radiates into the half-space in front: half a sphere of directions. At low frequencies, where the wavelength is much larger than the baffle, sound diffracts around the cabinet and radiates into the full space: the whole sphere. Engineers often call these "2π" and "4π" radiation, after the solid angle each one covers: For the same cone motion, radiating into half-space gives twice the sound pressure of full space: the baffle acts like a mirror, adding a coherent "image" source. Doubling pressure is a 6 dB rise, because sound pressure level is 20 times the base-10 logarithm of a pressure ratio: So as frequency falls and the radiation spreads into full space, a speaker's on-axis response steps down by up to 6 dB going from high to low frequencies. The transition happens where the wavelength is comparable with the baffle width: a few hundred hertz for a typical bookshelf speaker. This is the ideal figure: the real step is smoother, and nearby walls and floors change it. Designers compensate with baffle step compensation: usually a gentle shelf in the crossover that reduces everything above the step. In a real room, placing the speaker near a wall gives back some of the lost bass, which is why compensation is a judgement call. Key takeaways A bare driver has dipole cancellation at low frequencies. A baffle separates the front and rear paths. For fixed cone motion, a finite baffle can produce an approximately six-decibel transition; boundary placement changes it. Further reading Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue Helmholtz resonance — Joe Wolfe, UNSW Monopole and dipole radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State

sum: Ideal sealed and ported boxes have different low-frequency asymptotes.
x: Four ways to box a driver Sealed (closed box, acoustic suspension) The rear wave is trapped. The air inside acts as an extra spring on the cone, which raises the system resonance above the driver's free-air Fs. Below the system resonance, Fc, the response falls at 12 dB per octave (a second-order high-pass). Transient behaviour depends on system Q. Sealed boxes are relatively simple to model, and the trapped air adds restoring force at very low frequencies. Less efficient in the bass than a ported box of the same size. Ported (bass reflex, vented) A port tube (tube) connects the box air to the outside. The air in the port is a mass, the air in the box is a spring: a Helmholtz resonator, tuned to a frequency Fb. Around Fb, the port radiates strongly and in phase with the cone's front, adding bass output while the cone barely moves. More bass extension or output from the same box volume than sealed. Below Fb the response falls at 24 dB per octave (fourth-order), steeper than sealed. Below Fb the box provides progressively less air-spring loading on the cone: the suspension and motor still act, but the port increasingly relieves box pressure, so excursion can become excessive. Many ported systems use a subsonic high-pass filter to protect the driver. Ports can make noise ("chuffing") if the air speed is too high, usually because the port is too narrow for the output. Open baffle No box at all: the driver sits on a flat panel, open at the back. It stays a dipole, radiating front and back with opposite polarity and a null at the sides. No box resonances; many listeners like the spacious presentation. Front-to-back cancellation adds about 6 dB per octave of low-frequency roll-off relative to monopole radiation. The driver’s own response also matters: below its mechanical resonance, an unequalised ideal voltage-driven dipole can approach 18 dB per octave in total. Large baffles, displacement capability and EQ may be needed. The rear wave reflects off the wall behind, so placement matters even more. Transmission line The rear wave travels down a long, folded, damped duct before leaving through a vent. The line length is typically chosen as a quarter wavelength at the lowest frequency the design targets (often near the driver's resonance), so the line's output reinforces the front at low frequencies while the damping absorbs higher frequencies. To see how long that is, divide the wavelength by four: That is a starting estimate: stuffing slows the sound in the line and tapered lines behave differently, so real lines are tuned in modelling software. They're more complex to design and build than sealed or ported boxes. Type Roll-off Trade-off --------- Sealed 12 dB/oct Compact, controlled Ported 24 dB/oct More output; excursion below Fb Open baffle Additional ~6 dB/oct dipole loss Driver roll-off also contributes Transmission line varies Complex build Key takeaways Ideal sealed and ported boxes have different low-frequency asymptotes. A port reduces cone movement near tuning but unloads it progressively below tuning. Open baffles and damped transmission lines use rear radiation differently. Further reading Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue Helmholtz resonance — Joe Wolfe, UNSW Monopole and dipole radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State

sum: Moving mass and suspension compliance determine free-air resonance.
x: Thiele–Small parameters A driver datasheet lists Thiele–Small (T/S) parameters, measured at low levels where the driver behaves linearly. The three you use most: Fs: the free-air resonance (moving mass on the suspension spring). Qts: the total Q at Fs: how damped the resonance is. Purdue's notes put most drivers between about 0.2 and 0.5. Vas: the volume of air with the same springiness (compliance) as the driver's suspension. Fs: a mass on a spring The cone, voice coil and the air they carry are a mass; the surround and spider are a spring. Like any mass on a spring, they have one natural frequency: Qts: how damped the resonance is Two things damp the resonance. The suspension loses some energy as heat (the mechanical Q, Qms). The voice coil moving in the magnet generates a voltage that the amplifier's low output impedance loads through a low-resistance circuit, which brakes the cone (the electrical Q, Qes). They combine like resistors in parallel: With mechanical Q four and electrical Q 0.4, total Q is close to the electrical Q. That is typical: the motor does most of the damping. Q has no unit because it is a ratio (stored energy to energy lost per cycle, roughly). Vas: the suspension expressed as air Vas turns the suspension's springiness into "the volume of air that would be just as springy" under the same cone: So for a fixed cone area, larger Vas means a softer suspension. Because Vas grows with cone area squared, it is not a stiffness comparison across arbitrary driver sizes: a big woofer can have a large Vas with a stiff suspension. Key takeaways Moving mass and suspension compliance determine free-air resonance. Mechanical and electrical damping combine into total Q. Equivalent compliance volume depends on both cone area and suspension compliance. Further reading Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue Helmholtz resonance — Joe Wolfe, UNSW Monopole and dipole radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State

t: Estimate a sealed box’s resonance and Q
sum: Efficiency bandwidth product is only an initial enclosure-selection guide.
x: Driver choice and sealed-box alignment Efficiency bandwidth product A rough rule of thumb uses the efficiency bandwidth product (EBP): An EBP of 60 Hz sits near the sealed end. It's a starting point, not a design method: always model the full parameter set. Manufacturing tolerances are loose: Purdue's notes give typical factory tolerances of about ±15% for Fs and ±20–30% for Vas. Measure your own driver if accuracy matters. The sealed-box equations Put a driver in a sealed box. The air trapped in the box is a second spring pushing on the cone, alongside the suspension. A smaller box is a stiffer spring. The compliance ratio says how stiff the box air is compared with the suspension, and both the resonance and its Q rise with the square root of the total stiffness. These are the closed-box results (Small, 1972), used when you choose a box size: Consider a driver with 30 Hz free-air resonance, total Q of 0.35 and 60 L equivalent compliance volume, in a 20 L box: These equations ignore box losses and stuffing, and they assume the box is small compared with the wavelength (true in the bass). The sealed-box total Q sets the shape of the bass roll-off. The box-and-driver is a second-order high-pass filter, and for that filter the level exactly at Fc depends only on Qtc: Qtc Behaviour ------ 0.5 Critically damped, −6 dB at Fc 0.707 Butterworth: maximally flat, −3 dB at Fc ~1.0–1.1 Peak before roll-off, "boomier" The same sum for three box sizes, as code: The 20 L box gives a near-Butterworth alignment (a Qtc of about 0.7) with a 60 Hz resonance. A smaller box gives higher, peakier bass; a bigger one lower, more damped bass. Deep bass extension, reference efficiency and enclosure volume are coupled. “Pick two” summarizes the trade-off; real driver excursion, losses and power limits still constrain the design. (Filling the box with absorbent material can make it behave as if it were somewhat larger: Purdue's notes say up to about 15% in apparent volume, while also adding some effective moving mass.) Key takeaways Efficiency bandwidth product is only an initial enclosure-selection guide. A smaller sealed box raises both resonance and Q in the ideal model. Real losses, stuffing and measured driver parameters affect the finished alignment. Further reading Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue Helmholtz resonance — Joe Wolfe, UNSW Monopole and dipole radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State

sum: Box air acts as a spring and the port air as a moving mass.
x: Port tuning: Helmholtz intuition A port behaves like the neck of a bottle. The air plug in the port is a mass bouncing on the springy air in the box. That is a Helmholtz resonator, and its resonance (the box tuning) is: The air just beyond each open end of the port moves with the plug too, so the port acts longer than it is. That extra is the end correction: Because the area is under the square root and divided by the length, a wider port must also be longer to keep the same Fb. Worked example: a 30 L box with a 5 cm diameter port, 15 cm long, with a total radius-based end-correction factor of 1.46: The same sum as code: End correction moves the tuning by several hertz here. Real designs are modelled in software and checked by measurement (the impedance curve of a ported box has two peaks with a dip at Fb, which is an easy way to find the true tuning). Key takeaways Box air acts as a spring and the port air as a moving mass. Tuning depends on port area, box volume and effective length. End corrections are geometry-dependent; model and measure the actual cabinet. Further reading Loudspeaker parameters — D. G.
