Meyer, Purdue Helmholtz resonance — Joe Wolfe, UNSW Monopole and dipole radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State

sum: An alignment specifies a target bass response from driver and enclosure parameters.
x: Alignments, conceptually The driver plus box is a high-pass filter: second-order for sealed, fourth-order for ported. An box alignment is a choice of driver parameters, box volume and tuning that gives a particular filter shape, borrowed from electrical filter theory. Thiele (1961) and Small (1972–73) published tables of these; Butterworth (maximally flat), Chebyshev (some ripple, more extension) and quasi-Butterworth variants are common names. Modern practice is to simulate the response, excursion and port air speed in software, then measure. Cabinet resonance and bracing The box's walls are panels that vibrate. If they resonate at frequencies the driver produces, the cabinet itself radiates sound, smearing and colouring the output. Remedies: Stiff, dense material: MDF and birch plywood are common choices. Bracing: internal struts or shelves that stiffen large panels, pushing their resonances higher and reducing their amplitude. Damping: lining or filling the box with absorbent material reduces internal standing waves between parallel walls and can damp panels. Seal everything: air leaks in a sealed box change its behaviour and can whistle. If you build one Woodworking has its own hazards: control MDF dust with effective extraction and add suitable, correctly fitted respiratory protection where needed; a mask is not a substitute for extraction. Use power-tool guards and eye protection. Keep any amplifier electronics separate from the box-building and follow the power-amplifier units’ safety notes. Key takeaways An alignment specifies a target bass response from driver and enclosure parameters. Cabinet panels can radiate unwanted resonances. Use bracing, appropriate damping and controlled workshop methods; keep amplifier electronics separate. Further reading Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue Helmholtz resonance — Joe Wolfe, UNSW Monopole and dipole radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State MDF dust controls — HSE

sum: Passive networks filter speaker-level signals; active filters precede driver amplifiers.
x: A single driver faces substantial trade-offs in covering 20 Hz to 20 kHz at useful levels and with controlled dispersion. A woofer big enough for bass beams and breaks up in the treble (the loudspeaker-driver units); a tweeter small enough to disperse treble widely would be destroyed by bass excursion. So most speakers use two or more drivers, and a crossover sends each one only the frequencies it handles well. You already met filters in module 2 (synth filters). Crossovers use the same maths, with one extra demand: the outputs must add back together in the air into a smooth response. Passive, active and DSP Passive crossovers are inductors, capacitors and resistors between one power amplifier and the drivers. They carry full speaker-level current, so parts are large and the filter's behaviour depends on the drivers' impedance. Most hi-fi speakers use them. Active crossovers filter at line level (op-amp circuits), before a separate amplifier for each driver. Filter behaviour is predictable, each amp sees one driver, and a clipping woofer amp can't send its distortion to the tweeter. DSP crossovers are active crossovers done in software, as in most powered studio monitor loudspeakers and PA processors. They add delay, EQ and limiters per driver at little extra cost, and you can even use linear-phase (FIR) filters, with delay and latency determined by the design. Order and slope For the conventional analogue all-pole low-pass and corresponding high-pass families below, order sets the asymptotic stopband slope and total phase change. Arbitrary filters with additional zeros, delays or FIR structures need separate analysis: Order Slope Total phase rotation --------- 1st 6 dB/octave 90° 2nd 12 dB/octave 180° 3rd 18 dB/octave 270° 4th 24 dB/octave 360° The table follows one simple rule. Each order (each "pole" of the filter) adds 6 dB/octave of slope and 90° of phase rotation, so you can work out any row from the order alone: Why 6 dB? Far above its corner, a first-order low-pass halves its output voltage every time the frequency doubles, and halving the voltage is −6 dB (20 dB per decade, a tenfold change in frequency, says the same thing). A fourth-order filter approaches another 24 dB of attenuation per octave far into its stopband. Its absolute level one octave from the corner depends on the filter family. These are asymptotes: near the corner the real curve is gentler. Steeper slopes protect drivers better (a tweeter crossed with 24 dB/octave sees much less energy at its resonance than with 6 dB/octave) and reduce the overlap where both drivers play. The cost: more phase rotation, more complex circuits and, passively, more expensive parts. Key takeaways Passive networks filter speaker-level signals; active filters precede driver amplifiers. For the conventional families discussed, each order contributes roughly six decibels per octave asymptotically. Electrical filter response and actual driver response jointly determine the acoustic result. Further reading Crossovers — Linkwitz Lab Linkwitz–Riley crossover primer — Rane Filter circuits — Linkwitz Lab

sum: At a crossover both driver outputs contribute.
x: Making the outputs add up The low-pass and high-pass outputs have to sum to a flat response. Magnitude alone isn't enough: at the crossover frequency both drivers contribute, so their relative phase shift decides whether they add or cancel. Crossover levels are quoted in decibels, which come from the voltage (amplitude) ratio. These are the numbers you'll meet below: First order A first-order low-pass and high-pass at the same frequency are each −3 dB at the crossover, and they sum exactly to the input. Filter designers write a filter as a fraction of the input using the variable s: At the crossover, each output's size is about 0.707 of the input (−3 dB), but the two are 90° apart in phase, which is why two 0.707s can still add up to exactly 1. The catch: the two outputs are 90° apart at the crossover, the 6 dB/octave slopes give the drivers a lot of out-of-band signal to handle, and the perfect sum only holds on one axis with ideal drivers. Butterworth A Butterworth filter is maximally flat in its passband and −3 dB at its corner. For a second-order Butterworth crossover, the low-pass and high-pass outputs are 180° apart at the crossover, so: Wired with the same polarity, they cancel: a deep notch at the crossover. With one driver's polarity reversed, they sum with a +3 dB peak at the crossover (two −3 dB outputs adding in phase). This simple addition only works because, with one polarity flipped, the two outputs are exactly in step at the crossover. Key takeaways At a crossover both driver outputs contribute. A matched first-order pair sums exactly in the ideal aligned model. A second-order Butterworth pair needs a polarity choice and does not give a flat magnitude sum. Further reading Crossovers — Linkwitz Lab Linkwitz–Riley crossover primer — Rane Filter circuits — Linkwitz Lab

sum: Cascaded Butterworth sections give each Linkwitz–Riley output half amplitude at crossover.
x: Linkwitz–Riley summation Linkwitz–Riley Siegfried Linkwitz and Russ Riley's fix (1976) was to cascade two Butterworth filters of the same order on each side. Each output is then −6 dB at the crossover, half the voltage, and the two halves add to exactly 0 dB: LR2 (two first-order sections): 12 dB/octave, outputs 180° apart, so one driver is reversed in polarity. Sums flat. LR4 (two second-order Butterworths): 24 dB/octave. At the crossover the low-pass is at −180° and the high-pass at +180°, which is a 360° difference: the outputs are in phase at every frequency. They sum to a flat magnitude, and the total behaves as an all-pass filter: flat amplitude with smoothly changing phase. Why does LR4 sum flat at every frequency, not just at the crossover? Write each output as a transfer function, using the same normalised frequency variable as the first-order example, and compare the sizes of the top and bottom of the sum: The denominator polynomial has odd powers that the numerator lacks, so they are not identical polynomials and the sum’s phase still rotates. That's exactly what an all-pass filter is. Crossover Each output at crossover Sum at crossover --------- BW2, one driver inverted −3 dB +3 dB peak LR2, one driver inverted −6 dB 0 dB LR4 −6 dB 0 dB, in phase LR4 is a very common choice in active and DSP crossovers, including PA processors. Key takeaways Cascaded Butterworth sections give each Linkwitz–Riley output half amplitude at crossover. The correctly aligned LR4 sum has flat magnitude and varying phase. Ideal mathematical summation assumes suitable driver responses and equal path lengths. Further reading Crossovers — Linkwitz Lab Linkwitz–Riley crossover primer — Rane Filter circuits — Linkwitz Lab

t: Align drivers and protect the tweeter
sum: Distance offsets create frequency-dependent phase error.
x: Driver offset and phase The preceding units’ ideal sums assume both drivers' sound starts from the same point. Real drivers don't: a woofer's acoustic centre usually sits further back than a tweeter's on a flat baffle. A path difference becomes a time delay, and a time delay becomes a frequency-dependent phase shift that ruins the neat summation: The script below adds that delay to the woofer of an ideal 2 kHz LR4 crossover and prints the on-axis sum in dB. With the woofer 2 cm behind (58 µs), the dip is under 1 dB. At 8 cm (233 µs, almost half a period at 2 kHz) there's a deep on-axis hole at the crossover. Remedies: DSP delay on the earlier driver (easy in active/DSP systems). Stepped or sloped baffles to line up acoustic centres physically. Choosing the crossover frequency and filter shapes so the acoustic responses (filter × driver) hit the target, and checking the result by measurement. Even when on-axis is perfect, moving up or down changes the path lengths to the two drivers. That's lobing: the summed response changes with vertical angle. LR crossovers with aligned drivers keep the main radiation lobe pointing straight ahead, which is one reason they're popular. Filter choice also protects a driver The first-order and LR4 filters from the preceding units pass very different amounts of signal below the crossover. At half the crossover frequency, the ideal first-order high-pass is about seven decibels down, while LR4 is about twenty-five decibels down. The question works through the transfer-function calculation. This reduces the tweeter’s out-of-band input for the same source level. It does not establish a safe crossover or power rating: use the exact driver’s recommended filter type, minimum crossover and excursion and thermal limits, then measure the acoustic result. Key takeaways Distance offsets create frequency-dependent phase error. Delay or physical alignment can improve the target-axis sum. Steeper high-pass attenuation reduces out-of-band tweeter input but does not establish safe operating power. Further reading Crossovers — Linkwitz Lab Linkwitz–Riley crossover primer — Rane Filter circuits — Linkwitz Lab

t: Calculate passive values and recognise their limits
sum: The textbook values assume fixed resistive driver loads.
x: A first-order passive crossover, worked The textbook calculation treats each driver as a plain resistor equal to its nominal impedance. An inductor's opposition to current (its reactance) rises with frequency, and a capacitor's falls. A first-order filter's corner is where the part's reactance equals the driver's resistance, which gives: Worked example: crossover at 3 kHz, 8 Ω drivers. So a 0.42 mH inductor in series with the woofer and a 6.6 µF capacitor in series with the tweeter (nearest standard values in practice). Why it won't behave as calculated The formula assumes a constant 8 Ω resistor. The loudspeaker-driver units showed real drivers aren't: The impedance varies with frequency. If the tweeter can be approximated by a constant 6 Ω resistance throughout this region, the high-pass corner moves to about 4 kHz (calculated below). A single impedance measurement at 3 kHz cannot establish the real corner. The woofer's impedance rises through the crossover region because of coil inductance, so its inductor filters less than intended. The tweeter's resonance. Near its Fs (for a dome tweeter typically somewhere around 0.5–1.5 kHz; check the datasheet) the tweeter's impedance peaks and it can't handle much power. A gentle 6 dB/octave filter still feeds it a lot of energy there. The drivers' own roll-offs add to the filter's. What matters is the acoustic slope: electrical filter × driver response. A woofer that's already falling off adds its own slope and phase. Sensitivity differences. Tweeters are often more sensitive than woofers, so a resistor network (L-pad) is needed to bring the tweeter down. Here is the tweeter corner with the 6.63 µF capacitor from the 8 Ω design, when the tweeter is really closer to 6 Ω: This still assumes a constant resistance; a real driver's impedance is complex and changes with frequency, so only the full measured curve gives the true corner. Designers fix some of this with impedance-compensation networks (a Zobel network across the woofer flattens the rising impedance) and by designing from measured driver impedance and frequency response in simulation software, then measuring the built speaker. For a DIY project, using published, tested crossover designs, or a DSP crossover where everything can be measured and adjusted, is far more forgiving than calculating a passive one from nominal values. Passive crossover safety Passive crossovers sit after the power amplifier, at speaker-level voltages and currents. High-power speaker outputs can themselves present hazardous voltages and currents. Never open the amplifier; switch it off before changing speaker wiring and follow its discharge and connection instructions (the power-amplifier units). Key takeaways The textbook values assume fixed resistive driver loads. Real impedance, driver roll-off, sensitivity and acoustic-centre offsets change the result. Design from measurements and follow the amplifier’s safe connection guidance. Further reading Crossovers — Linkwitz Lab Linkwitz–Riley crossover primer — Rane Filter circuits — Linkwitz Lab

t: Voltage gain, current and load power
sum: An amplifier supplies output voltage and the current required by its load within its limits.
x: Your synth's line output can swing a volt or two into 10 kΩ or more (module 5). A loudspeaker needs tens of volts into a few ohms: amps of current and tens or hundreds of watts. A power amplifier bridges that gap. Safety: conceptual lesson only Power amplifiers contain mains wiring and, inside, high-voltage supply rails and large capacitors that can stay charged after unplugging. Valve (tube) amps run at hundreds of volts. Speaker terminals on a large amp can carry voltages that are dangerous to touch at full power. This lesson is about understanding and choosing amplifiers. Don't open, modify or build mains-powered amplifiers. Connect speakers with the amp switched off and the volume down, and leave repairs to qualified technicians. What a power amp does A power amp is a voltage amplifier with a very low output impedance that can deliver large currents: It multiplies the input voltage by a fixed voltage gain. It holds that output voltage steady whatever the speaker's impedance does (within its limits), by supplying whatever current the load demands. Power is a result. The amp sets the voltage; the speaker's impedance decides the current and so the power. For a resistive load, Ohm's law and the power formula tell you the current and power from the voltage: That's exact only for a resistor. A real speaker has complex impedance, so sinusoidal real power also depends on the voltage–current phase difference. Voltage gain vs power Amplifier gain is usually quoted in dB (voltage), or as input sensitivity: the input voltage that produces full rated output. To use a dB gain, turn it back into a multiplier: So an amp with 26 dB gain fed a +4 dBu signal gives about 24.5 V RMS: 75 W into 8 Ω. Gain and maximum output power are separate specifications. Higher power may require greater voltage swing, greater current capacity or both; different models may also have different gain. (26 dB is used here as an illustration: real amps range widely, and many quote sensitivity instead. Read the manual.) Key takeaways An amplifier supplies output voltage and the current required by its load within its limits. Gain and maximum clean output are different specifications. The simple voltage-squared power calculation assumes a resistive load. Further reading Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue

sum: Amplifier class describes output-device conduction.
x: Amplifier classes The amplifier class describes how the output transistors (or valves) conduct over the signal cycle. It's a broad guide to efficiency and linearity. Class A The output devices conduct over the whole cycle, biased at a high standing current even with no signal. Very linear: no switching between devices, so no crossover distortion. Inefficient: the ideal sine-wave amplifier power-stage efficiency depends on topology: 25% for a simple resistively loaded stage, and up to 50% in suitable inductively coupled or push-pull output-stage designs. Real designs at typical listening levels are far lower. Most of the power drawn from the mains becomes heat, all the time. Class B and AB A push-pull pair: one device handles the positive half of the waveform, the other the negative. Class B (each device conducts exactly half the cycle) has a maximum theoretical efficiency of 78.5% (see below), but suffers crossover distortion where one device hands over to the other. Class AB adds a small bias current so both devices conduct briefly around the handover, removing most crossover distortion. Efficiency sits just below class B's. It's been the standard design for linear hi-fi and PA amplifiers for decades. The class B figure comes from an ideal amplifier power stage swinging a full sine wave right up to its supply rails: Class D The output devices act as switches, fully on or fully off, switching far above the audio band (often at hundreds of kilohertz). The audio is encoded in the switching pattern (for example pulse-width modulation), and in conventional designs an output low-pass filter attenuates the switching carrier. Some low-power filterless designs instead use suitable modulation and the speaker’s electrical/mechanical filtering; external filtering and wiring constraints depend on the device. A perfect switch dissipates no power (either no voltage across it or no current through it), so class D is very efficient: over 80% is common and over 90% achievable with MOSFETs. Small, light, cool-running: the norm in powered speakers, PA amplifiers, car audio and portable devices. Trade-offs: the output filter's response can depend on the speaker load, the switching causes EMI that must be contained, and design quality varies. Good modern class D measures extremely well. Efficiency decides how much heat the amp makes. Everything drawn from the supply that doesn't reach the speaker becomes heat: The same sum for four efficiencies, as Python: Illustrative amplifier power-stage heat to deliver 100 W at the assumed efficiencies. The class D value is a practical example; these figures exclude power-supply and other losses. Heat means heatsinks, fans, weight and power bills, which is why class D dominates where size and power matter. Key takeaways Amplifier class describes output-device conduction. Ideal class-A limits depend on topology; class B reaches about 78.5 percent at full sine output. Class D reduces amplifier power-stage losses through switching; total system losses still matter. Further reading Class-D output filtering — Texas Instruments, SLAA701B Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue Class-A power-stage efficiency — ADI university course Class-A resistive and transformer coupling limits — ACS College of Engineering, pages 65–67

sum: Compare power ratings at stated load, bandwidth, distortion and test conditions.
x: Power ratings Continuous (average) power, often called "RMS power", is the meaningful figure: the average power the amp can deliver continuously into a stated load, over a stated bandwidth, at a stated distortion. "RMS power" is a loose name: it's the average power calculated from RMS voltage and current, not the RMS of the power waveform. Peak power. For a sine wave, peak instantaneous power is twice the average. A "200 W peak" amp may be a 100 W continuous amp. PMPO ("peak music power output") has no reliable conversion to continuous power without a defined test method and conditions. Treat an unexplained PMPO number as unsuitable for comparison. Where the factor of two for peak power comes from: a sine wave's instantaneous power swings between zero and a peak, and spends as long below the halfway line as above it. Example: a sine of 40 V peak into 8 Ω peaks at 1600 ÷ 8 = 200 W but averages 100 W, so "200 W peak" and "100 W continuous" can describe the same amp. This only holds for a steady sine into a resistive load. A complete specification looks like: "100 W continuous into 8 Ω, 20 Hz–20 kHz, at 0.1% THD". Missing conditions usually hide something, such as a rating taken at 10% distortion or at 1 kHz only. Key takeaways Compare power ratings at stated load, bandwidth, distortion and test conditions. Sine-wave instantaneous peak power is twice average into a resistor. A marketing peak label alone does not establish continuous output. Further reading Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue

sum: Lower impedance demands greater current at the same output voltage.
x: Load impedance and matching amp to speaker A solid-state amp is a voltage source, so lower impedance draws more current and more power: That's why amps quote power at several loads ("100 W into 8 Ω, 160 W into 4 Ω"). In practice power doesn't quite double into half the impedance, because the supply sags and the output devices have current limits. Matching rules of thumb: Check the minimum load. If an amp is rated for 4 Ω minimum, don't connect two 4 Ω speakers in parallel (2 Ω). Speakers' actual impedance dips below nominal (the loudspeaker-driver units), so nominal 4 Ω loads are already demanding. Parallel speakers halve impedance (two 8 Ω = 4 Ω); series doubles it. Power headroom. An amplifier’s clean capacity should accommodate the required peaks, but a higher rating can also destroy a driver. Avoid clipping and set gain and appropriate protection from the actual signal, driver limits and manufacturer’s guidance. Many manufacturers give a recommended amplifier power range; follow it. Bridged (BTL) mode drives one speaker from two channels in opposite polarity, doubling the voltage swing: in theory four times the power into the same load, but each channel sees half the load impedance, so bridging into 4 Ω asks each side to drive 2 Ω. Check the manual's bridged minimum load. The parallel and bridged rules come from these relations (for resistive loads): Valve amps are different Valve amps with output transformers do need the right load: running them with no speaker connected can damage the output transformer or valves. Always connect a speaker (or a proper load) before powering a valve guitar or hi-fi amp. Key takeaways Lower impedance demands greater current at the same output voltage. Two identical parallel speaker loads have half the impedance of one. Bridging doubles voltage swing ideally while each channel effectively drives half the load impedance. Further reading Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue Example valve-amplifier load warning — Fender 65 Twin Reverb manual, rear panel

t: Understand damping factor and cable loss
sum: Damping factor compares load impedance with amplifier source impedance.
x: Damping factor Damping factor is the ratio of the speaker's nominal impedance to the amp's output impedance: So an amp with 0.01 Ω output impedance into 8 Ω has a damping factor of 800. A low output impedance lets the amp's back-EMF path control the driver's motion near resonance (the loudspeaker-driver units: the driver is also a generator). Above a modest value (tens) the audible benefit is small, because the speaker cable and the driver's own voice-coil resistance dominate. The cable's resistance adds to the amp's output impedance: Ten metres of 1.5 mm² cable (20 m of conductor) turns DF 800 into about 34. Use thicker cable for long runs, and treat very high DF claims as marketing. Key takeaways Damping factor compares load impedance with amplifier source impedance. Both cable conductors contribute resistance. Long thin cable can dominate the amplifier’s own output resistance. Further reading Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue

sum: At equal peak voltage, a square wave dissipates twice a sine’s average power into a resistor.
x: Clipping and why it can kill tweeters An amplifier can't output more voltage than its supply rails allow. Ask for more and the output shows clipping: the waveform's peaks are flattened. Why that's dangerous for tweeters: More average power. A sine wave clipped hard towards a square wave carries up to twice the average power of the clean sine with the same peak voltage (worked out below). High-frequency harmonics. A square wave contains odd harmonics at 1/3, 1/5, 1/7... of the fundamental's amplitude (about −9.5, −14 and −16.9 dB, worked out below). Clip a loud bass or middle-frequency note and those harmonics land in the tweeter's band. The crossover passes them straight to a driver that normally receives only a small fraction of the total power, and its small voice coil overheats. A square wave sits at its peak voltage all the time, while a sine only touches its peak briefly: For example, a 1.5 kHz note clipped to a square wave puts its 3rd harmonic at 4.5 kHz, its 5th at 7.5 kHz and its 7th at 10.5 kHz: all above a typical 2–3 kHz crossover. So sustained clipping can overheat a tweeter; a larger clean amplifier can also damage it if level, spectrum or duration exceeds its limits. Watch for clip indicators, leave headroom, and use limiters in PA systems. Key takeaways At equal peak voltage, a square wave dissipates twice a sine’s average power into a resistor. Symmetric clipping adds odd harmonics. Driver damage depends on signal spectrum, duration, filtering and actual limits. Further reading Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue

t: Match a headphone output to its load
sum: Required voltage and current depend on headphone impedance and sensitivity.
x: headphone drive stages Headphones need far less power than speakers, but they vary enormously in impedance (roughly 16 Ω to several hundred ohms) and sensitivity: Low-impedance headphones need current; high-impedance ones need voltage. 10 mW is 0.57 V RMS into 32 Ω but 1.73 V RMS into 300 Ω (worked out below). A headphone drive stage should have a low output impedance, much lower than the headphones'. A high output impedance forms a divider with the headphones' frequency-varying impedance and changes their frequency response. Laptop and phone outputs can struggle with some headphones; compare required voltage/current and sensitivity with the source’s rated capabilities. A suitable dedicated amp or interface can help. The voltage needed for a given power comes from rearranging the power formula: The output impedance and the headphones form a voltage divider: In this illustrative example, 32 Ω headphones whose impedance rises to 64 Ω at their resonance, driven from a 10 Ω output, get about 1.1 dB more level at the resonance than elsewhere. From a 1 Ω output the difference would be well under 0.3 dB. (This treats the impedances as plain resistances; real ones also have phase.) Ears first Headphone amps can produce hearing-damaging levels very easily (the hearing units). Turn the level down before plugging in or switching sources. Verification gap The earlier historical headphone-output standard recommendation and broad output-impedance range are omitted because their original standard text and representative measurement basis were not reliably verified. Use the actual product specifications. Key takeaways Required voltage and current depend on headphone impedance and sensitivity. Source and load impedances form a voltage divider. A varying load can colour frequency response when source impedance is significant. Further reading Headphone amplifier load and output impedance — Texas Instruments, TIDUAW1 Amplifier principles and ratings — Crown Loudspeaker loads and damping — Purdue

t: Follow a console channel and its sends
sum: Each system stage has noise and overload limits.
x: Up to now we've looked at parts: microphones, drivers, boxes, crossovers, amplifiers. A sound system connects them so that a source (your synth, a voice, a drum) reaches listeners at the right level, with the right balance and without noise, distortion or feedback. Whether it's a desk in your bedroom or a festival PA, the principles are the same. The chain Every stage has a noise floor below the signal and a clipping point above it. The job is to keep the signal comfortably between them at every stage. The mixing console A console (mixer, desk) combines many inputs into a few outputs, with independent control over each. Digital consoles and DAWs (Ableton's mixer included) copy the analogue layout, so learning one teaches you the others. The channel strip Signal flows from top to bottom of a typical channel: Input and preamp gain (trim). Brings mic or line level up to the console's internal operating level. This is the most important control on the desk for noise and headroom. Phantom power and a pad switch usually live here. High-pass filter. Removes rumble and handling noise below the useful range of the source. Engage it only where removing those frequencies suits the source and the intended sound. Insert point. A send and return that loops the channel's signal out to an external processor (a compressor, say) and back, in series. EQ. Shelving and parametric bands for tone and to make room for other sources. Dynamics processing (on many digital desks): gate and compressor. Aux sends. Copies of the channel at an adjustable level to separate aux buses, used for monitor mixes and effects. Pre-fader sends ignore the channel fader: right for monitor mixes, so the front-of-house engineer's fader moves don't change what the performer hears. Post-fader sends follow the fader: right for effects like reverb, so the wet signal fades with the dry. Panning places the signal in the stereo bus. Fader sets the channel's level in the mix. Signal routing assigns the channel to the main mix and/or subgroups. Buses and subgroups A mix bus is any point where signals are summed. The main L/R mix is a bus; so are aux sends and subgroups. Subgroups sum related channels (all drums, all backing vocals) to one fader, so you can ride a whole section, or compress it together, with one control. VCA or DCA groups (on many consoles) are a variation: one fader remotely controls the faders of its member channels without summing audio. Key takeaways Each system stage has noise and overload limits. Pre-fader sends can keep monitor mixes independent of channel fader moves. Subgroups sum audio; VCA and DCA groups control channel gains. Further reading Setting system level controls — Rane Acoustic feedback — Rane Keyboard stage connections — Radial

t: Plan gain across the whole system
sum: Set input gain with representative source peaks and leave headroom.
x: Gain staging across the system Module 1 covered gain staging inside a digital synth. In a system, the same idea applies at every box: Set the preamp gain first, with the performer at their loudest. Aim for healthy levels with headroom to spare: on a digital desk, nominal levels around −18 to −20 dBFS leave room for peaks (module 1); on an analogue desk, follow its meter calibration and overload-warning guidance, allowing headroom for unexpectedly loud peaks rather than deliberately clipping. The system's signal-to-noise ratio is largely fixed here: noise added at the mic preamp is amplified by everything after it. Keep faders near their unity (0 dB) mark for normal levels, so there's travel in both directions. Set outboard gear to unity where possible, passing the full signal without clipping. Set amplifier input sensitivity as part of the system’s gain and protection plan. One approach maps the maximum clean system output to the required amplifier output; that output must also respect speaker and audience limits. Amp input controls are attenuators that set sensitivity, not "power" controls. To work out how much preamp gain a mic needs, start from its sensitivity (its output voltage at a reference sound pressure of 1 pascal, which is 94 dB SPL), add however far the real source is above that reference, convert to dBu, and subtract from the level the console wants. Example: an SM58 (sensitivity −56.0 dBV/Pa) picks up a singer at 104 dB SPL, which is 10 dB above 1 Pa: About 48 dB of preamp gain. A condenser about 25 dB more sensitive (the microphone units) would need only around 23 dB. Two common mistakes - Low preamp gain "made up" with faders pushed to the top: the console's noise is amplified as much as the signal. - Preamp gain set with the singer warming up quietly: the first chorus clips the input, and no fader can undo clipping that happened upstream. Key takeaways Set input gain with representative source peaks and leave headroom. A fader cannot repair clipping at an earlier stage. Coordinate amplifier sensitivity, limiter settings and speaker and audience limits. Further reading Setting system level controls — Rane Acoustic feedback — Rane Keyboard stage connections — Radial

t: Connect an instrument through a DI
sum: A suitable DI provides balanced mic-level output for a microphone input.
x: DI boxes A DI (direct input) box connects an instrument or line-level source to a console's balanced mic input: It accepts an instrument or line-level signal and provides a low-impedance, balanced, mic-level output. Passive guitar pickups often need a high input impedance; synth and keyboard line outputs are usually low impedance and may already be balanced. Choose the DI or direct line connection to suit both devices. That lets the signal travel down a long multicore to the desk with good noise rejection (module 5's balanced lines). Most DIs have a ground lift switch to break a ground loop between stage gear and the desk's ground (module 3), and many have a pad. Two types: Passive DIs use a transformer. No power needed; robust; the transformer gives galvanic isolation. Active DIs use a buffer amplifier, powered by phantom power or a battery. They load high-impedance sources (like passive guitar pickups) very lightly. For your synth on a stage, a DI is usually the right way into a PA, with the synth's output at line level into the DI's input (use its pad if needed). Key takeaways A suitable DI provides balanced mic-level output for a microphone input. Select its input impedance and pad for the actual source. A compatible balanced line connection may remove the need for a DI. Further reading Setting system level controls — Rane Acoustic feedback — Rane Keyboard stage connections — Radial

sum: main speakers, subs, fills, delays and monitors serve different coverage needs.
x: PA design A typical live PA has several systems, each with its own job: main speakers (front of house). Left/right or mono speakers covering the audience, flown or on stands. Larger venues use line arrays: vertical columns of boxes that control vertical coverage and lose level more slowly with distance over part of their range. Subwoofers. Below about 80–120 Hz. Usually on the ground. Several subs can be arranged (end-fire, cardioid, arc) to steer low frequencies away from the stage. Stage monitor loudspeakers. What performers hear: floor wedges aimed up at each performer, side fills, or in-ear monitors (IEMs). Fed from pre-fader aux mixes. Front fills. Small speakers along the stage lip for the front rows, who are below the main speakers' coverage. Delay speakers. Further back in large venues, where the main speakers have lost too much level. Delay speakers, worked At a chosen listener position, compare the path from the main speaker with the path from the delay speaker. Sound from the main speakers has further to travel, so without an electronic delay the delay speaker's copy would arrive first and pull the sound image towards it. The delay to dial in is the extra travel time, plus any difference in processing latency between the two paths: If the main speakers path is 40 m longer, about 117 ms aligns arrivals in this simplified example. It only holds exactly at the chosen position; listeners nearer or further away see a different path difference. A designer may choose an additional offset to favour the main speakers as the first arrival, but no universal 10–20 ms setting guarantees fusion or stage localisation. Those depend on signal, relative level, geometry and reflections; measure and listen throughout the overlap region. Exact universal precedence offsets are absent because reliable evidence for such a guarantee was not established. Studio vs live Studio Live --------- Goal Accurate monitoring Coverage, level Listeners One position Whole audience Speakers Near-field monitors PA, subs, wedges Feedback Rarely an issue Constant concern Room Treated (the room-acoustics units) Take what you get In a studio the monitors must tell the truth, so you can make decisions that translate to other systems. In a live system the goal is even, intelligible, sufficiently loud coverage for everyone, with controlled exposure and compliance with applicable venue limits. WHO’s 100 dB LAeq,15 min ceiling is one part of its safe-listening venue standard, not a guarantee that a whole event is safe at that level (the hearing units). Key takeaways main speakers, subs, fills, delays and monitors serve different coverage needs. Align a fill using acoustic-path and processing-latency differences. Verify timing, localisation, overlap and exposure throughout the audience area. Further reading Setting system level controls — Rane Acoustic feedback — Rane Keyboard stage connections — Radial

sum: Feedback depends on reinforcing loop phase as well as gain.
x: Acoustic feedback Acoustic feedback happens when the sound from a speaker re-enters a microphone, is amplified, comes out of the speaker louder, and so on. Sustained feedback can develop where the loop gain magnitude reaches or exceeds one (0 dB) and the phase reinforces the circulating signal. The precise stability and onset depend on the whole loop. Feedback develops at a frequency where both loop magnitude and reinforcing phase conditions are met: often a peak in a speaker's or mic's response, or a room resonance. How to get more gain before feedback: Get the mic close to the source. Halving the source-to-mic distance gives about 6 dB more source level at the mic (inverse square law), so 6 dB less gain is needed. Keep speakers away from mics, and put main speakers in front of the mic line. Use directional mics and their nulls. Put wedges in the null of the mic's pattern (the microphone units). Fewer open mics. In the usual approximate potential-acoustic-gain model, doubling similarly coupled open microphones (NOM) costs about 3 dB; actual loop paths can differ. Mute what isn't in use. EQ. "Ringing out" the system: raise gain until it starts to ring, identify the frequency, and cut it with a narrow EQ band. Automatic notch-based feedback suppressors do this live, but they typically add only a few dB of margin. In-ear monitors remove the wedge-to-mic path when wedges are actually removed from that mix. The 6 dB figure in step 1 comes from the inverse square law. For a small source in open air, the level change when you move from one distance to another is: Very close to a directional mic, the proximity effect also boosts the bass, and a voice is not a point source, so treat 6 dB per halving as a guide. The 3 dB figure in step 4 comes from the potential acoustic gain (PAG) model, where open mics that each pick up the PA about equally add up as uncorrelated signals: It's 10 rather than 20 because the PAG approximation treats the similarly coupled microphone signals as uncorrelated on average. They are summed as voltages physically; their mean-square contributions add under that modelling assumption. Real stages differ: mics nearer a wedge contribute more than the model assumes. Key takeaways Feedback depends on reinforcing loop phase as well as gain. Improve source pickup while reducing loudspeaker pickup at microphones. The open-microphone count rule is an approximation; geometry and individual coupling matter. sum: Ideal rectangular rigid rooms have axial, tangential and oblique mode families.
x: Put the best monitors in the world in an untreated, square, bare-walled room and you'll hear the room as much as the speakers. Below a few hundred hertz, a small room's response at your listening position can swing by 20 dB or more between neighbouring frequencies. Mix there and you'll correct for problems that only exist in your room, and the mix will sound wrong everywhere else. This lesson is about understanding what a room does, then placing monitors and treatment so you can trust what you hear. Room modes Between two parallel walls, a sound wave reflects back and forth. At frequencies where a whole number of half-wavelengths fits exactly between the walls, the reflections reinforce each other into a standing wave: a room mode (or resonance). To find those frequencies, start from the fact that one half-wavelength, two half-wavelengths, three and so on must fit the gap exactly, then use the link between wavelength, frequency and the speed of sound: For two walls 5.0 m apart, the first mode is 343 ÷ (2 × 5.0) = 34.3 Hz, the second 68.6 Hz and the third 102.9 Hz. The formula assumes rigid, parallel, flat walls; real walls flex and absorb a little, which damps and slightly shifts the modes. Those are axial modes: between one pair of surfaces. They usually carry the most energy and have the greatest influence on the low-frequency response. Tangential modes involve two pairs of surfaces and oblique modes all three. For a rectangular (shoebox) room, one formula covers all three kinds (exclude the all-zero mode-number combination, which is static pressure rather than an oscillating acoustic mode): When only one mode number is non-zero this reduces to the axial formula above. A tangential example, the (1, 1, 0) mode of a room with a 5.0 × 3.6 m floor plan: Like the axial formula, it assumes rigid walls and a perfectly rectangular room. Key takeaways Ideal rectangular rigid rooms have axial, tangential and oblique mode families. Mode frequency depends on room dimensions and mode numbers. Wall flexibility and absorption modify the ideal result. Further reading Monitor placement — Genelec Driving room modes — Dan Russell, Penn State Measured reverberation and Sabine’s equation — Dan Russell REW help — Room EQ Wizard

t: Relate modal frequencies to room position
sum: Coincident modal frequencies do not alone predict the response at a particular seat.
x: Room dimensions and listener position Worked example A small studio of 5.0 × 3.6 × 2.4 m. Using the axial formula for each dimension: The same calculation in Python, for the first three modes of each dimension: Notice that 3.6 ÷ 2.4 = 1.5, so the width's third mode and the height's second land on the same frequency, 142.9 Hz. Coincident modal frequencies can produce strong response peaks, depending on how the sources excite them, the listener position and damping. Rooms whose dimensions are simple multiples of each other (a cube has particularly extensive degeneracy) bunch their modes; unrelated dimensions spread them out more evenly. What a mode does at your seat depends on where you sit: For ideal rigid rectangular boundaries, each axial mode has pressure antinodes at its corresponding pair of walls. A general mode may still have nodes along other coordinates on a wall; corners are pressure antinodes of all these ideal modes. The first axial mode has a pressure null halfway between its walls. At the length midpoint, that ideal mode contributes no pressure; moving away can increase its contribution. The total response also contains direct sound and other modes, so it is not necessarily silent or boomy. So bass response varies dramatically with position. This is why many guides suggest avoiding the exact centre of the room for the listening position (Genelec suggests sitting in the front part of the room for music work, and at least 1 m from walls). Key takeaways Coincident modal frequencies do not alone predict the response at a particular seat. Source excitation, damping and listener position all matter. Avoid treating a node of one mode as silence in the total sound field. Further reading Monitor placement — Genelec Driving room modes — Dan Russell, Penn State Measured reverberation and Sabine’s equation — Dan Russell REW help — Room EQ Wizard

sum: Reverberation time describes a sixty-decibel decay.
x: Reverberation and RT60 After a sound stops, its reflections take time to die away. RT60 is the time for the sound level to fall by 60 dB. Wallace Sabine's empirical equation (from experiments at Harvard around 1900) relates it to the room's volume and absorption. Use it to estimate how live a room will sound, and how much treatment you'd need to change that: The total equivalent absorption area is each surface area multiplied by its frequency-dependent absorption coefficient, summed. Worked through for the 5.0 × 3.6 × 2.4 m studio with bare surfaces averaging an absorption coefficient of 0.10, then with 10 m² of surface swapped for panels with an absorption coefficient of 0.90: The same calculation as a Python script: Ten square metres of effective absorption halves the reverberation time. Two caveats: Absorption coefficients depend on frequency. A treatment that works at 2 kHz may do almost nothing at 100 Hz, so RT60 is quoted per octave band, and a room can be dead in the treble while still booming in the bass. Sabine assumes a fairly live room with diffuse sound. At higher broadly distributed absorption a diffuse-field Eyring model can improve the estimate; neither model is guaranteed for a strongly non-diffuse room, and in small rooms below the Schroeder frequency "reverberation time" is a rough description at best. Control rooms are typically much drier than living rooms; recommended targets vary by standard and room size, so treat any single number as a guide. Key takeaways Reverberation time describes a sixty-decibel decay. Sabine’s model uses room volume and equivalent absorption area. The diffuse-field and absorption assumptions limit its use, especially in small rooms. Further reading Monitor placement — Genelec Driving room modes — Dan Russell, Penn State Measured reverberation and Sabine’s equation — Dan Russell REW help — Room EQ Wizard

sum: The Schroeder estimate marks a gradual transition rather than a sharp frequency boundary.
x: The modal-to-statistical transition The Schroeder frequency At low frequencies, modes are few and far apart, and the room behaves like a set of resonances. Higher up, modes overlap so densely that the room behaves statistically, as reverberation. The crossover between the two is often estimated by the Schroeder frequency. It needs the room's volume and its reverberation time (RT60, the time sound takes to die away by 60 dB, defined in the reverberation unit): For the treated 43.2 m³ studio from the reverberation example, with an RT60 of 0.44 s: The transition is gradual, not a sharp line. Below it, think room modes (fix with placement and bass traps). Above it, think sound reflections and reverberation (fix with absorption and diffusion). Absorption vs diffusion Absorbers convert sound energy to heat. Porous absorbers (mineral wool, fibreglass, thick acoustic foam) work by friction as air moves through them. They're most effective where the air particle velocity is high, which is about a quarter wavelength from a hard wall. A thin porous panel against a rigid wall generally absorbs low frequencies poorly (the quarter-wavelength rule below puts numbers on this). An air gap can improve lower-frequency absorption. Diffusers scatter sound in many directions without removing much energy. They break up strong specular reflections and flutter echo (rapid repeats between parallel hard walls) while keeping the room feeling live. They need to be large compared with the wavelengths they diffuse, so they work mainly in the mids and highs, and need some distance from the listener. A good control room usually combines both: absorption where early reflections hit, diffusion or a mix at the back, and bass trapping in the corners. The quarter-wavelength rule For a normally incident plane wave reflected from an ideal rigid wall, the normal particle velocity is zero at the wall and has an antinode a quarter wavelength away. Oblique incidence and a real absorber modify that field. To see which frequency a porous layer of a given depth (or air gap) reaches, set its distance from the wall equal to a quarter wavelength: So a 10 cm panel corresponds to about 850 Hz, and reaching 60 Hz would need about 343 ÷ 240 ≈ 1.4 m. This is a rough guide, not a cut-off or a prediction of measured absorption: material flow resistance, thickness, mounting and the angle the sound arrives at all matter, and a panel still absorbs something below this frequency. Bass traps Bass wavelengths are metres long, so thin porous panels mounted against a rigid wall generally provide little bass absorption. Thin resonant panel systems are a different mechanism. Bass traps are: Thick porous absorbers (often 10–20 cm or more), commonly placed across corners. Straddling a corner leaves a large air gap behind the panel, which extends its effect to lower frequencies. Pressure-based (membrane or Helmholtz) absorbers tuned to specific low frequencies, which work by resonance and are most effective at pressure maxima such as walls and corners. For the ideal rigid rectangular model, corners are pressure antinodes for all the mode families. In real rooms, boundaries and coupling differ. Treating them reduces the peaks and decay times of modes across the low end. Key takeaways The Schroeder estimate marks a gradual transition rather than a sharp frequency boundary. Porous absorption depends on thickness, mounting and material properties. Quarter-wavelength spacing is an intuition aid, not a hard absorption cutoff. Diffusers scatter energy; resonant bass absorbers use a different mechanism from porous panels. Further reading Monitor placement — Genelec Driving room modes — Dan Russell, Penn State Measured reverberation and Sabine’s equation — Dan Russell REW help — Room EQ Wizard Modal-overlap transition — Treble Acoustic treatment and boundary interference — Genelec

t: Place monitors and locate early reflections
sum: Use symmetrical stereo geometry and the speaker’s specified acoustic axis.
x: Early reflections and the mirror trick The first reflections from the side walls, ceiling, desk and floor reach your ears a few milliseconds after the direct sound. Because they're close in time and level, they comb-filter with it (the acoustics units) and blur the stereo image. The mirror trick finds where to put absorption: Sit in the listening position. Have someone slide a mirror flat along the side wall. Wherever you can see a monitor's tweeter in the mirror, that's a first-reflection point. Mark it. Repeat for the other wall and the ceiling (with a mirror on a pole, or a laser and some geometry). Absorbers at those points reduce the strongest early reflections. The desk and the console surface are reflection points too, which is one reason monitors often go on stands behind the desk rather than on it. Near-field monitor placement Near-field monitors are designed for short listening distances, often around 1–2 m, which increases direct sound relative to reflected sound. Actual room contribution still depends on the room, directivity and frequency. Placement guidelines, largely as Genelec's placement guide sets them out: Equilateral triangle. The two monitors and your head form an equilateral triangle: 60° between the monitors, each aimed at the listening position. Ear height. The acoustic axis (usually between tweeter and woofer, or as the manual says) at ear level, typically 1.2–1.4 m from the floor for a seated listener. Tilt rather than lifting too high; Genelec suggests no more than about 15° of tilt. Symmetry. Place the setup symmetrically left–right in the room so both speakers see the same boundaries. Avoid half room height and the room's exact middle, where modes and floor-ceiling reflections line up badly. Key takeaways Use symmetrical stereo geometry and the speaker’s specified acoustic axis. The mirror method locates specular first-reflection paths. Listening distance alone does not remove the room’s contribution. Further reading Monitor placement — Genelec Driving room modes — Dan Russell, Penn State Measured reverberation and Sabine’s equation — Dan Russell REW help — Room EQ Wizard

t: Diagnose boundary notches and measure the room
sum: A reflected path can cancel direct sound at particular frequencies.
x: Boundary interference Wall distance and SBIR Sound radiates backwards from a monitor at low frequencies (it's omnidirectional there; the driver and enclosure units). That rear sound reflects off the front wall and returns. Where the reflected travel delays it by half a period, which happens when the distance to the wall is a quarter wavelength, it cancels the direct sound: speaker boundary interference response (SBIR). The reflected sound travels to the wall and back, an extra distance of twice the speaker-to-wall gap. The first cancellation happens when that extra distance is half a wavelength, so the wave comes back upside down: This assumes the wall is rigid and the reflection travels straight back (the wall-perpendicular path). Real notches are shallower than a perfect cancellation and are partly filled by other paths. The same calculation for other distances: Speaker to front wall First notch ------ 0.3 m ≈ 286 Hz 0.5 m ≈ 172 Hz 0.6 m ≈ 143 Hz 1.0 m ≈ 86 Hz Genelec’s guide describes deep cancellation notches and advises against fixing them by boosting EQ. EQ scales both direct and reflected sound: a perfect null remains zero, while a finite dip can be raised locally only at the cost of headroom and potentially worse sound elsewhere. EQ does not remove the reflection or its geometry. Their remedies: Flush-mount the monitors in a hard wall, which removes the rear reflection. Place them close to the wall: typically with the front of the monitor less than 60 cm from the wall, so the notch moves up to frequencies where the speaker radiates less backwards, while leaving at least 5 cm clearance for a rear port. The same cancellation happens with side walls, the floor and the desk at different distances, so varying those distances spreads the notches rather than stacking them. Measuring a room with REW You can't fix what you can't measure, and ears are bad at judging bass in a room. Room EQ Wizard (REW) is free room-acoustics software for Windows, macOS and Linux. With a calibrated measurement microphone (for example a USB mic supplied with a calibration file), it: Plays a swept sine through your monitors and records it at the listening position. Computes the impulse response, and from it the frequency response, waterfall plot (how each frequency decays over time, which shows ringing modes clearly) and decay / RT60 figures. Helps identify room modes and can calculate EQ filters. A practical workflow: Measure each monitor separately at the listening position, at a moderate level (the hearing units: protect your ears). Look for big peaks and deep notches below about 300 Hz, and long decay in the waterfall. Move the listening position and speakers first; that changes modes and SBIR far more than EQ can. Add bass traps and first-reflection absorption, and re-measure. Only then use EQ, mainly to cut peaks. Don't try to fill deep notches with boost: they're cancellations, and boosting them wastes amplifier power and driver excursion. Key takeaways A reflected path can cancel direct sound at particular frequencies. Placement and effective treatment change the reflection geometry; EQ does not remove it. Measure, change one cause and remeasure before applying final peak cuts. Further reading Monitor placement — Genelec Driving room modes — Dan Russell, Penn State Measured reverberation and Sabine’s equation — Dan Russell REW help — Room EQ Wizard Acoustic treatment and boundary interference — Genelec

sum: Distinguish observable features from numerical service targets, and let each request path have its own priorities.
x: System design is the work of deciding which components a system has, how they talk to each other, and where data lives, so that the system does what users need at the scale, speed, cost and reliability the business needs. Writing code answers "how does this function work?". System design answers bigger questions. Where does a request go first? What happens when a machine dies? How much will this cost when traffic grows ten times? There is rarely one right answer. A good design is one whose trade-offs are explicit and suited to the requirements. That is why every good design starts with requirements, not boxes and arrows. Why requirements come first Imagine two teams asked to "build a URL shortener". Team A builds for 100 internal users. A single Postgres instance and a small web app is perfect. Team B builds for a public service with 100 million new links and 10 billion redirects a month. They need capacity and failure-mode analysis; caching, partitioning or multiple regions may be justified by measured bottlenecks and availability/latency requirements, not traffic totals alone. Same feature list, completely different systems. The difference is entirely in the non-functional requirements and constraints. If you skip them, you'll either over-engineer (wasting months) or under-engineer (falling over on launch day). Functional requirements Functional requirements describe what the system does: the behaviours a user or another system can observe. For a URL shortener: Given a long URL, return a short code. Visiting /abc123 redirects to the original URL. Optionally: custom aliases, expiry dates, click analytics. A useful habit is to write them as user stories or API calls: Then prioritise. In an interview or a real project kickoff, agree which features are in scope for the first version. "Analytics is nice-to-have; the redirect path is the core." Even a tiny API line hides decisions that features drive. A 301 Moved Permanently is heuristically cacheable, so some repeat visits may bypass your servers. A 302 Found or 307 is not heuristically cacheable, but explicit freshness headers can still permit caching. Set an appropriate cache policy (for example Cache-Control: no-store) when each redirect must reach the service for analytics. If click analytics is in scope, that requirement quietly decides the status code and multiplies your redirect traffic. Non-functional requirements Non-functional requirements (NFRs) describe how well the system does those things. They are the "-ilities", and they drive most architectural decisions. NFR Example target ------ Latency Redirect p99 < 50 ms Throughput 100k redirects/s peak Availability 99.99% for redirects Durability Never lose a created link Consistency New link usable within 1 s Scalability 10x growth in 3 years Security Block malware URLs Cost < £5k/month infra Notice the targets are numbers. "Fast" and "highly available" are useless because nobody can test them. "p99 under 50 ms" can be measured, alerted on and designed for. Make NFRs differ per path Different parts of a system deserve different targets. The redirect path in a URL shortener must be very fast and very available. The analytics dashboard can be slower and eventually consistent. Saying this out loud is a sign of seniority. Key takeaways Clarify what the system does before choosing technologies. Replace “fast” and “available” with measurable targets, separately for each path. Redirect analytics depend on cache policy as well as the HTTP status code. Further reading The System Design Primer AWS Well-Architected Framework HTTP semantics (RFC 9110)

t: Scope a design around constraints and load
sum: Use team, budget, regulation and traffic assumptions to rule out unsuitable architectures before drawing them.
x: Requirements set the goal; constraints set the limits within which the team must achieve it. Traffic assumptions connect that goal to a practical capacity plan. Constraints Constraints are things you can't change (or can't change cheaply): Team: three engineers who know Python and Postgres. Time: must launch in four months. Budget: fixed cloud spend. Regulation: payment card data falls under PCI DSS; GDPR requires safeguards for transfers of personal data outside the European Economic Area; an organisation may additionally require EU-only residency. Such a residency rule is a specified policy, not a universal GDPR requirement. Existing systems: must integrate with the company's identity provider. Constraints often rule out "textbook" answers. A team of three probably shouldn't run its own Kafka cluster and Cassandra ring; managed services are usually the right call. Assumptions and scale Next, establish the numbers the design must support: Daily active users (DAU), and how many actions each performs. Read-to-write ratio (a URL shortener might be 100:1). Data size per item and retention period. Peak versus average load (a 2–10x factor is an illustrative planning range, not a universal statistic; measure the traffic shape). You'll turn these into queries per second, storage and bandwidth in the estimation lesson. The point here is that you can't choose components without them. A Postgres primary's sustainable write rate depends on hardware, schema, batching, durability and contention. Benchmark the intended workload before treating a guessed rate as a capacity limit. The read-to-write ratio is especially telling. At 100:1, almost all the work is reads, so caching and read replicas pay off and the write path can stay simple. A write-heavy system (logging, metrics, chat) pushes you towards partitioning writes and append-friendly storage instead. Common mistakes Jumping to technology "We'll use Kafka, Redis and Kubernetes" before knowing the requirements is the most common failure. Technology choices should be conclusions, justified by requirements. Designing for imaginary scale. Planning for a billion users when you have a thousand adds cost and complexity with no benefit. Design for roughly 10x your expected load and know how you'd get to 100x. Ignoring failure. Every component fails eventually. For each box, ask "what happens when this is down or slow?" Unquantified NFRs. "It should be fast" can't drive a decision. Ignoring operations. Who deploys it, monitors it and gets paged at 3 a.m.? A design the team can't operate is a bad design. One-size consistency. Not everything needs strong consistency; not everything can tolerate eventual consistency. Decide per data type. Key takeaways Constraints narrow the feasible design: team, time, budget, regulation and existing systems matter. Estimate behaviour, read/write balance, retained data and peak load before choosing components. Avoid imaginary scale, unmeasurable goals and systems the team cannot operate. Further reading The System Design Primer AWS Well-Architected Framework European Commission: international transfers

t: Walk a request and challenge its failure modes
sum: Build a simple architecture, trace the critical path, and use cache failure and ticket inventory to expose hidden risks.
x: Once the requirements and scale are clear, start with the simplest architecture that meets them. Trace a real request, then ask what happens when a component disappears or becomes slow. A repeatable approach Most practitioners use some variant of this sequence: Step 4: the high-level design Start with the simplest thing that meets the requirements, then evolve it. Walk a request through it: "A redirect hits the load balancer, goes to any app server, checks the cache, falls back to a read replica on a miss." Walking the flow catches missing pieces quickly. Step 5: deep dives This is where the real design happens. Pick the parts that are hard for this system: How are short codes generated without collisions across many servers? What happens if the cache cluster fails? What's the hot-key story when one link goes viral? The cache question decides whether the cache is an optimisation or critical infrastructure. The database normally sees only cache misses. At a 95% hit rate and 100,000 reads/s, it sees 5,000 reads/s. If the cache disappears and every miss falls through, it sees all 100,000 reads/s: twenty times its normal load. Can the database survive that jump? If not, plan admission control, bounded retries and a degraded response instead of allowing every request to fall through. This example assumes one database read per miss; retries can make an outage worse. Later modules cover the tools for these questions: caching, databases and partitioning, consistency and consensus, messaging, API design and reliability patterns. A worked mini-example "Design a ticket-booking system for concerts" Functional: browse events, hold seats for 10 minutes, pay, receive ticket. Non-functional: never sell the same seat twice (strong consistency on seat state); browse page p99 < 200 ms; survive a 50x traffic spike when a big tour goes on sale. Constraints: payments via an existing provider; 6 engineers; launch in 6 months. Implications: seat inventory needs transactions or conditional writes; the browse path can be heavily cached; the on-sale spike suggests a virtual waiting room or queue in front of checkout. Already the architecture is taking shape, and we haven't drawn a single box. Key takeaways Follow requirements, estimates, APIs, request flow, deep dives and explicit trade-offs. A cache at 95% hit rate hides a potential 20-fold database load increase when it fails. Ticket inventory needs concurrency-safe decisions; browse caching and a waiting room serve different goals. Further reading The System Design Primer AWS Well-Architected Framework

t: Separate latency from bandwidth and capacity
sum: Identify whether parallel capacity, fewer round trips or a faster link addresses the actual performance limit.
x: Two numbers describe the performance of almost any system: Latency: how long a single operation takes, from request to response. Measured in time (ms, µs). Throughput: how many operations complete per unit time. Measured in requests/s, MB/s, messages/s. They are related but not the same thing, and confusing them leads to bad designs. The pipe analogy Real-world analogy: parallel water pipes A longer pipe delays the first arriving drop. More pipes can carry more water at once. How it maps: Latency is the travel time; throughput is the amount delivered each second. Parallel servers can add capacity without shortening one request's journey. Where it stops: Networks carry packets and servers queue work; their delays depend on contention and processing as well as distance. You can increase throughput by adding servers without shortening a lightly loaded request. For an illustrative London–New York link, assume a 70 ms round trip. A signal still has to travel there and back; adding servers cannot remove that propagation delay. Moving work closer or avoiding an exchange can help. Bandwidth-bound or latency-bound? The pipe analogy gives a simple model for how long one transfer takes: a fixed cost for each round trip, plus the time to push the bytes through the pipe. For example, under this simplified model a 1 MB file over a 100 Mbps link with one 70 ms round trip takes about 150 ms. Sending the bytes and waiting for the reply both matter; server processing, protocol overhead and congestion would add more delay. Big transfers are bandwidth-bound: the size term dominates, so a fatter pipe or compression helps. Many small, sequential exchanges are latency-bound: the round-trip term dominates, so bandwidth upgrades do nothing and you must cut round trips (batching, parallelism, moving closer). Throughput limits show up as latency Users rarely see "throughput exceeded". They see slow pages and timeouts, because the queue in front of the bottleneck is growing. Throughput in practice Throughput depends on hardware, payload size, schema, batching, persistence, concurrency and the target latency percentile. A 10 Gbps link has a raw signalling rate equivalent to 1.25 GB/s before protocol overhead; that is not an application throughput guarantee. Content gap: verified throughput benchmarks Generic per-server rates for web APIs, PostgreSQL, Redis and Kafka are omitted. No reproducible workload and hardware configuration was provided for those figures, so they cannot be reliably verified as capacity guidance. Benchmark the intended workload and record its settings before using a rate in a design. Key takeaways Parallel servers increase throughput capacity without necessarily shortening one lightly loaded request. Large transfers are often bandwidth-bound; small sequential exchanges pay repeated round trips. Treat raw link speeds and per-server rates as inputs to measurement, not application guarantees. Further reading The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso) Service Level Objectives (Google SRE)

t: Predict queueing and leave capacity headroom
sum: Explain why queueing grows near saturation and why spare capacity matters during peaks and failures.
x: A server can have enough nominal throughput and still give poor latency because requests spend time waiting. Queueing models explain why capacity planning needs spare room. How they interact: queueing Latency and throughput meet through queueing. When requests arrive faster than a server can process them, they wait. Waiting time is latency. The M/M/1 queue assumes Poisson arrivals (independent random arrivals at a constant average rate), exponentially distributed service times, and one server serving one request at a time. The two M letters refer to the model’s memoryless arrival and service assumptions. For that model, queueing theory gives the average time a request spends in the system, waiting plus being served: For a modelled server with a 10 ms mean service time, 80% utilisation gives a 50 ms average response: most of that time is waiting. The table illustrates how quickly waiting grows: Utilisation Latency vs service time ------ 50% 2x 80% 5x 90% 10x 99% 100x This is why systems can appear to "fall off a cliff". As utilisation approaches 100% from below, the M/M/1 steady-state mean queue length diverges; at or above 100% the infinite-buffer model has no stable steady state. Capacity planning needs measured headroom rather than a goal of keeping every resource fully busy. Real servers aren't exactly M/M/1 (they have many workers, and service times vary differently), and the exact curve depends on arrival/service variability, scheduling and queue limits. Many real systems develop large queues near saturation; a deterministic or admission-controlled system need not follow this curve. Little's law: how many requests are in flight Little's law connects average throughput, time in the system and concurrency in a stable system, where work does not accumulate forever. If requests arrive at the same rate but each stays ten times longer, ten times as many are in flight on average. A slow dependency can therefore exhaust upstream threads or connections even without a traffic spike. The pool-sizing unit gives the reference relationship and discusses its limits. Headroom must also cover failures. If three equally sized zones normally share the load, losing one pushes its work onto the two survivors. Test that case separately from healthy operation; acceptable normal utilisation alone does not prove the survivors will meet the latency target. Key takeaways The M/M/1 model’s mean latency grows sharply near saturation; real systems depend on their workload, admission rules and scheduling. Little’s law multiplies throughput by time in the system to give average concurrency. Check both normal load and survivor capacity during failures; headroom must satisfy each target. Further reading Little’s Law (Marc Brooker) Handling Overload (Google SRE) MIT: basic queueing theory

t: Measure percentiles without hiding slow requests
sum: Interpret typical and tail latency, then aggregate and collect measurements correctly across a service.
x: A single average can hide the slow experience that matters to users. Percentiles identify positions in the latency distribution, but only if the measurements include the requests and waits you mean to represent. Why averages lie: percentiles Suppose 100 requests take these times: 98 take 10 ms, and 2 take 2,000 ms. The mean adds all durations and divides by the request count. It is 49.8 ms, which describes neither group's experience well. A percentile instead identifies a position after sorting requests from fastest to slowest. Under the nearest-rank convention, p50 picks the 50th request out of these 100 and p99 picks the 99th. Other percentile conventions can interpolate, so state the method when small samples matter. Applied to our 100 requests: Mean: 49.8 ms Median (p50), the 50th value: 10 ms p99, the 99th value: 2,000 ms The mean describes no real request. It's five times the typical case and 40 times better than the slow case. That's why we use percentiles: p50 (median): at least half of requests are at or below this threshold (ties and percentile conventions matter). The "typical" experience. p95, p99: roughly 95% / 99% of requests are at or below these thresholds. The experience of your unluckiest users. p99.9 and above: often called the tail. Latency distributions are almost never normal (bell-shaped). They have a long right tail caused by garbage-collection pauses, cache misses, retransmits, lock contention, noisy neighbours and queueing. Measuring percentiles correctly You can't average percentiles. The mean of 10 servers' p99s is not the fleet's p99. Aggregate raw histograms (e.g. HdrHistogram, Prometheus histograms) and compute percentiles from the combined data. Beware coordinated omission. A load tester that waits for each response before sending the next under-reports latency when the server stalls, because it stops sending during the stall. wrk2 corrects for this by recording latency from when each request was scheduled to start, even if its actual transmission is delayed. Measure at the client, too. Server-side timing misses network and queueing time before your code runs. Key takeaways The mean, median and tail percentiles describe different parts of the same distribution. Combine histograms or observations before calculating a fleet percentile; do not average server percentiles. Client timing and tests that account for coordinated omission expose waits a server-only metric may miss. Further reading Service Level Objectives (Google SRE) Histograms and summaries (Prometheus) The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso) wrk2: corrected latency measurement

t: Control the tail amplified by fan-out
sum: Explain why more parallel backends increase exposure to slow responses, and choose remedies for variability.
x: The previous unit introduced p99 and p99.9: thresholds near the slow end of a latency distribution. In a service that waits for many parallel backend calls, those rare slow responses can become the normal user experience. Why the tail matters more than you'd think Your heaviest users hit the tail most. A user loading a page that makes 50 backend calls is much more likely to experience at least one slow call. Amazon's Dynamo paper describes service-level targets set at p99.9 rather than the mean or median, so that every customer gets a good experience, including those with the longest histories and so the most expensive requests. Fan-out amplifies the tail. If a request fans out to several servers in parallel and must wait for all of them, it's as slow as the slowest. With independent 1%-slow backends, one call is rarely slow, but about 63% of requests waiting for 100 calls encounter at least one slow response. More calls create more opportunities for delay. The reference relationship is useful when estimating that exposure: The formula assumes each server is slow independently of the others. Correlated slowness (a shared overloaded database, say) changes the numbers. At 100-way fan-out, most requests (63%) wait for at least one server's p99-or-worse response, so a single server's tail becomes your typical latency. This is the central point of Dean and Barroso's paper The Tail at Scale. Mitigations include hedged requests (send a second copy after the p95 time elapses and use whichever returns first), tied requests, and reducing variability at the source. Tied requests let a replica cancel its queued duplicate when another replica starts the work. Isolating or scheduling background work reduces interference; returning partial results after a deadline can cap latency when the application permits missing results. Key takeaways A request waiting for every shard inherits the slowest response. Independent 1%-slow shards make about 63% of 100-way requests slow; shared causes change that model. Hedging, partial results and reducing background-work interference address tail variability, with their own costs. Further reading The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso) Dynamo: Amazon’s Highly Available Key-value Store

t: Compare latency orders of magnitude carefully
sum: Use hypothetical timings to spot important differences, then measure the actual workload before designing around them.
x: A useful estimate distinguishes nanoseconds, microseconds and milliseconds. Otherwise a small-looking number can hide a much slower operation. A microsecond is a thousand nanoseconds; a millisecond is a thousand microseconds. Use a timing table as a hypothesis The following values are hypothetical exercise inputs, not current hardware benchmarks: Operation Assumed time ------ L1 cache reference 1 ns Main memory reference 100 ns Random SSD read 100 µs Same-datacentre round trip 0.5 ms HDD seek 10 ms Distant-region round trip 70 ms Converting to a common unit shows that these operations can occupy very different scales. Under these assumptions, memory access is much cheaper than a random storage read, and a distant round trip costs far more than either. The useful conclusion is where to investigate, rather than a ratio to memorise. Content gap: reproducible measurements These assumed values do not come from one measured hardware and workload configuration. Do not use them as capacity promises. Measure payload size, access pattern, caching, concurrency and load on the intended system. A request can pay an expensive operation many times.
