Several sequential distant calls may dominate its latency even when each carries few bytes. Batching, overlapping independent work or moving computation near the data can avoid those repeated waits. Access pattern matters A storage device does not have one latency for every operation. A mechanical disk may need to move its head before a random read, whereas sequential access can stream nearby data. SSD behaviour also depends on size, load and device details. A network cache adds a network exchange even when its own data is in RAM. Use the table to ask specific questions: is this request waiting on many random reads, a distant dependency, or a saturated resource? Validate the answer with timings and traces. Throughput can be high while latency is poor Moving a large batch efficiently does not guarantee a fast first result. A bulk physical transfer can deliver a huge quantity per trip while taking hours to deliver any of it. That same distinction applies when buffering or batching network and storage work. Real-world analogy: a lorry carrying drives A lorry can carry many drives in one journey, but the recipient waits for the journey to finish. How it maps: Total data delivered per journey can imply high average throughput, while the time until delivery remains long. Bandwidth and latency answer different questions. Where it stops: Physical transfers have loading, handling and copying costs. They are useful only for suitable bulk jobs, not interactive requests. Key takeaways Compare durations in consistent units before deciding which cost matters. Illustrative timing tables suggest hypotheses; measure the actual workload and access pattern. Repeated sequential exchanges can dominate latency even with small payloads. High bulk throughput does not imply a quick first response. Further reading Service Level Objectives (Google SRE) The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso)

t: Translate availability targets into error budgets
sum: Distinguish availability, reliability and durability, and turn nines into measurable SLO budgets.
x: "Is the system up?" sounds like a yes/no question. In practice, availability is a number you design for, measure and trade against cost. This lesson explains how the target becomes a practical failure allowance. Availability vs reliability vs durability These words are often used interchangeably. They shouldn't be. Availability: the fraction of time (or of requests) the system is able to serve correctly. "99.9% of minutes this month the API returned successful responses." Reliability: the probability the system works correctly without failure over a period. A system that fails for 100 ms every minute is about 99.83% available but terrible for reliability: almost any long-running job or long-lived connection will hit a failure. Durability: the probability that stored data is not lost. Amazon S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability but offers a much lower availability SLA. Data can be safe yet temporarily unreachable. There are two common ways to turn availability into a number: count time, or count requests. Availability can count successful time or successful requests. Choose what counts as good service and the observation window before comparing targets. For a 30-day month, 99.9% time-based availability allows about 43 minutes of downtime. A request-based 99.9% target allows one failed request per thousand. These allowances differ when traffic varies or an incident affects only some requests. Time-based vs request-based Request-based availability is usually more meaningful for large services (Google SRE favours it), because a 5-minute outage at 3 a.m. affects far fewer users than one at peak. The nines Availability is usually quoted in "nines". Here's the equivalent downtime, using a 365.25-day year and an average month (year/12): Availability Downtime/year Downtime/month --------- 99% (two nines) 3.65 days 7.3 hours 99.9% 8.77 hours 43.8 min 99.95% 4.38 hours 21.9 min 99.99% 52.6 min 4.4 min 99.999% 5.26 min 26 s The formula behind the table: the fraction of time you are allowed to be down is 1 minus the availability. Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by 10x. The cost of achieving it depends on the architecture and failure modes; there is no universal cost multiplier. At 99.999%, you have 26 seconds a month. Manual detection and recovery can easily consume that budget, so automated recovery is usually essential. Think in error budgets If your SLO is 99.9%, you have a 0.1% error budget: about 43 minutes a month. Spend it on deploys, experiments and incidents. When it's gone, slow down releases. This turns availability into an engineering trade-off rather than a moral absolute. SLIs, SLOs and SLAs (briefly) SLI (indicator): the measurement, e.g. proportion of requests returning non-5xx in under 300 ms. SLO (objective): the target for that SLI, e.g. 99.9% over 30 days. SLA (agreement): a contract with consequences, e.g. service credits. AWS's EC2 Region-Level SLA specifies 99.99% under its stated multi-AZ deployment and measurement conditions; an individual instance has a separate commitment. SLAs are normally looser than internal SLOs, so you're warned before you owe customers money. The reliability and observability module goes deeper. Key takeaways Availability measures successful service, reliability measures failure-free operation, and durability measures retained data. Time-based and request-based availability weight partial and peak-hour outages differently. An SLI is a measurement, an SLO its target, and an SLA a contractual commitment; the remaining failure allowance is the error budget. Further reading Availability table (Google SRE) Embracing Risk (Google SRE) Service Level Objectives (Google SRE)

t: Model redundancy with capacity and shared failures
sum: Explain how redundancy depends on independent failures, working failover and enough survivor capacity.
x: Redundancy helps when another component can take over. Model that benefit using the survivors the workload actually needs, then account for failures that can affect every copy together. Components in parallel If the system works as long as at least one of several redundant components works, they're in parallel. The system fails only if all fail, so work out the chance that every one is down and subtract it from 1: For two independent 99%-available servers, with immediate switching and either able to carry the load, the model gives 99.99% availability. A third reduces the chance of all being down further. The gain depends on those assumptions. Redundancy needs spare capacity The parallel formula assumes one survivor can carry the whole load. If peak traffic needs both servers, losing either one at peak overloads the other, and the pair behaves like two components in series. Plan for N+1 (or N+2): enough servers that the system still meets its load with one, or one zone, gone. When some number of identical servers are needed out of a larger group (written "k of n"), the system is up while at least that many are up. For three 99% servers where any two can carry peak load, add up the chances of the states that work: all three up, or exactly two up. For three independent 99%-available servers where any two can carry the load, the model gives about 99.97% availability. This is lower than the any-one-of-three case because states with only one survivor now count as failures. The useful question is which survivor combinations can actually serve peak traffic, rather than how many copies exist. The big caveat: independence The formulas above assume failures are independent. In reality, they often aren't: Two servers in the same rack share a power supply and switch. Replicas running the same software share the same bugs (a bad deploy or a leap-second bug takes them all out at once). A bad config push hits every region. Failover itself can fail, or take minutes. The parallel formula assumes switching is instant; a 5-minute failover that happens four times a year is 20 minutes of downtime the formula never shows. Two 99% servers on the same host don't give you 99.99%. This is why cloud providers offer availability zones (separate power, cooling and networking) and why multi-region designs exist. It's also why staged rollouts matter: they stop a single bad change from becoming a correlated failure. Redundancy you haven't tested is a hope, not a design A standby database that has never been failed over to is likely to surprise you. Practise failovers regularly (game days, chaos engineering). Key takeaways Parallel availability improves only when surviving components can serve the required load. Two-of-three capacity has different availability from any-one-of-three capacity. Shared power, software, config and slow failover invalidate the simplest independent, instant-switch model. Further reading Availability and Beyond (AWS) AWS Well-Architected Framework

t: Find availability risks along a request path
sum: Identify required dependencies, distinguish redundant alternatives, and move optional work off the critical path.
x: The previous unit modelled redundant components in parallel. A real request usually also needs several different tiers to work together, so its availability combines both kinds of relationship. Components in series If a request needs every component to work, the components are in series. Assuming independent failures, the chance that all of them are up at once is the product of their availabilities: In this example, all three tiers must be healthy. Their independent modelled availability is about 99.84%, below each individual tier. A required dependency creates another way for the request to fail. The chain cannot be more available than its least available required tier; with independent imperfect tiers it is less available. Adding synchronous dependencies therefore consumes the request path's reliability budget. This is the mathematical reason to: Remove dependencies from the critical path (do work asynchronously). Degrade gracefully: show the page without recommendations rather than failing it. Be suspicious of deep synchronous microservice call chains. Combining them Real systems mix both. Compute parallel groups first, then multiply the groups in series: First identify the redundant alternatives inside each tier. Check that survivors have capacity and that failover works. Then treat the tiers the request still needs as a chain. Redundant app servers do not remove the database as a required dependency, and a shared failure can still affect several tiers together. Key takeaways A request needing every independent dependency has availability equal to the product of their availabilities. Calculate each parallel group first, then multiply required groups in series. Asynchronous work and graceful degradation reduce the dependencies that must succeed for the core request. Further reading Availability and Beyond (AWS) AWS Well-Architected Framework

sum: Use MTBF and MTTR to identify investments in detection, diagnosis, failover and verification.
x: Redundancy is only part of resilience. When service does fail, reducing the time users wait for recovery can be a more practical investment than trying to eliminate every failure. MTBF and MTTR Two quantities define steady-state availability: MTBF (mean time between failures): how long, on average, the system runs before failing. MTTR (mean time to repair/recovery): how long, on average, it takes to restore service. Over a long run, the system cycles between working (for MTBF on average) and being repaired (for MTTR on average). The fraction of each cycle spent working is the availability: The model assumes repeated working and recovery cycles at stable average rates. It describes long-run availability, not the duration or impact of a particular incident. There are two levers: Increase MTBF: better hardware, fewer risky changes, more testing. Decrease MTTR: faster detection, automated failover, quick rollbacks, good runbooks. Lowering MTTR is often cheaper and more effective. Cutting MTTR from 60 minutes to 6 gives the same availability gain as making failures 10x rarer. Recovery includes detection, diagnosis, repair or failover, and verification. Measuring those stages reveals where the delay actually occurs; faster repairs cannot help much if nobody notices the failure for an hour. Each piece suggests an investment: alerting on symptoms (detect), good dashboards and tracing (diagnose), automated failover and one-click rollback (fix). Related terms you'll see: MTTF (mean time to failure, for non-repairable parts) and MTTD (mean time to detect). Key takeaways Long-run availability depends on time working relative to time working plus recovery time. Making recovery ten times faster has the same modelled availability effect as making failures ten times rarer. Separate detection, diagnosis, repair and verification to choose concrete recovery improvements. Further reading Availability and Beyond (AWS) Embracing Risk (Google SRE)

t: Choose scaling strategies and expose hidden state
sum: Compare scale-up with scale-out, and identify the state that prevents an app instance being safely replaced.
x: A system is scalable if it can handle more load by adding resources, while keeping performance acceptable and cost roughly proportional to load. "Load" can mean many things: requests per second, number of users, data volume, write rate or number of concurrent connections. Always ask "scalable along which dimension?". A system that handles 10x more reads may not handle 10x more writes. Vertical scaling (scale up) Make the machine bigger: more CPU cores, more RAM, faster disks. Pros Usually no application changes. A bigger Postgres instance remains one Postgres instance, although configuration and resource limits may need adjustment. No distributed-systems problems: no network partitions between nodes, no consistency puzzles. Surprisingly far-reaching. Cloud instances with hundreds of vCPUs and multiple terabytes of RAM are readily available. Cons A ceiling. Eventually there's no bigger machine. Cost at the top end. On your own hardware, the biggest servers cost disproportionately more per unit of capacity. Cloud prices vary by instance family, region and purchase model. A continuously running fixed-size instance must be paid for even during quiet periods; compare current prices rather than assuming a universal cost curve. A single point of failure. One big machine is still one machine. Downtime to resize, in many setups. Don't dismiss scaling up Stack Overflow famously served huge traffic from a handful of powerful SQL Server machines for years. Scaling up is often the cheapest, simplest first move, especially for databases. A common path is: scale the database up, add read replicas and a cache for reads, and shard only when writes outgrow the biggest sensible machine. Horizontal scaling (scale out) Add more machines and spread the load across them. Pros Near-unlimited capacity, if the workload partitions well. Redundancy comes naturally: losing one of 20 nodes loses 5% of capacity. Commodity hardware and elastic autoscaling. Cons Requires load balancing, service discovery and distributed coordination. Data must be partitioned or replicated, which brings consistency trade-offs. More moving parts to operate and debug. Stateless vs stateful The single most important property for horizontal scaling is whether a component is stateless. A stateless service keeps no client-specific data between requests. Any instance can handle any request. Session data, uploaded files and caches live in shared external stores (a database, Redis, S3). Why stateless services are easy to scale: Add or remove instances freely; the load balancer needs no stickiness. An instance crash loses nothing except in-flight requests. Autoscaling, rolling deploys and spot instances become easier, but still require graceful shutdown, retry-safe requests and sufficient capacity in backing services. This is the "processes" factor of the Twelve-Factor App: processes are stateless and share nothing; state lives in backing services. A stateful component holds data that matters: databases, caches, message brokers, WebSocket connection servers, game servers. Scaling them needs answers to: Where does each piece of data live? (partitioning, or sharding) How are copies kept in sync? (replication) What happens when a node joins, leaves or dies? (rebalancing, failover) These are the hard problems covered in the databases, consistency and messaging modules. A common architecture pattern is to push state down into a few well-understood stateful systems (Postgres, Redis, Kafka, S3) and keep everything above them stateless. Hidden state In-memory authoritative sessions, unpersisted local uploads and uncoordinated rate-limit counters create hidden correctness-critical state. Disposable local caches can be compatible with a stateless service when correctness does not depend on their contents. Symptoms: users logged out randomly, rate limits that are 10x too lenient with 10 instances. Key takeaways Name the load dimension you need to scale: reads, writes, data or connections. Scaling up keeps a simpler architecture; scaling out adds coordination and data-placement work. Keep correctness-critical state in appropriate backing services; disposable caches differ from authoritative local state. Further reading The Twelve-Factor App: Processes Scalability

t: Find the serial and coordination limits of scaling
sum: Apply Amdahl’s law and node-pair growth to explain why more workers can stop helping or reduce throughput.
x: Once a workload can use several workers, the next question is how much speed-up they can provide. Fixed serial work and coordination overhead place different limits on that benefit. Amdahl's law: the limit of parallelism Some part of almost every job can only be done one step at a time (it is serial); the rest can be split across workers (it is parallel). Gene Amdahl pointed out in 1967 that the serial part limits how much faster extra workers can make the job. Measure the job's time on one worker as 1; the serial share still takes the same time, while the parallel share is divided between the workers: For example, if 5% of the original job is serial, even unlimited workers cannot make the fixed job more than twenty times faster. This assumes the parallel part splits perfectly with no coordination overhead; real overhead can reduce the benefit further. Parallel share Max speed-up ------ 50% 2x 90% 10x 95% 20x 99% 100x With 95% parallel, the ideal speed-up approaches a twentyfold limit as workers increase. For an entirely parallel job, this ideal model has no serial floor; practical communication and resource limits still apply. In system design, a shared bottleneck may play a similar limiting role. These components are not necessarily single-threaded, but each has finite capacity: A single primary database that handles all writes. A global lock or a single-threaded sequencer. A single coordinator service. Amdahl tells you that adding app servers won't help once you're bottlenecked on one of these. You must remove or partition the serial component. Universal Scalability Law Real systems often do worse than Amdahl, because nodes must coordinate (cache coherence, cross-node chatter). Neil Gunther's USL models two costs: contention (queueing for a shared resource, which is Amdahl's serial part) and coherence (nodes keeping each other up to date). Coherence cost grows roughly with the number of node pairs, which grows much faster than the number of nodes (illustrated below), so it can make throughput fall as you add nodes. The shapes are diagnostic. A curve that rises then flattens points to contention: find the shared bottleneck. A curve that rises then falls points to coherence: look for all-to-all chatter, global locks or broadcast cache invalidation. With eight nodes there are 28 distinct pairs; with sixteen there are 120. Doubling the nodes creates more than four times as many possible pairwise relationships in this example. If each node talks to every other on each update, coordination can grow faster than useful work. Gustafson's law gives the optimistic counterpart: as you add machines you usually also grow the problem (more users, more data), so the parallel portion grows and scaling stays useful. Scaling the different tiers Tier Typical scaling approach ------ Static content CDN Stateless app Horizontal + autoscaling Read-heavy data Cache + read replicas Write-heavy data Partition (shard) Async work Queue + worker pool Each technique gets its own lesson later. The pattern is consistent: find the bottleneck, apply the technique for that tier, then find the next bottleneck. Key takeaways For a fixed job, the serial fraction caps speed-up even with unlimited workers. Coordination between node pairs can grow much faster than the number of nodes. Treat curve shapes as clues, then measure the bottleneck and scale the tier responsible. Further reading Amdahl’s law Neil Gunther and the Universal Scalability Law Little’s Law (Marc Brooker) Gunther: quantifying scalability

t: Size concurrency pools with Little’s law
sum: Connect resource-holding time with concurrency, and predict why a slow dependency exhausts a pool.
x: Thread and connection pools limit how many requests can hold a resource at once. Little’s law estimates their average occupancy and shows what changes when a downstream call becomes slow. Little's law: concurrency, throughput, latency Little's law is one of the most useful equations in capacity planning. For any stable system (one where the queue doesn't grow forever), averaged over a long enough time: It holds regardless of arrival distribution, and applies to a single thread pool, a whole service or a coffee shop. Example 1: sizing a thread pool. A service handles 2,000 req/s, and each request spends 50 ms in the service (much of it waiting on the database): This workload keeps about 100 requests in flight on average. With one occupied thread per request, that means about 100 busy threads before headroom. Example 2: database connections. 5,000 queries/s at 4 ms each: About 20 connections are busy on average. This uses connection-holding time, not the whole request duration. A pool of 30–40 is a starting hypothesis, not a guarantee: burstiness, latency tails and database capacity determine the necessary headroom. A pool of 500 per app instance across 50 instances permits 25,000 connections and can impose substantial overhead; validate the total against database capacity rather than assuming more connections help. Example 3: what happens when latency rises. The database slows from 4 ms to 40 ms while traffic stays at 5,000/s: Average connection demand would rise to about 200 if the same throughput could be maintained. That is ten times the previous occupancy. The pool of 40 is exhausted; requests queue, latency rises further, and the problem cascades. Little's law explains why a slow dependency causes thread or connection-pool exhaustion upstream, and why timeouts and bulkheads (reliability module) matter. Key takeaways Average concurrency equals average arrival rate multiplied by average time inside a stable system. Use the time spent holding the resource you are sizing, with seconds matching the per-second rate. Longer resource occupancy requires more concurrency; pool headroom and database capacity must be measured. Further reading Little’s Law (Marc Brooker) Handling Overload (Google SRE)

t: Keep units and orders of magnitude straight
sum: Convert daily counts, powers of ten and network bits into consistent estimation units.
x: Back-of-the-envelope estimation is quick, approximate arithmetic that tells you which order of magnitude you're dealing with. Is this one database or a hundred? Gigabytes or petabytes? One server or a fleet? The goal is not precision. Being within a factor of 2–3 is fine. Being off by 1,000x because you confused MB with GB is not. Reference units, not a memory test Large counts and time Use thousand, million and billion consistently. Moving between decimal size prefixes changes the scale by a thousand each step. Write the units beside estimates so a missed prefix is visible. For daily counts, a day contains 86,400 seconds. Dividing a count per day by that duration gives an average per-second rate, not the busiest-second demand. A 365.25-day year contains about 31.6 million seconds; rounded estimates should say which convention they use. Daily events Average events/s ------ 1 million About 12 10 million About 120 100 million About 1,200 1 billion About 12,000 Use these as a scale check, then allow for the measured traffic peak. Size Unit Bytes In words --------- KB (kilobyte) 1,000 thousand MB (megabyte) 1,000,000 million GB (gigabyte) 10 to the power 9 billion TB (terabyte) 10 to the power 12 trillion PB (petabyte) 10 to the power 15 quadrillion Each step up the table is 1,000 times bigger. (Using powers of 10 rather than powers of 2 introduces an error of about 2% at KB, growing to about 13% at PB: a binary kilobyte is 1,024 bytes, 2.4% more than 1,000. That's fine for estimates. Strictly, the binary units are KiB, MiB, GiB and so on.) Illustrative object-size assumptions These are exercise inputs, not measured universal sizes. Content gap: no representative dataset is provided for a reliable generic object-size table; measure your own serialized records and media. Item Assumed size ------ ID / timestamp 8 bytes Short text post + metadata 300 B – 1 KB User profile row 1 KB Compressed photo 200 KB – 2 MB 1 minute of HD video ~40–100 MB Bandwidth Network speeds are quoted in bits per second; storage and file sizes in bytes. A byte contains eight bits. A 1 Gbps link therefore has a raw rate equivalent to 125 MB/s, and a 10 Gbps link to 1.25 GB/s. Application throughput is lower once protocol overhead and other limits are included. A claim that a 10 Gbps link sends 10 GB/s confuses bits with bytes. Key takeaways Estimate the order of magnitude and state what you rounded. Daily counts become average per-second rates by dividing by 86,400 seconds. Distinguish decimal and binary sizes, and divide bits by eight to obtain bytes. Object sizes in the table are illustrative assumptions; measure the records and media you will store. Further reading The System Design Primer Back-of-the-envelope calculation NIST: decimal and binary prefixes

t: Estimate request rates, records and cache memory
sum: Separate peak traffic, retained copies and a measured cache hot set before choosing capacity.
x: With the units established, use a sequence of explicit assumptions and small calculations. A URL shortener demonstrates why read traffic, stored records and cache memory need separate estimates. The method State assumptions: active users, actions per user, measured record size, retention and copies. Separate average from peak traffic. A daily total hides bursts; choose a peak factor from the actual traffic shape. Count retained data and copies. Longer retention and more full replicas both increase storage. Estimate delivered bytes separately. Reading an item many times adds delivery traffic without creating new stored records. Measure the cache hot set. Count distinct keys needed for the intended hit rate, then include memory overhead. Check the design implication. Compare each resource demand with a benchmark of the intended workload. A useful reference for record storage is: A URL shortener: what matters Assume 100 million new links a month, 100 redirects per new link, roughly 500 bytes per record, ten years of retention, and a threefold peak factor. These are exercise inputs. Using a rounded 2.5 million seconds per month gives about 40 writes/s and 4,000 reads/s on average. The assumed peak gives about 120 writes/s and 12,000 reads/s. Reads dominate, so a cache or read replicas may help; a large lifetime record count does not by itself prove the write path needs sharding. Ten years gives twelve billion records: about 6 TB for one copy and 18 TB for three, before indexes, metadata, backups and headroom. Shorter retention changes that storage budget without necessarily changing today's peak traffic. For cache memory, suppose access traces identify 80 million distinct hot links. Their raw payload is about 40 GB at the assumed record size. Add Redis object/index overhead, replication and spare memory before choosing nodes. Total requests or an assumed 80/20 rule cannot establish the number of distinct keys needed for a desired hit rate. These rates are candidates for a straightforward database-and-cache design. Benchmark the actual queries, contention and durability settings before choosing capacity. The estimate directs attention to read load, retained data, ID generation and availability; it does not certify that one particular database deployment will suffice. Key takeaways Calculate average traffic, apply an explicit peak factor, then estimate storage, bandwidth and hot-set memory. Retention and replication multiply record storage; cache payload still needs overhead and headroom. A hot-set size comes from distinct-key access measurements, not total requests or an assumed 80/20 rule. Finish with design implications and a workload-specific capacity check. Further reading The System Design Primer Fermi problem

t: Estimate media storage and delivery bandwidth
sum: Explain why media can dominate storage, repeated delivery drives egress, and simultaneous viewers determine streaming demand.
x: The preceding record estimate is only part of a media service. Large objects and repeated delivery can dominate the storage and network budget even when the metadata database is modest. A social feed: separate metadata from media Assume 200 million daily active users, each posting twice and viewing 100 posts daily. Ten per cent of posts contain a 500 KB photo; text and metadata take about 1 KB per post. These are exercise inputs, with decimal size units. Using a rounded 100,000 seconds per day gives about 4,000 posts/s and 200,000 post views/s on average. An assumed threefold peak raises these to about 12,000 and 600,000 respectively. The read-heavy pattern makes caching and precomputation candidates, subject to freshness and fan-out costs. The important storage result is the imbalance: One-copy payload Per day Per 365-day year --------- Text and metadata 400 GB About 150 TB Photos 20 TB About 7.3 PB Photos dominate even though they occur in a minority of posts. Keeping large media in object storage and keeping references and searchable metadata in the database is a useful starting design; the estimate does not require every byte to live in a database disk. Delivered bytes differ from stored bytes Assume ten per cent of the 20 billion daily views fetch a photo. That delivers about 1 PB per day, or roughly 80 Gbps using the same rounded day. A photo stored once can be downloaded many times, so upload volume alone cannot size egress. A CDN can serve repeat requests near users and reduce origin traffic. Its cache hit rate changes how much delivery load reaches the origin; it does not remove the bytes users receive. Measure geography, cacheability, payload sizes and peak demand. Say what an estimate changes A large result should lead to a resource or architecture question: where are the objects stored, which traffic can an edge cache serve, and can the origin survive misses? It should not automatically lead to sharding the metadata database. A streaming service: concurrency matters Assume one million concurrent viewers, each consuming an average 5 Mbps stream. Their combined peak delivery is 5 Tbps, equivalent to 625 GB/s. These assumed values explain why delivery placement and bandwidth can dominate a streaming design. The number of viewers watching at once matters here, rather than daily active users or uploads. Higher bitrate or more simultaneous viewers raises delivery demand directly. Provision measured server capacity with headroom and geographic redundancy; one generic network-card rate cannot determine the fleet. Netflix's Open Connect places delivery appliances inside ISP networks to serve traffic close to viewers. Key takeaways Photos can dominate storage even when only a small share of posts contain them. Estimate media bytes delivered as well as bytes retained, with bits and bytes kept distinct. A CDN supports offload, geography and redundancy; assumed NIC rates need workload-specific validation. Further reading The System Design Primer Netflix Open Connect

t: Turn workload estimates into a resilient fleet
sum: Use CPU time and concurrency to size capacity, then account for replicas, overhead, peaks and zone failure.
x: A traffic estimate becomes a fleet estimate only after you specify what consumes each resource. CPU work, concurrent connections and replicated writes are different constraints, and failure removes usable capacity. Worked example 4: servers needed Assumptions: 50,000 req/s peak, each request uses ~20 ms of CPU, servers have 16 cores, target 60% utilisation. These assumptions require about 105 servers before zone redundancy. If three evenly sized zones must survive losing one, the two remaining zones together need that capacity. Rounding to 53 servers per zone gives 159 servers total. This is an illustrative CPU estimate, not a guarantee about I/O, memory or tail latency. Common pitfalls Bits vs bytes. Network speeds are in bits; storage is in bytes. A 1 Gbps raw link rate corresponds to 125 MB/s before overhead. Forgetting peaks. Average QPS sizes nothing; capacity must handle the peak. Forgetting concurrency. For connections and sessions, use Little's law: the number connected at once is the arrival rate multiplied by the time each stays online. For example, 50 million daily users connected for 30 minutes each implies about one million connections on average, before the peak factor. Forgetting replication and overhead. Three replicas triple storage; index and metadata overhead depends on the schema and storage engine; state an explicit allowance or measure it. Forgetting growth. Plan for at least the next 1–2 years. False precision. "4,629.6 QPS" signals you've missed the point. Say "about 5k". Check your units at every step Write the unit next to every number. Most estimation errors are unit errors, not arithmetic errors. Key takeaways CPU-seconds arriving per second estimate busy cores; target utilisation determines usable capacity per server. Size the survivors for peak traffic when a whole zone fails, then provision the complete fleet. Connections require concurrency estimates, while replicated writes consume capacity on every required copy. Include units, peaks, overhead and growth; avoid false precision. Further reading The System Design Primer Little’s Law (Marc Brooker) Handling Overload (Google SRE)

t: Understand CAP through a two-node partition
sum: Use the exact definitions of linearisability and CAP availability to see why an isolated replica must choose.
x: The CAP theorem is the most quoted and most misunderstood result in distributed systems. Used carefully, it's a sharp tool for reasoning about what happens during a network failure. Used loosely ("Mongo is CP, Cassandra is AP"), it mostly causes confusion. The precise statement Eric Brewer conjectured it in 2000; Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch proved it in 2002. In their formulation: C (consistency) means linearisability: every read sees the most recent completed write, as if there were a single copy of the data. A (availability) means every request received by a non-failing node must get a non-error response. No time limit, but no "sorry, try later". P (partition tolerance) means the system keeps operating even if the network drops arbitrary messages between nodes. The theorem: in the presence of a network partition, a system cannot be both linearisable and available. Why it's true: the two-node argument Cut the network between the nodes before the write, so node 2 cannot receive it. Client X writes v = 1 to node 1 and receives a successful acknowledgement before Y starts reading. Client Y reads v from node 2. Node 2 has two choices: Answer with v = 0. It stays available but returns stale data: not linearisable. Choose A. Refuse or wait until it can contact node 1. It stays consistent but isn't available. Choose C. There is no third option. That's the whole theorem. Why “pick two of three” misleads The Venn-diagram version suggests you can pick consistency plus availability, consistency plus partition tolerance, or availability plus partition tolerance like menu items. But you don't get to choose whether partitions happen. Networks drop packets, switches fail, GC pauses make nodes unreachable, cloud zones lose connectivity. So for any system spread over a network, P isn't optional. The real statement is: The useful form When a partition happens, choose between consistency and availability. When there's no partition, you can have both. A design claiming both consistency and availability by excluding partitions has left that failure case outside its promise. A single node avoids inter-replica partitions, but remains a single point of failure. CAP consistency and ACID invariants They describe different properties. Term Meaning ------ ACID C Transactions keep invariants (constraints) valid CAP C Linearisability: reads see the latest write A single-node database can provide linearisable operations, but being single-node does not guarantee that every API or isolation level does so. ACID consistency is a separate question: application logic and constraints must preserve the intended invariants. Key takeaways During a partition, a replicated system cannot promise both linearisability and successful responses at every non-failing node. Partition tolerance is not a menu option that makes network failures disappear. CAP consistency concerns operation ordering; ACID consistency concerns application invariants. Further reading Brewer’s Conjecture and the Feasibility of CAP CAP Twelve Years Later (Eric Brewer) Gilbert and Lynch: perspectives on CAP

t: Choose a partition policy and plan reconciliation
sum: Separate CAP availability from operational uptime, and match refusal or conflict resolution to each data type.
x: The CAP proof identifies a constraint; the product still needs a policy. Decide which operations may continue during isolation and what the application must do when connectivity returns. CAP availability and operational uptime CAP availability is extreme: every non-failing node must respond successfully, even a node isolated on the minority side of a partition. Real systems usually mean something weaker by "highly available": most requests succeed most of the time. Systems using majority quorums (Raft in etcd, Paxos in Spanner, the similar Zab protocol in ZooKeeper) commonly refuse writes on the minority side during a partition. That consistency-oriented write policy does not establish that every read API is linearisable; ZooKeeper reads, covered below, may be stale. Yet such systems routinely achieve very high availability, because: Partitions are relatively rare. Clients on the minority side can often fail over to the majority side. Google Spanner offers a 99.999% monthly uptime commitment for multi-region configurations under its SLA measurement and credit conditions. This can coexist with refusing operations that cannot safely reach the required replicas; the SLA is not a CAP-availability promise. Guarantees matter more than labels Martin Kleppmann's essay "Please stop calling databases CP or AP" makes the case well. Most real systems are neither strictly: Many offer tunable consistency per request. Cassandra lets you pick ONE, QUORUM or ALL; DynamoDB offers eventually consistent or strongly consistent reads. Many aren't linearisable even without partitions (e.g. asynchronous replication with reads from replicas), so they don't satisfy CAP's C anyway. Many aren't CAP-available either (e.g. a leader-based system where nodes refuse writes when they can't see the leader). A system that is neither linearisable nor CAP-available is just... a system with other trade-offs. Describe its actual guarantees instead: "reads may be up to ~1 s stale", "writes are rejected on the minority side". Using this in a design Decide per data type, not per system. A bank's balance needs strong consistency; its "recently viewed" list doesn't. Ask what happens on the minority side of a partition. Refuse writes? Accept and reconcile later? Serve stale reads with a warning? Brewer's own example is an ATM: during a partition it can keep dispensing cash up to a small limit, accepting a bounded risk and reconciling (and charging overdraft fees) afterwards. If you choose availability, plan for conflicts. Last-write-wins (loses data silently), version vectors with application merge, or CRDTs. Amazon's original Dynamo merged conflicting shopping carts, occasionally resurrecting deleted items. If you choose consistency, plan for unavailability. Clients need retries, timeouts and clear errors. Quantify the latency cost. For an exercise, assume a same-zone quorum takes 1 ms and a cross-region quorum tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Real quorum latency depends on replica placement, protocol and workload; measure it. The distributed consistency and consensus module covers linearisability, quorums, Raft and conflict resolution in depth. Key takeaways A majority-quorum system may have high measured uptime while refusing requests on a minority side. Choosing to accept partitioned updates requires an application-appropriate conflict-resolution policy. Choosing consistency requires client-visible errors, timeouts and recovery behaviour. Choose per data type and quantify the latency and business risk of the policy. Further reading CAP Twelve Years Later (Eric Brewer) Eventually Consistent (Werner Vogels) Dynamo: Amazon’s Highly Available Key-value Store Spanner availability SLA

t: Apply PACELC to everyday replica latency
sum: Reason about consistency and latency during normal operation, using cross-region writes and local reads.
x: CAP alone does not explain the latency paid while every replica is healthy. PACELC asks how replica coordination affects normal reads and writes as well as partition behaviour. What CAP leaves out CAP only talks about behaviour during a partition, and only about one consistency model (linearisability) and one extreme availability definition. It says nothing about: Latency, which you trade against consistency all the time, not just during failures. Weaker but useful consistency models (causal, read-your-writes, bounded staleness). Node crashes, disk failures, or slow nodes (which are indistinguishable from partitions to the other nodes). That gap is what PACELC fills. PACELC Daniel Abadi proposed PACELC in 2010 (published 2012): The "else" half is the important addition. Even with a healthy network, coordinating replicated data can cost latency. A design that promises acknowledged writes will survive a zone or region loss must place the required copies before confirming them; linearisable reads may also need a leader or quorum. Linearisability alone does not require every write to wait for a distant durable copy: the replication and failure-survival contract matters. Classifying real systems These are approximate classifications; many are tunable. The table summarises coordination choices, not a promise that every read is linearisable. The next unit explains the read guarantees of Cassandra, etcd and ZooKeeper. System Partition Else --------- Cassandra (ONE reads/writes) PA-like EL DynamoDB Depends on API and global-table consistency mode Eventual or strong reads Spanner, CockroachDB PC EC etcd, ZooKeeper PC EC DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default and cost half as much read capacity as strong reads. ConsistentRead=true reflects all prior successful writes and is supported for tables and local secondary indexes, not global secondary indexes or streams. The public read contract does not specify which replica serves the request. Multi-Region eventual-consistency global tables replicate asynchronously across regions, though AWS now also offers a multi-Region strong consistency mode that pays cross-region latency on writes. Spanner pays commit latency for external consistency, using TrueTime and Paxos across replicas. Key takeaways PACELC adds the normal-operation trade-off between latency and consistency. Cross-region coordination pays network delay even when no partition occurs. DynamoDB read options and global-table modes have different contracts; local asynchronous reads can be stale. System classifications are approximate; check the API and deployment you will actually use. Further reading Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design DynamoDB read consistency CAP Twelve Years Later (Eric Brewer) DynamoDB global-table modes

t: Describe actual read guarantees and quorum overlap
sum: Use Cassandra and ZooKeeper to distinguish quorum intersection, freshness and linearisability.
x: PACELC classifications summarise choices, but a concrete operation needs a concrete guarantee. Replica counts and read behaviour explain why two systems with the same broad label can expose different values. Concrete read guarantees Cassandra with ONE reads and writes favours availability and low latency when at least one actual replica for the key is reachable, but can still time out or reject requests. With QUORUM reads and writes, it pays latency for stronger guarantees (though it still isn't fully linearisable without lightweight transactions). The rule behind this, quorum overlap, is worked through below. etcd serves linearisable reads by default, confirming with a quorum before answering. ZooKeeper commits writes through a quorum, but by default a client reads from whichever server it's connected to, which may lag: reads are ordered but can be stale. sync() is a useful freshness barrier, but is not a quorum operation and is not a strict linearisability guarantee under all failures. Same "CP" label, different everyday guarantee. Quorum overlap In a leaderless store like Cassandra, each key is copied to several replicas. A write is reported successful once some of them acknowledge it, and a read asks some of them and takes the newest answer. For a completed write and a subsequent read over the same fixed replica set, the groups must overlap when their combined replica counts exceed the number of replicas. This is an intersection guarantee; timestamps, concurrent updates and partially applied writes still affect which value is returned. With three replicas, QUORUM reads and writes each require two, so every read group intersects every successful write group. ONE reads and writes can use different replicas and miss an update. Overlap is necessary but not sufficient for linearisability: concurrent writes, last-write-wins timestamps and failed writes that partly landed still need extra machinery such as lightweight transactions. The everyday question PACELC's "E" half is the one you face daily. Partitions are rare; latency is paid on every request. "Do we need this read to be strongly consistent, at the cost of a cross-zone round trip?" is a question you'll ask constantly. Key takeaways Describe each API’s guarantees rather than relying on a CP or AP label. Read and write replica counts exceeding the replication factor force overlap under the model’s assumptions. Overlap alone does not provide linearisability in the presence of concurrent or partly applied writes. ZooKeeper follower reads may lag committed writes; etcd’s default linearisable reads use a different contract. Further reading Please stop calling databases CP or AP Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design ZooKeeper consistency guarantees etcd API guarantees ZooKeeper sync quorum discussion

sum: State the gain, cost, acceptable business behaviour and assumptions behind a choice of consistency.
x: Every interesting design decision gives something up. Senior engineers aren't distinguished by knowing the "right" technology. They're distinguished by naming what each option costs, quantifying it where possible, and matching it to the requirements. This lesson collects the trade-offs you'll meet again and again in later modules. A template for any decision When you choose between options, say these four things out loud: What we gain. "Reads are served from local replicas in ~2 ms." What we give up. "Reads may be up to 1 s stale." Why that's acceptable here. "Product prices change rarely; checkout re-reads from the primary." What would change our mind. "If we add live auctions, staleness becomes unacceptable." Point 4 is often skipped and is the most valuable. It records the assumption the design depends on. Consistency vs availability (and latency) The earlier CAP and PACELC units established this trade-off. In practice it appears as a spectrum: The diagram is only a rough trade-off sketch: weaker consistency does not guarantee faster responses or availability, and consistency models are not all points on a single total order. How to choose: Data Typical choice ------ Account balance, stock Strong Username uniqueness Strong User's own profile edits Read-your-writes Like counts, view counts Eventual Recommendations Eventual, even stale Mix within one system Most real systems use strong consistency for a small core of critical data and weaker models for everything else. An e-commerce site might serve the catalogue from a cache that's minutes stale, but decrement inventory with a transactional conditional write. Key takeaways State what an option gains, what it gives up, why that is acceptable and what would change your mind. Money, inventory and uniqueness need authoritative decisions; counts and recommendations often permit staleness. Consistency models do not form a simple speed guarantee; match the actual contract to each data type. Further reading Eventually Consistent (Werner Vogels) AWS Well-Architected Framework

t: Trade write acknowledgement latency against loss risk
sum: Compare PostgreSQL, Kafka and Redis acknowledgement controls, then use batching to share flush costs.
x: A successful write response makes a promise. Decide whether it means an in-memory update, a durable local flush or a required replicated commit, then account for the latency of keeping that promise. Latency vs durability When is a write "done"? The earlier you acknowledge it, the faster it is and the more you can lose. Acknowledge after... Additional work Remaining loss risks --------- Written to process memory Memory update Process or machine failure before persistence Written to OS page cache Kernel write OS crash or power loss before persistence fsync to local durable storage Storage flush Storage failure, corruption or later logical deletion Durably replicated to a second zone Replication acknowledgement Loss of required durable copies, common failures or logical deletion Durably replicated across regions Cross-region acknowledgement Protocol/storage failures, loss of required copies or logical deletion Content gap: generic durability latency figures Exact latency ranges are omitted because no representative measurements support them. Replication is not itself a promise that remote copies are durably flushed; verify the acknowledgement contract and failure model. Real knobs that control this: Postgres synchronous_commit: the default on waits for the WAL to be flushed locally (and, if synchronous standbys are configured, on them too). off acknowledges before the flush; a crash can lose up to about three times wal_writer_delay of commits (around 600 ms with the 200 ms default), but never corrupts the database. remote_apply waits until a synchronous standby has applied the commit, so reads there see it. It can be set per transaction. Kafka producer acks: 0 (fire and forget), 1 (leader only), all (all in-sync replicas), combined with the topic's min.insync.replicas. Kafka 3.0 changed the producer defaults to acks=all and idempotence on when settings do not conflict. A bug left idempotence off in 3.0.0 and 3.1.0 unless enabled explicitly; fixes shipped in 3.0.1, 3.1.1 and 3.2.0. min.insync.replicas defaults to 1; a value such as 2 with at least 3 appropriately placed replicas improves tolerance of one replica loss, but no setting alone guarantees zero loss under all failures. Redis persistence: no persistence, RDB snapshots (lose everything since the last snapshot), or the append-only file (AOF) with appendfsync always (slow, safest), everysec (the usual choice: lose about a second of writes) or no (let the OS decide when to flush). Batching (group commit) softens this trade-off: fsync once for many writes. A log that does one fsync at a time can only do so many per second, and each one can make a whole batch durable: For an illustrative log whose flush takes 2 ms, serial one-commit flushes allow about 500 commits/s. If each flush makes 50 commits durable, that same flush capacity can cover about 25,000 commits/s. The improvement comes from sharing the expensive flush, rather than weakening the durability acknowledgement. These illustrative ceilings assume flushes happen one after another and that there are always enough commits waiting to fill a batch. The price is latency: a commit may wait for the next batch, by an amount set by the batching policy, queueing and flush completion time. Kafka and most databases do this, which is why throughput can be high even with durable writes. Throughput vs latency Batching, buffering and compression can improve throughput while adding waiting or CPU work. End-to-end latency can still improve if they reduce a bottleneck: Kafka's linger.ms can wait to fill an incomplete batch, reducing per-request overhead; measure whether that improves throughput for the workload. Recent versions default it to 5 ms (it was 0 before Kafka 4.0); high-volume producers often raise it further. Nagle's algorithm in TCP delays small packets to coalesce them (often disabled with TCP_NODELAY for interactive traffic). Running servers at high utilisation is cheaper but increases queueing latency, as the latency lesson showed. Key takeaways The acknowledgement contract determines which crash and storage failures may lose a successful write. PostgreSQL commit settings, Kafka acknowledgement and ISR settings, and Redis persistence choices need explicit failure models. Group commit shares flush costs across a batch, while batching policy can add per-item waiting. Replicated data is not automatically durably flushed, and no single setting covers every failure. Further reading Asynchronous commit (PostgreSQL) Redis persistence Kafka producer configuration Kafka historical default changes Kafka topic durability configuration

sum: Compare the cost of downtime with resilience spending, and account for transfer, storage and idle headroom.
x: Technical resilience and cloud usage both consume a budget. Make the assumptions visible so a design review can compare the cost of the system with the cost of its failure. Cost Cost is a first-class requirement, not an afterthought. Each nine is expensive. Going from 99.9% to 99.99% often means multi-zone everything, automated failover and on-call staffing. Ask what an hour of downtime actually costs the business. Data transfer adds up. Some cross-zone and internet egress traffic is charged per GB; routes, service exceptions and free allowances vary by provider. A chatty cross-zone microservice architecture can cost more in transfer than in compute. Zone-aware routing (prefer a same-zone replica), compression and consumers that fetch from the nearest replica all cut the bill. Storage tiers. Hot SSD, object storage and archive tiers have different storage, request and retrieval prices; compare current provider pricing for the expected workload. Lifecycle policies move cold data down. Over-provisioning vs autoscaling. Headroom costs money; too little costs outages. To price a time-based availability target, combine its downtime allowance with an explicit cost per hour. A request-based target needs a model of affected requests and their impact. This is a budget scenario, not a prediction that the service will use every minute it is allowed. Compare the plausible reduction in downtime losses with the full extra infrastructure, staffing and operational cost. Include contractual and reputational consequences when they matter. Pricing the trade-off Suppose an outage costs £20k per hour. 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours a year (about £175k of downtime cost if you use the whole budget); 99.99% allows about 53 minutes (about £18k). The upgrade saves roughly £157k a year. If moving to 99.99% costs £300k/year in extra infrastructure and staff, it isn't worth it on these numbers, unless downtime also causes reputational or regulatory damage. Key takeaways An availability target is a business choice: compare additional infrastructure and staffing with the downtime risk it reduces. Cross-zone and internet traffic, retrieval prices and spare capacity can dominate costs. The downtime-budget calculation is a scenario, not a forecast that the full budget will actually be used. Further reading AWS Well-Architected Framework Embracing Risk (Google SRE) Magic Pocket (Dropbox)

t: Choose manageable complexity and record the decision
sum: Compare build with buy, distinguish reversible choices, and communicate the operating cost and assumptions.
x: A design must fit the people who operate it. Compare the value of a component with the complexity it introduces, decide which work the team should own, and leave a record future engineers can reassess. Complexity Complexity is the cost that's easiest to underestimate. Every component adds: Things to deploy, upgrade, monitor and secure. New failure modes and interactions between them. Knowledge the team must hold (and lose when people leave). Questions to ask: Could a simpler design meet the requirements? A Postgres table with SELECT... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is a perfectly good job queue at moderate scale. Is the complexity essential (required by the problem) or accidental (introduced by our choices)? Is the complexity reversible? Prefer decisions you can undo cheaply. Amazon calls these "two-way doors"; spend careful thought on the "one-way doors" (data models, public APIs, core storage). Microservices are the canonical example. They buy independent deployment and team autonomy, at the price of distributed failure modes, network latency, eventual consistency between services and much more operational work. Martin Fowler's advice is to start with a monolith unless you have a strong reason not to. Build vs buy Factor Favours build Favours buy/managed --------- Core differentiator? Yes No Team expertise Deep Thin Time to market Flexible Urgent Scale/cost at volume Huge Moderate Control needed High Standard Buy (or use managed) for undifferentiated heavy lifting: databases, queues, auth, email, payments, observability. Running your own Kafka or Elasticsearch cluster needs real expertise. Build when it's your core competitive advantage, when vendors can't meet a hard requirement, or when scale makes vendor pricing untenable. Dropbox moved most of its storage off S3 onto its own infrastructure ("Magic Pocket") only once it stored hundreds of petabytes. Watch for lock-in, but don't over-pay for portability you'll never use. Abstracting every cloud service "in case we migrate" is itself a cost. Other recurring trade-offs Normalisation vs denormalisation: storage and write simplicity vs read speed. (Databases module.) Push vs pull: precomputing feeds on write (fan-out on write) vs assembling on read. (Case studies.) Synchronous vs asynchronous: simple and immediately consistent vs decoupled and resilient. (Messaging module.) Generality vs specialisation: one flexible store vs purpose-built stores for search, analytics and caching. Freshness vs cost: cache TTLs, CDN expiry. (Caching module.) Communicating trade-offs In design reviews and interviews, it helps to: Present options, not just a conclusion. "We considered A and B; we chose B because..." Quantify. "Synchronous cross-region replication adds ~80 ms per write; our p99 budget is 200 ms." Write it down. An Architecture Decision Record (context, decision, consequences) lets future engineers understand why, and see when the assumptions no longer hold. Key takeaways Every additional component brings deployment work, knowledge and interacting failure modes. Spend careful effort on hard-to-reverse data and API decisions; test simpler reversible choices cheaply. Use managed services for work that does not differentiate the product when the team and costs favour it. Record options, consequences and revisit conditions in an Architecture Decision Record. Further reading Microservice Trade-Offs (Martin Fowler) MonolithFirst (Martin Fowler) Magic Pocket (Dropbox) AWS Well-Architected Framework

t: From a URL to a server address
sum: Trace the browser’s local checks and DNS lookup before it opens a connection.
x: "What happens when you type https://shop.example.com/cart into a browser and press Enter?" is the classic opening question in networking interviews. It's popular because a good answer touches almost every layer a system designer works with: naming, transport, security, load balancing, caching and the application itself. These short lessons walk the path end to end, then zoom into its naming, transport, security and routing decisions. The big picture The DNS arrow row names the hierarchy, rather than messages passed from root to TLD to authoritative servers: the recursive resolver queries each server itself. Roughly, the steps are: Parse the URL and check local caches. Resolve the name to an IP address with DNS. Open a transport connection (TCP, or QUIC for HTTP/3). Negotiate encryption with TLS. Send the HTTP request and receive the response, possibly via a CDN, load balancer and reverse proxy. Render the page, which triggers dozens more requests. Parse the URL and check caches The browser splits the URL into parts: Part Value ------ Scheme https (so port 443) Host shop.example.com Path /cart Query/fragment none Before touching the network, it checks a few things: HSTS list. If the site has sent a Strict-Transport-Security header before (or is on the browser's preload list), the browser upgrades http:// to https:// itself, skipping an insecure redirect. HTTP cache. If a fresh copy of the resource is stored, the browser can use it with zero network traffic. (Cache headers are covered in the caching module.) Existing connections. If there's already an open connection to this origin, it can be reused, skipping steps 2 to 4 entirely. That last point matters enormously. The first request to a site is expensive; later ones are cheap because connections are kept alive. DNS resolution Computers route IP packets by address. A browser may use the operating system resolver or its own resolver, including DNS over HTTPS. Cached answers may avoid a lookup; otherwise a recursive resolver resolves the name. If the recursive resolver has no cached answer, it walks the hierarchy: Ask a root server: "who handles.com?" Ask the.com TLD server: "who handles example.com?" Ask example.com's authoritative server: "what is shop.example.com?" The answer comes back with a TTL, telling every cache how long it may keep it. Latency depends on cache state, resolver placement and the authoritative path. Measurement gap No measured traces accompany this lesson. The timings below are illustrative assumptions, not measurements or universal latency bounds. DNS is also a routing tool The authoritative server doesn't have to give everyone the same answer. Large sites return different IPs depending on where you are, which is the basis of GeoDNS and CDN steering. More on that in the DNS and global traffic lessons. HSTS is learnt over a valid HTTPS connection or from a browser preload entry. Without a prior policy or another browser upgrade mechanism, an explicit first HTTP request still travels unencrypted before a redirect to HTTPS; a header received only on the later HTTPS response cannot protect that earlier request. Content-Length describes a content length in bytes. Changing that declared length does not remove DNS queries, handshakes or redirects; the useful shortcuts above come from cached state or a reusable connection. Key takeaways Local HTTP caches and existing connections can avoid network work entirely. HSTS upgrades known HTTP names locally; an unprotected first HTTP visit may still need a redirect. A recursive resolver follows root, TLD and authoritative referrals when it lacks cached answers. Further reading How browsers work (MDN) What happens when… (GitHub) HTTP Strict Transport Security (RFC 6797) HTTP semantics (RFC 9110)

t: TCP, TLS and the first HTTP request
sum: Understand connection setup, the distance floor and what HTTPS hides from an observer.
x: After resolving the name, a browser needs a transport connection and, for HTTPS, a protected channel. This unit follows a new HTTPS-over-TCP connection; QUIC combines transport and TLS setup differently. The TCP handshake With an IP address, the browser opens a TCP connection to port 443: Without TCP Fast Open, the client waits one round trip (RTT) before sending application data. Use 80 ms as an illustrative London–Virginia RTT, not a guaranteed route measurement. Most of that is physics. Light in fibre travels at roughly 200,000 km/s (about two-thirds of its speed in a vacuum), and London to Virginia is roughly 5,900 km in a straight line. The shortest possible round trip is the distance there and back divided by that speed, which is called the propagation floor: The 2 is there because a round trip goes out and comes back. The result is a floor, not a prediction: real cables don't follow the great-circle route (the shortest path over the Earth's surface), and routers add a little queueing, so measured RTTs are higher. For this assumed fibre path, software cannot beat that propagation floor, which is why putting servers (or CDN edges) close to users matters so much. The TLS handshake For HTTPS, client and server now agree on encryption keys and the server proves its identity with a certificate. TLS 1.3 needs one more round trip; a full TLS 1.2 handshake needs two. (The TLS lesson covers how resumption and 0-RTT shrink this further.) The browser checks that the certificate: covers the hostname (shop.example.com or.example.com), hasn't expired, and chains up to a certificate authority it trusts. The client also sends the hostname in the SNI extension, so a server hosting thousands of sites knows which certificate to present. SNI has traditionally been sent in the clear, so anyone on the path can see which site you're visiting even though they can't read the traffic. Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is a newer extension that hides it, and support is spreading through browsers and CDNs. The HTTP request and response Only now does the browser send: That's the HTTP/1.1 text format. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry the same method, path and headers in binary frames (the Host header becomes the:authority pseudo-header), but the meaning is identical. On the server side, the request might pass through several hops before reaching your code: Hop What it does ------ CDN edge Serves cached content, absorbs attacks Load balancer Picks a healthy backend Reverse proxy TLS, compression, routing App server Runs your code Cache / DB Supplies the data The app builds a response: a status line (200 OK), headers (Content-Type, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie) and a body, often compressed with gzip or Brotli. The HTTP block above is an illustrative request message, not an executable program or a complete packet capture. On a network without a VPN or proxy, a passive observer can see destination IP addresses and traffic timing. With plain DNS and no ECH, it can also learn the queried name and SNI hostname. TLS encrypts the HTTP path, cookies and body. Key takeaways A new TCP connection normally pays one round trip before TLS begins. Distance sets a propagation floor; software can reduce trip counts but cannot remove the physical path. HTTPS protects the path, cookies and response body; plain DNS and unencrypted SNI can still reveal the hostname. Further reading Building blocks of TCP (High Performance Browser Networking) TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446)

t: Count the trips before the first byte
sum: Calculate cold-request latency and explain how a nearby edge changes hits and misses.
x: The handshake path gives us a useful first-byte budget. The following timings are hypothetical inputs, with no loss, retry or additional processing unless a row explicitly includes it. Where the time goes Let's add up a cold first request from London to a single server in Virginia, with a round-trip time of 80 ms: Step Cost ------ DNS (uncached) ~100 ms TCP handshake 80 ms (1 RTT) TLS 1.3 80 ms (1 RTT) HTTP request/response 80 ms + server time Total before first byte ~340 ms + server The table follows a simple model: one DNS lookup, then a fixed number of round trips to the server, then the server's own work. Adding it up gives the time to first byte: Only the last of those round trips actually carries the page; the rest are setup. (The DNS round trips go to resolvers, not to Virginia, which is why that row isn't exactly one RTT.) If the server used TLS 1.2, add another 80 ms. Now put a CDN edge in London, with an RTT of 10 ms: Step Cost ------ DNS (cached at resolver) ~5 ms TCP 10 ms TLS 1.3 10 ms HTTP (cache hit) 10 ms Total ~35 ms The same model, with the shorter round trip to the edge and the edge's own trip to the origin on a miss: In these illustrative assumptions the total is about ten times lower (340 ms versus 35 ms, ignoring server time), combining a nearer endpoint, a faster DNS lookup and a cache hit. Note the hidden assumption: the edge had the response cached. On a miss, the edge must still fetch from Virginia, adding one 80 ms trip over a connection it keeps warm, so the total is closer to 115 ms. That's still about three times better than going direct. Most of this module is about techniques that shrink, skip or move these round trips. Interview framing Don't recite every step at equal depth. Walk the path briefly, then say "the expensive parts are the round trips: DNS, TCP and TLS. Here's how we cut them: caching, connection reuse, TLS 1.3/QUIC and edge termination." That shows you know what matters. Key takeaways A cold TCP/TLS 1.3 request pays DNS plus three server round trips and server work in the simplified model. A nearby CDN makes connection setup cheap; a miss still needs an origin trip. Reuse, caching and endpoint placement solve different parts of the latency budget. Further reading Primer on latency and bandwidth (High Performance Browser Networking) An overview of HTTP (MDN)

sum: Relate rendering requests and error symptoms to the layer that needs investigation.
x: Receiving HTML is the start of rendering, not the end of the page’s network activity. Apply the earlier connection budget separately to each unrelated origin, then use the error’s layer to narrow down failures. Rendering and the requests it triggers The browser parses the HTML and discovers more resources: CSS, JavaScript, images, fonts and API calls. A page may make many additional requests; the count depends on the page. Many go to the same origin and reuse the connection; others go to new origins (a CDN, an analytics domain), each paying its own DNS + TCP + TLS cost. This is why front-end engineers use hints like <link rel="preconnect"> and why consolidating origins can help. Failure modes along the path Every hop can fail, and each failure looks different to the user: DNS failure: "server not found" (NXDOMAIN or timeout). The 2016 Dyn attack took down Twitter, GitHub and others this way. TCP failure: "connection refused" (the host answered with a reset because nothing is listening on that port) or a timeout (a firewall silently dropping packets, or a dead host). Refused is fast; a timeout can hang for many seconds, which is why client connect timeouts matter. TLS failure: certificate warnings, often from an expired certificate. HTTP failure: a 502 Bad Gateway reports an invalid upstream response; a 504 Gateway Timeout reports an upstream timeout. Inspect backend health, the network and proxy configuration; the status alone does not prove which component is faulty. Knowing which layer produced an error is the first step in debugging production incidents. For setup questions, count only what the question asks for. DNS plus TCP plus TLS is the cost before an HTTP request can leave on a new connection; the response then needs another request/response trip and server work. Separate origins can perform setup in parallel, so adding their costs measures aggregate work rather than necessarily the elapsed page-load time. Key takeaways Resources on new unrelated origins may each require fresh DNS, TCP and TLS setup. A refused connection and a silent timeout suggest different transport failure behaviours. A 502 identifies an invalid upstream response; it does not prove which backend or proxy is faulty. Further reading How browsers work (MDN) HTTP semantics: 502 and 504 (RFC 9110)

sum: Follow a recursive resolver and explain why DNS needs both UDP and TCP.
x: DNS (the Domain Name System) maps names like api.example.com to the addresses and services behind them. It's one of the oldest and largest distributed databases on the internet, and it's on the critical path of almost every request. For a system designer, DNS matters for three reasons: It adds latency to the first request. Its caching decides how fast you can move traffic during a failover. It's a cheap, global load-balancing and routing layer. The cast of characters Component Role ------ Stub resolver Library in your OS; asks one resolver Recursive resolver Does the legwork, caches answers Root servers Know who runs each TLD TLD servers Know who runs each domain Authoritative server Holds the actual records There are 13 root server identities (a.root-servers.net to m.root-servers.net), run by 12 independent organisations. Each identity is served from many sites via anycast, and together they are deployed at many locations worldwide (the site count changes over time), so "13 root servers" is a naming detail, not a capacity limit. (The number 13 comes from fitting all their addresses into one small, original-size DNS response.) A full resolution, step by step The recursive resolver asks a root server, which replies with a referral to the.com servers. It asks a.com server, which refers it to example.com's name servers (from the NS records registered with the registrar). It asks the authoritative server, which returns the answer. The recursive resolver does iterative queries (it follows referrals itself); the stub makes a single recursive DNS query ("give me the final answer"). In practice, the root and TLD referrals are almost always cached, so most lookups need only step 3 or are answered entirely from cache. DNS normally runs over UDP port 53: one small packet each way, no handshake. If an answer is too big for the UDP size the client advertised (EDNS(0) lets clients advertise larger buffers; around 1,232 bytes is the common safe default since DNS Flag Day 2020, to avoid IP fragmentation), the server sets the truncated flag and the client retries over TCP. TCP support is mandatory, not optional (RFC 7766), and matters for DNSSEC-signed answers. DNS is also increasingly carried over TLS (DNS over TLS, DoT) or HTTPS (DNS over HTTPS, DoH) for privacy. Key takeaways A stub asks for a final answer; the recursive resolver follows referrals itself. Root server identities are served from many anycast locations. Large or truncated DNS responses need working TCP fallback; blocking TCP 53 can break resolution. Further reading Domain names: implementation and specification (RFC 1035) DNS transport over TCP (RFC 7766) Root server operators

t: Choose DNS records and apex aliases
sum: Choose record types and understand how a provider-resolved apex alias can alter CDN steering.
x: DNS records describe more than addresses. The record type determines what the next resolver does, which matters when a CDN uses the source of a DNS query to choose an edge. Record types you'll actually use Type Maps to Example use --------- A IPv4 address api → 203.0.113.10 AAAA IPv6 address api → 2001:db8::10 CNAME Another name www → shop.cdn.net NS Name servers Delegating a zone MX Mail servers Email for the domain TXT Free text SPF, domain verification SRV Host + port Service discovery CAA Allowed CAs Who may issue certs A few gotchas worth knowing: A CNAME can't sit at the zone apex (example.com itself), because the apex must also hold NS and SOA records and a CNAME cannot coexist with ordinary data at the same owner name (DNSSEC-related records have specific exceptions). Providers offer ALIAS/ANAME records or CNAME flattening to return address records without an ordinary apex CNAME. Supported targets differ: Route 53 alias records support selected AWS resources such as CloudFront, and eligible records in the same hosted zone; they are not aliases to arbitrary external hostnames. CNAME chains cost lookups. www → shop.cdn.net → edge.cdn.net → IP may need extra queries if the intermediate names aren't cached. HTTPS/SVCB records (RFC 9460) are newer: they can tell a browser up front that a site supports HTTP/3, saving a round trip of discovery. Aliases and location signals With an ordinary CNAME, the user’s recursive resolver looks up the CDN’s target name. With a provider-resolved ALIAS or flattening implementation, the DNS provider may perform that lookup itself and return address records. A CDN that chooses an edge from the query’s source address may then see the provider’s location instead of the user’s resolver. Client-subnet forwarding or a CDN-specific integration can change this; it is a deployment-dependent risk, not a universal defect in apex aliases. Test the apex and www from representative user networks before choosing the arrangement. Key takeaways A and AAAA point to addresses; CNAME points to another name. The zone apex needs NS and SOA data, so it cannot be an ordinary CNAME. Provider-side alias resolution can change the resolver-location signal seen by a CDN; behaviour depends on the integration. Further reading DNS clarifications: CNAME data (RFC 2181) CNAME flattening (Cloudflare) Alias versus CNAME targets (Amazon Route 53) Choosing a routing policy (Amazon Route 53)

t: TTL expiry and safe DNS changes
sum: Trace positive and negative cache expiry and plan a migration around existing cached answers.
x: DNS caching reduces query load, but a changed authoritative answer does not instantly reach cached copies. These examples separate ordinary expiry from clients or resolvers that retain old destinations longer. TTLs and caching Every record carries a TTL (time to live) in seconds. Any resolver can cache the answer for that long. Illustrative zone-file fragment, not a complete zone: Caching is why DNS scales: a popular resolver answers millions of queries for google.com from memory. But it creates the central DNS trade-off: Short TTL (30–60 s) Long TTL (hours–days) ------ Fast failover and changes Slow to change More queries, more latency Fewer queries, faster More load on your DNS Resilient if DNS is down Negative answers are cached too. If a name doesn't exist (NXDOMAIN), resolvers cache that for the zone's negative TTL: the smaller of the SOA record's own TTL and its MINIMUM field (RFC 2308).
