Forked snapshots copy pages changed during the snapshot and can require substantial memory headroom. Copy-on-write arithmetic is a first-order model; measure buffers, fragmentation and restart times for the actual deployment. Further reading Redis persistence Warm restart — Memcached

t: Reduce cache connections with a proxy tier
sum: Choose a cache topology and calculate the per-node connection count before and after adding proxies.
x: A large application fleet can create thousands of connections to every cache node. Proxies hide the fleet topology and concentrate backend connection pools into fewer clients. Topology choices Option Good for ------ Single node + replica Workload fits one node Client-side sharding Memcached fleets Redis Cluster Large, self-managing Proxy (mcrouter, Envoy) Many clients, simple config A proxy layer hides the topology from clients and pools connections, which matters when thousands of app instances would otherwise each open connections to every node. Each node holds one pool per client that connects to it: Facebook's mcrouter is a proxy of this kind for Memcached; it also routes invalidations and can replicate writes to pools of servers. Twemproxy (from Twitter) and Envoy's Redis proxy play the same role, and modern Memcached ships its own built-in proxy. Key takeaways A single node with a replica suits a measured workload that fits one primary; partitioning and proxies address different scaling pressures. Per-node connections are direct clients multiplied by each client’s pool size. A proxy tier simplifies routing and reduces backend connections but introduces another service to operate. Further reading mcrouter — Meta Built-in proxy — Memcached Redis Cluster specification

t: Bound duplicate rebuilds when a hot key expires
sum: Calculate a stampede and use bounded request coalescing with ownership-safe distributed locks.
x: A cache that works well becomes load-bearing. The database is sized for the miss rate, not the full traffic. So when the cache misbehaves, the failure is rarely gentle. The database's load scales with the miss ratio, so a change in hit ratio multiplies its load by: So a 99% hit ratio dropping to 0% means 100× the database load, instantly. The following failure-mode units cover these five ways it goes wrong and what large systems do about each. Failure Trigger ------ Stampede One hot key expires Hot key One key gets huge traffic Penetration Requests for keys that don't exist Avalanche Many keys expire at once, or cache dies Cold start Empty cache after deploy/restart 1. Cache stampede (thundering herd) A popular key, say the homepage feed, gets 5,000 requests a second and takes 200 ms to rebuild. It expires. How many requests pile in before the first rebuild finishes? Every request that arrives during the rebuild misses: About 1,000 requests all run the same expensive query at once. The database slows down, so each rebuild takes longer, so more requests pile up. This feedback loop is what turns a stampede into an outage. Fix A: request coalescing (single flight) Make sure only one request rebuilds a given key; the rest wait for its result. In-process, Go's singleflight or a per-key future/promise does this per server. With one coalescing group per server and no explicit forgetting, 50 servers allow at most 50 simultaneous rebuilds for the key; later calls can start new flights. Across servers, use a short lock in the cache: This is adapter-based pseudocode. publish_if_owner must atomically check the lock token and publish only while ownership is current; release must atomically compare-and-delete. A Redis Cluster implementation must colocate lock and data keys in one hash slot. The atomic lock-token comparison rejects publication after lease expiry on that Redis state. An asynchronously replicated lock can be lost during failover, allowing overlapping owners; this is duplicate-work mitigation, not a fault-tolerant mutual-exclusion proof. It also does not by itself order concurrent database invalidations. The lock TTL stops a crashed rebuilder holding it forever. This illustrative function returns its computed value to the caller even if its publication is rejected after lease expiry; a requirement for the latest value needs an additional version-aware read policy. Two details matter in practice: Release only your own lock. If a rebuild takes longer than 10 s, the lock expires and another caller may take it. A plain DELETE would then remove their lock. Store a random token and release with a small Lua script that deletes the key only if it still holds your token. Bound the retries. Waiters should give up after a limit and serve an acceptable stale value or fail with controlled load shedding; unbounded fallback rebuilds recreate the stampede, rather than spinning forever if the lock holder dies. Facebook's leases (the earlier invalidation units) are the same idea built into the cache. Key takeaways Duplicate rebuilds grow with request rate and rebuild time, creating a feedback loop under overload. Single-flight combines requests per process; an ownership-safe cache lock can coordinate across servers. Publish and release only under current ownership, bound waiting, and avoid falling back to unbounded concurrent rebuilds. Further reading singleflight package — Go Distributed locks — Redis Thundering herd problem — Wikipedia Scaling Memcache at Facebook — full paper PDF

t: Refresh stale values or expire them probabilistically
sum: Compare soft/hard expiry with XFetch’s random head start and calculate the early-refresh probability.
x: Readers need not all wait for a popular value to be rebuilt. A retained stale value can hide background work, and probabilistic refresh can begin that work before the nominal expiry. Fix B: serve stale while refreshing Store the value with a soft expiry inside it and a longer hard TTL on the key. After the soft expiry, one request refreshes in the background while everyone else keeps getting the slightly stale value. This is stale-while-revalidate applied to your application cache, so readers with a retained eligible stale value can avoid waiting; after hard expiry, eviction or loss they still miss. Fix C: probabilistic early expiration (XFetch) Instead of everyone noticing expiry at the same instant, each request independently decides to refresh a little early, with a probability that rises as expiry approaches. From Vattani, Chierichetti and Lowenstein (VLDB 2015), each request refreshes when: Because −ln(U) follows an exponential distribution with mean 1, the chance that a single request refreshes early, with some time Δ still left before expiry, works out as: So with a 0.5 s rebuild, each request 2 s before expiry has about a 1.8% chance of refreshing. In code (using 1 − random() so the logarithm never sees zero): With 5,000 requests a second, one of them almost certainly refreshes shortly before expiry, making expiry less likely under load; refresh failure or unlucky sampling can still let it expire. Rarely-read keys almost never refresh early, so you don't waste work on them. beta > 1 refreshes earlier; beta < 1 later. The refresh decision needs no lock or coordination, but overlapping refreshes are still possible; it does not guarantee exactly one rebuilder. Key takeaways Soft expiry permits stale reuse during refresh; hard expiry, eviction or cache loss still produces a miss. XFetch increases refresh probability as expiry approaches and as measured rebuild time grows. Probabilistic decisions reduce stampede risk without guaranteeing one refresh or preventing every eventual expiry. Further reading Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention (VLDB 2015) RFC 5861: stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error Cache stampede — Wikipedia

t: Relieve a single overloaded cache key
sum: Estimate local-cache fills and compare copied keys, read replicas and hot-key detection.
x: Adding ordinary shards spreads different keys, but leaves one exceptionally popular key on one owner. To relieve it, distribute reads for that value while meeting its staleness requirement. 2. Hot keys Sometimes a single key gets an enormous share of traffic: a celebrity's profile, a flash-sale product, a live match score. Partitioning doesn't help, because one key lives on one node. If that node handles 100k ops/s and the key gets 300k ops/s, it saturates regardless of cluster size. Fixes: Local (in-process) cache in front of Redis with a 1–5 s TTL. With 100 app servers, with per-server coalescing and no early eviction, Redis sees roughly 100 fills per TTL period for that key, rather than 300,000 a second: Key replication / splitting: store copies as score:match9#0 to score:match9#9 and have readers pick a random suffix. Load spreads over up to 10 nodes; writers update all copies. If the 10 copies really do land on 10 different nodes, each gets about a tenth of the reads: 300,000 reads a second becomes about 30,000 a second per node. Read replicas for the shard holding the hot key. Detect them: Redis has redis-cli --hotkeys (with LFU policy) and per-key monitoring in managed services. You can't fix what you can't see. Hot keys at Twitter-scale As an illustrative workload, suppose a celebrity with 100 million followers posts. Every timeline render that includes the tweet reads the same tweet object. Process-local caches can absorb repeated reads of the object when the allowed staleness fits; this is a design illustration, not a measured description of Twitter’s deployed system. Key takeaways One hot key can saturate one shard even when the rest of the cluster is idle. Per-process caches reduce Redis fills to roughly one per server per TTL when coalescing and retention assumptions hold. Copied keys or read replicas can spread reads, but copies need coordinated updates and suitable freshness guarantees. Further reading Redis anti-patterns Redis CLI hot-key detection

t: Cache missing records without hiding new records
sum: Use short-lived negative entries for repeated misses and invalidate them when a missing record is created.
x: A normal cache stores successful lookups. Repeated requests for absent records still reach the database unless the absence itself is represented in the cache. 3. Cache penetration Requests for keys that don't exist in the database are never cached (there is nothing to cache), so every one goes straight to the database. This can be accidental (a bug requesting user:undefined) or an attack: someone requests product:<random> 50,000 times a second. Fix A: negative caching Cache the absence: This adapter-based Python fragment illustrates storing a miss marker; it requires a database, cache and marker definition and has no console output. Use a short TTL, because the item may be created soon. Negative caching works well for repeated misses on the same keys. It does not stop an attacker using fresh random keys every time, since each is a new miss, and it fills the cache with markers. When the record is created, invalidate its negative entry as part of the write path. Otherwise readers can continue seeing the cached absence until that entry expires. A delayed negative fill can still race with creation and deletion; strict immediate visibility needs the same leases or retained version safeguards as positive values. Key takeaways Negative caching answers repeated lookups for the same absent key without returning to the database. Use a short TTL and invalidate a negative entry when creating that record so new users are not hidden. Fresh random keys defeat reuse of negative entries; validation, rate limits and set-membership filtering address different parts of penetration. Further reading Cache-aside pattern — Azure Architecture Center Negative cache — Wikipedia

t: Size and maintain a Bloom filter for valid keys
sum: Calculate memory from a false-positive target and preserve complete coverage before rejecting absent IDs.
x: A stream of random invalid IDs has no repeated key for a negative cache to absorb. A compact membership filter can reject most of them before the cache or database lookup. Fix B: Bloom filter A Bloom filter is a compact bit array that answers "is this key possibly in the set?" with no false negatives and a tunable false-positive rate. Put every valid id into it; check it before touching the cache or database. Sizing comes from the standard Bloom filter analysis. With the best number of hash functions, the bits needed per stored id depend only on the false-positive rate you accept: So 9.6 bits per element for a 1% false-positive rate, and the whole filter is: A random invalid id is rejected 99% of the time without any database work. The formula assumes a well-chosen number of hash functions (about 7 for 1%) and that every valid id has been added. Caveats: standard Bloom filters can't delete entries (use a counting filter or Cuckoo filter, or rebuild periodically), and new ids must be included before they become visible, or a negative result must fall back to the source while coverage is uncertain. A stale filter can otherwise reject a valid new id. Also: validate input (reject malformed ids at the edge) and rate-limit clients that generate many misses. Key takeaways A correctly populated Bloom filter rejects definite absence and permits some false positives. About 9.6 bits per valid ID gives an approximate one-percent false-positive rate with an appropriate hash count. Keep new IDs covered before relying on negative results; ordinary Bloom filters need a variant or rebuild strategy for deletion. Further reading Bloom filter — Wikipedia Network applications of Bloom filters: a survey

t: Spread mass expiry and protect the database
sum: Use TTL jitter for synchronised misses and layer capacity limits when the whole cache tier fails.
x: An avalanche affects many keys at once. Jitter addresses synchronised expiry; a cache outage also needs enough remaining capacity, controlled misses or degraded responses. 4. Cache avalanche An avalanche is a mass miss: many keys at once, rather than one hot key. Cause 1: synchronised expiry. A job warms 1 million keys at 09:00 with ex=3600. At 10:00 they all expire together. Fix: TTL jitter. This Python fragment requires random and base_ttl from its caller. It produces a random TTL and has no console output: With a one-hour base TTL the TTL jitter is up to 360 s, so the expiries spread over six minutes. A 10% spread over an hour turns one cliff into a gentle slope. One million keys expiring over 360 s is about 1,000,000 / 360 ≈ 2,800 expiries a second instead of a million at once, and only keys that are read again cause a reload. Cause 2: the cache tier fails. A Redis cluster goes down, or a network partition cuts it off. All traffic falls to the database. Fixes: High availability: replicas and automatic failover, spread across availability zones. Circuit breakers and load shedding: when the database is struggling, fail fast or serve degraded responses rather than queueing every request. Rate-limit misses: cap concurrent database rebuilds per key or per service. Multi-level caching: an in-process cache can carry the hottest keys for a while. A gutter pool (the earlier replication and gutter unit): Facebook sent traffic for failed memcached servers to a small pool of spare servers with short TTLs, so a few failed nodes did not become a database flood. Key takeaways Random TTL jitter spreads a batch’s expiry times; only keys requested again cause reloads. Replica availability, local caches and spare cache pools can absorb part of a tier failure. Compute residual database traffic and shed or cap misses when it exceeds sustainable capacity. Further reading Using load shedding to avoid overload — AWS Builders’ Library Scaling Memcache at Facebook — full paper PDF Key eviction — Redis docs

t: Bring a cold cache online within backend capacity
sum: Calculate a safe traffic ramp and compare pre-warming, peer fills, persistence and shadow traffic.
x: An empty cache behaves like a failed cache until useful keys are filled. Treat a restart, new region or key-format migration as a backend-load event and choose the traffic share from measured misses. 5. Cold starts and warming A new cache cluster, a restart without persistence, or a new region all start empty. With a database sized for a 1% miss rate, sending full production traffic to a cold cache is a self-inflicted avalanche. Warming strategies: Gradual traffic shift: route 1%, then 5%, 25%, 100% of traffic to the new cache over minutes, so it fills while the database copes. Pre-warm from data: load the most-requested keys, say the top 100,000 (from access logs or the old cluster's --hotkeys) before taking traffic. Warm from a peer: Facebook's cold cluster warm-up let a new cluster's clients read misses from a warm cluster's cache instead of the database, bringing cold clusters to full capacity in a few hours instead of a few days. To avoid copying a value that had just been invalidated, deletes in the cold cluster carried a two-second hold-off that made later adds fail; a failed add told the client to read the database instead. The paper records that an invalidation delayed beyond the two-second hold-off can still cause inconsistency; this timing safeguard was an operational trade-off, not a consistency guarantee. Persistence: Redis RDB/AOF restores a node warm after restart. Shadow traffic: mirror reads to the new cache before it serves users. How big can each traffic step be? At each step, the new cache sends the database its share of the traffic times its current miss ratio (traffic not yet moved is still served as before): If spare database capacity is 2% of full traffic, the new cluster alone uses that allowance at 5% traffic and a 60% hit ratio. Include the old cluster’s misses, warming work and other queries when comparing total load with capacity. In practice, leave headroom rather than stepping exactly at capacity. Deploys can flush caches Changing the cache key format (say, adding a field to the serialised object and bumping v2 to v3 in every key) makes every existing entry unreachable. That is a full flush on deploy. Roll it out gradually or run both versions side by side. Putting it together Each layer defends against a different failure. You won't need all of them for every service, but you should know which one you are relying on. Key takeaways Ramp traffic as the hit ratio rises, accounting for both the new cluster’s misses and traffic still served elsewhere. Pre-warming, peer fills, saved state and mirrored reads can reduce cold-start load, with correctness safeguards for copied values. A key-prefix change makes old entries unreachable; stage the transition or serve both key versions. Further reading Scaling Memcache at Facebook — full paper PDF Redis persistence Cache warming — AWS

sum: Use typed tables and ordinary constraints to reject invalid rows, and choose exact representations for money.
x: Relational databases are a common choice for transactional data: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, or a cloud variant such as Amazon Aurora. Before reaching for anything more exotic, you need to know what the relational model gives you for free. The relational model A relational database stores data in database tables (relations). Each table has a fixed set of typed database columns, and each database row is one record. A primary key uniquely identifies each row (users.id). A foreign key is one or more columns referring to an eligible unique or primary key, possibly in the same table (orders.user_id → users.id). The database can enforce that the referenced row exists. Constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK) push data rules into the database so that every application that writes to it obeys them. The schema is the set of table definitions. Relational databases are schema-on-write: data that doesn't fit the schema is rejected when you write it. Document stores often permit flexible document shapes, but many also enforce declared validation rules; readers must handle permitted historical shapes. Store money as integers total_p stores pence. Floating-point types can't represent 0.10 exactly, so sums drift. Use integer minor units or numeric. What ordinary constraints can express A foreign key alone permits NULL, so add NOT NULL when every order must name a user. A CHECK can test the row being written, such as a nonnegative total; PostgreSQL does not support a CHECK that continuously validates other table rows. A rule such as "invoice total equals the sum of its lines" needs a suitable redesign or another enforcement mechanism. Key takeaways A primary key identifies a row; foreign keys and NOT NULL work together to require a valid reference. UNIQUE and CHECK enforce declared rules, with limits on what a row constraint can express. Store currency in integer minor units or exact numeric values. Further reading PostgreSQL: Constraints

sum: Read a query plan, choose a join shape, and avoid LEFT JOIN filtering errors and N+1 round trips.
x: SQL separates the result you ask for from the access path that produces it. Use that separation to fetch related data in one deliberate query rather than many network trips. SQL is declarative You describe what you want; the query planner decides how to get it: which index to use, which join algorithm, which order to join tables in. This is a big deal. The same query can go from a full scan to an index lookup after you add an index, with no application change. The SQL fragments assume the tables and suitable rows already exist; results depend on those rows. The query above returns at most ten users, ranked by paid spend in pence. Run EXPLAIN in front of a query to see the plan the database chose, or EXPLAIN ANALYZE to also run it and report how long each step actually took. Because ANALYZE really executes the statement, wrap an UPDATE or DELETE in a transaction you roll back. Joins A join combines rows from two tables on a condition. Join Returns ------ INNER Only rows matching on both sides LEFT All left rows, NULLs if no match FULL All rows from both sides CROSS Every combination (rarely wanted) Under the hood the planner picks one of three algorithms: Nested loop: for each outer row, look up matches in the inner table. Great when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index. Hash join: build a hash table on the smaller input, then stream the larger one past it. Good for large, unsorted inputs with equality conditions. Merge join: sort both sides on the join key (or read them in index order) and walk them together. A WHERE clause can undo a LEFT JOIN users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id WHERE o.status = 'paid' silently drops users with no orders: their o.status is NULL, and the WHERE filters NULL out. To keep them, put the condition in the join: ON o.user_id = u.id AND o.status = 'paid'. The N+1 query problem An ORM loop that loads 100 orders and then runs one query per order to fetch its user makes 101 round trips. At 1 ms each that is 101 ms of round-trip latency before execution. A join can make one trip; fetching orders then users in bulk usually makes two. The name comes from the count: one query for the list, plus one more for each of the N rows in it. Because every query waits for a full network round trip, the time grows with the length of the list even when each query is fast: For the 100 orders above at 1 ms per round trip: A join replaces the N extra queries with none, so Q falls to 1. The formula assumes the queries run one after another; an ORM that batches or runs them in parallel changes the count, which is why you should check what your ORM actually sends. Key takeaways The planner chooses indexes and join algorithms from the query and data. Move a right-side filter into ON when a LEFT JOIN must retain unmatched left rows. N+1 loading makes one list query plus one query per row; joins or batching reduce round trips. Further reading PostgreSQL: Joins Between Tables PostgreSQL: Using EXPLAIN

sum: Trace a two-account transfer and separate database guarantees from application invariants and external effects.
x: A transfer changes two balances but represents one business event. Transactions let the database commit those row changes together; the application must still define which business rules make the transfer valid. ACID A transaction groups several reads and writes into one logical unit. ACID describes what the database promises about it. Atomicity: all of the transaction's writes happen, or none do. If the server crashes halfway through, the partial work is rolled back. "Abortability" would be a better name. ACID consistency: the transaction takes the database from one valid state to another, according to your invariants (constraints, foreign keys). This is mostly the application's responsibility; the database only enforces the constraints you declared. Transaction isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-finished work. How strong this is depends on the isolation level, which is a whole lesson later in this module. Durability: with a durable commit configuration and functioning storage, an acknowledged commit survives the failures covered by that configuration. In practice this means it has been flushed to a write-ahead log on disk (and possibly to replicas). The SQL assumes an accounts(id, balance) table with both rows present and a business decision that permits the transfer. Neither UPDATE by itself proves those prerequisites. If the process dies after the first UPDATE, atomicity guarantees that the debit is undone. No money vanishes. The C in ACID isn't the C in CAP ACID consistency means "invariants hold". CAP consistency means linearizability across replicas. Same word, unrelated ideas. Consistency models get their own module. Keep the guarantee within its boundary Atomicity covers transactional database row writes. It does not roll back an email already sent, and sequence values can remain consumed after an abort. A business rule such as "never overdraw" still needs a constraint or concurrency-safe application decision. Key takeaways Atomicity hides all transactional row changes from an aborted transfer. The database enforces declared constraints; the application must encode its other invariants. Durability depends on commit configuration, functioning storage and the failures that configuration covers. Further reading www.postgresql.org: tutorial transactions PostgreSQL: Write-Ahead Logging

sum: Remove duplicated facts, preserve historical prices, and maintain deliberate copies without losing correctness.
x: A fact copied into many rows is difficult to change consistently. Start by separating facts, then duplicate only a measured read path with a clear synchronisation rule. Normalisation Normalisation means structuring tables so that each fact is stored in exactly one place. The goal is to avoid update anomalies: if a customer's address is copied into every order row, changing it means updating hundreds of rows, and missing one leaves the data contradicting itself. The normal forms, informally: 1NF: each column holds one atomic value; no repeating groups like phone1, phone2, phone3. 2NF: each non-prime attribute depends on the whole of every candidate key, not a proper subset of a composite candidate key. 3NF: non-key columns depend only on the key, not on other non-key columns. ("The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.") For example, employees(id, dept_id, dept_name) breaks 3NF: dept_name depends on dept_id, which depends on id. Denormalisation Normalised data needs joins to reassemble. At large scale, or when one read path dominates, you may deliberately denormalise: duplicate data so that reads are cheaper. Normalised Denormalised --------- Writes One place to update Many copies to keep in sync Reads Joins needed Single lookup Storage Smaller Larger Risk Slow joins Inconsistent copies Common, sensible denormalisations: A comment_count column on posts, updated in the same transaction as the insert into comments. Copying the price into order_lines at purchase time. This one is actually correct modelling: the historical price is a different fact from the current price. Materialised views or read models built from the normalised source of truth. Rule of thumb Start normalised. Denormalise a specific read path when you've measured that it's too slow, and decide up front how the copies will be kept in sync (same transaction, trigger, or an async pipeline that tolerates lag). Why relational databases scale further than people think Single-node capacity depends on transaction shape, indexes, contention, hardware and recovery objectives. Measure these before introducing distribution. Universal throughput figures and company deployment anecdotes are absent because no matching benchmark or dated primary incident source is established here. The usual reasons to move beyond a single relational primary are write throughput beyond one machine, data volume beyond one machine, or very specific access patterns, all of which later lessons cover. Measure the read path before sharding If a primary is busy mostly answering reads, first investigate the slow query plans and suitable indexes. A cache and read replicas can offload eligible reads while writes remain on the primary. This adds freshness and failure trade-offs, covered in the replication units; do not send reads that require current primary state to a stale replica. Write rate or dataset size alone does not establish that sharding is necessary. Key takeaways Normal forms avoid partial-key and transitive dependencies that create update anomalies. A purchase price and a current catalogue price are different facts. Update transactional counters with their source writes; measure read bottlenecks before distributing data. Further reading PostgreSQL: Constraints www.postgresql.org: performance tips PostgreSQL: Hot standby

sum: Design exact-key and DynamoDB keyed access while checking session expiry, hot-item limits and Redis persistence.
x: "NoSQL" isn't one thing. It's a loose label for databases that drop part of the relational model, usually joins, a fixed schema or multi-row transactions, in exchange for something else: horizontal scale, a more natural data shape, or speed on one access pattern. The useful way to think about each family: what does it make cheap, and what does it make expensive? Key-value stores The simplest model: a mapping from keys to values, whether embedded on one host or distributed. You GET(key), PUT(key, value) and DELETE(key). In a pure key-value model the value is opaque; products such as Redis and DynamoDB also understand structured values and offer additional operations. Examples: Redis (in memory), Amazon DynamoDB, Riak, etcd, RocksDB (embedded). Cheap: lookups by exact key. Actual latency depends on deployment, payload, consistency, load and network distance. Expensive: anything else. "Find all users in Leeds" means scanning everything unless you build your own index. Check durability before treating an in-memory store as a system of record. Redis by default only snapshots to disk periodically (RDB), so a crash loses everything since the last snapshot. Its append-only file with appendfsync everysec narrows that to about a second of writes. DynamoDB extends the model a little. Each item has a partition key (PK, hashed to pick a partition) and an optional sort key (SK), and items with the same partition key are stored together, sorted by sort key. That lets you do range queries within one partition: A Query(PK = USER#42, SK begins_with ORDER#) returns that user’s orders in normalized date-key order; results larger than the Query page limit require pagination. This is the basis of single-table design: you model access patterns first, then shape keys to serve them. DynamoDB in numbers DynamoDB targets single-digit millisecond service latency for common operations, rather than guaranteeing every request latency; items are at most 400 KB, partitions of up to 10 GB, and each partition serving up to 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second. DynamoDB splits busy partitions automatically, but it can't split a single hot item, so hot keys hit those limits long before the table does. Switching to on-demand billing doesn't lift them. Expiry, ordering and another lookup Redis expires keys on access. DynamoDB TTL removes expired items asynchronously, typically within days, so check the session expiry timestamp in the application before accepting it. Cleanup timing is not an authentication deadline. For newest-first DynamoDB orders, use one fixed-width timestamp format and timezone in the sort key, and Query with ScanIndexForward=false. A lookup by order id needs another key mapping, such as a global secondary index (GSI); its reads are eventually consistent. A GSI is an extra index with its own keys, not a way to scan the table cheaply. A strongly consistent read of an item up to 4 KB uses one read unit; an eventually consistent read uses half. For a single hot 1 KB item, the 3,000-unit partition ceiling therefore permits at most 3,000 strongly consistent reads per second or 6,000 eventual reads per second. A read cache can help when stale values are acceptable, but it changes the freshness guarantee. Key takeaways Exact-key lookups suit sessions and other known access patterns. DynamoDB partition and sort keys support ordered queries within a key; an index supports a different lookup. Expiry cleanup and crash durability need explicit checks rather than assumptions. Further reading Amazon DynamoDB Developer Guide: What is DynamoDB? docs.aws.amazon.com: Query docs.aws.amazon.com: TTL Redis: Persistence

sum: Choose embedded or referenced data and keep growing arrays below document and workload limits.
x: A document groups data that belongs together. The useful boundary is a bounded aggregate that can be read and updated as a unit, rather than an ever-growing container for all history. Document stores A document store keeps self-contained, nested documents, usually JSON or BSON. Unlike a key-value store, the database understands the structure, so it can index and query fields inside the document. Examples: MongoDB, Couchbase, Firestore, and Postgres's own jsonb columns. Cheap: loading a whole aggregate (an order with its lines) in one read, without joins. Flexible schemas can ease evolution, but incompatible shape changes still need validation, migration or reader compatibility. Expensive: many-to-many relationships and cross-document joins. MongoDB has $lookup, but it's not what the engine is optimised for. The modelling rule is embed what you read together, reference what you share. Order lines belong inside the order. A product shared by thousands of orders should be referenced by id, not copied everywhere. Also keep embedded arrays bounded. A MongoDB document is capped at 16 MiB; an ever-growing array increases size and processing pressure, although updates and replication can use deltas rather than rewriting/transmitting the whole document. The bucket pattern fixes this: one document per device per hour, say, each holding that hour's readings. Schemaless isn't schema-free The schema still exists; it has moved into your application code. Every reader must handle every historical shape of the document. MongoDB's JSON Schema validation can put some of it back in the database. Transactions and arbitrary relationships MongoDB supports multi-document transactions, so "NoSQL" does not mean transactions are impossible. However, a new workload dominated by arbitrary joins and multi-entity updates can be simpler to model in a relational store. Compare the workload and complexity rather than assuming a missing product feature. Key takeaways Embed bounded data read with one aggregate; reference shared entities. Flexible documents still need schema compatibility and validation. Time buckets bound growing arrays; arbitrary joins and multi-entity updates can favour relational modelling. Further reading MongoDB: Data modeling www.mongodb.com: unbounded arrays www.mongodb.com: transactions

sum: Shape Cassandra partitions and clustering columns around a known query without growing one partition forever.
x: A wide-column schema begins with the query you need to answer. Follow the partition key to the owning data, then use clustering order to select a bounded range. Wide-column stores Wide-column stores group related cells into rows and column families, but their partitioning differs. Cassandra and ScyllaDB hash a partition key and order rows within that partition by clustering columns. HBase and Google Bigtable instead range-partition lexicographically ordered row keys; the Cassandra CQL example below does not describe their key layout. Here (sensor_id, day) is the partition key, and ts sorts rows within it. "Latest 100 readings for sensor X today" is a partition-targeted ordered query; multiple SSTables, replicas or storage reads may still be involved. Cheap: huge write throughput (they're built on LSM trees, covered in the indexing lesson), horizontal growth when key distribution and workload permit it, multi-datacentre replication. Expensive: queries that don't start with the partition key. No joins. You typically make one table per query, duplicating data across them. That's why the example puts day in the partition key. Keyed by sensor_id alone, a sensor reporting every second would add 86,400 rows a day to one partition, forever. The growth is simple multiplication: With day in the partition key, each partition holds at most one day of one sensor's readings and then stops growing. Huge partitions overload the replicas that own them and slow compaction and repair, so choose time buckets using measured serialized size, tombstones and query/repair behavior; a fixed size target is a rule of thumb, not a universal limit. Specific company deployment counts are omitted because this review did not establish a reliable dated primary-source basis for both claims. Key takeaways Cassandra hashes partition keys and orders rows within them by clustering columns. A day in the partition key bounds each sensor partition to one day of readings. Queries without a usable partition key can require expensive filtering across the cluster. Further reading Apache Cassandra: Data modeling

sum: Use explicit nodes and edges for multi-hop relationships while recognising traversal and sharding costs.
x: When a query repeatedly follows relationships, represent those relationships directly. The benefit depends on the amount of connected data visited, not just the label "graph database". Graph databases When the relationships are the data (social networks, fraud rings, recommendation, access control), a graph database stores nodes and edges directly, and some engines use direct adjacency structures. Edge traversal cost still depends on caching, representation and network placement; not every graph database uses the same storage design. The Cypher assumes existing Person nodes and FRIEND relationships. Returned names depend on that graph; LIMIT without ORDER BY does not promise which twenty appear. Examples: Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, JanusGraph, Dgraph. Cheap: multi-hop traversals ("within 3 hops"), path finding, pattern matching. Expensive: bulk aggregation over all nodes, and horizontal sharding (cutting a graph across machines makes traversals cross the network). A fixed-depth SQL traversal can use self-joins; variable-depth traversal can use a recursive CTE. Intermediate results can grow quickly with branching and depth, but indexes, pruning and the query plan determine the actual cost. Why adjacency helps Neo4j uses index-free adjacency: after locating a starting node, traversal follows its stored relationships. The work is proportional to the neighbours actually visited; a high-degree node or deep expansion can still be expensive. An SQL graph can use indexes and recursive CTEs too, so benchmark the real graph and query rather than expecting a universal speedup. Key takeaways Graph stores represent relationships directly and can follow adjacency structures efficiently. The work still depends on the neighbours visited, caching and placement. Splitting a graph across machines can turn traversals into network requests. Further reading neo4j.com: graphdb concepts neo4j.com: match

sum: Model timestamped metrics, choose tags and fields for the deployed engine, and bound retained detail.
x: Metrics are naturally organised by time. Their storage plan needs a retention boundary, an aggregation strategy and metadata choices that fit the specific engine. Time-series databases Metrics, IoT readings and financial ticks share a pattern: append-only writes, ordered by time, queried by time range and aggregated (avg per minute). Old data is downsampled or deleted. Examples: InfluxDB, TimescaleDB (a Postgres extension), Prometheus (for metrics), QuestDB. Tricks: columnar compression of timestamps (delta-of-delta encoding) and values (Gorilla-style XOR compression), time-partitioned storage so eligible old partitions or files can be removed together, and built-in retention policies and continuous aggregates. InfluxDB organises data into a measurement with tags (indexed metadata like host=web-1), fields (the values) and a timestamp. Each unique combination of tag values is a series. In InfluxDB 1.x and 2.x, watch cardinality: a tag with millions of distinct values (such as a user id) blows up the series index. InfluxDB 3 uses a different engine and supports high-cardinality tags; choose tags and fields from its version-specific schema guidance rather than carrying the TSM rule over unchanged. Bound the older detail For example, keep fine-grained CPU readings for seven days, then retain one-minute averages with a suitable longer retention period. In the InfluxDB 2.x TSM model, frequently filtered host names suit tags, while the measured CPU percentage is a field. Check the combined series cardinality and available resources, not just one tag in isolation. Key takeaways Time-series workloads append readings and query or aggregate time ranges. Retention and downsampling bound how much old detail is stored. InfluxDB tag-cardinality guidance depends on the engine generation. Further reading InfluxDB 2: Resolve high series cardinality docs.influxdata.com: schema design

sum: Explain near-real-time search visibility and compare the core strengths of the NoSQL families.
x: Search is a derived access path with its own visibility rules. A successful index write and a successful search for that write are different events. Search engines Elasticsearch and OpenSearch (both built on Apache Lucene) maintain inverted indexes: a map from each term to the documents containing it. They're excellent at full-text relevance ranking, fuzzy matching and faceted filters, and are usually fed from a primary database rather than being the system of record. They're also near-real-time: a newly indexed document becomes searchable only after the next index refresh, every second by default for actively searched Elastic Stack indexes; serverless deployments and OpenSearch settings may differ. Check the configured interval. Fetching a document by id is real-time. Search architecture is covered in the architecture module. Summary table Family Best at Weak at --------- Key-value Lookup by key Queries on values Document Whole aggregates Many-to-many Wide-column Writes at scale Ad-hoc queries Graph Multi-hop links Bulk analytics Time-series Time-range stats Updates, joins Search Text relevance Source of truth The lines are blurring Postgres has jsonb, full-text search and extensions for time series (TimescaleDB) and graphs (Apache AGE). MongoDB has multi-document ACID transactions. DynamoDB has transactions too. Pick based on the core access pattern, not the feature checklist. Key takeaways Inverted indexes map terms to matching documents. An indexed write becomes searchable after refresh; fetching by id uses a different visibility path. Compare the core access pattern and trade-offs rather than a product feature checklist. Further reading Elasticsearch: Near real-time search www.elastic.co: operation get

t: Estimate the cost of a table scan
sum: Calculate table pages and scan time, and compare the work with a selective indexed lookup.
x: Without a suitable access path, a database may need a full scan; partition pruning, zone maps or other mechanisms can sometimes reduce it. An index is an extra data structure, kept in sync with the table, that lets the database jump straight to the matching rows. Indexes can substantially reduce work for selective queries, but add storage and write cost. The cost of not having one Take a 100 million row orders table on 8 KB pages, about 100 rows per page: one million pages, or 8 GB. A full scan at 1 GB/s takes around 8 seconds. A B-tree lookup touches 3–4 pages: well under a millisecond if they're cached. To estimate how long a full scan takes, work out how many pages the table fills, how many bytes that is, and divide by how fast the disk can stream them: With the numbers above: This assumes the whole scan is sequential and nothing is cached; real scans can be faster if pages are in memory and slower if the disk is busy. Key takeaways Scan cost grows with the pages read rather than the few rows you hoped to return. The worked eight-second estimate assumes uncached sequential reads at the stated speed. Indexes trade a faster access path for extra storage and maintenance. Further reading www.postgresql.org: indexes PostgreSQL: Using EXPLAIN

t: B-tree depth and clustered row layout
sum: Estimate shallow tree depth and explain how InnoDB primary-key layout affects secondary indexes and inserts.
x: A B-tree reaches a key through a small number of wide pages. Its row-pointer design also explains why the same primary-key choice can affect the size and locality of every secondary index. B-trees The B-tree (strictly, the B+tree) is the default index in Postgres, MySQL InnoDB, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite. Each node is one database page (typically 4–16 KB) holding hundreds of keys, so the tree is very wide and shallow. With a B-tree fan-out of 500, four levels address 500⁴ ≈ 62 billion keys. Lookups walk root → leaf: O(log n), usually 3–4 page reads, and the top levels are almost always in memory. Here n is the number of keys in the index. Leaves are sorted and linked, so range scans (BETWEEN, >, ORDER BY) are efficient. Writes update pages in place. Inserting into a full page splits it into two. To survive crashes, every change is first written to the write-ahead log (see the storage internals lesson). Why so shallow? Each level multiplies the number of keys the tree can reach by the B-tree fan-out, the number of child pointers per page. So the depth only grows with the logarithm of the number of keys: For this simplified estimate, assume full internal pages with 500 children and full leaves with 500 keys. Actual occupancy and leaf capacity can differ. For a B-tree fan-out of 500: That is the meaning of O(log n) here: doubling n adds almost nothing to the height. The estimate assumes full pages; real pages are rarely completely full, which lowers the effective B-tree fan-out a little but barely changes the height. In InnoDB, the table is a B-tree clustered on the primary key, and secondary indexes store the primary key as their pointer. In Postgres, the table is an unordered heap and every index points to a physical tuple location. That design choice has practical consequences in InnoDB: A non-covering secondary-index lookup generally needs two B-tree walks: find the primary key in the secondary index, then find the row in the clustered index. Every secondary index entry carries a copy of the primary key, so a wide key (a 36-character UUID string) bloats every index. Rows are stored in key order, so random keys (UUIDv4) insert all over the tree and cause page splits, while increasing keys (auto-increment, or time-ordered UUIDv7) append at the right-hand edge. Such a query is covered by the secondary index, but InnoDB may still visit the clustered record for MVCC visibility. When a secondary index covers the result An InnoDB secondary index on email also carries the primary-key id. Queries returning just email or id, or counting matching entries, have all required columns there; returning name needs the clustered row too. Being covered does not remove every possible MVCC visibility visit to the clustered index. Covering PostgreSQL queries is explained in the unit on composite and covering indexes. Key takeaways Wide B-tree fan-out makes B-trees shallow; sorted leaves also support ranges. InnoDB clusters rows by primary key and copies that key into secondary indexes. Wide random primary keys increase secondary-index size and scatter inserts. Further reading www.postgresql.org: indexes MySQL: Clustered and secondary indexes www.rfc-editor.org: rfc9562

sum: Trace buffered writes, sorted-file flushes and compaction, and compare the trade-offs with B-trees.
x: An LSM engine improves write locality by collecting changes and flushing sorted runs. Background merging pays for that write path with additional read, rewrite and space work. LSM trees The log-structured merge tree takes the opposite approach: never update in place, always append. Writes go to an append-only log (for durability) and an in-memory sorted structure, the memtable. When the memtable fills (say 64 MB), it's written out as an immutable sorted file, an SSTable. Background compaction merges SSTables, discarding overwritten values and deletion markers (tombstones). Reads check the memtable, then SSTables from newest to oldest. Bloom filters let a read skip files that definitely don't contain the key. LSM trees power RocksDB, LevelDB, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, Bigtable, and the storage layers of CockroachDB, TiDB and YugabyteDB. B-tree LSM tree --------- Writes Random, in place Sequential, batched Reads One place to look Several levels Space Pages part-empty Old versions until compacted Latency Predictable Compaction spikes Rule of thumb B-trees favour reads and predictable latency; LSM trees favour write throughput and compression. Both are excellent; the details are in the storage internals lesson. Key takeaways Writes enter a WAL and sorted memtable before flushing to immutable SSTables. Compaction merges files and discards obsolete versions and eligible tombstones. Measure the write-locality benefit against read work and background compaction cost. Further reading RocksDB Overview

sum: Order index columns for a query, include needed payloads, and select a partial or specialised access path.
x: Design an index for the predicate, ordering and returned columns of a real query. Column order decides the contiguous range you can seek; extra payloads decide whether table visits are necessary. Composite indexes A composite (multi-column) index sorts by the first column, then by the second within ties, and so on, like a phone book sorted by surname then first name. This index serves: WHERE customer_id = 42 WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at > '2026-09-01' WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 with no sort step With many distinct customers, it may not efficiently serve WHERE created_at > '2026-09-01' alone, because entries for that date range are scattered across every customer. This is the leftmost-prefix rule. Some engines soften the rule with a skip scan (MySQL 8.0, Oracle, and Postgres from version 18): when the leading column has only a few distinct values, they probe the index once per value. With millions of customers that doesn't help, so design the index for the query rather than relying on it. Column order: equality first, then range Put columns tested with = first and the range or sort column last. With (created_at, customer_id), a conventional scan may cover September entries for many customers; skip scan and other planner choices can change that. Covering indexes Normally an index lookup finds a row pointer, then fetches the row from the table: an extra random read per row. If the index contains every column the query needs, the database can answer from the index alone. That's a covering index, and Postgres calls the resulting plan an index-only scan. These SQL fragments assume an orders table with the named columns. Returned values and whether a plan avoids heap visits depend on the data and visibility map. INCLUDE adds non-key payload columns to the leaves without affecting sort order. For a query returning 20 rows, that can avoid heap visits when the visibility conditions permit; avoided visits are not necessarily physical disk reads. In Postgres, index-only scans also depend on the visibility map: if a page has recent, unvacuumed changes, Postgres still visits the heap to check row visibility. Keep autovacuum healthy on tables where you rely on them. Other index types Hash indexes: equality only, no ranges. Rarely better than a B-tree in Postgres. Partial indexes: index only the rows you query, e.g. WHERE status = 'pending'. Much smaller. Expression indexes: ON users (lower(email)) serves WHERE lower(email) =.... GIN (inverted): for jsonb, arrays and full-text search. GiST/SP-GiST, BRIN: geometric data, and very large naturally ordered tables (BRIN stores min/max per block range and is tiny). Key takeaways Composite indexes sort by the first key, then by later keys within ties. Covering indexes contain the queried columns; PostgreSQL still needs sufficient visibility information. Partial indexes store only qualifying rows; other types serve expressions, documents or ordered block ranges. Further reading PostgreSQL: Multicolumn indexes PostgreSQL: Index-only scans and covering indexes PostgreSQL: Partial indexes

sum: Diagnose write overhead, HOT eligibility and sequential scans before adding or removing an index.
x: An index earns its place only when the work it saves is worth its maintenance. Diagnose the actual write cost and chosen read plan before adding another structure or removing an existing one. The cost of indexes on writes Each index adds maintenance for writes affecting its entries; partial indexes and HOT updates are important exceptions. An INSERT into a Postgres heap table with 6 B-tree indexes inserts one heap tuple and 6 index entries; InnoDB uses a clustered B-tree for the table itself. Each structure adds buffer, I/O and WAL work. An UPDATE touching an indexed column updates that index too. In Postgres, updating any column covered by a B-tree (or other non-summarising) index prevents a HOT update (heap-only tuple update), so ordinary indexes need entries for the new tuple version; summarizing indexes such as BRIN have different maintenance. A HOT update also needs free space on the same page, which is why hot tables often use a fillfactor below 100. Indexes consume memory. If they don't fit in the buffer cache, lookups and inserts start hitting disk. More indexes give the planner more choices, which occasionally means a bad choice. Audit unused indexes In Postgres, pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0 means no scans were recorded in the observed statistics window; it does not mean the index has no purpose. Before dropping one, check statistics resets, replicas, rare jobs and especially uniqueness, primary-key or exclusion constraints. Constraint enforcement is a reason to keep an index even without query scans. Why an index might not be used The query wraps the column in a function: WHERE date(created_at) =... can't use an index on created_at. Rewrite as a range. Low selectivity: if 40% of a 100-million-row table matches, a sequential scan of its million pages is cheaper than 40 million index lookups that jump around the heap. The crossover is often at a few percent of rows, and depends on how well the table's physical order matches the index. Type mismatch: PostgreSQL can reject a text-to-integer comparison unless you cast explicitly. Casting the indexed column may prevent an ordinary index seek; converting the parameter to the column type can preserve it. Leading wildcard: LIKE '%smith' can't use a B-tree (use a trigram GIN index). Stale statistics: run ANALYZE so the planner knows the data distribution. Key takeaways Indexes add storage and write work; PostgreSQL HOT updates can avoid ordinary index maintenance. Zero recorded scans alone do not establish that an index is safe to remove. Functions, low selectivity and stale statistics can make a raw-column index unsuitable. Further reading PostgreSQL: Heap-only tuples (HOT) PostgreSQL: Using EXPLAIN www.postgresql.org: monitoring stats

sum: Distinguish dirty reads, lost updates, phantoms and write skew from concrete interleavings.
x: The "I" in ACID is the slipperiest letter. Perfect isolation, serializability, means concurrent transactions produce the same result as some serial order. It's expensive, so databases offer weaker isolation levels that allow certain anomalies. Knowing exactly which anomalies your level allows is the difference between correct code and a race condition that only appears under load. The anomalies Dirty read Reading data another transaction has written but not committed. If it rolls back, you acted on data that never existed. Dirty write Overwriting another transaction's uncommitted write. Mainstream transactional engines prevent dirty writes, commonly through write locks; the exact mechanism is implementation-specific. Non-repeatable read (read skew) Reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting different values, because someone committed in between. A backup or report reading many rows across a long transaction sees a mixture of before and after states: totals that never existed at any instant. Lost update Two read-modify-write cycles interleave, and one overwrites the other. Phantom read A query's set of matching rows changes because another transaction inserted or deleted rows that match the condition. Row locks can't prevent this: the new rows didn't exist to be locked. Write skew Two transactions read the same data, make a decision based on it, then write to different rows. Each is fine alone; together they break an invariant. The on-call doctors Rule: at least one doctor must be on call. Alice and Bob are both on call, and both feel ill. 1. Alice's transaction: count(on_call) = 2, so she sets herself off. 2. Bob's transaction, concurrently: also sees 2, sets himself off. 3. Both commit. Nobody is on call. They updated different rows, so no write conflict was detected. This is write skew, and snapshot isolation allows it. Other examples: double-booking a meeting room, two users claiming the same username via a "check then insert" pattern, overspending a balance split across rows. Key takeaways Dirty reads use uncommitted data; dirty writes overwrite uncommitted work. Repeated reads and separate report statements can observe different committed states. Lost updates overwrite a concurrent change; write skew writes different rows and breaks a shared invariant. Further reading PostgreSQL: Transaction isolation Ports and Grittner: Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL

sum: Compare PostgreSQL, InnoDB, Oracle and SQL Server rather than treating a level name as a universal guarantee.
x: The anomaly traces explain what can go wrong. Now compare how each engine implements named isolation levels: the same name can protect a different set of reads and writes. The SQL standard levels Level Forbids ------ Read Uncommitted Nothing beyond dirty writes Read Committed + dirty reads Repeatable Read + non-repeatable reads Serializable + phantoms; must be serializable The standard defined these in terms of a few anomalies and is famously ambiguous: it doesn't mention lost updates or write skew at all. Real databases use the same names for quite different things. What each database actually gives you PostgreSQL (default Read Committed): Read Uncommitted behaves exactly like Read Committed; Postgres never shows dirty data. Read Committed takes a new snapshot per statement. Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation. Unlike the standard's minimum, it also prevents phantoms, and it aborts a transaction that tries to update a row someone else changed after its snapshot. Write skew is still allowed. Serializable is SSI, truly serializable (since 9.1). MySQL InnoDB (default Repeatable Read): Read Uncommitted really does allow dirty reads. Repeatable Read is a hybrid. Plain SELECTs read from a snapshot taken at the first read. But UPDATE, DELETE and locking reads (FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE) use current locking reads. Locking depends on the access path: a unique-index lookup of a unique key locks the record alone, while range scans generally use next-key (row plus gap) locks. There's no first-committer-wins check, so a read-then-write race silently loses an update, and write skew is possible. Serializable is Repeatable Read with plain SELECTs turned into SELECT... FOR SHARE (when autocommit is off): lock-based, effectively 2PL. Oracle (default Read Committed): Offers only Read Committed and Serializable (plus a Read Only mode). There is no Read Uncommitted or Repeatable Read. Its Serializable is snapshot isolation: it raises ORA-08177 on a write-write conflict but allows write skew, so it isn't truly serializable. SQL Server (default Read Committed, implemented with short read locks unless READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT is on, which it is by default in Azure SQL Database) offers a separate SNAPSHOT level that is snapshot isolation, and a Serializable level that uses key-range locks (2PL). Names lie "Repeatable Read" means snapshot isolation in Postgres and a snapshot-plus-locking hybrid in MySQL; "Serializable" means SSI in Postgres and snapshot isolation in Oracle. Always check what your database's level actually prevents. Jepsen's analyses have repeatedly found databases that didn't deliver the isolation they advertised. Follow current writes as well as snapshots InnoDB transactions also see their own writes. If a plain snapshot read counts ten new jobs, another transaction commits an eleventh, and an UPDATE changes all currently new jobs, that UPDATE can change eleven. A later plain SELECT can see all eleven changes because they now belong to the reading transaction. PostgreSQL Repeatable Read would not include the newly inserted job in that UPDATE. Key takeaways PostgreSQL Read Committed takes one snapshot per statement; Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation. InnoDB Repeatable Read mixes snapshot SELECTs with current locking writes. Oracle Serializable is snapshot isolation; the same names do not imply identical guarantees. Further reading PostgreSQL: Transaction isolation MySQL: Transaction isolation levels Oracle: Data concurrency and consistency

sum: Explain row-version visibility, retained-snapshot bloat and why snapshot isolation still permits write skew.
x: A snapshot chooses which row versions a transaction can see. Stable visibility is useful for reports, but it does not by itself protect every invariant across different rows. MVCC: how reads avoid blocking Multiversion concurrency control keeps several versions of each row. A writer creates a new version rather than overwriting, so readers can carry on reading the old one. Plain snapshot reads avoid row-level reader/writer blocking. Table locks, explicit locking reads and DDL can still block. In Postgres each row version has xmin (the transaction that created it) and xmax (the one that deleted or replaced it). A transaction's snapshot records which transactions had committed when it started; a version is visible if its xmin committed before the snapshot and its xmax didn't. Old versions are garbage-collected later: by VACUUM in Postgres, and purge of undo logs in InnoDB. An old retained snapshot or transaction-id horizon can delay cleanup and cause bloat; merely issuing BEGIN without acquiring such a horizon is not sufficient. Read Committed takes a new snapshot per statement. Snapshot isolation / Repeatable Read takes one snapshot per transaction (in Postgres, at its first non-transaction-control statement, not at BEGIN). Snapshot isolation Under SI, a transaction sees a consistent snapshot as of its start, and its own writes. On write-write conflicts, first committer wins: if T2 tries to update a row that T1 updated and committed after T2's snapshot was taken, T2 aborts. In Postgres, T2 first waits on T1's row lock; if T1 commits, T2 fails with could not serialize access due to concurrent update, and if T1 rolls back, T2 carries on. SI prevents dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, read skew, most phantoms, and lost updates on the same row. It does not prevent write skew, because the conflict check only looks at rows both transactions wrote. One snapshot for a report Separate Read Committed statements can add branch balances from different instants, even inside one transaction. PostgreSQL Repeatable Read uses one snapshot for the report, avoiding that mixture. The report can still retain old versions and take table locks; stable row visibility does not mean zero operational cost. Key takeaways Plain snapshot reads avoid row-level reader/writer blocking; table locks and DDL still matter. Old retained snapshots can delay cleanup and create bloat. Snapshot isolation rejects conflicting same-row writes but permits decisions that update different rows. Further reading PostgreSQL: Transaction isolation www.postgresql.org: explicit locking

t: Row locks, constraints and two-phase locking
sum: Fix lost updates and missing-row races, then trace the deadlock cost of lock-based serializability.
x: Choose the smallest mechanism that protects the decision you make. A SQL increment using the stored value, a lock on existing rows or an enforced uniqueness rule solves different kinds of race. Fixing races without full serializability The fragment assumes existing counters, doctors and bookings tables. It demonstrates three separate techniques; the doctors branch still needs the application decision described below. FOR UPDATE turns the read into a locking read: Bob's transaction blocks until Alice commits. Under Read Committed it then re-checks the rows and sees that Alice is now off call; under Repeatable Read it fails with a serialization error and retries. Either way, the invariant holds. It fixes write skew only when the rows you depend on already exist. For "check that nothing exists, then insert" phantoms, you need a unique constraint, a materialised lock row, or serializable isolation. Serializable, method 1: two-phase locking 2PL was the standard way for decades (still used by SQL Server's Serializable and MySQL's Serializable mode). Growing phase: acquire locks as you go. Reads take shared locks; writes take exclusive locks. Readers block writers and writers block readers. Shrinking phase: after releasing a lock, acquire no new locks. Strict 2PL retains exclusive write locks until commit/abort; retaining all shared and exclusive locks until then is often called rigorous 2PL. To stop phantoms, it locks ranges too: predicate locks or, more practically, index-range (next-key) locks. Costs: much lower concurrency, long waits behind slow transactions, and deadlocks (T1 holds A and wants B; T2 holds B and wants A). The database detects the cycle and aborts one transaction, which the application must retry. The application decision is still required The doctors example locks the rows, then the application must count the returned on-call doctors and refuse to remove the last one. The SQL fragment assumes that decision permits Alice to leave; it is not a complete invariant-checking stored procedure. The booking index enforces equality of a room and slot, not arbitrary overlapping time ranges. Key takeaways A single SQL increment removes the application read-modify-write gap. Row locks protect existing rows; a uniqueness rule or other mechanism is needed for absent-row races. Strict two-phase locking holds write locks until completion and can deadlock. Further reading www.postgresql.org: explicit locking PostgreSQL: Transaction isolation PostgreSQL: Constraints

sum: Use optimistic dependency tracking and bounded retries without repeating external side effects.
x: PostgreSQL Serializable adds dependency tracking to snapshots. It can reject a transaction whose decisions conflict with another, so the application must make retries part of its normal control flow. Serializable, method 2: SSI Serializable Snapshot Isolation (Cahill et al., 2008; in Postgres since 9.1) is optimistic. Plain snapshot reads avoid row-level reader/writer blocking, and the database tracks read/write dependencies. Ordinary write locks, explicit locking reads and table locks can still cause waits or deadlocks: It records what each transaction read (using SIREAD markers on rows and index ranges, not blocking locks). If T1 read something T2 later wrote (an rw-antidependency), and a dangerous structure of two such consecutive edges appears, one transaction is aborted, often at commit but sometimes at an earlier statement. In the doctors example, each transaction read the set the other wrote, so one of them fails with a serialization error and must retry. On retry it sees only one doctor on call and refuses. SSI can produce false positives: it tracks reads coarsely (a whole page or relation if many rows are read), so it sometimes aborts transactions that would have been fine. Proper indexes help, because they let it track narrower index ranges instead of whole tables. 2PL SSI --------- Approach Pessimistic Optimistic Plain read row locks? Yes No Failure mode Waits, deadlocks Aborts, retries Best when High contention Low contention Retries are part of the contract Under Serializable (and even SI), any transaction can fail with a serialization error (SQLSTATE 40001). Wrap transactions in a retry loop with backoff, and keep them short and free of side effects such as sending emails. Serializability on a single node is a different property from linearizability across replicas; that distinction, and distributed transactions, are covered in the consistency module. A retry is a new transaction Roll back after SQLSTATE 40001, then rerun the complete read-and-write logic with a fresh snapshot. Bound the attempts and surface exhaustion instead of silently dropping the operation. Atomic database work can be retried; an external email cannot be rolled back, so use an outbox and a downstream idempotency protocol when such an effect is needed. Key takeaways SSI tracks read/write dependencies using non-blocking SIREAD markers. A serialization failure requires rerunning the entire transaction in a fresh snapshot. Keep external effects out of retry bodies and use durable handoff with downstream idempotency. Further reading Ports and Grittner: Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL www.postgresql.org: mvcc serialization failure handling

sum: Compare physical and logical replication and distinguish durable standby acknowledgement from applied visibility.
x: Replication means keeping copies of the same data on several machines. You do it for three reasons: Availability: if one machine dies, another can serve. Read scaling: spread reads across replicas. Latency: put a copy near users in each region. Replicating data that never changes is trivial. All the difficulty is in handling changes. There are three main designs. Single-leader replication One node, the leader (primary), accepts all writes. It sends a stream of changes to followers (replicas, standbys), which preserve the required replication semantics; physical replay and parallel logical execution differ. Reads can go to the leader or any follower. This is how Postgres streaming replication, MySQL replication, SQL Server Always On, MongoDB replica sets and Amazon RDS read replicas work. This avoids independent multi-leader histories, but concurrent application transactions can still contend or conflict on the leader. What gets shipped varies: Physical log shipping: the raw WAL bytes (Postgres streaming replication). Replays physical page changes, so leader and follower need compatible formats and the same major version, and you can't replicate just one table. Logical (row-based) replication: "row X in table Y changed to Z" (MySQL row-based binlog, Postgres logical replication). Works across major versions (so it's a common way to upgrade with little downtime), can replicate a subset of tables, and is usable for change data capture into Kafka. Statement-based: replay the SQL. Some non-deterministic expressions and unordered operations are unsafe; MySQL explicitly handles NOW() using logged timestamp context, so it is not inherently unsafe. Row-based logging avoids many of these replay hazards. Synchronous vs asynchronous Synchronous: the leader waits for a follower to confirm it has the write before telling the client "committed". Asynchronous: the leader acknowledges after its local commit conditions without waiting for a replica acknowledgement. Streaming can already be sending changes while the transaction runs. Synchronous Asynchronous --------- Data loss on leader failure None if a durable acknowledged copy survives and is promoted Recent writes may be lost Write latency Waits for required remote acknowledgement No required replica acknowledgement Follower down Stalls if too few required acknowledgements remain Can continue subject to resources and policy Fully synchronous to every follower is fragile: any slow replica stalls all writes. PostgreSQL supports quorum synchronous replication, for example ANY 1 (s1, s2). MySQL semi-sync is a separate protocol with its own acknowledgement and timeout/fallback behavior. Aurora’s six-copy storage design uses a four-copy write quorum and three-copy recovery quorum; this does not mean every ordinary SQL read waits for three storage nodes. "Synchronous" also has degrees. Postgres's synchronous_commit decides what the leader waits for: Setting Standby has... ------ remote_write Written to its filesystem, possibly only in OS cache on Flushed it to disk remote_apply Applied it; visible to reads With on (the default once a sync standby is configured), a committed write is safe on the standby's disk but may not be visible there yet. Only remote_apply gives read-your-writes from that standby, at extra latency. Async means "committed" can be lost With async replication, if the leader dies 200 ms after confirming a write that hasn't shipped yet, and a follower is promoted, that write is gone. Whatever your users were told. Plan a logical-replication cutover For a major-version upgrade, check schema and type compatibility, initialise the target and stream changes before the switch. Logical replication does not automatically copy every object: schema definitions and sequence state need separate handling. Rehearse the write pause, catch-up check and client switch; logical replication alone does not guarantee a particular downtime. Key takeaways One leader orders writes; physical and logical replication carry different information. Synchronous durability requires the right surviving acknowledged history at failover. PostgreSQL on waits for standby flush; remote_apply also waits for replay visibility. Further reading www.postgresql.org: warm standby www.postgresql.org: runtime config wal www.postgresql.org: logical replication restrictions MySQL: Replication

sum: Diagnose stale and backwards reads and weigh report cancellation against retained-version bloat.
x: A replica can have less recent data than the leader, and two replicas can have different histories applied. Read routing needs to preserve the guarantees the user experience requires. Replication lag and its anomalies Async followers are behind the leader by some replication lag, usually milliseconds but seconds or minutes under load, during a long-running query on the replica, or after a network blip. This is eventual consistency: stop writing and the replicas converge, but at any moment they may be stale. Long queries on a Postgres replica create a specific tension. If the leader's vacuum removes row versions the replica's query still needs, the replica must either pause replay (lag grows) or cancel the query. The default 30 s max_standby_streaming_delay budgets total replay delay for received WAL, rather than granting every query thirty seconds. A conflicting query may therefore have less grace time before cancellation with conflict with recovery. hot_standby_feedback = on can prevent cleanup-related cancellations (not all recovery conflicts) by telling the leader to keep those versions, at the cost of bloat on the leader. Three classic anomalies: Reading your own writes A user updates their profile (leader) and reloads the page (served by a lagging follower). The change seems to have vanished. Fixes for read-your-writes consistency: Read data the user can edit from the leader (e.g. their own profile). For a short time after a write (say 10 s), route that user's reads to the leader. This is a heuristic unless replication lag is bounded; use log-position tracking for a guarantee. Track the log position of the user's last write (Postgres LSN, MySQL GTID) and only read from a replica that has caught up to it. Monotonic reads A user refreshes twice; the first request hits a replica 1 s behind, the second hits one 10 s behind. A comment appears, then disappears. Pinning each user to one advancing replica helps. Across failover or reassignment, carry a minimum observed log position/version and wait for it or use the leader; pinning alone cannot guarantee monotonic reads. Consistent prefix reads In partitioned systems, a reader sees an answer before the question that prompted it, because they were stored on partitions replicating at different speeds. Fix: write causally related data to the same partition, or track causal dependencies. These guarantees are part of a wider family of consistency models, covered in the consistency module. Key takeaways Async lag can violate read-your-writes, monotonic reads and consistent prefixes. Log-position tracking gives a stronger guarantee than an arbitrary post-write routing window. Standby feedback helps cleanup conflicts but can retain dead versions on the primary. Further reading PostgreSQL: Hot standby PostgreSQL: Replication settings

sum: Promote a replica safely while preventing stale leaders and external identifiers from corrupting associations.
x: Failure detection does not prove the old leader has stopped. A safe promotion needs both a chosen surviving history and an enforced way to exclude stale writers. Failover When the leader dies, a follower must be promoted. Detect the failure, usually by missed heartbeats over some timeout (say 30 s). Choose a new leader: ideally the most up-to-date follower. Agreeing on it is a consensus problem. Reconfigure clients to write to the new leader (DNS, a proxy, or a service discovery update), and make sure the old leader, if it comes back, becomes a follower. Tools: Patroni (Postgres, using etcd or Consul for leader election), MySQL Group Replication / Orchestrator, and managed services such as RDS Multi-AZ, whose failover duration depends on the service type, workload, recovery and client reconnection; measure it for the deployment. What goes wrong: Lost writes: with async replication, unshipped writes from the old leader are discarded. A lagging promoted replica may reuse identifiers whose earlier values remain in caches or external systems, leading to incorrect associations. A specific historical incident attribution is omitted because this review did not establish its primary report. Split brain: the old leader isn't dead, just partitioned, and keeps accepting writes. Two leaders now diverge. Enforced fencing prevents stale writes. Leases require reliable enforcement/watchdogs, and epoch tokens work only when every protected resource rejects stale epochs.
