Timeout tuning: too short and you fail over during a GC pause or traffic spike (making things worse); too long and you're down for longer. Key takeaways Failover needs failure detection, a chosen leader and client reconfiguration. Async failover can discard acknowledged history that caches or other systems still reference. Fencing must actually prevent stale writes; cooperative self-demotion alone is insufficient. Further reading www.postgresql.org: warm standby failover Patroni: Watchdog support

sum: Trade local regional writes for explicit conflict handling and compare last-write-wins, merging and CRDTs.
x: Putting a writer in each region removes a remote round trip from local writes. It also permits independent histories that must be reconciled after they meet. Multi-leader replication Several nodes accept writes, typically one leader per datacentre, and replicate to each other asynchronously. Benefits: local write latency in every region, and each datacentre keeps working if the link between them fails. Also the model behind offline-first apps (each device is a "leader") and collaborative editing. The cost: write conflicts. Two users edit the same record in different regions at the same moment; both writes succeed locally, then collide. Conflict resolution strategies: Last write wins (LWW): highest timestamp wins. Simple, but silently drops data, and clock skew decides the "winner". Merge: e.g. union of shopping cart items, or application callbacks. CRDTs: data types (counters, sets, text) designed so concurrent updates merge deterministically. Used by Riak, Redis Enterprise active-active, and collaborative-editing libraries such as Automerge and Yjs. Avoid conflicts: route all writes for a given record to one "home" region. Examples: MySQL/MariaDB multi-source setups, Postgres with BDR/pgEdge, CouchDB, and DynamoDB global tables (LWW in their default multi-region eventually consistent mode). Key takeaways Several leaders can accept local writes during an inter-region partition. Last-write-wins converges by discarding competing values and depends on timestamp ordering. Merging, CRDTs or a home region make different trade-offs for the application. Further reading DeCandia et al.: Dynamo, Amazon's highly available key-value store docs.aws.amazon.com: globaltables_HowItWorks

sum: Calculate quorum overlap and failure tolerance, then restore replicas with hints, read repair and anti-entropy.
x: A leaderless system asks several replicas to participate in each operation. Count the intersection and remaining replicas explicitly, then consider how missing writes are repaired. Leaderless replication Any replica accepts writes. The client (or a coordinator node) sends each write to all n replicas and considers it successful when w acknowledge; reads query r replicas and take the newest value. This is the Dynamo style, used by Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak and Amazon's original Dynamo. For a fixed replica set, durable successful writes and no concurrent writes, the quorum condition guarantees that a later read reaches at least one replica that accepted the last successful write. Assume the reconciliation rule recognises that version; overlap alone is not a general latest-value guarantee: Worked example with three replicas: The cost of raising w or r is latency and availability: each request waits for more replicas and fails if too few are up. How quorums behave under failure, and why they're weaker than they look (sloppy quorums, concurrent writes, clock-based conflict resolution), is covered in the consensus module. Repairing stale replicas: Read repair: a read that sees a stale replica writes the newer value back. Hinted handoff: if a replica is down, another node holds its writes ("hints") and passes them on when it recovers. Anti-entropy: background comparison with Merkle trees to find and fix differences. Single Multi Leaderless ------------ Write conflicts None Yes Yes Failover needed Yes Per DC No Write latency One region Local Quorum Compare a storage quorum In Aurora's simplified durability and recovery model, six storage copies are spread two per availability zone. Four-copy writes still have enough copies after one zone is lost; three-copy recovery reads can continue after a zone and one additional copy are lost. Any four-copy and three-copy sets overlap. This is storage arithmetic, not a statement that every ordinary SQL query reads three copies or that database compute is always available. Key takeaways Read and write sets overlap when their sizes sum to more than the replica count. Larger quorums raise acknowledgement latency and require more surviving replicas. Hints, read repair and anti-entropy converge stale replicas; overlap alone is not linearizability. Further reading DeCandia et al.: Dynamo, Amazon's highly available key-value store Verbitski et al.: Amazon Aurora design considerations

sum: Compare ordered-key locality with hash distribution and calculate why changing modulo placement moves most keys.
x: Replication gives you copies of the same data. Partitioning splits data into subsets; sharding distributes them among nodes. Systems use different physical units: MongoDB chunks/shards, Elasticsearch shards, HBase regions and Bigtable tablets. Cassandra virtual nodes own token ranges and are not the same thing as CQL partitions. You partition when one machine can't hold the data or absorb the write rate. The goal is to spread data and load evenly. A partition that gets far more than its share is a hot spot, and it caps the throughput of the entire system. In practice, each partition is also replicated, so a node holds replicas of several partitions: Range partitioning Assign contiguous ranges of the key to each partition, like volumes of an encyclopaedia: A–C, D–F, and so on. Pro: range scans are efficient. "All events between 09:00 and 10:00" touches the partitions overlapping that range; the number depends on boundaries and data volume. Con: hot spots when writes cluster in one range. If the key is a timestamp, all of today's writes go to the last partition while the others sit idle. Boundaries are usually chosen automatically, splitting a partition when it grows too big according to engine-specific policies and thresholds; verify these for the deployed version. Fix for time-ordered hot spots: prefix the key with something that spreads load, e.g. sensor_id + timestamp, so writes from different sensors land in different ranges. Range queries then need one query per sensor. Hash partitioning Apply a hash function to the key and assign ranges of the hash to partitions. A good hash spreads even sequential keys uniformly. The naive way to turn a hash into a partition number is to take the remainder after dividing by the number of partitions: For example, if hash("user42") came out as 1,000,003 and N = 10, the remainder is 3, so the key goes to partition 3. This spreads keys evenly, but it has a fatal flaw when N changes, described in the warning below. Pro: even distribution, no clustering. Con: range queries on the key are gone: adjacent keys are scattered. Cassandra's compromise is a compound key: hash the partition key, then keep rows sorted by the clustering columns within each partition. Never use hash mod N directly Going from 10 to 11 nodes, a key stays put only if its hash leaves the same remainder when divided by 10 and by 11, which is true for about 1 in 11 keys. Adding one node moves ~91% of the data. The general rule, for hash values spread evenly, when you add one node to N: For 10 nodes growing to 11: Why 1 in N + 1: a key stays only when its two remainders match, and over every run of N × (N + 1) consecutive hash values that happens for exactly N of them (the values 0 to N − 1 and their repeats). Key takeaways Sharding spreads both data and load; replication supplies copies of each partition. Range keys preserve range locality but concentrate monotonically increasing writes. Hashing spreads keys, but plain modulo placement remaps most keys when one node is added. Further reading DynamoDB: Designing partition keys to distribute your workload DeCandia et al.: Dynamo, Amazon's highly available key-value store

sum: Limit membership-change movement, colocate Redis keys and mitigate skew that even hashing cannot remove.
x: Membership changes and skew are different placement problems. Consistent hashing reduces remapping, while hot keys still need caching, splitting or another workload-specific response. Consistent hashing Place both nodes and keys on a ring of hash values (say 0 to 2⁶⁴). Each key belongs to the first node clockwise from it. When a node joins, it takes over keys only from its clockwise neighbour; when one leaves, its keys move to the next node. Only about one node's share of keys moves: Going from 10 to 11 nodes moves about 1/11 ≈ 9% of keys, against about 91% with plain modulo. Plain consistent hashing gives uneven ranges, and a newly added node only relieves one neighbour. The fix is virtual nodes: each physical node owns many small points on the ring (Cassandra historically used 256 per node, now 16 by default with a smarter allocation algorithm). Load evens out, and a new node can take small slices from many existing nodes, rather than necessarily every node. Used by Amazon Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak, and the client-side sharding in many cache libraries (such as memcached clients using the "ketama" scheme). A related approach used by Redis Cluster is a fixed set of 16,384 hash slots assigned to nodes. Redis Cluster only allows a multi-key command (MGET, a transaction, a Lua script) when all its keys are in the same slot. Hash tags make that possible: only the part inside {...} is hashed, so {user42}:cart and {user42}:profile always share a slot. Hot spots and skew Even with perfect hashing, a single hot key lands on one partition. A celebrity with 100 million followers, or a viral product during a sale, can overload it. Mitigations: Key splitting (salting): write to key#0 … key#9 (random suffix), creating ten logical keys that can spread load; they are not guaranteed to occupy ten physical partitions. Reads gather across those keys. Only do this for the few known-hot keys. Caching the hot key's reads in front of the database. Adaptive capacity: DynamoDB automatically shifts capacity to busy partitions and splits them, even isolating frequently accessed items on their own partitions. A single item still can't exceed one partition's limits (about 3,000 RCU / 1,000 WCU per second). Key takeaways Virtual nodes spread ring ownership and transfers over several physical nodes. Redis hash tags keep related keys in one slot for multi-key commands. Salting and caching can relieve hot keys; logical salts do not guarantee distinct physical partitions. Further reading www.cs.princeton.edu: chash.pdf Redis Cluster specification docs.aws.amazon.com: burst adaptive capacity

sum: Compare scatter-gather and global indexes, and choose DynamoDB LSI or GSI freshness and capacity deliberately.
x: An index on a field other than the shard key can change both query fan-out and write coordination. Distinguish the general local/global layout from DynamoDB's specific meanings of LSI and GSI. Secondary indexes on partitioned data Partitioning by primary key makes primary-key lookups easy. But what about "find all red cars" when cars are partitioned by car_id? Local (document-partitioned) indexes Each partition indexes only its own data. Writes: cheap, local to one partition. Reads: must ask every partition and merge (scatter-gather). Tail latency is the slowest partition's latency. Used by MongoDB, Cassandra secondary indexes, Elasticsearch. Global (term-partitioned) indexes The index itself is partitioned by the indexed value: all colour=red entries live in one index partition. Reads: go to one index partition. Writes: one row write may update index partitions on other nodes, so global indexes are usually updated asynchronously. DynamoDB global secondary indexes are eventually consistent, typically within a fraction of a second. Local index Global index --------- Write cost One partition Several Read cost All partitions One partition Freshness Engine-dependent (e.g. search refresh) Engine-dependent; often async DynamoDB's two kinds of index DynamoDB offers both, with its own twist on "local": A local secondary index (LSI) keeps the table's partition key and adds a different sort key. Because you must supply the partition key to query it, it reads one partition, not all of them. It supports strongly consistent reads, but you can have at most 5 per table, they can only be defined when the table is created, and each partition-key value's items (table plus LSIs) are capped at 10 GB. A global secondary index (GSI) can use any attribute as its keys. The default quota is 20 per table (adjustable), you can add or remove them at any time, but reads are eventually consistent only. Each GSI has its own capacity, and if a GSI can't keep up with writes, DynamoDB throttles writes to the base table. Fan-out makes tail latency matter A query waiting for all twenty shards completes at the slowest response. If their timings are independent, all must beat their individual 99th-percentile thresholds for the combined query to do so. Thus a per-shard p99 does not determine the combined p99; the full latency distribution and correlations matter. Key takeaways Local indexes make non-partition-key reads scatter across shards and wait for the slowest result. Global indexes change read routing but can require cross-node asynchronous maintenance. DynamoDB LSIs share a partition key and can read strongly; GSIs support other keys with eventual reads. Further reading DynamoDB: Global secondary indexes DynamoDB: Local secondary indexes research.google: the tail at scale

sum: Plan partition movement, routing and a verified migration while isolating unusually large tenants.
x: Moving data is a live operation with a routing change at its end. Keep capture, verification and rollback visible, and choose a layout that can move unusually large tenants independently. Rebalancing Over time, data grows, nodes are added, and load shifts. Rebalancing moves partitions between nodes. Goals: even load afterwards, keep serving during the move, and move as little data as possible. Strategies: Fixed number of partitions: create many more partitions than nodes up front (e.g. 1,000 partitions on 10 nodes), and move whole partitions when nodes join. Elasticsearch shards, Riak, Couchbase vBuckets and Redis Cluster slots work this way. Choose the count carefully: too few limits future growth; too many adds overhead. (Elasticsearch fixes an index's primary shard count at creation; changing it later means reindexing or the split API.) Dynamic partitioning: split a partition when it exceeds a size threshold, merge when it shrinks in engines that support those operations. Initial partition counts and split/merge policies vary; pre-split only when appropriate for that engine. Proportional to nodes: a fixed number of partitions per node (Cassandra's vnodes). Keep a human in the loop Fully automatic rebalancing plus automatic failure detection can cascade: a slow node is declared dead, its data is moved, the move overloads others, and they're declared dead too. Many operators require a person to approve rebalancing. Request routing Something must know which node holds which partition: Any node accepts a request and forwards it (Cassandra's gossip-based coordinator). A routing tier knows the map (MongoDB's mongos, Vitess's vtgate), often backed by ZooKeeper or etcd. The client knows the map (Redis Cluster clients, with MOVED redirects when it's stale). Resharding a relational database Postgres and MySQL don't shard natively, so teams shard at the application layer or use Vitess (YouTube, Slack, GitHub), Citus (Postgres), or a distributed SQL database (CockroachDB, Spanner, YugabyteDB, TiDB). Doubling the shard count online (say from 8 to 16) usually looks like: Create the new shards and start backfilling them from a snapshot. Capture ongoing changes reliably (for example CDC from the snapshot position), with replay, ordering and reconciliation; unrelated application dual writes can diverge. Verify: compare row counts and checksums. Cut over reads, then writes, shard by shard, with a quick rollback path. Clean up the moved data from the old shards. Pick the shard key to keep each request on one shard. For a SaaS product, tenant_id is the classic choice: every query includes it, and cross-tenant joins are rare. Tenant sizes are usually very skewed, though, so map tenants to shards through a directory (lookup table) rather than a formula: then a giant tenant can be moved to a dedicated shard on its own. Cross-shard transactions need distributed commit protocols, covered in the distributed transactions module. Coordinate the final switch For the tenant migration here, keep reads available while copying, then briefly queue that tenant's writes at cutover. Drain and reconcile captured changes before switching its write routing. Do not allow unrelated dual writes to pretend they form an atomic cutover. A dedicated tenant shard can itself need a second partition key if that tenant eventually outgrows one machine. Key takeaways Partition-count choices affect future growth and movement overhead. Coordinators, routing tiers or clients maintain the partition map. Backfill, capture changes, verify and coordinate cutover; tenant directories let outliers move independently. Further reading Vitess documentation Citus: Choosing a distribution column www.elastic.co: index modules

t: Choose from access patterns and invariants
sum: Estimate workload shape, identify transaction and regional constraints, and use a decision guide as a starting point.
x: "Which database should we use?" is one of the most common system design questions, and "it depends" is only a good answer if you can say on what. This lesson gives you a repeatable way to decide. Start with access patterns Write down how the data is read and written before thinking about products. What are the queries? By primary key? By ranges? Ad-hoc filters? Full-text? Multi-hop relationships? Aggregates over millions of rows? What's the read/write ratio? 100:1 read-heavy (a catalogue) and 1:10 write-heavy (telemetry) want different engines. How big is each item and the whole dataset? 1 KB rows × 100 million = 100 GB before indexes and overhead. Even 10 TB can fit on some machines; assess working-set memory, I/O, growth and recovery time rather than treating a data size as a universal single-node limit. What latency is needed? Sub-millisecond (in-memory), single-digit ms (OLTP), seconds (analytics). Are the queries known up front? Key-value and wide-column stores need them known; relational and search engines tolerate ad-hoc ones. Back-of-envelope 20 million users × 50 orders each × 500 bytes = 500 GB of orders. Peak 2,000 writes/s and 20,000 reads/s. That is a candidate for a Postgres primary with read replicas and a cache. Benchmark the actual transactions, indexes, contention and recovery requirements before deciding whether one primary has enough headroom. The size estimate in that example is a chain of multiplications, the same one you use for any dataset: Treat the result as a lower bound: indexes commonly add a large fraction on top, and every replica or backup multiplies it again. Consistency and transaction needs Do you need multi-row atomic updates, such as moving money or reserving stock? That points to a relational database or a distributed SQL database (Spanner, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB). Can users tolerate stale reads for a few seconds (feeds, view counts, recommendations)? Then eventually consistent replicas and caches are fine. Are there invariants across entities ("username unique", "no double booking")? Unique constraints in one database are far easier than coordinating across a distributed one. Do you need writes to keep working in every region during a partition? That pushes towards multi-leader or leaderless systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB global tables) and conflict handling. A decision guide Treat it as a starting point, not a rule. Postgres alone covers several of these branches (jsonb, full-text search, PostGIS, TimescaleDB) for moderate scale. Check the regional ordering requirement During an inter-region partition, independent writers cannot coordinate one immediately final strict conversation order. Choose provisional local acceptance with later ordering, or an authoritative ordering region with the resulting latency and partition-availability trade-offs. A named database does not remove that conflict. For bursty exact-key traffic, DynamoDB on-demand is a candidate, not unlimited capacity: validate key distribution, request sizes, warm throughput, previous peak and configured table/account limits against the rollout. Key takeaways List queries, item sizes, read/write mix and latency before comparing products. Cross-entity invariants favour a store that can enforce them together. Independent regional writes cannot immediately agree on one final order during a partition. Further reading DynamoDB: NoSQL design best practices PostgreSQL: Constraints docs.aws.amazon.com: on demand capacity mode

sum: Use measured bottlenecks, recovery objectives and team capability to evaluate distribution and database pricing.
x: A candidate database must meet measured service objectives and be operable by the team. Capacity, recovery time, billing and engineer effort belong in the same decision. Scale Be honest about it. A single well-run relational primary is a useful starting point; measure whether it meets this workload’s availability, throughput and recovery needs. Scale signal Typical answer ------ Workload fits a measured single-node budget One relational primary Read-heavy beyond that Replicas + cache Writes beyond one node Shard or distributed DB Global low-latency writes Multi-region store Scaling triggers worth acting on: cache misses cause unacceptable measured I/O or latency, write throughput nears the primary's limit even after tuning, or backups and restores take too long to meet recovery targets. Operational cost The database you can run well beats the theoretically better one you can't. Managed or self-hosted? RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, DynamoDB, Atlas and Astra automate parts of patching, backups and failover; you still own configuration, recovery testing, access control and application behavior, at a price premium (and with some loss of control). Team expertise. Operating Cassandra well (repairs, compaction tuning, tombstones) is a real skill. Postgres knowledge is widespread. Ecosystem. Drivers, ORMs, migration tools, monitoring, backups, CDC connectors. Cost model. DynamoDB on-demand charges per request, and provisioned charges per capacity unit-hour, which can be cheaper for steady, predictable traffic; compare current regional rates, utilization and commitments rather than assuming a fixed saving. Aurora charges for instances plus storage, and either per I/O or a higher flat rate on its I/O-Optimized configuration. Self-hosted charges in engineer time. Lock-in. DynamoDB's API is proprietary; Postgres-compatible services let you move between providers. Résumé-driven development Choosing a distributed database for a 50 GB dataset adds operational complexity. It can still be justified by regional availability, locality or throughput requirements; small size alone neither requires nor rules it out. Start simple, measure, and move when the numbers demand it. Apply the estimate to a retained sensor stream Two million sensors sending once every ten seconds produce 200,000 readings per second. At 100 bytes per reading, ninety days means about 155.5 TB before compression, indexes, replicas and overhead. A store keyed by sensor and a bounded time bucket is a candidate; benchmark ingestion, expiry and range queries instead of inferring an absolute single-node limit from this count. Key takeaways Tune and measure a primary before introducing distribution for a hypothetical bottleneck. Write saturation, working-set growth and recovery time are concrete scaling triggers. Compare current capacity prices and full operating costs, including recovery testing and engineer time. Further reading DynamoDB: Capacity modes www.postgresql.org: performance tips docs.aws.amazon.com: USER_WorkingWithAutomatedBackups

sum: Keep one source of truth per fact and derive search, caches and analytics through CDC or an outbox.
x: Several stores can serve different access paths, but each fact still needs one authoritative owner. Durable handoff connects that owner to derived views without relying on two independent application writes. Polyglot persistence Large systems usually use several stores, each for what it does best. This is called polyglot persistence. Typical example, an online shop: Postgres: orders, payments, inventory (transactions). Redis: sessions, carts, rate limits, hot product cache. Elasticsearch / OpenSearch: product search with facets. S3 + a columnar warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse): analytics. The costs of polyglot persistence Keeping stores in sync. Never "dual write" from the application (write to Postgres, then to Elasticsearch): if the second write fails, the stores silently diverge. Instead, make one store the source of truth and derive the others from its change log (CDC), or use the transactional outbox pattern: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the data, and have a relay publish it. These commonly use at-least-once delivery, conditional on reliable capture, retention and retries. Consumers must handle duplicates and ordering. A processed-event record only deduplicates an effect atomically when both are in the same transaction; external email or payment calls need a provider-supported idempotency protocol and reconciliation. More things to operate: backups, upgrades, monitoring, on-call for each. Consistency gaps: derived stores lag the source. Design the UX to tolerate it (e.g. a new product appears in search a second later). One source of truth per fact For each piece of data, name the system of record. Everything else is a derived, rebuildable view. If you can't rebuild your search index from scratch, it has quietly become a source of truth. Worked choice: a ride-hailing app Trips, payments, driver accounts: transactional, relational. Postgres (or Aurora), sharded by city if needed. Driver locations: millions of updates per minute, only the latest matters, queried by geography. Redis with geospatial indexes, or an in-memory grid service. Trip history for riders: a key-value or wide-column store keyed by rider id, sorted by time, because it's write-once and read by key. Surge pricing analytics: stream processing into a columnar store. Glue: CDC from the trip database into Kafka feeds history, analytics and search. Key takeaways Specialist stores can serve locations, history, search and analytics alongside transactional data. Ad-hoc dual writes can diverge after a partial failure. CDC or an outbox needs reliable delivery and duplicate handling; external effects need an idempotency protocol. Further reading debezium.io: outbox event router Resend: Idempotency keys Martin Fowler: Polyglot Persistence

sum: Trace durable commit before dirty-page flush and weigh checkpoints, full-page images and async commit.
x: Underneath every database is a storage engine: the code that lays bytes out on disk, survives crashes and answers lookups. Knowing how it works lets you predict performance, tune it and choose between engines. This unit goes one level below the earlier indexing units. Disks, pages and the buffer pool Disks read and write in blocks, and random I/O is far slower than sequential: a good NVMe SSD manages hundreds of thousands of random 4 KB reads per second (high-end drives exceed a million) and several GB/s sequentially; a spinning disk manages only ~100–200 random I/Os per second. These indicative hardware figures vary by device, queue depth, cache and workload; they are not measurements from this review. Measure the selected storage under the actual workload. These indicative hardware figures vary by device, queue depth, cache and workload; they are not measurements from this review. Measure the selected storage under the actual workload. So databases organise data into fixed-size pages: 8 KB in Postgres, 16 KB in InnoDB, 4 KB in SQLite by default. A page is the unit of I/O and of caching. The buffer pool (shared_buffers in Postgres, innodb_buffer_pool_size in MySQL) caches hot pages in RAM. A modified ("dirty") page is written back later, not at commit. That raises the question: what if the server crashes before it's written? The write-ahead log The answer is the write-ahead log (WAL), called the redo log in InnoDB. The rule: before any change to a data page reaches disk, the log record describing it must be on disk. A transaction modifies pages in the buffer pool and appends records to the WAL buffer. With durable commit settings, WAL is flushed using the configured synchronization method up to the commit record. That's the durability point. Dirty pages are written to their real locations later, in the background. A checkpoint periodically ensures all pages dirtied before a given log position are on disk, so older WAL can be recycled. Checkpoint spacing is a trade-off: further apart means fewer page writes (repeated changes to a hot page coalesce) and fewer full-page images, but more WAL to keep and a longer replay after a crash. After a crash, crash recovery replays WAL from the checkpoint redo position. Physical redo can include changes made by transactions that never committed. Postgres uses transaction status and MVCC to keep those versions invisible; engines such as InnoDB also undo uncommitted changes. Why it's fast: the WAL is a sequential append, while page writes are random. Commit costs one sequential fsync instead of many random page writes. Group commit batches several transactions' commits into one fsync. Torn pages A crash midway through writing an 8 KB page to a disk with 4 KB storage-atomic writes leaves half old, half new. Postgres guards against this by logging a full page image the first time a page changes after each checkpoint (full_page_writes); InnoDB uses a doublewrite buffer. The WAL also feeds replication (followers replay it) and change data capture. Durability knobs synchronous_commit = off (Postgres) or innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2 (MySQL) skip the per-commit flush. Throughput rises, but a power loss or OS crash can lose recently acknowledged commits: up to about 3 × wal_writer_delay (around 600 ms by default) in Postgres, and about a second in MySQL at its default background flush interval. MySQL scheduling and configuration can widen that approximate loss window; it is not a hard one-second bound. Neither corrupts the database; turning off fsync entirely is what does that. The Postgres figure comes from how often the background WAL writer flushes. The PostgreSQL documentation gives the worst case as three of its cycles: Raising wal_writer_delay widens the window in proportion. Lost commits are lost cleanly: recovery still ends at a consistent point. Key takeaways Pages are cached and modified in memory; WAL must reach durable storage before dependent data pages. Durable commit can finish before dirty pages reach their final locations. Checkpoint spacing, torn-page protection and async commit change recovery work and loss windows. Further reading PostgreSQL: Write-Ahead Logging PostgreSQL: Database page layout PostgreSQL: Asynchronous commit PostgreSQL: WAL configuration

sum: Compare tiered, leveled and time-window compaction without assuming universal amplification or free-space bounds.
x: The LSM write path leaves immutable files that need merging. The compaction strategy decides how much overlap, rewriting and temporary space a workload must tolerate. LSM trees in more detail Recap: writes go to the WAL and an in-memory memtable; full memtables flush to immutable sorted SSTables; reads merge across memtable and SSTables. An SSTable contains sorted key/value blocks (say 4–64 KB), a sparse index of the first key in each block, and a bloom filter. Deletes write a tombstone; the old value disappears only when compaction merges it away. Compaction strategies Size-tiered (Cassandra's long-standing default, STCS): when there are several SSTables of similar size, merge them into one bigger one. Low write amplification. But a key may exist in many overlapping files (reads check more), and a merge temporarily needs as much free space as its inputs (up to 2× space). Leveled (RocksDB, LevelDB, Cassandra LCS): level L1 is, say, 256 MB, and each level is 10× larger. Within a level (other than L0), SSTables don't overlap, so a key is in at most one file per level. The target size of each level grows geometrically: Because each level is ten times the previous one, the last level holds roughly 90% of the data, which is why leveled compaction keeps space overhead fairly low. Fewer overlapping candidate files for a point read and often lower space overhead; L0, snapshots and temporary compaction output prevent a universal 10% bound. But much higher write amplification: pushing data into the next level also rewrites the overlapping data already there, with amplification depending on overlap, file selection, retained versions and workload; a level-size ratio is not a universal upper bound. There's also time-window compaction, which suits time-series data with TTLs: whole expired windows are dropped as files. Cassandra 5.0 adds a unified compaction strategy that can be tuned anywhere between tiered and leveled behaviour. Treat the last-level share as conditional The roughly 90% last-level statement describes a well-filled geometric layout and RocksDB's dynamic level-size targeting. Static target settings, an underfilled last level, L0 and retained versions can change the observed share. It is a model for reasoning, not a universal space guarantee. Key takeaways Tiered compaction merges similarly sized files and can retain overlapping runs. Leveled compaction limits per-level point-key overlap while rewriting overlapping data. Peak free-space needs and amplification depend on versions, snapshots, overlap and workload. Further reading RocksDB: Leveled compaction cassandra.apache.org: lcs cassandra.apache.org: Apache Cassandra 5.0 Features Unified Compaction Strategy

sum: Measure physical work against logical work and compute a small-change page rewrite under explicit assumptions.
x: One logical write can create page writes, logs and compaction output. Compare engines by counting those physical costs under the same scope and workload assumptions. The three amplifications Write amplification: bytes written to disk ÷ bytes the application wrote. Read amplification: disk reads per logical read. Space amplification: bytes on disk ÷ size of live data. For example, if the application writes 1 GB a day and the engine writes 12 GB to disk, the write amplification is 12. Always say what you counted (WAL? compaction? the SSD's own internal copying?) because each choice gives a different number. B-tree LSM leveled LSM tiered ------------ Write amp Medium–high High Low Read amp Low Low–med Higher Space amp Depends on page fill and retained versions Depends on levels, versions and temporary output Depends on retained files and temporary output A B-tree's write amplification comes from writing a whole 8–16 KB page (plus WAL, plus full-page images) for a small change. The key variable is how many changes a page collects before it's written back: Sequential inserts or a hot working set that fits in RAM: many changes per page write, so the amplification is modest. Random updates to a table far bigger than RAM: perhaps one 100-byte change per 16 KB page write, which is over 150×, and InnoDB's doublewrite buffer doubles it. This is a worst case: it ignores the WAL and assumes no other change lands on the page before it is written. Leveled LSM amplification comes from compaction overlap and repeated rewriting. No universal 10–30× range or winner is supplied because a matched workload benchmark is absent. Compare measured read/write latency and amplification: an LSM read may check several levels, and background compaction competes for I/O. The RUM conjecture formalises the trade: you can optimise for two of Read, Update and Memory (space) overheads, at the expense of the third. Every engine picks a point; tuning moves it. On SSDs, write amplification also matters because flash cells wear out after a limited number of program/erase cycles. Key takeaways Write, read and space amplification compare physical cost with application work or live data. A whole-page flush for one tiny change can amplify writes sharply; coalescing changes reduces that cost. State what is counted and use measured workload values rather than a universal engine winner. Further reading stratos.seas.harvard.edu: designing access methods rum conjecture dev.mysql.com: innodb doublewrite buffer

sum: Calculate false-positive probability and distinguish candidate-file checks from disk reads and range-scan work.
x: Before searching an SSTable, cheaply rule out files that cannot contain an exact key. Bloom filters trade a small amount of memory for fewer candidate checks, with a controlled chance of false positives. Bloom filters A bloom filter answers "is this key possibly in this set?" using very little memory. It never gives a false negative, and gives false positives at a tunable rate. How it works: an array of bits, all starting at 0, plus a few independent hash functions. To add a key, hash it with each function and set the bits it lands on to 1. To check a key, test the same bits: any zero means "definitely not present". If all are 1, the key is possibly present, because other keys may have set those bits. With about 10 bits per key and the best number of hash functions (about 7), the false-positive rate is about 1%. A billion keys need ~1.2 GB of filter, a fraction of the data size. The standard approximation for a filter's false-positive rate, and the best number of hash functions, is: Worked example with 10 bits per key: The formula assumes the hash functions behave like independent random choices; real implementations come close. Each extra 4.8 or so bits per key cuts the rate about tenfold. In an LSM tree, each SSTable has a filter. A read for a missing key consults filters for every level and skips almost all of them, so a lookup may need far fewer candidate-file checks. False positives still require checking metadata or cached/disk blocks; there is no guarantee of at most one file read. RocksDB, Cassandra (bloom_filter_fp_chance), HBase and Bigtable all do this. Whole-key Bloom filters cannot exclude an arbitrary range using one membership test. A range iterator merges candidate sorted runs; key bounds and other metadata can still prune work. RocksDB's prefix bloom filters help when ranges share a prefix. Key takeaways A negative Bloom result excludes a key; a positive result only permits a follow-up check. Bits per key and hash count set the approximate false-positive rate. Exact-key filters do not solve arbitrary ranges; shared-prefix filtering serves a narrower use case. Further reading github.com: RocksDB Bloom Filter RocksDB: Prefix seek Wikipedia: Bloom filter

sum: Separate analytical scans from transactions and explain column pruning, compression, vectorisation and zone maps.
x: A transaction usually needs a few complete rows. Analytics often needs a few attributes from millions of rows, so it benefits from a different physical layout and execution path. OLTP vs OLAP OLTP OLAP --------- Query Few rows by key Scan millions Users Customers, apps Analysts, BI Writes Small, random Bulk loads Data size GB–TB TB–PB Large analytical scans can harm latency-sensitive OLTP workloads: a big aggregate evicts hot pages from the buffer pool and competes for I/O. That's why analytics moves to a separate data warehouse, fed by ETL or CDC. Column stores Row stores keep each row's columns together, which is ideal for "fetch order 42". But an analytical query like assumes an existing sales table and returns one aggregate per matching region; values depend on the rows. It reads only 3 columns of a 100-column table. A full row-store heap scan reads pages containing the other columns too, but covering indexes, cache residency and projections can change the I/O comparison. A column store keeps each column in its own file (or segment): Benefits: Read only the needed columns: 3 of 100 equally sized columns would mean roughly 97% less uncompressed column data. Actual I/O savings depend on column sizes, compression, indexes and row-group pruning. Compression: a column holds similar values. Run-length encoding (UK×3), dictionary encoding and bit-packing can compress repeated or correlated values; the ratio depends on the dataset and encoding. Vectorised execution: processing a batch of values from one column in a tight loop uses CPU caches and SIMD instructions efficiently. Zone maps: min/max per block let the engine skip blocks that can't match sale_date >= '2026-01-01'. Costs: a pure column layout may update many column chunks, so many column stores batch writes (often via an in-memory row buffer, LSM-style) and are poor at single-row updates. Examples: Snowflake, BigQuery (Capacitor format, Dremel engine), Amazon Redshift, ClickHouse, Apache Druid, DuckDB, and file formats like Parquet and ORC. Some databases are hybrids (HTAP): SQL Server columnstore indexes, TiDB with TiFlash, SingleStore. Key takeaways Large analytical scans compete with transaction latency for memory and I/O. Column layouts read only needed attributes and can compress and process values in batches. Zone maps prune blocks effectively when their value ranges are narrow; point updates have different costs. Further reading clickhouse.com: intro clickhouse.com: parts parquet.apache.org: overview

sum: Design retries for partial failure without repeating side effects or amplifying load.
x: A distributed system is a set of computers that cooperate over a network and, ideally, look like one machine to the user. You build one because a single machine can't give you enough capacity, availability or geographic reach. The price is that you inherit a class of problems that simply do not exist inside one process. Almost every technique in this module (quorums, consensus, fencing tokens, sagas, CRDTs) exists to tame the failure modes introduced here and in the following units. Partial failure A process crash or power loss can stop all work on one computer. Single machines can also suffer partial faults, such as a failed disk or a stuck thread; networking adds uncertainty about other machines whose state you cannot inspect directly. In a distributed system, failure is partial. Some nodes work, some don't, and some are in an unknown state. Worse, failures are non-deterministic: the same request might succeed, fail, or hang. Consider a client calling a remote service: When the timeout fires, the client has no idea which of these happened: The request was lost before reaching the server. The server is down or paused (e.g. a long GC pause). The server processed the request, but the reply was lost. The server is just slow and will reply in 5 seconds. All four look identical to the client. Cases 1 and 3 are the dangerous pair: in case 1 nothing happened, while in case 3 the side effect (charging a card, sending an email) already happened. This is why retries must be designed with idempotency in mind: an idempotency key lets the server recognise a duplicate and return its recorded result. This depends on the server's atomic deduplication and retention contract: a key forgotten after its retention window no longer protects a late retry. The core uncertainty A remote node can't tell "dead" from "slow" from "network broken". All it ever has is "I haven't heard back yet". Every failure detector is a guess. Living with timeouts Since a timeout is the only failure signal you get, its value is a real design decision. Too short: a slow but healthy node is declared dead. You fail over, retry or rebalance for nothing, and the extra work can make the overload that caused the slowness worse. Too long: a genuinely dead node stalls requests (and users) for the whole timeout before anything happens. A common starting point is to set request timeouts a little above the latency percentile you're willing to give up on (say the p99.9 of healthy calls), rather than picking a round number. Failure detectors used for cluster membership go further and adapt to observed latency; the failure-detection unit later in this module covers the phi accrual detector. Retries need care too Retrying after a timeout is natural, but naive retries cause their own outages: Use the same idempotency key on every attempt. A fresh key per attempt makes each retry look like a new request, which defeats the point. Back off exponentially, with jitter. If thousands of clients retry on the same schedule, they hit the recovering server in synchronised waves. Retry at one layer only. If three layers each make up to 3 attempts, one user request can become 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls at the bottom layer, just when it is least able to cope. The numbers multiply because every attempt at one layer starts a fresh set of attempts at the layer below. In general, when every layer in a stack retries independently: This is the worst case: it happens when every attempt fails, which is exactly what an overloaded database does. If only one layer retries (3 attempts), the bottom layer sees at most 3 calls per request. Key takeaways A timeout cannot tell whether a remote side effect happened; retry using the same idempotency key. Short timeouts can trigger needless failover and overload; long ones delay recovery. Back off with jitter and retry at one layer: independent retries multiply downstream load. Further reading Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (AWS Builders' Library) Making retries safe with idempotent APIs (AWS Builders' Library)

t: Network timing, partitions and process pauses
sum: Separate safety from progress when networks delay messages and healthy processes pause.
x: Timeouts reveal silence, not its cause. To reason about failover, distinguish network timing assumptions from the behaviour of the nodes themselves. The network is asynchronous Most real networks (Ethernet, IP, the internet) are asynchronous packet networks. They promise nothing about delivery time. A packet can be: dropped (a switch buffer overflows), delayed arbitrarily (queueing in switches, TCP retransmits, a busy receiver), duplicated (a retransmit after an ack was lost), reordered (different paths). TCP hides drops, duplicates and reordering from you, but it cannot hide delay, and it cannot tell you whether the far side processed your data once the connection breaks. Distributed systems theory names three timing models: Model Assumption ------ Synchronous Known upper bounds on delay and clock drift Partially synchronous Bounds unknown, or hold after an unknown stabilisation time Asynchronous No bounds at all Real systems are best described as partially synchronous: they behave well most of the time, then occasionally a link saturates or a VM is paused for 30 seconds. Algorithms like Raft are designed so that safety never depends on timing, and only liveness (making progress) needs the network to calm down. Network partitions A partition is when the network splits nodes into groups that cannot talk to each other, even though every node is still running. They happen far more than people expect: misconfigured switches, a cut fibre, a firewall rule, a NIC dropping only inbound packets. This is exactly the situation the CAP theorem talks about: during a partition, each side either refuses some requests (choosing consistency) or accepts them and risks divergence (choosing availability). PACELC adds that even with no partition you trade latency against consistency. Unreliable clocks and process pauses Every machine has its own quartz clock, and they drift (Google assumes up to 200 ppm, around 17 seconds a day if never corrected). NTP corrects them, but only to within a few milliseconds on a good LAN, and much worse over the internet. Clocks can even jump backwards when NTP steps them. Processes can also pause without noticing: a stop-the-world garbage collection (seconds, occasionally minutes), a VM being live-migrated or its hypervisor stealing CPU, the OS swapping memory to disk, a laptop lid closing. A paused thread resumes at its next instruction; a deadline check performed before the pause may now be obsolete. If it was holding a lease ("I'm the leader for 10 more seconds"), it may now act on a lease that expired long ago. The resource-fencing unit later in this module shows how fencing tokens defend against this. Key takeaways Asynchronous packet networks can lose, delay, duplicate or reorder messages; TCP cannot remove uncertainty about remote work. A partition separates working nodes, and one-way failures can give each side a different view. Clock jumps and process pauses make lease holders stale; timing assumptions control progress, not Raft log safety. Further reading Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (AWS Builders' Library) Jepsen analyses of real databases under partition

t: The eight fallacies and the cost of latency
sum: Recognise hidden network assumptions and calculate the cost of sequential remote calls.
x: A local-looking API call may cross a network with real latency and operational boundaries. The eight fallacies are a checklist for finding those hidden assumptions. The eight fallacies of distributed computing Peter Deutsch and colleagues at Sun Microsystems listed the false assumptions that newcomers make. Each one causes real outages. Fallacy What goes wrong ------ The network is reliable Lost requests, half-done operations Latency is zero Chatty APIs become slow over a WAN Bandwidth is infinite Large payloads saturate links The network is secure Unencrypted internal traffic is sniffed Topology doesn't change Hard-coded IPs break on failover There is one administrator Conflicting configs, firewalls Transport cost is zero Serialisation CPU, cross-AZ fees The network is homogeneous Mixed MTUs, protocols, versions Latency is not zero A page that makes 50 sequential calls to a service in the same data centre (0.5 ms round trip) spends 25 ms on the network. Move that service to another region (80 ms round trip) and the same page takes 4 seconds. Nothing in the code changed. When calls are made one after another (sequentially), each one waits for a full round trip before the next can start, so the network time is simply the number of calls multiplied by the round-trip time: This ignores the time the service spends doing the work, which adds on top. It only holds for sequential calls: calls made in parallel overlap, so 50 parallel calls cost roughly one round trip, not fifty. Key takeaways Reliability, latency, bandwidth, security, topology, administration, cost and homogeneity are all assumptions to check. Sequential calls pay one round trip each; moving a chatty service across regions can dominate its runtime. Parallel calls overlap network waits; service processing time remains an additional cost. Further reading Fallacies of distributed computing (Wikipedia) Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (AWS Builders' Library)

sum: Use the Two Generals argument to understand what retries and acknowledgements can promise.
x: A reply gives useful evidence, but asking the other party to acknowledge that reply starts the same uncertainty again. The Two Generals thought experiment isolates that limit. The Two Generals problem This thought experiment proves that no protocol over an unreliable channel can guarantee that two parties agree to act together. Two armies, A and B, camp on hills either side of a city. They win only if they attack at the same time. Their only means of communication is a message carrier who must run through the valley, where they might be captured. Suppose some protocol worked, and consider the shortest sequence of messages that results in both attacking. The last message in that sequence might be captured. Whoever sent it can't know whether it arrived, so the decision must not depend on it, meaning a shorter protocol also works. Repeat the argument and you reach zero messages, which obviously can't coordinate anything. Contradiction. What it means in practice You can't get certain agreement over a lossy network, so real systems settle for something weaker: Probabilistic confidence: send many message carriers; the chance all are lost shrinks quickly. Idempotent retries: keep retrying until acknowledged, and make repeats harmless. Agreement among a majority: consensus algorithms (covered later in this module) don't need every node to know; a majority is enough, and they tolerate lost messages by retrying. TCP's connection close runs into the same limitation: the final ACK can be lost, and the side that sent it can't know. That's one reason the TIME_WAIT state exists: it lingers so it can re-send the ACK if the peer re-sends its FIN. Two Generals vs Byzantine Generals Two Generals is about unreliable messages between honest parties. The Byzantine Generals problem is about dishonest or arbitrarily faulty nodes. Practical Byzantine fault tolerance (PBFT and its descendants) needs more than three nodes per traitor tolerated; most data-centre systems assume nodes are honest and only tolerate crashes, which needs a little over two nodes per fault. The next unit gives the exact counts for these quorum models. Key takeaways A final acknowledgement can always be lost, so another acknowledgement cannot create certain common knowledge. Retries, idempotency and majority agreement offer useful weaker guarantees under their own assumptions. Two Generals concerns unreliable communication; Byzantine Generals concerns arbitrarily faulty participants. Further reading Two Generals' Problem (Wikipedia) Byzantine fault (Wikipedia)

sum: Choose crash or Byzantine assumptions and understand the quorum counts and durable-state boundary.
x: A fault-tolerance claim is meaningful only with a fault model. A machine stopping is different from a restarted machine forgetting its votes or a node sending contradictory messages. Fault models When you read about an algorithm, check which faults it tolerates: Model Node behaviour ------ Crash-stop Fails by halting, never returns Crash-recovery Halts, may restart with its disk Omission Drops some messages Byzantine Anything, including lying Raft and Paxos assume crash-recovery with durable storage. Many blockchain protocols instead tolerate Byzantine faults. Choosing the model is a design decision: Byzantine tolerance is expensive and rarely needed inside one company's data centre. How many nodes you need The quorum model sets how many nodes a cluster needs to survive a given number of faulty ones. The counts below apply to majority crash quorums and the standard unsigned Byzantine quorum model, rather than every possible timing or signature model: Where the numbers come from: Crashes: decisions need a majority. If f nodes crash, the remaining f + 1 must still be a majority of the cluster, which first happens at 2f + 1 nodes. Any two majorities share at least one node, so no two decisions can contradict each other. Byzantine faults: a liar can tell different nodes different things, so a quorum must contain enough honest nodes to outvote it. With 3f + 1 nodes and quorums of 2f + 1, any two quorums share at least f + 1 nodes, and since at most f of those are liars, at least one honest node is in both. So tolerating 2 faults takes 5 nodes for crashes but 7 for Byzantine faults. That extra cost is why most data-centre systems assume crash faults only. The fine print matters. "Crash-recovery with durable storage" means a node that restarts still has everything it fsynced. A node that comes back with an empty or rolled-back disk (a replaced VM, a disk cache that lied about flushing) has amnesia, and that falls outside the model: it can vote twice in the same term and break safety. Likewise, silent data corruption is closer to a Byzantine fault than a crash, which is why storage systems add checksums. Key takeaways Crash-stop, crash-recovery, omission and Byzantine faults permit different node behaviours. Majority crash-tolerant groups and the standard Byzantine quorum model need different replica counts. Crash-recovery assumes durable state survives restart; amnesia and silent corruption can violate that assumption. Further reading The Byzantine Generals Problem (Lamport, Shostak and Pease) Byzantine fault (Wikipedia)

sum: Judge overlapping reads and writes using the single-copy contract and real-time order.
x: When data is replicated, different clients can see different values at the same moment. A consistency model is a contract that says which histories of reads and writes are allowed. Stronger models allow fewer surprising histories, at a cost in latency and availability. The CAP theorem's "C" means one specific model, linearizability. In practice there's a whole spectrum, and choosing the right point on it is one of the most important design decisions you make. The hierarchy From strongest to weakest (these are models for individual reads and writes, not multi-step transactions): Each level shown allows every history the level above allows, plus more. Session guarantees form additional, partly independent properties. Eventual convergence is a separate liveness promise and should not be inferred merely from a safety ordering model. Jepsen's map also places transactional models such as serializability alongside these. Linearizability Linearizability (also called atomic or strong consistency) means the system behaves as if there were one copy of the data, and every operation takes effect atomically at some instant between its start and its end. In the timelines below, x is a single stored value (one key) that starts at 0. write x=1 means a client sets it to 1, read x means a client asks for its current value, and each bar runs from when the client sent the request to when it got the reply. The key consequence is recency guarantee: once a write completes, every later read (in real-time order) must see it or something newer. And once any client has read a new value, no later read anywhere may return the old one. C's read overlaps A's write, so either answer is fine. B's read starts after the write finished, so it must return 1. These examples contain only one write. A later write can deliberately restore an old-looking value without violating linearizability; recency concerns operation/version order, not a number always increasing. A violation B saw the new value; C started after B finished, yet saw the old one. That's what happens with naive async replication: B hit an up-to-date replica, C hit a lagging one. Composability Linearizability is local (Herlihy and Wing call it composable): if every individual object is linearizable, the system as a whole is linearizable. You can shard keys across independent linearizable groups and still reason about each one alone. Sequential consistency does not compose: two objects that are each sequentially consistent can together produce a history that no single order explains. Where you need it Leader election and locks: everyone must agree who holds the lock. Uniqueness constraints: two users can't both claim username alice. Cross-channel timing: a user uploads a file, then a message on a queue tells a worker to process it. If the worker reads a stale replica, the file "doesn't exist". What it costs Linearizability needs coordination (a single leader with synchronous confirmation, or consensus). A replicated service must establish an authoritative order for writes and freshness for reads. Many protocols pay a quorum round trip; safe leader leases can permit local reads while their timing assumptions hold, so a network round trip is not required for every read. During a partition, the minority side must stop serving. That's the CAP theorem, and PACELC's "else latency" is the cost even without partitions. Linearizable vs serializable Serializability is about transactions over many objects: the result equals some serial order, which needn't match real-time order. Linearizability is about single operations respecting real-time order. Having both is called strict serializability. Spanner (which calls it external consistency) and FoundationDB provide it; CockroachDB provides serializability with somewhat weaker guarantees about real-time order. Key takeaways Linearizability places each operation at an instant between invocation and response, respecting real-time order. An overlapping read may return old or new; once a new value is observed, a later read cannot go backwards. Linearizability composes across objects and requires coordination; serializability concerns transactions. Further reading Consistency models map (Jepsen) Linearizability (Jepsen) Strict serializability (Jepsen) Linearizability versus serializability (Peter Bailis)

sum: Distinguish per-client order and transaction order from guarantees about real-time order.
x: The preceding lesson defined linearizability and strict serializability. Here the question is what remains when a system preserves an agreed order but does not promise that it matches real-time order. Sequential consistency Sequential consistency (Lamport, 1979) requires that all operations appear in some single total order that is consistent with each client's program order, but not necessarily with real-time order. So in the preceding linearizability unit’s violation diagram, if B and C are different clients with no communication, sequential consistency could allow it (order: C reads 0, A writes 1, B reads 1). What it forbids is a single client seeing time go backwards, or two clients disagreeing about the order of two writes. It's mostly of interest for CPU memory models and as a stepping stone. ZooKeeper is a real-world example of something close to it: writes are linearizable, but a read served by a follower may be stale, while each client still sees updates in one agreed order. Telling the three apart The names are easy to mix up, so compare them on two questions: what do they cover, and do they respect real-time order? Model Covers Real-time order? --------- Linearizable Single operations Yes Sequential Single operations No, only per-client order Serializable Multi-object transactions No Strict serializable Transactions Yes A quick test: if a history only looks wrong when you compare wall-clock times across different clients, it can still be sequentially consistent or serializable, but it isn't linearizable or strictly serializable. Key takeaways Sequential consistency preserves each client’s program order inside one total order, without requiring cross-client real-time order. Serializable transactions match some serial transaction order; strict serializability also respects real-time order. A stale cross-client read can fit sequential consistency or serializability even when it violates linearizability. Further reading Sequential consistency (Jepsen) Strict serializability (Jepsen) Linearizability versus serializability (Peter Bailis)

sum: Keep dependencies in order while understanding what partition availability and convergence leave unspecified.
x: Sequential consistency imposes a total order on all operations. Causal consistency relaxes that requirement for unrelated work; eventual convergence is a separate promise about what happens after updates stop. Causal consistency Causal consistency only orders operations that are causally related. If operation A could have influenced operation B (B happened after reading A's result, or they're in the same session), everyone must see A before B. Concurrent operations can be seen in different orders by different nodes. Without causal consistency, Carol might see Bob's "Congrats!" before Alice's posts arrive, or see the posts in reverse, which reads as Bob celebrating a sacking. Causal consistency is, in effect, the strongest model that remains available during partitions: each side keeps working and merges causal histories later. (Strictly, Mahajan et al. proved this for a slight strengthening called real-time causal, and it needs sticky availability, where each client keeps talking to the same replica.) Systems track causality with version vectors or dependency metadata; MongoDB offers causally consistent sessions. Eventual consistency Eventual consistency promises only that if writes stop, all replicas eventually converge to the same value. It says nothing about what you read in the meantime: stale values, values going backwards, writes out of order. It's what you get from Dynamo-style stores with low quorum settings, DNS, and asynchronous read replicas. It is cheap and highly available, and fine for things like like-counts and product views. But "eventually" has no bound, and convergence needs a conflict-resolution rule (covered in the CRDT units later in this module). Some systems offer bounded staleness in between: reads may lag, but by no more than a stated time or number of versions (Azure Cosmos DB offers this as a named level). That is stronger than eventual, because it gives a bound, but weaker than linearizable. Key takeaways Causal consistency orders dependent operations; independent concurrent writes need no common total order. Partition availability for causal histories needs suitable sticky replicas; moving clients may require waiting for dependencies. Eventual consistency promises convergence after writes stop, not bounded staleness or a particular intermediate read order. Further reading Consistency models map (Jepsen) Causal consistency (Jepsen) Please stop calling databases CP or AP (Kleppmann)

sum: Prevent vanished edits and backwards reads with version-aware session routing.
x: Eventual convergence can still make an edit appear to vanish on the next page refresh. Session guarantees add promises that follow a particular client without globally ordering every operation. Session guarantees Pure eventual consistency produces anomalies users notice immediately. Terry et al. (Bayou, 1994) defined four session guarantees that fix the worst of them cheaply, per client session: Guarantee Promise ------ Read-your-writes You see your own writes Monotonic reads You never see time go backwards Monotonic writes Your writes apply in order Writes-follow-reads Writes after a read are ordered after it Read-your-writes A user edits their profile, the page reloads from a lagging replica, and the edit has "vanished". They edit again. Read-your-writes prevents this. Implementations: Read from the authoritative leader for relevant data, or track a confirmed replication position. Routing to the leader for 60 s is only a heuristic unless replica lag is bounded below that interval. The client remembers the log position (LSN / timestamp) of its last write; a replica serves the read only if it has caught up past that point. Monotonic reads Fix: pin each user to a replica whose history never rolls back; when moving replicas, carry the last-seen version and wait for that version. Tracking versions is necessary across failover or rollback. Session guarantees are cheap They need only per-client metadata, not global coordination. Cross-device sessions are harder: the phone doesn't know what the laptop wrote unless the token is shared via the server. Choosing a model Need Model ------ Locks, leader, unique IDs Linearizable Comments, chat threads Causal Own profile edits Read-your-writes Like counts, view counts Eventual A common pattern is to mix them: strong consistency for a small core (account balances, inventory reservation) and weaker models everywhere else. Check the claims Jepsen has repeatedly found databases that advertise strong consistency but violate it under partitions or clock skew. Treat vendor claims as hypotheses and look for independent testing. Key takeaways Read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes and writes-follow-reads protect a client session. Carry confirmed replication positions across replica moves and failover; timed leader pinning alone is a heuristic. Cross-device sessions need shared metadata, and applications can choose stronger models only for their critical data. Further reading Original session guarantees paper (Terry et al.) Consistency models map (Jepsen) Causal consistency (Jepsen) Please stop calling databases CP or AP (Kleppmann)

sum: Choose the right clock for durations and see how skew can discard a later write.
x: Many distributed problems boil down to "which happened first?". Which write wins? Did this message cause that one? Is this lease still valid? On one machine the answer comes from a single clock. Across machines there is no shared clock, so you need to be careful about what "first" even means. Physical clocks and their problems Each server has two kinds of clock: Clock Use Behaviour --------- Time-of-day Timestamps Can jump back or forward Monotonic Measuring durations Only moves forward In Linux these are CLOCK_REALTIME and CLOCK_MONOTONIC. Rule one: never measure a timeout with the time-of-day clock. An NTP step can make an elapsed time negative. Drift and skew Quartz crystals run slightly fast or slow, and it varies with temperature. Drift depends on the oscillator and operating conditions. The 2012 Spanner paper used a conservative allowance of 200 parts per million (ppm): at that rate a clock gains or loses up to 200 microseconds every second. To see what that means over a day, multiply the drift rate by the time that passes: This calculation assumes a constant rate. Treat it as a bound only when the hardware and operating conditions justify that maximum drift rate; temperature can change the actual rate. A 10 ppm clock would build up less than a second a day. Skew is the difference between two clocks at one moment. Two clocks that drift in opposite directions grow apart at the sum of their rates. Last-write-wins with skewed clocks Node A's clock is 100 ms fast. A client writes v1 on A at A-time 10.100 (real 10.000). 50 ms later a client writes v2 on B at B-time 10.050 (real 10.050). LWW keeps v1 because 10.100 > 10.050, silently discarding the genuinely later write. This is a well-known hazard in Cassandra and other last-write-wins stores: any two writes closer together than the clock skew can be ordered wrongly. Key takeaways Use a monotonic clock for durations and timeouts; wall clocks can jump forwards or backwards. Drift is a clock’s rate error; skew is the difference between clocks at one moment. Timestamp last-write-wins can discard the later write in physical time when coordinator clocks are skewed. Further reading Spanner clock assumptions (OSDI 2012) Linux clock interfaces Network Time Protocol (Wikipedia)

sum: Calculate round-trip delay and offset, then identify the uncertainty caused by asymmetric paths.
x: Physical clocks drift, and synchronisation estimates their offset rather than discovering exact time. NTP’s round-trip exchange shows both how the estimate works and what it cannot observe. NTP The Network Time Protocol syncs a client with servers arranged in strata (stratum 0 is an atomic clock or GPS; stratum 1 servers attach to it, and so on). A client estimates offset from a round trip: The client records when it sent the request and when the reply arrived (on its own clock); the server records when it received the request and when it sent the reply (on its clock). From those four timestamps NTP works out two things: how long the messages spent on the network, and how far apart the two clocks are. Why the offset formula works: the difference t_1 − t_0 is the offset plus the outbound travel time, and t_2 − t_3 is the offset minus the return travel time. Adding them and halving cancels the travel time, but only when both directions take the same time. Worked example: the client sends at 100 ms, the server receives at 160 ms and replies at 161 ms, and the reply arrives at 120 ms (each time on its own side's clock): The offset formula assumes the network delay is symmetric. If the outbound path is slow and the return fast, the estimate is wrong by half the asymmetry: NTP has no way to notice this error from the timestamps alone. Typical accuracy: around 1 ms on a good LAN, tens of ms over the internet, and much worse under congestion. Managed time services differ: Amazon Time Sync supports NTP and, on supported EC2 hardware, a more precise PTP hardware clock. Google Public NTP uses leap smearing but explicitly provides no service-level agreement. Do not infer a universal sub-millisecond error bound from either provider's name. NTP corrects a clock by slewing (running it slightly fast or slow) for small offsets and stepping (jumping) for large ones. Steps are what make clocks go backwards. Key takeaways NTP uses four timestamps to subtract server processing time from round-trip delay and estimate clock offset. The offset estimate assumes equal one-way delays; its error is half the path asymmetry. Slewing adjusts a clock’s rate; stepping changes its reading abruptly, so wall time remains unsuitable for durations. Further reading Network Time Protocol Version 4 (RFC 5905) Amazon Time Sync options Google Public NTP FAQ Network Time Protocol (Wikipedia)

sum: Trace logical counters while avoiding the mistake that a smaller timestamp proves causality.
x: Wall time cannot reliably answer whether one event influenced another. Logical clocks start from the information that can actually flow between processes. Happens-before Lamport's 1978 paper defined order without clocks. It uses two pieces of notation: Event a happens before b (a → b) if: a and b are on the same process and a comes first, or a is sending a message and b is receiving that message, or there's an event c with a → c and c → b (transitivity: chains of happens-before also count). If neither event happens before the other, the events are concurrent. Concurrent doesn't mean simultaneous; it means neither could have influenced the other. Lamport clocks Each process keeps a single whole-number counter, L, starting at 0. Two rules update it: The first rule applies before every local event or send; the second on every receive. Worked example: P1's counter is 7 and P2's is 3. P1 sends a message, so its counter becomes 7 + 1 = 8 and the message carries 8. P2 receives it and sets its counter to the larger of 3 and 8, plus one, which is 9. The send (8) comes before the receive (9), as it must. The guarantee Lamport clocks give: Break ties with process id to get a total order consistent with causality. That's enough for things like a totally ordered mutex queue. Limitation: the converse fails. In the diagram, L(c) is 3 and L(b) is 4, so c has a smaller timestamp than b, but c and b are concurrent: no message path links them. A Lamport timestamp can't tell you whether two events are concurrent. Read the guarantee the right way round: A smaller timestamp means the event might have happened before the other, or they might be concurrent. Equal timestamps on different processes mean the events are definitely concurrent, because causally related events always have different timestamps. A larger timestamp means that event did not happen before the other. Either the other happened first, or they are concurrent. Logical clocks you already use Many systems contain similar logical epoch counters: Raft's term, Paxos's ballot number, Kafka's leader epoch, ZooKeeper's zxid. Each is a number that only goes up and is carried on messages, so a node that sees a higher one knows its own information is out of date. These counters track protocol generations; they do not necessarily assign a distinct Lamport timestamp to every application event. The resource-fencing unit later in this module uses ordered generations for fencing tokens. Key takeaways Happens-before follows local process order, message delivery and transitive chains; concurrent means neither event could influence the other. Lamport counters increment on local events and jump past both local and message counters on receive. Causality implies increasing timestamps, but increasing timestamps do not prove causality; equal timestamps on distinct processes imply concurrency. Further reading Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events (Lamport, 1978)

sum: Merge vector timestamps and compare every entry to distinguish causality from conflict.
x: Lamport clocks preserve causality but cannot detect concurrent events. A vector records each process’s progress separately, giving enough information to make that comparison. Vector clocks A vector clock keeps one counter per process. With N processes, each process holds a list of N counters, V[1] to V[N]: its best knowledge of how many events every process has had. For example, if P2's clock is [1, 4, 2] and it receives a message stamped [3, 1, 0], the position-by-position maximum is [3, 4, 2], and adding one to P2's own entry gives [3, 5, 2]. To compare two vector timestamps V and W: The last case is the one Lamport clocks can't see: distinct events are concurrent exactly when neither vector is less than or equal to the other in every position. Does event c precede the send on P2? Compare their vectors [3,0,0] and [2,2,0]: 3 > 2 in one position, 0 < 2 in another. Concurrent. Vector clocks can detect that, which is why Dynamo and Riak used them to keep both sibling values instead of silently dropping one. Cost: one entry per participant. With thousands of clients as writers, vectors bloat, so systems use version vectors keyed by replica (not client), or prune old entries (which can misclassify causal relationships). Key takeaways Each process increments its own vector entry; receive takes entry-wise maxima and then increments the receiver’s entry. One vector causally precedes another when no entry is greater and at least one is smaller. Vectors ahead in different entries are concurrent; metadata grows with the number of participants. Further reading Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events (Lamport, 1978) Vector clock (Wikipedia)

t: Hybrid logical clocks and uncertain reads
sum: Combine wall time with a counter and recognise when clock uncertainty requires a read restart.
x: Vector clocks expose causality but carry an entry per participant. Hybrid logical clocks keep a compact, time-like timestamp while retaining Lamport’s one-way causality guarantee. Hybrid logical clocks (HLC) HLC (Kulkarni et al., 2014) combines physical time with a logical counter. Each timestamp is a pair (l, c): l tracks the largest physical time seen, c is a counter that breaks ties when l doesn't advance. The rule on a send or local event: The counter c then decides ties. If l′ is the same as l (the wall clock hasn't moved past what was already seen), c goes up by one; otherwise the physical part has advanced and c resets to 0. As code: The update below is a fragment: l, c and pt are supplied by the surrounding clock implementation. It shows a local or send event, not the separate receive rule. On receive of a message stamped (lm, cm), take the max of l, lm and pt. If the new physical part matches both the old local part and the message part, use one more than the larger counter. If only one matches, increment that input's counter. If physical time exceeds both, reset the counter to zero. Properties: Respects happens-before like a Lamport clock (and, like one, can't detect concurrency).
