DynamoDB's MREC mode resolves conflicts per item, including different-attribute updates; it does not provide an attribute-wise merge. MRSC is a separately configured strongly consistent mode. Current AWS documentation permits combinations of three supported Regions, including Regions on different continents. You cannot change a global table's consistency mode after creation, so adopting MRSC for an existing EU/US MREC table still requires a migration rather than an in-place switch. Key takeaways LWW resolves a conflict by discarding one competing write; it does not merge independent whole-item edits. CRDT convergence relies on the data type's identity, durable state, merge and eventual-delivery assumptions. A counter merge does not enforce one-like-per-user, non-negative balances or unique reservations. Use atomic authoritative operations or bounded exclusive rights for invariants that merge semantics cannot preserve. Further reading AWS: DynamoDB global tables Wikipedia: Conflict-free replicated data type

sum: Apply an explicit residency requirement to every copy and contain local operational failures with cells.
x: Regional replication and conflict rules do not contain every bad deploy or runaway tenant. Combine home-region placement with smaller independent stacks and audit every data-copy path. Data residency Consider a hypothetical tenant whose contract explicitly requires EU-only storage and processing. The following is an architecture exercise for that stated requirement. Content gap Jurisdiction-specific legal requirements are not assessed here: no applicable contract, sector or legal analysis was supplied. This lesson does not assert that every EU customer has an EU-only obligation. Pin data to a region by tenant or user: EU customers' records live and are processed in EU regions, and are not replicated to the US. Separate global from local data: product catalogues and configuration can be global; personal data stays local. A global directory can map opaque tenant identifiers to home regions, but identifiers and routing metadata may themselves be personal data if they can be linked to a person; minimise and govern that data too. Watch the side channels: backups, logs, analytics pipelines, search indexes, caches and support tools all copy data. Residency applies to every copy. Disaster recovery inside the boundary: fail over from Frankfurt to another EU region, not to Virginia. Cell-based architecture Multi-region protects you from a region failing. But many outages are caused by you: a bad deploy, a poison-pill request, a runaway tenant, a configuration change. Shared dependencies can let such failures affect many customers. A cell-based architecture divides the system into many independent, identical copies called cells, each serving a subset of customers, with no shared state between cells. Blast radius: a cell-local failure can be contained to that cell if shared dependencies remain healthy. With 20 equally populated cells, one cell holds 1/20 = 5% of customers. Staged deploys: roll out to one cell, watch, then expand in waves. Known scaling limits: each cell has a fixed maximum size that has been load tested. Growth means adding cells, not scaling one system into unknown territory. Routing layer: a thin, extremely simple router (often a lookup of customer → cell) is a shared dependency to keep minimal and robust; audit other shared services and control-plane dependencies too. AWS uses cells extensively (it publishes guidance on the pattern), Slack migrated to a cellular architecture aligned with availability zones after zone-level incidents, and Azure calls the pattern Deployment Stamps. A related AWS technique, shuffle sharding, assigns each customer to a random combination of a few nodes, so that one customer's poison traffic overlaps fully with very few others. Cells and regions combine: each region contains several cells; a customer's cell lives in their home region; DR replicates each cell to a paired region. Putting it together A realistic design for a global SaaS: Users are assigned a home region (by residency or proximity) and a cell within it. A global directory and router send requests to the right cell, wherever the user connects. Each cell replicates asynchronously to a standby in a paired region inside the same jurisdiction (define objectives and verify recovery point and duration with drills). Truly global data (catalogue, feature flags) is replicated everywhere, read-mostly. Invariant-critical operations stay single-writer; commutative data (likes, presence, baskets) can be multi-writer with CRDTs. Why shuffled assignments reduce full overlap With fixed groups of four workers, a customer's traffic that breaks all four removes every worker for its whole group. Shuffle sharding instead assigns customers different four-worker combinations drawn from the larger fleet. Another customer loses every assigned worker only when its combination fully overlaps the failed one; partial overlaps can leave a healthy retry route. The combination calculation in the question assumes independent uniform assignments. It does not guarantee that every partially overlapping customer has spare capacity or that shared dependencies survive. Key takeaways A stated residency boundary covers backups, logs, analytics, search, caches and support paths as well as the primary. Cells isolate full serving stacks and bound tested scale; shared routers and control planes still require scrutiny. Staged cell deployment and tenant isolation reduce impact only when failures stay within the intended boundary. Shuffle sharding reduces full overlap between assigned worker sets, assuming healthy retry alternatives and sufficient capacity. Further reading AWS: What is a cell-based architecture? AWS Builders' Library: Workload isolation using shuffle-sharding Slack: Slack's migration to a cellular architecture Azure Architecture Center: Deployment Stamps pattern

t: Fan-out, timing faults and gray failure
sum: Recognise failure symptoms and why remote health checks can misclassify slow components.
x: This unit builds on fault models, leases and fencing in Distributed Systems. A fencing token is a monotonically increasing leadership epoch checked by the storage service: writes from an older epoch are rejected, even if the old leader resumes after a pause. At scale, failure is not an exception; it is the normal background noise. As an illustrative fleet calculation, 10,000 disks with an assumed 2% annual failure rate loses roughly 200 disks a year (10,000 × 0.02), or about four a week. Fan-out makes rare slowness common. If one request makes many independent downstream calls, the chance that at least one of them is slow is one minus the chance that every call is fast: This assumes the calls are slow independently of each other. Real delays are often correlated (one overloaded host slows many calls at once), and the answer also depends on where you draw the line for "slow". Reliability engineering starts by accepting this and asking three questions of every design: How can each component fail? If it fails, how much of the system goes with it? What keeps working, and does anyone have to wake up? The fundamentals module covered availability "nines" and how availability multiplies across hard dependencies in series. This lesson is about the shapes of failure behind those numbers and the structural tools for containing them. A taxonomy of failure modes Distributed systems literature classifies faults by how badly a component can misbehave. These categories highlight different symptoms; they are not a universal strict hierarchy. A Byzantine model permits arbitrary behavior, including omission or timing faults. Mode What happens Example --------- Crash Stops executing; detection may be uncertain Kernel panic, OOM kill Omission Drops some messages Full queue, lost packet Timing / latency Responds, but too late GC pause, noisy neighbour Byzantine Responds wrongly Bit flip, bug, attacker Crash failures The easiest to handle, because silence is unambiguous if you can detect it. Health checks, heartbeats and leases can suspect loss of responsiveness; a load balancer stops routing to the dead node and a container orchestrator replaces it. The catch: in an asynchronous network you cannot distinguish "crashed" from "very slow". Remote timeout-based detectors can be wrong; local process/OS notifications can also provide failure evidence. Omission failures The component is up but some requests or replies vanish. A saturated connection pool, a dropped UDP packet, a message broker that discards on overflow. Omissions look like timeouts to the caller, which is why they push people towards retries (next lesson). Latency failures: the dangerous middle A node that is slow but alive is often worse than a dead one. It still passes shallow health checks, still receives traffic, and ties up the caller's threads and connections while it dawdles. Microsoft researchers named this kind of fault gray failure (Huang et al., HotOS 2017): the system's failure detector sees a healthy component while the applications using it see a broken one. They argue that subtle faults like this, rather than clean crashes, are behind many major cloud availability breakdowns. Typical examples are a degraded disk, a NIC dropping a few per cent of packets, or a JVM stuck in GC. The fix is a combination of tight timeouts, latency-aware load balancing, and health checks that test real work, not just "is the process listening". Key takeaways Large fleets experience routine failures; fan-out increases exposure to independently slow calls. Crash, omission and timing faults present different symptoms; a shallow health check can miss gray failure. A timeout suspects a remote failure. Use fencing so a paused former leader cannot resume stale writes. Further reading Gray failure: the Achilles' heel of cloud-scale systems (Huang et al., HotOS 2017) Addressing cascading failures (Google SRE book) AWS Well-Architected Reliability Pillar

sum: Choose proportionate defences for wrong answers and identify single points of failure.
x: The previous unit covered silence and slowness. Here the component may answer incorrectly, or a shared dependency may disable every otherwise healthy replica. For the availability question, recall Fundamentals: independent hard dependency availabilities multiply, while independent redundant copies fail together only when all copies are down. Byzantine failures The component returns wrong answers: corrupted data, a buggy release computing the wrong price, or a malicious node. Tolerating liars costs far more replicas than tolerating crashes. Classic partially synchronous Byzantine consensus protocols such as PBFT need: For comparison, a crash-tolerant protocol such as Raft needs only three replicas to survive one crash, because a majority of two can still agree. Bounds differ with timing, authentication and trust assumptions; this is not a universal rule for every Byzantine-tolerant system. In practice, ordinary systems defend against the accidental Byzantine cases cheaply: Checksums on disk blocks and network payloads (S3, HDFS and Kafka all checksum data). Input validation of inputs and invariants at service boundaries. End-to-end data verification, e.g. reconciling ledgers nightly. Fail-fast is a design choice Failing fast on a detected broken invariant can contain corruption; consider redundancy and recovery before terminating a process. A process that detects a broken invariant and exits is far easier for the rest of the system to handle than one that keeps serving corrupt data. Single points of failure A single point of failure (SPOF) is any component whose failure takes the whole service down. The obvious ones are easy to spot: one database primary, one load balancer. The dangerous ones hide: Shared configuration: one bad config push to every node at once. DNS and certificates: an expired TLS certificate is a global SPOF with a calendar date. Control planes: your redundant VMs are fine, but you can't launch new ones because the provider's API is down. People and process: the only engineer who knows how to restore backups. Hidden dependencies: every "independent" region authenticates against one identity service in us-east-1. A useful exercise is to draw the request path and ask, for each box and arrow, "what if this vanished right now?" Key takeaways Classic PBFT needs four replicas to tolerate one Byzantine participant under its stated assumptions. Checksums, boundary validation and reconciliation address many accidental wrong-answer failures. Redundant app servers cannot mask a shared configuration, certificate, database or identity dependency. Further reading Byzantine fault (Wikipedia) Single point of failure (Wikipedia) AWS Well-Architected Reliability Pillar Practical Byzantine fault tolerance (Castro and Liskov)

sum: Calculate shuffle-shard overlap and limit the customer blast radius.
x: A single point of failure can disable the entire service. A fault boundary instead contains damage to a host, zone, region or cell. This unit asks how much damage one bad tenant or change can cause, even when the service remains partly available. Blast radius Redundancy stops a failure taking everything down. Blast radius asks the next question: when something does fail, how many users or requests are affected? Techniques for shrinking it: Cell-based architecture: split the service into independent full copies (cells), each serving a slice of customers. A bad deploy or poison request takes out one cell, not all of them. AWS uses cell-based architecture widely for this reason. The thin routing layer that maps customers to cells is shared by all of them, so it must be kept as simple and static as possible. Shuffle sharding: give each customer a random subset of workers. A customer who sends poison requests only damages their own subset. The number of different subsets ("shuffle shards") is a combination count (see the formula below). Availability zones and regions as fault boundaries, so a power or network event is contained. Staged rollouts: deploy to one host, then one zone, then one region (covered in the deployments lesson). How much does shuffle sharding help? Count the distinct subsets a customer could be given. Choosing k workers out of n, where order doesn't matter, is the "n choose k" count: Customers who share just one worker still have a healthy second worker and can continue at reduced capacity if retry/rerouting and survivor headroom support it. The calculation assumes shards are assigned at random and that a customer survives as long as one of its workers is healthy. Shuffle sharding in numbers AWS has described Route 53 shuffle sharding over 2,048 virtual name servers, giving each domain 4 of them. The number of possible combinations, 2,048 choose 4, is about 730 billion, so an attack against one customer's servers almost never fully overlaps another's. Key takeaways A cell contains a full serving stack for a slice of customers. Keep the shared cell router simple because every cell depends on it. Eight workers assigned in random pairs provide 28 possible shards; partial overlap can still degrade service. Further reading Workload isolation using shuffle-sharding (AWS Builders' Library) AWS Well-Architected Reliability Pillar

sum: Reserve enough existing capacity to survive planned failures without emergency provisioning.
x: Cells limit impact; redundancy keeps a serving path available. This unit assumes identical linear capacity and evenly redistributed work when calculating how busy the survivors become. Real load tests must also cover uneven work, peak demand and latency targets. Redundancy that actually works Adding a second copy helps against failures not shared by all copies; full statistical independence is needed for the simple product-probability calculation. Two servers in the same rack share a power supply and a switch; two databases in the same region share a control plane; two replicas running the same buggy binary fail together. Redundancy Protects against Doesn't protect against --------- N+1 instances One host dying Bad deploy to all Multi-AZ Data-centre outage Region control plane Multi-region Regional disaster Global config error Diverse software Shared bug Shared bad data Active-active vs active-passive Active-passive: a standby takes over when the primary fails. Simple, but an unexercised standby may hide faults until failover; drills and validation reduce this risk, and failover itself can fail. Active-active: all copies serve traffic. Normal serving paths are exercised continuously; failure paths still need testing, but you must handle concurrent writes and must keep enough headroom that the survivors can absorb the load. Capacity for failure: N+1 and static stability If you run 3 nodes at 80% utilisation and lose one, the remaining two need to carry 120% each. They fall over, and you have turned a single failure into a total outage. The total work stays the same when a node dies; it is just shared among fewer survivors: Setting U_after to 100% and solving for U gives the general rule: the highest safe utilisation before a failure. Treat U_max as a ceiling, not a target. At 60% the survivors land on 90%, and the queueing maths in the overload lesson shows that an illustrative M/M/1 model predicts mean response time ten times mean service time at 90%; this is not a universal latency multiplier. Real teams keep extra margin for traffic growth, uneven load balancing and the failure happening at peak. The rule also assumes load spreads evenly over the survivors. More, smaller units make redundancy cheaper, as the second formula shows: 3 nodes surviving one loss can only run at 67%, but 10 nodes can run at 90%. The same logic is why three AZs are more efficient than two: two AZs that must each survive the other's loss can run at only 50%: one of two equal zones survives. AWS calls the stronger version static stability: the system keeps working through a failure without depending on new provisioning or impaired control-plane operations, such as launching new instances or changing DNS. If you pre-provision capacity in each zone to survive losing another zone, you don't depend on a control plane that may itself be impaired during the event. Key takeaways Redundant copies need distinct failure exposure and regularly tested failover. Size survivors for the full redistributed load; the capacity ceiling assumes equal nodes and even work. Keep extra latency and traffic headroom below that ceiling. Static stability avoids impaired provisioning or management APIs. Further reading Static stability using Availability Zones (AWS Builders' Library) Addressing cascading failures (Google SRE book)

sum: Challenge independence assumptions and audit the complete failure path.
x: The preceding units separated fault symptoms, isolation and survivor capacity. Apply them together before accepting an availability estimate. Adding another copy changes the estimate only when its failure exposure and routing behaviour match the assumptions of the calculation. Correlated failure and the "it can't all fail" fallacy The probability maths of redundancy assumes independence. When two replicas fail independently, the chance both are down at once is the product of their individual chances of being down: That is only true if the failures really are independent. But real failures correlate: The same bad config or software release is applied to both. A load spike that kills one replica shifts its load to the other and kills that too (a cascading failure). Both depend on the same downstream service, DNS or certificate. Correlation also hides in time. Disks bought in the same batch tend to fail at similar ages, and a RAID rebuild puts heavy load on the surviving disks exactly when you can least afford another failure. Cascading failures are an important way redundant systems can go fully dark. The rest of this module covers the tools for stopping them: timeouts, retry discipline, circuit breakers, load shedding, and safe deployment. A checklist for any design List every component and dependency on the request path. For each, decide what crash, omission, latency and wrong-answer failures look like. Mark SPOFs, including config, DNS, certificates, control planes and humans. Decide the fault boundary (host, zone, region, cell) and the blast radius at each. Confirm survivors have headroom to absorb a failed peer's load. Prefer designs that are statically stable over ones that need a control plane to recover. Key takeaways Independent replica probabilities do not describe shared bugs, configuration or dependencies. A failed replica can overload its survivor and create a cascade. Audit component faults, shared dependencies, fault boundaries and survivor headroom together. Further reading Static stability using Availability Zones (AWS Builders' Library) Addressing cascading failures (Google SRE book) AWS Well-Architected Reliability Pillar

sum: Choose per-call timeouts from latency measurements and propagate one operation budget.
x: Gray failures hold caller resources while appearing alive. This unit bounds that resource use. A per-try timeout limits one attempt; an operation deadline limits the entire chain, including time already spent at earlier hops. Every remote call can hang, fail or succeed slowly. Timeouts bound how long you wait; retries turn transient failures into successes. Used carelessly, though, retries can contribute to large outages: they multiply load at the exact moment a system is weakest. The following units separate timeout selection, retry safety, backoff, amplification and budgets. Timeouts: every call needs one A call with no timeout can hold a thread, a connection and memory forever. Many client libraries default to no timeout or to absurdly long ones (some HTTP clients default to minutes). Under a gray failure (a dependency that's slow but alive), these calls pile up until the caller runs out of threads and fails too. There are usually several timeouts on one call: Timeout Bounds Typical value --------- Connect Connection establishment; TLS/DNS coverage depends on client Measure for the client and network Request / read Response wait or inactivity interval, depending on client Choose from measured latency Overall deadline Whole operation user's budget Choosing the value The AWS Builders' Library recommends picking a timeout from the dependency's latency distribution: choose an acceptable false-timeout rate (say 0.1%) and set the timeout at the matching percentile (p99.9), plus some padding. A percentile is read from measured latencies: p99.9 is the latency that 99.9% of calls beat, so only 0.1% of healthy calls take longer. If a dependency's p99.9 is 140 ms, a timeout at 140 ms reaches the roughly 0.1% healthy-call tail; padding it to about 150 ms should reduce false timeouts, but the precise fraction depends on the measured distribution. Very rare outliers (a 2-second GC pause at p99.99) are deliberately left to time out. Too short: you time out healthy-but-slightly-slow requests, retry them and add load. Too long: callers wait on doomed requests and exhaust their resources. Deadline propagation A user-facing request with a 2-second budget calls A, which calls B, which calls C. If each hop independently uses a 2 s timeout, C may keep working for seconds after the user has given up. The fix is to propagate an RPC deadline, rather than restarting a timeout at each hop. gRPC supports this when the language/runtime propagates the incoming context to outgoing calls. The remaining budget travels with the request; handlers must observe cancellation and stop their own work, because the deadline does not forcibly roll back or terminate every side effect. Each hop works out how much time is left from the one absolute deadline it received: Here p50 is the median latency of C's work: if less time remains than C usually needs, it is better to fail at once than start work nobody will wait for. Absolute deadlines assume the hosts' clocks roughly agree; gRPC avoids most clock skew by sending the remaining duration and converting it to a local deadline at each hop. Key takeaways Timeout scope depends on the client: connect, read and whole-operation deadlines are different. Choose an acceptable false-timeout rate and measure the matching latency percentile. Propagate the remaining duration and observe cancellation; a deadline cannot undo an already committed effect. Further reading Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (AWS Builders' Library) gRPC deadlines

sum: Distinguish retryable failures from unsafe repeated effects.
x: A timeout controls waiting; it does not prove that the server did nothing. Consider a payment whose response is lost after the charge commits. The question is whether another attempt changes the business result, rather than simply whether the network error looks temporary. Retries: when they help and when they hurt Retries are worth it for transient failures: a dropped packet, a connection reset, one overloaded host behind a load balancer, a leader election. A later attempt may reach a healthy instance; correlated failures can persist across retries. They are harmful when: The failure is persistent (bad request, auth error, bug). Retrying a 400 or 403 just wastes capacity. The dependency is overloaded. Retrying adds load to the thing that's already drowning. The operation is not idempotent. Retrying "charge £50" after a timeout might charge twice. Idempotency first A timeout tells you nothing about whether the server did the work. Before retrying writes, make them idempotent: The server coordinates concurrent requests and stores the key with the result. Stripe returns the stored result for the same key and parameters once execution has begun, including stored failures. Its keys may be pruned after at least 24 hours; reuse after pruning can execute a new request. External effects need compatible provider idempotency or reconciliation, because a local database transaction cannot atomically commit an external charge. What to retry Response Retry? ------ Connection reset / refused If no effect is possible, or operation is idempotent Timeout (idempotent op) If retryable and budget/deadline allow 429 Too Many Requests If safe to repeat; honour Retry-After and budget 503 Service Unavailable If safe to repeat, with backoff and budget 500 Maybe; often a bug 400, 401, 403, 404 Usually no blind retry; fix the request or follow a specific recovery protocol Key takeaways A timed-out write may already have committed. Retry only when repeated effects are controlled. Coordinate concurrent uses of an idempotency key and reject changed parameters. Respect deadlines, retry budgets and provider key-retention limits; external effects require provider support or reconciliation. Further reading Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (AWS Builders' Library) Limit retries (AWS Well-Architected) Stripe idempotent requests

sum: Spread retries over time without synchronising clients into repeated load spikes.
x: This unit assumes retries are safe and the operation still has time and budget. Backoff controls when to retry; it does not reduce the maximum number of attempts. The retry index in the formulas begins at zero for the first retry. Exponential backoff Retrying immediately after a failure hits the dependency again while it's still struggling. Exponential backoff waits longer after each failure: With base 100 ms and cap 10 s the waits go: Backoff gives the dependency time to recover and spreads load over time. But on its own it has a nasty property. Jitter: breaking the synchronisation Suppose 1,000 clients all fail at the same instant (a dependency restarted). With pure exponential backoff, they all wait exactly 100 ms, then all retry together, then all wait 200 ms, then all retry together again. The retries arrive in synchronised waves that look like a series of load spikes. Jitter adds randomness so retries spread out. Marc Brooker's analysis on the AWS Architecture Blog compared variants. Full jitter, the recommended default, picks a wait uniformly at random anywhere between zero and the exponential-backoff value: Key takeaways Backoff doubles delay until its cap, and the first retry has index zero. Full jitter spreads each retry across the entire current backoff interval. Backoff and jitter change timing; retry budgets and one retry layer still control work. Further reading Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (AWS Builders' Library) Exponential backoff and jitter (AWS Architecture Blog) AWS SDK retry behaviour (2026 opt-in)

t: Jitter variants and versioned SDK policy
sum: Compare jitter distributions and scope SDK defaults to the documented retry mode.
x: Full jitter, introduced immediately before this unit, chooses a delay from zero to the current capped backoff. The alternatives below change its minimum or how successive waits are related. Product defaults must be tied to an SDK mode and documented version. Equal and decorrelated jitter The two other variants keep a floor under the wait: For a 400-millisecond backoff, the equal-jitter calculation gives a wait between 200 and 400 milliseconds: In his simulations, full jitter used the fewest calls; decorrelated jitter finished slightly sooner but did more work; equal jitter was the loser, doing slightly more work than full jitter and taking much longer. Equal jitter's one attraction is that it guarantees a minimum wait. All three are vastly better than no jitter. The documented AWS SDK standard retry mode uses full jitter. In standard retry mode (as documented for the SDKs' updated 2026 retry behaviour, opt-in at first) the delay is written as a random fraction of the backoff, which is the same thing: The SDK documentation gives DynamoDB and DynamoDB Streams clients a shorter 25-millisecond transient base and four attempts by default. Long-polling operations also have special backoff behaviour. Check the exact client and operation, rather than applying the general example unchanged. Jitter everything periodic The same synchronisation problem hits cron jobs, cache expiry and health checks. Add jitter to TTLs and scheduled tasks too, or every client refreshes on the hour. Key takeaways Equal jitter keeps half of the current delay certain; decorrelated jitter chooses from the previous delay. The AWS simulation compares workload and completion time under its particular contention model. The quoted SDK values describe the 2026 opt-in standard retry behaviour; verify the SDK and mode actually in use. Further reading Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (AWS Builders' Library) Exponential backoff and jitter (AWS Architecture Blog) AWS SDK retry behaviour (2026 opt-in)

sum: Calculate worst-case and expected retry load and choose one retry layer.
x: Backoff and jitter spread work over time. They do not remove the multiplication caused by nested retry loops. Keep total attempts distinct from retries: three attempts means one initial attempt and two retries. Retry amplification across layers This is where retries cause outages. Suppose a request passes through three layers and each layer makes up to 3 attempts (1 try + 2 retries): If the database is completely down, one user request produces: 3 attempts at the API 3 × 3 = 9 at the service 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 at the database Each retrying layer multiplies the attempts of the layer above it: This is the worst case, when every attempt fails. The database, which was perhaps just overloaded, now receives 27 times its normal traffic and has no chance to recover. This is a retry storm. Partial failure amplifies too, just less dramatically. Take a single retrying layer making up to 3 tries. The first try always happens; the second happens only if the first fails; the third only if the first two fail: The same formula gives the rest of the table: Failure rate p Attempts per request ------ 10% 1.11× 50% 1.75× 90% 2.71× 100% 3× The extra load arrives exactly as the dependency gets worse, which is a positive feedback loop: more failures cause more retries, which cause more failures. Fixes for amplification Retry at one layer only. AWS's Well-Architected guidance is to implement retries at only one level of the stack. Usually that's the layer immediately above the failing dependency; every other layer fails fast and passes the error up. Retry budgets. Cap retries as a fraction of total traffic. Propagate "don't retry" signals. If a downstream is overloaded, return an error that tells upstream callers not to retry it. Google uses an explicit "overloaded; don't retry" response, so callers receiving that signal suppress retries. Key takeaways Worst-case attempts multiply across retrying layers. Expected attempts for three tries depend on the failure probability remaining independent and unchanged. Choose one retrying layer, propagate overload signals and bound retry traffic; jitter alone changes timing. Further reading Handling overload (Google SRE book) Addressing cascading failures (Google SRE book) Limit retries (AWS Well-Architected)

t: Retry quotas and a deadline-aware loop
sum: Bound extra retry work and combine quota, timeout and backoff in one call path.
x: The earlier retry units established safety, full jitter and one retry layer. Here the budget decides whether an otherwise safe retry is allowed. The displayed loop is a dependency-injected fragment: the RPC, clock, sleeper, retry predicate, quota and exception classes must be supplied by the application. Retry budgets and token buckets A retry budget limits retries to a proportion of requests, e.g. "retries may be at most 10% of original calls to this dependency". When things are healthy, the occasional failure gets retried. When everything is failing, the cap decides the load: The AWS SDKs implement a version with a token bucket (the "retry quota"): This executable event model keeps the original refill, charge and refund operations. The caller must invoke the matching method after each outcome. It assumes one fixed retry cost and serial access; it does not implement a production SDK, synchronization or a fractional traffic budget. When enough calls succeed, refunds keep quota available; retries still consume tokens and network resources. During a sustained outage the bucket drains and clients stop retrying. The documented 2026 opt-in standard behaviour starts with 500 tokens, charges 14 for transient-error retries and five for throttling retries, refunds the successful retry’s cost, and restores one token for a first-attempt success. A later success does not refund earlier failed retries. Other SDK versions and modes differ, and a finite initial bucket permits a burst rather than enforcing an exact traffic fraction. The bucket is typically per client instance; exact scope depends on SDK. A thousand hosts each with their own bucket still add up, which is why server-side signals matter too. Google's SRE book describes a similar pair of limits: a per-request cap (a request that has failed three times is not retried again) plus a per-client cap where retries must stay below 10% of requests. The book notes that the per-request cap alone can still triple load in the worst case, whereas the 10% cap limits growth to about 1.1×. Retries hide failures Retries make dashboards look green while users wait. Always emit a metric for retry rate. A rising retry rate is often the earliest sign of trouble. Putting it together Key takeaways A fractional retry budget caps aggregate extra traffic; a finite token quota has its own burst and refund behaviour. Client-local quotas add up across hosts. Retain server-side overload signals and capacity limits. Check the remaining deadline before calls and sleeps, and classify retryable failures narrowly. Further reading Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (AWS Builders' Library) Handling overload (Google SRE book) Addressing cascading failures (Google SRE book) AWS SDK retry quota

sum: Use an M/M/1 model to explain why high utilisation inflates mean and tail latency.
x: Timeouts bound waiting, but a healthy service also needs spare capacity. This unit uses an explicitly simplified queueing model to explain the shape of overload, rather than predict every multi-worker production service. Why overload is a cliff, not a slope With variable arrivals and service times, queueing delay can rise sharply near capacity. The simplest model that shows this is the M/M/1 queue: requests arrive at random (a Poisson process), each takes a random, exponentially distributed time to serve, there is one server, requests are served first in, first out (FIFO), and the waiting line has no size limit. For a stable M/M/1 queue, the average time a request spends in the system (waiting plus being served) is: The response-time multiplier is the inverse idle fraction: The model only holds while utilisation is below 100%; at or above capacity the unbounded queue never settles. Utilisation Latency multiplier ------ 50% 2× 80% 5× 90% 10× 99% 100× The tail is worse than the mean. In an M/M/1 queue the time in system is exponentially distributed, and for an exponential distribution any percentile is a fixed multiple of the mean: Where does ln(100) come from? For an exponential distribution, the fraction of requests slower than some multiple of the mean shrinks exponentially: Multi-worker systems and other arrival/service distributions have different delay curves; measure actual service behavior rather than treating M/M/1 as a universal bound. Key takeaways In the stable M/M/1 model, time in system rises sharply as utilisation approaches one. The exponential time-in-system distribution places p99 at about 4.6 times the mean. The model assumes random independent arrivals, exponential service, one server and FIFO; measure other systems. Further reading Using load shedding to avoid overload (AWS Builders' Library) Handling overload (Google SRE book)

sum: Calculate resource pressure from slowness and isolate dependency pools.
x: The preceding queue model showed why latency rises near saturation. Now follow the resources held by that waiting work. A bulkhead reserves a bounded share for one dependency; it helps only if other shared resources are isolated too. Two more facts worth carrying around: Little's law links traffic, latency and concurrency for any stable system, whatever the arrival pattern: So slowness alone exhausts threads and connections: the traffic didn't change, but the concurrent slots needed went up forty-fold. Without rejection or abandonment, sustained arrivals above service capacity have no finite steady-state queue. The queue grows at the gap between what arrives and what is served: Every request waits longer than the one before until something gives. Past saturation, latency rises until requests time out. Callers retry, adding load. Work completes after the client has given up, so the server does 100% work for 0% useful output. This is congestive collapse, and the patterns below exist to prevent it. Bulkheads Ships are divided into watertight compartments (bulkheads) so one breach doesn't sink the vessel. In software, a bulkhead isolates resources so one failing workload can't consume everything. Without bulkheads, a service with a 200-thread pool calling three dependencies can lose all 200 threads to the one dependency that's hanging: Bulkheads appear at many scales: Thread or connection pools per dependency. Separate instances for critical and non-critical traffic (e.g. checkout vs recommendations). Per-tenant quotas, so a noisy customer can't starve others. Cells and shards, the largest form of bulkhead (see the designing-for-failure lesson). Key takeaways Little’s law relates stable average in-flight work, arrival rate and time in system. Without rejection or abandonment, sustained arrivals above capacity build an ever-growing queue. Separate pools, quotas, instances or cells contain resource exhaustion from a slow workload. Further reading Using load shedding to avoid overload (AWS Builders' Library) Handling overload (Google SRE book) Bulkhead pattern (Azure Architecture Center)

sum: Fail quickly around a troubled dependency and keep degraded responses useful.
x: Bulkheads reserve resources. A circuit breaker goes further by stopping new calls when recent outcomes show a dependency is unhealthy. Decide what useful response remains, and ensure the fallback does not introduce another untested live dependency. Circuit breakers A circuit breaker wraps calls to a dependency and tracks failures. When failures cross a threshold, it "trips" and fails calls immediately without contacting the dependency. Martin Fowler popularised the pattern, building on Michael Nygard's Release It!. Closed: calls pass through; failures are counted over a rolling window. Open: calls fail immediately (or go to a fallback). No new calls through that breaker reach the dependency; existing calls and other clients can remain. Half-open: after a cool-down, a few trial calls go through. Success closes the breaker; failure reopens it. Why it helps The failing dependency gets breathing room to recover instead of being hammered. Callers stop wasting threads and time waiting on doomed calls; they fail without waiting for the remote timeout. It provides a natural place to return a fallback or degraded response. Tuning This illustrative YAML policy expresses the original thresholds; it is not any named library’s configuration format. Translate slow-call handling into the chosen library’s separate threshold, predicate or timeout controls. Counting slow calls as failures matters: it lets the breaker react to gray failure, not just errors. Resilience4j provides separate slow-call rate thresholds. Polly uses a configured failure predicate; combine it with an appropriate timeout strategy to classify slow operations. Envoy and Istio also provide host outlier detection, with different signals and configuration. Breakers can hide partial failure A single breaker per dependency may trip when only one of its hosts is bad, cutting off healthy hosts too. Per-host breakers or proxy-level outlier ejection give finer control. Graceful degradation When a dependency fails, serve a reduced but useful response rather than an error. Failed dependency Degraded behaviour ------ Recommendations Show bestsellers (static list) Reviews Hide the reviews panel Personalised prices Show list price Search ranking ML Fall back to text relevance Netflix is the classic example: if the personalisation service is down, the home page still renders with generic rows, and users can still press play. Fallbacks are dangerous if rarely exercised The AWS Builders' Library argues against complex fallbacks: a code path that only runs during outages may be poorly exercised, and it may put sudden new load on another system. Prefer static fallbacks (cached or precomputed data), or make the "fallback" the path you use all the time. Key takeaways Closed breakers admit calls; open breakers reject; half-open breakers allow limited recovery trials. Count enough requests and include slow calls using the library’s actual failure signals. Prefer simple, exercised, static fallbacks; a rare live fallback can fail under sudden incident load. Further reading Circuit breaker (Martin Fowler) Avoiding fallback in distributed systems (AWS Builders' Library) Circuit Breaker pattern (Azure Architecture Center)

sum: Preserve goodput by shedding excess work cheaply before expensive processing.
x: Goodput counts useful completions while throughput counts completed work regardless of usefulness. This unit protects the former. A capacity-limited server cannot make every caller happy, but early admission rejection can keep the accepted requests within their deadlines. Load shedding When a server is beyond capacity, it should reject excess work quickly rather than accept everything and serve it all late. An early 503 can cost far less than normal processing; a request that times out after doing 2 s of work costs 2 s of capacity for nothing. The AWS Builders' Library describes the principle: protect goodput (useful completed work) by shedding just enough to keep latency within the clients' timeouts. How to decide what to shed Concurrency limits: cap in-flight requests (e.g. 100). Above that, reject. Size the cap with Little's law (see the formula below), plus a margin. Adaptive versions (like Netflix's concurrency-limits library) adjust the cap from observed latency, TCP-congestion style. Queue time: if a request waited in the queue longer than the client's timeout, drop it if its useful work is tied to that deadline. Durable accepted jobs may still need completion even after a client disconnects. Some systems go further: Facebook's "adaptive LIFO" serves the queue newest-first when it builds up, because the newest requests are the ones whose clients are still waiting. Priority / criticality: shed lower-priority traffic first. Google tags requests as CRITICAL_PLUS, CRITICAL, SHEDDABLE_PLUS and SHEDDABLE, and sheds from the bottom. Sizing a concurrency limit with Little's law: The numbers here are illustrative. The admission check might look like this in code: This dependency-injected fragment assumes slots performs an atomic check-and-acquire and trusted policy has already assigned the request priority. The clock, limits, rejection response and processor are application dependencies. Make rejection cheap Shedding only works if rejecting is much cheaper than serving. Use cheap early admission checks before expensive body parsing or database access. Authenticate or validate any priority/tenant identity used for admission; never trust a caller-supplied criticality flag to bypass limits. Key takeaways Reject before costly parsing or database work, and release admission slots on every exit path. Discard work whose usefulness ended with its deadline; durable accepted jobs can have different obligations. Assign priorities with trusted policy and shed lower-priority work first. A concurrency limit must be measured under target latency. Further reading Using load shedding to avoid overload (AWS Builders' Library) Handling overload (Google SRE book)

sum: Reduce offered load upstream and bound every queue between producers and consumers.
x: The server-side admission unit rejected excess work at the service. Client-side throttling can prevent some rejected work from reaching it at all. Backpressure then carries a slow consumer’s capacity limit towards producers instead of silently accumulating an unbounded queue. Client-side throttling The Google SRE book describes adaptive throttling: each client counts the requests it has tried to make and the requests the backend accepted, over the last two minutes, and rejects new requests locally with this probability: With the tuning multiplier set to two, once the backend is rejecting more than half the requests, the client starts dropping some itself, and those rejected requests don't even cost the backend a network round trip. In steady state the client sends roughly twice the accepted request count when the multiplier is two, enough to notice quickly when the backend recovers. Lower K is more aggressive; higher K wastes more backend effort on rejections. The +1 in the denominator only stops division by zero when the client has sent nothing yet. Backpressure at the service level Backpressure means a slow consumer signals upstream to slow down instead of silently buffering. Unbounded queues are the enemy: they turn an overload into ever-increasing latency and eventually an out-of-memory crash. Bounded queues: when full, reject or block the producer. Protocol signals: HTTP 429 with Retry-After, gRPC RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, TCP flow control windows, Reactive Streams' request(n). Pull-based consumption: Kafka consumers pull at their own pace, so the broker never pushes faster than they can handle; lag grows instead (which you alert on). Backpressure must propagate all the way to something that can actually slow down: a user, a batch job, or a queue with spare capacity. Otherwise it just moves the overflow somewhere else. How the patterns fit together Key takeaways Adaptive throttling tracks all application attempts, including locally rejected ones, and backend accepts. Use bounded queues and propagate pressure to a producer that can slow down. Pull consumers can accumulate lag; durable queues still have finite capacity and retention. Combine these controls with admission, bulkheads and breakers. Further reading Using load shedding to avoid overload (AWS Builders' Library) Handling overload (Google SRE book)

sum: Translate recovery objectives into restorable, isolated data copies.
x: Earlier units kept a serving path available during ordinary failures. Disaster recovery also handles region loss and logical corruption. The key question is whether you can recover a usable copy within the business’s data-loss and downtime limits. High availability handles the failures you expect every week: a host dies, a zone blips. Disaster recovery (DR) handles the rare, large ones: a region goes dark, a ransomware attack encrypts your database, an engineer runs DROP TABLE in production, or a bug silently corrupts data for a week. DR planning starts with two numbers and ends with a drill. RPO and RTO Recovery Point Objective (RPO): the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time. RPO of 15 minutes means you can lose at most the last 15 minutes of writes. Recovery Time Objective (RTO): the maximum acceptable downtime, from disaster to service restored. These are business decisions, not technical ones. Ask "what does an hour of downtime cost?" and "what does losing an hour of orders cost?" Then compare against the cost of each DR strategy. These are illustrative business targets, not industry defaults. Workload Example RPO Example RTO --------- Internal wiki 24h 1–2 days E-commerce site minutes < 1 hour Payments ledger ~0 minutes RPO is driven by replication; RTO by automation RPO depends on how often data leaves the primary location (backup frequency, async replication lag). RTO depends on how much has to happen before you can serve: provisioning, restoring, DNS changes, and how many of those steps are manual. Backups: the foundation Replication is not a backup. If someone deletes a table, replication normally propagates the deletion to replicas; timing and replay behavior vary. Backups protect against logical failures (bugs, mistakes, attacks) that replication copies. Good backup practice: Point-in-time recovery (PITR): periodic full snapshots plus continuous write-ahead log archiving. Postgres with WAL archiving, MySQL binlogs, and AWS RDS PITR can recover to supported points within the available, continuous backup/log history, up to the latest restorable point. Your RPO is set by how often log segments actually leave the server: RDS, for example, typically uploads logs every five minutes, so its latest restorable time is usually a few minutes behind. 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, on 2 different media or services, with 1 off-site. Immutability: enforced write-once retention (such as S3 Object Lock compliance mode) protects retained object versions from deletion, including by administrators. Governance mode can be bypassed by authorized users. Protect encryption keys too: immutable ciphertext is useless if its key is destroyed. Separate account or project: backups stored where the production credentials cannot reach. Test restores regularly. A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup. The restore you didn't test Google's SRE book chapter on data integrity makes the point bluntly: nobody really wants backups, they want restores. Automate restore tests and measure how long a full restore takes, because that time is your RTO floor for backup-based recovery. Restore time maths Restore time often dominates RTO. The time to copy data back is its size divided by the speed you can actually restore at: Plus applicable log replay, validation and any rebuild work required by the backup format; physical database backups generally already include indexes. If the business wants a 1-hour RTO, a restore-from-backup strategy can't meet it. Key takeaways RPO limits lost data in time; RTO limits downtime. Targets come from business needs. Replication also propagates destructive operations. Retain independent point-in-time recovery history. Use enforced retention, isolated credentials and protected keys; measure full restores including replay and validation. Further reading Disaster recovery options in the cloud (AWS whitepaper) Data integrity: what you read is what you wrote (Google SRE book) Disaster recovery (Wikipedia) PostgreSQL continuous archiving Amazon S3 Object Lock Amazon RDS point-in-time recovery

sum: Choose a recovery strategy from tested targets, capacity and data-coordination limits.
x: Recovery objectives measure acceptable loss and downtime. The restore calculation in the previous unit provides a lower bound for backup-based recovery. Compare it with a rehearsed failover, not an assumed label such as “warm” or “active”. The four DR strategies The AWS DR whitepaper describes a spectrum from cheap and slow to expensive and fast. The ranges below are illustrative planning categories, not guarantees: backup plus continuous log archiving can have a low RPO, while active-active asynchronous replication can still lose acknowledged writes. 1. Backup and restore Back up data (and infrastructure as code) to another region. In a disaster, provision everything and restore. RPO: hours (backup interval). RTO: hours to a day. Cost: backup storage, copying, restore testing and recovery compute, with little continuously running application capacity. Fine for internal tools and batch systems. 2. Pilot light The core data layer runs continuously in the DR region (e.g. a cross-region database replica), but application servers are off or scaled to zero. In a disaster, scale up the app tier and switch traffic. RPO: minutes (replication lag). RTO: tens of minutes. Cost: the replica plus minimal infrastructure. 3. Warm standby A scaled-down but fully functional copy runs in the DR region and can take traffic immediately, at reduced capacity, while it scales up. RPO: seconds to minutes. RTO: minutes. Cost: a meaningful fraction of production. Big advantage: you can send a small amount of real traffic to it continuously, which exercises it; still test the complete failover and full target load. 4. Multi-site active-active Two or more regions serve production traffic simultaneously. Losing one means routing its share to the others. RPO: near zero (depends on replication mode). RTO: near zero. Cost: high in this planning spectrum; each region must have headroom to absorb the load displaced by the regional failures the design promises to tolerate. Hard part: data. Writes in multiple regions need conflict resolution (DynamoDB global tables' default mode replicates asynchronously and uses last-writer-wins), or partitioning so each record has a single home region, or synchronous cross-region replication or consensus (Spanner, or DynamoDB's newer multi-Region strong consistency mode), which adds coordination latency determined by region placement and protocol, and can preserve acknowledged commits under the supported region-failure model. This does not prevent replicated logical corruption. Strategy RPO RTO Cost ------------ Backup/restore hours hours+ £ Pilot light mins 10s of mins ££ Warm standby secs–mins mins £££ Active-active ~0 ~0 ££££ Key takeaways Backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby and active-active trade running cost for recovery work. Illustrative RPO/RTO bands are planning categories, never guarantees. Active-active still needs survivor headroom and an explicit multi-region write model; asynchronous writes can be lost. Further reading Disaster recovery options in the cloud (AWS whitepaper) Disaster recovery (Wikipedia) DynamoDB global table consistency modes

sum: Audit failover for stale writers, lost writes, routing delays and survivor capacity.
x: The previous units selected a recovery target and a strategy. Failover mechanics determine whether the promise holds during a real incident. Fencing prevents a still-alive former primary from writing; it does not itself copy missing acknowledged data. Failover mechanics Failover deserves explicit testing. Key questions: Who decides? Automatic failover reacts fast but can flap or trigger on false positives (a network partition makes the primary look dead). Many teams automate the mechanics but require a human to press the button for regional failover. Split brain: if the old primary isn't truly dead, two primaries accept writes. Use fencing to stop the old primary's writes before promoting. Enforce the fence at the storage or write authority, including existing sessions; a credential revocation counts only once its effect is verified. Capacity in the target: the surviving region must take the whole load. For equal-capacity regions with evenly redistributed traffic and tolerance of one region loss, the pre-failure utilisation ceiling is the fraction of regions that survive (see the formula below): 50% for two regions and about 67% for three. Reserve additional headroom for the desired latency. DNS TTLs: clients cache DNS. A freshly cached 300 s record can remain valid for five minutes; existing connections and client caching behavior can extend recovery. Preconfigured global routing can avoid waiting for DNS changes, but detection and reconnection still take time. Data loss on promotion: with async replication, writes that hadn't replicated are lost. That gap is the observed recovery-point loss; the RPO is the target it must meet (see the formula below). Failback: returning to the original region is a second migration, often forgotten in the plan. The capacity ceiling for surviving the loss of one of several equal regions: How much data an asynchronous failover loses depends on how far behind the replica was at that moment: Lag is not constant: it often grows during exactly the load spikes and network trouble that precede a disaster, so plan for the worst lag you have measured, not the average. Avoid control-plane dependencies during failover AWS's guidance is to rely on data-plane operations for failover (e.g. Route 53 health checks and pre-configured routing, which keep working) rather than control-plane actions like creating resources or editing records, which may be impaired during a regional event. Key takeaways Fence a former primary before promoting a replacement and rehearse failback too. Size already-running survivors for full target demand with latency headroom. Account for replication lag at the actual failure, DNS caching and reconnects; preconfigure data-plane recovery paths. Further reading Disaster recovery options in the cloud (AWS whitepaper) Data integrity: what you read is what you wrote (Google SRE book)

sum: Test a recovery hypothesis with measurable steady state and a limited blast radius.
x: A written recovery plan is a hypothesis. This unit describes how teams test it. The example is an experiment specification, not a runnable fault injector; it requires a controlled environment, a monitoring system and an authorised operator. Chaos engineering You only know your DR and redundancy work if you've seen them work. Chaos engineering is the discipline of running controlled experiments on a system to build confidence that it withstands turbulent conditions. Netflix's Chaos Monkey (built around 2010–11, open-sourced in 2012) randomly terminated production instances during business hours, forcing every team to build services that survive instance loss. Its successors simulated whole-zone (Chaos Gorilla) and region (Chaos Kong) failures. The principles (from principlesofchaos.org): Define steady state as a measurable output (e.g. successful plays per second), not internal metrics. Hypothesise that steady state will continue in both control and experiment groups. Introduce real-world events: kill instances, add latency, sever a dependency, fill a disk. Try to disprove the hypothesis by looking for a difference in steady state. Run in production where possible, minimise blast radius, and automate experiments to run continuously. The illustrative experiment compares user-visible checkout success and stops before a small experiment becomes a large outage: The injected recommendations failure rate is 100% for the selected 5% user cohort. These are illustrative thresholds chosen for the exercise, not recommended production defaults. Game days A game day is a scheduled exercise where a team simulates a disaster (e.g. "us-east-1 is gone") and executes the DR runbook for real. It tests people and process as well as systems: do on-call engineers know the steps, do they have the right access, is the runbook current? Google runs company-wide DiRT (Disaster Recovery Testing) exercises for this purpose. Key takeaways Define a user-visible steady state and compare control with experiment. Inject a realistic fault with a limited scope and explicit abort condition. Game days test runbooks, people and permissions alongside systems. Further reading Principles of chaos engineering Chaos engineering (Wikipedia)

sum: Choose metric types and aggregation that preserve meaningful latency measurements.
x: Recovery and overload controls require evidence. Metrics, logs and traces answer different questions. This unit focuses on metric types, costs and aggregation, building on the percentile definitions in Fundamentals. Monitoring tells you that something is wrong. Observability is the property that lets you work out why, including for failures you never predicted, by asking new questions of the telemetry your system already emits. A system is observable when an on-call engineer can go from "checkout p99 doubled" to "it's the new connection-pool setting on one shard of the inventory service" without deploying new code. The three signals Signal Shape Best for --------- Metrics numbers over time alerting, trends Logs discrete events detail, forensics Traces causal request tree latency, dependencies Each has a different cost and a different job. Mature systems link them: a metric spike leads to exemplar traces, and a trace span links to the logs it emitted. Metrics A metric is a numeric measurement aggregated over time, identified by a name and labels: This wrapped Prometheus exposition sample shows one counter value and its labels. Actual exposition writes the complete sample on one line; the wrapping here is only for the phone display. The common types (as in Prometheus and OpenTelemetry): Counter metric: accumulates nonnegative increments, with resets such as on restart (requests, errors, bytes). You graph its rate. Gauge metric: goes up and down (queue depth, memory in use). Histogram: counts observations into buckets, so you can compute percentiles across many hosts. With fixed-cardinality, periodically exported aggregates, metric storage primarily scales with series count, sample frequency and retention rather than individual requests. Instrumentation work still scales with observations. A million requests per second still produces one time series per combination. Cardinality explosions Never put unbounded values like user IDs, request IDs or full URLs in metric labels. Every distinct combination of label values is a separate time series, so the label counts multiply (see the formula below). The number of series one metric can create is the product of how many values each label can take: It is a maximum: only combinations that actually occur create series. But an unbounded label means there is no ceiling at all. Percentiles, not averages Averages hide the tail. The mean adds every latency and divides by the count, so one huge value barely moves it: Use percentiles instead. The p99 (99th percentile) is the latency that 99% of requests beat; p50 is the median. Track p50, p95, p99 and p99.9. You cannot average percentiles across hosts (the mean of each host's p99 is not the fleet p99). Aggregate histograms first, then compute percentiles. Histograms have their own catch: a percentile computed from buckets is an estimate, interpolated within the bucket it falls in. Put bucket boundaries at the thresholds you care about. For a classic histogram and an SLO of "at most 300 ms", put an upper-inclusive bucket edge at exactly 300 ms. This counts that threshold without within-bucket interpolation; strict "under" has different boundary semantics, and scraped rates still have measurement-window limitations. Key takeaways Counters measure accumulated events, gauges current state and histograms distributions. Bound labels: series combinations multiply, with histogram buckets adding series of their own. Aggregate histograms before percentiles and include bucket edges at the SLI thresholds you must count. Further reading Observability primer (OpenTelemetry) Monitoring distributed systems (Google SRE book) Prometheus histograms and summaries

sum: Make logs queryable, safe and affordable without losing useful error evidence.
x: Metrics summarise a service over time. Logs preserve individual events and the fields needed to reconstruct them. A request ID groups one request’s messages; a trace ID can correlate its journey across services, introduced fully in the next unit. Logs Logs record discrete events with context. The single most valuable practice is structured logging: emit machine-parseable key-value records (usually JSON) rather than free-form text. An unstructured event: The same event as a JSON record, with duration in milliseconds and a correlation ID: With structured logs you can filter and group fields instead of writing fragile regexes. For example, in a SQL-accessible log table, this native query selects slow Stripe events: The table and field types depend on the logging backend. The shown record matches this filter because its 3,012-millisecond duration is above two seconds. Good logging practice: Include a trace ID and request ID on every line, so logs can be joined to traces. Log at boundaries (request in, response out, external call) and on errors, not in tight loops. Never log secrets, tokens, passwords or full card numbers; redact PII. Sample high-volume debug logs; prioritize errors, but rate-limit or deduplicate error storms while preserving counters and useful examples. Log cost depends on event size, indexing, volume and retention. Estimate raw volume from request rate, log bytes per request and elapsed time: Indexing, replication and compression can make the stored size larger or smaller than this raw figure. Key takeaways Structured fields and trace IDs make events filterable and joinable. Record useful boundaries and errors, redact secrets and personal data, and control error storms. Estimate raw log volume before choosing retention; indexing, compression and replicas change stored size. Further reading Observability primer (OpenTelemetry) Monitoring distributed systems (Google SRE book)

sum: Keep causal traces connected across services and route them for outcome-based sampling.
x: A slow checkout metric tells you that users wait. A trace shows where that time went. This unit assumes counters and distributions from the metric unit; resource diagnosis with USE follows next. Distributed traces In a microservice system, one user request may touch 20 services. A trace records that request's whole journey as a tree of spans. Each span has a name, start time, duration and attributes; root spans have no parent. Span links can represent additional causal relationships, including across traces. Here the waterfall shows instantly that inventory, not payment, is the problem. Metrics alone would only tell you checkout is slow. Context propagation For the spans to join into one tree, each service must pass the trace context to the next. The W3C Trace Context standard defines a traceparent header: For linked instrumentation, propagate context using the supported carrier (such as HTTP/gRPC metadata or message properties). The displayed header is wrapped for readability; its wire value is one uninterrupted line. One service that drops the header breaks the trace into disconnected pieces; async boundaries like queues need explicit attention. Sampling Tracing every request at high volume is expensive. Strategies: Head-based sampling: decide at the start (e.g. keep 1%). The decision travels with the trace (the last field of traceparent contains flags, including the sampled bit). Parent-based sampling can keep decisions consistent, but this flag is a recommendation and downstream policy can differ. Cheap and simple, but you'll miss most rare errors. Tail-based sampling: buffer spans for a decision window and apply outcome-based policies, such as retaining errors and slow traces plus a sample of normal ones. Late spans, missing instrumentation, upstream sampling or buffer overflow can prevent retention of every interesting trace. Better signal, but needs a collector tier with memory to hold in-flight traces, and every span of a trace must reach the same collector instance (OpenTelemetry uses a load-balancing exporter keyed on trace ID for this). Google's Dapper paper, which inspired Zipkin and Jaeger, sampled as few as 1 in 1,024 traces and still found it useful for aggregate latency analysis. OpenTelemetry OpenTelemetry (OTel) is a CNCF project providing vendor-neutral APIs and protocols for generating and exporting telemetry. It provides vendor-neutral APIs and SDKs for traces, metrics and logs, plus automatic instrumentation for common frameworks, and the OTel Collector, which receives, processes (batching, sampling, redacting) and exports data to supported backends through configured exporters. Because instrumentation targets the OTel API rather than a vendor SDK, you can often switch compatible backends by reconfiguring collector exporters; backend-specific features, telemetry data formats and unsupported signals may require additional migration work. Key takeaways Trace spans record a request’s journey; propagate supported context across network and queue boundaries. Head sampling is cheap; tail sampling needs buffered spans and trace-consistent collector routing. OpenTelemetry supplies APIs, SDKs and a collector; backend migrations can still require work. Further reading Traces (OpenTelemetry) Context propagation (OpenTelemetry) Trace Context (W3C Recommendation) Dapper, a large-scale distributed systems tracing infrastructure (Google Research) OpenTelemetry tail sampling OpenTelemetry Python propagation API

sum: Separate user symptoms from resource causes when choosing dashboards and pages.
x: Metrics aggregate, logs explain events and traces connect the request path. These checklists decide which measurements deserve attention. The goal is a page that prompts useful action for users, with enough diagnostic signals to identify the cause. What to measure: RED and USE Two complementary checklists stop you drowning in metrics. RED: for every service (request-driven) Tom Wilkie's RED method, for each service or endpoint: Rate: requests per second. Errors: failed requests per second (or ratio). Duration: latency distribution (histogram). RED describes what users experience, which makes it a good basis for dashboards and SLIs. USE: for every resource Brendan Gregg's USE method, for each resource (CPU, memory, disk, network, connection pools, queues): Utilisation: how busy a resource is, such as busy-time percentage for a device or used capacity for memory and pools. Saturation: extra work it can't service yet (run-queue length, swap, queue depth). Errors: error events (disk errors, dropped packets). USE helps diagnose why a service's RED metrics went bad. Method Applies to Answers --------- RED services Are users OK? USE resources What's the bottleneck? Google's SRE book recommends the four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. That's essentially RED plus the most important USE question: how full is the service? Alert on symptoms, investigate with causes Page a human on symptoms users feel (RED metrics, SLO burn). Use cause metrics (USE: CPU, disk, GC) on dashboards for diagnosis. Paging on "CPU utilisation above 80%" wakes people for things that may not matter to users. Key takeaways RED measures service rate, errors and duration. USE checks each resource’s utilisation, saturation and errors. Page on actionable user symptoms and investigate their causes with resource telemetry. Further reading The USE method (Brendan Gregg) The RED method (Grafana Labs) Monitoring distributed systems (Google SRE book)

sum: Define measurable good events and distinguish internal objectives from customer contracts.
x: The observability units introduced measurements and actionable symptoms. An objective now specifies the acceptable user outcome over time. Use a clear event definition before choosing how many nines to promise. "Make it as reliable as possible" is not a target. Higher reliability targets generally require investment. Choose them from user needs and measured end-to-end behavior; the benefit depends on the workload and its other failure modes. Google's SRE approach replaces vague goals with three precise concepts, and turns the gap between perfect and good enough into a budget teams can spend. The fundamentals module covered what the nines mean in downtime per year. Here we use those numbers operationally. The vocabulary Term What it is Example --------- SLI a measurement % of requests < 300ms SLO a target for an SLI 99.9% over 28 days SLA a contract with penalties 99.5% or credits Error budget the failure the SLO allows 0.1% may fail SLI (service level indicator): a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of service, ideally a ratio of good events to total events. SLO (service level objective): the target value for the SLI over a window. SLA (service level agreement): a business contract stating consequences (refunds, credits) if a level is missed. SLAs should be looser than internal SLOs, so you notice and react long before you owe customers money. Choosing good SLIs The SRE workbook recommends expressing every SLI as: This gives a number between 0 and 100% that's easy to reason about and aggregate. Common SLI types by kind of system: System SLI types ------ Request/response API availability, latency, quality Data pipeline freshness, correctness, coverage Storage durability, latency Make SLIs reflect what users feel Measure as close to the user as practical. Server logs miss requests that never arrived (DNS, load balancer, TLS failures). Load balancer logs are better; client-side measurements or synthetic probes are closer still, but noisier. Define "good" precisely. "Availability" might be "HTTP status not 5xx", but a 200 with an empty search result due to a backend timeout is also bad. Latency SLIs need thresholds, e.g. "served in under 300 ms". Use percentile thresholds via ratios. "99% of requests faster than 300 ms" is a ratio SLI, so it can have an error budget. “a p99 below 300 milliseconds” is harder to budget. Focus on critical user journeys. For a shop: search, view product, add to basket, checkout. A slow "update avatar" endpoint matters less than a failing checkout. Exclude invalid events, such as health checks or requests rejected for bad input (4xx caused by the client). A concrete SLI spec "Proportion of POST /checkout requests, measured at the load balancer, that return a non-5xx status in under 800 ms, excluding synthetic health checks." SLO: 99.9% over a rolling 28 days. How many nines? Pick an SLO from what users need and what you can achieve, not from aspiration. Start from historical performance, then tighten if users are unhappy. Remember the maths of hard dependencies in series: a hard, synchronous dependency with 99.9% achieved availability caps its caller under the same measurement and failure conditions unless retries, caching or another recovery mechanism masks its failures. A dependency's contractual target alone is not a measured ceiling. Key takeaways An SLI measures, an SLO targets it over a window and an SLA states contractual consequences. Count valid events and define good outcomes precisely near the user. Choose critical journeys and realistic objectives; contractual dependency targets are not measured availability ceilings. Further reading Service level objectives (Google SRE book) Implementing SLOs (Google SRE workbook) Embracing risk (Google SRE book)

t: Error budgets, policy and burn rate
sum: Convert an objective into allowed bad events and a release policy.
x: Good and valid events from the SLI unit define the accounting boundary. This unit assumes that boundary remains consistent. Distinguish request budgets from outage minutes: a peak-time outage can spend a request budget much faster. Error budgets If the SLO is 99.9%, the error budget is the remaining 0.1%. It's an allowance of failure for the window, and you can count it in requests or in time: The time view assumes traffic is spread evenly; an outage at peak spends more of a request-based budget than the same outage at night. Error budget policy The budget becomes useful when it drives decisions. Google's example policy: Budget remaining: ship features freely; take risks (experiments, faster rollouts). Budget exhausted over the trailing four weeks: halt changes and releases other than urgent fixes and security patches until the service is back within SLO. Single incident consumes > 20% of the four-week budget: mandatory postmortem with at least one top-priority action item. With a rolling window, old events leave as new ones arrive. Remaining budget may rise or fall depending on their good/bad mix and request volume; it does not reset on the first of the month. This aligns product and SRE incentives. Product teams want to ship; SRE wants stability. The budget is an objective, pre-agreed way to decide between them, rather than an argument during each release. 100% is the wrong target If you're consistently using none of your error budget, your SLO may be too loose or you're over-investing in reliability. Spending budget on faster releases or planned maintenance is the point of having one. Burn rate Burn rate is how fast you're consuming the error budget relative to the rate that would exactly exhaust it at the end of the window. For the following exhaustion-time examples, assume steady traffic, a full initial budget and no additional old errors aging out. The time until the budget is gone is the window divided by the burn rate: Burn rate 1: you'll use exactly 100% of the budget by the end of the window. Burn rate 2: budget gone in half the window. Burn rate 14.4 with a 30-day window: budget gone in about 50 hours. Key takeaways The error budget is the share of valid events the objective allows to be bad. Agree the policy before incidents: examples freeze ordinary releases when the trailing budget is exhausted. Burn rate divides observed bad-event rate by allowed rate. Time-based spending estimates require steady request volume. Further reading Service level objectives (Google SRE book) Error budget policy (Google SRE workbook) Embracing risk (Google SRE book)

sum: Choose meaningful budget spending and reachable error thresholds for alerts.
x: Burn rate measures bad events against the allowed rate. Here we turn it into an alert threshold: how much budget should disappear, over how long, before a page or ticket is justified? The next unit adds short windows and derives detection time. Alerting on SLOs Naive approaches all have problems: Alert if error rate > SLO threshold (0.1%) over 10 minutes: fires on short blips that barely touch the budget; very noisy.
