Alert if error rate over the whole 30 days exceeds budget: precise, but you'd find out after the budget is already gone. The SRE workbook's recommendation is multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts. You choose burn rates that correspond to a meaningful fraction of budget consumed in a given lookback window: For request-based SLIs, the time-ratio calculation assumes roughly uniform request volume. The exact fraction consumed is bad requests in the alert window divided by the full-period request budget; traffic spikes can change it. Rearranged under that assumption, it tells you which burn rate to alert on: pick the fraction of budget worth waking someone for, and the window over which you want to notice it: The workbook's recommended starting point for a 99.9% SLO over 30 days (720 hours): Burn rate Long window Budget used Action ------------ 14.4 1 hour 2% page 6 6 hours 5% page 1 3 days 10% ticket Check each row with the budget-consumed formula: The burn rates are relative to the budget, so the same thresholds can be reused for other SLOs with the same period; only the error-rate thresholds change. Each threshold must also be reachable: even 100% errors can only burn so fast. For 99.99% the 14.4× rule fires at 0.144% errors. For a loose SLO such as 90%, the maximum burn rate is just 10, so a 14.4× rule could never fire. The workbook's full example configuration also adds a fourth, ticket-level rule (3× over 24 hours) between the 6-hour and 3-day rules. Key takeaways Choose a lookback and a meaningful share of budget to spend before alerting. The workbook’s example rates are relative to the objective; changing the objective changes the error threshold. A rule must be reachable even at total failure. Time fractions approximate request spending only under uniform traffic. Further reading Alerting on SLOs (Google SRE workbook)

sum: Combine long and short lookbacks and calculate which alert detects a sustained fault first.
x: The previous unit selected the example workbook thresholds: 14.4 over one hour, 6 over six hours and 1 over three days. Here a short lookback accompanies each long one so old failures stop paging after recovery. Keep those thresholds separate from the instantaneous incident burn rate. Adding a short window A long window alone has a slow reset: after you fix the problem, a 1-hour window keeps showing a high error rate for up to an hour, so the alert keeps firing. The fix is to require a short alert window (typically 1/12 of the long one) to be burning too: This executable policy fragment expects burn_rate to return the already measured ratio for a named lookback. It has no Prometheus server or scheduler; it simply chooses the most urgent action from the original conditions. The long window ensures the problem is significant; the short window ensures it's still happening. With both conditions, the 1-hour rule stops firing about five minutes after the errors stop, instead of nearly an hour later. In Prometheus this is usually built from recording rules for the error ratio over each window (ratio_rate5m, ratio_rate1h and so on), compared against the corresponding error-ratio threshold: Detection time How fast does a burn-rate alert fire? The workbook gives an approximate detection time for an error rate that starts abruptly, with a clean window beforehand and steady request volume (plus real-world scrape and alert-evaluation delays): For a full outage (100% errors) against a 99.9% objective, the burn rate is 1,000. The one-hour lookback reaches its 1.44% error threshold after: A burn-rate threshold of 14.4 is 72% of the actual burn rate of 20, so the rule needs 72% of the 60-minute lookback filled with these errors: about 43 minutes. Notice what stays constant: whatever the error rate, the 1-hour rule fires once about 2% of the budget has gone. Big outages page fast, small ones page slowly, but the cost at detection is the same. Errors burning below 14.4× are left to the 6-hour rule, and those below 6× to the ticket. Each rule trades detection speed against precision. Key takeaways A long window establishes significance while its paired short window confirms the problem continues. Under clean history and steady traffic, detection follows the time needed for window-average error to reach the threshold. Strong failures page fast; lower burn rates need slower rules. Real scrape and evaluation delays add time. Further reading Alerting on SLOs (Google SRE workbook)

sum: Adapt objectives and alerts when small event counts make one failure dominate.
x: Multiwindow alert maths assumes enough steady traffic for ratios to be informative. Quiet admin services violate that intuition: one event can dominate a whole hour. This unit closes the SLO sequence by adapting the policy and review process to the service. Low-traffic services With 10 requests in an hour, one failure gives a 10% hourly error rate and can trigger the fast page rule; longer windows depend on their own event counts. The workbook's options: Generate representative synthetic traffic to detect persistent failures; keep real-user outcomes visible so synthetic successes do not hide user-specific problems. Aggregate small services that share failure modes into one combined SLO. Change the product so a single failure matters less (client-side retries, for example). Lower the SLO or lengthen the windows, accepting slower detection where a brief failure has little real impact. Putting it to work Pick 2–4 critical user journeys. Define a ratio SLI for each, measured near the user. Set SLOs from historical data and user expectations. Agree an error-budget policy with product leadership before it's needed. Implement multi-window burn-rate alerts; delete cause-based pages that no longer add value. Review SLOs quarterly. Key takeaways A single failure in a quiet service can create a large measured error ratio. Use representative synthetic checks, meaningful aggregation or a revised objective/window while keeping real users visible. Agree objectives, policy and alerts as one process, then review them against user needs. Further reading Alerting on SLOs (Google SRE workbook) Implementing SLOs (Google SRE workbook) Error budget policy (Google SRE workbook)

sum: Compare capacity, exposure and rollback behaviour of two deployment shapes.
x: The SLO units explained when release policy permits change. Safe deployments control the exposure of that change. All strategies still need correct state compatibility and meaningful evidence of user outcomes. Deployments, configuration changes and migrations can trigger outages. Safe change processes reduce that risk. A universal outage percentage is absent here because a reliably applicable population and measurement were not established. Safe deployment rests on three ideas: Limit exposure: a bad change should reach as few users as possible before it's caught. Detect fast: compare the new version with the old automatically. Roll back fast and safely: undoing a change should be quicker and less risky than fixing forward. Rolling deployments Replace instances in batches: take a few out of the load balancer, upgrade them, health-check them, put them back, repeat. Pros: can use spare capacity in the existing fleet or a small surge; ensure remaining instances handle traffic while others are unavailable; it's the Kubernetes Deployment default, where maxSurge and maxUnavailable (both 25% by default) control the batch size. Cons: v1 and v2 serve traffic at the same time, so they must be compatible with each other and with the data. Rollback is another rolling deploy, so it's slow. Health checks only prove the process started, not that it's correct. A bad version can roll out to 100% if it passes shallow checks. Blue-green deployments Run two full environments. Blue serves production; deploy v2 to green, test it, then switch the router (load balancer, DNS or service mesh) all at once. Pros: fast routing cutover and rollback when the router, connections and shared state permit; you can test green with production config before switching. Cons: double the capacity during deploys; all users switch at once, so a bug not caught in testing hits 100% of traffic immediately. When both environments share a database, schema changes affect both and still need compatibility. Separate databases require their own synchronisation and cutover design. Watch out for long-lived connections (WebSockets) and in-flight requests at switch time; drain them. Key takeaways Rolling deployments mix versions and need capacity while instances are unavailable. Blue-green can switch routing quickly when connections and shared state permit; it needs a second environment. A process health check does not establish correct user-visible behaviour. Further reading Canarying releases (Google SRE workbook) Blue-green deployment (Martin Fowler) Release engineering (Google SRE book)

sum: Collect comparable evidence before widening exposure across hosts, zones and regions.
x: A rolling or blue-green release can expose many users before a rare bug is visible. A canary limits the population first. Expected error counts are evidence-volume estimates; observing ten errors or a difference in counts does not by itself prove statistical significance. Canary releases Send a small fraction of real traffic to the new version, compare its metrics with the old version's, and widen gradually. The key is comparison: the canary's error rate and latency are judged against a canary baseline group (the baseline running v1 at the same time, ideally on the same number of hosts), not against a fixed threshold. Tools like Spinnaker's Kayenta and Argo Rollouts run automated canary analysis. Considerations from the SRE workbook: The canary must get enough traffic to be statistically meaningful. 1% of a 100 req/s service is one request a second; a 0.1% error-rate increase would take a long time to detect (see the formula below). Bake time must cover slow-to-appear problems: memory leaks, cache expiry, daily batch jobs. Canary populations can be hosts, a percentage of requests, or specific users (internal staff first). How much evidence does a small canary collect? Multiply its traffic by the extra error rate you hope to spot: To detect small regressions sooner, send the canary more traffic, run it longer, or compare it with a baseline group of the same size so random variation is easier to separate from a real change. Staged rollouts at scale AWS describes deploying in waves: first a single box ("one-box"), then one AZ, then one region, then progressively larger groups of regions, with automated monitoring and rollback at each stage and bake time between them. A full global deploy may take days, deliberately. Combined with cell-based architecture, a bad change is usually caught while it affects a tiny fraction of customers. Strategy Extra capacity Rollback Exposure ------------ Rolling spare capacity or surge batch-dependent grows by batch Blue-green ~1× extra (~2× total) routing-dependent broad cutover Canary small fast 1% → 100% Automating the guardrails A mature pipeline does all of this without humans watching graphs: Build once; promote the same artefact through stages. Deploy to one box / canary; run automated analysis against baseline. Bake; check SLO burn rates, errors and latency. Proceed in waves, or automatically roll back on regression. Block deploys when the error budget is exhausted (see the SLO lesson) or outside safe hours. Key takeaways Compare a representative canary against a simultaneous baseline. Small canaries observe few errors: more traffic or more time may be needed to detect a small regression. Bake through delayed effects and widen in monitored waves with automatic rollback and budget gates. Further reading Canarying releases (Google SRE workbook) Automating safe, hands-off deployments (AWS Builders' Library) Canary release (Martin Fowler) Release engineering (Google SRE book)

sum: Separate code deployment from feature exposure while keeping persisted data rollback-compatible.
x: Canaries stage binary releases; flags stage behaviour already deployed. Both can require rollback. This unit joins those decisions to the formats written by a new path, because switching routing or a flag cannot reverse an incompatible stored effect. Feature flags: separating deploy from release A feature flag (feature toggle) wraps new behaviour in a runtime condition: This Python function-body fragment assumes an existing flag client, user context and two checkout functions. It shows routing behaviour, not a complete flag service. This splits two things that used to be one: Deploy: ship the code to production (dark, off). Release: turn the behaviour on, for staff first, then a small user cohort, then wider populations. Benefits: potentially fast behavior rollback by flipping a flag (subject to propagation and already-started effects), trunk-based development with unfinished features merged behind flags, and A/B experiments. Pete Hodgson's article on martinfowler.com classifies flags by longevity and dynamism: release toggles (short-lived), experiment toggles, ops toggles (kill switches for expensive features under load) and permission toggles. Flags are debt and config is code Every independent on/off flag doubles the number of possible configurations (see the formula below), although not every combination is reachable or a distinct execution path. Remove release flags once rolled out. And remember a flag change is a production change: stage it, audit it and monitor it like a deploy. Several major outages have come from a config or flag pushed globally at once. The number of possible configurations grows exponentially with the number of flags: Rollback safety Rolling back only works if the old version can run against whatever the new version did. AWS's guidance is that every change must be backwards and forwards compatible with the version on either side of it. The classic trap: v2 writes data in a new format. You roll back to v1, which can't read it, and now the rollback is causing the outage. AWS's solution is a two-phase deployment: Deploy a version that can read the new format but still writes the old one. Let it reach 100%. Deploy a version that writes the new format. Now rolling back from step 2 to step 1 is safe, because step 1 can read both. Key takeaways A flag separates deployment from release and can provide a fast kill switch under stated propagation and state assumptions. Flags multiply configurations and require staged, audited changes and removal. Deploy compatible readers everywhere before enabling new writers; a flag cannot make old readers understand new data. Further reading Automating safe, hands-off deployments (AWS Builders' Library) Ensuring rollback safety during deployments (AWS Builders' Library) Feature toggles (Pete Hodgson, martinfowler.com)

sum: Preserve compatibility through staged schema change and bound database-lock disruption.
x: Reader-first rollout keeps data formats compatible. Database columns need the same care across old and new application versions. “Zero downtime” is an engineering goal with explicit lock, writer-synchronisation and rollback prerequisites, rather than a guarantee from a command name. Zero-downtime schema changes: expand and contract You can't upgrade the database and every application server in the same instant. For some period, old and new code run against the same schema. So schema changes must be split into compatible steps. Martin Fowler calls this parallel change, or expand and contract. Example: rename column fullname to display_name on a large users table. Before switching reads, all active writers must synchronize both columns atomically (for example in one UPDATE), or use a carefully designed compatibility trigger. Complete and verify the backfill only after old single-column writers have retired; otherwise they can leave the new column stale after it was copied. During rollback, preserve that synchronization. The expansion and migration stages should support both old and new code. Contraction deliberately removes compatibility: drop the old column only after old binaries and the rollback window have retired. A destructive drop is not automatically reversible. Practical details Avoid locking DDL on large tables. In PostgreSQL, adding a nullable column is a metadata-only change, and since version 11 so is adding one with a constant (non-volatile) default. Many type changes rewrite the table under an exclusive lock; binary-compatible changes can avoid a rewrite. Where applicable, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids blocking ordinary writes, but can wait on transactions and leave an invalid index after failure; it cannot run inside a transaction block. For MySQL, tools like gh-ost and pt-online-schema-change copy the table in the background. Beware lock queues. Even an instant ALTER TABLE needs a brief exclusive lock. If a long-running query holds a conflicting lock, the ALTER waits, and every new query on the table queues behind it. Set a short lock_timeout (e.g. a few seconds) and retry, rather than stalling the whole table. Backfill in batches (say 10,000 rows at a time, throttled on replica lag), not one giant UPDATE that holds locks and floods replication. Never drop in the same release that stops using a column; wait until no running version references it, and keep a backup. Run migrations as a separate, observable step, not on application start-up from every instance at once. This SQL fragment uses named parameters supplied by a migration runner. It demonstrates a bounded, repeatable update; the runner selects ranges, commits batches and throttles from measured replica lag. It assumes the writer-synchronisation prerequisites above. Key takeaways Add compatible schema, retire old writers, verify synchronised backfill, switch readers and contract only after rollback retirement. Metadata-only DDL still takes locks; bound lock waits and inspect concurrent-index failure states. Batch and observe migrations in one coordinated pipeline step rather than racing every instance at start-up. Further reading Ensuring rollback safety during deployments (AWS Builders' Library) Parallel change (Martin Fowler) Release engineering (Google SRE book) PostgreSQL ALTER TABLE PostgreSQL CREATE INDEX PostgreSQL explicit locking

sum: Place layered encryption controls and identify what a compromised application can still read.
x: Security failures can also interrupt service. This unit assumes the authentication and authorisation distinction from API Design: proving a caller’s identity does not prove permission to read a particular record. Security is a reliability property: a breach, ransomware attack or DDoS can harm availability as well as confidentiality or integrity. In system design interviews and in real architecture reviews, security is judged on the same terms as everything else: what's the threat, what's the control, and what does it cost? The following units place the security controls on the diagram and explain their limits. Defence in depth No single control is perfect, so layer them. An attacker who gets past one layer should meet another. Encryption in transit Use TLS for supported application protocols across network boundaries (1.2 minimum, 1.3 preferred under current IETF guidance); use an appropriate encrypted transport for other traffic. TLS gives confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication via certificates. At the edge: HTTPS everywhere, with HSTS so browsers upgrade requests to HTTPS once a policy is learned (or preloaded); the initial visit is otherwise not protected by HSTS alone. Inside the network: historically teams terminated TLS at the load balancer and sent plain HTTP inside the "trusted" network. Zero trust (below) rejects this; internal hops should be encrypted too. Mutual TLS (mTLS): both sides present certificates, so the server also authenticates the client service. Service meshes like Istio and Linkerd issue short-lived certificates to every workload and do mTLS transparently, typically using SPIFFE identities. Automate certificates Expired certificates are a classic outage cause. Use automated issuance and renewal (ACME/Let's Encrypt, cloud certificate managers, mesh-issued certs with hours-long lifetimes), and alert well before expiry. Encryption at rest Encrypting stored data protects against stolen disks, mis-disposed hardware, leaked snapshots and some classes of storage-layer access. Layers, from coarse to fine: Layer Protects against ------ Disk / volume stolen hardware Database / object store encrypted copies without usable keys; not admins authorized to decrypt Application-level fields DB admins, SQL injection dumps Be honest about the limits: if an attacker compromises the application, which can decrypt, disk encryption doesn't help. Field-level encryption of the most sensitive data (card numbers, national IDs), with keys the database never sees, raises the bar further. Key takeaways Layer controls from the edge to audit, using TLS on network hops and mTLS for service identities where configured. HSTS protects after policy is learned or preloaded; automate certificate renewal. At-rest encryption protects stored copies, while a compromised authorised application can still decrypt. Identity authentication does not replace object authorisation. Further reading Secrets management cheat sheet (OWASP) AWS Well-Architected Security Pillar Recommendations for TLS and DTLS (RFC 9325)

sum: Keep bulk encryption local while controlling data-key use, rotation and destruction.
x: Storage encryption limits depend on who can use the keys. This unit separates a data encryption key (DEK), used locally for bulk bytes, from a key encryption key (KEK) that protects the DEK. AWS KMS product behaviour is scoped to the stated key type and mode, not every KMS service. Key management and envelope encryption Encryption moves the problem to key management. A plaintext key accessible to the same attacker as its ciphertext provides little protection; an encrypted DEK can safely accompany the ciphertext when its wrapping key remains protected. A Key Management Service controls key use through an authenticated API. AWS KMS provides HSM-backed key protection; Google Cloud KMS and Azure Key Vault also offer software-backed options. Select the required protection level explicitly and configure audit logging. The following envelope example uses AWS KMS-style data-key APIs. AWS KMS’s symmetric Encrypt API accepts at most 4,096 plaintext bytes per call. Sending terabytes as hundreds of millions of tiny remote calls would also require a secure framing and nonce/key design. Envelope encryption solves this: For AES-GCM, never reuse a nonce with the same key and respect the implementation's per-key/message limits. Prefer a vetted encryption SDK and framed format for large objects. Benefits: Bulk encryption happens locally and fast; KMS only handles tiny keys. The master key never leaves the HSM. Each KMS unwrap call is subject to access controls and audit logging. A cached plaintext DEK can decrypt many records locally without another KMS call, so KMS logs alone do not audit every data read. Key rotation need not rewrite bulk data. AWS KMS automatic rotation retains old key material for decrypting existing DEKs; moving to a different KEK may instead require re-wrapping DEKs. Crypto-shredding: destroy the relevant key material and every remaining plaintext or alternate-wrapped DEK, and ciphertext with no other recovery path becomes unreadable, which is useful for erasure requests and per-tenant keys. AWS services including S3, EBS, RDS and DynamoDB offer KMS integrations; exact key handling and defaults depend on the service and selected encryption mode. Key takeaways Encrypt bulk data with a local data key, protect its wrapped copy and retain nonce/tag information. Select the KMS protection level; cached plaintext keys bypass per-read KMS audit. KMS automatic rotation retains decryptable old material. Erasure requires destroying every remaining recovery path and obeying provider deletion timing. Further reading AWS KMS concepts AWS Encryption SDK concepts: envelope encryption AWS KMS Encrypt API AWS KMS rotation AWS KMS deletion

t: Workload identity, secrets and zero trust
sum: Limit compromised identities and avoid implicit trust from internal network location.
x: TLS protects a network hop and KMS controls key use. An authorised identity can still cause damage if its permissions are excessive. This unit limits that blast radius and explains why a trusted-looking source IP cannot substitute for access control. Least privilege and identity Every identity (human, service, CI job) should have only the permissions it needs, for only as long as it needs them. Scoped roles: the image-resizer service can read uploads/ and write thumbnails/, nothing else. Not s3: on. Short-lived credentials: workloads assume roles and receive temporary tokens (AWS STS, GCP workload identity) instead of long-lived access keys in config files. Just-in-time human access: engineers request elevated production access for a ticket, time-boxed and logged, rather than holding standing admin rights. Separate accounts/projects for prod, staging and backups, so one compromised credential has a limited blast radius. Over-permissioned roles turn small bugs into breaches The 2019 Capital One criminal complaint describes a misconfigured web application firewall that allowed theft of its WAF role credentials, then bucket listing and copying wherever that role had permission. Capital One reported about 100 million affected individuals in the US and six million in Canada. The SSRF/metadata scenario in this unit’s questions illustrates how such credential theft can occur; the complaint itself does not spell out that lower-level chain. Least privilege limits what a stolen role can read. Secrets management Secrets are database passwords, API keys, signing keys and tokens. Rules: Never in source control, container images, or plain environment files committed to the repo. Scan for leaks in CI (tools like gitleaks or GitHub secret scanning). Store in a secrets manager: HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager. Access is authenticated by workload identity, authorised per secret, and audited. Rotate automatically; better still, use dynamic secrets (Vault can mint a database user with a 1-hour lease per service instance). Never log them; redact in structured logging. Prefer identity-based auth (IAM roles, mTLS) to avoid long-lived shared passwords; temporary credentials and certificate private keys still require protection. Zero trust The traditional model was a castle and moat: a hard perimeter (VPN, firewall) and a soft, trusted interior. Once an attacker got in, by phishing a laptop for example, they could move laterally. Zero trust (Google's BeyondCorp, NIST SP 800-207) assumes the network is hostile everywhere: No implicit trust from network location. Being inside the VPC or office network grants nothing. Authenticate and authorise every request, user and device, based on identity and context (device health, location, risk). Encrypt all traffic, including service-to-service (mTLS). Least privilege per request, enforced by policy engines (e.g. Open Policy Agent) close to each resource. Continuous verification and logging rather than a one-time login. Key takeaways Grant narrowly scoped, short-lived permissions and isolate environments and backups. Manage secrets through authenticated identities, rotate them and keep them out of history, images and logs. Zero trust checks identity and policy at resources; internal network placement does not grant access. Further reading Secrets management cheat sheet (OWASP) NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture AWS Well-Architected Security Pillar

sum: Translate the 2025 risk categories into architectural controls and explicit failure behaviour.
x: The previous units added encryption, identity and secret controls. OWASP’s explicitly versioned 2025 list is a checklist of remaining web risks. A logged-in user must still be authorised for each object, and an unavailable security check needs a deliberate denial policy. OWASP Top 10 at a high level The OWASP Top 10:2025 ranks the most critical web application risks. The categories, in order, with the design-level response for each: Risk Design response ------ A01 Broken Access Control server-side authZ on every object A02 Security Misconfiguration hardened defaults, IaC, config scanning A03 Software Supply Chain Failures pinned, scanned, signed dependencies A04 Cryptographic Failures TLS everywhere, KMS, strong algorithms A05 Injection parameterised queries, output encoding A06 Insecure Design threat modelling at design time A07 Authentication Failures MFA, rate-limited login, managed IdP A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures signed artefacts, verified updates A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures audit logs, detections that page A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions fail closed, safe error handling What changed from the 2021 list: SSRF is no longer its own category; it's folded into A01 Broken Access Control. A03 broadens 2021's "Vulnerable and Outdated Components" to the whole software supply chain: build systems, distribution and dependencies. A10 is new: failing open, swallowing errors and leaking detail in error messages. A07 and A09 were renamed ("Identification and" dropped; "Monitoring" became "Alerting"). Broken access control is number one: insecure direct object references like GET /invoices/1234 that don't check the invoice belongs to the caller. The fix is architectural: authorisation enforced in a consistent layer, never just hidden in the UI. Fail closed A10 is a reliability lesson as much as a security one. If the authorisation service times out, the safe default is to deny, not allow. Decide the failure behaviour of every security check explicitly, because a check that fails open under load is a vulnerability that only appears during incidents. Key takeaways The 2025 list groups SSRF with Broken Access Control and expands supply-chain coverage. Enforce object authorisation server-side and validate unexpected inputs and outputs. Design exceptional security conditions to fail closed while preserving safe error handling and useful audit evidence. Further reading OWASP Top 10:2025 A01:2025 Broken Access Control (OWASP) Secrets management cheat sheet (OWASP)

sum: Match traffic attacks to edge absorption, origin controls and bounded expensive work.
x: Overload controls handled accidental demand. DDoS adds an adversary who deliberately maximises cost and bypasses simple limits. Network-volume attacks and apparently valid expensive requests require different layers, and all protection has finite capacity. DDoS mitigation A distributed denial-of-service attack floods you with traffic from many sources. Types: Volumetric (L3/L4): UDP floods, reflection/amplification (DNS, NTP, memcached). Measured in Tbps. Protocol: SYN floods exhausting connection tables. Application (L7): HTTP floods of expensive requests (search, login), which look like real users. Defences, layered: Absorb at the edge: anycast CDN or DDoS service (AWS Shield, Cloudflare, Google Cloud Armor) with huge distributed capacity. Anycast can distribute traffic across an operator's sites, depending on routing and source geography; it does not guarantee even distribution or unlimited capacity. Hide the origin: restrict origin ingress and authenticate your own edge (for example with mTLS or provider-supported origin authentication). An allow-list of shared CDN ranges alone may still admit another customer's traffic. Rate limit per IP, per API key and per user, at the edge and the gateway. WAF rules and bot detection for L7 patterns; challenges (CAPTCHA, proof-of-work) for suspicious clients. Make expensive endpoints cheap: cache safe responses, require appropriate auth and use bounded admission queues. Authentication alone does not make a costly request cheap. Combine with the load shedding and autoscaling from earlier lessons. Reduce attack surface: close unused ports, don't expose databases or admin panels publicly. Amplification maths A memcached reflection attack sends a ~15-byte request with a spoofed source address; the server replies with up to hundreds of kilobytes to the victim. Amplification factors above 10,000× were observed in 2018, which is how attacks passed 1 Tbps. Never expose UDP services like memcached to the internet. The arithmetic behind amplification: the attacker pays for small requests, and the victim receives large replies. The following ideal model uses the same payload accounting for sizes and bit rates. The 15-byte measurement is a UDP payload: IP/UDP headers, fragmentation and other network overhead lower the corresponding on-wire amplification. The 100 Mbps is illustrative. Real reflection attacks are limited by how many open reflectors exist and how much each one can send, not just by the factor. Key takeaways Layer edge absorption, authenticated origin access, rate limits, bot/WAF controls and cheap admission. Residential-IP application floods can defeat naive per-IP limits and random-query caches. Reflection amplification redirects much larger replies to a spoofed victim; close exposed reflectors and filter forged source traffic. Further reading AWS best practices for DDoS resiliency Denial-of-service attack (Wikipedia) Cloudflare memcached amplification measurements

t: Scope a design interview and budget the time
sum: Separate user actions from scale, latency, durability and availability requirements.
x: A system design interview is not a test of whether you know the "right" architecture for Twitter. There isn't one. It is a test of whether you can take a vague problem, turn it into a concrete one, and reason your way to a design that works, while explaining your trade-offs out loud. That means process matters as much as knowledge. Candidates with encyclopaedic knowledge still fail because they jump straight to drawing Kafka boxes. Candidates with modest knowledge pass because they ask good questions, size the problem, and make each decision for a stated reason. This lesson proposes a practice framework, not a universal hiring rubric. Timings, seniority signals and suggested answers vary by employer and interviewer; use the actual interview brief. This lesson gives you a method. Every case study in this module follows it, so you can see it applied six times. The shape of the interview For practice, assume a design round of 45 to 60 minutes. Take off five minutes of introductions and five of your questions at the end and you have about 35 to 45 minutes of actual design. That is not long. The single biggest failure mode is running out of time with half a design on the board. A reasonable budget for a 45-minute slot: Step Minutes ------ 1. Requirements 5 2. Estimates 3–5 3. API 3–5 4. Data model 3–5 5. High-level design 8–10 6. Deep dives 10–15 7. Wrap-up 2–3 The ranges add up to 34–48 minutes, so in a 45-minute slot you will be at the bottom of most of them. These aren't rigid. For this practice framework, spend less time on steps 1–5 once the design is clear, leaving time to demonstrate depth. Follow the interviewer's actual guidance. Step 1: Clarify requirements The prompt is deliberately vague: "Design a URL shortener." Your first job is to pin it down. Split requirements into two kinds. Functional requirements are what the system does, phrased as user actions: Users can create a short link from a long URL. Visiting the short link redirects to the long URL. Users can optionally pick a custom alias. Links can expire. Non-functional requirements are the qualities the system must have: Scale: how many users, requests per second, how much data? Latency: redirects under ~50 ms at p99? Availability vs consistency: is it worse to be down or to be briefly stale? Durability: can we ever lose a link? (No.) Write them on the board. Then explicitly scope out what you won't do: "I'll skip user accounts and billing unless you want them." Interviewers like this; it shows you can prioritise. Ask, then propose Don't interrogate the interviewer with twenty questions. Ask the three or four that change the design ("Is this read-heavy?", "Global or one region?"), then propose sensible defaults for the rest and ask if they're OK. Key takeaways Separate user actions from scale, latency, durability and availability requirements. Ask the questions that change the design and propose explicit assumptions for the rest. Use the time budget to finish an end-to-end design before deep dives. Further reading Amazon: SDE interview preparation System Design Primer: design approach

t: Convert daily workload into rate and storage
sum: Divide a daily count by 86,400 seconds, or state the 100,000-second shortcut.
x: A back-of-the-envelope estimate is useful when it changes a design decision. This unit establishes the rate and storage conversions used throughout the case studies. Step 2: Back-of-the-envelope estimates Estimates tell you which problems are real. A write count alone does not determine capacity: transaction complexity, indexes, contention, durability, hardware and latency targets matter. Don't compute to three significant figures. Round aggressively and keep powers of ten. Numbers worth memorising. The first one turns "so many per day" into "so many per second", which is how almost every estimate in this module starts, because servers and databases are sized by their per-second load: Rounding 86,400 up to 100,000 makes every rate about 13.6% too low (86,400 / 100,000 = 0.864), which rarely changes a design decision. Two anchors to remember: The rate above is an average. Traffic is not flat: it rises in the daytime and falls at night (diurnal skew), and campaigns or news events cause spikes. Capacity has to cover the busiest moment, so multiply the average by a peak factor: Real peak factors can be much higher than 3 (a push campaign or a sports final), so treat 2–3 as a placeholder until real traffic data exists. Storage works the same way: count times size. Using decimal units, where each step is a factor of 1,000: (Some tools count a kilobyte as 1,024 bytes instead. At estimation precision the difference, 2.4% per step, doesn't matter.) Content gap: universal capacity and latency numbers No reproducible benchmark supports a universal database writes/s, Redis operations/s, app-server throughput or hardware/network latency for this scenario. Those values are omitted. Use measured workload capacity or explicitly supplied hypothetical inputs when sizing. Key takeaways Divide a daily count by 86,400 seconds, or state the 100,000-second shortcut. State the peak factor as a scenario assumption until traffic measurements exist. Use decimal storage units consistently; raw bytes exclude replication and indexes. Further reading System Design Primer: design approach NIST: decimal SI prefixes

t: Turn a workload estimate into design constraints
sum: Compute reads, writes and retained bytes separately.
x: Use the daily-rate and decimal-byte conversions from the preceding unit. Here the objective is to explain what a concrete workload implies, rather than stopping after the arithmetic. A worked estimate Take a service with 100M (100 million) daily active users (DAU) who each make 10 reads and 1 write per day. First the rates: (Dividing by the exact 86,400 gives about 1,160 writes/s and 11,600 reads/s; the shortcut is close enough.) Then storage, assuming each write stores about 1 KB: Now you know: reads dominate 10:1 (cache them), 3k writes/s is a target to test against the chosen primary (and a partitioning strategy is useful if tests reveal a limit), and storage grows by tens of terabytes a year. Say what the numbers imply. "36 TB a year, nearly 200 TB over five years before replication, requires a storage, backup and recovery plan; I will evaluate partitioning, tiering and sharding against those constraints" is worth far more than the arithmetic itself. Make the assumption visible The 100-million-user example is hypothetical. The peak multiplier and record size are inputs to test, rather than facts about an existing deployment. A small change in record size can dominate a long retention period: indexes and replication are additional to the raw total. Treat the estimate as a decision record. Name the query that is expensive, the bytes that need retaining, and the failure or latency target a candidate store must meet. Benchmark the proposed workload before concluding that one machine or a shard is enough. This also explains why adding sharding merely because a daily count sounds large is premature. Key takeaways Compute reads, writes and retained bytes separately. A read-heavy ratio suggests caching; it does not establish database capacity. Include retention, replication, backups and recovery in the storage plan. Further reading System Design Primer: design approach

t: Size cache misses and surviving-zone capacity
sum: Only cache misses reach the database in this cache-aside estimate.
x: Continue the hypothetical workload: peak traffic is 30,000 reads and 3,000 writes each second. This unit turns it into a cache-miss budget and a fleet that survives losing one availability zone. From QPS to machines To turn a load into a machine count, divide peak load by what one unit handles, then add capacity headroom (spare capacity for failures and spikes). A cache in front of the database means only the misses reach it: How many database replicas that needs still depends on measured query capacity. For the app servers, assume each handles 1,000 requests a second (an assumption you would measure): The zone-loss factor comes from the surviving share of an evenly balanced fleet: Add further headroom for deploys, uneven traffic and measurement error. The model assumes the surviving fleet can receive the displaced traffic and that its dependencies also have enough capacity. Key takeaways Only cache misses reach the database in this cache-aside estimate. Use measured per-server capacity at the required latency. Size the surviving zones to carry peak traffic, with additional operational headroom. Further reading System Design Primer: design approach AWS: static stability and availability zones

t: Connect the API, access patterns and architecture
sum: Describe retries, pagination, authentication and rate limits in the client contract.
x: With requirements and estimates established, connect the external API to the data it reads and writes. Every architectural component should answer a stated requirement or measured constraint. Step 3: API design Define the contract between clients and your system. Usually a handful of REST endpoints is enough: Things to mention: authentication (API keys or OAuth tokens), pagination (cursor-based, not offset), idempotency keys for writes that might be retried, and rate limits. For live interactive features say how the client connects (WebSocket, Server-Sent Events, long polling) and why. Step 4: Data model Name the core entities, their key fields and, crucially, the access patterns: what you look up by what. The access pattern drives the choice of store and the partition key. "Look up a link by its short code" means a key-value lookup; any store works, and the partition key is the code. "Get a user's last 50 messages in a conversation" means a range scan ordered by time within a partition; a wide-column store such as Cassandra with partition key conversation_id and clustering key message_id fits well. Justify SQL vs NoSQL by the access pattern and scale, not by fashion. "Relational, because we need transactions across the order and payment tables" is a good reason. "NoSQL because it scales" is not. Step 5: High-level design Draw the boxes and arrows that satisfy the functional requirements end to end. Start simple: Then walk a request through it: "A redirect hits the load balancer, an app server checks Redis, on a miss reads the database, and returns a 302." Walking requests through the diagram catches gaps (where does the ID come from?) before the interviewer does. Only add components when a requirement or an estimate demands them. Every box should have a reason. A message queue appears because you need to absorb bursts or decouple a slow step, not because big systems have queues. Check the end-to-end contract For a retried write, the client needs to know whether a lost response means it should retry with the same idempotency key. The storage layer must enforce that key atomically with recoverable work; an API header by itself does not prevent duplicates. For reads, the pagination cursor should describe the ordering used by the query. A spatial query such as finding available drivers within two kilometres needs an index and query strategy that match location searches. Saying only that a database is reliable leaves the actual access pattern unexplained. Likewise, if representative benchmarks show a single relational primary meets the workload, latency and recovery targets, begin there and identify the evidence that would trigger replicas or sharding. These choices connect a contract to a concrete data path. Key takeaways Describe retries, pagination, authentication and rate limits in the client contract. Choose keys and stores from the queries and transaction boundaries. Walk a request through every component so gaps become visible. Further reading DynamoDB: conditional writes AWS: transactional outbox pattern

t: Use deep dives to explain failure and evolution
sum: Choose the hard parts specific to this design and compare alternatives.
x: Step 6: Deep dives This is where you earn the senior rating. Pick the two or three hardest parts of this problem and go deep: URL shortener: unique ID generation without coordination. Chat: delivering to a user connected to a different server. News feed: the celebrity with 100M followers. Often the interviewer will steer you here. If they don't, choose yourself: "The interesting part is fan-out; shall I go deep on that?" For each deep dive, show options and trade-offs, then choose. "We could hash the URL, use a counter, or use Snowflake IDs. Hashing needs collision handling; a counter needs coordination; Snowflake IDs need clock discipline. I'll use a counter with range allocation because..." Also cover failure: what happens when this node dies, this region goes dark, this queue backs up? Senior engineers think about failure modes by reflex. A useful checklist of probes that come up in almost every design, so you can raise them before you're asked: Hot keys and skew: one celebrity, one viral link, one huge group chat. Retries and duplicates: what is idempotent, and where is the dedup key? Data consistency: which reads can be stale, and for how long? Backpressure: what happens when a downstream dependency is slow, and does the queue grow without bound? Fail-open or fail-closed: when a dependency is down, do you allow the request or reject it? Multi-region: where do writes go, and what does a user see after a regional failover? Step 7: Wrap up and evolve Spend the last few minutes on: Bottlenecks: what breaks first as load grows? 10x scale: what would you change? (Shard further, add regions, move to async processing.) Operational concerns: monitoring, alerting, deployment, data migration. Cost: at staff level, say which component dominates the bill (often storage or egress) and one way to cut it. Finish with a one-sentence summary of the design and its key trade-off. It leaves the interviewer with a clear picture to write up. A practice review checklist Use these dimensions as a practice checklist; they are not asserted to be the scorecard of most companies: Problem navigation: did you clarify scope, or charge off in a random direction? Solution design: does the design actually work end to end and meet the requirements? Technical depth: can you go deep on at least a couple of components (database internals, consistency, caching behaviour)? Trade-offs: do you articulate alternatives and why you chose one? Communication: can the interviewer follow your reasoning? Do you respond well to hints? Seniority changes the bar. A mid-level candidate is expected to produce a working design with some guidance. A senior candidate drives the conversation, identifies the hard parts unprompted, and discusses failure modes. A staff candidate also talks about evolution, operability, cost and organisational trade-offs. Common mistakes Jumping to the solution. Drawing Kafka in minute two, before you know whether the system does 10 writes per second or 10 million. Over-engineering. Microservices, three caches and a service mesh for a system that fits on one database. Scale the design to the numbers. Buzzword architecture. Naming technologies without saying what they do for this problem. "I'll use Cassandra" means nothing without "because the access pattern is a partitioned time-ordered range scan and we need high write throughput". Ignoring the interviewer. If they ask "what about hot keys?" it's a hint, not small talk. Silent thinking. The interviewer can only score what they hear. Think out loud. Not finishing. A complete simple design beats a half-finished elaborate one. Get end to end first, then deepen. Pretending. If you don't know how something works, say so and reason from first principles. Bluffing is easy to spot. Estimates are a tool, not a ritual Some candidates spend ten minutes on estimates and then never refer to them again. Only compute numbers that will change a decision, and then use them. Key takeaways Choose the hard parts specific to this design and compare alternatives. Probe hot keys, retries, consistency, backpressure and regional failure. Describe the first growth bottleneck, a safe migration, cost and observability. Further reading Amazon: SDE interview preparation System Design Primer: design approach

t: Estimate redirect traffic and cache misses
sum: State the redirect ratio and peak multiplier explicitly.
x: A URL shortener looks trivial: map a short code to a long URL. That's why it's a favourite opener. The interviewer isn't interested in the mapping; they want to see how you generate billions of unique short codes without a bottleneck, how you serve a very read-heavy workload, and what you do about analytics. Step 1: Requirements Functional Create a short link from a long URL. Returns something like https://sho.rt/aZ3kQ9x. Visiting a short link redirects to the original URL. Optional custom alias (sho.rt/summer-sale). Optional expiry. Link owners can see click counts (by day, country, referrer). Non-functional Very read-heavy: assume 10 redirects for every link created. Low latency redirects: p99 under ~50 ms server-side. Highly available: a broken redirect breaks someone else's website, email or printed poster. Durable: a created link must never be lost or remapped. Avoid exposing sequential allocation through codes. Truly private links require authorization: at 10% namespace occupancy, a random probe finds some valid code about once in ten attempts, regardless of the permutation. Out of scope: user management, billing, link editing UI. Step 2: Estimates Assume 100 million new links per day and a 10:1 read:write ratio. Divide each daily count by the seconds in a day (rounded to 100,000), then multiply by an assumed peak factor of 3: Cache sizing using the 80/20 rule: if 20% of links get most of the traffic, suppose the chosen hot set contains 200 million distinct links. At 500 B each its raw payload is 100 GB, before cache overhead and replication. The 80/20 rule and a billion daily requests do not determine the number of distinct hot links; estimate that from access traces and the desired hit rate. The cache hit rate then sets the database read load, because only misses reach the store: So at a 90% hit rate, 30,000 peak redirects/s leaves about 3,000 reads/s for the store; at 99%, only 300. A skewed access trace can support high hit rates, but the achieved hit rate depends on the hot set, cache capacity and expiry policy. Measure it rather than assuming a universal link-lifetime distribution. Key takeaways State the redirect ratio and peak multiplier explicitly. Measure distinct hot links rather than deriving them from the 80/20 rule. Compare cache hit rates by the resulting database misses. Further reading RFC 9111: HTTP caching System Design Primer: design approach

t: Choose code length from namespace and retention
sum: Each additional base62 character multiplies the namespace by 62.
x: The scenario creates 100 million links a day and keeps ten years of mappings. Traffic and cache misses were sized in the preceding unit; now choose a code length that lasts for the retained dataset. Retention and code capacity Storage, keeping links for 10 years at about 500 bytes each (long URL, code, owner, timestamps), is the number of links times the size of each: How long must the code be? Using base62, each character is one of 62 symbols (a–z, A–Z, 0–9). Every extra character multiplies the number of possible codes by 62: To see how long a code space lasts, divide it by the links created per year: Six characters would run out in about 1.6 years. Seven gives 3.5 trillion, about ten times our 10-year need. That headroom matters for one of the ID strategies below. What the numbers tell us: writes are modest, reads are high but cache well, and storage (180 TB raw, over half a petabyte replicated) motivates evaluating horizontal partitioning, storage tiers and recovery costs; raw size alone does not prove a universal single-node limit. Key takeaways Each additional base62 character multiplies the namespace by 62. Size the namespace against retained link count and spare capacity. Retained bytes, replicas and recovery costs need their own budget. Further reading Python: numeric operations and divmod System Design Primer: design approach

t: Design the mapping contract and custom aliases
sum: Point lookup by code and listing by owner are different access patterns.
x: At the assumed peak, redirect traffic is 30,000 requests a second and creation is 3,000. The storage estimate uses seven-character generated codes; this unit connects those requirements to the API, data model and read/write paths. Step 3: API The create endpoint takes an API key and is rate limited per key (spammers love shorteners). It should accept an Idempotency-Key header so a retried request doesn't create two links. Step 4: Data model The core access pattern is a point lookup: code → long URL. No joins, no range scans. That suits a key-value or wide-column store partitioned by code: DynamoDB, Cassandra, or a sharded MySQL/Postgres with code as the shard key. Owners also want "list my links", which is a different access pattern (by owner_id). Handle it with a secondary index (a DynamoDB GSI) or a separate links_by_owner table, rather than scanning. Analytics data is a completely different shape (high-volume, append-only, aggregated) and lives elsewhere. Step 5: High-level design Create: the write API validates the URL (and checks an appropriate threat-intelligence service under its usage terms; Google Safe Browsing is limited to non-commercial use, while commercial users are directed to Web Risk), obtains a unique code, writes code → long_url to the links store, and returns. Redirect: the redirect service looks up the code in Redis; on a miss it reads the store and populates the cache. It returns a redirect and fires a click event to Kafka asynchronously, with bounded buffers and an explicit drop/backpressure policy so analytics do not block redirect completion. Read and write paths are separate services because they scale very differently: 30k reads/s vs 3k writes/s, with different latency targets. Custom alias uniqueness Custom aliases go in the same table using a conditional write ("insert if not exists": DynamoDB attribute_not_exists, or a primary key constraint in SQL). To stop a custom alias colliding with a future generated code, either reserve a distinct format for aliases (for example, require them to be 8+ characters or contain a hyphen) or have the generator skip codes that already exist. Key takeaways Point lookup by code and listing by owner are different access patterns. Make retried creates idempotent and keep click processing off the redirect path. Reserve alias formats or atomically skip codes already claimed by aliases. Further reading DynamoDB: conditional writes AWS: transactional outbox pattern Google: Safe Browsing usage

t: Compare hash collisions with Snowflake code length
sum: Uniform truncated hashes still need atomic code collision detection and retries.
x: Deep dive 1: Generating short codes This is the heart of the problem. You need billions of unique, short, ideally unguessable codes, generated by many servers without a global lock. Option A: Hash the long URL Hash the URL with SHA-256 and map it approximately uniformly into the base62 code space. The collision arithmetic below assumes uniform codes; naively taking leading digits of a variable-width integer encoding can introduce bias. Pro: stateless; any server can compute it. Con: collisions. Truncating to 7 characters leaves a 3.5-trillion space. By the birthday problem, the collision probability is about 39% by 1.9 million links and about 50% by 2.2 million (worked out below). With hundreds of billions of links you will collide constantly, so every write needs an atomic insert-if-absent and a retry on conflict (for example, appending a counter and rehashing). Con: same URL, same code. Two users shortening the same URL get the same link, which breaks per-owner analytics and expiry. You can salt with the user ID, but then you lose the dedup that was the main appeal. Where does "about 1.9 million" come from? The birthday problem asks how many random values you can draw from a space before two of them are likely to match. The answer grows with the square root of the space, which is far smaller than the space itself: At about 1.9 million uniformly random codes the chance of at least one collision is already about 39%. The approximation assumes codes are spread uniformly at random, which a good hash gives. A shortener issuing billions of links is a thousand times past this point, so collisions are routine, not rare. Option C: Snowflake-style IDs Snowflake, from Twitter, packs a 64-bit ID as: Each field's size in bits fixes how many values it can hold: Each worker has 4,096 sequence values per millisecond. Generation avoids per-ID coordination, but worker IDs must be assigned uniquely and restart/clock behavior must prevent reuse. Pro: fully decentralised, roughly time-ordered. Con: length. The original Snowflake layout has 63 usable bits. An ID above a quintillion (a 1 followed by 18 zeros) takes 11 base62 characters, not 7 (see below). For a shortener, that's a real cost. Con: clocks. If a machine's clock goes backwards (NTP correction), it can reissue IDs unless the generator refuses to run until the clock catches up. Why can it need 11 characters? Compare an assumed ID above a quintillion with the code capacities: Key takeaways Uniform truncated hashes still need atomic code collision detection and retries. The birthday threshold grows with the square root of the code space. Snowflake avoids per-ID coordination but needs unique workers, safe clocks and longer codes. Further reading Twitter: original Snowflake worker implementation Birthday problem

t: Allocate counter ranges and shuffle codes
sum: Allocate non-overlapping ranges durably and never reuse them after crashes.
x: The previous unit compared truncated hashes and Snowflake IDs. This unit develops the counter alternative: keep codes short and collision-free while moving coordination out of the per-link hot path. Option B: A counter, base62-encoded Give each link the next integer and base62-encode it. Base62 is ordinary place-value notation, like decimal, but each position is worth 62 times the one to its right instead of 10 times. With the alphabet ordered 0–9, a–z, A–Z: Longer codes just add positions worth 62², 62³ and so on. Pro: no collisions, ever. Codes are as short as possible. Con: a single global counter is a bottleneck and single point of failure. Fix: range allocation. A coordination service (a small database table, ZooKeeper or etcd) hands each write server a block of, say, 1 million IDs. The server allocates from its block in memory and only goes back for a new block when it runs out. At 3,000 writes/s, the coordinator is contacted once every few minutes (worked out below). If a server crashes, the rest of its block is simply wasted. With 3.5 trillion codes, wasting millions is irrelevant. Con: guessable. Sequential codes let anyone enumerate links (aaaaaab, aaaaaac...). Fix this by passing the counter through a reversible permutation before encoding: for example, multiply by a large constant that shares no factor with 62^7 (so not a multiple of 2 or 31) modulo 62^7, or use a small Feistel network keyed with a secret. It stays collision-free (it's a bijection) but looks random. The multiplication trick only hides the pattern from casual eyes (decoded codes from known consecutive counters reveal the multiplier through their modular difference); a vetted keyed permutation can hide sequence relationships, but a custom small Feistel construction is not established as secure here. How often the coordinator is contacted is the block size divided by the write rate: The multiply-and-wrap bijective shuffle from the "guessable" bullet looks like this: Option D: Pre-generated key service A key generation service pre-computes random 7-character codes, stores them in an "unused" table, and hands batches to write servers. It's essentially Option B with random rather than sequential codes. It works, but you have to store and manage billions of unused keys. Recommended answer Range-allocated counters with a bijective shuffle, base62-encoded to 7 characters. Collision-free and short when ranges are never reused; the bijective shuffle is not an access-control mechanism, and the coordinator is touched only once per million links. Key takeaways Allocate non-overlapping ranges durably and never reuse them after crashes. A coprime multiply-and-wrap mapping preserves uniqueness. A bijection is not authorisation or proof of cryptographic security. Further reading Python: numeric operations and divmod DynamoDB: conditional writes

t: Choose redirect caching and asynchronous analytics
sum: Choose Cache-Control explicitly for freshness and repeat click visibility.
x: A redirect that is reused by a browser or edge cache may never reach the origin. This unit connects HTTP caching semantics to click visibility and the analytics pipeline. Deep dive 2: 301 vs 302 Both send the browser to the long URL. The difference is caching. 301 Permanent 302 Found --------- Heuristic cacheability Yes Not normally; explicit freshness can permit storage Later clicks hit us? Depends on freshness policy Depends on freshness policy Analytics Cached visits may be missed Cached visits may be missed Updated target seen? Depends on cache policy Depends on cache policy A fresh cached redirect can bypass your service, hiding visits and delaying target or expiry changes. A 301 is heuristically cacheable; 302/307 can also be cached with explicit freshness. Use an explicit policy such as Cache-Control: no-store when repeat navigation should resolve through your service, and account for analytics delivery failures separately. Without explicit cache headers, browsers treat a 301 as cacheable and may keep it indefinitely; a 302 is cached only if headers say so. A permanent redirect can still use a short freshness lifetime or no-store; the status and cache policy serve different purposes. Content gap: live provider headers Exact Bitly, t.co and TinyURL cache-header claims have been removed. No reproducible set of representative URLs and dated response captures was supplied, so this audit cannot reliably present those variable deployment settings as provider-wide facts. So the real lever is Cache-Control, not only the status code. Say the trade-off explicitly; that's what the interviewer is checking. Deep dive 3: Analytics Never update a counter row synchronously on every redirect. At 30,000 redirects/s, a popular link would become a hot row and add latency to every redirect. Instead: The redirect service emits a click event (code, timestamp, country from IP, user agent, referrer) to Kafka, fire-and-forget, and returns immediately. A stream processor (Flink, Kafka Streams) aggregates events into per-link, per-hour buckets. Aggregates go into an OLAP store such as ClickHouse or Druid, which answers "clicks by country last 7 days" quickly. Raw events can also be written to object storage (S3) for reprocessing. If Kafka is briefly unavailable, the redirect must still work: buffer locally and drop analytics before you ever fail a redirect. Redirects are the product; analytics are a feature. Make the analytics guarantee explicit Returning quickly and recording every click are competing requirements during a log outage. A fire-and-forget event can be lost between process failure and publication, even if Kafka itself is durable after acknowledgement. A bounded local queue needs a size limit, retention policy and metric for dropped events. If the product requires durable click accounting, persist a recoverable event before acknowledging the operation or use an equivalent durable capture design, then measure its latency cost. For this availability-first shortener, redirect success takes priority and occasional missing analytics are accepted. Neither a 302 nor a no-store policy proves complete analytics: clients, bots and event delivery failures still need a measurement definition. Key takeaways Choose Cache-Control explicitly for freshness and repeat click visibility. Status codes and freshness policy are separate decisions. Keep analytics bounded and asynchronous; quantify tolerated event loss. Further reading RFC 9111: HTTP caching RFC 9110: redirect status codes

t: Keep expiry and negative caching race-safe
sum: Check logical expiry on reads instead of waiting for physical deletion.
x: The mapping store may replicate asynchronously, while redirect services cache both mappings and not-found results. This unit examines how those two optimisations can hide a new link and how to prevent that race. Deep dive 4: Caching and expiry The application uses cache-aside: check Redis, read the store on a miss, then populate Redis. Links are effectively immutable, so cache invalidation is easy; set a TTL (say, 24 hours) and evict on expiry or deletion. Two subtleties: Negative caching. Bots hammer random codes. Cache "not found" for a short time (60 s) so they don't all fall through to the database. A Bloom filter can reject absent codes only when it covers all committed codes relevant to that read; a stale filter must not suppress fresh links. Expiry. Check expires_at on every read (lazy expiry), and let a background job or the store's TTL feature (DynamoDB TTL, Cassandra TTL) physically delete rows later. Deep dive 5: Consistency after create A subtle bug lurks between negative caching and replication. A user creates a link and pastes it into a chat; a friend clicks within 200 ms. If the redirect hits a replica (or another region) that hasn't received the write yet, it returns 404 and caches the 404 for 60 seconds. The link looks broken for a minute. Fixes, roughly in order of preference: Write-through on create. The write API puts code → long_url into the cache as it writes the store, and deletes any negative entry for that code. Fall back to the primary on a miss. If the replica says "not found", retry against the primary (or home region) before caching a negative result. Misses on real codes are rare, so the extra cost is small. Keep negative TTLs short (seconds, not minutes) and only negatively cache after a cheap format rejection or a Bloom filter check whose completeness for relevant committed codes is guaranteed. Immutable mappings simplify replication, but deletion, expiry, abuse blocking, custom-alias uniqueness and stale negative-cache fills still need consistency rules. A create racing with an older miss can be overwritten by a late negative fill; version or condition cache writes, or avoid negative caching valid-looking codes when strict freshness is required. Bottlenecks and trade-offs Hot links: in a scenario where a viral link gets over 100,000 requests a second, compare that load with measured shard capacity. Add a small in-process cache on each redirect server, or serve the redirect from the CDN edge. ID coordinator: range allocation makes it nearly irrelevant, but run it replicated (etcd/ZooKeeper) so block allocation survives a node loss. Abuse: shorteners are used to hide phishing links. Scan on creation, rescan periodically, and be able to disable a link globally (another reason to keep browser caching of redirects short). Key takeaways Check logical expiry on reads instead of waiting for physical deletion. A stale replica or Bloom filter must not hide a freshly created mapping. Version cache fills and combine hot-link caching with bounded blocking delays. Further reading DynamoDB: time to live RFC 9111: HTTP caching

t: Expand the namespace and preserve regional uniqueness
sum: Seven characters cannot hold ten years at a billion new links a day.
x: Now increase the assumed workload tenfold: one billion new links a day and 300,000 redirects a second. Earlier units established cache freshness and non-reused ID ranges; apply both when expanding the namespace and serving regions. At 10x scale At 1 billion new links a day and 300k redirects/s: Seven characters is no longer enough for 10 years (3.65 trillion links vs 3.5 trillion codes; see the sum below). Move to 8 characters (218 trillion) for new links. An 8-character string can never equal a 7-character one, so new generated links use exactly eight characters (left-pad short encodings), with a fresh permutation over all 218 trillion 8-character values. Also revise alias reservations or atomically skip already-claimed aliases. Storage reaches petabytes (about 1.8 PB raw over 10 years). Expire links nobody has clicked for years, or move them to cheaper storage. Go multi-region. Redirects are read-only and links are immutable, so replicate the links store asynchronously to every region and serve redirects locally. Give each region its own ID ranges so regions never need to coordinate on writes. A link created in Europe might take a second to resolve in Asia; the primary-fallback from deep dive 5 covers that window. Push redirects to the edge. CDN workers (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) can hold hot mappings and reduce origin work; end-to-end latency still needs measurement, shipping click logs back in batches. Shard the analytics pipeline by code and pre-aggregate at the edge before sending upstream. The two 10x sums: Distinguish generated codes from aliases A region can create generated links during a bounded network partition while it still owns unused, durable ranges. It must stop or reject creation when its range is exhausted; disconnected regions cannot safely allocate the same new range. Custom aliases are different because a user can request the same text in two regions. Route that uniqueness decision to a home authority, or reject and defer alias creation while the authority is unreachable. Asynchronous replicas support local redirect reads with a documented freshness delay. A fallback to the home region improves a fresh-link miss only when that region is reachable. Abuse blocking and deletions need a separate propagation or authoritative check policy; immutable destinations do not make these changes instantly consistent. Key takeaways Seven characters cannot hold ten years at a billion new links a day. Use an exact new code length and revisit alias reservations. Disjoint preallocated ranges support partitioned creation; custom aliases still need global uniqueness. Further reading DynamoDB: conditional writes Python: numeric operations and divmod

t: Set limiter guarantees and estimate capacity
sum: Separate policy targets from measured Redis capacity.
x: A rate limiter caps how many requests a client can make in a period. It protects services from abuse and runaway clients, enforces pricing tiers ("free plan: 100 requests per minute"), and stops one tenant from starving everyone else. On one server it's an in-memory counter. The interview is about making it work across hundreds of API servers, at a million requests a second, adding no more than a millisecond, and staying correct when clients race each other. Step 1: Requirements Functional Limit requests per key (API key, user ID, IP address, or a combination) according to rules such as "100 requests/minute per API key on POST /charges". Support several rules per request (per-second burst limit and per-day quota). When a limit is exceeded, reject with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests and tell the client when to retry. Rules can be changed without redeploying. Non-functional Low overhead: the check sits on every request, so it must add under ~1–2 ms at p99. Highly available: if the limiter is down, the API should keep working. Approximately accurate: a small overshoot (a few percent) is fine; massively over-admitting is not. Distributed: limits are global across all API servers, not per server. Step 2: Estimates Assume an API fleet handling 1 million requests/s at peak, with 10 million active keys a day. Every request needs one limiter check, which is one Redis call (a single Lua script). The number of Redis shards follows from dividing the check rate by what one shard handles: Memory is keys times rules per key times bytes per counter: These are illustrative sizing inputs, not measured Redis capacity or memory bounds. Actual key strings, objects, allocator overhead, scripts, replication and network tails must be measured. A single atomic call reduces both race windows and network hops. Content gap: deployment benchmarks No reproducible deployment benchmark is supplied for the stated 1–2 ms target or per-shard throughput/footprint. Universal capacity and latency estimates are omitted; the calculation above uses explicit assumptions. Key takeaways Separate policy targets from measured Redis capacity. Count checks, active keys and rules independently. Choose the consequence of counter resets before selecting storage. Further reading Stripe: rate and concurrency limiting Redis: benchmark limitations

t: Choose identity, rule storage and shard routing
sum: Put checks before backend work and return useful retry guidance.
x: Step 3: API The limiter is usually an internal service called by the API gateway, or a library or sidecar inside it. Lyft's open-source Envoy rate limit service is a gRPC service with essentially this shape: To the external client, a rejected request looks like: 429 is defined in RFC 6585, and Retry-After is a standard HTTP header (RFC 9110). The RateLimit- headers above are illustrative, non-standard field names from an earlier draft. The IETF HTTPAPI draft evolves structured quota fields; check the current draft rather than treating these names as a final standard. Many APIs still use their own X-RateLimit- variants (GitHub sends x-ratelimit-limit, -remaining and -reset, the last as a Unix timestamp). Whatever the names, good headers matter: well-behaved clients back off instead of hammering you. Retry storms If every rejected client retries exactly at the Retry-After time, they all come back in the same instant. Client SDKs should add random jitter to retries, and the server can vary Retry-After slightly per client. Step 4: Data model Two kinds of data: Rules are small, read constantly, changed rarely. Store them in a database or config repo and push them to every limiter instance, which caches them in memory. Illustrative YAML configuration for this design, rather than an Envoy configuration format: Counters are tiny, extremely hot and short-lived. Keep them in Redis (or Memcached), keyed by rule and client: An illustrative Redis hash contains the balance and last refill time. These commands require a Redis connection; the timestamp is a fixture, not the current time. The hash contains 37 tokens and the supplied refill timestamp. Read, refill and decrement still need an atomic script; these two commands only demonstrate the stored representation. The braces are a Redis Cluster hash tag: only the part inside {} is hashed to pick the shard. Tagging the client key puts all of one client's counters (burst limit, daily quota) on the same shard, so one Lua script can check several rules atomically, while different clients still spread across shards. Tagging the rule name instead ({payments:/charges}) would be a classic mistake: every client of that endpoint would land on one shard. For this availability-first example, decide explicitly whether resetting counters is acceptable. A reset can grant a full new burst to every affected key, not merely a few percent overshoot. Security controls and billable quotas may require durable accounting or a different failure policy. Choosing the key What you limit by matters as much as the algorithm: API key or user ID for authenticated traffic: precise and fair. IP address for anonymous traffic, with care. Thousands of mobile users can share one carrier-grade NAT address, and an IPv6 attacker can rotate through billions of addresses in a /64. Limit IPv6 by prefix (often /64) and set IPv4 limits loosely enough for shared addresses. Combinations for specific abuse: per (account, IP) limits on login can reduce some abuse, but distributed credential stuffing needs additional account/global signals and monitoring. Step 5: High-level design Where to put it? In the client: never trust it; clients can be modified. In each service: duplicated logic, inconsistent rules. In the API gateway or a sidecar (Envoy, Kong, AWS API Gateway): one place, before traffic reaches backends. This is the usual answer. As a separate service the gateway calls: centralises logic, costs an extra hop. Envoy's model is a sidecar that calls a central rate limit service backed by Redis. Key takeaways Put checks before backend work and return useful retry guidance. Hash-tag the client identity to co-locate its rules without one endpoint-wide hot shard. Consider NAT sharing, IPv6 rotation and retry jitter when choosing policy. Further reading Envoy: global rate limiting Redis: cluster hash tags RFC 6585: HTTP 429

t: Compare fixed windows with rolling-count estimates
sum: Fixed windows allow a double burst across an aligned boundary.
x: A limiter rule might allow 100 requests per minute. The question is which minute: an aligned calendar interval or every possible rolling interval. This unit compares the counting algorithms before the next unit introduces a burst-and-average contract. Deep dive 1: Algorithms Fixed window counter Count requests in each calendar window (12:00:00–12:00:59); reject once the count passes the limit. One INCR plus an EXPIRE. Pro: trivial, one integer per key. Con: boundary bursts. With a 100/min limit, a client can send 100 at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00, so 200 requests in two seconds. Sliding request timestamp log Store a timestamp for every request (a Redis sorted set). On each request, drop entries older than the window and count what's left. Pro: exact for the chosen rolling request-count interval when pruning, counting and recording accepted requests happen atomically. Con: memory. A limit of 10,000/hour stores up to 10,000 timestamps per key. At 10 million keys, that's prohibitive. Sliding window counter Keep fixed-window counts for the current and previous window.
